en: *Cheng weishi lun shu chao*, Scroll One, composed by Dharma Master Lingtai of Beijing. Regarding the term "Yujing" (Jade Well):
some say there is a Jade Well in the region south of Ji; others say it is the name of a celestial mansion among the stars of the *Tian Tai* (Heavenly Terrace) constellation.

However, Tai (Thera) actually consists of ten stars: the four large stars at the corners and six stars forming the shape of a cart (saṃ). Those large stars at the four corners are named Yùjǐng (Jewel Well).
Furthermore, regarding the *Fahua jing* (Lotus Sūtra), in the commentary (*shū*), the character "fǎn" (返) may be read as "tiáo" (迢), and "fǎn" (返) as "lìng" (令).
This is because one obtains the correct characters from the transmitted books by using their phonetic reversals; these are the correct characters from the transmitted books.
The character "ren" (忍) is the "ling" (令) command transmitted within the scriptures; what we have here is simply the character for "zheng" (正) inverted to form the character for "ren.

This may be understood by referring to the first commentary [of the *Lotus Sūtra*] below. For a detailed explanation of the five joys and ten benefits, consult the *Fahua ji* (Record of the Lotus Sūtra).

Regarding the phrase "qie yi" (竊以): among the opening phrases of various texts, such as "xiang fu" (詳夫), "qie yi," "gai yi" (蓋以), "ruo fu" (若夫), and "fu yi" (夫以), all serve as introductory expressions.
"End" (duan). "End" means the beginning or the head. As will be seen in the following text, the current composition of this treatise is precisely the commencement.

To set forth, select, maintain, and point out the commencement is what constitutes the "Preface" (duanxu). However, herein the three teachings are contrasted and distinguished. Regarding the "subtlety of the six stages":
when the Yellow Emperor ascended the mountain, he beheld a divine spirit; upon its tortoise shell were five... [marks].
Regarding the hexagram texts and so forth, he eventually created the eight trigrams (*bagua*), such as Qian with three long lines and Kan with six short lines.
These eight trigrams each consist of three strokes. Subsequently, King Wen transformed these eight trigrams into sixty-four hexagrams, yet they were still called "the eight trigrams.
Within these sixty-four hexagrams, the eight trigrams serve as the primary heads, with the remaining seven trigrams following in succession.

There are eight trigrams; when these eight are combined with another set of eight, they are called the "pure" [hexagrams]. If one considers the single eight trigrams, each consists of only three lines.
If one considers the sixty-four hexagrams, within four of them there are six lines; therefore, they are called the "six positions."
Regarding the "six positions" (*liuwei*): as in the hexagram *Qian* above and *Kun* below, there are six lines;

likewise, in the hexagram *Zhen* above and *Li* below, and by extension for the others, all possess six lines, which are thus called the "six positions. Furthermore, these six positions are the most essential and subtle core among all written texts;
hence they are termed "refined and subtle" (*jingwei*). They rely on the images to assist in understanding the principles. As for "rely" (*zi*): it means...
This is indeed so. As the *Classic of Filial Piety* says: "One serves the ruler by means of one's father; one serves one's father by means of one's mother. Thus, the father embodies both roles.
When serving the ruler, one must revere him as one would a sovereign king; one must simply be respectful, for if a king were to become angry, he would execute one.
Therefore, it is a matter of reverence alone. When serving one's mother, one must simply love her; just as a mother feels only compassion and affection for her children.
One does not exercise killing. If one serves a father, one must both revere and love him; as in serving a father, one simultaneously exercises reverence and love.
Just as a father sometimes pities and loves his children, yet at times may even kill his children, so it is here.

"The Elephant" refers to the Ten Wings, such as the *Xiang* (Image) and *Xia xiang* (Lower Image). Since the *Xiang* is the foremost among the Ten Wings, the term "Elephant" is now cited to represent the Wings.
These are the Ten Wings (*Shiyi*). They assist and support the six positions (*liuwei*). It is only by means of the Ten Wings that one can explain the six positions.

As for what is called the "Ten Wings": first, the Upper Image (*shangxiang*); second, the Lower Image (*xiang*); third, the Upper Appendix (*shangxi*); fourth, the Lower Appendix (*xi*); fifth, the Upper Judgment (*shangtuan*); sixth, the Lower Judgment (*tuan*);

seventh, the Words on the Text (*wenyan*); eighth, the Explanation of the Hexagrams (*shuogua*); ninth, the Miscellaneous Hexagrams (*zaguā*); and tenth, the Sequence of the Hexagrams (*xuguā*), and so forth. Thus, the six positions rely upon [the Ten Wings].
Only with the Ten Wings does one finally obtain the underlying principles through the fishing-trap [of the text]. As it is said in the *Yijing*: the above clarifies the teaching of Confucius;
next, below, the teaching of Laozi is clarified. Regarding the profound and mysterious nature of the two chapters, these were composed by Laozi himself: the two chapters on the *Daode*.
Cultivation is called the Way (*mārga*); when the Way is perfected, it is termed Virtue (*guṇa*). This Way and this Virtue are both profound, mysterious, subtle, and wondrous.
Regarding the phrase "relying upon Mengzi and Liezi to explore the pivot": "relying upon" (*jiè*) means to borrow or depend upon; "Meng" refers to Mengzi;
"Lie" refers to Liezi—these being among the various masters of the hundred schools. Specifically, one must rely upon Mengzi, Liezi, Zhuangzi, Baopuzi, Huainanzi, and others of the hundred [schools].

The various sons of the house [studied] the two chapters on the Way and its Power (*Dàodé*) by Laozi. "To probe" (*tàn*) means to reach out and take with the hand; "the mechanism" (*jī*) refers to the essential point.
As for the phrase "how much more so," this serves as an illustration leading into the subsequent clarification of Buddhism. Just as within the two inferior teachings mentioned previously:

if it is the teaching of Confucius, the six positions (*liù wèi*) serve as the primary framework, and one then uses the Ten Wings (*shí yì*) to explain those six positions; if it is the teaching of Laozi...
The *Daodejing* and the *Zhuangzi* are taken as the primary texts; the various masters of the hundred schools are then used to explain these two works.

Now, within Buddhism, Buddhism itself is taken as the primary text; as with the aforementioned six sections and two treatises, the Bodhisattvas composed treatises to explain Buddhism, just as the ten appendices and the masters of the hundred schools explained the *Daodejing* and *Zhuangzi*. That which is neither existent nor empty is precisely Buddhism.
However, the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are all described as "neither existent nor empty. Now, we specifically adopt the Middle Way Mahāyāna teaching of "neither existent nor empty":
that which is conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*) is called non-existent, while that which is dependent (*paratantra*) and perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) is called non-empty.
"Cease the discussion of the fishing trap beyond the rabbit snare. "Cease" means to bring to rest. A "trap" (*quán*) is used for catching fish; a "snare" (*tí*) is used for catching rabbits.

"Discussion" (*biàn*) refers to the verbal teachings that can express [the truth]. Just as one relies on the trap and the snare to catch fish and rabbits, so too does one rely on verbal teachings to finally express and realize the underlying principle.
Once the fish and rabbits are caught, one discards the trap and the snare; once the principle is realized, [one discards the words].
This refers to the cessation of verbal teachings. The fish and the rabbit serve as metaphors for the principle (*li*); the trap and the snare serve as metaphors for the teaching (*jiao*).

That which is neither arising nor ceasing, which transcends names and marks at the ford of eternal quiescence, refers to the essential substance of the principle of *tathatā*. It is neither arising nor ceasing;

furthermore, it is free from names and phrases and free from formal characteristics, because its substance is without marks. Its substance is eternal and without cessation, and it is also because it is profoundly tranquil.
"Passage" (*jin*) refers to what is called the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*). Now, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the very foundation of the limit of reality for all phenomena.

"Ultimate awakening" (*zhìjué*) is none other than the Buddha. "Transcendent" (*huǐng*) means distant; "illumination" (*zhào*) means clarity; "patriarch" (*zōng*) means veneration; and "lord" (*zhǔ*) means honor.
The intended meaning is that the Buddha can distantly illuminate profound principles, and because these principles are worthy of reverence, [he is so designated]. Furthermore—
The "Sage" (ārya) refers to the Bodhisattva. If one is a Buddha, they are called the Ultimate Sage; if one is a Bodhisattva, they are called the Prospective Sage.
"Jian" (甄) means to discern or select; "zai" (宰) means to assist in governance. Previously, in the explanation of the Buddha, the term "patriarch" (zong) was used;

"patriarch" signifies the sovereign. Now, in the explanation of the Bodhisattva, the term "ruler" (zai) is used; "ruler" signifies the various officials. As stated below, it also says, "I am the sovereign."

To clarify this through contrast: furthermore, there are those who refer to it as "dregs" (*tsa*). However, because Bodhisattvas have not yet completely severed the two hindrances (*āvaraṇa*), they still possess dregs and impurities;
whereas because Buddhas have severed the two hindrances, they are free from all dregs and impurities.

Regarding the phrase "the wordless word" up to "the moon suspended," this refers precisely to the aforementioned teaching that is neither existent nor empty. Nevertheless, such is the principle-body (*tattva-mūla*) of the Middle Way Mahāyāna.
It is beyond words; thus, the fragrance is wordless. Yet, one must rely upon the words of the scriptural teachings to reveal the principles of the Mahāyāna;
therefore, they are spoken. Regarding the term "wind": it refers to the wind-like nature of the scriptural teachings.

As the worldly expression goes, "the wind of the instructions of the high-ranking official is heard and observed," "wind" here refers to the wind of the teachings of the twelve divisions of the scriptures, which awakens the sentiments of the multitude. However, there is...
The original text states: "The wordless word is the wind that gives warning. "Tao" (韜) means to conceal and then unfold. "Sui" (邃) means profound or remote.
"Gathering [the clouds] so that the moon hangs suspended" is like the clouds being dispersed and the mist rolled away, whereby one immediately beholds the moon in the heavens.
Now, by means of verbal teaching, one immediately beholds all the hidden and remote principles. "The existence of that which is not existent" is precisely this.
The "surging waves" refer to the linguistic expressions that articulate the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional.
"The ocean is profound because its chapters are serene and deep": here, "profound" means deep. The ocean serves as a metaphor for the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).

Just as one knows the great depth of the vast sea by seeing the surging of the water's waves, so too is it with this; if the water were shallow, the waves would likewise be small—as the worldly saying goes: "a foot of water [produces] a foot of wave."
One cannot produce a great wave without water; likewise, it is now because of the teachings on *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) that the profound principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is revealed.
If one did not obtain these teachings, one would not know the principle of *tathatā*.
"Fei" (匪) means "not. "Shu" (屬) means "attached to" or "belonging to. "Juti" (具體) refers to the Buddha. Thus, the Buddha is the embodiment of merit and virtue.
"Lin zhi" (隣智) refers to the Bodhisattva; because they are proximate to the Buddha's wisdom, this present meaning is explained as follows:
only those who are not merely attached to, nor merely embodied in, nor merely proximate to that wisdom can expound the profound and subtle principle of Vijñapti-mātratā. To expound...
This is the explanation. "Zé" (責) refers to that which is the most sublime within the sublime; it is named "Zé. As for "dào" (釣), it is spoken with the intention of capturing the Buddhist teachings.
Being able to expound the most sublime within the sublime and to "hook" the profound and far-reaching principles means that the conceptualization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is nearly exhausted.
This is said with the intention that the aforementioned teachings of the Middle Way, the Mahāyāna, and Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) are ultimate.
These are the essential points; they are the place where the mind comes to rest.

As for the "Ten Branches," these are: the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*, the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, and the *Yogācārabhūmi-viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* in three fascicles.
These last works clarify only matters such as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and do not explain other meanings, as well as the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*.
[The text continues with] "and so forth. Question: By whom were the names of the ten branches composed, and where are they located? Question:

Regarding the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*, this refers to the branch that briefly enumerates the names and numbers, continuing through the subsequent nine branches; all of these are merely such questions. Furthermore, there is the question concerning the branch that encompasses all meanings in their totality.
Consider this: what is the difference between these and the "branch that summarizes the great meaning"?
In the Mahāyāna, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* itself is taken as the trunk, while other treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* serve as its branches and leaves.
In the Hīnayāna, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and the *Kātyāyanīputra-sūtra* (or *Mahāvibhāṣā*) are taken as the trunk, while the six *Pāda-śāstras* are taken as the feet.
Regarding the white rainbows: when the Tathāgata entered nirvāṇa, twelve paths of white rainbows pierced the sun.
Here, that which is circular in the center is the sun, and those on its four sides are the white rainbows. Question: Why are there only twelve paths?
It does not say "eleven paths" or "thirteen paths. To ask again about "flying *jin*": this refers to evil vapors;

that is to say, when the heavens above sweep away stars, white rainbows, and the like, these are all *jin*. When various calamities and portents surge up into the air, they are called "flying. As for "plain" (*su*):
since the preceding phrase already mentioned "white," the following phrase uses "plain" in contrast to it. Thus, "plain" here refers back to...

This refers to the white color. "Suo" (索) means the hair-tuft; "hao" (毫) means the light of the hair-tuft. "Xiao" (銷) means to melt away or dissolve; "xiao" (宵) means night; "xiao" (霄) means the clouds and sky.
Together, these refer to the transformation occurring beneath the silk canopy. "Jing" (景) means brightness.

That is to say, when the Tathāgata was about to enter nirvana, wherever there were those with whom he had a karmic connection, he emitted the light of his white hair-tuft to illuminate them. Wherever that light shone, it did not take a thousand years [for the effects to manifest].

Or five hundred years; this must refer to when the holy teaching reaches [this land]. As for the Buddha’s desire to enter *nirvāṇa*, he emitted light during the night, so that the darkness was immediately dispelled;
thus it is said, "the scene is dissolved," or perhaps "the day is dissolved. Regarding the lines from "thread-flowers" to "even mistaking the day":
these four subsequent lines clarify that after the Buddha has entered *nirvāṇa*, all the sutras and teachings [are as follows].

All are erroneous and mistaken. Regarding the term "thread-flower" (xiànhuā): the warp (*sūtra*) is that which holds the woof; the warp is that which holds the meaning, just as a thread passes through a flower.

"Austere" (*ào*) means profound. As for the characters *fèng* (phoenix) and *fēng* (wind): when one writes the character *fèng*, one places the bird radical inside the "wind" radical, making it the name for a phoenix.
Some have erred and written the character *fēng*; that is, they place the "insect" radical inside the "wind" radical, thus writing it incorrectly.
The character "feng" (風) signifies that the scriptural teachings [of the Buddha] have been lost or corrupted after his parinirvāṇa. Regarding "palm leaves" (貝葉):
in the Western lands [India], all sūtras and śāstras are written upon *bhūrja* leaves. As for "the fish being mistaken for the sun":

this refers to how the secular character for "fish" (魚) should properly have the radical for "fire" (火) beneath the head of "lu" (魯); if one places the radical for "sun" (日) beneath the head of "lu," it is an error to write the character "lu" (魯).

The characters for "not flourishing" (不盛) and "Lu" (魯) are not [to be taken literally]. The intended meaning is that after the Buddha has entered nirvana, all his subtle teachings are what the observer perceives; this is the underlying principle.
"Vei" (惟) has the meaning of "deliberation. "Fǎbǎo" (法寶) refers to the scriptural teachings. "Sī" (斯) means "this.
"Xíng" (行) has the meaning of movement for a brief moment or an instant. "Zhuì" (墜) means to fall or sink. This is the intended meaning of the preceding commentary:
the reason I apply this deliberation is that within the fleeting instant of movement, one immediately falls and sinks into the Buddha-dharma. Some say "xíng" (行)...

The term "character" (字) here is not [the written sign]. It refers now to the practice of "characters," which is the interval between movements. If one is sitting or lying down, one can remain for a long time;
if one is moving, one can only do so for a brief moment.
"Tan" (誕) means birth. "Zi" (茲) means this. "Rong" (融) means comprehensive understanding;

it refers to having attained the Thirty Verses through cultivation, which is the attainment of birth and the attainment of comprehensive understanding regarding the teaching of Vijñaptimātratā. "Xiu" (秀) means solitary excellence. "Huì" (晦) means darkness.
"Guiming" (孤明) refers to the Mahāyāna; the realization of the Mahāyāna is called "solitary illumination," whereas the realization of the Hīnayāna is not so named.

"Solitary Clarity" (Guming). The intended meaning is this: the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu first employed skillful means to conceal his solitary, clear understanding of the Mahāyāna and entered the monastic life within the Hīnayāna.
There, he composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* to elucidate the tenets of the Sautrāntika masters.

One who "shows conformity with the mundane while asserting existence" is the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu. Although Vasubandhu entered the monastic order within the Hīnayāna school, [he remained] harmonious...
It illuminates while demonstrating conformity with the mundane dust. In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the doctrine of the Sarvāstivāda masters is clarified;

therefore, it is said that "existence is taught. Regarding the statement that "wisdom is bound" in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*: "wisdom-bound" refers precisely to the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because the cognitive obscuration is a bondage of wisdom, it is able to obstruct bodhi. The afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is termed "nature-bound," as it is able to obstruct nirvāṇa.
...the *pāda*. If the Hīnayāna adherents maintain that this is indeed the bondage of wisdom (*prajñā-bandhana*), the meaning is as follows:

Master Vasubandhu previously demonstrated that because there was an obstruction to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and a bondage of wisdom, he was obscured regarding the Mahāyāna; thus, he went forth into the Hīnayāna school.

Now, having abandoned the Hīnayāna for the Mahāyāna, he composed the *Triṃśikā-bhāṣya* (Commentary on the Thirty Verses). Thus, when Master Asaṅga perceived the illness of Vasubandhu, he [instructed] his disciples...

He acquired [the treatise]. As Vasubandhu was one of the disciples of Asaṅga, once he had completed his versification of the "Ten Stages" chapter, and after Vasubandhu had fallen ill, he composed the *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* to explain the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
This is precisely the "untying of the bonds of wisdom. Regarding the phrase "manifesting the vertical":
this refers to the period after Vasubandhu, during which the Mahāyāna flourished even more extensively, allowing the Great Vehicle to reach its ultimate fulfillment and spread widely.
Furthermore, "sages" refers to one sage appearing every five hundred years; "worthies" refers to one worthy appearing every thousand years. Regarding the commentary:

as for "discussing emptiness," since the preceding phrase spoke of "proclaiming existence," the following phrase speaks of "discussing emptiness"; these are likewise correlative. "To mirror" means to reflect or to illuminate.
The meaning is that the wisdom of the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu is able to illuminate all paths of meaning, exhausting them all completely and thoroughly. "Chia" (洽) means...

"Moistening" (*run*) means that the meaning explained by the Bodhisattva Maitreya is clear; it universally brings about benefit, happiness, moisture, and nourishment for all sentient beings without exception.
Therefore, it is said that "wisdom is pervasive and harmonious. "The ultimate mystery" (*xuanji*) refers precisely to these thirty verses.
This universally explains the profound, subtle, and ultimate principles of all sutras in their entirety.
As for the fact that the prose commentary (*vṛtti*) was not completed, it is simply because [Vasubandhu] composed only thirty verses (*śloka*) and had not yet produced the long prose commentary.

Regarding the term "returning to truth" (*guizhen*): the intended meaning is that the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu entered *nirvāṇa*, which is termed "returning to truth" and "ascending to the supreme. "Ascending" (*qian*) here means death.

The intended meaning is as follows: When Vasubandhu Bodhisattva passed away, [the questioner] asked about it but did not mention "middle" or "lower. Furthermore, when someone asked, "I humbly submit that the superior...
[he] did not mention "middle" or "lower. To ask again is to repeat; "redundant" (*fan*) means much, while "concise" (*yue*) means little.

The intended meaning is that although Vasubandhu Bodhisattva composed this verse, its wording is extremely brief while its significance is immense. As for "fountain source" (*quanyuan*): this refers to the *Vijñaptimātratā*.
The *Śāstra* is the very source of all dharmas. Regarding "twofold secrecy" (*punar-guhya*): it refers to a secret treasury. The intended meaning is as follows:
when the Buddha first entered parinirvāṇa, the principle of Vijñaptimātra was obtained and once concealed;
now, following the passing of Vasubandhu, the wisdom and principle of Vijñaptimātra have been concealed for a second time. Therefore, it is called "twofold secrecy."
"Yuan" (爰) refers to "at this point," specifically referring to Dharmapāla and others.

"Liquefying the mind" (*yiqing*) means that just as one sees a person's face when water is clear and pure, so too does one perceive the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) when the mind is clear and pure.

Regarding the "seven transformations" (*qizhuan*), among the eight grammatical cases (*aṣṭau vibhaktayaḥ*), the eighth—the vocative—is excluded, and the preceding seven cases are taken. "Ji" (激) means "to request."
It is like striking a bell: only when it is struck does its sound emerge. If someone requests the Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva then expounds the Dharma.
Regarding "eloquence like a flowing river": this Bodhisattva’s eloquence is like a cascading torrent. Regarding "praising the subtle": [the Bodhisattva praises] the profound and subtle [Dharma].
These same ten bodhisattvas composed a prose commentary (*gadya-vyākhyā*) to praise these subtle words of the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
"Spirit" (*shen*) refers to the mind. Regarding the eight consciousnesses: since both bodhisattvas and śrāvakas each have four collections (*piṭaka*), there are thus eight collections (*aṣṭapiṭaka*).
Among the Bodhisattva [piṭakas], there are four: first, that which elucidates meditative concentration (samādhi) is called the Sūtra Piṭaka;
second, that which elucidates ethical discipline (śīla) is called the Vinaya Piṭaka; third, that which elucidates the establishment of wisdom (prajñā) is called the Abhidharma Piṭaka;

and fourth, that which elucidates a mixture of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom is called the Miscellaneous Piṭaka (Kṣudraka). Furthermore, within the Śrāvaka Piṭaka, there are likewise four piṭakas.
The reason the Pratyekabuddhayāna does not establish the *piṭaka* is that it lacks distinct sūtras and teachings. Regarding the purification of that true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*):

although the principle of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) existed previously, it was not yet designated as "true consciousness" because the teaching of consciousness-only had not yet been established.

It is not called "pure. Now, by composing the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) to establish the principles of consciousness-only, one is said to purify that true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*).
True consciousness does not refer solely to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is also called true consciousness.

All three natures collectively are termed true consciousness; the three natures collectively are termed consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). "Ya" means "correct. [This refers to] the provisional and the ultimate.

Now, it is clarified that within the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only) there are two [positions]. The first states: the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) of indeterminate nature are provisional (*upāya*), while the bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment are real.

The second states: the *parasaṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body for others) and the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) are provisional, whereas the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body for oneself) and the *dharmatākāya* (dharma-nature body) are termed real.
However, within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, all three bodies are fully elucidated. "Ling" (陵) means to despise or slight.
Furthermore, the present *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* is even more sublime and profound; it utterly surpasses Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata*). "Vulture Peak" refers to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

Regarding the phrase "the principle penetrates the subtle and the ineffable": that which cannot be reached by sight is called "subtle" (*xi*); that which cannot be reached by hearing is called "ineffable" (*yi*).
These terms are borrowed from the language of Laozi. "To conceal" means to cover or obstruct. "Dragon Palace" (*nāga-bhavana*) here intends to signify the ocean.
The principle of this Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) is profound; it is as deep as the great ocean and as lofty as a mountain. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
within the Dragon Palace there are many sūtras and śāstras, yet this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* is even more excellent than those scriptures in the Dragon Palace.
Alternatively, one may consider the birds and beasts in contrast: in the preceding phrase "vulture" (*jīva*), the vulture is a bird; in the subsequent phrase "dragon," the dragon is a beast.

"Mainstay" (*kāṅ*) refers to the fundamental principles; "collar" (*lǐng*) refers to the collar of a garment; "gate" (*mén*) refers to that which can manage [the garment]; "essential use" (*yào*) refers to the sleeves.

From within the sleeves, the hand may emerge and thus possess essential utility. The intended meaning is that the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* serves as the mainstay and essential utility for all the sūtras.
"Cord" (*suò*) refers to unraveling; "hidden" (*yǐn*) refers to concealment. It refers to all the cords found within the various sūtras and śāstras.
The meaning of "concealed and hidden" is fully realized within this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. The term "to gather" (*duo*) means to collect; "extraordinary" (*qi*) means marvelous.

Within this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, one can indeed collect all the extraordinary meanings found throughout the various sūtras and śāstras, extracting and recording them all within the *Vijñaptimātra* system.

Regarding the "three valid cognitions" (*trividha-pramāṇa*), they are: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and authoritative testimony (*āptāgama*). These are erroneously [presented as] direct perception and sacred word.

Using these three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to refute the paths of outsiders is like the time of battle between two armies. If the army is victorious, its banners and standards remain firm;
if the army retreats and is weak, its banners and standards fall. This refers to the position of the *māmaka* (the retreating one).

As for the "two causes," these are the generative cause (*janaka-hetu*) and the revealing cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*) within the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*. The intent is to explain the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) of the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*).

Regarding the third principle: because the proponent establishes the cause of production (*janaka-hetu*), it serves as the cause of realization (*jñāpaka-hetu*) for the wisdom that overcomes adversaries.
This is analogous to the similarity between recitation and a spring. Thus, by employing the two causes of production and realization from the *Hetuvidyā*, one refutes the Hinayāna;

the Hinayānists are weakened and no longer follow the tracks. A "track" (*zhú*) refers to the hoofprints of an ox, while a "path" (*guǐ*) refers to the ruts of a chariot. The question asks how to distinguish the banners and avoid the chaotic tracks. [End of excerpt].
Regarding the text of the book: as for the further inquiry concerning "modeling" (yi), it refers to modeling the heavens and the earth in their simultaneous sustenance.

That Heaven can cover and Earth can sustain is intended to explain the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only); it means modeling the heavens and the earth in their capacities to cover and sustain.

"Pregnant" (*yun*) means to contain; it is like having a child within a mother's womb, which is called being pregnant. Regarding "contending its flow with the Yellow River," the waters of the Yellow River—
The flow of time is exceedingly swift. This *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* of mine is now circulating throughout all directions;
it flows even more rapidly than the waters of the Yellow River, as if competing with its current. Some versions read "the flow of the Huang (Huang)," but "Huang" is a name for stagnant water.
In the region east of Liu (Liu), there is a place called Wu (Wu), which is the name for the Han River. Since these two rivers flow together, it is referred to as "Huang."
"Wu zheng liu. The character "wu" is pronounced as the rising tone (third tone) of the character "mian. Furthermore, there is another version that reads "huang sheng" (yellow rope).
"Sheng" means "hu" (sudden/sudden burst). "Leiting" refers to "pilili" (thunderclap). Just as when a sudden thunderclap emits its sound, it can only be heard by those nearby.

The fame of my *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* now resounds far and wide, shaking the distant reaches of the world; thus, it is only fitting that its reputation should compete with the echoes of the past.

It was during the time of King Zhou Zhao that [the Master] was born, and during the era of King Zhou Mu that he entered *parinirvāṇa*. At midnight, he emitted a radiance that eclipsed the light of the stars.
At that very moment, the Buddha-dharma had not yet reached this land of Han. This is what is recorded in the *Mìzhě* (The Hidden).
"Zang" (藏) means to store. "The Ultimate Way" (至道) refers precisely to the Buddha-dharma. "Yü" (鬱) describes a state of flourishing. "Hanri Tōki" (漢日通暉)—"ki" (暉) means radiance.
This is like the places illuminated by the light emitted by the Buddha; even after a thousand years have passed, the Dharma of the Buddha will surely reach those places.
This occurred during the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, when Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna arrived carrying the scriptures on white horses.
Regarding "this land": as for the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), during the five hundred years of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), the Buddha-dharma had not yet reached this region;
it was only during the period of the Semblance Dharma that it finally arrived here. "Xia" (遐) means distant; it also implies being covered by or reaching unto.
Regarding those who translated the meanings of the Sūtras and Vinaya: the subsequent passage below clarifies this very point.

Since the Dharma first flowed to the East, there have been more than three hundred monks who translated the scriptures; they are like a flowing river that has never run dry. "Those who carry on the legacy" refers to their traces;
it means that the footprints of the monks who translated the scriptures from the Western lands have continued in succession. Thus, the Book says:

On the dais, one places the feet side by side (*buwu*); on the ground below the dais, one joins the footprints (*jiawu*). "Footprints" refers to the traces left behind. It is like when one sees a sovereign or an official:
if one reaches the base of the dais and walks there, the feet may move only one chi across the ground, yet this does not constitute a full step.
This is not a place for walking with wide strides. However, if one is summoned and must walk down from the dais, the feet should move only one cun at a time.
"Two inches of ground; one must not move even a foot of ground. *Duò* means "to encounter" or "to see. Regarding "the right of the Onion Range" (*Cōngyòu*):
if it is west of the Pamir Mountains (the Onion Range), it is called the Right of the Onion Range; if it is east of the Onion Range, it is called the Left of the Onion Range.

"Eminent" (*yīng*) refers to eminent scholars, that is, monks who comment upon the scriptures. The meaning of this passage is that since ancient times, there have been those [on the right of the Onion Range]...
The monks from countries such as Xiāo’āo Chángguó (Western Bird Long Country) and others, or those from other peripheral lands—these are all Hu (barbarian) monks;
they are not true Brahmins, nor do they speak the Sanskrit language. They have come here to translate the scriptures.

There is no one among the people here who has not dreamed of the various eminent masters within the five regions of India, yet they neither hear the true Sanskrit language nor [possess its knowledge].

[He] saw great arhats and bodhisattvas. Now, the Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang has personally traveled to each of the five regions of India, where he met various eminent scholars and received their personal instruction.
He has mastered the true Sanskrit language. As for the term "huang" (壤), it refers to the designation for fields and land.
To the west of the Pamir Mountains, within the small bordering kingdoms, since they are all entirely Hu (non-Chinese) lands, their speech and sounds are not correct. Not...
This is the language of Brahmā (Sanskrit), yet it does not resemble the Brahmā language of the five regions of India. "Mixed" means intermingled. Regarding "Gong" and "Yu":
these are the Gong among the five musical notes—namely, Gong, Shang, Jiao, Zhi, and Yu. "Hua" refers to the famous flowers of the Great Tang country; "Xia" refers to the Xia tribes;
and "Rong" refers to the various frontier states to the west, all of which are termed "Western Rong. These are not true Brahmins.
Nor is it the true speech of the Five Heavenly Emperors. Therefore, the various countries to the south of this land are called the Southern Man;
those to the north are called the Northern Di; those to the east are called the Eastern Yi; and those to the west are called the Western Rong.
The meaning of this passage is that the Rong and Hu languages of the western countries were translated into the Hua and Xia languages of this region, causing them to become intermingled.
The same applies; it is also erroneous because it is not the true Sanskrit language. Regarding the phrase "the characters are as far apart as heaven and earth":
if one were in the central kingdom of India, all written characters would be celestial writing (*devanāgarī*), and all spoken languages would be identical to the celestial tongue.

This is because it is the language of the Brahma King (*Brahmā*). As for the five kingdoms of India, these are called the Yuezhi Kingdoms (*Cīna*); just as the moon in the heavens is extremely cool and refreshing.
It is able to eliminate the heat of affliction. All the worthy and holy ones appeared in the five regions of India; they were able to remove the afflictions of sentient beings.
If the characters in this land of Han were created by humans, then they were fashioned by ancient figures such as Cang Jie and others;
these are human words. Therefore, since antiquity, the "Heaven" (Tian) character from the celestial language of India has been translated here as being identical to this [Chinese] character.
"Comparing human languages": this refers to errors or omissions. "Obscure" means dark or ignorant.

"Form and sound" refers to characters written according to their form and sound, namely those such as *xiàngxíng* (pictographic) and *zhuǎnzhù* (phono-semantic) characters. "Hu" refers to the language of Hu monks from the countries to the west.
"Jin" refers to the Han country of this region. The intended meaning is that [this applies to] all translations from ancient times onward.
These monks were all Hu monks from countries to the west; they understood only the Hu language and did not understand Sanskrit.
Consequently, they translated the scriptures using the Hu language, yet many of the meanings of the Way were erroneously rendered during the Jin period. "Zao" refers to wine dregs;
"po" refers to the fine essence within those dregs, which is called "po. However, they obtained only a small amount of these dregs and essences, failing to grasp the profound and mysterious depths.
"Sshang" means loss.
"Hong" means great. "Shi" means great. If there is great doubt, it is like being enveloped by mist; if there is great stagnation, it is like clouds coalescing.
When one is enveloped by great mist or when great clouds have coalesced, the sun and sky cannot be seen. If there is great doubt, [the same occurs].
If there is great stagnation, one will not perceive the profound principle. "Obscure" (*you*) means hidden; "brilliant" (*xuan*) refers to the fivefold patterns and colors.
"Repeatedly" (*lu*) means many times. The meaning of this passage is that all the hidden patterns within its principles have been explained numerous times above.
"In detail" (*xiang*) means to explain; it indicates that while the principles may be briefly stated, they can be fully understood through detailed exposition.
"Containing brilliance. "Brilliance" refers to literary elegance. "Gathering" means to assemble. This signifies the place where the Tripiṭaka Master and other people gathered together.
His name as the Tripiṭaka Master stood out beyond that of the others. "Illuminating" refers to what is seen by the eyes, which is termed illumination.
"Seizing" means to grasp. "The Spiritual Terrace" refers to the center of the mind. The intended meaning is: [the brilliance of] the Tripiṭaka Master.

The "mind-eye" refers to the heart-essence capable of grasping principles and meanings; "three years" refers to the period of accumulation. "Virtue" (*de*) means moral cultivation; "patriarch" (*zong*) means honorable.
The intended meaning is that the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty accumulated virtue within his person and occupied a position of supreme honor.
"Waves" (*yi*) refers to water; "marsh" (*zhao*) refers to a pond. The intended meaning is that within the body of the Tripitaka Master, the waters of wisdom surge forth inexhaustibly.

"Rushing forth" (*mù*) means to set out. "Three wheels" refers to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), instruction (*anuśāsana*), and reading the minds of others (*cetahparyāya*). "Track" (*zhú*) means the wheel-tracks of a chariot;
it signifies being far removed. "Advancing" (*jìn*) means to proceed forward. "Gold sand" refers to the river Aralavati in the West, which contains gold sand within its waters.
The meaning of this sentence is that the Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty proceeded far toward the Western Aralavati River.
[He] went to the banks of the Rohitī River. Regarding the character "Jin" (晉) used here: in the *Ping* (評), it states that "Jin" means "to advance" (進).

This corresponds to the "Jin" (進) in the word "advancing while running around" (走繞之進), as well as the "Jin" (晉) in "the land of Jin" (晉地). These two characters are identical in meaning: both signify "to go forward.
As for the "eight liberations" (八解), they are the eight *vimokṣas*. The intended meaning is that within the body of the Tripiṭaka, there are eight...
Within the context of liberation, *zhenbo* (眞波) means "water. *Liao* (遼) means "distant.
As for the "Jade Well" (*yùjǐng*), there is a country in the west where such a Jade Well exists; the intended meaning is that the Tripitaka Master traveled far toward that Jade Well.
Thus, the Jade Well corresponds to the "golden sand" mentioned in the preceding phrase. *Qū* (軀) refers to the body. *Xùn* (殉) means to seek after or pursue.
The meaning is as follows: Tripiṭaka forgot his physical fatigue because he was seeking the Dharma in the Western Regions. "Wei" (委) means to entrust oneself;

"qi" (祈) means to pray or entreat; and "tong" (通) means to attain penetration. This signifies that Tripiṭaka entrusted himself to the Triple Gem and made earnest prayers, thereby attaining penetration.
"Secretly harmonizing with the Heavenly Truth" means that the Tripitaka Master secretly harmonized [with the truth] and attained thorough penetration;
he attained harmony with the Heavenly Mind and his vows were fulfilled. "Subtle" (wei) means little; "aided" (zi) means to take up; "practiced" (xi) means to study.
This means that when the Tripitaka Master reached those Western countries, he used little effort yet learned many scriptures and treatises. "Fei" means not; "chi" means to unfold.
"Spread" (*pu*) means to extend. "Distinct" (*yi*) means to differentiate. This preceding phrase reveals that the wisdom of the Tripiṭaka is broad;
it is not merely that the wisdom is broadly spread, but that a person of divine spirit is what truly distinguishes them from others—hence, it is said to "reveal distinction.
"Firm" (*gu*) means steadfast. "Accumulation" (*yun*) means a gathering. "Distant" (*tiao*) means far-reaching. "Auspicious" (*xiang*) means good. This subsequent phrase is an eulogy.
The Tripitaka possesses merit. This implies that only those who have accumulated vast stores of merit within their firm bodies can travel far away on foot.
"Prepared" (bei) means broad; "to tread" (jian) means to walk upon; and "spiritual beings" (shen) refers to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the various noble disciples.
It is so. "Zōng" (蹤) means "traces. This signifies that wherever the Tripitaka reached in those Western lands, the traces of all the sages were entirely pervasive;
it also implies his actual treading upon them. "Probing the secret treasury": the "secret treasury" refers to the matters within the minds of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and other sages.
This signifies that when the Tripitaka went to those Western lands, he was able to exhaustively probe and extract [their essence].
One attains the secret essentials within the heart-treasury of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. "To behold" (*moku*) means to see.
"Former sages" refers to the various Dharma masters of this land from ancient times onward. "Pivot" (*shu*) refers to the essential mechanism. These two phrases above [constitute the title].

This intends to clarify meanings concerning the great virtuous ones of antiquity in this land that had not previously been seen; it shows that the Tripitaka masters have thoroughly mastered these, which reside within the pivot of the mind’s governance.
"In the past" (*nang*) means "formerly"; "left behind" (*yi*) means "lost. The meaning of the following two phrases is to clarify the meanings lost by the great virtuous ones of old;
it shows that the Tripitaka encompasses the ultimate depths of the mind.
"Vow" (*zhi*) refers to the will (*yi-zhi*). "Vast" (*hong*) means great. "Console" (*fu*) means to receive or welcome.

The meaning of this passage is that the fundamental intent of the Tripiṭaka Master was his vow and will to vastily console and welcome sentient beings. The preceding portion of the text praises the Master’s activities while in the Western Regions.
As for the phrase "returning to the old land," this refers to the subsequent portion of the text, which reveals that the Master departed from the Western Regions.
[He] returned to his native country. "Virtue" (*de*) refers to the Way and its Power (*daode*). "Appropriate" (*jian*) means fitting.
The meaning of this passage is that the Way and Power of the Tripiṭaka Master accorded with the mind of the Son of Heaven. "Extended" (*yan*) means far-reaching.

"Celestial refinement" (*tianzao*) implies that the Tripiṭaka Master was originally endowed with a natural talent bestowed by Heaven, not merely like human filial piety. "Precious verses" (*baoji*) refers to the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on the Thirty Verses) composed by Dharmapāla.

The *Daśa-śloka-vyākhyāna* (Explanation of the Ten Verses). When Dharmapāla was on the verge of death beneath the Bodhi tree, he had already composed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, but it had not yet been published for circulation.
At that time, there was a virtuous lay follower of the five precepts beneath the Bodhi tree who alone made offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla for three years.
Then, Dharmapāla took this commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and bestowed it upon him.
The Wise One Rests. At this time, once the Wise One had obtained this explanation of *vijñapti-mātra*, if another person were to look at this explanation from afar, they would obtain gold coins;
if one were to look at this explanation from nearby, they would obtain even more gold coins.
Because of the profound reverence for this explanation, the subsequent commentary states: "Although there were ten masters who composed this explanation, among them, Dharmapāla..."
His reputation for eloquence resounded alone; no other person could attain such verses.

As stated in the *Śūyao* (Essential Pivot), at a later time, the Tripiṭaka Master traveled to that Western land, crawling on his elbows and knees. When the Venerable One saw the Tripiṭaka Master approaching from afar, he...
Although he did not receive any money, he immediately provided the Tripiṭaka Master’s commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. As for "extolling to the south":
once the Tripiṭaka Master had obtained this commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, he extensively praised it before the King of South India and caused it to circulate widely.
Regarding the "golden tablet," the question asks: does the term "the Emperor's mind" refer to the King of the Western Country, or to the King of this country? If...

Regarding the statement "the Son of Heaven of this country": since the Tripitaka Master had already departed from this country, why does the subsequent text say "praising the South," specifically stating that he recited the precious verses while facing the territory of South India?
If one says it was the Son of Heaven of the Western Country (China), the Tripitaka Master had not yet arrived in this land;
why then does the preceding text state that he was "returning to his former home"? One should ask: according to my humble opinion, regarding what has not yet occurred...
It spread to South India during the Day (the Tang dynasty). Thus, it is not at all a fault to discuss both [traditions].

As for the "Golden Tablets flowing East," this refers to taking the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only) interpretation and bringing it toward the Eastern homeland. "Chang" means to expound; "yi" means to obscure or hinder.

"Dàng" (蕩) means to wash away or cleanse. "Yí" (疑) refers to the breath or vital energy (*qi*). The commentary states that since ancient times, there have been many instances of this "breath of doubt," which is pervasive and manifold.
"Rù" (縟) refers to the five colors. "Sī" (思) refers to the wisdom of contemplation; this character should be pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*).
"Yǐng" (穎) means to transcend or excel. "Tán" (彈) means to press down or constrain. "Jià" (駕) means to move or impel. This is the text.
The meaning is that the moral virtue and realization of the Tripitaka masters are able to suppress the heads of others;
it means that among all people, the Tripitaka masters stand out as uniquely eminent. "Ling" (陵) means to insult and oppress; "yan" (掩) means to cover and obstruct.

The meaning is that the moral virtue, realization, and understanding within the bodies of the Tripitaka masters have, for a thousand ages past, insulted and suppressed [the claims of others], and have covered and obstructed [their own faults].
"Jù yǔ fū zhě" (詎與夫者) is the opening phrase of the discourse; it is similar in its structural force to "qiè yǐ gài děng" (竊以蓋等).
"Jiāyī" (家依) refers to the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha; in Sanskrit he is called Paramārtha, which in Chinese is translated as Jiāyī.

"Xiáng" (驤) means to excel. "Yù" (譽) means reputation. "Shàn" (擅) means exclusive or sole. "Měi" (美) means excellent. "Shēngmíng" (聲明) refers to *śabda-vidyā* (the science of grammar and phonology). "Shēng" (聲) is sound.

This refers to the *Vyākaraṇa* (Grammar). The meaning of this passage is to show that although the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha had attained supreme and excellent renown at that time, he did not universally understand other sūtras and śāstras;
he was merely uniquely skilled in the *Vyākaraṇa*, like one who understands the speech of birds as soon as they cry out.
"Tongshou" refers to Dharma Master Kumārajīva. In Sanskrit, he is called Kumārajīva; here [it is rendered as] Tongshou.

Regarding the phrase "Master Kuṃārajīva": "Fāng" (芳) means beautiful or excellent; "tú" (徒) means empty or alone. "Madhyamaka" refers to the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, the *Śataśāstra*, the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, and so forth.

The intended meaning is that although Master Kumārajīva attained the beautiful reputation [of being a great translator], he only mastered the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, the *Śataśāstra*, and the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, and was not well-versed in other sūtras or śāstras. This is the intent and the explicit meaning.
"I, the Tripitaka Master, have attained a complete understanding of all sutras and śāstras. The phrase "only this much" (*yún'ér yǐrǐ*) is a term used to conclude a statement.

*Sī* (斯) means "this," and *huì* (彚) means "category" or "kind. The intended meaning is that this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) has ten masters as its categories [of commentaries].
"Shi" (釋) means to synthesize and compose into a single work; it means to deliberate and to summarize. "Hua" (華) is the name for this region, the Han country;
it refers to the heartland of China. "Fan" (梵) is the language of the West; "quan" (詮) means to explain and measure.

The meaning of this passage is as follows: When the Tripiṭaka Master translated the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, he deliberated upon the Chinese and Sanskrit terms and weighed the lightness and heaviness of the phonemes while translating.
"To mold and refine the distinctions among the various meanings"—here, "refine" (*zhen*) means "to accomplish.
This implies that when the Tripiṭaka Master translated these ten masters' interpretations, regarding those points where the ten masters' interpretations differed, he [resolved them]...
In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, when explaining a passage concerning a single meaning, it is appropriate to have many instances of "having meaning" (*yǒuyì*) and so forth;

this serves to distinguish them from three or five other instances of "having meaning. This is just as, for example, when explaining the "seeds" (*bīja*), there are the interpretations of three masters and so on.

Regarding the phrase "there are eleven masters' translations," *xié* means "to harmonize" or "to accord with. The intended meaning is that when the Tripiṭaka Master was translating the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, if he saw...
Regarding the explanation of "a single point of meaning" where ten masters share one interpretation:

at the time of translating this treatise, the interpretations of the ten masters were harmonized so that they concur on a single meaningful point, rather than adhering to many different meanings. *Hong* means great; *gang* refers to the fundamental framework or governing principles.

Regarding the statement "Establishing Consciousness-Only" (*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*), I shall first present the general outline. The term "banner" (*jīng*) signifies that upon seeing a banner, one knows there is a Son of Heaven beneath it;

upon seeing a banner or streamer, one knows there is a general and an army beneath it. Similarly, upon seeing the words "Establishing Consciousness-Only," one knows that the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* lies beneath them.

The term "mirror" (*jìng*) carries the meaning of reflecting or illuminating. As for "excluding the two Piṭakas": since this is a treatise (*śāstra*), it thereby excludes [the Sūtra and Vinaya Piṭakas].

Setting aside the other two collections of Sūtra and Vinaya, the Abhidharma-piṭaka alone is singled out as a "meritorious achievement. To explain this term *chéng* (成就): "achievement" (*chéng*) refers to the establishment of merit and the rectification of faults.

Thus, the *Biéxíng jiàojì* (Record of the Separate Transmission of the Teachings) states: "Achievement" is a designation for that which is capable of bringing something to completion; it establishes the grand design of the Great Meaning.
"Great Awakening" (*dàjué*) refers to the Mahāyāna, or perhaps the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*). Its "purport" (*zhǐyì*) is its underlying intent; it is "flourishing" (*lóng*).

"High" refers to loftiness. The intended meaning is that the assertion that external objects do not exist and that consciousness alone is established is precisely the lofty and far-reaching intention of the Mahāyāna.
"The root verses are established" means that when the thirty verses are successfully proven, the meaning of the Middle Way is revealed.
"Manifested" means made clear.

"Eliminating characteristics" (*miṅxiàng*): "eliminating" (*mǐn*) means to subsume. To subsume is to subsume the objective aspect (*xiànfēn*), which is why it is said that there is "consciousness-only.
"One who clings to existence loses their truth": this refers to the superimposition (*āropa*) of clinging to a real principle. "One who stagnates in emptiness deviates from its reality":
this refers to the denial (*apavāda*) of clinging to the true principle. "One who stagnates in emptiness deviates from its reality" means... [the latter half of the sentence continues as above].
This is the grasping at diminution (*apavāda*). The term "real" (*satya*) mentioned below corresponds to the character "true" (*tattva*) in the preceding phrase. "Obscure" means darkness.
"Long immersed in the two extremes" refers to being submerged in the extreme of superimposition (*samāropa*) and the extreme of diminution (*apavāda*).

Regarding the statement that "by means of this, that is established, which is called 'Establishment of Consciousness-Only' (*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*"): these thirty verses are named *Vijñaptimātra*, while the prose commentary is named... [the rest of the sentence continues].

This constitutes its establishment. That is to say, by means of this treatise, the thirty [verses] on Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) are established; therefore, it is called "the establishment of Consciousness-Only.
*Samāsa* refers to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound among the six types of compounds. In Sanskrit it is called *samāsa*, which here is translated as "dependent compound" (*yishu shi*).
However, in Sanskrit it is also called *ṣaṭ samāsāḥ*, which is translated as "the six types of compounded compounds."

*Sūtra* is a Sanskrit term; among the eight grammatical cases (*vibhakti*), it belongs to the seventh case, the locative (*ādhāra*), and is interpreted as a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative compound).
The "opponent" (*prativādin*) is the one who debates; the "proponent" (*vādin*) is the one who establishes the thesis.

As for "arraying," it means that the proponent and the opponent, these two associates, take their seats. Now, in any formal discussion, there must inevitably be an opponent and a proponent who engage in debate.

To establish a position and to refute it is what is called "discourse" (*lun*). When banners and drums are raised, this is because the method of debating doctrine is like two armies engaged in battle;
as banners and war-drums are sounded, one side retreats and the other prevails. Discourse is likewise:
one must strike the bell to assemble the multitude, wherein there is establishment and refutation, victory and defeat. Thus, the profound gate is opened wide.
"By means of this [treatise], all profound and obscure meanings that are difficult to understand within the discourses (*sūtra*) are fully understood and thoroughly penetrated.

'To respond' (*zhe*) refers to the most sublime among the sublime. Regarding 'establishing the teaching through the teaching': this refers to establishing the thirty verses (*kārikā*) by means of the prose commentary (*bhāṣya*) of the treatise.
Regarding 'relying on the teaching to establish the principle': 'relying' (*zi*) means taking up the prose commentary of the treatise and..."
The *Triṃśikā-kārikā* establishes the principle of Vijñaptimātra; thus, it constitutes this treatise (*śāstra*). "Constitutes" means that which establishes.

That which establishes is the treatise itself—the prose commentary and the thirty verses along with their underlying principles. These are what is established. The "treatise" refers to the instruction (*deśanā*).
This refers to the prose commentary (*gadya*) mentioned previously and the thirty verses (*kārikā*). The intended meaning is that these very [verses] constitute the treatise;
thus, it is called "the treatise" by way of a *karmadhāraya* compound, because they establish the principles of logic (*nyāyamukha*).

"Establishing principle by means of principle" means that "principle" refers to the principle of the prose commentary (*gadya*), and "establishing principle" refers to the principle of the thirty verses (*kārikā*).
The intended meaning is that the principle of the prose commentary is used to establish the principles of the thirty verses.
"Establishing the teaching by means of principle" refers to taking the principles of the prose commentary and the [thirty verses]...
The ten verses establish the teaching of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) through reasoning. Regarding this, "establishment" (*siddhi*) refers to that which establishes;
thus, "reasoning" (*yukti*) is what is termed the "establisher. As for "treatise" (*śāstra*), it is that which is established; since a treatise is precisely the teaching, it is the "established."

In this context, the principle (*li*) is that which establishes, while the teaching (*jiao*) is that which is established; therefore, the title "A Treatise on Establishment" (*Chengji lun*) is interpreted according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
"Mian" (*mian*) refers to shame and modesty. "Rong" refers to the ancient Master Rong. "Kai" refers to the ancient Master Kai. The intention of the author of the sub-commentary (*shu*) is as follows:
"I am ashamed before the ancient masters such as [Master] Rong and [Master] Kai. "Tian" (*tian*) means to be included in or to enter. "Pei" (*pei*) means to accompany.
"Pei-sui" (陪隨) means to accompany. "Yi-zhe" (譯者) refers to those who translate the sūtras and śāstras.
"Cai" (採) means to grasp or hold. "Gu" (觚) refers to the octagonal wooden tablets used in common parlance.
When a child wishes to pursue learning, they write the chapters of the twenty-five schools upon these octagonal wooden tablets; the child then mounts this octagonal wood.
One writes characters upon an octagonal wooden block. Once the writing on the octagonal wooden block is complete, one must wipe it away.
Having wiped away the characters written on the octagonal wooden block, one writes them once more.
When this child grows up, he will achieve personal virtue and lead a multitude as a leader. Thus, [it is from] the *Jiùjù biàn* (The Rush-to-Completion Primer).
Regarding the "Chapter on Mounted Persons": Within the Translation Institute (Fanjingyuan), there are also wooden tablets (mujianzi) about three or four feet long.
When it is time to translate a scripture, a Chinese monk holds a wooden tablet in his hand.
Once he hears a Brahmin monk recite the Sanskrit, the Chinese monk immediately writes it down upon the wooden tablet. Once the characters have been written, the assembly [proceeds together].
They deliberated upon these words. If the principles of these words were correct, they would transcribe them into the sūtras and śāstras;
if the words were not authentic, they would erase the characters on the tablets and send Brahmin monks to translate the Sanskrit, recording it back onto the tablets.
The assembly then deliberated again on this text. The intent of the commentary is that the Master humbly said of himself: "I possess no knowledge or understanding. On that day—
At that time, he was granted double the number of attendants compared to others of his rank and entered the Translation Institute (Yi-jing-yuan), where he held a wooden tablet (*mu-jian*).

Furthermore, it is said that the term "gu" refers to the handle of a brush; this signifies that the Master of the Commentary was holding a brush-handle while translating the scriptures within the Translation Institute.
As for Yan You, he was a principal disciple of Confucius—namely, Yan Hui and Zi You. This passage...
As for the meaning: the Master of the Commentary himself said, "My own studies are such that I feel ashamed when compared to the disciples of Confucius, namely Ziyou and Yanhui.
*Cè* (廁) means to participate in or to enter; it refers here to entering into the flow [of the teachings]. *Zī* (資) means to take up or to rely upon. *Hán* (函) refers to...

When the Dharma Master preaches the Dharma among the assembly, there must also be some small amount of open space before his seat to accommodate the *cintāmaṇi* staff held in the Dharma Master’s hand as he points toward the east and west. One must not allow people to sit too close to the Dharma Master’s seat.
As for the "staff," this refers to the *cintāmaṇi* staff held in the Dharma Master’s hand. The author of the commentary expresses self-deprecation, saying: "I..."
I have erroneously presumed to join the ranks of those who practice the dharma, ascending the high seat and grasping the *cintāmaṇi* staff.
"Exquisite blowing" (*yachui*) is a general term for music; "blowing the *yu*" refers to the *sheng* (reed organ). The meaning of these two lines is as follows:
In ancient times, there was a King of Qi (or Chu) who was extremely fond of music. He assembled a vast collection of musicians and ordered them to perform.
At that time, there was a man who, though he did not understand how to produce musical sounds, nevertheless took up a sheng pipe and began to blow it.

The King of Chu immediately summoned this man aside and commanded him to play the sheng. The man replied, "I do not know how. The King rebuked him, saying, "If you do not know how to play the sheng, why..."
[The king] asked why he was holding the *sheng* (double-reed oboe). He replied, "I saw that Your Majesty delighted in it; therefore, I held the *sheng* to please Your Majesty's mind.
The king did not become angry. This man holding the *sheng* was merely one among the other musicians.

Furthermore, when the state’s Grand Music Master (*da chang*) advances the musicians for a formal performance, if anyone among them holds a flute, a *pao*, a zither, or similar instruments, the gatekeeper [will act].
He was immediately admitted through the gate. If the gatekeeper saw anyone who did not hold musical instruments in their hands, they would not allow them to enter the Taichang Gate.

If there were others wishing to enter the Taichang Gate who were performers of *sanle* (scattered music), they likewise held *sheng* pipes and other instruments in their hands to blend in with the other *sanle* musicians. When the gatekeeper saw that this person had [an instrument] in their hand...

Regarding "musical instruments": this refers to those who deal with sounds; they too are permitted entry through the gate of the Imperial Court (Taichang). Sentient beings say, "I am also like this," yet they remain ignorant in all matters;
thus they also improperly enter the Translation Institute. Regarding "the leader": it is called "leading" because one leads by means of one's own body.

As for the name of the body, "skilled craftsman" refers to one who is proficient in the arts. The meaning of this passage is that the author of the commentary (*shuzhu*) speaks of himself with humility, saying: "I..."

In truth, I possess no knowledge; I have mistakenly joined the ranks of translators. It is like someone who does not understand the craft of fine craftsmanship, yet rashly grasps an axe and chisel, feeling ashamed when the king names him for tasks such as carpentry.

"Those who 'compile and narrate' are those who compose commentaries (*śāstra*). Those who 'direct and instruct' are those who received the personal guidance and teachings of the Tripiṭaka Master himself.

May those of future brilliance who possess profound discernment examine this in detail. Regarding this, the author of the commentary says: "Once I have completed the composition of this commentary..."

In the future, should there be those of profound discernment or eminent sages who come to examine this, they will know whether it is correct or not. The above concludes the explanation of the Preface.

From here on, we enter the main text. Regarding the three grades of spiritual capacity being different: although the Buddha taught the Dharma at three stages, all were intended for [the two vehicles].
Regarding the types of persons: these refer to those of indeterminate nature who attain enlightenment gradually, as well as those of determinate nature who attain enlightenment instantaneously.

As with those of indeterminate nature, from beginning to end, they possess all three grades [of faculties] within their very bodies—just as Kātyāyanaputra and others possessed the three faculties from start to finish.
This is evident when they first hear the Dharma wheel of the Four Noble Truths at Deer Park, the Āgamas, and so forth. Its...

Kauṇḍinya is designated as having inferior faculties because he was the first to enter the state of an ārya; thus, during that initial period, there were also śrāvakas of fixed lineage who attained the fruit of sainthood.
These śrāvakas of fixed lineage, from beginning to end, are designated only as having inferior faculties and are not called those of middling or superior faculties.
Furthermore, just as when the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other scriptures were preached immediately after his initial attainment of enlightenment, there were likewise śrāvakas present.
Some attained the fruit of a śrāvaka; others gave rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha, though it is not said that they attained the fruit.
There were also bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment who entered the first bhūmi and so forth. Thus we know that in the initial period there was both the sudden and the gradual.
Next, during the second period, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and other texts were taught. Even Kātyāyanaputra and others, having heard this sūtra, were no longer attached to...
Regarding the Dharma: those of indeterminate nature, such as Kauṇḍinya and his peers, are termed those of middling faculties.
During the second period, there were also śrāvakas of determinate nature who attained the fruits of the path, as well as bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment who attained the path.
Thus, one should know that within the second period there were both sudden and gradual approaches. During the third period, he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other teachings; those who—
When those of fixed nature, such as Kauṇḍinya and others, heard the preaching of the sūtra and turned their minds toward the Mahāyāna, they were designated as those of superior faculties.
At that time, there were also śrāvakas of fixed nature who attained the fruit of a śrāvaka, as well as bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment who entered the first bhūmi and so forth.
Thus, one should know that within the third period, there was both the sudden and the gradual. This is also the case for those of indeterminate nature.
Regarding persons such as Kauṇḍinya and others who pass through these three stages— beginning, middle, and end— within a single human body,
there exist faculties of three grades according to the sequence of beginning, end, and intermediate stages. Among these three stages,

those Śrāvakas who attain the fruit through sudden enlightenment are designated as having only "inferior faculties" (mūrdha-mūla), while Sudden Enlightenment Bodhisattvas may be designated as having "middling faculties."
Alternatively, it may refer to those of superior faculties; thus, within a single person's continuum, the three grades of faculties are not possessed simultaneously.

Regarding the term *āgama* in the commentary: whether they be Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna sūtras, they are designated as *āgama* because they have been transmitted sequentially from the Buddhas of past generations.
Furthermore, at the time of the compilation by the followers of the Hīnayāna, they took up everything that the Buddha had taught throughout his entire life.
The establishment of the four Āgamas refers precisely to the four Āgama sūtras. Those not included within the four Āgamas are termed "scattered sūtras" (kṣudraka).

Question: Since all sūtras may be designated as Āgamas, why was only that which was spoken by the Buddha throughout his entire life taken up during the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) council and named Āgama, while [the same was not done] for the Mahāyāna council?
Among all the sūtras, this [text] is not called Āgama. Answer: The Mahāyāna also speaks [of it as such]; for instance, within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there is the statement:
"The Āgamas are most profound."
The *Śāstra* states: "He heard the World-Honored One’s intended meaning of the secret significance... down to 'by this, the two sages each adhered to existence and emptiness.
Regarding the "two truths," these are the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional. Specifically, the Small Vehicle adheres to existence, while Bhāviveka adheres to emptiness.
Question: At that time, the Tathāgata had finished teaching the Second Period of the Dharma, but had not yet taught the Third Period of the Dharma.
At that time, it was not yet known whether the two sages, Bhāviveka and [Vasubandhu], had already appeared in the world.

If one says they did, how can it be said in the treatises that the division into the twenty schools of the Hīnayāna occurred only after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, and that the Bodhisattva Bhāviveka and the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla only appeared in the world after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa? If one says they did not, then after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa...

Regarding the statement "only later did they appear in the world": while the Buddha was still in the world, he had already taught the third period of the doctrine—that things are neither empty nor existent.
Since the Hīnayāna master Bhāviveka appeared later, he ought to have heard this as well; why then do you and he mutually cling to the views of existence and emptiness?
Furthermore, how can it be said in the commentary that the Tathāgata, in order to eliminate these attachments to emptiness and existence, expounded the definitive [teaching] during the third period?

Regarding the teaching on meaning: furthermore, when the Buddha preaches the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, he can only first give rise to a misconception and subsequently teach the doctrine to eliminate that ailment.
The ailment comes first and the medicine follows; it is not possible to first preach the medicine of the doctrine and only later give rise to the misconception and the ailment.

Since the ailment has not yet arisen, what is there to be eliminated? Furthermore, as for the denial of the two truths as being empty, I do not know whether this is the position of the Hīnayāna or of Bhāviveka.
The answer states: "The two sages" refers to two classes of noble ones (*ārya*). One class, upon hearing the teachings of the first period, clings to the existence of all phenomena (*dharma*).
Another class, upon hearing the teachings on emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the second period, clings to the fact that all phenomena are empty.
Therefore, they are called the "two sages. For example, during the teaching of the Buddha’s first period, there were śrāvakas who attained the fruits [of the path]. However...
There are those who adhere to the teachings on existence given during the first period; subsequently, during the second period, the teaching on emptiness was proclaimed.

Among them, there are some who, having heard the teaching on emptiness for the first time, cling to that emptiness; and there are others who, having already heard the teachings on existence from the first period, hear the teachings of the second period once again.

They then cling to emptiness. Later, the teaching of the third period was proclaimed. There are also those who, having heard the teaching of existence from the first period and the teaching of emptiness from the second period, hear again the teaching of the third period that it is neither empty nor existent.

Furthermore, there is a class of people who hear only the teaching of the third period and do not hear the teachings of the preceding two periods. According to the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, during the first period...
The first period was for delivering the śrāvakas; the second period was for delivering those of the Mahāyāna; and the third period was for delivering those of the three vehicles.
However, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the very first period, the various schools of the Hīnayāna clung to the existence of all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Next, during the second period, Nāgārjuna and others taught the emptiness of all phenomena. Subsequently, during the third period, Maitreya taught the *Yogācāra* and other systems, which are neither empty nor existent.
Furthermore, "having a method for realization and verification" means that method is precisely the principle; it refers to having the method and principle for verifying true suchness (*tathatā*).

"Skillfully able to retain or abandon" means that regarding the defiled portion of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one causes all evil dharmas to be abandoned, whereas regarding the pure portion of the dependent nature, one retains all wholesome dharmas.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "In the *Tathāgatotpattisambhava-guṇavyūha-sūtra*, regarding 'merit' (*guṇa*): Question:
Why is it called merit? Answer: Because that which is obtained only through the application of effort, exertion, and power, its virtue should be understood as being acquired first."
Furthermore, conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) that lack merit can only be newly acquired through the application of effort; thus they may be called "merit.
However, regarding the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), even if it possesses merit, that merit is not obtained through the benefit of sentient beings nor through the application of effort.
How, then, can it be designated as "unconditioned merit"? Question: In what passage is the text cited to prove the theory of Consciousness-Only (vijñapti-mātra)? What is it?
In the text, this *Abhidharmasamudgata-sūtra* is cited. The answer is that it refers to the verse on the Tathāgata’s stainless consciousness (*vimala-vijñāna*) mentioned below.

Regarding the six sūtras that are not yet known—where the subsequent treatise cites these six sūtras as well as the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and others to provide proof for the Yogācāra (Mind-Only) doctrine—the question is:
as in the proofs provided in the following text, why are further sūtras such as the *Cittotpāda-sūtra*, the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*, and the *Vimukti-sūtra* also cited? And...
Regarding other treatises and so forth: why is it that here only six scriptures and eleven great treatises are mentioned?
Why are other scriptures and treatises not listed? The answer is: these six scriptures and eleven treatises establish only the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
For this reason, only these six scriptures and eleven treatises are discussed herein. Within these six scriptures and eleven treatises, it is taught that there is *vijñapti-mātra*.
As for the principle: even if other sūtras, such as the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*, establish only the existence of seeds, they do not prove the principle of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātratā*).
Furthermore, just as the *Utpādanirodha-sūtra* only proves the existence of phenomena such as contact (*sparśa*) and sensation (*vedanā*), it does not prove the principle of Consciousness-Only.
Likewise, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* and others merely clarify the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*), yet they do not clarify the principle of Consciousness-Only. For this reason...
Does this not refer to other sutras and treatises concerning origination and cessation? Those who understand the characteristics of the Mahāyāna do so because it is taught through manifestation;

that which is not manifest is called "not understanding the characteristics. Regarding the differentiation of the three periods based on the gradual teaching methods for various capacities and principles:
Question: How are the three periods differentiated according to principle? Answer: Because there are varying depths in realization, in reality there are no three.
Regarding the three periods distinguished by years and months: if it is asked, "Since you speak of years and months, in what year and what month was the first period of teaching spoken?
