All noble ones (*ārya*) other than the Buddha constitute the Jewel of the Saṃgha. Regarding the phrase "the Dharma as previously explained," the question is: in which part of the preceding text is the Dharma elucidated?
The answer is: it is precisely in the preceding text, namely the passage concerning the teaching, reasoning, practice, and fruit (*śāsana-yukti-caryā-phala*).
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The Jewel of the Sangha comprehensively includes all noble ones (*ārya*) other than the Buddha. Question:

Since this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) belongs to the Mahāyāna, how can it universally pay homage to the Jewel of the Sangha of the three vehicles (*triyāna*)? If you say that it refers exclusively to the Mahāyāna Sangha, why does the text of the Commentary contain the phrase "comprehensively includes"?

This clearly shows that the author intends to include the Sangha of the three vehicles. Question: Regarding the rhinoceros-like solitary realizers (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa pratyekabuddha*), [how are they included?]
Regarding the question of which of the Three Jewels these various categories belong to according to different schools:

if one follows the Mahāyāna teachings, the rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddhas, the group-practicing pratyekabuddhas, householders who have attained the first two fruits [of the path], those among the six heavens of the desire realm who have attained the four fruits, and those in the two upper realms who have attained the third and fourth fruits—all of these are included within the category of the Saṃgha. Thus...
These are included within the Jewel of the Saṃgha. According to the many schools that assert the eighth [category], there are the rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddhas and those who travel in groups.

All the three faculties belonging to these rhinoceros-like and group-traveling [pratyekabuddhas]—namely, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has fully known"—are included therein.

Furthermore, once a bodhisattva has entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are two faculties (*indriya*): namely, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*).

These second faculties, along with those of the pratyekabuddhas—making three faculties in total—are all subsumed within the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*). How is this known? As it is said in that verse:

There are four kinds of verified purity (*avetyaprasāda*): namely, those regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the precepts. Regarding the Dharma, it refers in its entirety to the three truths, as well as the paths of the Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas.

One attains verified purity of the Dharma and the precepts upon seeing the three truths of suffering, origin, and cessation; upon seeing the path, one simultaneously attains verified purity of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. That is to say, [the Dharma] refers to the three truths of suffering, origin, and cessation.

This is the Jewel of the Dharma. Furthermore, Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas are also subsumed within the Jewel of the Dharma. If a Bodhisattva possesses the faculty of full knowledge (*ājñendriya*), they are subsumed within the Jewel of the Buddha.
Within the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), both the Buddha and the Sangha are present. There are householders who have attained the first two fruits;
there are those who have attained the four fruits in the heavens of the six desire realms, as well as Non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and Arhats within the two higher realms.
This is because they all belong to the category of the Saṃgha. If one is an ordained śrāvaka who has attained the four fruits, they are subsumed within the Jewel of the Saṃgha.

Why is this? Because those who have attained the four fruits of the śrāvaka share the same communal legal procedures (*karmavācanā*), and furthermore, they are seen to appear in great numbers together in the world.

Furthermore, in the *Śīla-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha, he prescribed the precepts solely for the four fruits of the śrāvaka. Because there are these four fruits of the śrāvaka, they are subsumed within the Saṅgha-ratna.
However, as for the pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas—whether it be a bodhisattva who appears in the world alone, or the two types of pratyekabuddhas—[they are not so included].
In worlds where no Buddha has appeared, all things are insentient and identical in their *karmic* nature; therefore, they are all subsumed within the practice of the Dharma Jewel.

Nevertheless, within both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, only untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena are taken as the essence of the Three Jewels; tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena are not taken as the essence of the Three Jewels.

However, within both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, the provisional "supporting" Three Jewels (*pratirūpaka-triratna*) are spoken of as the essence of the Three Jewels in a conventional sense. In reality...

It is not that they are not the Three Jewels; rather, it is because by revering the Three Jewels of distinct characteristics (*bhedalakṣaṇa*), one fully exhausts reverence for both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) merits.
Now, within the Three Jewels of distinct characteristics, all are encompassed by both the conditioned and the unconditioned.

For instance, within the Jewel of the Buddha, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is unconditioned, while the enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and responsive manifestations are conditioned. As for the Jewel of the Dharma, this refers specifically to the teachings and the principles.

The fruit of practice. Within this fruit, there is the principle of *nirvāṇa*, which is also unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Within that principle, there is also the principle of *tathatā* (suchness), which is likewise unconditioned.

However, within the teaching, the practice, and the entirety of the fruit, there is also a small portion that is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). This is just as the Jewel of the Sangha encompasses both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
For instance, a Bodhisattva of the ten stages is part of the Sangha; they have also attained a small measure of the unconditioned. That is to say:
The treatise states: "Bodhisattvas of the ten stages take conditioned and unconditioned merits as their intrinsic nature.
Thus, it is known that Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are called the Saṃgha. Regarding the two entities of the Three Jewels, this is as clarified in the preceding commentary:

namely, the Three Jewels of the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles, including the Three Jewels of common characteristics and distinct characteristics. As for "taking refuge and paying homage," it is...

As previously stated regarding the taking of refuge and paying homage to the field of merit, up to the homage paid to persons and non-Dharma, although the Three Jewels and the terminology of "taking refuge" and "paying homage" have been briefly explained above, the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of both the Three Jewels and the act of taking refuge—and the two-fold nature of these two—are both explained in detail in separate chapters;
therefore, it says "and their two-fold nature. Although there are four meanings [to this],...

To explain the first two lines [of the verse]: they constitute four meanings—first, revering the person but not the Dharma; second, revering the Dharma but not the person; third, revering both the person and the Dharma;
and fourth, revering the Three Jewels as a whole. This explains the two lines of the preceding verse.

Regarding the phrase "From the arising of wisdom, great compassion arises": the question is whether this refers to the arising of great wisdom and great compassion within the future fruition of the Bodhisattva’s own person, or whether it refers to the arising of great wisdom and great compassion within the future fruition of other sentient beings. Furthermore, regarding the question "I am An-hui," which refers to himself:
why did the preceding commentary text state in its general heading: [The text continues: "The Great Master of the Three Treatises, the Venerable Sthiramati... and so forth. Why was this stated there?
Regarding this first verse, Dharmapāla and others offer their homage to the Field of Merit, thereby indicating Dharmapāla’s own name;
furthermore, up until the explanation of the second half of the verse, it is stated that Sthiramati refers to himself. These two accounts appear contradictory.
The answer is that the single verse of homage at the beginning was composed as a separate verse of homage by each—Sthiramati and Dharmapāla—respectively. Now, as for the explanation...
Because it adopts the superior [interpretation]. The first half was composed by Dharmapāla, while the second half was composed by Sthiramati; there is no fault in this.

Regarding the commentator’s explanation of the meaning of "elucidation" (*vyākhyāna*) up to the point where he establishes the principles for respectful homage: Question: What is the distinction between these three interpretations herein? Answer:

The first interpretation explains [the subject] in terms of its profundity and manifestation, as well as its breadth and narrowness. That is to say, it first briefly designates [the term] as narrow, and subsequently discusses it extensively.
Therefore, it is called "Extensive" (*kuan*). As for the second interpretation, it refers to the capacity for understanding (*jī*) of sentient beings.
The third interpretation is distinct because it establishes the principles (*dào-lǐ*) through the formal presentation of the teachings (*jiàofǎ*).

Regarding the phrase "in order to briefly condense widely dispersed meanings," this is like the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Verses and Commentary), which, although composed in ten fascicles of concise text, nonetheless encompasses all the extensive meanings found within the various sūtras and śāstras.
This is the meaning [of the term]. As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on Yoga), fascicle 64: "Causing the Dharma to endure for a long time is itself self-benefit.
Question: For what reason does this passage appear? It says, "Therefore, it is called 'sentient being' (*sattva*) because there is no separate capacity";

this means that just as the eighth consciousness exists as the "sentient" (*sattva*) without a separate capacity, the non-Buddhists postulate a "Self" (*ātman*) as the capacity and sentient beings as that which belongs to it.
Thus, there is the capacity for existence; this is not the same as the non-Buddhists, which is why it is said that there is no separate capacity for existence.
The commentary further explains: "Alternatively, because the provisional entity possesses these mental consciousnesses.

Here, the provisional entity is the possessor, and the mental consciousnesses are what is possessed. Question: The Buddha is not a sentient being (*sattva*); why, then, is he included among the sixty-two types of sentient beings?
Regarding the Tathāgata as well, he is one who brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings. In response to the question of whether this excludes the Buddha to benefit others:

it is said that "benefit and happiness" refers to the majority of cases. Furthermore, if one says that the Tathāgata is not included among the sixty-two types of sentient beings, or if one says that the Tathāgata is a conventional sentient being and is thus included within those sixty-two types of sentient beings, there is no contradiction. If one says he is...
"Sentient beings" (*sattva*). One should know that these are all spoken of in terms of manifestation. Furthermore, as for "sentient beings," it means "those who possess craving.
Because sentient beings give rise to craving, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). Regarding the statement that "the Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*) is one":

[Question] There are four types of Wheel-turning Kings; why are these four combined into one? [Answer] It is because the four types of Wheel-turning Kings do not appear in the world simultaneously; therefore, they are combined.
This refers to the four types of wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*).
"Benefit" (*hita*) means that which provides subsequent relief; it is like teaching others to cultivate goodness in this life so that they may be born in a favorable realm in future lives.
"Happiness" (*sukha*) means that which provides immediate benefit; it is like teaching and transforming others in their present existence.

To "subdue afflictions upon [the stage] above" means to cause others to attain the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) in their present bodies, or to grant them the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
"Pure benefit" refers either to self-benefit alone or to benefiting others alone;

here, we take that which is solely for the benefit of others, as it resembles the conduct of a Bodhisattva, and do not take that which is solely for self-benefit, as that belongs to the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Because it is practiced. Regarding "mutual benefit," this refers to both self-benefit and the benefit of others. Regarding "the benefit consisting of the categories of peace and happiness," there are five distinct types;
therefore, they are called "categories. Regarding "the benefit subsumed under causes," this causes one to plant roots of goodness in the present life.

Regarding "the benefit subsumed under results," this likewise leads to rebirth in favorable realms in the future. Regarding "ultimate benefit," this means enabling others to attain the vehicle of the noble ones (*ārya-yāna*).
Regarding the "fruit" that is not ultimate: this refers to causing others to obtain the fruit of rebirth in the favorable realms of humans and devas.

As for the phrase "the cause of pleasure, namely, the factors associated with the pleasure of the sense-faculties and their objects conducive to pleasant feeling": just as the faculties act as causes to give rise to pleasant feeling, so too do desirable objects act as causes to give rise to pleasant feeling.
At the time of the cause, those mental states and mental factors that are associated with pleasant feeling are all [included therein].
One is able to experience pleasant sensations through the sense faculties and their objects. Because these serve as the causes for pleasant sensations, they are called "causes of pleasure.
Thus, through desirable objects and faculties, pleasant sensations are first initiated, which then give rise to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).

Likewise, through undesirable objects and faculties, painful sensations are first initiated, which then give rise to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*). This refers to the karma produced by pleasure.
"All are called 'caused by pleasure' because they are able to produce pleasure" means that karma produced by pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is termed "caused by pleasure.
This present passage refers specifically to the cultivation of causes within the lower three dhyānas and a small portion of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Just as in the lower three dhyānas, one cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) within a state of pleasant feeling; subsequently, this karma acts as the cause for further karma. Thus, this very karma serves as the cause.
Therefore, after death, one is reborn within the third dhyāna and experiences the desirable fruit of pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*).

That is to say, because one initiates karma for the sake of pleasant sensation, one subsequently experiences the fruit of pleasant sensation; since it is capable of giving rise to pleasure, it is termed "caused by pleasure" (*hetu-sukha*).
Thus, the text states that all karma initiated by pleasant sensation is called "caused by pleasure," as it is capable of [producing such results].
This is because it is pleasant.

If one were to say that even while maintaining the precepts within a mind of painful sensation, one will subsequently attain the pleasant sensation of the fruit, then this text should state that pleasure is what is induced by suffering;
it should not state that it is the karma produced [by the precepts]. This applies to the three types of sensation—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—within the desire realm.
Within the mind, one invariably experiences the fruits of suffering and pleasure. Furthermore, regarding the arising of the three types of sensation from within wholesome karma:
suppose there is a person who, with a wholesome mind, gives rise to pleasant sensation while observing the precepts; that person will immediately be reborn and experience the fruit of pleasure.
That which is pleasant both as cause and as fruit is precisely that karma produced by the pleasures of this world.

Alternatively, if a person maintains the precepts with a virtuous mind while experiencing painful sensations, that person will likewise experience pleasant sensations in the future; thus, the cause is suffering while the fruit is pleasure.
Or, if there are those who maintain the precepts with a virtuous mind while experiencing neutral sensations (*upekṣā-vedanā*), that person will likewise experience [pleasant results] in the future.
Virtue results in happiness. Regarding the arising of the three types of feeling within an unwholesome mind:

there may be someone who, from within an unwholesome mind, gives rise to a pleasant feeling—such as when one commits the ten unwholesome actions while in a state of pleasure. That person will subsequently experience the result of suffering; thus, because of the karma, the fruit is suffering.

Alternatively, there may be someone who, from within an evil mind, gives rise to a painful feeling while committing unwholesome deeds and so forth. That person... [will subsequently experience the result of suffering].
One will experience the fruit of suffering in the future; this is the case where the cause is suffering and the fruit is suffering.

Alternatively, there may be those who, from within a state of aversion, give rise to equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) and create unwholesome karma, thereby experiencing the fruit of suffering in the future; this is the case where the cause is equanimity and the fruit is suffering.
Since equanimity arises in all final moments of consciousness, if one interprets it in this way, one correctly grasps the meaning of this passage. Second:

Regarding the statement that "experiencing pleasure is the feeling of pleasure": although this speaks of experiencing pleasure, it does not refer solely to the feeling of pleasure within the category of universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).
Rather, it takes both together—namely, the feeling of pleasure among the universal factors and the pleasure of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). This refers to impure (*sāsrava*) pleasure.

That which is bound to the three realms and brings harmony and ease to body and mind is all termed "pleasure" (*sukha*). This does not refer to that which is categorized as pleasure among the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).
The intention here is to state that in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the third dhyāna, there is the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) because it gratifies the body;

this is the pleasure categorized among the universal mental factors. Furthermore, within the [first] three lower dhyānas, one also takes up the pleasure of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*). From the fourth dhyāna upward, however—

This is the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), which harmonizes and refreshes body and mind; it is designated as "bliss" (*sukha*). It is not the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) categorized among the mental formations (*saṃskāra*).
It is exclusively the pliancy found within the eleven wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*). For this reason, the name "bliss" applies throughout the three realms (*tridhātu*).

Feeling of pleasure, however, exists only from the third dhyāna downward, as well as in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Therefore, it is said that it is not merely the feeling of pleasure among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), but rather both are taken together.
Second: this refers to the pervasive feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) and the pleasure of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*).

Regarding the statement that "the untainted pleasure (*anāsrava-sukha*)—which pertains to both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—is the intrinsic nature of pleasure," the Noble Ones here take only the feeling of pleasure and not the others, because it is the most preeminent.
Furthermore, they take both together: namely, the pervasive feeling of pleasure and the pleasure of pliancy. Question: [Regarding] the untainted...

Since it has already been stated that "pleasure" (sukha) is accessible to those on the path of training (śaikṣa), it remains unknown whether those who have attained the first two fruits can possess pleasant sensation (sukha-vedanā). The answer is that they do.
According to the Mahāyāna, within the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) of the first two dhyānas, there exists the sensation of joy (prīti-vedanā).

Since those who have attained the first two fruits have acquired the initial threshold concentration (anāgamya-dhyāna), those who have attained the first two fruits can possess untainted pleasure (anāsrava-sukha). This is now explained according to the Mahāyāna; as for the Hīnayāna...

Regarding the fundamental principle: within all *anāgamya-samādhi* (preparatory concentrations), there is only the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*); there are no sensations of joy (*prīti*) or pleasure (*sukha*). Question:

If that is so, the Mahāyāna teaches that within the initial *anāgamya*, there is only the sensation of joy. In that case, those who have attained the first and second fruits [of the path] should obtain uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) joyful sensation.
How then do those who have attained the first and second fruits obtain uncontaminated pleasant sensation? Answer: Regarding the five sensations...

Regarding the clarification of the meaning: in the first two cases, the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration is designated only as the sensation of joy (*prīti-vedanā*) and cannot be called pleasure (*sukha*).
This refers to those who have attained the first three fruits [of the path], who obtain uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) joy; in their case, it is appropriate to apply the aforementioned critique.

However, if the meaning is clarified according to the three types of sensation, then joy may also be designated as pleasure, and it may likewise be designated as pleasure within the context of the three sensations. In this regard, those who have attained the first two fruits obtain the initial *anāgamya*.
Because it is the untainted bliss within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is no fault.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "the coarse and agitated feelings cease": this means that the feelings of suffering and pleasure, together with joy and equanimity, are termed "coarse and agitated.

In the question concerning the cessation of feelings within the bliss of meditative absorption, the state of non-percipient absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) was not mentioned. The answer is: here, the Bodhisattva employs these ten benefits and five joys to benefit sentient beings.
For this reason, when a Bodhisattva now employs the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) to benefit sentient beings, it is called "experiencing the bliss of abandonment" (*prahāṇasukha*);
they do not employ the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) to benefit sentient beings. Question: If sensation (*vedanā*) is present at that time, why is it not called "bliss"?
It is only when sensation ceases that it receives the name "bliss. Since this state is mindless (*acittaka*), where could there be bliss? One should state a verse: "The nature of the world..."
"Those" refers to the first and second [of the] ten benefits and joys previously explained, namely, the joy of being born into the world.

"Nature" refers to the third and fourth [benefits], such as the joy of embracing the wholesome and abandoning the unwholesome. Regarding the phrase "based on the conditions possessed, taking the previous explanation as the foundation," this refers to the preceding commentary which states:
"Now, in explaining this treatise, I shall cause the Dharma not to perish, for the sake of bestowing these benefits upon sentient beings."
Because of this joy, he explains that verse by means of two conditions. The preceding commentary is the interpretation of the Tripiṭaka Master;

therefore, it is said that the former explanation serves as the basis. According to the intention of the Tripiṭaka Master, in explaining that verse, the third line—"I now explain what was said"—means that one causes the Dharma not to perish, because one explains what was said. Thus, it causes the Dharma...

[The treatise] shall endure for a long time. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of benefiting and gladdening all sentient beings," this means that the purpose [of composing the treatise] is precisely to bestow such benefit and joy upon sentient beings. Thus, the Master of the Tripiṭaka explains these two phrases separately:
the former phrase means "to cause the Dharma to endure for a long time," and the latter phrase means "to benefit and gladden sentient beings. (2)
"Joy of seclusion" refers to that which arises in the second dhyāna through the distancing of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*);
it is called the joy of distancing from discursive thought. "Tranquility," meaning *nirvāṇa*, refers to the cessation of the defiled phenomena of birth and death within *nirvāṇa*;

therefore, it is called the joy of tranquility. Regarding the "joy of counteracting the three sufferings," why not take the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as joy? [The author] asks this again; thus, these three—
The masters are both persons and dharmas. Furthermore, Master Sthiramati says: "Those who are deluded and mistaken" refers to persons;
"because they give rise to correct understanding" and so forth refers to dharmas. Second, Master Dharmapāla: those who are deluded regarding *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) refers to persons;
"causing them to [realize] the two kinds of emptiness" and so forth refers to dharmas. Third, Master Dharmatrāta: those who cling to external objects... [refers to persons].

From the notion that "consciousness is not non-existent" up to various other attachments, these refer to persons (*pudgala*). To lead [beings] toward *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) and so forth refers to phenomena (*dharma*).

Therefore, these three masters all address both persons and phenomena. Regarding the statement that there is no contradiction in explaining the latter [the purpose of the treatise] by way of great compassion, the commentary (*śāstra*) states:
"Alternatively, within this verse, [it is said] because the fundamental aim of the Bodhisattva is to benefit others. This...
The text of the *Śāstra* (the commentary) is the master’s own explanation. Therefore, it is said that there is no contradiction in the subsequent interpretation. As for the master’s intended meaning:
he simply provides a general explanation of the two following lines together in one place; it is not possible to interpret them separately.

His intention is to say that because I now explain those words which speak of benefiting and bringing joy to all sentient beings, the two lines that "explain those words" are for the sake of all sentient beings.
Regarding "benefiting sentient beings": those who have faith and study rely upon this [teaching] to practice; thus, the Dharma abides for a long time.

Because it is for the sake of sentient beings that the Dharma abides for a long time, these two subsequent lines apply both to benefiting sentient beings and to causing the Dharma to abide for a long time.
"To initiate" (*fāduān*) is equivalent to expressions such as "to examine in detail" (*xiángfú*) or "privately considering" (*qièyǐ*); "to initiate" (*fā*) means to give rise to.

Furthermore, "end" (*duan*) means "head. This refers to the opening verse that initiates the treatise. Regarding "discerning and upholding" (*jianchi*): it means to set aside other treatises and uphold this one.

As for the seventh case [the locative] used in the sense of "toward" (*yu*) rather than the sense of "relying upon" (*yi*), it is because the word "toward" (*yu*) functions as the object of the action.

There are two types of the seventh grammatical case (*vibhakti*): first, "relying upon" (*āśraya*), and second, "toward" (*adhikaraṇa*). All those sentient beings to be delivered are the objects of the Bodhisattvas' cognitive focus (*ālambana*).
Regarding the object (*viṣaya*), the treatise states "for the sake of" (*yì wèi*).
[This refers to] Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and those in the evil destinies who have a false understanding of the principle of emptiness. Question:

What is the difference between the false understanding of the principle of emptiness held by those of the two vehicles and the false understanding of emptiness held by those who hold a nihilistic view of emptiness? Answer: If the two vehicles...
Although a person may lack such things as wrong views within the category of afflictions (*kleśa*), they still possess cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). One asks:

do wrong views, doubt, and so forth involve attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*)—that is, the grasping at all phenomena as being substantially real? It cannot be called a "wrong principle" to [assert] that phenomena are empty;

however, if one holds a perverted view of emptiness, such as repudiating cause and effect, this is entirely termed a "wrong understanding of the principle of emptiness. Correct understanding, in its essence, penetrates non-existence.
Regarding "outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and outflow-possessing wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*). Question:

Since it has now been stated that those of the two vehicles all possess what is called a "perverse understanding of the principle of emptiness," does the "correct understanding" herein give rise to Mahāyāna outflow-free and outflow-possessing wisdom, or does it give rise to Hīnayāna outflow-free and outflow-possessing wisdom?
Furthermore, regarding this term "outflow-free wisdom," does it refer to the [wisdoms] of seeing, cultivation, or no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)?

Regarding this "untainted wisdom" (*anāsrava-jñāna*): does it refer to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), the uninterrupted wisdom (*ānantarya-jñāna*), the liberation wisdom (*vimukti-jñāna*), or the superior progress wisdom (*viśeṣa-mārga-jñāna*)?

As for the statement regarding "tainted wisdom" (*sāsrava-jñāna*): does it refer to the innate wholesome merit (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) and the wholesome pertaining to the portion of merit (*puṇya-bhāgīya-kuśala*), or to the tainted wholesome arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā-maya-kuśala*), or to the wholesome of the provisions (*saṃbhāra-kuśala*), the preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśala*), the uninterrupted, the liberation, the preparatory application, or the superior progress? Answer: Tainted wisdom refers to the acquisition of the [four] directions... [text truncated].
Within that very goodness, one generates the aspiration for liberation and seeks the wisdom arising from hearing and reflection; this is called "clarity and sharpness.
For example, people of the present day may, even before having planted the roots of merit conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), give rise to a wholesome mind and aspire to transcendence.

This mind aspiring to transcendence is precisely what is called "wholesome by means" (*upāyakuśala*). Wholesome by means is a category within the wholesome factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
This skillful means of the flow-type can act as a remote condition to give rise to the wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*).
If one gives rise to skillful means while in the stage of the factors conducive to liberation, it is the companion to the wholesome roots of liberation itself.

As for the wholesome roots conducive to merit (*puṇya-bhāgīya*), these belong only to ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists who practice the contemplations of attraction and aversion, seeking rebirth within the cyclic existence of the two higher realms.
Because the wholesome factors of his merit and birth result in conduct that is entirely obscure, it is not called "right understanding"; it is merely "skillful means.
Because his nature is clear and sharp, it is called "right understanding."
What are the two kinds of emptiness? They are the emptiness of the produced dharmas (*jātidharma*). "Produced" is an ancient term for the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*).
If that were so, grasses, trees, and the like would have to be called sentient beings; thus, there would be confusion. The older tradition spoke of the "emptiness of persons" (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

If that were so, only the human realm could be called the emptiness of persons, while the other five realms would not; how then could they be called the emptiness of persons? The word "person" does not pervade all five [realms]. Now, it is said:

"Birth-emptiness" (jìngōng) subsumes the five destinies (*pañcagati*), all of which are termed "birth. Some older interpretations refer to this as the "emptiness of the person-self" (*pudgala-nairātmya*).

Although within phenomena (*dharma*) there is no sovereign entity called a "self," because they possess transformative function, they are also given the name "self. Thus, the character for "self" (*ātmaka*) is applied to both persons and phenomena; this is also a case of terminological confusion.
As for the phrase "like a vajra," this currently refers to the praise of the jade-vajra (*vajra-maṇi*); it is not [the diamond weapon].
Take another violet-colored vajra; this vajra is the color of barley and possesses facets. The large ones are the size of jujube fruits, while those for the Hīnayāna are the size of barley grains.

Question: Regarding the first four explanations, why are the two obscurations (*āvaraṇa*) mentioned, and how is it that by speaking of the two emptinesses (*śūnyatā*), other dharmas are also simultaneously included?
Answer: The meaning of this passage is that the preceding four explanations are made in reference to the names of the two obscurations.
Regarding the "heavy" [obstructions]: why do they obstruct the principle of *tathatā* (suchness)? It is because only the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) are mentioned.

When one wishes to eliminate these two graspings and give rise to understanding, it is said that the remaining two obstructions are severed along with other factors. These "other factors" refer to the remaining obstructions external to the two graspings;

thus, while the obstructions are broad, the graspings are narrow. Question: Regarding the fifth interpretation, which states that the heavy [obstructions] consist only of the two graspings, what is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the two obstructions?

This also applies to greed and the other afflictions. Why, then, are only the two emptinesses mentioned? The intent of this statement is that, within the fifth explanation, only the two types of grasping are designated as "heavy.

Since both types of grasping are abandoned, one establishes the emptiness of self and the emptiness of phenomena (*ātma-śūnyatā* and *dharma-śūnyatā*). As for the remaining two [afflictions], they manifest the attainment of the remainder.
Why are the emptinesses of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride not established? This is because such an objection would lack consistency.

This commentary merely explains the basis for the two attachments; even if the latter two phrases only explain the severance of the heavy obstacles, although there are two interpretations within this sub-commentary that answer the first two questions, their underlying meaning is similar.
If one answers the first question, it states that the two attachments are the root; therefore, it speaks only of how the two attachments can obstruct the two kinds of emptiness. If...
When the two types of grasping are severed, the two obstacles are also eliminated; for when the root is severed, the branches and twigs are likewise severed.

To answer the second question: the two types of grasping are the root. Therefore, at the time of realizing the principle, one speaks only of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Since craving, hatred, and so forth are merely the branches, when craving and the like are severed, one does not establish the emptiness of craving, hatred, and so on. This is based on...

Regarding the explanation that afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the ultimate stage: this refers to the paths of seeing and the ultimate paths of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
Within these, the grasping at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa*) and the afflictions are abandoned simultaneously;

that is, at the very moment the root is severed, all branches of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are also severed. This is not the case for other stages, where one first abandons eight grades of afflictions.

Regarding the statement that the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is severed only when the ninth category of afflictions is being abandoned: this is explained in terms of detachment from the stages (*bhūmi*).

For instance, although one who has attained the fruit of a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) has severed the six categories of afflictions belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they have not yet severed the grasping at a self.

Likewise, one who has attained the fruit of a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) has severed eight categories, yet still does not sever the grasping at a self. Therefore, it is said that "in other positions it is not so," referring to the fact that the first eight categories were previously severed [of the afflictions].
After the branches of the afflictions have been eliminated, it is only in the ninth stage that the root of the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is severed.

As for the statement that the view of self is likewise [eliminated] in the fourth stage: there are three types of afflictions. The first consists of greed, delusion, and pride, which arise simultaneously with the two views of identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
The second refers to the aforementioned views of identity and extremes in the preceding moment, which give rise to greed, delusion, and pride in the subsequent moment.

...and so forth. Among the three types of independent (*mukhya*) greed, hatred, delusion, and pride, those that do not arise simultaneously with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) or the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are as follows:

first, if greed, delusion, and pride arise together with these two views, then within the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), the two views of self-identity and extremes, along with the greed, delusion, pride, and so forth that arise simultaneously with them, are all suppressed (*vibhāvita*) during the fourth stage. As for those [afflictions] associated with the view of a self-identity...
It is observed that greed, delusion, and so forth, act as companions to afflictions that do not arise simultaneously with them.

Second, the power of the two views—view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—is able to induce the arising of subsequent moments of independent greed and so forth.

Those instances where greed and so forth arise simultaneously with the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes are called "simultaneously arising afflictions" (*sahaja-kleśa*). Those that induce subsequent moments of greed and so forth are called "non-simultaneously arising afflictions."
Those innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) and non-innate afflictions (*asahaja-kleśa*) have acted as constant companions since beginningless time.

Together with the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth, they are permanently severed in the fourth stage (*bhūmi*) because one practices the contemplations that constitute the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

Subsequently, the greed and other afflictions induced by those [innate ones] are suppressed and severed upon reaching the fifth stage. Thirdly, if greed, anger, delusion, and so forth do not yet [arise] in relation to the body...
Those [afflictions] arising through the power of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) consist of two types of greed, hatred, and so forth:
if they are weak, they are abandoned in the sixth stage; if they are subtle, they are permanently suppressed only in the seventh stage. The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states:
"First, the harmful accompanying latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), namely innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), which act as companions to non-innate afflictions. Upon reaching...

It is only from the fifth ground onward that [the afflictions] are never again practiced. This clearly shows that within the fourth ground, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is eliminated first, while the afflictions are severed later;

this is because even when the root is severed, the branches and twigs are not yet severed. After the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) have been severed in the fourth ground, the afflictions are severed in the fifth and sixth grounds. This is precisely the process of severing the root first and the branches later.

However, regarding the statement in this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* that "the two obstacles arise from the grasping at self and phenomena, and if one realizes the two emptinesses, those obstacles are accordingly severed," this too does not fully accord with the principle.

Why is this? Since this treatise states that if one realizes the two emptinesses, those obstacles are accordingly severed, it only encompasses the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the ultimate path (*niṣṭhāmārga*) of the three vehicles, as well as the fourth... [text fragment].

In the stages of the path, such as the abandonment of the [five] hindrances (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the [nine] levels (*bhūmi*), the afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned simultaneously with the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) and other secondary afflictions.
Thus, one first abandons the root of grasping and subsequently abandons the remaining afflictions. This treatise does not include the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the defilements of the stages;
rather, it first treats the remaining afflictions by category, and in the ninth category, it abandons the grasping at a self—thereby abandoning the branches first and the root later.

The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "As explained below in the ninth fascicle, within the stage of the Requisites (*sambhāra-avasthā*), there are two interpretations. [Question: To which passage does this refer?
(One should verify this). The *Śū* states:
"Regarding 'the hindrances are as stated in the main treatise, but only the two emptinesses are mentioned,' and 'as for anger, true concentration, and so forth'—there is..."
The Tang edition states: "As" (*ru*) refers to *tathatā* (suchness). "Fundamental" (*ben*) refers to the grasping at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-āgraha*).

Since this is spoken from the perspective of the root, it speaks of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvi-śūnyatā*) and does not speak of the emptiness of desire (*rāga-śūnyatā*) and so forth. "As" (*ru*) here means "thereby. The intended meaning is that, while obstructing [the path], one speaks of the two kinds of emptiness from the perspective of the root.

It is not said that greed and hatred are empty. Regarding the statement that "the six consciousnesses grasp external objects," this means that within the sixth consciousness, two types of grasping arise toward external objects;
furthermore, among the other afflictions, there are some afflictions that arise simultaneously with these two types of grasping. These afflictions—

This is precisely what is meant by "clinging within the six consciousnesses. Alternatively, there may be afflictions such as greed and delusion that arise solely in dependence upon the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and do not arise simultaneously with the two types of clinging.
These afflictions of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are termed "external to the clinging of the six consciousnesses.

Alternatively, even things such as attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) or anger within the five consciousnesses are also termed "external," because they do not coexist with clinging; thus they are called "external to clinging. If...
The afflictions within the seventh consciousness are always associated with the two types of grasping; there are no afflictions outside of the seventh consciousness.
Therefore, they are not mentioned here [in this context]. Thus, it is said that "grasping at the external" refers to what is called the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

As for those factors such as attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) and aversion (*pratigha*) within the five consciousnesses that are subsumed under the category of being born of maturation (*vipākaja*), the meaning of this passage is that [these exist] within the five consciousnesses.

Although there is no grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), within the five consciousnesses there are also afflictions such as greed and hatred that constitute cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

These greed, hatred, and so forth are subsumed under the "maturation-born" (*vipākaja*) among the four types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*), because this category is the most extensive; it is like the term "dominant condition" (*adhipati-pratyaya*), whose name and meaning are all-pervasive.
That which is definitely inferior in nature is the feeling (*vedanā*) within the sixth consciousness. For example, when one attains the first [dhyāna] through cultivation...

Having arisen from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one becomes attached to this concentration and refuses to further cultivate the second dhyāna. This is because the nature of that concentration is inferior.
Although other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) exist simultaneously, it is only the feeling (*vedanā*) that is grasped, as it alone is capable of experiencing [the object].

This feeling of attachment to concentration, which is an obscuration to the knowable (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), belongs exclusively to the sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it is the mental consciousness that is able to attain concentration. The five sensory consciousnesses do not possess craving for dharmas.

Hatred and the like are solely the final hindrances belonging to the category of the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that because one has exhausted [the afflictions] associated with sensation, one attains the unconditioned state of immovability (*āniñjya-asamskṛta*) of the fourth dhyāna.
Although one attains the unconditioned state of immovability by severing the defiled dharmas of the first dhyāna and so forth, the present explanation refers to the ultimate limit;
therefore, it says that by severing the defilements of the lower three dhyānas, one attains the concentration of the fourth dhyāna and thereby achieves [immovability].

Regarding the unconditioned state of immovability (*āniñjya-asaṃskṛta*): if it is other ordinary persons—namely, non-Buddhists who, through the practice of the sixfold cultivation, suppress their afflictions and attain the fourth dhyāna while suppressing the defilements of the lower three dhyānas—then those ordinary non-Buddhists obtain the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of immovability within the fourth dhyāna.
If it is an Arhat, they have severed the defilements of the lower three dhyānas and attained the fourth dhyāna concentration.

This is precisely the attainment of the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and immovability (*āniñjya*). Furthermore, because one has severed the arising of volitional mental experience (*manopavicāra*), one attains the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).
"Variable feelings" refer to suffering, pleasure, grief, and joy; "invariable mental feeling" refers to the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

This is explained in terms of feeling as maturation (*vipāka*) that is distinct from the afflictions (*kleśa*). Regarding the phrase "attaining the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*), this text refers to a certain class of Arhats, both those of dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*) and sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*).

For instance, there may be a dull-facultied Arhat who does not attain the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*) of the higher realms, but relies solely upon the preliminary stage of the first dhyāna (*anāgamya*). Although such a person has completely eradicated the afflictions of the three realms, they still do not [attain the unconditioned].

The four dhyānas and eight stages constitute the fundamental concentrations (*mauladhyāna*). Because these concentrations consist of sensations born of maturation (*vipākaja*) that are inferior in nature, once an Arhat has subsequently gradually suppressed and eliminated those sensations born of maturation which are obstacles to concentration, he then attains the higher concentrations.

He thereby attains the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the unconditioned state of immovability (*āniñjya-asaṃskṛta*), and the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and sensation (*saṃjñāvedayita-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*). If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) suppresses and detaches from the lower stages...

Once the afflictions have been suppressed, one immediately attains the fundamental concentration of the dhyānas. One immediately attains the unconditioned state of immovability (*āniñjya*), which is cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Just as when the afflictions of the desire realm have been suppressed, one immediately attains the fundamental concentration of the first dhyāna; and just as when the afflictions of the first dhyāna have been completely suppressed, one immediately attains the fundamental concentration of the second dhyāna;
and so on, until when the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) have been completely suppressed, one immediately attains [the corresponding fundamental concentration].

This is not a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). If one is a noble being (*ārya*), it is not necessarily so; for example, a person who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), although they have abandoned all discriminative afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*) of the three realms by relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*), still does not yet attain the fundamental concentrations (*mauladhyāna*) of the higher stages.
Regarding those who abandon [the afflictions] simultaneously with the afflictions themselves:

there is a class of individuals—whether of sharp or dull faculties—who, when they exhaust the afflictions of the three realms, simultaneously exhaust the resultant (*vipāka*) feelings and attain the four dhyānas and the eight fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*).
For example, when the afflictions of the first dhyāna are exhausted, one immediately attains the concentration of the second dhyāna, and so on.
Having severed the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one immediately attains the meditative absorption of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). How is this known?

There are those of sharp or dull faculties who, though being Arhats (*aśaikṣa*) and having exhausted all afflictions of the three realms, do not attain the fundamental absorptions of the higher stages.
Alternatively, there is a class of Arhats with sharp or dull faculties who, once they have exhausted all afflictions of the three realms, immediately attain the [fourth dhyāna].

The eight dhyānas are explained identically in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions. However, one is designated as "perfected" in terms of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) by virtue of being in the second stage of the path of training (*śaikṣa*) within the fundamental dhyānas;

one is designated as "perfected" in terms of faculties (*indriya*) and fruit (*phala*) by virtue of attaining the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). The meaning of this passage is that if one attains the third fruit, one is said to be perfected in terms of the fruit;

if one attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one is said to be perfected in terms of absorption; and if one possesses the nature of one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), one is said to be perfected in terms of the faculties.
If, among those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), one attains the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), one is said to be "perfected in concentration" (*samādhiparipūrṇa*).

If one belongs to the immovable lineage (*akopyagotra*), one is said to be "perfected in faculties" (*indriyaparipūrṇa*). Consequently, there may be cases where one is perfected in concentration but not perfected in faculties;

namely, those five types of persons of dull faculties who are subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) and yet attain the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Because they are of dull faculties, they are not called "perfected in faculties. Alternatively, there may be...

There are those who are full in faculties but not full in meditative concentration; these are individuals of the immovable lineage (*akopya-gotra*) who have not attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and thus are not called "full in concentration.

Because they possess sharp faculties, they are called "full in faculties. There may be those who are full in both faculties and concentration; these are the immovable ones who have attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and have attained the attainment of cessation.
There may also be those who are full in neither faculties nor concentration; these are the aforementioned individuals of the regressive lineage with dull faculties who have not [attained it].

Because the eight stages are fixed, we know that there may be those of sharp or dull faculties who attain the nine absorptions (*dhyāna*), while others of sharp or dull faculties do not attain the nine absorptions.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that those of sharp faculties necessarily attain the absorptions while those of dull faculties do not.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement "this feeling (*vedanā*) is also associated with absorption, and since feeling is the basis for the hindrances of absorption, only feeling is mentioned," the meaning of this passage is as follows:

Simultaneous with the feeling (*vedanā*), other universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viṣayaviśeṣa*) mental factors are also able to obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*). However, because feeling is the most prominent obstacle to concentration, it alone is mentioned.
Regarding the "two dharmas of the ten stages," these refer to the two dharmas of wisdom (*jñāna*) and principle (*tattva*).

The Commentary states: "That which is not the substance of liberation itself, but is the mental factor of resolve (*adhimokṣa*)," means that what is here called liberation is mastery and freedom from bondage;

it is not the mental factor of resolve among the distinct objects of cognition. This has true suchness (*tathatā*) as its substance, for it is not separate from suchness. This designation is applied metaphorically based on its substantial reality.

The Commentary states: "Fruit" refers to the fruit-benefit, which is that which accords with and benefits the cause; thus, the two superior fruits arise, being able to accord with the causes cultivated throughout the three kalpas.

As for the various practices cultivated by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)—which temporarily suppress [afflictions]—and those who, through the ascetic practices of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), reckon them as realizing *nirvāṇa*, these are all merely worldly paths for subduing delusions.
Whether they belong to ordinary beings or to the disciples of the Buddha, they are all "other" [than the true path]. If they are ordinary beings...
The mundane path cultivated by those [non-Buddhists] which suppresses afflictions is what non-Buddhists (tīrthika) cling to as *nirvāṇa*.
However, the mundane path that suppresses afflictions attained by the noble disciples (*ārya-śrāvaka*) of the Buddha is not reckoned as *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the principle revealed [by this path], those who cling to it as perfect quiescence (*parinirvāṇa*)—if one asks what kind of principle is revealed, the answer is that at certain times, one reveals only a single portion [of it].
The unconditioned state of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—taking this principle of cessation not through deliberation as *parinirvāṇa*.
When it is now said that "this is their *nirvāṇa*," it refers to the *nirvāṇa* attained by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), which is a portion of the Buddha-dharma’s *nirvāṇa*.
Because they possess a portion of the Buddha-dharma’s *nirvāṇa*, it is called "partial *nirvāṇa*" (*bhāga-nirvāṇa*); in reality, it is not true *nirvāṇa*. If [it were] the Buddha-dharma...
Attaining this in the interim is called true *nirvāṇa*. Because the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are exhausted, one attains *nirvāṇa with remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

When both body and cognition are exhausted, *nirvāṇa without remainder* (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) is manifested. Not abiding in either saṃsāra or *nirvāṇa* is called "non-abiding *nirvāṇa*" (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*).

Since these two types of *nirvāṇa* are subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is said that although the principle (*li*) [attained by others] is nominally called "true," one might ask:

why is the principle revealed by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also designated as "true"? The commentary below immediately states that the liberation attained by non-Buddhists and those of the Two Vehicles is not true liberation, but is merely provisional.
The answer is that while the preceding text says the principle is nominally called "true," [it does so only in relation to their own systems].
This refers to the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) manifested by the tenets held within the schools of the non-Buddhists themselves, which they grasp as true *nirvāṇa*.

The subsequent passage states that, according to the Buddha’s teaching, the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) obtained by those non-Buddhists through the suppression of afflictions is not *nirvāṇa*.
When those of the three vehicles have exhausted the afflictions of both the view-division and the cultivation-division, that which is revealed as perfect quiescence is alone named *nirvāṇa*.
Although they attain the two types of cessation and abide within these two, they are not non-abiding. These two cessations are the nirvana with remainder and the nirvana without remainder.

While the followers of the two vehicles abide within these two types of nirvana, because these are also conventional (*prajñapti*), both are analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and are not [non-analytical cessations].
Regarding "abiding": those of the Two Vehicles do not abide in the bodhisattva’s non-abiding nirvana; they are called "abiding" because they abide [in a limited state].
Because they still possess great compassion, they do not abide in nirvana; because they still possess great wisdom, they do not abide in saṃsāra.

This is because if those of the Two Vehicles were to abide in nirvana, they would be like ordinary beings who abide in saṃsāra. As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "It is not the practice of ordinary beings, nor that of the Two Vehicles..."

The practice of the vehicle is the practice of this Bodhisattva; it is precisely *apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding nirvana). Regarding the statement that "it is manifested by the cessation of the *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder)":

this refers to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). If there is reliance on *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder), it is manifested only after the afflictions have been completely severed.
If it is *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, it is manifested only after both body and cognition have ceased. That [nirvana] is merely conventional.

Regarding the phrase "not because of non-abiding": the meaning of this passage is that if the nirvāṇa attained by the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists is merely conventional, then those of the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists do not attain the bodhisattva’s non-abiding nirvāṇa;
non-abiding nirvāṇa is the ultimate truth. Question: The two vehicles attain liberation; how then do the non-Buddhists attain liberation? Answer: Indeed.

When non-Buddhists attain the first dhyāna concentration and are already able to suppress and detach from the afflictions of the desire realm, this is called "liberation from the afflictions of the desire realm," though it is merely a provisional designation for liberation.
This continues until the point when non-Buddhists detach from the afflictions of the sphere of nothingness;
at that time, it is called "liberation," though it is also merely a provisional designation for liberation from the afflictions of the sphere of nothingness. However, according to this commentary...

In the text, there are two interpretations. First, from the cultivation of ordinary beings up to that which is manifested through cessation; this constitutes the specific interpretation (*pṛthag-vyākhyā*).

Second, from the perspective of both the general and the specific, regarding those other than the two vehicles and non-Buddhists; this concerns the general interpretation of "true liberation" (*bhūta-vimukti*). Question:
Since the commentary already distinguishes the *nirvāṇa* attained by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages as not being true liberation, [how is this so? Part Two.
The two types of nirvāṇa—with remainder and without remainder—are conventional *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) and liberation, not the ultimate.
Now, regarding the fruit of Buddhahood, among the four kinds of nirvāṇa, which one is taken as true liberation? Answer:

The nirvāṇa with remainder and the nirvāṇa without remainder within the fruit of Buddhahood are also *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*; they are identical to the liberation of the two vehicles and are not [the ultimate].

True. If one takes *svabhāva-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity) as the true [nirvāṇa], then ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), followers of the two vehicles (*dvayayānika*), and bodhisattvas would all equally attain *svabhāva-nirvāṇa*;

consequently, the followers of the two vehicles and others should also attain true liberation. If, however, one takes *apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding nirvāṇa) as true liberation, then according to the tenth treatise below, one master says:
"By severing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one also attains analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)," which refers to the fourth [type of nirvāṇa].
Within *nirvāṇa*, the first is *tathatā* (suchness), while the latter three are all *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (analytical cessation);

these constitute non-abiding *nirvāṇa* and are also provisional liberations. If one were to say that all four types of *nirvāṇa* are not true liberation, why does the subsequent commentary state: [text follows]?
The essence of the two obstacles consists of the four wisdoms (*jñāna*) and the four nirvāṇas; reflect upon this. The *Śāstra* (commentary) states:
"Since *mārga* signifies 'the path to be traversed,' the ancient claim that it refers to the 'path to Bodhi' is incorrect. The intended meaning of this statement is as follows:
the aforementioned "Bodhi" is a Sanskrit term, which here means "awakening" (*bodha*). Regarding the ancient masters' interpretation, they take "Bodhi" [and proceed as follows]...
To claim that "path" (*mārga*) means "righteousness" (*dharma*) is incorrect; for in the Sanskrit it is *mārga*, which is precisely what is translated as "path. Question:

On what scriptural authority is it stated that "right understanding" (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) is "right awakening" (*samyag-bodhi*)? Answer: It is found in this very treatise and others. One who has severed the hindrances possesses right understanding.
Right understanding (*samyag-jñāna*) is a synonym for right awakening (*samyag-bodhi*). Regarding the establishment of the term "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*) based on that which is obscured:
the so-called "cognitive obscuration" (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) is named as such because it obstructs the knowable (*jñeya*).

Here, the term "knowable" does not refer to the objects of knowledge—the phenomena previously mentioned—but rather refers specifically to the uncontaminated noble wisdom (*anāsrava-ārya-prajñā*) that is capable of [penetrating] the emptiness of phenomena. It is this [wisdom] that is obstructed.
Because the wisdom that knows [them] cannot arise, it is called the "obstruction to the knowable" (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).
This very wisdom that knows takes its name from the various phenomena that are known by others; therefore, the wisdom that knows is itself termed "the knowable.

Fourth, because this obstruction can hinder the wisdom that knows, preventing it from arising, it renders one unable to cognize the two kinds of phenomena: the principles (*li*) and the facts (*shi*) that are to be known.

Therefore, the treatise states that what obstructs great bodhi is called the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This name for the obscuration is established by way of its obstructing the wisdom that knows;

it is just as in common parlance, when one sees a person who possesses learning and wisdom and is able to know all phenomena, one calls such a person "one who has something to know," rather than calling them "one who has the capacity to know. It is the same here: although ordinary beings...

Those who practice the two kinds of contemplation on the suchness of selflessness and cultivate great compassion for enlightenment are the bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*).
They vow to sever all evils that are like space and vow to cultivate all virtues that are like space.
Just as with space, all sentient beings wish to deliver one another; because the aspiration to do so is vast, it is called "Great.
Because it does not yet attain untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), it is not *bodhi*. While the *bodhi* of the two vehicles possesses untainted wisdom, their *bodhi* is not "Great.

[The alternative reading] states that the *bodhi* of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas is not "Great. However, within this second interpretation, it says regarding the causal stage of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*):
Regarding the statement that "the bodhisattva’s untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is called *bodhi*," this is explained in terms of five kinds of *bodhi*, namely:

the *bodhi* of generating the resolve (*cittotpāda-bodhi*), the *bodhi* of subduing the mind (*vinaya-citta-bodhi*), and so forth. Therefore, it is said that the untainted wisdom of the bodhisattva within the causal stage of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is called *bodhi*.

Furthermore, this serves merely to distinguish it from the wisdom of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); it does not mean that the wisdom of the Great Bodhisattvas is not *bodhi*. It is simply that [their wisdom] is "Great," whereas [the others'] is not *bodhi*.

Regarding the term "bodhi" (awakening): Why is it that the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) is called *bodhi*, whereas the untainted wisdom of a Bodhisattva on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is not so called?
The answer to this is the third interpretation. Its intent is to state that the untainted wisdom attained at the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*) of the two vehicles is named *bodhi*;
that is, it is the *bodhi* of the no-more-learners of the two vehicles. It is not [the same as] the fruit of Buddhahood.
Because all outflow-free knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is termed *bodhi*. The second treatise states that there are three kinds of bodhisattvas:

although a bodhisattva of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) possesses outflow-free wisdom, this outflow-free wisdom is merely termed "included within the practice of the cause" (*hetu-madhya-caryā-saṃgṛhīta*) and is not termed *bodhi*.
If that which is attained at the stage of Buddhahood is alone designated as *bodhi*, then the commentary states: "The Great [Vehicle] is not *bodhi*.

Regarding the three interpretations provided in the commentary, the third is superior. As for the statement that although ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) possess both types of selflessness, even the wisdom of ordinary beings is not both types—[the question is:
why is it that in the first interpretation the wisdom of ordinary beings is said to attain the name "Great," while in the latter two...
The wisdom of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) does not receive the name "Great. On what basis, then, are these three interpretations established? Answer:

Regarding the second interpretation in the commentary, it refers to non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) ordinary beings who, clinging to the views and precepts of their own schools through the wisdom of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*), take this as their correct practice and thereby attain superior meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
When the Buddha’s Dharma refutes this, it is termed "evil view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Therefore, [this refers to] that which belongs to non-Buddhists...

Giving rise to wrong views and the like is called "not great bodhi. Those who have entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are precisely those in the stages of accumulation (*saṃbhāra*) and preparation (*prayoga*) prior to that stage.
Since the word "prior" (*pūrva*) is used, it is known that they are indeed prior. If one were to say they have not yet entered the path of seeing, the word "prior" would not be necessary.
If the word "prior" is attached, then the word "not yet" (*na-yāvat*) is unnecessary. Regarding the mention of "four stages," [these are] accumulation and preparation...
The two paths are combined and termed "practice through understanding" (解行). Therefore, the three subsequent stages are identical [in this regard]. The Commentary states:

"Realizing emptiness and severing hindrances up to the ultimate stage. Question: Since the previous explanation of the third stage, the stage of cultivation (修習位), already contains the phrase "up to the ultimate," does this not imply that everything prior to reaching the ultimate path is already included?
Answer: This very phrasing [of "up to the ultimate"] clearly indicates that all stages preceding the ultimate path are designated as such.

This is the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*). Regarding the previous passage, "The preceding text explains," it means that from the commentary (*vṛtti*) one explains this treatise up until the point where correct understanding is produced.

The subsequent statement, "It is said below," reveals the fruit of realization and abandonment resulting from composing the treatise. Furthermore, the treatise states, "Understanding is produced in order to abandon the two heavy obstructions.
The subsequent statement, "This reveals the realization of emptiness," and so on, refers to the words in the commentary: "In this context, for the time being, it is explained..."
Because they are superior obstacles, they are said to be "distinct obstacles"; this shall be understood below.

The commentary above this point consists of the Master Tripiṭaka’s explanation of the preceding text as an initial interpretation, followed by the subsequent interpretation for those who are confused or mistaken regarding the two kinds of emptiness.
This refers to the period prior to entering the Dharma, up until this point, which constitutes the fourth stage of the seeker (*pṛthagjana*). This concludes the section above.
The *shu* (commentary) text refers to the commentary leading up to the explanation. In Sanskrit it is called Vātsīputrīya; here it is translated as the "Vātsīputra School.

Regarding the statement that these various internal and external paths all give rise to false wisdom and cannot contradict [this]: one might ask, "Does not the Hīnayāna also give rise to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*)?"

It is said that realizing the principle of the emptiness of arising is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), which also gives rise to subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) that integrates both the principle and phenomena.

Why, then, do those of the two vehicles not understand the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional? The answer is: because they have not fully exhausted [the realization] due to their limited capacity.
