This is also subsumed under the practice of "attaining Parinirvāṇa in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*). 3. One who attains Parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarābhava-parinirvāyin*): this person attains the state of *anāgāmin* in the present life but does not... [text fragment ends].

1. Arhat (who attains parinirvāṇa after casting off the body of the desire realm and receiving a body in the intermediate state between the two upper realms). 2. Upapadya-parinirvāyin (one who, upon being born in the first dhyāna, practices the path and attains parinirvāṇa before the end of that initial life, regardless of where one is born).

3. Sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin (the "attainer through exertion"; similar to the previous one in sharing the same body, but practicing the path with diligence and attaining parinirvāṇa at the end of their lifespan; this is called "attainment through exertion"). 4.

Anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin (also like the upapadya-parinirvāyin in sharing the same body, but not practicing the path diligently and attaining parinirvāṇa [at the end of] their lifespan; this is the "attainment without exertion"). 5. Abhāsvara (one who, within the upper realms, does not attain parinirvāṇa in the first body, but proceeds upward successively to the Bṛhatphala heaven, yet does not attain nirvāṇa there, but is born...).

...the formless realm). 8. Those with Joyful Wisdom (*prajñā-prīti*): among those in the higher realms who do not initially transmigrate upward through successive births, but reach the Bṛhatphala heaven without passing away [there], they are born in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).

9. Those Resolved by Faith (*śraddhādhimukta*): among the aforementioned persons, those of dull faculties are called "resolved through faith. 10. Those Who Have Attained Vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*): among the aforementioned persons, those of sharp faculties are called "attainers of vision. 11. Those Who Realize Through the Body (*kāyasākṣin*): among the aforementioned persons, those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

There are nine types of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): 1. Those of the Nature of Regression (*parihāṇadharman*): because of dull faculties, they necessarily regress from the attainment [of dhyāna]. 2. Those of the Nature of Guarding (*anurakṣaṇādharman*): because their faculties are slightly sharper, they attain the ability to protect themselves.

1. Guarding Non-retrogression (守不退). 2. The Mark of Death (死相): The faculties become sharp and one develops a deep revulsion for all states of existence (*bhava*). However, being unable to attain meditative concentration (*samādhi*), or fearing its loss once attained, one seeks revulsion [and speaks of oneself].

Hence it is called the mark of death. 3. The Mark of Abiding (住相): The *samādhi* already attained neither advances nor retreats, but increases further and becomes more excellent. 4. The Mark of Non-destruction (不壞相): The *samādhi* already attained is destroyed by various causes and conditions. 5. The Mark of Non-retrogression (不退相): This person’s supreme practice attains merit that is entirely without retrogression or loss.

6. Liberation through Wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*; 慧解脫): Among the aforementioned types of persons, one does not attain cessation (*nirodha*). 7. Double Liberation (*ubhaya-bhāga-vimukti*; 俱解脫): Among the aforementioned types of persons, one attains cessation.

Regarding the "exhaustion of meditative concentrations": the thirteen abodes consist of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) as ten, the provisions and preliminary practices (*sambhāra-prayoga*) as two, and the Buddha stage (*buddhabhūmi*) as one; thus, there are thirteen in total.

Just as ordinary beings have not yet been moistened by the water of the Dharma, they are called those of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*). Regarding the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the three vehicles, the first is the stage of dry wisdom;
this refers to the seed-nature (*gotra*) of the three vehicles, which is like fire that burns the fuel of afflictions (*kleśa*).

From the initial generation of the mind of awakening until the cultivation of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*) for the three vehicles, this is the stage of dry wisdom. Second is the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*).

This refers to those of the three vehicles (triyāna) who, while in the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), have attained certainty regarding their spiritual lineage (*gotra*). Thus far, these two [categories] apply to all three vehicles.
Third, regarding the "stage of the eighth person" (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*): in the older sūtras and śāstras, the "stage of the eighth person" refers to the four candidates and four fruits;
in the newer sūtras and śāstras, it is called the "eighth person," which refers to the candidate for stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*). From the Arhat...

The fruit of Arhatship is the first; the stage of approaching Arhatship is the second. Counting backward from the latter toward the former until reaching the stage of approaching the first fruit, this constitutes the eighth person.
Fourth, those who possess the ground of vision are those who have attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. Fifth, those on the ground of attenuation are those who have attained the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin;
having abandoned the delusions of view, they have also abandoned six grades of afflictions of the desire realm, which are light.

The sixth is the stage of "diminishing desire" (*tanū-bhūmi*); this is the fruit of the third [stream-enterer], so called because one has abandoned desire for the desire realm and is born in the eight higher stages.

The seventh is the stage of "having accomplished what was to be done" (*kṛtāvi-bhūmi*); this is the fruit of the arhat, so called because that which was to be done has been accomplished. The four stages following these exist only among the śrāvakas.

The eighth is the stage of the Pratyekabuddha, which refers to the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha. Question: Why, among these ten stages of the three vehicles, is the Pratyekabuddha established as only one stage?
Answer: Because this Pratyekabuddha achieves awakening in a single sitting, and furthermore, because he does not emerge from meditative absorption.

Therefore, among the Pratyekabuddhas, no separate stage for those "facing" the path (*pratipannaka*) is distinguished. Regarding the nine Bodhisattva stages, this refers to the ten stages of the Bodhisattvas and the ten stages of the Tathāgatas. The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Because there is no separate distinction made between the 'facing' stage and the 'fruit' stage.
The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states: "If the treatise were to speak of a person who has attained the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*)," [it would follow that they are not distinguished].

This refers to the candidate (*pratipannaka*). Although it mentions only the "stream-enterer" (*srotāpanna*) and not the fruit, it is clear that the candidate is also included within what is designated as "stream-enterer," for there is no separate distinction made.
Regarding the statement that one who moves against the flow of birth and death is called a "counter-currenter" (*pratisrota*), the meaning of this passage is as follows. The former masters said:
This refers to the *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer). Because they do not enter into [the realms of] form, sound, smell, taste, or touch, they are called "those who flow against the current.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "One who has definitively severed the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) within the three realms, or who has practiced to the fifth stage [of the path of cultivation], is established as having attained the fruit of stream-entry.

Regarding this, there are two interpretations. The first says: if one severs the first, second, or even up to the fifth stage of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the desire realm...

The [first] nine grades [of afflictions] all together constitute the stage of the candidate for the first fruit (srotāpanna-pratipannaka). If one has exhausted the eight grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the desire realm, this collectively constitutes the candidate for arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*).

The intent here is to provide a specific answer regarding the discourse on the four fruits and the four candidates. The abandonment of the first grade of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation is itself the second candidate.

If discussed in terms of the four fruits, from the time one reaches the path of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*) up until the sixth grade of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation has been abandoned, it is likewise [the second candidate].
This is the first fruit (*phala*). At the time of the sixth liberation path (*vimukti-mārga*), it is then the second fruit; up to the eighth [liberation path], it remains the second fruit.
Upon reaching the ninth preparatory (*prayoga*) and uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) paths, it is still the second fruit;
only at the time of the ninth liberation path does it become the third fruit. This applies likewise up to the stage of Arhat. This summarizes the progression toward the fruits.

This is because it is based on the fruit [of the path]. A second interpretation states: this text explains only in terms of the sequential and the leap-over [attainments], and does not clarify them by means of the four fruits.

Regarding the sequential [attainment]: one who has exhausted only the afflictions of the view-delusions (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) but has not yet abandoned even a single grade of the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is termed a sequential *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer).
If, however, one first uses the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) to suppress five grades of the afflictions of cultivation belonging to the desire realm...

That person later enters and realizes the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). Although they have completely abandoned the five grades of afflictions belonging to the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they are nonetheless called one who has "leaped over" the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Within the fruit of *srotāpanna*, there is only the leaping over of the grades, but no leaping over of the fruit itself.

As for those who follow the gradual sequence, they gradually abandon the six grades of afflictions of the desire realm and are named *sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner). As for those who leap over, if they first use the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) to suppress [the afflictions]...
The seventh and eighth categories. Once one has entered the Path of Seeing, that person is then called a *sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner).

If this text were intended to clarify the matter according to the four fruits of the spiritual life, the text should have stated: "The uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) that abandons the sixth category is all called the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*);
it is only upon reaching the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) of the sixth category that one is called a *sakṛdāgāmin*. Furthermore, it should have stated [this] up to the ninth..."

The path of uninterrupted transition for the first five categories is designated as the fruit of once-returner; it is only upon reaching the ninth path of liberation that one is designated as the fruit of non-returner.
Since the text states that one abandons five, seven, or eight categories, it is clear that this refers to both types of practitioners—the one who transcends and the one who proceeds by stages.
Furthermore, although this passage clarifies only the first two fruits and does not mention the third or fourth fruits, [the implication remains].
This is explained in reference to one who has abandoned six grades of afflictions within the desire realm.
The *Śāstra* states: "The two paths [of the candidate] are not fixed. The commentary explains: For instance, there are two types of those who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*):

first, the gradual practitioner; second, the one who transcends the stages. As for the gradual practitioner, they enter the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and abandon the delusions of vision; this is the fifteenth [moment].
The mind [at this stage] is called the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*). Upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind, it is called the first fruit (*phala*).

As for those of the "leap-over" type (*vyutkrāntaka*), having previously suppressed one to five categories of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm by means of the mundane path, they subsequently turn their minds to enter the path of seeing;
upon reaching the fifteenth moment of mind, it is called the candidate for the first fruit, and upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind, it is called [the first fruit].
The first fruit. A person who has attained the first fruit cannot skip over it. Next, regarding the second fruit, there are three types.

For one who proceeds by gradual stages, from the completion of the abandonment of the afflictions of the view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) up to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) for the first through the sixth grades of the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm, all are designated as the "second" stage.
Only upon reaching the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for the sixth grade does one truly attain what is called the second fruit. If one skips...

Regarding "leaping over" (*vyutkrānta*): having first used the worldly path to suppress the afflictions of the desire realm up to the sixth, seventh, or eighth grade, one subsequently turns the mind to enter the vision of the truths (*darśanamārga*).

Upon reaching the fifteenth moment of mind, one is called a candidate for the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*); upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind, one is called the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).
This surpasses the previous fruit of Stream-enterer. Regarding "leaping over grades": one first uses the worldly path to suppress the [afflictions] of the desire realm...

Regarding the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the realms: when one reaches the seventh or eighth category [of abandonment], upon subsequently entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one simultaneously abandons the eight preceding categories of afflictions.

Next, regarding the three fruits, there are likewise three types. First, as for the practitioner who proceeds sequentially (*anupūrva-kārī*): having first abandoned the afflictions of the path of seeing, they subsequently abandon the first category of the afflictions of the desire realm through cultivation, continuing up to the ninth category.
The uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the ninth category is termed the "candidate for the fruit of Non-returner" (*anāgāmi-pratipannaka*). As for the ninth category...

The path of liberation is called the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). If one is a leaper (*pluta*), having first suppressed the ninth grade of desire through the mundane path—from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness—and subsequently enters the vision of the truths (*darśanamārga*), reaching the fifteenth moment of mind, this is called the stage of the candidate for non-returning (*anāgāmipratipannaka*).
Upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind, it is called the fruit of non-returning; the two preceding fruits are not taken up. If...

Regarding those who transcend stages to attain the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), they are categorized as either "non-dharmic" (i.e., non-sequential) Arhats as previously described, or as "sequential.

Those discussed in the treatise as attaining the third fruit are called "transcenders" because they attain it from the first fruit, bypassing the three intermediate fruits. It is absolutely impossible for one to directly transcend from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) to attain the fruit of Arhatship.
This applies whether one is dealing with the nine grades of defilement in the first dhyāna, up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Regarding the nine grades of defilement: if one abandons these within the seven stages—either six grades or all nine—one is called a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and is also termed one "heading toward Arhatship" (*arhattvaphalapratipannaka*).
What is the meaning of this? For instance, take a practitioner who follows the gradual path:

having previously attained the first fruit up to the third fruit, they then abandon even a single grade of affliction in the first dhyāna, continuing until they abandon [the afflictions] of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
At the time when the nine grades of afflictions [of the form realm] are being abandoned, that person is called one "progressing toward arhatship" (arhattva-pratipannaka).

Alternatively, suppose there is a person who first uses the mundane path to suppress the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm up to the nine grades of afflictions of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

When that person later enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they are immediately called one who has attained the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*). Although that person has completely eliminated the afflictions of the sphere of nothingness, [they are not yet called an arhat].

For one who is seeking the fruit of non-returning, this is not called the fruit of arhatship. If one has abandoned the nine grades of afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), or if one has abandoned the nine grades of afflictions of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*)—whether by gradual or by leaping progression—one is designated solely as a candidate for arhatship (*arhattvaphalapratipannaka*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the two candidates are indeterminate": for those who attain the middle two fruits sequentially, there is sequential progress; for those who leap over stages, it is called "indeterminate progress toward the two.
As for the two individuals—the Non-returner (Anāgāmin) and the Once-returner (Sakṛdāgāmin)—if they progress sequentially, they abide solely in the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).

If they progress by leaping over, they abide within the first fifteen moments of mind of the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga). Thus, the progress of these two middle individuals pertains to both the Path of Seeing and the Path of Cultivation.

Therefore, it is called "indeterminate. However, the Upādhyāya spoke incidentally regarding the meaning of the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens. The other venerable masters (bhadanta) in the Upādhyāya’s lineage said:

"Regarding all matter (rūpa), mind (citta), and formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) within those five Śuddhāvāsa heavens, from what homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) do they arise?

They should be understood as being like the first untainted dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) in the Hīnayāna, which arises without a homogeneous cause," so say the various venerable masters.

Since he was unable to answer, [the Buddha] asked again: "In the first dhyāna there are two heavens. If one takes the seeds of the Brahmakāyika devas, will they be able to be born as Brahmā-purohita devas?
And if one takes the seeds of the Brahmā-purohita devas, will they be able to be born as Mahābrahmā devas?"
Master Guang replied: "It is not so. If that were the case, how could one steal [merit] and be reborn among the gods of the Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, or Bṛhatphala heavens?

If you say that it arises from seeds because they belong to the same level—just as those in the lower heavens of the three lower dhyānas cannot be born in the higher heavens—is it not also the case that being born in the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens should consist only of innate seeds?"
There are no newly perfumed seeds (*navābhinirvṛtta-bīja*), because since beginningless time it has been impossible to be born in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
The Upādhyāya explains that within the four dhyānas, the various heavens of each stage share the same type of seed;

thus, by means of the seeds of the Brahmakāyika heaven, one is born in the Brahmapurohita heaven, and by the seeds of the Brahmapurohita heaven, one is born in the Mahābrahmā heaven, and so on for the remaining dhyānas.
It is the same for the gods of Limited Light, Immeasurable Light, and so forth. It is like rice and grain in the world:
although they are of a single kind, depending on the different ways they are prepared by the cook, that which is excellently prepared is served to the Son of Heaven;
that which is moderately prepared is served to the high officials; and that which is poorly prepared is served to the common people. Now, this case is also like that.
Within those three heavens, the so-called "names and words" seeds are essentially the same; these seeds are like grains of rice.
However, the karma capable of inducing them differs in three grades, much like the hands that handle food. This is because the names and words seeds are induced by karma of the lower grade.

One is born in the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude due to the seeds of names and words (*nāma-vyañjana-bīja*) induced by middling karma; one is born in the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā due to the seeds of names and words induced by superior karma;
and one is born in the Heaven of Great Brahmā due to the seeds of names and words induced by superior karma. The same applies to the other dhyānas.
Therefore, it should be understood that there is no error in asserting that the newly perfumed seeds of the three heavens—Anabhraka and so forth—give rise to the five Pure Abodes. Thus, it is said:
The five Śuddhāvāsa heavens possess newly perfumed seeds and possess homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).

Regarding my statement that within the dharmas of the preceding category there are only twenty-four truths: [it is asked] if this is so, then within the preceding category of dharmas, the "self" (*ātman*) of the Vaiśeṣika school should be clarified among the twenty-four categories of substance (*dravya*), because the self is a substance and belongs to the preceding category.
Because it is included [in the aggregates]. Why is the self (*ātman*) not excluded? Answer: Here, that which is real should also exclude the self; the self is subsumed under the preceding category.
Regarding "the cause for the arising of a mass of honor": Question—what is meant by "honor" (*satkāra*) and what is meant by "mass" (*rāśi*)? Answer: "Honor" has the meaning of "mass."
The term "accumulation" (skandha) carries the meaning of "heaping up. This "heaping up" refers to eleven types of accumulations, which are designated as *skandhas*.
These eleven accumulations are as explained in the first chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* and the third volume of the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*. The eleven types of accumulations are:

first, the past, which refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that have already arisen and already performed their function; second, the future, which refers to the five factors that have not yet arisen.

1. That which has not yet performed its function is called the future. 2. The third is the present; that is, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) in the state of arising and performing their functions are called the present.

3. The fourth is the internal, referring to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). 4. The fifth is the external, referring to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). 5. The sixth is the coarse, referring to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), also called "resistant form" (*sapratigha-rūpa*). 6.

The seventh is the subtle, referring to the two higher realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*), also called "non-resistant form" (*apratigha-rūpa*). 7. The eighth is the superior, referring to wholesome states of mind (*kuśala-citta*).
Mental factors (*caitta*) and wholesome form (*rūpa*), etc., [are termed "distant"]. The nine inferior [factors] refer to unwholesome mind, form, etc., and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena.
Regarding the ten "near" [factors], there are three interpretations. First, it is said that those which have fallen into the past for one or two moments and beyond are called "near";
likewise, future phenomena, according to one or two moments, as well as the future and present, are also called "near. Second, it is based on location (*deśa*).
"Near" (*āsanna*) means that being separated by ten or five paces is called "near. A third [explanation] says:
because the cognizing mind takes as its object this proximate location and dharmas of the past or future, this very cognizing mind is also called "near.

Alternatively, it is said that the cognizing mind is called "near" because it takes the internal body as its object. Regarding the eleventh, "distant" (*viprakṛṣṭa*), there are three interpretations. The first says: [it refers to...]

Regarding future phenomena, those that follow more than ten moments of thought (*citta-kṣaṇa*) and have not yet reached the present are called "distant. Furthermore, regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and paths (*mārga*) of the past, those following more than ten moments of thought are called "distant.
Second, it is said that they are called "distant" in terms of spatial location; that is, being separated by more than ten *li* is called "distant.
Third, it is said that this refers to the cognizing mind (*ālambaka-citta*); that is, when the mind takes these distant phenomena of the past or future as its object.

Furthermore, this very mind that acts as the object-condition is also called "distant. It is also said that the mind acting as the object-condition takes the six external sense-objects as its objects, and thus it is termed "distant.

However, within the category of *dharmas*, these eleven meanings are not fully present. For while there are internal [dharmas], there are no external ones, because they differ in being internal versus external;

while there are coarse [dharmas], there are no subtle ones, because they are distinguished by being with resistance (*sapratigha*) versus without resistance (*apratigha*); while there are conditioned [dharmas], there are no inferior ones, because they are distinguished by being wholesome (*kuśala*) versus unwholesome (*akuśala*). Nevertheless, they are extremely numerous.
That is to say, within a single dharma there are only eight dharmas present. For example, when the five faculties arise, they simultaneously possess the past, future, and present [time periods].
Furthermore, they possess coarseness internally because they are obstructive matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*). Moreover, they possess inferiority, as they are the five faculties.

This is because they are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, there is a distinction between the distant and the near; however, this distance and proximity have no separate substantial entity.
If one follows [a sequence of] one or two moments of thought, it is called "near"; if one follows ten or five moments of thought and beyond, it is called "distant.

Yet, the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) do not possess subtlety, for they are not non-obstructive form (*anidarśana-rūpa*). Moreover, they lack superiority, as the five faculties are of an indeterminate nature and thus do not extend to the wholesome nature (*kuśala-dharma*).
Furthermore, there is no external [element], because the five sense faculties are internal bases (*āyatana*). Moreover, when the five objects arise, they likewise possess eight factors:
namely, the possession of the three times, as well as external proximity and distance, because the locations of the five objects involve distance and nearness;

furthermore, there is the inferior, which is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*); and there is the coarse, which is with resistance (*sapratigha*). If one takes the minimum, there are four factors, as follows:
After entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), all female bodies, as well as the eighth existence (*aṣṭama-bhava*) and so forth, attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
However, because a female body cannot arise [again], it has no past or present; there is only the future. Furthermore, there is that which is internal, coarse, and inferior.

That which is "born" refers to the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*). Since the twelve bases consist of the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) and the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), [the female body is included therein].

It is capable of producing consciousness. The "causes" are the eighteen *dhātus*. If the eighteen *dhātus* are manifesting consciousnesses, they arise from manifesting [consciousnesses] because the former induces the latter.
Furthermore, if the eighteen *dhātus* exist as seeds, they are also called causes. Moreover, the meaning of "sustaining" (*dhṛti*) is the meaning of *dhātu*.
Just as the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) can present themselves to consciousness, so too the substance of the seven mental *dhātus* is capable of sustaining [it].

[The term] "usage" (*yoga*) is applied here. The *Abhidharmakośa* likewise treats them as a single collection of doors of origination (*āyatana*). "Genus" (*gotra*) is the meaning of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

Regarding the other three types of expertise (*kauśalya*), the treatise intends to establish six kinds of expertise, namely: the aggregates, bases, elements, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), faculties (*indriya*), and truths (*satya*). This is why they are called "six.

Although the treatise mentions only three, it does so by using the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) to include the remaining three. Alternatively, there are four types of expertise; this refers to the present text.

These are the seven skills (kauśalya), namely: the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), faculties (indriya), truths (satya), and the possible and impossible (sthānāsthāna). These are called the seven.
The treatise mentions three; "etc. includes the remaining four.

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'places and non-places,' 'faculties,' 'worldly truth,' 'vehicles,' and 'existence and non-existence of the unconditioned': performing wholesome deeds and obtaining pleasant fruits is called a 'place' (*sthāna*);
performing wholesome deeds and obtaining painful fruits is called a 'non-place' (*asthāna*). 'Faculties' refers to the twenty-two faculties. 'World' refers to the three periods of time."
The truths refer to the two truths and the four truths; the vehicles refer to the three vehicles and the five vehicles.

Whether it be the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) or the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), although there is a distinction between their existence and non-existence, that which "exists" is precisely the dependent nature.

This is what is referred to in the holy teachings as the self and phenomena—meaning that the designation is based upon a substance, and the provisional establishment is based upon a substantial basis. It is not [ultimately] existent.
This refers precisely to the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). It is the real self and dharmas external to the mind as clung to by worldly non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*);
it is without intrinsic substance and is a mere conventionality following worldly sentiment. This is because it is a conventional designation based on what does not exist.

Regarding "following various worldly kinds of discrimination and arbitrary conceptualization," this means following the various non-Buddhists who, through their teachers and false teachings, cling to the existence of a real self.

Regarding the conditions for the self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-pratyaya*). Question: Just as within the sixth consciousness one may grasp at a self and phenomena according to various external, arbitrary conceptualizations of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), how does one grasp at a self and phenomena within the seventh consciousness according to external, arbitrary conceptualizations and other such conditions?
Furthermore, question: Does the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*) grasp at the existence of a self? If one says it does grasp at a self, then there should be bondage (*bandhana*) in that place.
Furthermore, how can it be said that the people of the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) lack the notions of "self" and "mine"?

Moreover, since there are no heterodox teachers there who propagate such arbitrary conceptualizations, if one were to say they lack these notions, then as those beings are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), how could they be devoid of self-clinging?

Furthermore, the treatise states that the two obstacles arise fully from the clinging to a self and to phenomena; since desire and other afflictions exist there, [how could they lack the obstacle of afflictions?]

Because all [afflictions] arise based on the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*). Furthermore, it was asked: "In the Mahāyāna, twenty root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are taught.
To what extent do the inhabitants of the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*) give rise to these?

Moreover, since there are no conditions such as false teachings in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and in the hells, how can they still grasp at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*)? Further questions were asked regarding the various proofs found in the holy scriptures (*āgama*).

Regarding "conditions" (*pratyaya*): it asks how the noble ones within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and so forth establish the self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*) in accordance with the various sacred teachings (*āgama*), and how they attain various unconditioned conditions (*asaṃskṛta-pratyaya*) in accordance with those sacred teachings.
Because they realize these unconditioned conditions, they are established as having attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
Furthermore, because they have abandoned the six grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm and realized the six grades of unconditioned states, they [are likewise established].
This is called the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*). If one realizes the nine grades of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) states, one is then called a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Up until the exhaustion of all afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) within the three realms—considering the three realms collectively, there are eighty-one grades of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is unconditioned;
therefore, it is said that there are "various unconditioned" states. According to the Sarvāstivāda school, within each of these grades, there are further [unconditioned states].
The measure of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is such that it is measured by the extent of the outflow-tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).

Since the unconditioned of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is likewise measured by that same extent, the subsequent treatise refutes the Sarvāstivāda on this point. Furthermore, regarding whether space (*ākāśa*) and so forth are one or many:

if space as an unconditioned phenomenon were many, it would be identical to the unconditioned of analytical cessation and the like. This passage constitutes a powerful refutation, particularly from the perspective of the Mahāyāna.
The *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states: "The essence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is solely one; it is only through its manifestations that there are different categories and numbers.

The commentary (*śāstra-vṛtti*) says: "Third, because it can remove the fear of non-self (*anātma-bhaya*). The explanation says: "For example, if sentient beings were to establish the existence of a self (*ātman*)," [and so forth].

Nevertheless, for my sake, one must separately cultivate the path. Since the "self" is non-existent, what is the purpose of cultivating the path, and for whom is the path cultivated to sever defilement and attain purity?
Therefore, it is necessary to establish that the self exists.
The Commentary states: "Fourth, because there exist [distinctions such as] self and other, defilement and purity, faith and understanding, and activities.
The Explanation states: If one posits a self, then there exists one's own body and the bodies of others. Birth and death are termed "defiled," while nirvana is termed "pure";

alternatively, ordinary beings are termed "defiled" and sages are termed "pure. Regarding "faith and understanding": if one posits a self, one then believes in the existence of a fundamental principle, ancestors, and parents.

Regarding matters such as those between sovereign and subject, or the great and the small: if there were no self, one would not believe in the existence of sovereigns, subjects, parents, and so forth;
nor would there be those engaged in worldly affairs or monastic affairs, nor the karma of the ten wholesome or ten unwholesome paths of action.
Because there still exists a self, all that has been stated above can be established. The term "etc. includes the three realms, the five destinies, and so forth.
If one does not assert the existence of a self, then there would be no phenomena of defilement or purification pertaining to self and other.

Regarding the two types of self and phenomena—the imputed and the dependent—the imputed refers to the self and phenomena of the mundane world which lack intrinsic nature and exist only according to conceptual attachment.
Regarding "provisional [designations] such as [the self]," if they depend on others, this refers to the provisional designations of the existence of the body and so forth as taught by the Sage.

"Transformation" means that the seeds within the eighth consciousness transform into manifesting states; this is the intended meaning of the passage. These are the seeds within the eighth consciousness.

The eight consciousnesses arise as active manifestations (*pravṛtti*). Regarding the transformation of these manifesting consciousnesses into seeds: the preceding seven consciousnesses act as the perfuming agents (*vāsaka*).

To be perfumed into seeds is itself a transformation. This corresponds to the passage in the treatise which asks how the perfuming agents produce various [seeds] that give rise to active manifestations.
Since the treatise states that the seed-consciousness transforms into active manifestations, the "seeing" (*darśana*) is included within those active manifestations.

Regarding the "objective aspect" (*nimitta-bhāga*): why does the subsequent passage also refer to the "perfuming" (*vāsanā*) as the "seeing and objective aspects"? Reflect on this; the seeing and objective aspects are precisely what is meant by the "manifestation of the mind.
If it were the actual *tathatā* (Suchness), it would not be described as either "dharma" or "adharma. Question: This text does not state that *tathatā* is neither dharma nor adharma;
however, in the preceding section explaining the teachings of the Noble Ones, it is stated that within the ten types of skillfulness, there is no... [text ends].

[The opponent asks: "Is it because they are designated as dharmas? Furthermore, in the previous treatise, within the section on the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), it was also stated that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are designated as dharmas.

Now, in this subsequent treatise, it is said that those characteristics are all provisionally established based on what is transformed by consciousness—that is, the self and dharmas are established upon the transformations of consciousness, rather than being established based on the nature of consciousness itself. Thus, there is a contradiction between the preceding and the following. [The author] answers this below.

Regarding the statement that "all subsequent attainments which manifest as [objects] are called dharmas": according to my own view, this is because the manifestation of *tathatā* (suchness) within the consciousness of subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is also called a dharma.
This refers specifically to the immediate dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). According to my view, it is the manifestation of *tathatā* by consciousness;

it is called "immediate" because it is manifested by consciousness. If *tathatā* were called "distant," then [it would not be so]. Furthermore, regarding the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)...
The dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) is proximate [to the mind], whereas True Suchness (*tathatā*) is remote from it.

The *Śāstra* states: "This means that while the objects [of the mental factors] do not necessarily arise simultaneously with the mind, [certain factors such as] greed (*rāga*) and faith (*śraddhā*) may not manifest. The commentary explains:
When the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) arises, the mental factors (*caitta*) also arise; for instance, there may be greed without faith, or when faith is present, the mental factor of greed arises.
Since it is indeterminate, one speaks only of the mind (*citta*) and cannot speak of the mental factors (*caitta*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because consciousness is primary and is able to produce them,” a question is raised: since the seeds of the mind and the mental factors are distinct, how can it be said that the mind produces the mental factors?
The answer is: they are called "produced" because they are induced by the predominant path (*adhipatimārga*). As for those five types:

When the five universal mental factors arise, they are accompanied by [the specific factors] such as greed or faith; these belong to the category of the five mental concomitants (*caitasika*). At times, they do not arise and cannot function simultaneously.

The Commentary states: "This is not so; for how could they be called 'knowledge of others' minds' or 'subsequently attained knowledge' (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*)? For these do not apprehend external objects. The Explanation says:
If there were no transformation of the objective aspect (nimittabhāga), how could it be called "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*)?

For instance, when subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) takes another's mind as its object, it relies upon that other's mind as the primary essence (*bimba*) and transforms itself to give rise to an objective aspect. This subsequently attained wisdom, which takes its own objective aspect as its object, is termed "external apprehension.

Question: How can it be said that this is not the case? Answer: If one says that the knowledge of others' minds directly perceives [the other's mind], then it would follow that it could arise with respect to another's mind.
The human mind is not like that; how then could it be called "knowledge of others' minds"? This is because subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) does not apprehend external objects.
When the knowledge of others' minds takes another's mind as its object, that other's mind serves as the substantial essence (*bhāva-svabhāva*).

Furthermore, this knowledge of others' minds also transforms and gives rise to a direct image-part (*sākṣāt-nimitta-bhāga*) which it then apprehends. When subsequently attained wisdom apprehends *tathatā* (suchness), it likewise transforms and gives rise to an image-part...
This is because [the consciousness] cannot take the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) as its object.
The commentary states: "These two are explained in detail below in the seventh and tenth [chapters]," etc. These two refer to the "seeing" (*darśana*) and "image" (*nimitta*) [aspects].

In the seventh chapter below, this is termed the "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*). Furthermore, at the end of the tenth chapter, there are three masters [who offer different interpretations].

Regarding the meaning: it clarifies that there are two parts, the perceived (nimitta-bhāga) and the seeing (darśana-bhāga). These three masters at the end of the tenth [chapter] were all disciples of Dharmapāla.

As for "arising through the transformation of what resembles the two parts' aspects and functions": "aspect" refers to the perceived part (nimitta-bhāga), and "function" refers to the seeing part (darśana-bhāga).

Regarding the "snail" (*kambūka*): *kambu* is the name of an insect; because its head has two horns resembling those of an ox, it is called a "snail. Although there are four [parts] on the head of this snail...
This refers to the horns. Here, taking two long horns as the metaphor and not taking two short horns is the point.

If the seeds were identical, then from the single substance of consciousness up to the distinction between the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) and the *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect), it would be superior in principle for them to have distinct seeds.

If the *darśanabhāga* and *nimittabhāga* shared the same seed, it is said that the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-verifying aspect), the *darśanabhāga*, and the *nimittabhāga*—these three factors—all arise from the same seed.
As for its essential object, it does not arise from the same seed as the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).

When it is said here that [an object] arises from the same seed, this refers exclusively to "solitary shadows" (*kevala-chāyā*), which arise solely from the seeing-part. If one were to say that the seeing-part and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) arise from entirely different seeds, [that would be incorrect].

It is then stated that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) arise from the same single seed; for the self-verifying-part is the essence of consciousness, while the seeing-part is its function.
Thus, the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) arises separately from them.
Now, regarding the statement that "the seeds of the discrimination of the perceived aspect arise," this refers precisely to the fact that the objective realm (性境) does not follow the mind.
A question is raised as to whether the perceived aspect (相分) and its original objective essence (本質境) arise from the same seed or different seeds.

However, what is meant here by "same seed" or "different seeds" is based on the explanation given at the end of the tenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which states: "The perceived aspects of consciousnesses such as those of the aggregates (蘊) do not necessarily all arise from the same [seed]."

This refers to the textual explanations concerning the characteristics of the three dharmas—cause, condition, and aspect—as being either identical or distinct. Now, regarding these two interpretations:

both the view that [the aspect] arises from the same seed as the object and the view that it arises from a different seed possess faults and do not fully accord with reason. This is because neither accounts for the "aspect with substance" (*sadravya-sākāra*) which penetrates both the mental state (*caitta*) and its basis (*āśraya*).
If one were to say that the aspect and the object arise solely from the same seed, then there would be no such thing as the real matter (*rūpa*) of the five sense organs and the five sense objects.

Because the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) arises from the same seeds as the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect), the *nimitta-bhāga* is subsumed under the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) and the mental factors such as the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

Therefore, there are only four aggregates, beginning with mind. Furthermore, when the sixth consciousness takes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object or conceives a self apart from the aggregates, it can be said that the objective and subjective aspects arise from the same seeds.
However, in the case of the five sensory consciousnesses, the eighth consciousness, and others, which take present phenomena as their objects...

Regarding the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) which are objective realms that do not follow the mind and so forth, how can it be said that the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) arise from the same seed?

If the latter teacher asserts that the image and seeing parts arise from distinct seeds, then this could be said for the five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness when they take present sensory objects and so forth as their objects;
however, if the sixth consciousness takes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) or [objects] beyond... [the senses] as its object, [this would not hold].
Regarding the conception of a self within the aggregates (*skandha*), how can one say that the aspect (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*) arise from different seeds?

Nor can it be said that they arise from seeds [of the same kind] to produce an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) substantial essence. Therefore, the current explanation states: both the simultaneous apprehension of the aspect and the seeing arise from both the same seed and different seeds.
This encompasses all phenomena exhaustively. It also includes those with a substantial basis (*sadravya*) that correspond to both the mental aspect (*ākāra*) and the objective essence (*ālambana*).

If they are of the same seed (*ekajātīya*), they include the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭhavijñāna*) perceiving unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and the conception of a self apart from the aggregates (*skandha-vinirmukta-ātman*). These are exclusively "sole images" (*kevalapratibimba*) arising solely from the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*).

If they are of different seeds (*bhinnajātīya*), they include the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭamavijñāna*), and a portion of the sixth consciousness that perceives present objects. Thus...
It is grasped as a real object that does not follow the mind. Furthermore, it is like the sixth consciousness itself perfuming seeds of ripening and neutral maturation within the sixth consciousness;

this is the "substantial with both phenomenal and noumenal aspects" (*sābhāsā-svabhāva-ālambana*) which penetrates both the mental and the fundamental. This is a principle extremely difficult to understand within the Mahāyāna. What is its meaning?
It is because the seeds of the seeing and image aspects (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness cannot perfume themselves; rather, it is by means of the five...
Consciousness and the six consciousnesses perfume the seeds of the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness;

if it is the sixth and seventh consciousnesses that perfume them, they form the seeds of the subject-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness. As previously stated regarding the matured, indeterminate mind within the sixth consciousness, it cannot perfume its own seeds.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "If a dharma possesses potent efficacy and is intense, it may be termed 'perfuming' (*vāsaka*). Thus, it is said:
Wholesome and unwholesome minds possess powerful and intense functional efficacy, and thus may be termed "capable of perfuming.
Because the resultant indeterminate mind lacks such powerful and intense functional efficacy, it cannot perfume itself.

For this reason, the seeds of the resultant indeterminate mind within the five consciousnesses cannot perfume themselves; rather, they are perfumed by the sixth consciousness, either simultaneously or by perceiving other objects.
Within the five consciousnesses, the maturation-neutral mind perfumes seeds of maturation-neutral [mind] within the five consciousnesses among their objective aspects (*nimittabhāga*).

This is just as when the sixth consciousness perceives the seeing aspect (*darśanabhāga*) of the eighth consciousness—whether perceiving it in the same moment—it perfumes the seeds of another eighth consciousness's seeing aspect within its own objective aspect. Its...
The image-part (*nimittabhāga*) cannot perfuse [the storehouse consciousness] by itself; it does so because it is carried along by the other, the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*).

Thus, the image-part is also able to perfume and form seeds, just as a weak soldier, although unable to strike the enemy himself, is said to "be able to strike the enemy" because he is struck down by the enemy alongside the preceding strong soldiers.
This case is likewise. If the seventh consciousness necessarily simultaneously takes the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness as its object, [it can perfume it].
It differentiates and perfumes the seeds of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.

As for the seeds of the neutral, maturation-resultant (*vipāka-avyākṛta*) mind within the sixth consciousness, how are the seeds of the maturation-resultant mind within the sixth consciousness perfumed?

This is because when the preceding sixth consciousness is actively engaged in wholesome or unwholesome states of mind, that maturation-resultant mind has either already ceased or has not yet arisen; thus, it cannot [be perfumed].
It is perfumed and formed as seeds of the retributive consciousness (*vipākacitta*) within the sixth consciousness itself.

Whether the sixth consciousness arises as a seed of retribution, or when the sixth consciousness arises as a retributive mind, it cannot perfume and form seeds, because that which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) cannot perfume.
Therefore, one should know that when a wholesome or unwholesome mind is actually arising within the sixth consciousness, it takes the preceding moment of the sixth consciousness as its object.
Within the consciousness, the maturation-consciousness (vipāka-citta) perfumes its own indeterminate seeds within the sixth consciousness among the image-aspects (nimitta-bhāga).

These indeterminate maturation-seeds within the sixth consciousness are subsumed under the "pervasive of the objective essence" (saviṣaya-sāmānya) category that includes both the mental state and the objective essence.
If the family of the objective essence is strong while the image-aspect is weak, then these newly perfumed maturation-seeds will produce another sixth consciousness.

The middle [aspect], the objective part (*nimittabhāga*), consists of the resultant mind and mental factors (*vipākacittacaitta*). Since the resultant mind and mental factors are the primary substance (*mūla*), this [aspect] pertains to the primary as well.
It does not produce the objective parts of the perfuming minds and mental factors, whether wholesome or defiled.

If the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is strong and the fundamental substance (*svabhāva*) is weak, then those ripening seeds (*vipāka-bīja*) will produce within the sixth consciousness the objective aspects of various perfuming minds—whether wholesome or defiled—which thus pertain to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
They do not, however, produce the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the ripening indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mind and mental factors.

To say that they "pertain to both phenomena and the fundamental" means that if the seeds produce the superior objective aspects upon wholesome or defiled minds, they are then termed as pertaining to phenomena.

Regarding the nature [of the seeds]: if they are the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the resultant (*vipāka*) mind and mental factors, they are designated as "pervading the basis" (*maula-vyāpin*), just as the seventh consciousness takes the seeds perfumed by the seeing-division of the eighth consciousness as its object.
These seeds, when subsumed under the seeing-division of the eighth consciousness, are termed "unobscured-neutral" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
However, if they are subsumed from the perspective of the seeing-division of the seventh consciousness, they are "obscured" (*nivṛta*). How can this be one?

The Dharma is half-defiled and half-pure, as clarified in the Abhidharma-śāstra. The Truth of the Path (mārga-satya) is also called conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because it arises from causes and conditions;
yet that same Truth of the Path is also called unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because it is not produced by karma or afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, the Truth of the Path is designated as both conditioned and unconditioned. The Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), however, is exclusively conditioned. This is also the case here.
It is so. The seeds acquired through perfuming do not necessarily produce the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, because that [seeing-part] is defiled.
Nor do they necessarily fail to produce the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness, because the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness lacks the capacity to perfume seeds.
As for the claim that consciousness serves as the support for the seeds of the evolving image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), while their functions differ and their natures are distinct—this is my own view.
"Transformation" (pariṇāma) means arising. That is, taking the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) as its support, it gives rise to the seeds of the image division (*nimittabhāga*).

Together, they produce the manifest activity of the image division, which perceives the self-witnessing division; thus, there is the function of cognitive engagement (*ālambana*). If the image division exists, there is the function of having an object of cognition (*ālambanavastu*). Therefore, their natures are distinct.
The Commentary states: "Because the characteristics arise only when consciousness undergoes transformation, it is like the primary elements (mahābhūta) producing derived matter (upādāyarūpa).

The Explanation states: "Just as when the seeds of the four great elements arise, the seeds of the derived matter then emerge; if the great elements themselves do not arise, the seeds of the derived matter cannot emerge.
Furthermore, the seed of the eye-consciousness follows along with the seed of the eye-faculty; when the eye-faculty arises, the eye-consciousness [arises].

It is just as when the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) of a blind person does not give rise to visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), it cannot produce the self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) of seeing.
If the objective part (*nimittabhāga*) arises first, the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) does not arise, and thus the objective part cannot arise. These two are real parts.

Regarding the phrase "because one relies on arising to form attachments" and so forth, up to "because it is the basis for the defiled part of the mind": [this asks] regarding the two parts, the objective (*nimitta*) and the subjective (*darśana*), and their relation to others...
Because the world takes the self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*) as its basis, it is termed the "basis of the defiled portion" (*saṃkleśa-bhāga-āśraya*).

As for the mind that takes the characteristics (*nimitta*), the views (*dṛṣṭi*), or other teachings and phenomena as its basis, it should be termed the "mind that is the basis of the pure portion" (*vyavadāna-bhāga-āśraya-citta*).

The answer is that it may indeed be termed the "basis of the pure portion," because from the Bodhisattvas below [the Buddha] up to those of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), all possess attachment to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*).

Question: Since An-hui (Sthiramati) already admits that there is attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) within the mind of the three natures, it is not yet known whether he admits that the untainted minds (*anāsravacitta*) of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages, as well as the untainted minds of those of the two vehicles, also possess attachment to phenomena.

Furthermore, since Bodhisattvas on the ten stages have already realized *tathatā* (suchness), why is it said that they still possess attachment to phenomena due to not realizing its true existence? Answer: Both cases exist.
The commentary states: "To claim that the link of ignorance (avidyā) is admitted to permeate all three natures (trividha-svabhāva) is the position of the master Ānanda-vṛttika.
This person was originally a non-Buddhist (tīrthika); later, he left the household life and entered the Buddha-dharma, whereupon he established this doctrine. Thus, it is a non-Buddhist tenet.
It is just like the masters of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, who were first within a non-Buddhist school and only later returned to the Buddhist school."

The Master of the Sautrāntika school, in composing the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, asserts that the four subtle particles (*catur-dhātu*) are the creators (*nirmāṇa*) and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the created (*nirmita*).
This is also not the correct principle. According to the correct principle of the Buddha-dharma, the four great elements are the creators and the four subtle particles are the created;
this is the correct principle. Regarding the second [point], the grasping of pervasiveness: on the aspect of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*),...

That is, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) and the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) are both pervasive. This is because one grasps the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), but does not grasp the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).
Question: Why is it not said that the grasping at phenomena is pervasive? Answer: It is because the grasping at a self does not arise based on the self-verifying aspect.

Furthermore, while the object-aspect and the seeing-aspect possess functional activity, if the self were also to possess such activity, it would depend upon the functional activity of these two aspects—the object and the seeing.
