therefore, according to the *Śāstra*, self-grasping does not arise based on the *svasaṃvitti*. Furthermore, since grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) merely conceives of the existence of an essence, it arises based on the *svasaṃvitti*.

Both ancient and modern schools, as well as both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, do not admit the existence of a *svasaṃvitti*. If this is so... [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument as presented.]

In ancient times, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools established only two parts [the apprehended and the apprehender]. It was only from the time of Dignāga onwards that three parts were established. Question:

Among the ancient Mahāyāna masters, did they not establish the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*)? Now that Dharmapāla has established the self-cognizing part, why do contemporary Mahāyānists not establish it as well?
Answer: When we refer to "contemporary" here, we exclude Dharmapāla and take other masters; this is to clarify the distinction between the subject and object of cognition.

Regarding the phrase "because it encompasses all phenomena": according to the view of the ignorant, the apprehending aspect (*grāhaka*) includes both the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) and the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*).
Since both the seeing aspect and the self-verifying aspect are termed "apprehending," this is called "encompassing all phenomena. Question:

What is the meaning of the self-verifying aspect, the seeing aspect, and so forth? If one says that "aspects" (*bhāga*) refers to divisions, then how can they be the very nature of the dharma that is being differentiated?

It may be called "segmented. For instance, regarding the seeing [consciousness], the self-cognizing [consciousness], and the self-cognizing-of-self-cognizing [consciousness]: since the self-cognizing [consciousness] is a single entity, how can it be called "segmented"?
Furthermore, if one follows Dharmapāla’s position that the seeing and the object-aspect are dharmas possessing substantial reality (*dravya*), then they may be designated as segments.

However, if one follows Sthiramati’s view that both the seeing and the object-aspect lack substantial reality, how can they be called segments? Moreover, what is the meaning of "cognizing" (*sākṣin*)? Answer: Although Sthiramati maintains that [they lack reality],...

There is no such thing as a "name" without a corresponding reality. If you establish three parts on the grounds that they are transformations of seeds, then the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*)—since it also arises from seeds—would likewise be called "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
This interpretation is incorrect; once "seeds" have been mentioned, how can it still be termed "representation-only"?
If one says that the four parts, or the three and four parts, further undergo transformation and are termed "consciousness-only," this refers to the self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) cognizing itself;

because self-cognition takes self-cognition as its object, it is called the "transformed essence of consciousness. It is for this reason that one teaching speaks of them transforming into one another.
This is an explanation of the principle. In its actual substance, it does not undergo mutual transformation. This should be analyzed through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): 1.

There are cases where there is an object-condition (*ālambana*) but no transformation, such as the objective essence (*bhāva*) of an external object or the objective essence of another's mind. These merely act from a distance and do not transform the objective essence of the other. 2.
There are cases where there is transformation but no object-condition, such as when seeds produce manifest activity (*pravṛtti*). Seeds are incapable of taking an object-condition.
Because it is the manifest consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), it is not called an "object-condition" (*ālambana*). Because the manifest arises from seeds, it is termed "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).
That which exists also undergoes transformation; this refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*). However, Master Huihu’s assertion of a fourth part is useless.

How could a single consciousness be established with a seeing-part, a self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), and a witness-to-self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-saṃvitti-bhāga*), such that there are three layers?
Just as a knife is able to cut objects, the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) is like that; the iron [of the blade] is like the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-cognizing aspect);

and the function of the knife is like the *darśanabhāga* (perceiving aspect). How could they be separate? Furthermore, since the iron filings are distinct from the iron body of the knife, how could they be one?

Nevertheless, the subsequent section establishes the existence of the "cognition of self-cognition" (*svasaṃvittisvasaṃvitti*) in order to protect against logical fallacies; thus it is established. As for the various mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), [the same applies].

The statement, "Although it is not separate from consciousness, because it is not the real nature of consciousness, it is also called 'consciousness-only' (*vijñapti-mātra*)," is redundant in this commentary.

This is because the preceding treatise text clarifies that the mind-associates (*caitta*) are what the mind relies upon; thus, the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) used here also encompasses the mind-associates as they are necessarily associated [with the mind].
Furthermore, since the preceding question itself did not inquire about the mind-associates, it would likewise be inappropriate for them to appear in this answer.

Regarding mental factors (*caitta*): furthermore, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states that they also serve as the basis for grasping (*grāhaka-āśraya*). This means that although True Suchness (*tathatā*) is remote from the objective essence (*ālambana-vastu*), it is nevertheless described as serving as the basis for grasping.
For example, when taking the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) True Suchness as an object, the transformation of consciousness gives rise to an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) which is then grasped.
This characteristic is both unitary and permanent; suchness is its essence, and therefore it is also the basis for grasping. As for their dissimilarity:
suchness is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), whereas the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Question:

How can the phenomena of the dependent nature and that which is grasped through conceptualization share even a slight degree of functional activity or formal characteristics such that they might be identical in substantial reality? [The answer is: They follow the mind that performs the grasping, arising anew at every moment.

"Arising" refers to the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*). This objective aspect arises anew with each moment, following the mind that performs the mental construction. Regarding the phrase "because those who have not yet trained rely on arising to form attachments":
if one has long practiced as a student, one does not grasp at *tathatā* (suchness) as a substantial entity;

rather, one knows that *tathatā* is the very nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, and that this nature is beyond verbal expression. If, however, one is a beginner, upon hearing the teaching of *tathatā*, they immediately grasp at *tathatā* [as a conceptual object].

This is true and real; there exists a separate substantial entity. Question: Regarding the attachment to the transformed marks (*nimitta*) as self and phenomena, it may be granted that both internal and external schools understand this to be based on the attachment to the transformed views (*dṛṣṭi*). Question:
How do the non-Buddhists know that they attach to self and phenomena based on the transformed marks? Furthermore, how do they attach [to them] based on the transformed views?

The *Fashu* (Dharmasāra? states that the non-Buddhists do not establish [the self] as the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*), but rather they conceive of the object of cognition (*ālambana*) as the self and its phenomena (*ātma-dharma*), and they grasp the subjective aspect (*grāhakabhāga*) as phenomena; this can be understood.

The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "Because the Vātsīputrīya school and others hold that the 'name' (*nāman*) is the seer, they grasp both aspects as being the self and its phenomena. The explanation says:

Those non-Buddhists and followers of the Hīnayāna do not establish the existence of the aspect (*nimitta*) of the object; they maintain only that there is a cognizing mind which takes an object as its support.
According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there are only two meanings. Regarding these "only two meanings," the *Saṃgraha* states:

"Only the measure (*pramāṇa*) and only the two [aspects]—all varieties are termed 'arising from many'. The root text of this *Saṃgraha* was composed by Asaṅga, while the commentary on the *Saṃgraha* is... [text continues].

This was composed by Vasubandhu and Asvabhāva. Regarding those who hold to the teachings of the world and assert a self and dharmas: "those who hold" refers to worldly people who maintain that there is a real self and real dharmas.

"Those for whom these have no essence and are merely conventional designations according to sentiment" refers to those within the sacred teachings for whom the self and dharmas exist as entities established through designation;
thus, it says "designated. Question: In the previous commentary, it was stated that they have no essence and are... [text continues]
"Sentient beings exist because they lack a basis; the meaning of 'existence' is established based on a substantial entity, and so forth. Both of these interpretations belong to Dharmapāla’s exegesis.
Why, then, does this commentary also state that Nanda and Bandhuśrī maintain that there is no substantial entity and that [existence] follows mere convention?

These two passages appear to be contradictory. Answer: As for those close associates of Nanda, Bandhuśrī, and Sthiramati, they likewise agree with Dharmapāla regarding the existence of a substantial entity. It is only in following mere convention...

Sentient beings exist because they lack a basis; the meaning of "existence" is established based on a substantial entity. Although the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) appears as if it were the grasper (*grāhaka*), it is nonetheless subsumed under the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
However, Master Nanda asserts that one clings to the self and phenomena only upon the object-aspect, and does not establish the self and phenomena upon the [seeing-]part itself.
Even if one were to cling to the seeing-part as the self and phenomena, this would simply be the transformation of this very clinging upon the mind that acts as the cognizer.
The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is also subsumed under the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*); therefore, one does not rely on the seeing-part to conceive of it as a self or phenomena.

Alternatively, if one speaks of [the consciousness] as being truly one part, as Ārya-Vasubandhu does, one might ask: why do other masters not say it is "real"? It is because Ārya-Vasubandhu speaks of it as real.

Answer: Briefly stated, they are not all mentioned, yet they should all be present. Alternatively, there may be a certain master who, having provisionally set forth various divergent views and investigated them extensively—even down to those held by contemporaries—presents them here for refutation. This refers to a particular master within the treatise who holds many such positions;
these are precisely the "certain meanings" clarified in the section on the seventh consciousness’s association with the five feelings (*pañca-vedanā*). (4)
The phrase "corresponding to sensation, etc. (*vedanā-saṃprayukta-ādi-artha*) refers to this. These four masters are all Dharmapāla, yet they appear to act as distinct teachers.
However, within the commentary (*śū*), it cites three masters from among those who explain the seeds (*bīja*). Among these three masters, Nanda is a separate teacher.
Dharmapāla and Candrapāla were one teacher; among the three teachers, two were the same teacher, while the one teacher was distinct.
How can this be cited as proof that many meanings are all from one teacher?

Or, if it is argued that a meaning which did not exist initially but was later stated to exist is superior because it appeared first—this refers to those masters mentioned within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
This clarifies that regarding the abandonment [of the seeds] at the stage of Arhatship, the first master holds the position that they do not exist, while the latter master asserts that they do exist;

thus, the first master represents the correct interpretation (*samyak-artha*). However, within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there is no such textual passage stating that the former holds the view that they exist and the latter holds the view that they do not exist;
such passages do, however, appear in other treatises. Alternatively, while both masters may state that they exist, the latter’s position is superior because it is supported by more authorities.

The *Shi* (The World) is the tenth treatise. It clarifies that regarding the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*), there is one interpretation that the retributive consciousness is abandoned at the moment of the adamantine mind, and another interpretation that it is abandoned during the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*). Of these, the latter master’s view is correct.
This refers to the previous general explanation followed by the subsequent logical inquiry (*yukti-pracchādana*).

This is the clarification of the passage concerning the abandonment of the eighth consciousness at the stage of Arhatship, which includes the doctrines of four masters. First, the general explanation states:

"Arhats encompass the stages of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) of all three vehicles," and so forth, up to "none of them mature the *ālayavijñāna*. Following this, the logical inquiry asks: "If..."
Why, then, does the *Nirṇayasaṃgraha* state that even non-retrogressive bodhisattvas do not bring the *ālayavijñāna* to maturation?
It explains: "That [text] refers to those of the two vehicles who, having attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), turn their minds toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).

Furthermore, there is one interpretation that from the eighth bhūmi upward, bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment also abandon the *ālayavijñāna*; there is another interpretation that it occurs at the first bhūmi.
The aforementioned Bodhisattvas also abandon the *ālayavijñāna* and receive the name of "Arhat" and so forth.

According to the interpretation of Dharmapāla, Nanda, and others, from beginningless time until the subsequent arising of the eighth consciousness, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses manifest as what appear to be a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*), because within the eight consciousnesses there is grasping (*grāha*) in all cases. [Question: Regarding this commentary, [what is the view of] masters such as Dharmapāla and Sthiramati?
Each of these has three levels of interpretation. What is the intended meaning clarified within these three levels of interpretation, and what are their differences? The answer is:

if the commentary states, "If one follows the interpretations of Dharmapāla, Nanda, and others... up until 'the subsequent consciousnesses arise and transform into what resembles a self and dharmas,'" this passage from the commentary explains the two phrases in the root treatise: "due to the power of the perfuming of the discrimination of self and dharmas."
If the *Śūchī* states, "The Dharmapāla commentary says that from the self-cognizing portion of consciousness...

up to 'acting as preceding and succeeding,'" this passage explains the two lines in the *Treatise* regarding how the various consciousnesses, when arising, manifest as what appear to be a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*).
As it is said in the world that one whose mouth does not catch fire when speaking of fire, so too in the Mahāyāna it is taught that sound may exist apart from its substance;
if one stands one or two paces from a bell, one hears the sound of the bell clearly, but once one has moved ten paces or more away, the sound gradually becomes faint.
If one moves ten *li* away, the sound becomes even fainter. It is like the light of a lamp at night:
if one is three or five feet from the lamp, one sees clearly; if one moves three or five paces away, the light gradually dims;
and if one moves a hundred paces or more away, one can no longer see objects. This is as explained in the Hīnayāna.

It is like when a bell is struck and a sound issues forth; although the sound moves away from the bell by the distance of a single atom (*paramāṇu*), it is still heard even at a great distance because the force of the sound is powerful, and thus it can be perceived.
This case is also like that: sound issues forth from the mouth, and upon that sound there exist names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*).
Since fire burns these names, phrases, and syllables, and since fire has already burned the names, phrases, and syllables...
Since names, phrases, and syllables are not separate from sound, and sound is also burned, and since sound is not separate from the mouth, the mouth too should be burned.

When one speaks the word "fire," it is clearly not intended to refer to the fire itself; for example, when one says "fire" with one's mouth, it immediately excludes the apprehension of other things such as water.

By this, it is also shown that one cannot abandon fire within the mouth by mere words. Thus, one relies on a self (*ātman*) corresponding to what is seen; this is solely through non-action (*anabhisamskāra*).
How could there be a reliance on the non-existent based upon the existent? Based upon the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), one clings to it as self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*).

That which is thus transformed appears like those false mental states and is therefore called "resembling self and phenomena. Those falsely grasped selves and phenomena do not truly exist and are ineffable.
Regarding the statement, "The cow's hair is not said to resemble the tortoise's hair; rather, it is said to resemble the mind," one asks:
Why does the preceding commentary state that "this dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is non-existent yet appears to exist;

in reality, it is not two parts, but because it resembles the two parts—the subject and object—of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), it is given the name 'resembling' (*sadṛśa*)"? Yet, in this current passage, it says, "This which is transformed appears like that delusion. How can these be reconciled?
[Objection: It cannot be like that which is conceptually constructed as external to the mind; one cannot say that cow-hair is like tortoise-hair.
[If it were so,] this would contradict the preceding and following passages. [Response: It is not contradictory either for it to be like the two parts (dvidhā) grasped by such deluded mental states.

Based on deluded mental states (*vikalpa*), there appear two aspects: the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*). These resemble that deluded mental state; because they exist as if they were real, self-realization (*svasaṃvitti*) itself is the deluded mental state.
Alternatively, the seeing-aspect is called the deluded mental state; thus, a single seeing-aspect differentiates itself into the semblance of subject and object.

Regarding Sthiramati’s explanation that "transforming into what resembles self and dharmas" has two interpretations up to eight consciousnesses arising and transforming into what resembles self and dharmas:

Question: If the Dharma-protector (Dharmapāla) establishes the existence of the two parts—the seen and the seeing—then it may be granted that there is the meaning of a provisional designation based on a real entity within the sacred teachings, where the provisional is based upon the entity.
However, since Sthiramati states that both the worldly and the sacred teachings are all mere conceptualizations (*parikalpita*), how can this be reconciled?
Furthermore, it does not establish the characteristics of the view (*dṛṣṭi-lakṣaṇa*).

Since these characteristics lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and since the commentary below states that from the passage "what is imagined by foolish people" onwards, there is only the interpretation of Dharmapāla and Nanda, and no interpretation of Sthiramati—how could Master Sthiramati possibly maintain the position that "provisional designations have an existent basis (*sadravya-prajñapti*) and that the provisional exists in dependence upon a real entity"? If one were to say that Sthiramati does not establish the existence [of such an entity]...

Regarding the provisional designations such as "having substance" (*sadravya*), since the text mentions both "the world" (*loka*) and "the holy teaching" (*āgama*), what kind of phenomena are established within that world and the holy teaching?

Furthermore, it is asked: Dharmapāla establishes the existence of the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*); since this seeing-part is precisely the cognitive consciousness (*vijñapti*), one might grant that in the world there are provisional designations based on non-substance according to mental states (*anurūpa-saṃjñā*).

However, regarding the provisional designation based on non-existence relying upon existence (*abhāva-niśrita-bhāva-prajñapti*), since Sthiramati does not establish the existence of the seeing-part, [how can this be accounted for?]
There should be no "provisional based on non-existence" (wuyi wujia) that follows worldly sentiment; there should only be "provisional based on existence" (yiyu jia).
If Sthiramati, despite regarding non-existence as non-existent, likewise establishes its provisionality as Dharmapāla does, then [we must consider this further]. Furthermore, it is asked:

regarding the world-protectors' view that the self and dharmas depend upon the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part), since the *darśana-bhāga* is a mental consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*), it may be termed a "provisional based on non-existence following worldly sentiment. If [Dharmapāla]...

According to Dharmapāla, the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) upon which the self and dharmas depend is not a sentient consciousness; and according to Nanda, the objective aspect upon which the self and dharmas depend is not a sentient consciousness.

How, then, can it be called "a designation without substance that follows convention"? If the objective aspect is not separate from the subjective vision (*darśanabhāga*), it may likewise be called "following convention.
Question: For what reason do other masters, such as Dharmapāla and Nanda, not speak of the "hearing-perfuming" (*śrutavāsanā*)?
An-hui alone specifically speaks of the "perfuming by hearing" (*śrutavāsanā*). Furthermore, how can there be perfuming by hearing within the seventh consciousness?

The answer is that, according to the combined [interpretations], it exists in all [consciousnesses]. This latter answer clarifies the former. Another explanation states that when the various consciousnesses arise, they manifest as what resembles a self and phenomena;
this means that upon the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-verifying portion), there is a semblance of a self. This is An-hui’s second interpretation. The explanation says:
This self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of Sthiramati’s system is termed "resembling self and dharmas";

that is, it is precisely the firm clinging to the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*) as being self and dharmas that constitutes the two portions of appearance and seeing, which are the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*).
This second interpretation in the commentary represents Sthiramati’s incorrect position; therefore, the preceding explanation in the commentary is superior. That is to say:
This is the correct interpretation of Sthiramati.

The Commentary states: "Below, regarding the analogy, because the dependent nature exists, that which appears as a self and dharmas transformed by consciousness seems to be the very essence of consciousness.
Sthiramati’s intention is to say that these appearances of a self and dharmas are precisely what establish the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva). This is because...

In the lower section of the treatise, it is stated that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) exists; it is clearly understood that what resembles a self and what resembles dharmas is precisely the dependent nature.

However, regarding the statement by Dharmapāla and others that "within the sixth, seventh, and even the eighth consciousnesses, there is grasping," according to my humble opinion, this commentary does not represent the third interpretation. This passage merely reiterates and examines the previous [arguments] of Dharmapāla.

"Dharma" refers to the meaning of "wisdom regarding phenomena" (*dharmapravicaya*) and so forth. According to the various previous commentaries, it refers to the *paratantra-svabhāva*—the phenomena produced by conditions—which are termed "resembling self and phenomena.

According to the interpretation of Dharmapāla, within the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, both the seeing and image portions (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*) are capable of grasping at a self and phenomena.
Due to the influence of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), when the eight consciousnesses arise, they all manifest as if they were a self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*).

According to the interpretation of Sthiramati, the seventh consciousness (*manas*) clings only to a self and does not cling to phenomena, whereas the sixth consciousness clings to both self and phenomena;

since the remaining seven consciousnesses—excluding the seventh—all cling to phenomena, the eight consciousnesses manifest as if they were self and phenomena when they arise. According to the interpretation of Master Nanda:
Among the six, seventh, and second consciousnesses, it is only upon the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) that the grasping of self and phenomena occurs.
When the latter eight consciousnesses arise, they all manifest as resembling self and phenomena; these two types are the *nimitta-bhāga* and the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect).

Regarding the initial interpretation by Sthiramati—that there is no support and no distinct support, but rather dependence on the universal—this refers to the preceding section of the text. Sthiramati has two [interpretations].

This is the first explanation within the [section on] "Understanding. Questioning Master Sthiramati: Regarding the world, the teachings of the Noble Ones, and my own Dharma—all of these possess a basis that is non-existent, yet they do not rely on anything else, but rather rely upon the universal.

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "This meaning [of the analogy] illustrates the passage of the main treatise beginning with 'the discrimination of self and dharmas' (*ātma-dharma-vikalpa*). Furthermore, the subsequent commentary states: "This analogy illustrates the passage of the main treatise beginning with 'all classes of sentient beings' (*sarva-sattva-jāti*).

Question: Why does a single analogy, such as that of one afflicted by a dream, serve to illustrate two passages from the main treatise? Answer: Within the main treatise itself, the analogies are distinct, just as in the case of being afflicted by a dream.

Specifically, the first analogy illustrates the passage concerning the discrimination of self and dharmas, while the second illustrates the passage concerning all classes of sentient beings. Thus, although the illustrative example is one, its application to the two textual passages is separate.
"The dreamer" and "suffering due to the power of the dream"— these two preceding phrases are metaphors for the power of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the discrimination of self and dharmas.
Furthermore, when the treatise states that "the mind manifests as various appearances of external objects," these two preceding phrases are metaphors for how,
at the time various consciousnesses arise, they transform and manifest as a self, and so forth, appearing as external objects due to discrimination.

However, as for the statement in the treatise, "Taking this as a basis, they grasp it as being a truly existent external object," these two preceding lines serve as a metaphor for the aforementioned classes of sentient beings who,

from beginningless time, have taken this as a basis and grasped it as a real self and real dharmas. Thus, the correspondence between the dharma (the subject) and the metaphor, as well as the aspects of the cognitive process (*ākāra*), can be understood.
*Cheng weishi lun shu chao*, Scroll One.

This commentary (*chao*) is like a luminous torch for dispelling the darkness of delusion, elucidating the *Ben shu* (the original commentary) by my elder brother. A manuscript of this work once existed at Guzhuansi Temple;

however, during the middle period, the text became scattered and lost. This has been a source of constant regret and lamentation for those devoted to the study of doctrine (*yixue*). How fortunate it is!

This year I obtained this transcription; it was truly like finding a boat or raft upon a river or sea. Relying upon it, I have guided my fellow elders and commissioned my dull-witted younger brother to transcribe it.
However, there are not a few errors regarding characters and orthography. Although I wish to correct them, what can be done if there is no original master copy?
I merely hope that future students will rectify these matters. Thus it is said.
Seen once on the twenty-sixth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Genbun era, the *ding-si* year. Recorded respectfully by Kihan.
*Commentary on the Cheng weishi lun*, Scroll Two.
The treatise says: "If that which is innate (*sahaja*) arises as a cause, it is the 'simultaneous acquisition' (*dharmasahabhū-prāpti*) of the dharma. However, the Sarvāstivādins establish..."

There are four kinds of acquisition (*prāpti*) by which things are acquired, and six kinds of phenomena (*dharma*) that are acquired. Regarding the four kinds of acquisition: first, there is acquisition prior to the arising of a phenomenon (*pūrvaprāpti*).

For example, in the case of the essence of the Dharma such as faith, when the essence of the Dharma exists in the future and has not yet arisen, there is an acquisition prior to it that extends across immeasurable hundreds of thousands of world-systems.
From the future, it flows into the past and functions to bring about birth in other stages (*bhūmi*).
When the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the faculty of existence (*bhavāṅga*) is severed, it does not arise; apart from this, it arises constantly.

As the ancients say, "One attains [the state] by being led by the ox-king," meaning that while the ox-king walks in front, the ox follows behind. If the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of a phenomenon arises, its acquisition (*prāpti*) can no longer arise.

Regarding those phenomena for which non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained within the future, their acquisition is simultaneous with the phenomenon itself—namely, the acquisition of the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
They coexist. Within a single dharma-substance (dharmatā), there is only a single "simultaneous acquisition" (prāpti-sahaja) of that dharma.

Because dharma-substances are immeasurable—numbering in the hundreds—it is said that simultaneous acquisitions are likewise immeasurable. When a dharma-substance arises, its acquisition also arises accordingly;

when the substance does not arise, the simultaneous acquisition does not arise either. The ancients called this "acquisition following the category like a shadow," meaning that it is constant, just like a shadow.
Regarding acquisition (*prāpti*) that accompanies [the dharma]: if the essence of the dharma (*dharmasvabhāva*) exists in the future, this acquisition also exists in the future;
if the essence of the dharma exists in the present, this acquisition exists in the present; if the essence of the dharma enters the past, this acquisition also enters the past.

Thirdly, there is acquisition subsequent to the dharma (*paścātprāpti*), which also exists in the past. If the essence of the dharma enters the past, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of such acquisitions subsequent to the dharma.
From the future, the fruit flows into the past. The remaining roots of merit should likewise arise in other realms.

"In accordance with the *Abhidharma*, it should likewise correspond to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* regarding the afflictions that have not yet been abandoned; being suppressed by *samatha*, they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and constitute the state of a noble one (*ārya*)."
It is acquired through birth because it has not yet been suppressed by wrong views. According to the *Abhidharma*, this should also be explained in the same way as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

It is in terms of its function that it is designated as "accomplished" or "unaccomplished. Regarding the fact that the innate wholesome (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) is the same as in the *Yogācāra* up to the point where it speaks only of its accomplishment being identical to the *Yogācāra*:
indeed, both the *Yogācāra* and the *Abhidharma* treatises alike state that the innate wholesome is the same. If...
If one is overcome by wrong views, it is not accomplished; if one has not been overcome by wrong views, it is called accomplished.

In these two treatises, the innate wholesome (*upapatti-lābha-kuśala*) is not mentioned. If one is born in this stage, it is called accomplished; if one is not born in this stage, it is not called accomplished.
Now, the intention of the commentator (*ṭīkākāra*) is that it refers only to the afflictions (*kleśa*) as explained in the *Abhidharma*. Regarding...
Regarding whether the essence and function are established or not, the innate wholesome [states] (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) should likewise be understood according to the *Abhidharma*:
if they have not yet been suppressed by the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), they are established; once suppressed, they are no longer established.

Now, as for these innate wholesome states, if one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the innate wholesome states of the desire realm are said to be "established," and one cannot give rise to those belonging to the two higher realms.
Because it is acquired through birth, the designation "innate wholesome" (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*) is established for those born in the upper realms who are born in the desire realm.
However, because one cannot give rise to the innate wholesome of the two upper realms while born there, the designation "innate wholesome" is not established for those born in the upper realms.

If one is born in the first dhyāna, the designation "innate wholesome" of the first dhyāna is established; however, the innate wholesome of the desire realm and that of the second dhyāna and above—[is not].

The designation "wholesome" is not established. This should be understood by analogy for other cases as well. Therefore, in the *Abhidharmakośa*, the attainment of the wholesome is not explained in terms of the levels (*bhūmi*);
rather, it is simply stated that as long as one has not been overcome by false views, one is said to possess [it]. This is consistent with the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

However, when one is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one is generally said to possess the afflictions (*kleśa*) of all three realms; this is because, having already given rise to the coarse afflictions of the desire realm, [the higher realms...]
Because even subtle afflictions can manifest, it cannot be said that while the body resides in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the afflictions of the two higher realms are not established.
Since there is no mundane path (*laukikamārga*) for suppressing the afflictions of the higher realms when one is in the desire realm,

if one gives rise to the afflictions of the first *dhyāna* of the higher realms while the body remains in the desire realm, this is termed the distinct establishment of desire-realm afflictions as they arise through the mundane path.

Because one lies within the intermediate path, the afflictions of the desire realm cannot arise. Therefore, afflictions do not arise simultaneously with the innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*).
When the body is in a lower realm, the innate wholesome states of a higher realm cannot arise; when the body is in a higher stage, the innate wholesome states of a lower realm cannot arise.
This is because when one is in another realm, the innate wholesome states of that other realm do not arise. Thus, [these states] exist only within their own respective realms.
This means that it is not called "attainment-born wholesome [states] of other realms. This is the general purport of the question:

if one’s body is in the first dhyāna, can one give rise to the attainment-born wholesome states of the second dhyāna? And if one’s body is in the second dhyāna, can one give rise to the attainment-born wholesome states of the first dhyāna?
When one is situated in the sphere of empty space (*ākāśāyatana*), can one give rise to the innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*)? This applies likewise to all other spheres.

If one gives rise to the innate wholesome states, this is permitted only within one’s own level; it is not allowed to give rise to the innate wholesome states of another level. The same principle applies to those that are acquired spontaneously (*anābhoga*).
The explanation is identical to what was stated previously.

Regarding the point that in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* only defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are discussed as being non-reliant [on the basis], and so forth, each according to a single specific meaning:

it is because within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, "accomplishment" and "non-accomplishment" are designated solely in terms of the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of afflictions (*kleśa*), and not in terms of the substance of the seeds (*bīja*) being accomplished or non-accomplished.
Therefore, in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it speaks only of suppressing afflictions through the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), and does not speak of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). If...
In the Abhidharma, whether a factor is "accomplished" or "unaccomplished" is determined by whether the seeds of the afflictions and their manifest activity have been extinguished.
For this reason, the Abhidharma speaks of both the mundane path and the untainted noble path; because it includes the untainted noble path, the textual corpus of the Abhidharma is extensive.
The *Nyāyānusāra* explains this based on a partial aspect. Therefore, we know that the two treatises each rely on a single meaning.

This "attainment" (*samanvāgama*) of the seeds refers exclusively to the seeds themselves and does not include their active manifestation (*samudācāra*). If one speaks of the attainment of active manifestations, it refers only to those active manifestations that are acquired at birth and are functional;
this is what is termed "attainment. Furthermore, it is not said that active manifestations are called "attainment of seeds. This is according to the *Abhidharmapitaka-śāstra*.
Within this [context], it speaks of innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) that have not yet been suppressed by wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth.
These innate wholesome states possess the functional capacity to produce manifest activity (*samudācāra*), which is termed "the accomplishment of seeds" (*bīja-samanvāgama*).

Furthermore, the accomplishment of seeds is not defined merely by the fact that innate wholesome states are currently capable of producing manifest activity; rather, when innate wholesome states are actually producing manifest activity, that itself constitutes the manifestation of those [seeds].
Regarding this inclusion, the *Śāstra* states:

"Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the failure to subdue the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth is not called 'accomplishment'; likewise, the failure to subdue greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and so forth is not called 'accomplishment.

This is because the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) can only subdue those afflictions that delude regarding phenomena (*vastu-moha*), such as greed, hatred, ignorance, pride, and so forth, which arise independently from indolence."

Because greed, hatred, delusion, and pride have been subdued, they are said to be "unestablished. Because one cannot subdue the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and the concomitant afflictions such as greed, they are called "unestablished," meaning they cannot be established.

If the greed, hatred, delusion, and pride that are independent and deluded regarding phenomena (*vastu*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) do not arise, then the remaining view of self and the conceptualized afflictions (*vikalpaka-kleśa*) will likewise not arise. That is to say, the conceptualized afflictions—...
Because afflictions (*kleśa*), the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), and so forth do not arise, they are termed "unestablished.

However, in this treatise, the terms "established" and "unestablished" are used in relation to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) with respect to the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Nevertheless, the aforementioned cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is considered defiled (*saṃkliṣṭa*) from the perspective of the bodhisattva.

This is also called "attainment" (*siddhi*), which is explained within the context of "seed-attainment" (*bīja-siddhi*). Regarding the statement that for one who has abandoned the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), attainment is never achieved [in the sense of seed-perfection], or alternatively, that it is not so and thus pertains to both attainment and non-attainment:

this text speaks provisionally in terms of the abandonment of defilements on the stages of the four fruits, such as the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and does not mention the bodhisattva because it does not concern the abandonment of defilements according to the [bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*). Or...

There are bodhisattvas of the first bhūmi who are able to sever the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) pertaining to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Alternatively, there may be bodhisattvas of the tenth bhūmi who are able to sever all cognitive obscurations pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). This passage is still incomplete;

one should explain the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in terms of their function and their essence. First, regarding their function: in the stage of accumulation (*sambhārāvasthā*), one is unable to suppress the afflictions that contradict the principle of reality (*tattva*).

Because they are currently active, their function is established. If one reaches the stage of application (*prayoga*), since the function of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) does not arise while active, the function of those afflictions of the path of seeing is not established.
If we consider them by way of their substance (*svabhāva*): prior to entering the path of seeing, the substance of the afflictions of the path of seeing is established.
Once the fruit of *srotāpanna* has been attained, [the afflictions of] the three realms of the path of seeing...

The seeds of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) on the path of cultivation are not yet established [as abandoned]. If the seeds of the afflictions on the path of cultivation and their essential nature (*svabhāva*) are established as such, then so long as one has not attained the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the seeds of the afflictions of the three realms on the path of cultivation are established as such. Once the fruit of Once-returner is attained, they are established as such;

however, up to the sixth grade of the six types of greed, anger, delusion, and pride that delude one regarding phenomena within the desire realm, they are not yet established as abandoned. This is based on the lower three [realms].

The [nine] grades [of afflictions], as well as the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, are established. If one attains the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are entirely not established. The establishment of the view of self occurs precisely at the ninth grade. If the view of self of the ninth grade is completely severed, then all nine grades of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm are no longer established. If one severs the remaining afflictions of the first eight grades but does not sever the view of self, then in the desire realm— [The text continues: ...the [afflictions] are not established. If one severs the view of self, then even if the other afflictions of the first eight grades are not yet severed, they are nonetheless not established. Why? Because the view of self acts as their root; since that root has been severed, they cannot arise again. The view of self regarding the realms (*dhātu*) is thus established. If it were not so, then [the argument] would apply both to what is established and what is not. According to the perspective of the ignorant:

if one has abandoned the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the desire realm, or if one has completely severed the view of self in the desire realm, then for those belonging to the six consciousnesses, [the view of self] is categorically not established.

If, at the time of leaving the defilements of the desire realm, one only severs the remaining afflictions and does not sever the view of self in the "self" of the desire realm, then for those [belonging to the six consciousnesses], [it is likewise not established].

Within consciousness, both the established and unestablished [positions] are addressed. Furthermore, regarding the question of the outflows of phenomena (*dharmāsrava*), it is explained exactly as above.
However, there are others who say that this commentary follows the "improper interpretation" (*apratyaya*) presented in the *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot).

They claim that the innate views of self and extremes (*satkāya-antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) within the sixth consciousness are not severed even upon the abandonment of desire; thus, the innate views of self and extremes within the sixth consciousness [are distinct from those of the other five].

The afflictions within the seven consciousnesses are severed simultaneously. According to the correct doctrine, at the time of detachment from desire, one severs the innate views of self and extremes (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) within the sixth consciousness;
that is, at the time of severing the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm, the afflictions of the six consciousnesses are consistently termed "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
If one does not refer to the time of detachment from the desire realm, [one must consider] the severance of the *satkāya* [view] within the sixth consciousness.

Regarding the phrase "the extremes and so forth": this refers to the claim that at the time of detachment from desire (*vairāgya*), the self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and other afflictions of the sixth consciousness are not abandoned.

This implies that among the afflictions within the six consciousnesses, some are "accomplished" (*siddha*) while others are "unaccomplished" (*asiddha*). It is called "unaccomplished" because other afflictions have been severed;
it is called "accomplished" because the view of a body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth of the sixth consciousness are not severed at the time of detachment from desire. This is incorrect.

If the innate wholesome dharmas (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-dharma*) possess a basis and function, and even if they are designated as "perfected" (*siddha*) in the case of future Buddhas, there are nevertheless four levels of these innate wholesome states.
First, regarding their presence in this consciousness, they are termed "perfected" when one is born in that stage, and "unperfected" when one is not born in that stage.
For example, when one's body is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the innate wholesome states of the desire realm are termed "perfected," whereas those of the two higher realms are not.
The designation "wholesome" is not established. If one’s body is in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the designation "wholesome acquired at birth" (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) is established;

one can acquire and give rise to the wholesome acquired at birth in the form realm, but cannot give rise to the wholesome acquired at birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The designation "wholesome acquired at birth" is not established for the wholesome acquired at birth in the desire realm, nor for the wholesome acquired at birth in both the desire and form realms. If one’s body is in the formless realm, [the wholesome] acquired at birth in the form realm...

The term "wholesome" (kuśala) is established [for the innate wholesome of one's own level]. However, the term "innate wholesome" (upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala) is not established for those born in the lower three realms, because when one is born in another level, the innate wholesome of that other level does not arise.
Nevertheless, since this innate wholesome belongs to a different realm, it lacks the necessary conditions and thus cannot arise.
It is not that they cannot arise because they are suppressed by wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), for there are no wrong views in the higher realms. The answer is the same as previously stated.

If we consider them in terms of seeds (*bīja*), then just as when one’s body is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) of all three realms are fully present, so too, even when one’s body is in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the seeds of the innate wholesome states of all three realms are accomplished. Second, the innate wholesome states.
That is to say, it is called "unperfected" because it is suppressed by wrong views; it is called "perfected" because it is not suppressed.
Among humans in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) may be severed by wrong views.

However, within the six heavens of the desire realm, as well as in the two higher realms, there is no severing of innate wholesome states by wrong views. Thirdly, this refers to the severing of the bonds of conditions (*pratyaya-bandhana*).

Although this is not explained in the Commentary (*Śāstra*), judging by the meaning, it refers to wholesome and neutral states (*dharma*). This is because the bonds of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratibandha*) are severed in all such cases.

It is just as when the defilements (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are completely severed, that which is called the "wholesome acquired at birth" (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*) of the desire realm arises; that is precisely the wholesome acquired at birth of the desire realm.

In that case, the designation of "wholesome acquired at birth" (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) in the desire realm would not be established. If one has not yet severed the defilements of the desire realm, one is said to possess (*samanvāgata*) that wholesome acquired at birth;
this applies likewise up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Fourth, regarding the substance of the seeds of the wholesome acquired at birth, only a Buddha is able to relinquish them;

even the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages all possess the wholesome acquired at birth. Question: When the followers of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) enter the state of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), [what happens to these seeds]?
Furthermore, there is no innate wholesome nature (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*). Why, then, does this passage speak only of the Buddha? Answer:

For the Buddha, that which arises from a remaining body (*avaśeṣa-kāya*) is called "accomplished" (*siddha*), whereas that which is innately acquired is not called "accomplished. Thus, they are designated as "accomplished" or "unaccomplished" in relation to each other.

If it were the case for those of the Two Vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*), once they have entered *nirvāṇa*, everything would be non-existent; how then could it be called "accomplished"? This is why the Two Vehicles are not mentioned.

This refers to entering nirvana by means of a vehicle. Regarding the nature of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it should be understood that they mutually constitute both accomplishment and non-accomplishment.
In this commentary, one takes the realms (*dhātu*) as the basis for the indeterminate; furthermore, there are two types of skillful deportment (*īryāpatha*) and those who are extremely inferior.
While taking a portion from the West, the indeterminate dharmas actually possess three levels of accomplishment and non-accomplishment. The first is, namely, the stage of birth (*upapatti-bhūmi*).

It is established. That which does not arise in this stage is called "not established," such as the indeterminate states born of maturation (*vipākaja*), including those associated with grasping (*upādāna*) or the fruits of karma.

If a phenomenon arises in this stage, it is called "established"; if it does not arise in this stage, it is not called "established," because one cannot separately give rise to the indeterminate states of maturation belonging to another realm while situated in this realm.
The same applies to the indeterminate states of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).

Second, these three are also explained in terms of the severance of the bonds of their objects, as being either accomplished or unaccomplished. If one has completely abandoned the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), then its [associated] indeterminate states (*avyākṛta*) are termed "unaccomplished.

If one has not yet abandoned the desire realm, they are also termed "unaccomplished. If one has not yet completely abandoned the defilements of the desire realm, those three indeterminate states are termed "accomplished.
This continues up until the complete abandonment of the defilements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), at which point its [associated] indeterminate states...

Regarding the names "realm" (*dhātu*), "conduct" (*airyāpathika*), "maturation-unspecified" (*vipākāvyākṛta*), and "supernormal power" (*nairmāṇika*), they are not established; if it were otherwise, they would be established.

Furthermore, if one has abandoned the defilements of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) entirely, the name "maturation-unspecified" is not established; if it were otherwise, the name would be established.
Thirdly, regarding whether the names are established or not based on the substance of the unspecified seeds: if it concerns Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), all [are established].
It is established by means of neutral (*avyākṛta*) seeds. If the Buddha were entirely devoid of neutral seeds, his designation [as such] would not be established.

Among the views, there is no false view to be suppressed; this is the first point. However, regarding the deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) categories, if they were to include an unwholesome nature, they would be treated identically to what was explained regarding the wholesome states of application (*prāyogika*) and acquisition (*upapattilābhika*). Since only the neutral is taken here, their absence is clarified in this context. If...

Regarding "wholesome dharmas produced through application": these are included within all wholesome states conducive to merit that consist of the application of wisdom born of hearing and reflection, as well as those comprised within the application of the provisions.
This is because such qualities all have the exertion of effort (*prayoga*) as their cause.
The merits within the Buddha’s body are all subsumed under the category of cultivated virtue (*prayoga-kuśala*).

If the merits within the Buddha’s body were not subsumed under cultivated virtue, then the three types of methods for maturation would be incomplete. Regarding the perfection of mastery (*vaśitā-saṃpad*):

This refers exclusively to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and does not include the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because the unconditioned does not arise from seeds, whereas the conditioned arises from seeds.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "The former two are merely seeds; mastery is attained only through the power of application (*prayoga*).

This means that during the stage of application, mastery is first designated when one engages in the mental orientations of application (*prayogamanasikāra*) consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. This explanation is based on the successive understanding of the phenomena.
This refers to persons; thus, it concerns those of the two vehicles.
It means that those who have practiced and become habituated in the arts and crafts, up to the mental states of deportment (*airyāpathika*), [attain this].

However, within this mastery, they for the most part grasp the mind and not the form (*rūpa*), because the mind possesses mastery. Thus, it is said that they take the mind of deportment as their condition.
The mind of deportment takes the mind of craftsmanship as its object and gives rise to the mind of craftsmanship.

Although there are instances mentioned in the texts where craftsmanship is not included, this is because Viśvakarman, the Devaputra, is the most skillful within the desire realm; thus, he is excluded from the category of deportment.

Those who possess deportment, such as the Bhikṣu Aśvajit and others, are all those who have attained extreme proficiency through long-term cultivation. However, regarding the deportment of daily conduct...
One takes these four objects (*viṣaya*) as the basis for the pathways. If one engages in craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), one further takes the five objects as the basis;

however, this separately gives rise to a specific category of *niṣyanda-rūpa* (evolved matter), which is termed the "pathway of deportment" (*airyāpathika*) and the "sphere of craftsmanship" (*śailpasthānika*).

Furthermore, one does not employ the external supporting dust (*upādāya-rūpa*) of another's body as the sphere of craftsmanship or the pathway of deportment. This is because the cited commentary states that there exists such supporting dust upon one's own body.

It is not correct to say that these are the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*). Question: Why do the spheres of craftsmanship exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?

If you say it is because in the desire realm one provides for others through craftsmanship, or by producing other goods to sustain one's life—as with the celestial artisan Viśvakarman, who produces various objects to sustain his life—then the answer is: it is simply because such phenomena exist within the specific realms and stages (*dhātubhūmi*).
Therefore, as explained in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this is subsumed below. Question:

Why does the Mahāyāna teach that the nature of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) lacks the craftsmanship of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) for sentient beings of the desire realm? Answer: It is because there is no lack of the arising of the mind of craftsmanship within the form realm.
If one follows the Mahāyāna teaching, all craftsmanship arising in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is for the sake of livelihood and the seeking of other things.

Since there is no livelihood in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), those who engage in craftsmanship there—such as Viśvakarman of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—are they creating such skillful works because they seek other wealth while living in the void? Answer: This is discussed here in its entirety...

Regarding the ritual procedure for the realms (*dhātu*): it refers only to those among human beings in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who, for the sake of sustaining their lives, engage in crafts and skills;
these are called "crafts and skills for livelihood" within the existence of desire (*kāma-bhava*). This is not a separate classification based on the five destinies (*gati*).

Thus, since the six heavens of the desire realm also belong to the desire realm, they likewise engage in crafts and skills for the sake of livelihood, just as when a single sentient being first enters [the womb].
Regarding the Avīci Hell: this refers to the very beginning of the respective injunctions. Question: Regarding the bodhisattvas who have entered the first bhūmi or above, they erect stūpas;

yet, for the Buddha, there is no effort or craft (*śilpa*). Answer: "Realm" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of being bound. This refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and others who lack such craft, not to Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
Although they rely upon the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), Buddhas do possess craft; those who transform the minds of others [do so through such skill].

Just as when bodhisattvas manifest playful supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) or produce emanations (*nirmāṇa*) and so forth not for the sake of benefiting sentient beings—as was the case with the arhats prior to the stage of the bodhisattva—[these are neutral].

However, if a bodhisattva on the seventh ground (*bhūmi*) produces supernatural powers and emanations with the intention of benefiting sentient beings, that mind is also of a virtuous nature (*kuśala*).
One should consider: under which category of virtue is this subsumed? It is [subsumed under] the virtue of "not acting for the benefit of others."
The supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). This excludes only those dharmas that are indeterminate by birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-avyākṛta*).

Regarding the term "by birth": it does not refer to being called "born" because it is a wholesome dharma acquired at birth; rather, within the category of the indeterminate, there are also two types of seeds.

The first is the indeterminate by birth, which refers to the indeterminate produced as maturation (*vipāka-ja-avyākṛta*). Whether it be the grasping of phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) or the mind’s attachment to results, these are all termed [indeterminate by birth].
The innate-unspecified (*upapatti-lābhika-avyākṛta*) is so called because it is acquired immediately upon birth.

Second is the preparatory-unspecified (*prayoga-avyākṛta*), which refers to the deportment (*airyāpathika*), the craft (*śailpasthānika*), and the supernormal fruit (*nairmāṇika*). These three types of unspecified states all arise only through the application of effort (*prayoga*).

Regarding the statement that "if one understands the function of the wholesome [states] of the preparatory stage, up to those that are with-outflows (*sāsrava*), they are abandoned": this question is based on the *Śāstra*.
The statement that "wrong view abandons innate wholesome states" does not say that wrong view abandons acquired wholesome states.

Why, then, is it said here that wrong view also abandons acquired wholesome states? Answer: When wrong view abandons innate wholesome states, it simultaneously constitutes the abandonment of the acquired wholesome states within the preparatory mental states (*prayoga-citta*) of the aforementioned wrong views; therefore, it is said that it abandons acquired wholesome states. There is no contradiction.
Commentary:
There are also cases where [the action] is accomplished by its application, yet not accomplished [in its essence], and even cases where it is not accomplished in its essence.

This passage from the sub-commentary clarifies that for those who have habituated themselves to the three types of neutral states—artistic (*śailpasthānika*), deportment (*airyāpathika*), and supernormal (*nairmāṇika*)—the method of performance follows the previous rule. Question: For what reason is "arising" (*jāti*) explained?

Regarding the passage on "attaining a favorable state": it states that one is born in this stage with the intention to achieve [realization]; a stage where such birth does not occur is termed "non-achievement.

If one speaks of "preparatory wholesome states" (*prayoga-kuśala*), and [the practitioner] is not physically in a higher stage—excluding those arising from a different stage—it is unclear whether one who is physically in a lower stage can attain all preparatory wholesome states of a higher stage;
or whether one who is not physically in a higher stage can attain all [preparatory wholesome states] of a lower stage.

Regarding the performance of wholesome deeds (*kuśala*), the same applies to those that are untainted (*anāsrava*). Answer: If it concerns wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha*) or neutral states born of maturation (*vipākaja*), one cannot give rise to wholesome states acquired at birth or neutral states born of maturation belonging to a different level (*bhūmi*).

Therefore, the commentary states: "That which belongs to the level where one is currently born is termed 'established' (*siddha*); that which belongs to a level where one is not born is termed 'unestablished' (*asiddha*).

However, this is not fixed for wholesome states produced through application (*prayoga-labdha*); for example, when one's body resides in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), [wholesome states of other levels may arise].
Regarding the deities of the realms (*dhātu*): one can give rise to the preparatory wholesome states of contaminated meditative wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) belonging to the two higher realms.

However, if one's body is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one cannot give rise to the preparatory wholesome states of hearing-wisdom (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) belonging to the higher realms; this is because those in their own level within the desire realm possess hearing-wisdom.

However, there is no Mahāyāna textual passage stating that the preparatory wholesome states (*prayoga-kuśala*) of the form realm, such as the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*), can arise [in a being of the desire realm];

this is because the wisdom derived from hearing already exists within its own level (the desire realm) itself. Nevertheless, there is likewise no Mahāyāna textual passage stating that the wisdom derived from hearing of the form realm can arise within the desire realm.

If one follows correct reasoning, it is also possible for one whose body is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to give rise to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

According to the Mahāyāna teaching, if one’s body is in the first dhyāna, one can immediately give rise to the preparatory wholesome states (*prayoga-kuśala*) of the second dhyāna and above, up to the level of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Just as one whose body is in the first dhyāna cannot give rise to the preparatory wholesome states of the desire realm, so too, even if one’s body is in the fourth dhyāna, [one cannot give rise to those of lower levels].

One can give rise to the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of the lower three dhyānas that are with-outflow (*sāsrava*), and even those of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) may likewise be either with-outflow or without-outflow (*anāsrava*).
One should ask the Dharma Master about this.
As for the seeds of the outflow-free state, it is the same up until the point where they are said not to be established; however, regarding the function of these outflow-free seeds, it is as follows:

One attains the first fruit (*phala*). The first fruit is termed "accomplished" (*siddha*). Abandoning what precedes and proceeding toward what follows is termed "not accomplished" (*asiddha*). This is like attaining the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*):

the fruit of no-more-learning is termed "accomplished," while one immediately abandons the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states of the three preceding fruits; those three preceding outflow-free states are termed "not accomplished."

Furthermore, it should be understood by analogy that when one attains the second vision, one immediately relinquishes the first stage (*bhūmi*) and so forth; in all such cases, one achieves a superior designation while relinquishing an inferior one.
Similarly, when the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*) arises, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is not yet established, and so on.

This statement regarding "abiding in happiness in the present life" refers specifically to contaminated concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*). Because one must rely on contaminated concentration as a cause in order to subsequently attain uncontaminated concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), there is thus regression.

Dwelling in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vihāra*) is termed the "receding from the outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). There are certain outflow-free concentrations that cannot induce the outflow-free state;

however, dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) also extends to the outflow-free. This "happiness in the present life" is precisely the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and is thus called "happiness in the present life.
One attains and dwells in this meditative concentration within the current body. Question: Does this involve abandoning both essence and function? Answer: One attains a superior abandonment.

At a time of inferiority, the substance of the inferior untainted seeds is also abandoned; thus, with respect to the substance of the noble state (*ārya-bhāva*), it is called "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*).

If one falls back from the "abiding in happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha-vihāra*), it is called "non-attainment" with respect to the function of abandonment, not with respect to the substance of abandonment.

This is like the case of an ordinary person’s abiding in happiness in the present life, which consists only of the active functioning of tainted concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*); because it cannot be termed "arising," it is called "non-attainment. As for that tainted concentration...
"Understanding" means not abandoning [it]. If it is dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), it is a contaminated concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*).
If it is an uncontaminated concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), one merely attains the Noble Path; it cannot be called "dwelling in happiness in the present life. Question:

In this context, one should also say that attaining the universally pervasive suchness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*) of the first stage is called "accomplishment," while not yet attaining the suchness of the second stage is called "non-accomplishment," and so on... up until... [already attained].
The same applies hereafter. Within this context, one also attains the eighty-one categories of the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) across the nine stages;

by contrast, the first [attainment] is also established under the designation of "unconditioned. This continues as before, and likewise for the subsequent stages, even up to the comparison with the principles of the Four Noble Truths.

Next, regarding the answer not being provided: it is understood that the name is established based on what has already arisen and is currently manifesting; however, there is no arising of the unconditioned (*anāsrava*) in its current manifestation.

The stage is not called "accomplished. Question: In this context, one should also say that it is "accomplished" when, from time immemorial while remaining a worldling, the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) activity has arisen and is manifest.
For example, obtaining the first fruit is called "accomplishment," and the manifestation of the uncontaminated activity of the first fruit is called "accomplishment.
However, as long as the uncontaminated activity of the second fruit has not yet been attained, it is called "unaccomplished," and so on.
The same applies thereafter. Furthermore, for a person of indeterminate nature who has attained the manifestation of the untainted [wisdom] of the two vehicles, this is termed "accomplishment";
yet, as long as they have not yet resolved their mind [for enlightenment] and have not attained the manifestation of the Bodhisattva's untainted [wisdom], it is termed "non-accomplishment.

This continues up to the point where, having attained the manifestation of the first bhūmi, it is termed "non-accomplishment," and having attained the manifestation of the untainted [wisdom] of the second bhūmi, it is termed "non-accomplishment," continuing in this manner up to the tenth bhūmi.

The manifestation of untainted (*anāsrava*) states is termed "accomplishment. The non-attainment of the manifestation of untainted states at the stage of Buddhahood is termed "non-accomplishment. Furthermore, this is relative to the nine stages:

for example, the attainment of the manifestation of untainted states in the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*) is termed "accomplishment," while the non-attainment of the manifestation of untainted states in the fundamental first dhyāna is termed "non-accomplishment.

The attainment of the untainted state in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is termed "accomplishment," whereas the non-attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is termed "non-accomplishment."
Furthermore, it is like the eleven views of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). For example, when the initial *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti* arises, the name [of that stage] is established;

as long as one has not yet attained *duḥkhe dharmajñāna*, the name is not established. This continues until the fifteenth moment of mind is attained, at which point the name is established; as long as the sixteenth moment of mind has not been attained, the name is not established.
In this way, the designation "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is applied only when it corresponds to its specific attainment and is not yet fully acquired.
Regarding those who possess a determined nature belonging to one of the three vehicles but are termed "unestablished":
if a person possesses only the śrāvaka [nature], the name "śrāvaka" is established, while the names "bodhisattva" and "pratyekabuddha"—which do not abide in that basis—are unestablished.

Alternatively, if a person possesses only the bodhisattva nature, the name "bodhisattva" is established, while the names for the two other vehicles—which do not abide in that basis—are unestablished. Those who abide in and have attained [the nature] are all bodhisattvas.

[Question: Seeds are not called "accomplished" (*siddha*). Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) can be accomplished through active manifestation (*samudācāra*), but within the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), such as the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) and the element of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*), there are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and so forth;

likewise, among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), how can the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) be said to be accomplished through active manifestation?

[Answer: This is stated from the perspective of the majority. [Question: As for those unconditioned phenomena and those existing within the five sense-objects (*viṣaya*) and the five sense-faculties (*indriya*), they also exist within the three types of accomplishment (*pariniṣpatti*).

[This is] included within the middle [category]. Since it was not answered that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and so forth are not subsumed under the threefold accomplishment (*trisaṃpada*), why did the Abhidharma previously state:
"All mundane and supramundane merits—among all merits—are conditioned"? And [why did it say]: "Among all merits, there are none that are unconditioned"?

Furthermore, the subsequent text states: "There is the acquisition (*prāpti*) of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and within the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), there are external objects such as mountains and so forth, as well as internal faculties and their objects;
these are included among the three types of accomplishment (*siddhi*). How then can the subsequent text say:

'The seeds are divided into two [types], while only one is established for the manifest'? Answer: Only those that are "one's own" include the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); others do not include the unconditioned. Is this not so?
Because they arise from seeds. The *Abhidharma* states: "All virtuous qualities" refers to other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). This is my own humble interpretation. Question:
Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) in relation to one another, among the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), that which is spontaneous (*anābhoga*) is subsumed within the category of seeds (*bīja*).

That which is habitual (*abhyāsa*) is subsumed within the category of mastery (*vaśitā*). That which arises from darkness (*tamas*) and is acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika*) is subsumed within the category of seeds. As for that which is produced through application (*prayoga*)...

"Wholesome [states] are subsumed under mastery (*vaśitā*). Why, then, among the afflictions (*kleśa*), are there both those that arise spontaneously (*svarasavāhin*) and those that are forcibly produced?
Why are these two not explained as being subsumed under those two categories? Answer: As will be explained below, they are common to both. There are three types of seeds:

innate seeds (*upapattilābhika-bīja*), seeds of applied wholesome states (*prāyogika-kuśala-bīja*), and fourthly, seeds of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta-bīja*). Among these, those that are spontaneous...
As for those that have been habituated, as well as the seeds of the afflictions of seeing and cultivation—these seeds are all subsumed within the accomplishment of seeds.
Second is the maturation of uncontrolled manifestation, which refers to the manifestation of the afflictions of seeing and cultivation.

The manifestation of innate wholesome states, as well as the spontaneous manifestation of a portion of deportment and craftsmanship—these are all subsumed within the accomplishment of non-autonomous manifestation.

Third is autonomous manifestation, which refers to the manifestation of applied wholesome states, as well as transformations, craftsmanship, deportment, and so forth; the manifestation of these dharmas is entirely within autonomy.
It is subsumed within actual manifestation (*samudācāra*). For example, just as there is the accomplishment of mastery alone, there is also the accomplishment of actual manifestation;
