from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, although afflictions do not manifest, one also partially attains such accomplishment. First, regarding the identification of the basis: now, to speak generally of the "other-dependent" (*paratantra*) non-sentient [basis].
As for the "basis," it refers to the attainment and so forth; it is explained that attainment occurs in relation to the bodies and other things of others. Question:

Since it is said that it accomplishes another’s body, does it accomplish another’s *upādāya-rūpa* (derived matter), or does it merely accomplish another’s five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*), or does it simply accomplish the objects (*viṣaya*) that can be experienced?

One belongs to what is acquired, namely, acquisition of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-prāpti*). The commentary explains: the dharma that is acquired is wholesome, and its acquisition is likewise wholesome; it is the acquisition of wholesome conduct.

Dharmas that are wholesome cannot be acquired [by a neutral attainment], nor can those that are unwholesome; these are acquired by the indeterminate (avyākṛta) attainment, because they are themselves indeterminate.
As for dharmas that are not acquired, these refer to conditioned dharmas (saṃskṛtadharma). Within conditioned dharmas, there are both out-flowing (sāsrava) and non-out-flowing (anāsrava).
If the dharma acquired is non-out-flowing, the attainment that acquires it is also non-out-flowing. If the dharma acquired is noble, out-flow-free, and wholesome...

The three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are equal [in this regard]. The acquisition (*prāpti*) that attains them is likewise of the three natures, such as contaminated wholesome (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and so forth.
Therefore, the acquisition that attains them is the substance of what is subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*). This is the interpretation of Master Chao Fa.

Second, regarding the path that attains [them], namely the acquisition of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): there is both contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). The commentary states: "If one employs the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) to sever..."
The acquisition (*prāpti*) of the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) obtained through the afflictions arises in opposition to the noble path that attains it;

this acquisition of analytical cessation is itself untainted (*anāsrava*). If ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and others suppress the afflictions by means of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), the acquisition of the analytical cessation obtained thereby arises in opposition to the nature of the path that attains it; thus, that acquisition of analytical cessation is tainted (*sāsrava*).
It is of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-dharma*).

This is also an explanation based on the *Abhidharmakośa*. The commentary states: "The three belong to what is acquired; that is, the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

However, within the future period, the acquisition of non-analytical cessation—which is manifested by a single simultaneous object-condition—is not at all part of the portion acquired by the present multitude. Now, regarding the Mahāyāna, even up to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā*)...
That the attainment of their cessation is also definitively associated with the Path is identical to the position of the Hīnayāna.

Second, regarding "belonging to the basis," the "basis" refers to the eighth consciousness, up to and including the Buddha-body. As for the statement that "false views and so forth do not arise within the Buddha-body":

since [the Buddha] perceives all things instantaneously and simultaneously, even if false views were present, they would not arise. Furthermore, to explain what it means for them "not to arise": it refers to the principle of false views themselves.

Regarding the term "and so forth" (*ādi*): after one has attained the vision of the path (*darśanamārga*), all such human bodies as those belonging to the three evil destinies, eunuchs, and so on, as well as the persons of no lineage (*agotrastha*), are ultimately not produced because they are objects of true discernment (*tattva-pravicaya*).
Their non-arising is comprised within both the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and that which is not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Since these [non-arising states] already possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their ultimate obstruction by conditions and subsequent non-arising is now attained.

Because it is a non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it belongs to the eighth consciousness. However, for those who lack the spiritual nature (*agotra*), they ultimately cannot enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*);
this is precisely the non-analytical cessation of a phenomenon that does not arise due to the absence of conditions. Why is this?

If there were a prior substantial entity, then at the present time, when conditions are lacking, one could obtain non-analytical cessation. Since there was no prior entity, even though conditions are lacking, one still cannot obtain non-analytical cessation. Therefore...

It does not belong to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Alternatively, regarding the second interpretation—that it belongs to the seeds which serve as its support because they reside within consciousness—when each [object] is perceived, it also takes non-existent phenomena (*abhāvadharma*) as its object; thus, these belong to consciousness itself as their seeds.
This is because the fundamental seeds of the root consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) are not separate from consciousness.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Thus, they pervade both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and their distinctions among the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*) are as explained in the *Abhidharma* (Dharmapada).

Specifically, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of uncontaminated dharmas is itself uncontaminated. Furthermore, the acquisition of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and the acquisition of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) within the Buddha’s body are both uncontaminated and of a virtuous nature (*kuśala*).

However, the acquisition of cessation not through deliberation via mundane paths (*laukika-mārga*), as well as the non-arising due to the deficiency of seeds (*bīja-vaikalyād anutpāda*), [are otherwise]."

Only contaminated (*sāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena possess acquisition (*prāpti*), which belongs to the phenomena it acquires; thus, it pervades all three natures (*tridharmasvabhāva*). This is the same as the Hīnayāna.

Furthermore, regarding the phenomena acquired, they also pervade everything; even though there are certain doctrinal points where this differs from the Hīnayāna, this [text] clarifies non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).

In the Mahāyāna, however, it is taught that non-acquisition pervades both the contaminated and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and likewise pervades both the conditioned and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Regarding sentient beings, there is non-possession (*aprāpti*); likewise, regarding external insentient things, there is also non-possession.

For example, one who has not obtained the seven treasures while born [as a wheel-turning king] possesses non-possession with respect to the sentient bodies of others. As for non-possession that is contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is exclusively of the nature of the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Furthermore, it is not said that non-possession arises from the statement that the three natures are non-accomplished (*asamanvāgama*) with regard to lower dharmas.

It is said that "non-acquisition" (aprāpti) pervades all three natures (*trisvabhāva*). For instance, when conditions are lacking at the time of craving and [the dharma] does not arise, that non-acquisition belongs to the seeds (*bīja*).
Later, when the seeds acquire arising and the acquisition of formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, one then regains [that dharma].
Now, regarding the question of relinquishing non-acquisition, this is precisely what occurs within the locus of non-acquisition. If the seeds lack conditions, there is ultimately no acquisition.

[This] arises. This non-acquisition (aprāpti) belongs to the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna). Just as once one has entered the [correct] view, one can no longer undergo [the state of being a worldly person], so too, although the bodies of the three evil destinies exist, there is a non-acquisition of that [state];

this non-acquisition belongs to the fundamental consciousness. If, for example, unwholesome dharmas and the like could never arise within the body of a Buddha, there would likewise be a non-acquisition;
this non-acquisition also belongs to the fundamental consciousness. Now, this non-acquisition is merely a semblance...

Regarding the acquisition of analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): according to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings, non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) belongs exclusively to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).

This non-acquisition is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), being of the nature of the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*); it does not extend to the wholesome (*kuśala*) or the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, non-acquisition is established only with respect to sentient beings; it exists only within the category of sentient beings, and for insentient things, there is no non-acquisition.

Furthermore, there is acquisition through the attainment of a dharma and through the transition of stages (*bhūmi-saṃcāra*). For example, at the moment one severs the roots of goodness, one simultaneously acquires [the state of being without roots of goodness];

later, when the roots of goodness are restored, one simultaneously matures that acquisition and abandons the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), such that what was previously acquired becomes entirely non-acquired. Moreover, it is as when one’s body resides in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
When one attains [a state] or non-attainment (*aprāpti*), at the time of being born into a higher realm, one immediately abandons all non-attainments pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

This applies equally when descending from a higher realm to a lower one. Non-attainment belongs exclusively to that which it pertains to, and it encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Question: What is this second interpretation? Furthermore, it is asked: when those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) extinguish their bodies and terminate their wisdom (*jñāna*), all seeds (*bīja*) and their supports (*āśraya*) are likewise extinguished;
to what, then, does their non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) belong? Answer: Regarding the first question, the first interpretation states:

"However, at the very moment the seeds arise, they fail to manifest due to the absence of conditions; this is termed 'attainment of cessation not through deliberation' (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-prāpti*). It is just as when afflictions (*kleśa*) are suppressed, they fail to manifest at that very moment."

When conditions are lacking and [a dharma] cannot arise, this is termed the "attainment of non-analytical cessation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-prāpti*). This attainment of non-analytical cessation belongs to the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa-bīja*).
If it concerns the uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) such that they cannot arise due to the lack of conditions, this attainment of non-analytical cessation belongs to the uncontaminated seeds.

Therefore, it is said to apply to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). According to the second interpretation, at the very moment the contaminated and uncontaminated seeds [are present], the conditions are lacking.

It cannot. That which arises is termed "non-analytical cessation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The attainment (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation is precisely the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

If it pertains to the ten stages (*bhūmi*), it belongs to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) eighth consciousness; if it pertains to the stage of Buddhahood, it is called the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) eighth consciousness.

This aforementioned [attainment] is itself the unsurpassed attainment. Regarding the answer to the subsequent question: since there is no substantial entity (*svabhāva*), one cannot distinguish between attainment and non-attainment (*aprāpti*).

Regarding the statement that the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* compound: Question: Why is it said that they are "conjoined" (*samāsa*), and how is the name of the dharma "conjoined"?
Answer: Both the ordinary person and the nature of an ordinary person are termed "conjoined" because both are explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Although these types are numerous: when a single instance of a mind with affliction (*sāsrava-citta*) arises, no other afflictions can arise;

thus, for each individual phenomenon (*dharma*), there is a non-possession (*aprāpti*). When an unwholesome mind arises, all other hundreds of thousands of wholesome and neutral states cannot be designated [as present];
each of these possesses its own non-possession. Therefore, it is said that "these types are numerous. And within the three realms...

Regarding the statement that "the seeds to be abandoned by seeing constitute the distinct nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*)," the afflictions of the two obstacles in the desire realm that are to be abandoned by seeing are termed "desire-realm ordinary beings.

They are not termed "form-realm or formless-realm ordinary beings. It is impossible for the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing across the three realms to be collectively called a single "ordinary being," because since the three realms are three, there are three types of ordinary beings.
As for the phrase "only the state where [the seeds] have not yet been destroyed is called the distinct nature," "state" (*avasthā*) refers to...
Regarding the stages: it is based upon the seeds of the two obstacles to be abandoned by insight that the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) is designated.

Alternatively, regarding the five or four aggregates: in the desire and form realms, sentient beings are constituted by the five aggregates; in the formless realm, sentient beings are constituted by the four aggregates.
It is said that this is provisionally designated upon both unwholesome and neutral dharmas. The explanation states:

while the basis (*āśraya*) of the hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) pertains to both natures (unwholesome and neutral), the dependent (*āśrita*) is the obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). Now, an objection is raised:

"Why do the two bases—the wholesome meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and the wholesome nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)—also rely on the two hindrances, given that these hindrances pertain to both natures, whereas the nature of an ordinary person is exclusively neutral? The answer follows.

Regarding the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*): if it were categorized as unwholesome (*akuśala*), this would be acceptable for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). However, in the two higher realms, false views are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

This nature of being an ordinary person, which is based upon them, is empty within the three realms; thus, there is indeed a real distinction, as the two natures—unwholesome and indeterminate—are distinct.

Therefore, it is only indeterminate that it may pervade all three realms without contradiction. Furthermore, among the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), there is the obstruction to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The "obstructions" (*āvaraṇa*) are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). That which is metaphorically established upon these two obstructions is likewise indeterminate.
Regarding the terms "birth" (*janman*) and "nature" (*prakṛti*): "birth" is the general designation for sentient beings of the five destinies (*pañcagati*), as all five destinies are termed "birth.
"Nature," on the other hand, is the specific designation for the seeds of the two obstructions within the continuum of one's own non-erroneous [mind] during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The Commentary states: "Regarding these four types of lineage (*gotra*). Question: Why does it not mention two or five lineages? Furthermore, regarding the capacity to obstruct, why is there no separate mention of those who lack the lineage (*agotra*)?

Answer: When the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) is established in relation to the obstructions, this refers to cases where both types of persons possessing the vehicle-nature (*yānagotra*) have within their continuum the two obstructions that can obstruct the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatājñāna*). If such [obstructions] exist...

Regarding the "lineage of the two vehicles" (*dvayayāna-gotra*): for such persons, the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are able to obstruct the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*).

Because they possess this lineage, based on these obstructing factors, one establishes the distinct categories of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-gotra*) according to their degree of superiority. As for those who lack the [Mahāyāna] nature (*agotra*), since they possess no [such] obstructions, [the distinctions do not apply].

Within the stage of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are not designated as "obstructors. Because they are not designated as obstructors, they do not constitute the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

Now, it is simply upon the seeds of these two obstacles that the nature of an ordinary person is established; thus, there is no contradiction in this designation. This is not explained in terms of being an actual obstructor.
Regarding its inclusion within the category of "a portion of the Noble Ones' provisions": for those of the Two Vehicles who have abandoned afflictions (*kleśa*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*), it is so named.

The Noble Ones (ārya) are not excluded from being called "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*) because they have not yet severed the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Regarding the statement that "similar speech and similar cognition should not arise":

it is like the case of living beings born among cattle or sheep; because the generic similarity (*nikāyasabhāga*) acts as the cause, those cattle and sheep all possess similar intelligence and similar speech.
Other cases should be understood accordingly. Furthermore, some say that "similar speech" refers to its production within the mouth.
Regarding the linguistic rule: "This horse is like that cow," it is because [the referent] is that cow and so forth.
The commentary (*śāstra*) states: "The *pramāṇa* says: 'In your school, the two fruits of wood should have distinct common factors (*sabhāgatā*), etc.
All the following commentary texts are refutations of the ancient Sarvāstivādins, because the Sarvāstivādins do not establish the existence of a "dharma" as a common factor; thus, it is so named.
This is difficult [to understand]. Regarding the *Abhidharma* established by the masters of the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma*, the *Abhidharmakośa*, and up to the *Nyāyānusāra*:

"Abhidharma" here refers to the *Ṣaṭpāda-śāstra*. Within the Hīnayāna, they take the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* as the foundational body (*kāya*), and upon that *Jñānaprasthāna*, they establish and compose [the other treatises].
The "six feet" (*ṣat-pāda*) are literally feet; thus, the *Ṣaṭpāda-śāstra* consists of six parts. The first is the *Vijñānakāya*.
The *Śarīra-prakaraṇa* (Body-Exposition) elucidates the various consciousnesses. Now, it is explained that "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is the "body" (*śarīra*) for that *Jñānaprasthāna* school;

therefore, it is called the *Vijñānakāya-prakaraṇa* (Consciousness-Body-Exposition). Second is the *Dhātukāya-prakaraṇa* (Element-Body-Exposition). "Elements" (*dhātu*) refers to the eighteen elements.

Taking those eighteen elements as primary, it further elucidates the aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*). "Body" (*kāya*) refers to the *Jñānaprasthāna*. This [text] elucidates that these eighteen elements are...
It is the feet of that *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*. Third is the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, which explains various categories (*prakaraṇa*) of phenomena in a miscellaneous manner;
if translated according to the old version, it is called the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, but in this new translation it is rendered as the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
Fourth is the *Saṃgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra*; within this treatise, various distinct matters are collected and arranged into a systematic method.
The *Mātṛkā* elucidates all dharmas. Regarding the five *Piṭakas*: the aforementioned five *Pādas* (Treatises on the Bases) were all translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang Dynasty;

there are extant versions of these in this country. As for the sixth, the *Prajñapti-pāda-śāstra*, there are extant versions of the *Prajñapti-pāda-śāstra* in the Western Regions, but there is no version in this country.
Within the Mahāyāna tradition, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* serves as the body and the basis, acting as its constituent branches—namely, the first [the *Maulī Bhūmi*].
1. *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Exposition of the Noble Teachings); 2. *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra* (Ornament of the Mahāyāna Sūtras); 3. *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra* (Compendium of the Mahāyāna); 4.

*Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only); 5. *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Twenty Verses on Consciousness-Only); 6. *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī-yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Compendium of Ascertainment on the Stages of Yoga Practice); 7. *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra* (Discrimination of the Middle and the Extremes); 8. *Vyākhyāyukti-śāstra* (Treatise on the Logic of Exegesis); 9.

*Ālambanaparīkṣā-śāstra* (Investigation of the Object of Cognition); 10. *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* (Treatise on the Five Aggregates); and 11. the ten root treatises of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. All of these rely upon yoga.

[The Abhidharma] was composed by Kātyāyanīputra. Question: For what reason is "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) not established within the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma*, whereas it is established in the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Nyāyānusāra*, and other such works?
Furthermore, one should seek to know whether, outside of the Hīnayāna, there exists "homogeneity" in things such as a piece of wood left behind.

Answer: Indeed, within the *Abhidharma-kośa*, the "human *nikāya-sabhāga*" (homogeneity of humans) is established solely with respect to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*), meaning that humans resemble humans and devas resemble devas, and so forth; however, a "dharma *nikāya-sabhāga*" is not established.
Later, one encounters the following critique from the Mahāyāna: "If you claim that devas resemble devas and humans resemble humans, then you [must admit]..."
If one were to posit a "homogeneity of persons" (*pudgala-sabhāgatā*) and so forth, then the eye should also be similar to the eye, the ear to the ear, and even wisdom to wisdom, and so on;
thus, one would likewise have to posit a distinct "homogeneity of phenomena" (*dharma-sabhāgatā*).

Having encountered this objection, the Master who follows the *Nyāyānusāra* posits the "homogeneity of phenomena" and so forth directly upon all phenomena; however, these are merely distinct factors that are the results of karma.
Regarding the statement that there are no *sabhāga* (homogeneous) factors: their arising and production both depend upon the *vipākaphala* (maturation fruit).
It is upon the *vipākaphala* that *sabhāga* is established; "factor" (*bhāga*) exists solely within the maturation fruit and does not extend to external things.

If it is accepted that [the term] is not restricted to karmic fruits alone, what prevents external phenomena from having *sabhāga*? Since *sabhāga* is established only for material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) that are maturations, this may be accepted.
External phenomena have no *sabhāgatā*. Nevertheless, it is also accepted that the *dharmasabhāgatā* is established upon matter that is a result of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*).

Since such matter of outflow extends to external existence, its *sabhāgatā* likewise extends to external existence. However, within this [category], there are general and specific types of *sabhāgatā*.

This is as explained in the *Compendium* (*Abhidharmasamuccaya*). The *Sub-commentary* (*Ṭīkā*) states: "Just as external phenomena such as the matter of maturation (*vipāka-rūpa*) may be absent. The *Exegesis* (*Vyākhyā*) explains: "The homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) is established based upon the fruit of maturation;

the five internal sense-faculties are of maturation because they are the retribution of prior wholesome or unwholesome karma. These are also of the nature of nourishment (*aupacayika-rūpa*), [such as] food..."
Because food serves as a sustenance, its maturation (*vipāka*) is homogeneous; it is not the case that external [matter] is not so. One interpretation states:

"The term 'homogeneous' (*sabhāga*) is established based upon the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). If wholesome matter gives rise to wholesome matter, and so forth, up to that which arises from a preceding cause of similar type (*sabhāga-hetu*), all of these are fruits of outflow; this also applies to external existence."
The Commentary states: "It should follow that one speaks only of the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) of sentient beings; it should not be explained as being the cause for all similar phenomena.
The Explanation clarifies: "If *sabhāgatā* were the cause only for pleasure and desire, then there would be *sabhāgatā* only for those phenomena [of pleasure and desire];
there should be no *sabhāgatā* upon other similar phenomena."

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "Furthermore, other difficulties are resolved solely by means of 'arising' (*jāti*). The Sub-commentary (*Vivaraṇa*) says: 'The Great Arising gives rise to the substance of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*); furthermore, there is a Small Arising that gives rise to it.
Since the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) is already capable of producing homogeneity, there must further be a 'homogeneity-producer' that produces homogeneity.'"

The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "This sets forth the opponent's defense of the *Sūtra*. This refers to the Sarvāstivāda school’s defense, which says: "Because there still exists the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity), the cognition of 'sameness' arises.
This is the defense of their own treatise (*śāstra*). Furthermore, this passage is a hypothetical construction of an opponent's defense to establish the logical principles of one's own treatise;
it is the underlying meaning beyond the literal words. If one were to include the "difference" (*visiṣṭa*), [the argument would be as follows].

The matured outflow (*vipākaja*) portion possesses many common characteristics, because it gives rise to the cognition of conventional expression regarding phenomena, just as in the case of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

Alternatively, matter and mind would otherwise have no distinction, since the cognition of conventional expression arises regarding them just as it does regarding the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*).
Furthermore, this is not so; for while the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) possess superior efficacy, the homogeneous character must likewise possess even greater superior efficacy.
"Capable" (neng): this passage represents the rebuttal of the opponent. Regarding the "four great elements" (mahābhūta): their substance is vast and pervasive, and thus they are called "great.
For example, the great rivers and great oceans are called "great"; the fierce, blazing fire is the fire element; and wind and so forth are the wind element.
As for the term "element" (dhātu), it has the meaning of "cause" (hetu). This is because they possess the five causes of production, dependence, establishment, maintenance, and nourishment.
Therefore, it is precisely by taking the four great elements as its cause that [matter] is able to produce the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

Since the five sense objects are produced in such a manner, they possess no superior capacity within their own homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*); they can only be identical with others of their own homogeneous class, and cannot further serve as the homogeneity for others.

However, since their substance is not one, and the subsequent arising of the cognition of "homogeneity" is not distinct from the phenomena themselves, how could there be no such thing as homogeneous character? This passage...

This is the Master of the Treatise challenging the opponent. He challenges them as follows: "In all other cases, the entities are not one, but rather consist of many entities. Yet, a cognition of commonality arises subsequently;
thus, one must establish 'homogeneity' (*sabhāgatā*) as a distinct entity upon those other dharmas.

Since the essence of homogeneity is similar [to others] and not one, it too consists of many entities. Furthermore, it is precisely because it arises as a cognition of commonality that this homogeneity is similar to other dharmas. Since...
There is no distinction. Upon that which is already a *sabhāga* (homogeneous), one would likewise have to establish another *sabhāga*.
Even if one were to expect this from the Vaiśeṣika school, it would still be difficult to understand;

for the Vaiśeṣika masters separately establish "commonness and difference" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) as real entities (*dravya*) because they possess the qualities of being both common and distinct across substances, qualities, and activities. Thus, the Sarvāstivādins wish to refute the superior arguments of those Vaiśeṣika masters.
Now, because this differs from other schools, they posit a distinct category of "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) apart from the substance of phenomena.

This homogeneity acts as the agent of similarity, while the substance of other phenomena serves as the object of that similarity. This is precisely what was refuted previously in the critique of the Vaiśeṣika school:

their positing of a separate "commonality" (*sāmānya*) external to substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*). Regarding how this commonality acts as the nature for substance, quality, and action, the objection was stated: "As for your commonality..."

If the nature [of a thing] were to act as the basis for the three—substance, quality, and activity—it would likewise follow that there must be a further "differentiation from differentiation" (anyānyatva) upon the "differentiation from differentiation" itself;
yet it has not yet become the nature of that differentiation from differentiation. Your Sarvāstivāda position is the same.

Specifically, regarding those who calculate that the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is established separately outside the essence of the dharma, the objection is raised: if the essence of the dharma possesses similarity, then why establish the *sabhāgatā* separately outside the essence of the dharma?

The *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) acts as a cause for the essential nature of phenomena; likewise, there should also be another distinct "homogeneity of homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā-sabhāgatā*) upon the *sabhāgatā* itself, which serves as the homogeneity for that [primary] *sabhāgatā*.
Thus, one should understand that the Sarvāstivāda masters regard it as being identical to the *sabhāgatā* of activity and desire.
It does not take the eye and so forth, nor external objects such as visible forms and contacts, as its *sabhāga* (homogeneous) factors. The commentary explains:
if it were said that *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is caused solely by activity, karma, cognition, or desire, then there would be no similar factors for the eye and so forth.

Since there is indeed a *dharmasabhāgatā* (homogeneity of phenomena), and since external phenomena are likewise similar, they too should possess *sabhāgatā*. Although this homogeneity applies to both the subject and the object...

Regarding the statement that "the present case belongs to the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) of the group," analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* compound (*yǔzhǔ shì*), the term "group" (*zhòng*) signifies a category.
Thus, with respect to that which is common—namely, the status of being a Brahmin—the many individuals who are Brahmins and so forth are called a "group.

Although "commonality" (*tóng*) applies to both the subject and the object, if it refers to the subject of commonality, it is *sabhāgatā*; if it refers to the object of commonality, it refers to the many Brahmins.

That which is capable of being the same as that which is already the same all possesses the sense of "sameness. Here, that which is capable of being the same refers to the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous character of a group).

Therefore, it is called the "homogeneous portion of the group," following the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound analysis. Regarding the phrase "the portion of the homogeneous character of the group" (*nikāya-sabhāga-bhāga*), the Hīnayāna explains it as follows:
"Group" (*nikāya*) means category; "same" (*sabhāga*) means similarity; and "portion" (*bhāga*) means cause. This homogeneous character serves as the cause for these [beings].
The present undertaking is likewise the same.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "the superior locus of support," this refers to the various sense faculties (*indriya*) and their associated material bases (*rūpa-prasāda*) within the bodies of sentient beings;

these are all considered "superior. As for the *Abhidharmakośa* and the Sautrāntika school accepting this: indeed, the Sautrāntikas also maintain that there exists a phenomenon (*dharma*) upon external phenomena.

This refers to the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity). Regarding the body that is abandoned and lies prostrate: according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, dying while lying on one's back is called "prostrate" (*jia*), and dying while lying face down is called "fallen" (*pu*).

That treatise raises an objection: "If it is acceptable to say as you have stated regarding death while lying on one's back or face down, what would one call someone who dies while lying on their side?
Furthermore, that same treatise states: 'Life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are mutually dependent, just as three reeds are dependent upon one another.'"

If that were so, at the time of wishing for death and actually dying, which of these three factors would be abandoned first? If you say that these three factors are not abandoned, then one should never die.

If you say that at the time of wishing for death one first abandons consciousness, then entering the two mindless meditative attainments (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti* and *nirodha-samāpatti*) should be called death.
If you say that one first abandons fear, then there are many people who, when frozen, have bodies that are indeed cold [yet do not die].

It appears they will not yet die; thus we know that at the time of death, one first relinquishes the life-faculty (*āyus*). Regarding the three factors—the life-faculty, the afflictions (*kleśa*), and consciousness—that abandon the body:

Question: This "warmth" (*uṣman*) is precisely the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) within the body. Why, among the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), is it specifically the fire element that is said to be relinquished?
The correct meaning lies solely in this. That is to say, it is taken from within this treatise, and it relies upon...
"It is the parents who produce the seeds of this consciousness; 'life' refers to that which is the root of life. This explanation applies to the five faculties, the mind, and so forth.
Since the Mahāyāna sūtras universally state that there is "life" and "roots," to which [phenomena] does "life" belong, and what is called a "root"?

There is also the view that life itself is the faculty. The answer is: here, the eighth consciousness in its active state (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) is designated as "life," while the functional capacity within the seeds is taken to be the "faculty";
thus it is called the "faculty of life. If one takes the functional capacity within the seeds to be the faculty, then...
The root of life (*jīvitendriya*). If one takes the functional capacity within the seed as "that which can sustain life," then life itself is the grasping root.

However, since the treatises state that the two mindless attainments (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti* and *nirodha-samāpatti*), the ripening of formlessness (*ārūpya-vipāka*), and the life-root are exclusively seeds, [the opponent's] position is not established.

The commentary explains: If light were not subsumed by form and were separate from consciousness, then life would be cited as an analogy for warmth; yet [the opponent] allows that warmth and consciousness may be separate.

If one were to separate [the object] from that which is established [as its support], then that which is established would not be accomplished as light. This is because color is not separated from consciousness;
thus, there is no fault in what is established.

The Commentary (*Shu*) says: "Fearing the loss of the general [principle]. The Explanation (*Jie*) says: "If one were to cite 'warmth' (*ūṣman*) separately as an analogy, one would lose the general category of 'form' (*rūpa*). Now...
If one takes all forms (*rūpa*) as the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), there is no fault, because they are certainly present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*). Question:
In the previous commentary, the inference (*anumāna*) specifically mentioned "warmth" (*uṣman*); why does this text not specifically mention "warmth"?
I fear it might lose the general sense. Answer: You were confused; now I shall correct you. It does not specifically mention "warmth," and thus there is no fault.
The *Śāstra* says: "If one gives rise to a dissimilar mind (*visabhāga-citta*) or an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), it is not that destination. The commentary explains:

Regarding "dissimilar minds," for example, according to the Sautrāntikas, they do not establish the existence of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) but gives rise to a mind belonging to the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), it is called a "dissimilar mind.

Since there is no life-faculty, it is not known to which level (*bhūmi*) such a person belongs. This also applies if one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness or the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The mind of the sphere of nothingness and the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are both termed "dissimilar minds" (*visabhāga-citta*).

If one is in a lower stage, one can give rise to all minds of the higher stages; however, if one is in a higher stage, one cannot give rise to a mind of a lower stage—except for the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body belonging to the first dhyāna, which may arise from the upper three dhyānas.
Furthermore, this excludes those born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) who rely on the category of the noble ones (*ārya*). *Śrī-mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā*, Fascicle [Number].

Regarding "arbitrariness" (*yadṛcchā*) or "one who acts arbitrarily": one in a higher stage cannot give rise to a mind belonging to a lower stage. Or, one may give rise to an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*).

An untainted mind does not tend toward the substance of rebirth (*janma-bhava*). [The text] says "does not know. What is the name of this person, and by which explanation is he subsumed? Please provide a complete account.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "Since the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneous character) was already refuted previously, there is no fault of being 'indeterminate' (*anaikāntika*).

The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says: "If light were not refuted, one could raise the charge of indeterminacy as follows: 'Is it like *sabhāgatā*, which, though not mental, can sustain the body; or is it like form (*rūpa*), etc., which, though not mental, cannot sustain the body?
Since light has already been refuted—along with the meditative absorption of non-conceptualization (*acittaka-samādhi*) and the Heaven of No-Characteristics (*āsaṃjñika-svarga*)—"

Three states are without mind; the remaining two both possess mind. This is not the same as the five stages of no-mind in the Mahāyāna. Therefore, it takes only one [of these] equally. The *Śū* (Commentary) says:

"Excluding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the remaining are matured phenomena (*vipākadharmas*). The *Jie* (Explanation) says: "Matured phenomena" refers precisely to the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

Furthermore, since the body consists of the [four] great elements and their derivatives (*bhautika*), one should exclude it [from being the sustainer], as it is that which is capable of being destroyed.

Therefore, the present objection is intended to show that while medicine can sustain the body, life-force (*jīvitendriya*) alone cannot sustain the body. Regarding the statement that in the two lower realms and in the mindless absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*), although [life-force] can sustain the body, consciousness (*vijñāna*) and warmth (*uṣman*) are not constant:
if it refers to the six consciousnesses, they are indeed subject to interruption; if it refers to warmth, it is not subject to interruption. This passage...

Regarding the term "beneficial warmth" (*uṣman*): this passage should state that although it can sustain the body, because consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not constant, it is merely "warmth at that location.
The Commentary (*Śū*) states: "Upon entering the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), there are three [factors]: life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and [consciousness]. This is one interpretation.

There is also another interpretation which holds that when consciousness enters the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), both matter (*rūpa*) and [the other factors] are entirely absent. Since [in the former case] there is warmth, the explanation says: in the Mahāyāna, these three are all the meaning of consciousness.
Because they are explained separately. Now, others raise an objection regarding the three natures: if there were no distinct mind, there would be consciousness [alone].

If the meaning of the three natures is explained as being one in essence, then when a person is without form (*rūpa*), there should be heat (*uṣman*). Although the realms (*dhātu*) also extend to other phenomena, this is because it is the true essential nature of the realm.

Regarding the nature of the destinies (*gati*) and births (*upapatti*): these consist solely of the maturation-unspecified (*vipāka-avyākṛta*). Furthermore, that which is about to arise is established as being included within the destinies.

It is not subsumed under the destinies (*gati*) within birth; that is to say, excluding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it comprises all phenomena of the three moral natures (*trividha-dharma*).

Whether internal sentient beings or external insentient things, such as rivers and other entities, are all the substance of the *dhātu* (element/realm). Thus, the substance of the *dhātu* is the most extensive. Question:

Since the substance of the *dhātu* already pervades everything, why is only the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) taken here as the substance of the *dhātu*? Answer: If it is the fundamental consciousness...
This is the very essence of the *dharmadhātu*. Because the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) exists, other phenomena are able to arise.

The *Śāstra* (sub-commentary) states: "The word 'this' serves to distinguish it from the seeds that directly produce other consciousnesses. Here, we take the term "directly producing" to distinguish it from the direct seeds of the seven consciousnesses;
this refers to the seeds of the eighth consciousness, which are drawn forth by prior karma and possess distinct functional capacities.
Regarding those who have attained certainty through distinct factors: by the drawing forth of prior karma, each [seed] possesses its own functional power (*śakti*).
This functional power is precisely that which sustains the body, such that one does not die for a hundred, a thousand, or fifty years.

It is this various functional power that is termed the "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*). Furthermore, while it separately takes up the essence of the seed, it does not take up this [specific] seed itself.
The meaning of the life-manifesting consciousness is termed the "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*).
If, at the time when the power of its subsequent functional capacity is exhausted, the seeds still exist within the body, one dies.

If these seeds lack this functional capacity—or even the capacity to sustain the other faculties and dharmas—"functional capacity" refers to the specific force inherent in the seeds. By means of this force...
Therefore, within the body, if there is no vital force (*śakti*), the body becomes cold.

Although it is by virtue of the superior force of the seeds that the manifest consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arises, this manifest consciousness is able to take the three kinds of objects as its cognitive domain and is able to sustain the five sense faculties, such as the eye.
Furthermore, by virtue of the power of seeds, it is established that the *uṣmagata* and consciousness possess a manifold capacity for maintenance (*dhāraṇa*).

First, by the force of the seeds, they are able to maintain the active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). Second, by means of the active consciousness, they are able to correspondingly maintain the five sense organs, such as the eye.

Regarding the intended meaning here, one takes only the seeds of the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the fundamental consciousness. [Question: Is this the same for the seeing division (*darśanabhāga*) and the self-witnessing division? [Answer: It is the same.
[The text] speaks of "seeds giving rise [to phenomena]. Why, in this context, does it take only the seeds of self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*) and not the other two types of seeds?
The commentary states: "The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) has no [specific] affiliation. This asks:

although the life-faculty itself is not a seed of consciousness, the seeds of consciousness are comprised within the aggregates (*skandha*), the mind-base (*manāyatana*), and the seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*). The functional capacity (*śakti*) upon that life-faculty is precisely the [unconditioned] non-disappearance (*avipraṇāśa*).

It should be included among the formations (*saṃskāra*). As for those formations that are dissociated (*viprayukta*), they are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) and are included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the constituent of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Why, then, is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) said to have no affiliation? If the life-faculty were not included at all within the aggregates and so forth, only then could it be called an "unaffiliated aggregate.

Now, when we speak of something having an affiliation, this designation does not depend on the dissociated factors; rather, it is called "having an affiliation" precisely because it is [included] therein. Now, in this very case...
Regarding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*): if it does not belong to the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) nor to the seeds (*bīja*), it is called the "unaffiliated life-faculty.

If it belonged to the seeds, it would have to be subsumed under the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). If it belonged to the seeds of consciousness, it would likewise be included within the aggregate of consciousness.

If it belonged to karma, it would be subsumed under the two aggregates of form (*rūpaskandha*) and formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); since karma permeates all bodies, it is thus the aggregate of form. If it were the seed of volition (*cetanā*)...
The son is already subsumed within the seeds of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and thus has something to which he belongs. How can you say that he has nothing to which he belongs?
Now, it does not belong to the seeds, nor to karma, nor to the manifesting consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*); rather, it is the functional power (*śakti*) upon the seeds induced by prior karma.

That the physical body (*rūpa-kāya*) does not cease at this time is called "life" (*jīvita*). Furthermore, if one explains the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as the seeds of consciousness and their characteristics:
That which is based on the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is superior; it is like the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth.

Since these four characteristics depend on multiple factors within the five aggregates, they are subsumed under the category of non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Furthermore, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is also established based on multiple factors and is likewise included among the non-associated formations.
If it were not so, then just as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is established based solely upon the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), it would be subsumed under the sense-base of form;

whereas since the life-faculty is established based solely upon the seeds of consciousness, it should be included within the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*), rather than being subsumed under the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). The objection states: "Since the life-faculty is established based upon multiple factors, there should be as many sentient beings as there are such factors.

The explanation says: It is like the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), which is established based solely upon the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and yet is posited with respect to the multiplicity of [defilements] to be abandoned.

It is merely a designation (*nāmamātra*). The same applies to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). [The opponent] says: "If the life-faculty is established based on many dharmas, then it should be called 'many sentient beings' (*bahusattva*);
likewise, since the nature of an ordinary person is also established based on many [dharmas], it should be called 'many natures of ordinary persons' (*bahupṛthagjanatva*).

This interpretation is superior. This [previous argument] was stated solely in reference to the text, according to the most prominent [view]. If both the "gate-king" (*dvārādhipati*) and the "gate" (*dvāra*) take the mental factors (*caitta*) as their object, then [the former] would not be seen.
This is an obstacle.
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Regarding the phrase 'the six bases have continued as such from beginningless time,' this refers exclusively to the sixth base. The explanation says:

This is like the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, which takes the name "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*) to refer to the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) within the sixth base, the mind-base (*manāyatana*).

It is a "son" (a derivative). It is called the "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*). This is like saying that there are no untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), or like the expression regarding the continuity of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).

[The commentary] explains: Just as the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* takes the name "six sense bases" to refer to the life-faculty, it refers to the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) within the sixth sense base, the mind-base (*mano-āyatana*). These are called the life-faculty. This is like the statement regarding the absence of untainted seeds.

Regarding the statement that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have been in continuous succession since beginningless time, it is said that the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) reside within the sixth mental base (*manāyatana*).
These untainted seeds exist within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); they are not contained within the five sense organs.

The untainted seeds are stored exclusively in the sixth [base], and the original untainted seeds within the consciousness do not reside as hidden stores within the five sense organs. This life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is said to pertain only to these six.

[The term] "seed" (bīja) refers exclusively to the seeds of the mental faculty (*manas*), and does not include the seeds of the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*). These constitute the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Question:
Within the three categories (*triskandha*), where are the seeds of the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) and the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*) subsumed?

If they are said to be subsumed under the category of "that which is supported" (*āśrita*), then since the manifest consciousnesses are themselves that which is supported, and following this logic up to the life-faculty, these would all be that which is supported by karma. What then of the eighth [consciousness]?

The manifesting consciousnesses are that which is supported (*āśrita*). If the functional capacity upon the seeds of its own designations within the eighth consciousness is called "that which supports" (*āśraya*), this refers to the eighth consciousness itself.

As for the statement that the mind (*manas*) is further termed the "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*), this refers to the supported consciousness; it explains that the functional capacity upon the seeds that support [the consciousness] is designated as the life-faculty.
This passage does not, however, mean that either the capacity or the seeds themselves are named the life-faculty; rather, it simply takes [the capacity] as such.

By the power of karmic seeds, the capacity within the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is induced; because this capacity can sustain the manifest state (*pravṛtti*), it is called "life" (*jīvitendriya*).
Thus, this text states that it "can sustain the seeds of karma. Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that the seeds of this consciousness refer to the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*):
one asks whether this second interpretation refers to the functioning of the five faculties or to the grasping of the seeds of the five faculties.

The "son" is called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). If one takes the five faculties as they manifest, how can the Sub-commentary state: "The aspect-division (*nimittabhāga*) is not separate from consciousness;
taken collectively, this is called the 'son' of that consciousness"? Furthermore, the Sub-commentary says: "Or it is of the class of seeds of the six sense-bases.
If one takes the seeds of the five faculties as the life-faculty, then the nature of those seeds of the five faculties is a constant, uninterrupted succession.

When these cease, the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) that are currently active are likewise interrupted. Why, then, does the sub-commentary state: "If one were to take up the seeds of the five sense-faculties, death would necessarily ensue"?
Furthermore, among the seeds of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), even if the seeds of five bases are severed, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) alone remains.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Although their functional capacities (*śakti*) are of one essence, there is a clear distinction between what is form (*rūpa*) and what is mind (*citta*).

This is because, when observing that the seeds of the same kind are all consciousness, it is said that their functional capacities are of one essence. The five sense organs are form, while the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is mind;
thus, it is said that if they are distinguished, each takes up its own respective seed-capacity.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Even if the [sense] bases (*āyatana*) are occasionally severed while the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) alone remains, this is not called death.

The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states: "Furthermore, at the time of passing away, the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are first relinquished; yet the fundamental consciousness still persists as it is about to be relinquished. How, then, could the five sense-faculties constitute the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?"

Furthermore, it is like at the time of initial birth, when the sense faculties (*indriya*) have not yet been fully formed; the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) alone exists. Or, it is like a person whose eye or ear faculties have been damaged;
because the fundamental consciousness alone remains, it arises such that the five faculties cannot be apprehended, serving as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Moreover, it is like being born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), where the five faculties are absent; by whom would they be severed, since the fundamental consciousness alone remains? It is through these [examples] that one knows [the existence of the fundamental consciousness].

The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are not the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Alternatively, because the life-faculty exists in the three realms, it is distinct [from the five faculties]. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states: "If one refers to the five faculties, they may be fully present in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*);

however, in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the five faculties do not exist, and thus there would be a distinction in their presence or absence. As for taking the 'seed' of the five faculties, it is..."

There must be death, because there is no functional capacity during the interval. This is like the case of humans who die prematurely, or those whose faculties—such as sight or hearing—fail through deafness and so forth;
such instances should be termed "death. Although one may be blind or deaf, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) should not be considered singular, because the seeds are not singular;
for since there are six types of seeds, the life-faculty should likewise be manifold.

Sixth: This passage does not fully capture the underlying principle. For instance, while the treatise speaks of the "seed-dharma" of consciousness alone, why would one prefer the seeds of the five [aggregates] here?
We do not observe a single karma that induces only the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and not the mental factors (*caitta*).

We know that from karma, both the mind-king and the mental factors are induced. Therefore, it is superior in principle to take this as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of life. This applies even to the previous interpretation.

What is the distinction? If one says that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) are of the same kind, this would accord with the explanation in this treatise [which states] that only the seeds of this consciousness are taken;

however, since it is said they are of the same kind as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), they should be subsumed under the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*). If, on the other hand, the seeing-part and the image-part are of different kinds, then the life-faculty must be of a different kind.
It should be subsumed under the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The treatise states: "That which can cause the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) to not manifest extensively. Question:

Why do those outside the school of the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa* all cite sūtra passages to substantiate their meaning, invariably saying, "As it is said in the Sūtra," and so forth? Why is this [distinction between] the two explained?

Question: Does this passage concerning the two mindless attainments (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti* and *nirodha-samāpatti*) not cite scriptural authority? Answer: This treatise [does] so; furthermore, there is no contradiction with the principles of these two attainments.
There are also sūtras that speak of them, as is clarified in the lower section of this treatise where both mindless attainments are explained.
In all cases, sūtra passages are cited as proof. When entering the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), there are likewise distinct real dharmas. Question: Regarding this passage...
Consider whether this refers to one who, while residing in the lower two realms, enters the formless attainments, or whether it refers to one who,
having been born in the formless realm, enters the formless attainments.

The *Śāstra* says: "If the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) possesses only mind and no mind, then there should also be cases where there is only matter (*rūpa*) and no mind. The commentary explains: This is merely challenging the other [party] without fault.

If it were certain that there is only mind and no mind, then there should indeed be only matter. You followers of the Mahāyāna loathe matter and enter the formless realm; [if so, you would be admitting such a case].
The formless is not the seed of form. One enters the mindless state through aversion toward the mind. As for the claim that the mindless state should be the seed of the mind:

according to the Mahāyāna, the two mindless absorptions (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti* and *nirodha-samāpatti*) are established based upon twenty-two types of seeds. This is why [it differs from] the views of outsiders.
It is difficult [to maintain] that the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) should not be seeds of the mind.

The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Even if, in the present case, material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are capable of producing revulsion toward the formless, this does not preclude them from being seeds of matter. The *Jie* (Exegesis) explains: "This statement is a rebuttal by way of inversion;

for it is held that matter is not capable [of producing revulsion], and that which is not capable cannot be a seed of the formless. Therefore, it is made clear that matter can generally be capable of producing revulsion."

What prevents this from being the nature of form? Therefore, mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) can universally function as both that which is weary of and that which is weary; material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), however, are exclusively that which is weary of.
The commentary states: "That which is universal and capable of being weary of is called 'formless' (*arūpya*)," referring to the Formless Realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*). It is exclusively...

That which possesses mind is called the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Regarding "tīrtha," it refers to a bathing place or ford; that is, the six dharmas themselves are like pits, and because one must descend into them, they are called *tīrtha*.
Regarding "setu," it refers to a dam or embankment; that is, a barrier constructed by piling up earth.

This is to exclude [the possibility of it being] water. If one holds that atoms are real and their aggregation is provisional—such as a jar or a *stūpa*—then a question is raised regarding the Sarvāstivāda:
since jars, *stūpas*, and so forth are admitted to be definitively provisional, then within gross matter there would be something half-provisional and half-real.

Why, then, did the previous text state that both the gross and the subtle are real? The explanation is: the previous passage clarified that, according to the Sarvāstivāda, both the gross and the subtle are real.

Regarding "the real": for instance, as with the many characteristics mentioned previously, even when broken down to a single atom (*paramāṇu*), they are all termed "generic form" (*sāmānyarūpa*) and do not further alter their reality.
This applies likewise to yellow and other colors; therefore, if blue and so forth are analyzed down to a single atom—

Furthermore, they are coarse because they are comprised of these [elements]. Now, with respect to the combination of the four particles to form things such as jars and robes, once those jars and robes are broken apart, their names are lost;
therefore, they are provisional. For instance, regarding things such as jars and robes from the perspective of conceptual discrimination:

If one says that the jar is a real entity, [it cannot be so], for the six consciousnesses [do not perceive it as a whole]. If one says that what is seen by the eye is the jar, that which is seen by the eye is merely color (rūpa), and thus it is insufficient to constitute a jar.
If one says that what is within [the parts] is the jar, that which exists between the parts is a conceptual construction (vikalpa) and is therefore not the jar.
If one says that what is smelled by the nose is the jar, that which is apprehended by the nose is fragrance; the same applies even to what is touched by the body.
Therefore, one knows that because jars and the like are conventional (prajñapti), within gross form (rūpa) according to the Sarvāstivāda school, there are both the conventional and the real.

The commentary states: "The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says, 'It is like damming a river. This citation refers to a distinct phenomenon and does not intend to use the conventional and the real as a metaphor.

The explanation says: In that treatise, regarding the objects used to dam a river, it is the embankment (*tīra*) that can dam it; it is not that something which is not a [substantial] thing cannot dam it.
However, regarding the metaphors for existence and non-existence, this treatise cites the *Tideng* (提塘) metaphor; its intended meaning concerns the conventional and the real.

Since even a conventional designation can serve as a negation, what need is there for a real dharma? Thus, the two treatises differ in their respective intended meanings regarding the metaphors for the conventional and real aspects of existence and non-existence.

As for "because one is weary of the coarse and agitated mind and mental factors, whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)," this refers to the preparatory application (*prayoga*) prior to entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) by those of the three vehicles.
Whether far or near, [this state] serves as an object of aversion for the tainted (*sāsrava*) mind. Is it an object of aversion for the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind?

If the tainted mind arises, one must inevitably exert effort regarding its lack of outflow; since it arises simultaneously with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is harmonious with the world—so why would the untainted mind be required?
Furthermore, when the mind arises with the thought "I shall cause [the mind] to become weary," does it cause itself to become weary, or does it cause another mind to become weary?
If it causes another mind to become weary, then that mind which performs the act of becoming weary—is it tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*)? It must be an untainted mind.

How is there aversion? Furthermore, as it is said in the Hīnayāna: when one is about to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, one gives rise to an outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) mind, and only then does aversion arise.

Regarding "one kalpa or more than one kalpa," this refers to entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), which lasts for only one or two kalpas of increase and decrease (*vivarta-kalpa* and *saṃvarta-kalpa*).
For example, when Mahākāśyapa entered the meditative absorption of cessation, his robe remained waiting until the time of Maitreya.
Regarding the cessation-concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*): one does not obtain the scriptural passage concerning the great formation and destruction kalpas.

Furthermore, even for Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above, they do not obtain the scriptural passage regarding entering cessation or the permanence of the Buddha. Why, then, would they not recollect entering concentration? As for the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*), there is likewise no question of obtaining the scriptural passage concerning the increase or decrease of kalpas.

The Commentary states: "As explained above, when one first enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) while still at the stage of a cause (*hetu-bhūmi*), it is not the result of long-term familiarization. The Explanation says:

"If one is newly practicing the absorption of cessation, one must apply preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and a mind of revulsion (*nirveda*) before being able to enter the meditative state. However, if one has long since become habituated through nature, such preparatory revulsion is unnecessary, as one enters spontaneously."

One is able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). If one contemplates the signless (*animitta*) spontaneously, one can then enter the Buddha’s absorption of the extinction of all outflows (*āsravakṣaya-samādhi*).

Although the Buddha does not rely on a mind of aversion, this is because the seeds of aversion have been fully perfected through habitual practice since beginningless time; thus, the essence of the Buddha’s absorption of cessation is conventionally designated upon the seeds of the distracted mind.
The Commentary states: "As for the distinction between the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of these two attainments:

if one enters the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), those clear and cognizant minds that seek the fruit of signlessness (*animitta-phala*)—which exist prior to the signless concentration—consist of subtle and extremely subtle minds."
One must first perform preparatory practices (*prayoga*) such as those for the "sick person" and so forth, before being able to enter the concentration of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*).

If one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one performs the mental visualization of the cessation of the mind as the preparatory practice. Among these three stages of the mind, at which stage does one seek the state of non-conceptuality (*asaṃjñin*)?
If one seeks the fruit of signlessness within all three stages of the mind, although this statement is general, its intent is to provide a clear explanation.

Regarding the phrase "because there is a distinction between the two fruits—the state with mind and the state without mind during the time of the mind": however, within the commentary (*śū*), there are two interpretations.

This is the first interpretation, which states: one takes the moment of the very first *sūkṣma-sūkṣma* (subtle-subtle) mind prior to meditative absorption (*samādhi*) as the point at which the seeds are infused.

Because this seed was initially perfumed, it possesses a specific potency; it thus constitutes the "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*) limb within the twelve links of dependent origination, which is capable of summoning the collective retribution (*vipāka*) of that [heavenly] realm.

This very seed of the subtle-subtle mind (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma-citta*), once the second moment of the state of non-consciousness has passed, its potency becomes weak, and it only summons the distinct individual retribution (*viśeṣa-vipāka*) of that heavenly realm. This...
Once the mindless state has passed, the seeds of revulsion in the mind become manifest; this is the time when the mind is clearly aware.

Thus, the seeds of revulsion are perfumed, yet their essence is no different [from the mind itself]. What is the meaning of this? Because these subtle and faint minds possess the nature of goodness, the seeds of revulsion are themselves karma;
they are thus able to extinguish the previously existing indeterminate mind of the sixth consciousness within that heavenly realm.

Manifestation: Due to the power of the seeds of the mind of renunciation arising from the previously extinguished distinct karmic fruits of wholesome action, it causes those devas to be unable to manifest the indeterminate *nāma-vyañjana* (name-and-phrase) seeds within their sixth consciousness for the duration of one life-span, lasting five hundred kalpas;
during this period, the indeterminate *nāma-vyañjana* seeds of the sixth consciousness cannot give rise to manifestation. This is the dharma-rule.
In that celestial realm, the seeds of indeterminate verbal designations (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*) of the sixth consciousness, which have been extinguished, ought to manifest as actualities (*pravṛtti*).

However, precisely because of the power of the mind of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇa-citta*) associated with the karma capable of extinguishing them, those seeds of indeterminate verbal designations of the sixth consciousness that have been extinguished are likewise prevented from arising as actualities.
Thus, within the sixth consciousness, one attains this "attainment of what has been extinguished" (*nirodha-prāpti*).

The neutral seeds of verbal designations (*nāma-kalpa-bīja*) serve as the basis for the arising of manifest activity; they constitute the essence of the maturation (*vipāka*) of the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

This is subsumed within the sphere of the "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*). It is, in fact, a single seed capable of producing two types of results: both collective retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*) and individual retribution (*viśeṣa-vipāka*).
At the initial moment when the mind first arises, it initially perfumes and acquires seeds capable of inducing the collective retribution (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*).

These seeds, in relation to the subsequent moments of non-mindfulness (unconscious states) and thereafter, are able to induce that heavenly realm. Within this sixth consciousness, there are seeds of indeterminate names and words (*nāma-pada*) for specific retributions (*asādhāraṇa-vipāka*);
because they rely upon the eighth consciousness, they each attain their respective maturations (*vipāka*). This is not because [the seeds] are distinct [from the eighth consciousness].

Regarding liberation: one contemplates the seeds of volition within its essence. If, from the first up to the third *karmavācanā*, these seeds of volition can bring about the fruit of collective retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*).

If one receives the precepts and subsequently commits violations throughout the duration of one's life, these seeds of volition that constitute the essence of the precepts can only bring about the fruit of individual retribution (*pratyeka-vipāka*).
Thus, a single seed of volition first brings about the collective grasping and subsequently brings about the individual [retribution].
Now this case is also like that; therefore, the substance of the seed is one, yet it universally brings about both collective and individual retributions.

However, the substance of the concentration of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika-samādhi*) is itself the member of volitional formations (*saṃskāra-aṅga*), because the non-perceptual maturation (*vipāka*) within the heavens is itself the fruit. As the text of the treatise below states:

"If one who has merely attained the concentration of non-perception subsequently falls away, they will later be born in the Heaven of No Clouds (*Anabhraka*) or the Heaven of Merit-Born (*Puṇyaprasava*)."

From the time one is born into the lower three dhyānas, one is able to cultivate the state of non-conceptual absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), with the sole exception of the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-deva).

This is because the Heaven of Non-conceptualization is the ultimate limit of the realm of form (rūpa-dhātu). Thus, it is known that non-conceptual absorption is the cause and the Heaven of Non-conceptualization is the fruit.

Furthermore, from the point when this mindless state has passed, the seeds of the mind that were weary of [conceptualization] are merely extinguished; at that time, the sixth consciousness within the heaven separately induces the five [sensory] consciousnesses.

Consciousness. Why? Because it is a maturation (*vipāka*) and cannot arise in a different stage (*bhūmi*). If the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is the karma of the fourth dhyāna, how could it induce the eye, ear, and body-consciousnesses of the first dhyāna, which belong to a different stage? Therefore, we know that it is only the sixth consciousness that is extinguished. Question:

Within the non-conceptual heaven (*asaṃjñi-deva*), there is the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*) and the indeterminate mind of name-and-form that are produced by the sixth consciousness. How is this so?

Regarding the dharmas that have existed since beginningless time as understood by the mind, the answer is: there are only six dharmas. Namely, the sixth mind-king (manas) and the five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
These six dharmas are called the "fruition of non-conceptualization" (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*). They are similar to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) of those gods.
Within that heaven, the eighth mind-king, the five universals, and so forth—these six dharmas are precisely what is termed the "collective retribution fruition. If, within that heaven...
Within the sixth consciousness, there are the five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) as well as the sixth mind-king (*citta-rāja*).

Because these six dharmas each constitute a distinct retribution-maturation (*vipāka*), although the five object-specific factors (*viṣaya-niyata*) arise simultaneously with the sixth consciousness in that celestial realm, their arising power is strong and induces for the most part wholesome fulfillment (*kuśala-pūrṇa*), rather than being predominantly maturation-neutral (*avyākṛta-vipāka*). This is why the sixth...

Within consciousness (*vijñāna*), only the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) are taken as the "fruition of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya-niṣyanda*), while the five object-specific factors (*viṣaya-pratiniyata*) are not.

Alternatively, if one takes the five object-specific factors, they too are included because these five also pertain to fruition. Thus, within the sixth consciousness of those gods, eleven dharmas are taken as the fruition of non-conception.
Since the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are bound exclusively to the first dhyāna, they cannot be included in the totality of the five consciousnesses [in that state].
Regarding the name: within the fourth dhyāna, there is the maturation (vipāka) of non-conception (asaṃjñika). If vitarka and vicāra exist only in the first dhyāna and the desire realm;

if kaukṛtya and middha exist only in the desire realm; and if the fundamental [dhyānas] are likewise complete according to these factors—then as for the eleven wholesome [factors], none of these exist within the fourth dhyāna.
Within the Heaven of Non-Conception (asaṃjñisattva), the sixth consciousness—if its faculties are subsumed under the maturation of non-conception—is absent.
Therefore, only eleven dharmas are taken. Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that "the former [explanation] up to the preceding one is superior," this refers to the second interpretation.

If we consider the seeds obtained within the gradually developing mind, these seeds are capable of inducing the retributive totality (*vipāka-sāmānya-phala*) of that heaven, which is the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). As for the seeds perfumed at the time of the gradually developing mind:
