It is capable of inducing the specific retribution of the non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi*) maturation within that celestial realm. Of the two interpretations [regarding its nature], both are superior.

Specifically, at the time when the mind gradually subsides, the seeds obtained through perfuming (*vāsanā*) constitute the essence of the non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Because the mind of aversion [toward conceptualization] is extremely intense, it constitutes the essence of the absorption.
To speak according to reality, one should also include the preceding distant preparatory stages (*prayoga*), which become increasingly subtle and refined.

Gradually, the mind is perfumed to acquire seeds, and one also takes up the gradual preparatory application (*prayoga*). It is not contradictory in principle for the various minds to combine to form the substance of the verbal expression.
This is because it is precisely due to the preceding distant preparatory application acting as the cause that one is subsequently able to acquire the proximate preparatory application.

This is just as the substance of the previously explained *prātimokṣa* vows is also acquired through the perfuming of the mind by the proximate preparatory application of the vow-substance, which was preceded by the distant preparatory application.
The seeds [of the precepts] serve as the essence of the precepts; furthermore, the seeds acquired through perfuming at the time of receiving the formal precepts serve as the essence of the precepts.

If one were to take only the moment of receiving the formal precepts [as the essence], there would be no time during which seeds are not being perfumed—so how could that alone constitute the essence of the precepts? Therefore, we know this.

Furthermore, regarding the position that the remote preparatory action (*dūre-prayoga*) constitutes the essence of the precept (*śīla-tattva*): this is like the third *karmavācanā*, when one abides in a state of non-consciousness (*acittaka*).
At the very moment of receiving the precepts, there is no failure to infuse seeds (*bīja*). How, then, could [the act at that moment] be the essence of the precept?

Therefore, it is known that taking the remote preparatory action as the essence of the precept is superior in principle. Generally, in discussing the paths of action (*karmapatha*), [one must consider] from the remote preparatory action all the way up to the point of completion.
Regarding the principle (*li*): there are two general explanations in the commentary (*shu*), and this passage from the commentary represents the first interpretation. The meaning here is as follows:

when the sixth consciousness arises within that heaven, it may give rise to a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or a defiled mind obscured by ignorance (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*), which refers to the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Alternatively, it may be an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mind; however, based on a wholesome or defiled mind, [the afflicted states] do not manifest (*na samudācarati*).

It is established as the substance of the maturation (*vipāka*) of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñika*), just as the seeds of the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) depend upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

Therefore, those two mindless attainments should be called "maturation-consciousness" (*vipāka-vijñāna*), because they are either the seeds of meditative attainment or are themselves uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);

and because the attainment of non-conceptualization is wholesome (*kuśala*). As for the claim that it is not called "maturation" because the seeds of the wholesome and defiled within that stage are [not so], in reality...

It is not itself a maturation (*vipāka*), but because it serves as the basis for maturation and thus receives the name "maturation," the treatise merely states that "the non-constant mental states and mental factors cease.

Furthermore, it has never been specified whether this is of a wholesome or defiled nature; however, in accordance with the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it refers exclusively to the cessation of the mental states and mental factors acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*).
This "maturation" is so called because as soon as a wholesome or defiled mind arises, it is immediately obtained.
This is called "attained at birth" (*upapatti-pratilambhika*). This consciousness, in terms of its three natures (*trisvabhāva*), is all termed "attained at birth.
That is to say, among the wholesome, it is already called "wholesome attained at birth"; when defiled afflictions arise, it is called "defiled obscured mind attained at birth";
and when neutral states arise, it is called "neutral attained at birth. Because these defiled minds are acquired precisely within that state of birth, they are so named.
It is called "innate" (*upapattiprātilambhika*). It is not that it is an indeterminate state resulting from maturation (*vipākaja-avyākṛta*) which is termed "innate.

Alternatively, the foundational consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) itself may be termed "innate indeterminate. Because the seeds of the virtuous mind, which depend upon it, rely on the foundational consciousness, they share the same nature as the foundational consciousness;
therefore, these dependent seeds are said to be "innate indeterminate. The above explanation is the traditional interpretation.
This is incorrect; it contradicts the seventh passage below. That passage states: "The initial moment of existence (bhava) is necessarily indeterminate.
The "innate indeterminate" (upapatti-lābhika-avyākṛta) refers precisely to the innate indeterminate mind within the sixth consciousness. Thus, it should be known.
Regarding the initial mind of those devas, it does not give rise to either defiled or wholesome minds.

Furthermore, the interpretation that "the sixth consciousness arises as the resultant equanimity, which is acquired at birth and is indeterminate (avyākṛta), or that it is established upon seeds because it is definitely non-obscured" constitutes the second interpretation.
This passage means that within the sixth consciousness of those devas, only the seeds of the resultant indeterminate state acquired at birth arise.

The seeds of the innately acquired (*upapatti-lābhika*) neutral (*avyākṛta*) maturation (*vipāka*) are precisely what are experienced during the state of mental exhaustion and thereafter in the state of non-conception;

these are the effects induced by those seeds. Thus, taking the innately acquired neutral seeds that do not function toward the extremes [of existence] as the "maturation of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti-vipāka*), this latter interpretation is superior.
This is because various treatises describe it as the maturation of non-conception, provided it refers strictly to the actual entity.
Among the five meanings of "dharma," the eighth consciousness is termed both *vipāka* (maturation) and *vipākaja* (born of maturation).

Other states, whether wholesome or defiled, are termed only *vipākaja* because they depend upon the *vipāka*. This state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*) should likewise be called "non-conceptualization born of maturation" (*asaṃjñika-vipākaja*).
That it is now described as "the maturation of non-conceptualization" (*asaṃjñika-vipāka*) is because it depends upon the true *vipāka*; thus, it is named "non-conceptualization."

It is a maturation (*vipāka*). Regarding the two initial meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) as *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds: Question: The essence of concentration (*samādhi*) is possessed of mind; only when there is mind is it called "concentration.
Now, these two [attainments] are each "concentrated" during their respective mindless states. In this case, is it a real concentration or a nominal concentration?
According to my humble opinion, it is a nominal concentration, as explained below in the treatise. Furthermore, how is it a *karmadhāraya*? Answer: If not yet...

If one attains the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*) of the higher stages, one cannot achieve tranquility and harmony in this present body. Only by attaining the fundamental absorptions of the higher stages can the body be made tranquil and harmonious.
According to the actual substance of meditative absorption, it consists solely of the mind; that is, it is the concentration (*samādhi*) among the five particular mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*).

Nor is it argued that any state of non-concomitance constitutes a fixed meditative absorption. Now, when the mind gradually becomes subtle prior to entering a fixed absorption, all such states are absorptions with mental activity (*sacittaka-samādhi*).
Having attained this absorption with mental activity as a preparatory practice (*prayoga*), one induces the state without mental activity (*acittaka*). Within the state without mental activity...
It causes the body to be peaceful and harmonious. Precisely at the time of this state of mindlessness, because the body is peaceful and harmonious, it is called "concentration" (*samādhi*).

Therefore, the treatise says: "Because it causes the body to be peaceful and harmonious, it is also called concentration. Since the mind also attains peace and harmony after the state of mindlessness, this peace and harmony of the body is termed "concentration.
Thus, the two mindless concentrations are called "mindless" (*acittaka*) in the sense of a descriptive compound (*karmadhāraya*).
These two types of meditative absorption (samāpatti) are also explained by way of the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. It is appropriate that absorption is essentially a state of mind;

since "concentration" (*samādhi*) is one of the five object-specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-citta*), it is termed "absorption. Because there is a subtle, extremely subtle state of mind prior to the attainment of the mindless state, it induces that mindlessness.
Thus, it is "the mindlessness of absorption" or "the absorption of mindlessness," which is explained by way of the *śeṣa* (possessive) compound. Absorption is precisely what precedes it.
There are meditative attainments with mind. If one speaks of the two mindless attainments, they are established as such by virtue of having emerged from cessation.

If one speaks of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is so named because all [mental factors] are extinguished therein; the same applies to the name "attainment of non-conception" (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*).

Regarding the term "fruition of non-conception" (*asaṃjñivipāka*), it functions both as a descriptive compound (*karmadhāraya*) and as a possessive compound (*tatpuruṣa*): "non-conception" refers to that very heaven.

In the middle [of the compound], regarding the indeterminate seeds of names and phrases (*nāma-pada*) of the sixth consciousness: when they do not arise as actual manifestations (*samudācāra*), they are termed "non-conceptualization" (*asaṃjñika*).

Because these seeds of non-conceptualization depend upon the eighth retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), this is an *upapadaka* (dependent) compound meaning "the retribution of non-conceptualization.
Furthermore, because the indeterminate seeds of names and phrases of the sixth consciousness are produced by other karma, they are themselves retribution (*vipāka*).
The compound "the perception of this" (*tad-ālambana-saṃjñā*) is an *upapada-karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative) compound.
*Cheng weishi lun shu chao*, Scroll Two; *Cheng weishi lun shu chao*, Scroll Three.
Composed by Lingtai of Beijing.

The second treatise states: "There are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned. There are three conditioned phenomena, which are the conditioned entities that possess these characteristics (*lakṣya*).
These three conditioned factors are the characteristics themselves (*lakṣaṇa*), namely: arising (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), and change (*anyathātva*).

The commentary states that when "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) is mentioned repeatedly, it is intended to reveal that the conditioned is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing; it does not indicate whether the conditioned is good or evil.
The sub-commentary says, "It is not like a young girl, who indicates her own goodness or evil. The explanation states: "If a young girl has a handsome face and head..."

If one gives birth to sons and daughters who are handsome and have good names, it is because this young girl has a beautiful face; if she gives birth to sons and daughters who are ugly, it is because her face is ugly.

This is how one can discern the goodness or badness of the children. Regarding the two explanations in the *Abhidharmakośa*, the first states: "Excluding those who abide [in the intermediate state]... and so forth, up to:
"...for the sake of inducing revulsion, they are explained together with the 'dissimilar'. Question: What is the difference between the assertions of these two masters? Answer: Indeed...

Regarding the initial master’s explanation of the three characteristics: sometimes the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) is excluded, and only the three characteristics of arising (*utpāda*), change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*nirodha*) are taught, as stated in the commentary regarding the exclusion of abiding. This is because, at times, the characteristic of abiding is simply another name for the characteristic of change;

thus, abiding is itself change. For example, "arising" (*utpāda*) is also called "origination" (*utpatti*); "arising" is a synonym for "origination. Likewise, "cessation" (*nirodha*) is also termed... [the characteristic of destruction].
Cessation (*nirodha*) is also called "extinction" (*kṣaya*); "extinction" is simply another name for cessation. Now, this "abiding" (*sthiti*) and "alteration" (*anyathātva*) are likewise:
it is called both "alteration" and "abiding-alteration. Therefore, since abiding is a specific designation for alteration, the Sūtra mentions only three characteristics.
The second master, however, speaks of abiding and alteration together, yet does not state that abiding is a specific designation for alteration.

This is because it is not stated that [the unconditioned] excludes abiding (*sthiti*). Thus, the two masters differ. Regarding the claim that the unconditioned possesses its own characteristic of abiding:

if one asserts that abiding is an active characteristic of the conditioned, then even if one says that the abiding of the unconditioned is called "unconditioned," it would still be a characteristic of the conditioned.
The Commentary (*śūtra*) says: "It is like showing Kālī together with Śrī. The Explanation (*vyākhyā*) says:

In the West, Kālī is spoken of in a manner similar to how people speak of a "red nose" [as a sign of good fortune]. In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is said that the goddess Puṇyavatī (Gongde Tian) is dark;

here, the goddess Puṇyavatī is a metaphor for saṃsāra, Kālī is a metaphor for death, and Śrī is a metaphor for birth. In this context, they are metaphors for subsistence and change: Śrī is a metaphor for subsistence.
Regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): the "Black-Eared Woman" (*Kālakanyā*) serves as an analogy for the distinct characteristics.

Specifically, the statement that "the arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) can also be discerned" is the scriptural passage itself. At that time, when this sutra was being taught, the Buddha [addressed] Nanda;

he spoke these words of the Dharma to Nanda because Nanda had taken a beautiful wife, developed a mind of attachment, and refused to renounce the world. The Buddha said: "Conditioned phenomena arise moment by moment (*kṣaṇe kṣaṇe*)."

Moment by moment, there is arising and ceasing; for this, the four characteristics are taught. The origination of conditioned phenomena can be understood, as can their cessation, duration, and change.
"Origination" refers to the characteristic of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*); "cessation" refers to the characteristic of destruction (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*). This is the summary verse (*uddāna*).

This "cloud-gathering giving" (yúnjíshī) carries the meaning of gathering and dispersing. By bestowing it upon sentient beings—that is, when a disciple preaches the Dharma of arising and ceasing—the intention is to cause those disciples to practice the contemplation of impermanence and to cultivate weariness toward birth and death; this is precisely the practice of impermanence within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

As stated in [the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*] 81: "Regarding that which has arising and ceasing, within 'arising' (*utpāda*), one already encompasses the three [phases] of birth (*jāti*), abiding (*sthiti*), and change (*anyathātva*). Birth...

The three characteristics—arising, change, and duration—are able to give rise to all phenomena. Cessation is the characteristic of extinction; therefore, within arising and cessation, the other four characteristics are also subsumed.

If, by means of these characteristics, one gives rise to contemplation of revulsion up to the point of detachment and liberation—if the disciples give rise to contemplation of revulsion, are able to leave behind craving and attain liberation—then that which is liberated is precisely the attainment of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*).

Because it ceases, the sutra refers to it as one of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). This is not, however, identical to the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) among those four, for it also includes arising (*jāti*).
As for the statement that "stability" (*sthiti*) and "change" (*anyathātva*) are spoken of in conjunction with arising because they exist within the same temporal period (*adhvan*):

the "impermanence" (*anityatā*) previously described as a single characteristic is not itself the four characteristics; rather, it is impermanence in its general sense. Thus, the four characteristics are collectively designated by the name "impermanence."

"Constant" refers to what was previously stated as "not non-constant. Therefore, it is said that within "arising" (utpāda), the three phases of arising, abiding, and change (sthiti-vyaya) are subsumed.
This is because abiding and change are explained in conjunction with arising; since they belong to the same temporal period, they are collectively subsumed under the name "arising.
As for why it is said that "arising is not eternally existent," and why it is called "arising-and-ceasing" (utpāda-nirodha): ceasing (nirodha) is the fourth [phase].

Because it is the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) among the [four] characteristics. Since arising and cessation together encompass all four characteristics, their collective designation is "impermanence" (*anityatā*).
Therefore, this impermanence does not merely refer to the characteristic of cessation among the four; it also encompasses all four characteristics.

That which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) exists and is eternally existent, and thus it does not become like the horns of a rabbit. That which is non-existent is eternally non-existent, and thus it does not arise.

Regarding the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that "up to the establishment of the category of cessation (*nirodha-varga*)," if birth (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), and change (*anyathātva*) are spoken of in a single location, this characteristic of duration and change is established as a partial category of birth because it is manifested by the characteristic of birth. Thus, one part is established as the category of birth. "Category" (*varga*) refers to a class or type.

These characteristics of birth, duration, and change are precisely the class-nature (*prakṛti*) and the extracted characteristics (*uddhṛta-lakṣaṇa*) belonging to the characteristic of birth; thus, one part is established as an extracted category. "Category" (*varga*) refers to...
The categories herein are the same as those in the *Saṃgītiparyāya*. Furthermore, regarding the reason for explaining the characteristics from impermanence up to the pair:
if one speaks of the characteristic of impermanence, it is precisely for the sake of explaining the two characteristics of arising and ceasing within this context.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "It appears similar to the second master of the *Abhidharmakośa*, yet the worlds are not the same. The Explanation says: "Regarding 'yet the worlds are not the same':
in the Mahāyāna, arising, abiding, and change are explained together; thus, their combined explanation appears similar to that of the second master of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
However, regarding 'yet the worlds are not the same': in the Mahāyāna, it is taught that arising, abiding, and change belong to the present world, whereas cessation [belongs to the past]."

The characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) exists in the past. According to the Sarvāstivāda of the Hīnayāna, it is said that the characteristic of arising exists in the future, while the three characteristics of duration (*sthiti*), change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*nirodha*) exist in the present.

Regarding the statement that the four characteristics are taught because their functional utility is fourfold, this refers to the subsequent treatise which explains the four characteristics for itself:

namely, that "arising" indicates that a dharma previously non-existent now exists, and so forth. Furthermore, it is said that the initial [moment of] existence is called "arising," and subsequently...

The phrases "the nameless" and "cessation," etc., all serve as explanations of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the bowl of Tiṣya and so forth, the present argument establishes an inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntika*):
Is it because the substance of form and mind possesses the sixth case (genitive) that one says the characteristics of the conditioned have no separate substance?
Or is it like the robe of Devadatta, where because there is a sixth case, one says the characteristics of the conditioned do have a separate [substance]?
Is it the substance? Or is it that the substance of the name itself—the solid nature of earth—is what is being scrutinized?
In the *Abhidharmakośa*, it refers to the substance of the name itself; in this treatise, however, it speaks of the substance of form and mind.

Thus, [the characteristics such as] arising and so forth are established as not being separate from the dharma. Furthermore, the formal argument states: "The characteristics of the conditioned certainly have no distinct substance. This is because they exist.
Therefore, just as with the essence of a name, the *Śāstra* states:

"To negate arising and so forth while asserting that there is definitely a distinct dharma which is categorically contradictory [to them]—this refers to the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) which are definitively without a separate essence.
The use of the sixth case (genitive) is like the essence of form (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*)."
The *Śāstra* says: "The essence of a Mahāsattva is the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity); the marks of a Mahāsattva refer to the thirty-two marks. The commentary explains:

If, according to the Sarvāstivāda, the essence of the *sabhāgatā* of a Mahāsattva is substantially existent (*dravyasat*), then the *sabhāgatā* serves as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the thirty-two marks serve as the characterized (*lakṣya*).

This follows the same principle as [the case where] birth (*jāti*) and so forth serve as the defining characteristics and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) serve as the characterized; the defining characteristics are all [simultaneously] present.

Because it is established as a conventional designation, it is established. If one takes the thirty-two marks as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the commonality of the group (*nikāyasabhāga*) as the characterized (*lakṣya*), then by that same analogy, [the case of] birth and so forth would not be established. How could it be that the defining characteristic is real while the characterized is conventional?

Therefore, the commonality of the group is taken as the defining characteristic, and the thirty-two marks are taken as the characterized—just as smoke indicates fire, where fire is the defining characteristic and smoke is the indicator.
[The thirty-two marks] serve as the characterized (lakṣya). The *Śū* states: "The Mahāyāna Sūtra school does not admit that [the marks] are known by what they characterize. The *Jie* explains:

"In the Mahāyāna, the commonality (sabhāgatā) of the Great Beings (*mahāsattva*) is a provisional [construction], whereas the thirty-two marks themselves are substantially existent (*dravyasat*). This is like the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*)."
White is real; all others are conventional designations. If the Sautrāntikas fundamentally do not establish the existence of *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneity), the commentary states:
"Therefore, in the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is countered with the objection: 'The characteristics of a Great Being differ from those of other Great Beings, and so forth.'"
...up to the point where he raises the objection of an "undetermined fallacy" (*anaikāntika*). In that treatise, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu clarifies the Sautrāntika critique of the Sarvāstivāda:
"The horns, peaks, hooves, dewlaps, and tails are not different [from the cow]; among these, the characteristics are not the marks of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

Being different from the marks of a Great Being, they are not different from the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*). The characterized (*lakṣya*) is equal to the characteristics themselves, just as within the characteristics there are five kinds of dharmas. First, if..."
If the central horn-tip is fine and small, it is auspicious within that context; if the central horn-tip is coarse and large, it is inauspicious within that context. Regarding the "two peaks":

this refers to peaks upon the head of the central [horn], like those in the *Wuchuanfang* translation of the *Mahā-*. This is auspicious; the "original" within the center is inauspicious. Regarding the "three truths":
if the original [portion] of the central hoof is large, it is auspicious within the center; if the central [portion] is thin, the hoof-kernel is inauspicious.
Regarding the four types of "bad" [omens], those that are head-downward or tail-downward belong to the level of the vehicle. Regarding the five types of "good" [omens]:

if the tail is level with the middle of the body and the tail feathers grow long enough to hang down to the ground, this constitutes the "good" type. If these five characteristics are reversed, they constitute the "bad" type.
These five characteristics are not different from the "Middle" (the ultimate reality). Now, regarding this "Fullness," we respond to your objection:

for you, Mahāsattva, the characteristics and the characterized phenomena of conditioned things do not possess a separate substantial entity. This is because of the word "identical" (*eva*). It is like the substance of form and mind.

Suppose you were to formulate a syllogism as follows: "The characteristics of a Mahāsattva and the characteristics of conditioned things must possess a separate substantial entity, because of the word 'identical,' just like [the substance of] form and mind."

Regarding the fire and its smoke, I now present this as an inconclusive [reason] (anaikāntika): Is it like the statement that the substance of form and mind exists, such that the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa) have no separate substance?
Or is it like the statement that the marks of fire and smoke exist, such that the marks of a Great Man do have a separate substance?
These two difficulties apply to both positions. As for the "separate Great Man," he is the Wheel-turning King (cakravartin) and the Buddha; the Wheel-turning King is able to govern universally.
The four continents are called the "Great Being" (*mahāsattva*). The characteristics of a Great Being are precisely the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśan-lakṣaṇa*).
To say that it is not the case that everything is non-existent means that smoke and fire are distinct in terms of the remote object (*ālambana*) and the subject (*ālambaka*).

However, since the Master of this treatise also maintains [positions] such as "it should be so," up to "existence and non-existence," this passage constitutes a critique by the Sarvāstivāda against the Mahāyāna. That...

The Refutation says: If your Mahāyāna school maintains that there are only conventional (prajñapti) four characteristics upon conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma), then there should likewise be conventional four characteristics upon unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).

If the Master [Dignāga] were to claim that while conventional four characteristics are established upon conditioned phenomena, no conventional four characteristics exist upon unconditioned phenomena, our own school would respond in the same way:
that while real (dravya) four characteristics are established upon the conditioned, they do not exist upon the unconditioned.

Regarding the phrase "because of characteristics": as for the statement that "there are also those that exist," this is because, in the case of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one does not establish the existence of four real characteristics;

rather, it is because [the unconditioned] possesses both existence and non-existence. As for the statement that "conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) possess transformation," and so forth, down to the question of what dharma establishes a provisional characteristic—this passage represents the Mahāyāna master’s explanation to the other Hīnayāna [opponent]. However, conditioned phenomena do indeed possess transformation and are manifold.
Because of their differentiation, the four provisional characteristics are established upon the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not undergo transformation and lacks such manifold differentiation, the four provisional characteristics are not established upon the unconditioned.

Furthermore, since there is no arising, aging, or cessation for the unconditioned, these three dharmas should likewise not be established as the characterizers (*lakṣaṇa*) upon the unconditioned; rather, the unconditioned is designated as the characterized (*lakṣya*), its very essence being [the absence of these].
Regarding the passage "there is no arising or ceasing, up to 'this meaning should be contemplated,'" this text represents the Mahāyāna interpretation.

For the essence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has neither arising nor ceasing, and furthermore, it is not a plurality of dharmas; because it is merely a distinction of states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*), one does not establish provisional characteristics (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*) upon the unconditioned.
Since the essence of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) possesses arising and ceasing and consists of a plurality of dharmas, one establishes provisional [characteristics] upon the conditioned.

This refers to the "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*). The outsider further says: "Even so, that which is conjoined with the characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*)—this passage establishes the reasoning and provides the explanation of the Sarvāstivāda masters.

However, because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) fall within the three periods of time, the conditioned phenomena that are characterized are made to exist by the characteristics such as arising (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), and so forth.
But the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not fall within the three periods of time; therefore, it is said that unconditioned phenomena [do not possess these characteristics].
"That which is capable of combining with arising, abiding, and so forth—this [unconditioned] also cannot [combine], up to and including the point that it is not established as combining.

This passage constitutes the Mahāyāna critique of the Sarvāstivāda: conditioned phenomena fall within the temporal world (*adhvan*) and thus combine with the four characteristics such as falling into the temporal world;
if unconditioned phenomena do not fall within the temporal world, they should instead combine with non-arising, non-ceasing, and other non-temporal characteristics. Great!

"Even the vehicle [of the Mahāyāna] must likewise not fall into the world of conventional designations (*prajñapti*). This passage represents the Sarvāstivāda school. They challenge the Mahāyāna by saying:
'The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not fall into the world; because it does not fall into the world, it lacks conventional designations.

Since the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) falls [into the world], it lacks conventional designations. This objection is incorrect. [If so,] how can one even establish conventional designations? This passage is...
This is the Mahāyāna interpretation. If there were numerous distinct dharmas, and furthermore, if they were worldly conditioned dharmas, one could establish provisional characteristics for them.
However, because [this dharma] lacks numerous distinctions and does not fall within the category of worldly unconditioned dharmas, such characteristics are not established.
The Commentary states: "The same applies to the inferential cognition (*anumāna*) regarding the three functions of abiding and so forth. The formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:

At the time when your function of abiding (*sthiti*) occurs, the functions of change (*anyathātva*) and cessation (*vināśa*) should also arise and be manifest as existing entities; for example, like [the function of] abiding itself. Furthermore, at the time when your change and cessation arise and function, the functions of arising (*utpāda*) and abiding should also arise and be manifest as existing entities;

for example, like the functions of change and cessation according to the other school. This refers to the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and their functions as held by the ancient Sarvāstivāda masters.
"Contradiction between the preceding and succeeding [phases] means they do not arise; even to the point of not reaching the preceding dharma.

According to the ancient Sarvāstivāda masters, because the functions of the four characteristics are mutually contradictory, they establish the four characteristics as being distributed horizontally across the preceding and succeeding moments, arising separately in the future. First, the characteristic of arising (jāti-lakṣaṇa) arises;

when it passes into the present moment, the characteristic of abiding (sthiti-lakṣaṇa) first arises; next, the characteristic of change (anyathātva-lakṣaṇa) reaches its turn; and finally, the characteristic of cessation (nirodha-lakṣaṇa) arises. Thus, the four characteristics occur sequentially.
[The objection] arises as follows: Those such as the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu challenge the ancient Sarvāstivādins, saying:

"If you admit that within matter (*rūpa*) the smallest unit is a single atom (*paramāṇu*) which lacks spatial parts, and that within time the shortest duration is a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), how can the three characteristics [of arising, abiding, and ceasing] occur sequentially?
If it is granted that the present lasts for only a single moment, yet the three characteristics are admitted to arise sequentially, then the same would apply to matter."

The smallest unit is a single atom (*paramāṇu*). It follows that this atom must possess spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*). Seeing that the ancient masters had been subjected to such criticism, the Master of Right Reasoning (*Nyāyācārya*) offered this defense:
"The three characteristics—abiding, change, and cessation—arise simultaneously and remain firm at one time.

If the characteristic of abiding is present, it can induce the subsequent moment and its superior outflow-fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*); if the characteristic of change weakens its power, it can induce the subsequent moment and its inferior [outflow-fruit]."
The outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) is the dharma of cessation. Therefore, it is known that in the present moment, the three characteristics arise simultaneously.

Regarding the term "outflowing fruit," it refers to that which is either equal to or superior [to its cause] as an outflowing fruit. For example, an inferior dharma acts as a cause capable of inducing an inferior or medium dharma;
however, an inferior dharma acting as a cause can only induce a superior fruit. It is absolutely impossible for a superior dharma to act as a cause and [induce] an inferior fruit.

This is the fruit of the inferior grade. If one asks whether its distinct characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and its characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) can induce a concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), the answer is no.

The Sarvāstivāda masters say that within the future world, there also exist the four characteristics—arising (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*nirodha*)—as substantial entities.
However, they do not separately exercise their functional activity. Nevertheless, these four characteristics, upon passing from the present into the past, also exist within the past world.

Regarding the four characteristics—arising, duration, change, and cessation—their essential nature persists and does not perish; thus, within the present state, they exercise their functions of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
However, when it is said that a future dharma intends to reach the present, it is the characteristic of arising (*jāti*) that possesses its function.
Once it reaches the present moment, it simultaneously possesses the functions of abiding, changing, and ceasing. Although these causes differ, [the characteristics are nonetheless simultaneous].
The characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) comes forth with force and is able to project future outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Its simultaneous [characteristics] and its distinct cessation (*vināśa*) are all likewise able to project future outflow fruits; however, the characteristic of duration is predominant.

Furthermore, let us discuss the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*). It can produce a concordant result (*niṣyanda-phala*) that is simultaneous with itself, as well as those that perish at different times or exist in the future;

all of these induce concordant results in the future. For example, when the four characteristics of the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) are present, they are able to induce a ripened result (*vipāka-phala*) in the future.

It can also induce future states such as faith; thus, there is a fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). Regarding the simultaneous and non-simultaneous characteristics, they are distinct and possess efficacy that can weaken their power.
The characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) possesses the power to cause cessation, for it has the efficacy to extinguish the essence of the dharma.

The three—stasis (*sthiti*), change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*nirodha*)—all exist simultaneously and are not divided by temporal sequence. If this is so, should the characteristic of cessation not itself cease, and stasis not [cease]?
Regarding the phrase "because they are contradictory": this must be asked concerning whether this "abiding" (sthiti) belongs to the preceding clause or the following clause (and so forth).

As for the statement "now, that which is of the same substance is also inherently present," the Sarvāstivādins maintain that within the three time periods, there are the four characteristics—arising, abiding, change, and cessation—as their essential nature.
Among these, arising, abiding, change, and cessation manifest their activity only in the present. "Conditions" refers to the other three conditions.

Regarding the three conditions: namely, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). As for the word "condition" (*pratyaya*) used above, it refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); thus, three are mentioned rather than four.

[The statement that] "the substance of the seed is inherently existent, and so forth, that it logically should not arise," etc., [is as follows: [Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* or a related treatise concerning the nature of seeds (*bīja*) and their arising.]

This passage constitutes the Sarvāstivāda’s critique of the Mahāyāna. If [the opponent] argues that because [things] are provisional, they only arise when real conditions converge—this is precisely the Sarvāstivāda’s refutation of the Proponent’s [Mahāyānist] defense and their establishment of their own position through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If the Proponent says: "Because seeds are provisional, they require the convergence of conditions before they can produce [their fruit]; my school is likewise: all phenomena are real..."
Therefore, [the effect] must depend upon conditions to arise. [The opponent asks: "If your real entity (dravya-dharma) actually exists as a condition, why does it not arise at all times?
Since the conditions for your [entity] exist constantly, why does it not arise instantaneously? This passage represents the Hīnayāna challenging the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, it says: "How can your real dharma serve as an analogy [for our case]? However, this point should be considered. The explanation states: Regarding that external objection, since the seed is constant...
There are seeds of the three realms that simultaneously produce the seeds of the five destinies; these arise in accordance with the mind. The commentary explains:

although the immediate cause (the seed) exists, if external conditions do not converge, it cannot produce [the result]. Furthermore, since this [external condition] is insubstantial and hollow, while the mind is substantial, how could it serve as a precedent?

Therefore, it is said that this meaning is to be considered. Regarding the analogy to the substance of the immediate causes and conditions: the commentary explains that the Sarvāstivādins maintain [this view] regarding the past.
The dharma of cessation (*vigama-dharma*) serves as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for past dharmas.

Regarding the statement in the commentary that "causes have degrees of proximity and distance, and the same applies to conditioned dharmas (*pratyaya-dharma*)," the proximate causes are namely: the associated cause (*samprayukta-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
Vipāka (maturation) and sabhāga (homogeneous)—these five causes all possess the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). The remote cause refers to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*);
the proximate condition refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); and the remote conditions refer to the remaining three conditions.

The Commentary states: Since there exists a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and because it is held that a single entity can arise over many moments, past dharmas serve as homogeneous causes for present dharmas;
past dharmas serve as homogeneous causes for future dharmas; and [present dharmas serve as homogeneous causes for] future dharmas.
A past dharma does not act as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for [past dharmas]. Why? Because the effect would precede the cause.
A present dharma does not act as a homogeneous cause for a presently existing [dharma], because a present dharma lasts for only a single moment;
therefore, this is impossible. A present dharma acts as a homogeneous cause for future dharmas. If it were otherwise, there would be no homogeneous causes in the future world.

By means of these dharmas, this homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) has not yet arisen; it shall only arise for the five afflictions of the meditative states (dhyāna-kleśa), each acting as its own cause, with the ground of its own realm and its own arising level serving as the cause.
Other matter and mind serve as homogeneous causes, just as in the case of the present mind-king (citta-rāja).
It is capable of inducing the five aggregates of the future.
The commentary states: "The same applies to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Here, the inference can be understood through its contrapositive. The explanation says: "Your conditioned phenomena..."
It should follow that [unconditioned phenomena] are subject to arising and so forth, because their combined essence is eternally present— just as you claim unconditioned phenomena arise and so forth,
because their combined essence is eternally present, just like conditioned phenomena.
The *Śāstra* says: "The term 'non-eternal' (anitya) is used to exclude unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). The commentary explains:

If one does not say "non-eternal," but speaks only of the past and future, they would certainly not be substantially existent, because it is argued that they are not present. Thus, unconditioned phenomena do not fall within the three periods of time;

consequently, the subsequent [category of] unconditioned phenomena becomes indeterminate. This is because it is argued that, like unconditioned phenomena, they are not present. Now, as for the past and future periods...

If [the opponent] asserts that [past and future entities] truly exist as real, yet they are not manifest—just like flowers in the sky—and thus combines them with the past and future worlds, is it not the case that they lack true existence?

If [the proponent] offers "non-eternality" alone as the reason, without stating that they are not manifest to others, then the opponent may raise the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*), asking:

"Is it because the present world is non-eternal that it is truly existent, and thereby you intend for the past and future worlds to be truly existent? Or is it because they are non-eternal, like flowers in the sky and the like, that they are [unreal]?"
Therefore, it is asked: "Are the past and future not substantially existent? Thus, both terms—“neither present” (*na pratyutpanna*) and “not eternal” (*na nitya*)—are used.
The term “not eternal” excludes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), while “neither present” excludes the present.
The Commentary states: "As for the claim that the essence of arising and ceasing are mutually contradictory," [it asks:

"If arising can be contradictory, how is it that the Hīnayāna teaches that the Great Vehicle’s arising can produce the Small Vehicle’s ceasing, and even that the Great Vehicle’s ceasing can produce the Small Vehicle’s arising? [It answers:

"If within the Mahāyāna, the very essence of the characteristic of arising were the characteristic of ceasing, then existence would be non-existence; this would constitute a contradiction between existence and non-existence. Such an arising could not produce..."
Cessation. This cessation cannot give rise to prior arising. According to the Sarvāstivāda school, the dharmas of arising and cessation both exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*).

Since dharmas that exist substantially do not contradict one another, it is said that the characteristic of arising can produce the existence of cessation, and the characteristic of cessation can produce the characteristic of arising, and so forth.
Thus, the characteristic of cessation is the "capable dharma" (*śaktadharma*), while arising is the "agent of production" (*janaka*) within the world. Arising...
There is functional efficacy. Up to the point where it is said that "only the present [dharma] possesses the function of grasping a fruit," the *Śū* (Commentary) states:

"However, the masters of the *Nyāyānusāra* [hold that] future [dharmas]... This passage represents the masters of the *Nyāyānusāra* establishing a distinct interpretation to rescue the ancient Sarvāstivāda position.
They assert: "The five [causes] grasp a fruit; only two [causes] give a fruit, and these two also possess both functions."
Regarding causes: first, those that take up results exclusively in the past; second, those that take up results exclusively in the present.

Among the six causes, the five—namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), and the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)—are able to take up results only when they are in the present state, and not through the past or future.
However, the enabling cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is excluded because it is indeterminate. Second, those that are capable of both giving and taking results.
That is to say, the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

These two causes, with respect to the present mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and mental factors (*caitta*), when viewed in relation to one another in the present, act as the past and present for the two causes;

these are precisely the two causes of similar type (*sabhāga-hetu*) and universal (*sarvatraga-hetu*). If these two causes are immediate [to the effect], then the present fruit is also given its fruit in the present. If outflows (*āsrava*) arise, then it is the present...
Regarding the appropriation of the fruit (*phalādāna*): the past gives the fruit. That which gives [the fruit] exclusively in the past is the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).

Only the present appropriates the fruit, and it is the past that gives the fruit. As for this ripening cause, it necessarily does not give the fruit in the present, because once an action has been performed, its result is not experienced in the same world-moment.

This is also like when one enters the mindless meditative attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*); at that time, this [attainment] causes the mind to cease, yet it is able to appropriate the fruit, and subsequently, upon emerging from it...
The concentrated mind is able to bestow its fruit. To speak of "taking the fruit" means that it takes [the fruit] for the sake of that seed; thus it is called "taking the fruit.

Just as when a person borrows an object from another, if they bestow [a return], it is called "bestowing the fruit" because they are recompensing for that effort, just as a person sends an object back to the other.
When the characteristic of arising in the future occurs, the ripening cause bestows its fruit only when it is in the past.
However, the ancient Sarvāstivāda masters maintained that within the past, there exists the activity of producing a fruit— namely, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*),

the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in its entirety, and one portion each of the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) which causes the outflows (*āsrava*) to be grasped.

All of these possess the activity of yielding a fruit within the past; furthermore, you maintain that within the future, there are three dharmas—the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), light (*āloka*), and the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*)—which possess activity within the future.

Regarding this, the Sautrāntikas, Vasubandhu Bodhisattva, and the ancient Sarvāstivādins say: "In your system of the three time periods, [the characteristics such as] the characteristic of arising and light..."

If these three dharmas—namely, the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñānakṣānti*)—have functional activity within the future, then the outsiders also claim that within the future there are the characteristics of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), light, and the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*); these three dharmas likewise have functional activity within the future.
Regarding this, the Sautrāntikas and the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu refute the ancient Sarvāstivādins, saying: "You maintain [the existence of] the three times..."
Regarding phenomena (*dharma*): if their activity has not yet arisen, they are called "future"; if their activity is currently arising, they are called "present";

if their activity has already ceased, they are called "past. You maintain that the past possesses the activity of giving a fruit, and that the three factors—such as future birth and so forth—possess activity.
Since the past and future worlds thus possess activity, and because those past and future worlds possess activity, [they must exist].

It should be called "present," not "past" or "future. When the masters of correct reasoning (Nyāyācāryas) saw that the ancient masters had been thus challenged, they carefully examined the past and future times and found that there exists within them "functional activity" (*kāritra*). They then offered this defense:

that which gives rise to a fruit in the past time is merely termed a "capacity" (*śakti*), not "functional activity. Likewise, the three factors such as "arising" (*jāti*) in the future time are also merely termed [capacities].

"Efficiency" (*śakti*) is not called "activity" (*kāritra*). If it were to exercise activity, it would exist only in the present time; taking an effect within the present time is precisely what is called "activity.

If, within the present time, the associated (*samprayukta*), co-existent (*sahabhū*), homogeneous (*sabhāga*), and pervasive (*sarvatraga*) [causes], as well as a portion of the universal (*sarvatraga*) cause, give their fruit, these are also called "efficiency," but not "activity. This, too, is not correct. Why?

"Knowing that all dharmas of coming and going possess functional capacity (*sāmarthya*). This passage represents the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*) challenging the Sthavira (the "Proponent of Correct Principle"):

"If you claim that within the future world there exists the functional capacity of the three dharmas, such as arising (*jāti*), and that within the past world there exists a portion of the universal (*sarvatraga*) and homogeneous (*sabhāga*) causes, as well as the entirety of the retributive (*vipāka*) cause, and that the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) possesses the efficacy for yielding a fruit..."
As for "capacity": why is it not understood that all phenomena arising in future lives possess capacity?

Why is it asserted exclusively that the three factors—future birth and so forth—possess capacity, as well as the remaining capacity of past maturation causes (*vipāka-hetu*) and the like, which can produce results that are non-functional (*akāritra*)?
Furthermore, these are also non-functional; this applies even to all past phenomena, which should constantly [produce results].
Regarding the "result": in this passage, the author of the treatise further clarifies that [opponent's] position and refutes it.
If you say that in the future, the three factors such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth do not constitute actual activity (*kāritra*), but are merely termed "capacities" (*śakti*);

and if you say that in the past, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), the divisible [cause], and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and others are able to produce results, yet these are not actual activities—[then your position is untenable].
As for the term "function" (*śakti*): since all future phenomena possess function, it would follow that these future phenomena should arise at all times.

How then could there be any phenomena within the future that do not arise? Furthermore, regarding past causes such as the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), which possess the function of yielding their fruit, it follows that all past phenomena likewise possess [such function].

Regarding "efficacy" (*kāritra*): all dharmas are capable of yielding results. Why, then, are only the *vipāka-hetu* (maturation cause), the *sabhāga-hetu* (homogeneous cause), and so forth specifically designated as "yielding results"?
If one speaks of "activity" (*vṛtti*), this refers to the present; if one speaks of "efficacy," it refers to the past and future.

If one claims that what possesses efficacy in the present is designated as "past" or "future," this passage constitutes the Master of the Treatise’s critique, clarifying the distinction between these two concepts.

If you say that there is "taking of the fruit" (*phalādāna*) in the present—wherein "taking of the fruit" is defined as activity (*kāritra*), whereas the past and future lack such taking—and that although the past possesses "giving of the fruit" (*phaladāna*), it is merely termed a "capacity" (*śakti*);

we then raise this objection: If the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) established for the present must be fully present, then the simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and those parts of them that arise in immediate succession would all, being in the present, be capable of giving their fruit. Since [the giving of fruit]...

Regarding what is called "functional capacity" (*śakti*): if these [factors] currently possess functional capacity, they ought to be designated as belonging to the past or future, and not to the present time.

If it is argued that the state of "arising" (*jāti*) is termed "activity" (*kāritra*) because it grasps its fruit (*phala*), whereas the "maturation" (*vipāka*) that has ceased cannot grasp its fruit and is thus merely "functional capacity"—and therefore not of the present—this commentary is indeed erroneous.
If the author of this commentary were to say [that this is the Sarvāstivāda view], then... [the text continues with the refutation].

There are many schools of thought. To claim that the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) is able to grasp the fruit while the characteristic of cessation (*bhaṅga-lakṣaṇa*) is not, is incorrect.

If one explains the four characteristics in a general sense, it is said that the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) causes future dharmas to transition and flow into the present, while the characteristic of abiding [maintains them] in the present.

The phase of arising (*jāti*) can project subsequent moments and so forth as superior outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*). The phase of difference (*jarā*), by weakening its power, can project subsequent moments as inferior outflow fruits.
The phase of cessation (*nirodha*) is that which extinguishes the dharma. Can it then be said that the phase of duration (*sthiti*) projects outflow fruits?
Here, it is clarified that regarding the grasping of fruits, as explained when refuting the Sarvāstivāda school: all three phases—duration, change, and cessation—are capable of grasping fruits.
How is this known? That school asserts that when a single dharma of form arises from the future and flows into the present, there are nine dharmas:

namely, the essential body of the primary dharma (*mūla-dharma*), along with the great arising, the great abiding, the great change, the great cessation, the minor arising, the minor change, the minor cessation, and the minor abiding.
However, each of these four great characteristics (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*) possesses three names; for instance, if one takes the great characteristic of arising, it is also called...

The primary characteristics (mūla-lakṣaṇa) are termed "primary arising," "primary change," and "primary cessation. As for the secondary four characteristics (anuloma-lakṣaṇa), they follow the primary four characteristics;
thus, the primary and secondary are paired. These two—the primary four characteristics—are simply called the "four characteristics," meaning they are merely arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
If one considers the four minor characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) in relation to the four major characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), each of these minor characteristics receives its subsequent name:

namely, "birth-of-birth" (*jāti-jāti*), "staying-of-staying" (*sthiti-sthiti*), "alteration-of-alteration" (*jarā-jarā*), and "destruction-of-destruction" (*anityatā-anityatā*). This constitutes the correspondence between the singular and the plural. If one considers the four major characteristics in relation to the four major characteristics themselves, they are simply called the "four major characteristics.

The characteristics that follow them (the minor ones) are called the "minor characteristics. This constitutes the correspondence between the major and the minor. If one considers the fundamental dharma (*mūladharma*) in relation to itself, it constitutes the whole.

The essence of the dharma consists of four causes. Regarding these four sets of four causes: they are the four minor characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Because they lack power, they cannot act as causes to produce the fundamental dharma;
thus, they are called the "four non-causes. The four causes are the four major characteristics, which are able to produce the essence of the fundamental dharma.

This means that great arising (*mahā-utpāda*) can cause the essential nature of the primary dharma to arise; great abiding (*mahā-sthiti*) can cause the essential nature of the primary dharma to abide;

great alteration (*mahā-anyathātva*) can cause the essential nature of the primary dharma to alter; and great cessation (*mahā-nirodha*) can cause the essential nature of the primary dharma to cease. If one considers great arising in relation to the eight factors, it is both co-existent (*sahabhū*) and a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
This great arising can produce great abiding, great alteration, and great cessation, as well as the essential nature of the primary dharma itself.

It is capable of producing the four minor characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). If the eight dharmas are considered in relation to the major production (*mahā-jāti*), there are five causes and three non-causes.

As for the three non-causes, they refer to the minor difference (*paratva*) and the minor cessation (*nirodha*); these three minor characteristics are all incapable of producing the major production, and therefore they are not causes.
As for the five causes: first, the essential nature of the dharma produces the major production; second, the major duration (*sthiti*) is able to sustain the major production.
The three great *asādhāraṇa-śaktis* give rise to the great *mahābhūta*. The four great [elements] that cease can cause the cessation of the great [elements] that arise.

The five minor [factors] that arise give rise to the five minor [factors] that arise, which in turn can give rise to the great [factors] that arise. These five factors can serve as causes for the great arising; therefore, they are called "causes" (*hetu*).

If one considers the great abiding in relation to the eight factors, it is necessarily a co-existent [cause]. Because the great abiding is a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), it is able to cause the eight factors to abide. If...

The "Great Abiding" (mahā-sthiti) depends upon eight factors. These consist of five causes and three non-causes. Regarding the three non-causes, they are: minor change (pariṇāma), minor cessation (nirodha), and minor abiding (sthiti).
These three minor characteristics lack the power to produce or sustain the "Great" [characteristics]. The five causes are:

the primary dharma itself, the Great Arising (mahā-jāti), the Great Change (mahā-pariṇāma), the Great Cessation (mahā-nirodha), and the Great Abiding (mahā-sthiti). These are able to produce the Great Abiding and so forth. This should be understood as explained above. Thus...

Regarding the great cessation (*mahā-nirodha*) in relation to the eight factors: it is a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*). Because the great cessation is a co-existent cause that is capable of ceasing the eight factors, it functions as a cause.
If one considers the eight factors in relation to the eight factors themselves, there are five causes and three non-causes.

As for the three non-causes, they are minor birth (*upapatti*), minor duration (*sthiti*), and minor change (*anyathātva*); these three factors are incapable of ceasing [the others]. As for the five causes, they are... [as previously defined].
That is to say: great arising, great abiding, great change, and great cessation; as well as the abiding of the essence, and minor cessation—these five dharmas all constitute "great cessation.
If there is minor arising, it can only give rise to the great arising of that which arises, and cannot further give rise to the other seven dharmas.
If there is minor abiding, it can only abide the great abiding, and does not further abide the other seven dharmas. If there is minor change...
The great [non-conceptual] cessation can only differ from the great [non-conceptual] cessation; it cannot further differ from the other seven dharmas.

If the small [non-conceptual] cessation can only cease the great [non-conceptual] cessation, it cannot further cease the other seven dharmas. Furthermore, regarding the method applied to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), it is as follows:

when the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) arises, the mental factors are at most ten universal ground factors (*mahābhūmika*), namely: contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), [faith, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom].

Mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are all mind-kings (*cittarāja*). Each of these eleven factors possesses four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)—namely, the four minor characteristics—and the essential body of the factor itself;
thus, there are both the primary factors and their secondary attributes. Calculating these eleven factors together with their attributes results in ninety-nine factors in total.
The unwholesome mind-king is able to produce other factors and acts as their simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*). What is the meaning of this? It is like the mind-king.
At the moment of arising, upon the back [of the mind] there are immediately the four major and minor marks;
its mental sovereign (*cittarāja*) turns backward and is thus able to produce the first level of the four major marks. When evil arises, it is able to produce the fourteen marks of the second level.

When that mental sovereign turns forward, it can produce the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-caitta*) of the first level; when the mental sovereign turns forward, it is greatly able to produce [them].
The second layer consists of the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-caitta*). Each individual mental factor possesses the four great characteristics (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*) of arising and so forth.
When this mind-king (*citta-rāja*) moves forward, it can produce two layers of phenomena: namely, the ten universal mental factors and their own secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*).
When this mind-king moves backward, it can also produce two layers of phenomena: namely, itself and the four great characteristics upon its back.
And the minor four characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*). That is to say, the primary and secondary [characteristics] each can produce two layers.

However, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) cannot produce the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-caitta*), nor the third layer of minor four characteristics on their back, because they are too remote.
This calculation totals that the mind-king, as the producer of dharmas, can produce ten universal mental factors as the ten [produced entities], and can also produce ten [instances of] mind.

The four major characteristics (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*) of each [of the fifty-eight factors] thus constitute forty. Furthermore, upon the back of the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*), there are the four major and four minor characteristics, as well as eight other dharmas.
In total, the sovereign mind is able to produce these fifty-eight dharmas. Thus, from the perspective of the sovereign mind toward these fifty-eight dharmas, they are "co-existent" (*sahabhū*).
The co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) refers precisely to the sovereign mind and its mental factors (*caitta*). Is this not so?

Regarding the cause by way of association (*sahabhū-hetu*): if one considers the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) in relation to the other forty-eight factors consisting of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they constitute mutual association and the cause of association.

Within the fifty-eight factors associated with the mental faculty (*manas*), excluding the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), the remaining forty-eight factors are related to the mind-king in this manner.

Just as it is with the mind-king, the same applies when the ten other mental concomitants (*caitasika*) are considered in relation to one another. Furthermore, as in the method explained above, this one...
There is one mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and ten mental concomitants (*caitta*), making eleven dharmas in total. Within these eleven dharmas, there are secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*).

Since there are ten other dharmas [excluding the primary characteristics], if we consider the totality in relation to those ten other dharmas, they are all capable of producing two types of characteristics—both preceding and following.
These characteristics, in turn, can produce the first major set of four characteristics (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*) from their own backs as they face forward. These characteristics...
Furthermore, it can produce a second set of four minor marks on its back, which face forward toward the first set.
These [first] marks can produce ten other primary entities; likewise, the second set can produce another ten.
However, these four major marks on the back cannot produce those other ten dharmas, as they are remote from them. This refers to the four minor marks on the back. Its...

These [twenty-two mental factors] can, in turn, give rise to fifty-eight other dharmas; when these fifty-eight are mutually related to one another, they constitute nine types of co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
This applies to the remaining nine mental factors as well; their mutual non-occurrence as dharmas should be understood according to this same principle.

This continues up until the arising of a wholesome mind in the desire realm, wherein there are twenty-two mental factors—namely, the ten universal ground factors (*mahābhūmika*) and the ten specific factors (*paritta-bhūmika*), excluding the mind-faculty (*manas*) itself.

...and so forth. Regarding the ten great wholesome grounds (*mahābhūmika*), the remaining wholesome roots such as non-delusion (*amoha*), and the factors such as vitarka and vicāra, one should understand that each is to be treated according to the method of mutual correlation as previously explained.

Furthermore, regarding the arising of unwholesome mental factors—whether they are numerous or few—as described in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, their functioning as causes for one another is also as stated before.
Therefore, it is known that for present phenomena, the three characteristics of duration (*sthiti*), change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*bhaṅga*) all...

It is capable of grasping the fruit. If it is argued that activity cannot grasp the fruit and is therefore merely a manifest characteristic rather than a functional capacity, and if they offer this defense:

"Just as present dharmas are co-existent yet do not grasp the fruit—meaning that while matter has the activity of obstructing space, the mind has the activity of taking objects"—the difficulty is raised: if one claims that the present...

If a dharma possesses activity yet does not necessarily grasp its fruit, then the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) in the future would likewise possess activity but be unable to grasp its fruit;
it would then be an activity rather than what is called a "capacity" (*sāmarthya*). How, then, can one say that the characteristic of arising possesses such a capacity?
The *Śāstra* (Vibhāṣā) states in its third [section] that the three dharmas of the future possess functional activity (*kāritra*). The commentary explains:
"The three dharmas of the future are: first, the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), which can cause the future to arise and reach the present;

however, among the [other] three characteristics—duration (*sthiti*), change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*anityatā*)—only the characteristic of arising possesses functional activity, because the other two do not initiate their function. Second, the characteristic of light (*āloka-lakṣaṇa*) exists in the future world and can dispel..."

In the future, it is impossible for [the first dharma] to arise again. If light reaches the present, once the inquiry has ceased and there is no further light, there is no need for a third [moment] for the arising of patience regarding the dharmas.
The first dharma of the present arises simultaneously with the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*).
At the time of the present, it is able to empty the nature of an ordinary being, rendering it inferior by means of the power of non-accumulation. Furthermore...

It cannot project a subsequent moment of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) from within the storehouse of the future, just as a lingering resentment remains extremely similar [to its source].
This is like the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), which possesses the power to project the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) in the future;

once this receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena exists, it can exclude any other nature of an ordinary person that might otherwise exist in the future, so that such a state can no longer be obtained.

[The Vaibhāṣika] asks: "If, when [a dharma] arises, its patience (*kṣānti*) regarding that dharma flows on into the present, and it simultaneously transcends the state of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*) at the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), then for what reason does this dharma possess efficacy and activity while residing in the future store?

Furthermore, how is this reconciled? To this, they respond according to the explanation of the masters who follow correct reasoning (*samyuktanyāyavādin*): "In the future, there are three dharmas, namely the characteristics of arising (*jāti*) and so forth."

To claim that both are termed "capacities" (*śakti*) but not "activities" (*kāritra*), and that only those [dharmas] in the past that give rise to results are termed "capacities," contradicts the third explanation in the *Pūrvavaibhāṣika* (Old *Mahāvibhāṣā*).

Therein, it is stated that the three dharmas—arising and so forth—in the future are termed "activities" but not "capacities," and that even those in the past that give rise to results are termed "activities.
Since these two [definitions of activity and capacity] are contradictory in nature, they cannot coexist.

Regarding "existence": if your [position] regarding the entities were contradictory, then the four characteristics could not exist simultaneously. Furthermore, their functions would not be mutually exclusive.
Why? Because if one challenges the Ancient Master (Pūrvācārya), it would imply that the functions of the four characteristics all arise at the same time, rather than arising sequentially.
If one challenges the Master of Right Reasoning (Nyāyācārya), then your [position] implies that the function of arising must coexist with the functions of abiding, change, and cessation.
It arose during the time of the three emperors.
Furthermore, the commentary states: "Abiding, cessation, and difference belong to different worlds... even 'attainment' is according to correct principle.

If the first two extremes encounter their own school, or if they fall back from between the two, these are all considered "falling back" when referring to other schools; this is specifically established even if it were your own school.

Regarding the statement that "having attained [cessation], one immediately abides in it," if one claims this refers to abiding in cessation within a different birth (*jāti*), or if one claims it refers to abiding in cessation within a different world-system (*loka*), then one contradicts one's own school’s tenets.
This explanation follows the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* of the Hīnayāna and the tenets of the Mahāyāna school.
If [the cessation] abides in a different world from that which has ceased, it would contradict the tenets of our own Hīnayāna school.

If, on the other hand, one were to concede and agree with the Hīnayāna school by asserting that [the cessation] abides in the same world as that which has ceased, this would likewise contradict the correct reasoning of the aforementioned inference (*anumāna*).

The *Śāstra* says: "Then 'difference' would not constitute a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). The commentary explains: This refers to the *Abhidharmakośa*. It means that the aforementioned means of cognition does not establish difference.
Since the preceding phenomenon is a single entity, to posit difference within that single entity is untenable; thus, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu [states this].

Regarding the refutation of their distinct characteristics: as for the claim that "the preceding [moment] does not establish difference," you maintain that this subsequent moment’s characteristic of difference is identical in substance to the dharma characterized by the measure of the preceding abiding moment.

However, if they were indeed identical in substance, then how could one say that cognition apprehends two distinct dharmas? Since it would be impossible to speak of measuring them, the preceding measure cannot establish this subsequent moment.

Regarding the distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): if they share the same essential substance (*svabhāva*) as the preceding momentary state (*kṣaṇasthiti*), yet the phenomena (*dharma*) are of different measure, then in reality the preceding [moment] would not be a single phenomenon.

How, then, could one say it "depends on a single phenomenon"? Furthermore, since the four characteristics of time depend upon multiple phenomena, the cognition you grasp based on the aforementioned distinction of the four characteristics of time is untenable.
The *Śāstra* says: "Regarding the term 'Hetuvidyā' (Logic), there is no fault, because it explains that non-attainment is the cause of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The commentary explains: This objection refers to the Saṃmitīya school’s [position on] the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) existing over a long duration. One establishes a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to refute them as follows:

"At the beginning of the eon (*kalpa*), [the characteristics] must have been present, because they destroy conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), just like [the characteristics] at later times. Furthermore, this does not negate their prior non-existence. Moreover, the inference states: "I..."
The essence is certainly non-existent, because its essence is absent, like the horns of a rabbit.
The Commentary states: "Although four meanings are separately explained for a single dharma, these four exist in relation to one another within the emergence of the essence of that single dharma.
As the Sūtra says: "Bhikṣus, you should know: you are now being born, aging, and perishing"—this refers to a single [dharma].
Within a single *kṣaṇa*, there are four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). The Commentary states:
