If the mind takes as its object a self that is a dharma among the aggregates, since the external essence of the self cannot be subsumed under its characteristics (nimitta) by following the substance (dravya),
then if the mind takes as its object a self that is a dharma among the aggregates, and the external essence of that self is subsumed under its characteristics by following the aspect (ākāra),

then the four aggregates are merely "shadow-only" (pratibimba-mātra) derived solely from the aspect, because they cause the aspect to arise from the same seed as the aspect itself. If one discusses this in terms of the distinction between nature and function, it is identical to the "person-aspect" (pudgala-ākāra).
This is a matter of classification. If the atom lacks substantial reality, then it is a solitary reflection arising solely from the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*).

The Commentary states: "This refers to the impure preparatory minds (*prayoga-citta*) prior to the seventh stage; all these are said to take empty space as their object and the sphere of space (*ākāśa-dhātu*) as their condition, giving rise to discriminative minds that perfume and form seeds.
As for those who have entered the stages: this refers to those who have entered the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and those who have entered the fruition (*phala*).

One immediately attains the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path]. For bodhisattvas from the seventh stage downward, within their untainted subsequently attained wisdom (*anāsrava-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), as well as within the subsequently attained wisdom of those who have attained the four fruits, they are all able to take as their object the emptiness of the dharmatā within their preceding non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

Furthermore, this untainted subsequently attained wisdom can also remotely take as its object the true suchness (*tathatā*) sought for realization within their preceding preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*).

Furthermore, through personally hearing the Buddha’s teaching on space and so forth, within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), space and such are mutually perfumed to form the seeds of space.
From the eighth stage onward, the subsequently attained wisdom also takes space as its object and perfumes it to form the seeds of space;

this subsequently attained wisdom can also take the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*)—the emptiness of dharmatā—as its object, and it can also remotely take the preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) as its object.

In the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that follows the mind’s pursuit of true suchness (*tathatā*), such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the subsequently attained wisdom of the Bodhisattva again manifests the appearances of space and so forth;
this is because it is accepted that [this wisdom] takes all phenomena as its object.
The Commentary states: "There is one contaminated consciousness as the cause, two uncontaminated consciousnesses as the result, and three uncontaminated wisdoms.

Alternatively, when it speaks of "eight consciousnesses," this passage refers to the dharma-consciousness within the causal and resultant [stages] that takes the unconditioned (*asamskṛta*) as its object, whereby the mind transforms and gives rise to the consciousness that transforms the unconditioned.
Within the contaminated [consciousnesses], only the sixth consciousness takes the unconditioned of space (*ākāśa-asamskṛta*) as its object, and upon the mind, it transforms...

Regarding the statement "arising as the cause of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)" and "the two untainted (anāsrava) consciousnesses": these refer to the wisdoms of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), namely, the wisdom of wondrous contemplation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Following these two wisdoms, within the former [wisdom of wondrous contemplation], they are able to take the unconditioned space (*ākāśa-asaṃskṛta*) as an object and transform it to produce the fruit of the appearance of the unconditioned.

Regarding the "three untainted wisdoms," this is the first interpretation; if one does not state that the wisdom of accomplishment (*krtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) takes space as its object, then the remaining three [wisdoms] [would be meant].
The subsequently attained wisdom following gnosis can take the unconditioned as its object and transformatively give rise to an aspect-part (nimitta-bhāga) that is unconditioned.

This is the second interpretation, which explains that the subsequently attained wisdom of the "accomplishment of what was to be done" (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna) can take the unconditioned of emptiness as its object and transformatively give rise to an aspect-part that is unconditioned.

Thus, this second interpretation is superior. That is to say, the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom) cannot possess the *mūla-jñāna* (fundamental wisdom) that can realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
However, the *pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna* (subsequently attained wisdom) following the all-accomplishing wisdom can also take the unconditioned as its object and manifest the appearance of the unconditioned.
The Commentary states: "This [object] lacks a substantial essence and is a transformation of mind alone, like atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth.

This means that when one takes atoms as an object, the atoms lack a substantial essence; there is only an image. Space likewise lacks atoms with a substantial essence. Both cases are similar in this regard.

The *Śāstra* states that there is no transformation; this is because, in terms of the fundamental substance (*svabhāva*), it is non-existent. Since the *śāstra* discusses the essence as being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is subject to transformation. The *Vyākhyā* states:

"If the direct objects (*ālambana-pratibimba*) of tainted cognition (*sāsrava-jñāna*) are for the most part subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), [this refers to] the indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*)."

Conditioned by the unconditioned [state] of space (*ākāśa-asamskṛta*), it is subsumed solely under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). If there is a specific wholesome mind that takes the unconditioned state of space as its object, it is subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

A mind of inferior capacity is likewise also subsumed under the Truth of Suffering. Question: Just as with unwholesome minds such as wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), how can they take unconditioned states such as space as their objects?
Answer: It is like when a person with wrong views feels anger toward someone who has attained liberation; if another person says to him: "There is..."
Regarding unconditioned phenomena such as space: when a person with wrong views feels anger toward another person, they discern that what is spoken by that other’s mouth includes space as well.

Therefore, one with wrong views can take space and the like as an object. However, the Hīnayāna does not allow that a person afflicted by defilements takes space or non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—which are unconditioned—as objects, because space is not [an object of the mind].

Because it is a defiled phenomenon (*kliṣṭa-dharma*), it does not have a different object of cognition (*ālambana*). Because it is not an augmented object, it is not the object of hatred (*dveṣa*). Because it is not a Truth (*satya*), it is not the object of false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).

The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that, for the most part, it is subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); however, when an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) takes it as its object, it is subsumed under the Path (*mārga*).
That is to say, regarding whether it is subject to arising and ceasing or not: if this consciousness transforms into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), [it is not subject to arising and ceasing].

Because they arise and perish from moment to moment, they are indeed characterized by arising and perishing. These unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) that are thus transformed remain similar across preceding and succeeding moments;
being devoid of change, they are conventionally designated as "permanent. This is precisely the gate of non-arising and non-perishing.
The treatise states that "emptiness and non-self" refers to the attainment of the wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness.

The commentary says: "Where the movements of the mind cease and the path of discourse is cut off" refers to the sphere of the true suchness of suffering (*duḥkha-tathatā*), which is beyond the coarse mind of conceptual discrimination.

Not being attached to conditions means that the sphere of mental activity has ceased. If one were to speak of this *tathatā* (suchness) through words, it could not be named, for the path of speech is severed.
This intrinsic nature is pure by its very essence and not produced by wisdom; thus it is called "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
That is to say, within the substance of *tathatā*, there is primordial purity, which is termed "cessation not through deliberation. As for the substance of *tathatā*, it is distinct...
Because it is through the preceding wisdom that one discerns suchness, and only then does suchness attain purity, suchness is by its very nature pure;

this is termed "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Regarding the Sarvāstivāda school of the Lesser Vehicle, their interpretation of cessation not through deliberation holds that it is manifested solely by the absence of conditions;
they do not designate suchness as "cessation not through deliberation" on account of its being pure by nature.
Why is this? In the Hīnayāna, it is not that true suchness (*tathatā*) is not established; however, how could one say that true suchness is "inherently pure by nature"?
In the Mahāyāna, true suchness is established as existing, and because the essence of true suchness is pure, it is designated as "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Regarding those who become free from desire for the third dhyāna: if an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) uses the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) to suppress the afflictions of the lower three dhyānas and attains the fourth dhyāna-concentration, that immovability is comprised within the unconditioned state of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

If it is one who has attained the fruit of a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), having severed the defilements of the lower three dhyānas and attained the fourth dhyāna-concentration, that immovability is comprised within analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). However, this commentary...

In the text, the statement "having become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna, one attains the unconditioned of immovability," and the statement "having become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness,

one attains the unconditioned of the cessation of perception and feeling," refer specifically to the explanation of freedom from defilement according to the stages of the two vehicles and ordinary worldlings.

If one is free from the defilements of a lower stage, one attains the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of a higher stage; if one attains the meditative concentration of a higher stage, one seeks to become free from the defilements of the lower stage.

This commentary does not speak with reference to Bodhisattvas. For if a Bodhisattva were not free from the defilements of a lower stage yet attained the meditative concentration of a higher stage, they would not relinquish that higher stage and would instead be reborn in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Therefore, it is known that although they may give rise to the active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) of the Desire Realm, [they do not fall back].
They are also able to attain the unconditioned state of immovability in the higher stages and the unconditioned state of the cessation of sensation.

If a Bodhisattva from the first stage up to the seventh stage still receives a body of segmented birth (*prādeśika-kāya*), such as that of a lay Bodhisattva, it is permitted for them to have parents, wives, children, and so forth;
consequently, they may give rise to afflictions of the desire realm through the power of their mental faculty. If from the first stage...

Regarding those who have departed to receive a transformation body (*pariṇāmika-kāya*): although they have suppressed and extinguished the pervasive arising of afflictions (*kleśa*), they still give rise to afflictions to a small degree by virtue of their power.

If one seeks the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-asamskṛta*) while remaining apart from desire for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), this is because it is subsumed under the path of the affliction of craving (*rāga*).
Thus, desire-craving (*kāmarāga*) is said to exist within all three realms. This is so even for an Arhat.

The cessation of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the attainment of the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-asamskṛta*) are subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

If a person who has attained the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) exhausts all afflictions of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and attains the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling, it is likewise subsumed under analytical cessation. Alternatively, that which is attained through suppression (*vibhava-prāpti*) is subsumed under non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Regarding the cessation of painful and pleasant feelings: among the five types of feeling (*pañca-vedanā*), why is it not mentioned that there is the cessation of sorrowful (*daurmanasya*) and joyful (*saumanasya*) feelings?
If [the afflictions] are extinguished, how can one speak of suffering and pleasure? Answer: Suffering and pleasure are themselves craving; sorrow and joy are themselves narrowness.

Since sorrow is eliminated in the first dhyāna and suffering is eliminated in the second dhyāna, they are thus [regarded as] the craving for suffering. Therefore, it is said that craving is suffering, and that sorrow is subsumed within suffering.

*Prīti* (joy) is subsumed within *sukha* (pleasure). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The second dhyāna transcends suffering; although it is not [present as] actual seeds, it is termed 'coarseness' (*dauṣṭhulya*).
If the third dhyāna transcends that [second], there still remains the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) within it. Thus we know that *sukha* is broad while *prīti* is narrow.
Furthermore, suffering and pleasure pertain generally to all six consciousnesses, whereas grief and joy exist only within the sixth consciousness. Therefore, there is...

Regarding the breadth and narrowness [of the scope]: for this reason, this treatise mentions only suffering and pleasure (*duḥkha* and *sukha*), but does not mention sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and joy (*saumanasya*).

The Commentary states: "The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (or *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*) also states that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) such as suffering are a temporary dissociation (*visamyoga*);

this refers to the two natures among the unconditioned phenomena, which are explained by combining the existence and non-existence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) within the latter three natures. The Explanation says: "In that *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*..."

It is said: the unconditioned state of immovability (*āniñjya-asamskṛta*) and the unconditioned state of the cessation of feeling (*vedanā-nirodha-asamskṛta*). These two unconditioned states are dissociation at the time of being bound;

both are non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), as they both consist in the temporary absence of conditions whereby neither painful nor pleasant feelings function, and neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*) does not function.
For this reason, these two unconditioned states are subsumed under non-analytical cessation. These two types of unconditioned natures are contaminated (*sāsrava*).

Regarding transformation (*pariṇāma*): if it is impure transformation, it is subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) as being dependent-arising; if it is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) transformation, it is subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), and is also subsumed under the nature of dependent-arising (*paratantrasvabhāva*).

As for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is subsumed under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), which is the thoroughly established nature (*pariniṣpannasvabhāva*) common to both [the dependent and the perfected].

Regarding the combined explanation of existence and non-existence within the three natures below: if one relies on the two natures (dependent and perfected), they exist; if one calculates them according to the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*), they do not exist.

This is precisely non-existence; therefore, it is said that existence and non-existence are taught in combination. In other treatises, "immovable" refers to the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*), which consists of both analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
When the mundane path temporarily suppresses the cessation of painful and pleasant feelings, one attains the analytical cessation of the immovable state.

This analytical cessation constitutes the third fruit [of the *anāgāmin*]. As for the upstream (*ūrdhva-srotas*) *anāgāmin*, they sever the outflows (*āsrava*) and the transformations associated with the lower three dhyānas.

One attains the unconditioned state of immovability (*āniñjya-asaṃskṛta*), which is the unconditioned state of the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of feeling and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*).

This also includes the unconditioned state of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), as in the case of a body-witness *anāgāmin* who enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). By entering this attainment of cessation, one is able to suppress the outflow-tainted equanimity (*sāsrava-upekṣā*); this is precisely the attainment of cessation.
The unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*) of the cessation of sensation and perception is precisely analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

If an Arhat is able to sever contaminated equanimity (*sāsrava-upekṣā*) and enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), thereby severing this unconditioned state of the cessation of sensation and perception, it is subsumed under analytical cessation.

Therefore, in various treatises, both the unconditioned state of immovability (*āniñjya-asaṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayita-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*) are both encompassed by analytical cessation. Furthermore, these two natures are non-existent...
Regarding the statement that "existence and non-existence are taught in combination," this very treatise explains the two natures as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

That is to say, the unconditioned which is the transformation of consciousness is subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). This teaching [concerning] the two characteristics, up to the two natures, refers to the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

If the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). However, regarding the subsequent passage which mentions space, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), under which nature are these three subsumed?
If they are all subsumed under the third [the perfected nature], this is from the perspective of grasping the mind that clings to the unconditioned;

thus, the unconditioned would be the imaginatively constructed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). If the mind transforms into the unconditioned, it is subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). If the nature of phenomena is unconditioned...

It is subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Since the first nature is non-existent while the latter two natures are existent, it is said that existence and non-existence are taught in combination.
Regarding the statement that the true suchness (*tathatā*) of wholesome phenomena is, when discussed in terms of its designation, a single entity in essence: [the question is] why, in this context...
It is taught that there are only six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), and it does not teach that the *tathatā* (suchness) of wholesome dharmas and so forth [is unconditioned], and so on.

The commentary states: "The four formless attainments, from the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception," refers to the teaching of the four schools such as the Mahāsāṃghika.
This is because the Desire and Form Realms possess physical bodies; since the mind and mental factors depend upon the physical body, they are able to take them as objects of cognition.

Regarding all phenomena: these four formless bases (ārūpyāyatana) are "formless" because they serve as the support for the body and life. The mind of the formless realm depends solely upon the "non-existent";

because it depends on the non-existent, that mind of the formless realm can only take as its object phenomena of its own level or higher levels, and cannot take as its object any phenomena of lower levels.
Thus, for example, the mind of the sphere of infinite space takes as its object only its own level and those above it.

The [formless] stages cannot take a lower stage as an object; even the mind of the sphere of nothingness takes only its own stage or higher stages as objects, and does not take the lower sphere of infinite consciousness as an object.
The same applies to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Furthermore, the unconditioned state of the sphere of infinite space is not the unconditioned state of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) is not the unconditioned of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
All four formless spheres (ārūpyāyatana) possess the unconditioned.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Regarding the eight [points] on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and its nature (*dharmatā*): it is as stated in the Sūtra.

This dharma of dependent origination—whether a Buddha appears or does not appear—the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) remains eternally constant. Regarding this, the Mahāyāna-Sarvāstivādins explain the Sūtra as follows: "Dependent origination refers to the twelve links.
From 'ignorance conditions volitional formations' up to 'old age and death,' whether a Buddha teaches them or not..."
It is said: "The essential nature of these links of dependent origination is eternally constant; within birth and death, the bonds of conditions are never severed.
Furthermore, it is not because the Buddha taught the links of dependent origination that these twelve links exist as the bonds of conditions within birth and death;
rather, they are called the eternally constant *dharmatā*. If the Mahāsāṃghika and the other four schools interpret this sutra, they say: "Dependent origination is precisely..."

These are the twelve links. That which is the eternally abiding nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). These twelve links take the unconditioned as their essential nature.
Because ignorance (*avidyā*) relies upon the unconditioned, that ignorance is itself outflowing (*sāsrava*).

Because it exists, ignorance can ascend and take formations (*saṃskāra*) as its object, yet it cannot take consciousness (*vijñāna*) as its object, and so on up to birth and old age and death. The link of formations relies upon the unconditioned.
For this reason, the superior practice is able to take the *vijñāna* link as its object, and furthermore can specifically take *nāmarūpa*, up to and including *jarāmaraṇa*, as its objects;

all subsequent cases should be understood according to this principle. These twelve links are based upon the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and for this reason they are eternally fixed, being called the "ever-abiding dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*).
That which is unconditioned is itself eternal; it is the very nature of the twelve links. While their twelvefold substance is subject to arising and ceasing, [their underlying nature is not].
It is impermanent. Therefore, the four schools and others alike [hold that] these factors of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda-anga) are unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).

These four schools have misinterpreted the scriptural passage. When it says, "Whether a Buddha appears or not, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is eternally abiding," this scriptural passage cited in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* does not serve as proof [for their position].
The *Śāstra* states: "Regarding the nature of the nine factors of the noble path," the Sūtra says: "These thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

Here, the intention is to take up the seven factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). Whether these factors of the path belong to the Buddha-dharma or to the mundane world, they are not subject to arising;

their dharma-nature is eternally abiding. Regarding this, the Mahāyāna masters and the Sarvāstivādins explain the Sūtra as follows: "If the Buddha speaks of them, they are immediately capable [of functioning]."

Regarding the teaching on the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*): it is the inherent nature (*dharmatā*) of the factors of the Noble Path (*āryamārgāṅga*) that they are all capable of abandoning afflictions;
it is not by virtue of the Buddha’s teaching alone that they can abandon afflictions, because these factors of the Noble Path are ever-present.

If the four groups, such as the Mahāsāṃghika and others, all interpret this sutra as saying "the factors of the Noble Path," this refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*). This also includes the seven factors of awakening (*sapta-sambodhyaṅga*) and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
The eight branches of the noble path constitute its [the path's] constituent factors. That which is eternally abiding in its dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Because the branches of the noble path rely upon the unconditioned, and because the noble path takes the unconditioned as its essence, it is able to be ever-present and able to sever worldly delusions;
thus, the branches of the noble path are established as unconditioned. These four sections are a misinterpretation of the scriptural text. However, within this context, they are assigned as follows:

In the preceding Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), although there are eight factors, because they have already reached the middle grade of the Path of Seeing, they are designated as the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) and are not called the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

In the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), although there are the seven factors of enlightenment, because they reach the middle grade of that Path of Cultivation, they are designated as the eightfold noble path and cannot be called the seven factors of enlightenment. In the Path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), although there are the eightfold noble path...

Regarding the Path: within the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), one attains only the ten dharmas of no-more-learning; they are not termed the "ten dharmas of no-more-learning," nor are they termed the "eightfold noble path" (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

The commentary states: "The four immovable unconditioned [factors]—formerly called 'non-self' was an error. This means that the former interpretation took them to be for the sake of eliminating the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*).
Therefore, it is called the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) of non-self. Now, when one is unmoved by feelings of suffering or pleasure, it is called the unconditioned of immovability (āniñjya-asaṃskṛta).
The *Śū* states: "The suchness (tathatā) of the five wholesome dharmas, up to the suchness of the seven indeterminate dharmas.

If, according to the Hīnayāna, the suchness underlying wholesome dharmas belongs only to the indeterminate category and does not extend to the wholesome or unwholesome, this differs from the Mahāyāna. In the Mahāyāna...
The suchness (tathatā) underlying indeterminate phenomena extends even to the suchness underlying all wholesome phenomena; thus, it pervades all dharmas.

As for the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of the Hīnayāna, it belongs exclusively to the contaminated (sāsrava). There are many such unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) analytical cessations of contaminated phenomena.
In the Mahāyāna, however, when the extreme of severing the roots of goodness is eliminated, it reveals a portion of the same suchness, which is merely designated as "analytical cessation."

As for the "Tathatā of the Eightfold Path" and the "Tathatā based on Dependent Origination," the interpretation of this Mahīśāsaka school is the same as that of the previously mentioned four schools, such as the Mahāsāṃghika.
The commentary states: "Regarding the statement that the Dārṣṭāntika masters posit the three unconditioned [phenomena] as having no substantial nature (*svabhāva*):
the Dārṣṭāntikas are none other than the aforementioned Kumāralāta. Kumāralāta is the patriarch of the Sautrāntika school. As for the 'unconditioned'..."

That is to say, space (*ākāśa*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) exist only as provisional designations; they possess no substantial reality whatsoever. This is identical to the tenets of the Sautrāntika school.

Regarding the statement in the commentary that "among the three types of cessation according to the Vibhajyavādins, even impermanent cessation (*anityatā-nirodha*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)," the term *Vibhajyavādins* refers to those known as the *Vibhajyavādins* (or *Vibhajjavādins*), who are a specific sub-sect among the various schools that interpret the meaning [of the scriptures] incorrectly. They are collectively so designated.

It is called Vibhajyavāda. If one interprets the principles of meaning according to the *Sautrāntika* school, they are called Saṃmitīya-vādin; this is translated as "Correspondent Master" (*xiāngyìng lùnshī*).

This Vibhajyavāda establishes both analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because by severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), one realizes the attainment of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thus, they establish non-analytical cessation as an unconditioned phenomenon. If it is the Sarvāstivāda...

Mostly. The unconditioned phenomenon of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) pertains to ultimate abandonment. That which is not ultimate refers to the establishment [of cessation] solely upon the basis of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
If it is the unconditioned phenomenon of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it belongs to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and is exclusively ultimate. In the Mahāyāna...

The *Sārvastivāda* [school] shares the same principle of "one faith and double the characteristics" (*ekasamaya-dvisvabhāva*) as the others; it is established by overturning the other schools and is identical to the Mahāyāna. This interpretation is correct.

Regarding the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 53, that the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the two emptinesses is mentioned: [the question is] why that treatise... only [mentions this]?

Does this teaching of the two unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta)—emptiness (śūnyatā) and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha)—mean that no other unconditioned phenomena are mentioned? The answer is found in that treatise:

it speaks of these two unconditioned phenomena by way of what is commonly known by the world. For example, as it is commonly known in the world that there is space (ākāśa), and because it establishes what is commonly known in the world as a phenomenon characterized by the absence of conditions (pratyaya-vaikalya).
If one speaks of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), it refers to the abandonment of specific categories [of defilements]; if one speaks of the immovable (āniñjya)...

Regarding "perception and feeling" (*saṃjñā-vedanā*): this refers to the abandonment of these two feelings. If one speaks of the *tathatā* (suchness) of wholesome phenomena, the *tathatā* of unwholesome phenomena, and the *tathatā* of indeterminate phenomena, this refers to the exposition of principle through treatises.
Here, the names of the three natures of phenomena (*tri-svabhāva*) function as the expression (*nāman*), while the *tathatā* underlying the three natures functions as the principle (*artha*).
If one speaks of *tathatā* (suchness) as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), this refers specifically to the various substantial entities.

The Commentary states: "One should discuss four [unconditioned phenomena] and not two, such as 'immovability' (*āniñjya*) and so forth; these two are, in fact, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Regarding the mention of "four," they are: suchness, space, analytical cessation, and non-analytical cessation. As for the reason why "immovability" and "the cessation of perception and feeling" (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*) are not mentioned: if these two were [merely] mental...

That which is ultimately severed is subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This [state of] immovability, the cessation of perception and feeling (*asaṃjñi-vedayita-nirodha*), when it is a temporary cessation, is subsumed within non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Therefore, the unconditioned state of the immovable cessation of perception and feeling is not mentioned [as a separate category].
The Commentary states: "Because the perspectives regarding the conventional expression (*vyavahāra*) and the ultimate principle (*tattva*) differ.

When we now speak of "the suchness of wholesome dharmas" and so forth, this is spoken in terms of conventional expression; thus, there is the suchness of wholesome dharmas, the suchness of unwholesome dharmas, and so on—these are the three distinctions.

However, if one discusses it from the perspective of the ultimate principle, the three natures and the [three] non-conditioned phenomena are all subsumed within a single suchness as their essence. Herein, the discussion is based on conventional expression.

The principles that are revealed—namely, the phenomena of the three natures such as the wholesome and so forth—are called "designations" (*prajñapti*). The true suchness (*tathatā*) inherent within those three natures is the "principle" (*artha*).
Therefore, it is said that the referents [of these two terms] are distinct.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "That which is based on a provisional entity can all be described as either provisional or real; it can likewise all be described as determinate.
If [these] pervade the three natures and exist throughout both existence and non-existence, the explanation says: "That is to say..."

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "That which is the principle itself possesses outflows (*sāsrava*), up to being designated as 'wholesome' (*kuśala*) and so forth. Furthermore, according to the text of the Treatise (*Śāstra*): "These five are all *tathatā*.

That which is conventionally established as *tathatā* is also a designation based on provisional construction (*prajñapti*). Thus, the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are all termed 'provisional.

If one speaks of the unconditioned by means of linguistic expression (*abhilāpa*), it is termed provisional; if it is the unconditioned as transformed by consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*), it may likewise be said to be provisional."

That is, the six unconditioned phenomena (*asamskṛta*). Based on the conventional (*prajñapti*), they are still [unconditioned]; thus, the six unconditioned phenomena can all be said to be conventional.

If one refers to the nature of the six unconditioned phenomena, that is *tathatā* (suchness), because it is beyond words; based on the six unconditioned phenomena as real entities, the six unconditioned phenomena can all be said to be real.
If one includes all three natures, then it includes the three natures such as the imagined (*parikalpita*) and so forth; because it is pervasive...

Regarding "existence and non-existence": True Suchness (tathatā) pervades both the non-existent nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) and the existent nature of the dependent and perfected (paratantra and pariniṣpanna).
The Commentary states: "The cessation of other feelings is not established as unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). This was posed as a question by an opponent:

"Why is the cessation of change (anyathātva) and the cessation of feeling not established as two types of unconditioned phenomena? Why is it that the cessation of the feelings of grief (daurmanasya) and joy (saumanasya) is not established as unconditioned?"

The commentary states: "For now, regarding the obstacles to superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), these are precisely feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*). If, within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), feeling is predominant, there is the equanimity-feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*) and the pleasure-feeling (*sukha-vedanā*);
conversely, joy (*prīti*) arises because it is a mental activity (*citta-saṃskāra*). Thus, one experiences the inferior nature of the concentration, as when attaining dhyāna."
He is fixed; that is, he personally experiences the feeling of joy and bliss of the first dhyāna and is unwilling to cultivate the concentration of the second dhyāna.

Just as with the second dhyāna, he personally experiences the feeling of joy and bliss within the concentration on the signs of the second dhyāna and is unwilling to advance to cultivate the excellence of the third dhyāna concentration.

This is because the signs of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) are powerful. He speaks of the perception of the sphere of infinite space, the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the perception of the sphere of nothingness. Thus...
Even reaching the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one can also reach reality. Other defiled states, such as craving and so forth, all obstruct meditative concentration;

now, by severing these remaining defilements, one also attains the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Here, because we are considering specific modes of activity, two unconditioned states are attained: through the cessation of painful and pleasant feelings, and through the cessation of neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
It is not that one attains many unconditioned states by excluding everything; rather, it is calculated that one emerges from the first dhyāna.

Sorrow (*daurmanasya*) should likewise be associated with the unconditioned state of immovability (*āniñjya-asaṃskṛta*). However, among the types of sorrow to be abandoned, there are hundreds of thousands of varieties within that sorrow;

because it is said that there are hundreds of thousands of kinds of sorrow, one attains hundreds of thousands of instances of the unconditioned state of immovability upon emerging from the second dhyāna.

If it is also appropriate that this be associated with the unconditioned state of immovability, then within suffering (*duḥkha*) as well, there are likewise hundreds of thousands of varieties, which are now being abandoned.
One also attains hundreds of thousands of unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*) through hundreds of thousands of types of painful feelings (*duḥkhavedanā*);
this is likewise true for neutral feelings (*upekṣāvedanā*). Furthermore, within greed (*lobha*), there are hundreds of thousands of millions of types;
by severing even a single instance of greed, one severs hundreds of thousands of millions of types of greed, and by severing each individual seed of greed, one severs all such seeds.

When one attains a single instance of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) [attainment], and when one desires to sever a single instance of greed, one attains hundreds of thousands of millions of instances of the unconditioned;

this applies likewise to anger and the other afflictions. Since this is explained here in terms of the point at which transformation, loss, and sensation are exhausted, the fourth dhyāna is established as the "immovable" (*āneñjya*) unconditioned.

Furthermore, when one severs the equanimity-sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*) of the fourth dhyāna, one also attains the unconditioned of the cessation of perception and sensation (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*), and so forth.

All the above cases are likewise so. Since the present discussion concerns the initial limit of exhaustion, it speaks of the attainment of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) following the abandonment of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Regarding the question in the sub-commentary (*śāstra*)—“Does one attain the unconditioned through the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)?”—the tenth fascicle below provides two explanations; alternatively, the object...

The "obstructions of knowledge" (jñeyāvaraṇa) are able to obstruct non-abiding nirvāṇa (apratisthita-nirvāṇa). Their abandonment is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), or it is said that they cannot be attained; all these points will be clarified below as explained.
The commentary (*śū*) states: "Within this, there are further internal and external [aspects], even as explained elsewhere," which refers to the repeated explanation regarding the unconditioned.

The commentary states: "Regarding the established and the non-established truths: if one follows the path of seeing according to the Hīnayāna, when taking the non-established truth as the object, one enters the path of seeing by relying on emptiness and selflessness as the preliminary practice (*pūrvaprayoga*). If, however, one practices the contemplation of the established truths..."
One enters the path of seeing (darśanamārga) by means of the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) based on suffering and impermanence.

Subsequently, as the stream flows like a reflection, once one has emerged from the first of the sixteen moments of the path of seeing, one does not give rise to the wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*), because these have already become obscured; nor does one give rise to a distracted mind (*vikṣiptacitta*).

Returning to the initial stage of the wisdom of the fixed nature (*niyāma*) that has not yet been reached, there are three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*). What are they? All of them may be attained;

alternatively, one may employ mental attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and impermanence (*anityatā*). Question: One attains the fruit by abandoning the previous [preparatory] stage of application (*prayoga*) through the contemplation of suffering and impermanence.
How is it that after having attained the first fruit (*prathamaphala*), one again performs the contemplation of suffering, impermanence, and so forth? Answer: If...
In the stage of application (*prayoga*), when one performs the contemplations of suffering, impermanence, and so forth, one is simultaneously performing a partial observation of the truths (*satya*).

This involves the observation of the eight truths across the upper and lower realms. "Eight" refers to observing the suffering of the lower realm, as well as the suffering and other characteristics of the upper realms.

The term "and so forth" (*ca*) excludes those [contemplations] that follow from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), such as the contemplation that all three realms are suffering or that all three realms are impermanent. This is because such [universal] observations do not constitute a partial analysis.
Because it differs from the preceding preparatory stage (*prayoga*), one also abandons the previous path of application (*prayogamārga*) upon attaining the fruit.
The commentary states that the term *tathatā* (suchness) has twelve names, among which is "dharma-dhātu. Here, *dhātu* has the meaning of "nature" (*svabhāva*). Thus, "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*)...
These are the various essential natures. Regarding the nature of non-falsity: conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are false, whereas True Suchness (*tathatā*) is not false.

Regarding the nature of immutability: conditioned phenomena are subject to change, whereas Suchness is immutable. Regarding the nature of equality: conditioned phenomena are of an unequal nature, whereas Suchness is equal.
Regarding the nature of freedom from arising: it means that the essence of conditioned phenomena is not permanent.
"Abiding" means that the unconditioned essence is eternally constant. Regarding "the fundamental nature of the realm of empty space":
True Suchness (*tathatā*) is able to contain all phenomena, whereas the conditioned cannot. Regarding "the limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*): "Reality" refers to the limit itself;

it is the true limit, meaning the ultimate limit of the Dharma. Regarding "inconceivable": coarse consciousness, being conditioned, can be conceived by the intellect; however, True Suchness is subtle and thus inconceivable.
It is inconceivable. Regarding the three types of self clung to by non-Buddhists and followers of other vehicles, they are like the various phenomena mentioned previously. Question:

While it may be possible for those of the Lesser Vehicle to eliminate their clinging to the three selves through the realization of the emptiness of phenomena, how can non-Buddhists do so while still clinging to these three kinds of phenomena? Furthermore, question: why is that which is conditioned called "self"?
The term "self" (ātman) is subsumed under the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); however, [the definition] explaining it does not subsume the unconditioned.

Furthermore, the Commentary asks: "If there is the fault of partial agreement," this means that if one were to formulate an inference (*anumāna*) stating, "Unconditioned phenomena that are necessarily dissociated [from mind] are definitely outflows (*sāsrava*)," then there would be no fault.
If, however, one speaks generally of the three types of self-phenomena, they are certainly not distinct from mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
There is the fallacy of mutual contradiction in establishing [this]. For example, regarding "all cognitions that take this cognition as their object":

those cognitions that take this cognition as their object consist of both the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the cognizing mind itself. As for "that which takes this cognition as its object," this refers to the mind that is the object of perception (*ālambana-citta*).

Furthermore, there is also an inferential conclusion (*anumāna-nigamana*) following the section on the prior grasping at a self (*pūrvātma-grāha*); that is to say, in the first fascicle mentioned above, after both the Hīnayāna and the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) have been refuted.
There is a structural outline to the text: first, it refutes the real self as the object of perception; next, it refutes the small self-view that acts as the perceiving subject.
This is likewise the case within the refutation of phenomena (*dharma*): first, it refutes that real phenomena external to the mind can definitively be the objects of perception;
next, it refutes that the perceiving mind which takes those external phenomena as its objects can definitively perceive them.
The Commentary states: [Question] If it is the case that the mind which is the perceiving subject of external objects does not definitively perceive them, [then what follows]?
The Commentary states: [Question] If that is so, regarding the relationship between mind and object—if there were no prior object, how could the mind still be "mind"?
Thus, there would be no distinction between mind and object; how then can one speak of "Cognition-Only" (*vijñaptimātra*)? The intent of the question is as follows.
The treatise states: "If one clings to consciousness as being truly existent, such clinging is a form of attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*), just like clinging to external objects. Question:
As stated in the tenth fascicle below, consciousness exists only internally, whereas objects also extend externally; for fear of confusion with the external, [the text] speaks only of the internal.

Regarding the term "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*), an objection is raised: because the object (*viṣaya*) is confused with that which is external, one should speak only of "consciousness" and not "consciousness-only. Furthermore, since consciousness also includes the *parikalpita* (imagined) nature, external consciousness should not be called "consciousness-only. The explanation states: as for the remark below that "the object also extends to the external," [it means that while the object is indeed external, it is subsumed within the category of consciousness]. Thus, even though the object is external, because it is ultimately nothing other than the manifestation of consciousness, it is designated as "consciousness-only. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Even if one were to say "consciousness-only," this would not exclude external objects; rather, it indicates that the object is not separate from consciousness. Consequently, the term "consciousness-only" is established to refute the notion of an external object distinct from consciousness. This is why it is said that the object also extends to the external.

Regarding the statement that "the object extends to the external": this means the object extends to the external substantial essence (*bhāva*). There are cases where it is not an object grasped through the conceptual construction (*parikalpita*) of attachment.

If it were an object of the conceptually constructed nature, then the aforementioned difficulties and contradictions would apply. However, if it extends to the external substantial essence, there is no such contradiction.

Furthermore, the external substantial essence extends to both the insentient and the sentient; yet, it is exclusively the sentient aspect that is subsumed [within the mind], because it is a derivative transformation from the mind.
In the end, it returns to its source; therefore, it is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
The Commentary states: "As for those who previously clung to [phenomena] as arising from no intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*)," this refers to the essence of nature itself.

If this clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) were to arise with a separate essence from the clinging to persons (*pudgala-grāha*), then how could an Arhat have only the clinging to phenomena arising without an essence, while lacking the clinging to persons?

The Commentary states: "Because there are those that arise solely from the seeds of the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). This means that there are still instances where one continues to practice the clinging to phenomena;

"solely" refers to arising from the seeds of the clinging to phenomena, not from the seeds of the clinging to persons (*pudgalagrāha*). Since they share the same substance, there is no case where the clinging to persons arises solely from its own seeds.

This is because when one speaks of a person, it is said that within that person there is both a mind that clings to persons and a mind that clings to phenomena; thus, the mind clinging to persons and the [mind clinging to phenomena]...

[Objection: It is held that [the two types of grasping] arise from seeds of the same kind; thus, for those who maintain that the grasping at a person arises solely from the seeds of the grasping at a person, and not from seeds shared with the grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha), there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, since the similar-appearances of self and phenomena that are both transformed by the [eighth consciousness] are likewise [distinct], there is no obstacle to this objection. This is just as, among the appearances of self and phenomena transformed upon the mind, there are those that appear as a self.
Thus, because phenomena undergo transformations that resemble [other] phenomena, there is no self that could give rise to something resembling a self.
Since these resemble phenomena arise from the same seed as the phenomena themselves, it is not the case that what resembles a self arises from a separate seed.

The Commentary states: "If external objects that conform to phenomena (dharma) are [regarded as] phenomena rather than self (ātman), this reveals that internally there are things that are neither unitary nor permanent.

This means that regarding external objects that conform to phenomena, one gives rise only to the grasping of phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) and does not give rise to the grasping of a self (*ātmagrāha*), because they are identical in being neither unitary nor permanent.

Thus, one knows that the "self" of phenomena is itself non-self. This indicates that even regarding internal phenomena, one likewise gives rise only to the grasping of phenomena and does not give rise to the grasping of a self.

The Commentary states: "That the seventh consciousness also possesses only the grasping for self (ātman-grāha) and lacks the grasping for dharmas (dharma-grāha), while the grasping for dharmas also extends to the eighth consciousness—this, moreover, is precisely the position of Master Sthiramati."

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Thus, the fundamental characteristic (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*) of the self is simply called 'aggregates' (*skandha*); as for calling its fundamental characteristic 'elements' (*dhātu*) or 'bases' (*āyatana*), this is because the meaning of the self's activity [is expressed by them].

Therefore, it is said that the aggregates are without function; since the self is reckoned as small, [it is not perceived]. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states: "Regarding 'the fundamental characteristic of the self':

the fundamental essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) of the conceived self arises only with respect to the aggregates. Thus, the Sūtra says: 'All things depend upon the five aggregates of clinging.'"

The aggregates arise; the essential nature of those phenomena likewise exists only within the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*). For what reason? It is because one does not conceive of the bases and elements as the self.
Regarding the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), these include the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Among those who conceive of the unconditioned as the self, there are few—only those who, based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, conceive of the Buddha-nature as the self. Those who conceive of the aggregates as the self are many.
That is to say, all the bases (*āyatana*) arise from the aggregates (*skandha*) upon which the self predominantly relies.

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, by taking as objects the various aggregates, bases, and elements transformed by consciousness, one gives rise to the images of one's own mind and clings to them as real dharmas;

this is the same as the two interpretations regarding the self [discussed] previously. One interpretation says: "One clings to the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and grasps it as being determinate."

Regarding the Dharma: secondly, it refers to the grasping at the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which is the delusive appearance grasped according to one's own mental inclinations and clung to as a real phenomenon.
Within the former school [of thought], these two types also exist.
The Commentary states: "Because the Buddha-nature does not lose its own essence" means that the Buddha-nature possesses an essence that maintains itself.

Regarding this essence, as in the preceding text, that which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is called "grasping" (*upādāna*), while that which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is called "maintaining" (*dhṛti*). However, the fundamental characteristic of the self is simply referred to as the aggregates (*skandha*).

As for the fundamental characteristic of phenomena (*dharma*), it extends to all cases, being explained through both general and specific presentations of the three categories (*triskandha*). Question: In this passage of the Commentary...

There are three interpretations. What is their distinction? The answer is: from "the original characteristic of the self" (*ātman*) up to "because the essence of phenomena (*dharma*) is not so," including the passages concerning the bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth—this constitutes the first interpretation.
Regarding "the original characteristic of the self," the intended meaning is the essential characteristic of the objective basis (*ālambana-svabhāva*) of the grasping at a self.
Regarding "the original characteristic of phenomena," it refers to the essential characteristic of the objective basis of the grasping at phenomena. This is the intended meaning.
It is said: if there were a permanent function, one would reckon it as the self; therefore, one reckons only the aggregates (*skandha*) as the self.

If there were a substantial entity, one would reckon it as a phenomenon (*dharma*); thus, "clinging" refers to the attachment to the three categories (*triskandha*). The commentary text refers to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
To explain the commentary text in detail, follow what was previously cited and explained. Furthermore, from the phrase "also," it refers back to the original essence.
The commentary from "even unto" up to "having thus taken the words" constitutes the second interpretation.
This second interpretation explains [the matter] by means of the similarity and dissimilarity of the primary substance (*bimba*).
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, regarding the explanation based on the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and its similarity or dissimilarity:

according to that *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the conceptualized Buddha-nature is taken as the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the aspect (*bhāga*). It is similar [to the seeing-aspect] because both are equally conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). As for their dissimilarity:
it is held that while the self-characteristic of the aspect is conditioned, the essential nature of the Buddha-nature is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); thus they are dissimilar. However..."

This treatise states that the aspect of the self-conception which takes the aggregates (*skandha*) as its object is similar in essence to the aggregates themselves, because they both share the same characteristic of being conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) and are likewise aggregates.
This treatise explains [the analogy] based on such similarity; when it says "the former conforms to the latter," the preceding instances include the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).

Previously, when grasping at a self, one relied solely upon the view of self regarding the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). Now, in clarifying the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), the terms "bases" (*āyatana*) and "elements" (*dhātu*) are added for distinction.
While previously the grasping at a self was limited to the aggregates of clinging, and the grasping at phenomena was limited to the [aggregates], one must now add the bases and elements;

thus, one calculates a self across all three categories (*triskandhaka*). This is based on the teaching that the bases and elements are established through mutual conjunction. Since these already include the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), such as nirvāṇa...

The sutras calculate that the Buddha-nature is the self (*ātman*). Since the Buddha-nature is untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), to cling to the mark of a self is precisely to be tainted and conditioned.

The Commentary states: "From here on, following the previous [logic], one should exclude the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*); one should speak only of the aggregates (*skandha*). Why? Because since the elements and bases..."

There is a portion that adheres to the characteristics of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma-lakṣaṇa-varga*), which consists exclusively of contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskṛta*).

Because these do not resemble their objective essence (*svabhāva-tathatā*), they are categorized as the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*). Since these aggregates are both conditioned and contaminated, they resemble the aspectual division (*nimitta-bhāga*).

Consequently, the subsequent text excludes the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*). Furthermore, the statement "I have only summarized... up to... regarding the teaching of the three categories (*traya-nikāya*) is precisely the third interpretation.
However, that which is designated as "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) is distinct; it exists only within the dharma-dhātu and the dharma-āyatana.

As for the grasping at a self (ātma-grāha), because it functions by way of a general synthesis, it grasps only the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) as the self, but does not grasp the dhātus or āyatanas as the self, since there exist distinct unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) phenomena within the dhātus and āyatanas.
Therefore, within the grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha), all three categories (traya-skandha) are collectively reckoned as "phenomena."

Regarding the seventh consciousness being of a nature that repeatedly arises throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*): Question: When one traverses the ten stages, does one abandon the seventh consciousness?
Answer: It is not said to be abandoned because it is subtle. It is of a wholesome, non-obscured, and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature.
Because it is associated with afflictions (*kleśa*), it is termed "unwieldy" (*akarmaṇyatā*). This [state] exists even in the body of an Arhat.

Within this [stage], there exists an insensitivity (*akarmanyatā*) that is incapable of bearing [the path]. This is the case, for example, with Pratyekabuddhas who are on the verge of manifesting their transformation, or when Śrāvakas give rise to compassion and so forth.
Therefore, within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one only abandons the coarse, heavy, and insensitive nature (*dausthulya-akarmanyatā*) among the first six consciousnesses.

Regarding the statement here that it is "subtle" because, in terms of its categories, it is said to be difficult to sever: if one asks about its mode of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*), it resides precisely in the ninth category.
As for those of the Two Vehicles, having first severed the preceding eight grades, they subsequently give rise to the path-conditioning [wisdom] and only then sever the grasping at a self;

thus it is said that the grades of grasping at a self are subtle and difficult to sever. Now, since this dharma is said to have subtle grades, it should reside within the ninth grade among the nine grades.
Likewise, a Bodhisattva should also first sever the preceding eight grades and only then sever the grasping at dharmas; thus one may say "subsequently. If...

Regarding the followers of the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*), because they possess the detachment from the stages (*bhūmi-vairāgya*) and so forth, there are Bodhisattvas of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) who have abandoned the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
One might argue that for them, the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) can still be discussed as existing in subtle categories. The answer is: not so.

When the text states that the innate clinging to self and phenomena (*sahaja-ātma-dharmagrāha*) is abandoned within the ninth category (*navama-prakāra*), this refers specifically to the abandonment of the afflictions by the first two vehicles through the detachment from the stages. If it concerns a Bodhisattva...
Regarding the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*), one cannot say that innate self-clinging (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) is abandoned in the ninth stage (*navama-bhūmi*).

This is because there is no stage among the ten bodhisattva grounds (*daśabhūmi*) where innate self-clinging is not being abandoned; it is only upon reaching the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*) that the innate self-clinging within the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭha-vijñāna*) is finally severed.
However, although a bodhisattva abandons the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) without designating specific stages, it is nonetheless abandoned in nine grades within each stage.

There are Bodhisattvas of the first stage (*bhūmi*) who can bear the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). There are also Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage who can sever the cognitive obstructions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

It is also possible for them to first give rise to subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) to sever the remaining cognitive obstructions, and subsequently give rise to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) to sever the cognitive obstructions of the desire realm;
this is because they have already realized the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), whereas the categories of grasping at substantial entities (*dravyasat-grāha*) are subtle.
Regarding the statement here that it is "subtle" in terms of its category and is said to be "difficult to sever": attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) resides in the lowest-of-the-low grade;
hence it is called "subtle. Because it can be eliminated only by the highest-of-the-high wisdom, it is said to be "difficult to sever."

The Commentary states: "Because there are distinctions between entering, abiding, and emerging within the first stage (*bhūmi*), each of the ten stages possesses both the nature [of the path] and the path itself.

Someone raises an objection: "Since the first stage is the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) and thus only severs the afflictions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpavāsanā*), how can it now be said that the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) throughout the ten stages is able to eliminate subtle clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*)? The explanation says: "It is just as the first stage has eight moments of mind for abiding and emerging; if one enters..."

The mind then severs the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-vikalpa*). By abiding in the "emerging mind" (*niṣkrama-citta*), one eliminates and severs attachment to subtle phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Therefore, there is no contradiction. The *Śāstra* states:

"The cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) known by the five consciousnesses are also severed in the first stage (*bhūmi*), because they cannot give rise to attachment through the nature of wisdom that deliberates via non-conceptual activity.
This means that the conceptual cognitive obstacles of the five consciousnesses are induced by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). If [the obstacle] were conceptual...

The nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) that deliberates and evaluates exists only in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); it does not exist in the five sensory consciousnesses. Therefore, there is no grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

The Commentary states: "It is not the case for those various non-outflow minds (*anāsrava-citta*) involved in contemplative observation," such as the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms (*mūla-prsthalabdha-jñāna*) of the path that abandons afflictions.

All of these are modes of contemplative observation (*paryeṣaṇā*). Alternatively, practicing the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) for the sake of disciplining the mind is also a mode of contemplative observation.

This is as in the case of the Buddha’s ten powers (*daśabala*): the first four have no fruit and are fundamentally modes of contemplative observation, whereas the untainted (*anāsrava*) states constitute the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*). Nevertheless, regarding the path of superior progress...

There are two types. One type is the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) within the four paths, which serves as the category of the path of advancement; it proceeds by surpassing what came before.
Another type consists of distinct stages of superior progress, namely the ten powers of a Buddha (*daśa-bala*) and so forth; these are all distinct paths of superior progress.

Regarding the statement that "the Hīnayāna and so forth are all termed 'erroneous' (yā)": this is because within the Hīnayāna, one clings to the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) as being substantially real.
This directly contradicts the Mahāyāna wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna).

Therefore, in comparison to the Mahāyāna wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena, the aggregates, bases, and elements as conceived by the Hīnayāna—indeed, even the names, phrases, and sentences [within those teachings]—are erroneous. This applies even up to the point where one clings to bodhi and nirvāṇa [as being real].
They truly exist. "Extremely" (*parama*) refers to the *ya* [view]. Regarding these two, there are also general and specific conditions;

this is because all twenty views and the sixty-two [views] possess the truths. However, within the aforementioned grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), there are already the sixty-five views and so forth.

If there is grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*) regarding the faculties, there must necessarily be grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), because grasping at phenomena and grasping at a self arise as a single entity.
Since grasping at a self consists of sixty-five phrases, twenty phrases, and so forth, within this grasping at phenomena there are likewise sixty-five phrases and twenty phrases.
Even in the Hīnayāna, they maintain that there exists a self and phenomena that are neither identical to nor separate from the aggregates (*skandha*). This is superior [to other views].

The term *pudgala* refers to the "self" (*ātman*). However, since there are twenty phrases, sixty-five phrases, and so forth regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), these [conceptions] likewise exist within the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*).
Although one does not specifically cling to the eye as the self while failing to cling to other faculties such as the ear, by analogy, such [clinging] can still occur.
This is just as, among the sixty-two views, even though [the view of] the four types of finite existence (*antavān*)...
There is no fourth alternative; that is, the position that things are neither finite nor infinite. Nevertheless, in terms of the number of permutations, it should also be included.

This is similar to the method used regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*). If one analyzes the objects of activity (*ālambana*) without analyzing the arising [of the cognition], then within the twelve bases there are forty-eight permutations.
For example, as when one grasps the eye-base as "this is my eye" or "this is my necklace."
The eye: "This is my servant; the eye is my house. Grasping the ear: "This is my ear; this is my ornament;
this is my servant; this is my house. And so on, up to grasping the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*):
"This is my phenomenon; this is my ornament; all are my servants; all are my houses. Within these twelve spheres (*āyatanas*), there are thus twelve distinct entities.
I see thirty-six instances of "mine" (*mama-ātmīya*); when totaled, these constitute thirty-eight propositions.
The eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are likewise; within these eighteen elements, there are seven sets of two propositions, namely: grasping the eye-element as "my eye."

"The eye is my servant; it is my house. ... up to "clinging to the consciousness-element (*vijñāna-dhātu*) as 'I,' [thinking] the consciousness-element is my ornament, the consciousness-element is my servant, and the consciousness-element is my house.
Altogether, there are eighteen instances of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). There are further fifty-four instances of the view of "mine" (*ātmīya*). In total, there are seventy-two.

[This is the] phrase. If one discriminates that the objects of the spheres (*āyatana*) are empty, and also discriminates that the places from which discrimination arises are empty—within these two [categories], one clings to the eye-sphere as "self" and the remaining twelve spheres as "mine. That is to say: "The ear is my ornament;
the ear is my servant; the ear is my dwelling," and so on, up to calculating the dharma-sphere as "my ornament" and dharmas as "my servants."

Disciple: The Dharma is the dwelling place. Initially, the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is taken as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); the remaining eleven parts are taken as "mine" (*ātmīya*).
Within these eleven components of "mine," there are one hundred and thirty-three propositions. Including the view of self, there are thus thirty-four propositions.

Taking the sense-base of the eye as the self, there are thirty-four propositions; this continues up to taking the sense-base of mental phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*) as the view of self, while taking the remainder...

Regarding the eleven bases (*āyatana*), there are thirty-four propositions concerning what belongs to the self (*ātmiya*). Specifically, there are twelve types of views regarding the self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), while the remaining three hundred and ninety-six propositions concern what belongs to the self.
As for the arising of conceptualization (*parikalpa*), there are four hundred and eight propositions; the same applies to the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
Within these eighteen elements, there are likewise eighteen types of views regarding the elements, while the remaining nine hundred and eighty-eight [propositions] concern what belongs to the self.
"Self" (*ātman*) refers to what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*). Within the eighteen *dhātus*, there are a total of nine hundred and thirty-six phrases.
However, the twenty-four truths (*tattva*) of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the six categories of meaning (*padārtha*) adhered to by non-Buddhists are all subsumed under false views;

they are included within the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and do not constitute attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). Their adherence to intrinsic nature should properly have been clarified in the preceding section on attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*). It is not [here].

In this context, all [instances] are explained as the locus of grasping (*grāha-sthāna*). If the two vehicles grasp at the aggregates, bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu*), this is precisely the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*);

thus, it should be included in the explanation of the locus of grasping at phenomena. As for what was previously discussed in the section refuting the self (*ātman*), namely the self as grasped by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), that is explained as the locus of grasping at the self (*ātma-grāha*).

Since the twenty-four principles (*tattva*) and the six categories (*padārtha*) and so forth are phenomena (*dharma*), they are therefore [included in the locus of grasping at phenomena]. Thus, [it is said]:

"Nature," etc. This question concerns the locus of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Now, if one were to formulate the categories of this attachment to phenomena by analogy with the attachment to self (*ātman-grāha*), one should say as follows:
among the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), those with fewer categories are the attachment to form (*rūpa*) as a phenomenon;

by analogy with the "ornament" form, it is the attachment to form; by analogy with the "servant" form, it is the attachment to the house; and so on, up to the attachment to consciousness (*vijñāna*) as a phenomenon.
Consciousness. This consciousness is the ornament of the Dharma; this consciousness is the servant of the Dharma; it is the dwelling of the Dharma.
Is it the same for the sixty [elements] and the spheres (āyatana)? Furthermore, according to the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) below, one should understand that there are sixty-five.
For what reason does this text here state sixty-two? The answer is: according to the text below, "the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*)" refers to one hundred and twenty-eight.
Regarding the root afflictions and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the objects of attachment are likewise one hundred and eight and so forth;
thus it is known that within the grasping for a self (*ātma-grāha*), there are twenty phrases, sixty-five phrases, and twenty-six phrases of self-grasping.

At all times, one is necessarily accompanied by attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Since the intrinsic nature of this attachment to phenomena arises simultaneously with the aforementioned attachment to a self (*ātman*), there are likewise twenty phrases for attachment to phenomena;
thus, [the total] amounts to sixty-five phrases. However, it is not appropriate to state the number of phrases separately.

"Form" refers to the form of phenomena, such as necklaces and the like. Nevertheless, according to this [text], there are sixty-five phrases herein. However, in the *Śū* (Commentary), there is an error.
This refers to the sixty-two phrases. The Commentary states:

"Regarding the three moments of mind, if two moments of mind sever [the afflictions], they are called the first and second paths; the third path is designated as the 'first' in relation to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Among these three moments of mind, if the first and second categories [of afflictions] are severed, it is called the first; the third moment of mind is called the latter. If [the remaining categories] are severed...

Regarding the second and third moments of mind in relation to the subsequent path of cultivation—wherein "subsequent" refers to the path of cultivation—the characteristics of these second and third moments are termed the "initial abandonment.
As for the reckoning of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth as being possibly existent, or the reckoning of self-nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth as being definitely existent:

it is asked whether there are also three types within the absence of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). First, reckoning phenomena as identical with the aggregates; second, reckoning phenomena as separate from the aggregates; and third, reckoning them as neither identical with nor separate from the aggregates.

[Question: Regarding "separate from the aggregates," the answer is that it refers to the existence [of a self] arising simultaneously with the aggregates. As for the calculation that the *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) and so forth are definitely non-existent:

[Question] If the twenty-three principles (*tattva*) of the six categories (*padārtha*) as calculated by the non-Buddhists are all subsumed under the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and not under the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), why are the *svabhāva* and so forth explained here within the context of the clinging to phenomena?
