[Answer] The explanation given immediately prior is also applicable here.

The Commentary states: "Whether sudden or gradual; one should know this upon reaching the following section. This means that the severance of delusions within the single mind may be either sudden or gradual, as will be explained in the ninth fascicle during the discussion on the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*).

The Commentary states: "The *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says that, with the exception of ordinary beings, the knowledge of others' minds does not know the objects manifested by a Buddha. What is this *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*?
If one seeks to understand it through the analysis of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).

The verse asks: "How does the knowledge of others' minds know its object as it truly is? Some say that when persons of the two vehicles or bodhisattvas take another's mind as their object, they cannot know it through analytical discernment.

Even when in meditative absorption and taking another's mind as their object, although it is an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they take it only in its general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and cannot know the other's mind with detailed clarity, just as one knows one's own mind.
The similarity of cognition is also like when a subsequent moment of mental consciousness takes the immediately preceding moment of mind as its object;

although it does take that as its object, it cannot apprehend it clearly. When Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles take another’s mind as their object, the knowledge of others' minds is likewise.
That it cannot be like the Buddha’s domain means that it cannot, like the Buddha’s wisdom, discern the mind with such clarity and subtlety. This is the interpretation of Sthiramati.

It says: "Because the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) of Bodhisattvas and those of the two vehicles still possess attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), they do not know the minds of others as they truly are when perceiving them.
When there is attachment to phenomena while perceiving another's mind, it is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This explanation is incorrect; we shall not accept it here. If one proceeds...

The supernormal powers (abhijñā) of ghosts, the heavenly realms, and the mind-reading of others are "born-acquired" (upapatti-lābhika). This is because they are acquired immediately upon being born into those respective classes. Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds is not direct perception (pratyakṣa).
As the Commentary states: "As for that which is not an object [of perception], it is like the object of sound; it is not an object of the visual consciousness and so forth."

The Commentary states: "If it were not so, there would be consciousness that is not merely representation-only (vijñaptimātra). When the Buddha takes another's mind as an object, if there were no objective aspect (nimittabhāga), it would not be representation-only;
therefore, in taking another's mind as an object, there is an objective aspect."

The Commentary states: "As for the claim of the Sthavira school and others that the mental factors associated with a single assembly (*ekasamūha*) are capable of taking [their objects] as conditions, this refers to the masters of this school who hold that, just as when visual consciousness arises, sensation (*vedanā*) can directly take as its object the primary mind (*citta*) arising simultaneously with it, and even the primary mind itself can directly take as its object other mental factors (*caitta*) arising simultaneously; so too it is when auditory consciousness arises."

The ear is directly conditioned by its own specific characteristics. With the exception of the inquiry regarding the conditioning of an aggregate, this "self-aggregate" cannot take as its object the distinct mind and mental factors within that same self-aggregate.
It cannot take those mind and mental factors of the self-aggregate as its object.
The Commentary states: "The Mahīśāsaka school asserts that [the sense organs] take co-existent dharmas as their objects;

the Western masters assert that even the matter (rūpa) within the body belongs to the category of the faculties because it is of the same kind. Regarding the term "Westerners" (xifang): this does not refer to what we call the "Western Country" (Xiguo) in this Great Tang Empire.
In the Western lands there are two countries: the country of Kaśmīra and the country of Gandhāra, which is called the West.

A master from the West, belonging to the Mahīśāsaka school, states that wisdom coexists with the five aggregates; he asserts that the five consciousnesses rely upon the five forms, and based on the five material sense-faculties, they arise above [them].
For example, the wisdom associated with visual consciousness is able to directly perceive the mental factors that are simultaneous with it.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the colors and so forth within the body are of the same category as the sense-faculties," this refers to the four objects (dharmas) that support the faculties within the body—namely, color, odor, taste, and tangibility.
Because these belong to the category of form, they constitute the five sense-faculty elements (*indriya-dhātu*).

Since wisdom (*prajñā*) can also take these four supporting objects as its cognitive domain, there are two explanations. One states that the wisdom co-arising with visual consciousness takes only the eye as its object.

The sense-faculties (*indriya*) do not take as their object the *āśraya* (the physical support) of the faculties. Second, wisdom (*prajñā*) is also able to exclude the taking of the eye-faculty as its object, and it also excludes the taking of the objects that support the faculties.
This extends even to body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), which can [perceive] the five aggregates (*skandha*): the five material faculties are called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*);

the consciousness existing simultaneously with them is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*); the sensation existing simultaneously with them is called the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*); and the perception arising simultaneously with them is called the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*). Same.
At that time, there are the four characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) and volition (*cetanā*), which constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Because these—the physical sense faculties and the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*)—exist simultaneously with wisdom (*prajñā*), wisdom is able to take them as objects; thus they are called "co-existent factors" (*sahabhū-dharma*).

With wisdom as the primary factor, visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*) is likewise able to take the eye faculty, the mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*), and the four characteristics equal to wisdom as its objects; it is able to take all of these as its objects.

Consciousness is also called the five aggregates co-arising with consciousness (*vijñāna-sahabhū-pañca-skandha*). This applies even up to feeling, perception, and volition, which should be called the five aggregates co-arising with feeling (*vedanā-sahabhū-pañca-skandha*), as it is only wisdom (*prajñā*) that is termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
The same exclusion applies to the remaining consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue, and body; these are simply the five scattered consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*).

Question: Regarding these masters, how many mental factors (*caitta*) do they establish? Answer: In works such as the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra*, the number of mental factors established by the Mahīśāsaka school and others is not specifically clarified.

However, since the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra* does specifically clarify the number of mental factors and so forth for the Hīnayāna schools, this refers to the number of mental factors mentioned by the Master [of the Commentary] when citing various accounts. This is the case whether it be the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra*.
Regarding the fact that the number of mental factors (*caitta*) is not explicitly stated therein, even the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) does not clarify it. The Commentary states:

"The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) relies solely upon the immediately preceding mind (*anantaraniruddhamanaḥ*). Since its basis is non-material (*arūpin*), it cannot perceive the types of form (*rūpa*) and so forth within the co-existent body.
This is the position of the Mahīśāsaka school. They say: when the sixfold mental consciousness arises based on the intermediate mind... [the former... relies upon the previous [mind].

The mental faculty (*manas*) is the equal-and-immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Because the mental faculty is not material (*arūpa*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cannot take as its object the four types of sensory objects (*viṣaya*) that support the faculties within the body.
This is because the four types of sensory objects supporting the faculties within the body do not belong to the same category as the locus of the mental faculty.

Since the supports of the faculties are material, whereas the mental faculty is not material, the mental consciousness cannot take the objects that support the faculties as its objects. This, then, is the state of distraction.

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not take the sense-bases that support the faculties as its object; it takes only the mutual objects of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) as its object.

Regarding the four aggregates (*skandha*), there is no wisdom (*prajñā*) [present]; with the five aggregates, there is wisdom. If one enters a contaminated meditative absorption (*sāsrava-samādhi*), there is then that which is concomitant with the absorption (*samādhisaṃprayukta*).

Regarding the form (*rūpa*) [of the absorption], there is wisdom taking it as its object; simultaneously with that form, there are the mind and mental factors concomitant with the absorption. Through these, the five aggregates accompanied by wisdom are obtained. If one enters a contaminated meditative absorption, they are concomitant with the form.

Wisdom (*prajñā*). When it arises together with its objects at the same time, within the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*)—consisting of the mind, mental factors (*caitta*), wisdom, and their simultaneous [concomitants]—are established.

If one enters the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*), there is the morality concomitant with the path (*mārgasamvaraśīla*); this can take as its object both form and wisdom, as well as the simultaneous mind and mental factors, and the four characteristics such as arising (*jāti*).
Thus, the five aggregates concomitant with wisdom are obtained. If it is any other distracted wisdom of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), then there is no wisdom [concomitant with the path].

These are the five aggregates associated with both [wisdom and consciousness]. Here, we clarify the factors that coexist: those associated with form through meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahagata*) and those associated with form through the Path (*mārga-sahagata*), as well as the four characteristics such as acquisition (*prāpti*).

Since all these are associated with wisdom (*prajñā*), wisdom takes them as its objects; therefore, they are called the "five aggregates associated with wisdom. Above, wisdom was cited as the primary factor;
however, consciousness (*vijñāna*) also takes these as its objects, including the factors that arise simultaneously. Thus, they may also be termed the "form aggregate associated with consciousness."
The perception and feeling [skandhas] can also take co-existent dharmas as their objects; they may likewise be termed the five aggregates of characteristics and co-existence.
Regarding the other mental factors co-existent with feeling, one should understand them all by analogy with wisdom.
The Commentary states: "The Mahāsāṃghika and other schools assert that the mind and mental factors can take their own substance as an object simultaneously with [the arising of] the Great Vehicle.
The intention of these masters is that the mind can still take its own substance as an object, and mental factors can likewise do so.

If one uses the analogy of the Great Vehicle’s view of the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvedana*) taking the seeing aspect (*darśanabhāga*) as its object, would it not be similar? It is exactly like this.
The vehicle possesses a self-realized seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). This is the same as the Mahāsāṃghika school and the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the two views—that the Buddha’s境智 (objective-cognitive wisdom) and so forth, even if not false, must all be the seeing-part in order to share the same object of cognition (*ālambana*)—there are two interpretations in the commentary.
The former master’s position is not the correct doctrine; the latter master’s is correct. The former master says: "As for that Buddha..."

Regarding the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), it is similarly shown that both mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) admit that there is no lack of indirect cognitive apprehension (*viprakṛṣṭa-jñāna*).

Since their respective seeing-parts (*darśana-bhāga*) equally take the preceding object as their condition, they constitute a single common objective support (*eka-samālambana*). As for the various self-witnessing parts (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), if they take their own seeing-parts as objects, they constitute universal knowledge (*sarvajña*).

A later master states: although the mind and mental factors at the stage of Buddhahood do not engage in direct mutual cognition (*sākṣāt-paraspara-ālambana*), they also exclude indirect mutual cognition (*viprakṛṣṭa-paraspara-ālambana*).

Thus, universal cognition is established. Just as when other mental factors [cognize] the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of a mind, and when that mind and its mental factors mutually cognize each other's seeing-aspects, the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the mind-king takes its own seeing-aspect as an object, thereby becoming one in terms of the focal object (*ālambana*).
The Commentary states: "Because the self-verifying aspect (svasaṃvedana-bhāga) takes its own substance as its object to the full extent, it is called 'omniscient' (sarvajña).

Although the mind and mental factors do not take one another as objects, each self-verifying aspect takes its own seeing aspect (darśana-bhāga) as its object; therefore, it also constitutes omniscience.

The Commentary states: "The objects of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) must necessarily be the same as those of the self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), with the exception of the mind itself and its mental factors.

If they were each distinct, then while the seeing-parts of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) would equally perceive all external objects such as wisdom (*jñāna*), the individual minds and mental factors would not all be perceiving the same object."
The self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) is able to reflexively perceive the respective objects of the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*).
The Commentary states: "Because the Buddha manifests those images upon the seeing portion, it is called 'omniscience' (*sarvajñatā*).

Thus, each individual self-cognizing portion shares the same object as its associated mental factors and the seeing portion; this is what is meant by "having the same focal object" (*samālambana*). For example, regarding the seeing portion of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*):

At the same time, the mental factors (*caitta*) associated with the mind all manifest upon the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*). Furthermore, the mind-king and the mental factors mutually manifest upon each other’s seeing-parts.
This is just as when the various mental factors undergo a common transformation of images and take the seeing-part of the mind-king as their object;

at that time, the substance of this king’s seeing-part cannot itself take the mind-king as its object. Rather, it is the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) that takes the seeing-part as its object, and thus they function together.
All mental factors (caitta-dharma) have the same object of cognition (ālambana). One should understand that the cognition of minds and mental factors follows this same principle.

Therefore, it is also established as "universal knowledge" (sarvajñatā), as explained below. Furthermore, another interpretation states: "Just as the Buddha, by means of the self-verifying aspect (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) of his own mind, can manifest the objects seen by other mental factors.
This latter interpretation is difficult to establish; the former interpretation is superior.

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, while it negates the direct object of cognition (*sākṣāt-ālambana*), it does not fail to exclude that [same object] as the indirect object of cognition (*parokṣa-ālambana*).

According to the principles of *Hetuvidyā* (Logic), although it merely negates the direct objects of cognition held by other schools, what prevents it from also excluding the indirect objects of cognition?

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that although this negates their direct objects of cognition, it does not fail to exclude their indirect objects of cognition; for the direct and indirect objects of cognition are distinct."
Both [positions] are refuted; therefore, the method of *hetuvidyā* (logic) is one of negation (*paryudāsa*).

Furthermore, since the Sthavira school and others cannot maintain that there is self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) because they do not posit a self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) to perceive the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*), the mind cannot perceive itself.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The question, 'When the mind takes feeling as its object, does feeling itself take [it] as its object?

and so forth, up to 'feeling and the others cannot take themselves as objects,' is a question posed within this Mahāyāna [tradition] to the Sthavira school. For instance, while other minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) collectively apprehend a preceding object, those minds and mental factors likewise take that preceding object as their common object;
yet when those minds and mental factors take feeling as their common object, that feeling does not [take] the others..."

This question asks: "If the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) do not take their own associated feeling (vedanā) as an object, then the principle that they share the same object (ekālambana) would not be established.
There is no answer to this in the commentary (*śū*). An answer outside the commentary states: "I [the self] share the same object."

The object of cognition (*ālambana*) is exclusively that which the noble ones take as their objective field; thus, the principle of "sameness" (*sabhāgatā*) is established. This is not intended to argue that a mind takes itself as its own object, nor that it takes its own associated mental factors (*citta-samprayukta-dharma*) as its object.

The *Śāstravṛtti* (Commentary on the Treatise) explains the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* as follows: "These commentarial passages are precisely those from the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* refuting the Sthavira Dharmaguptaka school.
The Sthaviras maintain that the mind and mental factors are established as being identical and directly apprehend one another as objects; however, the mind does not take itself as its own object."
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Refuting the dharmas such as form that arise simultaneously with conditions and are shared;

these are shared dharma-substances, as explained extensively in the ninth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*. It says there, according to the Sarvāstivāda: "Mind and mental factors do not take one another as objects;

furthermore, they cannot take as objects the four characteristics, such as arising (*jāti*), which exist simultaneously with the mind. Refuting the Mahīśāsaka school, it says: "It is like the soles of two people's feet being together."

Regarding the observation of form (*rūpa*) and so forth: because these two [the eye and consciousness] can only perceive external objects, they cannot see each other’s own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

The same applies to the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*); since they both take the same external object as their focal point (*ālambana*), they likewise cannot take each other as their focal point.

Regarding the refutation of the four characteristics such as "attainment" (*prāpti*): for example, when visual consciousness observes an external form, it cannot see its own eye; this is because the eye serves as the path [for the consciousness].

It is seen that the four characteristics (lakṣaṇas) accompanying each moment of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are likewise [unable to perceive themselves]. Because they are too proximate, they cannot take themselves as objects.
The *Śāstra* states: "The Mahāsāṃghika school holds that the mind perceives itself; this is an obstacle," following the second master mentioned previously. The commentary explains:

In the Mahāyāna, it is established that there is self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) which takes its own seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as an object; thus, there is no obstacle of self-perception. However, for the Mahāsāṃghikas, the self-cognizing part does not take [itself] as an object.
Regarding the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*): there is no contradiction in its taking its own seeing-part as a common object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

The *Shu* (Commentary) cites the *Thūpana-sūtra* (*Thūpana-sūtra*), which explains: "Because the merit of those who read and recite this sūtra is thickly adorned (*thūpana*), it is named the *Thūpana-sūtra*.
This sūtra exists in India, but it was not present in the Great Tang.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'there must be common dharmas such as the general function of goodness,' whether it be phenomena transformed by the mind or real selves and phenomena external to the mind, all possess both good and evil; these are termed 'common'."

The Commentary states: "If, at the time of aggregation, it is called 'dependent' because of a presiding subject, this refers to [the self]; even if it were as subtle as an atom, it would still be called a 'dharma.
If the essence of the self were not produced from a distinct seed, whereas dharmas are produced from distinct seeds—even if they are as subtle as atoms, they may still be designated as 'dharmas.
Regarding external selves and dharmas, since true entities do not exist, [this applies] even to their meanings and attributes."

Regarding the "provisionality of essence" (*tǐjiǎ*), the *Shū* (Commentary) states: "Now, there is nothing external to the mind. A person asks: "If there were real dharmas external to the mind, then there would be provisional dharmas internal to the mind.

If there are provisional dharmas internal to the mind, then there would be the objects of discourse; thus, there would be an object of meaning that is established based upon an essence. If [external real dharmas] do not exist..."

If real dharmas external to the mind do not exist, then internal mental dharmas likewise cannot be established. Since there are no internal mental dharmas, there is consequently no basis for the designation of objects in dependence upon consciousness.
Furthermore, since the designations of the transformed [objects] are non-existent, even the designation of a "substantial entity" (*tattva-prajñapti*) would be impossible.
An opponent objects: "If there were real dharmas external to the mind, then there would also be real dharmas of consciousness within the mind. Regarding these dharmas...

The [opponent] initiates the discourse, asserting that there are provisional persons and phenomena. If there were no external phenomena apart from the mind, then internal mental phenomena could not be established.

As for the intent of the *Agnivaiśeṣika-śāstra* in refuting [the opponent] by means of real external phenomena: its meaning is that the previous examples of fire and so forth were used to illustrate external form;
the claim that "there is real fire" is precisely what the Master [Vasubandhu] refuted in the preceding fascicle through the analysis of the six categories (*ṣaṭkoṭi*).
In the section on "Meaning" (*yi*), the substantial fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) is refuted.

The commentary (*shu*) states: "The term 'kind' (*lei*) signifies a specific distinction. Humans are of the same kind, while animals and so forth are different; animals and so forth are of the same kind, yet they differ from humans.
Because animals possess both sameness and difference by which they are distinguished, it is called "specific" (*bie*). Now, we take up the aspect of sameness.
They are distinct, whether as humans or as animals, because they are mutually separate. As stated in the following passage, the "Great Existence" (*mahā-sattā*) is not itself grasped;
for the Great Existence is like the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*), being a single entity that pervades all real phenomena.
The Commentary states: "That school maintains that the fourteen qualities prior to the stages [of the path], as well as other forms, depend upon the nature of earth. Question:
Why does the Commentary in the previous fascicle state, "If there are color, odor, taste, and touch, these manifest earth," and so on, up to "only touch manifests earth, wind, and so forth"?
Yet here it says that earth possesses fourteen [qualities] and so on? What is the reason for this?
This is contradictory. The answer is that the preceding text refers to the "specific qualities" (*asādhāraṇa-guṇa*);

it speaks of the four qualities and so forth existing on the earth element, and this applies even to wind. However, in this context, because it refers to the "common qualities" (*sādhāraṇa-guṇa*), it is stated that the earth possesses fourteen qualities.
The *Śāstra* states, "It is also called 'sharp' (*li*). This character *meng* (fierce) is termed "sharp," meaning it is the fierce intensity of fire.

The *Śāstra* further states, "Or perhaps it is because there are those who possess the quality [of fierceness] but lack the human nature. For example, although the Great [Element] and the Mutually [Dependent] possess the qualities of fierceness and redness, they lack the human nature.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "If it is said that fire resides in qualities (*guṇa*), and since quality is a real entity (*dravya*), it is by virtue of the similarity of qualities that fire is said to depend on the real entity; yet, if it is said that fire resides in the person (*pudgala*), then it should be by virtue of the similarity of the person that it is called fire, rather than saying fire depends on the real entity. The Explanation says: You claim that wind and fire reside in qualities because of the similarity of qualities; however, the qualities of intensity and redness exist upon the person as well, and these qualities of intensity and redness likewise exist upon fire. Furthermore, [you argue] that fire resides in qualities because of the similarity of qualities. But the qualities of intensity and redness exist upon the person too, so why does fire not reside in the person? Why is it not said that fire depends on the person? Why do you say fire depends on the real entity? This is because you fail to understand the principle of the mutual dependence between substance and attribute. If you say that fire resides in qualities because of the similarity of qualities, then since the qualities of intensity and redness exist upon the person, fire should reside in the person. Why do you not say that fire depends on the person? Why do you insist that fire depends on the real entity? "Because it resembles [fire], it is called 'resembling fire' (sādṛśya-agni). As for the statement that 'fire depends on reality,' the objection is as follows:

Since the description of fierce, red fire already exists in the person, then two persons who resemble each other should be called 'conventionally designated fire' (prajñapti-agni), and one should not say that fire depends on reality. This is because what resembles fire depends on the person;
it is to explain that the quality of fierce, red flames exists upon the person. Now, the Hīnayāna schools and others establish their own definitions of real entities based on the preceding argument.

Regarding the "three matters," this is the first interpretation: it refers exclusively to establishing that the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a real entity is beyond the reach of linguistic expression (*prajñapti*).

That is to say, the conventional does not depend upon the real. Alternatively, this may refer to those entities accepted as real by both non-Buddhists and Buddhists, where even the conventional does not depend [upon them].
This is the second interpretation, which states: for both non-Buddhists and Buddhists, apart from their own [respective] real entities, verbal expressions do not [apply].

Furthermore, because conventional cognition (*prajñapti-jñāna*) does not take [ultimate reality] as its object, conventional designations do not rely upon real entities (*vastu*). Nevertheless, there is a distinction:
if one follows the non-Buddhists or the Hīnayāna, they accept that external self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are called "real entities.

If one follows the Mahāyāna, they accept that the internal self-characteristics transformed by consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*) are called "real entities. If, in the preceding text, the person carrying fire was used as an objection, this refers to the outsider [the non-Buddhist].
The Master [Dao]li held that the real self external to the mind is a true entity, while the provisional self internal to the mind is a semblance entity.

In this present text, "true" refers to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth. Whether in non-Buddhist schools or in the Buddha-dharma, all are provisional designations and cannot be attained [directly], because they depend directly upon the specific characteristic.

To say they are provisional means they do not rely on the true; however, it is also permitted that they may be attained through indirect dependence. A "true entity" refers to the specific characteristic.

The *Treatise* states: "Conventional wisdom (*prajñapti-jñāna*) and that which abides in designations (*vyavahāra*) are both not the object [of direct perception]. This is because the essence of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-svabhāva*) is free from names and expressions;

thus, it is not something that can be apprehended by verbal designation. Therefore, the aspect of the specific characteristic is the object of conventional wisdom. Furthermore, this [conventional wisdom] is the object of conventional designation (*prajñapti-vyavahāra*).

Because it is an object [of cognition], and because it is called "neither of the two" as an object, it refers only to the mind of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which attains its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

The commentary states: "The sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises subsequently following the five sensory consciousnesses, and even when taking this wisdom as its object, it gives rise to speech and so forth.
Here, "wisdom" refers to the name of the subsequent moment of independent sixth mental consciousness, termed "conventional wisdom" (*prajñā*). "Taking this as its object" means...

This refers to the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) acting independently in a subsequent moment, taking as its object the same realm that was previously perceived by the five sensory consciousnesses.

What is intended here is that, just as the sixth consciousness simultaneously perceives the five sense-objects with the five consciousnesses, this [subsequent perception] is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it apprehends the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

In order to transcend verbal designation, once the preceding moments of the six consciousnesses and their respective objects have fallen into the past, the subsequent moment of the sixth consciousness takes as its object the domains previously perceived by those six consciousnesses; this subsequent sixth consciousness is termed "conceptual cognition" (*prajñapti-jñāna*).

Consequently, when speech is produced to designate a preceding object, this is precisely "provisional designation" (*prajñapti*). Through this, one apprehends the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). The *Śāstra* states:

"In this school, this is established as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), not because it is universally accepted. This means that while this means of cognition is established based on another school’s tenets, it does not mean that one's own school accepts [the existence of] that which is the objective support (*ālambana*) for the conceptualizing person;
rather, it refers to the "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) residing within the person who possesses the conceptualization.

The Commentary states: "This is not because there is no firm grasping or appropriation. This refers to the mental engagement with universal characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), such as innate virtue (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*) and the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) and reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*).

When the mind takes universal characteristics as its object, there is no grasping whatsoever. However, if one were to grasp universal characteristics as being real, then it would indeed involve grasping.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the statement that among blue, yellow, and other such categories within a single location, each category is called its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*):
'one category' refers to a single class of specific characteristics. Yellow is a specific characteristic; likewise, red, white, and blue—each being distinct—is a specific characteristic."
The Commentary states: "Since the universal is neither universal nor particular, it serves as a mutual negation.

This means that since the universal lacks an intrinsic nature, both the particular and the universal could be described as the particular and the universal; yet, since the particular itself lacks an intrinsic nature, it is also not a particular.

This is because their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are beyond verbal expression. However, when they are explained individually—such as emptiness, selflessness, and so forth—they can each be understood separately;

this does not mean that a collective understanding is being formed. This is just as in the aforementioned stages of the equipment (*saṃbhāra*) and the practice (*pratipatti*), where within the mind of the wisdom arisen from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*), one may contemplate all phenomena as empty, or contemplate all as impermanent, or conceive of them as selfless.

Within this wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*), the contemplations of emptiness, selflessness, and so forth, all pertain to common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and are conventional cognition (*prajñapti-jñāna*).

They do not apprehend specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). While the essence of emptiness and selflessness pervades all phenomena, one merely engages in the conceptual resolution (*adhimukti*) of emptiness, selflessness, and so forth within the mind of hearing and reflection.
Thus, contemplating emptiness, selflessness, and so forth by means of this wisdom of hearing and reflection constitutes the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Therefore, one subsequently induces the contaminated wisdom of cultivation (*sāsrava-bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) to enter this uncontaminated path of cultivation (*anāsrava-bhāvanāmārga*).
One truly contemplates all phenomena (*dharma*), perceiving each and every one as attaining its own essence; this is called "attaining the specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Even within the contaminated wisdom of cultivation, contemplating emptiness, selflessness, and so forth, is also called the "specific characteristic," because one directly attains the essence of the phenomena (*dharmatā*). Thus, it applies to the contaminated wisdom of cultivation in general, as well as the eighth [moment].

Consciousness—namely, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and so forth that arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses—all obtain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and this is termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If one were to separately and independently contemplate impermanence, emptiness, and so forth, and if these were dharmas possessing a real substance, then the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) would be said to directly apprehend the specific characteristics of those dharmas.
However, since impermanence, emptiness, and so forth lack any substantial nature (*svabhāva*), how could the concentrated mind take them as its object and yet obtain their specific characteristics?

Is it a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)? Answer: It is designated as such because it serves as a single gateway for realizing the lower *tathatā* (suchness); this is called "attaining the specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*), as will be explained in detail below.

If the independent, distracted mind does not give rise to grasping, and when the wisdoms of hearing and reflection take all phenomena as their objects, one attains only the "common characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*);

this is inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, it is not by taking all phenomena as objects that one immediately attains the specific characteristic; rather, it is by taking many [phenomena] as objects...

Because it is a dharma, one immediately attains the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Why is this? For example, although the sixth consciousness takes all things as its object, when a single moment of wisdom produces the cognition of "blue," that is the common characteristic.

Conversely, if it were like [the case of] emptiness (*śūnyatā*), although it takes many dharmas—such as emptiness and selflessness—under the four truths as its objects, those would be specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Now, this also refers to the state within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), whether it be with outflows (*sāsrava*) or within concentration, or when taking a single [object].

A phenomenon (*dharma*) may take many phenomena as its object, because it is designated by the term "attainment through detachment" (*vairāgya*). These are all termed "specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*).

However, when the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), as well as the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*), take either one phenomenon or many phenomena as their object, they are termed "general characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) because they carry names and concepts (*nāma-pada*) and because cognition is a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
This is a mind of inference (*anumāna-citta*). Furthermore, within the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, if [it takes... as its object...

Both specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) are objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is just as when Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, within their untainted subsequently attained wisdom (*anāsrava-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), give rise to conventional verbal expressions for the sake of sentient beings, saying:
"O sentient being, upon the surface of your sixth consciousness, you take blue as an object and form a conceptual construction."

The blue [color] pervades all that exists above it. When Buddhas and Bodhisattvas explain this conventional designation of "blue" for the sake of sentient beings, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take the common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) as their object.
If they did not take the common characteristic as their object, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would not achieve omniscience (sarvajñatā).

There is only the cognitive activity of the apprehending consciousness; that which perceives the true common essence as being without an object of perception exists only upon the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
It is not the cognitive activity of impermanence, nor is it the common essential nature of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the statement in the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-gāthā*... *Gāthā* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "verse on dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda-gāthā*).
If a verse follows immediately after a preceding prose section (*gadya*) and restates its meaning for emphasis, it is called a "repetitive verse" (*geya*).
If it does not appear within the preceding prose section, it is called a "stand-alone verse. As it says in a sutra: "His countenance was most wondrous and sublime."
This is so. Furthermore, in the third fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Great Brahmā King speaks in verse. These are all "isolated verses" (*ku-qi-ge*).
If one says, "Desiring to restate this meaning, he spoke these verses," such verses as these are "repetitive verses" (*zhong-song*).
When awakening to the present as being like a dream arises, since both the seeing and the object have already ceased to exist, how could it be permitted that [this is]...?
Regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): this refers to the Mahāyāna refutation of the Sarvāstivāda and Sāmmitīya schools' position that the six consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously.
The Sarvāstivādins maintain that the five sensory consciousnesses are exclusively direct perception;

even though the five consciousnesses of the preceding moment have fallen into the past, when the sixth consciousness arises immediately thereafter, it also apprehends its object as direct perception. If the Mahāyāna explains it in relation to the five [consciousnesses]...

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises simultaneously with the [sensory] consciousnesses is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Once the five consciousnesses have subsided, the subsequent independent mental consciousness is inference (*anumāna*).
For example, when visual consciousness is arising and apprehending an object as direct perception, mental consciousness may also arise;

yet, even though visual consciousness has attained direct perception at that time, the five consciousnesses do not themselves say, "I have attained the object of direct perception. It is just like a dream.
One takes as an object that which was perceived within a dream. Furthermore, while one is actually perceiving an object within a dream, one does not even know, "I am dreaming.
Once one has subsequently awakened, both the objects perceived within the dream and the mind that perceived them have all fallen into the past.
It is only upon waking that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) realizes that the objects previously perceived were what was seen in a dream.

At the moment when the visual consciousness has ceased and the mental consciousness subsequently arises, it perceives the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the objects seen by the five sensory consciousnesses during their active phases. Thus, the mental consciousness can arise subsequent to them.

It is permissible to admit that there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This refutes the idea that the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*), arising independently at a later moment, possesses direct perception.
However, if it is the five sensory consciousnesses, one may indeed admit they possess direct perception.

As for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) taking as its object a realm that has already ceased, this further proves that the activity of observational wisdom (*vipaśyanājñāna*) remains present; for when a term expresses "blue," it simultaneously excludes yellow, red, and so forth.
Regarding "form" (*rūpa*): if one says "blue lotus," this excludes peaches, pear blossoms, and so forth; it excludes other forms and other flowers.
However, speaking from the standpoint of ultimate reality, the nature of that blue lotus is beyond words, and thus even the verbal expression cannot reach it.

For now, we do not exclude it because its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is apprehended. This is like how, for the time being, the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is said to be apprehended.
Speaking according to reality, one cannot obtain a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) either.
The *Śāstra* states: "There is only the essence of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and the essence of the common characteristic is entirely absent.

This means that while the essences of particulars such as blue or yellow are admitted to exist, there is not even a single instance of "blue" that pervades all instances of blue throughout the world; therefore, it is known that there exists only a conceptual construction (*prajñapti*).
In reality, there is no such thing as a universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

The Commentary states: "If one says that the universal characteristic exists only as a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the observing mind that universally perceives both the particular (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) and the universal, then within the untainted subsequently attained wisdom (*anāsrava-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of Bodhisattvas and Buddhas from the first through the tenth stages, the perception of blue and so forth is a particular, and it is also manifest."

It is apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Whether it be the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of suffering, emptiness, and impermanence, or their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), because one personally realizes the essence of the dharma, both are indeed direct perception.
By taking suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self as internal [objects], one subsequently realizes the principle of the specific characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā-svalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, even that which takes common characteristics as its object is called a "specific characteristic"; this is the untainted (*anāsrava*) cognition of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
In the state of post-attainment direct perception (*prsthalabdha-pratyakṣa*), one takes the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of blue and so forth as objects;

furthermore, when preaching the Dharma to the multitude, one gives rise to conventional designations that express various sentient beings. These are the conceptual understandings (*kalpanā*) upon the sixth consciousness, which are termed "common characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Since Buddhas and Bodhisattvas also take these as objects and thereby achieve universal knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), they speak of principles such as suffering, emptiness, and impermanence as common characteristics. These are exclusively...
Within a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one directly realizes the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of suffering, impermanence, and so forth.

In other states of distracted mind, there is nothing that is not directly realized as the common characteristic of suffering and impermanence. If a phenomenon’s specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is attained according to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then that specific characteristic extends to the five distracted sensory consciousnesses as well as the eighth consciousness; all of them directly realize their own specific characteristics, because they are direct perceptions. [The same applies to] common characteristics.

Regarding the statement that "characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are also obtained through inference (*anumāna*)," the intended meaning is as follows: The sixth consciousness provisionally understands the commonality (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of blue and so forth only when it is in a state of distraction consisting of the wisdom of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā*, *cintāmayī-prajñā*), as well as other states of distracted mind; it only obtains a provisional understanding of the commonality of blue.

It does not understand characteristics such as suffering (*duḥkha*) or impermanence (*anityatā*), because those possess specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Thus, the provisional blue and the provisional designation arise based upon specific characteristics.

Because conventional cognition expresses [objects], it is said that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is "conventionally blue. Regarding the phrase "because it is the basis for conventional expression," this means it serves as the basis for the convention.

The treatise states: "The specific characteristic is established as the basis for the convention; for instance, when there is the specific characteristic of blue, a conventional verbal expression arises immediately."

As for "the speaker," this refers to the arising of a conceptual construction based on the provisional [designation] "blue" and the formation of an understanding of its existence. This is an indirect basis (*parokṣa-āśraya*), not a direct basis (*sākṣāt-āśraya*);

it merely excludes the direct [basis]. Alternatively, because there are provisional verbal expressions that express the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of blue and so forth, sentient beings possess specific characteristics that are distinct from names and words.
If there were no verbal expressions to express these specific characteristics, the minds of sentient beings would not [function].

It is known that there is an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Because it is provisionally known and designated based on the similarity between the transformation of the signified object and its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is called 'provisional' and thus considered a remote condition (*parokṣapratyaya*);
it cannot directly [grasp] itself. Furthermore, when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) records the blue specific characteristic, it is in fact...
The arising of the aspect of the blue image: this upper image is an accomplished object-condition (*pariniṣpanna-ālambana*).

It is accepted that this aspect, together with its primary essence (*bimba*), is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the "great" [blue]. When one perceives a single instance of blue, it penetrates through all instances of blue;

this is the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) that pervades blue. This conceptual construction is an impermanent object; because there is one blue that is able to penetrate all blues, we know it to be such.
This is a conceptual understanding (*vikalpa*) based on the mind; it does not encompass the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the essential reality (*svabhāva*).

Since the mind does not grasp the object, this conceptual understanding of "blue" is similar to the essential reality itself; thus, the blue of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) serves as a remote condition (*viprakṛṣṭapratyaya*).

Therefore, one should know that the own-characteristic is not the basis for the conceptual [understanding]. This own-characteristic is not the direct basis for the designation of the conceptual "blue."

The Commentary states: "Because one forms the cognition of blue and so forth regarding the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form, it is said that the self-characteristic is the basis for the conventional (*prajñapti*).

This is because there exists the self-characteristic of blue; it is upon this that the eye produces the cognition of blue as a conventional blue. If the self-characteristic of blue did not exist, the mind of conventional blue could not arise.
Therefore, it is said that conventional cognition relies upon the self-characteristic, and thus the self-characteristic is called the basis for the conventional."
The treatise states: "That which is designated by conventional cognition regarding the mind arises based on sound.
Now, within this treatise, when it says that conventional designations arise based on sound, it refers specifically to their arising based on sound as explained within this Sahā world;
it does not refer to other world-systems. In those other regions, conventional designations may instead arise based upon objects such as light, subtle fragrances, exquisite tastes, and so forth.

This refers to the arising of conventional designations (*prajñapti*). Furthermore, when the treatise states that conventional cognition arises in dependence upon sound, this is said specifically with reference to the two realms of desire and form.
Within these two realms of desire and form, conventional cognition arises in dependence upon sound;

therefore, this treatise does not speak of it in relation to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Although conventional cognition exists within the formless realm, it does not arise in dependence upon sound.
Furthermore, "provisional designators" refers to the names that serve as designators. These names arise based on sounds accepted by oneself, or through hearing the sounds of others;

once provisional cognition has taken them as its object, one subsequently gives rise to the names and so forth accepted by oneself. In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), however, this does not occur by means of sound.

If one is born with the capacity to cognize all dharmas as sounds, and is born having attained that formless realm concentration, then upon being born in that formless realm, all [cognitions] take sound as their object;
this is the mental consciousness taking sound as its object. Since there is no faculty of hearing, it is also impossible for ear-consciousness to arise and take sound as its object.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Regarding 'designation' (*abhilāpa*), it refers to names (*nāman*) and so forth, up to each being based on its own predominance.

This means that for names, phrases (*pada*), and so forth, they are predominant as the "designators" (*vyañjaka*), while manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) is subordinate. Conversely, regarding the substance of sound (*śabda-dravya*), it is predominant as the "manifested action," while its function as a designator is subordinate.

Furthermore, among phenomena, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) takes names as its object, whereas the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) takes sounds as its object; thus, sound is predominant when contrasted with the Abhidharma’s specific categories. This reasoning is not tenable, just as in the case of a rat hearing [a sound].
Regarding the phrase "from the sound of a cat up to excluding those in the formless realm," this commentary contains two interpretations. The first interpretation states:

Even the provisional wisdom of the formless realm arises based on sound. This is because, since beginningless time, while dwelling in the lower realms, one has heard others speak of the existence of meditative absorptions in the formless realm; having heard these sounds from others, one then cultivates and attains them.

Regarding the formless realm concentrations (*ārūpya-samāpatti*): after death, one is reborn within the formless realms. Therefore, it is known that even the provisional wisdom within the formless realms arises based on sound.
Regarding this, the Master [Hui]tan comments on the initial interpretation in this commentary, saying: "If this person, from time immemorial..."

When one arises in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and gives rise to a mind of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), hears sounds of the lower realms, and possesses the seeds of wisdom acquired through the concentration of the formless realm, that person, upon attaining it, is born in the formless realm. It may be said that this conventional cognition (prajñā) of the formless arises based on sound.
It is said that such wisdom exists. That person previously resided within the lower realms;
while hearing the teaching on the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), they gave rise to a mind of the lower realms, thereby perfuming the seeds of the lower-realm mind.

Since they did not actually give rise to a mind of the formless realm, how can it be said that birth [in the formless realm] results from hearing the teaching on the formless absorptions in the lower realms, which then perfumes the seeds?
Furthermore, one may be reborn in the formless realm, yet it is said that conventional cognition arises in dependence upon sound.

For example, consider a Bodhisattva of the *pāramitās*, or a Śrāvaka of extensive wisdom who has attained the fruit of non-returning; having previously attained only the concentration of the formless realm in the lower realms, they comprehend all phenomena with a mind belonging to the form realm.
When such a person gives rise to a formless mind and hears another’s voice explaining the formless concentrations, [conventional cognition arises].

These perfumes form seeds. Later, when that person is born into the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one might say that conventional cognition arises based on sound and thus possesses inference (*anumāna*).

If this were so, then among those born in the Formless Realm—namely, the Bodhisattvas of the Perfections (*pāramitā*) and the Śrāvakas of Vast Wisdom (*vipula-prajñā*)—who possess only inferential knowledge, it would be said that conventional cognition depends on sound.
However, as for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in that state who are born into the Formless Realm, [this should not apply].
The Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu) should not possess conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), because the mind of the Formless Realm cannot comprehend all phenomena (sarvadharma).
Therefore, it is known that the first interpretation in the Commentary is incorrect. Furthermore, the second interpretation in the Commentary states:

"As for this treatise’s statement that conventional knowledge arises based on sound, this refers exclusively to conventional knowledge arising based on sound within the lower realms; the subsequent passage concerning the Formless Realm speaks of something else."
However, mice, lice, and so forth all possess inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*).
The *Vyākhyā* states: "It is not so; here it is taught that the knowledge of the lower realms arises based on sound, with the exception of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
In the formless realm, this inferential knowledge exists, yet it does not arise based on sound. If this were not the case, then this treatise would apply only to...
In the desire realm, conventional wisdom mostly arises based on sound; this is stated in the treatise according to the majority of cases.
Excluding the formless realm, although wisdom exists in the formless realm, it does not arise based on sound.

The treatise states: "Where sound does not reach, this [designation] does not function. This means that where sound does not reach its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), this conventional cognition (*prajñapti-jñāna*) cannot apprehend it.
Conventional cognition is precisely the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) functioning as a provisional understanding. "Designation" (*abhilāpa*) refers to verbal designation;
this verbal designation designates the essence of the specific characteristic, yet it also cannot [apprehend it], because the sphere of mental activity has ceased. Provisional...
Because the path of language is cut off, provisional designations cannot be obtained; because the sphere of mental activity has ceased, provisional cognition cannot take it as its object.
Provisional cognition and provisional designations do not arise with respect to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); rather, they arise through conceptual transmission.

This is like when the sense organs of smell, taste, and touch come into contact [with their objects], up to and including sound. Question: What is the intent of this passage? Why is "form" (*rūpa*) not mentioned?
Regarding "sound": these three objects—smell, taste, and touch—are explained specifically here because they are cognized through contact (saṃyoga).

As for visible form, sound, and so forth, they are not mentioned here because they are cognized through separation (viyoga). Nevertheless, all five types of objects are established according to their locations;
it is by means of these locations that they are clarified.
The *Śāstra* states: "Because both the designator and the designated are not self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), one knows that conventional designation does not rely on real entities.

If it is argued that the designating names and so forth, as well as the designated meanings such as impermanence, are all conventionally understood by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the explanation is as follows:

because the mind takes as its object the designating name and the designated meaning, the designator and the designated are collectively termed the "common characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Although names and so forth possess their own self-characteristics, here [we are] considering...
Because it is conventionally explained by others, it becomes a universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Conventional designation functions solely in dependence upon universal characteristics;

conventional designation does not depend directly upon the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Why is this? Because the particular characteristic is free from verbal expression (*nāman*), whereas conventional designation of universal characteristics carries verbal expression.

How could there be a universal characteristic that carries verbal expression while directly depending on a particular characteristic that is free from verbal expression? Even if indirectly, the same [contradiction] would apply.

Regarding the statement that "these signifiers are names, phrases, and so forth": although sound possesses its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is apprehended solely by the auditory consciousness, the signifiers—names, phrases, and phonemes—do not have a separate substantial entity.
They are like the conceptualizing cognition (*prajñā*) that arises as a mental construct upon the sixth consciousness.
The individual and universal characteristics (svalakṣaṇa and sāmānyalakṣaṇa) are mutually dependent and are all devoid of intrinsic substance; furthermore, they lack anything to be signified.

This is because the conventional understanding of universal characteristics and so forth, as well as speech, apply universally across all cognitions, and because they are the means of signification; thus, they are not individual characteristics.
The Commentary states: "As for the phrase 'it functions with respect to its own-characteristic just as it does with respect to sound':
if conventional wisdom (*prajñapti-jñāna*) only apprehends the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), then that conventional wisdom does not apprehend the own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

This is just as, in the case of sound, sound only realizes the common characteristic of sound and cannot express the own-characteristic, because the own-characteristic is beyond names and expressions (*nāma-vyavahāra*). It should rather say: "as it is with respect to a name that is inadequate."
The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is called "without substance. Therefore, it is said to be based on what is taught; thus, it is stated, "just as in the case of sound. Question:
If one does not apprehend the specific characteristic, and so forth, up to not grasping the objective reality (*vastu*), why is this not an attachment?
Should it not be like the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) that occurs within an unwholesome mind, since it likewise does not grasp the objective reality? Answer:

Regarding the statement, "If the mind that clings to phenomena (dharma-grāha) were to be subsumed [within the object], it should be called 'attaining the substance' (*tattva-lābha*)," there are two interpretations within this commentary.
The first interpretation in the commentary states: "When taking an object as a condition, if it is a reflection that corresponds to the original substance (*bimba*)."

That which is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) apprehends the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). If, when taking an object as its condition, it does not correspond to the mental image (*pratibimba*), then it is an inferential cognition (*anumāna*) that apprehends the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
This objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is wisdom; it is the wisdom of conceptual understanding upon the sixth consciousness, which is similar to the objective aspect.
If one follows the latter interpretation in the *Śūchí* (Commentary), it states: "If it corresponds to the mental image, it is direct perception, and thus [apprehends the particular characteristic]."

Regarding the object of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*): if it does not correspond to the underlying reality (*bhāva*), nor does it apprehend a mental image (*pratibimba*), yet a mind of grasping arises, this is an inferential cognition (*anumāna*) that attains a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
If it neither apprehends the underlying reality nor the mental image, yet a mind of grasping arises, [this is likewise an inferential cognition].

This is precisely non-valid cognition (*anumāna*). If one maintains that the mind is non-valid cognition—specifically, if a mind of the three natures such as joy (*prīti*) and so forth takes a jar or a basin as its object, it is termed non-valid cognition.
Although there are two interpretations in the Commentary (*śāstra*), one may choose between them as one pleases.

Not only does it fail to apprehend the primary essence (*bimba*), but because the mind adheres firmly to this direct image-part (*sākṣāt-bhāga*), it is called "clinging" (*abhiniveśa*). This applies if the mind clings...
That is to say, it does not grasp the essential image (*svabhāva-bimba*). The essence of the essential image is not substantially real; furthermore, it is neither a self, nor permanent, nor pure.
That grasping mind takes the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and so forth to be a self, to be substantially real, and to be permanent and pure.

Because this direct object of cognition (*sākṣāt-ālambana*) appears as if it were a truly existent dharma within the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), such grasping is [false attachment].

Therefore, it is said that the grasping mind does not encompass the essence of the image. Nevertheless, at the moment the grasping mind arises, what appears upon the mind is the actual universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
This objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is the object of perception for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and so forth, because it is a mind arising from conditions.
Thus, although it is a grasping mind, it still possesses an objective aspect. If one were to formulate this as an inference: the mind is indeed commensurate with the objective aspect of the image.
The Commentary states: "Alternatively, if the mind of inference (*anumāna*) and so forth takes the direct image-part (*sākṣāt-bimba-bhāga*) as its object, these too would not be mutually inclusive.

If one follows the previous interpretation, this [statement] is a provisional explanation. To say that the image-part is mutually inclusive means that the image is provisionally explained as being blue, yet even as a provisional explanation, it is not actually blue.

Therefore, it is said that they are mutually inclusive. If this latter interpretation is adopted, then this metaphorical cognition of blue (*nīla-anumāna*) is not mutually inclusive with the reflected image (*pratibimba*).

Why? Because the portion of the blue aspect (*nīla-ākāra-bhāga*) of the reflected image is either smaller than this inferential cognition, or because within the mind of metaphorical cognition, it merely encompasses all blues in the world.
Therefore, the metaphorical cognition of blue is not mutually inclusive with the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*). This latter interpretation is superior to the former.
Regarding the interpretation of mutual inclusion, this is not acceptable.

The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "If that were so, since the five objects such as form have their own distinct cognizing subjects, they would possess [cognitions] of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*);

the same would apply to the five sense organs such as the eye and their seeds, because they are the objects of wisdom-consciousness. If this were the case, then for the time being, according to the coarse cultivation of the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the intention is as follows:

Regarding the five objects, such as form and so forth, there are the five consciousnesses and the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), each of which perceives them individually; these are their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
As for the five sense organs and their seeds, they are perceived by the mental consciousness through inference; thus, they should be called common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states: "For now, this discussion is based on what is commonly accepted. It is also said that the five objects, the five sense organs, and their seeds [are perceived]. Second...

The eight consciousnesses directly perceive them; these are also the objective spheres of the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). The intent of the question here is this:

if the five sense objects are perceived simultaneously with the five consciousnesses, as well as by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the fundamental consciousness, then all of them obtain the objective sphere of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

This question asks: "If the five faculties such as the eye, along with their seeds, are apprehended by the eighth consciousness and thus attained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), thereby attaining the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of those faculties;

then, as for the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), which are conceptual objects of expression (*abhilāpa-viṣaya*), is it not the case that they too attain direct perception of their own specific characteristics?"

The Commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "If one says that the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) can take this [object] as its cognitive object, it would not be a direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*)," and so on, up to "like other distracted states of mind.
This is the position of Master Sthiramati and other masters of incorrect tenets.

They maintain that, setting aside the Buddhas, the knowledge of others' minds possessed by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), which takes the minds of others as its object, is an inferential cognition (*anumāna*).
Since this is an inference (*anumāna*), it is clearly known to be a state of distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*). As the verse says:

"Knowing an object as it is not [in reality], like knowing the mind of another"—this refers to the subsequent mind within a distracted state taking the preceding mind as its object; this is precisely the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) cultivated in a distracted state.
This is also a state of distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*).

The *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) states that Dharmapāla’s explanation—namely, that "all self-attesting portions (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of ordinary beings and sages constitute direct perception (*pramāṇa*)"—is because the self-attesting portion takes the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object and is thus a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This interpretation does not fully capture the underlying principle. One should rather say that the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) takes another's... [text truncated]

The cognition of another's mind is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). As previously stated regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the cognition of a jar or a garment is what is commonly known by the world;

these are cognitions of inference based on the sense faculties (*indriya-anumāna-jñāna*). However, when one takes another’s mind as an object, this is direct perception. Furthermore, when taking another’s mind as an object, one is able to do so only while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
thus it is clearly understood to be direct perception.

The Commentary states: "Because these are the fruits of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); just as supernormal powers are included within realized wisdom (*pramāṇa-bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), the six supernormal powers within the Buddha-body are all termed 'fruits.

This is because they are obtained through the cultivation of causes over three *kalpas*, and because they are the supernormal powers existing upon the stage of Buddhahood; thus they are called 'fruits.
When these powers take another's mind as their object, it is like the supernormal power of the divine eye taking objects. The supernormal power of the divine ear takes sound as its object."

Furthermore, just as the supernormal power of recollecting past lives takes the past as its object, and the supernormal power of death and rebirth takes future objects and so forth, when these take such objects, they are all direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Since they are both wholesome and derived from meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*), they are necessarily [the result of] meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The Commentary states: "As it is said in the verses of the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, up to the phrase 'because of the false attachment of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

This passage represents the interpretation of Sthiramati. Sthiramati says: When a Bodhisattva of the One Vehicle gives rise to the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and takes another's mind as its object..."
All of these are inferences (*anumāna*) by which one apprehends the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), but not the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of another’s mind.

Since the verse states that "the object of knowledge is not as it truly is," it is clear that this is inference. Being an inference, it therefore takes the common characteristic of another’s mind as its object;

for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses grasping. This master has misinterpreted the verse; his understanding of the defiled factors (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) is deficient. The verse says: "Since it takes another’s mind as its object..."

Because it takes [the object] as its focal point within meditative concentration, it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). To say that it does not accord with reality means that it does not know the minds of others as they truly are, for it cannot know them in their full detail.

If it were to arise as the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), when taking another person's mind as its focal point, it would know in every single detail the various matters such as the desires and inclinations present within that person's mind. Furthermore, the Buddha spoke of the knowledge of minds.
When greed arises in the mind of another person, one immediately knows the greed that has arisen in that person.

One should observe such and such conduct to recognize that greed, or perhaps a single instance of a greedy mind; by observing in this way, one attains the severance of this greed upon first realizing the Path.
Alternatively, the greed of another person should be observed as being severed only when the Buddha turns the Wheel of Dharma. Or, [the greed] of another person...

Regarding greed: one should sever this greed by viewing it as being merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). Or, there may be a certain greed that should be severed by viewing the Buddha’s entry into *parinirvāṇa*.
Or, when a person sees a certain greed, they should sever that greed by viewing the distribution of the Buddha’s relics after his passing.
This applies to all other afflictions as well; for example, as in the case of greed and so forth arising in the minds of sentient beings due to the condition of the color blue. (1)
A portion of clarity: to know in detail that which can counteract [a state] is called "conduct" (*caryā*), up to eighty-four thousand types of conduct.
If a Bodhisattva or one of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) gives rise to the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), it is merely a knowledge of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Even if they know that the person before them has a mind of greed, they do not yet know the specific conduct that serves as the antidote to that greed. Because their own recollective mind takes the other's preceding mind as its object, they only perceive it through general characteristics and cannot [know it specifically].

Because one knows [the minds of others] with clarity and in detail, it is called the "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*). How does it know its object? It does not know it as it truly is, unlike the knowledge of reality (*yathābhūtajñāna*) or the knowledge of the mind (*cittajñāna*).
If it is the knowledge of others' minds, it takes as its object only the three natures of mind within the six consciousnesses of another person;

it does not take the seventh or eighth consciousnesses as its object. The seventh and eighth consciousnesses can only be known by a Buddha; other Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) do not perceive the seventh or eighth consciousnesses at all.
The treatise states: "That which functions solely by relying on the thing (*vastu*) refers to that which resembles the thing, namely the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Conventional cognition, verbal designations, and so forth, function by relying upon this universal characteristic; they do not rely upon the true thing’s own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)."
The *Śāstra* states: "Sound functions by depending on an augmented semblance. This means it arises depending on an augmented universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

The *Commentary* states: "This applies to all three natures" (*trividha-svabhāva*), meaning that taking a universal characteristic as an object pertains to wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral minds alike.

The commentary states: "Because the mind that grasps must contradict the characteristics of the image. To grasp this image as permanent or as a self contradicts the fact that these characteristic portions (nimitta-bhāga) are impermanent and non-self;
it is a contradiction because they share the same objective field. A mind that conceptually understands the common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) does not contradict the characteristic portion.
If one firmly grasps this conceptualized characteristic portion, then that common characteristic is subsumed [by the grasping].

Regarding the mental image (*pratibimba*): if one considers it from the perspective of a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) whose mind takes this very common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) as its object, then it does not cast a reflection.
