The first thought-moment serves as the cause for the outflow-free state; thus, while the initial moment lacks causal conditions, subsequent moments of outflow-freedom possess them.
This "patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) is termed a single moment (eka-ksana). This single moment is outflow-free.
Because it arises without a cause, this single moment—among the six causes—possesses only the associated, co-existent, and enabling causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Because its nature is pure, there is no pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*). Because it is newly acquired knowledge, there is no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*);

and because there is no homogeneous cause, there is also no outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*). However, if it were subsequently uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it would also be possible for it to have a homogeneous cause; [this refers to] the outflowing [fruit].

This is the result. According to this master’s interpretation, following the Sarvāstivāda view of momentariness, that school posits five types of phenomena: first, nurtured (aupacayika); second, outflowing (naiṣyandika);

third, ripening (vipākaja); fourth, momentary (kṣaṇika); and fifth, substantial (dravya). Since the untainted (anāsrava) patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) at the initial moment of the Hīnayāna is not material form, it is not nurtured.
Furthermore, from the beginningless past, there has never been anything untainted [prior to its arising].

Because it acts as a cause, it does not arise from a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*). It is not of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*), because it is untainted and wholesome (*anāsrava-kuśala*) rather than indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
It is not of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*), because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It is not substantial; it is merely designated as "momentary."
Thus, at the first moment of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), there arises the patience of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñānakṣānti*).

Since this is an untainted wholesome factor, when subsequent moments of the untainted arise from the preceding patience of dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*), there exists a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*); consequently, the subsequent moments possess its outflow (*niṣyanda*).

In the Mahāyāna view of the Path of Seeing, if one takes the originally existing untainted factors as the outflow, then there exists a causal condition (*hetupratyaya*). Upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*).
In the first moment, there are newly perfumed untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*). In the second moment, they do not produce an active manifestation (*samudācāra*). Why is this?

Because the seed of the knowledge of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya-jñāna*) regarding the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) does not produce the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) directed toward the higher realms.

Why is this? Because the paths are distinct. This applies even up to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which likewise cannot produce an active manifestation; for these are seeds of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
This gives rise to the path-knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārgajñāna*). Because this seed only increases, it is the transformation of the seeds of the *śaikṣa* (one still in training).

Since there are three grades [of these seeds], if one transforms the meaning of the state of being a *śaikṣa*, then upon reaching the subsequent path of cultivation, these newly perfumed seeds from the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) are also able to produce actual manifestations (*samudācāra*), because these seeds consist of only a single grade. This continues until one reaches the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
This refers to the transformation of the seeds of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) to produce the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "In this context, there are also those who are still in training (*śaikṣa*), etc., in contrast to those with innate outflows (*sahaja-sāsrava*).

Now, this treatise also uses the Buddha as a challenge to that [position]. If one were to challenge that [position] by means of the noble one in training (*śaikṣa-ārya*), then it would also be possible for afflictions (*kleśa*) to arise once again.

There are cases where that which is untainted (anāsrava) gives rise to that which is tainted (sāsrava); this is precisely like using untainted karma as the cause for undergoing the projection of birth and death (saṃsāra).

The treatise states: "If one were to raise the objection that the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), though untainted, produces what is tainted when assumed by another, such an objection is called 'difficult to resolve'."
The commentary states: "If it were said that wholesome [dharmas] and so forth should serve as seeds for unwholesome [dharmas] and so forth, this would be acceptable for the Hīnayāna;

however, regarding their being 'homogeneous causes' (sabhāga-hetu), the commentator has cited this erroneously. In the Hīnayāna school, there is no instance of wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas] serving as homogeneous causes; there are only [unwholesome dharmas acting as such]."
Wholesome dharmas can serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for those that are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
This is also like the case of the two views—view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*)—giving rise to obscured dharmas such as anger.

Those who hold these views, namely the Sarvāstivādins, the Vibhajyavādins, the Vaibhāṣikas, and those who misinterpret the meaning, are collectively termed "teachers who confuse the mind. Furthermore, unwholesome dharmas serve as homogeneous causes, as do those that are obscured. Regarding the body...

The two extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*) for unwholesome states such as hatred (*dveṣa*). Regarding the "teacher who muddies the mind," this refers to what the treatise says:

"That which is adventitious (*āgantuka*) with respect to the faculties (*indriya*) can be discarded and known; it is termed 'adventitious. That which is untainted (*anāsrava*) and cannot be discarded is termed 'the master' (*mūla*).
Question: Defilements (*kleśa*) can be discarded and known; is it not the case that these defilements themselves are called "dust" (*rajas*)?
Guest: "The afflictions (*kleśa*) can be abandoned and known; these afflictions are precisely what are called 'adventitious dust-like afflictions' (*āgantuka-rajas-kleśa*).

When the followers of the Two Vehicles enter the vision of the two [truths] and reach the state of the remainderless *nirvāṇa*, their path is likewise seen as something that can be abandoned and known.

Should the noble path (*āryamārga*) then be called 'adventitious dust'? Regarding the statement found in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*: "That sūtra also says, 'The nature of the mind (*cittaprakṛti*) is not pure.'"
Regarding the phrase "the afflictions of earth and adventitious dust," it refers to such passages as "because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled.

If one were to say that the preceding untainted essence perishes and the subsequent untainted essence takes its place, this would be an error in the commentary; it should rather state that the preceding tainted essence perishes and the subsequent untainted essence arises.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Regarding the statement that one should enumerate how many types of wholesome factors each of the various masters posits, as explained in the separate notes:

if it is a Mahāyāna master, they posit eleven types of wholesome factors, namely faith, gradual cultivation, and so forth. If it is the Sarvāstivāda, they posit ten types of wholesome and unwholesome factors, and do not posit the wholesome roots of non-delusion.
If it is the Mahāsāṃghika school, they posit three types of wholesome factors, namely [non-greed, non-hatred, and] non-delusion."
The roots of goodness are non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. One may establish one root of goodness, or two, or even up to four roots of goodness and so forth.
As stated in the treatise, there are four types of phenomena: namely, wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and unobscured-neutral.
This is explained in the commentary (*śāstra*). Regarding the passage in the commentary which says, "If form and sound were wholesome, they would lack faith and so forth," form and sound are...
Because it is wholesome by way of origination (*samutthāna*), it is like the untainted (*anāsrava*) and so forth.

The response, "It is dissociated (*viprayukta*) and not of the nature of mind (*cittasvabhāva*)," means that if, among the dissociated factors, there were [factors] such as acquisition (*prāpti*) and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), this would imply the existence of manifest outflowing (*sāsrava*) mental nature. Since the nature of mind is pure, it is like the Buddhas and other noble ones (*ārya*).
The Buddha is such an example. Furthermore, even that which is wholesome by way of origination does not possess association (*saṃprayoga*) with faith (*śraddhā*) and the other [faculties].

The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'this refers to defilement' and 'this refers to all three natures': if one speaks of 'defilement,' it encompasses both the wholesome and other two natures;
if one speaks merely of 'affliction' (*rajas*), it refers exclusively to the unwholesome and the obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Since there exists a nature of the mind that is with outflows (*sāsrava*), how is it that here the purity of the nature of the mind with outflows is explained as the cause, using the Buddha as the causal analogy?"
The reason does not fail to apply to the example. The answer is that the Buddha fundamentally possesses no mind-nature that is subject to outflows (*āsrava*).
If one relies on the commentary (*śū*), the inference (*anumāna*) contains a logical fault. Now, the inference in the commentary should be revised as follows:

"In the state of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the outflow-free [mind] must be manifest, because it is admitted that the nature of the mind is pure, just like the Buddhas and other noble ones (*ārya*). This is without fault.
The Commentary states: Regarding the explanation of the transformation of the mind within the "Three Transformations of the Basis" in the tenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*:

as for the three transformations of the basis, first is the transformation of the mind, which is suchness because it is the nature of the mind; second is the transformation of the heavy impurities (*dausthulya*), which refers to the afflictions that are the objects to be countered;
third is the transformation of the path, which refers to the untainted noble path that serves as the counteragent.
The *Śāstra* states: "The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* fully explains this meaning," and it also says, "the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*).

Regarding the statement in the treatise, "I say that the essence of the mind is not affliction, and therefore its nature is fundamentally pure": Question: Since the mental kings (*citta-rāja*) and so forth are all pervasive of an unwholesome nature, how can they be called "fundamentally pure by nature"?
Answer: While it is true that the six consciousnesses as mental kings, along with the five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), are [pervasive], [the following distinction applies]...

The five objects and the four indeterminate states (*aniyata*) and so forth, although they pertain to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*), are called "naturally pure" because their essence is not affliction.
Thus, the mental states of an evil mind and other phenomena of the three natures are collectively termed "naturally pure by nature."
The Commentary states: "Regarding the statement that the four yogas and fifty-four [dharmas] are likewise so for mental factors (caitta) and the rest:

this refers to the fourteen mental factors, such as the universal (sarvatraga), the object-specific (viniyata), and the four indeterminate (aniyata). The essence of these fourteen mental factors is not affliction; they are also termed 'factors of purification'."

The Commentary states: "Later perfuming produces seeds" means that even for humans on the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), there are both innate (*sahaja*) and newly perfumed (*navasaṃskṛta*) untainted (*anāsrava*) seeds.

When first entering the Path of Vision, the first moment of the present activity perfumes and acquires untainted seeds. These newly perfumed seeds do not produce a manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) by the second moment.
Why? Because the first moment is either the activity itself or the seeds of the wisdom of the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*).

The subsequent thought can realize the principle (*tattva*). It does not produce the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the wisdom realizing the principle by means of seeds of abandonment or realization, because the wisdom that abandons and the wisdom that realizes cessation are distinct.
These newly perfumed seeds from the initial thought are only able to produce the actual manifestation after a long period of time;

thus, they are collectively termed "naturally pure" (*prakṛti-viśuddha*). At the time of hearing the true Dharma, due to the presence of actual manifestations of outflow-tainted states and one's own...
Regarding the statement that "the impure seeds perfumed by causes and conditions act as a dominant condition": Question:
Now, do the impure manifest states (*sāsrava-samudācāra*) provide support for the pure seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), or do the impure seeds themselves provide support for the pure seeds?
Answer: If one is in the stages of the provisions (*saṃbhāra-avasthā*) or the application (*prayoga-avasthā*), it is the originally existing impure seeds [that provide support].
Son, [if it were so], one would be unable to support the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) and cause them to increase.

For, since beginningless time, although there have been innate (*sahaja*) seeds of the provisions and the preparatory practices (*prayoga*), none of these tainted (*sāsrava*) seeds have been able to support other untainted seeds and cause them to increase.

Now, however, one does indeed support and take up the seeds of both the manifest activity (*samudācāra*) and the newly perfumed (*navasaṃskṛta*) [seeds] from the stages of the provisions and the preparatory practices. These manifest...
Only when the practice and the newly perfumed seeds possess sufficient power can they assist other untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) to grow.
What is now being explained is that the newly perfumed seeds can indirectly assist other untainted seeds to grow;
this is just as previously mentioned tainted wholesome and unwholesome karma can indirectly assist other ripened (*vipāka*) indeterminate seeds of name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*) to grow.

This is also the same case here. It is asked: regarding the transformation within the Buddha-body of one who has perfected the household, how is it that the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (wisdom of accomplishing activities) and the *ādarśa-jñāna* (mirror-like wisdom), which are originally of the highest grade, are called "transformed" (*parāvṛtta*)? [It is said... It is asked: regarding the bodies of other vehicles and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),...
Regarding the question, "How can there be the transformation, exhaustion, and cessation of the three natures which are contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*)? the answer follows.
The commentary (*śūtra*) states: "The wholesome factors of the stage of certainty (*niyāmāvakrānti*) are also contaminated, and so forth, because they are distinct.

This means that while in the preparatory stage (*prayoga-mārga*) prior to the [first] ground, the contaminated hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*) resulting from hearing the teachings act as auxiliary conditions for the perfuming (*vāsanā*), thereby enabling the [uncontaminated wisdom].
The seeds of outflows gradually increase. The wisdoms of hearing and reflection that possess outflows act as the causes for increasing these seeds;
they are thus called both "outflowing" and "non-outflowing" seeds. That which is increased is also called "non-outflowing. Thus, the two types are distinct from one another.

The *Śāstra* states: "That which induces a superior maturation (*viśiṣṭa-vipāka*)" refers to the wholesome deeds performed during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), which are capable of inducing the superior maturational fruits of rebirth among humans and gods, or the fruit of seven rounds of coming and going (*saptakṛtvaḥ-parama*).
This text does not define a "superior maturational fruit" by reference to the result of the ten kings of the reverse order of existence (*viparyāsa-deha-daśarāja-phala*).
If one follows the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, the stages of equipment and application (*prayoga-avasthā*) mostly refer to the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). If one follows the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*...

Regarding the stage of the application of the accumulations (*sambhāra-prayoga*), it is generally said that these pertain to Bodhisattvas. Alternatively, one may speak of them collectively as the attainment of superior maturation (*viśiṣṭa-vipāka*) without needing to differentiate between them.
This includes the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the ten kings (*daśarāja*) of the Mahāyāna, as well as the sevenfold superior maturation of the Hīnayāna.
The Commentary states that the fifty-first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of "experiencing general and specific retributive fruits.

According to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) interpretation, one experiences both general and specific retributive fruits during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), and one likewise experiences both general and specific retributive fruits during the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*).

Regarding the attainment of specific and general results in the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*): according to the Mahāyāna interpretation, in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), one attains both general and specific retributive results.
Regarding the stage of application, there are two views. One states that one creates only karma for specific retribution, which can induce specific retributive results.
If one were in the stage of equipment, being deluded regarding cause and effect, one might create general karmic retribution; however, in the stage of application, one does not create such causes.
[The opponent says: "It does not produce collective retribution (*saṃvartanīya-karma*). [The proponent replies: "The second view holds that it produces both collective and individual results. Why?
Because the treatise discusses the unique ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*) of noble learners (*śaikṣa*), stating that because they have eternally severed [ignorance], they do not create new karma;

it speaks only of the noble ones (*ārya*) not creating collective retribution, but does not say that ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) do not create collective retribution. Since one is still an ordinary person while in the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-avasthā*),"
Furthermore, those with clear knowledge can also create karma that results in collective retribution.

Moreover, according to the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, if an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) within the internal dharma is heedless, it is said that three types of ignorance serve as conditions for the arising of formations (*saṃskāra*).

If an ordinary person within the internal dharma is not heedless, it is said that latent ignorance (*anuśaya-avidyā*) serves as the condition for the arising of formations. These "formations" are precisely the "formations" among the twelve links [of dependent origination].

[Answer: Branch. If karma is capable of inducing a collective retribution (*saṃnipāta-vipāka*), that fruit of retribution may be termed the "branch of formations" (*saṃskāra-aṅga*). If it induces only a specific individual retribution (*pratyeka-vipāka*), it is not termed the branch of formations.

Since it is said that [the stage of] "initiating formations" (*pravartaka-saṃskāra*) occurs, it is clearly known that at the stage of formations, one is able to create the collective retribution-inducing karma of the branch of formations.

Even after attaining the four fruits of the path, one can still create karma for specific retributions; this is just as when an Arhat discards his robes and bowl and subsequently falls back [to a lower state].
The formations of life (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) are all newly created *vipāka*-karmas. Upon reaching the stage of the provisions (*sambhāra-avasthā*), the originally existing seeds of the provisions arise;
upon reaching the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), the originally existing seeds of application arise. Thus, the causes do not intermingle.

First, regarding those who truly understand the primary causes and conditions: as the aforementioned treatise states, "That which is of an untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharma*) is not subsumed under cessation (*prahāṇa*)."

It serves as the direct cause and condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for supramundane dharmas. Regarding the second [type], the superior dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for maturation, the treatise states:
"This direct cause and condition is subtle and hidden, difficult to comprehend; it is explained through skillful means as the seed of the supramundane mind. The answer says:

In terms of contaminated (*sāsrava*) formations, there are superior, middling, and inferior grades; however, the stage of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) belongs to the inferior grade of the contaminated.
Therefore, because that which can support the contaminated (*sāsrava*) is of an inferior grade, the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) it supports is also of an inferior grade.

If the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*) are of a medium grade among the contaminated and can support the contaminated, then since they are of a medium grade, the uncontaminated they support is also of a medium grade.
If the stages of Patience (*kṣānti*) and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) are of a superior grade, then that which can support the contaminated is already... [superior].
If it is of the superior grade, that which it supports—the untainted (anāsrava) seeds—is also of the superior grade.

The Commentary states: "If one relies on the view that [seeds] exist only as innate (*prakṛtistha*) or only as newly perfumed (*navavāsanā*), or even if they are treated as being of the middling grade, etc., then these seeds—whether exclusively innate or exclusively newly perfumed—consist of only a single grade of untainted seeds:
namely, the superior, middling, or inferior grades. These are thus categorized according to whether they are exclusively innate or exclusively newly perfumed.
As the perfuming gradually becomes superior, the inferior grade essence must be extinguished and transformed into the medium grade.
As the medium grade essence is perfumed, it gradually becomes extinguished and is transformed into the superior grade. When it becomes the medium grade, the inferior grade is extinguished;
when it becomes the superior grade, the medium grade is extinguished. This stage is called "transformative extinction" (parāvṛtti-nirodha). It extinguishes the medium...
The lower [grade] brings about the upper.
The Commentary states: "Now, the third master holds that there are three grades of seeds, which refers to the meaning of 'transformation and equality.

This is the school that maintains the combined application of both newly perfumed and originally existing [seeds]. There are three grades of seeds; by means of the arising of lower-grade outflows-free [states], they support the distinctness of the middle-grade seeds."
It is superior. When the seeds of the medium grade arise later, the seeds of the medium grade are also able to support the power of the seeds of the inferior grade, making them superior.
Although the inferior and medium grades are similar in their vital force (*bala*), it is only the seeds of the medium grade that can produce actual manifestation (*samudācāra*);

the seeds of the inferior grade, despite having a distinct vital force, cannot manifest. This is because the seeds of the medium grade of outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states arise as actual manifestations; therefore, those [inferior seeds]...
It is capable of assisting the superior grade of untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) to increase until they reach their full potential;

even when the superior grade of untainted seeds arises, it can assist the inferior and middle-grade seeds, such that their power becomes exceptionally superior and equal to that of the superior-grade seeds.

Following the principle of the superior-grade untainted seeds being able to produce actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*), the middle-grade seeds cannot produce actual manifestations of their own fruit. Superior...

Just as the seeds of the path of seeing can nourish the growth of the untainted seeds of the path of cultivation, so too, when the seeds of the path of cultivation subsequently arise, they can in turn nourish the seeds of the path of seeing, making their power superior. Because the power of the seeds of the path of seeing is thus superior, the seeds of the path of seeing—
The nature and power of the seeds of the [Śaikṣa] stage are equal to those produced by the arising of the Path of Cultivation;

therefore, when they assist the seeds of the Aśaikṣa stage and increase the arising of the Aśaikṣa path, they are also able to assist the power of the seeds of the Path of Seeing and the Path of Cultivation.

However, while the seeds of the Paths of Seeing and Cultivation reach the stage of Aśaikṣa through the power of the seeds of the Aśaikṣa path, it is only the seeds of the Aśaikṣa stage that can produce actual manifestation (*samudācāra*); the seeds of the nature of seeing cannot produce such manifestation.

This refers to their active manifestation (*samudācāra*). Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that [the seeds] are either exclusively innate (*prakṛtistha*) or exclusively newly perfumed (*navasaṃskṛta*), and so forth, up to the point of "in the midst of performing and performing":
if one establishes only the position of the new perfuming school, they establish only a single category of seed, concerning which there are two theories. One says:
from time immemorial, there have existed only the seeds of the mundane wholesome *mokṣabhāgīya* (factors conducive to liberation) and the mundane... [text fragment].

The seeds of the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are themselves the untainted seeds (*anāsravabīja*). Second, it is said that since beginningless time, prior to the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), and because they have not yet undergone perfuming (*vāsanā*), there are neither the seeds of the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) nor the seeds of the stage of penetration.

It is only at a later time, through hearing the teachings, that one newly perfumes the seeds of the stage conducive to liberation; and it is only through the practice of contemplation of the truths (*satyadarśana*) that one begins to perfume [the seeds of penetration].

Regarding the seeds of the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (stages leading to penetration), they are gradually cultivated through perfuming; thus, from contaminated seeds, uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) actualities are newly produced.

Upon these uncontaminated actualities, uncontaminated seeds are formed through perfuming. Just as upon first hearing the teachings, one immediately perfumes and acquires the seeds of the inferior *mokṣabhāgīya* (stages conducive to liberation), so too, by subsequent gradual cultivation, one refines those previously acquired inferior seeds and develops them into the middling.
In this stage, one further cultivates the medium grade of extinction until it becomes the superior grade.

Next, one eliminates the seeds of the superior *mokṣabhāgīya* (factors conducive to liberation) and produces the inferior seeds of the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (factors conducive to penetration). Then, by eliminating the inferior, the medium is formed; again, by eliminating the medium, the superior is formed.

Subsequently, one eliminates the *uṣmagata* (heat) and *mūrdhan* (summit) stages to form the *kṣānti* (patience), continuing until one eliminates the *laukikāgradharma* (supreme mundane dharmas) to produce the untainted (*anāsrava*) vision.

The Path: Within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one eliminates the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and gives rise to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*).

In this manner, up until one eliminates the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge ’nvayajñānakṣānti*) and gives rise to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge ’nvayajñāna*). Furthermore, within the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), one eliminates the mind of entry (*praveśacitta*) and gives rise to the mind of abiding in the stage (*bhūmisthiticitta*);

one eliminates the mind of abiding in the stage and gives rise to the mind of fulfillment of the stage (*paripūrṇabhūmicitta*). This continues until one eliminates the mind of fulfillment of the stage.
The mind enters the second bhūmi from within the [first] bhūmi; this continues in the same manner up to the final ninth bhūmi.

Because one becomes a Buddha by extinguishing the Vajra-mind, there is only the attainment of Buddhahood, not the extinction of the Teacher. That is, by extinguishing the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga), one accomplishes the Path of Buddhahood;

by extinguishing the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), one accomplishes the Path of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa-mārga). Thus, by extinguishing the first bhūmi, one accomplishes the second bhūmi; by extinguishing the second bhūmi...

The seeds of the three stages are extinguished, and so on until the seeds of the ninth stage are extinguished to form the tenth stage; the seeds of the tenth stage are extinguished to form the Buddha-stage.
Therefore, according to those who maintain only the theory of newly perfumed seeds (*navābhyāsa-vāda*), only a single grade of seed is established as it undergoes transformation and extinction.

This is because the inferior grade is extinguished and transformed into the middling grade, and so forth. If one were to maintain only the theory of innate seeds (*prakṛtistha-vāda*), then since they have existed from beginningless time, there would be only a single grade of existence.

Regarding the seeds of the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the stage conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), there is only a single category of untainted seeds (*anāsravabīja*).
Precisely through the arising of hearing and reflection, these original, inferior seeds of the stage conducive to liberation increase and cause their actualization (*samudācāra*).
Furthermore, by means of this actualization as a support, the inferior seeds are extinguished and become intermediate; then, the intermediate are extinguished and become superior. Thus...

The same applies to the three grades [of seeds] at the stage of initiating the preparatory application (*prayoga*). That is to say, during the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and preparation, the currently active auxiliary causes and the originally existing untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) increase.
Subsequently, upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the untainted mind arises as an actual manifestation, whereby the originally existing untainted seeds are further increased;
this is because no new seeds are produced through fresh perfuming (*vāsanā*). As for the eighth stage and beyond, there is only...

The outflow-free (*anāsrava*) manifestations arise, which support and cause the increase of the originally existing (*prakṛtistha*) outflow-free seeds, until finally the seeds of the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*) are extinguished and Buddhahood is attained.
Thus, it is established that only one category of seed is transformed and extinguished.

Now, regarding the third master’s position that there are three categories of seeds, the principle of their simultaneous transformation would be consistent with Master Huiyuan’s view that both newly perfumed (*navasaṃskṛta*) and originally existing seeds are combined.

Regarding their application within the continuum: from time immemorial, there have existed the seeds of the provisions (*sambhāra*), the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), the sixteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the three moments of entering, abiding, and emerging within each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the four wisdoms (*jñāna*) of the Buddha-stage.

Each of these dharmas possesses its own innate seeds (*prakṛtistha-bīja*). Thus, for instance, in the stages of the provisions and the preparatory stage, there are respectively three grades of innate seeds.

Son, just as in the stage of the equipment for the path (*mārga-sambhāra-avasthā*), when seeds of an inferior variety arise as actualities (*samudācāra*), they are able to perfuse and form perfuming seeds (*vāsanā-bīja*).
Those inferior actualities directly support their own seeds of an inferior variety, causing them to increase;
if they can also support seeds of a middling or superior variety, they cause those too to increase, skillfully generating actualities.

This should be understood accordingly hereafter. When the seeds of the medium grade arise through successive cultivation, the seeds of the inferior grade can no longer give rise to their manifest activity (*samudācāra*).
When the manifest activity of the medium grade arises, it can nourish its own seeds of the same grade as well as the seeds of the superior grade;
yet [the seeds of the inferior grade] can no longer give rise to their manifest activity. Thus it is for the superior grade.

When seeds produce manifest activity (*pravṛtti*), they subsequently perfume and produce newly perfumed seeds. When a superior-grade manifest activity arises, it is immediately able to directly support its own superior-grade seeds of the same class;
subsequently, it indirectly supports the three types of seeds within the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The middle-grade manifest activity arising in the stage of preparatory application should be understood accordingly. Thus, in general, it is said that [the manifest] acts as a support.
When the manifest activity of the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) arises, that manifest activity can directly support the seeds of the stage of equipment;
it can also proximately support the seeds of the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*); and it can distantly support the seeds of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

However, those seeds [of the stage of equipment] cannot support the nature [itself]; rather, they can directly support the seeds of the stage of equipment and can also proximately support the seeds of the stage of application.

The seeds [of the path of preparation] can also remotely support the seeds of the path of seeing. However, the active states (*samudācāra*) of the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) cannot support the seeds of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) or the path beyond training (*aśaikṣamārga*), because they are too remote and thus lack the power to provide such support.

When the seeds of this stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*) produce their active states, those active states of the stage of application are then able to directly support the seeds of their own stage of application.
My son, it can also proximately support the seeds of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and it can distantly support the seeds of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
However, the seeds of the path of cultivation cannot support the seeds of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).

When those seeds of the path of seeing arise as actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*), they can directly support the seeds of the path of seeing, proximately support the seeds of the path of cultivation, and distantly support the path of no-more-learning.

Regarding the seeds: next, when the seeds of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) arise as actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*), they can directly support the seeds of the path of cultivation and also proximately support the seeds of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

From the stage of application (*prayoga*) until the completion of the first arising of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the seeds acquired through perfuming (*vāsanā*) within the first uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) cannot produce the manifestation of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) at the third moment, because [the obstacles] have been severed.
The seeds of delusion arise from afar because they are the seeds of the wisdom that realizes cessation and the path; this is for the sake of one's own benefit.

Furthermore, the seeds acquired through perfuming within fundamental wisdom cannot produce the actual manifestation of subsequently attained wisdom, because the wisdom that realizes principle and the wisdom that takes phenomena as its object are distinct.
From the first stage up to the fifth stage, these are the seeds of fundamental wisdom.

Only the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) can produce its own manifest activity (*samudācāra*); the seeds of fundamental wisdom cannot produce the manifest activity of subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), nor can the seeds of subsequently attained wisdom produce the manifest activity of fundamental wisdom. The seeds of subsequently attained wisdom can only produce subsequently attained wisdom;
all are produced from their own respective seeds. Thus, when the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) arises, it arises solely from [the seeds of] suffering.

The seeds of the *dharmajñānakṣānti* arise; that which is perfumed by the *duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti* constitutes a single acquisition of seeds, yet it cannot produce subsequent moments of *duḥkha-dharmajñāna* and so forth.
The same applies thereafter: what precedes does not produce what follows. Next, the second moment.

When the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) arises, its seed—the patience toward the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*)—can no longer arise as an actualized state (*pravṛtti*).

It is immediately able to enter into the seed of the patience toward the dharma-knowledge of suffering. The answer is that the power of this seed of the patience toward the dharma-knowledge of suffering is equal to the power of the dharma-knowledge of suffering itself.
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvayajñānakṣānti*) arises as an actualized state, it is immediately able to support [it].

The receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the seed-force of the dharma-knowledge of suffering combine to equalize the seeds of the two preceding knowledges with the power of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Consequently, the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering and the seeds of the dharma-knowledge of suffering can no longer produce their actualized manifestations (*samudācāra*);

they have already been superseded by the abandonment of the inferior for the sake of the superior outflow-free state (*anāsrava*). This process continues in this manner until the seeds of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) arise.

At the time of its manifestation, it utilizes the power of the seeds of the preceding fifteen moments of mind, causing that power of the seeds of the preceding fifteen moments of mind to become equal to the power of the sixteenth moment of mind;
this is called "equal transformation. Furthermore, it is termed "attaining the superior" and "abandoning the inferior," because it abandons the inferior and attains the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Thus, those seeds of the preceding fifteen moments of mind no longer give rise to manifest activity; in this way, one enters [the state].

Once the path of cultivation has been developed, when the wisdom of the path of cultivation arises and manifests, it immediately supports the power of the seeds of the previous path of seeing, causing the seeds of the path of seeing to become equal in strength to the wisdom of the path of cultivation. Those seeds of the path of seeing do not manifest again.

As in the first bhūmi there are three moments of mind—namely, the entry (*praveśa*), the abiding (*sthiti*), and the fulfillment (*pūraṇa*)—when one reaches the moment of the abiding mind, that is, at the time the abiding mind is manifesting, it also draws upon the power of the seeds of the preceding entry mind. The power of the seeds of the entry mind and the power of the abiding mind are equal;

both are termed "the abandonment of inferiority" (*hīna-parityāga*) within the untainted (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, those seeds of the entry mind do not again give rise to manifest activity (*samudācāra*). Thus it is.

The "fulfillment mind" (pūrṇa-citta) is the actual manifestation of that fulfillment mind. It supports the power of the seeds of the preceding minds of entry and abiding, causing the power of the seeds of the fulfillment mind to become equalized.
Those seeds of entry and abiding reach the stage of fulfillment, yet they no longer produce actual manifestations thereafter.
This principle applies to the entry, abiding, and fulfillment of all nine stages. Thus, when one enters the second stage, it immediately supports...
The seeds of the preceding first bhūmi are equal in strength to the seeds of the second bhūmi, and so on until one enters the tenth bhūmi;
at that time, they draw upon the power of the seeds of the preceding nine bhūmis so that their strength becomes equal to the seeds of the tenth bhūmi.

While remaining equal to the seeds of the preceding nine bhūmis, they no longer give rise to active manifestations (*pravṛtti*). Thus, the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) acts as the perfuming agent.

The victor causes that which is perfumed to be identical with the seed; the power of the seed is equal to a vajra, and it is also equal to the functional efficacy and power of the preceding nine stages.

It is like the human method of raising silkworms: as a celestial silkworm gives birth to a maiden of the *parīttābha* (Limited Light) realm, and that maiden of the *parīttābha* realm can likewise cause her parents to age simultaneously, so it is here as well, even within the tenth stage.
The uncontaminated seeds obtained through perfuming are such that these uncontaminated seeds are equal in their generative power to those of the ten preceding stages (*bhūmi*).
Thus, when Buddhahood is attained, all the seeds of the Bodhisattvas from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) through the ten stages are fully present within the Buddha-body;
those seeds of the ten preceding stages are entirely contained within the Buddha-body.
The seeds of the preceding ten stages no longer give rise to active manifestations; therefore, they are called "transformed and equalized.
If the Buddha’s body lacked the seeds of the preceding ten stages, then the qualities within the Buddha’s body would not be complete.

Furthermore, when one enters the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), although the seeds of the preceding path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) exist within the body, those seeds of the path of seeing [belong to] the stage of the path of cultivation.
It cannot be called the "seed of the path of seeing. The seeds of the path of seeing are collectively termed the seeds of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Thus, when one enters the second stage (*dvitīyabhūmi*), although the seeds of the previous first stage still exist within the body, those seeds of the first stage have already reached the second stage.
The seeds of the first stage may not be renamed as the seeds of the first stage; rather, the seeds of the first stage are collectively termed the seeds of the second stage.

This continues until one attains the body of the tenth stage. Although the seeds of the preceding nine stages exist within the body of the tenth stage, those seeds of the preceding nine stages may no longer be called "seeds of the ninth stage" once they are within the tenth stage; the seeds of the ninth stage are collectively termed the seeds of the tenth stage.

Son, when one thus enters the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*), although the seeds of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) exist within the Buddha-body, once those seeds of the ten stages have reached the stage of Buddhahood, they can no longer be called "seeds of the ten stages.

The seeds of the ten stages are collectively termed the "stage of Buddhahood," because by means of the seeds, one attains [the fruit] and abandons inferior causes. It is like a person who has first become a general...
Later, when that person becomes *kaṅkha* (rigid), all their previously categorized functions (*puruṣakāra*) are judged to be functions of dissolution.

Although this person’s body was formerly that of a *sīdhu* (fermented liquor) at its time of ripening, now that it has become [something else], once it has become so, one can only call this person by the name *kaṅkha*; one can no longer call it *sīdhu*. Thus, this person later...
At the time when one becomes a prime minister, although that person’s body remains as it was before—old and worn—the body is made to perform the duties of a prime minister;
yet, one may only call this person by the title "prime minister," and one may no longer call this person by his former name.

This is likewise the case here: although one has entered the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*), even though the seeds of the ten preceding grounds remain, they are collectively designated by the name "Buddha-ground."
Virtue. Furthermore, one does not yet obtain the seeds of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Now, there are thirty-one categories, which consist of thirty-one volitions (*cetanā*).
The inferior outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) that abandons the body refers to the ten stages. Each of the ten stages possesses three moments of mind: the entry, the abiding, and the exit.
Entering the stage called "entering the mind" (*cittapraveśa*) is termed the medium grade; abiding in the stage called "abiding in the mind" (*cittasthiti*) is termed the superior grade.
Thus, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) constitute thirty grades, and the Buddha stage (*buddhabhūmi*) constitutes one grade, totaling thirty-one grades.

Now, speaking from the perspective of the ultimate limit, this refers to the moment of attaining liberation upon achieving Buddhahood, at which time one abandons the inferior outflow-free states (*anāsrava*). However, according to the actual reality, this occurs at every stage.
It is the relinquishing of inferior untainted [dharmas]. Therefore, the Abhidharma states: "Within the ten stages, one always attains the superior and relinquishes the inferior.

Based on this, one should formulate a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*): there are cases where [dharmas] are abandoned but not relinquished, namely, tainted wholesome dharmas and neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas.
Within each stage (*bhūmi*), one practices both tainted wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and indeterminate states (*avyākṛta-dharma*). This refers to the abandonment of objects;

regarding the abandonment [of defilements], even within the bodies of Arhats and Non-returners (*anāgāmin*), they may still give rise to tainted wholesome minds and indeterminate states pertaining to the three realms, which is termed "not abandoning.

There is also "abandoning" that does not constitute "abandonment," namely, the abandonment of inferior untainted states (*anāsrava*) in the ten stages while attaining superior ones, which is termed "transformation."

It is "equal" (*samatā*) because its essence is untainted (*anāsrava*); it is not "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*). There are cases where there is both abandonment and relinquishment, namely, deep-seated dharmas such as greed and so forth.
The fourth phrase is easily understood. If, within the Hīnayāna, this refers to attaining the fruit and relinquishing the stage of application (*prayoga*), one might ask:

why is it that each of the stages prior to the [first] ground—the stage of equipment (*saṃbhāra*) and the stage of application—each possesses three grades of seeds, rather than relying on the inferior grade?

Within the [stages of] morality (*śīla*), a medium grade does not rely upon a medium grade to become a superior grade; thus, there is no sense of "transformation and completion" (*parāvṛtti-pūrṇatā*).

However, within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), a lower grade relies upon itself to become a medium grade, and a medium grade becomes superior; in this case, is there not the meaning of "transformation and completion"? Answer:

The stages prior to the [ten] stages consist of outflowing phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) which can be severed and abandoned. Therefore, they do not rely upon lower or medium grades to become superior, and thus there is no "transformation and completion."

Regarding the meaning: if the stages from the first ground (*bhūmi*) onward were untainted (*anāsrava*), then because that which is untainted is not a dharma subject to abandonment, there would be the sense of "transformation" and "attaining equality" as the lower grades serve to perfect the higher.
This would be acceptable only for those who maintain the position of "newly perfumed" (*navavāsanā*) alone within the ten grounds.

There are, however, the wisdom of wondrous observation and the wisdom of equality. If one wishes to attain Buddhahood, one may newly cultivate the wisdom of the great perfect mirror and the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done.
If these exist solely as innate factors, then since there is only a single category of seeds, the path of seeing would be extinguished upon becoming the path of cultivation;
the first stage would be extinguished upon becoming the second stage; the second through the ninth stages would be extinguished upon becoming the tenth stage, and so forth.

Within those ten stages (*bhūmi*), the sixth consciousness may possess the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), and the seventh consciousness possesses the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*).

However, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, since the seeds already exist within the mind and no new seeds are produced through perfuming (*vāsanā*), how could the wisdom of the great perfect mirror (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) be obtained? Therefore, one knows that these two wisdoms are lacking in the state of Buddhahood. If...

Only those who maintain the theory of "newly perfumed" (navābhyasta) claim that the *samatājñāna* (equality wisdom) perfumes the *ādarśajñāna* (great perfect mirror wisdom), and that the *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (wonderful observation wisdom) perfumes the *kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna* (performance of duties wisdom). How could this not contradict the treatise when it states that the eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms?

Therefore, we know that taking both the "newly perfumed" and the "original" (mūla) positions as correct is the right view. Since the untainted (*anāsrava*) [consciousness] does not exist [in the state of being perfumed],...
Regarding the statement that "it is a natural law (*dharmatā*) that one should not speak of 'perfuming' (*vāsanā*)," this text serves as a counter-argument to reveal the fundamental point:

namely, that since seeds have existed from time immemorial, they have never been perfumed. Therefore, there must be naturally occurring (*dharmatā*) untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*). Thus say the various masters of the Dharma.
All [these factors], such as the protection of the Dharma and liberation, involve the arising of new seeds.

However, prior to the composition of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the various Dharma masters of antiquity taught that during the stages of the *sambhāra* (provisioning) and *prayoga* (preparatory application), due to the habituation of hearing and reflection involving outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas, a distinct new untainted (*anāsrava*) seed is produced upon top of the originally existing untainted seeds. This is the current explanation.

Not so. The meaning of "arising" should be understood as occurring during the stages of the provisions (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*), wherein the contaminated (*sāsrava*) perfuming of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*) indirectly supports the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [seeds] to cause them to increase.
As the *Ben-shu* (Original Commentary) states: "Because there is no arising without cause and condition, and because beginningless obstructions would not be severed.
Since there are no naturally existing uncontaminated seeds (*dharmatā-bīja*) to serve as their cause, the fruit of the Path cannot arise where such [seeds] do not exist.
The innate, untainted seeds of the path that serves as the antidote do not permanently sever the two obstacles which they counteract,
because they lack a substantial entity to serve as an antidote to the tainted seeds.
Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Excerpts from the *Śāstra*), Scroll Four;
Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Excerpts from the *Śāstra*), Scroll Five (Part One of the Third Section of Master Ci’en’s Commentary).
Composed by Dharma Master Lingtai of Beijing.
The *Śāstra* states that dharmas consist of five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Question: Since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is a single entity, it is not a dharma produced by aggregation.
Yet, this text speaks of "five aggregates of dharmas. Why, then, does it state that the unconditioned is an aggregate? Answer:
This statement that the unconditioned is an aggregate follows the explanation of the Sarvāstivāda school. However, the Sarvāstivādins do indeed assert that the unconditioned is an aggregate. Its...
The substance [of unconditioned phenomena] is one. However, if it refers to the unconditioned phenomenon of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), its substance is manifold.
Just as there are as many conditioned phenomena as there are in measure, there are likewise as many instances of the unconditioned phenomenon of analytical cessation.

Since there are as many instances of the unconditioned phenomenon of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as there are conditioned phenomena, non-existent phenomena (*abhāva-dharma*) are numerous. This is why.

It is called "unconditioned harmony" (*asaṃskṛta-sāmagrī*). If, within the Mahāyāna, the unconditioned is not a harmonious phenomenon (*sāmagrī-dharma*), then in this Mahāyāna context, this text should state that "dharmas are of five kinds," rather than using the term "harmony.

Furthermore, regarding these five harmonies, they refer to the mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitta*), matter (*rūpa*), non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Question: Why is the unconditioned called "harmony"? Answer: Because the essence (*svabhāva*) of the unconditioned is not...

Because they are harmoniously assembled, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not included among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). By grouping the six types of unconditioned phenomena into one, the six meanings of the seed (*bīja*) are further clarified;
this thereby subsumes the seven meanings of the *Nāpika-yoga*.
Regarding the second section, "Distinguishing the Self-Abode and Establishing Other Gates," which further elaborates on the distinctions of the self-abode by means of exclusion:

However, within each of the six characteristics of seeds, one establishes a second gate to exclude and distinguish it from its own seed-abode, while the first [gate] expresses the seed itself and the second excludes other dharmas.

For example, as in the case of momentary destruction... [the first gate] expresses the seed, and the second excludes other dharmas. Thus, in the middle of [the discussion on] momentary destruction... [it is stated: "The first... etc.

First, regarding the seed of the manifest [action], it perishes as soon as it arises, yet possesses a superior functional power. Second, this excludes unconditioned permanent phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharmas*).
Next, regarding the coexistence with the fruit: first, the seed of the manifest [action] is conjoined with the manifest fruit that it produces.

Second, this excludes [the possibility of the seed existing] before or after [the fruit], or being permanently separated from it. Next, regarding its constant persistence: first, the seed of the manifest [action] is singular...
Regarding the "similarity of the continuum": the second [point] excludes the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and so forth. Next, within the determination of nature:

first, the seeds of the first category arise as the three natures—wholesome and so on—in accordance with the power of their causes; second, it excludes the Sarvāstivāda position that a cause of a different nature produces a fruit of a different nature.
Next, regarding "waiting for various conditions": first, it means that the seeds of the first manifest [action] can only produce their actual manifestation when they await other factors;
second, it refutes the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) attachment to a spontaneous cause (*svabhāva-hetu*). Next, regarding "drawing forth its own fruit":

first, the seeds of the first manifest refer to the seeds of form, mind, and so forth, which exist as the causes for the actual manifestation of form, mind, and so forth; second, it refutes the externalist attachment to a single, sole cause.
It gives rise to all fruits and so forth. Furthermore, that which is subsumed within the first moment clarifies the seed's own locus;
others are established for the sake of mutual distinction, just as [the first] excludes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) by being subsumed within the first moment.

The second, "simultaneous with the fruit" (*phala-sahabhū*), excludes the Sautrāntika view of causes and effects occurring at different times. The third excludes those that persist continuously, namely the seven [mental factors].
The evolving consciousnesses and so forth—indeed, all four, five, and six categories—are excluded for the purpose of eliminating other faults;
thus, the remaining five categories are established to exclude one another.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*) that "Yaśomitra [explains] this comprehensively," the phrase "each of these is explained by him himself" refers to Yaśomitra’s own commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. As for the passage in the *Śāstra*:

"In the state of transformation, the grasper possesses a superior functional power to yield a fruit; it is in this sense that the cause arises in the present. This means that at the stage of transformation, the subjective grasper has a predominant efficacy in producing its result, and thus it is established as a cause arising in the present.

"Activity" (*kriyā*) is defined as taking up a fruit (*phala-grahaṇa*). "Recompensing" (*pratyupabhoga*) a cause is defined as giving a fruit (*phala-dāna*). This extends even to the production of seeds of their own kind; thus, there is the sense of both taking up and giving a fruit.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The twelvefold dependent origination is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) because it is subject to transformation," this passage of the commentary [is incomplete].
It is certain. One should say: For that Sautrāntika master, the twelve links of dependent origination are not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

for us of the Mahāyāna, the twelve links of dependent origination are indeed conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and are not unconditioned, because they are subsumed within the category of the non-arisen (*anutpāda*).

The Commentary states: If it is argued that because there exists a superior functional power at that time, and because the substance remains one, it is like the previous state—this is the assertion of the Saṃmitīya school.
They maintain that when the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) undergoes cessation during a subsequent kalpa, there is a superior capacity to grasp the fruit;

thus, even after a hundred years have passed within a single lifetime, it is only at the moment of death that it is able to grasp the fruit, such as in the performance of postures and deportments (*iryāpatha*). This refers to... [the end of the passage].

At the time of the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), it is also able to take up its fruit. The following section constitutes the Mahāyāna, which employs two types of inference (*anumāna*) to refute the Saṃmitīya school.

Because [the dharma] exists during the period of destruction at the end of the kalpa, it is said that it must also possess a substantial entity (*svabhāva*) at the beginning. Just as it exists later, it should likewise exist at the beginning;

since the substance is one, it is not the case that it lacks activity. Thus, the marvelous initial moment possesses a superior functional power such that it exists immediately upon arising, and does not necessarily depend on a subsequent time.

The intended meaning is as follows: He challenges the Saṃmitīya school by stating that if the four characteristics exist over a long duration, then the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha*) should occur at the very moment of arising;
it need not wait until a later time before cessation occurs. Regarding the claim that eternal dharmas such as the *puruṣa* (Self) act as causes:

[the questioner asks] how this differs from the previous [critique] regarding the Sūtras, or why one would allow non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) to hold that the *puruṣa* is the cause. [The answer is: It is just like their own tenets concerning Mahābrahmā, Time (*kāla*), Space (*dis*), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "space and the self" (*ākāśa-ātman*): this refers to grasping at a divine self (*puruṣa*) as the cause of all phenomena of birth and death. Furthermore, it is like the Vaiśeṣika masters who grasp at the self as the agent;
since the agent is the cause, they grasp at the divine self as the cause. As for the term "divine" (*deva*), it is simply another name for the "self.
That which is grasped by non-Buddhists is called the "self," and it is also called the "divine," and it is also called the "suchness" (*tathatā*).
"Suchness" (*tathatā*) is simply another name for "self.

According to the Commentary (*Śū*), because the seventh consciousness of those who lack the spiritual lineage (*agotra*) is not called a "seed," and its fruit does not manifest, the term "manifestation" (*prabhāsvara*) serves to exclude that [seventh consciousness] of the pure ones.
Someone raises an objection, saying: "In those who possess the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), the seventh consciousness manifests as actual functioning (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*)."

At a later time, when the noble path (*āryamārga*) undergoes transformation, it is no longer called a "seed," just as in the case of the seventh consciousness of those lacking the nature [for liberation].

Once that [seventh consciousness] has ceased its activity, it necessarily becomes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Since the noble path constantly follows and transforms [the basis], for a person lacking the nature [for liberation], the seventh active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) should be called a "seed.
Now, the explanation states: that which is called a "seed" refers to the causal seed; once it has become submerged and hidden, the manifest [result] it produces...

The manifest result of practice is designated as such and is not called a seed. Now, for those of no-nature (icchantika), the seeds produced by the perfuming of the seventh manifest consciousness are termed "submerged and hidden.

Because the seventh manifest consciousness acts as the perfuming cause and that cause is thus made manifest, one cannot say that the seventh manifest consciousness of those of no-nature serves as a seed; this is because it is the cause of the manifest [result].

This reveals that the fruit of the seed is latent [at the time of its arising]. As for the statement, "The fruit arises spontaneously because it exists within cessation," this is the position of the master Saṃghabhadra.
That is to say, that master maintains that while the cause is arising, it draws forth the fruit; and when the cause ceases, it repays the debt to the cause.

Regarding the claim that "the cause exists in the state of cessation while the fruit exists in the state of arising," this is the position maintained by the Sthavira school. That is to say, at the time of arising, it repays the debt to the cause; and at the time of cessation, it draws forth [the fruit].
This is the result. For instance, as the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states regarding dharmas that are extremely rapid in the present:

"Because there are two moments—arising and ceasing—at the beginning and end, [the dharma] repays the cause at the time of its own cessation while inducing the result. Question: The preceding passage stated, "The cause exists at the time of arising, and the result exists at the time of cessation.

Yet, the subsequent statement says, "It is called the cause existing at the phase of cessation and the result existing at the phase of arising. These two passages appear contradictory. Answer: Regarding these two passages, the former and the latter...
All of these are the tenets of the Sthavira school; they differ according to their respective perspectives and are not contradictory.

If the subsequent passage states that "the cause exists in the phase of cessation while the fruit exists in the phase of arising," this is a distinction made between the causes and effects of arising and ceasing with respect to the single substance of a dharma.
However, that school asserts that the essence of cessation is existent and is not a dharma lacking essence, just like the present.

There is a dharma-substance (*dharmatā*). When this dharma-substance is in the phase of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), it is immediately called the "fruit" (*phala*), because it repays the cause that was previously extinguished.
Therefore, the fruit exists during the phase of arising; as the subsequent passage states: "At the time of arising, it repays the cause.
If this present dharma reaches the phase of extinction (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), it is then called the "cause. This phase of extinction is precisely what is called the cause. This extinction...

The characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) acts as the cause, capable of inducing the subsequent moment of dharma; therefore, it is said that "the cause resides in the characteristic of cessation. Thus, the following passage states: "At the time of cessation, it induces the fruit.

If the text says, "The cause resides in arising and the fruit resides in cessation," this refers to two distinct dharma-entities viewed in relation to one another according to the conventional teaching (*saṃvṛti-dharma*).
That is to say, when the preceding moment of dharma reaches the stage of the characteristic of cessation, it is able to act as a cause and induce the subsequent moment of dharma. Upon reaching...
At the time of the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), it is precisely the dharma of the subsequent moment that reaches the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*).

Thus, the cause—the characteristic of cessation of the preceding moment—exists simultaneously with the effect—the characteristic of arising of the subsequent moment. Therefore, it is said that "the effect exists during the arising.

Regarding the phrase "the effect exists during the cessation," one should understand this as being the reverse of the former: namely, that the effect which is the characteristic of arising upon the dharma of the subsequent moment is itself the dharma of the preceding moment.

The preceding [passage] concerns the cause of the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), while the following one reveals both [characteristics] together. Therefore, although the meanings intended by these two preceding and following passages differ, they are not mutually contradictory.

As for the objection that there would be the fault of two destinies (*gati*) arising simultaneously: the characteristic of cessation belongs to the human destiny (*manuṣya-gati*), while the birth occurs in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*).
Otherwise, there would be the difficulty of two destinies arising simultaneously. Furthermore, according to the Sautrāntika school, cause and effect also occur at different times;
that is, a seed from a preceding moment gives rise to a manifest activity in a succeeding moment.

The Commentary raises an objection: regarding those who maintain that the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) perceives its own self-substance as being simultaneous—for example, when the seeing-part of the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes the seeing-parts of the first five consciousnesses as its object, at the very moment the seeing-part of the mental consciousness is perceiving those five seeing-parts, the two seeing-parts are simultaneous in substance.
Or, for example, when the seeing-part of the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manas*) takes the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object.

This is also simultaneous. Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*) that although the seeing [aspects] are simultaneous, cause and effect do not constitute the meaning of "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*): Question: How can the seeing [aspect] be called cause and effect in relation to the seeing [aspect]?

Answer: Although the seeing aspect of the *darśana-bhāga* (the perceiving part) in relation to the seeing [aspect] is like the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) in the state of Buddhahood, [it is so designated].

As for the fruit: because it is the mind that takes [the object] as its cognitive support (ālambana), if the other three are the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) acting as the cause, then that which is the cognitive support—the objective field—is the fruit, while that which is the cognitive support is the cause.
Thus, the subject that cognizes is the fruit, and the object that is cognized is the cause.

Commentary: If that were so, then the same would apply to the seeds in relation to their manifesting counterparts. In that case, when the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) takes the seeing-part as its object simultaneously, it would not be a causal seed;
and since they arise simultaneously with the active manifestation (pravṛtti-vijñāna), they would not be causal conditions.

Regarding the passage: "Therefore, one must further explain that if a seed is held to be simultaneous with [another] seed... up to not allowing a subsequent seed to produce a fruit again," the meaning of this text is as follows:
If it were granted that a seed produces a seed simultaneously, then within a single moment, an infinite number of subsequent seeds would arise horizontally;
thus, seeds would become excessive. Since it is not granted that a seed of the preceding moment [produces a seed of the same moment], [the fault does not apply].
Regarding the production of a subsequent momentary seed from a seed: if the subsequent moment were not continuous, that seed would simply cease.
Therefore, the arising of the preceding momentary seed produces the subsequent momentary seed as its causal condition; thus, the seed is not severed.
This is because it is accepted that the seed gives rise to the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) simultaneously with it, and it is likewise accepted that the seed is simultaneous with the seed [itself].
Regarding the phrase "because it is not admitted that a subsequent seed can produce a further fruit": the meaning of this passage is as follows.
If one were to admit that a seed produces a seed simultaneously, then within a single moment, an infinite number of subsequent seeds would arise horizontally;
thus, the seeds would be too many. Since it is not admitted that a seed of the preceding moment produces the fruit of a seed of the succeeding moment, [if the seed were to persist] after...

If mindfulness does not continue, its seeds are immediately severed. Therefore, the arising of the seed of the preceding thought serves as the cause and condition for the production of the seed of the succeeding thought;
thus, the seeds are not severed. This is because it is accepted that the seed and the manifest activity (pravṛtti) arise simultaneously.
As for the statement, "The same should apply to the relationship between a seed and its own kind," this constitutes an external objection. The external objection states:

If it is claimed that within a single moment, an active manifestation arises directly from a perfumed seed, and that subsequent active manifestation perfumes to form a new perfumed seed, then this new perfumed seed could not produce another active manifestation within that same single moment.
This is because within a single moment, two simultaneous active manifestations—such as two eye-consciousnesses—cannot arise; likewise, within a single moment, its newly perfumed [seed]...

The seed and the perfumed seed cannot coexist. It should be that within a single moment of thought, two seeds cannot coexist, just as within a single moment of thought, two manifest activities (pravṛtti) do not coexist.

The opponent replies: Although this is not so, there is nonetheless clear scriptural authority stating that within a single moment of thought, two manifest activities do not coexist; namely, that it is nowhere possible for them to be identical.
At that time, two visual consciousnesses may arise simultaneously in the same location and so forth.
Since that sūtra does not intend to say that two seeds cannot coexist within a single moment, we know that two seeds can indeed coexist within a single moment.

The Commentary asks: "If that is so, how is it that those who possess innate [seeds] (sahaja) can simultaneously give rise to newly perfumed [seeds]? The intent of this question is to introduce the meaning of the "Teacher" (ācārya).
Regarding the passage in the Commentary from "As in the first dharma... up to "...the loss of the seeds," all subsequent commentary text is already [established by] ancient authorities.

This is the section on the "Establishment of Dharmas," which explains the gateway. It means that when one is about to enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the untainted seeds (*anāsravabīja*) are nurtured by the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Because these untainted [seeds] are thus nurtured, they are able to indirectly induce a new perfumed seed.

At the time of entering the path of seeing, the originally existing untainted seeds and the indirectly perfumed untainted seeds together produce a single manifestation of the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).

It is "activity" (*pravṛtti*). That is, it is manifest activity. Furthermore, it perfumes and produces a new, perfumed seed. Thus, within a single moment of thought (*citta-kṣaṇa*), there are four factors: first, the innate seed;
second, a new perfumed seed produced by the lateral perfuming of the innate seed; third, the manifest activity that is produced; and fourth, the new perfumed seed produced by that manifest activity.
Therefore, there are four factors within a single moment of thought. This is the view of the ancient masters.

"Correct. Now, the explanation that this is not so—that from the "inherently existing seeds" (*prakṛtistha-bīja*) down to "therefore there are only three dharmas"—is the first interpretation, and it is also incorrect.
This passage [states] that both the inherently existing seeds and the manifest activities (*samudācāra*), when compared to the newly perfumed seeds, are all causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, the interpretation that from the "inherently existing seeds" down to [the phrase] "acting as causal conditions" is the second interpretation.
This is precisely the correct principle.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that the Prātimokṣa up to the dhyāna-precepts are similar: in the concentration of the Path (mārga-samādhi), there is only a single momentary manifestation;
there are no two simultaneous manifestations. This is merely because its function is predominant, and thus the Prātimokṣa precepts likewise manifest only through their function.
[The number of] instances increases, yet the substance does not increase; this is similar to the precepts of the *samāhita-śīla* (precepts of meditative concentration).

Regarding the statement in the previous commentary, "This means that, according to the preceding [explanation], both the substance and function of the *prātimokṣa-śīla* (individual liberation precepts) increase," this refers to the explanation of *avijñapti-rūpa* (non-informative matter) in the second fascicle of the previous commentary. It clarifies that even when an *ācārya* transforms a white disciple while the disciple abides in a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), the commentary explains [the following]: [The ācārya] says: "Disciple, you have committed such-and-such a transgression. At that time, although the disciple is in a state of mindlessness, the *avijñapti-rūpa* arises. Furthermore, when the disciple subsequently returns to a state with mind (*sacittaka*) and confesses the transgression, the *avijñapti-rūpa* is severed. This is because the *avijñapti-rūpa* produced by the *ācārya*’s instruction exists as long as the disciple remains in the state of mindlessness; once they return to a state with mind and perform the confession, it ceases. Thus, the substance and function of the *prātimokṣa-śīla* increase through the arising of new instances, even though the underlying substance itself does not multiply. This is the meaning of the previous commentary.
When one attains [the path], the substance of the sevenfold seeds increases manifold; this very passage from the commentary clarifies that there are innate (*sahaja*) untainted (*anāsrava*) seeds.
Within a single moment, through lateral perfuming (*paribhāvanā*), a new perfumed (*abhinava*) untainted seed is produced, whereby the substance of the aforementioned sevenfold seeds increases.
This is the doctrine of the ancient masters (*pūrvācārya*).
Why is it so? Regarding the phrase "because it is capable of perfuming": why is it that the seed which takes up the fruit must be co-existent with it? The answer is:

if the seed produces a manifest fruit, this seed was previously produced by a manifest state capable of perfuming. Therefore, [the text] here specifically excludes seeds of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-bīja*).

This is because it is not produced from the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the perfuming agent (*bhāvakatva*).
