This passage is distinct from the preceding text; for now, it refers primarily to the increase of active manifestations (*samudācāra*), whereby the perfuming agent acquires newly perfumed seeds (*navavāsanā-bīja*).

From these newly perfumed seeds acting as causes, active manifestations arise. However, speaking according to reality, there are also innate seeds (*prakṛtistha-bīja*) that give rise to active manifestations.
The second fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "That which does not produce an active manifestation is called 'arising by way of its own kind' (*jātisamudācāra*)."

Regarding the statement that "that which is called a seed at that time" is the explanation found in the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary), it also does not fully accord with reason. Let us consider the primary seed first:

when it is actually producing a manifest state (*pravṛtti*), it is called a "seed. If one were to say that a seed is called a "seed" even when it has not yet produced a manifest state at this present moment, but will produce a manifest state later on, then it would merely be categorized as a "type" (*jāti*). How then could Saṃghabhadra explain it as being "not identical"?

"From the moment of arising until it has no further seeds"—this passage is difficult for Sthiramati to resolve, because that master maintains that cause and effect belong to the same temporal period (*adhvan*).

How, then, can he explain the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*’s statement that "impermanent phenomena act as causes for their own intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*)? It is not the case that this very [moment] is identical to that [cause];
rather, if one follows Dharmapāla’s interpretation, this means that a seed gives rise to a seed, and not that this very moment [is the cause].

Therefore, the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of preceding and succeeding moments are such that the cause perishes and the effect arises. Question: This commentary states, "How does Saṃghabhadra explain this?
It is not the case that [the cause and effect] are identical within this same moment (*kṣaṇa*), because he maintains that cause and effect belong to the same temporal period (*adhvan*).

The preceding passage further states, "This is merely Saṃghabhadra's provisional explanation; it is not the actual application of the Sthavira's view. Answer: The "application" (*yoga*) is precisely what is meant here. Why?
Regarding the subsequent explanation of "arising without seeds": when a seed produces a seed, it is called "arising without seeds.
If a seed produces a manifest phenomenon, it is called "arising with seeds."
The treatise says: "A certain class of continuity reaches the ultimate stage. Question: If the seeds of the two categories are dharmas that can be severed, one may say they reach the ultimate stage.
Question: If the seeds of the two categories are dharmas that can be severed, one may say they reach the ultimate stage;
this applies to all [seeds], including those of contaminated wholesome [dharmas], indeterminate seeds, and uncontaminated seeds.

[Question: It is always present and follows along; its nature as a seed is not a phenomenon subject to cessation. How, then, can it be said to reach the ultimate stage? [Answer: One interpretation is as follows:
It is precisely the untainted (anāsrava) seeds that, upon attaining the superior and relinquishing the inferior, are also called "reaching the ultimate path" (*niṣṭhāmārga*).
As for the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) seeds and so forth, when they reach that path, they also relinquish the indeterminate tainted [seeds]; therefore, they too reach the ultimate path.
The second interpretation states: here, the discussion refers exclusively to the seeds of afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth, up until the ultimate path of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).
It does not refer to the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), because even upon reaching the ultimate path of counteraction, the untainted seeds are not severed.

Therefore, this treatise merely states that [the seeds] "can perpetually evolve," which fully captures the underlying principle; for [this applies to] both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena.

This is because both are termed "constantly evolving" (*anuvartaka*). If they are contaminated seeds (*sāsrava-bīja*), they constantly evolve in accordance with the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭamavijñāna*);

thus, when the path of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) eventually arises, they are abandoned. If they are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they constantly evolve in dependence upon the eighth consciousness;
therefore, until the end of the future limit (*anāgata-koṭi*), they are never abandoned. However, among the six characteristics of seeds (*bīja*) in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*:
The third is called "that which follows along" (*anubandha*). It refers to the stage of the counteractive path (*pratipakṣa-avasthā*). The intended meaning of that treatise is as follows:

the seeds of afflictions (*kleśa-bīja*) constantly reside within the eighth consciousness, following along with sentient beings; subsequently, at the stage of the counteractive path, one abandons those seeds of affliction.

Regarding the statement that they are called "ultimate" when reaching the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*): the separately manifest afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*) are severed immediately upon reaching the culmination of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
As for the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), they are severed upon reaching the culmination of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Therefore, the subsequent text states:

"For example, among those in the desire realm, such as sensual craving (*kāmarāga*), if one attains the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), one severs the sensual craving of the desire realm, up to and including the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*)."
It is severed by the abandonment of desire; this is called the ultimate state of names. This clarifies the principle that the preceding seeds give rise to the subsequent [states].

As for the fact that the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* does not contain this [passage], the commentary text [you cite] is likewise not the correct interpretation. It states that when a seed is actually producing a manifest state (*pravṛtti*), it is designated as a "seed.
If a seed were not currently producing a manifest state, then after the seed has been established, the manifest state would arise [only later].
At the time of its functioning, this seed is still called a "seed" and is not [otherwise] called a "seed. Question:
Since the seventh consciousness is also severed only upon reaching the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*), why is it not called a "seed"?

If the *Saṃgrahaṇī* does not contain this, then although the *Saṃgrahaṇī* has the third category of the "ever-continuing" (*anuvartaka*), there is no textual passage regarding seeds of its own kind for each individual [consciousness]. Only this...
The treatise is complete. This treatise explains that the seeds reach their ultimate state based on excellence. Why is this?

It is because, just as with the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they are severed when the path of seeing reaches its ultimate stage of counteraction (*pratipakṣa*). If it concerns the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they are severed when the path of cultivation reaches its ultimate stage of counteraction.
If one were to say that the seeds are severed upon reaching the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*), this would apply to the afflictions of the path of seeing.

The affliction (*kleśa*) is severed only upon reaching the Vajra-like Mind during the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Alternatively, it is like the seeds of contaminated virtue (*sāsrava-kuśala-bīja*) produced by birth in the case of the Two Vehicles, which are not severed until the Path of Cultivation;
thus, one knows that its severance at the ultimate stage is superior, and this is precisely what makes this treatise superior.
Regarding the commentary’s response in the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* and other texts concerning "transformation" and "the ease with which the object of cognition is relinquished":

within the *Daśabhūmi*, from the fifth bhūmi and prior, when the fundamental wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) within the seventh consciousness cognizes *tathatā*, that seventh consciousness gives rise to the fundamental wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), which likewise cognizes only *tathatā* and is unable to cognize the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Its...

Within the sixth consciousness, when subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) arises and takes conventional phenomena as its object, the seventh consciousness likewise gives rise to the subsequently attained wisdom of equality and takes the ālayavijñāna as its object. This occurs from the fifth bhūmi onward within the sixth consciousness.

When untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) arises and transforms its perception to take both the ultimate and conventional truths as objects, the seventh consciousness likewise gives rise to untainted wisdom, transforming its perception to take suchness (*tathatā*) and the eighth consciousness as its objects.
Regarding the ten kinds of equality, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* provides three interpretations:
first, that one attains the ten equalities from the first bhūmi upward; second, that one only attains them from the fifth bhūmi upward.
Regarding the ten equalities: some say that one attains the ten equalities only from the eighth bhūmi upward.

Since it is stated within the context of the ten equalities that "one gives rise to equal love and joy," the seventh consciousness does not only take the eighth consciousness as its object; the seventh consciousness can also take other sentient beings and so forth as its objects.

Therefore, it is said that the objects it perceives are easily abandoned. As for the statement regarding the seeds of the aspect of the exhaustion of sensation and so forth: [this refers to the fact that these seeds are not yet eliminated].
Furthermore, for example, regarding the characteristics of the exhaustion of seeds: it is like the fragrance of incense stored in a casket. Initially, there is only the scent;
after a long period of time has passed, the fragrance is then exhausted. It is the same with the seeds of good and evil:

although they initially possess the power to counteract the force of the roots of goodness and the force of the inclinations toward [defilements], and though they can give rise to good and evil karma and counteract the power of bodily actions, [they eventually exhaust their potency].

Once it is exhausted, that itself is impermanence. These seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma continue in their own essence; when the power capable of counteracting and destroying the body is exhausted, that itself is impermanence.
When they can no longer counteract, they are called "seeds with the characteristic of exhaustion through experience" (*sopabhoga-kṣaya-lakṣaṇa-bīja*).

As for those "seeds without the characteristic of exhaustion through experience" (*anupabhoga-kṣaya-lakṣaṇa-bīja*), they are like being in the air: even if burned by fire or soaked in water, they remain in the air.
It is ever-present, unchanging, and non-transmigrating; the seeds of the aspect of inexhaustibility are likewise so. These are called the seeds of conventional expression (*nāma-vyañjana-bīja*).

When a person is born among humans or animals under the influence of a single wholesome name, once they have died, these old seeds of conventional expression are subsequently extinguished by the attraction of karma, yet they arise again as manifest activity (*samudācāra*).
In this manner, through hundreds or thousands of cycles, one repeatedly produces the old seeds of conventional expression.
Because this single designation arises again and again hundreds and thousands of times, designations have no characteristic of being exhausted;

for since the experience of their fruits is inexhaustible, there is no characteristic of exhaustion. Seeds that possess no characteristic of exhaustion are the *niṣyanda-vāsanā* (homogeneous habitual tendencies).

Seeds that possess a characteristic of exhaustion are the *vipāka-vāsanā* (ripening habitual tendencies). Question: What is meant by "exhaustion" and what is meant by "characteristic"? Answer: As for "characteristic," it refers to the mark (*nimitta*).

This explains the meaning of the *dharmaparyāya* (dharma-gate) titled "The Dharma-Gate of the Phenomena Having the Characteristic of Exhaustion through Appropriation and the Phenomena Having the Characteristic of Exhaustion without Appropriation. The response states:
"That [text] refers to the sense of having a portion for the production of fruit, up to the point where the perfuming of names and words is called 'perpetually following and evolving.

Within this passage, there are only two interpretations. The first is an interpretation based on whether [the seeds] have been countered or not yet countered. If the Master of the Sūtras [refers to] the path of counteraction, then these seeds—
The water is immediately cut off. If the path of counteraction has not yet been attained, the substance of the seed must still be present. To explain:

if it is categorized by its distinct nature, it is called the "characteristic of non-exhaustion through experience"; if it is that which evokes a ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*), it is called the "characteristic of exhaustion through experience."

Nor can it be said that because they are of different natures, they are called "possessing the characteristic of the exhaustion of grasping. This is just as non-meritorious formations (apuṇyābhisaṃskāra) are said to attract the seeds of names and words for the three evil destinies;
meritorious formations (puṇyābhisaṃskāra) attract the seeds of names and words for humans and gods, which are neutral (avyākṛta);

and immovable formations (āniñjyābhisaṃskāra) attract the seeds of names and words for the two upper realms, which are also neutral. In these cases, one may say that things of different natures mutually attract one another, and thus they are called "possessing [the characteristic]."

Regarding the characteristic of being subject to exhaustion (*parikṣaya-lakṣaṇa*): within the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-avasthā*), there are also tainted (*sāsrava*) wisdoms derived from hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*, *cintā-mayī-prajñā*) that can nourish untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*).
These are also termed "of a different nature" (*vijātīya*) and should be designated as having the characteristic of being subject to exhaustion.

For this reason, they are designated as having the characteristic of being subject to exhaustion only insofar as they correspond to the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*). In the second interpretation, this refers specifically to the three lower types of perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Explanation: That which consists of the perfuming of conceptualization (*vikalpa-vāsanā*) is termed the "characteristic of exhaustion with sensation" (*sopabhoga-kṣaya-lakṣaṇa*);

that which consists of the perfuming of names (*nāma-vāsanā*) is termed the "characteristic of exhaustion without sensation" (*nirupabhoga-kṣaya-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding all the syllables mentioned herein, there is no separate interpretation; they simply serve to exclude other dharmas, as they are not seeds (*bīja*).

The Commentary specifically uses the two principles of constant revolution (*nitya-parivṛtti*) and arising-and-ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*) to clarify the meaning of seeds (*bīja*). Among the six preceding meanings, "arising-and-ceasing" distinguishes [seeds] from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
"constant revolution" clarifies that seeds mutually induce their own kind, thereby clarifying the meaning of seeds. The remaining categories are established based on these.
This merely excludes other alternative views. Therefore, it distinguishes that the seventh consciousness (*manas*), which is the presently active mind, is not the seed.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "this [seed] of its own kind... nor does it contradict the characteristics," this is the first interpretation within the commentary;
it is entirely an incorrect position. The meaning of this passage is as follows: if the seed combines with other conditions, that seed is then capable of [producing its fruit].
That which arises as a manifest activity (pravṛtti) is precisely what is called a seed (bīja).
If a seed has not yet encountered the convergence of conditions at the present time, that seed cannot produce a manifest activity; however, at a later time, it can produce a manifest activity.

Because that which has not yet produced a manifest activity at the present time is designated by the term "category" (jāti), the *Nirabhilāpyadharmatā-siddhi* states: "This reveals the distinction between two stages. If the seed produces [the manifest activity]...
That which is currently active as a result is called a seed. If the seed has not yet produced what is currently active, it is called a "type" (*jāti*).

Now, this discussion concerns its essence (*svabhāva*) in terms of that which is not currently active; thus, when the treatise generally refers to it as a "seed," it is speaking of the essence of the seed itself.

Whether the seed produces what is currently active, or whether this seed later encounters conditions and thereby produces what is currently active—[in all such cases, it is the essence of the seed that is being discussed].

As for this: if, once one has entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), all seeds of a female body can ultimately never arise as manifest activity, then these seeds—within this very consciousness—are collectively termed "seeds.
Therefore, this does not contradict the doctrine of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

This interpretation, however, is also not exhaustive of the principle. If it were the case that after the seeds [have been transformed], they could subsequently arise as manifest activity, then [the distinction between the two] would be obtainable.

It is called a "seed. However, in cases such as entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), and so forth, how can that which will never arise again be designated as a "seed"?
Therefore, this interpretation does not fully accord with reason.

The Commentary states: "If one distinguishes between the two stages—up to the point where the potential for seeds is fully present and their power increases, even in those of no-nature (agotra)—this is the intent of the *Treatise on No-Nature* (*Asvabhāva-śāstra*).
When seeds and conditions coincide, and the functional activity of producing manifest results arises, they are termed 'seeds.

If conditions have not yet coincided such that manifest results do not arise, even if they were capable of producing manifest results later on, that which is currently absent is termed [the state of no-nature]."
It serves as a category to manifest the distinction between the two [types of seeds]. This first interpretation is correct in its origin; the subsequent explanation is the definitive one.
Regarding the interpretation that "it manifests the seeds up to the state of non-ideation," this second interpretation is the correct meaning.
That is to say, it refers to whether the seeds, upon meeting with conditions at the present time, produce manifest results, or whether they remain unmanifest at the present time.

Regarding the meaning that "a result" refers to that which is capable of producing a manifest result at a later time, all such things are termed "seeds. This intends to capture the sense of producing a result;

thus, although they do not possess the six characteristics at present because the manifest has not yet arisen, if they encounter conditions at a later time and produce a manifest result, they are seeds.
This possesses all six meanings. If that which is ultimately non-arising manifests, it is termed "homogeneous" (*nikāya-sabhāga*).

For example, those who have entered the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and so forth—all that is ultimately non-arising—is subsumed under the category of the homogeneous. Regarding "beings lacking the nature [of Buddhahood]" (*icchantika*) and those who are not even seeds:
previously it was stated that only when a seed exists simultaneously with its manifestation and its fruit can it be called a "seed. As for beings lacking the nature [of Buddhahood], first...

The seven consciousnesses can perfume seeds; they possess only the characteristic of the simultaneous existence of the seed and its fruit, because they lack the simultaneous existence of a manifest fruit. Therefore, they are not [themselves] seeds. Question:

For a person of the nature of having outflows (*sāsrava-dharmatā*), it may be admitted that after the seventh consciousness attains the subsequently attained wisdom of a noble one (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), there is a transformation into the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), which is called the "transformed consciousness" (*parāvṛtta-vijñāna*).

However, for a person of the nature of being without outflows (*anāsrava-dharmatā*), the seventh consciousness is always with outflows. How, then, can it be called a "transformed consciousness"? Please explain further.
Regarding those [defilements] to be abandoned by the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*): speaking according to reality, the substance of the seeds still remains;

it is only the capacity of the seeds to produce future fruits that is severed. Once this has been attained, all seeds—such as those for a female body, the eighth rebirth, birth from eggs or moisture, and the three evil destinies—are never again to arise;
these are comprised within the category of "seeds of the same kind" (*nikāya-sabhāga*). Furthermore...

Just as when one has entered the first stage (*bhūmi*), all seeds of the three evil destinies and the acquisition of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) mean that one no longer receives a body of fragmented birth (*prādeśikakāya*);
all such seeds of fragmented birth are forever non-arising, for they are all comprised within their own respective categories.

The Commentary states that if it were not so, the principle of severing [the seeds] within a single realm would not be established. For example, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, regarding the maturation of seeds:

even if one is born in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) and does not manifest [defilements] belonging to the two higher realms, one is still said to possess the seeds of all three realms, which have all reached maturity.
This is because, when born in the two higher realms, both [types of] seeds of the three realms have matured; this is explained in terms of completion.
That which ultimately does not arise is called a "homogeneous class" (*nikāya-sabhāga*). For example, the single category of the yellow [perception] in the Path of Seeing is such.
If a seed has not yet arisen at the present time but possesses the potential to arise later, it is also termed a "seed" and is named a "homogeneous class."
The commentary refutes the Sarvāstivādins and others who claim [that all dharmas] act as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) even for those that are not remedied;

for example, hatred that is not remedied acts as a homogeneous cause for the two views of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*). Since these two views are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), this interpretation is correct.

Therefore, the statement in the previous commentary that "wholesome dharmas of the Hīnayāna serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for unwholesome dharmas" is an error in that preceding commentary.

Furthermore, regarding the passage in the commentary stating that "the same applies even to the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) acting as a cause," the treatise says that their nature is determined (*niyata-svabhāva*), which excludes the [indeterminate] *saṃskṛta*.
Bhadanta [Vasumitra] asserts three kinds of causes: first, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*); second, the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*); and third, the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).

That school maintains that these three causes are all of the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Regarding the similar-type cause: for instance, unwholesome states characterized by hatred serve as the similar-type cause for obscured views regarding the extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*);
or, obscured views regarding the self and what belongs to the self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) serve as the similar-type cause for unwholesome states such as hatred.

Regarding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), these are contained within the eleven factors under the category of "Origin" (*samudaya*), which are capable of producing the five categories of teachings.
Other afflictions up to the condition as cause (*hetu-pratyaya*) have already been explained previously. As for the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), it should be understood accordingly.

Now, among the four kinds of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), we take that which is "leaking beyond" (*asravatīta*) as being of the nature of the condition as cause (*hetu-pratyaya*), and do not take [the other types].

The remaining three are the fruits of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). Regarding the statement that the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and others have the nature of maturation (*vipāka-dharmatā*) as their fruit:

since the universal cause is itself a defilement, it is exclusively of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala-svabhāva*). It acts as the cause for that which is unwholesome; for example, hatred (*dveṣa*) acts as the cause for hatred, and an unwholesome nature acts as the cause for the obscured-unwholesome nature (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-svabhāva*).
This is just like how hatred and the like act as causes for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and so forth.

Furthermore, there is the nature of being obscured (*nivṛta*), which serves as the cause for that which is of an obscured nature; for example, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) serve as the cause for subsequent moments of those same views.

Additionally, that which is obscured serves as the cause for that which is unwholesome (*akuśala*); for example, the aforementioned view of a self-identity and view of extremes serve as the cause for subsequent moments of anger (*dveṣa*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) takes the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*), the immediate fruit (*anantaraphala*), and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) as its results.
As for this: those that are simultaneous in thought are subsumed under the causes of association (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and co-existence (*sahabhū-hetu*).
If they differ in thought, they are the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*), as well as the cause of human effort (*puruṣakāra-hetu*) with an intervening interval. However, the Sarvāstivādins say:
when a wholesome mind or an unwholesome mind arises simultaneously, it constitutes both the cause of association and the cause of co-existence; being simultaneous, it is thus established.

Regarding the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*): if it occurs in subsequent moments or thereafter, it is termed a fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), and it may also be a fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
If it is simultaneous with indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) minds and mental factors, it constitutes a cause of association (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and a cause of coexistence (*sahabhū-hetu*);

these also obtain the fruit of human effort. If it occurs in subsequent moments when they are tainted (*sāsrava*), it is termed a fruit of uniform outflow. This is likewise true when untainted (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors arise.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of virile fruits (*puruṣakāra-phala*): first, the simultaneously arising virile fruit;
second, the immediately succeeding virile fruit; third, the temporally separated virile fruit; and fourth, the non-arising virile fruit.
When wholesome or unwholesome minds and mental factors arise, they are associated within the same moment; as simultaneous co-existent causes, they obtain [their fruit] at that very time.
Simultaneously arising *puruṣakāra-phala* (human effort fruit): that which arises simultaneously indeed receives the name of actual *puruṣakāra*.

If [the action] has already passed through gradual or transcendent progression, it then obtains the *niṣyanda-phala* (outflow fruit). Although the *niṣyanda-phala* is also conventionally designated as the "immediately subsequent *puruṣakāra-fruit*," in reality it is the *niṣyanda-phala*.
If [the action] has already passed through many moments, it then obtains the *vipāka-phala* (ripening fruit). Ripening...
The fruit is also conventionally designated as the "remote human-effort fruit" (*puruṣakāra-phala*), though in reality it is subsumed under the "ripening fruit" (*vipāka-phala*).
When the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) arises and is able to sever the afflictions so that they never arise again, one attains the "fruit of dissociation" (*visamyoga-phala*);

this very fruit of dissociation is also conventionally designated as the "non-arising human-effort fruit," because the afflictions never arise again. Question: Regarding the fourth [topic], the determination of the nature (*gotra-niyama*).

What is the difference between this and the sixth [category], which projects its own fruit? Is it not the case that the sixth, which projects its own fruit, is already included within the fourth category, namely "the seed as a certainty"? Please explain further.

Regarding the statement, "Therefore, seeds of their own kind are not called seeds unless they are combined with conditions": it is only when conditions combine to produce a manifest state (*pravṛtti*) that something is designated a seed.
Seeds of their own kind do not possess the combination of conditions; thus, they are not called seeds, though they are still subsumed under the category of "kind."
If there are conditions that conjoin to produce a virile fruit (*puruṣakāraphala*), it may also be called a seed.

The commentary states: "The assertion that [dharmas] exist in all three time periods and that their substance exists at all times" refers to the refutation of the Sarvāstivāda school; they maintain that [dharmas] are eternally existent.
The commentary states: "If that which conditions is eternally present, it should eternally produce its fruit... down to: 'because that which conditions is eternally absent.
This passage establishes the reasoning of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The Sarvāstivādins take wholesome form as the cause with respect to the four aggregates," their school [asserts this] by means of the four present aggregates.

It can attract the future aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) by acting as its causal condition (*hetupratyaya*). By taking the aggregate of form as its cause, it gives rise to the other four aggregates, serving as their own-object condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
However, the Sarvāstivādins have five interpretations. One states: "Form is the cause of form; mind is the cause of mind.
This means that the aggregate of form is the cause of the aggregate of form, and the [other] four aggregates are the causes of the [other] four aggregates. This is the cause.

The second [position] states that the four aggregates serve as causes for the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), because mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) possess a powerful capacity for induction; thus, the four aggregates are the causes of the aggregate of form.

Furthermore, it states that the four aggregates act as causes, whereas the aggregate of form cannot act as a cause for the four aggregates, because material phenomena lack functions such as cognitive engagement (*ālambana*).
The third [position] states that the aggregate of form serves as a cause for the four aggregates, but the four aggregates do not...

[The first view] holds that [the four aggregates] can serve as causes for the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). [The second view] holds that because the four [mental] aggregates are themselves [the seeds], they serve as causes for the aggregate of form, and the aggregate of form serves as a cause for the four aggregates.
[The third view] holds that the five aggregates serve as mutual causes for one another.

If one were to say this is so, then since these manifest states (*pravṛtti*) are not *hetupratyaya* (causal conditions) with respect to their own kind and are not perfumers (*vāsaka*), it follows that the seeds [must be established] within this context.
The manifest fruit produced by a seed is called "drawing forth its own fruit. How so? Because the intervening words state that it is not capable of perfuming;

therefore, we know it is not [the case]. Furthermore, the verse cited says: "As long as conceptualization does not exist externally... Here, "heaven" refers to the twenty-eight heavens and the lunar mansions;
"earth" refers to the great earth; "wind" refers to the winds that move through space and so forth; and "void" refers to the form of the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*).
Regarding the "form of the space-element" (*ākāśa-dhātu-rūpa*), it is the emptiness of consciousness (*vijñāna-ākāśa*).

However, the aforementioned consciousness and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not this actual empty space, because the unconditioned phenomenon of space is not the "space-form element" within this context.

That which is beneath the earth where there is no water is called "that" (*tat*); that which has water is called "other" (*anya*). These directions are termed the "ten directions" (*daśa-diś*). All such [distinctions] are...
It is the activity of consciousness; it does not occur outside of the mind. To say that discrimination is neither external nor internal means that "discrimination" has two interpretations.

First, discrimination is an alternative name for the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*), because the preceding heaven, earth, and so forth are all transformations produced by the discriminating mind.
Second, "discrimination" carries the sense of "explanation," meaning it explains heaven and earth.
They do not exist externally. Question: This wind is said to have motion as its nature, while earth has solidity as its nature.
Since the wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala) is its substance, it should be mobile and not solid; how then can it be said that its substance is solid?
If its substance is solid, it should be called earth; how then is it wind? If one were to speak according to the majority of the sūtras, then water should also be defined by moisture.
Nature. Fire has heat as its nature; earth has motion as its nature (and so forth).

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "because it is heavy and substantial, it is not a seed, like the eye [organ]," this means that just as the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*)—the seed of the visual faculty and its cognition—first substantially attains birth and can produce the manifest visual faculty, so too does the manifest visual faculty, being heavy and substantial, [arise from] external seeds.

It is so. First, the seeds of the mutual [external] forms are transformed by the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); subsequently, when the barley and other such seeds arise, the consciousness transforms them again.
Therefore, they are not [the original] seeds. According to principle, the eighth consciousness first takes the seeds as its object;

those subsequent manifest forms (*pravṛttivijñāna*) likewise do not constitute a second layer of objective images (*nimittabhāga*) within the eighth consciousness. As Asvabhāva states: "Just as the internal seeds of consciousness... [are] the remote fruit."

Regarding "that which induces": for example, when the seeds of the eighth consciousness’s own names and phrases (nāma-pada), which are neutral (*avyākṛta*), directly produce the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) of the eighth consciousness, these seeds of names and phrases are the "causes of production" (*janaka-hetu*). That manifest eighth consciousness is termed the "proximate fruit" (*āsanna-phala*).

Furthermore, with respect to the fruits of the eighth consciousness—such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)—the seeds of names and phrases of the eighth consciousness [function as the cause]. As for that eighth...
The seeds of designation (*nāma-vikalpa-bīja*) of the consciousness are the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) in relation to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth;
thus, name-and-form and the rest are its remote effects. The production of the body from external seeds should also be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, just as ignorance (*avidyā*) is the producing cause (*janana-hetu*) for the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*), the seeds of ignorance can, in the distant future, produce formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so on; these are thus called projecting causes.

From this it may be inferred that after the transformation has occurred, the loss [of the original] is likewise so. Furthermore, Wu-xing says: "It is like the movement of drawing a bow, which is called the 'inducing cause' (*ākṣepa-hetu*);
the movement of releasing the string is called the 'producing cause' (*janana-hetu*). That is to say, when one first wishes to shoot an arrow, one first pulls back the bowstring."
This is called the distant cause of drawing the bow. At the very moment the arrow is released, this is called the cause;
the arrow thus released is called the distant effect and the proximate effect.

As Vasubandhu stated, "From the internal seeds... up to what is called the 'projecting cause' (ākṣepahetu)," this refers specifically to the internal seeds that produce the twelve links [of dependent origination].
That is to say, from ignorance (*avidyā*) through to the link of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), these constitute a single lifetime.
These internal seeds are termed "internal," and the twelve links and so forth are the actual results (*phala*). What is now referred to as "dying" is precisely the process of being about to die.

Furthermore, if the corpse were identical to that which has already died, then Vasubandhu would have based his analysis on the physical body as it exists in the present, designating it as "projected internally" (*ākṣiptāntara*) and so forth.
After death, he names it "projected internally"; this is a figurative explanation wherein the seeds of that "projected internally" are termed "projected internally."
It is established through the seeds of names and conventions. By means of a single karmic seed, a human body is produced; this seed is called the "cause of birth.
Once the body has died, one may either be reborn in a higher realm or enter nirvāṇa. A present corpse is, in fact, a sentient being of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Since the fundamental seeds capable of transformation never fail to transform, they are metaphorically designated as "internal" and termed "projecting causes" (*ākṣepa-hetu*). These project and manifest the "causes of skeletal production.
Regarding the term "skeletal": if one refers to that which exists internally after death, it is called a "corpse" (*śava*);
if, after a long period has passed, there remains only bone without further cause for growth, it is called a "skeleton" (*kaṅkāla*).
As for the commentary stating, "Now, because the two explanations are distinct, they are spoken of as two":

there is only the internal seed of production (*janman*), which is metaphorically designated as the drawing-in cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*). Therefore, regarding the internal production, the drawing-in cause is explained;

since this is precisely the internal seed of a single birth, it is called the productive cause (*janana-hetu*) because it has the capacity to produce the present body from upon the present seed. Furthermore, it is the immediate [cause] of this present seed—
Because it possesses the power to draw forth the subsequent corpse, it is called the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
To speak according to reality, at the internal stage [of the embryo], there is as yet no corpse or the like; the same applies to external seeds.

If it is argued that those who possess both causes throughout the four modes of birth have a superior principle of "no-nature" (niḥsvabhāva) because they transform birth and death such that no corpse remains;
and if, regarding the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), when these seeds produce manifesting consciousnesses, they are considered proximate fruits for the production of the fruit,

yet those same seeds are considered distant fruits in relation to name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and so forth— then all sentient beings of the three realms, five destinies, and four modes of birth possess [these seeds].
The seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) produce seeds, which in turn produce the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) of the fundamental consciousness.

Since the three realms, five destinies, and four modes of birth (*yoni*) also possess name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), [the distinction between] the cause of production (*janakahetu*) and the cause of attraction (*ākṣepakahetu*)—whereby the former is proximate to the fruit and the latter is remote—is established based on the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). This, moreover, applies universally to all four modes of birth.

If Devaśarman establishes that the "result of the established" (*pratisthita-phala*) and the "residual result" (*avaśeṣa-phala*) apply only to egg-birth, moisture-birth, and womb-birth—since these three types of birth all have a corpse after death, which is termed "residual"—then they do not apply to miraculous birth (*upapāduka*). This is because there is no corpse or skeletal remains after the death of one born by transformation. Question:
If there are no corpses after the death of those born by transformation, how is it that Maheśvara took the bhikṣu Sūkṣma to the ocean?
On the edge [of the precipice], he saw a woman carrying a copper or iron vessel filled with boiling water, in which she was cooking her own body.
Once her body was cooked, it was called a "transformed body" (*nirmāṇakāya*), and she ate her own flesh. This is what occurs after the transformation of birth and death, leaving behind a corpse.
To answer according to the facts: the raw meat within the iron vessel has not yet died; this is a sentient being who has come to this woman.
As for their bodies—specifically those female bodies—they do not actually die. This is because they have not yet exhausted their karmic characteristics and are thus compelled to eat their own flesh.

Furthermore, although the bodies of sentient beings in the *Nārī-avaśeṣa-kvathita* (Female-Remnant-Boiling) Hell become utterly decomposed from being boiled, they still remain in a state of unconscious stupor.
In a brief moment, they return to life. Furthermore, it is like the Hell of Severing with Spikes:

although the sinners are cut into thousands or tens of thousands of pieces, because their coarse flesh is severed, yet their fine tendons and veins remain unbroken, they are still sentient beings and cannot be said to be dead;
they merely fall into a state of unconsciousness and later awaken. This woman is just like that. Therefore, it is said in the Mahāyāna that there are other Avīci hells.
In the seven remaining outer hells and the minor hells, those who die there merely faint from being beaten with clubs; they do not actually die.
Furthermore, once one has died in the body of a specific hell, one does not return to receive that same body in that very place again.
However, if one dies in the body of a specific hell, it is also possible to be reborn in another minor hell. According to the Mahāyāna...
Because he slandered the sūtras, he immediately underwent death in the Avīci Hell. Once his body there had perished, he again received another Avīci body.

In this manner, within the Avīci Hell of this world-system, he underwent twenty bodies for the duration of a *kalpa* of abiding (*sthiti-kalpa*). Because there are twenty [intermediate kalpas], he underwent twenty bodies.
When this period reached the time of the *kalpa* of destruction (*saṃvarta-kalpa*), he then moved toward a world-system in the eastern direction.
During one kalpa, he undergoes twenty lifetimes. When the kalpa of destruction reaches the eastern direction, this very region is in its period of emptiness (*śūnyakalpa*);

the person then proceeds toward the southern direction and undergoes twenty lifetimes in the Avīci Hell. When the kalpa of destruction reaches the southern direction, this region is in its period of formation (*vivartakalpa*).
The person then proceeds into the world-system of the western direction and undergoes twenty lifetimes there; in the western direction, the period of suffering is brief.

Regarding the body: when the kalpa of the western direction is destroyed, one again passes through this direction to undergo the Avīci hell; this direction, in turn, shall likewise pass through a kalpa.

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, it is said that when a sinner undergoes the retribution of hell, once that person has died, they do not again receive a physical body for that specific hell location.
This applies even to one who has committed all five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*); such a person receives only the [retribution of] Avīci.

In the intermediate state of hell (*antarābhava*), one undergoes suffering that is five times greater than in the [actual] hells. Furthermore, according to that school, once the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and form (*rūpa*) have been severed, they cannot be restored.
It is like when a person has their limbs cut off; even if the body is hacked into thousands or tens of thousands of pieces, how could it ever be reconstituted?
Although they are severed, in reality there are still subtle channels (*sūkṣma-nāḍī*) connecting them that remain unbroken. This is similar to [the case of] a large...
The vehicle is the same.
As for the statement that Vasubandhu’s commentary is concise while Asaṅga’s is extensive, yet they do not contradict one another:

when it is said that Vasubandhu’s commentary is concise, it is not called "concise" because it is small in length; rather, it is called "concise" because its explanation of the meaning is sparse. What does this mean? For example:

Ignorance (*avidyā*) may be admitted as the cause of production for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). Just as it is said that ignorance is the cause of production for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), so too, up to birth and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), all are called causes of production;
therefore, know that [the previous statement] was spoken in a general or abbreviated manner.

As for the statement that "the broad explanation of the natureless" is not called "broad" because many [factors] are simultaneously present, but rather because—within the stage of being already moistened—it explains that the seeds of production give rise to manifest formative forces as the cause of production with respect to name-and-form.
From form (*rūpa*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), these serve as the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*). This is indeed an interpretation that accords with the meaning.

Although it accords with the meaning, it still includes things such as withered corpses and remains; thus, the skeletal remains are not fully exhausted. Now, we primarily adopt the two interpretations of Vasubandhu and Asaṅga.

Only by taking the "projecting cause" as birth (*janman*) are all phenomena fully encompassed. Furthermore, Vasubandhu’s explanation is concise while Asaṅga’s explanation is extensive, yet they do not differ [in their essential import].

Regarding the contradiction: however, the Commentary states that if there is no understanding of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), the seeds of consciousness produce the manifest consciousness as its proximate fruit (*āsanna-phala*) as a generative cause;

in relation to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth, it is the remote fruit (*viprakṛṣṭa-phala*). As for the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*), it pervades the three realms, the five destinies, and the four modes of birth.

This means "broad" or "extensive. However, Vasubandhu’s classification—designating only the present body and so forth as the "cause for the production of the actual fruit" (*samyak-phala-utpatti-hetu*) and designating other factors such as the corpse as the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*)—is both superficial and incomplete.

This is because it fails to account for beings in the two upper realms, the six heavens of the desire realm, and the various hells; in these places, beings are born by transformation (*upapāduka*), and thus no corpse remains after death. Furthermore...

Regarding the statement that it "pervades the human realm and the animal destiny, including a portion of those born by transformation": because humans, ghosts, animals, and others born by transformation leave no physical remains after death, [the text] refers to them.
As for Vasubandhu’s interpretation, it applies only to a portion of those born from a womb, an egg, or moisture within the human, ghost, and animal destinies;
this is because those born from a womb, an egg, or moisture do leave physical remains after death. Therefore, Vasubandhu’s explanation is abbreviated.

However, the Upādhyāya says: "Regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), Vasubandhu’s commentary is extensive because it establishes the causes of production and so forth with respect to both sentient and insentient things.

If one explains it according to the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), the explanation is concise, as it establishes the causes of production and projection only with respect to sentient beings;
there are no causes of production or projection regarding insentient things."
The commentary’s verse states: "Withering and perishing result from the projecting cause, like that which ceases spontaneously at the end.

This treatise must have been composed by Asaṅga; the prose commentary was written by Vasubandhu. Since Vasubandhu, in his commentary on Asaṅga’s verses, stated: "There is withering and perishing within the intermediate state," this reveals that Vasubandhu studied under [Asaṅga].

It is appropriate to understand that there are two causes for projection and production. Regarding the phrase "like that which ceases spontaneously at the end": (Note: The original text contains a lacuna marked by □, which has been interpreted as referring to the context of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the relationship between the two masters.)
The flame of a lamp and its oil serve as the causes for its arising, giving rise to the flame as the result. If there is oil, the flame of the lamp persists;
if there is no oil, the flame spontaneously extinguishes itself. The oil is a metaphor for the seed that serves as the cause of arising.
The flame of a lamp is a metaphor for the body. If the seeds that cause birth exist within the body, it may endure for a long time;
however, if those seeds of birth are absent, this corpse will naturally perish on its own after no more than fifty or one hundred years.
"Withered" refers to external withered plants, grasses, and the like. "Perished" refers to the corpses of dead people and so forth. Vasubandhu explains:
"If there were no projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*), there would be no results of withering and perishing, as if they ceased spontaneously later.
However, it is always taught that because there is a projecting cause, such things as withering and perishing occur even after the death of sentient and insentient beings alike."

If there were no projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*), then after death there would be no such things as withering or decay; it would simply be like a lamp flame extinguishing spontaneously, and the same would apply to the lamp flame itself.

Regarding the statement in the *Śūnyatāsaptati-ṭīkā* that "the absence of nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) refers only to the distance between the cause and the fruit within a seed already moistened: if one follows this principle, [it means that]...

In that case, the projecting cause (*ākṣepahetu*) comes first, and the productive cause (*abhinirvṛttihetu*) follows. However, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts, the projecting cause comes first and the productive cause follows.
For instance, ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth up to contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are all projecting causes because they are distant from the fruit.

Craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) are productive causes because they are proximate to the fruit; thus, the projecting cause precedes, while the productive cause occupies the subsequent position.

Later, the present explanation is not so; the points of reference differ. The "cause of arising" (*utpatti-hetu*) and the "inducing cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*) established by Vasubandhu are explained in terms of the stage of having already been moistened by craving and being subject to aging.

The karmic seeds within the womb are able to produce the actual manifestation (*pravṛtti*) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) and cause the karmic seeds to arise; viewed in relation to the consciousness, these are called the "cause of arising.

Once the fundamental consciousness has received birth, the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) gradually increases through the karmic seeds; thus, viewed in relation to the name-and-form, the karmic seeds are—

It is called the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*) because it is remote. Regarding the state of having already been moistened, the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) establishes the "projecting cause" as the cause of birth (*janma-hetu*).

In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, with respect to the states of being moistened and not yet moistened—the seven links prior to being moistened are called the projecting cause, while craving, grasping, and becoming, which have already been moistened, are called the cause of birth.

Thus, the establishment of the cause of birth and the projecting cause differs according to their respective perspectives, yet they are not contradictory. If Vasubandhu has already taken up the corpse...

"Et cetera. "As for the remaining fruits," etc., this is a citation from the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*. Regarding the phrase "because they are dharmas of sentient beings": internal seeds are dharmas of sentient beings. As for the commentary's phrase "or by way of causing [them to arise]":
it means that they serve as the cause for the arising of the perfuming active manifestations (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*); thus, they perfume the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

This is the process by which consciousness arises. It proceeds from the ability of the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*) to strike the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), thereby enabling the perfuming agent to activate seeds within that fundamental consciousness.

Within this [process], there are three parts: first, the analysis of the object of perfuming (*bhāvyamāna*) and the number of conditions it possesses; second, [the discussion] up to the third, which explains the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*); and so forth. Question:

Regarding this topical outline (*kośasthāna*), how does it relate to the previous brief indication that there are three [parts], up to the third: "causing seeds to grow and develop"? This is called [the section on] the conditions for the growth of seeds.
This is the outline for the section on "perfuming" (*vāsanā*) and so forth; reflect upon what distinguishes them.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "it excludes the matter of the sense organs, objects, and the matter within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)," this refers to the five kinds of matter: those belonging to the sense organs, the objects, and the fivefold matter within the sphere of mental objects.
All are excluded. This is because those born in the formless realm have severed them all.

The treatise states that this exclusion applies to both the wholesome and the defiled. If one were to say that "wholesome" refers broadly only to what encompasses wholesome and unwholesome natures, it would not encompass the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Now, within the category of the wholesome and defiled, it does indeed encompass the unwholesome nature of the desire realm, as well as—
This is a concise summary of the obscured and defiled phenomena within the three realms.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “like a person who practices equanimity” (*upekṣā-cārī*): Question: Why is such a person called one who “practices equanimity”?

What is the meaning of “practice” (*cāra*) here? Answer: If a person of neutral temperament is called “equanimous,” and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are called “practice,” then their negation is termed “equanimity-practice.”
The Commentary states: "This is the same as the later explanation that [the seeds] are exclusively non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

This means that if, among the eight consciousnesses, one first explains that which is of a non-obscured neutral nature is capable of receiving perfuming (*vāsanā*), then these two types of neutral natures are likewise [capable of it].

Furthermore, there are two points in the world where the texts agree: namely, that the causal characteristics (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), the resultant characteristics (*phala-lakṣaṇa*), and the self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Regarding the statement in the commentary that "because there is superiority or inferiority, they cannot receive perfuming (*vāsanā*)," "superior" means excellent, or perhaps superior in duration. If this were so, it would follow that the Buddha possesses both superiority and inferiority.

Regarding the statement that "the nature of the [earth] element is not solid and dense": Question: What is the difference between this solidity and the previous solidity? Answer: That [previous solidity] was designated as "solid" based on a single type of continuous stream;
this [present solidity] is distinct because it refers to a superior quality.
The Commentary states: "If that is so, then conditioned phenomena such as 'arising' upon consciousness are simply the distinct states of arising, abiding, and ceasing within consciousness.
Furthermore, this should state: 'If it were not solid, dense, substantial, and sovereign,' and so forth, up to the phrase 'because it cites what is now being explained.'"
However, in the present treatise, it should have been stated in full: "If it were not firm, possessed of substance, and autonomous, then it could receive perfuming.
Yet, the current treatise merely says that it depends on the other-dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) as being firm and dense.

As for the fact that the treatise does not explicitly state, "If it were not firm, dense, possessed of substance, and autonomous, then it could receive perfuming," this is because such an elaboration is explained in the commentary (*śū*), or perhaps because it was already [stated] previously.
Regarding the phrase "not firm, not dense, having substance, and autonomous" in the treatise: [it is] because the present treatise text states it so.

Furthermore, as for the question of why one must exclude [the possibility that] this does not refer to something truly existing as a substance: however, in the body of the treatise, it simply states that the dependent nature is firm and dense.

This immediately excludes mental factors (*caitta*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). Regarding the fact that the treatise does not state "having a real substantial entity" (*dravyasat-svabhāva*) as a means of excluding conventional phenomena (*prajñaptidharma*):

because conventional phenomena do not exist prior [to their conceptualization], they are excluded by way of being [mere] phenomena; therefore, the treatise does not state "having a real substantial entity.
As for the term "wholesome and defiled": if one were to say "wholesome and evil," it would only include the wholesome and would not include the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

The Commentary states: "If one says that True Suchness (tathatā) is not non-defined (avyākṛta), [one must say] it is not the same as non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) or other conventional dharmas such as co-arising;

for these reasons, it should be as in the first [case] above. The Explanation states: Since the treatise text already excludes the "wind-difference" (vāyu-viśeṣa), the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) subsumes all six unconditioned phenomena.
If one says that True Suchness is what is called "having a nature" (sasvabhāva), then True Suchness...

They do not receive perfuming (*vāsanā*). Because both cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*), they cannot receive perfuming, just like birth and other such factors.

Regarding the statement in the Commentary that "ignorance perfumes True Suchness" (*tathatā*), this refers to the citation of the *Asamyag-manas* (the "improper mind") by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu within the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
The Master of Meaning explains the meaning as follows: Because the True [Nature] is perfumed by wholesome dharmas, one is able to attain nirvana;

because True Suchness (tathatā) is perfumed by ignorance, sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death. This is like a person who has first completed the stages of the equipment (sambhāra) and application (prayoga);
because that person is perfumed by their spiritual lineage (gotra), wherever they are born, they always encounter a Buddha.

The Commentary states: "If it is asked how the arising of the manifest and the seed can occur at different times, and thus one knows that this very principle is correct—if cause and effect were at different times, then the seed would only arise after the manifest has already ceased;

in that case, the principle of simultaneous arising and ceasing would not be established. If cause and effect are simultaneous, then the principle of simultaneous arising and simultaneous ceasing is established. If...
Regarding the statement that cause and effect occur at different times: how can this be reconciled with the meaning of "associated and simultaneous"?

If it is argued that when both [matter and mind] maintain the seed, there is the fault of one kind producing two sprouts, [we ask]: since both matter and mind maintain the seed, this is actually two kinds producing one sprout;
why then do you say one kind produces two sprouts? [We answer]: If we speak of matter and mind, "mind" here refers to the six consciousnesses.
If seeds were held in two locations, one would have to say that there is the fault of two seeds producing a single sprout, because there are two bases [for the seed].
Nor is there the fault of a single seed producing two sprouts.

The Commentary states: A composite whole (*samudāya*) cannot sustain distinct [elements] such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, because that which possesses these—the jar—is a conceptual construct (*prajñapti*). It is not the substance itself, but rather the physical form;
the four sensory objects, such as form and so forth, are the real dharmas (*dravyadharma*) that sustain the substance.

Regarding the statement that "the non-associated [factors] are not the same as matter, mind, and so forth": since non-associated factors are merely specific states (avasthā) of matter and mind, they cannot maintain seeds;
likewise, things such as jars, which are conventionally established based on the four sense-objects, also cannot maintain seeds.
The Commentary states: "If it is a provisional designation, it can also receive perfuming, even to the point of being able to receive the perfuming of others.

The term "one" (者) refers to the principal; it carries the meaning of sovereignty. This refers to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) when speaking of the "principal," namely, the eighth mind-king which is capable of receiving perfuming.
It is like the example of a wealthy man who is called the "master" (*svāmin*); the "master" is one who possesses enduring wealth. Now, this [eighth consciousness] is that master.

This is so. Alternatively, if one were to provisionally state that even such provisional dharmas as "arising" and so forth can receive perfuming, this would be according to the conventional standpoint;

however, speaking from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is only the self-substance (*svabhāva-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness that receives perfuming. As follows. What is the meaning of "left" (*zuo*)?
"Left" signifies "prior and posterior. That is to say, the meaning to be explained is subsumed within the preceding and following passages, thereby departing from a person-centered interpretation.

As for this: if a matter has already passed, it is termed "left" (*zuo*); for example, after first stating that such-and-such a matter has been completed, one subsequently says, "the aforementioned items," and so forth.
If a matter has not yet passed, it is termed "left"; for example, when one first says, "as on the left," and only later specifies the particulars of that matter.
Regarding the exclusion of unconditioned causes by means of the aforementioned six meanings:

as for the question of why the aforementioned perfuming is called "born of maturation" (vipākaja) with respect to the attachment to dharmas, the answer is that this attachment, when viewed from the perspective of the two vehicles, is called "born of maturation" because it is of the nature of non-obscured indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta).

Because it does not manifest that [subsequent] arising. If viewed from the perspective of a Bodhisattva, it is of the nature of being obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) or unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta), because it can manifest that arising.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The two types [of minds], such as the maturation-mind (vipākacitta), produce no superior function," this refers to when the maturation-mind arises.
1. It arises from the seeds of indeterminate conventional designations (*nāma-vyavahāra*). 2. It is precisely due to the seeds of others' wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that the case of the untainted (*anāsrava*) [seeds] within the causal stage is likewise so because there are superior, middling, and inferior seeds:
if the seventh consciousness (*manas*) of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) also possesses increasing and decreasing untainted seeds, some say that when they reach the superior grade, they are so designated.
"Increase" refers to the lower grade, which is indeed a decrease; it is that which leads to the attainment of the fruit, not anything else.
"Middle grade" is also a decrease; it is that which leads to the attainment of the fruit, not anything else. As for "neither middle nor equal things":

if the resultant (*vipāka*) indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mind and mental factors are termed "middle things," then "middle things" refers to that which is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, being situated in the middle.
Therefore, intermediate things cannot also perfume [the seeds]. As for "equal things," this refers to the stage of Buddhahood;
because the untainted (*anāsrava*) active manifestations are neither increasing nor decreasing, they are called "equal. Thus, the wholesome factors of the Buddha-fruit also cannot perfume seeds.
Just as "birth" (*jāti*) is termed "arising" (*utpāda*), birth and arising, as well as cessation (*nirodha*) and exhaustion (*kṣaya*), are all synonyms for the same essence.
Regarding the statement that manifest activity gives rise to seeds: if one asserts they occur at different times, how does one explain these [passages]?
If one says that cause and effect occur at different times, how does one explain the meaning of their being associated and simultaneous?
Regarding the passage in the Commentary stating, "From the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) up to 'it should not be a perfuming agent'": Question:

Just as before sentient beings have attained the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), their seventh consciousness is also a perfuming agent; how then can there be increase or decrease in the seventh consciousness? [The author] asks further.
Regarding the commentary on the phrase "from wrong views and so forth, up to the fulfillment of the four meanings":

as stated in the Sūtra, one who severs the roots of goodness through a single grade of wrong view does so according to the discussion concerning the interval between the exhaustion [of the lower grades] and the superior.

As with the superior grade of wrong view, even if one severs the first eight grades of the roots of goodness, it is still not termed "severing the roots of goodness," because a lower grade of the roots of goodness still remains. However, if one gives rise to the highest-of-the-high (上上品) grade of wrong view...
[The text] says: "Seeing. When the mind severs the lowest-of-the-low grade of wholesome roots, it is called 'severed and exhausted.

Just as it is said that wrong view severs wholesome roots at the highest grade, yet this does not preclude the existence of the other nine grades [of afflictions]. Although the seventh consciousness is said to have only 'lower' afflictions, what prevents there being eight grades of detachment from them?
This clarifies that the seventh consciousness has nine grades, which are categorized by analogy with the highest grade of wrong view. Regarding the seventh [consciousness]:

In the Chapter on Consciousness (*Vijñāna-varga*), there are nine grades associated with the name. False view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) likewise possesses the four conditions for being able to perfume (*vāsana*).

If one adopts the first interpretation, the seventh consciousness would increase exclusively; this presents a difficulty. The objection states: [If it were so,] there would be no arising through non-conceptualization (*avikalpa-utpatti*);

gradual clarification and gradual increase would not occur, and the fruit would not reach fulfillment. Since the seventh consciousness, lacking intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), becomes increasingly deluded and dark, it should also reach full completion at a later time.
When it is fulfilled, and when the subsequent fruit reaches completion through the gradual increase of non-conceptual arising, one experiences happiness.
Furthermore, when the seventh consciousness gradually darkens, at that later time, the seventh consciousness will constantly enter hell. Again, an objection is raised:

if the seventh consciousness of a sentient being with the potential for enlightenment (gotra) remains in the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), it is identical to that of a sentient being without such potential. As for those sentient beings without the potential...
If [the seventh consciousness] were bound and further obscured, then the seventh consciousness of sentient beings who possess such a nature would also be obscured.
Consequently, past sentient beings would have attained Buddhahood by practicing the path for only two great kalpas; this would apply to all future sentient beings as well.
One must practice the path for one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* before finally attaining Buddhahood. Thus, we know that the first interpretation does not preclude adopting the second interpretation.
Regarding the nine stages (*bhūmi*) within the three realms (*tridhātu*), they represent the nine grades of superiority according to their coarseness or subtlety.

Furthermore, because the seventh consciousness of sentient beings who lack the [Buddha-]nature is constantly and mutually expansive—and likewise subject to increase and decrease—it constitutes a category of sentient beings' vehicles (*yāna*). Why is this discussed in the treatise?

Regarding the statement that the path of the lowest-lowest grade (*adhamādhama*) of the stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) simultaneously and instantaneously abandons [the afflictions], a question arises:

if the lower treatise states that the lower [path] and the lowest-lowest afflictions are abandoned simultaneously and instantaneously, why does this text speak of the "lowest-lowest grade of the path"?

This passage does not intend to designate the Noble Path itself as the "lowest-lowest grade"; rather, its meaning is to refer to the Noble Path that effects the abandonment of the lowest-lowest grade of afflictions belonging to the stage of the Peak of Existence.

The Path is able to sever the clinging to a vehicle within the seventh consciousness. If this is so, when a Bodhisattva in the tenth stage suddenly and simultaneously severs the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), at the time that Bodhisattva suddenly severs the afflictions across the ten stages, there is no moment when the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*) does not arise;
it is solely for the sake of the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*) regarding the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). This is why the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage severs the afflictions.
Regarding the question, "Is there not already a sense of 'attainment' (*prāpti*) in the prior sudden severance?"—this master of the treatise counters by questioning the opponent:

"If you raise the objection that because the Bodhisattva does not obstruct the stages (*bhūmi*), he only obstructs the mental application (*manasikāra*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and thus leaves it behind, then must there not also be a sense of 'attainment' through sudden severance for the Bodhisattva prior to the seventh stage? The outsider replies: "No, prior to entering the [Bodhisattva] stages..."

Regarding the severance of afflictions (*kleśa*), the Master of the Treatise says: Since you do not admit that they are severed, these afflictions of the seventh consciousness likewise do not obstruct those in training (*śaikṣa*).

Therefore, there is no fault in their being suddenly severed at the moment of the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*), as they consist of nine grades. This is because they are considered non-obstructive afflictions for those in training.

The Commentary states: "If, as in the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a Bodhisattva, the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) to be abandoned in each stage pertain to all three realms, how can there not be multiple grades?
Although the abandonment in each stage pertains to all three realms, does it follow that within a single stage there are no nine grades?

Therefore, one should know that there are indeed nine grades. Thus, although the seventh consciousness is abandoned all at once by the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*), within it there are likewise [nine grades]."

This refers to the nine grades [of afflictions]. Just as the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the nine stages within the three realms pervade the stages of entering, abiding, and completing throughout the ten grounds, one likewise knows the objects of the nine stages within the three realms.

Just as the cognitive obstructions of the nine stages within the three realms pervade the obstructions of the ten grounds, there are obstructions that hinder entry into the first ground during the mind of entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
At the very moment of entering the illumination of the first ground, one simultaneously and completely severs the portions of the three realms and nine stages.

This is distinct from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). For instance, among the nine stages of the three realms, there is a certain class of cognitive obstructions that can obstruct the time of entering the first stage of abiding in the mind;
at that moment, upon entering the first stage of abiding in the mind, one simultaneously cuts off the innate cognitive obstructions associated with all nine stages of the three realms.
Furthermore, within the nine stages of the three realms, there is another class of cognitive obstructions that can obstruct the time of the final stage of abiding in the first stage.

When that bodhisattva reaches the stage of full completion (*pūrṇa-citta*) in the first ground (*bhūmi*), they also universally abandon the cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) of the nine stages within the three realms.

Just as it is with the three phases of entering, abiding, and completing in the first ground, so it is for the three phases of the second ground, and likewise for the three phases up to the tenth ground.
Therefore, throughout the ten grounds, in each and every ground, during the phases of entering, abiding, and completing, [the bodhisattva] universally abandons [the cognitive obstructions].

The cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) pertain to the three realms and nine stages. Thus, one should know that within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the cognitive obstructions are divided into ten categories.

Subsequently, they obstruct the ten stages (*bhūmi*) in general; since each stage is treated as a single category, the cognitive obstructions of the desire realm—which are capable of obstructing the ten stages—are therefore divided into ten categories.
This continues up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), where the cognitive obstructions are numerous, yet they too are divided into ten.

Because of this classification, one cannot say that the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the desire realm are abandoned in the first stage (*bhūmi*), those of the first dhyāna in the second stage,
and so on, up to the abandonment of the cognitive obstructions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) in the ninth stage.
The Commentary further states: "Moreover, as with a Bodhisattva who, having been born in a higher realm, does not sever the lower realms or does not obstruct them, this analogy should likewise apply.

This refers, for example, to how the afflictions within the six consciousnesses of one in the third fruit must necessarily sever the lower [afflictions] when they predominate; it is also like the case of those of the Two Vehicles or ordinary worldlings.

If one has not yet abandoned the full [defilements] of a lower stage, one will certainly not attain the meditative concentration of a higher stage; if one attains the meditative concentration of a higher stage, one must have abandoned the full [defilements] of the lower stage.

Furthermore, if one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one will necessarily lose the meditative concentration of the higher stages; if one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one must have suppressed and exhausted the full [defilements] of the desire realm.
It is not so for the Bodhisattva: from the very first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, they have already accomplished the lower stages. Thus, when the Bodhisattva is born in the form realm...
