Because they have not severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), even though they are born in the higher realms, they give rise from afar to the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of the afflictions of the desire realm.

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas are born in the desire realm, they do not lose their meditative attainments (*samādhi*) of the higher realms, and they obtain those higher attainments; or, when they are born in the higher realms, they do not sever the afflictions of the desire realm.
Moreover, when Bodhisattvas are about to give rise to afflictions, their preceding preparatory minds (*prayoga-citta*) are all for the sake of the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
Because of this causal condition, when a bodhisattva gives rise to afflictions, they immediately attain hundreds of thousands of merits. Question:

Can a bodhisattva born in the higher realms give rise to the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of afflictions belonging to the desire realm? Furthermore, can one born in the formless realm give rise to afflictions belonging to the form realm?

Answer: When the body is in a lower realm, one cannot give rise to any afflictions of a higher realm. If a bodhisattva’s body is in a higher realm, there is certainly no arising of afflictions of a lower realm.
For example, when the body is in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one does not give rise to the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm itself.
Likewise, if the body is in the second dhyāna or above, even up to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one does not give rise to the afflictions of the two lower realms.

Regarding the commentary’s essential point that one must reach the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*) before being able to retroactively abandon lower [defilements]: for example, when one attains the fruit of No-More-Learning while still in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), one is able to abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the two higher realms;
it is only upon reaching the fruit of No-More-Learning that one is finally able to abandon them collectively. [In this context], the character "却" (què) should be changed to "改却" (gǎiquè).
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage is born in Akaniṣṭha and attains the fruit of Arhatship,
if they were to ascend to the formless realm or descend to the desire or form realms, all afflictions would temporarily merge there and would not yet be severed.

If one were to sever [afflictions] specifically in the lower realms, it might be called "severing the lower," yet only those *anāgāmins* who "flow upwards" (ūrdhvasrotas) are born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Only upon attaining the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa-phala) does one subsequently sever the afflictions within the seventh consciousness of that particular stage (*bhūmi*). Based on this, one should formulate a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*):

there are cases where the body resides in a lower realm while one severs the afflictions of a higher realm; for example, when attaining the first fruit (*prathamaphala*), one severs the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) belonging to all three realms.
Or, for example, when one’s body resides in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) yet attains the fruit of no-more-learning, one also severs [the afflictions] of the two higher realms.

Regarding innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*): there are those who possess a body while severing the afflictions of lower stages. This refers to those like the *ūrdhvasrotas* (one who flows upward) *anāgāmin*, who, having been born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), attain the fruit of *aśaikṣa* and thereby sever the afflictions within the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭamanas*) of the lower stages. There are also those who possess a body in a lower stage while severing the afflictions of that lower stage;
such as a *sakṛdāgāmin* or *anāgāmin* who has not yet severed the afflictions of the lower desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) but attains [the respective fruits].

Regarding the second and third fruits [of the path]: when one exists in a higher realm (*ūrdhvabhūmi*) and abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*) of that higher realm—just as in the case of a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who, having been born within a higher sphere, abandons the afflictions of the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭhavijñāna*) and so forth—the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the sixth consciousness does not constitute a difficulty because it lacks the latter two meanings.
However, an external objection states: "In the seventh consciousness, the view of a self and so forth are of a single class..."

Therefore, they are severed at the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*). Since the innate view of self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and other afflictions within the sixth consciousness belong to the same category, they too should be severed at the diamond-like mind.
Answer: Regarding the innate view of self and other afflictions within the sixth consciousness, among the four meanings—

Because these three meanings do not exist, this does not constitute a valid objection. That is to say, the innate views and so forth associated with the sixth consciousness undergo a transformation according to the three types of sensation (*vedanā*).

If one is in hell, they are associated with the sensation of suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*); if in the third dhyāna of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they are associated with the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*);
and if in the two lower dhyānas and so forth, they are associated with the sensation of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*). This is because the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is common to all.
The sixth, the innate view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), can be associated with four types of feeling; this is clarified by the lower section of the treatise itself.

Furthermore, its objects are easily accessible, meaning that the innate view of a self-body associated with the sixth consciousness may grasp the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as the self, or it may grasp the other four aggregates as the self and so forth.
Moreover, it does not persist [as a continuous stream]. This innate view of a self-body associated with the sixth consciousness is exclusively obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Regarding "nature," there are only three natures that do not change. It is incorrect for the *Śū* (Commentary) to state that the latter meaning does not exist.
As for the passage in the *Śū* which says, "Because of this meaning, it instead establishes [the view] from beginningless time until today;

today serves as an addition, and only then does the previous interpretation become established"—the intent of these words is as follows: the main purport of the *Śū* adopts the first of the two previous interpretations. If [one follows] Master Zhì and others...
The following is the measure of the scholar’s teaching. If one wishes to adopt the second interpretation, it is superior from the perspective of principle.

Regarding the passage in the *Śū* [the Sub-commentary] which states, "If those sentient beings who lack the nature [for enlightenment], up to those of the 'unfit' category, could be called 'perfumed' (*vāsya*)," this represents a specific master offering such an interpretation.
The author of the *Śū* now cites and establishes this very point in order to refute it within the *Śū*.
The Commentary further states: For instance, regarding the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) abandoned at the first stage (*bhūmi*), these pertain to all three realms.

Among them, there is a category of cognitive obstructions belonging to the [lower] nine stages that the first stage is able to abandon. Furthermore, there is a category of cognitive obstructions belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) stage.

It is capable [of being severed] at the first stage (*bhūmi*). It is at the first stage that [the obstacles] can be severed. It cannot be explained as follows: "The coarse cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the desire realm obstruct the first stage and are severed there;

the cognitive obstacles of the first dhyāna cause them to be severed at the second stage; the second stage severs both types of obstacles; the cognitive obstacles [of the second stage] cause them to be severed at the third stage;
and so on, up to the subtle cognitive obstacles of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), which are caused to be severed at the tenth stage. Why is this? Because...
At the summit [of existence], there is a certain category of subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). On the first stage (*bhūmi*), one also abandons the obstructions of the summit.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "it does not preclude that the first category of cognitive obstructions in the desire realm generally obstructs all ten stages, yet they are abandoned individually on each stage":

the present mention of the "first category of the desire realm" is because the nine stages are collectively divided into nine categories; thus, it refers to the cognitive obstructions of the desire realm.

The cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the first dhyāna are of the upper-middle grade; those of the second dhyāna are of the upper-lower grade; those of the third dhyāna are of the middle-upper grade;
those of the fourth dhyāna are of the middle-middle grade; and so on, until the cognitive obstacles of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are of the lower-lower grade.
Thus, throughout the three realms, there are nine grades in total. Although it is said that the first grade pertains to the desire realm, within that—
The remote [obstructions] consist of nine grades, which are combined into one. Because they collectively obstruct the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they are severed individually. Question:

When it says "the first grade of the desire realm," does this mean that the ten superior grades of the nine grades of the desire realm are collectively named the "first grade," or does it mean that the nine grades of the desire realm are categorized as a single grade and named the "first grade"?
Answer: It is indeed so; however, regarding the chapter on severing obstructions, it refers specifically to the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

One cannot establish eighty-one categories by dividing the nine grounds; rather, it is because the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the three realms can obstruct the ten grounds that these cognitive obstructions are divided into ten categories.
The Commentary merely states that "that which can initially obstruct this is severed upon realizing this.

Regarding the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, if the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) can obstruct this first stage (*bhūmi*), then upon realizing the suchness (*tathatā*) of this first stage, those very cognitive obstacles are severed.
If the cognitive obstacles can obstruct this second stage, they are severed at the time of realizing this second stage; this logic applies up to the tenth stage and need not be discussed further.

Chapter. In the first stage (*bhūmi*), one abandons the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the desire realm; in the second stage, one abandons the obstructions of the first dhyāna and so forth.
Within the nine stages of the three realms, whichever stage has an obstruction that can hinder that specific stage, the Dharma eliminates it.

Commentary: Regarding the preceding four [types of perfuming] among those corresponding to the perfuming of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-vāsanā*), up to the point where it says "arising through provisional questioning":

the first four perfumers are all included within the textual discourse on the arising of phenomena. Question: If it is said that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is a perfumer, it should also be able to include and give rise to a passage concerning the existence of one [entity] with arising and ceasing.
If arising and ceasing were the perfumers, then the maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) and its mental factors would be inferior.
If those that are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and so forth were to be called "perfumers" (*vāsaka*), this would refer to the passage stating that two [of the three natures] possess superior function.

If one says that possessing superior function constitutes being a "perfumer," then the wholesome dharmas of the Buddha-fruit should be called "perfumers"; this refers to the passage stating that three [of the four fruits] involve increase or decrease.
If one says that having increase or decrease constitutes being a "perfumer," then one's own body perfuming another body should be named a "perfumer. Thus...
Regarding the statement that those which arise in conjunction with the four [conditions] and the perfumed (bhāvyamāna) must each arise individually according to the treatises:

as for the commentary’s question, "If it is the objective aspect (nimittabhāga), what dharma acts as an obstacle... up to 'because it is only perfumed'?"—this refers to the ripening consciousness (vipākacitta) and so forth.

Since it cannot be perfumed by itself, if a wholesome or unwholesome mind can perfume seeds of maturation (*vipāka-bīja*) within the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), there is likewise no obstruction.
As for what dharma acts as an obstruction—what further dharma could act as an obstruction to perfuming within the objective aspect? The meaning is that there is no obstruction.
It is not the case that the wholesome or unwholesome [states] of the perceiving mind cannot perfume seeds of maturation within the objective aspect of that perceiving mind; rather, its capacity...
Within the aspect of the object (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), seeds of the three natures can also be perfumed.

If [the mind] is able to perfume within the self-witnessing aspect (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*), seeds of good and evil are perfumed; these seeds possess power and subsequently function as karma to extinguish the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
If, however, the seeds of good and evil perfumed within the objective aspect, they can subsequently only produce their own kind.

The mind [itself] cannot perform karma such as good or evil. Therefore, it was previously stated that only the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness can receive perfuming;
thus, we know that the perfuming capacity of the first seven consciousnesses also resides in their respective self-witnessing divisions, which are able to perfume seeds.

Because the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) is capable of perfuming seeds, it follows that the seeing and image divisions (*darśana- and nimitta-bhāga*), which it carries with it, are also capable of perfuming seeds.

This is just as when soldiers and a general can both defeat an enemy: while the general can defeat the enemy because he leads the troops, the soldiers and the general together are also able to defeat the enemy.

[Objection: Since the seeing-consciousness (*darśanacitta*) can take external objects as its object and can also take the image division as its object, it may be granted that the seeing division is capable of perfuming.

If the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) cannot take the external object or the image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its object, how can it be said that the self-witnessing division perfumes seeds?
Answer: The seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) is the function, while the self-witnessing division is the substance of consciousness.

Although the self-witnessing division can take the image-division as its object, it does so precisely because the self-witnessing division carries the image-texture (*nimittākāra*). Therefore, both the self-witnessing division and the image-division are capable of perfuming the mind. Within the image-division...
Because it possesses the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and so forth, the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is also capable of perfuming (*vāsana*).

However, the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) is merely a functional activity and thus cannot perfume seeds. Therefore, one should know that for material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), there is no sense of "simultaneous existence" (*sahabhū*);

that is, within such phenomena, there is no simultaneous relationship between the seven consciousnesses acting as perfumers and the eighth consciousness acting as the perfumed, as there is in the case of incense perfuming clothing and the like. And...

The analogy of the flower and the incense, as explained by Vasubandhu, also refers to simultaneity. As for the subsequent citation of two dharmas and two analogies to illustrate the two types of cause and effect:
this refers to the active perfuming agent (*pravṛtti-vāsanā*) acting as the cause, which directly perfumes to produce the seed-result;

because they are simultaneous, it is so called. Regarding the result of the newly perfumed seed, it likewise depends on the perfuming cause; thus, these too constitute a relationship of mutual dependence between cause and effect. If it is a newly perfumed seed... [passage continues].
After the second moment of thought, they manifest separately, and their seeds likewise differ.
Furthermore, when the manifest fruits of the seven evolving consciousnesses arise, they proceed directly from seeds; it is not that seeds which produce manifest fruits arise [again].
Rather, one takes the production of the manifest itself as the causal relationship of mutual dependence between cause and fruit.
Regarding the two meanings of cause and effect illustrated by the analogy of the two dharmas: this refers to when a manifest state arises from a seed, the manifest state then depends upon the seed;
thus, these two dharmas are mutually dependent. Furthermore, when a seed is perfumed by a manifest state, [the manifest state likewise depends upon the seed].
That is to say, newly perfumed seeds depend upon actual manifestations; this is likewise the mutual dependence of two dharmas.

As for the example from the Hīnayāna regarding the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) acting as the cause for co-existent dharmas: it is like when a single material form (*rūpa*) is produced, there is a complete set of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Therein, the earth element and the water element act as causes and conditions, being able to produce the water element, because they exist simultaneously.

The water element can produce the earth element and acts as its efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*); thus, the water element is the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the earth element is its dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
This applies even up to the fire element producing the wind element: the fire element is the efficient cause, and the wind element is its dominant fruit.
When the four great elements are considered in relation to one another, they each act as co-existent causes for one another, and they each act as dominant fruits for one another.

This is the result. The four great elements (mahābhūta) do not serve as simultaneous causes (sahabhū-hetu) for [unmanifest form]. Why is this? It may be so that, just as when one is in meditative absorption (samāpatti), the four great elements act as simultaneous causes for the unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa) produced at that same time;

however, these four great elements cannot be simultaneous causes for the unmanifest form during the subsequent period of a single lifetime, even though it arises from the four great elements at the time of the initial reception [of the vow].
This is because, although the unmanifest form exists by virtue of the four great elements at the time of its reception, [the elements] no longer persist as such in the subsequent state.

Because these [elements] exist subsequent to the sensation (vedanā), they do not constitute simultaneous causes (sahabhū-hetu). This [simultaneous causality] applies only to the four great elements (mahābhūta) at the same time.
Regarding the atoms (paramāṇu) of the four great elements, some say that they are spread horizontally beneath the matter (rūpa), while the atoms of matter abide above them.
Some say that the atoms of form (*rūpa-paramāṇu*) are in the center, while the atoms of mind (*citta-paramāṇu*) are on the four sides, adhering to their interior.
This applies even up to the mental factors (*caitta*). They are mutually simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) and efficient fruits (*puruṣakāra-phala*). Question:
In the Hīnayāna, since fire and water are mutually contradictory, how can the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) be established as simultaneous causes in relation to one another, as previously stated?

Regarding the statement "the *Vyākhyāyukti* clarifies that [this] is refuted": this refers to the nature of causal conditions (*pratyaya*). It is just like the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), as well as when the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise;
they merely support one another. How then can it be said that the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) possess the nature of causal conditions?

This is refuted at length in that treatise (*Vyākhyāyukti*). The third fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* also states that they are causal conditions; this is because the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is the same in this regard.

As for the objection: that treatise also states that the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) are able to produce the various consciousnesses and so forth, serving as their causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
For example, regarding the nature of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), it is not established that they function as causal conditions simultaneously;
thus, according to the meaning of the co-existent cause, in the Mahāyāna system, seeds give rise to seeds and actualities give rise to seeds. However, in that [Hīnayāna] school...
The co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) of the Mahāyāna is indeed similar in meaning to the simultaneous [condition].

Specifically, the seeds of the Mahāyāna that give rise to the manifest and so forth constitute the co-existent cause; this is the condition of causal efficacy (*hetu-pratyaya*). Your Small Vehicle’s co-existent cause consists of one manifestation (*samudācāra*) acting as a co-existent factor toward another manifestation.
Since it is a case of one manifestation acting toward another manifestation, it does not constitute a condition of causal efficacy. Furthermore, there are also manifest...

Regarding the phrase "because the [active] states cannot perfuse": this refers to the manifestation of the resultant mind and mental factors, as well as the manifestation of the mind and mental factors at the stage of Buddhahood;
however, these are unable to perfuse.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) further states: "Regarding the case where the present [moment] in relation to the present, or the non-present in relation to the present, is subsumed under the category of causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*):

for example, when a preceding moment of wholesome form (*rūpa*) in the Śrāvaka vehicle gives rise to a subsequent moment of wholesome form, the preceding moment acts as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and the subsequent moment is its outflowing effect (*niṣyanda-phala*);
both are causal conditions. Furthermore, it is like the case where, within the causal stage of the Truths (*satya-hetu*), a preceding instance of anger acts as the homogeneous cause."

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) at the end of the body (*kāya-paryanta*) is cited as its outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*). Now, this refers to the relationship between the unwholesome and the obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Furthermore, wholesome or unwholesome matter (*rūpa*) of a preceding moment induces the four aggregates (*skandha*) of a subsequent wholesome moment; these also function as similar-type causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) and outflow fruits. Regarding the present:

next, within the critique of the Hīnayāna, it is not transmitted that a manifest state (*pravṛtti*) serves as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for a manifest state. If a manifest state were merely a predominating condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), [the argument would follow accordingly].
This is subsumed under the category of superior objects. Now, when one relies upon the seeds of the Mahāyāna, they correspond to both [the cause and the effect].

Just as the homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) of the Śrāvaka vehicle mutually induce one another before and after, so too is this the meaning of mutual induction between preceding and succeeding moments. This is precisely what constitutes their causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Specifically, the seed produced by the seed of the Mahāyāna in the preceding moment is the homogeneous cause; this is the actual causal condition. If it were like the homogeneous cause of the Śrāvaka vehicle, it would not be a [true] cause.

This refers to conditions (*pratyaya*). If the Mahāyāna explains that preceding wholesome form induces subsequent wholesome form, it is subsumed under the category of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

The treatise states: "These two are of the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) with respect to the fruit. Regarding these two: first, the perfuming agent produces seeds, and the seeds give rise to actual manifestations;
second, seeds of the same kind produce one another across successive moments. Therefore, these two types are causal conditions.
Regarding the discussion of why these other dharmas, such as the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), are called "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*):

if the seven evolving consciousnesses, when viewed in relation to their own actualization (*samudācāra*), are causal conditions for one another, then it should be understood that all dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*, chapter forty-two, is designated as "causal condition" by way of metaphorical designation (*prajñapti*).

This is because that treatise follows the metaphorical designations of the Hīnayāna; specifically, it refers to what appears as the "concomitant cause" (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the "arising-in-turn cause" (*anuvartaka-hetu*). This follows the Hīnayāna.
It is called "conforming" (*anuvartana*) because it is explained according to principle; in the Mahāyāna, it is called "the true principle.

It is also like the case where taking life results in a short lifespan, or stealing results in the retribution of poverty, and so forth. In the verse, one should have said: "The location is clearly such that it cannot be known beforehand.
However, in the current treatise, for the sake of brevity, the phrase "previously" is omitted; thus, the treatise does not explicitly state "knowable" or "appropriated" (*upātta*).
Once it has ceased, it cannot be known as something prior.
Regarding the statement "the aspect (*ākāra*) is the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*); likewise, the substance (*svabhāva*) is also so": in consciousness, the function of discerning is the aspect;

consciousness reaches out through the function of discerning as its own essential nature (*svabhāva*). This is like saying that the transformation of color is itself the object; thus, that which transforms is itself [the object].

Regarding the "intrinsic nature of form" and its "aspects" (*ākāra*): the term "aspect" carries the meaning of "traversing" or "wandering. It refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and so forth, which traverse their respective objects.
Furthermore, the aspect is the seeing-part itself. As for the first interpretation stating that "aspect" refers to the essence (*lakṣaṇa*):
even True Suchness (*tathatā*) can be termed an "aspect," because it is neither characterized by marks nor devoid of marks; it is the ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

True Suchness (*tathatā*) also possesses essence and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). However, regarding the statement that it "originally has only the meaning of the aspect of activity (*ākāra*)," the first interpretation holds that "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the essence (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, the interpretation that "the aspect of activity is so called because it acts upon the characteristic of the object" is the original explanation of the Tripiṭaka Master [Xuanzang].

The latter two interpretations are those of the Commentator [Kuiji]. Alternatively, "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) may refer to a formal appearance (*ākṛti*); thus, the formal appearance of the object of activity is termed "aspect of activity."
Regarding "aspect" (*ākāra*): this second interpretation states that the character *xing* (行) should be pronounced with the level tone (*ping sheng*).

Here, "aspect" refers to the mode of appearance, which is the perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) that operates upon the mode of appearance of the perceived object; thus, it is called the "aspected aspect.

Alternatively, "the mode of understanding and appearance that operates within the object"—this is the third interpretation, wherein the character *xing* should be pronounced with the departing tone (*qu sheng*).

This refers to "understanding" (*avabodha*). "Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to appearance. That is to say, when the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) perceives an object, understanding proceeds upon the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "From here below, it will be extensively explained according to those respective locations," these "locations" refer to the various [sections] as stated in the treatiment below.
This is explained extensively in the Commentary (*Śāstra*) regarding "matured" (*vipakva*) and other locations.
As for the statement, "That which is capable of producing sensation (*vedanā*) by means of apprehending and receiving [objects] is called 'appropriation' (*upādāna*)," etc.:

because the eighth consciousness apprehends the five sense organs as its objects and maintains them so that they do not perish, it is upon the basis of the body-organ (*kāyendriya*) that body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) arises.

Regarding "simultaneously": when one experiences pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*), there is also the acquisition of nourishment (*puṣṭi*) and so forth. With respect to this nourishment and so forth, it is not merely sensation;

rather, it is subsumed within the object-field of tangibles (*spraṣṭavya-viṣaya*). It is included within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*). This is because, upon the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), there is a state of well-being (*prasrabdhi*);

this well-being is [itself] within the object-field of tangibles. Furthermore, upon one's own mind-faculty (*manendriya*), there is weariness (*parikheda*); this weariness is [also] within the object-field of tangibles. This occurs by way of both body and mind.
Because there is the experience of pleasure or the exhaustion of labor, this passage speaks of "feeling" (*vedanā*), which is identical to the explanation in the lower treatise.

Whether one has entered meditative absorption or is not in absorption, there is the pervasion of distinct volition or the pervasion of non-volition; in principle, there are many ways in which the body arises.
There may be ease and well-being, or there may be weariness and exhaustion. This ease and well-being, as well as this weariness and exhaustion, are precisely the sensations (*vedanā*) of this world.

These states of ease and well-being, or weariness and exhaustion, are not the sensation (*vedanā*) among the mental factors (*caitta*). This ease is the attainment of a light and upright tactile contact upon the body;
it is the taking of breath from within the four types of subtle contacts. Breath itself is the ease. Whether it be ease or weariness—
"Damage" (*upaghāta*) refers to physical pain. This "exhaustion and damage" (*pariśrama-upaghāta*) is precisely the "fatigue" (*klamatha*) among the twenty-four types of contact (*spraṣṭavya*).
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Chapter Five, states that what is "appropriated" (*upātta*) consists only of the five sense faculties and a portion of the four objects.

By saying it is "appropriated," it means that it is solely the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) which, being born with pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*), receives nourishment through contact and so forth; subsequently, the five consciousnesses depend upon these five [faculties].

The origination from the faculties (*indriya-samutthāna*) occurs within the feelings of pleasure and so forth. Regarding the statement in the *Pañcaṣaṣṭika* that "the five faculties in their entirety and a portion of the five objects" [are the contact], it is as previously explained:
just as the objects of touch such as pain and nourishment can subsequently give rise to various feelings.

If the meaning of "the basis upon which consciousness relies and clings, up to the point of experiencing" refers to taking something as its object, then "the basis upon which consciousness relies and clings" specifically reveals the five faculties and...

Regarding seeds and so forth: because the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is able to grasp and maintain the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*), it is only then that one possesses the five sense organs and so on, and is born with pleasant sensations.
As for what is said regarding "consciousness," this refers specifically to the eighth consciousness of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Its reliance upon the five sense organs is the same as stated in the following passage: "The *ālayavijñāna* relies predominantly upon the various fundamental consciousnesses (*mūlavijñāna*)," referring here to the physical sense organs (*rūpīndriya*).
Thus, they attain simultaneous growth and do not perish. Furthermore, within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the eighth consciousness depends upon the five sense organs;
therefore, that eighth consciousness also attains growth and remains uninterrupted. If the five sense organs are absent, the eighth consciousness is relinquished;
if the eighth consciousness is absent, the five sense organs are also severed. Consequently, their security and peril are identical, and they arise in union.
This is "long" (*dīrgha*). It clarifies that the eighth consciousness is able to grasp and maintain the five sense faculties as well as their seeds, taking them as its objects of perception.
However, within this context, one should distinguish by saying: if the five sense faculties and their seeds depend upon the eighth consciousness, [then they are maintained by it].
This refers to "constant concentration" (*nitya-samādhi*). If the eighth consciousness were absent, its seeds and the five sense organs would be severed.
If the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) were to depend upon the five sense organs, it would not be constant;

for while one may say that in the desire and form realms the fundamental consciousness depends on the five organs, when born in the formless realm, the eighth consciousness does not depend on the five organs. Thus it is said.

Regarding the statement that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is indeterminate with respect to its seeds: for example, when it causes [phenomena] not to arise in the desire realm, the storehouse consciousness is already a manifesting consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
This manifesting consciousness depends upon the neutral (*avyākṛta*) seeds of its own designations (*nāma-vyañjana*) which cause [those phenomena] to arise; this is what is meant by "determinacy."
If, within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), the seeds capable of producing the eighth consciousness in successive future lives,
as well as the seeds of the other seven consciousnesses and so forth, were all not the support of that fundamental consciousness, they would therefore be called "indeterminate. However,

if one sets aside [those] and causes the fundamental consciousness to arise from the seeds of "naming and expression" (nāma-vyañjana) within the consciousness of the subsequent life, then the fundamental consciousness manifests, which is precisely the subsequent life.

The seeds of names and phrases are that upon which the fundamental consciousness relies. If those seeds of names and phrases have already been abandoned such that they no longer arise, they are no longer the support for the fundamental consciousness;
this should be understood accordingly for all subsequent cases as well.

Second, regarding the statement that "taking this as a basis, one can produce the discourse on all sensations, up to the point where they are indestructible, and can produce the awareness of sensation":

this text refers specifically to the dependence upon the five sense-faculties (*indriya*). The fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is able to grasp and sustain these five faculties, thereby enabling the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*) to equally produce the awareness of pleasure and other sensations within it, which then take pain as their object and provide nourishment. Furthermore, according to this interpretation, the five faculties serve as the bases for the six consciousnesses.

Therefore, the six consciousnesses arise within the factors of enlightenment such as joy (*prīti*). This is because, by maintaining that the five sense faculties are unimpaired, one is subsequently able to give rise to various sensations (*vedanā*).

If one speaks according to the ultimate principle—even though the actual reality is not so—one says that the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) arises within the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), thereby obtaining the experiences of gratification, pain, or nourishment within the sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavya*).

"Pain-nourishment and so forth" refers to the cessation of pain (*vedanā-sthiti*) among the twenty types of contact (*spraṣṭavya*). By analogy, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) obtains the remaining four faculties and their respective physical bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

There is no case where it does not obtain the tactile object (*spraṣṭavya*) of pain-nourishment and so forth, because the remaining four faculties and their bases occupy the same location as the [body-]faculty.
Thus, at the time when the body-faculty attains the awakening factor of pain-nourishment (*vedanā-sambodhyaṅga*), the remaining four faculties and so forth are said to "attain" it as well.
Regarding "feeling" (*vedanā*):

the Commentary (*Śāstra*), based on the fact that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are inseparable from their manifest activity and even pervade the eighteen bases (*āyatana*), [concludes] that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* refers only to the four great elements that act as the creators (*nirmātṛ*) of the five sense organs.
This is because the five sense organs, which are the created (*nirmita*), are possessed of appropriation (*upātta*). Thus, they are the creators of the organs.

Regarding these four great elements (*mahābhūta*), there are also appropriated (*upātta*) four great elements which, being conjoined with and attached to the same location as the five sense faculties (*indriya*), subsequently produce sound.
Or, the characteristics of the four great elements that can produce the five sense faculties strike one another and produce sound.

Or, the four great elements that can support the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) strike one another and produce sound. This sound is also [sometimes] appropriated. If this sound strikes or contacts [an object], or...
When the blood vessels flow internally, there are three hundred conduits within the body. Over the course of one day and night, these three hundred [conduits] circulate;
the blood flows through the body from top to bottom, long and pervasive. "Ying" (營) refers to the blood.
"Thorough-pervasion" (*cheda*) refers to the channels (*nāḍī*). This is because [the breath] flows everywhere through the channels.

It is the flesh within the embryo that grows long within the body. If the blood and channels do not circulate, pain arises. Therefore, one who attains the pure divine ear hears the sound of the blood and channels flowing within the body.
However, with respect to the time of taking birth, the vital energy (*prāṇa*) first enters; thus, it initially arises from the fourth dhyāna.

When that breath has already entered, if one is at the point of death, yet while still in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) intends to enter the fourth *dhyāna*, the breath will arise as the concentration is attained.
However, when born among the gods of the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), there is also warmth within the body, as well as the sound of flowing and the sound of arising;
at other times, there is no such sound. If it is the same within the body to the utmost degree...
If subtle, there is no sound. How is it known that the subtle lacks combined sound? The meaning here is as follows: in the desire realm, if [matter] is subtle, there is no sound.
If sound occurs throughout the body, there are times when sound is not produced. How is it known that there is sound within the body?
Just as in the external world, even up to the Heaven of Non-perception (asaṃjñisattva), the body possesses all ten bases (*āyatana*), namely the five sense organs.
There are three objects (*viṣaya*): form, sound, and touch. This is because the other two—odor and taste—are absent there, as those two do not exist in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Furthermore, this includes the original sense-sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). Within the *dharmāyatana*, there is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*). Regarding their inclusion within the ten elements (*dhātu*) and spheres (*āyatana*):

according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, if sound is also included, then because there are five faculties and five objects, they are comprised within the ten elements. This is like the case of the eye.

The eye-pupil occupies the same location [as the other sense organs]. Thus, there is the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) in that same location. Furthermore, there are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that constitute the visual faculty in that same location.

Moreover, there are the "dust-like" atoms (*anu*) that support the visual faculty in that same location. Additionally, there are the four great elements that constitute those supporting dust-atoms in that same location.
Finally, because the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is also present, one experiences pain when the eye-pupil is struck; therefore, we know it is the eye-pupil.
In the same location, there exists the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). Furthermore, there exist the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that constitute the body-faculty in the same location.

Moreover, there exist the four objects (*viṣaya*) that support the body-faculty in the same location. Additionally, there exist the four great elements that support the objects which, in turn, support the body-faculty in the same location.
There is also nutritive matter (*aupacayika-rūpa*); this nutritive matter likewise exists in the same location as non-retributive matter (*avipāka-rūpa*). Furthermore, there is also... [growth].
Above the nourishing matter (*puṣṭi-rūpa*), there are the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that can produce it, existing in the same location.

Furthermore, there is the resultant matter (*vipāka-rūpa*) existing in the same location, and above that resultant matter, there are the primary elements that can produce it—just as in the case of the eye-organ, where these many factors exist together.

As for the nose, tongue, ear, and body organs, they likewise possess fleshly matter that is matured and nourished; thus, do not all schools of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) explain them in this same way?
Regarding "differentiated great atoms" (*mahāparamāṇu*): this means that the great atoms of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the atoms of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) are all inseparable;
thus, they are termed "unreal. Question: Since the Mahāyāna does not posit the existence of atoms, why is it said here that there are atoms?
Answer: Although in the Mahāyāna there is no accumulation of multiple atoms, coarse objects are nonetheless established [as such].

Regarding form (*rūpa*): even within what is distant from the body, there exist subtle and most minute atoms (*paramāṇu*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 53, states that there are fifteen kinds of atoms:

namely, the atoms of the five sense organs, the atoms of the five sense objects, the atoms of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and the atoms of the real matter (*dravya-rūpa*) subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Thus, there are fifteen kinds. According to the Sarvāstivādins, there are [atoms of] the four sense objects and so forth.
Each individual [object] of form, odor, taste, and touch possesses its own distinct set of four primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as its creator.

In the Mahāyāna, however, it is not maintained that a small portion of the primary elements can create many forms. This is just as the solar disk, though small, emits light and color that pervade the entirety of space.
This is the intended meaning found in the fifty-first fascicle [of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*], in this treatise, and elsewhere.
This refers to the seeds and the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) that are contacted; these are called the two types of appropriation (*upādāna*).

The commentary asks: "If non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) also depend upon consciousness... This question is an abbreviated reference to what follows.

One should state that it asks whether the mental factors associated with the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), as well as non-informative matter and the seventh [consciousness], share the same security and peril as the fundamental consciousness—that is, they arise and perish together with it.

This question was formulated in collaboration with others; it is merely abbreviated here in the commentary (*śāstra*). Regarding the response, "because it is not an object of cognition (*ālambana*), as will be explained," this refers to the analysis of the teaching on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) as clarified below, which shall be explained in its own turn within the counter-argument (*prativāda*).
The commentary states: "It is like a hair-circle (*keśonduka*). The fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) perceives its objects with such subtlety that it is like the fineness of a hair.
Regarding the term "hair-circle": if one has an eye disease (*timira*), a circular eye-disease will perceive a circle in the empty space outside;

if the cataract on the eye is straight and elongated, one sees elongated forms in the empty space—all of which are essentially like hairs. [Question: What is the name and substance of this? [Answer: It is simply sound, and so forth.

Therefore, regarding that which is called "name" (*nāman*): here, "name" and "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) may refer to a general explanation of names, rather than being restricted to the "name" and "characteristic" among the five dharmas;
alternatively, they may indeed refer to the "name" and "characteristic" within the five dharmas. Consequently, this commentary contains four interpretations.

According to the first interpretation, it explains by means of the "characteristic" and "name" within the five dharmas; thus, "name" refers to that which consists of phrases (*pada*), words (*vyañjana*), and so forth.

The basis (*āśraya*) is precisely sound; sound is that which expresses. "Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the five sense faculties, the objects of the senses, the physical world (*bhājana-loka*), and so forth, because these are what is meant [by the term].

However, regarding "Yoga," it refers to the questions and answers concerning the five factors (*pañca-dharma*) in relation to one another; this should be verified in the subsequent text of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

It is not so that the mental factors (*caitta*) associated with it are its objects (*ālambana*). If one does not say that the substance of "name" (*nāma*) is simply sound, then sound would be perceived by the eighth consciousness.
If one takes each of the four aggregates [as the object], then those associated [factors] would be the objects of that eighth consciousness;
for the remaining [reasons], since the Sūtra states that the fundamental consciousness perceives both "name" and "characteristic" (*nimitta*), "name" refers to this very [entity].
Regarding "sound": because the eighth consciousness can take sound as its object, it is said to take "names" (nāman) as its object. Another interpretation states:

if one adheres to the school that emphasizes characteristics (lakṣaṇa-vāda), then the associated mental factors (caitta) and the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) are excluded, for the seeing-part is not a characteristic.

If one does not adhere to the school that emphasizes characteristics, then the seeing-parts of the five associated mental factors are said to be the fundamental consciousness. These three interpretations are found in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) below.

The general explanation of "name" and "characteristic" does not refer to the "characteristic" among the five dharmas. However, within the third explanation, "name" refers to the four aggregates (*skandhas*).

In the text of the question and answer, it further mentions the objects experienced by the five simultaneous mental factors associated with the eighth consciousness. it does not exist in the external vessel-world, which is comprised merely as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

In certain passages of the *Śāstra*, it is stated that the various consciousnesses must necessarily rely upon objects (*ālambana*), as has already been explained previously. This is interpreted through two meanings:
first, they maintain the present non-substantiality (*anātman*) as their object; second, they maintain [the seeds] so that they do not perish, thereby enabling the arising of views and feelings.
Regarding the phrase "because there is a substantial essence (*svabhāva*) up to the teachings (*śāsana*)," this is just as explained in other treatises such as the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*. If...
When the six consciousnesses perceive the five sense objects, they take those actual five sense objects as their objective basis (*ālambana-pratibhāsa*).

If the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) perceives the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), it takes what has been transformed by others as its objective basis. If the fundamental consciousness perceives seeds and the five sense faculties, [it likewise takes them as its objective basis].
It has no substantial essence (*svabhāva*), because the seeds of sentient beings are not all equal, as explained in the section on the four conditions below.

If one takes "tortoise hair" or the "self distinct from the aggregates" as objects, or calculates [them] according to the dharmas of other realms, these are all cases where the name serves as the substantial essence.

"Transformation" refers to the differentiation between the ripening and non-ripening of internal fruits; that is, because the seeds have matured, they give rise to active manifestations (*samudācāra*). This is called...

The distinction between the produced (*jāta*) and the producer (*janaka*). Furthermore, the arising of actualized manifestations (*pravṛtti*) from seeds is termed the "ripened cause" (*vipāka-hetu*); that which is the seed while not yet manifest is termed the "producer.
According to the view of the ignorant, the "producer" is the causal capacity (*hetu-śakti*), while the "transformer" (*pariṇāma*) is the resultant capacity (*phala-śakti*).

Regarding the statement "the first is the producer-transformation," even up to the meaning of "immediately transforming into manifestation": [it is asked] within this transformation, is it solely the aforementioned causal capacity that transforms?

Within the transformation of conditions (*pratyaya-pariṇāma*), that which was previously described as the "fruit-transforming" (*phala-śakti-pariṇāma*) is [included]. Why, then, are both the transformation of arising (*utpatti-pariṇāma*) and the transformation of conditions considered to be "provisionally fruit-transforming"?

Answer: This transformation of arising is precisely the "cause-transforming" (*hetu-śakti-pariṇāma*). That is to say, it refers to seeds giving rise to manifest activities (*samudācāra*), manifest activities giving rise to seeds, and seeds giving rise to seeds, and so forth;
these are still the cause-transforming. It is only when the seeds subsequently give rise to the fruit-transforming manifest activities that they are termed "fruit-transforming."
Therefore, here we take only that which can produce seeds as the cause to be "transformation" (*pariṇāma*); we do not take the transformation of the fruit.

If, within the context of the second condition (the object-condition), it is called "transformation," then we take only the transformation of the fruit—namely, the manifest self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) transforming to give rise to the seeing and image portions (*darśanabhāga* and *nimittabhāga*).
If, however, it is called "transformation" in the sense of "producing," then the eighth consciousness producing the seven consciousnesses and so forth is all termed "transformation."
This refers to the arising of the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the first seven consciousnesses from the seeds within the eighth consciousness.
When seeds give rise to active manifestations, it is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). As for the seventh consciousness giving rise to the eighth, this is also termed "transformation":
that is, the seeds capable of transforming [into the seventh] exist within the eighth consciousness; thus, it is called "transformation. Question: This passage is based on...

Do the seven consciousnesses perfuse and produce the "seeing" and "image" aspects of another eighth consciousness, and do the seeing and image aspects then give rise to the eighth consciousness? Answer: This is also the case.

Regarding the statement, "One should know that the seeds produced by conditions of the outflow-free (anāsrava) are analogous to this," the phrase "conditions of the outflow-free" refers to what has already been explained:

if the eighth consciousness of the Buddha-fruit is outflow-free and can take outflow-free seeds as its objects, then because the outflow-free [consciousness] possesses these conditions, it is grasped [as such].

Therefore, there are three types of "substantiality" (*dravya*): substantiality by way of arising, substantiality by way of being accompanied by grasping, and substantiality by way of being the cause.

If the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) within the causal state were impure (*sāsrava*), it would be unable to take pure seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) as its object, because it would lack grasping; thus, it would not possess substantiality by way of being the cause.

However, when one attains the stage of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) or the first bhūmi of the Bodhisattva—the single stage of the noble ones (*ārya*)—the pure seeds cannot produce their manifest activity (*samudācāra*). This refers precisely to the pure seeds within the causal state.

Because there is birth, there is the reality of existence (*sat*). If one has not yet attained the state of a noble one (*ārya*), then because there is no birth, there is the reality of non-existence (*asat*).

Therefore, with respect to those who have not yet attained the state of a noble one, the eighth consciousness lacks all three realities—namely, the reality of being an object-condition (*ālambana*), the reality of grasping (*upādāna*), and the reality of birth (*janman*). Thus, these three realities are entirely absent.

If one expects to attain the state of a noble one (*ārya*), the eighth consciousness is "real" in the sense of being merely that which arises, and it is also "real" because it lacks cognitive objects (*ālambana*).

If, however, "reality" refers to the fact that seeds give rise to actualities (*pravṛtti*) and actualities give rise to seeds, then this is what is called the "causal transformation" (*hetu-pariṇāma*) and the "resultant transformation" (*phala-pariṇāma*); it is precisely these conditions that are termed "real."

Furthermore, regarding the statement "one should know that seeds arise conditioned by the uncontaminated (anāsrava)": "conditioned" (pratyaya) here has the sense of "relying upon" (upādāya), not the sense of "pervasive condition" (sarvatraga-pratyaya).
Relying upon contaminated seeds, one can produce the manifest activity (pravṛtti) of contaminated consciousness; relying upon uncontaminated seeds, one can produce uncontaminated manifest activity.
If there were a transformation, conjunction, or manifestation upon the uncontaminated [seeds], then—excluding the Buddha—all others would be limited to ten [stages].
In the stage of the Bodhisattva’s One Vehicle, that which is called "arising from untainted seeds" refers to the manifestation of actual functioning.

Even when untainted actual functioning perfumes and forms untainted seeds, all such cases are termed "transforming the real. This is designated as the arising of the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) upon untainted actual functioning consciousness; that is to say, it is the process of transformationally arising and transformationally withdrawing.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “From the various contaminated consciousnesses up to what should be inferred accordingly,” this refers to the transformation and manifestation [of objects].

Upon the eight consciousnesses, the seeing and image divisions (darśana-bhāga and nimitta-bhāga) are transformed and produced. The fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) takes its own image division as its object, while the first six consciousnesses all likewise take the image division as their object.
Therefore, it is said that one should reflect upon this. Regarding the statement that the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and seeds possess the two meanings of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*):

it means that seeds have two types of transformation—namely, they are called "transformations" because they give rise [to effects], and they are called "transformations" because they grasp [objects]. Furthermore, they are called "transformations" because they lack [independent] conditions.

If the five sense-faculties also possess two [meanings], they are called "transformations" because they take conditions [as objects], and they are called "transformations" because they grasp [objects]; however, they are not called "transformations" because they lack [the capacity to] give rise [to effects]. As for the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), it only...

First, regarding the external receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*): it is real by virtue of being conditioned, but it is called "transformative" because it is devoid of grasping, and it is called "transformative" because it arises.
However, this is generally stated with reference to a limited portion; as for the sense faculties (*indriya*), they are spoken of only in terms of manifest phenomena (*samudācāra-dharma*).

Seeds possess both types of transformation, while the external receptacle possesses only one. If one considers that which fully possesses transformation, seeds and faculties possess two transformations, whereas the external receptacle possesses [only] one.

Second, regarding transformation (*pariṇāma*). As for "the seeds possessing two types of reality": this means that because seeds are able to produce all phenomena, they possess the name "arising" and are thus called transformation;
furthermore, because the eighth consciousness is able to maintain impure seeds, it possesses "grasping" and is thus called transformation;

additionally, because the eighth consciousness is able to take impure seeds as its object, it possesses "cognition" and is thus called transformation. Regarding "the faculties possessing two types of transformation": [the same applies].
This means that because the five sense faculties arise from seeds, they are called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) since those five faculties possess arising.

Furthermore, because the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) can take the five faculties as its objects, it is called "transformation" since it possesses the capacity for objective apprehension within the five eyes.

Moreover, because the fundamental consciousness can maintain and uphold the five faculties, they are called "transformation" since the five faculties possess the state of being maintained. Regarding the external receptacle world possessing two types of transformation: this refers to the external receptacle world arising from...

Because it arises from seeds, it is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) due to its very arising. Furthermore, because the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) can take the external vessel-world as its object, that external vessel-world is called "transformation" because it possesses an object.
Since the fundamental consciousness cannot grasp or maintain the external vessel-world, the external vessel-world is called "transformation" because it lacks grasping.

If so, within both the state of Buddhahood and the causal stage, the primary meaning—the sense-faculties and their seeds—possesses two types of transformation, while the vessel-world [possesses only one].

The [ālayavijñāna] possesses only one transformation, which is likewise the same as the meaning within that [preceding] context. As for the statement that "the sense-faculties and seeds possess two transformations, while the preceding seven consciousnesses and the [ālayavijñāna] itself possess only one," it is because the first seven consciousnesses merely arise [from it] that they are called "transformations."
The Commentary states that the term "unchanging" can be understood based on these two gates. To explain:

the "two gates" refer to the aforementioned *pariṇāma* (transformation) within the *pariṇāmin* (that which undergoes transformation), namely *pariṇāma-pariṇāma* (transformative change) and *vyañjana-pariṇāma* (manifestational change). *Pariṇāma-pariṇāma* collectively constitutes the change of arising.

*Vyañjana-pariṇāma* refers to the differentiation of characteristics; it changes because it is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for this gate. The "three gates" are formed by adding "grasping" (*abhiniveśa*) to the aforementioned two gates.
Regarding "unchanging": apart from these two or three categories, there is no further change. Since there is no meaning of change outside of these three types, it is said to be unchanging.

The Commentary states: "If the image-mind were not necessarily present, up to the point that the object lacks substantiality"—if one says that when the mind arises, it arises bearing the aspect of that [object], this is explained in accordance with the teachings of the Hīnayāna; yet it does not fully accord with reason, because when taking True Suchness (tathatā) as an object, no aspect is borne.
If one says that the mind arises from a substantial entity—whether taking True Suchness as its object or arising through the realization and perception of that object—[this is the correct view].
Each [of these] has a substantial entity that gives rise to the mind; this interpretation fully accords with reason and is the exclusive Mahāyāna interpretation.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “As in the previous case where the vehicle and the view, up to the Mahāyāna, are all distinct,” it refers to the interpretation provided earlier in the first commentary regarding the section on "the solitary non-arising" and "the simultaneous non-arising of the capacity to arise."

The *Śāstra* states: "If it were not so, the object-sphere (*ālambana*) of the resultant consciousness would be too narrow. The phrase "in this context" (*atra*) carries the sense of exclusion and inclusion.

"Exclusion" refers to the exclusion of the other seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), which instead take the eighth consciousness as their support. Furthermore, "exclusion" refers to the exclusion of the eighth consciousness at the stage of Buddhahood, because [the text] takes the eighth consciousness of the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*) as its support.
Thus, "in this context" also refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) of the causal stage with respect to its own objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Regarding the three types of objects, as well as the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), [the ordinary consciousness] cannot take others as its objects.

If one does not exclude the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) at the stage of Buddhahood, then the fundamental consciousness at the stage of Buddhahood would also comprehend these three types of objects;

that is, the objects perceived by the fundamental consciousness at the stage of Buddhahood would become its objects of perception. However, upon reaching the untainted state (*anāsrava*), it universally perceives all things. As the subsequent text states: "In the untainted..."

The stage of outflows (*āsrava*). It is able to take as its objects the faculties, the sense-fields, and consciousness. "Faculties" refers to the six faculties; "sense-fields" refers to the six objects;

and "consciousness" refers to the six consciousnesses—that is, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), which is also able to take the eighteen elements as its objects.

Second, regarding the statement that "the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) serves as the gate for the aspect [of cognition], up to the point of having the same object of focus": if the immediate part (*sākṣādbhāga*) constitutes the mode of activity (*ākāra*), then it is the various consciousnesses.

The presence or absence [of the object] is not fixed; that is to say, when taking other forms (*rūpa*) and so forth as objects, these are precisely the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). When realizing *tathatā*, there is no objective aspect.
When the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of "the same object of cognition" (*ekālambana*), this refers specifically to the immediate objective aspect.

Regarding the statement that "all consciousnesses have indeterminate objects, being sometimes present and sometimes absent": when it says "the aspect-part (nimitta-bhāga) is called the mode-of-apprehension (ākāra)," this refers to cases where it takes other things as its object.
When the objective field transforms and gives rise to an aspect-part, then there is an aspect-part, and that aspect-part functions as the mode-of-apprehension.

Alternatively, it is "absent" in cases such as when self-cognition (svasaṃvitti) takes the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) as its object, or when the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) takes True Suchness (tathatā) as its object; in both these instances, there is no aspect-part functioning as a mode-of-apprehension. Therefore [it is said they are indeterminate].

This refers to the fact that the object of cognition (*ālambana*) is not fixed. Whether it be the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) or the aspect (*ākāra*), when realizing *tathatā*, there is also a seeing-part.
Regarding the commentary’s statement "or [the view] that it is a separate entity from the Hīnayāna" up to "because it is the same as the Hīnayāna": if this refers to the Mahāyāna seeing-part...
To designate the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) as the aspect (*ākāra*) is to treat them as having the same substance; this interpretation is exhaustive of the principle.
If the image-part were the aspect, they would have distinct substances, because the image-part and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) are differentiated.

Now, when the Mahāyāna speaks of the image-part as the aspect, it does so because this is common to the Hīnayāna and because it is a shared [teaching]. Therefore, it is stated thus. Although there are two such explanations in the Mahāyāna, this...

In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is stated that the *nimittabhāga* (image-part) is the object (*ālambana*), while the *darśanabhāga* (seeing-part) is called the mode of activity (*ākāra*), and the *svasaṃvitti* (self-cognition) is called the substance (*vastu*).

However, in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, it is stated that the external primary object (*bimba*) is the object, the *nimittabhāga* is called the mode of activity, and the *darśanabhāga* is called the substance.
This differs from the latter interpretation. Now, this [text] also relies on the fixed nature of the various consciousnesses. Some say that in this treatise...
In this [text], the explanation that the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) is called the "aspect" (*ākāra*) is based on the fact that all consciousnesses possess a seeing-part;
thus, the seeing-part is designated as the aspect, and self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is designated as the "entity" (*vastu*).

This differs from the explanation in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, which states that the external objective essence (*bimba-viṣaya*) is the "object-condition" (*ālambana*), the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) is the aspect, and the seeing-part is the entity. Here, too, it is based on...

Regarding the certainty of the various consciousnesses: some say that in this treatise, when the "aspect" (*ākāra*) is identified as the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*), it refers to all consciousnesses because they all possess a seeing-part.
This means that even when the seeing-part takes true suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, that seeing-part itself is called the aspect;
thus, the "image-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*) is not said to be the aspect. If the image-part were said to be the aspect, then later wisdom realizing true suchness...

At that time, because there is no differentiation, the objective part (*nimittabhāga*) constitutes the aspect (*ākāra*). Thus, the various consciousnesses do not necessarily possess [an objective part].

Because it is not fixed, this treatise does not state that the objective part constitutes the aspect. Alternatively, those of the Hīnayāna who assert distinct entities claim that the reflected image constitutes the aspect.
As for "because it is a cause for the Hīnayāna," this treatise, however, speaks of the subjective part (*darśanabhāga*).

Regarding those who assert that the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is the mode of activity (*ākāra*): this refers to those who explain it as being distinct in substance from the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*).
That is to say, while the Hīnayāna asserts that the objective aspect is the mode of activity, the present Mahāyāna asserts that the subjective aspect is the mode of activity.

Thus, the subjective aspect consists of only four aggregates (*skandha*), whereas the objective aspect possesses all five aggregates; therefore, the objective and subjective aspects are distinct in substance. If one asserts that the objective aspect is the mode of activity, then...

Because it is the same as the Hīnayāna, the latter interpretation is preferable. However, in the first interpretation alone—and not in the second—up to the point where the verse mentions "two interpretations," the eighth consciousness simultaneously takes the five objects, such as seeds, as its objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

This is because there are no external primary objects or seeds [in that case]. Therefore, in the second interpretation, the aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) functions as the subjective mode of apprehension (*ākāra*). This is because...
The five mental factors (caitta) that arise simultaneously with the eighth consciousness have object-aspects (nimittabhāga) and modes of apprehension (ākāra) that are similar;
this is termed "having a single common object" (*ekālambana*). As for the object-aspects of other mental factors, they all possess practical utility.

However, regarding the object-aspects of the five mental factors associated with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), one does not consider them [to be real], because real sense-faculties lack the function of producing consciousness, and real seeds lack the function of producing fruits.
Regarding the statement that the Sarvāstivādins and others do not admit that there are mental aspects (*ākāra*) or even a self-substance (*svabhāva*) as objects of cognition:

that Sarvāstivāda school asserts that external objects serve as the objective condition (*ālambana*). They designate the "image-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*) as the aspect (*ākāra*) and the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) as the substance (*vastu*).

[They hold] that there is no mind or mental factor capable of cognizing itself. In the Mahāyāna school, however, there is an image-part consisting of a reflection upon the mind, which is not separate from it. This is the explanation.

Therefore, it is said that the mind and mental factors are "able to take themselves as objects" (*svasaṃvedana*). Alternatively, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the self-cognizing-part (*svasaṃvitti*) are mutually able to take one another as objects; this too is called being "able to take themselves as objects.

The Sarvāstivādins do not establish the existence of an image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), but rather maintain that external objects are apprehended by the mind; for them, there is no such thing as being "able to take themselves as objects.
This explanation—that the subject and object are subsumed within the seeing and image parts—refers to what this treatise calls the "semblance of the object" (*ālambana-nirbhāsa*).
The aspect [of the object] is called the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part). That which resembles the aspect of the cognizing subject is called the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part).
Regarding the relationship between the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) within these two parts, it is as follows:

if that which is capable of resembling [an object] is the dependent nature, then that which is resembled is the imagined nature. Here, we take the dependent nature—which is capable of resembling—as the seeing and image parts, and do not take the imagined nature—which is what is resembled.

This is called "the two parts. Regarding the phrase in the *Śāstra* (Sū), "or like the object of another person": the inference (*anumāna*) is as follows. When the mind is currently perceiving blue, that mind must be unable to perceive the blue object;

this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is admitted that there is no objective aspect (*ālambana-nimitta*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: like a sound that is not being perceived by another [mind].
The object (*viṣaya*). Or, it is illustrated by the objects of other persons. However, the objects of other persons can only be apprehended by those other persons;

one's own self cannot apprehend the objects of other persons, and thus this serves as the illustration. "Other persons are likewise" means that just as other persons cannot apprehend the objects of my own school, I likewise cannot apprehend them.
Regarding the objects of other persons, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is now established as follows: the minds of other persons...

It should also directly perceive the object of its own thesis (*pakṣa*). This is the thesis. The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is admitted that there is no aspect of an object of perception (*ālambana-nimitta*).

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: like my own mind perceiving the object of my own thesis; or, my mind may also perceive the objects perceived by others, because it is admitted that there is no aspect of an object of perception.
The example is: like the minds of other persons perceiving the objects of other persons. [The opponent says: "Others..."

"It is also thus. However, the *Śū* (Commentary) states the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "Other phenomena, such as sounds, odors, and so forth, external to visible form, should also be the objects of the mind that takes visible form as its object.

The reason (*hetu*) is: because they lack the characteristic of being an object (*ālambana-lakṣaṇa*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: like the visible forms and so forth that are themselves the objects [of that mind].
Regarding the formal argument for both self and other, it says "it should be admitted. This refers to visible forms external to the object that are themselves the objects of one's own body.
The object (*ālambana*) should also be the object for this mind of another that takes another as its object. The reason is stated: "because it has a signless (*animitta*) object.

This is illustrated by the example of one person taking another's own object as their own. Alternatively, regarding the two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) mentioned in the treatise, the first [pair] corresponds to the former [category] and the latter to the latter;

within the treatise, "one's own object" (*svaviṣaya*) is assigned to the preceding case, just as in other instances. If [the subject refers to] the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), [the same principle applies].

There is no characteristic of an object of cognition (*ālambana-nimitta*), and [cognitions] are likewise unable to take their own objects as objects. If others were like oneself, they would correspond to what was stated previously;
otherwise, each [cognition] would have to be able to take all things as its objects.
The commentary states that only that which possesses an aspect (ākāra) is called an object of cognition (*ālambana*); otherwise, as previously stated, there would be logical fallacies.

If one does not posit the existence of an objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*), then just as with its own [perceived] object, it would likewise not take other objects as its support—or conversely, other objects would be like its own object—because the objective aspect is absent.
This refutes the Saṃmitīya school.
In the *Fodi lun* (Treatise on the Buddha-bhūmi), the third chapter discusses the three controversies regarding whether the four wisdoms possess an objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*).
That treatise clarifies that these four untainted wisdoms (*anāsrava-jñāna*) constitute the objective aspect; however, there are three masters who dispute whether they lack an objective aspect.

One interpretation holds that the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) possesses both the seeing aspect (*darśanabhāga*) and the objective aspect, as it cannot be said to be incapable of realizing the truth. Another interpretation holds that for the other wisdoms, the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) possesses the seeing aspect.
The characteristics are non-existent; there is meaning. The three—wondrous observation, great perfection, and equality—are the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Regarding the statement in the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) that if the concentrated mind and so forth possess the function of an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), one must admit they have a real function:
