if the mind were to possess a real function apart from its objects, it would contradict the teaching of the Noble Ones (*ārya*). For the Noble Ones teach that all phenomena lack real functions. Therefore, it is known that [the function] exists.

Regarding the statement in the Commentary, "The object has no mind," which suggests that the point can be understood by analogy with what follows: it further states that the mind must necessarily possess the function of being an apprehending subject (*ālambaka*), because it grasps objects, just like a lamp.
However, this inference is not established, for the analogy of the lamp lacks the function of being an apprehending subject.

The Commentary further states: "The Mahāsāṃghika school holds that the mind has its own objective condition (*ālambana*), and so forth, up to those who agree with this; they assert that external objects are the objective conditions.
The image-part (*nimittabhāga*) is called the mode of activity (*ākāra*), and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) is called the substance (*vastu*)."

Regarding the statement that "it is not so for those whose conditions are their own substance," the four schools, including the Mahāsāṃghika and others, agree in saying: the mind itself takes the mind as its object.

If it were to take other objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, then a distinct mental aspect (*ākāra*) would arise. However, when the substance of the mind takes the substance of the mind as its object, it is not said that a distinct mental aspect arises;
rather, the mind that acts as the subject of cognition (*ālambaka*) takes the mind as its object (*ālambana*). The object is the [mind].

The cognitive faculty (*ālambaka*) and its object (*ālambana*) do not possess separate substantial entities; rather, the mind’s own mode of understanding is itself the object, which means it arises as a distinct aspect (*ākāra*).
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, they do not admit that the mind and its mental concomitants (*caitta*) can simultaneously take one another as objects.
This is like two people facing each other looking at their own reflections; although they are together, they cannot see one another. Thus, the mind and [its concomitants]...

Regarding the dharmas that share the same object: they do not mutually perceive one another. Furthermore, the mind and mental factors cannot take the four characteristics (lakṣaṇas) that arise simultaneously as their objects.

Just as the eye-consciousness does not see the eye itself because it is too close, the mind and mental factors do not take the four simultaneous characteristics as their objects for the same reason—they are too close.

The Commentary states: "The 'aspects of the seen and the seeing' in the Mahāyāna are precisely the names for the 'object-condition,' 'mental aspect,' and 'substantial entity' in that [Hīnayāna] school.

That Hīnayāna school possesses only three terms: first, the object-condition (*ālambana*); second, the mental aspect (*ākāra*); and third, the substantial entity (*vastu*). That school does not establish the terminology of "aspects of the seen and the seeing.
Now, at the time of the Mahāyāna, one takes the Mahāyāna’s own terms for the aspects of the seen and the seeing and applies them to those [terms] of the Hīnayāna.
The *zong* (thesis) establishes the name "form" (*rūpa*).
Regarding the statement in the *shu* (commentary) that the term "aspect" (*ākāra*) does not establish [categories] such as "wholesome" (*kuśala*) and so forth, this is based on their similarity;

it continues until the point where there is no distinction. In the previous explanation of "aspects," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) was not used; it simply stated "similarity" and "similar to similarity," with nothing further.
"Similarity in meaning" means that they are equal and without distinction.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (Commentary), "The aspect and the seeing [parts] should each have these two dharmas, just as the mind and its objects," this is an inference (*anumāna*).

As for the statement, "There is no separate cognition of the aspect-part and the seeing-part," this is spoken from the perspective of consciousness (*vijñāna*) based on the remaining outflows (*āsrava*); it is because the aspect is identical to consciousness. If...

According to the proponents of differentiation (*viśeṣavādin*), the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) encompasses all five aggregates (*skandha*), while the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) consists of only four aggregates.

The objective aspect encompasses all eighteen elements (*dhātu*), while the subjective aspect consists only of the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), together with the seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*). This is because these two factors possess distinct entities from one another, just as the mind and its mental concomitants (*caitta*) do;

or like the relationship between the primary mind (*cittarāja*) and its objects. Thus, whether it be the mind and its mental concomitants, or the minds of oneself and others, they are neither identical nor different.
Thus, there is indeed a difference.

Regarding the statement in the Commentary that "the Mahāyāna mind attains self-objectification": this explains that the *svasaṃvitti* (self-cognizing division) takes the *svasaṃvitti* itself as its object; hence it is called "the mind attaining self-objectification.
The Mahāyāna establishes the existence of the *svasaṃvitti*, which separately functions as a reflexive cognition (*pratyavekṣaṇa*). The Hīnayāna does not establish such a self-cognizing division.
This establishes that there is no returning condition (*pratyaya*).

Regarding the argument that "if this [cognition] did not exist, one would not be able to recollect mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta-dharma*), because one cannot recollect an object that has never been experienced," the term "experienced" (*anubhūta*) means "gone through" (*anubhūta*).
Just as an object previously gone through is explained as having been previously perceived (*pūrvānubhūta*), so too at a later time can one...

"Recollection" (smṛti) means that which has been previously experienced and is now remembered. That is to say, the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) is apprehended by the subjective aspect (darśanabhāga).

Just as with a thing never before seen, the subjective aspect cannot be recollected. It is like when two people who have met for the first time later encounter each other again and subsequently say, "I recall where we met before.
The "aspect of meeting" is precisely the subjective aspect; the subjective aspect, in turn, is self-attested (svasaṃvedya). Self-...

Because they can be divided into aspects. It is by means of the self-witnessing aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) that the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) is perceived. While the seeing aspect experiences past events, the self-witnessing aspect is able to describe them. Regarding the commentary’s statement:

"The mind of the past or present never takes itself as an object, even to the extent of taking what has not yet occurred as its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*)," this is because [the mind] does not take what has not yet occurred as its objective aspect.
That which has already been established as the mind is the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). This is what is meant here:

if the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) has previously been perceived by the seeing-part, then later, when the seeing-part is perfumed by that object-part, it will be able to take that object as its sphere.

However, if the object-part has never been perceived by the seeing-part, then later the seeing-part cannot take that object-part as its sphere. The same applies to this seeing-part: if the seeing-part has previously been...

Regarding the object-condition of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*): at a later time, when the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) has already ceased, the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*)—if it was never previously experienced by self-awareness—cannot be recollected by self-awareness at a later time.

This is just as when a person who met someone several days ago, upon seeing that person's appearance later on, asks, "Where did I see you before? or "When did we ever meet?"—words that imply a prior encounter.
This indicates that self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) has previously taken the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object. This, too, is a proof based on coarse characteristics.

However, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) also establishes the self-cognition part; it states, for instance, that if self-cognition did not exist, one would necessarily be unable to remember, just as one cannot remember an object never previously experienced.
All such logical principles are similar to the reasoning in this question. Nevertheless, throughout the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there is...
Regarding the textual passages from the two sections, why are the initial and final passages subject to such objection?

[The objection asks: "If there is no real self (*ātman*), how can there be such phenomena as memory and recognition? The Master of the Treatise replies: "By means of repeated perfuming (*vāsanā*), such phenomena as memory and recognition come to exist.
This interpretation is the best: by means of excellent and frequent practice, one acquires memory, recognition, and so forth. It is just like a student who, through repeated...
Through repeated perfuming (*bhāvanā*), there arises recollective cognition (*smṛti-vijñapti*); subsequently, one is then able to understand the meaning. Furthermore, as stated in the passage below:

"Because perception (*saṃjñā*) serves as the cause for mindfulness (*smṛti*), mindfulness is able to recollect and cognize. That is to say, by means of perception grasping the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it acts as the cause for mindfulness;

subsequently, mindfulness is able to recollect that which was previously cognized. This interpretation is also excellent. If, in this current passage, it is said that [cognition] exists because of the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).
Only then do functions such as recollection and cognition occur. This passage from the treatise is not as extensive as the two preceding passages from the treatise.
Regarding the commentary’s exclusion of the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of others' minds:

for instance, when the Buddha’s knowledge of past lives takes his own past events as its object, it is a recollection of what he has previously experienced; likewise, when it takes the past events of other sentient beings as its object, he is able to know them all.

This is precisely what is meant by "recollection of that which was previously experienced," because it belongs to the category of recollection of that which was previously experienced. As the subsequent text states:

"Mindfulness is able to take as its object the categories of things previously practiced. In this current commentary, the focus is strictly on the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), not on the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

While the arising of the knowledge of others' minds takes the arising of the present mind as its condition, it cannot take past events as its object; however, it may be taken in conjunction with the knowledge of others' minds.

Knowledge (*jñāna*) can take the present mind as its object, and it also possesses objects that have been previously experienced. As for the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*), it can take the objects of future lives as its domain.
Regarding the distinction from the Hīnayāna based on the fact that the essential natures of consciousness (*vijñāna*), feeling (*vedanā*), and so forth differ:

however, within the Hīnayāna, only four types [of distinctions] are established—namely, those of time, basis, aspect (*ākāra*), and object (*ālambana*). These four aspects of knowledge are all identical; for instance, it is like the eye.

When consciousness arises simultaneously with the mind-king (citta) and its mental factors (caitta), they rely upon the same sense organ, such as the eye; this is called "sameness of basis" (*āśraya-samatā*).

Furthermore, since the mind and its factors arise at the same time without any sequence, this is called "sameness of time" (*kāla-samatā*). This sameness of time and sameness of basis is similar to that of the Mahāyāna, and thus there is no dispute between them.
However, regarding the object of cognition (*ālambana*) and the mode of activity (*ākāra*), there are differences between the Great and Small Vehicles.

It is different. If, according to the teachings of the Hīnayāna, the objective essence (*vastu*) is the object-condition (*ālambana*), then having the same object-condition is called "sameness of object-condition" (*ālambana-samatā*).
If, however, it refers to the aspect (*ākāra*), then when the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) simultaneously perceive blue and so forth, they all possess the aspect of blue;
this similarity is called "sameness. In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the term "aspect" is clearly explained as that which constantly possesses a characteristic while perceiving.
Regarding the aspect (*ākāra*): although the ancient Sarvāstivādins assert that there is an aspect, they do not explain it clearly.

In the Mahāyāna, however, it is taught that based on the causal conditions of the object—such as a blue substance—the mind and mental factors that correspond to that object arise with a distinct "blue-aspect-part" (*nīlākāra-bhāga*).
This is because this aspect-part resembles [the object]. If one analyzes the aspect, the aspect itself is a part.

Because consciousness has "discernment" as its mode of activity (*ākāra*), whether the mind apprehends a general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) or whether the mind apprehends a specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) that is concomitant with it, there are five factors established in the Mahāyāna:
namely, time (*kāla*), basis (*āśraya*), object (*ālambana*), mode of activity (*ākāra*), and substance (*vastu*).
If the Mahāyāna teaches this, the Hīnayāna schools likewise maintain five factors: namely, time, basis, object, mode of activity, and substance.
This treatise states: "Because the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) is designated as 'object' (vastu), it is the same as the Hīnayāna.

If the Hīnayāna were to say that not only the mind has the capacity for cognition, but other factors such as perception (saṃjñā) and feeling (vedanā) can also cognize; and that while feeling alone has the capacity for experiencing (anubhava), other minds and other mental factors such as perception can also experience;
and that while perception alone has the capacity for grasping images (nimitta), other minds and mental factors can also grasp images."

However, among these, there are those that are primary and those that are auxiliary. If the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) arises, it is capable of discerning; the other mental factors (*caitta*) are what assist in this discernment.
If sensation (*vedanā*) is present, it is capable of experiencing and receiving; the other mental factors are what assist in this reception.

If perception (*saṃjñā*) is present, it is capable of grasping images; the other minds and mental factors grasp images as well. Although the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) are difficult to distinguish from one another, they are extremely similar to them.

Regarding the statement, "When blue is the object, all its aspects are blue; they are similar and thus identical in name," the intended meaning here is that this is precisely the same as the passage in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

However, this is an interpretation according to the text of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. That treatise states: "That which has the same object of cognition (*ālambana*) refers to the blue aspect-part (*nimitta-bhāga*);
it is 'similar and identical in name' in the sense that it corresponds to the intent of the passage in this [Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi] treatise concerning the similarity of the object."
It is the same. Alternatively, this treatise may be interpreted as follows: that treatise and this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* share a similar object of cognition (*ālambana*).
"Similar" here means "identical. Thus, this treatise states that it is "similar to that," meaning the two treatises have the same object of cognition.
Within this context, regarding the phrase "the aspect (*ākāra*) and the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*)... therefore, one aspect," it refers to—
Because all the various objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) are mutually similar in their deep blue color, they are called "objects" (*viṣaya*). Taken collectively, they are termed "one";
however, because the seven subjective aspects (*darśana-bhāga*) are each distinct, they are termed "similar. Nevertheless, in this treatise, the discussion is based on the actual reality (*dravya*).

It is said that they are similar in terms of their objects (*ālambana*), because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are distinct. Thus, each of the two treatises relies on one specific meaning, and there is no contradiction between them.

Furthermore, the Commentary states that regarding the distant object-condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*) and so forth, it is not a case of contradiction. This second interpretation says: "The Yogācāra..."
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Having the same object" (*ekālambana*) refers to the indirect object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), because its essential substance (*svabhāva*) is one;

or it is spoken of in reference to the wisdom of the fundamental essence (*mūlaprajñā*) perceiving true suchness (*tathatā*), because both the essential substance and true suchness are of a single nature, and are thus termed "the same.
As for what this treatise [the *Triṃśikā*] calls "similarity of the object," it refers to the direct image, namely the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). Mind...

The many *nimitta-bhāga*s (objective images) associated with the King [of consciousnesses] are all said to be "similar. This treatise speaks in terms of the direct objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

This treatise also states: "At that time, they rely on the same object-base (*ālambana-vastu*) and so forth. Since it mentions "object" (*ālambana*), it refers specifically to the direct objective image.
Thus, these two explanations are not contradictory. Furthermore, this treatise relies upon the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) according to the *Yogācāra*.
This treatise explains the realization of *tathatā* (suchness) from the perspective of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Regarding the phrase "What is the meaning of 'fruit' (*phala*)?

It is the meaning of the fulfillment of the cause": all fruits indeed carry the meaning of fulfillment. For example, when a person wishes to measure an object with a ruler, their primary intention is to know the number of units on the preceding part of the ruler;
knowing that number of units on the preceding object is precisely what constitutes the meaning of fulfillment. Now, in this case...
It is likewise. When the mind cognizes an object, its primary intention is to determine whether the preceding object is ultimately real or unreal, and whether it is good or bad.

When the mind knows the reality or unreality, and the goodness or badness, of the preceding object, that is the completion [of the process], which is called the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
Regarding the statement "there are two masters" and so forth, concerning their differing natures: as for the two masters, one is the master prior to Dignāga.

The masters who appeared after Dignāga are called the "Second Masters. As for the various masters prior to him, they merely stated that at the time of cessation and cognition, there is a grasping mind termed the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) and the grasped object termed the "image-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*);

they held that the grasper is simply the substance of consciousness itself, and they did not separately explain the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*pramāṇaphala*). After Dignāga appeared in the world, he [Dharmakīrti] distinguished them.

The three valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) are established as follows: the aspect of appearance (*nimittabhāga*) is the object of cognition (*prameya*); the aspect of seeing (*darśanabhāga*) is the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*);

and the aspect of self-cognition (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) is the result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). After Dharmapāla emerged [from this tradition], he further distinguished four aspects, taking the self-cognition that cognizes itself as the result.
Thus, these two masters—Dignāga and Dharmapāla—respectively explain the result of cognition. Furthermore, regarding these two masters, they refer to Vasubandhu and [Dignāga].
Prior to that, he established the two parts of the seeing (*darśana*) and the seen (*nimitta*). From Dignāga onwards, he established three parts, which is the same as the first interpretation.
It is like the external scriptures stating that Fuxi created the eight trigrams (*bagua*); only after him did written texts begin to emerge.
Subsequently, based on those eight trigrams, the sixty-four hexagrams (*liubashi gua*) were translated and produced. Afterward, Confucius, based on these sixty...

The four *guā* [hexagrams] were established above, and the *Shiyì* [Ten Wings] were composed to explain them. "Wings" (*yì*) refers to the *shàng huàn* (upper judgment) and so forth. Who is the one who measures? As stated in the previous discussion on measurement:

"The third, the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), should also have a separate result, because it is a cause that is capable of being an object of cognition, just like the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*).
Regarding the question and answer as to whether direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) serves as an inference (*anumāna*) rather than a direct result, the external objection states: "Direct..."

[Objection: Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) should be the fruit of inference (*anumāna*), and inference should be the fruit of direct perception. [Response: Self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is internal;

it serves as the fruit for that which is seen externally. The seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) is external; therefore, it cannot serve as the fruit for that which is internal. As for the difficulty regarding the analogy between the internal and external, the external objection states:
"If self-cognition is internal and can serve as the fruit for that which is external, then the seeing-portion, being external, should likewise [serve as the fruit for that which is internal]."
It can serve as an internal fruit. The answer states: the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part) only takes the external as its object; it cannot serve as a fruit for the internal.

Because the essence of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is internal, it serves as the object for the internal and thus acts as a fruit for the external. The opponent objects: "The perceiving part taking the appearing part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its object is called 'bondage by signs' (*nimitta-bandhana*)."
"Self-realization (svasaṃvitti) that takes the seeing-aspect as its object should be called 'bondage by view' (dṛṣṭibandhana). Answer: "It may be so; it is also called bondage by view.

Commentary: Regarding the objection that while taking the aspect (nimitta) as an object is admitted to be 'bondage by aspect' (nimittabandhana), self-realization that takes the seeing-aspect (darśanabhāga) as its object should likewise be called 'bondage by view,' and that there would be no fault in this being a bondage—the external critic says: "According to the coarse [level of analysis]..."

To speak generally, this is called "bondage by characteristics" (*nimitta-bandhana*). To explain in detail: the self-cognizing [manas] taking the seeing [aspect] as its object is "bondage by the seeing" (*darśana-bandhana*).
As explained in the commentary on the five consciousnesses, the bondage of the five consciousnesses taking objects with characteristics is subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);

likewise, in the section on the manas, the five consciousnesses taking objects with characteristics is indeed subsumed under direct perception, while the self-cognizing [manas] taking the seeing [aspect] as its object is named "bondage by the seeing," which is also direct perception.

This is complete. Just as within the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), although afflictions (*kleśa*) arise, they are considered direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because they take the essential nature [of the object] as their immediate realization.

However, within the seventh *manas*-consciousness, since afflictions are inherent, it is not subsumed under [valid] cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nevertheless, in the subsequent text, the section concerning the seventh consciousness is titled the "Chapter on *Manas*.
This refers to the simultaneous liberation from the bondage of characteristics (*nimitta-bandhana*) and the bondage of the seen-portion (*dṛśya-bhāga*).

Regarding the point that it is invalid because of contradiction: one cannot say that when the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) takes itself as its object within a single moment, it simultaneously arises as invalid (apramāṇa), for that seeing-part is also direct perception (pratyakṣa). Furthermore, that seeing-part does not serve as the effect of those three [cognitions].
Because there is no contradiction regarding the temporal duration [of the cognitions].
Regarding the commentary’s point that "if the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) were a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it would entail the difficulty of being a third result":

the external objection states that if the seeing-part were an inference (*anumāna*) or an invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*), it would not be admitted as a result of a third [cognition]. However, if the seeing-part were a direct perception at that time, it would [entail the aforementioned difficulty].
Regarding the third fruit: the answer is that the fourth [fruit] is exclusively internal and is also fundamental; therefore, it can constitute the third fruit.

Although its aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) may be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it takes external objects as its objective condition (*ālambana*), and because it has not yet attained [the ultimate realization], it cannot serve as the third fruit.
The commentary states that this direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) likewise does not take the three as its object.

This means that when this seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is about to arise as a direct perception, the seeing-part itself cannot directly perceive the third, self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*). This is because the seeing-part perceives the arising mental image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).
The *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of a concentrated mind cannot also take [that same objective aspect] as its object.
The commentary answers: "This principle may also be so; since this text is an implicit indication (*chāyā-prakāśana*), there is no fault.

This means that when the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) takes the *nimitta-bhāga* as its object, the *darśana-bhāga* can also be designated as an "object" (*ālambana*), using the term "sphere" (*viṣaya*) as its name. The subsequent passage in the treatise refers to this very point.

They are termed "consciousness of name" up to "consciousness of dharmas"; this is naming them according to their objects. This also implies that while they may be named after the sense faculties, they can likewise be named after the objects, as these designations are mutually reflective.

Furthermore, just as the knowledge of others' minds takes another's mind as its object, when a person is able to take a mind as an object, the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) is termed the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Difficulties concerning form and so forth should all be considered accordingly,” an external objection is raised:

“If it is granted that seeing which takes the external as its object is called ‘external,’ then seeing which takes form as its object should be called ‘form-consciousness. The answer is: “That may be so; that is to say, the five consciousnesses are named after their objects.”

The Commentary states: "If the mind that constitutes the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) were necessarily not one [with the subjective aspect], or even if it were a preceding or succeeding mind, then the self-witnessing (*svasaṃvitti*) would take the objective aspect as its object.

Furthermore, regarding the distinction of their essence: according to this, the four aggregates [of the objective aspect] and the essence of the mind that constitutes the objective aspect are distinct;

thus, they are produced from different seeds than the perceiving subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*). Alternatively, the mind constituting the objective aspect may arise by taking another person’s mind as its object, or a subsequent mind may take it as its object."

If each preceding mind takes the subsequent mind as its object, and all these are merely the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the mind, then they would be unable to engage in cognitive reflection (*ālambana*).

Regarding the question, "When taking the fourth moment [of consciousness] as an object, what serves as the fruit? and so forth—this point should be considered—the external critic objects: "The initial *nimitta-bhāga* is the object of cognition."
The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is the cognitive faculty (*ālambaka*). It is impossible for the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) to be the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*).

This is because, just as when the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) takes the seeing-part as its object, the objective aspect cannot be its result; likewise, when the third part takes the fourth part as its object, it too would be impossible for the objective aspect to be the result of valid cognition.
This is the response, based on the reason that the objective aspect [is not the result] even in such cases. As with the fourth...

Regarding the second [cognition] as the third condition: there is a distinction in that the second [cognition] is common to both types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas the object of cognition (*ālambana*) cannot be the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
This is just as the fourth condition relates to the third. The third [cognition], being exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and internal, takes the very object already cognized as its result.

The fourth [cognition] relates to the third; being exclusively direct perception, it takes the object of cognition as its result. By analogy with this cause, the formless [objects] are likewise excluded.
The statement that "the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), and so forth, is as previously explained" is the correct interpretation.

Just as the seeds are attached to the self-witnessing-division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), the seeing-division abides by taking the functional capacity of the seeds within the self-witnessing-division as its object.

That self-witnessing-division, in turn, takes the functional capacity of the seeing-division as its object. As for the seeing-division, it takes only the functional capacity of the seeds within the self-witnessing-division as its object.
The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) cannot, however, take as its object the functional capacity of the seeing-part that resides upon the self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*).
Regarding the statement in the treatise, "either valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), or direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*)," one asks:

since it has already been stated that it is not non-valid cognition, and the meaning of direct perception and inference is already established, why is it necessary to include the two preceding words "or valid cognition"? The answer is: the phrase "or valid cognition" is used in contrast to the aforementioned "non-valid cognition."

This constitutes a pair. However, because there are no many distinctions within the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the subsequent section does not further clarify the distinctions existing within the aforementioned means of valid cognition.
Thus, there are two types: namely, either this direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*). As for the Buddha, it is not so; as in the two types of responses found in the following text:

first, it is said that on the level of the fruit of Buddhahood, the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) realizes the self-realized part (*svasaṃvitti-saṃvitti-bhāga*); if it were to take the external as its object, [it would be otherwise].

To claim that on the level of the *svasaṃvittisaṃvitti* (self-cognition of self-cognition), it is called the "arising of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) as a real object," is a confused interpretation.
If this were on the level of a distinct consciousness, one could allow for the transformation and arising of an objective aspect;

however, since this occurs on the level of a single consciousness, to call the objective aspect that arises upon the *darśanabhāga*, the *svasaṃvitti*, and the *svasaṃvittisaṃvitti* "transformed" would mean there are three layers of objective aspects within a single mind. Therefore, this is untenable. For this reason...
The second interpretation further explains: Within the state of Buddhahood, it is solely the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) that is able to cognize all objects without exception;
therefore, it constitutes "omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*). As for the third and fourth aspects (*bhāga*), they likewise cognize only the internal and do not cognize the external.
The commentary states that the two parts—the third and the fourth—are subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because they are derived from self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).

That which possesses both the capacity and the object is precisely the third part. Since this third part is also the fourth part, it is referred to as "two parts. This refers to the third and fourth parts.

These two parts serve as mutual objects for one another; both are subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and possess the capacity to be perceived. Regarding this, there is an objection from those such as the Sarvāstivādins, who argue:

"Just as in our own school it is said that the 'arising of arising' (*jāti-jāti*) and the 'nature of arising' (*jāti-svabhāva*) [are established], so too [the following must be considered]: if one accepts that acquisitions (*prāpti*) and births (*jāti*) have acquisitions and births, then non-acquisitions (*aprāpti*) and non-births (*ajāti*) would not be established as a fourth category.

Furthermore, if one posits an acquisition and a birth for these, then... This passage refers to the Sarvāstivādins and others. Their objection states: "In our school, it is held that the 'arising of arising' and the 'nature of arising' [are established]."
The great arising does not arise by itself; it must depend on the small arising for the great arising to arise. No fourth arising is established.

Just as the great abiding abides in its own fundamental dharma, the great abiding does not abide by itself; it must depend on the small abiding of the dharma for the great abiding to abide. No fourth abiding is established.

Likewise, the great differentiation differentiates from its own fundamental dharma; the great differentiation does not differentiate by itself; it must depend on the small differentiation of the dharma. No [fourth differentiation is established]. Further...
A fourth distinct [destruction] is not established. That is to say, the "great destruction" destroys the primary dharma, yet the great destruction does not destroy itself;

it must be destroyed by a "small destruction. Furthermore, a fourth destruction is not established. That is to say, the "great acquisition" acquires the primary dharma, yet the great acquisition does not acquire itself;

it must be acquired by a "small acquisition. Furthermore, a fourth is not established. Your "great self-view-part" takes the "object-part" as its object, while the "self-attesting part" takes... [the self-view-part] as its object.

As for the objective aspect (*viṣayabhāga*), what further need is there for a fourth aspect? Within the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) it is taught that "acquisition" (*prāpti*) is similar to "arising" (*jāti*).

That is to say: the primary arising gives rise to the essence of the primary dharma; the secondary arising gives rise to the primary arising, which is equivalent to the primary acquisition giving rise to the essence of the primary dharma;

and the secondary acquisition gives rise to the primary acquisition. Furthermore, there are two kinds of acquisition: first, the acquisition of a dharma (*dharmaprāpti*), which is the primary acquisition; second, the acquisition of acquisition (*prāptiprāpti*).
This refers to "attainment" (prāpti). Great attainment and small attainment are both types of attainment within the category of non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

If there is small birth and great birth, these are the characteristic of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) within non-associated formations. This is as established by the Sarvāstivādins, who posit three kinds of dharmas.

First, the minor acquisition (*anuprāpti*); second, the major acquisition (*mahāprāpti*); third, the fundamental dharma (*mūladharma*). The minor acquisition acquires the major acquisition, and the major acquisition acquires the preceding fundamental dharma.
Furthermore, the major acquisition also acquires what follows. Above the minor acquisition, one does not further establish a "minor acquisition of the minor acquisition.

Again, the "great birth" (*mahājāti*) of the arising-dharma produces the fundamental dharma, and it can also produce the "small birth" (*parīttajāti*). The small birth and the great birth do not further establish a fourth "small birth."

The arising [of consciousness] consists of only three factors. You of the Mahāyāna should see that it takes the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) as its object, while in turn taking the *svasaṃvitti* (self-cognition) as its object;
thus, you should not establish a fourth factor. The "original dharma" refers precisely to such things as volition (*cetanā*) and so forth.
The commentary states: "That which merely possesses the capacity for maturation and growth. Here, "maturation" refers to great attainment (*mahā-lābha*) and small attainment (*alpa-lābha*).
"Growth" refers to great arising (*mahā-utpāda*) and small arising (*alpa-utpāda*). Based on these distinct capacities, they are designated by different names; yet, these are not separate entities.

They are alternative names for the same essence and function (*tattva-vyāpāra*), rather than being distinct. However, this first interpretation—that they are not identical—is similar to the second interpretation.

There is a slight distinction. That is to say, the *nimittabhāga* (image-part) is the functional capacity of the apprehended (*grāhya*), while the *darśanabhāga* (seeing-part) is the apprehending (*grāhaka*).

If it is the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-verifying part), it is the functional capacity that takes the *darśanabhāga* as its object. If it is the *svasaṃvittisaṃvittibhāga* (part that verifies the self-verification), it is the functional capacity of the very essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-svabhāva*).

According to the first interpretation, because the functional capacities of these four parts are distinct, they are said to be "not identical. Although the functions of the four parts are different, their substance (*svabhāva*) is not [different].

"Non-separation" (a-paricchinna) means not being distinct; it refers to the fourfold division [of consciousness], which is precisely *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). The second interpretation states: the four divisions consist of the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*) and the objective perceived (*ālambana*).
"Non-identity" (*a-tad-bhāva*) means they are not substantially identical; "non-separation" means they do not arise from separate seeds.

However, this [second view] also applies to objects such as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the past, and the future—so-called "solitary images" (*pratibimba*)—wherein the four divisions are said to share the same seed. This does not apply to the present, where they are neither identical nor non-distinct.
Because they are seen within the spheres of the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), they arise from distinct seeds. Between these two interpretations, the former is superior.
Regarding the "entanglements" (*paryavasthāna*) of the grasped and the grasper mentioned in the treatise, these do not refer to the eight entanglements and so forth. Why?

Because if the fourfold division of aspects—the seeing and the appearance—existed only within defiled minds, one could say they are the eight entanglements and so forth; however, since they exist within all minds of the three natures that are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Regarding the fourfold division, it should be understood that the term "envelopment" (*paryavasthāna*) does not refer to the eight envelopments.

Rather, it refers to the sense of mutual support, mutual dependence, and mutual entanglement that arises when the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the mind and mental factors manifests; this is what is called "envelopment."

Regarding the two bonds of coarse characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and heavy dysfunction (*dauṣṭhulya*): whether they be the seeds of afflictions or an unserviceable state (*akarmanyatā*), both are termed "heavy dysfunction.

As for the claim that *tathatā* (suchness) is not external because it does not function as an external object of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), and thus cannot be taken as an object—nevertheless, according to the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, when discussing internal and external phenomena, that treatise states: "What phenomena are called internal? What phenomena are external? The answer is: [as follows].

Among the eighteen *dhātus*, the six sense-faculties (*indriya*) are called "internal," the six objects (*viṣaya*) are called "external," and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are called "intermediate. Furthermore, it is asked:

within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the five sensory objects are called "external"; in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all things including wisdom (*prajñā*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are collectively termed "internal.

However, in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are still the three sensory objects of visible form, touch, and sound; since the minds of those in the form realm frequently take these as their objects of perception, they [are classified accordingly].

Collectively, these are termed "internal. However, in this present commentary (*śāstra*), the designation of *tathatā* (suchness) as "internal" follows the explanation given in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

Furthermore, within this treatise, the latter two [the seeing-part and the self-verifying-part] are termed "internal," while the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) is termed "external. Because the seeing-part takes the image-part as its object, the seeing-part is likewise designated as "external.
Although *tathatā* is termed "internal," the seeing-part is also able to take it as an object; nevertheless, the text of the commentary...
Regarding the statement that "it also cannot take [them] as an object," this is an error in the commentary. Question: The six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are subsumed under the external;

since *tathatā* (suchness) is subsumed within the sense-object of mental phenomena (*dharmaviṣaya*), how is it that *tathatā* is not the object of cognition? If *tathatā* is not the object of cognition, how can the aspect of seeing (*darśanabhāga*) fail to take it as its object?

Answer: This is because the perspectives from which they are considered differ. If *tathatā* is regarded as the ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) that serves as the true nature of all phenomena, then its *tathatā*—[is as follows:]...

That which is termed "internal" is as follows: if suchness (*tathatā*) is the objective sphere (*ālambana-viṣaya*), it is subsumed under the sense-field of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*);
in that case, suchness is termed "external. To say that it cannot be taken as an object is an error.
The Commentary states: "If that were so, the internal mind would not be the external fruit; this meaning can be understood by analogy. This refers to an external objection:

"Since the seeing-aspects of the internal and external are distinct, they do not function as fruits for one another. Because the internal and external are different, the internal does not act as the fruit of the external. The response is: The external seeing-aspect is accessible to the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and takes the external as its object;

it cannot obtain a separate internal fruit. However, the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvitti*) is essentially direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); because its substance is internal, it can serve as the external [fruit].
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) sometimes subsumes [the four] into three because their essential nature (*svabhāva*) is one. Thus, it establishes a system of three parts:

namely, the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) is the object of cognition (*prameya*), the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) is the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying aspect) is the fruit of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). Therefore, among these three parts, the essence of the fruit is only one; thus, the four are subsumed into three.
These four aforementioned categories are called "one distinct meaning," yet they are all... [not... (Note: The final phrase appears to be incomplete in the source text.)

Regarding the statement that they are all termed "only" (vijñapti-mātra) because they are apart from consciousness: as for the mention of "four categories," does this refer to four parts, or does it refer to the four categories of the aforementioned consciousness, mental factors, matter, and suchness?

The commentary’s verse states: "Grasping at one's own mind as false; therefore, the mind is present. Regarding "false": this refers to the cognizing mind (*ālambaka-citta*), because it does not realize reality.
Regarding "grasping at one's own mind": this refers to the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*).

Since the image-division is not separate from the mind, yet is not itself called "mind," the phrase "therefore the mind is present" means that both the seeing-division and the image-division are simultaneously present. If one discusses...
"Internally apprehended by one's own mind" refers to the verse from the new translation. This verse does not mean that there is only a single mind and no other distinct entities as objects;
rather, its intended meaning is that within this verse it is stated that there is "only the single mind," and that within the sphere of objects, there is nothing else apart from this single mind.
The phrase "like the objects" implies that beyond the single mind, there are further various phenomena such as forms, sounds, and so forth.
Question: Within this treatise, is it sometimes subsumed as three, according to the three parts of Dignāga;
or sometimes subsumed as two, according to the two parts of Nanda; or sometimes subsumed as one, according to the single part of Sthiramati?
Answer: Herein, all of this is the doctrine of Dharmapāla; it is not the doctrine of other masters.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the third [moment] takes the fourth as its objective aspect (*ākāra*), and so on, up to the point where the principle of reciprocal repetition is equal":
the third moment takes the fourth as its object; the fourth is the fruit (*phala*); the fourth is the self-nature (*svabhāva*); and the third is termed the objective aspect (*ākāra*).
The fourth [cognition] takes the third as its object; the third serves as the result, which is to say, the third constitutes its own essence.

The fourth is termed the "aspect" (*ākāra*); thus, the logic of their mutual relationship is symmetrical. Furthermore, the objection states that while the second cognition is neither valid nor invalid, the remaining two parts are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This passage assumes a thesis for the sake of argument, because the treatise states that the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) is invalid, while the other two [parts] are... [direct perception].

This division is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, the opponent provisionally assumes that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) while the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) is not, and thereby raises an objection against the thesis:
"If the image-part is not valid cognition, then the seeing-part should likewise be distinct from the defiled, the pleasant, and the neutral;

furthermore, if these two parts were excluded, it would follow that [the mind] is undefiled, and so on, up to being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*). Second, regarding the defiled and the non-defiled: that which is non-defiled is precisely...
Regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): that which is defiled is not valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding the commentary’s point that the distinction between valid and non-valid cognition must differ in terms of pleasure and equanimity, the external objection states: "Secondly, [regarding] valid and non-valid cognition..."

The remaining two parts are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The second [part] exists in the diversity of pleasure; the remaining two parts are exclusively the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). The answer states: because the words and their meanings are identical.

From "this is the sensation of equanimity" onwards, there are three pairs: first, the pair of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*); second, the pair of the four truths (*catur-āryasatya*) and the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*);
third, the pair of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*). As previously stated, this is due to the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*).
Sometimes the measure of non-triplicity is not the measure of the three natures; the latter three are invariably direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, it should be understood that all these [statements] regarding the arising of comprehension are spoken in reference to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*).

The Commentary further states: If the mind were to take itself as its own object, there would be cause and effect; because the object serves as the cause for the arising of the mind, the object is the cause and the mind is the fruit.

If considered in terms of the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) is the object of cognition (*prameya*), the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) is the fruit of valid cognition, and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) is the cause, with the self-verifying part being the fruit. This is because the seeing and image parts arise from the self-verifying part.
In this context, self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is the cause and the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is the effect. Regarding the agent and the object of action:
self-cognition is the agent and the seeing-part is the object of action. The seeing-part as the agent is the mind; that which is acted upon is virtuous or non-virtuous karma. An objection is raised:
there should be only the mind as the agent, but no object of action; or else, the agent is the mind and the object of action is the house.
Regarding the "establisher" and the "established": the establisher is the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), and that which is established is the so-called seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*).

The subsequent cases should all be understood by analogy. The establisher is the cause; the cause is the mind itself. That which is established is the fruit. Regarding the "that which leads" and "that which is led":
the leader is the cause of the mind, and that which is led is the objective sphere (*ālambana*), or rather, it is the fruit led forth by the mind. This is the producer.

This refers to that which can produce this mind; that which is produced is precisely all objective phenomena (*ālambana-dharma*). Regarding the relationship between the subject and the object: they are like a servant and a master.

The subject is that which exclusively presides over the master, while the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is that which belongs to it; the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) acts as the agent of manifestation, and the objective aspect is that which is manifested.
Regarding the binder and the bound: just as a rope is the binder and a person is the bound, so too the afflictions and the mind are the binder, while all objective spheres are the bound.
Regarding the characteristic and the characterized: the mind that subdues the various characteristics of all phenomena is the characteristic of the mind;
this is because the two types of mental activity give rise to the phenomena that are characterized. Regarding the perceiver and the perceived: the perceiver is the mind, and the perceived is...
All phenomena are thus. If there were no phenomena external to the mind, then all the aforementioned phenomena could not be established.

Furthermore, the Commentary should not state that "consciousness arises from two conditions" or "consciousness arises from the conjunction of the three. Regarding "consciousness arising from two conditions," the subsequent treatise further states:
"The eye and forms serve as conditions to produce visual consciousness; visual consciousness arises by virtue of the two conditions of the sense organ and the object. Since...

If there were a self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvitti*) that gives rise to the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*), then consciousness would also give rise to consciousness; thus, the two conditions would not be established, because it is taught that consciousness arises from three conditions.

As for "arising from the conjunction of three," this refers to the triad of faculty (*indriya*), object (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Now, since there is already a self-cognizing portion that gives rise to the seeing portion...

It should also be recognized that consciousness arises from consciousness; thus, the "threefold conjunction" (trikasamnipāta) is not established, because there would be a "fourfold conjunction" for the arising of consciousness.
Furthermore, the Commentary should not state that the entire substance of an unwholesome mind is entirely "wooden" (insentient). An external objection states:

If the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) and the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), etc., are equally both valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), then one might admit that the seeing-part is unwholesome, but the self-witnessing-part would also [be so].

[Objection: "Evil" refers to the substance (*svabhāva*) of the mind being evil. The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is not evil; its self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) must be correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*), because the self-cognizing part is able to take as its object the arising of evil and thus cognize it as evil. How can it be called correct cognition? If the seeing-part is evil and unwholesome while the self-cognizing part is correct cognition, then an evil mind would not pervade its entire substance. [Response: Although the self-cognizing part is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [it is not so in this context]. It is like the case where one says, "I am eating," when in fact one is merely tasting the flavor. In that same way, although the self-cognizing part is a means of valid cognition, it is not [correctly termed] "correct cognition" here. Furthermore, the seeing-part is not necessarily evil; for example, when one sees a beautiful form, the seeing-part is wholesome. Therefore, it is not the case that the substance of an evil mind does not pervade [the whole]. Thus, the view that the self-cognizing part is correct cognition while the seeing-part is evil is unreasonable. This is because the self-cognizing part is the very nature of the seeing-part; they are not distinct entities. If the seeing-part were evil, the self-cognizing part would also be evil. Since the self-cognizing part is the substance of the seeing-part, how could it be correct cognition while the seeing-part is evil? If the seeing-part were not evil, then the self-cognizing part would not be correct cognition. Therefore, the claim that the self-cognizing part is correct cognition while the seeing-part is evil is untenable. This is also evil and unwholesome because it shares the same category of views as that which is evil. If direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) were not itself evil, then since the five consciousnesses possess evil, they would not be direct perceptions.
Therefore, we know that the existence of evil is not predicated in relation to direct perception.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) should likewise have no distinction, up to the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna)," this is because:

the foundation of mindfulness of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna) takes as its object the eleven types of form within the body; the foundation of mindfulness of sensation (vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna) arises by taking the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) as its object;

the foundation of mindfulness of mind (cittasmṛtyupasthāna) arises by taking either the six or eight consciousnesses as its object; and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) consists of the mental factors (caitta) external to the first three foundations of mindfulness.

Dharma. Or rather, it is wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth. These four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) all have wisdom as their essential nature. If the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) were to take the seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object, then wisdom would also be taking wisdom itself as its object;
this would merely be called the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*), because the self-witnessing portion of wisdom takes the seeing portion of wisdom as its object.
In that case, the other three foundations of mindfulness would all fail to be established. Wisdom, therefore, exists within the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas.

Because it is included [in the category of the foundations of mindfulness]. Now, regarding the objection concerning the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), the commentary states: "From the arising of the Four Truths up to the arising of the Path," and so forth.

However, within this commentary, there are instances where the Four Truths are treated in relation to untainted consciousness (*anāsravacitta*) as its object, rather than being established within tainted consciousness (*sāsravacitta*).
Therefore, since the treatise asks whether both the tainted and the untainted constitute the contemplation of the Four Truths, what [distinction] exists among the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*)?
Regarding the distinctions: when one performs the contemplation of the Four Truths and so forth within the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), there are four distinct truths, namely:

the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*). When that untainted mind takes the Four Truths as its object, there are the knowledges that take the truth of suffering as their object, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of cessation.
If the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the untainted mind takes its own seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object, there is only the knowledge of the truth of the path. Thus...

The three remaining knowledges (*jñāna*) are [the knowledges] of the truths (*satya*). This is because they take as their object the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) by means of the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the uncontaminated path.

If one practices the contemplation of the four truths (*catur-āryasatya-vipaśyanā*) within a contaminated state of mind during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), that contaminated contemplative mind is subsumed under conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
However, when the mind does not take itself as its object, there arises the knowledge of the four truths, such as taking suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) as objects.

This is a distinction. If the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of that which is with outflows were to take the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*) as its object, there would have to be only knowledge of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-jñāna*) regarding that which is with outflows, yet there would be no knowledge of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-jñāna*).
This is because the Truth of the Path is untainted (*anāsrava*), and the Truth of Cessation is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and [the self-verifying portion] takes the mind as its causal condition.

The commentary further states: "Moreover, the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) would also fail to be established as a cognition, because it cognizes the present. This is because the knowledge of past lives takes the past as its object;

however, the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the present cognizes the present, and the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*) takes only present phenomena as its object. Therefore, the knowledge of past lives would not be established [as a cognition of the present].
Furthermore, the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*) would also fail to be established. Why? Because that knowledge of death and rebirth takes as its object—
Since the cognition of death and rebirth is a self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) that takes the present seeing-aspect (*darśanabhāga*) as its object,
it would likewise be impossible for the cognition of death and rebirth to take the future as its object.
The Commentary further states: "If one knows another as oneself"—if the knowledge of others' minds takes another's mind as its object, it may be called 'knowledge of others' minds.

However, if that knowledge of others' minds takes its own seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object via its own self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), it is then called 'knowledge of one's own mind,' not 'knowledge of others' minds.'"
Regarding the statement, "The Master knows that the refutation from the opponent's perspective is likewise," the external objection is as follows:
If one knows another's mind just as one knows one's own mind, then knowing one's own mind should also be called "knowing another's mind."
The Commentary further states that because there are two functions, the essence (*tattva*) should not be one. The explanation says:

"The two functions" refers to the two functions of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*). "The essence should not be one" refers to the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*). An external objection is raised:
"Since there are already the two functions of the seeing-part and the object-part, the essence of the self-verification should likewise consist of two distinct bodies of the self-verifying part."
The commentary states: "The analogy of a lamp illuminating itself is not established as an analogy because it lacks a cognizing subject (*ālambaka*), whereas the mind possesses a cognizing subject.
Thus, there is the fault that the reason contradicts its own specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa-viruddha-hetu*) and that the thesis to be proven (*sādhya*) is unestablished. The explanation says:

If there were no cognizing mind within the lamp itself, then—since the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) does possess a cognizing capacity—the lamp would only illuminate other minds and would be unable [to illuminate itself].
[The opponent] says: "It is self-illuminating (*svaprakāśa*). According to inference (*anumāna*), the mind must necessarily have the capacity to be a causal condition for illumination;

therefore, it is like a lamp. This [argument] is subject to the fault of the unestablished thesis (*asiddha-sādhyadharmatva*). Within the analogy of the lamp, there is no property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) that serves as the basis for establishing what is to be proven;

for the lamp-analogy only illuminates itself and does not further illuminate anything else. If the mind were something distinct that possesses the capacity to illuminate, then since this would constitute an inference (*anumāna*), there would be no point of similarity (*sādharmya*).
This involves the fallacy of the example (*dṛṣṭānta-doṣa*). Furthermore, there is the fallacy of contradicting the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-viruddha*) of the subject. An opponent says:

"Your mind certainly lacks the causal capacity to illuminate an object, just like the example of a lamp. This inference follows the intent of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* to establish that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the mind possesses a distinct faculty of cognition, which is the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).

The Commentary further states: "If the nature of a lamp is illumination, why would it need further illumination? The nature of the lamp is itself capable of illuminating; one does not discuss a separate entity as that which illuminates it.
Likewise, the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) is itself capable of cognizing; one does not further discuss the self-witnessing (svasaṃvitti) as being the cognizer."

The Commentary states: If it were not illumination, it would follow that it is not the essence of that which illuminates; its nature would then be darkness. If the lamp were darkness, it could not illuminate.
If the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) were darkness, it should likewise be unable to take darkness as its object. Therefore, [it must be illumination].
However, in the third fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, there is an explanation for the objection regarding the lamp’s illumination, yet there is no such explanation for other objections.
That treatise raises only the objection that a lamp does not illuminate itself; it does not resolve the other objections as to how the mind can take itself as its own object.

Regarding the statement that "the explanations for these objections are based on the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*)," this refers to objects such as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) of other realms and untainted objects (*anāsrava*), which are explained based on the seeing-part and not on self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). Thus, [the objection] is external.
The objection states: If the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) takes the seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object, then the mind would be taking itself as its object.

Consequently, [the cognition] of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), untainted phenomena (*anāsrava*), or those belonging to other realms would all fail to be established. That is to say, when the mind takes an unconditioned phenomenon as its object, if the self-witnessing portion were to take the seeing portion as its object, it would have to be called "taking the conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
To take the conditioned as its object is not called "taking the unconditioned. Furthermore, it is like an impure mind taking an unconditioned phenomenon as its object.
When a defiled mind takes the untainted as its object, that which is self-attesting and takes the seeing-part as its object should be called "defiled" and not "taking the untainted as its object.

Furthermore, when the mind takes another realm as its object, if the mind were to take itself as its object, it would be a mind of its own realm taking dharmas of its own realm as its object, and thus could not be called "taking another realm as its object.
If one speaks according to the aspect of self-objectification, then the various difficulties previously mentioned will arise.
This refers exclusively to the statement that [cognition] takes the fundamental object (svabhāva) as its object based on the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga). Thus, there are no obstacles or difficulties.

As for the aforementioned cases of taking objects in other realms, taking unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) as objects, taking untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) as objects, and the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), the knowledge of past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), and so forth—all these are recorded as taking the fundamental object as their object based on the seeing-part; thus, there is no fault.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) further states that what is termed "non-valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*) due to its stubborn adherence is called "non-valid cognition" because it is neither inference (*anumāna*) nor direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The explanation says:
However, because the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of wrong view possesses false adherence, it does not directly realize the object; therefore, it is called non-valid cognition.

If, however, the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of wrong view takes the seeing-part as its object, then because the seeing-part directly realizes [the object] and attains its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is a form of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is merely a provisional [distinction].
The self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of an afflicted mind is also seen to be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the self-cognition of the five consciousnesses, such as greed and anger, is subsumed under direct perception," although the self-cognition portions of the other six consciousnesses are also subsumed under direct perception, when they are in an afflicted state, all three parts [of the cognition] are collectively afflicted; this is not the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

If the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvedana*) is not defiled, then it is not defiled; thus, all three parts are collectively defiled. Furthermore, it is like the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*):

although they may be defiled by greed, hatred, and delusion, they are either induced from within the five consciousnesses by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), or even though the five consciousnesses are defiled, because they directly cognize their own essence, they are all direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The same applies to the self-cognizing portions within the other consciousnesses; even if they are defiled, what harm is there?

If it is argued that because the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is defiled, its self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) would also not be valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then since the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are also subject to defilement, they too should be invalid.
Therefore, we know this is untenable; for although the five consciousnesses possess defilement, they are nonetheless direct perceptions.
This does not preclude the fact that within the sixth consciousness, wholesome and indeterminate mental states are not invalid cognition.

Regarding the eight consciousnesses, the three types of wisdom, and the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within the causes and effects [of the path] as explained in the *Śāstra* on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: in the causal stage, the fifth and eighth consciousnesses are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);

the sixth consciousness is common to all three means of valid cognition; and the seventh consciousness is exclusively inferential cognition (*anumāna*). If one reaches the resultant stage, all eight consciousnesses are direct perception.

Regarding the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*): within the stage of a causal practitioner, the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭhavijñāna*) possesses the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*).

Among these, the wisdoms of hearing and reflection are inferential cognition (*anumāna*), while the wisdom of cultivation is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). From the eighth ground (*bhūmi*) onward, it is explained that both the wisdoms of hearing and reflection are also direct perception.
As for the other seven consciousnesses, they do not possess these three wisdoms. Upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, all eight consciousnesses [possess them].
Within [these] all is cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement: “If the principle of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātratā*) is that which transforms as nothing but one's own mind... it is also called the ‘non-common characteristic’ (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*).

This refers to the “common within the common,” because all sentient beings transform [it] in the same location and because it is similar [to them]. It cannot [be otherwise]. The above is the cessation [of this discussion].

They are obtained separately. These are transformations of both self and others, which are termed "common. If analyzed according to the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), all are transformations of one's own mind that obtain their own specific functions.
Transformations such as mountains and rivers are all "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) characteristics, because they arise from their own respective seeds.
[Commentary: Regarding the "common within the common," such as mountains and rivers, they are not used exclusively by one realm of existence; other realms of existence can also utilize them.

Regarding the phrase "others can also use them": these mountains, rivers, and so forth are not only used by those in the human realm—for instance, taking wood for fuel—but other realms (*gati*) may also utilize them.
For example, animals such as foxes, wolves, and lions that dwell in the mountains are likewise able to make use of them.
This can be understood by reading this commentary with a long pause (i.e., as a continuous phrase).

The commentary below raises an objection, stating: "Although the faculties are indeed transformations, they are 'common among the uncommon'; thus, the category of 'uncommon among the uncommon' is missing.
This master's position is incorrect. If one does not admit that the faculties themselves are transformations, then there is indeed the sense of being "uncommon among the uncommon."

Since the commentary (*śāstra*) already contains these four [meanings], when they are individually correlated with the subsequent text, the treatise (*śāstra-pada*) simply states that all of them possess these four meanings—
such as the "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) and so forth— and they are correlated accordingly as they are explained.

The Commentary asks: "Is it also the case that among the dharmas of form (*rūpa*), such as shape and shadow—which are provisional (*prajñapti*) dharmas—the eighth consciousness does not take them as objects?
Shape refers to things such as long and short; shadow refers to things such as light and shade, brightness and darkness.

If the eighth consciousness does not take provisional dharmas such as the shapes of long and short as its objects, then what of shadows, light and shade, brightness and darkness, smoke, clouds, dust, and mist, which are themselves blue, yellow, red, and so forth?"

Regarding the distinctions among manifest colors (*varṇa*): both the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) are all capable of taking light and shadow as their objects.

If one says that "light" (*āloka*) refers to a radiant illumination that possesses a vital force (*sattva*) when it shines upon a person, then lights such as those from a spark or other similar sources are all termed "luminosity" (*prakāśa*).

If one is near a fire, even if the force [of the light] departs from the fire, or if one sees the fire's light from afar, there is no longer that vital force; for this reason, it is merely termed [luminosity].
"Clarifying: Only that which is called 'light' (*āloka*) is named as such; the vapor of fire becomes smoke, and the momentum of air becomes clouds. Fine earth rising upward is called dust (*rajas*);

the vapor of earth and water is called mist (*nīhāra*). The answer says: "It does not take [these] as objects, as in the verse you have composed... up to this being correct. Furthermore, it is explained:
However, the eighth consciousness, among the objects of form (*rūpa*), takes only the four kinds of real entities—blue, yellow, red, and white—as its objects, and cannot [take others].
Regarding the light of reflected images, darkness, and so forth: these lights of reflected images and darkness are merely distinctions within manifest color (*varṇa*).

The eighth consciousness perceives only the real four great elements (*mahābhūta*) within the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*); it cannot perceive the twenty-four kinds of conventional touch, such as roughness and smoothness, which exist within the locus of touch.
Question: If this is so, how was it previously stated that the eighth consciousness apprehends the object of touch?

The middle [consciousness] passes through. It encounters the afflictions of resistance and fatigue. The eighth consciousness only perceives the real four great elements within the object-field of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*).
As for the six consciousnesses, within the gateway of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), they perceive the objects of tangibility such as fatigue and rest.

Alternatively, from the fundamental consciousness, when the eighth consciousness perceives real blue and so forth, it also perceives the conventional [notions] of length and so on; however, this is based solely upon blue, yellow, and the like.

Because they are established as equal. If the eighth consciousness perceives the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) among the objects of touch (*spraṣṭavya*), it also perceives tactile qualities such as roughness and smoothness.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that when perceiving the derivative [matter], it perceives the four great elements as their real substratum—just as it perceives length and so forth—if the root consciousness...
When one perceives blue, it is precisely [the perception of] length and so forth. If one perceives the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), it is precisely the perception of roughness and smoothness.

However, while length and shortness are specifically explained as being conventional (*prajñapti*) within the categories of phenomena (*dharmamukha*), roughness, smoothness, and the like are not separately distinguished.

Rather, they are conventionally designated based upon the four great elements; their reality is the four great elements themselves, for the four great elements do not produce conventional phenomena such as roughness and smoothness. Question: Regarding the two aforementioned...
