Within the realms (*dhātu*) and the ten stages (*bhūmi*), as well as in the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and within the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of the three realms, it is said that even down to the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, and the great elements—among these, it is not yet known whether there are both common and uncommon [aspects] for all four [types of seeds].

Question: Regarding the objects perceived by the sixth consciousness, when it forms a shared conceptualization (*sādhāraṇa-vikalpa*), it is then able to perfume [the seeds] such that they become common.

Regarding the seeds of common characteristics (*sādhāraṇa-nimitta-bīja*): at the time when these seeds subsequently arise as manifest activity (*pravṛtti*), they are able to transform into mountains, rivers, and so forth.

However, when the first five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) perceive their objects, they do not yet possess the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of "commonality. How, then, can they perfume (*vāsayati*) and thereby establish the seeds of common characteristics? Answer:
Although it is not the case that the five consciousnesses themselves produce the conceptualization of commonality, the seeds perfumed within the five consciousnesses are [the cause for] the second...

Because they belong to the same category as the six consciousnesses, the seeds produced by perfuming within the five consciousnesses are termed "seeds of common characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-bīja*).
Regarding the answer, "because of the similarity of karma," and so forth, up to "because of the obstruction or non-obstruction of one's own mind": "similarity of karma" refers to...

Because the sixth consciousness perceives mountains and rivers, it is not the case that all [beings] can simultaneously produce mental engagement (*ākāra*) and understanding; rather, they each perfume seeds accordingly.

This is precisely what constitutes "common karma" (*sabhāga-karma*). When these seeds subsequently arise, they collectively transform into mountains, rivers, and so forth, such that there is no obstruction.
Thus, within a single location, many people may occupy the same space together without mutual hindrance. Question: If the sixth consciousness perceives...
Regarding the object: when one forms the conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) that it is shared, one is then able to perfuse the seeds of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-bīja*).

When these seeds of common characteristics later give rise to their actual manifestation (*pravṛtti*), they are then able to transform into mountains, rivers, and so forth. However, as for the first five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) perceiving their objects, they are unable to form the conceptualization that the object is shared;
how then could they perfume the seeds of common characteristics? This point should be further questioned of the Dharma Master; is the previous explanation not correct?
"Similarity" refers to the fact that within one's own mind, things such as stones possess resistance (*sapratigha*). Regarding "the common transformation of karma":
it is like hemp growing within a forest, or a forest growing within hemp; they do not obstruct one another. It is the same with their coexisting and simultaneous transformation.
Because of what arose previously, the sixth consciousness takes earth, water, and mind as its objects, forming a collective interpretation rather than a distinct interpretation. Upon encountering...
It perfumes and forms seeds of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Now, within this life’s common characteristics, when these seeds arise, they transform in the same location;

thus, others do not encounter non-common obstructions. Since beginningless time, the mind has produced the conceptualization of obstruction toward wood, stone, and so forth, thereby perfuming and forming seeds.
Consequently, in this life, wood and stone appear as obstructive upon the mind. This is just as when one’s own hand strikes another person’s body—it is likewise [an obstruction] for oneself.
When there is mutual obstruction between minds, the *āśraya-rūpa* (supporting matter) of another person’s body obstructs one’s own mind-transformed *āśraya-rūpa*.
Because it shares the same location as that other person’s supporting matter, it damages one’s own supporting matter, and that other person likewise dies immediately.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Because they accord with the characteristics of bondage, they arise in mutual conformity": the meaning of this passage is that because many people collectively perform the same karma, they mutually conform to one another;
consequently, even objects such as wood and stone, which mutually conform to one another, do not obstruct each other in that same location.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that although the four types of sensory objects (*catur-viṣaya*) described there are similar to those here—such as mountains, rivers, and so forth—that *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* merely states that the four types of sensory objects of the external vessel-world transform together in the same location.
If this treatise were to include the secondary sensory objects (*anugraha-viṣaya*) upon the body as well, [the comparison would not hold].

The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are established as being in the same location and transforming together. Regarding the phrase "on another's mind" up to "this meaning should be contemplated," the intended sense is as follows:

on one's own mind, one manifests hundreds of thousands of lamps and lights; these hundreds of thousands of lamps and lights do not obstruct one another in their nature, and thus they mutually reflect and illuminate without hindrance.
This is like a small lamp, which would conflict with the great brilliance of the sun and moon if it were placed in the sunlight. If one were to place that light within the sunlight...
In the case of light, the characteristics themselves are mutually obstructive; for example, when the light of the sun is present, the light of a lamp does not manifest.

Thus, the light of a lamp is contrary to [the light of] the sun. Now, this case is also like that: it is called "hundreds of thousands of lamps upon the mind" because they do not obstruct one another.
This is used as a metaphor for many people together, just as the minds of many people, or wood and stone, do not obstruct one another. If the light of a lamp and the sun...
This is contrary to the light; it is like using wood or stone upon one's own mind to obstruct the wood or stone upon that very same mind.

Regarding the passage in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts which asks, "To whom does this transformation of the external vessel-world belong?"—the intent of this question is to cite the text of the *Yogācāra* as a point of inquiry.
The meaning of the *Yogācāra* is that the external vessel-world of the desire realm is produced by the collective karma of the sentient beings of the desire realm.

Regarding the statement that "all shared transformations are distinctions of the scriptural text," since the scriptures are the common transformation produced by the dominant influence (*adhipati-pratyaya*) of the karma of all sentient beings, it is not yet known whose transformation the higher realms are; therefore, this question is asked.
Regarding the statement that the Brahmā King Śaṅkhakeśa is also of this class: Question: What level of dhyāna does this Brahmā King belong to?

The text identifies him as a bodhisattva of the [tenth] stage; he is the Brahmā King mentioned in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*. Answer: This king is a bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), and he is also capable of transforming a pure land.

The commentary states that this includes the various small bodhisattvas of the two vehicles. Both the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are unable to undergo transformation;
rather, it is the eighteen perfections of the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* (Enjoyment by Others) land from the stages onward.
Thus, when "pure lands" are mentioned here, they all refer to the pure lands of the eighteen perfections.
Commentary on this term "Sahā World": Formerly it was called *Saha*, but now it is called *Sokha* because their sounds are similar.
Its translated name is "Endurance" (*Kṣānti*). In the pure lands of other directions, when Bodhisattvas practice, there are no evil people, evil events, or afflictions to cause distress;
therefore, they are not called "Endurance. In this direction, however, when practicing, there are many [such things].
Because this Bodhisattva is able to endure being troubled and disturbed by evil people and evil events, this world is called the "Endurance World" (Sahā-lokadhātu).
Furthermore, it is explained that although the sentient beings of this region are afflicted by manifold sufferings, there are none who do not seek liberation;
consequently, they take birth in this place. Thus, these sentient beings are called "enduring," and for this reason, this land is so named.
It is named "Endurance" (*kṣānti*). The subsequent interpretation is superior.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Also in this realm, on Vulture Peak Mountain, etc.," it refers to those who hold the view that there is [a teaching] within the mountain. If one speaks of the path of the *vipākakṣetra* (retribution land), it is not said that it exists only here;

rather, it is spoken of as being present throughout the ten directions. Within all mountains of this current land, it is not said that it exists solely here. Thus, it is pervasive across the ten directions.
Because it is currently so. This treatise [states] that the truly pure lands and pure realms all preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

While at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, it also indicates that [the Buddha] constantly dwells on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa as well as other various abodes. Regarding impure pure lands, external dharmas truly arise, and there are also those capable of perfuming them.
It is said that within the great transformation of the impure, there are bodhisattvas dwelling in the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) who are capable of transformation.

One is born therein. If it concerns Bodhisattvas in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) or external phenomena that produce the fruit of birth, they are unable to produce the great transformation-clouds (*mahā-nirmāṇa-megha*).
Prior to the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of external phenomena also transform through distinct dharmas.

Within the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), the great transformation-clouds seen are those with outflows (*sāsrava*). From the tenth stage of dedication (*daśama-praṇidhāna*) onwards, one is indeed able to transform.
Question: It is said that there is "Great Transformation" (*mahānirmita*). From which sutra or treatise does this emerge? Answer: It is from the *Brahmanasūtra*.

That which surrounds the thousand-petaled lotus is all "Great Transformation," and thus it is called the Buddha of Great Transformation. Question: Why are they called "outsiders" (*bāhya*) and "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*)? Answer:

If one reaches the seventh mind of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), one is non-retrogressive and is called an "insider" (*adhyātma*) ordinary being, because this is the Buddha-dharma. Those such as the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), however, are outsiders.
They are called "external dharmas" and "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*), because they are not established within the Buddha-dharma.
One commentary states: "Next, 'birth' refers to transformation; that is, sentient beings of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth.

Having already received this present body, their subsequent body becomes one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Although such sentient beings have their bodies within the form realm, they also possess the eighth consciousness."
Regarding the statement "the desire realm": if one must pass through many bodies before being born into the desire realm, the eighth consciousness does not transform into the desire realm.
As for the second case, "one who is about to be born," such a person will be born into this desire realm after having passed through ten births;

at that time, the eighth consciousness also transforms into the desire realm. In this current explanation, we take the case of "one who is about to be born," whose transformation has continued up until the completion of the kalpa. Now...
One is born in this place. If one takes the former interpretation—that one is to be born there—it would be like being in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) intending to be reborn in a lower realm;
yet, without abandoning the desire realm, one would accomplish the *anāgāmin* fruit through "leaping over" (*pluta*). This interpretation does not surpass the latter one.

The Commentary asks: Why does the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (51) state that "that consciousness does not take the actual receptacle as its object"? [It says this] because if one is a noble being (*ārya*), one does not descend [to lower realms];

thus, that consciousness does not take the receptacles of the lower realms as its object. This master [Vasubandhu], regarding the object as indeterminate, [argues] that it takes the receptacle as its object;

for if one is a noble being, one does not descend, and therefore that consciousness does not take the receptacles of the lower realms as its object. This is stated with respect to the indeterminate [nature of the object].

This is the meaning of that master’s incorrect interpretation. According to the correct system, this passage from the *Yogācārabhūmi* indicates that the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) in the higher realms does not transform the lower realms;
thus, it does not take the external vessel-world as its object.

The Commentary asks: "If a noble one (*ārya*) is certainly not reborn in the Avīci hell, and so forth, up to the Heaven of Long Life (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva*), then since a noble one does not take birth in the Avīci hell where sinners are reborn, nor in the Heaven of Long Life where non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are reborn, they should not be reborn there;
yet they should not fail to be reborn [in other places]. As for the "Heaven of Long Life," it refers to the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) within the Fourth Dhyāna. This is so.
It is said that this refers to the birthplace of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The Commentary answers this question by stating: "Because it is the very realm of earth where they currently reside, they obtain [it]. To explain:

although a Noble One (*ārya*) may even descend into hell while still in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), because they possess the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they do not undergo transformation into a sinful state despite going to hell, and they are likewise able to enjoy [the fruits of their merit].

It is transformed because they belong to the same level (*bhūmi*). If a noble one (*ārya*) is born in the Heaven of the Fourth Dhyāna, he transforms the Heaven of Long Life (*Āyuṣmat*), because they are of the same transformational nature.

According to another interpretation: if that were so, when the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) is about to be destroyed, since there would be no inhabitants currently residing there nor any who are to be born there, the kalpa would be destroyed;
and once the kalpa has been destroyed, there would be twenty intermediate kalpas (*antara-kalpa*) of emptiness. Once those twenty kalpas of emptiness have passed, it would immediately form as before.
After fourteen or fifteen days had passed, a sentient being from the upper realms died and was reborn in the Great Brahma Heaven as a Brahmā King.

This king dwelt alone in the half-Vimāna; for many kalpas his mind remained solitary, and he was not yet joined by the other Brahma-sons who were subsequently born into the Brahma-Pariṣadya Heaven and other such realms.
Thus, when there is a Brahmā King in the First Dhyāna, there is also the eighth consciousness present in that First Dhyāna.

Transformation. Furthermore, within the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), since there are sentient beings, the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) of those sentient beings transforms [the environment] in the same way as it does for the wind-circle below, up to the seven golden mountains and the great earth. Moreover, during the kalpa, as sentient beings gradually arise above, so too does the great earth and fire [extend upward];
as sentient beings are born above, reaching up to the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations, so too does the light extend to the First Dhyāna.
At the time of the Brahmakāyika devas, when the Great Brahmā King has just passed away and ascended, there is not a single sentient being remaining in this world.
After ten thousand years, thirty thousand years, or even thirty thousand years have elapsed, the world is then consumed by fire until nothing remains; this is the end of the kalpa of destruction.

At the initial stage of formation, the palace of the Great Brahmā King lacks the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*). This continues as it evolves up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; at the very beginning of formation, it is likewise so for the physical environment (*bhājana-loka*).

At the time of correct inference: since sentient beings of the desire realm have already been born in the higher realms and within the first dhyāna, and sentient beings there have likewise been born above, there are currently no [beings] residing in the desire realm or the first dhyāna, nor any who are about to be born there; thus, the fires and so forth of that desire realm [cease].
"By whom is the eighth consciousness transformed? Thus we know that transformation by a co-realm (samabhūmika) and lateral (pārśvavartin) [consciousness] is predominant.
Regarding the statement "the present realm of desire is reversed," this refers to sentient beings of this realm who are about to be born; this passage represents the third master mentioned later.
Regarding the desire realm according to correct reasoning, first I shall refute the second teacher.

You, the second teacher, for what reason do you speak only of those currently residing in the desire realm as undergoing lateral transformation (*pārśvavikāra*), and not of those in other worlds who are identical to those in the desire realm?
This desire realm is the same stage (*bhūmi*) and the same sphere (*dhātu*); why then do you say that only those within the upper three dhyānas of this very world undergo such transformation?

Sentient beings of the desire realm transform the desire realm. Why, then, is it not said that those who are to be born in the three higher dhyānas of other directions also undergo transformation here in this desire realm?
Furthermore, when the receptacle world is formed, the three dhyānas of other directions and so forth are likewise [formed];
therefore, I now refute [this]. The later master says: "Just as in this direction two intersecting sets of three thousandfold world systems arise, so too do the lower three dhyānas."

When, subsequently, the receptacle world of the lower three dhyānas is formed in this direction, sentient beings in the third dhyāna of another world-system undergo lateral transformation into the receptacle world of the third dhyāna here.

Once the receptacle world of the third dhyāna has been formed in this direction, sentient beings die from the third dhyāna of that other world-system and are reborn here in the third dhyāna; thus, they become the Śubhakṛtsna gods.
O Deva, as for those who undergo the sixty-four [kalpas], even down to the receptacles of the lower two dhyānas, their capacity to endure is likewise destroyed;
therefore, I grant that the sentient beings of the third dhyāna undergo lateral transformation.

As for this very third dhyāna, why did your former teacher allow only the sentient beings of the fourth dhyāna to descend and take birth in the three lower dhyānas, while remaining in the higher stage to transform the three lower dhyānas? Your former teacher—
"Granting and granting is correct" refers to the explanation of the current dwelling place; that is, the sentient beings of this trichiliocosm, wherein the upper [realms] transform the lower.

As for the commentary stating, "The Mahāsāṃghika school holds that there is form in the formless realm," this school grants that the six consciousnesses and the six [objects] exist within the formless realm.
Consciousness must necessarily rely upon the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) in order to arise.

Although the Mahāsāṃghika school maintains that there is a material body (*rūpakāya*) even in the four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), how does this differ from the desire and form realms? Their teacher replies:
"Although there is a material body in the formless realm, it is called 'formless' because it is subtle; the other two realms are coarse. Again, he is challenged: "In the formless realm..."

Since the form-body (*rūpakāya*) exists [in those realms], they are called "formless" (*ārūpya*) because their bodies are subtle. The form-bodies of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are subtler than those of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*);
therefore, in comparison to the Desire Realm, they should be called the Formless Realm. That teacher replied: "The form-bodies of the Form Realm are not the most subtle;
because they are only intermediate in subtlety, they cannot be called 'formless. It is the form-body of the Formless Realm that is the ultimate limit of subtlety."

Regarding the reason for being named "Formless" (*ārūpya*), another objection is raised: If the Formless Realm is named "Formless" because it is subtler than the preceding Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*), then the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)—when compared to the three lower formless realms—is the subtlest of all. Thus, the Peak of Existence alone [should be called "Formless"].
It is called "formless" (*ārūpya*). Since the three lower formless realms are coarser than the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they should not be called "formless.
For this reason, that [position] is not the same as what is stated here. This is a passage from the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* refuting the Mahāsāṃghika school’s claim regarding the formless realm.
It says: "The teachers of the Mahāsāṃghika school assert that there is a physical body (*rūpakāya*) in the formless realm; thus, they say 'formless'..."
The form realm (*rūpadhātu*) has distinct locations, which are established because they exist above the form realm.
However, according to the Mahāyāna and other schools, it is not asserted that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) has distinct locations.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that the Brahmā King transforms the ground below him separately: when the Brahmā King reaches the ground of the Desire Realm, it is like oil being poured onto sand—the oil immediately sinks straight down;
or like standing in the midst of flour; or like walking through clouds—all of these involve sinking directly into the substance.
It must necessarily transform other regions according to the dharma for it to remain stable. This is also as stated in the second fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. As it says:
If one wishes to travel upon the grounds of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is necessary to specifically transform [the body] into a vajra; only then can one proceed as if walking or standing.
Why is this? Because the grounds of the desire realm are coarse and solid like the earth; if one does not transform [the body], one would simply sink in as if entering the ground itself.
It must be modified.

The commentary states: "If that were so, regarding the fact that noble ones [abide] in their own level within the Brahma-palace and in their own level within hell—if one refers to the noble ones of the Hīnayāna, it is granted that they may be born in the Brahmakāyika or Brahmapurohita heavens, but they certainly do not arise in the Mahābrahmā heaven. Since they do not arise there, it should..."
It is unchanging. This applies both to the realm where the Great Brahmā King dwells and likewise to the hells.

At present, even the initial noble ones of the Hīnayāna are not reborn as Great Brahmā when they inquire; however, this is not the case for Bodhisattvas, who are indeed reborn in the Heaven of Great Brahmā.
This refers to Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), all of whom become Great Brahmā Kings of the First Dhyāna because they have attained mastery (*vaśitā*).
As for those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*), they are not born in that heaven;

since there exists in that heaven a Brahmā King who holds the false attachment to the vehicle of existence (*bhavayāna-satkāyadṛṣṭi*), they are not born in the Mahābrahmā Heaven. The intended meaning is that Non-returners (*anāgāmin*) cannot be born there.

O King, as for those who have attained the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmin) and are born in the Brahmakāyika heaven, because they do not see Mahābrahmā, they are not reborn in the realm of Mahābrahmā.
Although the realm of Mahābrahmā and the Brahmakāyika heaven belong to the same level (bhūmi), these noble non-returners do not transform their own level to dwell in the palace of Mahābrahmā;
for it is known that only those noble ones who realize emptiness are born in the Anabhraka and Bṛhatphala heavens.
Among the heavens, that eighth consciousness does not transform into the formless celestial palaces, because the noble ones do not take those heavens as their proper abode.

Furthermore, because noble beings of the desire realm never again enter the hells, the eighth consciousness of such noble ones transforms only the location of the hells, but does not transform the instruments of suffering such as Mount Kālaśaila. However, speaking according to reality, since these non-returners are already noble beings...
He is also called the Great Brahmā King. As for that Sage, his eighth consciousness is also capable of transforming into the Great [Brahmā] and those below.

Now, because this refers to the general characteristic, it is said that he is born in the Brahma-realm and fills the heavens. Whether sage or ordinary person, none see the Brahmā King, nor does he transform into the word "Brahmā."
Just as the transformations of Mahābrahmā and those of the solitary hells (pratyeka-naraka) transform according to the number of sentient beings, it is asked:
Can the sentient beings in hell also transform other superior places among humans? The answer is:

Because they share the same level (*bhūmi*), they can indeed transform them—just as Mahābrahmā transforms only the palace of the Great Brahmā King; if it is said that one person alone enjoys it, then there is only one.
This refers to a solitary hell, wherein this person alone undergoes the suffering of that solitary hell.

Because *Rakṣapāla* (Hùyuè) perceives all three realms, he takes as his object even the lower receptacle-worlds down to those that are utterly useless. Question: Regarding the previous discussion on taking the receptacle-world as an object—
There is only Candragarbha, but no Rāhula. For what reason do you now say that Rāhulamitra does not exist?
Because of the color-aggregate (rūpa-skandha) of the lower vessel, this teacher Candragarbha is none other than the teacher Rāhula; they are not different.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "the seeds which take the formless [realms] as their object" (*ārūpyālambana-bīja*), there is an interpretation which says: the phrase "up to and including those that take only seeds as their objects" refers to this Master Arcaṭa (Hugüeyuè).

According to his view, the Sūtra states that while the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) dwells supported by the seeds, the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) takes the seeds as its object; this refers to the seeing-part of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
It is permitted that [the mind] takes the form of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) of the lower realms as its object.

Regarding the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that it "takes seeds as its object," this refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) taking the objects of its respective self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) as its own objects, while conversely taking the forms of the lower realms as its objects. This is precisely the meaning of the present treatise;

the positions of the first two masters are not correct, whereas the position of the third master is correct. As for the statement that "true suchness (*tathatā*) is the self-verifying-part," the intended meaning is that true suchness is itself...
It is the self-substance (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Regarding the statement in the Commentary that "the Buddha’s seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes the self-substance as its object, even unto that which is not an object of characteristics (*nimitta*)," it means that the Buddha’s seeing-part, in turn, takes the self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) as its object;
that is, the dharma turns back and takes the characteristic-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its object. Thus, there are four parts. This is so provided it does not undergo transformation (*pariṇāma*).
If that which is perceived as the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) were itself the object of cognition, then the doctrine of the four aspects would be untenable.

If it is argued that, in such a case, the mind would not cognize an object and should therefore be called "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*), the intent of this question is as follows: because the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) depend upon consciousness and are realized by the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of consciousness, these seeds are not separate from consciousness and are thus termed "transformations of consciousness.
However, because their true nature is True Suchness (*tathatā*), they are designated as "consciousness-only. Since mental factors (*caitta-dharma*)... [text truncated]

This is the nature of the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*). Furthermore, it is not the same as the seeds. Based on the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), the mental factors (*caitta*) are distinct.
Material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are transformations of consciousness; therefore, those mental phenomena should also be termed "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).

As for that which does not constitute the self-substance of the mental factors: however, mental phenomena do not abide within the self-nature division of consciousness. Thus, the mental factors are distinct [from the mind]. Material phenomena are...
The mental factors (caitta-dharma) that are transformations of consciousness should be termed "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "They should be termed 'bound to the desire realm' (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta); this point should be reflected upon": if they arise as actual manifestations (samudācāra), they then pertain to the bonds of all three realms.
If it were a seed, it would be bound to only one realm (*dhātu*). Furthermore, regarding the meaning of being bound to a realm, three [interpretations] are untenable.
It is better to follow the view that it is bound to a realm according to the consciousness; the latter explanation is superior, while the former is not good.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (Commentary): "The seeds of afflictions should also follow consciousness, yet they are not themselves afflictions;

all such cases are in accordance with reason," there are two interpretations. First, according to the preceding discussion on cause and effect: because they possess the nature of being wholesome and so forth, if the seeds of affliction were themselves wholesome and so forth, then these afflictions would be able to perfuse the active state (*samudācāra*), thereby extending even to the unwholesome (*akuśala*).

Furthermore, since the active states they produce would also extend to the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), [the seeds of affliction] are [distinct from the afflictions themselves]. Thus, the seeds of affliction...
My son, it is because that which cannot be followed by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) is designated as "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).
The Commentary asks: "How can this be so greatly at odds with the fact that the original object (*ālambana-bhāva*) is the very basis, and even the mental image (*pratibimba*) follows it?

Now, this question concerns the objects of the eight consciousnesses—the original substance and the mental image—which are all collectively termed the "objective aspect" (*nimitta-bhāga*) and are all said to follow the "perceiving aspect" (*darśana-bhāga*). As for oneself...
Question: Regarding the attachment to the stages (*bhūmi*).

The commentary states: "In this life, there is a transformation [of consciousness] that takes the upper realms as its object, even extending to taking the body of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as its object.

This means that when a person in the desire realm is about to die, their sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) gives rise to the factors of craving and views belonging to the upper realms, while taking the body of the desire realm as its object. [This is said] because of fear...

After death, one is born into an evil realm; this constitutes the portion of craving and views belonging to the higher realms (*ūrdhva-dhātu*). Taking the body of the desire realm as an object, the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) arises from craving.

Because the objective aspect follows the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), it is bound to the same level (*samāna-bhūmi*) within those higher realms. This is what is meant by the following passage:

When one is born in the desire realm, one immediately gives rise to craving for the desire realm; when one takes birth in the form realm, one immediately gives rise to feeling belonging to the form realm;

and when one takes birth in the formless realm, one immediately gives rise to craving for the formless realm. These are the nine types of death-moment consciousnesses (*cyuti-citta*), because they are accompanied by simultaneously arising craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Since these [death-moment consciousnesses] possess both the aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), they are all bound to the same level (*bhūmi*). Why, then, are the aspect and seeing aspects of the eighth consciousness not bound to different levels?
The eighth consciousness consists of seeds bound to a single realm (dhātu), yet it pervades all three realms.

It is likewise with the object-part (nimittabhāga) of the eighth consciousness as perceived by the seventh consciousness: the object-part produced by the seventh consciousness is also bound to the same stage (bhūmi) as its seeing-part (darśanabhāga).

The Commentary states: This is not a case of a Bodhisattva being born there as a transformation-body. If it is a Bodhisattva on the [Ten] Grounds (*bhūmi*), they are not born in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If it is a Bodhisattva prior to the Grounds (*pṛthagjana-bodhisattva*), it is also permitted that they produce the fragrance of a palace through the transformation of consciousness.

Alternatively, it may be a Śrāvaka of Extensive Wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) who is also capable of such transformations. Because this Śrāvaka possesses abundant wisdom, he is called "Extensive Wisdom" (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*); thus, he is said to be of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*).
The Commentary further states: "When Bodhisattvas enter that meditative absorption, they transform it so that the fragrance of the palaces is abundant.
This is a transformation performed by Bodhisattvas on the bhūmis, which enables other Bodhisattvas of the same class to obtain it."
The commentary states: "This is the same as the previous objection; why labor to provide proof? This is the language of the commentary’s interrogation and objection.

Your objection stated that "the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) and its object (nimitta-bhāga) belong to the same stage (bhūmi). Now, it is explained that the object and the seeing-part can also be bound to different stages. Furthermore, this passage is a question. Its meaning is:
if you were to provide an interpretation such as the one previously mentioned, would you still be able to resolve the previous objection? Why then labor to cite [this proof]?
This serves as textual evidence. For this reason, the commentary below provides a further alternative interpretation, which is superior.

If the commentary were not to do so, it would follow that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) would also merely follow the mind, and so on, until there would be no consciousness to maintain [the seeds].

If one does not allow that the "seeing" and "image" aspects (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*) of the fundamental consciousness belong to different stages—such that the fundamental consciousness of the desire realm is not allowed to maintain the characteristics of the divine eye and ear of the form realm—[then the aforementioned fault follows].
Regarding "arising separately": the divine ear-faculty is protected and maintained by non-consciousness; it should be understood that it is indeed maintained by non-consciousness.
[Commentary: If, within a single body, bodies belonging to two realms were both substantially existent, then within a single body of the desire realm...

If one were to claim that the divine eye and ear faculties arise while the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) of the desire realm does not sustain them, yet they nonetheless possess a separate, substantially real entity, then there would be two bodies present in the desire realm:

the body of the desire realm itself and the body of the divine eye and ear. Since these two bodies would both be fully accomplished, the realm of sentient beings would increase, because there would be two distinct entities of a body that have been accomplished.
However, this commentary is also logically sound: if the eighth consciousness sustains the divine ear, how could...

The divine eyes and ears of the eight consciousnesses—do these belong to the Desire Realm? Therefore, one should know that although the eighth consciousness of the Desire Realm sustains those divine eyes and ears, they nonetheless belong to the higher realms.
Regarding the fact that the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) and *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) do not necessarily share the same nature:

if we discuss this in terms of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), then the eighth consciousness consists of "solitary shadows" (*kevala-pratibimba*) which follow only the *darśana-bhāga*; these are the seeds of the three natures.

In accordance with the substance of the eighth consciousness, all are termed indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). This extends even to the five sense organs and the five sense objects, as they are all of an indeterminate nature.

Speaking in terms of their nature, when the eighth consciousness takes seeds and so forth as its objects, these are all "solely shadowy images" (*kevala-chāyā*) arising solely from the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*).
If discussed in terms of the realms (*dhātu*), the eighth consciousness is an objective realm (*vastu*) that does not follow the mind; however, its seeds do follow the mind.
That is to say, these seeds pervade the consciousnesses of all three realms, yet they cannot be restricted to the seeds of only one single realm.

Although the eighth consciousness itself is bound to only one realm, it is able to take the seeds of all three realms as its objects; thus, the eighth consciousness takes the seeds of the three realms as its cognitive objects.
This refers to the fact that "the objective realm does not follow the mind.

As explained in the Commentary (*Śū*), this concerns cases such as when one in the second dhyāna or above initiates the visual, auditory, or tactile consciousnesses of the first dhyāna, or when the *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived aspect) and *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) are bound to different levels (*bhūmi*).

Regarding this, there are two interpretations. The first states: "Alternatively, there may be a certain class of beings whose bodies are born within a particular realm [of existence], yet they obtain the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) of the first dhyāna."
The ear-faculty gives rise to the visual and auditory consciousnesses of the first dhyāna, which take the forms of the desire realm as their objects.

These [faculties], along with the body, belong to the desire realm, while the consciousness belongs to the first dhyāna. Thus, the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) belongs to the desire realm, while the subjective aspect (darśana-bhāga) belongs to the first dhyāna.

This applies even when, based on the divine eye or ear-faculties of the first dhyāna, one produces the forms of the first dhyāna; in that case, both the objective and subjective aspects belong to the first dhyāna. Furthermore...

When one is in a body belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and possesses the mind of the second dhyāna, one obtains the divine eye and ear faculties (*divyacakṣuḥ-śrotra-indriya*) of the second dhyāna, which give rise to the visual and auditory consciousnesses (*cakṣur-vijñāna* / *śrotra-vijñāna*) of the first dhyāna.

These take the forms (*rūpa*) of the second dhyāna as their objects. Thus, the body is bound to the desire realm, while the eye is bound to the second dhyāna and the consciousness is likewise [bound to the first dhyāna].
The seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) belongs to the first dhyāna. The image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) belongs to the second dhyāna.

This continues until the body is in the fourth dhyāna and the eye-faculty is also in the fourth dhyāna, yet it gives rise to an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna that takes the forms of the second dhyāna as its object.
In this case, the image-portion consists of the faculties and the body of the second dhyāna, while the consciousness is of the fourth dhyāna; the seeing-portion, however, belongs to the first dhyāna.

The rest should be understood by analogy. That is to say: when one is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), if one produces the eye and ear faculties of the first dhyāna, they can take as objects those things belonging to the desire realm and the first dhyāna.

Furthermore, when one is in the desire realm, if one produces the eye and ear faculties of the second dhyāna, they can take as objects the forms (*rūpa*) of the desire realm, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the first dhyāna, and the second dhyāna.

This continues up to: when one is in the desire realm, if one produces the eye and ear faculties of the fourth dhyāna, they can take as objects... [the forms of the desire realm through the fourth dhyāna].

Regarding the four dhyānas and the objects of form and sound in the desire realm: even when the body is in the first dhyāna, one can give rise to the eyes, ears, and so forth of the second through the fourth dhyānas.
All of this should be understood according to what was previously explained. One should cite the verse from the *Abhidharmakośa*:

"The eye is not lower than the body; Form and consciousness are not higher than the eye. As for form, it is in all [stages] relative to consciousness; The same applies to the other two (ear and nose) relative to the body. This is just as it is for the eye and ear.

It is likewise. The next three [consciousnesses] all belong to their own level (*svabhūmi*). Body-consciousness belongs to its own level or a lower level. It should be understood that the mental consciousness (*manas*) is indeterminate.
These two verses are common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; one should consult the *Abhidharmakośa-vyākhyā* for an explanation of these verses.

However, while it is permitted for the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) to arise separately with respect to their "bondage" (*saṃyojana*), they cannot be bound separately by different realms (*dhātu*). "Realm" carries the sense of "bondage. Now, this has been discussed in relation to the eye- and ear-consciousness.

Furthermore, when the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) makes this statement, it refers to the five sensory consciousnesses and the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), all of which obtain distinct levels of connection between the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).

However, regarding the actual meaning: as stated in the second [section], because the eighth consciousness is taught to be both a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and to possess practical utility, the seeing-part and the image-part can arise with distinct connections.
Since the preceding seven consciousnesses are transformations of discrimination (*vikalpa-pariṇāma*), that which is transformed— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]
Because the object lacks practical utility, the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) are both bound to the same level as the superior [level].

For example, when one is in the second dhyāna and the divine eye or ear faculty produces a consciousness of the first dhyāna that takes the forms or sounds of the second dhyāna as its object, the image-aspect is explained as being of the second dhyāna, while the seeing-aspect is also bound to the same level as the first dhyāna.
This continues up to the point where, because one is in the fourth dhyāna, the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna—or perhaps that of the desire realm—[arises].

Regarding the matter of the realms (*dhātu*) and form (*rūpa*): either they take the form of the third dhyāna as their object, or the characteristics of form are explained from the perspective of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). All of these are bound to the first dhyāna.

As for forms of the third dhyāna and those above it, they are all permeated by the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because there is no permeation by visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Regarding the statement that the five consciousnesses, such as those perceiving form (*rūpa*), should lack material obstruction (*sapratigha*), there are two interpretations. The first states:

The objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the five consciousnesses possesses obstruction; after the seeds have been perfumed (*vāsita*), the primary object (*mūlapadārtha*) arises, and thus the objective aspect also possesses obstruction.

The second states: The objective aspect transformed by the five consciousnesses is without obstruction. If this is so, how can seeds be perfumed within an unobstructed objective aspect? Subsequently...

At the time of arising, are there obstructive forms (*sapratigha-rūpa*) and so forth? Answer: Although there is no obstruction at the initial moment of perfuming, when the seeds subsequently produce their actual manifestations (*samudācāra*), they do indeed possess obstruction.
It is just as grass and trees have no fruit when first sprouting, yet later the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) become solid; this case is also like that.
First, the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) is unimpeded. Once the image-part has been perfumed as an unimpeded [seed], it subsequently produces the objective essence (*ālambanavastu*).
Regarding the statement "if it is that which is transformed by the fundamental consciousness" (*mūlavijñāna-pariṇāma*) and so forth, the question is: does this text constitute a critique?

Is the "First Master" (*prathama-ācārya*) mentioned in the commentary the same as the First Master in the main treatise? This passage leads directly to the following discussion concerning other sense organs (*indriya*) and so forth.
Because it is a formal treatise (*śāstra*), the commentary first provides this question and answer. This constitutes the objection to the subsequent passage in the treatise which states:
"In the treatise, there is also the sense that [the object] transforms by means of the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth. This refers to the position of the first master.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “one should exert effort as if it were one’s own eye-faculty,” all the preceding textual passages of this commentary constitute what is not the correct meaning.
Although one should indeed exert effort, the commentator separately seeks out divergent views to provide a detailed response. This causes the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* itself to fall into error;
therein, the Sautrāntikas challenge the Sarvāstivādins, and there too, there is much that requires effort and the separate seeking of divergent views.
[The word] "text" refers to this very passage composed according to that school's tenet.

Regarding the phrase "because it is an external object for the real sense-faculties of others," the commentary below provides another interpretation: it acknowledges that the transformed [faculties] are real.
The commentary states: "However, those faculties are not substantially functional. This and the following passages constitute the second interpretation:
they are called "pseudo-faculties" because they are admitted to be real in another sense while appearing as faculties; there is nothing that does not transform from a real faculty.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that expressions such as “transforming another’s form” or “resembling another’s form” have practical utility: transforming the forms of the sense-objects that support the faculties within another’s body all possess actual efficacy.
The commentary answers this by stating that these cases serve as examples; while they are real, those things resembling another’s form and so forth are not actually possessed by that other person.
Regarding "functioning": it is like one's own consciousness transforming another person's body and its sensory objects (āyatana), whereby one still functions by means of that other.

In reality, however, one does not function [by means of it]; this is as explained in the *Śū* (Commentary). As for the phrase "one should reflect upon this"—namely, that one's own consciousness does not transform another's sense organs (*indriya*)—this is why it says "one should reflect.
All the preceding text above this point consists of incorrect questions and answers. Only the text of the *Śū* from this point onward represents the correct meaning.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase in the *Śāstra*: "Among the uncommon [factors], the uncommon are like one's own faculties, up to being like [the elements] such as space. If it is the uncommon among the previously mentioned uncommon factors, these are the five internal sense-faculties (*indriya*).
If they are common, such as in the case of visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth—those that exist in visible forms and so forth—are the *anuparivartin* (subsidiary) faculties.
Regarding the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*): here, both are present. First, the five sense organs are "unshared among the unshared" (*asādhāraṇa-asādhāraṇa*).
Second, the objects that support the sense organs (*indriyādhiṣṭhāna*) are "shared among the unshared" (*asādhāraṇa-sādhāraṇa*).

If one allows for the transformation of another's sense organs, then those other organs are likewise "shared among the unshared," because what was previously called "unshared" is now termed "shared. Thus, what was previously described as "unshared" refers precisely to the supporting objects within this context.
Regarding the sense-objects (*viṣaya*) that support the faculties: these are both uncommon and common.

For instance, regarding the bases of the nose and tongue belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), up to the point where it should be that there are no two [types of] faculties, the former master says:

"If you, following the Master [Vasubandhu], maintain that the eighth consciousness does not transform the five faculties of others because the five faculties of others lack the function of producing consciousness, then as for those that do not transform... [it is] just like the case of form.

Regarding the elements of the nose and tongue faculties (*ghrāṇa-jihvendriya*), although they lack the function of producing consciousness, it is still admitted that the nose and tongue faculties undergo transformation.

This is because if the nose and tongue faculties did not exist, their respective *upādāya-rūpa* (the sensory bases that support the faculties) would also not exist. Therefore, one should know that although these [faculties] lack the function of producing consciousness for the other five faculties, it is nonetheless admitted that one's own consciousness transforms the faculties of others.
If one were to say that only the *upādāya-rūpa* (sensory bases) of others are transformed while the five faculties themselves are not used, then...
If it were unchanging in that way, there would be no nose or tongue faculties in the form realm, because the nose and tongue faculties would lack the function of producing consciousness;

they would possess only the *āśraya-rūpa* (the physical support). As for those such as those born blind, although they possess the eye faculty, their fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) also transforms into the eye, yet because there is a defect upon the pupil, it cannot produce consciousness.
Although my [consciousness] truly takes another's faculty as its object, it can still independently produce [its own cognition].

It is consciousness (*vijñāna*). If the eye were identical to the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), then the other five kinds of form within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)—namely, "extremely condensed form" (*paramāṇu-saṃghāta-rūpa*) and so forth—and the five and eight consciousnesses would not take them as objects.
However, if these are actual forms within the sphere of mental objects, then both the five and eight consciousnesses of ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*) are able to take them as objects.
The intention of the Commentary (*śāstra*) in maintaining that there is but one consciousness is as follows:

however, the old verses only state that the eighth consciousness can transform the sense organs, objects, and so forth, and do not state that the other seven preceding consciousnesses can transform matter; therefore, it specifically mentions the eighth consciousness, intending to maintain that there is but one [transforming] consciousness.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) the faculties of nose and tongue cannot be absent because they arise from other [causes], whereas in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) this is not the case: the Master of this treatise then says,
"Even if it were granted that the faculties of nose and tongue could be absent in the Form Realm because of the absence of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*),
how could the faculties of nose and tongue be absent in the Desire Realm, given that odors and tastes exist there as edible food?"
The Commentary states: "If that is so, since beings in the desire realm also manifest and experience the superior bodies of others, why do they not transform their sense organs?

The intent of this objection is as follows: for example, when a Universal Monarch (cakravartin) of the desire realm also manifests excellent palace ladies and maidservants whom the monarch himself perceives, why does he not transform the sense organs—such as the eyes and ears—of those other women to experience them [as his own]? Or...

If other people can likewise obtain excellent wives from the [desire] realms, as well as illusory elephants, horses, and so forth, why do they not transform their own five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) to enjoy them?
This reasoning is incorrect... [up to] ...as for what could serve as an analogy: you yourself admit that those in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) transform their own five [faculties].
Regarding the statement that "the roots cause the transformation of other roots within the desire realm," what serves as the illustration?

The commentary asks: "If one's own body is one's own sentient experience, it truly lacks a basis for the sense organs, nor does it possess external objects; since they are not one's own experience, why must there necessarily be sense organs?
The explanation says: If one's own eighth consciousness transforms the *upādāya-rūpa* (sustaining matter) upon its own body, then that object (*viṣaya*) indeed exists.
The "auxiliary" (扶) refers to the fact that it supports the five sense organs of one's own body. Therefore, it belongs to the eighth consciousness itself.

If the eighth consciousness did not experience the five sense organs upon its own body, then there would be no five auxiliary organs upon that body; since the auxiliary [organ] lacks the locus for supporting the sensory objects upon the body, the support for the organs would likewise not exist.
If the eighth consciousness itself were to transform into an auxiliary [organ] upon the body of another, [it would function as such].
The "dust" (viṣaya) refers to the auxiliary dust (upādāya-rūpa) upon other bodies; this is subsumed under the category of insentient things. Why is this?
If it were the auxiliary dust that supports the five sense organs of one's own body, then that auxiliary dust could be reckoned among sentient beings.

However, although one’s own consciousness may transform the auxiliary dust upon another’s body, that auxiliary dust on another’s body cannot support the five sense organs of one’s own body; therefore, it is subsumed under the category of non-sentient things.
From the eighth consciousness onward, it cannot transform the five sense organs (*indriya*) of others. If this is so, why does one incur the sin of killing when taking life?
Although one kills another sentient being, one still causes damage to the faculties and objects (*viṣaya*) transformed by one’s own consciousness.

If one were to kill the supporting objects (*upādāya-rūpa*) of another, that would constitute grasping at phenomena external to the mind; however, [the killing occurs] upon the supporting objects transformed by one’s own eighth consciousness.
To harm another by supporting a minute particle (*paramāṇu*) constitutes killing because it causes the life-force of that other being to be severed.
If this is so, how do we reconcile this with the earlier passage which states that "the forms and so forth transformed upon one's own mind" obstruct the forms transformed upon one's own mind?

If the forms transformed upon one's own mind did not obstruct the forms transformed upon another's mind, then at the time of the fruition of the act of killing, one would only obtain the [karmic] acquisition (*prāpti*).

The *upādāya-rūpa* (supporting elements) transformed by one’s own consciousness should not damage the *upādāya-rūpa* transformed by another; likewise, their results should also be subject to treatment [of the afflictions].
Furthermore, regarding things such as the earth and grasses, which are all collectively transformed by all sentient beings:

when one digs them, one should be digging the earth transformed by one’s own consciousness and making it into something transformed by the consciousness of another, yet it does not become so. If one were to kill [them]...
When cutting down a tree, one should only cut the tree transformed by one's own consciousness; one should not damage the tree transformed by the consciousness of another.
For this reason, if one cuts a tree and damages the earth transformed by one's own consciousness, one also damages the earth transformed by another.

Thus, it is known that the form (rūpa) transformed upon one's own mind also obtains the form transformed by another. Although it is understood that the sense bases (indriya-sthāna) each transform their own and others' [objects],...
"Others also obtain the conditions for [perceiving] them or not. This passage serves as the introduction to the following treatise.

Although it is known that one's own and others' eighth consciousnesses (ālayavijñāna) undergo transformation to manifest as the primary and secondary objects (adhiṣṭhāna and upādāya-rūpa) of oneself and others, the eighth consciousness is likewise capable of taking the secondary objects of others as its cognitive objects.
Regarding "not occasionally borrowing consciousness": what is the meaning of these five kinds of power? What constitutes the essence of this power?
When asking about the majestic power of the Dharma and the power of great vows, how is it known that the transformed bodies and environments are such?
Furthermore, why are the transformed bodies and environments not fixed? The answer is as explained below.

Regarding the statement that "the *sūtra* may arise by borrowing consciousness": if it borrows the power of consciousness, then while the body is in one of the three higher dhyānas, it borrows the three consciousnesses—eye, ear, and body—from the first dhyāna to see forms, hear sounds, and touch objects. This is not what is directly intended here;

rather, it is a case where the primary meditative concentration (*samādhi*) takes secondary objects. If this refers to the primary intention regarding what is transformed by the eighth consciousness, then it takes only [that which is so transformed].

Regarding the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*): if one speaks of this in relation to the first six consciousnesses, it pertains to its own level (*svabhūmi*). This includes the power of borrowed consciousness (*jia-shi*), yet does not include the power of dharmas or the power of others.

That which is transformed by the power of others—namely, the bodies, vessels, and so forth of other levels—is indeterminate. By means of this power of concentration, one is able to transform objects such as bodies and vessels.
Furthermore, as a secondary provision, one may see lower levels while on a higher level, or see higher levels while on a lower level; thus it is cited.
"By borrowing the power of consciousness" refers to the actual grasping.

Regarding the commentary’s alternative explanation of "by the power of great vows": if a Bodhisattva on the [first] grounds wishes to transform sentient beings, they take birth in accordance with their vows;
if a Bodhisattva on the grounds, by means of the sixth mental consciousness, transforms pure (anāsrava) images within the mind of contemplative practice (vipaśyanā).
Regarding the fish body and so forth, the sound itself is transformed from the eighth consciousness. It manifests the body of a great fish to allow sentient beings to perceive it as such.

This great fish body manifested by the Bodhisattva serves as the objective basis (*ālambana-pratyaya*); the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) of the sentient beings then transforms into a fish body and devours it.

Now, speaking from the perspective of this objective basis, it is called a "result of meditative concentration" (*samādhi-phala*), meaning that [the Bodhisattva] does not actually transform into a fish body.

Therefore, when sentient beings take fish or meat, the Bodhisattva experiences no suffering. If a Bodhisattva prior to the stages (bhūmi) perceives sentient beings during an era of famine and gives rise to a mind of compassion, he then transforms his own fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) into the body of a fish as food and scatters it.

From the perspective of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), this is called a "result of meditative concentration" (*samādhiphala*). However, because it does not transform [the Bodhisattva's own body] into the body of a fish, [it is distinct from ordinary transformation].

When sentient beings take fish or meat, the Bodhisattva experiences no suffering. However, if a Bodhisattva prior to the stages (bhūmi) perceives sentient beings during an age of famine and gives rise to a heart of compassion, they then make a great vow:

"May my own body transform into the form of a fish so that when it is taken by others, I may experience pain. If, for the sake of all sentient beings, they enter into hell, they likewise experience pain.
Regarding suffering: although there is pain, by giving rise to a mind of weary detachment (*nirveda*), that suffering is immediately eliminated. As it is said in the *Madhyama Āgama*:
In a past life, the Buddha was a great king who saw a meteor appear in the heavens, portending twelve years of great drought.

He then made a great vow and transformed himself into the body of a massive red fish, seven hundred *li* in length, to relieve the hunger and deprivation of all beings. This is the [story from the] *Dì* [Sūtra].
Former Bodhisattvas, by the power of their great vows, manifested transformed bodies as fish and other such beings; even when their flesh was taken, they experienced suffering.

Regarding the phrase "or by the power of the Dharma," it is as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "By virtue of hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one attains the purification of the six sense faculties."

This refers to Bodhisattvas prior to the stages [of the ten bhūmis]. Even at the stage of the four roots of goodness (catur-kuśala-mūla), they do not attain the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*) merely by hearing the sūtras;
rather, it is solely through practicing the conduct of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā-caryā*) that they attain the purity of the six sense faculties.

This is also like the various devas of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), who attain clarity and purity in their celestial bodies by practicing the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action (*pañca-śīla-daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*). Why then would one doubt these Bodhisattvas? Much more so... [the rest of the sentence is omitted in the source].
At that time, through cultivation, one attains the purity of the sense-faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*). This Bodhisattva does not see or hear with the divine eye or ear;
rather, it is with the physical eye and ear that they are able to see the trichiliocosm. As for "the power of the Dharma," this refers to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
The power of the Dharma is the Dharma of the six *pāramitās*, which possesses such efficacy. It is precisely by means of the Bodhisattva...
Because one practices giving, one eliminates stinginess in the present and attains great wealth and so forth in the future; the same applies to the remaining [perfections].

According to the commentary, these [five perfections] apply to all consciousnesses. As for the eighth [consciousness], it possesses the power of meditative concentration and supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), through which it transforms bodies, objects, and so forth.
If we speak in terms of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), all such powers are induced by the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭha-vijñāna*).

Within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the seventh consciousness possesses no fixed supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) or the power of the Dharma (*dharma-prabhāva*). Within the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), there also arises the power of borrowed consciousness;

this refers specifically to the divine eye and divine ear. Regarding the power of the Dharma, there is also that which is obtained through hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, whereby one attains the six [supernormal powers].

This refers to the purity of the faculties (*indriya-viśuddhi*). This power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*) exists only within the sixth consciousness; the other consciousnesses all lack this power of concentration.

If, by means of the power of concentration, one transforms the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), then it pertains to all six consciousnesses as they take the "form produced by concentration" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) as their object.

[The other consciousnesses] all lack this power of concentration. If, by means of the power of concentration, one brings forth the five sense objects through transformation, then it pertains to all six consciousnesses as they take [these objects] as their object.

Regarding the matter of *nirmāṇa-rūpa* (created forms) and the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*): these also take *nirmāṇa-rūpa* as their object. This excludes only the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*).

As for those possessing supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), these powers pertain to three consciousnesses—namely, the sixth consciousness and the visual and auditory consciousnesses—which constitute the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) and the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*).
Through these supernormal powers, the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are manifested; these are also objects perceived by the aforementioned six consciousnesses, as well as the eighth.

Consciousness also takes this as its object, with the exception of the seventh consciousness. Question: In the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, it is stated that the untainted (*anāsrava*) seventh consciousness lacks the power of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).

How can this be so, given that since the untainted seventh consciousness abides [in its state], it must necessarily be accompanied by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and furthermore, that the seventh consciousness attains the ten kinds of the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) and manifests according to the inclinations of sentient beings? Why would it not be considered a supernormal knowledge?

[This is the] power. What kind of power is this? Answer: It is the power that can manifest various Buddha-bodies, or manifest gold, silver, and so forth, causing sentient beings to transform and experience [them as] objects of enjoyment;

thus, there are also forms that are the fruits of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*). According to the Sarvāstivāda, there are three kinds of retrogression: first, retrogression from what has already been attained (*prāpti-hāni*).
This refers to a certain class who either lose the fruit of Arhatship and also retrogress from the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha-vihāra*). Second...
First is "retrogression from what has not yet been attained," as in the case of arhats and others who have not yet attained the ten powers and four fearlessnesses within the Buddha-body;
regarding such unattained dharmas, all are termed "retrogression. Second is "non-retrogression despite not having attained," as in the case of bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward;

although they have not yet attained the ten powers and so forth within the Buddha-body, because they shall gradually attain them, this is called "non-retrogression despite not having attained. Third is "retrogression from enjoyment," as in the case of the six supernormal knowledges of a Buddha.
If one gives rise to the knowledge of rebirth (*upapatti-jñāna*), one cannot simultaneously give rise to the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*).

Just as when one gives rise to the knowledge of rebirth to observe the future, one cannot give rise to the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) to observe the past—because, according to that school, the six consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously—so it is with those [knowledges] that cannot arise together.

Regarding the "retrogression from enjoyment" (*paribhoga-vihāni*): according to the Mahāyāna interpretation, within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), a bodhisattva can simultaneously give rise to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

Question: Is it unknown whether there are śrāmaṇeras among arhats? Answer: The various schools differ on this point. According to the Mahāsāṃghika school, those in the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) across the three vehicles are all of the same category;
just as when one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), one simultaneously acquires the corresponding precepts. [This concludes] the answer regarding the Buddha’s attainment.
When practicing the path, one may become a Pratyekabuddha; such a person arises only in a world where no Buddha exists, because they do not receive [instruction] from a human teacher.
Therefore, they attain the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). The same applies to those who become Arhats.

Regarding the Mahāyāna Sarvāstivāda school, their tenets are identical to those of the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas. As for the nature of an Arhat, there are also śrāmaṇeras and srotāpannas who possess this nature.

Regarding "precepts": this refers to the fruit of the first stage (srotāpanna). Since one received the five precepts in a previous life, and that life has already been separated from the present, those five precepts have been relinquished.
Because one has not yet attained the fruit of the first stage, one remains within the nature of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Thus, regarding the five [precepts] such as not killing living beings and refraining from sexual misconduct, although one may have a legitimate wife and children, because one is still a layperson, one does not engage in external sexual misconduct; by nature, one does not commit such wrongs. This, however, does not mean that one possesses the [formal] precepts.

This is called "natural precept" (*prakṛti-śīla*). If one is a person of wrong conduct, it obstructs those who have attained the first two fruits [of the path]. If one engages in sexual desire, one is separated from the third fruit.

This is because even the attainment of the first fruit involves the presence of sexual desire. Even for an Arhat, by their very nature (*prakṛti*), they do not commit such acts; thus it is termed a "natural precept.
Even before one has received the Prātimokṣa vows, within the body of an Arhat there is already this precept, even though it has not yet been formally undertaken.
Upon receiving the precepts, one may still attain entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

However, if one possesses fixed karma (*niyata-karma*) for the three evil destinies, one cannot attain the first two fruits of the path. If an Arhat possesses fixed karma, they cannot enter the fixed path;
such fixed-karma individuals must undergo seven more rebirths among humans and devas. Only after completing these seven fixed-karma bodies does one finally attain the fruit of Arhatship.
If there is indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karma*), one may likewise enter the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*). The power of consciousness (*vijñāna*) thus extends through all four types of consciousness.

For example, when the body is situated within the three higher dhyāna stages, one borrows the three consciousnesses—eye, ear, and body—from the lower first dhyāna to perceive objects in those higher stages;

furthermore, one borrows the sixth consciousness (mental consciousness), along with its functions of vitarka and vicāra, from the first dhyāna to produce speech and inquire about the three higher dhyānas.
[Question: Among these, the sixth consciousness that arises simultaneously with the three consciousnesses of the divine eye, divine ear, and body—of which stage (*bhūmi*) is this sixth consciousness?
[Answer: That sixth consciousness is precisely the sixth consciousness of the First Dhyāna. Why is this?

Because, just as the three consciousnesses of the eye and so forth rely on their respective bases (*āśraya*), they must necessarily belong to the same stage. Furthermore, it is impossible for the eye, ear, or body consciousnesses of a lower stage to [arise] within the First Dhyāna.
Regarding the reliance upon the four consciousnesses of the upper [realms], these four consciousnesses are exclusively of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*); this is the Mahāyāna teaching.
The four consciousnesses borrowed [from below] are subsumed under "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) among the four types of indeterminate states.

Since "born of maturation" is broad in scope—much like a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*)—it is not the case that the four consciousnesses within the first or third dhyānas could be of a wholesome nature simply because the higher stages are not distant from the lower stages.

Because it is wholesome. This applies with the sole exception of an Ārya born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) who, relying on a lower stage, exhausts the remaining afflictions. If one’s body is in the Desire Realm, this is not fixed;
for example, Mahāmaudgalyāyana quickly entered the meditative absorption of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*).

His sixth consciousness was then a mind of the Sphere of Nothingness, yet he subsequently gave rise to an ear-consciousness of the Desire Realm and heard the trumpeting sound of a wild elephant in the Desire Realm. This is [an instance of] the Desire Realm.
Regarding the elements, ear-consciousness, and the faculties distinguished by the sphere of nothingness:

Question—Is it possible for a noble one who has not yet attained full knowledge, while residing in the fourth dhyāna and entering the four formless attainments, to give rise to eye- and ear-consciousness of the first dhyāna that take objects belonging to the desire realm? Answer—There is no such case.
If the body is in a lower stage, one may give rise to all [consciousnesses] of a higher stage; this is just as when the body is in the desire realm.

Among the four dhyānas, one may attain the neutral *abhijñā-phala* (fruition of supernormal powers), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), wholesome meditative absorption (*kuśala-samādhi*), and obscured afflictions (*nivṛta-kleśa*).

If the body is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one can give rise to obscured afflictions and wholesome meditative absorption belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), with the sole exception of the fruition of supernormal powers, because the fruition of supernormal powers does not exist in the formless realm.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, if the body is in the upper three dhyānas, one borrows [the faculties] from the first dhyāna.
The consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and so forth are all of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). They are subsumed under the category of indeterminate deportment (*airyāpathika-avyākṛta*).

This category of indeterminate deportment is broad, like a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). If one speaks of "power" (*prabhāva*), it extends throughout the first six consciousnesses; within each, there is the power of the Dharma.

For example, by upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one attains the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*). However, this refers specifically to the six faculties of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*); it does not include the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*).
Regarding the function of the sense faculties: the nose produced by one's parents in the desire realm can perceive the fragrance of the palaces in the formless realm.
As for the eighth consciousness perceiving the fragrance of those palaces, some say it can perceive it, while others say it cannot. Question: Since the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states this...

There is the power of the noble ones (*ārya-prabhāva*), the power of the Dharma (*dharma-prabhāva*), and the innate power (*sahaja-prabhāva*). Why, in this context, is only the power of the Dharma mentioned, while the other two powers are not included?
Answer: Prior to entering the stages (*bhūmi*), these are distinguished as individual powers; once one has entered the stages, they are collectively termed "the power of the noble ones.
