Commentary 1: Unwholesome [actions] that result in undesirable fruits refer to extremely evil dharmas; this refers to the eleven unwholesome destinies, as well as dharmas such as anger, resentment, and malice.
Commentary 2: Unwholesome [dharmas] by nature that lack skillfulness refer to defiled dharmas; this refers exclusively to obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) dharmas.
This is correct.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that the three natures are "unpeaceful" (*an-āśvāsika*) and "unwholesome" (*akuśala*), meaning "impure phenomena" (*sāsrava-dharma*), some interpret this as referring exclusively to non-obscured neutral phenomena (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Others explain it as including impure wholesome phenomena (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) as well. These impure wholesome phenomena, when contrasted with pure phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), are [considered] impure.
Because they are wholesome dharmas, they become unwholesome.
Regarding the "associated indeterminate" mentioned in the commentary, which refers to all indeterminate minds and mental factors:

if these are the mind and mental factors of the eighth consciousness, then six dharmas are of an indeterminate nature; if they are the associated mind and mental factors of the seventh consciousness, there are eighteen in total.

The *dharma* is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). Within the sixth consciousness, there are nine fundamental mental factors; among the remaining twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), there are the seven minor ones;
and including the four universal, specific-object, and indeterminate factors, there are thirty-six in total, one of which is of an indeterminate nature.
Furthermore, in the higher realms, one should understand accordingly that pride and the [faculties] such as the eye are excluded. As for the first five [consciousnesses]...

Within consciousness (*vijñāna*), there are six factors: the five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) that possess the meaning of "grasping" (*upalabdhi*), together with the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).

This is because the other five specific object-determining factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya-niyata*) do not abide within the five sensory consciousnesses. Therefore, within each of the five consciousnesses, every factor consists of these six dharmas.

Regarding the view that the five specific object-determining factors exist within the five sensory consciousnesses, those five consciousnesses would then possess eleven factors; this is their indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*).
If afflictions and so forth are added, the subsequent [sections] may be understood by analogy. Second, non-associated indeterminate [factors]:

this refers to indeterminate matter that is non-associated with formations (*saṃskāra*). Question: While it is appropriate to call formations "non-associated," how can the category of matter (*rūpa-dharma*) be called "associated"?
Furthermore, regarding the term "indeterminate matter" used here, does it refer to the five sense organs and their supporting objects (*upādāya-rūpa*), or does it refer to...?
Regarding the five external sense objects: the answer is that they are not the mind. Third, regarding "ultimately indeterminate" (*paramārtha-avyākṛta*):

the question asks what distinction there is between ultimate indeterminacy and the previously mentioned ultimate indeterminacy (*paramārtha-avyākṛta*). The answer is: it is in contrast to conditioned phenomena, which are illusory;

since space and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they are termed "ultimate. Furthermore, it is in contrast to the aforementioned conditioned conventional [phenomena] that...
Space and analytical cessation are what are termed the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Regarding "wholesome states associated with [the mind]," this refers to the mental states and mental factors associated with faith and so forth; specifically, it takes up the eight consciousnesses as the primary minds (*citta-rāja*).

Together with the five universal [mental factors], the five object-specific ones, and the four indeterminate ones—these twenty-two factors that possess the nature of wholesome phenomena are all termed "associated wholesome" (*saṃprayukta-kuśala*).

However, this must be distinguished: if one reaches the stage of Buddhahood, these eighteen factors—the eight mind-kings, the five universals, and the five object-specific ones—are called associated wholesome. If, however, one considers the causal stage, in the desire realm...

In the midst [of this], during the stages of hearing, reflecting, and meditating, within the category of wholesome factors conducive to merit (*puṇyabhāgīya-kuśala*), one takes the six consciousnesses as the mental kings (*cittarāja*), the five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyata*), and the four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*).
These dharmas are subsumed under the nature of associated wholesomeness (*saṃprayukta-kuśalatva*). The same applies to innate wholesome factors (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*).

If one attains the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā) of the higher stages, one correctly takes as the basis the sixth consciousness-king, along with the five universal mental factors, the five object-specific mental factors, and vitarka and vicāra;
these thirteen dharmas are subsumed under "associated wholesomeness" (saṃprayukta-kuśala), because remorse (kaukṛtya) and torpor (middha) are bound exclusively to the desire realm.

Within that cultivation of wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*), although it primarily apprehends the sixth consciousness, it also concurrently apprehends the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). This is because there is penetration within the eye-consciousness.
However, in the Mahāyāna it is taught that the six consciousnesses also possess innate goodness (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*), merit-partaking goodness (*puṇyabhāgīya-kuśala*), and cultivated wisdom.
If innate goodness arises within the sixth consciousness and induces the five consciousnesses, then innate goodness also arises within the five consciousnesses.

Regarding innate wholesome states: within the sixth consciousness, there arises the wholesome pertaining to the category of merit (*puṇyabhāgīya*). This induces the arising of the wholesome pertaining to the category of merit within the five sensory consciousnesses;

thus, within the five sensory consciousnesses, the wholesome pertaining to the category of merit also arises. Its substance is meditative wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), which properly belongs to the sixth consciousness.

As for the substance of the preceding five consciousnesses, it is not the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) or reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), yet it also includes that which is accomplished through cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*). That is to say, the first five consciousnesses may also be termed "wisdom accomplished through hearing."

This refers to the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Furthermore, within the Mahāyāna school, it is taught that even the five sensory consciousnesses may be conventionally designated as "wisdom born of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

For example, when Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, while in a state of meditative concentration within the sixth consciousness, evoke the five sensory consciousnesses such as the visual consciousness.
The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, may also be termed "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*), because they are induced by that which is outflow-free.

Furthermore, what is induced by these five consciousnesses may also be termed "cultivated wisdom" (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*), because it is induced by the cultivated wisdom within the sixth consciousness. This is analogous to the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

It may also be termed "untainted" (*anāsrava*). This is because the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is induced by the untainted, and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is likewise capable of inducing the untainted.
Within the category of tainted wholesome states, the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is subsumed under partial wholesomeness.

Within the category of untainted wholesome states, the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is also termed "wholesome by way of state" (*avasthika-kuśala*). To explain these types of wholesomeness, see the following explanation of the fifty [dharmas].
Within the section on the "single-mind" (ekacitta), each entry is explained by itself; this should be verified by consulting the subsequent text.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The three types of wholesome [states] refer to contaminated wholesome form and non-associated formations, and so forth," the same principle applies by extension.

That which is virtuous by way of origination (*samutthāna-kuśala*) is so because the mind is virtuous; it causes the body and speech to perform such acts as joining the palms and prostrating, whereby even the physical form (*rūpa*) becomes virtuous.
Furthermore, both informative form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) and the non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) derived from it are also virtuous forms by way of origination.
Because the manifesting mind that perfumes is virtuous, the seeds formed by that perfuming are also virtuous. As it is asked: "What is a seed?"

Excellent. One should answer: seeds are subsumed solely under "wholesome by way of origination" (*samutthāna-kuśala*). Furthermore, the seeds of the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) are also subsumed under "wholesome by way of origination.
Moreover, the four characteristics such as acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth are likewise subsumed under "wholesome by way of origination."

Commentary: First, regarding those that are unwholesome by nature (*svabhāva-akuśala*), namely the ten mental factors such as shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) which are exclusively unwholesome mental concomitants: these are the ten unwholesome mental states:

(1) anger (*krodha*), (2) enmity (*upanāha*), (3) vexation (*pradāsa*), (4) avarice (*mātsarya*), (5) envy (*īrṣyā*), (6) concealment (*mrakṣa*), (7) harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), (8) shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), (9) lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), and (10) hatred (*dveṣa*).

These ten types are subsumed under the category of being exclusively unwholesome in nature. Second, regarding those that are unwholesome through association (*samprayoga-akuśala*), they are as follows:

Within the fundamental [afflictions], there are five: namely, greed (*rāga*), delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, from among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), eleven factors are taken:
namely, the eight great secondary afflictions, along with flattery (*śāṭhya*), deception (*māyā*), and arrogance (*mada*). Thus, one takes these eleven factors from the afflictions.

Additionally, the universal (*sarvatraga*) factors, the five object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) factors, the four indeterminate (*aniyata*) factors, and the six primary consciousnesses (*citta-rāja*) are taken. These constitute the universal and object-specific [mental factors].
Among the six objects of the six consciousnesses, those that universally take on an unwholesome nature are all "unwholesome by association" (*saṃprayukta-akuśala*).

This includes the thirty-six factors previously enumerated, which are subsumed under unwholesomeness by association. The ten factors—greed, hatred, anger, and harm—are subsumed as "unwholesome by intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-akuśala*).
The commentary states that because they give rise to the unwholesome, the seeds of unwholesome form and non-associated formations are likewise so.

This refers to manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti-karman*); because the mind is unwholesome, the form produced is also unwholesome, such as the form of the unwholesome restraint (*dauḥśīlya-saṃvara*) of a butcher.
Furthermore, the four characteristics, such as acquisition (*prāpti*), are likewise [unwholesome] because the active mind is unwholesome. Thus...
The perfuming that forms seeds is also an unwholesome seed; it is subsumed within "unwholesome by way of origination" (*samutthāna-akuśala*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "ultimately unwholesome refers to contaminated phenomena" (*sāsrava-dharma*), this refers exclusively to wholesome contaminated phenomena.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the first type of transformation consists of the indeterminate mind-kings and mental factors": this refers to the *vipākaja-citta* (mind born of maturation) within the first six consciousnesses that is produced by karma;
specifically, it is the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) and the seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) which transform to give rise to the image portion (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Furthermore, the self-witnessing portion and the seeing portion of the eighth consciousness are also included.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The indeterminate [dharmas] transformed by the two [minds], up to their seeds, are likewise so”: this refers to the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*).

This is comprised within the indeterminate matter that is transformed; it is the seed perfumed by the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika-citta*), which is termed the "indeterminate seed of co-arising" (*samutthāna-avyākṛta-bīja*).
As for the "indeterminate of the three stages," this refers to the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) such as acquisition (*prāpti*), and so forth.
The treatise states that the processes of transmigration and cessation would not be possible;

however, since nirvāṇa constitutes the realm (dhātu) and all sentient beings are within the realm of nirvāṇa, their wandering through birth and death is itself the origin of suffering (duḥkha-samudaya). Now, because the noble path is directed toward nirvāṇa, [cessation is established].

This is called "returning. Therefore, the Truth of the Path is named "returning. It is like fleeing from one's home, which is called "transmigration," whereas returning to one's dwelling is called "returning."

Regarding the statement that "the same applies to the inversion in the evil destinies": because they are unwholesome, it is known that they cannot serve as a basis for the attainment of the wholesome.

Second, regarding the statement that "because the essence of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas is superior to indeterminate dharmas, they are therefore called 'determined' (*niyata*)," the term "superior essential nature" refers to the wholesome with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*). The term "harmonious" refers precisely to the wholesome with outflows. The term "discordant" refers precisely to the [unwholesome].
[This refers to] outflowing unwholesome karma. Regarding that which is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), even if one were to say it is likewise for this reason, [the author] asks:
Why does the first master state that only the indeterminate nature of the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is cited as an analogy, and not further cite other categories?
The answer is: In the verse it is stated that these are "unobscured-neutral" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), and it is added that "contact and so forth are likewise.

Since it says immediately after the mention of the neutral that "contact and so forth are likewise," it follows that contact and the others are taken here as being exclusively of a neutral nature. This is the intended meaning of this master.

For example, regarding the substance of consciousness, five meanings are identical. Even though it is said that "there are only four," if one cannot establish a separate category for the "unknowable," this master would instead apply it to the five categories: first, maturation; second, the object and aspect, both of which are unknowable;
third, the objects of cognition, which are the three types of objects mentioned within the third category, and which have no separate substance apart from that. Its...
The aspect (*ākāra*) is the discernment (*vijñapti*) of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*). Because it functions by means of aspects, it apprehends only that which is unknowable.
It has three conditions, three types of objects, four or five associated mental factors, and is undefiled-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). This is excluding the gate of the unknowable.

There are only four categories: first, maturation (*vipāka*); second, the three types of objects as conditions; third, association with the five factors; and fourth, being non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Regarding the question in the *Śāstra*: "Do the five factors, such as contact (*sparśa*), coexist in the fundamental consciousness? and so forth—even other similar examples pose the same difficulty—this is the question posed here.
Regarding the five factors such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth: among these ten categories, one takes the *vipāka* (maturation) category as an example;

from the category of the three types of objects, one takes the *saṃprayukta* (associated) category as an example; and from the category of the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), one takes the "unknowable" category as an example.
Since the mind and mental factors alike contact their objects through contact and so forth, and since it has now been stated that the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is always accompanied by contact—
They are associated. However, the mind-king (citta-rāja) is associated with the five mental factors (caitta-dharma), such as contact (sparśa) and so forth;
yet these six dharmas each have distinct modes of activity (ākāra). That is to say: consciousness has the mode of activity of discerning; contact has the mode of activity of contacting the object;

feeling has the mode of activity of experiencing; attention has the mode of activity of alerting the mind; perception has the mode of activity of grasping images; and volition has the mode of activity of forming an impulse.

Regarding their modes of activity (*ākāra*): the substance of these six modes of activity is distinct for each. However, if one considers their mutual interpenetration, contact (*sparśa*) is also associated with five factors;

that is, contact itself is associated with mind, attention (*manasikāra*), volition (*cetanā*), and feeling (*vedanā*). As for feeling (*vedanā*), excluding its own self-substance, it is associated with the other four.
This means that feeling (*vedanā*) is associated with contact (*sparśa*), mental intention (*manasikāra*), volition (*cetanā*), the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), and so forth.
Thus, the mind-king can be associated with five factors. However, according to the verse, it is not stated that it is always associated with existent factors;

therefore, in the treatise, mental concomitants (*caitta*) cannot be obtained [as being the mind-king itself], because they are associated with the mind-king. Consequently, mental concomitants such as contact and the rest are excluded from the mind.

Regarding the king [of mental factors]: contact (*sparśa*) and the others can only be associated with four [mental factors]. That is to say, contact—excluding contact itself—is not associated with contact;

thus, contact is associated only with the four factors of attention (*manaskāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*). As for feeling, excluding the substance of feeling itself...
Feeling (*vedanā*) does not associate with feeling; feeling also associates with contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), and mental factors (*dharma*).
This applies likewise up to perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth. Now, regarding this intermediate point: the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) can indeed associate with five factors.
Since the mind-king can associate with five factors, the mental concomitants (*caitta*) are taken as an analogy for the mind-king; thus, those mental concomitants can only associate with four.

It is associated with the dharma. However, among the five [factors] such as contact (*sparśa*), is there perhaps one that is so? Now, regarding the mental factors (*caitta*) as well, they follow the same principle as the primary mind (*cittarāja*) in their mode of activity (*ākāra*).
Do these mental factors also possess the capacity for discernment (*prativijñapti*)?

The Commentary replies: Since the other gates are common [to all], they may all be treated as analogous. As for the statement that the aspect of "discernment" (*vijñapti*) is already established, how can it be claimed that contact (*sparśa*) and the others are analogous?
Because the other gates, such as the gate of maturation (*vipāka*), are common to all five [mental factors], contact and the others may indeed be treated as analogous.

Furthermore, while the five factors beginning with contact are merely analogous to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), they are associated with four factors; namely, contact is associated with feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), intention (*cetanā*), and [volition].

Regarding "correspondence" (*saṃprayukta*) and so forth: this refers to the four points of identity and one point of difference between the mental factors (*caitta*) and the mental sovereign (*cittarāja*). As for the one point of difference:

it means that contact (*sparśa*) and the other mental factors cannot be analogized to the aspect of activity (*ākāra*) of the mental sovereign, because they also possess the function of discernment (*vijñapti*).

Discernment belongs exclusively to the mental sovereign; since contact and the others are mental factors, they cannot be analogized to the sovereign in its discernment. This fails as a defense, and so on, up to the point regarding contact.

Regarding the point that "contact and the others should likewise be associated with themselves": the intent of this objection is as follows. The mind-king (citta-rāja) is associated with contact (sparśa) and the ten material factors (daśa rūpa-dharmāḥ).

Since contact and the others are treated by analogy with the mind-king—just as the mind-king is associated with contact—so too, by analogy with the mind-king, contact should be associated with contact.
Likewise, feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā) should be associated with feeling. [The opponent] asks: what was the objection in the preceding text?

[Question: You have also caused [the mental factors] such as contact (*sparśa*) to follow the same pattern as the mental king (*citta-rāja*), [asserting that] their mode of activity (*ākāra*) is likewise "discernment" (*vijñapti*). Now, I raise a further objection:

would this not contradict the previous objection by making contact itself correspond to contact? [Answer: There is a slight difference, but the general meaning is the same. This reasoning is incorrect.
According to what is appropriate, even the feeling (*vedanā*) associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*) should also be [considered] "feeling," and so forth.

Regarding the establishment of the example: this is precisely a counter-objection directed at the opponent. If other mental factors such as contact (*sparśa*) were to correspond with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), then they would be identical [to the case of contact].
However, among the mental factors, feeling (*vedanā*) itself does not correspond with the feeling of equanimity, because feeling cannot correspond with feeling.

Therefore, it is a counter-objection directed at the opponent. Fourth, as for discernment (*vijñapti*), it resides in consciousness (*vijñāna*); by analogy with contact, discernment is the same, yet it differs from equanimity.
Regarding association with feeling (*vedanā*): when feeling is acquired, it is associated with equanimity; once feeling has been acquired, it cannot be associated with equanimity.
Therefore, one should know that it cannot be analogized to the mental king (*citta-rāja*), which performs the function of discerning (*vijñapti*).

The "unconscious" (*asamvidita*) is not included alongside the others. Excluding the previously mentioned "gate of specific characteristics," there are seven gates: first, the single maturation; second, all seeds; third, the unconscious;

fourth, the appropriated basis; fifth, the gate of association with contact and so forth; sixth, the gate of association with the feeling of equanimity; and seventh, the gate of the non-obscured neutral.
According to the structural principles of this treatise, even when it is not necessarily a distinct teaching, this passage refers to the single [unconscious] itself.

According to the intent of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, if one follows the correct doctrine of the ten masters, wisdom (*prajñā*) and discernment (*mati*) are combined into a single meaning for the sake of clarification.
However, regarding the erroneous doctrines of the heterodox schools, they are provisionally established as separate masters; thus, these four [masters] represent many different interpretations.

Regarding the *Vyākhyā* on Vasubandhu’s *Triṃśikā-bhāṣya*, which explains the four criteria for being a perfumable basis (*bhāvanīya*) by separately establishing the criterion of "possessing mastery" (*vaśitva*), this commentary actually combines it with the explanation within the four criteria for being a perfumable basis. It is now cited here.

The author of the *Vyākhyā* also considers that, in addition to the four [criteria] for being a perfumable basis in Vasubandhu’s *Triṃśikā-bhāṣya*, one must further add the criterion of "possessing mastery" for something to truly be a perfumable basis.
The Commentary answers the question regarding the cause, stating: "That which possesses power and is capable of perfuming, yet is not itself perfumed, is the present activity acting as the perfumer;

'perfuming' here refers to the cause. Regarding the statement that "the mental factors (caitta) that can perfume—namely, the object-aspect (nimittabhāga) and the seeing-aspect (darśanabhāga)—merely follow the five categories and so forth," the question asks:
"How can they be said to merely follow the five categories when there are six kinds? The intended meaning is that there are five [categories].
Regarding mental factors (*caitta*): when they act as perfumers (*vāsaka*), there are five corresponding perfuming mental factors that perfume and form five seeds.

For example, in a single aggregate (*kalāpa*) of mind and mental factors, there are the five omnipresent (*sarvatraga*) factors and the five object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) factors, together with the mind-king (*cittarāja*), totaling eleven [factors] which perfume and form five seeds.
Thus, within a single aggregate of mind and mental factors, there are the five omnipresent factors and the five... [object-specific factors].
Regarding the object-specific mental states (*viṣaya-viniyata*) together with the mind-kings (*citta-rāja*), there are eleven factors capable of perfuming (*bhāvaka*).
When these take the eighteen spheres (*dhātu*) as their objects, at the very moment the mind-king arises simultaneously with form (*rūpa*), eighteen seeds are perfumed within a single thought-moment.
This is because even sensation (*vedanā*) perfumes eighteen seeds; thus, within each of the eleven positions of the mind-kings, eighteen seeds are all individually perfumed.
If ten dharmas take one hundred dharmas as their objects, there is a mind-king (*citta-rāja*) that, within a single moment, acquires one hundred seeds;
likewise, the remaining ten mental factors (*caitta*), each within a single moment, individually perfume and acquire one hundred seeds.
The rest should be understood accordingly. Furthermore, it is like ten mental factors acting as the perfuming agents for one [mind].
The fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*). As for those ten mental factors (*caitta*), they merely follow their own capacity to perfume;
repeatedly, each individually perfumes the seeds of the ten seeing-parts (*darśanabhāga*) and image-parts (*nimittabhāga*) of the fundamental consciousness.

Among these ten mental factors, not each one individually possesses all six [perfections]. If the five [aggregates] are the perfumable matter, then the ten perfuming mental factors perfume and produce the six [perfections].
There are ten types [of seeds], which would entail the contradiction of having six fruits.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "If the six dharmas receive perfuming and subsequently arise individually," even within the minimum number of perfuming factors, it refers to one mind-king and five mental associates—these six dharmas. Since the perfumer and the perfumed are of one essence, at the time of perfuming...
Accordingly, there are six types of seeds. If there are six [factors] capable of perfuming, and six [factors] that are perfumed, then their substance consists of six;
thus, there are thirty-six seeds (six times six). If the seeds of the seeing-part and the seen-part are distinct, there are now seventy-two seeds.
If there are ten [factors] capable of perfuming the mind and mental factors, and six [factors] that are perfumed, then together there would be sixty seeds.

The Commentary asks: Regarding the lack of contradiction in the case where the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) produces six fruits simultaneously, it is as follows:

just as the fundamental consciousness is not self-perfuming but must rely on the perfuming of the preceding seven consciousnesses, consider for instance when the seventh consciousness takes the eighth consciousness as its object.

At that time, the mind-king and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the seventh consciousness together comprise eighteen entities. These eighteen minds and mental factors all take the fundamental consciousness as their common object.
Consciousness: within a single thought-moment, it perfumes and forms eighteen seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

Later, when the actual manifestations (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise, there is also the simultaneous arising of eighteen consciousnesses; such is the objection regarding the multiplicity of fruits. The intent of the question is as follows:
"What prevents me from asserting that what is perfumed now will later give rise to six fruits simultaneously? Since those mental factors (*caitta*) are also like that, even if other [factors]..."

The six consciousnesses and their associated mental factors arise simultaneously with their respective objects; furthermore, the five categories of mental factors also perfume [the seeds] in multiple ways.
Consequently, when they arise later, there would likewise be the logical fault of multiple fruits arising all at once.
One cannot discuss the production or non-production of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) regarding the six kinds of objects thus perfumed.

What is being discussed here is the image produced by the mental factors (*caitta*) arising upon the remaining consciousness (*jñāna*). This refers to the understanding that the mind-king (*cittarāja*) produces the essential nature and so forth;
one must not discuss its essential nature. One should further inquire into the stage where the image is produced.
The commentary states: "This is also not the case; the analogy for being perfumed should be thus, up to the phrase 'the images produced. This is an intentional analogy used as an explanation.
Mental factors (*caitta*) are not what is perfumed. Just as mental factors cannot produce an original substance (*bimba*), they can only produce an image (*pratibimba*)."

"The mind-king (*cittarāja*) is capable of receiving perfuming (*vāsanā*), because it gives rise to the essential nature (*svabhāva*); thus, the principle of 'receiving' should be understood accordingly.

This second interpretation, which states that "according to the true meaning, when seeds are perfumed by the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), there is likewise no logical error regarding [its acting as] an object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) or even a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*"), is also not the correct doctrine. It belongs to the master *Ratnamati*, who established only...

Regarding the originally existing seeds: when a perfuming mind and its mental factors take the fundamental consciousness as their object, that perfuming mind merely perfumes the originally existing seeds within the consciousness, thereby increasing one such originally existing seed.
This alone gives rise to a single entity of the fundamental consciousness and serves as its direct cause (hetu-pratyaya).
When it subsequently perfumes the mind and its mental factors, although there are many such instances, they are all subsumed under the category of the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
Thus, there would be no obstacle to the simultaneous production of six fruits, nor would there be any obstacle to the production of a single sprout from multiple seeds.

If that were the case—that numerous newly perfumed seeds produced the fundamental consciousness—then there would be the fault of many seeds producing a single sprout; this, however, is not the correct principle.
Furthermore, another interpretation is that this commentary text means: the seeds of karma nourish a single seed of name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*) within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

Just as when a single thought arises, the volition (*cetanā*) at that same moment is the essence of karma; simultaneously, during the time of the other four aggregates—contact, feeling, and so forth—they are termed "seeds of karma.
The attendants of these seeds of karma are also designated by the name "karma. Thus, it is said that many karmas collectively bring about the fundamental [consciousness].

One should understand that there is a seed of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*) that is innately present. This seed of names and phrases produces a manifestation of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

In this process, the seeds produced by the collective karma of many beings act as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), while the seeds of the fundamental consciousness itself act as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
As for the term "innately present seed," it is called an innately present seed because it was already perfumed (*vāsita*) in the past.
It is not that seeds existing from the beginning (hon-yū) are called "existing from the beginning"; rather, it refers to a single seed of name-and-form (myōgon).

Because this gives rise to the actual manifestation (gen-gyō) of the fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna), there is no fault of a single sprout being produced from multiple seeds. This interpretation, however, is also not the correct doctrine.

The Commentary further posits that each perfuming agent individually perfumes a seed within a single fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), because the substance of the consciousness that maintains them is one;
this is the third interpretation, which represents the orthodox view of Master Hu.

When perceiving the fundamental consciousness, although the perfuming minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are numerous, each individually perfumes a seed within the single fundamental consciousness. Later, perhaps ten...
There is no contradiction in [multiple] seeds of the same kind arising together as a single entity of the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Alternatively, five seeds or even seeds belonging to two different realms may arise together as a single manifest activity (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). This is just as many atoms within a single grain of barley collectively produce a single sprout;
is it not the same here? However, it is absolutely impossible for multiple seeds of different kinds to arise together as a single manifest activity.
This interpretation is the correct meaning. Regarding the point that there is no contradiction in six types [of seeds] arising together to produce a single fruit:
it is asked, if many seeds arise together to produce a single manifesting state (*pravṛtti*), then should not a single seed also be able to produce many manifesting states?

Furthermore, they should also frequently manifest and collectively permeate to form a single seed. Moreover, it should be that a single preceding moment [of consciousness] produces one [subsequent] kind.
If you say that such dharmas do not exist, how can multiple [causes] together produce a single manifestation?

If you say that multiple [causes] produce one manifestation—just as many atoms within a single grain of barley together produce a single sprout, and within that single sprout there is one... [atom]—then [the same principle applies here].

[Objection: "Subtle particles (*paramāṇu*). Your analogy is equally unestablished. It is not that many subtle particles within a single sprout produce many [subtle particles]; rather, it is that many [subtle particles] together produce one subtle particle.

This would mean that multiple types produce multiple manifest activities (*pravṛtti*), and thus your analogy is also unestablished. Furthermore, the textual passage has not yet shown that multiple types produce a single sprout.
[Response: The answer is that the subsequent [moment] is able to sustain the preceding multiplicity.
Regarding the statement that although there are six types of perfuming agents (*bhāvakavijñāna*), they do not manifest separately as a single fruit produced by co-arising causes and conditions:

there are six perfuming agents, and they in turn perfume to form six seeds. It is absolutely impossible for these six manifesting perfuming consciousnesses to act together to perfume and produce a single resultant seed through any other cause and condition. Such a thing cannot exist.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) receive their retribution within a single lifetime”:

the five deeds of immediate retribution consist of five seeds of karma that collectively induce a single body for entry into the Avīci Hell. This is because the retribution for the offenses is fivefold.

This explanation is formulated from the perspective of the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving portion) acting as the perfuming agent; however, this *darśana-bhāga* takes the *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived portion) as its object, and it is within the *nimitta-bhāga* that the perfuming is established.

Regarding the seeds of the eighth consciousness: Question—As with the seventh consciousness, it perfumes seeds of its own seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) within its objective-image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).
How is it that the objective-image-part lacks the perfuming of cognitive apprehension (*ālambana-vicāra*), while the seeing-part possesses seeds of cognitive apprehension?

Answer—Because the seeing and image parts of the eighth consciousness do not perfume each other, it is able to perfume seeds of the eighth consciousness’s own seeing and image parts within the objective-image-part of another [consciousness].
Regarding the seeds:
according to the old and new commentaries on causes and conditions, there are six types of perfuming factors, down to a single grain of barley containing many atoms (*paramāṇu*).
However, if these newly perfumed seeds and the originally existing seeds of the same kind both encounter their respective conditions, then these two seeds will now arise together.

It is also possible for a single manifest activity (*samudācāra*) to arise. Alternatively, it is also possible for only those seeds existing by nature (*prakṛti-stha*) to encounter conditions and give rise to a single manifest activity.
Or, it is also possible for newly perfumed seeds (*navasaṃskṛta-bīja*) to likewise give rise to a single manifest activity.

Or, it is also possible for ten seeds of the same kind or twenty seeds of a similar class to simultaneously encounter conditions and together produce one manifest activity. For example, as in the case of one [person].
Within a grain of barley, there are many atoms that arise together to produce a single sprout.

[The author] refutes the Sautrāntika position that material form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) each have their own seeds and arise together to produce a single fruit, asserting instead that seeds are maintained within both the material and the mental;
thus, with seeds present in both locations simultaneously, they arise together to produce a single sprout.
The Commentary states: "In this context, it is easy to understand that this has a measure, as it says:

'When your initial seed arises, the seed also produces an impression (vāsanā), because they are simultaneous and equal in force, just like the initially produced seed. It is difficult [to deny] that the initially produced seed is likewise so."
Regarding the statement that Maheśvara has three eyes on his face: this is not what is taught within the Buddha-dharma; rather, it is a claim made among the monastics of the West (India).
They say that in the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*), Maheśvara has three eyes on his face.

Furthermore, the monastics of that Western land do not maintain that the palace of Maheśvara is located in the Heaven of Ultimate Purity (*Akaniṣṭha*), because they lack such knowledge. As for that Buddha...
It is stated in the Dharma that Maheśvara has only two eyes; however, Maheśvara is none other than those gods within the Bṛhatphala Heaven.
The Buddha-Dharma further explains that this refers to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā and the Dharmakāya of liberation.
When these three conditions are complete, it is just as described in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi* regarding Maheśvara; it is similar to that. Question:
The Dragon King has eighty thousand eyes; what sacred teaching should this be abandoned as?

Furthermore, just as a person’s two eyes have but one visual consciousness, [is it the case that] in the two eyes of a human, consciousness arises simultaneously from both, or does it arise sequentially?
Regarding eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*): the answer is that two eyes simultaneously produce consciousness; it is not the case that eye-consciousness is produced sequentially.

As for the "fruit" (*phala*), the commentary does not provide a separate illustration here. Why is this? Because the mind-king (*cittarāja*) transforms the seeds of the sense organs (*indriya-bīja*) and material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), all of which possess actual efficacy.

If the seeds transformed by the five [sensory consciousnesses] were the sense organs, they would lack practical utility; however, the matter (rūpa) they transform possesses the utility of resistance (sapratigha). If one objects:

"Because this matter is transformed by mental factors (caitta), because it lacks sovereignty, and because matter has the utility of non-resistance, then the matter transformed by the mental factors associated with the five consciousnesses should also possess the utility of non-resistance.
[To this we reply: That which is transformed by the mental factors of the five consciousnesses...

Form (*rūpa*) is characterized by the function of resistance (*pratigha*). If this principle is applied by analogy to the five objects of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), one knows that within a single moment, the five objects of the fundamental consciousness can possess two types of sensation (*vedanā*).
This is the same for the mental factors (*caitta*) of the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*).

According to this interpretation in the *Chao*, and furthermore according to the Sarvāstivāda masters, the present four great elements (*mahābhūta*) act as simultaneous causes (*sahabhūhetu*) for the present form; they exist at the same time as they are perceived.

Regarding the sensation produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) at a distance, and the non-resistant derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) that follows it, the derived matter is not a simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for those [elements].

This is because one must avoid the case where distant non-resistant matter is not a simultaneous cause; thus, it is also made so that present derived matter does not constitute a simultaneous cause for present great elements.
Since the Master of the Commentary (*Śāstrakāra*) does not accept the five [factors] of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*)...

Regarding the five unimpeded [objects] transformed by various mental factors (*caitta*), they too should not possess the function of being impeded, as the matter transformed by the five consciousnesses and their mental factors is obstructive.

Rather, it should be that only the five consciousnesses as mental kings (*cittarāja*), together with the matter transformed by the mental king of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), possess the function of being obstructive.
Thus, together with the Sarvāstivādins, one must set aside the case of non-obstructive form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) that is distant.

This would cause the present four great elements (*mahābhūta*) to simultaneously produce derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), which would also fail to establish them as simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*). As for these six faculties, such as the eye, which exist at the same time:

the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*) each transform into a complete set of five faculties; these six sets of five faculties all occupy the same location and exist at the same time.

They do not inquire of one another. Furthermore, the treatise states that fire is incapable of burning its own user. According to this text, within the Great Mirror [of the Mind] there are lateral [manifestations].
In reality they do not exist, yet they appear as if they do.

The commentary states that there are two types of appropriation (*upādāna*): first, the five material sense-faculties up to the seeds, which are both capable of being appropriated and are themselves objects of appropriation.
If one were to offer this defense: "In the third section on 'all seeds,' it clarifies the conditions for seeds;

whereas in the fourth section on 'appropriation,' it merely speaks of appropriating the sense-faculties and the body, and taking the sense-faculties and the body as its object. [The opponent argues: "In the fourth section, appropriation is not explained [in the manner of the third]."

[Regarding] the seed: because it takes the seed as its object. Now, they raise this objection: "Just as in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the seeds and the five sense organs, along with their supporting objective fields (*viṣaya*), are said to be grasped (*upātta*) together within the same gateway and to have the same single location as their object; why do you [then] claim that [the ālayavijñāna] takes the seed as its object?"
That is to say, in the third gate, it grasps the appropriated body and takes that body as its object; and in the fourth gate, it concerns the seeds.
It is not permitted for [the seeds] to be explained separately from the body within the gate of appropriation. Therefore, you should know that what you have said is incorrect.
The commentary’s examples are the same as those for the five gates; now, adding the *āśraya* (basis) gate up to "it may be known by analogy with the meaning," [the following are excluded]:

first, the gate of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); that is, excluding the gate of all-seed (*sarvabījaka*), the gate of the modes of consciousness (*vijñāna-ākāra*), and the gate of being constantly associated with contact (*sparśa*).
Why? Because contact is not constantly associated with itself. If one speaks merely of the gate of association (*saṃprayoga*), it may also be applied by analogy.
[The term] "taking" (upādāna) [is used]. If one follows the gate of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), it must also be excluded, because feeling cannot be associated with equanimity itself.
If one excludes feeling, the remaining factors such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth can indeed be associated with equanimity.
However, this cannot be analogously applied to the abandonment (*prahāṇa*) gate. Why? Because in the state of an Arhat, only the *ālayavijñāna* of the mind-king is abandoned.
The term "ye" (ya) refers to the name for the non-interruption of the five mental factors (*caitta*). Therefore, one cannot take it to mean "interruption.

Furthermore, if one were to interpret it broadly according to its meaning within the prose section, it would refer to the substance of the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), which the Bodhisattva relinquishes when about to attain enlightenment.

Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas abandon [the storehouse consciousness] upon entering the nirvāṇa without remainder; thus, we know that when they abandon the vipākavijñāna, they also abandon the mental factors (caitta).
Therefore, one may also understand this through the gate of "severing and abandoning" (prahāṇa). As for the others who take [the ālayavijñāna] as common, it should be understood accordingly.

Regarding the exclusion of those schools who hold [the self] to be neither eternal nor annihilated: this is to distinguish them from the Śrāvaka schools who maintain that the substratum of the saṃgha (saṃgha-āśraya) is eternal by its very nature (svabhāva-nitya); therefore, it is said to be "non-[eternal]."

"Permanent" (*nitya*): This is stated to distinguish [the ālayavijñāna] from the Sautrāntika view that material form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) maintain the seeds; thus, it is said to be "not interrupted. Regarding the four characteristics—"1.

indeterminate," "2. stable," and so forth up to "4. associated"—which are capable of being perfumed by consciousness: First, "indeterminate nature" (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*) refers to what was previously described in the treatise as "one class of continuity" (*eka-jāti-prabandha*), because it is the basis for the designation of realms (*dhātu*), destinies (*gati*), and births (*yoni*).
Second, "stable" (*dṛḍha*) refers to what was previously described in the treatise as "nature that is firmly maintained" (*dṛḍha-dhṛti-svabhāva*).
First, it must be capable of being perfumed (*bhāvya*). Second, it must be impermanent; because it is not permanent or unitary, the preceding cause ceases and the subsequent fruit arises.
Third, it must be "perfumable" (*vāsya*); that is, it can be perfumed by the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), as illustrated by the analogy of water provided in the following text.

As stated in the seventh [chapter]: "It is like the waves on water, which follow its quantity and so forth"—this is the point. Question: How is it that it is "constantly revolving" (*nitya-parivartana*) like a torrent?

Regarding the gate of the constant non-interruption of cause and effect within the "flow": it takes only the seeds as cause and effect; however, it also takes the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) and so forth as cause and effect.

The answer is that this refers specifically to the eighth consciousness in its active manifestation, which revolves perpetually like a violent torrent. As for "flooding the water above and below": [it means]...
Question: Can water float upon water? How is it called "floating"?
The commentary states that the Saṃmitīya school and others hold that the past and future exist. However, the Saṃmitīya also establishes the existence of the past and future time-periods.
As for the mention of the Black Mountains (*Kṛṣṇaparvata*) as an analogy: according to the calculation of the Brahmins of the Western Regions, when the sun sets, nine black mountains [arise].
Mountains can reveal the sun. The Master of the Commentary (Suzhu) here cites a common worldly phenomenon.

In the context of the Buddha-dharma, if the sun is at a great distance, when one eats facing due west and the sun sets, it is as if a person standing nearby sees clouds or stars rising upward, yet from a distance those same clouds appear to be entering the earth; the setting of the sun is likewise.
Regarding the phrase "the former perishes and the latter arises": according to the preceding section of the treatise, this refers to the former perishing and the latter arising.

Regarding the statement in the commentary, "First one merely refuted annihilation; now one also refutes permanence": "first merely refuting annihilation" refers to the passage in the preceding treatise which states:
"Since the past and future are not substantially existent, it may be granted that they are not permanent, but how can they be non-annihilated? and so forth.
Furthermore, it is difficult for [the cause] to remain constant even now. As the treatise states: "While in the state of simultaneous presence, the subsequent fruit has not yet arisen;

because the subsequent fruit has not yet arisen, there is no subsequent fruit. This constitutes the difficulty regarding cessation. At the time when the fruit is present, the preceding cause has already ceased.
If the fruit manifests as the fruit of something, then at the time when the fruit manifests, the preceding cause would be without its fruit.
Since it would not arise from a cause, it would be eternal. If the essence of cause and fruit already exists in the future, then according to the principle of causality:
if that which is the cause exists prior [to the fruit], and that which is the fruit exists simultaneously [with the cause], then it follows that the past must be the cause.
That is, the present and future serve as the fruit. If the present serves as the cause, then the present and future serve as the fruit;
thus, the cause precedes and the fruit follows. How, then, does this text state that there is a cause in the future?

Answer: This is now based on the Sarvāstivāda school. It is not [stated] according to the literal meaning. If one sets aside the causal activity (*kāritra*), then the causal activity exists in the present. If...

Regarding their essential nature: within the three time periods, they all possess the nature of having causes. If we consider the corresponding cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahajāta-hetu*), the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), and the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*)—these four causes are established based upon the very substance of the phenomena themselves. Therefore, throughout the three time periods, these same four causes exist;
for instance, as for the existence of these four causes within the future time period, it is because the maturation cause exists therein due to the presence of the mind.

Because it is a mental factor (*caitta*), it possesses the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*). Because it possesses the substance of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of acquisition (*prāpti*), it possesses the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Because it possesses the substance of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it possesses the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). The same applies to the remaining present and past [dharmas].
Therefore, these four causes are established based on the nature of the dharmas (*dharmatā*).

As for the two causes—the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)—they are not established based on the nature of the dharmas themselves, but rather are established solely based on their sequential positions.
Consequently, these two causes exist only in the present and the past, because these two time periods consist exclusively of preceding positions; they do not exist in the future.

These two causes are so called because they are posterior in nature. This explanation—that the cause precedes and the effect follows—refers specifically to the universal (sarvatraga) and homogeneous (sabhāga) causes which share the same object-condition (*ālambana*).
Furthermore, it refers to the other four causes, as they exercise their functional activity;

since these also have the cause preceding and the effect following, this statement regarding "cause" applies to them as well, provided that the cause exists prior [to the effect], such as in the case of co-existent (*sahabhū*) causes. If the essence of the cause...
The future exists. Previously, following the counter-argument, one challenged only the notion of permanence; now, following the dual challenge, one also refutes the view of annihilation.
Regarding the first point—following the counter-argument and challenging the position on permanence—it refers to the preceding passage stating:

"If the past and future were substantially existent, they could be admitted as non-annihilated; how then could they not be permanent? For even permanence does not accord with the correct principle of dependent origination. Now, following the dual [challenge]...
The refutation of the view that [the effect] is annihilated is stated in this very text: "If the fruit already exists inherently, why would it depend on a prior cause?

Thus, if the essence of the fruit exists inherently and does not rely upon its cause, it must be eternal. Since the meaning of 'cause' is thereby non-existent, how could the meaning of 'fruit' possibly exist?"
If cause and effect were entirely non-existent, that would constitute nihilism. Now, there are two ways in which the three times are non-existent:
if a dharma moves through time, then "past" is designated as prior and "future" as posterior. In this treatise, cause and effect are precisely the dharma moving through the three times.
If there are three time periods, then the past is called "after" and the future is called "before," just as cause and effect exist within human life;

this is the dharma-practice of the three times. If one turns away from these three, then the past is called "after" and the future is called "before," just as a person's childhood is called "after" and their old age is called "that [the former].
As for the statement regarding a standing person, what distinction is there that is not yet clear?

If one knows [this], then that which is yet to come is called "prior. Furthermore, it is like when a person walks along a road: the place already traversed is called "posterior," and the place not yet traversed is called "prior.
This is similar to the case of a house with a gabled roof; likewise, the past is called "posterior" and the future is called "prior."

Regarding the statement in the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary): "The activity [of arising] that is postulated must exist in the future, because it is not separate from its essence"—this present inference takes as its object the very activity of giving and receiving results within the past and future periods.

If one were to raise an objection against the characteristic of arising (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa*) by claiming it is identical to the cause of arising in the future—which the opponent also admits to existing—then there would be a fallacy of proving what is already accepted (*siddha-sādhana*). However, since the present objection concerns the activity of giving and receiving results, there is no such fault.
Furthermore, if one were to apply this inference (*anumāna*) against the ancient Sarvāstivāda masters, it would entail the fault of contradicting their own tenets.

For the ancient Sarvāstivāda masters assert that future phenomena also possess functional activity (*kāritra*). Specifically, regarding the "arising-phase of light" (*āloka-jāti-lakṣaṇa*) and the "patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), one should infer as follows:
apart from the three factors such as light, which are admitted [to exist] in the future, there is no other functional activity.
All phenomena (*dharma*) must necessarily exercise their activity, for it is no more difficult to establish their nature than their essence itself.
Furthermore, this inference (*anumāna*) presented in the commentary is established even when directed against the masters of the *Nyāyānusāra*, who follow the new Sarvāstivāda school;

for those masters of the *Nyāyānusāra* admit that the three types of future phenomena possess only capacity (*śakti*), but do not constitute actual activity (*kāritra*). Thus, the inference in the commentary stands in opposition to the *Nyāyānusāra*.

Master of Principle, there is no contradiction here. Your [position that] past and future phenomena are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) would follow because they possess the essence of a phenomenon (*dharmatā*) but lack functional activity (*kāritra*), just like unconditioned phenomena. If one applies this inference from the commentary against the ancient Sarvāstivādins:
In that case, there would be the fallacy of one or the other being unestablished (*anyatarāsiddha*).

However, because the ancient Vaibhāṣika masters accept that the three dharmas—light and so forth—possess functional activity (*kāritra*) even in the future, this inference, when directed against those ancient Vaibhāṣikas, suffers from the fallacy of one or the other being unestablished.
If, however, this inference from the commentary is applied against the masters of the *Nyāyānusāra*, there is no such fallacy of one or the other being unestablished.

According to the Master who follows the Correct Principle (Sthiramati), it is maintained that while past and future dharmas possess functional capacity (*śakti*), they lack actual activity (*kāritra*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement in the commentary that "the dharma which has not yet manifested should be unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*): according to the Sarvāstivāda school, the substantial body (*svabhāva*) of a dharma exists within the future time period.

Thus, there would be no characteristic of arising and ceasing. That which has returned [to its source] has not yet arisen; as for activity in the past, since it has already performed its function, there is likewise no characteristic of transition.
If it were a present phenomenon, then there would be the four characteristics of transition. Therefore, this measure is employed to refute [the opponent's position].
The *Śāstra* further states that the future possesses the activity (*kāritra*) of the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), while the past possesses the activity of giving fruit (*phala-dāna*).
This refers to the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*): it takes the fruit in the present and gives the fruit in the past.

If the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) possess the activity of giving fruit in the past—specifically regarding those similar-type causes that are separated by an interval—then their fruit-activity likewise arises in the future.
"Because they have utility. This is the objection raised in the *Śāstra* (the Commentary): "The past and future lack utility; therefore, they should be designated as 'present'.
The *Śāstra* now states that "utility" refers to the utility of grasping and giving. This passage constitutes the rebuttal of the Hīnayāna.
Their rebuttal says: "Your Mahāyāna objection is logically untenable. When I speak of 'utility,' I mean the utility of grasping and giving."

The commentary raises an objection: "Regarding the claim that the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) takes up its fruit in the past—if the equal-and-immediate condition, at the time of the preceding moment's affliction, is able to induce the subsequent moments of mind and mental factors, then taking up the fruit would likewise occur in the past while giving the fruit occurs [in the present]."
The Commentary states: "If there were half a functional activity (*kāritra*) in the past, then that which possesses the function of grasping the fruit (*phala-grahaṇa*) would [exist];

with the exception of the five causes such as association (*samprayukta*) and coexistence (*sahabhū*), all [causes] grasp [their fruits] in the present and cannot grasp them in the past. The same applies to the other three conditions (*pratyaya*).

Only the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) can grasp its fruit in the past, because it possesses half a functional activity. Now, this is discussed in response to the objection regarding the past."
Half [of the function] exists. The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "In this regard, there are four types of characteristics of the state (*avasthā-lakṣaṇa*).

It is best to establish the 'present' based on the first function, which is distinct from the third [the future]. Furthermore, another interpretation says: "The past *samanantarapratyaya* (equal-and-immediate condition) takes up the fruit;
according to the explicit teaching of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, it must therefore be past. This is because it possesses half of the function, namely, the function of taking up the fruit. This is the text.
One should say: the present [condition] is able to grasp the fruit; the past possesses the activity of giving the fruit, yet the past lacks the activity of grasping the fruit.

An objection is raised: within that past time, only the equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*) and so forth possess the activity of giving the fruit, while the past lacks the activity of grasping the fruit; thus, it is called "half-possessing activity. Regarding that past...
Other dharmas within the world are all incapable of yielding a fruit; this constitutes half of their lack of functional activity.
Likewise, other dharmas within the past are all incapable of yielding a fruit; this constitutes half of their lack of functional activity.

Regarding the three dharmas of the *śāstra*—the function, the light-characteristic (*āloka-lakṣaṇa*), and the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*)—when the light-characteristic arises in the future, the present darkness is in the state of being abandoned. If the light arises, the darkness is already eliminated.

If the light were to exist as a functional activity in the present, it would be coexistent with darkness; therefore, it possesses function in the future. If the characteristic of arising exists in the future, it [possesses function].

Regarding their function: if they exist in the present, then abiding, change, and cessation possess function. If it is the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), then in the present moment, it arises simultaneously with the function of the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*);
however, its power to destroy that state of being an ordinary person is weak. This is the case for the Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma regarding Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).

When [the Path] arises in the future, at the moment it is in the state of "arising" (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), it possesses the power to exclude and sever the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) so that it does not arise within the future.

When the Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma regarding Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises and reaches the present, the preceding Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) and the nature of an ordinary person have already been extinguished.
Why is this? Because one cannot simultaneously possess both [the mundane path and the noble state]; one must necessarily abandon the former to proceed toward the latter. Regarding suffering...

The Dharma-knowledge-forbearance (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) is the half [of the path of seeing]; the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) are the "approach" (*pratipannaka*), and they are also the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The commentary raises an objection: "Since these three possess function in the future, they should be designated as 'present'."

The commentary states that when the function of giving fruit has ceased and then ceases again, it loses the function of grasping the fruit; when the subsequent arising occurs and arises again, it loses [the function of] arising.
This is also like the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), or the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and its outflow (*niṣyanda*).

Upon reaching the present world, having already ceased once, it falls into the past. Within the past world, it once again possesses the function of giving fruit, and thus ceases yet once more. Therefore...
It is said that [the characteristic of arising] ceases after it has ceased. At the time when the characteristic of arising occurs, it has already arisen once;

furthermore, upon reaching the present world, it is again able to grasp its fruit, which constitutes another instance of arising. This is precisely the loss [of the characteristic] after it has arisen; therefore, this objection is raised.
Commentary: If it is argued that the fruit of suffering consists merely of a capacity and lacks the function of "grasping" (taking) a fruit,

then this would entail the fault that the final mind of an Arhat, being unable to grasp a future fruit, should be designated as having the function of a past indeterminate fruit rather than a present one.
The Commentary further states: "If this mind initially lacked any activity, it should be called 'extinguished' (nirodha).

Even regarding that which exists in the final state, if one speaks of 'extinguished,' then since the final mind of an Arhat lacks grasping and function, life itself is extinguished; how then could there be further extinction thereafter?"
The Commentary further asks: "If their capacity (*śakti*) is renamed 'activity' (*kāritra*), how does this differ [from our position]?

This is because that school simply renames the three dharmas—non-luminosity and so forth—in the future as "capacity," and likewise renames the partial non-existence of activity in the past, such as grasping and giving, as "capacity.
Therefore, this text should state: "Furthermore, what they call 'activity' is precisely what we call 'capacity. Furthermore...

This is difficult to explain. Since your school asserts that the past possesses the capacity to yield a fruit, which is termed "activity" (kāritra) in the present, it remains unknown what distinction exists between this general capacity and the activity of the present.
To this objection, one must reply that there is no distinction, as they are merely different names for the same thing, like the words "eye" and "organ of sight.

As the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The five [faculties] grasp their fruits only in the present," meaning that the associated (*samprayukta*) and co-existent (*sahabhū*) [causes] act in the same way.

The universal concomitant causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and the retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*)—these five [types of causes] possess the power to grasp the fruit (*phala-grahaṇa*) while abiding in their present state.

Only the remaining "functioning cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*) does not grasp the fruit in this manner; thus, it is the same for the two [other types of causes] regarding the giving of the fruit (*phala-dāna*).

When the fruit arises as a recompense for the cause, this is termed "giving the fruit. This refers to the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), which, while abiding in their present state, [give the fruit].

They are able to take up their fruits. The primary mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) mutually provide assistance; at the moment they cease in the present, they mutually bestow their fruits.

Regarding the two causes that operate in the past and present, these refer to the two causes of similar type (*sabhāga-hetu*) and universal association (*sarvatraga-hetu*). At the stage when the present [moment] abides, it allocates its portion.

If the fruit is contiguous, when the two preceding causes are in the phase of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) and the subsequent fruit is in the phase of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), they are said to "give the fruit.
If these two causes arise and enter the past—whether after three or five moments—and the subsequent fruit arises in the phase of arising, then they are able to give the fruit;
thus, the two causes that give the fruit exist in the past. They give it simultaneously.
The *Śāstravibhāṣā* states: "That which 'gives fruit' refers to that seed; this present dharma possesses an inherent power capable of producing other dharmas.
That power which is currently producing them is called 'giving fruit. Question: Since the Sarvāstivāda school does not posit the existence of seeds, [how can this be so?]
How is it that this serves as their seed? Why is it asked again, "for the sake of being their seed"? The answer is: what is called the "seed" is the cause.
Regarding the phrase "only the past": this refers to the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).

While it takes its fruit during the phase of abiding in the present, it is only when the ripening cause has fallen into the past that it is able to yield its fruit. For example, if one performs a single unwholesome karma in the present life, this karma—

That which is capable of grasping a future body—this cause has already fallen into the past, perhaps having passed through many moments or many lifetimes—and when the subsequent effect arises at the moment of its "characteristic of arising" (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), it is then the fruit of that past ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*). Therefore, the ripening cause gives its fruit as it moves toward the past.
Regarding the two causes [the associated and co-existent] at the moment of actual cessation: these are the mental king (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) existing at the time of their cessation.

Thus, they mutually bestow their fruits. Regarding the three causes that bestow fruit upon that which is currently arising: these are the pervasive (*sarvatraga*), the homogeneous (*sabhāga*), and the retributive (*vipāka*) causes.

When the subsequent fruit of these three causes arises while in the state of the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), they are said to "bestow fruit. As for the other two conditions, they function contrarily:

as for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it takes up its fruit when the mind and mental factors are currently abiding in the state of the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*), at the time they are correctly perceiving an object.

When they exist in the state of the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), they can give their fruit. If it is the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it exclusively takes [the fruit] when past;
at the moment the preceding mind and mental factors cease, it opens the way and is able to induce the subsequent mind and mental factors, thereby being able to take the fruit.

If the subsequent mind and mental factors arise, it is called "giving the fruit" because it exists separately in the state of the characteristic of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*). These two— [the condition that gives the fruit while existing and the condition that gives the fruit after having ceased]—are...

Explaining by way of distinction: if a cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya) acts as a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) in grasping a fruit, it is not explained separately here because it is not distinct from the five previously mentioned causes.
Furthermore, if an unconditioned phenomenon (asaṃskṛta-dharma) serves as an efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu), it likewise does not grasp a fruit.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāvibhāṣā*) that "the correct text should name it as 'present,'" this commentary repeatedly cites what is the "correct teaching of the *Vibhāṣā*.
Here, the commentator of the present work quotes that correct principle from the *Vibhāṣā* to raise an objection.

If it is argued that [the final mind of an Arhat] is not capable of taking up a fruit because it is not the final mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), nor even because it is not an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), then if that school offers the following defense:
It is not that the final mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is incapable; rather, the intended meaning is that the final mind of one beyond training is indeed able to take up a fruit.

However, if the conditions for subsequent moments are lacking, the fruit cannot arise. An objection is raised: "If you say that the final mind of one beyond training can take up a fruit, you contradict your own tenet.
Your tenet asserts that after the final mind of one beyond training, it is no longer possible to take up a fruit."

It is not an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). If you say that the final mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) can take up a fruit, then the final mind of one beyond training would have to constitute an equal-and-immediate condition.
Furthermore, as for your statement that the present final mind cannot take up a fruit:
This contradicts your own tenet. [According to you,] it is taught that all phenomena exist in the present and possess the activity of grasping a fruit (*phalagrahaṇa*).

Since the final mind cannot grasp a fruit, it should be designated as "past. Furthermore, since it lacks the activity of grasping a fruit, it should be designated as a "capacity" (*śakti*). It is not as you previously explained.

The previous explanation followed the literal text. However, since it is also taught within the Mahāyāna that the final mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is not an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), the following passage states:
"If this consciousness is immediately followed by the arising of that consciousness as a certainty, it may constitute an immediate condition."
If this consciousness were not followed immediately by a subsequent consciousness, it would not constitute an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Regarding the argument that if there is no attainment of a fruit, yet the conditions are not deficient and it is certain that [the fruit] arises from this, how could it be that the fruit cannot be produced?
If they offer this defense: "If the conditions for the final fruit are not deficient, then that subsequent fruit can be produced," because...

Because the conditions for the subsequent fruit are lacking, the subsequent fruit cannot arise. To this, an objection is raised: "Since the cause has its conditions unimpaired, it possesses functional activity;
why then can it not produce the fruit? Since the final mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) exists as the cause, the remaining conditions should likewise be unimpaired;
it should possess functional activity, and the subsequent fruit must necessarily arise. If the cause cannot produce the fruit, then [the present...]"
"In the Dharma, this is useless. The objection states: "When your mind and mental factors arise, they are produced by possessing the four conditions.

Since your final mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) likewise possesses the four conditions, that final mind of one beyond training should constitute a cause that has functional activity, and thus it should be able to produce a dharma and obtain a fruit."

Regarding the question, "How can it be said that the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are beyond verbal expression?"—this refers to the passage on "true attainment" (*bhūtāpti*) mentioned previously, namely the text concerning "specific characteristics" and so forth.

Consequently, the name "result" (*phala*) is applied to the object-referent (*ālambana*) and the aspect-part (*nimittabhāga*). The answer is: it is precisely the aspect-part. This does not depend on whether the aspect-part is direct or indirect;
