rather, it refers to the time when [the seed] is a grain of millet or the like, which is the aspect-part. The intended meaning is as follows: just as in the springtime there is the sound of the cause for the sprout.

At that time, the fruit has not yet arisen; one speaks of this "spring-time sound-seed" as being about to produce the "autumn-time fruit," which is a provisional designation for the future fruit in relation to the present cause.
Furthermore, when the autumn-time sound-fruit exists, its cause has already ceased;
one speaks of the "autumn-time fruit-sound" as arising from the "spring-time cause," which is a provisional designation for the past cause in relation to the present fruit. Thus...
The same applies to the causes of good and evil. This *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains that both cause and effect are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*).

That is to say, it refers to the text stating that one provisionally establishes the future effect in relation to the present cause, and provisionally establishes the future cause in relation to the present effect, and so forth.

When it says that both cause and effect are provisional, this is explained according to the second of the two ultimate truths (*paramārtha-satya*), and not according to the four conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
If it is explained according to the four conventional gates, then all causes and effects are merely provisional designations and conceptual constructs.

This refers to what is explained according to the second gate, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and not according to the four conventional gates. If it is not explained according to the four conventional gates, then all causes and effects are substantially existent (*dravyasat*).
Regarding that which "recompenses" prior characteristics, such as the characteristics of maturation and transformation, yet the fruit... [desires] to... [is about to]... [occur].

When something arises, it must reach maturity and undergo transformation before it can produce a fruit. Thus, observing that the present body is a fruit born from past wholesome karma, one regards the past as the cause;
then, observing present wholesome and unwholesome karma, one regards it as the cause for what will be the future fruit.
Although the fruit exists in the future, one provisionally designates the present phenomena as the cause. Furthermore, observe:
Regarding the present ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*): when one observes that there is a good capacity for giving, one knows that past virtue existed;
thus, by observing the present fruit, one provisionally designates a prior cause. As for the statement "the fruit is also like this": because its nature is beyond words, it is not [itself] a fruit.
Rather, because it possesses functional capacity, the fruit arises to repay the cause; it is not a separate fruit.

"To remain far removed from the two extremes" means to remain far removed from the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. This answers the previous objection regarding the state of dharmas subject to arising and ceasing.
For the preceding treatise stated: "It is challenged by the Hīnayāna opponents that it is identical to the state of existing [in the present], since the subsequent fruit has not yet arisen;

thus, they argue it cannot avoid the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. The present treatise answers: "Such things as cause and effect are all merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*)."
The designation has already been explained in terms of the stages of prior arising and ceasing. As for those who interpret it differently below, they follow the interpretation provided thereunder.

The paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning all involve the understanding of untainted true wisdom (*anāsrava-bhūta-jñāna*). Because one knows through principle, it is called "conforming to the Path" (*mārga-anuloma*).
"Principle" (li) here does not refer to the principle of True Suchness (tathatā). Rather, it is the Way that is neither interrupted nor eternal;
it is this principle that can give rise to the manifestation of outflow-free (anāsrava) states, thereby conforming to the Middle Way through the principle of being neither interrupted nor eternal.
If one clings to interruption or to eternity, one will be unable to give rise to the Middle Way of the outflow-free state.
Regarding the statement that "the time periods are established based on seeds by way of the sense of what has been and what will be":

however, in that *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the principle of the three time periods based on seeds is precisely the ultimate exhaustion of reasoning—that which is fixed in sequence and fixed at all times.
That is to say, seeds give rise to seeds, thereby distinguishing the three time periods; namely, this present seed arises from the past...
Regarding the seed of the preceding thought-moment: that which is the seed of the preceding thought-moment is designated as the cause, while the present seed is the effect.
Furthermore, from this present seed, at the time of the subsequent thought-moment’s seed, that subsequent seed is the effect and the present seed is the cause.

This *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) explains that cause and effect exist throughout the three periods of time; this is established according to the principle of coarse characteristics (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*).

There are three time periods. Specifically, when one contemplates the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of the present human body as arising from a previous birth, the present body is said to be the fruit and past wholesome karma is the cause.
Furthermore, because one observes that the present [person] still performs immovable karma (*āniñjya-karman*), they will attain rebirth in the two higher realms in the future.
Due to the causes such as the active performance of meritorious karma (*puṇya-karman*), they will obtain a human existence in the future.
The body: by performing meritorious karma in the present, one obtains birth in the three fortunate realms with a body composed of the five aggregates in the future.
Furthermore, just as through giving in the present one obtains great wealth in the future, so too by maintaining [virtue] with the present body one obtains a great body in the future;
and because of patience in the present, one obtains a great retinue and so forth in the future. Thus, by observing the coarse causes of the present world, one attains [the results] in the future.
[This refers to] the fruit.

It is stated that there are six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), and so forth, up to the point where it is said that even though they are not seeds, they nonetheless exist across the three times. [The text] asks:

what is the difference in the objects (*ālambana*) conditioned by the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledge of the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*)? Furthermore, it asks: the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 56, and other sources state that these possess seeds.
Regarding the three periods of time: within the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only) school, it is taught that the three periods undergo transformation (*pariṇāma*).
What principle underlies these three instances, and what is their distinction? Answer: This is clarified in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) below.

Furthermore, as for the "functional capacity" (*śakti*) which modifies the activity of the text, in that school, the functional capacity refers to the modification of the activities of the three dharmas—light and so forth—in the future; it also refers to the modification of the past [dharmas] in taking and giving results.
Because it is the activity [of a dharma] that is designated as its "efficacy" (*kāritra*). This passage should be stated as follows: Furthermore, that activity is renamed "efficacy.

The knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows take as their object the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) state where afflictions have been exhausted. Although the unconditioned does not belong to the three time periods (*adhvan*), it is nevertheless said to exist by way of designation.
The unconditioned is present; it exists because it is one of the paths belonging to the three time periods, and even by way of conventional explanation it belongs to the three time periods.
Thus, both external and internal seeds possess the significance of the three time periods. Regarding the three time periods of external seeds, they are as previously explained in the *Saṃgraha*.
As for internal seeds, it is as observed: when one sees a person with an excellent body in the present, it is said that this person arises from the cause of virtuous karma in the past;
thus, the prior cause is provisionally established in contrast to the present fruit. Furthermore, seeing that this person performs wholesome deeds in the present, then...

When it is said that by practicing this in the future one will obtain the fruits of good human and celestial rebirths, this is a provisional designation of a future fruit in contrast to a present cause.
Regarding the second point, concerning the realization of the three periods of time through supernormal powers:

when knowledge of past lives and so forth arises, there is, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), the functional capacity to take the three periods as its object. Since the phenomena perceived through such supernormal power are not products of a deluded mind, [they are valid].
Because all that is seen is real;
because the second [type of person] still gives rise to the purities of conviction (*avetyaprasāda*);

and because they also manifest reflections of the three periods of time, having extensively cultivated dharmas such as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they thus know past events and so forth, whereby their knowledge of former abodes (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) eliminates the three [obstructions].
Because worldly affairs are manifested and universally manifest, that which is perceived—the past, future, and present—is entirely real.
According to its power, even when one asks about events spanning many kalpas, in principle, the characteristics of the object and the seeing that takes it as an object are actually present.
Because one forms conceptual constructions regarding the three periods of time within the mind, wisdom takes the future as its object.

When that which is seen in the future arrives, it is no different from the object seen by present-time wisdom; there is no further distinction between them. Regarding the difference in capacity between ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*):
if an ordinary being possesses supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they can know eighty eons of formation and destruction beforehand, and likewise eighty eons afterward.

Ten kalpas constitute a cycle of formation and destruction. If śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess supernatural powers, they can know eighty thousand cycles of formation and destruction in the past, and likewise eighty thousand cycles in the future.
If a bodhisattva of the first bhūmi possesses such powers, they can know one hundred cycles of formation and destruction in the past and one hundred cycles in the future;
from the second bhūmi upward, they know even more. As for a Buddha, [their knowledge extends through] boundless kalpas.

Regarding the third point, "relying on consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra) up to the fact that the characteristics of the past and future are in reality only present": this principle applies only to the first two types.

That is to say, the aforementioned reasoning and supernormal powers (abhijñā) both refer to the substance of the three times as being consciousness-only; apart from these first two types, there exists something else.
Regarding the substance: its three periods of time—past, future, and present—are for the most part transformations of the falsely discriminating mind.

This is because, in terms of actual reality, the subjective cognizers of the past, future, and present are all themselves present. Alternatively, to further explain even those points that seem to contradict the text, one may inquire about their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

these are subsumed within "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*), meaning they are included within the three types of consciousness-only based on the principle of "only-consciousness. Fearing [confusion regarding] the divine...

Because they overlap with and are confused by false conditions (*mithyālambana*), the three periods of time are divided into three types. However, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are never cognitions based on false conditions;

rather, within the three periods of time as *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only), there is one portion that consists of cognitions based on false conditions, such as the independent, distracted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) taking the past and so forth as its object.

Regarding the establishment of four [periods] and the negation of three, or the establishment of the remaining six, or the establishment of four kinds of three periods, or the negation of three: [these are the various formulations].

The application of the principles of cause and effect according to the master Vasumitra is similar to that of the Sthavira.
Vasumitra states: "This very same single seed has two moments: at the time of arising, it repays the cause; at the time of ceasing, it projects the effect.
Thus, the subsequent dharma is called the "prior effect"; this very present dharma, upon reaching the moment of its characteristic of cessation, gives rise to the subsequent dharma.
It stands. That which has ceased serves as the cause, and that which arises serves as the effect; therefore, it is called the "subsequent cause.

Within the single dharma-substance of the present, when the dharma-substance arises, it is the effect. Because at the moment of its initial arising it recompenses the preceding cause, the time of arising is termed the "effect.

When this very present dharma-substance is in the state of the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), it is able to serve as [the cause] for the dharma of the subsequent moment, because at the time of cessation—

Regarding the drawing forth of the fruit (*phala-ākṣepa*): the functions of the three characteristics do not occur simultaneously. The following passage represents the position of the Sthavira school.

As for the statement that "the subsequent fruit arises only at a different time," it should be stated that "it arises only at the time of cessation. Alternatively, one might say that it should be simultaneous with cessation.

Regarding the statement that these two characteristics—arising and cessation—are identical to the dharma itself and have no separate essence: these refer to the two characteristics of arising and cessation.
This is distinguished within the very substance of a single dharma; that is, because within a single dharma there exist the two characteristics of arising and ceasing.
This is because if these two characteristics of arising and ceasing were separate from the substance of the dharma, they would have no distinct essence of their own.

As for the Sarvāstivādins, although the four characteristics and the self-characteristic (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*) are distinct from the dharma, they do not exist as a separate essence apart from the dharma. In the case of material dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*), which are sluggish, there are three characteristic functions.

Substance (*dravya*). At the moment the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) first occurs within a conditioned phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*), it constitutes a fruit; it coexists with the causal path of the preceding dharma, such that these two dharmas exist together.
However, at the time of the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*), it exists alone, and there are no two dharmas concurrent. Thus, this characteristic of duration is not a fruit.

When it reaches the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), it can act as a cause, existing concurrently with the fruit of the subsequent dharma. These are the two dharmas: the cause of cessation and so forth.

That is, the subsequent dharma serves as [the effect]. Regarding the statement that "that which is discussed here is the single essence of the dharma," and that "the dharma functions across two times":

this means that when the subsequent dharma arises, it repays the causes such as the cessation of the preceding dharma; thus, the subsequent dharma becomes the effect. That is, the characteristic of arising of the subsequent dharma, as an effect, coexists with the characteristic of cessation of the preceding dharma as its cause.
If this present dharma reaches the characteristic of cessation, it then [coexists] with the characteristic of arising of the subsequent dharma.

Furthermore, regarding the two dharmas, one distinguishes the moments of arising and ceasing. These moments of arising and ceasing both exist within a single present thought-moment (*cittakṣaṇa*), reaching a point where arising and ceasing do not contradict one another.

This constitutes the presence of two temporal phases within these two dharmas. Therefore, the text below states: "The preceding cause is in the process of ceasing, while the subsequent effect is in the process of arising.
Thus, according to this treatise, it is said that at the time of arising, one repays the cause, and at the time of ceasing, one induces [the subsequent state].
Regarding the fruit, it is distinguished within a single dharma. That is to say, when this present dharma first arises, it immediately functions as both cause and fruit;
it acts as a fruit because it repays the cause of the preceding dharma, and it acts as a cause because, upon reaching the phase of cessation, it can induce the fruit of a subsequent dharma.
This arising and ceasing within a single dharma cannot occur simultaneously in one time-period; they must necessarily be sequential and mutually exclusive.

This is distinguished from the perspective of a single dharma. Although the essential nature (*tī*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the two moments of arising and ceasing differ, both are equally existent.
When it says "the essence," it refers to the essence of the dharma; when it says "the characteristics," it refers to arising and ceasing. Regarding the question posed by those who speak emptily:
"What dharmas are included by the word 'etcetera' in the phrase 'such as understanding and delusion,' etc.? Understanding is wisdom (*jñāna*); delusion is ignorance (*moha*).
Because they are mutually contradictory, like [the cases of] the ignorant and the wise.
Furthermore, regarding the statement in the Commentary that this is based on the fact that the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) of the two vehicles is slight and thus not mentioned:

when one reaches the stage of the diamond-like mind, the grasping at a self (*ātman*) no longer functions; it should therefore be called "abandoned. It is simply not mentioned because it is slight. Moreover, from the eighth stage upward...
It does not function for one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*. Now, this is discussed in terms of the complete state; therefore, it is said that [the seeds] are abandoned at the stage of an Arhat.

If it concerns those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), by the time they reach the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), they have completely severed the manifest activity of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*).

At the time of the diamond-like mind, they are still subsumed under the stage of training (*śaikṣa*); only upon reaching the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) do they become those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Here, however, we speak only of...
The statement that those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) relinquish the name "ālayavijñāna" is spoken in reference to a long duration;

it does not mention the ālayavijñāna at the moment of the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*), because that period is brief and thus is not discussed. Regarding the two interpretations for Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage according to their respective applications:

if one follows the first master’s explanation, Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage may also be called *arhats*, and they likewise relinquish the name "ālayavijñāna. Furthermore, this is based on the [text] *Vibhaṅga*.
Regarding the statement, "The one born in segments is called 'unborn' (ajāta)": the intended meaning is that an Arhat may also be designated as "unborn.
This is because among the three names [for an Arhat], it is said that he "should never again undergo birth in segments" (*pratisaṃdhi*); thus, an Arhat receives the name "unborn.
Furthermore, because an Arhat has severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), he is also designated as a "slayer of thieves" (*vadhaka*).

Regarding the statement in the Commentary that the name "appropriated" (*upādāna*) is used solely in reference to bondage: the current mention of "abandoning the *ālayavijñāna*" is based on objective bondage (*ālambana-bandhana*).

As for the Sarvāstivāda school, they maintain that even dharmas already severed serve as causes for those not yet severed, just as it was previously when one was still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

The defilements such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) serve as the cause for the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). When one subsequently enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), although views such as the view of a self-identity may still arise within the continuum of one who is training (*śaikṣa*), these defiled states arising in the body of the learner are distinct from those previously abandoned on the path of seeing. Specifically, the defiled states that arise in the body of the learner during the subsequent stage are not the same as the views of a self-identity and other such views of the afflictions of seeing that were previously severed. Because it is produced by what is induced by the Path, the afflictions that arise subsequently during the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) merely cause [the result] to be given and do not grasp it;
that is to say, they are dharmas already abandoned that serve as causes for those not yet abandoned.

Furthermore, according to that school, because sentient beings are bound by the afflictions through the coexistence of preceding and succeeding dharmas, they cannot attain liberation; the arising of the Noble Path can only sever [the afflictions] from above.
To cause that which is associated not to proceed is what is called "being free from bondage.
For example, when afflictions are associated with the mind and mental factors, those past mind and mental factors that have fallen away remain constantly bound by those afflictions.

Merely causing present afflictions not to arise is what is called "being free from bondage. In the Mahāyāna, one severs the bondage of association as well as defiled phenomena; if [one is] associated with afflictions...

The mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that arise simultaneously with affliction (*kleśa*) are also all severed. However, according to the Hīnayāna explanation, since the bond of association (*saṃprayoga-bandha*) is identical to the bonds of greed and so forth, the primary mind (*citta-rāja*) experiences them simultaneously.
When the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are acquired, they constitute the bond of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-bandha*).

Furthermore, since the four characteristics acquired upon the afflictions of greed and so forth are themselves bound by greed and so forth, this is called the bond of association. It is taught that the state of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) is not established at the higher stages.
However, it is only at the stage of the tenth bhūmi bodhisattva that the seeds of afflictions along with their residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are severed;
upon reaching the state of Buddhahood, the habitual tendencies are permanently and completely eliminated. Even arhats still possess residual habitual tendencies.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "As in the case of the arising of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth": this refers to the *Abhidharmakośa* verses concerning offerings made to the Buddha, the Sangha, and so on, which distinguish between the "old" and "new" Sanghas.

The commentary explains that "new" refers to: (1) the new [attainment] of the path of seeing; (2) the new teaching of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); (3) the new emergence from the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*);

(4) the new emergence from the samādhi of non-contention (*araṇasamādhi*); (5) the new emergence from the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); and (6) the new [emergence] when someone makes an offering.
One obtains great merit. Later, after a long time, when making offerings while entering into a mundane state of mind, one obtains different merit because of this distinction.
Question: Is the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) acquired through training (*śaikṣa*) or acquired beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?

Furthermore, among the six types of persons beginning with the Buddha as the foremost, how many obtain much merit when offered to, and how many obtain little merit? Further question: There is the "ripened" (*paripakva*) [person]...

It is the *ālaya-vijñāna*, not the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). Regarding the first proposition—that those who enter the state of mindlessness [do not have evolving consciousnesses]—the question is:
if ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the state of mindlessness also possess the seventh consciousness, how can it be said that the evolving consciousnesses are not present?

Furthermore, since practitioners of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) who enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) all possess the seventh evolving consciousness, how can it be said that the evolving consciousnesses are not present? The answer is: this refers to the aforementioned...
This is explained in terms of the six evolving consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ vijñāna-kāya*), not in terms of the seventh consciousness; thus, there is no contradiction.

Among those of the two vehicles (*dviyānika*), a person who has attained the third fruit immediately enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Those who have attained the first two fruits also experience the states of mental dormancy, deep sleep, or fainting.

Furthermore, all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) may enter the meditative absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or be born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñi-deva*); moreover, those in the Heaven of Non-conception may also enter [the absorption of cessation].
Deep sleep and fainting—these are called "mindless" states. The *Śāstra* says:
"All Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are likewise. Question: Among the Pratyekabuddhas, there are both those who are like rhinoceroses (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa*) and those who live in groups (*vargacārin*).
Why does it not say "all" [Pratyekabuddhas], but instead say "all" specifically regarding the Arhats? Furthermore, [the question asks about] the Pratyekabuddhas...
Thus, each attains its own distinct name; however, it is only the śrāvaka who receives the general designation of "arhat.

In this way, one should be called a pratyekabuddha, and a pratyekabuddha should be called [an arhat] in such a manner. Answer: A pratyekabuddha cannot sever the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);
therefore, they do not receive the name "in this way" (i.e., as an arhat). Because they can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), they receive the name "arhat."
The treatise states: "To suddenly sever the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa* is) to become an Arhat and to become a Tathāgata. Question:

Regarding the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*), one may say that the cognitive obstructions are suddenly severed; however, since they are gradually severed throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*), to what extent can it be said that they are suddenly severed?

As stated in the commentary itself: "Question: Within the Abhidharma, why is it that among the ten epithets, when describing the attainment of Buddhahood, it is said only that one 'becomes an arhat,' and the other titles are not mentioned? The answer can be understood through reflection."
"Already attained non-retrogression" refers to the realization of non-retrogression (*avivartana*).
"Also attained non-retrogression" refers to the non-retrogression of practice (*caryā-avivartana*).

For Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, regarding dharmas not yet attained that are destined to be attained, even if adverse conditions arise, they cannot act as obstacles. As for those on the first stage...
For Bodhisattvas above this stage who have not yet attained the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), even when adverse conditions arise, these cannot act as obstacles.
For Bodhisattvas from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward, regarding qualities not yet attained, there is only the obstacle of hindrance;

if adverse conditions arise, they are unable to attain those qualities and thus undergo regression. The initial teaching and the subsequent teaching concerning the turning of the mind are called "non-regression."
Regarding those who regress: this refers to those from the preceding stages up to the "directly proceeding" ones, who are exclusively oriented toward non-regression.
Now, as for the statement here that a non-regressing Bodhisattva abandons the name of *ālayavijñāna*, this specifically refers to the fourth stage of non-regression, which is designated as "Arhat.

Furthermore, regarding these two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) who have attained no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), even though they have not yet reached the "tenfold increase" and so forth since their initial turning of the mind, such individuals— [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.]
Thus, they are called only "non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas. If such a person reaches the tenth stage at the time of the sixth mind, that person obtains two names:
they are called "non-retrogressive in faith" and also "non-retrogressive in afflictions.
If that person reaches the seventh mind and beyond of the ten abidings, they are called "non-retrogressive in rank" and also "non-retrogressive in afflictions."

Regarding "retrogression": if such a person has reached the first stage (*bhūmi*) or beyond, they also receive two names: namely, they are called "one who has realized non-retrogression" and also "one who is non-retrogressive regarding afflictions.

If such a person reaches the eighth stage or beyond, they also receive two names: namely, they are called "one who is non-retrogressive in practice" and "one who is non-retrogressive regarding afflictions.

When those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) turn their minds toward [the Mahāyāna], they immediately obtain the name of being both non-retrogressive. That is to say:
These are called: non-retrogression in faith, non-retrogression in stage, non-retrogression in realization, and non-retrogression in practice regarding afflictions.

If one is a bodhisattva who proceeds directly [to Buddhahood], there are only the remaining four types of non-retrogression, excluding non-retrogression regarding afflictions. If one specifically refers to this context, it concerns non-retrogression regarding afflictions;
however, if one explains non-retrogression in a general sense, then all the other four types of non-retrogression are included.

Regarding the commentary on "the first stage of faith being non-retrogressive, which is the sixth of the ten stages of faith": during the first five stages of mind, one may retrogress and thereby sever the roots of goodness;
however, upon reaching the sixth stage of the ten stages of faith, one no longer retrogresses and can no longer sever the roots of goodness.

The Commentary states: "If even the seventh mind of the Ten Abodes is 'good' such that one does not regress from that stage, it is because within this stage one no longer regresses into becoming a follower of the Two Vehicles.

The Commentary further explains: "Because one has attained 'verified purity' (samyaktva-niyāma), one does not regress into the arising of afflictions; this is precisely what is meant by verified purity."

The Commentary also states that "non-retrogression in faith" refers to those who have not yet reached that stage. This includes those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) in their state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) who have turned their minds toward the Great Vehicle;
although they have not yet reached the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), because they possess definitive faith in the Mahāyāna, they are also called "non-retrogressive in faith.
This kind of non-retrogression exists only in the Mahāyāna; if it were of the Lesser Vehicle, even Arhats would still be subject to retrogression and loss.
The commentary states that there should be five [types of non-retrogression]. Now, within this commentary, there are five forms of non-retrogression:

first, the tenth stage of the sixth mind is called "non-retrogression of faith"; the seventh mind of the Ten Abidings is called "non-retrogression of position"; and third, "non-retrogression of realization."
From the first stage through the seventh, there is no regression in the four practices. From the eighth stage upward, there is no regression in the five afflictions;
these are those who, having attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle.
Commentary: Fourth, if those of the three vehicles who have attained no-more-learning all abandon the name "ālayavijñāna," these are the three types of persons.
Furthermore, adding those of no-more-learning who have turned their minds toward enlightenment, called "non-retrogressive bodhisattvas," constitutes the four types of persons.

The commentary states that "twenty thousand kalpas from the initial generation of the mind" refers specifically to those of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) who turn their minds [toward Bodhi].
At the outset, this is ten times the duration of the initial mind; that is, they proceed toward Nirvana. For a *srotāpanna*, it is eighty thousand kalpas;
for a *sakṛdāgāmin*, sixty thousand kalpas; for an *anāgāmin*, forty thousand kalpas; for an *arhat*, twenty thousand kalpas; and for a *pratyekabuddha*, ten thousand kalpas.

These types of individuals whose minds have turned toward the Great Vehicle must pass through this number of kalpas before they are first ranked as those of the Great Vehicle with ten times the resolve of an initial practitioner.
Regarding these "intermediate kalpas" (antarakalpa), the calculation is based on the great kalpas of formation and destruction.

However, from the time an Arhat first gives rise to the mind of the Great Vehicle until their attainment of Buddhahood, they are all termed "non-retrogressive regarding afflictions. Once they have turned their minds [toward the Great Vehicle],...
This is precisely what is called a Bodhisattva abiding in the stage of non-retrogression; thus it is termed "non-retrogression.

Regarding the statement that the *Abhidharmakośa* does not mention this for those in the stages of training (*śaikṣa*) of the Three Vehicles up to the position of the diamond-mind (*vajracitta*), the question is:
why is it also called "diamond-mind" and "diamond-like concentration" (*vajropama-samādhi*)? Furthermore, based on the nine minds of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) discussed below:

The eight associated minds are unified as one; yet, since there are eight associations, they constitute eight [moments]. Now, within the context of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*), this refers to insight (*vipaśyanā*) rather than serenity (*śamatha*).
Thus, it is explained in terms of wisdom (*prajñā*). Here, the meaning of "abandoning" refers exclusively to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*);
it is not called "diamond-like wisdom. The so-called "diamond-like mind" is precisely the diamond-like concentration, because it is the mind itself. Therefore, in the Sūtra:

The training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*) is also called the training of the mind (*citta-śikṣā*). Here, the concentration that serves as the basis is mentioned, with the intention of including the wisdom (*jñāna*) that depends upon it, because wisdom can arise through concentration.
Thus, the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) is used as a metaphor for concentration; it is not called "diamond-like wisdom" (*vajropama-jñāna*).

However, in other treatises, it is also termed the "diamond-like path" (*vajramārga*), and since the path is itself wisdom, [the two are identified]. Nevertheless, in this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other treatises...
In this context, it refers to the ultimate path of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), which is called "vajra" (*vajra*).

Alternatively, the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be severed—being as difficult to overcome as a vajra—or the wisdom (*jñāna*) capable of severing them—being as firm and solid as a vajra—are both metaphorically termed "vajra. Thus, in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, [it is stated:]...
This refers collectively to the three paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning, which are termed "vajra. Regarding "in the ocean of signlessness":

if true suchness is signless like an ocean, and the fundamental wisdom that realizes true suchness is like a person on a boat—specifically, the boat of the noble path of the Bodhisattva vehicle—then by crossing the ocean of signlessness, one shall likewise attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

This refers to one who initiates superior practice through the wisdom of skillful means regarding emptiness. "Emptiness" here refers to the Bodhisattva; they give rise to the fundamental wisdom of emptiness.
When contemplating *tathatā* (suchness), there is skillful means upon that fundamental wisdom. "Skillful means" is an exalted term for this.

"Existence" refers to subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*). When one correctly realizes true suchness (*tathatā*) through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), this wisdom is able to give rise to subsequently attained wisdom, whereby one initiates various physical activities and ascetic practices, relinquishing body and life, and so forth, in order to teach and transform sentient beings.
Just as there is neither arising nor ceasing, one observes all modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*).

From before the initial arising, one practices one of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) within a single practice, up until the point where one arises through the power of the Buddha's clarity. This applies from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to and beyond the sixth stage.
One then practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*): namely, practicing generosity (*dāna*) in the first stage (*bhūmi*), up to cultivating wisdom (*prajñā*) in the sixth stage;

if one cultivates skillful means (*upāya*) in the seventh stage; if one cultivates the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*) in the eighth stage; if one cultivates power (*bala*) in the ninth stage; and if one cultivates clear wisdom (*jñāna*) in the tenth stage.
From this eighth stage onward, one is able, in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), to transcend the two [preceding] stages.
Regarding the statement that "the merit and wisdom practiced over an *asaṃkhyeya* [kalpa] increase twofold": this is the case from the entry into the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onwards.

Upon reaching the ninth stage and beyond, the cultivation of the path in the first moment of thought already exceeds the [merit of the] eighth stage by twofold. The cultivation of the path in the third moment of thought exceeds the first moment by even more than twofold;
and so on, with each subsequent doubling following the same principle as before. Question: What is meant by this term "merit" (*puṇya*)?

Regarding the phrase "those with much wisdom": does this mean they have acquired many seeds through perfuming (*vāsanā*), or that their [wisdom] gradually becomes clear and sharp, or that their mind is courageous? Answer:

In this context, it refers to the attainment of many qualities such as merit and wisdom, because these gradually become increasingly distinguished, clear, and sharp. It does not refer to the abundance of seeds acquired through perfuming.
For this reason, if a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) practices the path for one year, they can surpass those prior to the stages (*pūrvabhūmi*).
During the great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), if one practices the path for a single day, it surpasses a Bodhisattva of the first stage practicing for a hundred years;

subsequent cases should be understood accordingly. If a Bodhisattva of the ninth stage practices the path for two moments of thought, it surpasses one who has practiced for an entire eon (*kalpa*) on the eighth stage;
likewise, if a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage practices the path for a single moment of thought, they transcend the ninth stage. [The same applies] up to the tenth stage.

"Regarding the statement, 'This also explains that each [of these] possesses the three meanings of an Arhat,' this refers to possessing the three meanings of being a Worthy One (Arhat), having slain the thief, and not undergoing further birth in the realm of分段生 (*bhava*)—that is, the three meanings of being a Worthy One, a slayer of the thief, and one who does not receive further segmented birth. Regarding the phrase, 'The two knowledges are the fundamental and the subsequently attained,' the question is: however, as for this passage..."

[Question: Since it is stated that [this] refers to the true reality revealed by the two kinds of emptiness, how can the text here say that the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) do not correspond with the other two types?
[Answer: When we speak here of "fundamental and subsequently attained wisdom," this also includes the wisdoms regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Regarding the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*): within its fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), there is also the fundamental wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-mūla-jñāna*) and the fundamental wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena.

Within its subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it also subsumes the subsequently attained wisdom of the emptiness of persons. Alternatively, the two wisdoms are the wisdom of the emptiness of persons and the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena.
Within the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena, both the fundamental and the subsequently attained [wisdoms] are subsumed; the same applies to the wisdom of the emptiness of persons.
Within this [wisdom], there are also both fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms. This is similar to what was previously discussed regarding "attainment.

As for the commentary’s statement that it is discussed solely in terms of the six *pāramitās*, up to the point where it says "because within each individual practice one is able to cultivate all practices":
if a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*bhūmi*) practices any one [of these] among the six *pāramitās*...

This differs from the previous case because, when Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above practice the eighty-four thousand pāramitās, they are able to perform all practices therein. Thus, it is distinct from what preceded.
The commentary states that one who gives rise to delusion without first moving a defiled mind is a person whose mind is inverted.

When Bodhisattvas give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*), they do so with a mind of correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), and thus they do not allow themselves to be associated with those afflictions; this is for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.

The intended meaning is that ordinary persons and small-minded individuals, when wishing to perform acts of good or evil karma, must necessarily give rise to a mind of either goodness or evil—just as when [one performs] a construction...
Regarding evil deeds: it is only when one gives rise to afflictions and a truly evil mind that one can commit an evil act such as striking another.

If one gives rise to a wholesome mind at that time, one cannot commit an evil act such as striking another. Likewise, if one wishes to perform a wholesome deed, it is necessary to give rise to a wholesome mind;
only then can one perform a wholesome deed. If one gives rise to an unwholesome mind, one cannot perform a wholesome deed. Thus it is with the Bodhisattva.
It is not so; otherwise, it would contradict [the principle] in two ways. For instance, when a bodhisattva gives rise to an evil mind, they may immediately perform a virtuous deed;
or when they give rise to a virtuous mind, they may perform an evil deed. These are performed within a state of compassion. Even when there is an evil mind, it is a virtuous deed;
or when a virtuous mind arises, the performance of an evil deed is entirely performed within a mind of compassion. As the sutra says:
It is stated in the *Madhyama Āgama*: In the past, when the Buddha was the Bodhisattva Jñānaguṇa, he saw another person slandering a Mahāyāna sūtra and thought to himself:
"If this person continues to slander the sūtras, they will certainly enter the Avīci Hell for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.

It would be better for me to kill this person so as not to let them slander the sūtras. With a heart of great compassion, he killed him; yet, at the end of his life, the man went to the Avīci Hell. And...
Three thoughts arise, as in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. First, the answer is given: there is no similarity to a king.

It is like the case of the "stump-removing" medicine (*khaṇḍa-bhaiṣajya*) and so forth, which causes transformation and causes poison. Because it transforms medicine into poison, it is due to a distinct dharma—the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

This is because Arhats still possess conceptual discrimination and attachment to dharmas (*dharma-abhiniveśa*), and thus do not harm others. Alternatively, by means of other excellent medicines and the like, [the poison] within the poisonous medicine is caused to...
The transformed poison is powerless. Third, it does not harm people.

Regarding the phrase "because of the view of a self in phenomena" (*dharmātman-dṛṣṭi*): phenomena possess functional activity, and this is termed "self. Alternatively, because it shares the same essence as the self of persons (*pudgalātman*), it is termed the "self of phenomena.
Because it shares the same essence as the common afflictions (*sāmānya-kleśa*), this passage should state that [it exists] by virtue of its presence.
Regarding the essence:
[The text] states that the afflictions (*kleśa*) arising in a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) constitute a fault. Question:
Since afflictions no longer arise from the eighth stage upward, how can this text speak of "afflictions arising in a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage"? Answer: This text merely...
This is a general explanation of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). It should be stated that the afflictions (*kleśa*) arising in a Bodhisattva of the seventh stage do not constitute a fault.

As for the statement in the treatise: "However, the Arhat has completely exhausted the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of the afflictions within this consciousness," it refers to the ultimate exhaustion [of those specific residues].

According to the view of the ignorant, a careful examination of this passage reveals that since it speaks of "severing the heavy latencies (*dausthulya*) of the afflictions," it is clearly the position of the first master and not that of the second master.

This is because the second master asserts that even a Bodhisattva who has proceeded directly to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) still suppresses the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the seventh consciousness’s afflictions,
yet is nonetheless termed one who has "abandoned the *ālayavijñāna*."
The treatise states: "An Arhat, having no consciousness that sustains the seeds, at that moment enters nirvana without remainder.
Based on this passage, it is said that one enters nirvana without remainder; this is the position of the first master. Question:

If those of the two vehicles enter nirvana without remainder because they have no consciousness sustaining the seeds, how can a Bodhisattva—who possesses uncontaminated seeds—enter nirvana without remainder? That is to say...
The meaning of "accumulation" (*upacaya*) is the meaning of "mind" (*citta*).

Up to the point where it can perfume seeds, once these have been accumulated within this consciousness, regarding the subsequent arising of dharmas and so forth—what is the difference between the twelve explanations in this commentary? One should further inquire of this master.

As the initial understanding of the ignorant [suggests], it refers only to the accumulation of seeds within consciousness (*vijñāna*). The subsequent understanding, however, refers to the accumulation of all seeds which subsequently arise as manifest activity (*pravṛtti*);

this is what is called the essence of mind (*citta*). In this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, that which explains "mind" is precisely the statement that the faculty of intellect (*manas*) can cognize the characteristics of various objects;
this is what is termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). Now, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is itself the "mind" among these three types.
...the mind (*citta*). Briefly stated, it refers to the locus where seeds are accumulated.

Regarding the "mind" among the triad of mind, mentation, and consciousness (*cittamanovijñāna*) mentioned in the Commentary: that which is called "mind" is the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); that whose nature is deliberation is called "mentation" (*manas*).

As for the statement in the *Abhidharmakośa*, Chapter Two, regarding the meaning of "mind" and so forth, even when speaking from one perspective—[the questioner] asks: since this treatise already states...

Because it is perfumed by the clouds of seeds and because it is the accumulation of seeds, this text states that there is only the collection and accumulation of seeds, and no arising of defiled active manifestations (*pravṛtti*);
this is also stated from one perspective. The answer is found in the first proof at the beginning of this treatise:

"That which collects the seeds of phenomena and is capable of giving rise to active manifestations is the meaning of 'mind' (*citta*). Furthermore, in the *Abhidharma*, that which possesses only seeds is designated as "mind."
There is no arising of active manifestation (*samudācāra*). This is stated from one perspective.
The *Commentary on the Compendium of Ascertainments* (*Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*), fascicle 1, states: "As the basis... [it] does not apply to all noble ones (*ārya*). That same *Compendium* says:
"Ādāna" (appropriation) means that which is able to maintain the seeds of all phenomena and is able to appropriate the physical sense-faculties and their bases.

Because it is now able to appropriate the continuity of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), that treatise—referring to the appropriation of the continuity of rebirth and referring to the moment of actual birth—states that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) serves as the basis for appropriation;
thus, that which is the basis is the body. [Question: Is this "appropriator" [the same as the appropriating consciousness]?

Regarding the question of how the *upādāna* (clinging) within the twelve links serves as the basis for [the *vijñāna*]: one asks, "For those who have attained the first two fruits of the path, their bodies must necessarily give rise to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) upon contact with the sense bases;
thus, it serves as the basis for *upādāna*. How then can you say that this does not apply to all noble ones (*ārya*)? The answer is:

The *upādāna* intended here is not the *upādāna* link among the twelve links of dependent origination. Rather, it refers to the *upādāna* of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because one undergoes birth from that state.

That is to say, it refers to obtaining birth; "appropriation" (upādāna) means grasping at the existence of birth (upapatti-bhava), and this is what is termed "appropriation. It causes the continuity of birth and death.
Furthermore, it is the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) that serves as the basis at the time of taking birth. Question: Regarding the explanation of *ādāna* in the preceding text...
That is to say, it possesses two meanings: the appropriation of seeds and the various material sense-faculties (rūpindriya). This will be explained below:
ādāna-vijñāna is that which maintains the seeds, maintains the material sense-faculties and their bases, and grasps the continuity of rebirth.
This possesses four meanings and involves two textual contradictions. The answer is that this is stated by way of emphasizing the preeminent.
That is, regarding "this basis of the knowable" from the first chapter, the *Basis of the Knowable* (*Jñeyāśraya*), of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, that treatise states:
"The basis of the knowable refers to the eighth consciousness. This "basis of the knowable" is the most excellent among all other dharmas within the category of the knowable. It is this.

Therefore, regarding the statement that the phenomena of the three natures all exist only by depending upon this consciousness: this refers to the three natures—dependent, imagined, and perfected. Question:
How does the eighth consciousness serve as the basis for the perfected nature and the imagined nature? Answer:
Within the eighth consciousness, there still exist the seeds of the mind capable of imagining; the seeds within that consciousness are all that which is imagined.
Regarding the objects of cognition: the objects that are the basis of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) serve as the support for that very pervasive conceptualization.

Furthermore, when the seventh consciousness universally cognizes the eighth consciousness and gives rise to the grasping of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*), that eighth consciousness serves as the real support for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and so forth.
"Support" here means a reliance; it is not like the visual consciousness relying on the eye-faculty and other organs. It is precisely by virtue of the eighth [consciousness]...
Within the mind, there are seeds of afflictions and seeds of outflow-free (anāsrava) dharmas.

When the outflow-free seeds give rise to their actual manifestation and one realizes True Suchness (tathatā), one is then able to sever the seeds of affliction within consciousness; only then does one manifest True Suchness.
If the eighth consciousness did not exist, there would be neither the seeds of affliction nor the outflow-free seeds, and one would be unable to manifest True Suchness.
Therefore, it is said that True Suchness (tathatā) relies upon the eighth consciousness.
Regarding the first [of the three meanings of *citta*] mentioned previously as "mind" (*citta*), it signifies the sense of accumulating seeds within it. The commentary states:

If one were to explain "mind" in a general and distinct manner, there are two meanings: first, it refers to that which can accumulate the seeds of all phenomena (*dharma*) and can also give rise to their actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*).

If the mind is clearly understood as the seed-consciousness, that mind possesses only one meaning: namely, that the first [meaning] of "mind" (*citta*) is the sense of being the locus where seeds are accumulated;
it clarifies the seeds by means of the locus of the manifest consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) which serves as their support. Thus, what is now called "seed-consciousness" [is established].
This clarifies that the seeds within consciousness have the capacity to produce manifest activity; thus, there is a distinction between the two.

Regarding the statement that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) possesses "divisions" (*bhāga*), it is asked: if this refers to the fundamental consciousness as existing throughout all stages—according to the text, "having" (*yōu*) refers to the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), and "division" (*fēn*) has the sense of "cause"—how can this be reconciled with the untainted stage of Buddhahood? [The answer is: within the fruit of old age (*jarāphala*), one proceeds from the cause.
This is for the sake of designation; that is to say, it is taught that such [a person] is also called a *pudgala*. However, the term "person" (*pudgala*) is used because of the causal basis.
Yet, the Buddha is not a *pudgala*; this case is likewise so. When it is said that the Buddha possesses "consciousness of the portion," this too is designated according to its causal state.
The commentary states: "That which is the mind in the state of continuous grasping" refers to the four names—such as "mind" (*citta*) and so forth—which apply universally across all states.
This is explained in reference to the *ālayavijñāna* in its state of continuous grasping, because the *ādānavijñāna* (appropriating consciousness) pervades all causes and effects.
Furthermore, when one begins this treatise, this capacity for grasping and storing (*upādāna-ālaya*) also extends to the untainted (*anāsrava*), even functioning as the capacity for [grasping] that.
Regarding the meaning of "store" (*ālaya*): it is intended to mean that the eighth consciousness is the "storer" (*ālaya*), while the sense organs, the body, and the seeds are the "stored" (*ālaya*).

Speaking from the perspective of its continuity from beginning to end, this fundamental consciousness acts as the storer; furthermore, this applies to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), because the fundamental consciousness of the Buddha-fruit is also termed the storer.
That which is the stored does not apply to the uncontaminated, for "the stored" carries the meaning of being susceptible to perfuming (*vāsanā*) and being the locus of the "self."

Regarding "storing" (*ālaya*): because the Buddha is free from perfuming and lacks the grasping of a self, the Buddha has nothing that is stored. If the seventh consciousness, as the grasping of a self, takes the eighth consciousness as the self, then the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) becomes the "object stored" (*āśrita*), and the grasping of a self becomes the "subject that stores" (*āśraya*). Speaking in terms of the beginning and the end, this consciousness is the object stored; it does not extend to the untainted (*anāsrava*), but exists only in the tainted (*sāsrava*) state. As for the fundamental consciousness of the Buddha-fruit: [The remainder of the text follows: ...it is neither the subject nor the object of storing. Why? Because it is free from the grasping of a self. Furthermore, the Buddha’s fundamental consciousness is not perfumed by afflictions, nor is it perfumed by the outflows (*āsrava*). Therefore, it is neither the subject nor the object of storing. Moreover, the Buddha’s fundamental consciousness is not the object stored, because it is free from the grasping of a self. It is not the subject that stores, because there is no perfuming. Thus, the Buddha’s fundamental consciousness is neither the subject nor the object of storing. This is the meaning of the statement that the Buddha’s fundamental consciousness is neither the subject nor the object of storing. This concludes the section on the storehouse consciousness. Next is the section on the transformation of the support (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*). What is meant by the transformation of the support? It means that the seeds of the afflictive obstructions and the cognitive obstructions within the storehouse consciousness are eliminated, and the pure seeds are fully developed. Through this, the support is transformed, and one attains the three bodies of the Tathāgata. This is called the transformation of the support. What are the three bodies? First, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); second, the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); third, the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Among these, the Dharma-body is the support of the other two bodies. The Enjoyment-body is the support for manifesting the pure lands and the enjoyment of the Dharma. The Transformation-body is the support for manifesting various forms to benefit sentient beings. These are called the three bodies. This concludes the section on the transformation of the support. Next is the section on the attainment of the fruit. What is meant by the attainment of the fruit? It means that through the power of cultivation, one gradually eliminates the obstructions and realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. This is called the attainment of the fruit. This concludes the section on the attainment of the fruit. This concludes the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. May all beings attain the supreme enlightenment. May all be well. "Because it is not the storehouse for the grasping of a self; because there is nothing that does not undergo perfuming.
Regarding the statement, "The first master [says] the third follows reason and should be taught":

the question is, since there were three masters' explanations regarding the stage of Arhatship at the preceding time, if the first two masters represent the correct meaning, then the third master does not represent the correct meaning. [This is stated] in the Commentary.

One should say that the second explanation of the first master accords with reason and should be stated. Why, then, is the third [explanation] attributed to the first master? Answer: Because he cites the beginning and the end.

Furthermore, one should question the Dharma Master: Regarding those who are "defiled" (saṃkliṣṭa), do they consist of the three natures of the outflowing (sāsrava) and the dharmas of the three natures of the outflowing?
As for non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas and the Arhats of the Two Vehicles, they all possess outflowing defilements.

Regarding the phrase "stained seeds": how is it that this statement—that those who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and non-regressive bodhisattvas possess no stained or mixed dharmas—is explained?

The answer is that it is also spoken with reference to the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*). For this reason, as for the statement that "the seeds give rise to active manifestations at different times, and only when they arise do they manifest," this master asserts that at the moment of entering the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*), one abandons the seeds of the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), and only the ripening consciousness itself manifests.

Now, that which arises simultaneously with the *vajracitta* (diamond-like mind) is precisely what is called "equanimity" (*upekṣā*). Since that bodhi is yet to come in the future, it is termed "about to be attained.
This master’s view is also not orthodox. This interpretation is the explanation of a disciple of Master Dharmapāla.

The seeds of consciousness belonging to the period prior to birth have already ceased by the time of the *vajracitta*; as for the seeds of consciousness belonging to the period after birth, they coexist with the [diamond-like mind].

It is simultaneous with the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*). The preceding moment’s manifestation of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) arises together with the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) that is abandoned along with the adamantine mind.

Regarding the five lines in the commentary on the "Gates" (*dvāra*), these are all the teacher's incorrect interpretations; for in the main text of the treatise, it is stated in every instance that cause and effect are simultaneous.
Regarding the statement in the *Commentary on the Buddha-bhūmi* (Fodi lun) that "it is explained among the four purities, etc.," this refers to that treatise’s elucidation of all pure dharmas.

Regarding the statement in the commentary, "If explained in terms of abandonment, then from the stage of the two vehicles' no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) down to the previous [stage], the former is superior," this refers to what is being discussed.

Regarding those in the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) and Arhats who "abandon the ālayavijñāna," this is designated as such in terms of severing the bondage of its objects (*ālambana-bandhana*), yet they do not abandon its substance (*tattva*).

Therefore, at the time of becoming free from the defilements of their own respective stages, they are all said to "abandon the ālayavijñāna. However, it is only at the moment of the Vajra-like mind (*vajropama-citta*) that its substance is abandoned.
Based on this, one should establish a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi-vibhaṅga*), such as "severed but not abandoned" and so forth, as explained in the previous notes.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) classifies the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*) according to its objective referent (*ālambana*) into three types. If the subjective perceiver is classified according to its objective referent, there are three:

the state of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*), the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), and [the remaining two]. If the objective referent is classified according to the subjective perceiver, there are three:

namely, the *ālaya-vijñāna*, the *vipāka* (maturation), and the *ādāna* (appropriation)—these being the names for the subjective perceiver and the objective referent. The former is long and the latter is short; that is, from beginningless time...
"Coming. The grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) constantly takes the *ālaya-vijñāna* as its object; therefore, it is called "prior. If one considers its substance (*tattva*), it is the *ālaya*.

This is like being tall in front and long behind. As for the substance of the *ālaya*, it is only upon reaching the stage of the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-citta*) and when the followers of the Two Vehicles enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* that one finally abandons the substance of the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
As for the grasping at a self that acts as the perceiving subject (*ālambaka*), if one considers its substance, it is likewise "prior."
"High in the beginning, short at the end. Since beginningless time, the grasping at a self has coexisted with its objective support, the ālayavijñāna; therefore, it is called "high in the beginning.
When one reaches the eighth stage, or the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*) of the two vehicles, the substance of this grasping at a self is severed; therefore, it is called "short at the end."

The attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) takes the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) as its object; its subjective aspect (*ālambaka*) likewise arises either simultaneously with it or subsequently.
Because this attachment to phenomena has existed from beginningless time and constantly takes the ripening consciousness as its object, it is called "arising prior" (*pūrvotpanna*).

When one reaches the stage where the followers of the two vehicles enter the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), or when a Bodhisattva reaches the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), they simultaneously abandon the ripening consciousness and sever the attachment to phenomena.

Therefore, it is called "high in the latter part. When the *samatājñāna* (wisdom of equality) takes the *ādānavijñāna* as its object, it is "long in the former and high in the latter," meaning that upon attaining Buddhahood, it continues until the end of the future, as the *samatājñāna* constantly takes the *ādānavijñāna* as its object.

If explained in terms of the subject that perceives [the object], it is "short in the former and high in the latter," meaning that one only attains the *samatājñāna* upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*); thus, it is designated as such.
It is short. Once Buddhahood has been attained, the *samatājñāna* (wisdom of equality) continues in a constant state;

thus it is always coexistent with the *ādānavijñāna*. This is called "high in the rear. If we consider the *ādānavijñāna* as the object of perception, then it is "long in the front and high in the rear.
Since the beginningless past, the *ādānavijñāna* has existed; this is called "long in the front."

Regarding the commentary’s statement that, as explained in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, all conditioned and untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas do not receive perfuming (*vāsanā*), the intended meaning is this:

if one says that untainted dharmas do not receive perfuming, one should also say that wholesome (*kuśala*) and defiled (*kliṣṭa*) dharmas likewise do not receive perfuming; only those that are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) are capable of receiving perfuming.

Regarding the two explanations concerning Bodhisattvas such as Vajracitta and others, if it is said that they do not arise because there is little time remaining once [the stage] has already begun, this refers to the tenth fascicle.
According to one explanation, the time of Vajracitta is precisely the time when the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) arises.
Why is it not mentioned? Because the moment of the vajra-mind (*vajracitta*) is brief, it is described only as the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).

Furthermore, one tradition states that the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) does not arise at the stage of the vajra-mind, but arises only upon the path of liberation. Moreover, this fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is not perfumed by factors of the three natures—such as the wholesome or the defiled;
only that which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is said to be characterized by self-love (*ātmasneha*), and only the indeterminate is capable of receiving perfuming.

However, regarding the distinctions among these three states of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*): they are the state of being stored through the grasping of self-love (*ātmasneha*), the state of being the fruit of wholesome and unwholesome karma, and the state of continuous maintenance.

When the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun), in its second chapter, explains that the *ālayavijñāna* is the nature [of all phenomena] and so forth, and does not mention the names of the Hīnayāna therein, it is because this text of the *Saṃgraha* first clarifies the eighth consciousness as being like a great king.
Following this path, one then establishes the function of the eighth consciousness, taking the *ālaya-vijñāna* as its nature.
This eighth consciousness has "mind" (*citta*) as its essential nature; this eighth consciousness takes the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness) as its essence.
If the fourth [consciousness] is referred to merely as *ālayana*, it refers to the *ālayana* of the Sarvāstivāda school—the sense of being fond of, delighting in, and rejoicing in [existence].
Therefore, in the fourth [section], there is no mention of the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Regarding the commentary’s previous first explanation, “because *citta* and so forth are common,” the same applies here, up to the phrase “knowing by analogy with the meaning.

Since the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) is used, it inclusively takes the three names from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*: *ālayavijñāna*, *vipākavijñāna*, and *ādānavijñāna*. Furthermore, it inclusively takes *sattva*.
Bhadanta loves the *ālaya*-mind; since this is a general term for which various treatises provide different names, it is collectively designated as "mind" (*citta*).
Regarding the statement that "the two types of contaminated states are called the first abandonment," the inclusion of these two states refers to the ripening (*vipāka*) *ālaya*.
The *Śāstra* provides two explanations regarding "imminent attainment" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and "attainment" (*ājñendriya*): both are termed "imminent attainment" here.
At the time of the diamond-like path of uninterrupted transition (*vajropama-ānantarya-mārga*), enlightenment (*bodhi*) exists in the future; thus, it is called "imminent attainment.

As for the commentator’s analysis of the stages—wherein the texts distinguish between "imminent attainment" and "attainment"—the term "imminent attainment" is used as a general designation in the treatise. One interpretation states that [the seeds] produce the manifest.
Regarding the phrase "simultaneously having two, up to... thus it is called 'about to attain,'" there are two interpretations within this commentary, both of which constitute the correct meaning.
First, the initial master says: at the time of the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), it coexists with the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*);

since that diamond-like mind perishes simultaneously with the ripening consciousness, the relinquishing of the ripening consciousness by the diamond-like mind is precisely its "correct relinquishment."

This is called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*). As it is taught in the Hīnayāna, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) arises simultaneously with the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), much like riding upon an enemy.
Thus, the Supreme Mundane Dharma is able to contain the nature of an ordinary person, and the nature of an ordinary person is able to coexist with the Supreme Mundane Dharma;
their simultaneous abandonment is what is termed "abandonment. This master’s position represents the correct interpretation. As for the gold... [text fragment ends].
When the mind is firm, Bodhi is present; this is called "about to attain. Regarding the statement that Bodhi arises simultaneously with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*):

if one asks whether Bodhi is itself wisdom, and yet it is said to arise simultaneously with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom—of the eight consciousnesses, in which consciousness does this Bodhi consist as wisdom?
Furthermore, since the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is itself Bodhi. Answer: Bodhi is the Path of Liberation.
The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) consists of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, which are the two wisdoms of equanimity and sublime observation (*samatā-vipaśyanā*).
When the sixth consciousness gives rise to the diamond-like uninterrupted path (*vajropama-anantarya-mārga*), it induces the path of liberation within the seventh consciousness.

If one defines the uninterrupted and liberation paths based on the severing of afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*), then these uninterrupted and liberation paths belong exclusively to the sixth consciousness; [the other consciousnesses] possess the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

In the middle [stage], there is only the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*). Therefore, the present sixth consciousness’s path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is co-existent with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).

Regarding the statement in the commentary that "attainment" (*prāpti*) and "maturation" (*paripāka*) are distinct entities: according to the Sarvāstivāda, the initial acquisition is termed "attainment," while subsequent development is termed "maturation.
This treatise, however, distinguishes itself from the Sarvāstivāda position; thus it says "about to attain. To speak according to reality, attainment and...

"Maturation" (*vipāka*) is a synonym for "the same essence" (*eka-rasa*). When the maturation has previously ceased, at that moment of the vajra-like [samādhi], it is called "abandoning" because it has already been relinquished.

According to the second explanation, at the time of the vajra-mind, just as when the "receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises in the Hīnayāna, one is said to abandon the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*);
it is called "abandoning" because it has already been relinquished. This case is likewise so. These two explanations are as follows in the [next] section.
This is the explanation given in the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*. Regarding the seeds giving rise to the manifest [state], they differ in timing; this is the same as the initial explanation.

At the moment the Vajra-like Samādhi arises, the seeds of the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) have already ceased, and only the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) of the ripening consciousness remains, arising simultaneously with the Vajra-like mind.

That which is called "attainment" at the beginning is termed "maturation" at the end. However, this passage is explained according to the Sautrāntika masters. As for the restoration of the roots of goodness...

Regarding the roots: when the wholesome roots reach the stage of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), they are termed "attained" (*prāpta*). If the wholesome roots reach the present time, they are termed "matured" (*paripakva*).

This is distinct from [the previous case of] maturation; here it is likewise so. If [the path] is at the stage of the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), it is termed "attaining enlightenment" (*bodhi-prāpti*);
thus, by attaining that name, it is called "attained. If it reaches the stage of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it is termed "correctly attained," which is [what is meant by] maturation.
[This refers to] Bodhi.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "These and those disciples [of Vasubandhu], up to the divergent views of the two schools," one asks: in the subsequent passage, there is no mention of Dharmapāla;
yet in this current passage, it refers to the disciples of Dharmapāla. Thus, there are divergent views between the two schools. Furthermore, if it is Mahāyāna...
People do not understand that this is a discourse on the ultimate suchness (*tathatā*) as the gate of non-extinction.

Yet, when that treatise asks what distinguishes the nirvāṇa without remainder of a śrāvaka from that of a Buddha, it answers that there is no distinction; this is because, according to the three vehicles, all are alike in being devoid of a body that serves as the basis for suffering.

When those of the two vehicles have entered the remainderless [nirvāṇa], their bodies and their arising perish together. Although the Buddha lacks the basis for suffering, he attains an uncontaminated body of the five aggregates that is eternal, and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "because the mind and so forth are universal, one should explain according to the meaning," if this refers to the *ālayavijñāna*:

That which is called "mind" (*citta*), that which is called the "basis of the knowable," that which is called "seed-consciousness," and that which is called "appropriating consciousness" (*ādāna-vijñāna*)—
at the time of the Vajra-mind of the two vehicles and when Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above relinquish the *ālaya-vijñāna*,

these are also termed the "relinquished mind," the "relinquished basis of the knowable," and the "relinquished appropriating consciousness. The maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is termed "mind" and...
As for its being called the seed-consciousness, the support of the knowable, and the *ādāna* (appropriating consciousness):
