when that Bodhisattva’s adamantine mind abandons the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), as do those of the two vehicles upon entering the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*)—at the time of abandoning the ripening consciousness—it is also called abandoning the mind that is the support of the knowable, the seed-consciousness, and the *ādāna*.
It is like the stainless consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*), which persists until the end of the future.
Because it is not interrupted, that which is known by the mind—namely, its support (*āśraya*) and so forth—is likewise not interrupted.
Some say that the "state with outflows" (*sāsrava-avasthā*) reveals both the former two and the latter one.

The former two refer to the state with outflows wherein there is only the self-characteristic aspect (*svalakṣaṇa-mukha*) of the *ādāna-vijñāna*, and only the other-characteristic aspect (*vilakṣaṇa-mukha*) of the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*). As for the latter one:
And finally, there is the door of relinquishment at the stage of arhatship. These three doors exist only during the contaminated (sāsrava) state;

since they were explained in detail previously, they will not be discussed here. Regarding the statement that "the causal characteristics are entirely unknowable because they revolve constantly together with relinquishment, pervading both cause and fruit":
if the five doors pervade both cause and fruit, there is first, the door of all types of causal characteristics, and second, the unknowable...
[This refers to] the gate of knowing; third, the gate of the cognitive aspect (*ākāra*) of consciousness; fourth, the gate of being accompanied by the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*);

and fifth, the gate of constant revolution like a violent torrent. Question: Since it is said that "constant revolution" applies even to the Buddha-fruit (*buddhatva*), and it is stated regarding the Buddha-fruit that it is "constantly revolving like a violent torrent," there are the three types of dharmas and metaphors mentioned in the preceding text, such as the flowing water of a torrent and so forth. Answer: Indeed, regarding the Buddha-fruit, first...
The eight evolving consciousnesses constantly revolve like a flowing stream. They also possess a small portion of the preceding [consciousness], and the preceding water serves as a metaphor;

however, they lack such functions as floating, sinking, or moving upward. Regarding the "gate of the unknowable": Question: Ordinary beings at the stage of the cause do not possess universal knowledge (*sarvajñāna*);
thus, while their eighth consciousness and its objects can all be known, why is it said that the "unknowable" applies even to the fruit of Buddhahood? Answer: It is also as follows...
Regarding the eighth consciousness in its causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*) and its corresponding objects, it is "knowable" insofar as all Buddhas know them;
yet, because other ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not know them, it is "unknowable. The present case is likewise:

although the eighth consciousness in the state of Buddhahood (*buddhatva-phala*) and its objects are known by all Buddhas—and are thus "knowable"—this status applies only in relation to the state of Buddhahood.

However, regarding the concern that this might be confused with the stage of a cause (*hetu-avasthā*): the eighth [consciousness] during the causal stage is associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), as it is the master of the ripening retribution (*vipāka*).
In contrast, the feeling of equanimity at the stage of Buddhahood is not the master of ripening retribution.

Therefore, because there is a fear that the feeling of equanimity at the level of the fruit (*phala*) might be confused with the feeling of equanimity during the causal stage, this treatise here also maintains that it is associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity.
This is correct. Because within the absence of diminution of desire (*chanda-akṣaya*), there is the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

Here, the term "absence of diminution" (*akṣaya*) refers to what is called the "absence of diminution of desire," as well as the "absence of diminution of mindfulness" (*smṛti-akṣaya*) and so forth. In newer sūtras and śāstras, these are referred to as the "non-retrogression of desire" (*chanda-aparihāṇi*) and the "non-retrogression of mindfulness" (*smṛti-aparihāṇi*), and so on.
The Tathāgata possesses no such uncertainty or retrogression. Regarding the mind: since [the question] concerns the Buddha’s eighth consciousness...

There is a meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Among the nine successive concentrations (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), which one is this? The answer is: it is exclusively the initial realization of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) for those of the lower stream (*adhogāmin*).

It pervades both the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Within the forty stages (*bhūmi*), there are also various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) within that very Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

If, during the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*), a single moment of mind simultaneously possesses both desire and mindfulness, even so, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) within a single thought-moment cannot take the past or future as an object.
However, at the level of the Buddha-fruit (*buddhatva-phala*), within a single thought-moment, desire can take the future as its object and mindfulness can take the past as its object.
Within the causal stage, although the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) occurs in a single moment, it is unable to take the past as its object.

No. Only [the sixth consciousness] can take the present as its object. If it is the sixth consciousness within the causal stage, it can only take a small portion of the past and future as its object and cannot do so for a long duration.
However, at the stage of Buddhahood, all eight consciousnesses can take the three periods of time as their objects within a single moment.
The desire [of the supernormal knowledge of death and rebirth] takes the future as its object; the recollection [of the supernormal knowledge of past lives] takes the past as its object.

Therefore, it is said in the Mahāyāna that these six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and ten powers (*daśabala*) arise simultaneously within a single moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). This means that within a single thought-moment, all eight consciousnesses arise together;

thus, when the knowledge of past lives arises, it takes the present as its object, and immediately the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*) arises, taking the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of the present as its object. When [the knowledge of cessation] arises...
Through the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*), one takes as objects the mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) and fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*) of the eight stages.

Immediately thereafter, one gives rise to the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*) to take form as its object, and gives rise to the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-abhijñā*) to take sound as its object.

For example, in a single moment, a Bodhisattva of the first stage can also know a hundred kalpas past and future, and can see a hundred Buddha-worlds; even their bodies can travel there. Thus, one should know that [the power of] the Great [Vehicle] is such.
Within a single thought-moment, the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) arise simultaneously. According to the teachings of the Hīnayāna, however, the six consciousnesses cannot arise simultaneously;

thus, there are three types of regression (parihāṇi): first, regression from what has already been attained; second, regression from what has not yet been attained; and third, regression from enjoyment.

A person of dull faculties who is an Arhat possesses all three types of regression; that is, having already attained the latter three fruits, they may regress from those latter three fruits, continuing until—

Regarding the first fruit (*prathamaphala*), it is termed "already attained. Furthermore, regarding qualities not yet attained within the Buddha’s body, even a noble one (*ārya*) does not attain those qualities within the Buddha’s body;

this is termed "retrogression from the unattained" (*aprāptaparihāṇi*). If a noble one gives rise to the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), they cannot simultaneously give rise to the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*).

If they give rise to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*), it cannot arise while taking the past as its object. If they give rise to the supernormal power of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*), it takes [the present] as its object.
Regarding the future: when one [mental state] arises, the others cannot arise; this is called "retrogression from enjoyment" (*parihāṇi*), because the six consciousnesses cannot arise simultaneously.

If one is an Arhat of the non-inferior nature (*an-avamardanīya-gotra*), there are only two types of retrogression: namely, retrogression from what has not yet been attained and retrogression from enjoyment;
there is no retrogression from what has already been attained. Such a person does not attain the qualities within the Buddha-body; this is termed...

There is no falling away from what has not yet been attained. As for enjoyment, it is as previously explained. If, within the Buddha’s own body, there is only one kind of falling away, it is solely the falling away from enjoyment;

that is, there is no falling away from what has already been attained nor falling away from what has not yet been attained. However, according to the Mahāyāna and the Sautrāntika school, there are likewise three kinds of falling away.

For example, even an Arhat of dull faculties may fall away from three things: the attainment of the nine meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the state of being beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the blissful abiding in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).

If one now regresses from what has already been attained, it is called "regression from what has been attained" (*prāpti-parihāṇi*). If it concerns regression from what has not yet been attained, it is explained in the same manner as in the Hīnayāna.

If we consider the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), they can arise simultaneously. However, within the first eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), there is "regression from enjoyment" (*upabhoga-parihāṇi*);

for example, when the first two liberations arise, these two liberations are the mind of the first dhyāna (*prathama-dhyāna-citta*), and one cannot further give rise to the remaining liberations. As for the other liberations...

This is because the stages upon which they rely are distinct. Furthermore, just as when one gives rise to the liberation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*), one cannot simultaneously give rise to the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*) and so forth, because minds belonging to two different stages cannot arise concurrently. Moreover, within the body of a Buddha, all three types of retrogression are entirely absent.

The commentary states: "Because the Tathāgata has attained the four kinds of verified purity (*catur-avetyaprasāda*). The four verified purities refer to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the precepts (*śīla*).

Because he has personally realized these four, and because they are untainted (*anāsrava*), they are called "pure. Because he possesses profound faith in these four, it is termed "unshakeable faith" (*akopya-prasāda*).
Thus, we know that the Buddha also possesses faith. Question: Regarding the eight consciousnesses of the state of Buddhahood, have all of them attained verified purity?

As stated elsewhere, the Commentary maintains that it is not logically contradictory for [vitarka and vicāra] to also pertain to the untainted (*anāsrava*), because in the untainted minds of Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, there are also untainted vitarka and vicāra;
thus, vitarka and vicāra also pertain to the untainted. However, in the case of a Buddha’s untainted mind, there is no vitarka.
It is *anuprekṣā* (investigation). The commentary states that it cannot be shaken, unlike other forms of wisdom. Question: In what sense is it called "shaken"? Answer:

If, during the causal stage of the ten bhūmis, the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is still subject to interruption, it is called "shaken. Furthermore, [the questioner] asks regarding the wisdom of equality of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

It is also associated with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). How is it that its nature is not like that of other types of wisdom? Answer: The eighth wisdom of the Buddha-fruit, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), is exclusively associated with the sensation of equanimity.
As for the other three wisdoms, they may be accompanied by either joy (*prīti*) or bliss (*sukha*).

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states that the supramundane supernormal powers (*anāsrava-abhijñā*) which range through the six stages of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) are those that course through these levels.

Regarding the "six [stages] of the form realm," these refer to the four fundamental dhyānas, the intermediate dhyāna, the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna, and the four fundamental concentrations of the formless realm.
However, such true merits as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*) exist only in the fourth dhyāna.
As for the remaining nine stages, by analogy they possess uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) contemplation; however, they lack such genuine functional efficacy.

Why is it that only the initial *anāgamya* stage is taken, while the other seven higher *anāgamya* stages are not? This is because those [higher stages] lack the uncontaminated path and are thus unable to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*);
for this reason, they are not included.
Regarding the statement, "The manifestation of this wisdom occurs only in the fourth dhyāna, as it mostly relies on the celestial abodes (devasthāna) and frequently gives rise to great compassion":
if the Buddha’s wisdom manifests, it occurs only in the fourth dhyāna and not in other stages. Thus, among the celestial abodes, he dwells in the fourth dhyāna;
within that dwelling, he mostly dwells in the ten powers (daśabala), and within those, he mostly dwells in the realization of emptiness (śūnyatā).

[He] is liberated. If, among the Brahma-abodes (*brahmavihāra*), one dwells predominantly in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)—the Brahma-abodes being loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—the commentary states that there is no logical reason to preclude [the existence of such a state], and thus there is a mind in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that possesses universal objectification (*sarvālambana*).
If one takes five stages, then the initial *anāgamya* (preparatory stage) is excluded. If one were to sever the defilements of the desire realm, the initial *anāgamya* would be required;

however, since this does not intend to sever the defilements of the desire realm, the initial *anāgamya* is not produced. One takes only the four fundamental dhyānas and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
Regarding the fact that the commentary (*śāstra*) should state "five stages" and further mention [them], it refers to the three lower dhyānas, the initial *anāgamya*, and the intermediate dhyāna.
This refers to dhyāna. The previous interpretation is superior. If one takes all six stages generally, this includes the initial *anāgamya* stage.

If it concerns the mind and mental factors of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they can universally take the mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) as their object; however, they cannot universally take the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) of that stage as objects, because such factors do not exist there.

Regarding the statement that although the four lower stages still possess only the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*): these "four stages" refer to the four stages consisting of the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*) and the fundamental dhyāna of the first dhyāna.
According to the Mahāyāna school, all of these generally admit of the sensations of joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*), as explained below in the exposition of the three sensations.
Although they generally admit of all four, these four stages still possess only the sensation of equanimity because of their profound tranquility (*śānta*). [This] excludes...
Regarding the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the Mahāyāna accepts it as being associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
As for the commentary’s statement that "the ālayavijñāna is accompanied by equanimity and proceeds uninterruptedly throughout all three states of sensation":

this means that while among the first six consciousnesses there are the three sensations of joy, pleasure, and equanimity, the eighth consciousness always possesses the sensation of equanimity; therefore, it is said to "proceed together" [with them].
[The commentary] concludes: "It should be understood that the remaining three feelings are produced by mental attention (*manasikāra*), even unto their distinct manifestation.
Question: Is the feeling of joy and pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) associated with attaining the state of Buddhahood also produced by mental attention? Answer: To a small extent.
It is also produced through volition (*manasikāra*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “in this stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*), it is similar to the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) and cannot give rise to the two sensations of pleasure (*sukha*) or joy (*saumanasya*), because these are induced by volition,” the meaning is as follows:
within the state of the Buddha-fruit, the eighth consciousness is characterized by the sensation of equanimity. As for that Buddha-fruit...

The eighth consciousness is also characterized by the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Even within the state of Buddhahood, although the preceding seventh consciousness may give rise to feelings of joy or equanimity, the fundamental consciousness (the ālayavijñāna) remains constantly in a state of equanimity because it functions spontaneously (*svarasena*).
If it were associated with feelings of joy or pleasure, it would involve volitional effort (*cetanā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
"Taking up" means to bring about.
The commentary states that in other stages there are none at all, totaling sixty-eight; it further says that such merits mostly rely on the fourth stage. The explanation says:
since the previous commentary text stated that there are none at all in other stages, yet the subsequent commentary passage says that such merits rely solely on the fourth stage.

Regarding dhyāna: the preceding passage states that it is entirely absent [in the higher realms], while the subsequent passage states that it mostly relies on other stages (*bhūmi*) and also includes a small portion.
Since these textual statements contradict one another, we know that it is said to exist in a small portion of the other stages as well.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "although this arises in both the form and formless realms, up to all such wisdoms":

if one is in the causal stage of the ten bhūmis, one attains the cultivation and increase of those seeds; however, if one is in the resultant stage of Buddhahood, one cannot cultivate the increase of seeds either.
Although these exist in the other nine bhūmis, they cannot produce them; only the fundamental stage of the fourth dhyāna can produce them in its actual manifestation (*samudācāra*). As it is said:
The three types of peripheral knowledge (*prāntakoṭika-jñāna*) of the Hīnayāna are also like those of ordinary persons who, from beginningless time, have practiced only the paths of non-Buddhists.

They give rise to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and suppress the afflictions through the six modes of practice. Therein, there are only the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation, but they cannot give rise to the truth of the path. They feel revulsion toward the suffering of suffering in the lower realms; this is the truth of suffering.

They feel revulsion toward the coarse nature of the lower realms; this is the truth of origin. They rejoice in the tranquility and subtlety of the higher realms; this is the truth of cessation. There is no truth of the path.
Truth. Although one may give rise to impure conventional knowledge (*sāsrava-saṃvṛti-jñāna*), it is not called the untainted Truth of the Path (*anāsrava-mārgasatya*).

For example, when one is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and gives rise to the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of the first dhyāna, one suppresses and exhausts the nine grades of defilement of the desire realm;

yet, it is only after one has already aspired to the superior first dhyāna that one actually attains the first dhyāna. If one feels revulsion toward the lower stage as being suffering and coarse, this constitutes the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*). Aspiration...
The higher stages are characterized by tranquility, subtlety, and detachment; these constitute the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Even the contaminated fundamental concentration (*sāsrava-maula-samādhi*) of the first dhyāna cannot free one from the defilements of the first dhyāna itself or those of other levels.

One must attain the concentrations of the second dhyāna or above before one can finally become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna, continuing in this manner up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
From the first dhyāna stage upward, in each successive stage, one feels revulsion for the lower level and aspiration for the higher.

However, the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) cannot be subdued, because there is no further state above it toward which one could aspire. This is like a centipede: only when it has moved its front legs can it move its hind legs.
If it reaches the very tip of the inverted peak, where it moves, if it cannot move its front legs, it likewise cannot shift its hind legs. Now, this case is exactly the same.

If one is established in the eight dhyāna stages and there is a higher stage to be delighted in, one is then able to weary of and subdue the defilements of one’s own lower stages, up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
One then delights in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above as being tranquil, sublime, and detached, while wearying of the lower sphere of nothingness.

Regarding the suffering, coarseness, and hindrances as objects to be suppressed, one subdues the defilements of the sphere of nothingness. The first leg is like the path of liberation characterized by tranquility, subtlety, and detachment.
As for the latter two legs, they are analogous to the path of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*), which involves revulsion toward the lower stages as being suffering, coarseness, and hindrances.

However, upon reaching the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), because there is no higher stage to be sought after, it does not constitute a path of liberation; since it does not constitute a path of liberation...
The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) likewise cannot subdue the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), nor does it constitute the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Later, when one becomes a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*) and enters the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the "patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises as the path of uninterrupted transition, severing the afflictions beneath the truth of suffering in the desire realm.

Then, the "patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises, severing the afflictions beneath the truth of suffering in the two higher realms, continuing up to the fourth [moment] of the subsequent knowledge of suffering.

At the time of wisdom (*jñāna*), because the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) that previously existed in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)—which suppresses the afflictions through the six modes of practice—remains within the future store (*anāgata-garbha*), it can no longer arise from within that future store.
There is only a single dharma in total, which was previously acquired and serves as the precursor for the subsequent arising of the inferential knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*).
Since its meaning is expressed by the term "dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), what exactly is this dharma-knowledge of suffering?
"Before this [realization] arose, I merely used conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) to suppress the afflictions; yet I could not do so even a hundred times.
I could not suppress the afflictions of the lower stages to be born in the higher, nor, having been born in the higher, return to be born in the lower.

I could only suppress the Truth of Suffering from the Sphere of Nothingness downward, and the path for abandoning the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Today, however, I have completely severed all the afflictions of the three realms—how magnificent! I thought.

Worldly knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) arises in the future and does not give rise to the afflictions of the three realms. The same applies to the knowledges of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) and cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).

Regarding the "limits of the subsequent knowledges" (*anvaya-jñāna-pakṣa*): these are the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*), and the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*).

Because these three occur at the final limit [of their respective categories], they are called "limits. The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) is likewise; it does not arise in other stages, just as worldly knowledge does not.

It arises. The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśajñāna) attains its manifest activity in the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), just as the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) attain their manifest arising.
In the older sūtras and śāstras, it is said that "conventional wisdom" (*samvṛtijñāna*) is possessed by all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) throughout the four modes of birth;
thus, the new [translation] refers to it as conventional wisdom.
The commentary states: "Because it takes the eighteen realms as its object, whether conditioned or unconditioned, it is therefore called 'thorough knowledge' (*parijñā*).
This explanation of thorough knowledge is most excellent and correct. *Cheng weishi lun shu chao*, Scroll Six.
*Cheng weishi lun shu chao*, Scroll Seven.

Regarding the five teachings and ten principles that prove the existence of the foundational consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) in the commentary: as for the "five teachings," the text of the commentary does not explain them clearly.
Here, there are three general interpretations. The first interpretation explains two passages from the *Abhidharma-sūtra*.

The verses [of this treatise], the verses of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and the commentaries—these and other such immeasurable Mahāyāna sūtras, such as those in the *Prakaraṇāryavāca-śāstra* (or *Xianyang lun*), the sūtras concerning ordinary beings who are shrouded by ignorance and bound by the fetter of craving, and the *Pañcabīja-sūtra*—all these aforementioned sūtras are exclusively those not commonly accepted [by other schools]. Now, they are all combined together into one. [End of section]

The "Sūtras" category consists of two parts: those accepted by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna (the Lesser Vehicle), which are divided into four, and those accepted exclusively by the Mahāyāna, which constitute one.

Specifically, the four accepted by both vehicles are: first, the *mūlavijñāna* (root consciousness); second, the *bhavāṅgavijñāna* (consciousness of the constituent of existence); third, the *saṃsāraparyantaskandha* (aggregates at the limit of birth and death);

and fourth, the *ālaya-vijñāna* characterized by attachment, delight, and joy. As for the one accepted exclusively by the Mahāyāna, it refers to the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*. Thus, they are called the "Five Teachings. Another interpretation states: first, [the Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra]...
The *Abhidharma-sūtra*, although having explanations in three locations, constitutes a single teaching as a whole. Second, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*;

third, the verses of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*; and fourth, within the prose sections of that same sūtra—within these and other such immeasurable Mahāyāna sūtras, it is all specifically stated that this eighth consciousness exists.
Thus, this commentary states: "As in the fifth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*..."
A cited sūtra states: "Enveloped by ignorance and bound by the fetters of craving, the fool brings about a body possessed of consciousness.
Furthermore, it says, "It is like the five seeds," and so forth, up to "it is called the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna)," etc.; these are all what is being illustrated.

The "five" refers to the *Mahāsāṃghika Āgama* and other such texts, which name it the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the partaking-of-consciousness (*bhavāṅgavijñāna*), the aggregate that reaches the end of saṃsāra (*āsaṃsārikaskandha*), and so on; this is the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) perspective.

The *Sammatīya-sūtra* (or *Sādhāraṇa-sūtra*) is taken as a single teaching [for the first category]. Regarding the third interpretation: it takes only the Mahāyāna *asādhāraṇa-sūtras* (non-common sūtras) as the five teachings.
First, the verses of the *Abhidharma-sūtra*; second, the verses of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*; third, the verses of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*;
fourth, the passage beginning with "Fools are shrouded by ignorance and bound by the fetters of craving"; fifth, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, it is like the five... [and so forth].
The *Pañcabījaka-sūtra*, which is accepted by both [Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna], serves as proof for the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*).
Although it is believed within our own Mahāyāna school, it is not accepted by the Hīnayāna; therefore, we adopt the first interpretation, taking the sūtra accepted by the Hīnayāna as superior.

As for the statement regarding "annihilationism and eternalism" from [the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*] up to "it is not exclusively based on this," this is explained according to the preceding clarification that the *ālayavijñāna* is not...
Within the section on severing [the views of] annihilation and permanence, it is stated that the *ālayavijñāna* is neither annihilated nor permanent because it has been evolving continuously.

If the eighth consciousness were to evolve continuously and without interruption during the causal stage, then one could say that the *ālayavijñāna* is neither annihilated nor permanent, because the *ālayavijñāna* exists as a cause.
However, regarding the present state of Buddhahood, there is no *ālayavijñāna* upon the level of the Buddha-fruit.
Regarding the *ālayavijñāna*, there is only the meaning of the stainless consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) which perpetually functions in a manner that is neither interrupted nor eternal.

Now, concerning the eighth consciousness at the stage of Buddhahood, within the state where cause and effect are uninterrupted and non-eternal, the term "ālaya" is used as a name derived from its causal state.
However, the previous question was broad in its scope while the terminology used was narrow.

When the previous question asked whether the *ālaya* is subject to cessation or permanence, it encompassed all inquiries regarding the eighth consciousness, whether in the causal stage or at the fruit of Buddhahood.

Yet, in the subsequent inquiry concerning the associated mental factors (*samprayukta*), it specifically states that from time immemorial until it is transformed, the *ālayavijñāna* is always associated with these in all states.

Regarding the association with the five mental factors (*caitta*): this name "ālaya" applies universally to those in the two vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) as well as to Bodhisattvas on the ten stages;
all possess the designation "ālayavijñāna" and are associated with these five factors.

Therefore, speaking from the perspective of reality from the eighth stage upward, while those in the two vehicles who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) and Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage do indeed possess ālayavijñāna, [they are not yet fully so].

In the case of birth, it is associated with the five sense-bases. If one is a Bodhisattva from the eighth stage upward, then regarding the ālayavijñāna, when it is said to be associated with the five sense-bases, there is no longer the ālayavijñāna;
rather, there is only the vipākavijñāna (retribution-consciousness) associated with the five sense-bases.
Now, regarding the statement that [the ālayavijñāna] "co-exists" with those above the eighth stage, this is also a designation made within the context of the "co-arising cause.
This indicates that it is named according to its initial relinquishment, whereas the term "that mind" (tad-manas) indicates that it pervades all stages.

However, when the term *ālayavijñāna* appears in the text of this specific fascicle, it is designated according to its initial relinquishment; whereas in other passages, whether preceding or following, when it says—

Regarding the eighth consciousness: its name is established by manifesting its pervasion across all stages. Furthermore, according to what is explained below, among all states of existence (*bhava*), it is that which destroys the five appropriated aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) and is not a locus for attachment;
it is that which is reckoned as having no separate self-substance apart from form (*rūpa*) and so forth. This refers to the second interpretation and others.
The term "others" (*ādi*) includes the remaining [aggregates] such as form. Therefore, below, when refuting the Sarvāstivāda, it first addresses the five appropriated aggregates.

Nor is it a locus for true attachment. Since it speaks of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is included therein, the five aggregates are taken collectively.
As for the statement in this fascicle that "this nirvāṇa is not an object of craving, and therefore it is not discussed," regarding the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth:

One immediately gathers the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and takes up the fifty-one mental concomitants (*caitta*). One gathers the existence of real dharmas (*dravya-dharma*), which consists of taking up the twenty-four non-associated provisional dharmas such as acquisition (*prāpti*).
Furthermore, one equally takes up the eleven types of form (*rūpa*); thus, one equally takes up all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), for these are the objects of craving and attachment.
One does not unequally take up unconditioned *nirvāṇa*, because *nirvāṇa* is not a true object of craving and attachment; it is the state of being free from [such] commonality.

Regarding the statement that there is no separate entity apart from the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), the word "separate" (*li*) in the commentary is an error; it should read "commonly accepted" (*gong*).

Thus, it means that the five aggregates are universally acknowledged as the true object of attachment. If one considers anything other than the five aggregates of clinging—such as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas—that is not the true object of attachment.
Furthermore, another interpretation states that the meaning is that both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools commonly accept that there is nothing else apart from the five aggregates.
Because the eighth consciousness is their very nature, the adherents of the Hīnayāna now maintain that there are only six consciousnesses.

This is because the Hīnayāna maintains that apart from the six consciousnesses, there is no separate nature of an eighth consciousness; they define the aggregate of consciousness as consisting of these six.

Therefore, the Hīnayāna now challenges the eighth consciousness, asserting that it has no distinct nature apart from the eye-consciousness and the others. "Māna" (量) refers to the act of measuring or evaluating.
Regarding the statement, "The meaning of *niyama* (ascertainment) should be understood as it is usually [explained]," one asks:

how can the correct principle (*nyāya*) of the teaching be called "ascertained" (*niyata*), such that it is said that the correct principle of the Noble Teaching (*ārya-śāsana*) is to be understood by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? One asks: the correct principle of the Noble Teaching is to be inferred.

If the three types of valid cognition are called "cognition" (*pramiti*) because they measure, yet these are not found in various treatises—such as the *Śāstra-saṃgraha*—which are identical to this same sūtra, then what of this fascicle?
In the *Abhidharmasūtra*, there is the verse on the "dhātu from beginningless time," and in the *Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra*, there is the verse beginning with "The ādānavijñāna is profound and subtle.
These two verses from the present sūtra are also found in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises.
However, as for the subsequent verse beginning with "Like the ocean encountering the condition of wind," this exists only in this [present] consciousness; it is not found in other treatises.
This is a verse.

The Commentary does not state that it is "countered" (*pratya*) in relation to "possessing phenomena" (*sadharmaka*); rather, it says it is "countered" in relation to "phenomena" (*dharma*). Therefore, one should not raise this as an objection. Now, let us explain the title of the scripture:

*Abhi* means "countered" (*prati*), and *Dharma* means "phenomenon" (*dharma*). This name also applies to the case of being "countered" by "possessing phenomena. Why, then, is it said to be "countered"?

Regarding the term "dharma" (dharmas) used in reference to *abhidharma*, the answer is as follows: If "dharma" refers to the *āśraya* (the substratum), it possesses only the sense of "supporting" (*dhṛti*) and lacks the sense of "guidance" (*niyama*).

If one speaks of *abhidharma*, it must combine both the senses of guidance and support. This is because, in the context of *hetuvidyā* (logic), "dharma" is named as that which supports, while "adharma" is named as that which provides guidance.

Furthermore, within *hetuvidyā*, "dharma" may be treated as the subject (*pakṣa*), or it may be treated as the predicate (*sādhya-dharma*). For example, for the Sāṃkhya teacher, the "Self" (*ātman*) is such a dharma.

Regarding "existent phenomena" (*bhāva-dharma*): "thought" (*cetanā*) is called a phenomenon because it, along with existent phenomena, is not fixed [in its nature]. One cannot raise an objection against this. As for the term *Abhidharma*:

"toward" (*abhi*) means "directed toward" the Dharma, which consists of teaching (*śāsana*), practice (*pratipatti*), and realization (*adhigama*). There are three interpretations: first, teaching is directed toward principle (*nīti*);

second, practice is directed toward the fruit (*phala*); third, realization is directed toward the object (*viṣaya*). There are also two other interpretations: one says that if there are existent phenomena...

There is only the "retention" (dhāraṇa) without the "norm" (nyāya). If a phenomenon (*dharma*) is to possess both norm and retention, then what is now called *Abhidharma* (the "counter-phenomenon") must consist of both norm and retention within that phenomenon;
it does not refer merely to the counter-entity of a phenomenon. If one were to say it refers only to the counter-entity of a phenomenon, there would be only retention without norm.

Second, according to the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic), both the phenomenon and its counter-entity are indeterminate. For example, volition (*cetanā*) and so forth are intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), whereas the self (*ātman*)— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the partial nature of the source.*
The distinction lies in [the Sāṃkhya's claim that] the self (*ātman*) is non-mental. However, the Sāṃkhya maintains that the self is precisely thought (*cetanā*);

thus, the self is the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), while thought is its specific modification (*vikāra*). Since both the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) would be indeterminate, we speak only of "counter-dharmas" (*dharmapratipakṣa*), not of "counter-substrata."

Regarding the first two phrases of the commentary, they are called "the words that bring about a single meaning. However, the first phrase only mentions the four characters "since beginningless time" (*anādikālam āgatam*);
the intent is to reveal that the second phrase below also contains "since beginningless time. The second phrase contains the three characters "all dharmas" (*sarvadharmāḥ*);
the intent is likewise to reveal that the first phrase also contains the three characters "all dharmas. Thus, they mutually clarify one another. Therefore, the first...
The first phrase speaks only of "since beginningless time," while the second phrase speaks only of "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*); these two phrases mutually clarify one another.

Regarding the statement that "among the seeds, manifestations, and consciousnesses, it is the seed-consciousness," this means that the seeds of all phenomena reside within the eighth manifesting consciousness;
therefore, the eighth consciousness is called the "seed-consciousness. This eighth consciousness is capable of maintaining [the seeds].
"Consciousness" refers to the seeds that are simultaneously supported [by it]; thus, the name "supporting consciousness" is established.

Although the active manifestation (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) is also called the "causal characteristic" (*nimitta*), this refers to the eighth consciousness in its active state acting as the supporting cause for all phenomena.
This passage is to be understood in the same way as the previous explanation regarding the "characteristic of the cause of all seeds."

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that although the eighth consciousness and the five sense organs alike serve as supports for various phenomena by undergoing transformation together, they are explained separately:

the eighth consciousness also serves as the support for all phenomena; likewise, the five material sense organs serve as the supports for the seven visual consciousnesses and other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Although the sense organs and the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) share the same status as supports, why are they not explained in the same way? The answer is: if the five material...
The faculties serve as the support (*āśraya*). Furthermore, encountering conditions serves as the causal factor (*pratyaya*), or the visual faculty undergoes transformation;

although this is called "transformation," if the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is taken as the support, it is eternally unchanging. Therefore, what is discussed here is the retributive fruit (*vipāka*).

According to my humble opinion, the eighth consciousness is the support for the five faculties, the sensory realm, and the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the first seven consciousnesses; it acts as the support for all form and mind, and is therefore so named.

Although they are the same in terms of being the basis (*āśraya*), as for "transformation" (*pariṇāma*): the eighth consciousness is able to take as its object the transformation of the five sense organs, the receptacle world, and so forth.
As for "not transforming," this refers to the eighth consciousness not being able to take as its object the transformation of the seven active consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

Therefore, regarding the distinct explanation in the *Pramāṇa*: it is because of "transformation" that the treatise speaks of it as "transforming. It is because those [seven] do not transform [in that way] that the treatise speaks of them as "not transforming."
Another explanation states that it is "transformed" or "untransformed" because it serves as the basis for those [seven consciousnesses]. This is explained differently in other treatises.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "[the eighth consciousness] does not take the transformed fruit of the seven consciousnesses as its object": the eighth consciousness does not take the active manifestations (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) of the seven consciousnesses as its objects;

the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) only takes the matter (*rūpa-dharma*) of the five sense organs—which are the fruits of transformation—as its object. These are precisely the five sense organs, the world, and so forth. Although... [the eighth consciousness] is the first... [it does not take them as objects].
That the eight consciousnesses, from the manas up to the sixth consciousness, take [the eighth] as their support for transformation—this is the first interpretation.
To explain the meaning: the eighth consciousness acts as the simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) for the seventh consciousness;

furthermore, the seventh consciousness takes the seeds within the eighth consciousness as its causal condition support (*hetu-pratyaya-āśraya*), and the seventh consciousness also takes the active manifestation (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) of the eighth consciousness as its simultaneous support.
There is a basis. Furthermore, the seventh consciousness takes the eighth consciousness as its object.
Now, it is only the active (pravṛtti) seventh consciousness that serves as the basis for the active sixth consciousness; thus, the active sixth consciousness depends upon the seventh.

This clarifies only the co-existent faculty (sahabhū-indriya) as the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya), without mentioning the seed as the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya), nor the equal-and-immediate mental faculty (samanantara-manas-indriya). Moreover, the seventh...
Regarding the statement that "the eight consciousnesses, up to the seventh, rely upon the eighth," this is the second interpretation.
It means that because the eighth consciousness serves as the support for all [other] supports, it is only then that the seventh relies upon the eighth. Furthermore, the sixth relies upon the seventh;
thus, this second interpretation differs from the previous one.
The Commentary states that regarding whichever of these transgressions applies, one must first establish that the sixth faculty with roots (*sendriya*) is precisely the *manas*. As for this *manas*:

currently, the Hīnayāna does not admit the existence of a seventh consciousness. If, within the causal state, it were said to be subsumed under the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), [it would follow that it is not the seventh].
The Hīnayāna does not admit the existence of the seventh *manas* consciousness, as it is subsumed under the category of evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

Consequently, among the reasons [adduced], at least one lacks the property of being established for that school. Furthermore, others do not admit the existence of the eighth consciousness; therefore, we shall first establish the existence of the seventh consciousness.
The *Pramāṇa* states: "The sixth consciousness definitely exists, because it is subsumed under the simultaneously arising and non-common sense-faculty (*indriya*).

The five consciousnesses and that sixth consciousness both possess a non-common sense-faculty, which is precisely the manas. Only then is the existence of the manas established as having a sense-faculty;

only then should it be said that the seventh and sixth consciousnesses definitely possess a simultaneously arising sense-faculty, because they are subsumed under the evolving consciousnesses. This [is what] exists.
Regarding the claim that the five consciousnesses constitute an "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) fallacy: one raises the inconclusive objection as follows:
Is it the case that, although the five consciousnesses possess the nature of consciousness, they do not take the seventh consciousness as their co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*)?

Or is it the case that, because the sixth consciousness possesses the nature of consciousness, it takes the seventh consciousness as its co-existent support? Since the five consciousnesses are consciousness and possess the nature of consciousness, this constitutes an inconclusive fallacy.
If it is argued that, because the sixth is of the nature of consciousness and not one of the five consciousnesses, it takes the seventh as its co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*);
and likewise, because the seventh is of the nature of consciousness and not one of the five consciousnesses, it does not take the seventh as its co-existent dharma—this is also not the case.
For it is accepted that the seventh consciousness has no support.

The Commentary states: "Alternatively, if it were not so, the preceding manas would have the fault of being indeterminate with respect to the eighth consciousness as its co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), because the eighth consciousness is already established as a co-existent support.

This is because the fundamental intent of this treatise is to clarify that the first seven consciousnesses depend upon the eighth consciousness. Therefore, in order to avoid the fault of indeterminacy, the text establishes the eighth consciousness as the co-existent support for the seventh.
As for the formal inference (*pramāṇa*): [the seventh consciousness has the eighth consciousness as its co-existent support, because it is a consciousness that arises simultaneously with it].

It is said: The seventh consciousness takes the eighth consciousness as its co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), because it is of the nature of consciousness, just like the first six consciousnesses.

[The opponent objects: "This is indeterminate, as it is 'made by another' (*parakṛta*). [The proponent asks: "Is it like the eighth consciousness? Since it is of the nature of consciousness, it has no co-existent support.

Does the seventh consciousness then lack a co-existent support? [The proponent replies: "Or is it like the first six consciousnesses? Since they are of that nature, they possess a co-existent support. The seventh [consciousness] likewise..."
There is a basis for this. Now, the treatise establishes the eighth consciousness in order to prevent this fault of indeterminacy.

It does so by establishing that the seventh consciousness serves as the simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) for the eighth, and that the eighth consciousness, being of the nature of consciousness, likewise uses the seventh as its simultaneous support. Since the seventh is of the nature of consciousness, it employs the eighth as its simultaneous support;
and since the eighth is of the nature of consciousness, it also employs the seventh as its simultaneous support.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) does not dispute the *samanantarāśraya* (immediately preceding support), as it concerns the cause of seeds;

since the cause of seeds was already addressed in the preceding section, it disputes only the *sahabhv-āśraya* (simultaneous support). Herein, we dispute only the simultaneous support and do not dispute the immediately preceding support, nor do we discuss seeds.

This is because the support of seeds was already clarified in the preceding section concerning the "beginningless element" (*anādikāliko dhātuḥ*), for the element is itself the seed. Thus, the former [section] has already explained it.
The discussion on the basis of the seeds is concluded; it shall not be further debated here.

In this commentary, the passage from "these defiled seeds can produce actual manifestations" up to "all sentient beings thus transmigrate through birth and death" refers to the defiled seeds that accord with actual manifestations.

The commentary states that all birth and death are "concordant with what precedes and subsequent to it" in terms of their essence being concordant with their function. This means that the preceding afflictions serve as causes capable of being concordant with what follows.

Furthermore, just as ignorance (*avidyā*) can be concordant with volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) to produce the fruit of the suffering of birth and death, their essence does not descend [upon one another], yet their nature and characteristics are mutually concordant.
It is through the arising of the function of ignorance that volitional formations are subsequently set in motion.
The treatise says: "Alternatively, it is produced by karma. Question: What is the difference between this and the other passages concerning afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering (*duḥkha*)?
Furthermore, what should be asked regarding the distinction between this statement that [beings] are born into the realms of form (*rūpa-gati*) and those others?

In this commentary, the explanation regarding the "grasping and maintaining" of all phenomena that accord with the process of transmigration, up to its similarity with the previous explanation, is as follows:
just as the five sense faculties rely upon the eighth consciousness, the eighth consciousness grasps and maintains the five sense faculties, like holding a staff in one's hand.
The manifesting afflictions and karma are not the five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*); these are what are termed "appropriated" (*upātta*).

Here, however, only the support (*āśraya*) is discussed because the eighth consciousness is called "the appropriator" (*ādāna*). Thus, the manifesting eighth consciousness serves as the support for the manifesting afflictions and karma; the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) is likewise so [supported].
The intended meaning here is that the manifesting fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) acts as the objective support (*āśraya*) for the manifesting afflictions and karma. That is to say:
This refers to the rule of adhering to names. Since [the afflictions] may manifest, they are themselves active manifestations; that is, they are active afflictions.
If karma is the manifestation of volition (*cetanā*), the eighth consciousness cannot directly take those active delusions and karma as its objects of adherence or support.

It takes as its objective sphere the manifest afflictions and karma; these are not like the five [sensory] objects such as form, which are called "guiding and supporting" (*ādhāra*) because they are insentient.
If it is the eighth consciousness, it can directly guide and support the five material sense-faculties, causing them not to be confused, and takes them as its object.
The commentary states that the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) is the basis for the realms of existence (*gati*), and so forth, up to being called the "limb of joyful experience.

Regarding this, the first interpretation holds that the external receptacle world, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and so on, are all the requisites for the realms of existence, and thus these five are called "realms of existence" (*gati*). The second interpretation...
That is to say, only afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma are taken as the "requisites" (*pariṣkāra*), because afflictions give rise to karma, and karma is capable of inducing birth.

This is as stated in both the Mahāyāna and the Sautrāntika school of the Hīnayāna. For example, just as the feeling of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*) is a "concordant dharma," so too are the five universal (*sarvatraga*) and specifically objective (*viṣayapratiniyata*) mental factors, the mental concomitants (*caitta*) and non-associated formations (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*), and the co-existent (*sahabhū*) factors—all these are called "concordant. Concordant...

Because it is associated with joy, the mind and mental factors, as well as acquisitions (*prāpti*) and so forth, along with the sensation of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*), are collectively termed the "joy factor of enlightenment" (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Here, too, it is the same: the body is the "destination" (*gati*); the afflictions and karma are the "factors conducive to the destination"; and the requisites for the destination are also "factors conducive to the destination.

Among these, all are termed "destinations. Furthermore, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is merely that which is capable of going to a destination, just as in the case of the [intermediate] state.

One who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) is necessarily unable to turn their mind toward the Mahāyāna. Such a person belongs to the category of those with indefinite lineage;
one who turns their mind toward the Mahāyāna will certainly not receive the body of an antarāparinirvāyin.

Regarding the commentary on "the formation of the world": because the seeds of the provisions (*sambhāra*) contained within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), as well as the seeds of the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), all reach maturation by depending upon the eighth consciousness, it is called "the formation of worldly purity" up to "the formation of the purity of afflictions.

All these are explained below in the tenth section, "Defilement Following the Mind" (*cittānuvartin-saṃkleśa*). If there is one who dies in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*) and is reborn in a non-equipoised state...

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* and other texts also state that [the seeds] accord with the manifest activity (*samudācāra*), up to the point where it says: "The afflictions serve as the support for the manifest path, enabling the realization of nirvāṇa.
However, within this, there are two layers: that which accords with the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) and that which accords with the untainted manifest activity (*anāsrava-samudācāra*).

The manifestation of the untainted (*anāsrava*) is that which accords with the *nirvāṇa* to be realized; it is the manifestation of the eighth consciousness (*vijñāna*), which serves as the support for the manifest path.

This interpretation accords with the first master’s explanation below regarding the meaning of the "path that can realize": that it is a category (*jāti*) of that [nirvāṇa] but not its essence (*svabhāva*).
This means that while it is not the Path itself, it is a category belonging to the family of Cessation (*nirodha*); it truly does not belong to the Path.
The essence of cessation (*nirodha-svabhāva*) is in fact of the same category as the [other] factors; its reality is that cessation itself is not that path. Question:

Why is it called "pure cessation" (*nirodha-śubha*)? It is said to be so because it extinguishes the afflictions (*kleśa*). If that which is called cessation—that is, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—is also able to give rise to the noble path (*āryamārga*), then it should be called "pure production" (*utpāda-śubha*), and so forth.

The commentary states that "attaining nirvāṇa, where the former accords with the latter," means that the path of seeing (darśanamārga) accords with the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), and the path of cultivation accords with the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga).

Regarding the statement, "the afflictions comprise worldly attainment because they are distantly realized as nirvāṇa," this interpretation refers specifically to the stage of the provisions (sambhāra).

The preparatory stage (*prayoga*) consists of contaminated wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*) that can support the uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), causing them to increase. At a later time, the uncontaminated seeds give rise to manifest activity (*pravṛtti*), which is able to realize *nirvāṇa*.

The commentary states that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) serves as the basis for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); this is because there exists the eighth consciousness in its manifest state (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
Because it serves as the support for the seventh consciousness, the seventh consciousness is further able to engage in grasping.

Because the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) serves as the support for the sixth consciousness, the sixth consciousness is further able to give rise to grasping. This means that it is not only the path that is "returning" (reverting).
...up to: "These are categories (*paryāya*) of that [cessation], but they are not its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Now, cessation is a category of returning home, yet cessation is not the essential nature of returning. Returning is a category of cessation, yet returning is not the essential nature of cessation.
Regarding these three explanations, those who should understand them according to the verses are the three masters mentioned in this very text; the first is as follows:

The first master takes that which can realize the Path; the second master takes that which can be realized, namely Nirvāṇa; the third master takes both that which can realize the Path and that which can be realized, namely Cessation (*nirodha*).
Regarding the statement "the afflictions (*kleśa*) all manifest simultaneously, because 'realm' (*dhātu*) has the meaning of a causal nature":

Question: What is the difference between this second interpretation and the first interpretation? Answer: As for the passage from "However, the preceding... up to "...is precisely the manifesting consciousness," this refers to the first [interpretation].
The first interpretation refers to the functioning eighth consciousness (ālayavijñāna) acting as the locus and support for all other defiled and pure seeds of wholesome phenomena.

The second interpretation refers exclusively to the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) in their defiled and pure functioning states, which depend upon the functioning eighth consciousness mentioned in the third phrase—namely, that which is called "the support of all dharmas" (*sarvadharmasamāśraya*). This very functioning eighth consciousness is what is meant here.
From this, there is the movement toward active manifestation (*samudācāra*) and the attainment of *nirvāṇa*; this is precisely the pure active manifestation.
That "element" (*dhātu*) is the cause of nature refers to the word "element" in the first line of the preceding verse. Regarding the phrase "from this there is retribution;
the movement is the dependent defiled phenomena, up to because it pervades both the defiled and the pure": "from this there is" refers to two [meanings] within this commentary.
Explanation: One interpretation states that the term "existence" (*asti*) belongs exclusively to the specific dependent phenomena of defilement and purity;
it is by virtue of this that the phenomena of the various realms of existence (*gati*) exist, and by virtue of this that the pure phenomena of nirvāṇa exist.

This "existence" does not, however, belong to the capacity of the general substratum (*āśraya*). The second phrase refers to the capacity of the substratum of perception (*saṃjñā*). The third and fourth phrases are as follows:
It is both the possessor and the possessed. Some say: "It belongs to both the support and the supported, because it pervades both the possessor and the possessed.
This is the second interpretation. Regarding the phrase "by virtue of this existence," the word "existence" (有) here pervasively belongs to both the supported and the possessed.
The second line [of the verse] refers to that which is the possessor and also the support; the final two lines refer to the defiled and pure phenomena, which are the supported.
The first [line] refers to the existence that serves as the basis (*āśraya*). The following two lines refer to the specific existences that depend upon it, which constitute the general basis.

The first [line] is the general capacity (*bhava*) of the specific existences; if one takes the second line, it refers to the existence that is the basis for perception (*saṃjñā*), which is a specific dependence and also a specific possession of the general capacity.
However, regarding the statement that "birth and karmic causation both pertain to suffering and origination": "birth" is itself suffering.

That is to say, if they are afflictions, karma, or suffering, they are all subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya), because the Truth of Suffering is broad in scope. If they are afflictions or karma, they are subsumed under the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya);
if they are [the state of] abiding, they are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering.

Furthermore, regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* stating that within the Mahāyāna there arise phenomena such as suffering that are not accumulation (*saṃudaya*), up to those that are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*):

in the Mahāyāna, "suffering" (*duḥkha*) is broad while "accumulation" is narrow; that is to say, what is accumulation is necessarily suffering—just as it is said that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) things are suffering, and just as all twelve links are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
However, there are things subsumed under the Truth of Suffering that are not accumulation, namely, the maturation (*vipāka*) produced by karma.

This is because it is not an affliction (*kleśa*). Just as in the Hīnayāna, the discernment of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are a single entity because they are cause and effect; they are not two.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*), and even the Abhidharma are not taken [as distinct] because they are identical":

if, within the stage of equipment, one generates tainted hearing and reflection (*śruta* and *cintā*) that proceed in accordance with the eight periods of practice, these can also serve as equipment for the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), causing them to increase.

That which provides the support is contaminated (*sāsrava*), while that which is supported is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, those uncontaminated seeds that are supported may also be designated as the wisdoms accomplished through hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-maya*, *cintā-maya*, and *bhāvanā-maya* prajñā), because the category of "accomplished" is broader.
These wisdoms accomplished through hearing, reflection, and cultivation are comprised within the five aggregates (*skandha*) and the twelve bases (*āyatana*);

specifically, they are comprised within four bases: namely, the base of form (*rūpa-āyatana*), the base of sound (*śabda-āyatana*), the base of mind (*mano-āyatana*), and the base of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*).

Regarding their bases: the two [hearing and reflecting] pertain to all ten realms—namely, the seven mind-realms (*cittadhātu*), the two realms of form and sound (*rūpadhātu* and *śabdadhātu*), and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

If one speaks only of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, these are subsumed solely within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) and are included within the dharma-realm; specifically, they are the wisdom (*prajñā*) among the five object-specific mental factors (*pañca viṣayapratiniyataviṣayāḥ*).

If the ancient masters established only the three types of wisdom—those consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation—they did not establish [the categories of] "that which is produced" and so forth.

Consequently, they held that the morality obtained through formal reception and the virtues of application were included within the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation; specifically, the Prātimokṣa vows obtained through reception were included within the wisdoms of hearing and reflection, as there was no other category to subsume them.
However, since the New Abhidharma treatises establish the three [wisdoms] beginning with that consisting of hearing...

Regarding wisdom (*prajñā*), it is as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: it is established through hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*). "Established" means that which is brought about;

thus, the three types of wisdom—those consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation—are explained. Among these, the prātimokṣa vows received within the mind are subsumed under the innate wisdom acquired through hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and are also gathered within the wisdom acquired through reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). If one employs the wholesome states of application (*prayoga-kuśala*), they are received within the wisdoms of hearing and reflection.

The prātimokṣa vows. The prātimokṣa vows belong to the category of preparatory virtue (*prayoga-kuśala*) and are subsumed under the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayi-prajñā*) as well as the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmaya-prajñā*).

Since the perfuming by hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*) permeates both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it is not only the contaminated seeds that are perfumed at the time of hearing the true Dharma mentioned in the preceding text.
This is because they are identical in the Abhidharma (*Abhidharma-samuccaya*); that is to say, this is according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
In the *Śāstra*, the explanation of the perfuming of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*) is identical to that explained in the *Abhidharma*.

If one speaks of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), it is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) and does not extend to the tainted (*sāsrava*), because [the latter] gives rise to grasping (*abhiniveśa*). Regarding the statement that "all destinies (*gati*) still have rebirth in those destinies," this first interpretation says:
because the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is established, there arises the capacity for pervasive conceptualization.

Because the grasping mind arises from the grasping mind that performs universal conceptualization (*parikalpa*), one consequently creates wholesome and unwholesome karma within the five destinies (*pañca-gati*).

Because one creates and acquires such wholesome and unwholesome karma, at a later time, one either arises [in] the midst of the five destinies or gives rise to the grasping of precepts (*śīlavrata-parāmarśa*) by taking them as an object.

This [grasping] arises because of that; it is of that nature. Alternatively, one gives rise to the grasping of precepts by taking the five destinies as an object; this grasping still takes [them] as its object.

"Because it arises from that, it is of the nature of that parikalpita-svabhāva. Furthermore, there is another interpretation: "Alternatively, by taking various arisings as an object, one gives rise to adherence to precepts;
because this arises from that, it is of that nature. Regarding this second interpretation, it says: "The 'destinies' (gati) are precisely the *pudgalas*."
This refers to the "self" and "mine" toward which one repeatedly inclines; because there are five destinies of self, one gives rise to grasping based upon them.

Due to the arising of this self-grasping, one subsequently creates karma for the five destinies. Since this grasping arises by depending on those [destinies], it is of the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
"Or, it is a 'tendency toward views' because it gives rise to two types of clinging"—this third [explanation] is interpreted according to the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*).

Because views arise, by virtue of that very intention, there is once again clinging to both self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*). Alternatively, it refers to the arising of the two types of clinging: to a self and to what belongs to a self (*ātman-ātmīya-grāha*).

Regarding the "four dharmas of purity" in the Commentary (*Śāstra*): as for these four pure dharmas, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra*, chapter five, states: "The eight similes illustrate the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
that which is said to be nameless is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). If one speaks of the four purities, they constitute the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

The eight similes refer to those such as reflections in a mirror and the moon in water. One should consult that text [for the full list], which includes: (1) True Suchness (*tathatā*), (2) Nirvana, and (3) Non-existence... [etc.]

The Noble Path is untainted (*anāsrava*). There are four factors that give rise to the untainted. Because of hearing the teachings, one immediately cultivates the Noble Path, abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*) to realize *nirvāṇa*, and manifests the *dharmakāya*.

This is precisely *tathatā* (suchness), which is the untainted dharma. Regarding the statement that the four dharmas—conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), pure (*viśuddha*), and the dharma of reality (*bhūtatā*)—constitute the perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna*): according to the subsequent text, the conditioned untainted [dharma] reaches its ultimate limit through detachment.

The same applies to the pervasive excellence of its function. If this [term] is so named, then could the untainted seeds within the bodies of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) also be called "perfectly established" (*pariniṣpanna*)?
Furthermore, one might ask whether that untainted wisdom can be called "pervasive in its excellent function" and, possessing these three meanings, be termed "perfectly established.
Among the four kinds of purity, the first is the purity of the basis (*āśraya-viśuddhi*), which refers to the Buddha’s body as the basis.

Since the supporting body consists of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), what superior function does it possess that allows it to be called "perfectly established" (*pariniṣpanna*)?
One should respond by referring to the text of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Regarding the four lines in the *Śālistambasūtra* that collect [the truths of] suffering, origination, cessation, and the path: the first line is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).

The second line is the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). The third line is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*); the meaning of "various destinations" (*yoni*) is precisely nirvāṇa, which is the place toward which one proceeds.
The fourth line is the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*); "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*) refers to the truth of the path, and this realization is the means of realization (*sākṣāt-karaṇa*).

It is the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*). Regarding the phrase "because the destination (*gati*) is the principle of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) toward which the three vehicles proceed":
if it is the Truth of Cessation, it is the place to which the three vehicles return; therefore, the Truth of Cessation is designated as the "destination.

This refers to the "capable store" (*nibandhana-ālaya*) for the purpose of explaining the *ālayavijñāna*. ... [omission] ... This correctly describes the meaning of the name *ālaya*. However, as for the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they [regard] the dharmas...
Prakṛti (the Primal Nature) is the concealer, and the remaining twenty-three principles are the concealed. This is not like that [Sāṃkhya] system where there is only one [Prakṛti].

Regarding this Ālayavijñāna and all phenomena being neither identical nor different: according to the Sāṃkhya teaching, when the Unmanifest (avyakta) has not yet undergone transformation, the store of mahat and the other principles is of one essence within the Supreme Nature (pradhāna). In my present Ālayavijñāna, however, the seeds of the wholesome are stored.
"Son, [the self] and all phenomena are neither identical nor different.

Regarding the statement that "the commentary is even more difficult than the treatise," it means that the treatise is more difficult than this [text]. The *Saṃghabhadra-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or similar text), concerning the "superiority of abiding" (*sthiti-viśeṣa*) and so forth, is consistent with the arguments in this treatise.
The treatise states: "Furthermore, that which can grasp and take up the continuity of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi-bandha*). Here, "grasping" (*upādāna*) carries the sense of "taking hold of" (*parigraha*).

This means that because the preceding moment of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) passes away at death, or because it grasps a subsequent body within the five sense faculties so as not to allow for interruption, it is not the afflictions themselves that are called "grasping" (*upādāna*).
Regarding those who can realize and understand the *ālayavijñāna* according to the treatises:

even Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are unable to perceive the seventh and eighth consciousnesses; they only contemplate the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). From...
This is because one knows that all these tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), and because there is only such knowledge capable of this realization.
As it is said in an objection: when the followers of the Two Vehicles first contemplate the Four Truths, they do not know of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses;

nevertheless, because they also realize the Truth of Suffering by way of its general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), they are likewise able to sever the afflictions within the seventh and eighth consciousnesses. Furthermore, others...

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can know the first six consciousnesses, but it cannot know the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, because the consciousness of others is a coarse consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "opening the capacity and attributing it to the dharmas," this means that one opens the capacity and attributes it to the dharmas.

As for the statement in the second fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun) that there is only the initial word and no subsequent explanation: in that treatise, all Bodhisattvas are termed "superior" (*vibhu*). The *Saṃgraha* states... [text fragment ends].

Third: Regarding "having no initial seeds. However, among the three meanings in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the passage stating that it "merely maintains the basis of the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and is also able to grasp and connect the continuity of rebirth" is precisely the same as the preceding passage concerning its ability to maintain the seeds of all phenomena.
Question: Within the twenty-four types of contact (*sparśa*) produced by the bases, since they are all conventional (*prajñapti*), how can they [be established]?
It is called "derived" (*upādāya*). Its substances—form, sound, the world, and so forth—possess substantial reality and can thus be termed "derived" (and so on).
If viewed from the perspective of seeds, it is then termed "retaining" (*dhṛti*), up to "grasping all forms of existence" (*bhava*). Within this first interpretation, the first [point] is as follows:
