thus, the untainted (*anāsrava*) state of an Arhat at a later time should permeate (*vāsita*) the prior untainted state of a trainee (*śaikṣa*) as well as the prior ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

The establishment of permeation by that which has outflows is likewise so. Alternatively, it may refer to a different body. This text refers specifically to the present life, from the stage of an ordinary person until the attainment [of the fruit].
Having attained the fruit of the learner (*śaikṣa*), one subsequently attains the fruit of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) from within the body itself.

Thus, the untainted (*anāsrava*) state of an Arhat in a later life perfumes the untainted states of the learner in previous lives; likewise, the untainted states of the learner in previous lives perfume the untainted state of the Arhat in the later life.
The treatise states: Furthermore, the faculties such as the eye, or other dharmas—even those of the same category as the faculties—should mutually perfuse one another.
Regarding "mutual perfusion": it is difficult to maintain that the preceding consciousness is perfused by the subsequent moments of its own kind; thus, they are called "mutually perfusing.

It is also difficult to maintain that the consciousnesses themselves simultaneously and reciprocally perfume one another. The text below investigates these faculties and dharmas, namely: the faculties, the faculties of the faculties, and the remaining dharmas.

Furthermore, regarding that which you do not accept, we now raise this objection: If it is granted that there is mutual perfuming because they belong to the same category of consciousness, then within consciousness itself there exists the preceding moment of the mental faculty (*manas*) as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

Since the mental faculty is of the same kind as a faculty, it must be granted that the preceding moment of the mental faculty acts as the perfumer, and its seeds are perfumed within the succeeding moment of the mental faculty. As for the five material faculties (*rūpīndriya*), however...

Now, the mental faculty (*manas*) is likewise of the same category as a faculty; it should therefore also be that the preceding moment’s five faculties act as the perfuming agent, and the seeds perfumed therein reside within the subsequent moment’s five faculties.
Those five material faculties should also mutually perfume one another. As for what was previously called the "successively ceasing mental faculty":

Now, regarding what is called the "immediately preceding mental faculty" (*manas-indriya*): since it is designated as the support for the five consciousnesses, it refers to the immediately preceding mental faculty of the prior moment.

Just as the five aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth are all termed "dharmas" because they possess the characteristics of maintaining their own nature and supporting others, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is likewise a category of dharma.
Therefore, it is accepted that the prior moment [of consciousness] perfumes the subsequent one. As for the other four aggregates and the aggregate of consciousness, since they are...
Because they are of the same category as phenomena (*dharma*), those four aggregates (*skandha*) must likewise [be established] through preceding and succeeding moments.

Furthermore, since all eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are phenomena, the seven mental elements (*citta-dhātu*)—being of the same category as phenomena—must be admitted to receive perfuming (*vāsanā*) from preceding moments.

Since the other five external objects and the remaining mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) are of the same category as phenomena as these seven mental elements are, the same applies to the other six external objects and the mental factors.

The dharmas should likewise have their preceding moments perfuming their succeeding moments. Alternatively, since the five faculties such as faith and the mental faculty (*manas*) belong to the same category of faculties, the mental factors (*caitta*) such as faith should also have their preceding moments perfuming their succeeding moments.

Why, then, do you allow only the mind-king (*cittarāja*) to receive perfuming, while not allowing the mental factors to also be capable of receiving perfuming? However, [you] cannot [maintain this] without the three unconditioned [dharmas]...
Regarding the objection concerning the faculty of outflows (*āsrava-indriya*): it may be that this is raised because the Sautrāntikas do not accept [such a faculty].

However, the Sautrāntikas do accept that a "homogeneous class" (*nikāya-sabhāga*)—which, like a saw, is always in a continuous stream and is of one kind of neutral (*avyākṛta*) nature—is able to maintain the seeds.

This continues even when entering the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), where its homogeneous class remains constantly uninterrupted, much like the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) in the Mahāyāna. Even after being born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), [it persists].
At that time, from seeds within the category of similar type (*sabhāga*), the five types of desire-realm consciousness arise.

Or, after entering a mindless absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*), at a later time, the mind arises again from seeds within the category of similar type. As for the substance and activity of consciousness, it is like the teeth of a saw;
just as the teeth of a saw are sometimes high and sometimes low, being unstable, so too is the subsequent activity: it may give rise to the wholesome, the unwholesome, or the indeterminate mind.

At times, the mind is not recorded [by seeds], or there may be interruptions. Regarding the dharmas of the eye and so forth, as well as non-dharmas—the latter being the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*)—the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are dharmas.
The external five sense objects are likewise of the same category as the eyes and so forth; they constitute the five secrets (*pañca-rahasya*).
Furthermore, these should also mutually receive perfuming (*vāsanā*) and maintain the seeds (*bīja*).

As for the commentary’s statement that “the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) should likewise consist of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), because it belongs to the same category as the faculties,” the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* refutes this.

Thus it says: “If the immediately preceding mental faculty is permitted [to produce seeds] because it shares the same faculty-category as the five physical faculties, then since the five physical faculties also share the same faculty-category, the seeds of the five types of form within the subsequent moment of existence should likewise be infused by the preceding moment of the mental faculty.”
The faculty (indriya) is precisely the mental faculty (manas-indriya) that arises immediately after [the preceding moment], which is of the nature of derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
Since it is of the same category as the five physical faculties, the immediately preceding mental faculty should likewise be of the nature of derived matter.
The Commentary states that there are three types [of Sautrāntikas]: first, Kumāralāta and others;
in reality, these constitute a single school, the Sautrāntika. They maintain the transformation of dharmas (*dharmapariṇāma*) as the correct principle.
Śrīlāta was considered a Sthavira by the Sautrāntikas, though he was not a Sthavira of the Sthavira school. However, Śrīlāta composed the *Sautrāntikavibhāṣā*. As for "Vibhāṣā," it means...

"Vai" means different, extensive, or superior. "Bhāṣā" refers to what is called an extensive exposition (*vaipulya-bhāṣā*), a superior exposition (*viśeṣa-bhāṣā*), or a distinct exposition (*viśiṣṭa-bhāṣā*).
Question: How many schools within the Sarvāstivāda possess the *Vibhāṣā*? Furthermore, if many people together compose a treatise, [how is it designated]?
It may be said that "Vibhāṣā" refers to diversity. If it were composed by a single person alone, how could it be called *Vibhāṣā*? Furthermore, in this region there are numerical designations.
Now, regarding the composition of the *Vibhāṣā* treatise: the answer is that although it was composed by a single individual, it is designated as one *Vibhāṣā*.
Within a single meaning, there are ten interpretations and five interpretations; these may also be called "different names" or the "Noble Teachings.
In this region, there is only the *Vibhāṣā* of the Sarvāstivāda school, but no *Vibhāṣā* of the Sautrāntika school.
Regarding the tenet that establishes the causal principle wherein the preceding moment of one's own mental form serves as the seed for the subsequent moment of its own kind: Question:

According to the calculation of this Sthavira school, does that which serves as the seed for what follows actually possess the nature of a seed? Furthermore, does that school maintain that such seeds exist?
Answer: It is not a seed. As the Sarvāstivādins say, it is called "appropriating the fruit" (*phalaparigraha*) because it acts as the cause for that seed.
Regarding the term "Sautrāntika":

since the *Śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*) takes the sūtras as its authority, it refers to them as the Sautrāntikas. Does this refer to the Sautrāntika school that exists within the Mahāsāṃghika (specifically the Utsūtrāntavāda branch of the Mahāsāṃghika), rather than the Sautrāntika masters mentioned in the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*?
The *Vyākhyā* on Asvabhāva’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* states: "Because two moments of thought do not coexist, they cannot undergo perfuming. That treatise refutes the Sthavira school by saying:
"If it were the case that the preceding two moments could both receive perfuming, [it would be so]; however, since the preceding and succeeding moments do not coexist..."
[The Buddha] cannot be perfumed.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "the term 'extremely established' excludes the Buddha because he is indeterminate, as [that status] is not extremely established":

if, according to the Sarvāstivādins and other schools, it is held that the Buddha is identical to the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) in entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and thus extinguishing both body and wisdom, then from the perspective of the Mahāyāna...
Furthermore, [the two vehicles] together with the Mahāyāna enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. However, the Buddha of the Mahāyāna does not calculate entering *nirvāṇa*;
thus, [the reason] would not be established. If one does not state "established by consensus" (*prasiddha*) as a qualification, it becomes an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason.

Is it like the Buddha, who enters *nirvāṇa* because he has eliminated that which can act as a cause? Or is it like the practitioners of the two vehicles, who previously admitted that [it] can act as a cause?
"Is it possible to enter nirvāṇa? Now, since the statement is extremely established and concise, there is no fault.
Regarding the commentary’s previous explanation being "the original," this refers to the interpretation of the Tripiṭaka Master.

That is to say, the commentary states that after the Sautrāntika masters below saw the Elder (Sthavira) refute this objection, they subsequently formulated the alternative calculation regarding the "outflowing text" (*niṣyanda-vākya*). This is the [Tripiṭaka Master's] view.
The Tibetan master’s commentary explains: if one follows the latter interpretation in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*), that is the interpretation of the author of the sub-commentary himself.
Regarding the statement that there is no fault in various forms and minds arising after a formless state or a mindless state: this is the tenet of the Sautrāntikas.

They maintain that, for example, in the case of ordinary beings, when one is born from the Formless Realm into the Form Realm after the physical matter of the Formless Realm has long since ceased, matter arises directly from the seeds of the mind.
It is like entering the mindless meditative absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*): although the mind is not extinguished, at a later time the mind arises from the seeds of form (*rūpa-bīja*).
Although the Commentary states that because the mind with form can give rise to form, it mentions only "mind," this refers to the convergence of these two categories.

This convergence of the two categories means that when this sutra speaks of "mind," it refers to that which is powerful and capable of giving rise to both mind and form; form, however, cannot [give rise to mind].
Because of the arising of the mind, the Sūtras state that the mind is the seed of the body.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Because it is not of the nature of a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and because it lacks the function of grasping the fruit": although the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) grasps the fruit even when past, it is not of the nature of a causal condition.
The five causes (*pañca-hetu*), being of the nature of causal conditions, grasp the fruit only when present; therefore, there is no fault.
[Omission]. Regarding the fifth point, that of Bhāviveka’s “signless Mahāyāna” wherein even ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is empty:
Question: How can it be called the "signless Mahāyāna"? If it is called the signless Mahāyāna, does it not also imply the existence of a "sign-possessing Mahāyāna"?

Furthermore, if both Bhāviveka and those [other] systems explain the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as being within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), how do these two schools differ? As for that ultimate truth...
Regarding the statement that emptiness is taught within the [four] truths, what is the distinction between the two types of emptiness? The answer is as follows:

concerning the "signless" (animitta), Bhāviveka asserts that the dependent and perfected natures of the ultimate truth are neither empty nor existent; however, the imagined nature is empty in its essence.

This is said to be a semblance of inference (*pramāṇābhāsa*), because you do not accept my ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Furthermore, among the four kinds of conventionalities (*saṃvṛti*), each is subsumed accordingly.
Regarding this, within the four supreme truths (*paramārtha*) of that Dharma school, none are empty. That is to say: first, the supreme truth of being like an illusion is neither empty nor non-empty;
second, the true nature of cause and effect is neither empty nor existent; third, the true nature of the two kinds of emptiness is neither empty nor existent;
and fourth, the true single reality-dharmadhātu is neither empty nor existent. If the first conventional truth were merely empty, [the others would likewise follow].
If the latter three are conventional, they are all present within the gateway of the supramundane truth (*lokottara-satya*); thus, there is no sense in which they are not empty.

Regarding the phrase "because each is subsumed according to its respective [category] among the superior," even within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as taught in the Madhyamaka Mahāyāna, the existence of seeds (*bīja*) is admitted.
This means that within the first ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there are also seeds. Because seeds arise from others, they are called "fruits" (*phala*);
because they can produce others, they are called "causes" (*hetu*). This is because the second ultimate truth consists of the nature of cause and effect. If one follows the Hīnayāna:

If that [subject] were truly existent, it would contradict one's own tenets. If Bhāviveka were to establish this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) against the Hīnayāna, then since the Hīnayāna tenets themselves maintain that all phenomena are truly existent, Bhāviveka’s establishment of this *pramāṇa* would contradict the internal meaning of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna Buddhism.
Furthermore, this passage does not define "self" as Mahāyāna and "other" as Hīnayāna; rather, it takes the Hīnayāna as...

If one [asserts] that for oneself it is Mahāyāna while for others it is not, this greatly contradicts both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings; such is called "contradicting one's own vehicle" (*svayānabādhana*).

If, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are held to exist, then for Bhāviveka to state that "conditioned phenomena are empty" would constitute the fault of contradicting one's own tenets (*svasiddhāntavirodha*).

If, however, one accepts that even within the Saṃmitīya school it is taught that phenomena are empty, then if the true nature (*tathatā*) is that conditioned phenomena are empty, the word "empty" (*śūnya*) should be understood as referring to that [true nature].
The analogy of an illusory handkerchief involves the fault of the "unestablished nature of the subject" (*asiddha-dharmin*).

This is because while the property to be established (*sādhya-dharma*) exists in the actual entity, it does not exist within the analogy. If one were to take a real rabbit or a true illusion as the analogy, it would be established.

Furthermore, if the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that [the object] is unreal, and one takes the aspect of the empty flower in the consciousness (*cittākāśa-puṣpa-ākāra-bhāga*) as the analogy, then the subject to be established is not truly established. The... [text ends].

The thesis is not established as having no real object of proof, because it does not apply to the actual example cited. If one takes "emptiness" [as the subject], it is likewise not even universally established (*prasiddha*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "If one follows your own tenet, it is likewise not even universally established": although Bhāviveka asserts that both [the subject and the predicate] are empty, he now addresses [this point].

Regarding those who establish inference based on the equality of phenomena (*dharma-sāmya*): their *prajñā* possesses a specific attribute (*viśeṣya*), which entails the fallacy of non-establishment (*asiddha*).

To eliminate this illusory adversary, the commentary seeks the son of a barren woman; this encompasses the blossoming of empty flowers and the formation of fruit, as if you were to conceive and give birth to a child from nothingness to serve as a military force.
Within your [position], one may briefly omit these three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and their existence or non-existence. This is a brief exposition of the *Tattvasaṃgraha*.
Regarding Bhāviveka’s original intention in citing the right and wrong of the two views to determine the falsity or correctness of the dual nature:

the former nature is non-existent, while the latter two natures are existent; this refers to the "bodily experience" (*kāyānubhava*) among the eight proofs. Question: For what reason is this mentioned in the scriptural passage? Answer:
Within the ten proofs of this treatise, it is found specifically within the proof of maturation (*vipāka*), where matters such as bodily experience occur. Therefore, that...
The title of this treatise is "Realization through Internal Bodily Experience. Regarding the phrase "nourishing form and so forth like a flash of lightning":
it is just as when a person eats wholesome food, whereby they obtain the nourishment of fat, marrow, and flesh upon the body.

This fat, marrow, and flesh are what constitute "nourished form," meaning that it pervades the locations [of the body] and its characteristics of growth and increase become prominent. When one later becomes weary, its coarse characteristics [become apparent].
The "nourished matter" (*aupacayika-rūpa*) that is "fat" does not exist [in that state]. Therefore, it is said that nourished matter is interrupted.

However, if subtle nourished matter still persists, then because it coexists with the maturation [matter] (*vipāka*), there must necessarily be nourished matter. This is like a city wall protecting a subordinate city;
there is nourished matter, though it does not necessarily have to have maturation matter. For example, the divine eyes and ears possess only nourished matter.

There is matter, yet no matter born of maturation (*vipākaja*). The nourished matter (*aupacayika*) of the divine eye and ear faculties also has interruptions, just like the divine eyes of humans, which possess only nourished matter and no matter born of maturation. The nourished matter of the divine eye and ear faculties likewise has interruptions;
for example, when the body is on a lower plane, one may induce [the faculties] from a higher plane.
The earth element, the divine eye and ear faculties, and the four great elements that support these faculties:

when such a person gives rise to the supernormal powers of the divine eye and ear, they immediately bring forth the divine eye and ear faculties, which then support the divine eye and ear consciousnesses, enabling them to see forms and hear sounds from afar.
If such a person does not give rise to the supernormal power of the divine eye, those divine eye and ear faculties are then severed and cease to exist.
By this, the divine eye and ear faculties possess only the *sabhāga* (functioning) faculty and lack the *tatsabhāga* (non-functioning) faculty.

Whether it be the five faculties that are maturation (*vipāka*), if they are apprehending their respective objects, they are *sabhāga* faculties; thus, they possess only the *sabhāga* faculty and lack the *tatsabhāga* faculty.
However, when these faculties give rise to consciousness but do not apprehend an object, those faculties are then *tatsabhāga*; therefore, the maturation faculties [possess both].

It is a constant continuity, just like the homogeneous matter (*niṣyanda-rūpa*) within the body. For example, when a person exerts effort while holding up their arms, those arms become firm and rigid, thereby inducing homogeneous matter;
yet when one ceases to exert effort while holding up the arms, the hands are no longer firm or rigid, and there is no homogeneous matter.
This case is exactly the same: when the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear arise, they likewise induce [homogeneous matter].
Regarding the divine eye and ear faculties, as well as their simultaneous supporting elements (mahābhūta) and derived matter (upādāya-rūpa):
when the supernormal powers of the divine eye and ear are not activated, that person possesses no [divine] eyes or ears, but rather possesses the physical eyes and ears of ordinary flesh.

If one is born within the fourth dhyāna, then one obtains both types of eyes—namely, the divine eye and the physical eye. However, when the supernormal powers are not activated, one likewise lacks the divine ear and eye.
Because these divine eyes and ears are *aupacayika-rūpa* (nourished matter) and possess interruptions, this text cites them as a metaphor.
Even if the divine eye and ear were to arise simultaneously with the fleshly eye, the two faculties would necessarily not function concurrently.

When the divine eye arises and produces a divine visual consciousness (*divya-cakṣur-vijñāna*) taking form as its object, it is impossible for the fleshly eye to arise and produce [a fleshly visual consciousness].

Consciousness perceives form. For example, when the eye-faculty gives rise to visual consciousness that takes form as its object, it is impossible for celestial-eye consciousness to arise simultaneously to take form as its object;

this applies likewise to the ear-faculty and so forth. Question: Since it has been stated that the celestial-eye and celestial-ear faculties repeatedly interrupt [their activity], how can they perceive?

How does the treatise explain that the five physical sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) are in constant continuity? The treatise speaks only of the constant continuity of the five *vipāka* (maturation) faculties;
it does not refer to the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Consequently, there are those who possess the divine eye but lack the fleshly eye, such as Aniruddha;
and there are those who possess both the divine eye and the fleshly eye, such as Śāriputra and others. Question: Regarding the body...

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), when one attains the superior divine ear and eye faculties (*divya-śrotra-cakṣur-indriya*), one generates consciousness of the higher realms based on those divine ear and eye faculties.
If one employs the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), one generates consciousness belonging to the desire realm. Thus, there are two kinds of consciousness:

it is impossible for the divine eye faculty to generate consciousness of the desire realm, nor for the fleshly eye faculty to generate consciousness of the higher realms. Now, it is stated that upon being born within the four *dhyānas*, one immediately attains [the divine faculties].

The faculties of the eye and ear—the physical eye-faculty and the physical ear-faculty—and since the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) is of two kinds, the consciousnesses they produce are likewise of two kinds.
Regarding these two faculties of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown," do they produce one kind of consciousness together, or does each faculty produce its own distinct consciousness?
Now, regarding consciousness, if it is said that two sense organs together produce a single consciousness, then the same should apply to the inverted perceptions of the desire realm. Answer:
Although they belong to the desire realm, their specific desires differ; thus, the production of consciousnesses does not occur simultaneously. This is as explained above. Question:
If it is said that the divine eye and ear faculties do not possess *vipāka* (maturation), why does the Sūtra state that in the past, Aniruddha was a thief who gathered lamps to provide illumination?
The Buddha’s roots of goodness have now resulted in the karmic retribution of the divine eye; thus, one knows that the divine eye and divine ear are also results of maturation (*vipāka*).
If other persons do not cultivate goodness, they likewise do not obtain the divine eye or divine ear. [The Buddha] asked Āniruddha, saying, "You have obtained the faculty of the divine ear."

Regarding the statement that they are "the same as the divine eye," there are also cases where one does not obtain the divine ear. Whether this refers to cultivation at the time of the cause or cultivation at the time of the induction, it should be further examined in detail by consulting the preceding and following contexts.
Alternatively, if one argues that there is no fault of "concordance" (sādhya-sama) because [the subject] is not any of the six consciousnesses up to [the point of being a sentient being], we ask:

since that school also admits that within the six consciousnesses there are wholesome and unwholesome natures which are not true maturation (vipāka), how can there be no fault of concordance? Furthermore, we ask:

if a "sentient being" (sattva) is a conventional designation (prajñapti), it refers to the five sense faculties; thus, what is designated as a "sentient being" is merely the five faculties. This is like your own acceptance of the term "sound" [as a mere designation]. This is not [the position of] the Mahāyāna.
This is because it is admitted to be born of maturation (*vipākaja*). However, within the Mahāyāna, sound is also subsumed under that which is born of maturation.
In the Hīnayāna, it is not subsumed as being born of maturation induced by karma. This [position] is specifically directed against the Sautrāntikas; thus, one is able to act as a Sautrāntika master.

There are five states of mindlessness (*acittaka*): namely, sleep, fainting, the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*).

Therefore, this [explanation] specifically addresses the Sautrāntikas. According to the Sarvāstivādins, there are only three states of mindlessness: namely, the two mindless attainments and the maturation of non-conception.

As for those who enter these attainments—whether they be ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) or noble ones (*ārya*)—whether the attainments are contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it is as follows: [they enter] existence...

Regarding the taintless (*anāsrava*) and tainted (*sāsrava*) meditative absorptions: after emerging from the absorption, one only then perceives the tactile sensation of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) within the body.
Just as when one is correctly entering a mind-concentrated absorption (*citta-samādhi*), one induces the tactile sensation of pliancy belonging to the higher realms;

taking that attainment of the higher-realm pliancy as a condition, at the moment of emerging from the absorption, one immediately induces the pervasive sensation of joy (*prīti*) belonging to the desire realm. As for "reflecting according to reality" (*yoniśo-manasikāra*): it is like when a person cultivates wholesome qualities...

It is not that the body becomes weary; rather, it is only after the action has passed that one then perceives whether the body has been benefited or harmed. It is also like a person who seeks to learn:

only after the task has been completed does he then perceive the exhaustion of his body. As for "not necessarily involving conceptual reflection," this refers, for example, to when a person commits an evil deed.
This refers to one who, having become negligent through bodily craving and engaging in improper conduct, only later realizes matters such as physical exhaustion and injury;
or it refers to one whose nature is not contemplative, which is the state of being without mind, or the subsequent state of the faculties and so forth, which is the state of having mind.

The commentary states that "whether in meditative concentration or in the distracted state" means that there is also bodily sensation within meditative concentration, and there is also bodily sensation in the distracted mind.

Regarding "when the mental consciousness does not take a profound and subtle principle as its object": this refers either to attaining meditative concentration and realizing the truth, or to being focused single-mindedly on concentration while in meditation—whether for the duration of a meal or for an entire day—and subsequently emerging from concentration with the body still [in that state].
There is a touch of pliancy and pleasant satisfaction. Furthermore, whether one is in meditative absorption or not, there may be distinct mental deliberation (*vitarka*).

Question: Is it the case that both in a state of concentration and in a distracted state of mind, there can be both distinct mental deliberation and the absence of distinct mental deliberation? Answer: It is so.
Regarding the passage: "Furthermore, there are no five consciousnesses, nor any separate objects of perception," and so on, up to "at a later time, for the benefit or detriment of the body":

**Question:** Since weariness and fatigue are merely conventional (*prajñapti*) contacts within the category of the tactile object (*spraṣṭavya*), such as exhaustion and rest, how can the eighth consciousness experience these conventional objects?
For the eighth consciousness does not take conventional entities as its objects. **Answer:** This is not so. The eighth consciousness only perceives that which constitutes weariness and fatigue.

The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that constitute [the objects of] inhalation and exhalation must already exist, for it is only when these four primary elements are present that one can produce the tactile sensations of fatigue, breath, and so forth.
Thus, both the eighth consciousness and the body-consciousness take as their objects the actual primary elements that constitute the tactile sensations of fatigue, breath, and so on.

Regarding what is called "bodily sensation" (*kāyikī vedanā*): either such bodily sensation exists within these states, or it is first acquired upon entering these states. Even if one has previously attained [it], [it is here that it is fully realized].

At that time, one does not yet perceive the sensations of fatigue, rest, and so forth. Only after emerging from these states does one then perceive the sensations of lightness, rest, and so forth upon the body.
Therefore, we know that these sensations manifest the previously mentioned eighth consciousness; it is certainly through the faculty of touch that this object is apprehended.

The eighth consciousness, which is capable of receiving [sensory objects] at its peak, is the cause; at a later time, the contact of physical fatigue, rest, and so forth upon the body is called the fruit.

This is like a meditation master who, while in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), has a mind that perceives other objects; even if there is bodily injury, this is said with reference to one who has not yet attained *samādhi*.

However, regarding the time of seeking *samādhi*, one simply performs the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of noble intention, directing one's focus toward and concentrating upon the meditative state.
Although at first the body does not perceive weariness or injury, it perceives them only later. This indicates that the subsequent state of fruition presupposes the prior existence of its cause.
Furthermore, this does not refer to the category of "feeling" (*vedanā*); rather, it is the object-field of contact (*spraṣṭavya*).

If one experiences pleasure, it is the "contact of tranquility" (*praśrabdhi-sparśa*) among the twenty-four types of contact; if the body experiences injury, it is the "contact of fatigue" (*klamatha-sparśa*) among the twenty-four types of contact.

Therefore, this "feeling of the body" (kāyavedanā) is precisely the object of contact (spraṣṭavya) within that meditative absorption; it is not [itself] a member of the aggregate of feeling (vedanāskandha).
In the commentary (*śāstra*), it does not say "not for the Buddha," but rather says "sentient beings have the fault of indeterminate [states]," and so on, up to "for the sake of sentient beings."

This is an inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntika-doṣa*). Since a Buddha is included within the category of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgṛhīta*), at times when a Buddha’s wisdom is accompanied by other virtuous minds and so forth, there would be no maturation (*vipāka*) [of that wisdom].
Yet, at such times, because he is still categorized as a sentient being, would it follow that there is actual maturation during those moments of wisdom or other virtuous minds?

Alternatively, if you claim that because he is established as being included among sentient beings, he must possess actual maturation, then a Buddha would also have to manifest emanations (*nirmāṇa*) as having maturation.
If it were established that the mental consciousness (*manas*) possesses a true maturation (*vipāka*), it would contradict the fault of one's own school’s tenets.

If one were to use the eighth consciousness of this school as an analogy, it cannot be said that "both [the subject and the analogy] are unestablished," because that school does not assert its existence.

However, within the context of an analogy, there are cases where both are unestablished and cases where neither is unestablished. If the eighth consciousness were used as the analogy, that school would admit that they possess an eighth consciousness.

Therefore, regarding the "unestablished probans" (*asiddha-hetu*): since that [opponent's] school does not admit that I possess an eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*), if one takes the eighth consciousness as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), then because the substance of the eighth consciousness does not exist for them, both the probans (*hetu*) and the thesis (*pakṣa*) within that example are unestablished.
This is called "non-establishment of both. If that school does not... [text truncated]

Granting that I accept the existence of the eighth consciousness, it is neither the case that "simultaneous non-establishment" (俱不成) applies, nor is it the case that "simultaneous establishment" (有俱不成) applies.
Furthermore, a sūtra states: "Sentient beings transmigrate through the five destinies (gati), the four modes of birth (yoni), and so forth. Question:
Why does the commentary (*śāstra*) not state that this third sūtra is subsumed within the eight proofs? Moreover, this sūtra mentions only the five destinies and the four modes of birth.

It does not mention the three realms. Furthermore, [the opponent] asks: "If one simply says 'birth' (*jāti*), why is it necessary to say 'destiny' (*gati*)? If one simply says 'destiny,' that would suffice;

why is it necessary to say 'birth'? (This can be understood by reflecting upon it. This statement is precise and substantial, as it distinguishes the factors that lead toward a state from those that merely resemble such a destiny or birth.

That which is taken up upon proceeding to a destination and constitutes the body is called the "substance of the destiny" (*gati-vastu*). Furthermore, neither the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) nor the karma that is capable of giving rise to it is called the "birth of the destiny" (*gati-janman*).

"Outside the [fundamental] concentrations" refers to other preparatory wholesome states (*prayoga-kuśala*) and their remaining indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mental states and mental factors, as well as the nourished (*aupacayika*) and outflowing (*naiṣyandika*) forms.
If these are innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*), they cannot arise [in a higher stage]; innate states arise only within their own respective level (*svabhūmi*).

If they are among the preparatory wholesome states, the wisdoms of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) and reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*) cannot arise in a higher stage. As for the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) within the preparatory stages, although the body may be in a higher realm, it [can still arise].
Those that can arise as cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) are all wholesome through application (*prayoga-kuśala*). This refers to entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*) at a higher level.

As for defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*), once one has abandoned the defilements of a lower stage, nine of the ten afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the higher stage—excluding only anger (*pratigha*)—can all arise;

this applies even up to the higher realms. The afflictions of the higher stages are as explained below in the section on "denying liberation" (*vimukti-vipratipatti*). This is what is meant by the term.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, [minds] can arise from a lower realm; however, the two higher realms cannot give rise to afflictions of a lower realm.

Among the four types of neutral minds (*avyākṛta*), the mind of maturation (*vipākaja*) must belong to the same level (*bhūmi*) and cannot be acquired from a different realm or level. As for the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*), it cannot arise from a lower level to produce one of a higher level, nor does such a mind exist in the higher levels.
If it arises from a lower realm, it may also produce one of a higher level; however, this applies to the mind of supernormal power (*nairmāṇika*), which does not exist in the higher realms.
It records the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*). When the body is in a lower realm, one attains a higher realm concentration (*dhyāna*) through sitting;

that the body is always clean, pure, and lustrous is entirely due to the "nourished matter" (*aupacayika-rūpa*) of the higher realm, for it is nourished by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*). In the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), there is no such nourished matter.
Regarding derived matter (*niṣyanda-rūpa*), that which belongs to a lower realm cannot arise from a higher realm. Generally speaking, there are three types of continuity (*srotas*):
first, the continuity of outflow (*niṣyanda-srotas*); second, the continuity of maturation (*vipāka-srotas*), which refers to wholesome and unwholesome karma that brings about neutral results;

and third, the continuity of nourishment (*puṣṭi-srotas*), which, whether through the power of meditative concentration or otherwise, consists of successive states that are similar to one another. Regarding the continuity of outflow...

Regarding matter (*rūpa*): that which belongs to a lower realm cannot arise from a higher realm. However, if it is matter produced by nourishment (*aupacayika*) and termed "outflow" (*naiṣyandika*), then matter of a higher stage may also arise from a lower realm;
yet matter of a higher stage cannot give rise to matter of a different kind belonging to a lower realm.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the seventh consciousness is not included herein because it is not common": the seventh consciousness also possesses the four characteristics of being real, constant, pervasive, and unmixed;
however, it is excluded here because these qualities exist exclusively within the Mahāyāna as its unique (asādhāraṇa) feature. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
even when one's body is in a lower realm, one can still give rise to the *niṣyanda-rūpa* (outflow-form) of a higher stage, as was the case with the Bhikṣu Aśvajit when he went to...
Within the realm of form (rūpadhātu), when one sees that Brahmā King, one necessarily gives rise to the divine eye (divyacakṣus).

Once the speech of Brahmā King is heard, one must also give rise to the divine ear (divyaśrotra) before the sound can be perceived. Furthermore, when Brahmā King speaks, it is necessary for the divine eye to arise;
and when Brahmā King speaks, it is necessary for the outflowing matter (niṣyandarupeṇa) to be produced first before he can initiate speech.

It also includes matter that is the result of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala-rūpa*). According to this principle, in the lower realms as well, one can give rise to matter that is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of a higher stage;

or, for example, when a person attains supernormal powers, whether [the objects manifested] are large or small, they are all matter resulting from supernormal power. If it refers to wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*), it is named after its object;

if it refers to wisdom derived from reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*), it is named after its associated mental factors; and if it refers to wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), it is named after its essential nature. [This applies to] meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The essence is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), because it is attained through successive stages. As for wisdom (*prajñā*), when it coexists with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called a "stage. Regarding wisdom:

in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), but no wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is wisdom derived from hearing and wisdom of cultivation, but no wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is only wisdom of cultivation, and lacks both wisdom derived from hearing and wisdom derived from reflection. As for innate goodness (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*), it proceeds from its source...

It is named after the body upon which it depends. Furthermore, in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no nurtured matter (*aupacayika-rūpa*). When one is born in the formless realm or enters the concentration of the formless realm (*ārūpya-samādhi*), there is then no nurtured matter.
Even if the body remains in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), when one attains the concentration of the formless realm while seated, [there is likewise no nurtured matter].
All the luminous, well-nourished forms possessed by the body are exclusively nourished forms of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); they are not nourished forms of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Why is this? For example, when a person attains a concentration of the formless realm while seated, they must first sit in a concentration of the form realm.

However, it is only after first attaining the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) that one subsequently attains them while seated. Is the nourished matter (*aupacayika-rūpa*) of this present body the same as the nourished matter of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
Certainly not; one cannot attain the formless absorptions while seated without first attaining the form realm absorptions.
Even if one were to leap over stages, one can only leap over one stage at a time; one cannot leap over four stages.
If one’s body is in a lower realm, it is possible to attain the eight higher meditative absorptions (dhyāna), because these are all wholesome states resulting from application (*prayoga-kuśala*).

It is accepted that wholesome states resulting from application may arise in a different level (*bhūmi*) as well as in the same level. Furthermore, it is also accepted that defiled states (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) may likewise arise in a different level;

however, if one has not yet abandoned the defilements of a lower level, one cannot give rise to the afflictions of a higher level. Conversely, if one has already abandoned the defilements of a lower level, one can then give rise to them.
These are the afflictions of the higher stages. As for the remaining indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) minds and mental factors, these are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the higher stages;

it is also admitted that those of the lower stages can give rise to the indeterminate supernormal powers of the higher stages. "Nourishing matter" refers to the sense organs of the divine eye and divine ear.

It is also admitted that the divine eye and ear faculties of a higher stage can arise in one belonging to a lower stage. However, there are differences between the explanations of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Within the Hīnayāna, among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the divine eye and ear powers consist solely of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mental states and their associated factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*); they do not extend to the wholesome (*kuśala*) nature.

Nevertheless, by means of the sixth [power], one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of a higher stage as a cause; yet at the time of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), it has still not been attained.

Regarding the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear: they arise only at the time of attaining liberation; thus, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) serves as the cause that gives rise to the divine eye and divine ear, which are termed their "fruits.

Within the supernormal power of knowledge regarding the movement of the psychic faculties (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*), there is also a portion that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), namely the fourteen transformation-minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*). As for the remaining three supernormal powers—knowledge of others' minds and so forth—they are all...

This is of a virtuous nature (*kuśala*). If one speaks according to the Mahāyāna, with the exception of the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear, the remaining four supernormal powers are all of a virtuous nature.
As for the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear, they are both of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*); this is the same in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

However, one does not take the divine eye and divine ear faculties as the essential substance (*svabhāva*) of these powers; rather, one takes only the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) of the divine eye and divine ear as their substance.

Because this [consciousness] pervades the entire body, it is called "pervasive" (*vyāpya*) in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. It refers exclusively to the wisdom associated with the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear.
In the Mahāyāna, it is taught that if the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear are known through conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), they are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Now, within this pervasive consciousness, both the primary mind and its mental factors possess eleven dharmas; namely, the five universal (*sarvatraga*) factors, the five object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) factors, together with the [mental factors of] the eye and ear.

The consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the mental king (*citta-rāja*). If the divine eye and divine ear arise for the sake of benefit and happiness, they are associated with both mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) and are of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*);

thus, they are associated with twenty-one dharmas. The essence of the divine eye and divine ear consists of the ten universal (*sarvatraga*) and specific-object (*viṣayapratiniyata*) mental factors, plus the ten wholesome factors excluding *praśrabdhi* (pliancy), because *praśrabdhi* is absent among the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). This includes the visual consciousness as the mental king. As for the divine eye and divine ear that arise from it...
"Universal. This refers to the inclusion within the category of "arising-good" (*samutthāna-kuśala*). Question:

Among the four types of goodness, if ten or eleven [mental factors] are intrinsic goodness (*svabhāva-kuśala*), and the eleven associated with the desire realm are associated goodness (*saṃprayoga-kuśala*)—namely, the specific objects, the universal [mental factors], and so forth—then since the supernormal powers of the divine eye and ear arise together with goodness, they ought to be associated goodness. Why, then, are they described as "arising-good"?

"Is it wholesome? He replied, "In principle, these are associated wholesome states. For example, when the wisdom of application (*prayoga*) derived from hearing and reflection within the sixth consciousness induces the five sensory consciousnesses, those five consciousnesses are themselves wholesome through application, wholesome through the wisdom of hearing, and nominally wholesome through the wisdom of reflection.
If we include the present case, since the supernormal powers of the divine eye and ear are induced by the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) within the sixth consciousness..."

Regarding the mental factors (*caitta*) of the supernormal powers of the divine eye and ear: these five mental factors are also nominally subsumed under the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

However, the mental factors of the divine eye and ear that are induced by the wisdom of cultivation belonging to the sixth consciousness cannot [be so categorized], because the divine eye and ear themselves are subsumed under the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
It is by means of the wisdom of cultivation within the sixth consciousness that the supernormal powers of the divine eye and ear are induced.
Regarding mental factors (*caitta*): the mental factors associated with the supernormal powers of the divine eye and ear are taken as being "virtuous by way of origination" (*samutthāna-kuśala*).
In reality, however, the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are by nature distracted (*vikṣipta*) and do not pertain to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

Just as the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha-indriya*) is metaphorically designated as "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*), so too, within the outflow-free sixth consciousness of a Bodhisattva, the faculty of suffering is induced within the five sensory consciousnesses for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.

Because the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) is induced by untainted cultivated wisdom (anāsrava-bhāvanāmayī-prajñā), this faculty of suffering may also be designated as being subsumed under untainted cultivated wisdom;

furthermore, this faculty of suffering is also comprised within the category of "wholesome by origination" (samutthāna-kuśala). However, according to the ultimate reality, the faculty of suffering does not extend to the untainted state.
Now, the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear are called "wisdom derived from cultivation" (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*); the same applies to [the supernormal power of] suffering.

Furthermore, within the Mahāyāna, the five consciousnesses induced by the sixth consciousness when it gives rise to wholesome states of applied effort (*prayoga-kuśala*) are themselves also wholesome states of applied effort. If, within the sixth consciousness...

This refers to innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*). The five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) that are induced [by them] are also innate wholesome states, because the five consciousnesses cannot necessarily be wholesome on their own, whereas the sixth consciousness can.
According to the teachings of the Hīnayāna, there is no applied wholesome state (*prāyogika-kuśala*) within the five consciousnesses;
thus, the five consciousnesses are not induced by the sixth consciousness when applied wholesome states arise within the sixth consciousness. As for those [states] within the five consciousnesses...

It further gives rise to the wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*). It is also said that among the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), there are only afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*); these five are abandoned solely by cultivation.
Regarding the categories of phenomena such as maturation (*vipāka*) and nourishment (*aupacayika*), if one follows the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), five types of dharmas are established;

however, in reality, they exist moment by moment. If one follows the Mahāyāna, only three types of dharmas are established: first, maturation (*vipāka*), which refers to neutral (*avyākṛta*) phenomena produced by karma.
This is so. Second is that which is nurtured (*aupacayika*), namely the faculties of the divine eye and divine ear, as well as other such nurtured matter (*rūpa*).
Third is that which is of similar outflow (*naiṣyandika*), referring to all remaining afflicted phenomena (*dharma*) other than the first two;

thus, both preparatory wholesome states and neutral (*avyākṛta*) minds and mental factors are subsumed within the category of similar outflow. Furthermore, matter of a lower level can arise from a similar outflow of a higher level.
Question: Just as when the body is in a lower realm, how is it that one cannot give rise to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) belonging to a higher realm?
Furthermore, does this commentary state that the wholesome of application (*prayoga-kuśala*) also includes the wholesome pertaining to the portion of merit (*puṇyabhāgīya-kuśala*)?

Moreover, does this "wholesome of application" refer specifically to the wholesome of application belonging to the provisions (*sambhāra-prayoga-kuśala*)? However, within the Mahāyāna, there are two explanations: one says that the body’s suffering belongs to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
One can give rise to the *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing) pertaining to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). One view maintains that it is permitted to arise [there].

If one’s body is in the form realm, a non-male (*apaṇḍaka*) cannot give rise to the *śrutamayī-prajñā* of the lower desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). As for the claim that the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manas*) is not included therein because it is not commonly accepted [in that context]:

[this is] a question regarding how the seventh consciousness possesses the four characteristics of being real, constant, pervasive, and so forth. For instance, when one whose body is in a lower realm gives rise to [the wisdom] of a higher stage...

The *dharmadhātu-śūnyatā* is the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*. Its seventh consciousness, the *samatā-jñāna*, follows the sixth consciousness and is likewise subsumed under the higher stages (*ūrdhva-bhūmi*).

Its preparatory application (*prayoga*) is not termed "mixed. If one uses the eighth consciousness of this school as an analogy, there is no case where both [the probans and the subject] are unestablished (*ubhayāsiddha*).

However, within the analogy itself, there exist cases of both being unestablished and neither being unestablished; thus, upon the analogy, the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*) and the locus of the argument (*dharmin*) do not exist.

The name [of the subject] is not established, nor is the [logical reason] established. Since that school does not admit the existence of an eighth consciousness, taking the eighth consciousness as an analogy is impossible because the substance of the eighth consciousness does not exist;
thus, both the probans (*sādhana*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) are unestablished.

In the *Śāstra*, it is explained that among the resultant (*vipāka*) forms there are nine bases, excluding sound; furthermore, throughout the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), those [bases] are entirely absent.

Within the body, the five faculties (*indriya*) and their respective material supports (*upādāya-rūpa*) are all produced by karma and are thus termed "resultant forms. According to the Hīnayāna school, these nine bases are produced by karma, with the sole exception of sound.
Now, according to the Mahāyāna, the five faculties, their five material supports, and the five objects (*viṣaya*) are all produced by the power of karma.

[Feeling. Now, regarding the nine bases excluding sound: this is a door of reasoning that follows [the general principle]. Within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), there are the five consciousnesses and mental factors;
these do not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
In the commentary, it states that among the five types of form, those produced by karma—namely suffering, pleasure, and equanimity—exist in the formless realm today. However, the five...
Within consciousness (*vijñāna*), there are suffering, pleasure, and equanimity; these are the maturation (*vipāka*). Within the mind (*manas*), there are suffering, pleasure, joy, and equanimity;
these are the maturation, with the sole exception of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The Commentary states: From the second dhyāna upward, there are no uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) distinctions of form.

Although from the second dhyāna upward there are likewise forms of shape (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), color (*varṇa-rūpa*), and informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*), there is no vocal action (*vāk-karman*). This is because vocal action, being sound, is bound only to the first dhyāna and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
other sounds, however, may also exist there. Furthermore, there are two kinds of form: odor (*gandha*) and taste (*rasa*).

Commentary: Although it is said here that this is an "exclusive cause" (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*) because it exists even above [the seventh consciousness], two causes that together exclude a single phenomenon are called a "shared cause" (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*). If a single cause excludes only a single phenomenon, it is called an "exclusive cause.
For example, the seventh consciousness is also real, pervasive, and unmixed; yet, it does not constantly enter the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), as has already been established.
Because they are subject to change, that which is exclusively and eternally constant is excluded; this is what is called the "unshared cause" (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*).

For example, among the five colors, those produced by karma are indeed real and unmixed, yet they are not eternal and not pervasive; thus, they are excluded by both the [requirements of being] eternal and pervasive.
There is one phenomenon that possesses all three causes for exclusion: namely, when a body in the desire realm initiates the *māyā* (deceit) of the first dhyāna.
Deceit (*māyā*). Although this deceit of the first dhyāna is real, it is not pervasive (*avyāpin*), because it does not exist from the second dhyāna upward.
It is also mixed (*vyavakīrṇa*), because [states] of lower realms can arise within the higher stages. Furthermore, it is not constant (*anitya*), because there are times when it does not arise.

Now, by stating "pervasive, unmixed, and constant," these three causes exclude [deceit]. There is one dharma that possesses all four causes; this excludes [the others]. All remaining [defilements] are to be understood through reflection (*cintā*).

The commentary does not merely distinguish each [factor] individually as being non-karmic fruit; rather, when two causes are used together to distinguish a single dharma, it is termed "common" (*sādhāraṇa*).
If one common [cause] is used to distinguish only a single dharma, it is termed "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*). If one says that the truth...
The retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is also distinguished from other dharmas, because those other dharmas are not true retribution.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the seventh consciousness is not co-existent" and so forth up to "because it undergoes transformation": as for that seventh consciousness—

The third cause, the character *heng* (constant), excludes it. For instance, as for the seventh consciousness, after entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), it may either transform into the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) or enter the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya-darśana*), whereby the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) no longer functions; thus, there is also a transformation and change, and it is not constant.
Although it is likewise pervasive, real, and without admixture, because it is not constant, it is excluded.

The Commentary states: If that Sarvāstivāda school did not already admit those [factors] to be dissociated (*viprayukta*), then, as previously stated at the end of the first fascicle and the beginning of the second fascicle, because the Sarvāstivāda exposition of the fourteen dissociated factors was refuted, it is said that they do not admit such dharmas.

All these are instances of arising; that is, they are the *jīvitendriya-sabhāgatā* (homogeneity of the life-faculty) and the *pañcendriya-sabhāgatā* (homogeneity of the five faculties). These are all the substance of rebirth in the destinies (*gati*).

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are no five faculties; here, we take the *sabhāgatā*, the life-faculty, and so forth. This is the position of the Sarvāstivādins regarding all unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena.
The commentary states: "Because the noble ones of the two vehicles are not subsumed under birth" and so forth, up to "should be abandoned and eliminated.
With the exception of the Buddha alone, the remaining Arhats of the two vehicles are all subsumed under birth.

Furthermore, as with the *ūrdhvasrotas* (one who flows upwards) Anāgāmin who reaches the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), since there is no path for severing afflictions at the Peak of Existence, they must instead give rise to [the path] belonging to the lower realms. There is none [else].

The untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) is capable of severing the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). If it were the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), then for one born in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there would be no body in that realm.
Furthermore, when the sixth consciousness gives rise to the untainted path of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), at that time, to which place of birth does it belong?
Does it belong to the place of birth in the Peak of Existence, or does it belong to the place where the mind arises? It belongs to neither.

If there were a place within the realms of existence (*gati*), it would entail the fallacy that two realms would simultaneously undergo cessation and separation. As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun), fascicle 3, states:
"Regarding birth in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), [the explanation] should be understood according to the preceding.

However, even if we were to grant the Lesser Vehicle’s assertion that the contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena of the three natures constitute the essence of the realms of existence and birth, we now raise this objection: how could contaminated phenomena of the three natures constitute the realms?
Consider, for instance, one who has been reborn as a human being in the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and gives rise to an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*).

At that time, this untainted mind is not the substance of the destiny of birth (*gati-janman*). Furthermore, when the untainted mind is actually arising, it is impossible for a separate tainted sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭha-vijñāna*) to arise as the substance of the destiny of birth, because two consciousnesses cannot coexist simultaneously. Since the sixth consciousness is untainted, [it cannot serve as the basis for such a destiny].
The untainted (anāsrava) is not a realm of rebirth (gati), for its essential nature is that of cessation and detachment.

Furthermore, when one who has attained the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmin) is born in the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) and subsequently descends to the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), at the time of the untainted mind, there is already untainted dharma within that Stage of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
If [the state] were the very essence of rebirth, then within the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), there would be no essence of rebirth;

furthermore, the untainted mind (anāsrava-citta) of the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) would not be the essence of rebirth, resulting in the fallacy that both destinies (gati) would be entirely absent.

If, however, one follows the Mahīśāsaka school, they establish the existence of a "level-headed" (samamūrdha) *pudgala*, such as an Anāgāmin born in the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra); that person, then, with...
At the limit of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), that person no longer needs to intentionally arouse an untainted mind of the lower sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*);

rather, their afflictions are exhausted spontaneously, and they attain the fruit of Arhatship. Furthermore, this refers to one who is born for the very last time in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)—one who is neither an ordinary being nor a noble one among those subject to rebirth.
Question: Does this final passage from the treatise clarify only the noble non-returner (*anāgāmin*)? Why?

The passage concerning "ordinary persons" (pṛthagjana) is answered as follows: The preceding text states, "If this mind were non-arising and did not exist in the formless realm, then its arising during states such as the cultivation of wholesome qualities would mean it is not a 'destiny-born' (gati-janman) being.

This clarifies that [the subject] is an ordinary person. As for the subsequent text, which posits that even if it were granted to be destiny-born, it would even contradict correct reasoning, this clarifies that [the subject] is a noble one (ārya).

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "outflows (*sāsrava*) have the meaning of 'realms' (*dhātu*"): all phenomena of the three periods of time that are outflowing possess the meaning of "bondage.

As for wholesome phenomena, they are bonds by way of being objects of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*). Regarding "futile proliferation" (*prapañca*): those outflowing phenomena are like children who spend their entire day playing in sand and dust, merely wasting their efforts in vain.

The Commentary states that those in the human realm are called "miraculously born" (*upapāduka*) because the Buddha’s body is a transformation (*nirmāṇa*) and is not included within the [ordinary] modes of birth;
for it is karma or fetters that are designated as the four types of birth.
Regarding the statement that "the five sense organs within one's own body are not one's own *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), whereas the five sense organs of another's body are," this means:

if the five sense organs belong to one's own body, they are capable of being grasped by oneself and are thus one's own *nimitta-bhāga*. If the five sense organs belong to another's body, they are not one's own *nimitta-bhāga*, as they are mutually not grasped or appropriated by oneself.

This passage concerns those that are "appropriated by support" (*āśraya-upādāna*) rather than "appropriated by production" (*janman-upādāna*). This text [states]: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the continuation of the original text.*

One should also understand the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* regarding this point. However, when the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of sound as being "appropriated" (*upātta*), it refers to sound based on the appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*), not based on the appropriated [seeds] that give rise to them.
That sound is produced by the four primary elements which serve as its basis; since those producing primary elements are themselves appropriated, the derived [sound] they produce is likewise so.

Sound is also called "appropriated sensation" (*upātta-vedanā*). If the *Abhidharma* treatises state that sound is not appropriated, this refers to the sense of being produced by appropriation (*janmopādāna*), not in the sense of being based upon appropriation (*āśrayopādāna*). Sound itself is not produced by appropriation;

rather, it gives rise to sensations such as suffering and pleasure, yet it cannot perceive pain, nourishment, and so forth. When the body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*) arises, it is termed "appropriation."

This refers to the sense-faculties that are "functioning" (sabhāga). That is to say, when the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) actually gives rise to body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), it is called "functioning.
As for the statement, "Even when body-consciousness does not arise, it is called 'appropriated' because it belongs to that class," this refers to those that are "non-functioning" (tatsabhāga).

Although that body-faculty does not give rise to body-consciousness, it is still called "appropriated" and is termed "non-functioning" (*tatsabhāga*). Furthermore, this is because it is based on appropriation, rather than being produced by appropriation.

As for this: if the five faculties (*indriya*) and the four objects (*viṣaya*) are constantly grasped by the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), they are able to arise; if it does not grasp them, they immediately decay and perish.

This death is not called "arising. If one were to say that arising consists in being grasped, then even though sound relies upon the five faculties and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as its creators, the fundamental consciousness does not grasp it in the same way it grasps the five faculties and the four objects. It is like a person's hand grasping a bronze gong. The bronze...
Because the hand does not grasp the cymbal when it is struck. The fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is like the hand; the copper cymbals are like the five sense organs;

and the removal of the four objects (*viṣaya*) is like the sound within the cymbals. The fundamental consciousness does not grasp [the objects], which refers to one of the eight proofs for the grasping of the appropriated body (*upādāna*) among the five reasons.
This refers to the eight proofs in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. It states that because the six consciousnesses are each distinct, they do not [grasp the body].
Regarding the claim that [the first six consciousnesses] can universally grasp [their objects]:
they say this is like visual consciousness, which relies on the eye-faculty as its basis, yet that visual consciousness cannot universally grasp or maintain the eye-faculty itself;

this applies likewise up to auditory consciousness. If the eighth consciousness universally relies on the five faculties, then that eighth consciousness is indeed able to grasp and maintain those five.

This refers to the sense faculties (*indriya*). Regarding the "proof by the Buddha’s physical faculties" within this context, the intended meaning is that the eighth consciousness of the Buddha-fruit also serves as the appropriating agent (*upādātṛ*) for the five faculties of the Buddha-fruit stage.
As for the term "proof," it refers to the eight proofs presented below. It does not mean to manifest that only the purely maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is the appropriating agent;
rather, it is to prevent the conclusion that the Buddha’s physical body would lack an appropriating agent. This is the proof by the Buddha’s physical faculties.
This refers to the eight proofs among the five reasons for the appropriation [of the body] by consciousness. These are the eight proofs found in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
Regarding the statement that the six consciousnesses cannot appropriate [the body] because they each have distinct supports:

this means that just as visual consciousness has its own specific sense organ as its support, that visual consciousness cannot appropriate the eye faculty; and so it is for the other consciousnesses up to auditory consciousness. If it were the eighth consciousness...
Regarding the five sense faculties: the eighth consciousness is precisely that which can grasp and maintain (*upādāna*) the five sense faculties.

Herein, the phrase "the eighth consciousness of a Buddha is proven by the physical sense faculties" means that the eighth consciousness of the stage of Buddhahood is likewise able to grasp and maintain the five sense faculties of the stage of Buddhahood.

The term "proven" refers to the treatise below; it does not intend to show that only the *vipāka* (maturation) consciousness can grasp and maintain [the faculties], lest one conclude that the physical faculties of all Buddhas...
"Because the body is without appropriation" refers to the realization of the Buddha’s physical sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*).

This encompasses one category entirely—the single category of maturation-neutral (*vipāka-avyākṛta*)—and thus encompasses both categories simultaneously. Regarding the statement that there are "three [causes] now," the question is:

Why were five causes previously explained for the eighth consciousness, whereas only the latter three causes are explained here for the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*)? The answer is: The previous discussion concerned prior karma.
That which was previously cited as being neither virtuous nor defiled is now stated to include the first two causes within this single category.

Within this single category, the term "maturation" (*vipāka*) includes what was previously described as "induced by prior karma," while the term "neutral" (*avyākṛta*) includes what was previously described as "neither virtuous nor defiled.
If one speaks of the eighth consciousness within the Buddha-body as a single category, it is exclusively one.

[The text] states: "In this regard, the Buddha also possesses appropriation (*upātta*). If one asks whether that which is maturation-neutral (*vipāka-avyākṛta*) is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), [the answer is no].
Therefore, among the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), only the latter three causes are mentioned, while the former two causes are not.

Furthermore, regarding the clarification of the similarities and differences between the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) and the evolving consciousnesses through the former two causes—this is the second interpretation. It means that the eighth consciousness is induced precisely by prior karma; it is not..."
Regarding the present conditions: if it refers to the first seven consciousnesses, then it is indeed by way of present conditions.

Furthermore, because the essence of the eighth consciousness is neither virtuous nor defiled, if there were a fixed fault [in that argument], one would further question why the first seven consciousnesses—being either virtuous or defiled—are not [the subject].

It is not to manifest that the mind capable of appropriation (*upādāna*) is exclusively the maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*). As for the statement that "the Buddha’s appropriating mind is indeterminate," how does one formulate the inference (*anumāna*) such that it exists?
This is the fallacy of the "undetermined" (*anaikāntika*). In the commentaries, the phrase "and so forth" includes the minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and so on;

although among the four types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) states of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), there is indeed the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*), this [present discussion] refers to the manifest dependent origination (*pratyutpanna-pratītyasamutpāda*) within the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), as opposed to what was previously stated regarding that which is neither wholesome nor defiled, etc.
The term "hence" (gu) refers to what was previously induced by the karma of the eighth consciousness.

Hereafter, when clarifying the first seven consciousnesses, the mention of their being wholesome, defiled, and so forth, refers to their being non-wholesome, non-defiled, and so forth, in contrast to the previous eighth consciousness.
The commentary (*śāstra*) states that this is equivalent to what the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* describes as "arising impurity.

That *Saṃgraha* clarifies mundane purity, namely the three types of wisdom—listening, reflection, and cultivation—as well as the wholesome roots of the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). It further clarifies supramundane purity.
This refers to the untainted dharmas such as those of the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning. It clarifies the three kinds of impurity:

namely, the impurity of afflictions (*kleśa-aśubha*), the impurity of karma (*karma-aśubha*), and the impurity of birth (*janma-aśubha*). This is the text of the old translation. Now, in the new translation, it says:

"namely, the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and the defilement of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*). [The inclusion of] "the defilement of form (*rūpa-saṃkleśa*)" does not exclude the text of the old translation; now, in the new translation, it says: "namely..."

The defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and the defilement of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*). "Defilement" (*saṃkleśa*) is precisely what is meant by impurity.

From this point onward in the treatise, it merely serves to reveal by contrast that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) receives the name "maturation" (*vipāka*) due to five causes; there is no other means of proof through inference (*anumāna*).

The commentary (*śāstra*) states: "As for those who previously composed these five reasons and even went so far as to examine the eight consciousnesses, yet did not find this passage in the first [section on] 'appropriation' (*upādāna*), they merely know how to read in vain.

The author of the commentary demonstrates that the text of this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* is superior. If one reads the eight proofs in the various *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* treatises and does not see these five reasons from this treatise, such a person merely knows how to read in vain.

However, the five reasons of the older [commentary] are compared as follows: [Insert comparison of the two sets of five reasons here. ...is superior to the former. Therefore, it is known that the text of this treatise is indeed excellent.
