Furthermore, regarding the eight proofs in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, if one does not see these five reasons from this treatise, that person merely knows how to read in vain. Thus, the five reasons of the older [commentary] are compared... [end of fragment].
"Valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) refers to the five types of present examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). "Present" means that within this treatise there are three types of present examples;

each of these three present examples can individually function as an inference (*anumāna*) by applying it to all five logical reasons (*hetu*). This demonstrates the master’s skillful ingenuity (*upāya-kauśalya*).
Regarding the three similes: they are like sound, wind, and so forth; like non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); and like lightning, and so forth.
If one excludes these five causes and three similes, then even if one reads other treatises, it is merely a vain reading.
Within this context, the cause of mutual support refers to the explanation of the support of the three dharmas, which is precisely the textual passage from the *Āgama*. Or, that...

If one were to assert that while the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) possess the function of sustaining [the body], they do not sustain it constantly, and take this very point as the ultimate logical reason (*parama-hetu*):
if one merely accepts the proposition that the evolving consciousnesses do not sustain [the body] constantly, then there is an interruption;

and since such interruption is admitted by both parties, it constitutes an ultimate logical reason. This analogy has a precedent: namely, that vitality (*āyuḥ*) and warmth (*uṣman*) are not the sustainers [of the body].

Regarding the phrase "because it is consciousness": the intended meaning is that if one says something can "sustain consciousness," only consciousness itself may be called that which sustains consciousness.
Vitality, warmth, and so forth are not what sustain consciousness; to claim here that they do so is an error.

The commentary states: "Non-life-force and consciousness are also like warmth. Since warmth exists in the desire and form realms, while consciousness and life-force extend to the formless realm, [the opponent asks:
"Are non-life-force and consciousness not also like warmth in that they do not extend to the formless realm?"
The commentary should not [apply] to the three natures or to the untainted (anāsrava), just as with life-force and warmth.

Since life-force and warmth are of an indeterminate nature (avyākṛta) and are also tainted (sāsrava) births, if it is stated that the six consciousnesses can maintain them, should they not then be exclusively indeterminate and exclusively comprised within the tainted?

The Commentary states: This is also not the case. Regarding the passage, "Just as life-force can sustain warmth, and so on, up to 'it is not non-outflow,'" this is the objection raised by the Hinayana:

"O Mahayana, if you claim that consciousness is non-outflow and permeates all three natures, then since life-force and warmth are exclusively indeterminate and outflowing, you do not allow them to sustain one another.
The objection continues: "Just as life-force can sustain warmth, warmth itself is not [the sustainer]."

Life-force (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*) are each distinct. Just as consciousness (*vijñāna*) is able to sustain warmth, what prevents life-force and warmth from being either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*), while consciousness—being of all three natures—is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)? This is because the two are distinct.
Furthermore, just as life-force can sustain warmth and thus be called "life-force," if [warmth] were not different from that which sustains life-force, then life-force would not be life-force.
The commentary states that this interpretation is incorrect. Regarding the use of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) up to life-force (*āyus*) as examples to establish the point:

first, the Mahāyāna responds to the Hīnayāna from the perspective of its own school’s tenets. In the Mahāyāna, consciousness is the *darśana-bhāga* (the perceiving aspect), while warmth (*uṣman*) is the *nimitta-bhāga* (the perceived aspect).

Life-force is likewise a functional capacity residing upon the seeds (*bīja*). Since all these are equally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and equally tainted (*sāsrava*), they do not [serve as valid examples].
The visible portion (*dṛśya-bhāga*) is untainted (*anāsrava*), while the objective image portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) is tainted (*sāsrava*). How could the former be cited as an identical objection?

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "this example applies to all [cases]": it is like when the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is able to see form; it is subsequently designated as "eye-consciousness."

Visual consciousness does not see itself; should it therefore not be considered non-visual consciousness? This is discussed in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Root Chapter) regarding the question of which among the three—vitality (*jīvitendriya*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—is abandoned first at the time of death. As stated in the fifth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*, vitality is abandoned first.
If one were to say that warmth is abandoned first and only then the other two, that would contradict the fact that there is no warmth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

It should be called "the end of life" and so forth, as has already been explained in the previous notes. However, here [it is argued that] the functional capacity within the seeds of consciousness constitutes "life.

Thus, when the manifest life-force is compared to its seeds—until it lacks the power to project and produce that which can sustain what has previously existed—this passage constitutes an external objection.
Regarding the meaning of "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is not necessary that they must be capable of perfuming (*vāsanā*) in order for this term to be established;

this is the answer. Now, when we speak of "causal conditions," these are not direct causes (*sākṣāt-hetu*). Rather, it means that at the time a phenomenon arises, it must rely upon causes and conditions in order to be able to manifest.

"Manifesting" (*prādurbhāva*) means to become evident. If a seed of evil were able to arise through its own power alone, without relying on the power of others, then [the distinction between] names and words (*nāma-vyavahāra*)... [would not hold].
Regarding the indeterminate seeds: they lack the power to arise by themselves; must they not rely on the induction of wholesome or unwholesome [karma] in order to arise?

For instance, when a single present wholesome karma induces a single present consciousness—the so-called "seed of names and words"—and causes it to manifest as an actual activity (*pravṛtti*), this seed of names and words possesses two powers:
it can produce a manifestation within the same moment, and it can also induce a seed of subsequent wisdom in the following moment. This...
Subsequent moments arise as manifest activity again within the same stream of thought, and they can also induce seeds for subsequent moments;
thus, this process continues without interruption, and all that follows is likewise so, because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are by nature subject to momentary extinction.

Furthermore, just as seeds induce one another across preceding and succeeding moments without depending on a perfuming agent (*vāsanā*), this is also a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Manifest consciousnesses are able to maintain all these seeds. All...

The seeds that produce their respective manifest activities (*pravṛtti*) are also *hetu-pratyaya* (causal conditions), as they rely upon the perfuming agent (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, this applies to both seeds and manifest activities alike.

However, although the eighth consciousness in its manifest state cannot perform perfuming, it is nonetheless not a *hetu-pratyaya* with respect to its own seeds of designation (*nāma-vyañjana-bīja*), because the manifest consciousness of the eighth does not exert power over the seeds; rather, it is through the manifest consciousness that the seeds are maintained.
My son, if there were no evolving consciousness capable of maintaining [the seeds], those seeds would be lost, and so forth.

Therefore, the evolving consciousness is able to maintain the essence of life, while the seeds are able to maintain the evolving consciousness. Furthermore, warmth also remotely maintains consciousness;
for if the body lacks warmth, one abandons the eighth consciousness. Thus, warmth is able to maintain consciousness.
The treatise states: "At the time of birth and death, one necessarily abides in a distracted state of mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), not in a mindless absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*).

Question: In that same passage, it says that this sūtra applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Within the Hīnayāna, it is taught that at the time of birth and death, one always abides with a mind (*sacittaka*).

Furthermore, even the Sautrāntika school of the Hīnayāna establishes five states of mindlessness (*pañca-acittakāvasthā*). How, then, can it be said that the mind arises at the time of birth and death?
How does the Sautrāntika school explain this? Check further.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that those who are no longer in training (*aśaikṣa*) first enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and only afterwards enter the remainderless [nirvāṇa] (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), and so forth, until it concerns how the consciousness at the moment of death (*cyuti-vijñāna*) is established therein:
if one relies on the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) of sharp faculties, when they wish to enter the remainderless [nirvāṇa], they first traverse various...

Regarding the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*): this refers to the contaminated states in forward and reverse order. Immediately following these, one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Within the attainment of cessation, one enters *nirvāṇa*. If a person of dull faculties cannot enter the attainment of cessation, do they still enter *nirvāṇa*? It is by means of the six consciousnesses that they enter *nirvāṇa*.
If the eighth consciousness is taken as the consciousness at the moment of death, then their entry into *nirvāṇa* would be with a mind present.
It is not a state of no-mind, nor is it a state of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). It is established as being neither [no-mind] nor [absorption].

If one were to take the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭhavijñāna*) as the consciousness at the moment of death, then for an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*) who enters nirvāṇa while in a mindless absorption, it would be impossible for there to be a "scattered" state of having a mind—this is because such a state is beyond description.
This is explained with reference to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Thus, the "extinction attainment" (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is so named.

Regarding "the intermediate state of meditative concentration": those of sharp faculties who are about to enter *nirvāṇa* first enter the eight concentrations with mental activity (*sacittaka*), and subsequently enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) before finally entering *nirvāṇa*.
Because the attainment of cessation lies between these stages, it is called "intermediate."

Question: If it is said that only those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) who are *aśaikṣas* first enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and subsequently enter *nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*, while those of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*) do not, why is it taught that there are attainments where the faculties are complete but the attainment is not, and attainments where the attainment is complete but the faculties are not, and so forth?

Furthermore, when those of sharp faculties who are *aśaikṣas* in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) wish to enter *nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*, how are they able to traverse the various meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*)?
Yes. If it is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that undergoes birth and death, and so forth, without contradiction—this text belongs to the Mahāyāna.
How then does the Hīnayāna maintain this second interpretation?

It is precisely by positing the sixth consciousness as the consciousness that undergoes birth and death, rather than explaining it in terms of the eighth consciousness. Thus, it accords with the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

The treatise states: That claim—that one who has attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and enters *nirvāṇa* without the six consciousnesses existing—is due precisely to the power of the vow (*praṇidhāna*) of that one who has attained no-more-learning.

However, when the sūtras speak of passing away while possessing a distracted mind (*vikṣiptacitta*), this refers to the passing away of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*).
It is because they are ordinary worldlings, and it refers to the passing away of those in training. It is their [passing away].
To claim that those born as learners (*śaikṣa*) and those undergoing birth and death both possess the sixth consciousness is an incorrect interpretation.
However, the *Yogācārabhūmi* includes these two stages of birth and death—even up to the state of fainting—within its enumeration.
That treatise speaks of six states of mindlessness (*acittaka*), yet it does not separately mention birth and death; rather, the two stages of birth and death are [included therein].

This is included within the state of fainting (*mūrcchā*). As for the current statement that "fainting" refers to being rendered unconscious by ghosts, medicinal drugs, and the like, outside of the context of birth and death—this refers to what the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "Just as in sleep without dreaming, it is also included at the time of fainting;

it is also included at the time of fainting when one is rendered unconscious by ghosts, medicinal drugs, and so forth. Thus, this does not define fainting solely in terms of the time of birth and death.

Regarding the phrase "because there is no mind": according to the Sarvāstivāda school, there are only three states of consciousness where there is no mind—namely, the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*).
This is because all other states, such as the moments of death and rebirth, as well as the states of sleep and fainting, are all possessed of mind.

Regarding the commentary’s initial explanation of "there are two [interpretations]": one might ask, among the eminent Dharma masters of former ages, did they already possess these two interpretations?

If it is said that this person states, "In this land, since ancient times, there have been these two interpretations," and thus calls them the "prior explanations" (*pūrva-vyākhyāna*), then why—given that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (the *Abhidharma* treatise) had not yet been explained by those predecessors—did those masters of antiquity immediately cite the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*?
Take the Dharma as your witness; reflect upon this.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that one dies only with a neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind:

in the Mahāyāna, it is taught that for those who die gradually, the distant mind is permitted to be of all three natures, while the proximate mind is defiled (*kliṣṭa*). This refers to the nine types [of craving], such as the craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) which moistens rebirth through wisdom.

Because it arises simultaneously with the mind at the end of life and is accompanied by craving. If [the mind] were strictly neutral (avyākṛta), then according to the Sarvāstivāda school, the minds of one about to die and the mind at the very moment of death would all pertain to all three natures, as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa-vyākhyā*.
Now, I cite the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* to prove that the mind at the end of life is exclusively consciousness and exclusively of a neutral nature.
The Commentary states: "If this were not the case, why would the state of being without mind (*acittaka*) not be mentioned separately, up to the point where it says 'only five states'?
The latter master explains: This implies that at the moment of birth and death, the sixth consciousness is always present.
If there were no sixth mental consciousness at the time of death, why does the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speak of only five states without mind—namely, the two [meditative] states without mind..."

The meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), the absorption of signlessness (*animitta-samāpatti*), the gods of the perception of existence (*āsaṃjñika-sattva*), as well as sleep and fainting, are not mentioned separately.

Likewise, the state of being without mind at birth and the state of being without mind at death constitute the worldly state of being without mind; since these are not mentioned separately, there is no state of being without mind in the two positions of birth and death.

If one were to say that the sixth consciousness does not exist in the position of death or the position of birth, then regarding the Yogācāra teaching of the seven states of being without mind, it refers to two... [text truncated].

In the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*), sleep, fainting, and the states of birth and death—therefore, these five other states are collectively called "mindless.
Thus, one might wonder: does the sixth mental consciousness exist during the states of birth and death?
The commentary on the former master’s interpretation states: “...because they are subsumed within the [five] stages.

The former master says that those who are mindless during the two stages of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) are also subsumed within the state of fainting; therefore, he does not separately enumerate a sixth stage of mindlessness.
Since there are only five stages of mindlessness, one knows that the sixth consciousness does not exist during the stage of birth-and-death.

The Commentary now provides an auxiliary explanation, stating: "This is because it refutes others," and so on, up to "the two masters regarding inference. The author of the Commentary provides this auxiliary explanation:

the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that at the time of birth and death there is no sixth consciousness, but only the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), in order to refute the Sarvāstivādins' position that a sixth consciousness exists during the process of birth and death.
However, according to the actual principle, the state of initial birth and the state of death likewise possess [the sixth consciousness].

Regarding the manifestation of the sixth consciousness, does this not only adopt the first master’s position but also incorporate the second? To speak according to the facts, this passage adopts only the first master’s view;
it concerns solely the dispute over whether the eighth consciousness exists during the state of birth and death, and does not concern the sixth consciousness.
The reason for this is that even all [masters] collectively receive the various teachings in common.

As for the explanation: here, it is taught that during the state of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), when there are no evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), the cause is dullness and ignorance (*mūḍhatā*).

This is precisely the meaning upon which all the [Abhidharma] masters rely. All who abide by the Holy Teachings agree in stating that in this state of birth and death, there are no evolving consciousnesses, and that the eight [consciousnesses] have dullness and ignorance as their cause. This applies from the time of the master Nanda up to those currently being pointed out.

This refers to masters such as the Sthavira Nanda and others, all of whom maintain that at the moment of rebirth (*pratisandhi*), three causes are deficient, and thus they intend to express the meaning that [the mental consciousness] cannot arise.
They take the mental consciousness at the stage of rebirth (*upapatti-bhava*) as the correct position, being constantly and repeatedly discussing this doctrine.
Question: When it says "the treasury of the True Dharma" (*saddharma-piṭaka*), does this refer to the Dharmaguptaka school? Or...
Within the Mahāyāna, there is a distinct treasury of the True Dharma (Saddharmapiṭaka). It is well to further inquire of those who abide [in it].
As for its application, the land of Pañcālaka is named the "Country of Causes" (Hetu-deśa); this refers to the Buddhas of the three periods.

Among all the teachers of the Pratyekabuddhas, they manifest the ability to eliminate the afflictions arising from the power of sentient beings' greed and hatred, thereby attaining coolness—just as the moon in the heavens can eliminate the power [of heat] and bring about coolness.
It means "cool and refreshing. Formerly it was called "Tianzhu" (India); because the character "Zhu" was considered inauspicious, it was thus named Tianzhu.

This is like when an elderly person reciting the sutras [mispronounces] the fruit of *srotāpanna*; because the character "Huan" is unseemly, they change that character "Huan" and call it the fruit of *srotāyuan*.

...and so forth. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it says "gathering firewood and fruit" (*píng*). Because the character *píng* (屏) is considered vulgar, those who recite the sutra or produce its commentaries have changed it to *bù* (布).
Formerly, this land was called Shendu; now it is newly called Shendu, and is also known as Pañcāla (Five Indias).
Because five great masters of the treatises appeared in the world, it is named "Five Moons" (*wǔ yuè*) or "Five Suns" (*wǔ rì*). As for "light" (*guāng*), it means manifestation.
Furthermore, "transformation" (hua) means bestowal (shi). It is so named because it pervades the five regions of India;

thus, when praising and extolling the present [teaching], the intended meaning is that the principle of the three causes being absent at the stage of birth is also superior to the doctrines established by contemporary Dharma masters.

Contemporary Dharma masters are likewise unable to produce a doctrine as sublime as this; this is precisely what the various treatise masters praise as being prior to and superior to the incorrect [views].

"Yi" (義) shall be taken as "correct meaning. Regarding the phrase "those of no discernment" (無識之籌): the subsequent commentary (*shu*) constitutes the Master of the Commentary’s refutation of masters such as Nanda;
thus, they are termed "the class of those without discernment. "Chou" (籌) means "class" (*lei*). This refers to the Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang.

At the end of the Western [commentary], it briefly refutes this incorrect [position]. The interpretation of the Tripiṭaka Master’s intent accords with the meaning found in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.

Furthermore, when the Master of the Sub-commentary examined this [text] within the context of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, he refuted this incorrect position which lacked three causes, thereby further augmenting the prior faults of Nanda and others.
Now that the commentaries on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* by the ten masters are all complete, one has designated this as a single primary source.

Commentary: This is the "Cloud Assembly of the Ultimate Meaning" (*Paramārtha-megha-samāja*). All that follows regarding the "sheep-like" [ignorant] realities consists of refutations of prior incorrect doctrines.

For instance, some might argue that the five consciousnesses arise first, followed by the objects, or that the objects are primary. However, the correct doctrine should state that a single consciousness gives rise to the five forms.
Now, this master [the opponent] claims that the five consciousnesses first perceive the five sense-objects, and only thereafter does the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arise. Or...

Due to hearing the instructions of others, one engages in mental activity that gives rise to distinct cognitions and views; or, with meditative concentration as the cause, one subsequently arouses a distracted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
It is said that at the moment of death, due to the five sensory consciousnesses, the instructions of others, and so forth, the mental consciousness may indeed exist.

However, this applies only when it arises specifically with the cause of being in a state of torpor or dullness at the time of death; for although the five [sensory] consciousnesses may still be present...

Consciousness and the instructions of others serve as its causes; however, because it has torpor and delusion (*styāna-middha*) as its cause, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cannot arise at the time of death.

Regarding the statement in the commentary that "since the state of death is the same, there is no further divergent explanation," and even further adding this explanation: at the time of death, the mental...

The masters agree that when consciousness is昏昧 (obscured), it does not depend on the three causes; therefore, the present [text] does not discuss the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) at the stage of birth.
Since it must be made to depend on the three causes, there are other masters who provide a distinct explanation for this.
The commentary extracts the passage concerning "the person who increases" (*pudgala-vardhana*) and asks: "Why is this not mentioned, up until the point where it must necessarily be so?

This is a question posed by that master [the opponent], who asserts that there is also a "solitary mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*) that arises independently of the three causes—the five sense objects and so forth—arising as a solitary grasping of a person or a solitary grasping of dharmas.
That master replies: "If mental consciousness must rely upon these three causes before it can arise, then perhaps it is the visual consciousness..."

Seeing other objects and hearing other sounds, consciousness first arises based on the five sensory cognitions. When the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes the five sense-objects as its conditions, does it not necessarily arise independently?

The commentary states that [wholesome states] may be induced by application (*prayoga*), such as the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*), or by innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika*).

If one is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is only through the induction of the wholesome wisdoms of hearing and reflection via application that one can enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*); this is because the factors of the desire realm lack the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*).
Thus, one must rely on hearing and reflection to first enter absorption. As for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is induced by the wholesome wisdom of hearing via application, and then...

One is able to enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This is because the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) lacks the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), yet possesses the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) and the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

Its innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) can also, though distantly, induce meditative concentration. In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), both the wisdoms of hearing and reflection are absent; there exists only the innate wholesome state.

Is it present throughout the three realms? However, within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), immediately following an outflow-free mind (*anāsrava-citta*), one evokes the cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) of the formless realm;
that cultivated wisdom then evokes the innate wholesome states (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*). Thus, the outflow-free mind does not directly evoke the innate wholesome states.

If, however, within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), immediately following an outflow-free mind, one either directly evokes the heard wisdom (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) of the form realm... [text continues]... heard wisdom.

Wisdom (prajñā) subsequently induces innate wholesome states, or immediately follows upon an untainted mind (anāsrava-citta), or directly induces the wisdom of hearing (śruta-mayī-prajñā) within the form realm;
the wisdom of hearing subsequently induces innate wholesome states, or immediately follows upon an untainted mind, or induces the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā) in the form realm;
the wisdom of cultivation subsequently induces innate wholesome states, yet it does not directly induce them immediately following an untainted mind.

It is the acquisition of the wholesome. For instance, within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), immediately following an outflow-free mind (*anāsrava-citta*), one either directly gives rise to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) within the realm of form, and only then does that wisdom give rise to the innate wholesome (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*);

or, immediately following an outflow-free mind, one directly gives rise to the wisdom derived from hearing within the realm of form, and only then does that wisdom give rise to the innate wholesome; or, immediately following an outflow-free mind, one gives rise to...

The wisdom cultivated through meditation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is that which directly and immediately gives rise to the innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*).
Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), an outflow-free mind (*anāsrava-citta*) can directly and immediately give rise to the innate wholesome states of the desire realm;

or, immediately following an outflow-free state, it can directly give rise to the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*) of the desire realm. Question: Why is it that an outflow-free mind of the higher realms cannot directly [give rise to these]?

Regarding the production of innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*): within the hearing [of the Dharma] in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), can the untainted (*anāsrava*) state immediately and directly induce the innate wholesome states?
Answer: If the desire realm is a state of distraction (*vikṣepa-bhūmi*), then the innate wholesome states therein are clear and sharp.

However, since the two upper realms are states of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bhūmi*), the innate wholesome states there are obscure and weak. Therefore, regarding the innate wholesome states of the upper and lower realms...
There is a distinction. At the time of his initial birth, [the sixth consciousness] had never previously arisen. However, that master says:
"By the power of habitual practice in the lower realm, when one is subsequently born in the formless realm, it arises manifest in the second moment.
If there were no sixth consciousness at the very first moment of initial birth, the present objection states: "Since it is by the power of habitual practice in the higher realm... [and so forth].
At the very moment of birth, during the very first thought-moment, it should also be the sixth consciousness; yet now, its arising is difficult to establish.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that it is "either innate goodness (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*), or afflictions (*kleśa*) frequently practiced, or skills (*śailpasthānika*) long cultivated," the critic challenges the Master, saying:

"It refers to the innate goodness frequently practiced in previous lives, or frequently practiced afflictions, or minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) long cultivated."

The first thought at the moment of birth should likewise arise. If you attempt to defend this by saying that even in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one must necessarily give rise to a distinct [consciousness], or if you say that at the time of initial birth, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cannot arise because of its state of torpor (*mūḍha*), we now raise this objection:
this is precisely the cause for the various real objects of the six sense-fields; for both at the stage of death and the stage of birth, there is invariably a state of torpor.
This is the cause. Why labor over explaining it separately?

Regarding the statement in the Commentary that the fundamental [proponent] allows for the co-arising of both the coarse and subtle mental consciousnesses (*manovijñāna*): that school’s fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) maintains that the two mental consciousnesses arise simultaneously.
When challenged by the Mahāyāna position that two consciousnesses cannot arise simultaneously, they immediately offer a counter-argument, stating: "The coarse and the subtle..."
Regarding the two intentions: it is impossible for them to arise simultaneously, as they occur sequentially.
The *Vivṛti* (Commentary) on Asaṅga’s *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "The two mental consciousnesses (*manovijñāna*) should be understood to function simultaneously," and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because [the object] is defiled and skillful, and because at that time the object of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mental consciousness cannot be obtained," that treatise [cites] the Sthavira school as saying: "Two consciousnesses..."
They cannot arise simultaneously. As it is said in the Sūtra: "There is no place where it is possible for two consciousnesses to arise together;
there is no place, no possibility, for two Buddhas to appear in a single location; there is no place, no possibility, for two wheel-turning monarchs (*cakravartin*) to be born together;

there is no place, no possibility, for two solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha*) to appear together. There are three reasons for this. First, regarding the dependence on defilement (*saṃkleśa*), there are two...
Explanation: One interpretation states that the eighth consciousness relies on the defiled manas-consciousness as its simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*);

this is called "relying on the defiled. This interpretation is not definitive, because the sixth consciousness also relies on the defiled manas. Second, regarding the desire for rebirth at the time of death:
at the moment of death, within the sixth consciousness, there arises craving and attachment, which then nourishes the eighth consciousness for the sake of rebirth. It relies [on the manas].

Because the sixth consciousness involves defiled craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*), one attains rebirth. As the treatise states: "The nine types of death-minds are accompanied by co-emergent craving.
Thus, we know that because it relies on the defiled [sixth consciousness], it is proven that at the moment of death there is only the eighth consciousness.

Now, we adopt the latter interpretation: those who are suddenly beaten to death do not give rise to the craving that moistens rebirth (*upapatti-tṛṣṇā*) in the same way as those who die gradually. If...

Regarding "one who dies from a gradual illness," this refers to the arising of defiled craving for renewed existence (*punarbhava*). Regarding "because there is no interruption at that time," this demonstrates that the eighth consciousness is constantly uninterrupted.
These two preceding reasons both serve as *prasajyapratiṣedha* (reductio ad absurdum) to demonstrate the existence of the eighth consciousness at the moment of death.
As for the third point, "the object of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cannot be apprehended," this constitutes an inference (*anumāna*) that refutes the Sthavira school.
At the time of death, your school maintains that there is a subtle mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). [We] say:

At the time of your death, it is certainly not mental consciousness, because its object of cognition (*ālambana*) cannot be apprehended, just like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Thus, you use your own reason to refute yourself.

Furthermore, in the passage below, if it were indeed mental consciousness, its mode of activity (*ākāra*) and object of cognition would necessarily be apprehendable. If, within the Mahāyāna, one intends for death—
The final returning mind may be associated with any of the three natures. If it is the mind proximate to death, it is exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*).

According to the Sarvāstivādins, both the final returning mind and the proximate mind at the time of death may belong to all three natures. Now, this [discussion] relies on the defiled cause, which exists only in the Mahāyāna;
that is, the eighth consciousness. Does it not exist in the Hīnayāna?

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Furthermore, this basis is the seed-consciousness, up to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*," the subtle mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the Sthavira school is precisely what I [the Mahāyānist] take to be the eighth consciousness of my own Mahāyāna. This involves adopting the tenets of other schools as one's own;

as stated in the aforementioned treatise, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the part-containing consciousness (*bhāgavijñāna*), and so forth of the other Hīnayāna schools are all taken collectively.

Do you take this to be the eighth consciousness of the Mahāyāna? Hitherto, the Dharma masters who have lectured on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* have understood only the position of the Sthavira school, which maintains that two mental consciousnesses cannot arise simultaneously.
This was because they failed to consult the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (the *Śatadharma-vidyāmukha-śāstra*) and thus lacked understanding;
they simply took the subtle mental consciousness of the Sthavira school and identified it as their own Mahāyāna eighth consciousness. Furthermore, those who previously lectured on the *Saṃgraha*...

Although the Dharma masters and others have seen in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* the refutation of the two consciousnesses arising simultaneously with the manas, as well as the scriptural passage beginning "because it is defiled," they—these various masters—did not realize that this *Saṃgraha* was refuting the Sthavira school.

Only by reading this text of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* does one come to know that it is indeed the Sthavira tenets being refuted. This refers to those who maintain that two mental consciousnesses do not arise concurrently.

The Theravādins say: "In our school's sūtras, it is taught only that there are no three Buddhas appearing simultaneously in the world, no two wheel-turning monarchs born at the same time, and no two pratyekabuddhas appearing in the world together.

Since it is only in these three classes of sūtras that it is stated—and not permitted—that two mental consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously, do you therefore allow for the simultaneous arising of two mental consciousnesses?"—the Sautrāntikas.
The Sarvāstivāda masters, for this reason, do not permit the simultaneous arising of two consciousnesses based on the scriptural texts;
they further maintain that because the six consciousnesses cannot arise simultaneously, each arises individually.
Furthermore, regarding the *Nyāyapraveśa* [Treatise on Logic] stating that "the reason has three characteristics" up to "it is not a direct inference":

if one were to formulate this as a formal proof (*pramāṇa*)—namely, "The eighth consciousness is definitely the mind at the time of death; because it is based on defilement and its continuity is uninterrupted"—then there would be no similar example (*sapakṣa*).
Although the first characteristic exists—that is, the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—it lacks the second characteristic. And yet...
To take these two reasons—namely, that [the object] does not definitely exist in similar instances (*sapakṣa*)—as a means of inference (*anumāna*) is a logical fallacy.

Regarding the statement in the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) that "the object of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is unknowable," up to the phrase "the consciousness that is thus conceived": this refers to the Mahāyāna.
You, of the Sthavira school, say: "The subtle mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that you speak of, whose object is unknowable, is precisely what I [assert]."
Regarding the Mahāyāna seed-consciousness: because it cognizes the inequality of the body and the vessel-world [the physical environment], it is unknowable.
Therefore, you, the Elder Master, why trouble yourself with concern for our eighth consciousness? Is it perhaps your own subtle mental consciousness?

Regarding the commentary’s statement that there is a difficulty concerning the simultaneous arising of the first two [visual consciousnesses]: this refers to certain other Dharma masters who employ the following inference (*anumāna*) to challenge the Sthavira school.

The commentary should also include the following inference: that the two eye-consciousnesses, coarse and subtle, arise simultaneously and are subsumed under the *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses), just like the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is the inference.

There is an indeterminate result. Is it the case that because [the ear-consciousness] is subsumed under the category of consciousness, there are no two types of consciousness—the coarse and the subtle?

Or is it the case that because [it] is subsumed under the category of evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), like the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), there are indeed the two types of consciousness—the coarse and the subtle?

Therefore, within our school’s tenets, one should state that the first five consciousnesses also possess both the coarse and subtle types of consciousness arising simultaneously, because they are subsumed under the category of evolving consciousness, just like the mental consciousness; thus, there is no fault.
[Objection:
How can a commentary follow mere personal inclination? It must reject the sacred teachings [of others]. To refute the Sthavira school, he says:
"How could it be that because this statement is not found within our own school’s scriptures, it is therefore not the sacred teaching?"

Regarding the statement in the Commentary, "These three reasons are not valid measures," this means that if these three reasons are employed to establish an autonomous inference (*svatantra-anumāna*), they are subject to logical fallacies.
If one were to first state the thesis (*pakṣa*) as: "The eighth consciousness is necessarily the mind at the time of death," and provide the reasons (*hetu*) as:

"Because it relies on the defiled [mind]," "Because its continuity is uninterrupted," and "Because the objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are unknowable," there would be no similar instance (*sapakṣa*). Therefore, it is not a valid inference.

Regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): the first two reasons mentioned above do not constitute an inference (*anumāna*), but merely serve to reveal by way of reductio (*prasaṅga*) that the mind at the moment of death is the eighth consciousness.

Only the third reason constitutes a reductio that reveals an inference. Both [the reductio and the inference] are free from fault, as explained in the commentary; the aforementioned inference may be understood accordingly.
The commentary states that the formulation of the syllogism beginning with "up to... just as in the case of form, etc. refers here to the first reason (*hetu*) of the inference;
it is the third reason found within that *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*.
The Commentary states: "Only the third reason constitutes an inference (*anumāna*), [and so on] up to 'how can one attain awakening?

regarding the inquiry. This means that only the third reason functions as a reductive inference (*prasaṅga-anumāna*), stating: "Because your life at the time of death is unknowable, it is like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). One might ask:

"Do not the first two reasons merely function as reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and not as inferences? Indeed, the Dharma masters who have lectured and debated thus far have treated both of the first two reasons as [inferences].
Is it not an inference? How can you raise this objection in vain?
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "wholesome karma cools from the bottom up, while unwholesome karma cools from the top down, until finally there is relinquishment":

it is like a person who has previously committed evil karma and is destined for rebirth in the miserable realms; when that person is about to die, [the cooling sensation] proceeds from the head down to the heart.
First it becomes cold. After that, from the heart and wisdom [center] down to the feet, it gradually becomes cold all at once.
If one has previously performed virtuous deeds, at the time of death, it first becomes cold from the feet up to the heart; thereafter, from the heart to the head, it becomes cold all at once.
Regarding the "remaining fallen flower" (yǒu yú luò huā), Master Shì explains: if the heart and everything below the ankles become cold simultaneously.
If that person’s heart and feet and knees become cold simultaneously, they enter the realm of animals.

If the heart, waist, and everything below them become cold simultaneously, they enter the realm of hungry ghosts. If the heart, chest, and everything below them become cold simultaneously, they enter the human realm.
If the heart and everything from the crown of the head downward become cold simultaneously, their [destiny is as follows].
A person may attain birth in heaven. If the mind and the crown of the head cool simultaneously, that person enters the state of a noble one (*ārya*).
The subsequent explanations above are all incorrect principles. However, this mass of flesh that is the mind is what arises first and is what is abandoned last;

that is to say, it is what arises at the very beginning and ceases at the very end. Thus, when first entering the womb, the body is about the size of a *māṣa* bean, and at that moment, there is already this mass of flesh.
It is the mind. Furthermore, at the time of actual death, it is this physical heart-mass that is the last to be relinquished. Second, it is like the kalpa-ending fire:
the palace of Mahābrahmā arises first, and though the fire persists thereafter, it is the palace of Mahābrahmā that is the last to perish.
Third, it is like the kalpa-ending water: the palace of the Ābhāsvara Heaven also arises first, and later, when [the destruction] occurs...
It is also most permitted that they perish during the calamity of water. Furthermore, at the time of the kalpa-ending wind disaster, the palaces of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven first arise;
later, when the calamity of water arises, they are the last to perish. Likewise, at the time of the kalpa-ending wind disaster, the palaces of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven first arise;
later, when the wind disaster occurs, they are the last to perish. The Three Deep Pits.
Among these, the water in that [deep] pit reaches it first; only later does it reach the other shallow places.
Later, when the water is about to run out, the water in that deep pit is the last to disappear. Regarding the "flesh-ball of the heart" (*māṃsapiṇḍa-hṛdaya*):

because it is grasped at birth and finally abandoned at death, it has been heard said that "this consciousness arises first, and this consciousness ceases last. Furthermore, at the time of initial birth, there is also the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
How can it be said that this mind alone arises for the first time? [One might ask: In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is likewise an initial arising and a final relinquishing;

yet one is not born into the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Since these are also instances of birth, they too possess such phenomena as an "initial arising" and so forth.
Furthermore, after dying from the form realm or the six heavens of the desire realm, one may also be born into other realms of existence, whether wholesome or unwholesome. Regarding this...
In the six heavens of the desire realm within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is likewise a distinction based on the gradual arising of cold touch from the lower to the upper parts [of the body].
Those who die in the northern continent (*uttarakuru*) will necessarily be reborn in the heavens; for them too, there is a gradual arising of cold touch from the lower to the upper parts of the body.

This applies analogously even to those in the four miserable destinies (*apāya*), the persons who have attained the four fruits of the path, and the bodhisattvas of the first seven stages (*bhūmi*). Question: Is there also [a gradual death] for those whose life ends gradually?
Regarding the phrase "first abandoning the body of the five consciousnesses": a question is raised as to what happens in the case of one who dies instantaneously.
The treatise states: "The sixth mental consciousness does not abide in the body... because it is constantly continuous.

This means that while the five consciousnesses each rely upon their respective five material sense organs and may thus be said to abide in the body, if the mental consciousness does not rely upon the material sense organs, it is termed "not abiding in the body."
Furthermore, the objects are not fixed. Moreover, the mind may take form as its object, or it may take sounds, odors, tastes, and other such objects.

Regarding the phrase "pervadingly resting within the body," it should rather be said "pervadingly relying upon the body. As for "pervadingly": if it takes the same objects as the body-consciousness, then it is "pervading."
Or is it because it shares the same objects as visual consciousness and so forth that it is called "non-pervasive"? Regarding the phrase "constantly continuous":

this means that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises perpetually, unlike the five sensory consciousnesses which are frequently interrupted; for, except during the five states of mindlessness when it does not manifest, it arises constantly at all other times.
However, if one considers the sixth consciousness in relation to the eighth consciousness, the sixth consciousness is likewise intermittent.

The sixth consciousness arises constantly and manifests perpetually; it encounters objects and takes them as conditions immediately. Unlike the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which dwells for a long time upon a single object and must necessarily take that specific object as its condition, this [sixth consciousness] encounters an object and takes it as a condition immediately. This refers to the independent sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Alternatively, when it relies on the five sense organs as its gateway and takes the same objects as the five consciousnesses, the eighth consciousness serves as the objective sphere for the five sense organs.

This refers to what is stated in the passage below: "Within the ālayavijñāna, there is one class of thinkers who maintain that it is driven by the winds of karma, universally relying upon all the sense faculties, and perpetually evolving in a continuous stream.
If it is argued that if the sixth consciousness were able to grasp and maintain [the body] by relying on the faculties, then the same would apply to the eighth;
that is, if the eighth consciousness can grasp and maintain the five faculties without relying on them, then the same should hold for the sixth consciousness.

Nor does it maintain the five sense-faculties [independently], for it must be able to grasp and maintain them. Thus, the eighth consciousness, by depending upon the five sense-faculties, is able to grasp and maintain those very faculties.
If it were not dependent [on them] to perform this grasping and maintaining, and if the eighth consciousness were considered indeterminate, the point being made is this:
if the sixth consciousness did not depend on its faculties yet could still grasp and maintain them, then the same would apply to the eighth consciousness. However, it does depend [on them].

The five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are capable of being appropriated (*upādāna*). If it is argued that the eighth consciousness is capable of appropriation because it does not depend [on physical organs], then the sixth consciousness would likewise be incapable of appropriation despite its dependence [on such organs].
Since the eighth consciousness is established as indeterminate matter (*rūpa*), the formal inference (*prayoga*) stated outside the text is as follows:

The sixth consciousness is certainly unable to grasp and maintain [the body], because it does not pervade the five sense organs, just like external wind, sound, and so forth. Now, regarding the transformation that is not fixed as past:

is it because, unlike the eighth consciousness which does not rely on all [parts of the body], the sixth consciousness cannot grasp and maintain? It is precisely because the eighth consciousness is able to grasp and maintain [the body] that it is so.
Your sixth consciousness does not have a pervasive basis, yet it is able to grasp and maintain [the body], just as wind, sound, and so forth do not have a pervasive basis;
therefore, your sixth consciousness cannot grasp and maintain [the body]. Thus, we know that the eighth consciousness has a pervasive basis and is able to grasp and maintain [the body].
Regarding the phrase "that which is comprised of the fruit projected by its nature": the question is whether this term "projected fruit" refers to the remaining fruit projected previously.

As for the gloss "the four aggregates [of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness], which are non-material in terms of name and status," there are many interpretations according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. To begin with, one explanation states:

Because within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) there are names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*), are the remaining four aggregates—feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*)—collectively termed "name"?
Furthermore, another explanation states: the four aggregates, consisting of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), can manifest objects (*viṣaya*), just as names can express objects.

Because it is designated by way of analogy, these four aggregates are called "name" (*nāman*). This interpretation of "name" applies throughout the Mahāyāna. Regarding the passage below concerning the "head," the "object," and "name":
as stated in the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra* (Treatise on the Different Schools), *arbuda* is translated here as "bubble. Its gradual development...

*Gijjha* (Vulture): This refers to [the state] like a festering sore. *Ubbhida* (Closed/Coagulated): This is translated as "gradually coagulating. It refers to when the [corpse] has become fully pervasive;
it is also called *ubbhida*, meaning the same. When it has grown and solidified, it is called *kunapa*. *Kunapa* means "thick" or "dense. The *Pañcavidha-bhava-sūtra* states:
on the first seven days it becomes putrid; on the second seven days it is like a sore; on the third seven days it is like a sore; after the third seven days it has coagulated; on the fourth...
Over seven days, it gradually thickens. When the Bodhisattva enters the womb, he does not rely on impurities, nor does he grow incrementally.

This means that if the fetus were already endowed with the sense faculties (indriya) and the great elements (mahābhūta), then since these would all be suddenly perfected, it would reach the stage of *praśākhā* at five weeks.
*Praśākhā* is translated here as "endowed with sense faculties. This stage is so named upon reaching the fifth week. Question: Is this stage prior to the stages of the path (*bhūmi*), or is it...?
The Bodhisattva on the Ground further asked: "Regarding the fact that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas undergo five types of gestation, how do they differ from Bodhisattvas?

As for the statement that 'consciousness conditions name-and-form' and 'name-and-form conditions consciousness,' why is it that among the twelve links of dependent origination, it is said that 'consciousness conditions name-and-form' and 'name-and-form conditions the six sense bases,' which differs from the wording of this sūtra?
Is it not rather that these [links] condition one another mutually? He further asked: "In this context, what is meant by the term 'consciousness'?"

[The interlocutor asks: "In the twelve links [of dependent origination], are these [the two] consciousness and name-and-form? [The respondent] answers: 'This is the explanation of Wu-xing (Asvabhāva):

both of these take consciousness as their designation. Regarding the term 'causal condition' (*pratyaya*): the questioner asks, 'Is this a direct causal condition (*sākṣāt-pratyaya*)? The answer is: 'It is still called a causal condition.
Furthermore, he cites simultaneous cause and effect as an example, such as the two bundles of reeds. [The questioner asks: "Regarding the two bundles of reeds..."

How can there be cause and effect? The answer is: because it is still designated as cause and effect. If one claims that there is only the *manas* (mind), and that the *manas* itself constitutes consciousness (*vijñāna*), then according to the Sarvāstivāda school, at the moment of initial conception, there exists the sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This mental consciousness is what is referred to here as "consciousness external to name" (*nāmabāhyavijñāna*).

In reality, however, there are only three aggregates, because there is no aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) [separate from the other four]. As for the statement "it does not correspond with name," this is the intention of this master.
It is said: "The sixth consciousness is designated as the 'consciousness external to names,' while the eighth consciousness is not fixedly designated as the 'consciousness within names';
therefore, the sixth consciousness does not correspond with names. Regarding the Sautrāntika masters and others whose reasoning is the same as this:

if one asks whether the tenets of the Sautrāntikas are also the same as those of the Sarvāstivādins, and what other schools are included by the term "others," the answer is: it refers to the final [concluding] section.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “the simultaneously existing faculties are called ‘form’ (rūpa), while the intervening faculties are called ‘name’ (nāma)”: this treatise provides a general explanation of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and is not a point of contention.
Does it mean that the five material faculties are called “form” because they are simultaneously existing, while the immediately preceding moments [of consciousness] are taken as “name”?
The second interpretation further states: “The five material faculties, the primary elements upon which those faculties depend, and the physical locations of the faculties [are called form].”

Regarding that which is capable of producing the primary elements (*mahābhūta*): it is said that "form" (*rūpa*) exists therein in four kinds. First, the derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*) of the five sense organs (*indriya*).
Second, the four primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that constitute the five sense organs. Third, the objects that support the sense organs (*indriyāśraya*).
Fourth, the four primary elements that constitute the objects supporting the sense organs. These four kinds are called "form. As for the four primary elements that constitute the five sense organs:

The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the most intimate; they are able to support the five sense faculties (*indriya*). Next are the derivative forms that support the objects of the senses (*viṣaya*), which are also capable of supporting the faculties, though at a greater distance.
As for the four great elements that act as the producers of these supports for the faculties and their objects, these elements are only able to support themselves and their own derivative objects;
they do not directly support the five sense faculties. However, in a more remote and partial sense, they are also capable of supporting them.
The commentary states that the remaining four names must necessarily involve consciousness, and so forth; thus, there is little to be understood [otherwise]. The explanation says:

the remaining mental states and mental factors are called "name" (*nāma*). The eighth consciousness is able to grasp and maintain the five sense organs (*indriya*) along with their objective fields (*viṣaya*);

these are also the characteristics of "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). This does not exist in the Hīnayāna. Question: Among the twelve organs mentioned below, the material organs (*rūpīndriya*) are already included within the six...

[The five faculties] are subsumed within the "basis" (*āśraya*). Why, then, are the five faculties said here to be included within "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*)? This will be explained below. The *Śāstra* states:

"The eye and other [faculties], being subsumed under the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), are included within 'name'. Question: Does this "name" mean that the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are included within "name"? Answer:
The subsequent passage states that at the stage of the *kalala*, when the five consciousnesses are absent, [the faculties exist]. Thus, it refers to both the upper and lower [stages].
The preceding text is internally contradictory. Answer: The subsequent text refers to that which exists from the seventh-day stage onward; thus, there is no fault.

That which is termed "intermediate consciousness" (antarābhava-vijñāna)—what is its function? It is the seventh consciousness. Question: Since the seventh consciousness is not produced by karmic retribution, how can it be a form of consciousness?
Answer: Here, we are merely considering them in terms of mutual dependence; we do not rely on the distinction between being produced by karmic retribution or not. There is another...

Regarding the statement that “the manas is the consciousness within the name”: the question is, this text speaks for now of the seventh consciousness as being the consciousness within the name, yet it is not so taken among the twelve links [of dependent origination] below.
Furthermore, since the seventh consciousness is not produced by karma, how can it be designated as the consciousness within the name?
According to my humble opinion, as for the statement that the seventh consciousness is the consciousness within the name, in the Mahāyāna, it is for the time being based on...

Regarding the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) associated with affliction (*saṃkleśa*), it is taught that even those which are not [inherently] factors are also designated as "factors. This is because the positions of the Hīnayāna have already been refuted.

In this commentary, it is also stated that the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) are likewise subsumed under name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). If one explains this according to the non-afflicted perspective, the seventh consciousness and the five [sensory consciousnesses] are not subsumed under form (*rūpa*).
This interpretation is also found in the eighth fascicle of the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) below.

The commentary, summarizing the treatise, states that the consciousness of odor regresses; this refers to those bodhisattvas who, having faith in the existence of the eighth consciousness, practice this contemplation.
Reaching the stage of old age and death, they contemplate that this old age and death arise from "birth" (jāti) and, by virtue of the truth of origination (samudaya-satya), come into being.
The truth of origination (samudaya-satya) is both coarse and subtle. If the branch of birth (*jāti*) is the coarse truth of origination, it is because it brings about present birth, aging, and death.

If the branch of existence (*bhava*) is called the subtle truth of origination, then one contemplates from the branch of aging (*jarā*): by what is this aging and death caused? It is caused by the branch of birth.
Next, by what is the branch of birth caused? It is caused by the branch of existence. By what is the branch of existence caused? By...
The link of appropriation exists because of existence. By what does existence exist? It exists because of craving. Why does craving exist?

It exists because of the link of feeling produced by the link of contact. Furthermore, it is precisely the feelings produced by contact associated with ignorance that serve as the condition for the arising of craving;
if they were not feelings produced by contact associated with ignorance, they could not serve as the condition for the arising of craving. This continues up to name-and-form.

By virtue of what does the link of *aṅga* exist? It exists by virtue of the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*). One contemplates up to the link of consciousness and then stops further contemplation, immediately withdrawing.
This is because one contemplates that the links of consciousness and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are mutually dependent; having already done so, one now does not contemplate their mutual projection.

The link of consciousness is the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Now, citing the meaning of that passage: "Because the head [of existence] possesses the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). If...
The wisdom of bodhisattvas prior to and upon the stages delights in this contemplation. There are bodhisattvas who do not perform the contemplation of the thirty-four knowledges;

however, those belonging to the vehicles of the two realms do perform the contemplation of the thirty-four knowledges. Furthermore, those belonging to the vehicles of the two realms perform the contemplation of the forty-four knowledges, namely:
contemplating old age and death, the origin of old age and death, the cessation of old age and death, and the practice leading to the cessation of old age and death.
Old age and death are themselves the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). That which is the origination of old age and death is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).

That which is the cessation of old age and death is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). That which is the practice leading to the cessation of old age and death is the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).

This means that because the essence of this old age and death is oppressive, it is the truth of suffering. One considers from what cause this old age and death arises; old age and death arise from the link of birth (*jāti-aṅga*).
Therefore, the birth-link (*jāti-aṅga*) is called the fruit of aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*). What is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*)?

It is precisely the attainment of the cessation of this aging-and-death, which must be realized through the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). How is this cessation to be realized? It is by means of the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).

In this manner, up to the formations (*saṃskāra*), the origination of formations, the cessation of formations, and the practice leading to the cessation of formations, there are only forty-four knowledges (*jñāna*). This is because ignorance (*avidyā*) has no cause.
Because ignorance does not arise from the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), there is no mention of the Four Truths above [ignorance].
Regarding the statement, "If consciousness were not to cease, name-and-form would increase," this is incorrect; however, this text contains a redundancy because it is actually a question.
This passage should rather state: "If how could name-and-form alone increase? This is because the four [truths] are not being praised.
World-Honored One.
*Commentary on the Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only*, Scroll Seven;
*Commentary on the Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only*, Scroll Eight.
Composed by Lingtai of Beijing as a commentary.

Now, regarding those who explain this differently from what has been stated here, there are three masters whose views differ. Therefore, it is said in the long prose section that the meanings of the three masters differ.
As for the phrase "some have established alternative theories" (*po she yi ji*): *po* means "to establish. This refers to certain masters; however, below this...

Regarding the three masters mentioned within the section on "clearly explaining sensation" (*vedanā*): they are all protectors of the Dharma who merely adopted divergent views; however, their underlying intent was the same as that of the first transformation.

This is why they were not mentioned [separately]—this very text represents the correct interpretation. Since the seventh consciousness, like the eighth consciousness, is characterized by the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), it is not mentioned again within the second transformation.

As for the emergence of the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) from within the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*): [it is because it arises from the cessation of the sixth consciousness].

The intended meaning is that in the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), both mind and mental factors are extinguished; therefore, the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is absent, and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is extinguished as well.
The Commentary states: "This seventh consciousness is associated with a type of predominant sensation capable of projecting the fruit of karma, and takes that karmic fruit as its object.
This is the assertion of this master. To explain it further: suppose there is a person who commits three [types of] actions...
At the time when karma for the miserable realms arises, that evil karma arises together with the feeling of sorrow (*daurmanasya*).

Since that evil karma has arisen together with the feeling of sorrow, at a later time, when it brings about the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and one is born into the three miserable realms, the seventh consciousness takes as its object that eighth consciousness which has been brought about by the evil karma associated with the feeling of sorrow; at that time, the seventh consciousness is likewise accompanied by sorrow.
It is associated. For instance, suppose there is a person who performs the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions.

Those five precepts and ten wholesome actions arise simultaneously with the experience of wholesome feeling (*sukha-vedanā*). Later, as a result of those ten wholesome actions and five precepts, one attains rebirth in the eighth consciousness within the human realm or the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
At that time, when the seventh consciousness takes the eighth consciousness as its object, it is associated with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*). Furthermore, it is like this...
When one attains the first two fundamental meditative absorptions (*maula-dhyāna*) in this life, their immovable karma (*āniñjya-karma*) is associated with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*).

This immovable karma, coexisting with the feeling of joy, brings about the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) as it arises in the first two dhyānas; thus, the eighth consciousness is the result of karma that accords with the feeling of joy.
As for the seventh consciousness (*manas*), it takes as its object the eighth consciousness produced by that immovable karma which accords with the feeling of joy.
At the time of consciousness, its seventh consciousness is associated with the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*).

In the third and fourth dhyānas, it is likewise induced by the pleasantness of mental activity and by wholesome feelings of pleasure and equanimity; thus, it is designated as karma that accords with the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanīya-karma*).
This refers to the ripening of the fruit of karma associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanīya*). However, according to this master’s interpretation, the two upper realms are exceedingly excellent.

Because one attains the first and second dhyānas through sitting, immovable karma (*āniñjya-karma*) is conjoined with the feeling of joy (*prīti-vedanā*). If one attains the third dhyāna, that immovable karma is conjoined with the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*).
If one attains the fourth dhyāna, that immovable karma is conjoined with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). At a later time...
This immovable karma brings about the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) when one is born within the four dhyānas.
When the seventh consciousness takes that eighth consciousness as its object, that seventh consciousness may arise in association with joy, bliss, or equanimity.

If, however, a person in the desire realm performs karma associated with unwholesome states—that is, karma associated with the sensation of sorrow—and subsequently brings about the eighth consciousness, [the seventh consciousness] takes that eighth consciousness...

This refers to karma that accords with the experience of feeling. It is logically consistent that the seventh consciousness takes the eighth consciousness as its object while being associated with feelings of mutual distress (*daurmanasya*).
Alternatively, there may be cases where a person, at the very moment they commit an evil deed, is associated with feelings of joy (*saumanasya*) or pleasure (*sukha*).

Since they have already produced evil karma, which is accompanied by feelings of joy and pleasure, how could the eighth consciousness arise in an evil realm? When its seventh consciousness takes that eighth consciousness as its object...

That seventh consciousness is associated with joy and pleasure. Furthermore, when a person performs unwholesome karma, their precepts—which are wholesome karma—are associated with pleasant feeling to be experienced.

Since this wholesome karma is associated with pleasant feeling to be experienced, how could the seventh consciousness, within the realms of humans and devas, not be associated with wholesome karma and pleasant feeling to be experienced? (Mahā-śāstra)
It is said: If one craves present pleasure, one creates non-ripening karma (*avipāka-karma*). When creating evil karma, there may still be pleasant sensations and so forth.
If one craves future pleasure, one creates meritorious karma (*puṇya-karma*). If one craves the pleasure of future meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one creates immovable karma (*āneñjya-karma*).
The text states: "If one provides material requisites, one bestows present pleasure; if one causes [them] to go forth into homelessness, one bestows future pleasure. If...
Causing one to sit in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and so forth immediately bestows happiness upon the present and the future.

The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Furthermore, regarding the statement that before the stage of concentration there is superior pleasant sensation (*adhimātra-sukha-vedanā*), which exists only in the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*)," this refers to the second interpretation herein.
As for the seventh consciousness (*manas*) following other sensations: when one is born into the fourth dhyāna, the seventh consciousness [is likewise affected].

It is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Among the mental factors (*caitta*) belonging to that level, there is equanimity. If one is born in the third dhyāna, within that third dhyāna there is the pleasure (*sukha*) of that level;
thus, the seventh consciousness is associated with the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), because the mental factors of the third dhyāna level are the feeling of pleasure.
Therefore, the seventh consciousness is associated with the feeling of pleasure. If one is within the three evil destinies (*durgati*), it is mostly accompanied by sorrow (*daurmanasya*).

They are both associated with sorrow and suffering. That is to say, within the five sensory consciousnesses there is sorrow; likewise, the sixth consciousness is also associated with sorrow, though not with suffering.

Even when performing karma that leads to the evil realms, although it may be accompanied by joy or pleasure, because the fruit is experienced by the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), there is the feeling of sorrow at the place where the fruit is received.
As for the seventh consciousness, it is associated exclusively with the feeling of sorrow. This applies to those among humans and the heavens of desire.
For the most part, it is accompanied by joy and bliss; the sensation of bliss resides within the five sensory consciousnesses, while the sensation of joy is concomitant with the sixth consciousness.

Furthermore, the seventh consciousness is also accompanied by joy and bliss; the sensation of bliss resides precisely within those associated with the five [sensory] consciousnesses. This is even when one performs meritorious karmic actions.

There is the experience of sorrowful suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*). Due to the birth induced by it, the eighth consciousness arises. Others have joy (*prīti*); the seventh consciousness, for its part, is associated with joy.

Furthermore, above the dhyānas, the karma of the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is predominant. Above the four superior dhyānas, it is said that the seventh consciousness is associated with the feeling of equanimity.

If one is among humans or the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), although there is the feeling of equanimity, the karma of the feeling of equanimity is weak; thus, [the seventh consciousness] is associated with joy.
Pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is superior; therefore, it is not mentioned [in that context]. There is a seventh consciousness which is associated with neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

Although neutral feeling also exists within the three miserable destinies (*durgati*), because the karma of neutral feeling is inferior there while painful and sorrowful feelings are predominant, it is likewise not said to be associated with neutral feeling.
This explanation is superior to the interpretation found in the previous commentary.

The *Śāstra* says: "As for the statement that feelings of suffering and pleasure exist only in the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) and do not coexist with projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*), nor are they mentioned in this context—the teacher [Vasubandhu] explains that if it is the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it can create both projecting karma and completing karma (*paripūraka-karma*). These two types constitute giving.

If it is the first five consciousnesses, they can only create completing karma and cannot create projecting karma. Furthermore, there is no projecting karma associated with the feeling of mental distress (*daurmanasya*)."

It is predominant. Within the five consciousnesses, one cannot speak of the feeling of sorrow alone. In the fundamental mental stages (*manobhūmi*) of the first and second dhyānas, there is only the category of joy (*saumanasya*).
If it is said that there is the feeling of pleasure (*sukha*), is this always a figurative designation?

If *praśrabdhi* (serenity) is what is called "tranquilization" (*damana*), then if one says [pleasure] exists, one must say it is a pervasive satisfaction (*prasāda*). In the first and second dhyānas, the pleasure and the satisfaction differ in five respects.
