if the sixth consciousness gives rise to the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) alone during the first moment, then the attachment to the phenomenon of consciousness within the seventh consciousness remains active. If the latter two moments of mind arise, then that sixth [consciousness]...

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises solely through the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya-vipaśyanā*), which directly opposes the seventh consciousness; thus, the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) no longer functions.

However, according to the correct interpretation (*samyak-artha*), only the single "uninterrupted" (*anantarya*) and the single "liberated" (*vimukti*) moments are taken as the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). This is the correct position.

As for the three-moment path of seeing, these are all considered the "path of seeing with signs" (*sanimitta-darśanamārga*). If one follows the non-correct interpretation, then the three-moment path of seeing is indeed accepted as being the true path of seeing.

The Commentary states: "Regarding those noble ones whose minds are either in a state of natural dispersion or in a state of concentration—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*):

whenever they are in a state of natural dispersion, or in a state of concentration with outflows, or in a mind with outflows, or in a mind without outflows, they all possess attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*)."
However, regarding the contaminated (*sāsrava*) meditative concentrations, there are four types. The first is the "part conducive to decline" (*hānabhāgīya*).

If a bodhisattva from the first to the seventh stage enters this concentration—whether it be the first dhyāna or another such state—their power is inferior, as is the case for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Entering this meditative absorption, one tends toward the arising of various afflictions; this is called the "part conducive to decline" (*hānabhāgīya*). Second is the "part conducive to maintenance" (*sthityanukūla*), which means being conducive to one's own level (*svabhūmi*).

For example, ordinary beings, followers of the Two Vehicles, and Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage, when entering meditative absorption, are conducive to their own level of the first dhyāna if they enter the first dhyāna, to their own level of the second dhyāna if they enter the second dhyāna, and so on, up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

It is likewise. Regarding the third stage, the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*): it refers to Bodhisattvas who, having already entered the first stage (*bhūmi*), enter into contaminated meditative absorption (*sāsrava-samādhi*) that is capable of conforming to their future Bodhisattva penetration and discernment;
it does not refer to the aids to penetration belonging to the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-avasthā*).
When a Bodhisattva on the grounds attains the fruit of non-arising, they do not give rise to the preparatory stage directed toward it;

rather, they possess only the noble wisdom of discernment that accords with the first ground. Regarding the four factors conducive to superior progress, for Bodhisattvas from the seventh ground downward, as well as for the noble births of the two vehicles and so forth, if they enter the first dhyāna concentration, they are able to induce the second dhyāna concentration. If they enter the second...

The second dhyāna-samādhi can then lead progressively to the third dhyāna-samādhi and accord with subsequent superior progress, even up to the meditative absorptions of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).

Is this the case for all? If it concerns those who have attained gradual or sudden realization—whether they be śaikṣas, aśaikṣas, or bodhisattvas of sudden awakening from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) and above whose power is comparable—if there are śaikṣas and aśaikṣas of both gradual and sudden awakening who reach the eighth stage and beyond...

[They] depart because they are able to subdue the self-grasping so that it no longer functions. This is because those of gradual awakening who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) possess great power from the eighth bhūmi onwards.

As for those of gradual awakening who have attained no-more-learning, they are able to sever the afflictions; however, this applies to the stage prior to the seventh bhūmi. As for those of gradual awakening who are still in training (śaikṣa):
This is also similar for Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment.
The Commentary states: "If one cannot bestow [the gift], one should then give rise to the contemplation of dharmas (*dharmānupaśyanā*), and so forth.

If this is taken as proof, then since those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward maintain only a continuous stream of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharma-contemplation, how could they give rise to attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*)? Therefore, we know that they too give rise to [birth].
Regarding the contemplation of emptiness: the seventh consciousness arises based on the clinging to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).

Since the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) and beyond, the untainted mind (*anāsravacitta*) is constantly continuous, and there is no longer any tainted mind (*sāsravacitta*) to serve as its object. Using this as proof, we know that from the eighth stage onward, the tainted mind never exists.

Regarding the statement in the treatises and sūtras that from the eighth bhūmi upward all afflictions (*kleśa*) can no longer manifest, and that only the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) remain as their basis (*āśraya*):
there are currently two interpretations of this "basis. The first states that the cognitive obstructions themselves are the basis.

The afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are that which depends [upon a basis]. Since the afflictions no longer exist, only the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which serves as their basis, remains established.
Therefore, a sutra says: "It is like a tree that has once been felled yet continues to grow depending upon the earth. Even if the tree has been destroyed, it still relies on the earth;
likewise, these dharmas of the afflictions all depend upon the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) to grow. If the ground of ignorance did not exist, those afflictions...

This is also not the case; traditionally, everyone has held this interpretation. Second, the seventh consciousness is the supporting faculty (*āśraya*) for the sixth consciousness, while the sixth consciousness is that which is supported (*āśrita*).

It possesses only a supporting faculty. Regarding the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the seventh consciousness, Zhi-fa once asked the Master of the Commentary about this point, and the Master of the Commentary approved of this interpretation.

The Commentary states: "It is not observed that at other times the sixth consciousness possesses only the grasping of phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) and lacks the grasping of a person (*pudgala-grāha*) at all times.
This is intended as a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), for [if it were otherwise], one would not observe [the absence of person-grasping] during the remaining eight stages up to the tenth stage.
Throughout the course of one kalpa, within the sixth consciousness, only the grasping at phenomena (dharmagrāha) arises, while the grasping at a self (ātmagrāha) does not arise.
Thus, we know that during this one kalpa, because the seventh consciousness gives rise to the grasping at phenomena, the sixth consciousness remains constantly untainted (anāsrava).
If, however, it is a bodhisattva prior to the seventh stage, the sixth consciousness within them still gives rise to the grasping at phenomena.
The Commentary states: "Thus there is a distinct name; this is not among those [others], nor is it any of the other three. One interpretation says:

the dharmas of the three natures are collectively termed "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*). Since they arise from maturation, all four types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas are called "born of maturation.
Now, this indeterminate dharma is indeed born of maturation, whereas the other three are not born of maturation; this refers to [the exclusion] within that collective designation.
Regarding the specific names: however, the distinction of "unspecified (avyākṛta) born of maturation" is not included within those specific names such as "postures," "crafts," or "transformations.
This unspecified state born of maturation is subsumed under "maturation" within the general category.
To say that there are four types of the unspecified is to refer to the general category; "born of maturation" is a specific name for one among these four general categories.
Those not subsumed under those three categories, and those not subsumed by the other three, are all comprised within that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Just as with the four conditions: although the first three conditions are also predominating conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*), they are distinguished separately to manifest their specific differences;

thus, those not subsumed by the first three conditions are all comprised within the predominating condition. All four types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*) are born of maturation, in order to demonstrate this.

Because of the distinction [of categories]. Just as with the other three types of neutral (avyākṛta) states, those not included among the other three neutral states are all subsumed under "neutral born of maturation" (vipākaja-avyākṛta).

Furthermore, regarding the three kinds of matter (rūpa), although nourished matter (aupacayika-rūpa) also arises from homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu), it consists only of substances such as fat and flesh;
it merely increases the physical form by depending on "matter born of maturation," which is induced by prior wholesome or unwholesome karma, or is [the result of] prior...
They are born of the same kind. However, regarding whether they arise from wholesome or unwholesome karma, they are designated solely as "ripened matter" (*vipāka-rūpa*).

These two types of matter are not included within "matter that is a result of outflow" (*niṣyanda-rūpa*), because [the former] is excluded from the four types of indeterminate matter mentioned above. Regarding matter that is a result of outflow, it is called "posture" (*airyāpathika*) when it arises from a mind directed toward posture or when it initiates a mind of posture.
Furthermore, in the second dhyāna, the *Vaibhāṣikas* maintain that the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) is borrowed from the first dhyāna.

The ear-consciousness is all termed "borrowing from the deportment. These divine eyes and ears are not produced by karma, nor are they resultant minds (*vipāka-citta*). A resultant mind does not borrow from another stage (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, when taking craftsmanship as an object, or when giving rise to a mind of craftsmanship, it is called a "mind of craftsmanship" (*śailpasthānika-citta*).

If one gives rise to a mind of karmic transformation or a mind of supernormal transformation, it is called a "mind of transformation" (*nairmāṇika-citta*). Or, it refers to the production of transformed matter and so forth.

[The nature of the mind is] indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Question: Since the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the result-minds (*phala-citta*) all arise based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), how can a wholesome concentration serve as the cause for producing an indeterminate supernormal power or result-mind?

Answer: If one is within a wholesome concentration, a separate indeterminate supernormal power or result-mind must necessarily arise; for among the various wholesome concentrations, such a phenomenon does not exist. [Question:

Does the evil [mind] arise only after one has already entered concentration, or does it give rise to the supernormal power or result-mind? Answer: [It arises] after one has already entered concentration.
Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Sheng weishi lun shu chao), Scroll Eight;
End of Scroll Nine (Explanation of the Second Part of the Fifth Commentary).

The five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are incapable of transforming the mind to initiate karma; they merely do not follow along in initiating karma... up to and including the four [applications of mindfulness].

The commentary states that [the first dhyāna] possesses all three [types of volition], excluding that of transformation. When a mind of the first dhyāna initiates karma, it is exclusively the sixth mental consciousness.

Just as when killing was previously initiated, first there is the deliberative volition (*santīraṇa-cetanā*) associated with the sixth consciousness, which deliberates on what matter should or should not be killed.
Having given rise to this deliberative volition, one immediately gives rise to the volition of determination (*niścaya-cetanā*), resolving to kill.
Because it is a preceding [mental state], the sixth consciousness acts as the "antagonistic cause" (*virodhahetu*) and so forth.

Later, when one intends to kill, the five sensory consciousnesses—such as the visual consciousness—must seek out weapons such as knives or staves; these five consciousnesses can only arise following the sixth consciousness and are thus termed "conforming arising" (*anuvartaka-karma-samutthāna*).

They act as the "proximate cause" (*āsannakāraṇa*) and the "arising cause" (*samutthānahetu*). Therefore, the sixth consciousness is also capable of acting as the proximate cause and the arising cause. Now...

These are the four types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) states. First is the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja-citta*); this pervades the six consciousnesses, and its meaning is as explained in the regular commentaries.

Second is the path of deportment (*airyāpathika*). If one speaks of "deportment" alone, its substance consists of bodily action (*kāyakarman*), namely the manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) of walking, standing, bending, and stretching.
However, one takes only the manifest form and not the shape (*saṃsthāna*). One takes only the colors—blue, yellow, red, and white. If...

Among the three types of matter constituting the *airyāpathika* (postures), only the *naiṣyandika* (outflowing) matter is taken. This is because the scope of *naiṣyandika* matter is broad, as it does not include the other types, such as *vipākaja* (maturation-born) or *aupacayika* (accumulation-born) matter.
If one speaks of the *airyāpathika*, it takes only the objects (*viṣaya*), yet it also takes the bases (*āyatana*) for those three objects;

thus, there are also the three [objects] of fragrance, taste, and tangibility, since they are never separated from the object of visible form. Therefore, fragrance, taste, and tangibility are also [included].
It is the path of deportment (*airyāpathika*). With the exception of the sense-object of sound, there are now two types. First, "path" may refer to the actual road;
that is, deportment itself, because one traverses, comes and goes, walks out, and moves about upon the road. Thus it is also called the "path of deportment.
Second, it refers to a specific category of derivative matter (*niṣyanda-rūpa*)—namely, odor, taste, and touch—which is produced on the body; this is deportment itself.
Because it is the basis for manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*), the four objects on the body are also called the "path of deportment" (*airyāpathika*).
That which is the basis is termed a "locus" (*sthāna*) and a "path" (*mārga*). This is the explanation of Master Chao.

If the sixth consciousness can also initiate deportment, it is because it can also take as its object the manifest form of bodily action (*kāya-karman-vijñapti-rūpa*), which is the substance of deportment; thus, the manifest form that is the substance of deportment is perceived by only two consciousnesses, namely, the sixth.

Consciousness, as well as visual consciousness—if visual consciousness can also take the course of deportment (*airyāpathika*) as its object, it does so because it takes visible form (*rūpa*) as its object;
furthermore, because it can produce the moments of deportment and the deportment induced by that motivating cause (*samutthāna*), there is also a mind that takes deportment as its object.

If auditory consciousness can produce the moments of deportment, because it produces deportment through its motivating cause, it acts as a pervasive cause (*sāmānyahetu*); [however], the motivating cause [itself] does not...

It can take the substance of deportment (*airyāpathika*) as its object; however, because there is no substance of deportment within sound, it cannot also take the path of deportment as its object, for sound is neither the basis of deportment nor that which is traversed by it.
As for the three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body, they can only produce the momentary arising (*kṣaṇasamutthāna*) and the concomitant arising (*anuvartakasamutthāna*) of deportment;
they can also [take] the paths of deportment as objects, as the three objects—odor, taste, and touch—are [the bases of deportment].
Because it is that upon which deportment (*īryāpatha*) relies and through which one moves, the substance of deportment cannot be taken as an object.

The substance of deportment is precisely bodily action (*kāyakarman*), because it consists of informative matter (*vijñaptirūpa*) such as long and short [postures]. Thus far, all six consciousnesses can initiate deportment;

two consciousnesses can take the substance of deportment as an object—namely, visual consciousness and mental consciousness can take the substance of deportment as an object—while four consciousnesses take the paths of deportment as their objects.
This refers to the four consciousnesses of the eye, nose, tongue, and body. As for the essence of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), it apprehends only the two objects of form and sound.

For example, when there is a melodic modulation within sound—such as in the singing of a song—that is the essence of craftsmanship; whereas the sound upon which it depends is the basis of craftsmanship (*śailpasthāna*).
The term "curvature" (*kuṭila*) reveals its basis. Since sound has no distinct substance, its very substance is the sense-field (*āyatana*).

If it refers to engraved patterns, carvings, or curves upon a form, these are all the substance of craftsmanship (*śilpa*). If it refers to the supporting form-object (*rūpa-viṣaya*), then that is the sense-field of craftsmanship.

For example, in the case of painted images on a wall and so forth, craftsmanship consists not only of the form-objects; when one object exists, the others [the other four aggregates] are also present.

Because fragrance, odor, and tangibility are inseparable from form, fragrance, odor, and tangibility, although they are not the substance of craftsmanship itself, are also bases of craftsmanship (*śailpasthāna*).
For example, the construction of houses and the like are also bases of craftsmanship.

If the sixth consciousness takes the substance of craftsmanship as its object, it can also [engage with] the bases of craftsmanship, because it gives rise to the five types of skillful arts; thus, it also possesses the remote causes and so forth.
Regarding the momentary origination (*kṣaṇasamutthāna*) and the simultaneous origination (*tatsabhāgasamutthāna*):

if the two consciousnesses of eye and ear can also take the sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthāna*) as their object and can also initiate craftsmanship, they likewise possess both momentary origination and simultaneous origination.

If there is the essence of craftsmanship and the sphere of craftsmanship within the objects of form and sound, then the three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body can also initiate craftsmanship. [Momentary...]

That which follows and turns [the mind] (*anuvartaka*) can initiate karma; it can also take as its objects the sensory fields of craftsmanship (*śailpasthāna*), namely odors, tastes, and tangibles, because these constitute the field of craftsmanship.
However, it cannot take the essence of craftsmanship itself as an object. The above clarifies that all six consciousnesses are capable of initiating craftsmanship.

Three consciousnesses can take the essence of craftsmanship as their object—namely, the mental consciousness, the visual consciousness, and the auditory consciousness. These three consciousnesses can take the essence of color-form and sound as craftsmanship;
the five [sensory] consciousnesses can take the sphere of craftsmanship as their object. Now, regarding the sphere of deportment and the sphere of craftsmanship:

"Are these sentient beings or non-sentient things? The answer is: those belonging to the *airyāpathika* (postures) and *śailpasthānika* (crafts) categories are comprised within the class of sentient beings.

Question: If that is so, how is it that you previously stated that one takes up external non-sentient things—the visible forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles of the upper paths—and names them *airyāpathika*;
and that one takes up external non-sentient things, namely wood, stone, houses, and walls?
Regarding such things as painting and so forth, they are called "bases of craftsmanship" (*śailpasthāna*). To answer according to the actual reality:

it refers only to the derivative matter (*niṣyanda-rūpa*) produced within the internal body, consisting of visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects, which are termed the "bases of deportment" (*airyāpathika*) and "bases of craftsmanship.

That is to say, one takes the derivative matter of the body—namely, the four sensory objects of odor and so forth—and calls them "bases," just as when a person performs the bodily expressions of deportment such as walking or standing. All [of these] are...
Based on the derived matter (*niṣyanda-rūpa*) of the body’s hands, feet, and so forth, the derived matter of this present body serves as the basis for postures (*airyāpathika*).
Therefore, the derived matter of the body is called "the path of postures" (*airyāpathika*).

For example, when a person performs hymns of praise and the like, it is by depending upon the lips, tongue, teeth, throat, and so forth that sound is produced to perform those hymns. Now, depending upon the lips...

The tongue, teeth, throat, and so forth, as well as the five objects of sensory experience (*pañca-viṣaya*) that are their outflow (*niṣyanda*), are called the bases of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).

Furthermore, when a person performs dance or other crafts, the outflowing matter (*rūpa*) of the hands, feet, and other parts of the body upon which they depend, along with the five objects of sensory experience, constitute the bases of craftsmanship.
Moreover, when a person grasps a pen with their hand or foot to write, or grasps an axe or similar tool in their hand to work, [these are likewise the bases of craftsmanship].
When woodwork is being performed, that which is a derivative (*niṣyanda*) of the five sense objects based upon the hand is called a "field of craftsmanship" (*śailpasthānika*).
Because this meaning is intended, both the "path of deportment" (*airyāpathika*) and the "field of craftsmanship" are also sentient; they are not insentient.
Therefore, the derivative matter (*rūpa*) induced by the body is taken as the path of deportment and named the field of craftsmanship. As for the path of deportment and the field of craftsmanship...

[If it were so,] there would be interruptions. If the *upādāya-rūpa* (derived matter) of the body were [the object of] the *śailpasthāna* (arts and crafts) and the *airyāpathika* (modes of deportment), then those bases (*sthāna*) and paths (*mārga*) should be constantly continuous; however, this is not the case, as the *upādāya-rūpa* of the body is not taken as the path.

Furthermore, if the eighth consciousness cannot take the *vijñapti-rūpa* (informative matter) of deportment as its object—because informative matter is merely conventional (*prajñapti*)—it likewise cannot take it as its object.

Since the body of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) is also conventional (*prajñapti*), for this reason, the previous statement that visual consciousness and so forth take as their object the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) of deportment (*airyāpathika*),

as well as the admission that visual and auditory consciousnesses take as their object the body of craftsmanship— all these are admissions that the five consciousnesses take the teacher as their object.
If one does not admit that the five consciousnesses are conventional, then visual consciousness and the others would not take the body of deportment as their object.

And it is the substance of craftsmanship. If explained according to its meaning: since manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) is not separate from the objective field of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*), and since it has been stated that the eighth consciousness can take the objective field of form as its object, it is metaphorically said that the eighth consciousness can also take the substance of deportment (*iryāpatha*) as its object.

Since those four [subtle] objects are substantially existent entities, it is therefore said that the eighth consciousness can take the five objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) as its objects; thus, it is said that the eighth consciousness...
It can also take the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthāna*) as its object. However, the names, phrases, and syllables upon sound are not themselves the spheres of craftsmanship;

rather, it is only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that takes these names, phrases, and syllables as its objects, for the five sensory consciousnesses cannot take names, phrases, and syllables as their objects.

Since the Buddha’s vocal articulations constitute craftsmanship, and craftsmanship is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*), if there were such articulation upon form (*rūpa*), it would be called "craftsmanship of form."

Form and craftsmanship are also merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*). If one allows that the five consciousnesses take the provisional as their object, then it is said that the two consciousnesses of eye and ear can take the essence of craftsmanship as their object.
To speak according to reality, since the essence of craftsmanship is provisional, the eighth consciousness cannot take the essence of craftsmanship as its object.
If it is said that the essence of craftsmanship is not separate from the two objects of form and sound, then this is the meaning.

This explains that the eighth consciousness takes craftsmanship as its objective essence (*ālambana*). If it brings forth the essence of deportment (*airyāpathika*), it takes the manifest color (*vijñapti-rūpa*) from among the hundred dharmas as its essence.
The essence of this manifest color consists of the long, short, square, round, high, low, and so forth found within the category of form (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, as stated in the preceding text, the substance of manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) consists of long, short, square, round, and so forth; these are the forms of shape (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*).
If such qualities as length, shortness, squareness, or roundness exist upon the five external sense objects, they are termed "external matter" (*bāhya-rūpa*).
If such qualities as length, shortness, and so forth exist upon the internal body, they are termed "manifest form. Manifest form is precisely the shapes of long, short, and so on.
Because of the distinctions in higher states, the substance of deportment (*iryāpatha*) is precisely color such as long and short.
Due to shadows, light, darkness, and so forth, there are further distinctions of color such as blue and yellow; this is also a synthesis. As for the seventh consciousness:
None of these can resolve [the issue regarding] craftsmanship, deportment, and so forth. As for transformations (*nirmāṇa*), they belong exclusively to the sixth consciousness;

the five sensory consciousnesses do not possess the capacity for transformation. Within the five sensory consciousnesses, there exists only the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*), such as the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear.
Although these possess the capacity to perceive distant forms, they cannot effect transformations. Wherever there is such transformation, it must necessarily be a supernormal power.
Fruit. For example, the transformation of gold, silver, and so forth is such. There are supernormal powers that are fruits [of supernormal power] but are not transformations;

for example, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is such. Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of death and rebirth within the sixth consciousness, which—by means of the eye-door—is able to perceive distant matters such as death and rebirth in future lives, this cognition is comprised solely within the category of the fruit of supernormal power and is not a transformation. Moreover, this...
Among the three types of wisdom (prajñā), this transformation is subsumed solely under the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā).

If one speaks only of the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā), then "thinking" (cintā) is a portion of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha), specifically the wisdom among the five object-specific mental factors (viśeṣa-viṣaya-citta). If one says it is accomplished through the wisdoms of hearing, thinking, and cultivation, then it pervades all five aggregates;

it also pervades ten of the eighteen elements (dhātu)—namely, the seven mind-elements, the element of form, the element of sound, and the element of phenomena (dharma-dhātu)—that is, excluding the five material sense-faculties.

And as for odors, tastes, and tangibles: for instance, regarding the *prātimokṣa* discipline of the *vyañjana-saṃvara* (dispersed discipline) within the desire realm, when a person who is well-versed in the sūtras and śāstras intends to receive the precepts, they generate a resolve and make a vow to sever all evil and to clarify all that is wholesome.

At that moment, within the sixth consciousness, the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā* and *cintā-mayī-prajñā*) arise as preparatory application (*prayoga*), whereby the *prātimokṣa* [discipline] is acquired.

Regarding the precepts: these scattered restraints (*vyañjana-saṃvara*), which are the form (*rūpa*) of bodily and vocal actions, are all comprised within those produced by the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation;

therefore, they pertain to all five aggregates (*skandha*). If one does not understand this when receiving the scattered restraints according to the sūtras and śāstras, [it occurs] within the sixth consciousness.
When one receives the precepts through an innate wholesome mind (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*), these precepts are subsumed under the category of innate wholesomeness.

If it concerns cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), since this pertains to the higher realms or is unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*), it necessarily includes the meditative precepts (*dhyāna-samvara*). Question:

In the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, how many natures (*svabhāva*) do the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) possess? Answer: In the Mahāyāna, transformation bodies, supernormal powers, and so forth, possess two natures. If they are for the purpose of benefiting and gladdening [sentient beings]...

When sentient beings manifest transformations such as the supernormal power of transformation (*nairmāṇika-ṛddhi*) or the fruit of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*), these are of a virtuous nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*).

However, when [deities] such as apsaras manifest supernatural transformations for the sake of play and sport, all of these are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). By extension, the transformations and fruits of supernormal power belonging to the Hīnayāna are also subsumed under the category of the indeterminate.

Question: Within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are also minds that take postures (*īryāpatha*) as their object, and there are also minds that take crafts (*śailpasthānika*) as their object;

if these did not exist, how could one speak of *vipaśyanā*? How could Bodhisattvas of vast wisdom or Śrāvakas—whether in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) or in birth (*upapatti*)—comprehend the phenomena of the three realms by means of a mind belonging to the formless realm?
Answer: Furthermore, within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and so forth.
Since the mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) universally takes its objects within that form realm, it also takes as its object the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika-citta*). Question:

When Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above enter the meditative absorptions of the formless realm (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), can they also manifest deportment (*airyāpathika*)? Taking deportment as an object and taking craftsmanship as an object—do these not both cease?
Question: One should examine the previous notes regarding the essence (*svabhāva*) and locus (*sthāna*) of craftsmanship, as well as the essence and path (*mārga*) of deportment.
Does it also include the results of maturation (*vipāka*), growth (*aupacayika*), and outflow (*naiṣyandika*)? Answer: Regarding the outflow, it is as stated above. Question:

Why is it that, concerning the essence of the path of deportment (*airyāpathika*), one takes only informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) and not shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), even though informative matter itself consists of length and so forth?
Answer: Regarding the internal [dimensions], such as length and height, it is as stated above. Questioner:
Does the Buddha’s body possess the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) that support the faculties, and does it consist of the *airyāpathika* (postures) and *śailpasthānika* (crafts)?

If one takes the sensory objects supporting the body to be the *śailpasthānika* and *airyāpathika*, then those bases and paths should be constantly continuous; they would only be of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) and would not extend to the wholesome or unwholesome.

Answer: It is precisely that which can induce a certain category of *niṣyanda-rūpa* (homogeneous matter) within the body, serving as the basis for the modes of deportment (*iryāpatha*) and the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*).
This is why the paths of deportment and the arts and crafts are subject to interruption. Furthermore, it does not grasp the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) that support the body.

Regarding the pathways of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*): if it was stated in the preceding section that one takes up particles of dust and so forth to perform acts of craftsmanship, deportment, and the like, this should now be clarified.

To conclude the discussion on sounds: those sounds produced by craftsmanship, such as the vocal sounds used for chanting and singing, are appropriated (*upātta*) and are subsumed under the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of sound. If, however, one is able to play the *vīṇā* lute and other instruments with the hands, or [with the mouth]...
The chanting of the Buddha’s birth and so forth is subsumed under the category of "causal sound" (*hetu-śabda*). Question:

If one takes the inflections (*vaikṛtya*) upon sound as being "craft" (*śailpasthānika*), and it is said that the auditory consciousness takes craft as its object, then according to the aforementioned treatise, these inflections upon sound are themselves subsumed under names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*).
How, then, can the ear perceive names, phrases, and syllables? [For] names, phrases, and syllables are [the same as] the craft upon sound.
What is the distinction regarding "skillful contractions and curves"? Question: Regarding the essence of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), among the one hundred dharmas, what constitutes its essence?

Answer: It is provisionally subsumed under the category of real objects (*dravya*). Question: For what reason are qualities such as length and shortness, which exist upon external matter, specifically termed "shape-color" (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*)?

It constitutes shape and color (*saṃsthāna-varṇa*). If it exists within the body, it is termed manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*). Furthermore, as stated in the aforementioned treatise when refuting the Sarvāstivāda position on manifest form:
"If one says it is shape, then it is not substantially existent (*dravyasat*), because atoms (*paramāṇu*) such as length and so forth cannot be apprehended."

Therefore, it should be known that what is manifested externally based on the internal body—such as shortness and so forth—is also called "shape" (*saṃsthāna*); it is upon shape that "manifest action" (*vijñapti*) is conventionally established.

Question: What is the difference between the essence of bodily craftsmanship and the *śailpasthāna* (bases of craftsmanship)? Answer: They differ in terms of being conventional (*prajñapti*) and real (*dravya*).
The Commentary further states that the five consciousnesses do not have two moments following one another, nor do they arise alternately.

This master [Sthiramati], based on his previous explanation of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), maintains that according to the first master’s view, the five consciousnesses obtain only a single moment.

Two moments cannot occur in immediate succession. Furthermore, it is not the case that the ear-consciousness arises after the eye-consciousness has ceased, nor that the nose-consciousness arises after the ear-consciousness has ceased, and so forth.
Rather, immediately after the eye-consciousness ceases, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) arises; immediately following that, the ear-consciousness arises;

and when the ear-consciousness ceases, the mental consciousness arises again. Thus, among the five sensory consciousnesses, whichever one arises, it does so in dependence upon the fundamental consciousness—the seventh and sixth consciousnesses.

It always functions simultaneously with three [consciousnesses] and the three [mental factors]. If that were so, then when the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) arises together with the five sensory consciousnesses, it would function simultaneously with seven;

therefore, one should know that this is not the correct principle. Furthermore, according to this master, the first six consciousnesses always arise as a single nature and cannot arise as two natures.
It arises. Furthermore, just as there is a distinction such that when one visual consciousness is wholesome, the other four consciousnesses do not arise;

if the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is defiled by its object, it is simultaneously defiled along with one auditory consciousness, and the others cannot arise because they would be bound by fetters.

The five consciousnesses and the three natures are all induced by the mental consciousness (*manas*). If the five consciousnesses were to arise simultaneously with the three natures, then the mental consciousness would likewise possess the three natures.
The commentary states that this is because it discerns both the fixed objects of perception and the various objects of perception. Regarding "fixed objects of perception":
These noble ones take as their meditative objects either the truth of suffering—such as impermanence, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth—or the truth of origination, cessation, and so on.

While this concentration is present, the mental consciousness does not merely take the meditative object as its domain; within that concentration, it is also able to take sounds and other objects together with the ear-consciousness.
Because these noble ones possess sharp faculties, their minds in the formless realm are able to take three [realms] as objects.

Is it the dharma of the realm (*dhātu*)? Furthermore, another interpretation states: that which takes the object of concentration as its focus does so while within the state of meditative absorption, focusing solely on the principle of signless *tathatā* (suchness), or focusing on the single principle of impermanence.
Thus, within concentration, one focuses solely on the principle and not on phenomena (*vastu*) or various other objects of focus.
As for the statement that concentration and [other mental states] do not coexist, this refers to the initial stage.

Although the Master speaks of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and although he allows that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) may share the same object as the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*)—

namely, the sound-object— he maintains that the mental and auditory consciousnesses must necessarily be of the same moral nature (*jāti*), for they cannot be of different natures. Consequently, within meditative concentration, since the mental consciousness is wholesome (*kuśala*),
an auditory consciousness of a wholesome or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature cannot arise.

The commentary states that "simultaneous" (*sahabhū*) is spoken of in reference to multiple moments of thought; the analogy provided is as follows: it is like saying that a single mind is not a single arising-and-ceasing [moment].
This is the analogy.
The commentary further cites the Sūtra: "The arising of one mind or many minds" refers to when the Tathāgata first attained enlightenment, [at which time] Śakra...
While in the heavens, conceit arose within him. The Buddha addressed his twenty-two celestial ministers, saying: "In Jambudvīpa, a Buddha has appeared in the world;
we do not yet know whether he is genuine or false. Now let us pose a question to the Buddha. If the Buddha can answer it, he is indeed a true Buddha.
He asked: "What is the highest? What is the heaviest? What is the swiftest?"
"What is the most numerous? Among the twenty-two ministers, one minister replied: "The Heaven of the Thirty-three is the highest;
Mount Cakravāḍa is the heaviest; the flight of the hawk is the swiftest; the people of Magadha are the most numerous.
Śakra said: "This is neither heavy nor numerous. Another minister then replied: "Space is the most numerous."
"Which is high? Which is heavy? Which moves most swiftly through the air? And which is most abundant? The Great Earth is heavy; the wind moving through the sky is swift;
and the grasses and trees of the great earth are most numerous. Śakra then gave his approval. This minister had brought this question from afar to ask the Buddha.
Upon reaching the Buddha's presence, he questioned the Buddha. The Buddha, knowing his intention beforehand, replied: "Wisdom is higher than the sky; merit is heavier than the earth. He was cautious.
Thought is swifter than the wind; distracted imaginings are more numerous than blades of grass. Now, I shall explain the intended meaning:
the Buddha’s wisdom is higher than empty space, yet empty space itself is not "high. It is because the Buddha’s merit is so profound that he can cause the earth to quake in six ways.

The great earth is not called "heavy," yet at the moment a single thought arises, it immediately pervades and conditions all phenomena. The movement of the wind is not called "swift," yet sentient beings—

Regarding the signs of aversion: because they arise within a single day, the great earth grasses are more numerous than the scattered thoughts; conversely, the scattered thoughts are fewer than the great earth grasses.
Now, that which is "many-minded" is precisely what constitutes scattered thought.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) asks: "What is meant by 'one thought-moment' (*ekakṣaṇa*)? It refers to a single moment of conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*), not a moment of actual origination (*utpatti-kṣaṇa*).

For example, regarding the sixteen moments of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), such as the 'patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering' (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), it may take three or five moments for the mind to enter and give rise to the realization of the Dharma.
Although many moments may elapse before the matter is fully accomplished, it is collectively termed 'one mind. This is what is meant by conventional discourse."
"One-mind" does not refer to a single moment of arising and ceasing; it is called "one-mind. What is here termed a "moment of one-mind" is superior because it contains multiple minds within it.

Regarding the seven [afflictions] being defiled and the sun being indeterminate (*avyākṛta*): although they possess the three natures (*tridhātu-svabhāva*), this master’s intention is to say that while he does not permit the six consciousnesses to possess the three natures simultaneously, he does permit the eight consciousnesses to possess the three natures simultaneously. For example:

When a single wholesome visual consciousness arises, because the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are always intrinsically indeterminate (avyākṛta), there is the coexistence of all three natures (tridharmasvabhāva).
If one takes the eight consciousnesses as being characterized by the coexistence of the three natures, then all mental factors (caitta-dharma) likewise possess the coexistence of the three natures.
Now, we take only the meaning of the first six consciousnesses possessing all three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the *nisyanda* [homogeneous] is frequent while the *ābhoga* [sudden] is rare," this refers to the eye-consciousness, which possesses wholesome *nisyanda*, and the ear-consciousness, which possesses unwholesome *nisyanda*;
thus, there are two types of *nisyanda*. Furthermore, it refers to the nose-consciousness arising as a sudden mind; thus, there are two types [of sudden mind].
The *niṣyanda* (outflow) is one, while the *ābhoga* (sudden/arbitrary) is many;
thus it is said that *niṣyanda* is much and *ābhoga* is little. The commentary states:

"In this context, the meaning is that either two consciousnesses have much *niṣyanda* and one consciousness has little *ābhoga*, or one and two are contrasted, such that 'two' is called 'much' and 'one' is [called] 'little'."

Fewer [mental states] may occur, such as two or three in relation to one another. Among these, two consciousnesses arise as *saterila* (sudden), while three consciousnesses arise as *nisyanda* (outflowing).
Thus, two constitute the "few" and three constitute the "many. Alternatively, there may be *saterila* in three consciousnesses and *nisyanda* in two consciousnesses.

Whether comparing more with fewer or fewer with more, all such configurations are possible. Herein, for the time being, the initial *saterila* and the subsequent *saterila* and *nisyanda* minds are cited.
Because one makes a determination therein, the methods for seeking defilement and purity are all merely the performance of mental acts by means of a mind that is impulsive or continuous;
this differs slightly from the previous explanation.
The *Śāstra* states: "If [the mind] were always directed toward the same object, then from unwholesome volition (*akuśala-cetanā*) up to this point, it would be as established by the former master.

The meaning of this passage in the *Śāstra* is that it represents the interpretation of the former master, who asserts that the three natures do not coexist and that the five consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously.

Regarding the statement in the *Vyākhyāyukti* that the mental consciousness co-arising with the five [sensory consciousnesses] must necessarily be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), this treatise does not fully capture the principle.
This is because the mental consciousness simultaneous with the five consciousnesses is admitted to encompass both direct perception and inference (*anumāna*).
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "the Sārvastivāda masters heard it only after they had emerged [from concentration]":

because the Sārvastivādins maintain that the six consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously, one in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) gives rise only to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and cannot have the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*). Therefore, while actually in concentration, there is only the mental consciousness.

Only after emerging from meditative absorption do the five sensory consciousnesses arise. This is because, just as a person possesses mental consciousness while asleep but the five sensory consciousnesses only arise upon waking, so too, once one has emerged from absorption, the five sensory consciousnesses arise and are then able to hear. Is this not the case?

Regarding the statement that "the Śrāvakas of Broad Wisdom, whether in training (śaikṣa) or beyond training (aśaikṣa), take the dharmas of the three realms as their object by means of a mind belonging to the formless realm":
this concludes the discussion on the vipaśyanā of the Bodhisattvas and the Śrāvakas of Broad Wisdom, whether in meditative absorption or in birth, by means of a mind of the formless realm.
Regarding the comprehension of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), among the Arhats, only the Immovable Arhat (*akopya-arhat*) possesses the sharpest faculties.
While remaining in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), they can give rise to the meditative absorption of the formless realm (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and take all phenomena as their object.

Furthermore, while within the formless absorption, they can give rise to the ear-consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and thus hear sounds; this is called "if in meditative absorption" (*yadi samāpannaḥ*). "If born" (*yadi jātaḥ*) refers to when the body is actually born in the formless realm.

Within the realms, one uses a mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) to comprehend the phenomena of the three realms. Furthermore, among those who are Non-returners (*anāgāmin*), specifically those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) who are able to enter the meditative absorption of the formless realm, their minds take the phenomena of the three realms as objects while they are also able to enter the meditative absorption of the formless realm.

They may then give rise to ear-consciousness of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to hear sounds; if the sound is that of a Śrāvaka, it is one of sharp faculties. As for Bodhisattvas, this may occur at the stage of first generating the mind of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*).

As for the "lesser" [bodhisattvas], they are unable to give rise to ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) and so forth while in meditative absorption (*samādhi*). As for great bodhisattvas, although their power of wisdom is generally superior, there are still distinctions between sharp and dull faculties.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas prior to the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*) may be reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), yet they fully comprehend all phenomena.
However, bodhisattvas who have attained the four roots of goodness are born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Why is this? It is because they utilize a body belonging to the desire realm.
One enters the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). By means of this, one is not reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Question:

When entering the Path of Seeing according to the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna, in what kind of body does one enter? Answer: For those of the Mahāyāna and the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), entry into the Path of Seeing occurs by relying on nine locations.

These are: the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as six locations; the three continents (excluding the Northern Continent, *Uttarakuru*) as three locations; and [the remaining locations]. That is to say:

In all nine abodes, one may enter the Path of Seeing; this is common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Furthermore, within the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), one must necessarily enter the First Fruit (srotāpatti).
If one attains it there, one enters directly into the Third Fruit, because of having already abandoned desire. Question:
After the death of a person from Uttarakuru, it is unknown where they will be reborn, nor is it known what karma they have created. Regarding the death of a person from the Northern Continent...
Thereafter, they will certainly not be reborn in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru). After their lives end, they will certainly be born in the heavens. Why is this?
Because during their previous lifetimes while practicing the path, they fully engaged in the erroneous view of emptiness (durgṛhīta-śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi) and became attached to the view of emptiness.

Due to their prior preparatory mind being a virtuous state of mind, they were consequently born in Uttarakuru; however, due to having practiced the erroneous view of emptiness, they were consequently born in a borderland.

Regarding difficult circumstances: because one practiced the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) in a previous life, one is born in this life with the realization that wives, children, clothing, and so forth are entirely devoid of self or what belongs to a self (*ātman* or *ātmīya*).

However, due to ignorance (*avidyā*) and karmic formations (*saṃskāra*), even those in the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*) cannot perform such practice. Because they rely on their wholesome or unwholesome karma, they are all reborn in the heavens after death.

If one were to practice a perverted grasping of the contemplation of emptiness, one might be born in the Northern Continent; however, if one were to repudiate cause and effect, [the result would be far more dire].

They immediately enter hell and cannot be reborn in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru). Furthermore, as for those in the Heaven of No-Thought (Asaṃjñisattva), after their lives there end, they will necessarily be reborn among humans;

yet, if they have residual evil karma, they may enter hell. This is because, while previously cultivating the karma for the Heaven of No-Thought, they either denied cause and effect or [committed acts] that result in retribution in a future life, and thus such karma ripens, causing them to enter hell. Regarding "the side of the Monkey Pond" (Markaṭahrada): [this is] asked whether it refers to a pond.
He is named "Monkey" because he was a monkey by the side of a pond; thus he is called "Monkey. Furthermore, regarding the question:

"How is it that upon hearing a sound, the ear-consciousness (śrotra-vijñāna) becomes associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and so forth, until emerging from it because of hearing within concentration?"—this passage explains the phrase "from concentration" found in the treatise.
There are three interpretations. The first interpretation holds that it refers to the arising of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) within concentration to hear the sound. This is termed...
Regarding "arising from meditative concentration": according to the second interpretation, this refers to the arising of auditory consciousness from within meditative concentration to hear sounds;

thus it is called "arising from concentration. According to the third interpretation, since one hears sounds as a person (a conventional entity), it refers to emerging from within meditative concentration.

The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Exposition of Manifestation) explains that "various meanings" refers to the fact that within the aforementioned causes, the capacity to understand various objects through sound is termed "various establishments."

The Commentary states: This is not the original text of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, but rather the interpretation of Siṃhabuddhi. As for the previous masters who cited it as proof, [the author] now explains it:
the statement that the five consciousnesses do not exist during the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*) is an explanation of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*. Furthermore, Siṃhabuddhi says:

It is not that Asaṅga did not compile this treatise; rather, in all other treatises composed by Asaṅga, it is stated that the five consciousnesses are admitted to exist within the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).

Thus, he does not admit that the six consciousnesses can coexist with all three natures (*trisvabhāva*) simultaneously. He cites this very point as proof that within meditative concentration, there is only the wholesome (*kuśala*);
one cannot give rise to the auditory consciousness of sudden, indeterminate (*īryāpathika-avyākṛta*) nature. This is because the five consciousnesses cannot arise within meditative concentration.

Therefore, the commentary generally presents two meanings: first, "many consciousnesses," and second, "many persons. Regarding "many consciousnesses": among the five consciousnesses, one cannot give rise to the other four;
only a single auditory consciousness can arise. Hence, it is called "many consciousnesses. Regarding "many persons": this refers exclusively to the Immovable [Stage].
An Arhat can give rise to ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), whereas other noble ones (*ārya*) cannot; therefore, it is said that "many people" [can do so].
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Only [an Arhat] can give rise to ear-consciousness, not the other four consciousnesses, because they are not Bodhisattvas": Question:

When one gives rise to the fundamental [realization] or the correct understanding of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there may also be sound at that time, and thus ear-consciousness could likewise arise. Is this not the case for those who have attained the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a Bodhisattva?

Sāriputra, you should also answer this question accordingly. Furthermore, it is asked: when persons of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) abandon the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), can the five sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) also arise at that time?
And when Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) realize True Suchness (*tathatā*) and abandon the obstacles that arise, can the five sense-consciousnesses also arise at that time?

Furthermore, it is asked: regarding the four dhyānas and the eight "not-yet-arrived" concentrations (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of the two vehicles, can [the five consciousnesses] arise from within the intermediate state (*dhyānāntara*) in the desire realm?

"Does the ear-consciousness [arise]? He further asked the followers of the Two Vehicles: "When entering the four formless attainments, whether at the fundamental stage or the preparatory stage, can the three consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and body of the form realm also arise? He further asked: "As in the case of Mahāmaudgalyāyana, because a sound-object has arrived..."

In that case, auditory consciousness would arise; furthermore, it could also arise during the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). Likewise, other objects such as visible forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles should also give rise to their respective consciousnesses.

These four questions have not been answered. Moreover, regarding the final question, it is explained that for those of broad wisdom—namely, the followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*)—only auditory consciousness can arise within emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the other four consciousnesses cannot arise. Thus it is said.

"Extensive wisdom" (*vipula-prajñā*) refers to those of the lineage of "followers by dharma" (*dharmānusārin*) and "those who have attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), who possess sharp faculties and are endowed with the arising of wisdom.
As for others of the lineage of "resolute belief" (*śraddhādhimukta*), they are of dull faculties; although they do give rise to wisdom, it is not called "extensive wisdom.
Regarding the bodhisattva who is able to speak of *vipaśyanā*: *vipaśyanā* is likewise the arising of wisdom, which is the same as the aforementioned "extensive wisdom."

The names are similar. Question: Since the names have already been stated, why does [the text] not say "Bodhisattva Vipaśyanā" or "Śrāvaka Vipaśyanā," and so forth, up to "Bodhisattva Vipaśyanā" and "Śrāvaka Vipaśyanā"? Answer:
If one were to repeat the term "Vipaśyanā" above both the Bodhisattvas and the Śrāvakas, the names would be redundant. Now, for the sake of the flow of the composition, it says:

Vipaśyanā refers to Bodhisattvas and those Śrāvakas of extensive wisdom. If a Bodhisattva is in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), all five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are capable of arising.

As the *Sūtra on Contemplation* states: "Whether emerging from or entering into concentration, one hears the wondrous Dharma. That sūtra is similar to what is described here regarding hearing various sounds.
Furthermore, a Bodhisattva can also give rise to visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*) while in concentration, just as in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

It is said: There are Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have attained the true divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). While in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), they are able to see the three thousandfold world-systems of Buddha-fields.

In the preceding discussion, it was established that the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*) possess two natures; while both in absorption, upon hearing a sound, they are either wholesome or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

This is because there is no textual evidence for the simultaneous arising of all three natures (*tridharmasvabhāva*), and because of the extensive wisdom (*vipula-prajñā*) and other such factors. This concludes [the section].
Regarding the four characters "Li, Ji, Guanghui, etc. (*li jí guǎng huì děng*) in the commentary: why is this?

Since the preceding passage already stated that the śrāvaka Guanghui (*guǎnghuì*) could, within meditative concentration, give rise only to auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) and not the other four consciousnesses, how can the subsequent passage further state, "not because of Guanghui"?
Thus, one knows these characters are superfluous.

The Commentary asks: "How can the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) within meditative absorption experience the same object as the ear-consciousness? This preceding passage is an inquiry into the necessity [of this]. The intention of the question is:
since this is the meditative absorption of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), its mental consciousness consists of the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*);

whereas the ear-consciousness belongs to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) and possesses the three feelings of suffering, pleasure, and equanimity. Thus, the mental consciousness can possess all three feelings—suffering, pleasure, and equanimity.
The ear-consciousness obtains its cause through fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* from "at the time of its initial arising, it is necessarily dull and inferior" up to "it will certainly not arise," this is the intended meaning of the response herein.

When auditory consciousness first arises during a state of sudden, impulsive attention (*saterika-citta*), it is both dull and impulsive; thus, it necessarily abandons mental consciousness and shares the same object as the auditory consciousness—namely, sound.

Since mental consciousness is associated with neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*), and auditory consciousness is likewise associated only with neutral feeling, they share a single, distracted sound as their common object.

Regarding the passage from "Because when the ear-consciousness first arises, it is necessarily dull and inferior" up to "it necessarily does not arise": the intended meaning of this response is as follows.

When the ear-consciousness first arises during a state of sudden, impulsive attention (*ābhoga*), it is both dull and impulsive; therefore, it is necessarily associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Since the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes the same sound as its object as the ear-consciousness, and the mental consciousness is associated with the feeling of equanimity, the ear-consciousness must likewise be associated with the feeling of equanimity. Thus, within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is definitively so.

One can give rise to the ear-consciousness associated with the sensations of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). However, when entering the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of joy and pleasure (*prīti-sukha-vedanā*) in the second dhyāna or the first dhyāna, or the meditative absorption of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) in the third dhyāna, one certainly does not give rise to the sudden, indeterminate (*āveṇika-avyākṛta*) ear-consciousness; it simply cannot arise.

This interpretation represents the view of the master who maintains that the three sensations do not coexist, but it is incorrect. Answer: For instance, when a Bodhisattva enters the lower three dhyānas...

In meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the sixth consciousness is accompanied by joy, pleasure, or equanimity. However, for the sake of sentient beings, that Bodhisattva may give rise to the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) within that very concentration;

or, when experiencing suffering or pleasure for the sake of sentient beings, there is the sensation of suffering within the five sensory consciousnesses, while within the sixth consciousness there are the sensations of joy and pleasure.

Therefore, it is known that even the six consciousnesses can simultaneously give rise to different sensations of suffering. Thus, it is known that [the preceding... *Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "故知。前" (Thus, it is known. The preceding...).*
This explanation is incorrect. Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (Sū):

"Although the two explanations are the same in terms of their object, what prevents them from being different? It is permitted that their nature may also differ"—this explanation is precisely that all three feelings are permitted [to coexist];
this is the correct principle. Even if the sixth consciousness enters meditative absorption, it is [characterized by] joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*).

It is possible for an ear-consciousness accompanied by equanimity to be induced by an equanimous state; it is also possible for a sixth consciousness that is equanimous to definitely induce an ear-consciousness accompanied by equanimity.

When entering the meditative absorptions of the Sphere of Infinite Space or the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, one can also give rise to ear-consciousness, which is similar to the Sphere of Nothingness.
However, if one enters the meditative absorption of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one cannot give rise to ear-consciousness. This is because...

Because the mental faculty (*manas*) is dull and weak, this is understood by inference. Since this treatise states that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises from the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) while the ear-consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) belongs to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), it follows that this is an ear-consciousness of a lower stage (*adhobhūmi*) whose sense-base (*indriya*) is analyzed by the sixth consciousness of a higher stage (*uparibhūmi*).
Furthermore, the *Shu* (Commentary) explains: "Question: How can the mental consciousness within meditative absorption (*samādhi*) share the same object of perception (*ālambana*) as the ear?"

The above text constitutes the question. The intent of the question is as follows: Since it is the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), its mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) consists of the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
However, the ear-consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) belongs to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and possesses all three feelings—pain, pleasure, and equanimity.
How can the ear-consciousness, which possesses these three feelings, share the same object as the mental consciousness of equanimity? [How does] the distracted mind enter into equanimity?
Regarding the phrase "feeling and so forth do not arise even mutually," this refers to the preceding passage, which constitutes the answer.

The intended answer is that by means of a distracted mind, one enters the meditative absorption of equanimity-feeling in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), which then induces the ear-consciousness associated with equanimity-feeling belonging to the desire realm.

Because auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) is, at its initial occurrence, associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), it is able to share the same object [as the mental consciousness].

However, if one enters the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the two lower realms, such as those characterized by joy (*prīti*) or bliss (*sukha*), one cannot give rise to auditory consciousness accompanied by the feeling of equanimity. This is the first interpretation.

To claim that within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) there is no distinct feeling for sound would be incorrect. Therefore, the second interpretation provided in the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) should be taken as the correct position. (*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*)
Regarding the treatise’s statement that the three states beginning with *saurya* (sudden/impulsive) are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and so forth, up to the question of how many minds can arise:

this section contains two questions. The intent of the first question is as follows: it cites the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which states that among the five types of mind, the first three are indeterminate.

How, then, can these [three] coexist with meditative concentration? Furthermore, how can the seeking mind (*paryeṣaka-citta*) arising from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) be wholesome (*kuśala*)?

Regarding the nature [of these minds], the second question asks: among the five types of mind, how many can arise within a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*)? Only the first two minds can arise.
Within that concentration, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) gives rise to only two minds, namely, the "sudden" (*ābhoga*) and the "seeking" (*paryeṣaka*) minds.

When the seeking mind arises, one has already emerged from concentration; it is no longer possible for the three subsequent minds—namely, the "determinative," the "defiled," and the "pure outflow"—to arise.
Answering the second question:
The commentary states, "If one is scattered, the first three of the five minds are neutral (*avyākṛta*), and so on, even extending to the wholesome (*kuśala*) and others. This second answer says:

"Now, when hearing a sound while in a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) is initially sudden (*ābhoga*) and is of a neutral nature. If it is associated with concentration..."
Simultaneously, the sixth consciousness’s initial seeking mind (*saṃtīraṇa-citta*) is of a virtuous nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*). As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The first three minds are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)," this refers to the other interrupted, distracted, and deluded states of the six consciousnesses.

Since a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) is a virtuous dharma, even the initial seeking mind regarding sounds within sound and so forth are all virtuous. For this reason, [the preceding statement] holds true.

Regarding other distracted minds: when one is focused on a Buddha image with a virtuous mind, if other sounds or objects suddenly arise, the resulting *saurer* (sudden) mind, *paryeṣaka* (seeking) mind, and *viniścaya* (determinative) mind are all of a virtuous nature.

Conversely, when committing an evil act or focusing on an evil object, if other objects suddenly arise, the *saurer* and *paryeṣaka* minds are both of an unvirtuous nature. As for the eighth [consciousness]...

Regarding consciousness: there is only the *saṃtīraṇa* (investigative) and *niścaya* (ascertaining) mind. If the object of the first sound arrives, there is also the *ābhoga* (initial attention) mind;

this is so stated in terms of its conventional meaning. As for the seventh consciousness (*manas*), it is also conventionally said to possess the *niścaya* (ascertaining), defiled, and *nisyanda* (outflowing) [minds], because it lacks the *ābhoga* (initial attention) and *paryeṣaka* (seeking) minds.

Regarding the commentary’s statement: “Furthermore, the five consciousnesses must be induced by vitarka and vicāra, because this mind entering meditative absorption—even up until the stage where there is no vitarka or vicāra—is such that when the five consciousnesses arise five times, they are all induced by vitarka and vicāra;
yet since this mind entering absorption belongs to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), it is devoid of vitarka and vicāra. If one enters the first dhyāna absorption, whatever vitarka...

Investigation (vicāra) induces the five sensory consciousnesses. When the five sensory consciousnesses arise in the second dhyāna or above, they arise because they are induced by the absence of applied thought (vitarka) and investigation (vicāra).
Regarding the commentary stating "as in the seventh fascicle, under vitarka and vicāra," the seventh fascicle of the treatise says: "This indicates that [the consciousness] mostly arises from them;
it does not mean that it is associated with them. The commentary explains this as follows: if one considers the desire realm and the first dhyāna, where vitarka and vicāra exist...

On the level of the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), [the arising] is mostly due to *vitarka* (applied thought), because all consciousnesses are induced by both *vitarka* and *vicāra* (sustained thought).
Furthermore, even when the five consciousnesses themselves are present, they do not arise through the induction of *vitarka* and *vicāra*; therefore, it is said to be "mostly" so.

If one is on a level from the second *dhyāna* upward where *vicāra* is absent, and one borrows the three consciousnesses of the first *dhyāna*, their arising must necessarily depend upon the *vitarka* and *vicāra* of the first *dhyāna* in order to be able to initiate the first *dhyāna* [consciousness].

This refers to the three consciousnesses. When a consciousness of a different level arises, it must necessarily be induced by vitarka and vicāra; therefore, it is said that they are mostly induced by those two.

Why is this? Although a mind of a different level may induce an ear-consciousness of a different level, because the body belongs to the desire realm and the ear-consciousness likewise belongs to the desire realm, even though it is induced by a mind of a different level, it lacks both vitarka and vicāra.
The Commentary further states: "As for whether this concentration is exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or also includes that which is without-outflows (*anāsrava*):

if all that is without-outflows is inseparable from the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*), then if it is not the contemplation of the emptiness of persons, it must be the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena;

and if it is not the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena, it must be the outflow-free concentration on the emptiness of persons. This is because all [such concentrations] are inseparable from the contemplations of these two emptinesses."
The Commentary further asks: "Is it permissible that an ear-consciousness of the desire realm is induced by a mind of a different stage, even down to a mind devoid of vitarka?
This question may be understood as follows: it restates the previous answer and poses a query based upon it.

Since it was stated that a mental consciousness of the sphere of nothingness induces an ear-consciousness of the desire realm belonging to a different stage, then [it follows that] what is devoid of vitarka and vicāra induces [a state] from the second dhyāna onwards.

Regarding the statement that when the three consciousnesses of the first dhyāna first arise, they should be without vitarka and vicāra, [the question is]: does the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) induce the five sensory consciousnesses?

The commentary answers: "When the five consciousnesses first arise, they must be induced by vitarka and vicāra," and so forth, up to the point of stating that even the *nisyanda-citta* (evolving mind) and others do not permit this.
The intended meaning of this response is as follows: from the second dhyāna upward, when the initial *ābhoga-citta* (spontaneous mind) of the three consciousnesses of the first dhyāna first arises...
It must be induced by vitarka and vicāra before reaching the subsequent *niṣyanda* (outflow) mind. When the three consciousnesses arise, there is no induction by vitarka and vicāra;

this is explained in the commentary, though it is not the correct principle. One should rather say: when the three consciousnesses arise in the second dhyāna and above, because they are consciousnesses of a different stage (*bhūmi*), one must necessarily borrow the vitarka and vicāra of the first dhyāna.
It is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that can give rise to the three consciousnesses; if it does not obtain vitarka...

Because sustained thought (*vicāra*) cannot give rise to the three [sensory] consciousnesses, they must necessarily be induced by both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) when belonging to a different level.

Although the mind of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) induces the ear-consciousness of the Desire Realm— which belongs to a different level— because the body and the ear-consciousness belong to the same level of the Desire Realm,
when the ear-consciousness arises, it is not induced by applied and sustained thought.
Regarding the commentary’s mention of “recording divergent views in a separate excerpt”: this refers to recording the similarities and differences between two masters, as explained in the *Shuyao*.

As for the commentary stating that if the fifth consciousness and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) have distinct objects and [the latter] takes only the *dharmāyatana* as its object, [it would follow that] it could not be associated with [mental factors], because there are not merely one type of dissociated formation (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), but rather hundreds of thousands of millions of types of dissociated formations; thus, the sixth consciousness has distinct objects within the *dharma*-sphere.
Regarding the "pairings": they may take the five types of colored forms as their object, or the twenty-four non-distinctive associations, or the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and so forth.
The sixth consciousness, however, takes different objects than the five sensory consciousnesses.
The Commentary states: "By this, it is known that the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* and other treatises—even those cited as evidence [for the absence of grasping at phenomena]—are based on this.

This concludes the section. Within this commentary, the statement that the mental consciousness arising simultaneously with the five [sensory consciousnesses] is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) follows the position of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*.

In making this commentary, not all [explanations] are fully presented within this sub-commentary. According to the treatise below, the fifth consciousness—the mental consciousness that arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses—is admitted to encompass all three moral natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral).
Although this mental consciousness may sometimes take names, teachings, and so forth as its objects, it is nevertheless subsumed under the category of inference (*anumāna*).
