Alternatively, when a visual object reaches the eye and serves as a condition for visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), it does not preclude mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

At that same time, the visual consciousness is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), whereas the mental consciousness is inference (*anumāna*). When auditory consciousness hears a sutra, it is direct perception;

even if the mental consciousness at that time conceives of a self (*ātman*) as being eternal and omnipresent, it is subsumed under non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Or, when there is an auditory object and auditory consciousness, it is likewise [direct perception].

It is subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If it is accompanied by the arrival of the object, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the five [sensory] consciousnesses arise together, perceiving the same object simultaneously;

this is because the mental consciousness concomitant with the five (*pañcavijñānakāya-sahabhū-manovijñāna*) is necessarily direct perception. Regarding this, various masters hold differing views concerning this cognitive wisdom (*buddhi*), as is detailed in separate notes.
Regarding this, various masters hold differing views: some say that the mental consciousness concomitant with the five [sensory consciousnesses] is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
some say it is inference (*anumāna*); and others say it is non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement that in the stages of the two vehicles and ordinary beings at the eighth ground, the three natures may arise simultaneously within the six consciousnesses:

if one considers bodhisattvas from the eighth ground onward, even within the five sensory consciousnesses there exists the nature of outflowing indeterminate [states], which arise from homogeneous causes of a preceding moment.
These are also termed "natural indeterminate" (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*). As for the sixth consciousness of bodhisattvas from the eighth ground upward...

Within consciousness, it is always uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Within its five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), there are also both wholesome (*kuśala*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) natures;
these two natures arise together, but there is no unwholesome nature. It is the same for those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

For Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, within their sixth consciousness, they constantly give rise to uncontaminated wholesomeness; within their five sensory consciousnesses, they can also give rise to the indeterminate. They likewise all converge upon this. Great!

Maudgalyāyana, even when one enters the untainted goodness (*anāsrava-kuśala*) that has no fixed location, there also arises the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). [Question:
Since your former teacher did not allow for two natures to coexist within the six consciousnesses, this point is now established. [Answer:

It is permitted that two natures coexist in Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and in those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the state beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*). Since it is permitted that two natures coexist, it is known that the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) can coexist within the six consciousnesses.

Is it because they arise? In this commentary, the statement that Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage give rise to the three natures within their six consciousnesses cannot be said to mean that the six consciousnesses of Bodhisattvas above that level can only give rise to two natures; rather, it refers to Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage.
Since the sixth consciousness arises as a defiled mind, it can give rise to minds of the three natures.

Regarding the transformation of the five consciousnesses according to the stages explained by the two aforementioned masters, there are two masters' explanations for the transformation of the five consciousnesses:
some say they are attained in the first bhūmi, while others say they are transformed at the stage of Buddhahood.

Regarding the commentary on the Bodhisattvas who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) among the three vehicles: among the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which of the six consciousnesses arises together with what nature?
If the subsequently attained wisdom is for the sake of maturing sentient beings, the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) it induces is entirely of a virtuous nature.

Since this suffering arises as a derivative of a virtuous nature, by which virtue is it subsumed? It is not subsumed under innate virtue (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*); therefore, since this faculty of suffering is induced by cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), [it is subsumed under that].

This refers to the cultivation of wisdom that accomplishes the roots of goodness. If, as in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), auditory consciousness arises, it is like ordinary auditory consciousness triggered by sound;

such is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). Therefore, one should know that it is induced by subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), as it is pervasive across all indeterminate states.

Furthermore, if the five sensory consciousnesses were present during the causal stage, there would necessarily be no meditative concentration; it is only when the five consciousnesses arise as transformations of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) that concentration exists. It is from this that [the aforementioned] arises.

From the first bhūmi onwards, the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of Bodhisattvas and those of the three vehicles is induced by that [wisdom] and thus encompasses both the nature of the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

As for persons of the two vehicles, their untainted (*anāsrava*) subsequently attained wisdom of the sixth consciousness—the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—is able to induce the divine eye and ear, as well as the indeterminate states resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*) and the wholesome states resulting from supernormal powers. This is just like the case of the subsequently attained wisdom of one beyond training in the two vehicles.

Within the wisdom attained therein, one is also able to give rise to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and so forth. Transforming the five sensory objects (*pañcaviṣaya*) and moving the body through space to come and go are all subsumed under the supernormal power of the basis of psychic power (*ṛddhiviṣayābhijñā*).

As for those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the two vehicles, within the subsequent attainment wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that is untainted (*anāsrava*), they are only able to induce the naturally indeterminate (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*) within the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*). This naturally indeterminate is also termed "equal" (*sama*).
The outflowing indeterminate (*niḥsyanda-avyākṛta*) is itself indeterminate by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*), yet it is not included among the four types of indeterminate states.

This is because there exists a distinct category of indeterminate by nature that is categorized as "indeterminate by way of arising" (*utpatti-avyākṛta*), which is separate from the four types of indeterminate states.

Furthermore, that which arises subsequent to the outflowing [state] does not induce [further states]. Within the five consciousnesses, this refers to the indeterminate state born of maturation (*vipākaja-avyākṛta*). As for the two vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), they do not... [possess it].

The post-attainment wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) that follows from the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) is weak; therefore, within that very post-attainment wisdom, it cannot induce the five consciousnesses, such as those involved in deportment (*īryāpatha*) or craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).
This is because when the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*) abide in a wholesome meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are unable to initiate deportment and so forth.

If, like the followers of the Two Vehicles, one were to separately initiate [such activities]—for instance, by going out to beg for alms—that would constitute the sixth [consciousness] of the follower of the Two Vehicles.

When consciousness enters the neutral mind of the transformative (*nairmāṇika*) or fruition-of-supernormal-power (*abhijñā-phala*) states, it is then able to give rise to transformative minds and so forth.

It is absolutely impossible for one to give rise to the fruition-of-supernormal-power neutral state while remaining within a wholesome meditative absorption (*samādhi*). If, however, one is on the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) may be induced by the Bodhisattva’s subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*);
these five consciousnesses also possess a small portion of innate neutrality (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*). As for that which is untainted (*anāsrava*)...

It attains wisdom and is also capable of inducing the five consciousnesses. Within the five consciousnesses, the majority are of a virtuous nature, because they are induced by the subsequently attained wisdom of the untainted state.
That which is virtuous within these five consciousnesses is the wisdom produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), subsumed under the category of preparatory virtue (*prayoga-kuśala*).

Within that subsequent non-outflow wisdom (*anāsrava-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it does not induce the innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) arising within the five sensory consciousnesses, because those innate wholesome states are obscure and inferior.

Within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of a Bodhisattva, the non-outflow subsequent wisdom can also induce non-outflow states; it gives rise to the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika-citta*) and also has as its object a limited portion [of phenomena].
It also gives rise to the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) by taking craftsmanship as its object, through the sixth consciousness, which is non-outflow.

Within subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one is also able to give rise to the minds of deportment (*iryāpatha*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) among the five sensory consciousnesses.
Therefore, even while a bodhisattva remains in meditative concentration, they can manifest physical deportment such as walking and so forth for the sake of sentient beings.

The aforementioned arising of deportment, craftsmanship, and so on, is exclusively comprised within the nature of the wholesome; it is precisely the wisdom produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) and is a wholesome state of preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśala*).

Regarding their inclusion: the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Those of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) pertain to all three natures.
Those of supernormal power (*nairmāṇika*) pertain to only two natures, namely the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the indeterminate.

Therefore, those [mental factors] arising within the non-outflow subsequent knowledge (*anāsrava-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of a Bodhisattva are all wholesome by nature, as they constitute deportment and craftsmanship. Alternatively, this may be understood through the non-outflow subsequently attained wisdom (*anāsrava-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
It can also induce a small amount of neutral (*avyākṛta*) deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) within the five consciousnesses.
The deportment and craftsmanship thus induced are subsumed under the categories of deportment and craftsmanship themselves.

Furthermore, although the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) state continues constantly within the sixth consciousness of Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, they are likewise able to induce wholesome (*kuśala*) deportment and craftsmanship within the five consciousnesses.

The *kauśalya* (skillful) and *nirmāṇaphala* (fruition of emanation) minds also induce a small amount of neutral (*avyākṛta*) states, such as those of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).

Therefore, the previous commentary states: "In Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above, there is also the neutral within the five sensory consciousnesses," which is the same as what was previously explained.
If it is for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, the supernormal powers (abhijñā-phala) that arise are of a wholesome nature.

If it is for the sake of play or sport, the supernormal powers that arise are of an indeterminate (avyākṛta) nature. For Bodhisattvas from the seventh stage downward, because they still engage in play, their supernormal powers also include the indeterminate nature.
From the eighth stage upward, because there is no play, the supernormal powers that arise are exclusively [wholesome].
This is of a wholesome nature. Therefore, Bodhisattvas also possess uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) deportment, craftsmanship, and so forth. How is this known?
That Bodhisattvas possess uncontaminated craftsmanship is evident, for example, in the images of the Subduer of Māra created by the Bodhisattva Maitreya after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
all such works are produced through the mind of a Bodhisattva’s craftsmanship. Furthermore, within the uncontaminated wisdom of a Bodhisattva on the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), there is also...

It can give rise to [them]. The five consciousnesses are tenfold; they are neutral by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*). They are neutral by nature, nor are they subsumed under the four types of neutral states;
rather, they constitute a distinct category that is neutral by nature. They are neutral by nature, nor are they obtained through the retribution of karma;
they are neutral by nature, just like external mountains and rivers. External mountains, rivers, and so forth are also not [subsumed under] the four [types of neutral states].
It is included within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Why? If among the four types of indeterminate, that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is indeed sentient beings;

as it is categorized under the name "born of maturation," it is the fruit of karma. Since external things such as mountains and rivers are merely dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*) and not fruits of maturation (*vipākaphala*), they are not included within the indeterminate born of maturation. These external mountains, rivers, and so forth are likewise...
It is not due to deportment (*airyāpathika*) or craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*). Deportment and craftsmanship are comprised within the category of sentient beings;
they are produced by the mind of deportment and craftsmanship, as well as by the minds that initiate deportment and craftsmanship.

Therefore, with respect to external objects such as mountains and rivers, it is not due to deportment or craftsmanship. Furthermore, those mountains, rivers, and so forth, are also not transformations (*nirmāṇa*).

This is included within the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). These mountains and rivers are produced by karma; because they are subsumed under the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), their intrinsic nature is indeterminate.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains that there are five kinds of indeterminate phenomena: first, the indeterminate by intrinsic nature (*svabhāvāvyākṛta*).

Regarding that which is indeterminate by intrinsic nature: it refers to external mountains and rivers, as well as the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*), nasal mucus, saliva, and the five sense faculties.
The first part: the nourishment (*puṣṭi*) of the five faculties (*indriya*). All of these are neutral by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*).
Regarding the five faculties, there are two kinds of conditions: first, maturation (*vipāka*), which refers to those obtained through the influence of karma;
such matured five faculties are not termed "neutral by nature. Second, nourishment, which refers to that which is nourished by things such as food and drink. This nourishment...

The cultivation of the five faculties is, by its very nature, indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). These two types of five faculties are neither the substance of deportment (*īryāpatha*), nor the paths of deportment;
they are neither the substance of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), nor the bases of craftsmanship. Why is this?
Because these five faculties are subsumed under the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), whereas deportment, craftsmanship, and so forth, are comprised within the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
Therefore, the two types of five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are neither postures (*airyāpathika*) nor craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).
Furthermore, the subtle particles that support the body (*upastambha-rūpa*) are also neither postures nor craftsmanship. Why is this?

Because those subtle particles supporting the body are nurtured by food and drink, whereas postures and craftsmanship are produced by the very acts of posture and craftsmanship, and furthermore, they depend upon an objective referent (*ālambana*).

Because deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) are objects of the mind, it is known that by giving rise to a mind of deportment, a specific type of informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) is produced, which is then perceived by the visual consciousness. Likewise, by giving rise to a mind of craftsmanship, a specific type of matter such as craftsmanship or sound is produced.
Furthermore, the five sense faculties and the physical supports (*adhiṣṭhāna*) upon the body are neither paths of deportment nor craftsmanship.

As for the bases (*sthāna*): first, by means of generating a mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika-citta*), one separately generates a specific category of mind of craftsmanship; this is called the "basis of craftsmanship" (*śailpasthāna*).
Furthermore, by means of generating a mind of deportment (*airyāpathika-citta*), one separately generates a specific category of the four objects—visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects;

this is called the "course of deportment" (*airyāpathika*). Second is that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*), namely the fruit of karma. Third is deportment (*airyāpathika*), and fourth is craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*). These are the general categories.

Therefore, within the subsequent attainment wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the untainted (*anāsrava*) stage of a Bodhisattva on the ten grounds, that which arises within the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is called "indeterminate by nature" (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*).
This "indeterminate by nature" is not among the four types of indeterminate states.

For example, due to conditions such as the mountains and rivers mentioned previously, sentient beings at the mental level of Bodhisattvas from the seventh ground downward also possess the four types of indeterminate states. As for the Tathāgata...
There are also untainted (*anāsrava*) minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and supernormal fruition (*nairmāṇika*).

If there are retribution bodies (*vipākakāya*) and transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), there are also minds of deportment such as walking and standing. The Buddha of craftsmanship also possesses craftsmanship.

If it is said that the Buddha lacks deportment, does this mean the Buddha lacks walking, standing, and so forth? If the Buddha lacked craftsmanship, would he not be clumsy compared to other ordinary beings?
[The Buddha] arose. The Buddha also possesses majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*), craftsmanship (*śilpa*), and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Question: Since there are five eyes, there should likewise be five kinds of eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Furthermore, regarding the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) mentioned [in the scriptures]:

since there is no internal ear-faculty, within that ear-faculty there should also exist the five kinds of ear-faculties, such as the Buddha’s ear-faculty; and ear-consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) should likewise be of five kinds.
[The same applies] to the other types [of faculties], up to and including the body faculty (*kāyendriya*). Question:

Since the Sūtras state that a Bodhisattva manifests various modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), when a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) is actually entering the eight fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), [how can this be so]?

When entering these contaminated meditative attainments (*sāsrava-samādhi*), as well as when entering the fundamental uncontaminated meditative attainments (*anāsrava-maula-samādhi*), one is also able to take postures (*iryāpatha*) and crafts (*śilpa*) as objects of cognition.
This is because the treatises state that the two types of wisdom—the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*)—arise in practice.

This is mutually contradictory. To say that hearing and reflection are brought into correspondence means that if one speaks of "hearing sound," this occurs within the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*).

However, what is called "wisdom born of hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is not so named because it hears sound; rather, wisdom born of hearing is that which takes the names, phrases, and syllables of the teachings as its cognitive object (*ālambana*).
Therefore, wisdom born of hearing exists only within the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and not in the ear-...

Regarding "consciousness and so forth," this refers to the absence of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), because the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) is unable to take phrases and syllables as its objects.

The *Śū* (the Sub-commentary) states that what was cited there also applies to that which is accomplished [by the wisdoms], because within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), there may be the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation;

consequently, the five consciousnesses are also designated as being accomplished by the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Among these accomplishments, they pertain to all five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

If non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and so forth are all induced by the three types of wisdom—listening, reflection, and cultivation—and have already been attained and established as such, do they receive the name "accomplished through cultivation"?

If within the mental consciousness one enters the wisdom of cultivation, the goodness induced therein within the five sensory consciousnesses—the phrase "goodness within the five sensory consciousnesses"—is designated as being subsumed under what is accomplished through cultivation.
As for other ordinary beings who employ the wisdoms of listening and reflection, their minds...
The prātimokṣa precepts received therein are also called those produced by hearing and reflection (*śruta-maya* and *cintā-maya*).

Later, when one wishes to give rise to wrong views and sever the roots of goodness, at the moment of the preparatory mind for those wrong views, one immediately relinquishes the prātimokṣa precepts obtained within that state of hearing and reflection.
If, however, one receives the prātimokṣa precepts within a state of innate goodness (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*), [they are not lost in the same way].
Liberation and the prātimokṣa are also subsumed under innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*).
Later, when wrong views arise, one immediately gives rise to this grade of wrong views, which then severs these nine grades of innate prātimokṣa.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The wisdom of accomplished action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) is itself cultivation (*bhāvanā*): this is because the wisdom of accomplished action consists solely of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), and lacks the wisdoms of hearing (*śruta-mayī*) and reflection (*cintā-mayī*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “All these arise by being induced according to intention, up to the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*): if it refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arising as a part [of that process]...

Separate afflictions also induce the afflictions of discrimination within the five consciousnesses. If the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) gives rise to innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), it also induces the innate afflictions arising within the five consciousnesses.
If the mental consciousness gives rise to unwholesome discriminative [afflictions] that project karma, it also induces the five consciousnesses;
since there are thus discriminative afflictions, these are abandoned by penetrating the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). If the mental consciousness...

In the intermediate state, there arises the wholesome [state] acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*). This also induces the five consciousnesses; furthermore, both the wholesome acquired at birth and the cultivated wholesome (*prāyogika*) take these as objects.

As for the statement in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* that "the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the desire realm extends even to the obscured-unwholesome nature," this refers, for the time being, to the mental consciousness.
Deep darkness gives rise to craving; this consists of nine types, as they arise simultaneously with the end of life. Thus, it is of an obscured nature (*nivṛta*).

Others, such as bhikṣus who maintain the precepts or practitioners who cultivate the path, for the most part constantly give rise to wholesome minds. Even if they do not attain awakening, [their state is different].
Once delusion has given rise to greed, ignorance, pride, and so forth, one immediately gives rise to shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*) and repents one's transgression.

Because these afflictions are suppressed by shame and remorse, the afflictions that have arisen cannot incite karma, nor do they constitute an unwholesome nature; they are merely designated as being subsumed under the category of "obscured-neutral" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Regarding the statement that "the conditions for non-transformative marks are subsumed under the four types of transformation":
if the five consciousnesses possess only the supernormal fruit (abhijñā-phala), they actually lack transformation, as transformation exists only within the sixth consciousness.
Because the supernormal fruit resembles transformation, one metaphorically says that the five consciousnesses possess transformation; however, the five consciousnesses actually lack transformation.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that the five consciousnesses, though taking postures (*īryāpatha*) and craftsmanship (*śilpa*) as their objects, cannot produce postures or craftsmanship:

the five consciousnesses take postures and craftsmanship as their objects as previously explained. The present statement that the five consciousnesses cannot produce postures or craftsmanship means that the five consciousnesses are incapable of acting as the remote cause (*dūre-samutthāna*) for the production of postures and craftsmanship.
Furthermore, the five consciousnesses are also capable of [acting as] the momentary cause (*tatkṣaṇa-samutthāna*).
"Arising" refers to the arising of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*). These [two], deportment and craftsmanship, encompass all three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

If they are born of maturation (*vipākaja*), they are exclusively of the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). If they are attained through supernormal powers (*nairmāṇika*), they encompass two natures: namely, the indeterminate and the wholesome (*kuśala*) natures. Question:
Why does this text state that the five consciousnesses take deportment and craftsmanship as their objects? Why does the commentary immediately below state, "Furthermore, the four..."?

"Consciousness conditions deportment and craftsmanship. This response to the question serves as a general heading; therefore, it says, "The five consciousnesses condition the mind of deportment and so forth.
The subsequent text provides a detailed explanation, specifically stating that "the four consciousnesses condition deportment."

The commentary stating, "It is not the five consciousnesses; it truly belongs to the realm of birth (upapatti-bhūmi-saṃgṛhīta)," based on what is similar within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), is an inconvenient reading of the text.
It should rather be: "It is indeed a transformation (*nirmāṇa*); it does not exist in the five consciousnesses, but truly exists within the mental consciousness.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "it is not bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-saṃgṛhīta*), but truly belongs to the higher realms," this is because the transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) of the higher realms is immediately followed by that of the desire realm, and is thus so designated.

Regarding "transformations of the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-nirmāṇa*): since these transformations actually belong to the higher realms, the Commentary (*Śāstra*) states that they are called "transformations of the desire realm" because the objects transformed resemble those of the desire realm;

or, because the objects transformed appear as if within the desire realm, they are termed "desire realm. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that in the Mahāyāna, the mind itself is capable of transformation. It is the mental consciousness (*citta*) that undergoes transformation.
Regarding the transformed object: it follows the consciousness that performs the transformation and is thus bound to the higher realms.

For sentient beings of the desire realm, the eighth consciousness takes the transformed objects of those higher realms as its substantial basis and subsequently transforms them into a visual object. This transformed object within the desire realm is itself bound to the desire realm.
Regarding the statement that "the transformation produced by birth (*upapatti-labdha-nirmāṇa*) is comprised solely within the *vipāka-citta*":
this refers to cases such as the dragon kings and spirits of the desire realm, all of whom are able to produce transformations through birth.

For instance, when dragons and others produce transformations through birth in the sky to cause rain or other phenomena below, if that transformation produced by birth is virtuous, it is subsumed under the wholesome; if it is a transformation produced by an unwholesome mind, it is unwholesome.
If a transformation produced by an indeterminate mind is categorized as being born of maturation (*vipākaja*), it actually pertains to all three moral natures;

however, when it is specifically termed "indeterminate," it is included within that which is born of maturation. Furthermore, the lower heavens of the desire realm also possess transformations acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*).
Moreover, among the various devas of the desire realm, there are those who do not exercise supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) but rely solely on the power of transformations acquired at birth.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that the form realm lacks craftsmanship and the like: since there is no construction of houses and such in the form realm, it therefore lacks craftsmanship.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that the formless realm further lacks deportment: since there is no body in the formless realm, it therefore lacks deportment.

It is *īryāpatha* (posture/gait). The *Śāstra* states: "The four consciousnesses take *īryāpatha* as their object; the five [sensory] consciousnesses take *śailpasthānika* (artistic/craft) as their object. If it were not so, they would be subsumed under *vipākaja* (born of maturation). The commentary explains:
"Visual consciousness can take the substance of *īryāpatha* as its object, as well as the paths of *īryāpatha*. Auditory consciousness, however, cannot take either."

This refers to deportment (*iryāpatha*). As for the three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body, they can also take deportment as their object, but cannot take the substance of deportment as their object.
As for the two consciousnesses of eye and ear, they can take the substance of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) as their object, and also take the locus of craftsmanship as their object.

As for the three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body, they can only take the locus of craftsmanship as their object, but cannot take the substance of craftsmanship as their object. Both Mahayana and Hinayana agree on this point.

This was already explained in the previous excerpt: if something is not included within the categories of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), it is then subsumed under that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Now, whether in terms of their objects or their arousal, both are termed "deportment-minds" (*airyāpathika-citta*); the same applies to craftsmanship and the rest.
The Commentary states that [this] differs from the Hīnayāna in its classification of the "mind of deportment" (*airyāpathika-citta*).

While the term "mind of deportment" is broad and the "mind born of maturation" (*vipākaja-citta*) is narrow, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, among the neutral (*avyākṛta*) minds, the other three are narrow while the mind of deportment is broad.

That which is not included among the other three types of neutral states is subsumed under the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*). Furthermore, there is a distinct category established as "deportment-like.
For instance, in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the gods of the upper three dhyānas borrow the three consciousnesses—visual, auditory, and tactile—from the first dhyāna.

This mind of borrowed consciousness from a different level is not the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) among the four neutral states, for there is no such thing [of craftsmanship] in the realm of form.

Because they are produced by craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), they are not comprised within that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*). This is because that school maintains that a mind born of maturation does not allow for arising in a different level (*bhūmi*);
thus, these visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses of a different level are comprised within the category of the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and are termed "of the deportment class.
If, according to the Mahāyāna, one borrows the three consciousnesses of the first dhyāna from a different level while in the upper three levels, these three consciousnesses of a different level—

Consciousness is comprised solely within that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*). Furthermore, in the three higher dhyānas, one borrows the three consciousnesses—eye, ear, and body—from the lower first dhyāna.

These eye, ear, and body consciousnesses are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) and are thus comprised within that which is born of maturation. In the Mahāyāna, "born of maturation" is a broad category;
those other three types of indeterminate states not included [in the specific categories] are all comprised within that which is born of maturation. If this is so, as for the mind...
Regarding the statement that "the universal [factors] should be called mental concomitants (*caitta*)," the intent of this question is as follows:

Since the mind-king (*cittarāja*) also arises by being alerted through attention (*manasikāra*), and furthermore, since the mind-king only arises through the conjunction of contact (*sparśa*), it would follow that the mind-king depends upon the mental concomitants.
If the mind-king depends upon the mental concomitants, then the mind-king itself should be designated as a mental concomitant.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation: "The mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is not called 'the object' (*vastu*), because it does not belong to the mind.

This passage provides a second interpretation, which itself contains a third interpretation. In that third interpretation, it says: "That which is bound to the mind" correctly explains the meaning of mental factors (*caitta*).
Now, in this second interpretation, it says: "That which is not bound to the mind" means that the mind-king is not called an object, as it is not [bound to] the mind.
Because of the mind.

Although the *shu* (commentary) prescribes two types of seals, it specifically designates the *xian-cheng* (prefectural vice-president) as the seal for the second rank. This is because the *xian-cheng* is the official prescribed for the second rank.

As for the *xian-wei* (prefectural commandant) and others, they are not called seals of the third rank; this is because, as seen on the official tally (*fu*), they possess only the image [of the seal].

The military unit consists of two men and no more. The County Magistrate (*xianling*) represents the mind-king (*cittarāja*); the County Vice-Magistrate (*xiancheng*) represents the mental factor of attention (*manasikāra*).

Furthermore, it also represents the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the mind-king, as well as the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all other mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).

The County Commandant (*xianwei*) represents the remaining mental factors that grasp specific characteristics. Question: Since the analogies for sensation (*vedanā*) and contact (*sparśa*) only grasp specific characteristics, they may be considered equivalent to the County Commandant.
One knows distinct objects and uses them as metaphors for the other mental factors, such as contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*).

These other mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*) are likewise able to grasp the general characteristics of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), yet they also possess their own apprehension of specific characteristics. How can one use the example of the district magistrate (*xianwei*) to illustrate this?

Since these other mental factors are already able to grasp general characteristics—just as the aforementioned district vice-magistrate (*xiancheng*) grasps both general and specific characteristics—what difference is there between them and feeling, which is capable of cognizing this "grasping" (*parigraha*) and so forth?

"Regarding this: the term 'appropriation' (*parigraha*) is a synonym for 'reception' (*anubhava*). As for the statement that 'this attention (*manasikāra*) regarding the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object can also cognize it,' the question is:

if it is now said that attention can cognize the specific characteristics of the object, then when attention takes up the specific characteristics of the other fifty mental factors (*caitasika*), does the attention act in the same way as those other mental factors?"

The distinct characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object-conditioned [mind] is precisely what is called the distinct characteristic of the other fifty mental factors (*caitasika*) conditioned by that attention (*manasikāra*).

If one says that the distinct characteristic of the [object-]conditioned is what takes the distinct characteristics of the fifty mental factors as its object, then [this would apply to] the remaining factors such as contact (*sparśa*), and so forth.

When the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is perceived as the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) [of one mental factor], contact (*sparśa*) should likewise be called the specific characteristic of the other fifty mental factors.

Furthermore, when attention (*manasikāra*) takes the aspect-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the other fifty mental factors as its object-condition, it is called "attention grasping the specific characteristics of the other mental factors."

It is said that attention (*manasikāra*) carries the aspects (*ākāra*) of other mental factors (*caitasika*), such as the aspect of being agreeable and so forth, or the act of experiencing (*anubhava*) and so forth.
Thus, it is stated that the cause for the name "attention" is its grasping the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of other mental factors.
If attention were to carry the aspects of other mental factors, what further need would there be for those other mental factors? For attention itself would already possess all aspects.
The nature of the mental factor of attention (*manasikāra*) is that which performs the function [of directing the mind]; it is capable of both experiencing [objects] and initiating [mental activity].

To say that other mental factors would be useless is to imply that even the grasping of the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*) by other mental factors should be questioned in the same manner. The phrase "as explained below" refers back to the preceding word "this" (*idam*).

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (Commentary), "This term [in the sūtra] indicates the grasping of the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*)," the word "this" (*idam*) in the treatise refers to what was previously understood as "this is the general characteristic of this mind-king.

That is to say, within this very treatise, it is stated that contact (*sparśa*) which is capable of cognizing "this" possesses a contact of general characteristics, because it is capable of cognizing the general characteristic of this mind-king.
As for "the characteristics such as being agreeable," these are precisely those things cognized by contact.

This refers to the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the statement in the treatise that "feeling (*vedanā*) can cognize this and that," this refers to the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of mental factors (*caitta*), because feeling can cognize the general characteristic of the mind-king (*cittarāja*).
Regarding the phrase "it apprehends such characteristics as feeling," this refers to the specific characteristic of feeling itself, because feeling can cognize its own specific characteristic.

The same applies to all other mental factors (*caitta*). Up to and including the remaining fifty-one mental factors, they all take the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*) as their object.

That is to say, while each mental factor possesses its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and distinct characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), they are all able to take the general characteristic of the sovereign mind as their object. Each mental factor has its own distinct characteristic;
this should likewise be stated for the five object-specific factors (*viṣaya-pratiniyata-ālambana*), such that desire (*chanda*) is able to apprehend what is desirable.

Regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*): resolve (*adhimokṣa*) understands these as determined characteristics; mindfulness (*smṛti*) understands these as characteristics resulting from habitual cultivation;

concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) understand these as characteristics such as gain and loss, and so forth. Furthermore, within the eleven wholesome mental factors, one should likewise say that faith (*śraddhā*) understands these as having the characteristic of mental purity;
shame (*hrī*) understands these as the characteristic of being noble and virtuous; and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) understands these as the characteristic of being evil, and so forth.

Up to the root afflictions such as greed (*rāga*), which are able to cognize the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of this defiled attachment and so forth— and since the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are subsumed under the [root] fetters—

all fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*) are able to cognize the general characteristic of the mind-king (*cittarāja*), while each individually takes the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the mental factors as its object.

Only attention (*manaskāra*), although it takes the general characteristic of the mind-king as its object, shares the same substantial entity (*ekadravya*) with the other mental factors in its objective apprehension.

Mental attention (manasikāra) has no distinct characteristic of its own, yet it takes that [characteristic] as its object; thus, the distinct characteristics of the other fifty-one mental factors constitute the distinct characteristic of mental attention.
However, when mental attention apprehends the general characteristic of the sovereign mind-king (citta-rāja), [it does so in this manner].

The momentum is immediately understood. The characteristic of being agreeable upon contact and so forth, and the characteristic of equanimity upon feeling and so forth, are precisely the distinct characteristics of the other mental factors (caitta).

Taking these as the distinct characteristic of attention (manasikāra), this applies even up to the distinct characteristics of all fifty-one mental factors, which constitute the distinct characteristic of attention.

The treatise states: "Desire (*chanda*) is also able to cognize objects that are desirable," and so on, up to "even concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) lack such characteristics as gain or loss.
This concludes the discussion of the text. Regarding the word "also" (*api*) used within the context of the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣaya-niyata-kausalika-citta-dharma*):

it indicates that desire also possesses the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*). By including the character "also," it is meant that desire is able to cognize the general characteristic of the mind-king; desire also [cognizes] itself.

The specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the objects of desire that are to be enjoyed, and so forth, up to the point where concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) can discern the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the preceding mind-king (*citta-rāja*).

Furthermore, that concentration and wisdom are also able to discern the specific characteristics of their own attainment or non-attainment of concentration and wisdom. The "distinctive characteristics" (*visabhāga-lakṣaṇa*) of the mental factors (*caitasika*) are called "distinctive characteristics" because they are distinct [from the mind].
This refers to the specific characteristics of the mental factors.

The commentary [states] "fifty-three" and "fifty-five"; the numbers differ because of the opening and closing of the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*) and the inclusion or exclusion of wrong desire (*mithyā-chanda*) and wrong resolve (*mithyā-adhimokṣa*).
This concludes the discussion on how the texts at two points in the *Yogācārabhūmi* differ: in one passage, the five views are opened out while wrong desire and wrong resolve are combined;
thus, there are fifty-five mental factors (*caitasika*). In another passage, wrong desire and wrong resolve are opened out while the five views are combined.
There are fifty-three mental factors (*caitta*) in total. If the five views (*dṛṣṭi*) are combined [into one], there are fifty-one mental factors.
Although these three textual accounts differ, the version taking fifty-one mental factors is correct.

Regarding the statement that five specific mental factors (*pañca-viniyata*) may arise with respect to four objects: the "four objects" refer to the object of pleasure, the determined object, the previously experienced object, and the object of recorded names; these are termed the "four objects."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The term ‘equal outflow’ (niṣyanda) refers to that which is induced by a similar type; it does not mean an equal outflow in the sense of preceding and succeeding moments,” this passage serves to distinguish it from the aforementioned fruit of equal outflow.
This latter fruit arises exclusively at different times, sequentially: that is, a similar-type cause in a prior moment induces an equal-outflow fruit in a subsequent moment.
This is just as was stated previously regarding seeds, where members of the same category produce one another in succession. It is like the analogy of a lamp.
Does the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) produce a result of similar outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*)?

Now, these twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are provisionally established upon the states (*avasthā*) of the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*); because they resemble the root afflictions, they are called "results of similar outflow.
These secondary afflictions may arise in the same moment as the root afflictions, or they may arise before or after them. This is not restricted by...
The preceding similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) draws forth a subsequent outflowing fruit (niṣyanda-phala); because the preceding and succeeding moments draw each other forth, it is called "outflowing.

Regarding the statement that they "coexist at all times," this reveals their universal nature (sarvatraga), for they always arise together at all times and are associated with the afflictions (kleśa).

Regarding "or both": the five subtle [faculties] arise together. As for "time," it means that as soon as the mind arises, they exist; thus, the two are distinct. Regarding the term "time": it may mean that all minds possess them;
or that they have no beginning and are not comparable; or that they take everything as their object.
To explain "all times" in general terms: there are three kinds. The first refers to all moments when the mind exists.
First, its arising; second, its uninterruptedness from beginningless time. Regarding "uninterruptedness from beginningless time": it means that at the very moment the mind arises, it arises [again];

it is not merely that it has been continuously succeeding one another since beginningless time—this is what is called "uninterruptedness from beginningless time. Third, it refers to the time when it takes all objects as its conditions.

It arises immediately; therefore, it is said to exist "at all times. It does not take all objects as its conditions, nor is it a continuous succession, because there is no [ordinary] mind [to be absent].

Thus, regarding the term "time," these three questions above are the reversals of the three factors explained previously. That is to say, they reverse the previous statement that "all minds" possess this [nature];
by reversing that, it is called "the non-existence of mind" which is actually "existence. By reversing the previous statement of being "uninterrupted from beginningless time," this question is posed.
It is also not a continuity; that is to say, it reverses the previous [position] by taking all objects as its domain. This very question then asks: "Does it not take all objects as its domain?

According to the Commentary (*Śāstra*), if it is as stated in the first case, it refers to the majority; alternatively, if one adds the practitioner, it is as in the previous case where the nine stages are called "all."
Regarding "ground" (*bhūmi*): it refers to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) prior to the dhyāna of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because it is there that "pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*) is so designated.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The meaning of what is not present here should be carefully distinguished": since *mada* (intoxication/arrogance) also extends throughout the three realms, [the distinctions are as follows]:

if one sees with the eye, it is called "seeing" (*darśana*); if one hears, it is called "hearing" (*śravaṇa*); that which is termed "cognition" (*jñāna*) refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); and that which is termed "perception" (*vijñapti*) refers to the three [faculties] of nose, tongue, and body.
"Discernment" (saṃjñā) is that which can discern matters such as suffering and pleasure. If one considers the Mahāyāna perspective, it is understood in the same way as the Hīnayāna:

namely, the three discernments of nose, tongue, and body. This refers to discernment within the sixth consciousness; it is not a discernment distinct from the mind of thought (*manovijñāna*). This is a secondary point. Regarding the statement "because they are superior, give rise [to sensation], and are even called 'feeling' (vedanā), they are pervasive":
if one were to say that the five faculties of feeling (*pañca-vedanendriya*) themselves constitute [discernment], then the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) would not [be included].

It subsumes the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*). The faculty of sorrow corresponds to the sixth consciousness. The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) resides in the five sensory consciousnesses.

If one says that the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) does not subsume the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), it is because the faculty of pleasure extends across all five sensory consciousnesses, whereas the faculty of joy exists only in the sixth consciousness; therefore, they are designated as distinct faculties.
If one speaks of the three feelings (*vedanā*), the scope is broader: that is to say, the feeling of pleasure subsumes the feeling of joy. If one speaks of sorrow...
Since feeling (vedanā) includes painful feeling (duḥkhavedanā), it is said that feeling is "pervasive" (sāmānya).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The basis for the accumulation of form and the basis for the accumulation of the formless are distinct; thus, they are called ‘distinct bases of the body’,” that treatise asks:

“What is meant by ‘bodily feeling’? It is so called because it is the basis for the accumulation of form. This refers to the sense-faculties (indriya) which are formed by the accumulation of many subtle atoms (paramāṇu) of matter.

Feeling (*vedanā*) is the dependent (*āśrita*), while the five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) are its support (*āśraya*). Because the five faculties are the locus of feeling, it is called "bodily feeling" (*kāyikī vedanā*).

What is meant by "mental feeling" (*cittikī vedanā*)? It is so called because it collects upon a non-material support. Since the substance of the mind (*citta*) is not a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*), it is said to be "non-material" (*arūpa*).

At the same time as the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*), there are numerous factors such as attention (*manasikāra*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*); therefore, it is said to "collect."

Furthermore, these very minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are the basis (*āśraya*), while sensation (*vedanā*) is that which depends upon them (*āśrita*). Because the physical sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) differ in character, they are termed "bodily sensation" (*kāyikī vedanā*);

because the mental organ (*manas-indriya*) differs in character, it is termed "mental sensation" (*caitasikī vedanā*). Regarding the phrase "depending separately on the body," this means that each of the sensations and so forth depends individually on the five physical sense organs;
or, the seventh consciousness is called "depending separately on the mental organ"; or, the eighth consciousness pertains to both the defiled and the pure.

The general basis is the five material sense-faculties; these are the specific bases. Question: The *Abhidharmakośa* states that the basis for the collection of matter is called "bodily sensation" (*kāyikī-vedanā*).
This implies that a body is formed by the aggregation of numerous atoms, and thus it is termed a "collection.

This contradicts what was stated previously in the first treatise, which explains that in the Mahāyāna, when the various consciousnesses undergo transformation, they manifest instantaneously as a single image according to its size, whether large or small.
It is not that a multitude of distinct atoms undergo transformation to combine and form a single entity. How then does that treatise speak of the body being formed by the aggregation of atoms?
Answer: It speaks of it as a conventional designation (prajñapti).

The Commentary (Śāstra) states: "The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha*) are both capable of [arising]... even up to being all-pervasive and including the untainted (*anāsrava*).

This passage from the current commentary explains the "suffering sensation" (*duḥkhavedanā*) mentioned in the main treatise (*śāstra*), as it likewise arises as untainted. There are two interpretations of this text; this is the first interpretation.
If one were to say that the five faculties [are meant], the scope would be too narrow; if one refers to the faculty of suffering alone, it would not include the faculty of sorrow.
If the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) does not include the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), then the faculties would be narrow.
If one says that the three feelings (*vedanā*) are broad, then within suffering (*duḥkha*) the feeling of grief (*daurmanasya*) is included, and within joy the feeling of pleasure is included.

Now, in this treatise, it is even stated that the feeling of suffering also arises from the untainted (*anāsrava*). Since it is called the "feeling of suffering," it includes the feeling of grief; thus, both the feelings of grief and suffering are common to the untainted.
If it is said that both the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha*) can induce the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), this statement is general in nature.
One should rather say that the faculty of sorrow can induce the outflow-free, because the faculty of suffering is itself induced by the outflow-free.

Regarding the statement that "feeling (*vedanā*) is broad while the faculties (*indriya*) are narrow": if one speaks merely of "pleasant feeling," it encompasses both the faculty of joy (*saumanasya-indriya*);

if one speaks merely of "painful feeling," it encompasses both the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya-indriya*). This is because "feeling" is a general term. However, if one speaks of the "faculty of pain," it does not encompass the faculty of grief;

and if one speaks merely of the "faculty of pleasure," it does not encompass the faculty of joy. This is because the meaning of "faculty" is narrower in scope. In this context of the general [classification], the term "faculty" does not refer to that which gives rise [to sensation].

Regarding the meaning [of "faculty" (*indriya*)]. Furthermore, there is another interpretation: the meaning of "faculty" is explained solely in terms of the sense of "illuminating with clarity" and the sense of "predominance.

This is the second interpretation. The intent here is that although the treatise mentions only "painful sensation" (*duḥkhavedanā*), it is because this too arises from the untainted (*anāsrava*). Thus, one should know that within the treatise, it refers only to suffering.
This is explained in terms of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*). In this treatise, it is not explained in terms of the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*). Why is this?

If the faculty of suffering were universally applicable, it would be present in all bodies, including those of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). However, if the faculty of grief were universally applicable, it would apply to those in training (*śaikṣa*) but would not be present in the bodies of those beyond training.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "the faculty of suffering exists because it is induced by the sixth consciousness free from outflows (*anāsrava*), up to [because of] diligence and so forth," and specifically the phrase "because it is induced by the sixth [consciousness] free from outflows":
this text here encompasses both the outflow-free [minds] of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) as well as those of Bodhisattvas and others.
It means that by means of the outflow-free [state] within the sixth consciousness, one gives rise to painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*). This is just as Mahāmaudgalyāyana attained [it].

Having completed the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), he then used his eye of the Path (*mārgacakṣus*) to survey the world. He saw that his mother had been reborn among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).

... [and so on] ... Maudgalyāyana cried out and hurried back to inform the Buddha. Since it was stated that this was known through clear knowledge (*vidyā*), it must have been induced by untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*).

However, this does not constitute the feeling of sorrow (*daurmanasya*), because the feeling of sorrow has already been abandoned through the relinquishing of desire (*vairāgya*). Alternatively, it may only arise within the scope of subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "the five consciousnesses, etc.," this passage refers exclusively to Bodhisattvas and not to those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). This is because the two vehicles lack subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Thus, it concludes that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, when the untainted sixth consciousness gives rise to subsequently attained wisdom, the Bodhisattva enters the fires of hell for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
Once the fire has already pressed against their bodies, the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) arises. If the Bodhi...

The Bodhisattva’s mind gives rise to weary detachment (*nirveda*), and he immediately becomes free from that suffering. Or, within the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), there may be the suffering of fatigue due to diligence;

all such instances are induced by the untainted (*anāsrava*). These are not considered here as fetters (*saṃyojana*). This applies even to cases such as manifesting in the body of a fish and experiencing the suffering of being taken for its flesh.

A Bodhisattva on the bhūmis manifests in the body of a fish because they are free from suffering; whereas although a Bodhisattva prior to the bhūmis may also manifest as a fish, this is not induced by untainted (anāsrava) karma.

The commentary clarifies the gateway of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*). Regarding this statement, it means that within the gateway of the tainted and untainted in that *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, these very points are clarified.

The commentary states: "Dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*) is not non-outflow (*anāsrava*), because although it can serve as a preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the non-outflow, it does not even arise simultaneously with it.

This means that if the faculty of dissatisfaction were to induce the non-outflow, it would still not arise simultaneously with the non-outflow; nor does the non-outflow induce the faculty of dissatisfaction.

However, the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha*) may indeed arise simultaneously with the non-outflow, such as in the case of Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward during their sixth [consciousness].
Within the consciousnesses, they constantly give rise to the outflow-free (anāsrava). For the sake of transforming sentient beings, they may even enter into fire.

Because these Bodhisattvas also give rise to painful sensations within the five consciousnesses, even though the sixth consciousness enters meditative absorptions of joy and bliss, it is accompanied by the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) through the five consciousnesses;
thus, it arises either before or after the outflow-free state. This is just as it is with the five consciousnesses prior to the seventh stage.

Within these [categories], there is also the experience of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*). Alternatively, an untainted state (*anāsrava*) may arise in a preceding moment, which then induces suffering in a subsequent moment.

In the Mahāyāna, the faculty of "knowing the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is the most extensive; it comprises the fifteen moments of mind prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), as well as the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*).
These two stages prior to the path are also designated as the essence of the faculty of "knowing the unknown," because they are conducive to the untainted state.

Because it is a phenomenon (*dharma*), it is conventionally designated as "untainted" (*anāsrava*). Taking the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) as the substance of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), if there is a substance of investigation (*vitarka*), it is included.

This includes all conditioned untainted phenomena (*saṃskṛtānāsravadharma*) and tainted preparatory wholesome states (*sāsravaprayogakuśala*), with the exception of innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhakuśala*) and factors such as sleep (*middha*) within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Since all these are termed "in training" (*śaikṣa*) or "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*), it is the most extensive [category]. Question: For what reason is it called "untainted"?

Regarding "training" (*śaikṣa*): wholesome states acquired within the body of one in training are subsumed under both training and beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*). Likewise, sleep occurring within the body of one beyond training is subsumed under both training and beyond-training.

Furthermore, because the morality associated with the path (*mārga-saṃvara*), the morality of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*), and the morality of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*) all pertain to both training and beyond-training, [the state of being] "not-yet" [perfected]—according to the Sarvāstivāda—is reckoned as referring only to the fifteen moments of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

One should know the essence of the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*). If there is a person in training (*śaikṣa*), the untainted conditioned factors within their continuum are called the essence of one in training.
Furthermore, taking the untainted conditioned factors within the continuum of a person beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) constitutes the essence of one beyond training.

Regarding the essences of those in training and those beyond training, these consist of twenty-nine dharmas: namely, the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the five object-specific factors (*viśeṣabhūmika*), and the ten wholesome universal factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*).

Excluding the roots of goodness that are "without doubt," as well as unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), the two—vitarka and vicāra—and the four characteristics of acquisition, arising, and so forth, together with the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), these constitute twenty-nine dharmas.
This is because they constitute the essence of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).

All contaminated wholesome dharmas and so forth existing within the bodies of those who are learners or non-learners are subsumed under the category of "neither learner nor non-learner. These are the contaminated [dharmas].
"Good. It is not the untainted conditioned phenomena within the person of one in training (*śaikṣa*); therefore, it is called 'neither-in-training' (*na-śaikṣa*).
It is not the untainted conditioned phenomena within the person of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); therefore, it is said to be 'not included among those beyond training.

Furthermore, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are also included among those neither-in-training nor beyond-training. This also includes the wholesome states conducive to birth and death, such as the merit of humans and devas."

All are categorized as being neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*). If it refers to the morality associated with the Path (*mārgasamvara*), it applies to both learners (*śaikṣa*) and non-learners (*aśaikṣa*).
However, the Prātimokṣa morality and the morality associated with meditative concentration (*samādhisamvara*) do not apply to both learners and non-learners.

This is because the morality associated with meditative concentration and the Prātimokṣa morality are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*); thus, the Hīnayāna perspective is narrow. Now, when it says "neither-learner-nor-non-learner," [it refers to this].
This is neither training (*śaikṣa*) nor beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); it is called "neither-training-nor-beyond-training.

It is just as the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is neither suffering nor pleasure, yet is named the "feeling of equanimity. According to the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), this is because mental grief (*daurmanasya*) and physical pain (*duḥkha*) do not extend to those beyond training.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "a portion is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and a portion is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)," this refers to the seven material faculties (*rūpīndriya*), the five feeling faculties (*vedanendriya*), the mind faculty (*manas-indriya*), and the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
In this present commentary, it is stated in general terms; strictly speaking, one should say: "the five feeling faculties and the mind faculty."

They pertain to all three types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*). If they arise together with discriminative afflictions (*vikalpita-kleśa*), their mental faculty is abandoned by its own nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*), which means it pertains to abandonment through seeing (*darśana-heya*).

If the five feelings arise together with innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), they are also abandoned by their own nature, and they also pertain to abandonment through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

If the five feelings and the mental faculty are of a wholesome or neutral nature, they also pertain to abandonment through the severance of objective fetters (*ālambana-bandhana-prahāṇa*). That is to say:
They are abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). If they were to include the untainted (*anāsrava*), they would not be subject to abandonment;

that is, the three—joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—actually do include the untainted. This is as follows: within the third dhyāna there is untainted bliss, and within the first and second dhyānas there is said to be no joy.

The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) both pertain to both types of abandonment. If the faculties of mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and physical pain (*duḥkha*) are called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*), they are merely nominally outflow-free.

As for the five material faculties, the two sexual faculties, and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), these also pertain to both types of abandonment. Furthermore, once one has entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and beyond, the non-arising of the three evil destinies and so forth is also a form of non-arising;

this subsequently pertains to both abandonment by seeing and abandonment by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*). As for indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas, they pertain to both objects of cognition and bondage.

Abandonment. This applies to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). As for the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), as well as the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), if they are impure wholesome dharmas (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*), they are also abandoned by way of the bondage of conditions; thus, they are generally abandoned through cultivation.

As for the five faculties beginning with faith, as well as the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," if they are impure wholesome dharmas, they are also abandoned by way of the bondage of conditions; thus, they are generally abandoned through cultivation. The five faculties beginning with faith... [repeated].

The faculties (*indriya*), as well as the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), are untainted (*anāsrava*) and are also included within that which is not to be abandoned (*aheya*).

Regarding the statement in the commentary that the seven material faculties and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) are included among those abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) because they are categorized by way of non-arising: if this refers to the Mahāyāna, [it is as follows].

Thus, there are three types of abandonment: first, non-abandonment, which pertains exclusively to what is abandoned through the path of seeing; second, abandonment by way of conditions and fetters, which pertains exclusively to what is abandoned through the path of cultivation;
and third, abandonment by way of intrinsic nature, referring to afflictions and the like, which applies to both what is abandoned through seeing and what is abandoned through cultivation.

In the Hīnayāna, there are only two types of abandonment: abandonment by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*) and abandonment by the severance of conditions (*ālambana-bandhana-prahāṇa*), which is to say, non-arising abandonment (*anutpāda-prahāṇa*).

For example, once one has entered the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one abandons the bodies of the three evil destinies, the bodies of eunuchs and women, those born from eggs or moisture, as well as the bodies of those in Uttarakuru and the long-lived heavens. Having attained the Path of Seeing, one will never again be reborn in such states.

Because they are not produced through rebirth: once one has entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*), the male and female faculties, and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) can no longer arise within the three miserable destinies (*durgati*), among eunuchs, or in female bodies.

Since these are abandoned by being rendered incapable of arising (*anutpāda-prahāṇa*), it is said that the seven material faculties and so forth are abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*). However, from the perspective of their separation from bondage (*bandhana-vigama*), they are also abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Thus, the seven...
The material faculties, the life-faculty, and so forth, pertain exclusively to what is abandoned by insight and what is abandoned by cultivation; they do not pertain to what is not to be abandoned.

Now it is said that the five faculties, the male faculty, the life-faculty, and so forth, do not pertain to what is not to be abandoned. Now it is said that the five faculties, the male faculty, the life-faculty, and so forth.
Regarding the statement that they do not pertain to what is non-abandonable (*aheya*): this refers specifically to the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) and the bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

That is to say, within the bodies of those of the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas of the ten stages, the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*);

because they do not extend to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), the five material sense organs (*pañcarūpendriya*) and so forth do not pertain to what is non-abandonable. If, however, one speaks in reference to the body of a Buddha, it is the five material sense organs [that are meant].
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) also pertain to the untainted (*anāsrava*) and are not to be abandoned (*apraheya*).

Since the Buddha’s body possesses the five untainted material faculties (*rūpendriya*), as well as the life-faculty and the male faculty, these five material faculties, the male faculty, and the life-faculty all pertain to that which is not to be abandoned.
Therefore, when speaking in reference to the Buddha’s body, thirteen faculties pertain to all three categories of abandonment—namely, the five material faculties and the male faculty.

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the five feeling-faculties (*vedanendriya*), and the mind-faculty (*manendriya*): these thirteen faculties are indeed common to both those abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) and those not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).
Now, in this commentary, it states that "the first six and the last six"—these twelve—partially pertain to abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) and are also not abandoned;

this is also based on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the two vehicles and Bodhisattvas, and is not spoken with reference to the Buddha-body. However, regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) herein:

Regarding abandonment through the severance of fetters that take [these factors] as objects: as for those abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), consider, for instance, the nine stages within the three realms.

In each stage, there are nine grades of afflictions. For example, when one abandons the first eight grades of afflictions of the desire realm, this constitutes abandonment solely by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*);
at that time, one does not yet abandon the wholesome or indeterminate factors. However, when one abandons the ninth grade of affliction...

Affliction (*kleśa*) is the abandonment of its own nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*). If one abandons wholesome or neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas, it involves the abandonment through both the object-condition (*ālambana*) and the fetter (*bandhana*).

This applies likewise up to the stage of afflictions (*sāsrava-bhūmi*). Question: Since the male and female organs are considered ugly, and even the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) lack the male organ, why is this so?
Answer: Because they are untainted (*anāsrava*), and because they attain Buddhahood; they possess the fundamental body retained within the realms.

Regarding those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): if that were so, then a male *śrāvaka* of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) who turns his mind [toward enlightenment] and becomes a bodhisattva of sudden awakening would possess a body of the form realm;
yet, since he lacks the male organ (*puruṣendriya*), he would acquire it later upon attaining Buddhahood.
Furthermore, it is said that even within the hells there is no male organ, as it serves no purpose; nor could there be any expectation of sexual desire within the Great Avīci Hell.
This is illogical; how much more so in the case of the Tathāgata’s body? What use would a male organ be there?

If you claim that this male organ is required among the thirty-two marks to adorn the body, then since it is a "fine thing," the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) should also all possess male organs.
One should not say that the male organ is ugly. [This] should be further examined in the commentary. Question: By what entry...

Because they pertain to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Within the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*) and among those who have entered the long-lived heavens (*dīrghāyus-deva*), the five faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*) can no longer arise;
thus, it is taught that the five faculties beginning with faith are also abandoned by seeing. Why, then, does the treatise not state that the five faculties such as faith are abandoned by seeing?

Regarding these twenty-two faculties, when viewed from the perspective of the Tathāgata’s teaching, since the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) already exists...
