Regarding the statement that "they are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and also pertain to abandonment through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*"), this was not yet answered; the explanation follows immediately below.

If one intends to clarify them according to their respective applications, the meaning here is as follows: it is not only the seven material faculties and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) that pertain to abandonment through non-arising during the path of seeing;

rather, the five feeling faculties (*vedanendriya*), the mind-faculty (*manendriya*), and among the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), these also pertain to abandonment through non-arising during the path of seeing.
This refers to the period prior to entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), when one may be born in the three evil destinies, the northern continent (*uttarakuru*), or as a woman, and so forth.

Within those bodies of the three evil destinies and so on, the five feelings such as suffering and mental distress (*daurmanasya*) arise, as do the five faculties of the mind such as faith (*śraddhā*).
However, once one has entered the Path of Seeing and beyond, these can no longer arise within the bodies of the evil destinies and so forth.

There are the five faculties of faith and so forth, the five faculties of feeling, and the mental faculty and its associates, which never arise again. Therefore, among these, the five faculties of faith and so forth are also not produced as severed [from their objects].
Now, it is said that these—the five faculties of faith and so forth, the five faculties of feeling, and the mental faculty and its associates—when spoken of according to reality:
This also applies to the non-arising abandonment (*anutpāda-prahāṇa*) of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Now, as for the seven material faculties, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and so forth, because they do not coexist with discrimination (*vikalpa*), they are therefore instances of non-arising abandonment within the path of seeing.

As for the five feeling faculties (*vedanendriya*) and the mind faculty (*manas*), although they too are indeed non-arising abandonments, since these five feeling faculties and the mind faculty arise together with discriminating afflictions (*kleśa*), the five feelings... [are not].

The faculty of mind (*manas*) is, within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), comprised of abandonment by its own nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*); it is not abandonment through non-arising (*anutpāda-prahāṇa*).

Although wholesome factors such as faith (*śraddhā*) are also comprised of abandonment through non-arising within the path of seeing, these five factors beginning with faith are here comprised within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) as abandonment through the severance of objective fetters (*ālambana-bandhana-prahāṇa*).

The commentary states that there are six preceding and six subsequent [roots]. Regarding the six preceding: these are the five faculties of sensation (*pañca-vedanendriya*) and the faculty of mind (*manendriya*).

The five faculties of sensation and the faculty of mind constitute the "preceding gate," which clarifies the fourteen faculties. Since it has already been clarified that these are subject to abandonment through both the path of vision (*darśana-heya*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they are called "preceding.

Regarding the six subsequent: these refer to the five faculties beginning with faith (*pañca-śraddhādīndriya*) and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*). These eight constitute the three untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties, beginning with faith.

The "roots" refer to the aforementioned fourteen roots, from which eight have already been excluded. Since those eight roots do not pertain to being abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) and so forth, it says "the latter six.

Regarding why the *Śāstra* does not mention that the untainted (*anāsrava*) [roots] induce [other states], the *Śāstra* merely states that sorrow (*daurmanasya*) can induce the untainted. The *Śāstra*...
Nor does it say that the untainted (anāsrava) gives rise to sorrow, because it would serve no purpose. Furthermore, the treatise does not state that sorrow arises simultaneously with the untainted.

The treatise merely states that the untainted gives rise to the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya), nor does it say that suffering arises simultaneously with the untainted, nor that suffering can induce joy or pleasure;
thus, it is only by way of being associated with the untainted that [the faculty of suffering] obtains the designation "untainted."
Because they arise simultaneously.
Regarding the statement in the commentary, "It cannot be said that among the six [faculties] it is the life-faculty...

up to 'therefore it is not possible,'" this means that one cannot say that among the aforementioned six, one might exclude the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) and add the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as the sixth; for the life-faculty is common to both [the wholesome and the unwholesome].

[It is] abandoned. As for the claim that "because the Buddha’s body possesses the untainted life-faculty (anāsrava-jīvitendriya)," if that were so, then the five material faculties would also have to be non-abandonable, since the Buddha’s body likewise possesses the five untainted faculties. Therefore, one must know that the life-faculty cannot be taken as one of the first six [faculties].

Since it exists in the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), this refers specifically to the Buddha; it does not include the state beyond training of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). This is the intended meaning.
Because the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) exists within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), the five faculties of sensation and the mind-faculty (manas-indriya) are now taken as the first six.
This is stated in reference to those beyond training and those in training of the two vehicles, as well as Bodhisattvas of the ten stages; it is not spoken in reference to the stage of Buddhahood.
Regarding the statement that "the five faculties beginning with faith, up to those that are to be abandoned through cultivation, are untainted and not to be abandoned":

if the five faculties beginning with faith are tainted (*sāsrava*), they are abandoned by means of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). If the five faculties beginning with faith are both tainted and untainted (*anāsrava*), they are not abandoned.

As for the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), since it pertains to all three stages, it is termed "unknown" during the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and the preparation (*prayoga*).

One should know that the faculties which are with outflows (*sāsrava*) are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). If, prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), during the first fifteen moments of mind, they are untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), they are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvy-ajñendriya*); these are not to be abandoned.

The commentary states that "that which conforms to it is itself that. The explanation says: if there is a body of one in training (*śaikṣa*) possessing various feelings of suffering and pleasure, it is called "training";
if there is a body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) possessing suffering and pleasure, it is called "beyond training."
The two faculties of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*) are both associated with those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

As for the faculty of sorrow, it exists only in those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) or the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*). For those in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*) or the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), there is no faculty of sorrow, because the faculty of sorrow has been abandoned through the relinquishing of desire.
As for the faculty of suffering, it is accepted that all persons in the four fruits who have their bodies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) possess this faculty of suffering.

The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is coarse and heavy; it is abandoned upon the departure from desire (*vairāgya*). If the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is subtle, it is not abandoned even upon the departure from desire, just as with sleep.

For example, those who have attained the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) or the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), though their bodies remain in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and they have severed the defilements of the desire realm, can still experience sleep.
The faculty of suffering is likewise; therefore, it exists [even for them]. If persons who have attained the first or second fruits, while their bodies remain in the desire realm, turn their minds...
Regarding the turning toward the Mahāyāna: up until the seventh bhūmi, it is admitted that even with outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) minds, the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) may arise.

From the eighth bhūmi onward, there is a constant continuity of the untainted (*anāsrava*). Thus, for those who have attained the latter two fruits and turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna, there is no faculty of sorrow throughout the ten bhūmis.

Furthermore, for a bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment whose body remains in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there may still be subtle faculties, or [faculties] belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding the realms: for those born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), both the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) are entirely absent.

As for the treatise’s division into four categories—namely, the wholesome (*kuśala*), the unwholesome (*akuśala*), the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), and the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)—this textual passage speaks in terms of general characteristics and does not provide a detailed analysis;
its intent is to clarify that the three types of sensation (*vedanā*) pertain to the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the obscured-unspecified.
The four natures arise together. In this initial explanation, among the three types of feeling (*vedanā*), any one of them may be associated with the four natures;
this is what is meant by "attainment" (*prāpti*). It does not mean that each individual feeling must possess all four natures, such as the wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth.

Regarding the attainment of a pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) associated with the wholesome nature: for instance, the pleasant feeling within the third dhyāna when entering a wholesome meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is precisely that pleasant feeling.
It can coexist with a wholesome nature (*kuśala-dharma*). Furthermore, as when entering the second dhyāna, pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) also coexists with a wholesome nature.

Likewise, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), when one sees the Buddha and so forth, and a mind of longevity arises, pleasant feeling also coexists with a wholesome nature. As for pleasant feeling arising together with an unwholesome nature (*akuśala-dharma*):

it occurs when anger (*dveṣa*) encounters a favorable object; because joy and pleasure coexist [with that object], and since anger is of an unwholesome nature, [the pleasant feeling] is thereby obtained.

It is accompanied by joy and pleasure. Furthermore, for example, when one first gives rise to joy and pleasure in the mind through acts such as killing, or experiences pleasure through engaging in misconduct and so forth, then the feeling of pleasure is associated with an unwholesome nature.

If the body is within the lower three dhyānas and one gives rise to afflictions belonging to those lower three dhyānas, then the feeling of pleasure is associated with the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta). If, in ordinary circumstances, one gives rise to pleasure...

Feeling that is neither wholesome nor unwholesome is feeling associated with the non-obscured neutral nature (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Regarding the joy-feeling (*saumanasya*) arising together with the four [mental states] such as the wholesome:
this is explained by analogy with the previously discussed pleasant feeling (*sukha*). As for the equanimity-feeling (*upekṣā*) associated with the wholesome nature:

this refers to entering the fourth dhyāna concentration up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) concentration; all of these are equanimity-feelings associated with the wholesome nature. Equanimity-feeling...
That which arises simultaneously with the unwholesome nature refers, for example, to the commission of transgressions by human beings.

That which is associated with the sensation of equanimity and the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) nature refers to the arising of afflictions from the fourth dhyāna and above, up to and including the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
That is to say, equanimity arises together with the nature of obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta). Equanimity may also arise together with the unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) nature.
It should be understood that if it is the feeling of sorrow (daurmanasya), it can only arise together with the two natures of wholesome (kuśala) and unwholesome (akuśala).

If the sorrow concerns wealth, color, wife, children, and so forth, then the sorrow is associated with the unwholesome nature. If it is a longing or grief for the unsurpassed Dharma, then it is sorrow [associated with the wholesome nature].

It coexists with a wholesome nature (*kuśala-dharma*). As for the sensation of sorrow and suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*), it is like a bhikṣu who, while practicing the path with diligence, undergoes hardship;
he immediately attains coexistence with a wholesome nature. He cannot, however, coexist with either the obscured (*nivṛta*) or unobscured (*anivṛta*) natures.

If a sensation of suffering coexists with an unwholesome nature (*akuśala-dharma*), such as when one commits many transgressions and experiences physical exhaustion and pain, then that sensation coexists with an unwholesome nature.

If one does not perform wholesome or unwholesome karma—such as when a person engages in ordinary livelihood activities—the painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*) is associated with the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

That pain cannot be associated with the obscured nature (*nivṛta*). However, according to this treatise, it is only admitted that on the mental level (*manobhūmi*) there are four sensations—joy, pleasure, sorrow, and equanimity—each according to its characteristic; within that mental level, there is no painful sensation. If [one is] in the lower three [levels]...
Within dhyāna, because there is mental pleasure (*manas-sukha*), there is also pleasure within the mind. The treatise states:
"There is one interpretation that the three feelings (*vedanā*) each may be divided into four [types], up to being indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). However, this master...
He then analyzes them in detail and records the three types of feeling (*vedanā*). Each and every feeling can be associated with the four natures, such as the wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth.
If it is the three feelings of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), each may be associated with the wholesome nature, as previously explained.

As for suffering (*duḥkha*), if it arises in association with the wholesome nature, the unwholesome nature (*akuśala*), or the non-obscured neutral nature (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), this is also as previously explained. Regarding that feeling of suffering, its association with existence...
Because it arises simultaneously with the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) nature and is thus difficult to discern, it is now analyzed.
If the afflictions of the upper realms are exclusively of an obscured nature, yet there is no sensation of suffering (duḥkhavedanā) therein, it is therefore analyzed as follows:

if a person within the five consciousnesses (pañcavijñāna) of the celestial beings of the desire realm already possesses the sensation of suffering, then within those five consciousnesses, there exists innate greed and delusion that do not give rise to non-informative action (avijñapti).
This is precisely what constitutes being "obscured" (nivṛta). Thus, one knows that the acquisition (*prāpti*) of painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*) coexists with the state of being obscured.

Furthermore, within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in the midst of the most extreme suffering of the three evil destinies, the feeling of grief (*daurmanasya*) exists only in the mental consciousness.

Since there are no afflictions involving conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) in such places of extreme suffering, they are of an obscured nature. Therefore, one knows that the acquisition of painful feeling coexists with the state of being obscured. This is the intended meaning here.

In the middle [dhyāna], all five feelings are present. Within the minds of the lower three dhyānas, there is the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*). If one is within the hells, there is the feeling of suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*).

Each of these feelings may be of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*), an unwholesome nature (*akuśala-svabhāva*), a nature obscured by defilements (*nivṛta-svabhāva*), or an unobscured nature (*anivṛta-svabhāva*).

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The five consciousnesses all possess these four natures" means that within the five consciousnesses, there exist wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, and unobscured-unspecified natures.
This treatise says: "There is an interpretation that each of the three feelings is divided into four.
This master explains the intention in detail: regarding the wholesome nature having the three feelings, it is like a bhikṣu who is weary from diligent progress on the path of clarity.
Regarding suffering and so forth: wholesome states may be associated with the sensation of suffering, such as when the body has just emerged from meditative absorption.

However, wholesome states that are peaceful are associated with the sensation of pleasure, as is the wholesome mind of pleasure within the third dhyāna; both of these may also be associated with the sensation of equanimity.

As for unwholesome states, such as performing evil deeds or other unwholesome acts, they may be associated with the sensation of pleasure, such as when one experiences pleasure from committing a transgression or from the fatigue resulting from such unwholesome acts. They may also be associated with [the other sensations].

It is associated with painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*). It is associated with all [types] of neutral feeling (*upekṣāvedanā*). Since sorrowful feeling (*daurmanasyavedanā*) is of a wholesome or unwholesome nature, it cannot be of the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) type;
this is what is analyzed in the present treatise. The detailed explanation is as stated above.
Regarding the statement, "Because hatred (*dveṣa*) is unwholesome (*akuśala*), it is excluded here": Hatred is unwholesome because it can coexist with mental distress (*daurmanasya*);

therefore, it is excluded here. Regarding the statement, "Because the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the two views—the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—are entirely neutral (*avyākṛta*)": [this refers to] the afflictions of the path of cultivation...
One portion—those that do not incite karma—is comprised within the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

As for the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), if they arise through discrimination (*vikalpita*), they can incite karma and are thus unwholesome (*akuśala*); if they are innate (*sahaja*), they are all obscured-unspecified.

Question: Regarding the mental level (*manobhūmi*) within this miserable realm (*durgati*), one should consider with how many primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) it arises concomitantly.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If [afflictions] arise spontaneously (*svarasena*), they are all associated with every faculty.
Here, "spontaneously" refers to innate (*sahaja*) afflictions. It further states that these are all found to manifest in connection with the three types of feeling (*vedanā*).
The intended meaning is as follows: innate afflictions can arise simultaneously with the three feelings of pleasure, pain, and equanimity.

If they were to pervade all classes of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) and be associated with all faculties (*indriya*), it would imply that greed, hatred, and delusion pervade the six consciousnesses. This is because [the sūtras] state that these three afflictions are pervasive across the six consciousnesses.

This refers to those within the hells who create karma for collective retribution (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka-karman*). While they remain within the hells, there is no time when they can emerge from them.

However, according to this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, because the sinners within the hells lack discernment (*vikalpa*) and their suffering is especially intense, they are unable to create karma for collective retribution. Nevertheless, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that while within the hells, the sinners...
Because they lack discursive thought (*avikalpa*) and because their suffering is so extreme, they are unable to create karma that results in a collective retribution (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka-karma*).
However, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that when a sinner in hell is exhorted by King Yama, the sinner refrains from creating such collective retribution karma.

As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, once the twenty intermediate kalpas (*antara-kalpa*) of formation have been completed and the period of the abiding kalpa (*sthiti-kalpa*) begins, [the gods] cause a single person to...
He becomes King Yama. Next, there are various sinners born within the hells.
Then, the Ox-Headed Jailers arrive at the location of the sinners, desiring to inflict suffering upon them. The sinners do not submit and strike back with clubs.
Consequently, the sinners and the Ox-Headed Jailers engage in mutual combat and blows; when they cannot endure the punishment due to their lack of strength, King Yama immediately arrives.
The wardens address the sinner, saying: "Stay! Arise! Where is this place? The sinner replies: "This is hell. They ask again:
"Do you know from where your previous body came? By what karma were you created so as to be born here? The sinner then realizes for himself that he came from the human realm;
it was by committing the ten non-virtuous actions, such as taking life and so forth, while among humans, that he has come to be born here.

"Because of their karmic paths, they have come to be born in this place," he reported to the King in full detail. The King said, "Since you yourself created these karmas, it is you who must experience the results of your own actions.
Why do you further resist Zhang Niutou and the others? If you set your mind upon receiving your punishment..."

There will then be a limit to its duration; at what time can one emerge? Because you further engage in transformation, dispute, give rise to anger, and create karma, there will be no time of emergence.
When a sinner is exhorted by the King, and the King does not further reject or obstruct them, they are left to their own four calculations.
Now, as for the place where they are taken: the sinners within that hell [suffer] first because of their lack of discernment, and secondly because their suffering is exceedingly heavy.
Second, because there is exhortation and admonition. Due to these two conditions, the offender does not create karma that results in collective retribution (*saṃghāta-karma*).

However, in other realms such as those of hungry ghosts and animals where suffering is mixed with lighter forms, there are also discerning afflictions capable of creating karma that results in collective retribution.

Here, an objection is raised: "Because it is the most extreme suffering among all forms of suffering, the hells lack discerning sorrow (*daurmanasya*); and because they lack sorrow," [they cannot produce such karma].

There are no afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) [in the third dhyāna], because it is the ultimate bliss among all forms of pleasure. The third dhyāna is indeed non-conceptual joy (*nirvikalpa-prīti*);
because there is no [ordinary] joy, there are likewise no afflictions of views. The third dhyāna is the most extreme bliss, precisely because it is non-conceptual joy.

There are afflictions of views in hell, the place of extreme suffering, because there is non-conceptual sorrow (*nirvikalpa-daurmanasya*). The answer is: in hell, there is the suffering of oppressive sorrow. It is extreme.

There is no room for interference. Because there is no room for interference, there are no afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). In the Third Dhyāna, there is supreme bliss; in the hells, there is pleasure.

It is permitted that there is room for interference. Because there is room for interference, there are afflictions of view. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If it pervades all groups of consciousness... and so forth.

Regarding those associated with all faculties on the mental level (*manobhūmi*): in the human realm and the hells, the greed, delusion, and so forth of the five consciousnesses that are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) are all concomitant with the three feelings;
this principle is reasonable. However, as for the two views—view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—of the sixth consciousness...

In the hells, there is the nature of obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta). Regarding how this is acquired: if it is held that [the obscured-unspecified] can coexist with all three feelings, then all three feelings would be admitted [therein].

If, however, in the case of humans and devas, the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the sixth consciousness are of the nature of obscured-unspecified, they could likewise coexist with the feelings of pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

But regarding the eighth consciousness of humans and devas, since it should be understood as being devoid of suffering (*duḥkha*), how can it be said that it possesses the characteristics of all three feelings?

[The opponent] says: "It should be so; however, in all these cases, the meaning is not established. Now, speaking in terms of the majority, the word "all" (皆) is said to be extremely difficult to interpret.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (Sūtra-commentary), fascicle 57: "One faculty (*indriya*) is wholesome by taking the three natures as its object, and among the twenty-two faculties, it is also not other dharmas," this means that within the twenty-two faculties, only the single faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is exclusively of a wholesome or unwholesome nature, and not [of an indeterminate nature].

Because it is associated with the indeterminate (avyākṛta). Sorrow takes the three natures—wholesome and so forth—as its seeds; however, only the mental faculty (manas) is wholesome or unwholesome, whereas the other faculties are not, as they pertain exclusively to unwholesome states.

Regarding "excluding three, the remainder": as for excluding three, if these are the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), this refers to their potential presence within the six consciousnesses.
In the hells, they are definitely not present in actual manifestation (*samudācāra*). If one follows the masters of the First Dhyāna, these are the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity.

Regarding the six consciousnesses: according to the later master, the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, with the exception of three—namely, the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and sorrow (*daurmanasya*)—these three do not definitely manifest within the hells.
Some say that with the exception of three, these are the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*); they definitely do not manifest [there].

Regarding the statement in the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary), "Those who are exclusively suffering—the hungry ghosts and animals are also like this": if one refers to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it says, "those who are exclusively [in the realms of] hungry ghosts and animals are also like this";

whereas if one refers to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, it says, "the realm of hungry ghosts and the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*) consisting solely of suffering are also like this. Thus, the two texts differ.

The Commentary states: If one who experiences mixed sensations also manifests the latter three [feelings]—namely, pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—then, even if they are ghosts or animals experiencing mild sensations, they may still achieve the former;
according to the first master, they achieve pleasure, joy, and equanimity, while according to the latter master, they also achieve sorrow (*daurmanasya*). Thus, they achieve them as well.

Regarding the statement that the five faculties beginning with faith and the two sexual organs (male and female) may either be manifest or not, and that there are cases where they are both present or absent, this is because for those who have not severed the roots of goodness, even while suffering within the great hells, they occasionally experience weariness toward suffering and seek happiness;
thus, the five faculties beginning with faith can become manifest. This is as stated in the treatise: "May I... [and so forth].
At that time, one must relinquish this life; thus, it is for the sake of causing me to experience happiness that one knows the arising of the five faculties, such as faith.
Just as a person who loathes suffering seeks a place of happiness, if one has severed the roots of goodness, then the five faculties, such as faith, cannot arise.
Furthermore, because both male and female faculties are entirely absent within the eight cold and eight hot hells, the subsequent text states: "No."
Regarding the possibility of sexual desire within the Avīci Great Hell, the treatise briefly cites this place of extreme suffering as an example where neither male nor female faculties exist.
However, speaking according to reality, the other hells such as Saṃjīva also lack these two faculties.
Yet, in reality, if one considers the other realms of hungry ghosts and animals, both male and female faculties can be present; thus, their presence or absence varies between them.

This means that if the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) is present, the female faculty (*strīndriya*) is not; if the female faculty is present, the male faculty is not. Thus, it is said that they are mutually exclusive.

Regarding the inclusion of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) within the indeterminate category, the former master stated: "Because there is suffering within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*). Within the five sensory consciousnesses...

Regarding suffering: as in the hells, or during states of fainting or the transition between death and rebirth, there is no faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*); however, at other times when other sensations are present, the faculty of suffering exists.
Therefore, it is said that [the faculty of suffering] enters into the indeterminate category.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra*: "If it were not so, the other three would be non-existent," the former master said:

For example, within the hells, among the five consciousnesses there is constant suffering and within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) there is constant grief; thus, joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) are certainly not established.

If one does not take the possibility of equanimity (*upekṣā*) into account, then among the three that are not established, if equanimity is taken as the third, then among those three factors, only the two factors of joy and bliss are not established. That is to say:
This is because there is no third [feeling] of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) that would not be established.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "If one says that joy and bliss further take on another form," and so forth, up to "because there is neither the absence of form nor the presence of both forms":
this refers to the reasoning established by the former master, who argued that if one does not admit the possibility of equanimity, it cannot be established as the third [feeling].
Regarding those who have attained [the form], they may take the form of a male or the form of a female as the third [category].
This is because it is not permitted for one who possesses a single body within the miserable realms (durgati) to possess both male and female sexual organs.
The Master replied: "How could even ghosts or animals lack two sexual organs? Indeed, among ghosts and animals, there are those who possess both male and female organs.

As for the five faculties such as faith, the two sexual organs, and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), these all fall within the category of the 'indeterminate' (*aniyata*), because they may or may not be present."
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that the sensation of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure is not discussed because it is eclipsed and overwhelmed by pure suffering:

although the former masters maintain that even for a portion of hungry ghosts and animals there is occasionally a neutral state of equanimity (*upekṣā*) that is neither painful nor pleasant, it cannot be called "equanimity" because it is eclipsed and overwhelmed by pure suffering.
This is like the third dhyāna, where there is also the sensation of equanimity, yet it is mentioned only briefly because it is subtle.
It is called "pleasure. Although ghosts and animals possess neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations, because [their existence] consists purely of suffering, it is designated solely as "suffering.
In this treatise, the former master is Ārya Asaṅga, and the latter master is Dharmapāla.
The commentary states: "If the six consciousnesses are sometimes absent and thus do not constitute the mental faculty (*manas*), this refutes the previous master’s position.
Why is it that you [the opponent] claim that the support (*āśraya*)—which is the capacity to receive—is non-existent, yet claim that the six consciousnesses possess such a support?
Just as those supports are non-existent, the six consciousnesses, which are like the supported capacities to receive, should likewise be non-existent."
The preceding master’s statement that "that [state] is itself the stage of birth-and-death and does not exist separately" is explained as follows:
it is like the state of fainting, which is subsumed within the stage of birth-and-death and does not exist separately from it.

The Commentary states: If one maintains that the consciousnesses of the body and so forth are in constant succession until the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is interrupted and the five sensory consciousnesses continue, then the original intention of the former master was to take the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) as the eighth.

Now, since it is argued that grief is subject to interruption, he has shifted his position to take the faculties of grief and suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) as the eighth, on the grounds that the five sensory consciousnesses, such as that of the body, are always in continuous succession. If this is the case, then suffering (*duḥkha*) is taken as the eighth.

Furthermore, since the five consciousnesses possess suffering, the five consciousnesses should be constantly continuous. Since the faculty of grief exists within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and yet this faculty of grief is not established [as continuous], the mental consciousness should likewise be intermittent.
The Commentary asks: According to the second chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are some beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*) who possess all their sense faculties (*indriya*).

Here, it is intended that beings born by transformation possess their faculties instantaneously; thus, they must possess both male and female faculties. Since those in the hells are born by transformation, [they too must possess these].
Why? Because they lack the male and female faculties (*puruṣendriya* and *strīndriya*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “all five faculties experience suffering”: if it is contact that is suffering, it is apprehended by body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*); if it is the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*), then all five faculties possess it.
In the intermediate states of the minor hells (*kṣudranaraka*), there are male and female organs;

however, in the Saṃjīva and other such hells, these organs are absent, and thus no sexual intercourse occurs, yet sexual desire (*kāmarāga*) arises. Even in the great hells (*mahānaraka*), there is likewise no sexual desire.

According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, however, even within the great hells there exists a mind of lustful desire and sexual acts; it is said that they may see [others] and become attached to them.
If consciousness and so forth were to come into contact with one another, the body would immediately be ground to dust. Question:
For what reason does the Sūtra state that men embrace copper pillars and women lie upon iron beds? Furthermore, how can it be said that there is sexual desire within those hells?
If male and female sexual organs were present, it might be granted that sexual desire manifests in hell; but if they are absent, how could such desire arise?

Furthermore, if it were held that desire serves as a condition such that a single sexual organ is required for one's painful feelings— even if many organs were required as conditions for those painful feelings—
and if in the hells one might obtain a male form or take on a female form and so forth as a condition for experiencing suffering,
then every sentient being within the hells would necessarily have to possess both sexual organs upon their bodies.
Because they currently undergo much suffering, it may be that a single sentient being has hundreds of thousands of male and female forms upon their body,
as these many forms serve as the conditions for their suffering.
Regarding the commentary’s reference to the explanations of the Sarvāstivāda and other schools within the Hīnayāna: there are three interpretations presented in this commentary.
The first interpretation relies on the Hīnayāna, while the latter two rely on the Mahāyāna. This is the first interpretation, which explains according to the Hīnayāna.

According to the Sarvāstivāda and other Hīnayāna schools, there are no neutral (*avyākṛta*) pleasant sensations resulting from maturation (*vipāka*) in either the great or small hells; they consist exclusively of suffering.

In those [realms], it is also admitted that there is pleasure of outflow (*niṣyanda-sukha*). As for "pleasure of outflow," this refers to the pleasure within the minds of deportment (*īryāpatha*) and craftsmanship (*śilpa*), or the pleasure within virtuous or non-virtuous minds;
such is called the pleasure of outflow. If it were the pleasure of maturation (*vipāka-sukha*), it would be the feeling of pleasure that is of a neutral (*avyākṛta*) nature resulting from maturation.
According to the interpretation of the Dharma Master, because suffering exists within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the hells, it is therefore designated as "pleasure."
In reality, there is no pleasure. It is like a person who places their heavy right thigh upon the left; this is also called "pleasure," yet within it, there is truly no pleasure.
Regarding the statement that "maturation (*vipāka*) is not a pleasure of outflow (*niṣyanda*"), there are two interpretations in the Mahāyāna. The first interpretation states:
This refers to other mixed locations of sensation where there is a pleasure of outflow, but no pleasure of maturation—excluding the hells. Within the hells, [there is no such distinction].

Furthermore, because there is no ripening (*vipāka*) pleasure, hell is a place where one experiences exclusively suffering. According to a second interpretation, within that hell, while there is no ripening pleasure, it is admitted that there is pleasure of concordant outflow (*naiṣyandika*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "This is called 'pure suffering' because none of it exists," this commentary text specifically restates [the previous point] to adopt the first interpretation from within the Mahāyāna.
Within the Mahāyāna, it is taught that in the hells there is no pleasure of outflow (*niṣyanda*) and no pleasure of maturation (*vipāka*).
It speaks of the name "hell. Because there is no pleasure of outflow (*niṣyanda*) and no pleasure of maturation (*vipāka*), it is called hell; thus, it is said to be a place of pure suffering.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Or, following the Sarvāstivāda and other Hīnayāna schools, because it is accompanied by intense anger within the present mental consciousness," if [it refers to] the Sarvāstivāda...
Regarding the tenets of the Bhadanta school: greed is associated with joy and pleasure; hatred is associated with sorrow and suffering.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 59, from verse 58 onwards, it says that they manifest based on coarse characteristics.

That treatise also states: "Lust is accompanied by joy and pleasure; hatred is accompanied by grief and suffering. This is also spoken according to the coarse characteristics as explained in the Hīnayāna.
If one distinguishes them subtly, however, lust is accompanied by grief and suffering, and hatred is accompanied by joy and pleasure—as stated in the subsequent section of that same treatise.
Greed is accompanied by sorrow and suffering when encountering adverse conditions, whereas hatred is accompanied by joy and pleasure when encountering favorable conditions.

The Commentary states: "In response to the question of why they are called 'greed' and 'food,' it is because they are provisional designations. Thus, in the hells, consciousness-food (*vijñānāhāra*) predominates;
among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), thought-food (*manahsaṃcetanāhāra*) predominates; and among animals (*tiryagyoni*), contact-food (*sparśāhāra*) predominates."

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "in the Mahāsāṃghika school, all consciousnesses arise together, and suffering and grief continue in succession": in this school, the six consciousnesses arise simultaneously;

the five sensory consciousnesses possess suffering (*duḥkha*), while the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses grief (*daurmanasya*). Therefore, it is said that suffering and grief continue in succession.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states that according to the tenets of the Sthavira school, up to the proponents of "mere designation" (*prajñaptivādin*), these schools maintain that within the nine states of mind there is a "consciousness of division" (*vibhaṅgavijñāna*), which is called the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation consciousness). Therefore, this treatise says "immediately following maturation" (*vipākānantaram*).

Furthermore, when the "mind of elicitation" (*ākṣepakacitta*) and the "mind of seeking" (*paryeṣakacitta*) arise, these are precisely the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*), or they continue in association with sorrow and suffering.
The Commentary states that according to the Sautrāntika school, vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) exist only within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The reason the Sautrāntikas maintain that vitarka and vicāra exist only in the mental consciousness is that they are associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya*);

if, as the Sarvāstivādins calculate, vitarka and vicāra existed in the five sensory consciousnesses, then because the five consciousnesses are present from the first dhyāna upward, [vitarka and vicāra would be present there as well]. Thus, regarding whether vitarka and vicāra arise or do not arise within the mental consciousness:
Regarding the commentary’s statement that, according to the Mahīśāsaka school, there is also a resultant (*vipāka*) mental consciousness because mental consciousness arises:

"Mahīśāsaka" means the *Mahīśāsaka* school (the School of the Earth-Makers). They maintain that there is a mental consciousness termed "resultant fruit," and this mental consciousness is associated with sorrow.
[This is] asked regarding those sixty-six [states] among the various realms of existence, and so forth; therefore, it should now be explained within this context.

The intent of the question is as follows: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the other six classes of gods in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as well as the human realm and so forth, possess sorrow and suffering;

thus, sorrow and suffering are real. This is not in accordance with the claims of others, such as the followers of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). Since the *Yogācāra* and other treatises state this regarding the hells:

Regarding the statement that there is "sorrow and so forth," this means that according to the teachings of other followers of the Hīnayāna, it is said that there is sorrow within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the hells.

As for the commentary’s question, "What is wrong with saying there is [sorrow] as well?": although the first two *sāmantaka* (preparatory stages) possess pleasant sensations (*sukha-vedanā*), they are so slight that they are not mentioned;
they are simply designated as "joy" (*saumanasya*). As for the mention of "winds between the internal organs in the hells," this refers to when cool breezes arrive within the hot hells.

Sometimes [the wind] enters through the pores and into the internal organs; sometimes it enters through the mouth. Thus, external wind enters the internal body and, by being within the organs, functions as *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra* (edible food).
However, according to the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), when a sinner swallows glowing iron balls and the like, the moment they first enter the stomach is also termed *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*.
If one attains the first stage (*bhūmi*) of a Bodhisattva, one immediately enters into *pariṇāmika-jarā-maraṇa* (transformational birth and death).
Those born in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) likewise lack the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*).
The commentary states that regarding those with retribution (*vipāka*), with the exception of sorrow, the remaining four feelings (*vedanā*) all involve retribution.

The commentary further addresses the stages where these are severed: the first dhyāna (*prathamadhyāna*) severs sorrow; the second dhyāna (*dvitīyadhyāna*) severs suffering (*duḥkha*); and the third dhyāna (*tṛtīyadhyāna*) severs joy (*saumanasya*).

Regarding the statement that "in the fourth dhyāna, pleasure is abandoned; within the meditative absorptions, joy and pleasure are [abandoned], and the *saterī* (initial) ear-consciousness possesses only the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*)," it is because when the sixth consciousness enters the lower three dhyānas, that sixth consciousness—which consists of the sensations of sorrow, joy, and pleasure—can likewise give rise to the sensation of equanimity belonging to the *saterī* ear-consciousness.
Therefore, one should know that even in the preceding texts, different sensations can arise simultaneously. In this context:

Regarding the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*): this refers to the time of attaining Buddhahood, or alternatively, the attainment of the untainted (*anāsrava*) state at the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*).
Within this commentary, there are two kinds of fruition: first, the ultimate fruition, which refers to attaining the untainted state of Buddhahood;
second, the non-ultimate fruition, which refers to attaining the untainted state of the first ground. One correctly attains seven or six [of these], while not incorrectly attaining five.

Regarding the statement that they are "untainted" (*anāsrava*) because they do not sever the outflows (*āsrava*): if it refers to the feelings of joy and pleasure, these would indeed be untainted, as they are capable of severing the outflows.
However, when joy and pleasure are conjoined with the untainted noble path (*āryamārga*), they are called "untainted" in the sense that they can sever [the outflows].
As for the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), since it cannot sever the outflows, it is designated as "untainted" only because it is induced by the untainted [path].
The Commentary answers: "Existence" is like tears; when tears fall like rain, there is a locus for the fixed eye, though it is not a real sense-faculty (indriya).

Thus we know it exists. The Explanation says: Therefore, one knows that within the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu), the falling of tears is not actually the eye-faculty itself, but serves as an example for the existence of its supporting form (rūpa).
Thus, one knows that in the Formless Realm, there are the five untainted (anāsrava) faculties of a Buddha.
The commentary is as explained in the section on the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
There are certain seeds that do not manifest there, as stated in the seventh fascicle of the treatise below; this has also been mentioned above.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that the three higher dhyānas of the form realm possess untainted (*anāsrava*) fivefold consciousnesses, taking this as an illustration:
for instance, the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue are bound only to the desire realm; the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body are bound to both the desire realm and the first dhyāna.

As for the five material sense organs, they are bound to five levels—that is, the fivefold tainted (*sāsrava*) consciousnesses are bound to two levels. In the three higher dhyānas, there are no tainted fivefold consciousnesses.

Regarding consciousness: the five uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses pertain to all five stages. Now, as for the five contaminated (*sāsrava*) faculties, they are bound only to the five stages.
Although the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) lacks the five contaminated faculties, what prevents the five uncontaminated faculties from existing throughout all six stages?
[Commentary: If this is so, why are the seventh and eighth uncontaminated [consciousnesses] associated only with equanimity (*upekṣā*)? This is the underlying intention.
The first six consciousnesses exist throughout the three lower dhyānas and are associated with joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*).

As for whether the untainted seventh and eighth consciousnesses also exist throughout the three lower dhyānas and are likewise associated with the mental sensations of joy, bliss, and equanimity (*upekṣā*): [the answer is yes].
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because its ultimate merit is superior”: within a single stage (*bhūmi*), it is the most excellent;
among the four dhyānas, it is the fourth dhyāna that is the most supreme. Furthermore, within the fourth dhyāna, there are superior and inferior grades;
because this is the highest grade, it is the most superior grade within that stage. That which is most superior is termed "ultimate" (*prāntakoṭika*). There are six such types.

There are four kinds: first, the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*); second, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*); third, the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
One attains these three kinds of analytical knowledge only upon entering the limit of the fourth dhyāna (*caturtha-dhyāna-sīmāntika-samādhi*).

As for the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), because it pertains to sounds, it is bound to the first dhyāna (*prathama-dhyāna-niyata*). Fourth is the *vimala-samādhi* (stainless samādhi). There are Arhats who [possess this].

He is the supreme field of merit among humanity. Since those who have attained the first three fruits do not equal him, this Arhat, when about to enter a city for alms, first forms this thought during his preliminary preparation:
"All sentient beings fall into the hells solely because they take afflictions as their cause. Now that I am an Arhat, the most supreme in merit among humans..."
"O Kāśyapa, there are those who make offerings to me; they will certainly attain the Noble Path, or encounter various Buddhas, or be reborn in the heavens.
However, because those who give rise to afflictions toward my person fall into the evil realms, I now practice impure conduct.
If someone scorns me, I immediately sit down; if they scorn my sitting, I immediately walk away; if they scorn my walking, I immediately sit down, and so forth. I reflect in this way:"
Having done so, he immediately enters the fourth dhyāna, the supreme limit of concentration, the *anirjita* (unconquered) samādhi. Fifth, regarding how the Buddha knows:
if he wishes to know the minds of all people and so forth, he enters the fourth dhyāna, the supreme limit of concentration, and only then is he able to know them.
Sixth, the method for extending life: as when an Arhat’s life is about to end, he immediately forms this thought in his mind...
He reflected: "If I were to remain long within the Buddha-dharma, there would be great benefit.
He then immediately relinquished his robes and bowl, entered the Saṃgha, and attained the fourth dhyāna, the supreme limit-concentration (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*).
Because this fourth dhyāna, as a superior concentration, constitutes the limit-concentration, its merit is preeminent; for this reason, he was also able to prolong his life.

The *Śāstra* states that the Abodes of the Great Compassionate One (*mahākāruṇika-vihāra*) and others are mostly based upon the fourth dhyāna. First is the Celestial Abode (*deva-vihāra*), which refers to the heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

All levels of the Form Realm are termed "celestial abodes," and because one dwells together with these deities, they are called the Celestial Abode. Among these celestial abodes, the Buddha primarily relies upon the fourth dhyāna.

Second is the Brahma Abode (*brahma-vihāra*), which consists of the cultivation of the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*): loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Therefore, one is subsequently born in the third heaven of the First Dhyāna as the Great Brahmā King, dwelling among the Brahmās; hence it is called the "Brahma-abode" (brahmavihāra).
In a single realm, there is only one Brahmā King. Those who practice with inferior cultivation are born in the Heaven of the Brahma-Assembly (Brahmapāriṣadya);
those with middling clarity are born in the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita); and those with superior clarity are born as the Great Brahmā King. This is the Brahma-abode.

Among these, the Buddha frequently dwells in the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness. Third, regarding the Buddha’s dwelling, it consists of the one hundred and thirty dharmas that are not of the nature of suffering;
within this dwelling, he frequently dwells in the ten powers (*daśabala*) for the purpose of subduing the celestial Māras.

Fourth, regarding the noble dwellings (*āryavihāra*), these consist of the liberations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and wishlessness (*apranihita*), which are attainable by all three vehicles. Nevertheless, among the noble dwellings, the Buddha frequently dwells in emptiness.
Regarding samādhi: because it enters the śūnyatā-samādhi, it is able to counteract the māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*).

Since the remaining [samādhis]—the signless (*animitta*), the wishless (*apraṇihita*), and the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*)—cannot counteract afflictions, one does not abide in these four higher abodes. All of this is formulated with respect to the Buddha-body of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*);
it is not formulated with respect to the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Because the causes for transforming fragrance are lacking": this is because within the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is no edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*);
consequently, there are no seeds of odor and fragrance, nor is there any karma capable of inducing odor and fragrance.

Thus, because the causes of odor and fragrance are absent, one cannot transform odor and fragrance within the Form Realm. Since the objects of perception (*ālambana*) do not exist, the consciousness that perceives them likewise [does not arise].
No. Furthermore, there are no seeds for nose-consciousness and tongue-consciousness.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "It is not so; even for the Hinayana, odors and tastes exist, and even nose- and tongue-consciousness exist," the portion beginning with "It is not so" constitutes the answer.
However, according to the Hinayana teachings, it is not admitted that odors and tastes exist in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Furthermore, it is accepted that there are śrāvakas of extensive wisdom (*vipula-prajñā*). Indeed, the Mahāyāna accepts that such śrāvakas of extensive wisdom—bodhisattvas practicing the *pāramitās*—are capable of transforming the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) within the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*).

Moreover, when there is no transformation of objects in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), these are merely termed the fruits of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*), and cannot be termed the fruits of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*), because they do not involve the application of both concentration and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "above [the third dhyāna], there are no three consciousnesses that are outflow-free (anāsrava), yet they should be said to exist":

the intent of this objection is that since the upper three dhyānas lack the three outflow-afflicted (sāsrava) consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body, one should likewise say that the three outflow-free consciousnesses also exist in those upper three dhyānas.

Regarding the commentary’s question, "How can there be those [five consciousnesses] when they are fundamentally non-existent in the higher stages and lack their own kind?"—the five consciousnesses are fundamentally non-existent in the three higher dhyānas;
therefore, the three higher dhyānas are not admitted to possess the five consciousnesses, whereas the five consciousnesses are admitted to exist in the first dhyāna.
Thus, one may freely adopt any of the three interpretations provided here in the commentary. However, the question within the commentary [concerns] the eight...
The first interpretation is that [the seventh and eighth consciousnesses] exist in all stages (*bhūmi*), even up to their manifest activity (*samudācāra*).
The second interpretation is that they exist only in the fourth dhyāna; since the seventh and eighth consciousnesses do not exist [in other stages], how could they exist there?
The third interpretation is that within the four *dhyānas*, they exist just as the seventh and eighth consciousnesses do. As for the fourth interpretation, it is as follows:

In the third explanation, the sub-sections are distinguished. However, the Master further explains that the fourth explanation is actually the second explanation, from which the sub-sections are derived.
Yet, regarding the first explanation—which states that the eight consciousnesses exist throughout all eight stages—there is a difficulty:
it asks, "If there are seeds in other stages that do not arise, how does this differ from having no seeds at all? If [the seeds] were...
Regarding the statement that "within the dhyānas, all possess the five faculties": there are seventeen heavens in the four dhyānas, excluding the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva).
How could a single Buddha-body possess seventeen sets of the five faculties? Furthermore, if consciousness arises, it is unknown upon which level's five faculties it relies to arise.
Moreover, according to the second interpretation, the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] reside in the fourth dhyāna, while the sixth consciousness is permitted to pervade all levels.
The five consciousnesses of the eighth stage are admitted to exist in the level of the first dhyāna; how could they exist in the fruit of Buddhahood?

If the transforming consciousness belongs to a higher stage while the transformed five sense-faculties belong to the first dhyāna, then the five consciousnesses of a lower stage and the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) of a higher stage would arise at all times.

Furthermore, when one possesses a body in a lower stage and gives rise to the divine eye of a higher stage, there would be times when that divine eye does not arise [if it were restricted to its own level]. Therefore, this is untenable.

Furthermore, it is not yet known whether the five consciousnesses of the first dhyāna rely on the power of consciousness or arise through the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*); it remains unknown which consciousness arises.

Moreover, among the ten stages (*bhūmi*) within the causal state, the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) and the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇajñāna*) exist from the first dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
However, in the resultant stage of Buddhahood, the Wisdom of Equality does not follow the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation. This is the third interpretation.

[In the] middle [section]: If all eight consciousnesses rely upon the fourth dhyāna—as stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*—then bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above, when born into the fourth dhyāna, still give rise to the vitarka and vicāra of the first dhyāna within their subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Since preaching the Dharma necessarily relies upon vitarka and vicāra, this implies that higher stages can give rise to the mental factors of lower stages; how then could the Buddha be inferior to such bodhisattvas? If the...

Regarding the six consciousnesses relying solely on the fourth dhyāna: according to the treatise below, the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (wonderful observation wisdom) and the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (accomplishing what is to be done wisdom) are intermittently severed and cease entirely upon entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
This is because it is only permitted that the *ādarśa-jñāna* (great perfect mirror wisdom) and the *samatā-jñāna* (equality wisdom) continue uninterrupted.

Thus, it is known that the sixth [consciousness] also enters the cessation attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Furthermore, it would follow that one could transcend the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), which is untenable. Now, to assist in the explanation:
the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), the seventh consciousness, the five consciousnesses, and the five sense organs are always based upon the fourth dhyāna;

this is the interpretation. However, this is extremely difficult to understand. Among these three interpretations, one may choose and adopt whichever one pleases. Regarding the point "if one encounters the mental faculty" (*yadṛcchika-manas*), the commentary states: Question—
The first interpretation is that from the eighth stage upward, these [mental factors] do not manifest.

The second interpretation is that they range from the fourth dhyāna upward, owing to their superior nature. The commentary states: "Furthermore, all four dhyānas possess the five consciousnesses, etc."

The text merely emphasizes the second interpretation, without providing a separate one. Furthermore, from the subsequent explanation, it is shown that only the fourth dhyāna possesses seven or eight consciousnesses; this constitutes the third interpretation.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "the eight untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses should be grouped according to their objects," as explained by various masters, there are three interpretations within this *Śāstra*, all of which are the explanations of the author of the *Śāstra*.
It should be stated: there are eight untainted consciousnesses that exist throughout the eight stages (*bhūmi*).

One interpretation holds that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses reside in the fourth dhyāna, while the five sensory consciousnesses reside in the first dhyāna. Another interpretation holds that all eight consciousnesses collectively rely upon the fourth dhyāna. Furthermore...
The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra states: "The Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*). The fleshly eye sees forms within obstructions;

the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) sees forms beyond obstructions but does not see those within them. If both the fleshly and divine eyes were required to see both the internal and external, why would the fleshly eye be necessary?"
Furthermore, a sutra states: "There are small Sumeru mountains, great Sumeru mountains, small Cakravāḍa mountains, and great Cakravāḍa mountains.

This refers to a single four-continent world-system (*cāturdvīpaka*), wherein there is one small Sumeru mountain; and for a single trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*), there is one great Sumeru mountain.
Master Zhao challenged the author of the commentary, saying: "Take, for instance, the case where there is one small Sumeru mountain within a four-continent world-system. As for Sumeru..."
On that mountain there are the minor Four Great Kings, the minor Heaven of the Thirty-three, and so forth, up to the heavens of the First Dhyāna.
Since it is said that within a single trichiliocosm there is one great Mount Sumeru, there must likewise be great Four Great Kings dwelling upon the mountain,
and there must likewise be a great Heaven of the Thirty-three dwelling there, as well as the great Brahmā and Tuṣita heavens, O Dharma Master.
For several days he did not respond. Later, he explained: "The Great Mount Sumeru belongs exclusively to the *vyūha* (adorned) world-system, nor are the various devas stationed there;
furthermore, this is a secondary meaning (*pārśva-artha*). Seeing the secondary clarifies that the seeds are not its active manifestations (*pravṛtti*).
This 'seeing the secondary' is as explained in the seventh fascicle of the treatise. Regarding the term *Brahmāvarta*, in this region it is called the "Han Kingdom" (*Hán-guó*). That is to say—
The Westerners call this land of China "Gengqieguo" (根且國). In Sanskrit, it is called Mahācīna;
this is translated as "Dàtángguó" (大唐國). Thus, the Westerners call this Great Táng country "Mahācīna."
Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun shu chao), Fascicle Nine, End; Fascicle Ten, Part One.
Composed by Dharma Master Lingtai of Beijing.
The explanation of the four kinds of ignorance pervading the three realms; the clarification of the eighty-four thousand mental activities (*citta-carita*).

It clarifies that there are benefits in two lifetimes, whereas being clear-sighted regarding only one lifetime is not called "good. It clarifies that the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) can give rise to the four types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*).

It clarifies the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). It clarifies the number of persons. It clarifies the objects of focus for the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). Halfway down, it clarifies the sixty [types of beings].
Regarding the two views, it clarifies the fourteen points of "indeterminate matters" (*avyākṛta*).

The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "That which generally exhorts the arising of the teaching" refers to the passage in the treatise [that says], "Now, one should extensively manifest those. This refers to the "distinctive characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

It generally exhorts the wisdom of others; that is, my explanation of the meanings of the universal (*sarvatraga*), object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*), and other mental factors is intended to instruct them so that they may give rise to faith.
Thus, the teaching of Vijñaptimātra was established.

Regarding the commentary’s question as to whether the mental factors (caitta) and the mind (citta) are identical or distinct, this will be addressed later in the treatise under the passage concerning whether these six categories are identical to or distinct from the mind.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the initial question by Satata and others concerning why only the five universal factors are mentioned, this will be addressed in the subsequent treatise text with the passage:
'Are these six identical to or different from the mind?'"
The Commentary states: "First, regarding the Sarvāstivāda and others. Question: It is only the five universal mental factors (*pañca-sarvatraga*) [that are so called].

However, in the Sarvāstivāda school, the five universal factors and the ten specific-objective factors (*pañca-viniyata*) are named "universal" (*sarvatraga*). These arise separately from the mind. Now, in the Mahāyāna, it is said that there are five universal factors.
Therefore, I now pose this question.
The *Śāstra* commentary states: "The Sautrāntikas and others ask why there are five real [mental factors] that function as universal.

However, according to the Sautrāntikas, only sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*)—these three—are universal; they exist whenever the mind arises. Yet, although contact (*sparśa*) and attention (*manasikāra*) are also...
Although they are pervasive, they are conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*). Now, in the Mahāyāna, the five vehicles and the five pervasive factors are all substantially existent (*dravyasat*).
Therefore, the present inquiry concerns the conventional and the substantial; it does not inquire into the ultimate meaning of "pervasiveness."
The Commentary states: "From the fifty-sixth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* up to the *Udayavibhaṅga-sūtra*":

within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, this *Āgama* scripture is also cited to clarify contact (*sparśa*). Furthermore, in the preceding third fascicle, the *Udayavibhaṅga-sūtra* is also cited to establish the existence of contact.

The Commentary states: "It is designated as a 'skandha' because it serves as the basis for the three dharmas of feeling, perception, and volition; it is mentioned here as the most prominent. Feeling, perception, and volition are subsumed under the [other] three skandhas.
Now, contact is the basis for feeling, perception, and volition; it is designated as a skandha because it is the most prominent basis for those three skandhas.

The *Śāstra* states: "That which corresponds to the *Hastipadopama-sūtra* (The Elephant’s Footprint Simile Sūtra). This sūtra clarifies that by means of the tracks of an elephant—such as its likeness—one knows the elephant and knows its location;

it is for this reason that the worldly name [is applied]. The *Śāstra* states: "The four [aggregates] without the aggregate of contact are always in harmonious union, etc. It further clarifies: "They are the aggregates of form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*), which are always in harmonious union."
Because they are conjoined. The treatise states: "If one attends to this, one cognizes this; if one attends to this, [it is] this.
Here, "this" refers to the object. The meaning of this passage is that the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and attention (*manasikāra*) always arise in mutual association. If one attends to this...

Regarding the statement, "The mind itself is that which discerns this": when attention (*manasikāra*) relies upon this object, there is simultaneously a mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*) that relies upon it together with it;
thus, there is "attention accompanied by mind. Furthermore, because it also takes the same object as the mental sovereign, there is indeed "attention."
The *Śāstra* states: "The fifty-fifth [chapter] cites the *Sūtra*, while the remainder cites the *Śāstra*.

However, regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fifty-fifth chapter) and this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, when these cite *sūtra* passages to prove the meaning of the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), they clarify the meaning of the universals themselves.

When citing other works such as the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, they cite textual evidence from those treatises to prove the meaning of the universals, rather than citing the *sūtras*.

[The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*] states: "Attention causes the mind to incline toward its own object. If, at the very moment one is correctly attending to this object, it is already termed "another's object" [i.e., an external object].
The treatise states that there is no instance where the mind arises without being accompanied by at least one [of these mental factors].

Regarding the statement that "contact necessarily arises from existence": as for "contact arising from that [existence]," it is said that contact is produced because of the coming together of the three.
As for "necessarily by virtue of existence," this means that it is precisely by virtue of the existence of contact that the three characteristics come to be.

However, this treatise is identical to the third section of the preceding treatise. That "contact arises dependent on that [object] and causes that [consciousness] to know the conjunction" is the same as the preceding statement that "contact arises dependent on that.
That "this 'that' definitely gives rise to contact" is identical to the preceding statement that "it causes them to conjoin.
As for the argument in the treatise stating, "When a thoughtless state arises, it is because of a single following," such a thought does not arise.

At that time, among the three types of feeling (*vedanā*), one does not possess all three simultaneously. Rather, it is accompanied by either a single painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*), a pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*), or an indifferent feeling (*upekṣāvedanā*).
This is because, within the category of feeling, all three cannot arise concurrently, as they are mutually exclusive;
thus, when the mind arises, only one feeling can arise accordingly. Regarding the statement that "among volition (*cetanā*) there is also one or another," this refers to that same volition.

It is also capable of producing wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral karma; since it pervades all three moral natures, when a single moment of mind arises, only one—such as a wholesome nature—can arise.
Because these three natures cannot arise simultaneously, it is said that there is no "concomitance with any one [of them]."

Question: Regarding the five omnipresent factors (*sarvatraga*), if in the passage concerning clarity, volition, and feeling it is stated that one obtains "any one" (*anyatama*) of them, why is it not stated that "any one" of the others—contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), and mental aspect (*ākāra*)—is obtained? Answer: Indeed, within those [others] there are three categories;

thus, one should also say "any one. Furthermore, among contacts, there are agreeable contacts (*iṣṭa-sparśa*), disagreeable contacts (*aniṣṭa-sparśa*), and contacts that are neither. Within these contacts...

The text is abbreviated and does not state it explicitly; however, it should logically be included here, as it is identical to the case of *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought).
If *manasikāra* (attention) were capable only of verbal expression and only of grasping the object—functioning solely within its own limited scope—it would not have multiple categories.

Therefore, in the text, when clarifying *nimitta-manasikāra* (attention to signs) and so forth, it does not say "any one of them. However, *vedanā* (feeling), *saṃjñā* (perception), and *cetanā* (volition) all possess three types; therefore, in the text...
This refers to "one of them. Since there are three types of contact, at the moment a single thought arises, it likewise corresponds to one specific type of contact.
The commentary states, "it is not non-blue," which means that it is blue and not something else, such as yellow.

The commentary states: "The objects of focus (*ālambana*) and the spheres (*āyatana*)" is a general designation for the objective field. "And the spheres" refers to the specific limits or boundaries of apprehending the object;
that is, taking one sphere or two spheres as the object, and so on, up to sometimes taking the twelve spheres (*dvādaśāyatana*) or the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*) as the object.
This passage describes the mental activity of causing the mind to apprehend the characteristics of the correct cause and so forth, which constitutes wholesome action (*kuśala-karman*).

"Et cetera" (*ādi*): "Cause" (*hetu*) refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that grasp the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). "Aspect" (*nimitta*) refers to the aspect of the object of perception (*ālambana-viṣaya*).

The meaning of this passage is that it is precisely because of the aspect of an unwholesome object (*akuśala-viṣaya-nimitta*) that the mind and its mental factors give rise to an unwholesome state of mind.
As stated in the treatise: "The arising of the unwholesome occurs due to three conditions. First, the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) such as greed have not yet been abandoned..."

First, because [the roots] have been permanently severed; second, because an object conducive to affliction has appeared before one; and third, because improper attention and sleep arise in the present.

Furthermore, this also transcends the characteristics of wholesome objects, which are the causes for the arising of a wholesome mind. When a wholesome mind arises, it likewise possesses three conditions.

First, because the seeds of the wholesome have not yet been impaired; second, because a mental state conducive to the wholesome is present before one; and third, because correct reflection and cultivation arise manifestly.

By virtue of these meanings, when wholesome mind and mental factors pass beyond an indeterminate object and give rise to an indeterminate state, that which arises from the indeterminate also possesses two bases:
it takes the indeterminate seeds as its object, and those seeds have neither been impaired nor are they conducive [to change].
Because the object is present before one, and because half of the mind is correctly manifesting.
The commentary states that since the subsequent section says desire can give rise to right effort (*samyak-vīrya*), the former interpretation is superior;
this refers to the previous explanation that effort can be said to have faith as its basis, meaning desire serves as the support for the exertion of diligence.

The commentary states: "Regarding the phenomena that can be conventionally designated as 'outflowing' (*sāsrava*) or 'outflow-free' (*anāsrava*), and even those that can be ultimately designated as 'objects of pursuit' (*heya-dharma*):
