To speak according to ultimate reality, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) are objects of pursuit. The Truths of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and Origination (*samudaya-satya*) are phenomena to be loathed;

this is precisely what is meant by "wholesome desire. Now, regarding the correct meaning herein: if one takes delight in phenomena of the three natures—unwholesome (*akuśala*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*)—all such things are termed [objects of pursuit].
It can be abandoned (*praheya*). This refers to the two natures of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the path (*mārga*); it does not refer to cessation (*nirodha*).
That which is untainted (*anāsrava*) is called "that which can be abandoned. The commentary states: "If within one's own body there is that which is loathsome, it is not appropriate [to remain];

even when the subsequent consciousnesses depart from their state, down to things that are not loathsome—this dharma is a loathsome thing, and wherever there is a loathsome thing, there must necessarily be something that can be abandoned. Based upon such things as 'that which can be abandoned,' [the mind] arises..."
Because of desire. For example, when one develops revulsion toward the internal body, one must necessarily develop attraction toward external objects.
Thus, regarding the internal body, there is no desire for that which is repulsive; regarding external objects, there is desire for that which is attractive.
Or, if one develops revulsion toward external objects, it is likewise that one develops attraction toward the internal body. [The opponent] asks this teacher: "If [it is] an external object..."
One gives rise to revulsion. This immediately produces a sense of loathing toward the internal body. How could both delight and revulsion arise within a single moment of mind?

When one contemplates that which is to be reviled, this applies to all six consciousnesses; or, it may refer to only six [of the eighteen elements]. This is as when one practices the contemplation of loathing toward the three realms:

at that time, the contemplations of delight and revulsion cannot be performed simultaneously. If one is correctly performing the contemplation of revulsion, the desire realm is perceived as suffering, coarse, and obstructive.

At that time, the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) cannot yet constitute the contemplation of excellence (*udārāpekṣā*). If one contemplates excellence as being "calm," "sublime," or "detached," it is then the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Furthermore, at the time of contemplating excellence, its essence consists of a portion of non-hatred (*adveṣa*) associated with the desire realm;

if it is a state of aversion (*vidūṣaṇā*), its essence consists of a portion of non-attachment (*alobha*) associated with wisdom (*prajñā*). However, according to the Mahāyāna, the distinction between aversion and detachment should be analyzed through a fourfold logical permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is aversion that is not detachment. This refers to the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) which takes the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and origination (*samudaya-satya*) as its object;

because it involves a profound aversion toward suffering and origination, it possesses the quality of preparation, yet it is unable to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus is not called detachment. There is detachment that is not aversion.

This refers to the immediate path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) which take the truths of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the path (*mārga-satya*) as their objects; because they are able to sever the afflictions, they are called detachment. As for that cessation...

The Path (mārga), although it is something to be pursued, is called "non-repugnant" (anudvega). There are those that are both repugnant and abandoned; these refer to the Truths of Suffering and Origination within the path of liberation immediately following [the realization of] the Truths of Suffering and Origination.
Because the Truths of Suffering and Origination are objects to be repugnant, they are called "repugnant"; because they can sever the afflictions (kleśa), they are also called "repugnant.

There are those that are neither repugnant nor abandoned; these refer to the Truths of Cessation and the Path. Furthermore, regarding the preparatory path (prayoga-mārga) of the Truth of the Path, it is said that Cessation and the Path are... [to be pursued].
It is not that [the seventh consciousness] lacks aversion; it is simply that it cannot sever the afflictions.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Although the seventh consciousness, or perhaps only the sixth, possesses this desire," if the seventh consciousness were to possess desire, it would clarify that the seventh consciousness is not the correct tenet among the first three masters. As for the fourth master, [he holds that] within the seventh consciousness...
"Without desire.

The Commentary states: "The entirety of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, as well as a portion of the sixth consciousness—namely, the maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-citta*) and so forth—that functions spontaneously by following the power of its objects;
if it is the seventh consciousness, it perceives its object by following the power of its own arising; if it is the eighth [consciousness]..."

Regarding "consciousness" and "a portion of the six consciousnesses that is maturation-consciousness": this refers to the spontaneous engagement with objects by the power of the causes of those [minds], which are themselves wholesome.

As for the question of why the scope of "desire" and "consciousness" differs across these three positions—whether it is only the first six consciousnesses or only the sixth—it is asked: what is the purpose of these three masters' differing explanations? It is said that the first master may be interpreted as follows: [The first master holds that] desire is broad while consciousness is narrow; [the second master holds that] desire is narrow while consciousness is broad; [the third master holds that] both desire and consciousness are equally broad. Thus, their respective assertions differ according to the specific context of the treatise. This is because the first master’s position is based on the principle that the term "desire" (*kāma*) primarily refers to the objects of enjoyment, whereas the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) primarily refers to the subjective mind. Since the objects of enjoyment are vast and manifold, he asserts that desire is broad. However, because the maturation-consciousness is restricted to the five sense-faculties and their objects, he asserts that consciousness is narrow. The other two masters, conversely, prioritize the subjective mind over the objects of enjoyment, and thus they assert that consciousness is broad while desire is narrow. Therefore, there is no contradiction among them. Furthermore, the first master’s view can be understood as follows: [text continues].

The locus of aversion (nirveda) pervades all six consciousnesses, or it may be restricted to the sixth alone. Regarding the objects within this context, it is common for all eight consciousnesses to be involved.
The second master states that it pertains only to the first seven consciousnesses, or specifically to the sixth, because desire exists therein, and so forth, up to the point of aspiration and hope.
The third master states that it pertains only to the first six consciousnesses; whether it is the six or only the sixth, this can be understood through reflection. There is [a teaching].
Regarding "right" and "wrong," the *Śāstra* states, and so on until it concludes: "Liberation is firm and ultimate nirvāṇa.

This refers to the explanation of the Master of the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, who says that one generates desire for unwholesome dharmas, and even generates desire for the wholesome dharmas of humans and devas.
Even regarding nirvāṇa, one gives rise to desire; thus, one knows that desire is omnipresent (*sarvatraga*). As for "firm liberation":

if it were of a worldly nature, or if it were to arise again at a later time, it would be called "not firm. However, because the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*) has severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) and they will never arise again, it is called "firm.
From this, it is further known that entry into the first path is due to the wholesome (*kuśala*).
Regarding "the desire for the Dharma": In response to this question, various sūtras and śāstras all clarify the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) at the beginning;

they all state that faith is the primary gateway for entering the Dharma, and that faith is the basis for desire. Yet, in this specific context, it is stated that desire itself is the primary gateway for entering the Dharma. Answer:

If one is considering the initial stage of an ordinary person who understands the events and dharmas of a sūtra through conditions, then faith is indeed the primary gateway. However, in the present case...
When investigating the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), desire is taken as the primary starting point;
yet each [explanation] relies on a single meaning and is not mutually contradictory. The commentary states, "up to liberation as the final limit":

the total exhaustion of afflictions (*kleśa*) is termed "liberation" (*niḥsaraṇa*), because *nirvāṇa* is the ultimate limit of saṃsāra. Alternatively, "liberation" is simply another name for *nirvāṇa*.
The Commentary states: "Each of the three time periods can be understood through comparative analysis. Regarding the previous explanation concerning the three masters:
if it refers to the first two masters, since desire takes the objects of aversion as its domain, that desire only takes the future as its object and does not take the past as its object.

If it refers to the third master, desire takes all three time periods as its object, because desire is able to take the objects of aversion as its domain. The Treatise states: "Resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*)."
This is because, just as when a person develops doubt regarding phenomena of the three natures—such as the wholesome—and thus fails to reach certainty, they are not said to be "superior.

Later, when they understand these phenomena of the three natures, the teacher says, "Perhaps this understanding is it," because the mind that understands is superior to the extreme state of the [doubting] mind.
Therefore, it is called "resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*). Resolute conviction pervades all three natures. The Dharma Master says that "conviction" (*adhi*) means "to resolve.
If one speaks of it specifically in terms of what is superior, then when it arises toward the dharmas of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, it may be termed "resolute conviction."
It is not identical to the phenomena of birth and death. This preceding section concerns resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), which is exclusively of a wholesome nature (*kuśala*).

Regarding the statement in the commentary, "By the reasoning of the Sautrāntika school, it is established through the power of realization and so forth": that which is external to the Buddha's teaching is called a false path (*mithyāmārga*);

the principles expounded by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are called false principles (*mithyānaya*); and the four dhyāna-concentrations attained by non-Buddhists are called false realizations (*mithyāsākṣātkāra*).
The Commentary states: "It is absent even as a minor portion within a defiled mind. If there is doubt within a defiled mind, there is no resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
Likewise, within wholesome or neutral states, if one has not yet reached a decision regarding the object, there is also no resolute conviction."
The commentary states: "The 'intention of the masters of the Abhidharma' refers to the Abhidharma treatises as conceived by the masters of the Sarvāstivāda.
Since this [text] primarily refutes the Sarvāstivāda, [it refers to them]."
The Commentary states: "If a certain dharma exists in other sūtras here as well, it should likewise exist even in the higher stages. To this, an objection is raised:

"To examine the case where 'resolute conviction' (adhimokṣa) is permitted in some places while it is denied in others—where it is said that there is no resolute conviction—if one also says that there is resolute conviction [there], then one must also admit that vitarka and vicāra exist in the desire realm and the first dhyāna; would they not also have to exist in the higher stages where they are absent?"

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Therefore, the mental factors of mindfulness (*smṛti*) are the traces of concentration (*samādhi*) and are firm. Non-greed (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adveṣa*) are the causes of ethical discipline (*śīla*);

mindfulness is the cause of concentration; and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) is the cause. "Traces" (*traces*) has the meaning of "causes. Question: Greed, hatred, and delusion—these three—are the roots of unwholesomeness (*akuśala-mūla*).
Now that these three roots have been established as the roots of wholesomeness (*kuśala-mūla*), why are only non-greed and non-hatred established as the "traces of my ethical discipline"?
These two [ignorance and hatred] can obstruct the precepts; furthermore, because ignorance pervades all defiled minds, it cannot obstruct the precepts.
The commentary states: "Some have already received its substance, up to the point of being driven by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take other realms as their objects.

Regarding "having already received its substance," this refers to the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), because ordinary beings have previously taken these five sense-objects as their objective basis. Alternatively, regarding "not yet having obtained its substance," it is as follows:
Regarding the truths of cessation and the path: because ordinary beings have never before attained them, their defiled minds and so forth are as follows.
For example, a person with wrong views has never before realized the untainted (anāsrava) cessation and path; they merely hear the names of the cessation and path of the Buddhas and noble ones.

Upon first hearing the names of cessation and the path, the mind undergoes a transformation and gives rise to the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) of cessation and the path. Taking cessation as its object, it conceives [of it] as non-existent.
One forms the understanding that there is the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is neither arising nor ceasing.

If the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) also transforms into being conditioned yet untainted (*anāsrava*), this is the culmination of such understanding. Later, when the Truth of the Path is extinguished, one again takes as an object of perception its aspect of non-arising and non-ceasing;
this is called "taking that cessation and the path as its object. Because this is the untainted cessation and the path, it consequently...

They do not take [the object] as their direct support; they merely take that class [of phenomena] as their object. When taking the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) perceived upon the mind through the power of vision, all such [cognitions] are with-outflow (*sāsrava*).

Now, this is the primary explanation regarding the fundamental nature of the remote objective condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*). As for why those [cognitions] directed toward the outflow-free (*anāsrava*)—namely, the path of cessation and the path of abandonment—each take their own mind’s immediate image-part as their object, it is because when taking objects that are with-outflow, or when employing the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), or when taking phenomena belonging to other stages (*bhūmi*), [they likewise take their respective immediate image-parts].
None of these are established; they all take as their object the single *sākāra-bhāga* (objective aspect) of one's own mind. First, regarding false views:

when they take uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) knowledge of others' minds as their object, or take phenomena belonging to another stage (*bhūmi*) as their object, these are all explained in terms of the primary substantial object (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

This is why they are established, even up to the case of taking phenomena of another stage as an object, which is also called "taking that category" as its object. As for the Sarvāstivāda school, when a contaminated mind takes the uncontaminated path as its object...
It does not constitute a condition (*pratyaya*), because its nature as a condition is not concordant.

Just as gold that is solid and firm does not allow the force of coarse afflictions (*kleśa*) to enter within it, so too when a mind with outflows (*sāsrava*) takes an object with outflows, the nature and characteristics of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) gather and enter within it, thereby becoming outflowing.
For this reason, the bodies of Buddhas and the minds of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) among the two vehicles are [considered] outflowing.

Due to the condition of afflictions (*kleśa*), poisonous vapors enter and thereby become outflowing (*sāsrava*). Regarding these texts, there are four interpretations for the substance of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the categories of the object-condition.
Furthermore, this does not rely on the immediate (*sākṣāt*) image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*). To explain the substance and categories of the object-condition:

if one takes the first immediate part, it is because wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) takes the first untainted (*anāsrava*) [dharmas] as its object; conversely, when taking the image-parts of dharmas belonging to other stages, all are termed "immediate grasping" (*sākṣāt-grahaṇa*). Therefore...

Now, I shall briefly explain the conditions (*pratyaya*) for the sake of understanding. This text constitutes the first [section], which explains the nature and categories of the conditions based on whether they are contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and regarding the feelings (*vedanā*) already experienced.

If one recollects as if it were direct perception (*pramāṇa*), then within a mind that is not a valid cognition (*apramāṇa-citta*), the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and so forth that were previously conditioned are all acquired through feeling;
this is termed the "nature of the condition. If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) has never before attained [such realization]...

Because they are untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas. For example, when wrong view takes the untainted truths of cessation and the path as its object, it is called "taking the category" (*ālambana-jāti*), not "taking the substance" (*ālambana-dravya*).

Furthermore, there are four interpretations. First, within the tainted (*sāsrava*) [dharmas]: a dharma that has already been experienced is called "taking the substance," which falls under past dharmas;
a dharma not yet experienced is called "taking the category," which is designated as future. This refers to taking what is proximate and immediate; "proximate" means immediate.

"Condition. Up to "having completed the conditions of others and the conditions of the elements"—this is the second interpretation, which is essentially the same as the first proximate interpretation.

When one recollects and takes as an object phenomena belonging to one’s own level (*svabhūmi*), it is called "taking the substance as an object" (*dravyālambana*), because it pertains to one’s own level.

If one recollects and takes as an object phenomena belonging to another realm (*dhātu*) or another level (*bhūmi*), it is called "taking the category as an object" (*jātālambana*), because it pertains to a different level; thus, one does not become attached to them.
The term "proclivity" (*anuśaya*) refers to what is called *anusaya* in the newer sūtras and śāstras. In the older sūtras and śāstras, afflictions (*kleśa*) are referred to by the term "proclivity."
If afflictions and unwholesome dharmas are like the master, then indeterminate dharmas are like the servants.

Thus, they afflict other wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas, thereby constituting the state of being "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) and "unwieldy" (*akarmanyatā*). As it says in the older sūtras:

"That is to say, one is driven by the latent tendency of greed, driven by the latent tendency of hatred, driven by the latent tendency of delusion," and so forth. However, the Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty, having observed...
Having finished this, he immediately raised an objection, saying: "If it is simply because they are 'proclivities' (*anuśaya*), how could the 'breath' of a person enter into the body of a slave?
When afflictions act as proclivities toward wholesome or neutral states, do those afflictions actually enter into the substance of the wholesome states and so forth?"
For this reason, in the new translations of sūtras and śāstras by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty, the term *anuśaya* is used.

In the Mahāyāna, *anuśaya* is explained as "following along" (*anugata*), meaning it lies dormant within sentient beings and so forth. The Hīnayāna also explains *anuśaya* as in the *Abhidharmakośa-vyākhyā*:

it refers to the state of being unserviceable (*akarmanyatā*) and so forth that arises within the substance of tainted wholesome and neutral phenomena due to the conditions of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Thus, it follows along.
Sleep is defined as that which conditions past latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Furthermore, another interpretation states:

regarding "distant" and "near," if there is a person who, because the dharmas attained in this present life are not forgotten, [those dharmas] are termed "conditioning the substance" (*ālambana-vastu*); whereas those dharmas forgotten over many lifetimes that are later recollected, [are termed "conditioning the object"].

This refers to the category (*jāti*). Regarding the statement that subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) taking conditioned, untainted phenomena as its object is also called "taking that category as its object":
the third point concerns subsequent wisdom. It is called "taking the substance as its object" if it takes [the substance] as its category;

if subsequent wisdom takes conditioned, untainted phenomena as its object, it is called "taking the object," because they are mutually inclusive in terms of their characteristics. If subsequent wisdom takes true suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth as its object, it is called "taking the category as its object. It is not...

Because it is directly apprehended. If subsequent cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) takes the Truth of the Path as its object, it is said to "take that essence as its object," because it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

If subsequent cognition takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, it is said to "take that category as its object," because there is a distinction between the conditioned and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

[in this case], it is the ultimate characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that takes True Suchness as its object, yet it does not directly realize it. The fourth [point] explains the taking of the essence by way of both fundamental (*mūla*) and subsequent cognition.

Regarding "categories" (*jāti*): fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) attains the essence (*tattva*) by taking true thusness (*tathatā*) as its object, whereas subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) attains the category (*jāti*) by taking true thusness as its object.

However, when the first moment of subsequently attained wisdom takes true thusness as its object, it also takes the essence as its object because it directly realizes it; thus, it is also called "taking the category as its object," just as one practices the path that accords with the category of true thusness.
Therefore, the preceding stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*) is questioned, for at that time, the name "true thusness" itself constitutes the contemplation of true thusness.

That is to say, when this very first moment of non-conceptual [wisdom] takes True Suchness (tathatā) as its object, it is—considering it from the perspective of a single moment—that True Suchness is precisely that which was previously heard under the name "I" during the stage of preparatory application (prayoga). Therefore, it is said to take that category as its object; thus, it is indeed so.

This is because it has already been heard that the substance of the "I" is [True Suchness]. If one considers the second, third, and subsequent moments, they too should be called "taking [it] as an object."

The essence (*tattva*) and the category (*jāti*). This refers to the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) of the second moment, which directly realizes suchness (*tathatā*); this is called "taking that essence as its object.

Furthermore, this very suchness is of the same category as the suchness of the first moment’s self; it should likewise be called a "category. This applies up to the intermediate stages and the stage of Buddhahood.

Non-conceptual wisdom realizes the truth, and all [realizations] possess a "substantial category" (*tattva-jāti*). It is called a "substance" (*tattva*) because it is directly attained as a substance;

the "category" (*jāti*) refers to the class of this very *tathatā* (suchness). If one does not give rise to any thought regarding such categories as *nirvāṇa* and so forth, one is like other worldly people who, having never heard the name of *nirvāṇa*, are unable to give rise to thoughts directed toward *nirvāṇa*. This is the case for those who study the Buddha-dharma.

Having heard the name of *nirvāṇa*, one immediately gives rise to a mental representation (*saṃjñā*) regarding *nirvāṇa*. As for the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvedanabhāga*) serving as the cause for subsequent recollection, this is taught in three places throughout the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only):
first, at the end of the first fascicle, it states that by the power of the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), they are able to serve as the cause for recollection;
second, it is as when establishing the capacity of the self-witnessing division to serve as the cause for subsequent [recollection].
In this regard, the recollection is identical [in both systems]. Thirdly, as for the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic) being able to serve as the cause of recollection:
taking the grasping of mental images (*saṃjñā*) as the cause of recollection is acceptable to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Question:

As explained in the subsequent text, when the mind and so forth grasp an object, the perfumed capacity (*vāsanā*) remains within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). This serves as the cause for recollection at a later time due to the power of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). How is this so?
There are such phenomena as memory and cognition; how does this differ from the treatise? The answer is that they are similar.

If one asserts that a functional activity (*kāritra*) is established upon a previously existing entity, the meaning of this passage is that because the preceding moment possesses a self-verifying essence (*svasaṃvedana-svabhāva*), it is itself divided into [the aspects of] essence and function.
Regarding the subsequent thought that perceives the differentiation of functions and is able to recollect the essence of wholesome thoughts:
the commentary states, "This is because it arises subsequently from a deluded mind. This means it arises subsequently from a defiled meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

"That is to say, as when a deluded mind arises after absorption" means, for example, as when a person attains an absorption of a higher realm and, upon emerging from that state of concentration, [a deluded mind arises].
Furthermore, delusion can also arise [from it], just as when a "red" concentration (*rakta-samādhi*) is immediately induced from a pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*).

In "red" concentration, a mind of delusion exists simultaneously; this is also like a temporarily distracted mind bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Upon emerging from concentration, a mind of delusion can likewise arise.
The Commentary states: "When tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*) arises, it can know its object and apprehend its characteristics.

However, when these two types of people are within a tainted meditative concentration (*samādhi*), their wisdom can know what is lost but cannot know what is gained. Once they have emerged from concentration, they know what is gained but do not know what is lost.
If a bodhisattva is within an untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), they are simultaneously able to know both gain and loss.
The commentary states: He [the opponent] counters by asking, "If there is no state of mind within concentration, and even in the absence of mind one seeks defilement for oneself..."

The adherents of the Hīnayāna raise this objection: "If one could abide in a single object even when lacking a concentrated mind (*samādhi*), then at the time of experiencing the relish (*āsvādana*) [of meditative absorption], the mind would necessarily be defiled.
Since the mind cannot be defiled when free from greed (*lobha*), we know that it is only when concentration is present that the mind can separately attain stability in a single object."

The Commentary states: "This [objection] is not so. Even when focusing intently on an object of observation (*ālambana*), how could it be that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is necessarily assumed here?
If many moments of mind focus intently on an object of observation, this is due to concentration.

However, if even a single moment of mind abides in its object, it does not do so by virtue of having concentration. This is because once a phenomenon has arisen, it abides for that single moment of its own accord."
The Commentary states: "It is not the case that because greed and so forth do not exist, defilement cannot be established. Does this passage make sense? It should rather state:
"Defilement is not established by means of greed and so forth."

The Commentary states: "As for the statement that although the dharmas such as mindfulness (smṛti) have volition (cetanā) as their essence, they are not identical to it, this refers to the Sautrāntika masters.

According to them, only feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and volition (cetanā)—these three—are real, because they are the constant [factors] among the aggregates. When mindfulness, wisdom (prajñā), greed (lobha), hatred (dveṣa), and so forth arise, they are merely conventional designations established upon the basis of volition."
The Commentary states: "It is not the case that all who are deluded do so because of wrong views. Regarding those who are predominant:

if one is deluded and yet relishes [the state], then there is no wisdom. If one possesses only delusion without relishing it, then there is wisdom; for example, a person with wrong views, though deluded, does not relish it.

The Commentary states: "The arising of the stages is also without the simultaneous presence of 'mine' (mamakāra) or 'I' (ahaṃkāra). This treatise follows entirely the Sarvāstivāda school. The Commentary further states:
"This is the position of Sthiramati, which is now collectively criticized. According to the tradition of the Brahmin masters, it is transmitted that the Westerners criticize Sthiramati, saying:
"Sometimes [a cognition] arises as one; regarding what is desired, it arises only as desire," and so on, up to "because the object is not determined. There is none.

Regarding "resolute conviction" (*adhimokṣa*): in this passage, if it is argued that although the object is not fixed, resolute conviction can nevertheless arise, then the fact that the initial desired [object] does not give rise to resolute conviction would contradict the subsequent text. The subsequent text states: "Greed and delusion cannot arise simultaneously;
because there is no decisive determination regarding the object, there is no stained attachment. This is because the *Mūla-śāstra* states that it is the object of wisdom (*prajñā*). However, only...
Regarding the explanation of consciousness (*vijñapti*): it is because the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) was composed based upon six sūtras and eleven treatises.

Those six sūtras and eleven treatises are all the fundamental sūtras and fundamental treatises. However, that which is definitively taken as the object of contemplation is precisely what has already been mastered through the names [of those teachings] via the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-mayī*, *cintā-mayī*, and *bhāvanā-mayī* prajñā).
The Commentary states: "One who merely fixes the mind on the space between the eyebrows without being able to discern the object of this meditative concentration" refers to a person who,

although having heard from a teacher that one should dwell with the mind fixed between the eyebrows, or having personally sought it in the sūtras and śāstras and seen mentions of dwelling between the eyebrows,
observes such fixation— whether on the space between the eyebrows or on a lamp flame— and is even able to recognize that this [object] is suffering.
It is empty; we do not know what corresponds to it. Furthermore, this form is always form, yet it is only because the mind is bound to it.

If a person is distracted, they should bind the mind between the eyebrows; or at times, practice counting the breath; or for one who practices desire, contemplate the impurity of the heart and so forth.

The *Śāstra* says: "This second interpretation, from 'or the object of observation' up to 'from the majority of others,' interjects that this state of delusion possesses concentration (*samādhi*) but lacks superior wisdom (*prajñā*).

If it refers to the first interpretation, it concerns the initial stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-avasthā*), wherein there exist the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-mayī*, *cintā-mayī*, and *bhāvanā-mayī* prajñā).
Subsequently, at the time of correctly observing the space between the eyebrows, there is concentration but no wisdom. If this [refers to] the latter..."

[Commentary: Regarding the statement, "If the preceding preparatory mind lacks the two types of wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī* prajñā*), and this person lacks wisdom, from what state of mind would they learn to attain this understanding?

Furthermore, it is asked: "Regarding the phrase 'the corners of the eyes meet with a wrathful gaze' (*krodha-prajñā-koṇa-netra-saṃprekṣaṇa*), does 'wrath' (*krodha*) constitute a separate entity [from anger] (*pratigha*)?
Moreover, the sub-commentary states: 'Or, if greed (*rāga*) arises, how can it be called wrathful anger (*krodha-pratigha*)? [This refers to the distinction between] greed and hatred."

Because they do not arise simultaneously. Furthermore, how can these [notions of] horns and eyes be so named? Moreover, as for the objects of this deluded thought and agitated wisdom, how can they be called "objects of observation"?
Such reflection does not proceed by way of the principles of the Four Noble Truths, nor at times by way of logical reasoning.

The Commentary states: "Alternatively, the principle of the later time" refers to the principle of the Four Noble Truths; alternatively, it refers to the principle of time. All that is explained herein is based on the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*).

However, this is here provisionally designated as the "stage of the cause" from a limited perspective. That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is the cause, and that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is the fruit.

Furthermore, the fruit is not defined by reference to the Buddha-stage; this is just as in the case of the ten excellences (*viśeṣa*), where the six perfections (*pāramitā*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are included.
The [five] objects are called the "causes," while the six perfections (ṣaḍpāramitā) on the stages (bhūmi) are called the "fruits.

Now, according to the actual state of affairs, all untainted minds (anāsrava-citta) possess the five specific objects (viśeṣālambana), because untainted minds are all endowed with twenty-one mental factors (caitasika-dharma).

If within tainted cultivated wisdom (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā), it likewise possesses the five specific objects and thus also has twenty-one factors. However, within the wisdom derived from hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā), they are not as numerous; that is, the five specific objects may—[or may not].
At that time, three grades arise. If within the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), it is also like the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*).

Regarding the statement "from the arising of the sudden mind (*ābhoga-citta*) up to the uniform flow (*nisyanda*), one should know this according to the principle": if it is the sudden mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there are no five object-specific factors.

If it is the mind of seeking (*paryeṣaka-citta*), there is only the absence of resolve (*adhimokṣa*). As for the minds of determination, defilement, purity, and so forth, which constitute the uniform flow, [the same applies].
It is half-existent and half-nonexistent. In the state of Buddhahood, within the *sater* (impulsive) mind, there are also the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyatālambana*).
In the eighth [consciousness], the mind of uniform outflow (*nisyanda-citta*), there are likewise no five object-specific mental factors.
The Commentary states: "Intrinsic distraction" refers to the inability to enter meditative absorption within the five sensory consciousnesses;
this is intrinsic distraction (*svabhāva-vikṣepa*). It consists of six types: (1) internal distraction, which refers to improper concentration such as lethargy (*styāna*) and so forth;

(2) external distraction, which refers to restlessness (*auddhatya*) and regret (*kaukṛtya*), because they take the five external sense objects as their objective conditions; (3) intrinsic distraction, which is precisely the five faculties and the five consciousnesses. However, [this contradicts...].
The five mental consciousnesses are like thieves that together cultivate and accumulate [karmic seeds] over successive lifetimes; thus, they gather what is near and new.
However, when the eye perceives a form, the sixth mental consciousness does not follow along to perceive that object. Therefore, it is said that "the forms one sees are like those of a blind person."

Within this previously established meditative concentration, there is the concentration of hearing sounds. In this state, other mental consciousnesses do not follow the auditory consciousness to grasp at sounds, because it is like a newly transformed being.

There are four types of distraction regarding the signs: first, the distraction of craving for fame, which is the desire to let others know that one has already attained the signs of seated meditation;
second, the distraction of the five coarse heavy states, which is the mental reflection thinking, "I alone am capable of performing such meritorious deeds on the path."
The thought "I am a good person" arises from the mind and is thus a coarse and heavy state.

Sixth is inferior distraction (*hīna-vikṣepa*), which refers to not forming the intention to attain a lesser fruit, but seeking only unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*). If one engages in these six types of error, they are called distractions;

to be contrary to these five [types of distraction] is non-distraction. When one correctly enters the fundamental meditative absorption (*mauladhyāna*), the five sensory consciousnesses do not function, and the five [faculties] are induced.

Because of wisdom. Although the five consciousnesses, like the sixth consciousness, recollect objects previously experienced, [the text] states that they all induce the arising of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).

Question: Why does this passage state that that which takes a present object as its condition is called "conditioning by category" (*ālambanavarga*), and thus the five consciousnesses are said to be "conditioning by category"?

Furthermore, it states that taking a past object as its condition is called "conditioning by substance" (*ālambanadravya*). According to the preceding text, [this refers to] taking a past object as its condition.

Because it is remote, it should be called "conditioning by category" (*jāti-pratyaya*). If it conditions a present object, because it belongs to the [present] time, it should be called "conditioning by realization" (*sākṣāt-pratyaya*).

According to this text, one should know that the text ought to have stated "conditioning objects of another stage. Based on the essence of the conditioning, that which conditions its own or another's object is called "category" (*jāti*).
Reflect upon this.
The commentary states that "meditative equipoise" (samāhita) refers to concentration that is not distracted; it possesses mind and is not without mind.
Furthermore, because it is a stage (bhūmi) named "the stage of equipoise," the treatise says: "The stage of equipoise and the non-stage of equipoise. If it is meditative concentration (samādhi)...

The "attainment of dispersal" (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*) applies to states with mind, but not to those without mind. If it refers to meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), it applies to both states with mind and without mind.
Because there is tranquility even within the state with mind, and because one is able to reach this tranquility within the state without mind, it is called an "attainment.
Therefore, other treatises speak of the "attainment of signlessness" (*animitta-samāpatti*) and the "attainment of cessation" (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
The Commentary states: "That which is the nature of tranquility and harmony existing within all states of the body and mind.

However, at the time of entering meditative absorption, there is also a pervasive bliss upon the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and upon the great element of mind (*citta-mahābhūta*). This is the nature of the body-faculty; yet, at the time of entering absorption...

Above the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), there is also a pervasive satisfaction (*prasrabdhi*). This faculty of satisfaction is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) in nature and is not called pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

Pliancy is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*) in nature. As for the mind: if it is within the mental continuum, sometimes there is a mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and yet no body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
Regarding those who lack body-consciousness, within meditative absorption (*samādhi*) there is always the sixth consciousness; it is always the sixth.
Within consciousness there is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), and this is of a wholesome nature. A junior teacher asked the Master:

"Regarding the blue [object] induced by the mind within the five consciousnesses, since these too possess a state of being well-tempered and flowing, how can there be peaceful harmony (*anugraha*)? The answer is:

Because when one is in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), if the five consciousnesses are induced, they are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) and thus lack the well-tempered pliancy. However, if [they are induced] by means of meditative absorption...
The five consciousnesses induced by [the power of] effort are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). That is, they possess the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) of being well-regulated and tranquil.

If the five consciousnesses induced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are of a virtuous nature (*kuśala*), then within those five consciousnesses there is likewise the pliancy of being well-regulated and tranquil;

for pliancy is of a virtuous nature. Thus, for Bodhisattvas from the sixth stage upward, the five consciousnesses that arise from the virtuous nature produced within meditative concentration—those five consciousnesses are...

This refers to pliancy and lightness. Even the wholesome natures of the divine eye and divine ear consciousnesses that arise within the meditative minds of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles likewise possess pliancy.
The Commentary states: "Or, there is innate wisdom (*upapatti-pratilambhikā prajñā*), up to 'because it is of that same nature. The five consciousnesses also possess innate wisdom.

If one says that the essence of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation consists solely of supramundane and meditative consciousnesses, then when these three wisdoms induce the five consciousnesses within this mental consciousness, the five consciousnesses also come to possess what is produced by the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. These productions likewise belong to this mental consciousness.

Within consciousness, there are the categories of the three types of wisdom—those arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Therefore, if the mental consciousness gives rise to innate wisdom (*upapattilābhikī prajñā*), it induces innate wisdom within the five sensory consciousnesses as well.
If wisdom arising from hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*) arises within consciousness, it likewise induces wisdom arising from hearing within the five sensory consciousnesses.

If the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) arises within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it also induces the wisdom consisting of reflection within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).

If the wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) arises within the mental consciousness, it also induces that which is produced by the wisdom consisting of cultivation within the five sensory consciousnesses.

This is just as, for instance, when Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward constantly enter into the wisdom consisting of cultivation within their sixth consciousness, thereby inducing a virtuous nature within the five sensory consciousnesses; [the virtue] within the five sensory consciousnesses [is likewise induced].

The nature [of these] is comprised within that which is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*). If they arise within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), then that indeterminate nature is not comprised within what is produced through cultivation.
Why is this? Because the three types of wisdom—those consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation—as well as those produced by hearing and so forth, are not indeterminate;
they are exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*). This is because Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward lack the wisdoms of hearing and reflection.

Therefore, among the five consciousnesses, there is only that which is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*); there is none produced through hearing (*śruta-maya*) or reflection (*cintā-maya*).

Furthermore, for ordinary beings, followers of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage, if the sixth consciousness is in a state of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) for the sake of play, the resulting visual and auditory consciousnesses are neutral (*avyākṛta*). That which is neutral is not an ultimate attainment produced by cultivation.
If one says that the consciousnesses of the divine eye and so forth—which are indeterminate—are produced by wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), then one should counter-interrogate:
"The divine eyes and ears are also produced by wisdom born of cultivation; therefore, the divine eyes and ears should likewise be included among those things accomplished through cultivation.
Thus, it is known that although the divine eye-faculty and so forth are produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are not...
These are comprised within that which is produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*). The same applies to the five neutral sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).

As for the divine eyes and ears produced by the mental consciousness—whether attained through birth or through meditative concentration (*samādhi*)—and those induced by the two vehicles and by Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage, these enter into the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) for the sake of benefiting and gladdening others. These are the divine eyes and ears of consciousness that they bring forth.
The divine eye, divine ear, and consciousnesses are of a virtuous nature; therefore, their respective stages are subsumed under what is produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*).

Furthermore, the mental faculty (*manas*) is also capable of inducing the divine eye and divine ear for the sake of benefit and happiness. Moreover, within that which is produced by cultivation, all five aggregates (*skandha*) are present simultaneously:

the consciousness present at that time is the aggregate of consciousness; the feeling, perception, and volition present simultaneously are termed the three [mental] aggregates. If these are with outflows (*sāsrava*), [they are further categorized as such].

Regarding concentration (*samādhi*): there is the precept associated with concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*), which separately restrains the seven branches of body and speech; this is called the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). If it is untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), it is the meditative absorption associated with the Path (*mārga-saṃvara*);

because it is designated as "form," it is included therein. Among those produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), the five aggregates obtained upon reaching the fruit [of the path] are likewise included.

Furthermore, within the Hīnayāna, the deportment, craftsmanship, supernormal powers, and results of maturation (*vipākaja*) are exclusively of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*); they do not extend to the wholesome or unwholesome. If...

The arising of good and evil is subsumed within other dharmas; there are four types of inclusion under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, among these, the maturation (*vipāka*) is of an indeterminate nature;
the deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the skillful (*śailpasthānika*) pertain to all three natures; and the supernormal fruit (*nairmāṇika*) pertains to two natures.

The *Śāstra* states: "It is admitted that [the wisdom of] skillful supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vidyā*) and so forth are for the most part subsumed under the wisdom of profound discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*). A question is then posed to the latter master:
"If the wisdom of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*) also exists within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), then it would accord with the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.

However, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that among the six supernormal powers, only the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-abhijñā*) is detailed; this is because it is admitted that within the stage of Buddhahood, [this power] exists in the four grounds."
All possess them. As for the other five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they are all subsumed under the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).
It is not said that the five consciousnesses possess the wisdom of the divine eye or divine ear. To answer according to the actual reality:

the essence of the divine eye and divine ear is not the two consciousnesses themselves, but rather the wisdom associated with those two consciousnesses, as well as the wisdom associated with the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). If it were merely the divine eye alone...

The supernormal power of the ear (*śrotra-abhijñā*) takes preceding objects as its domain. Since there is no simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the objects seen and heard are like perceptions within a dream;
they cannot be clearly discerned, nor can one speak of them with certainty. It is only when the simultaneous mental consciousness is present that one can perceive objects with clarity.
Furthermore, this is because [the supernormal powers] are luminous, and because the divine eye and ear are frequently interrupted, whereas the mental consciousness has many aspects.

Because it is a continuation [of the preceding]. Therefore, regarding the stage of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-bhūmi*), speaking in terms of reality, it also takes as its object the wisdom associated with the divine eye and ear consciousnesses (*divyacakṣuḥ-śrotra-vijñāna-samprayukta-jñāna*).
According to the Sarvāstivādins, the six consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously. For instance, when the Bhikṣu Aśvajit went to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

When conversing with the Brahmā King, one who has produced the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear—having already engaged the visual consciousness regarding the body of that Brahmā King—then produces the auditory consciousness.
When the Brahmā King speaks, the auditory consciousness ceases; then, the mental consciousness arises again to produce speech and question that Brahmā King.
Furthermore, the divine eye and divine ear consciousnesses arise as they do for those of the Two Vehicles who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or perhaps knowing what is above them.

The minds of sentient beings in the lower realms are mostly [known by] the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). If a Buddha were to arise [with regard to] all sentient beings, he would do so solely through the arising of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) that knows them.
The Commentary states: "It is not like the case of the cause, where among the five consciousnesses, one only contemplates the category of the object.

If, among the five consciousnesses at the stage of the cause, they only take the present as their object, then all that takes a present object is called "contemplating the category. If, however, the five consciousnesses at the stage of the fruit take the three periods of time as their objects, then they take the substance of the object;
thus, those taking a past object are all called "taking the substance of the object."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “as previously explained,” the commentator has mistakenly referred to a preceding section of the treatise.

In that preceding section of the treatise, there is no discussion whatsoever regarding whether [the mental factors] are concomitant or non-concomitant within the category of the five object-specific mental factors (*pañca-viṣaya-niyata*).
The Commentary states: "This is explained from the perspective of other schools, asserting that the five consciousnesses lack desire and so forth. This explains the preceding point.
However, among the five masters' views on consciousness, the five [sensory] consciousnesses lack the five [mental factors] such as desire, while the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) possesses them.
Since there is already the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*) within the mental consciousness, could desire and the others also be associated with suffering?

The Commentary states: "Regarding the third character of the eighth [category], the five [mental factors] such as the object-specific ones (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*) also pertain to the three trainings (*triśikṣā*).

Within the person of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), these object-specific factors exist; however, they are specifically designated as being subsumed under 'neither-training-nor-non-training' (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣya*)."

The Commentary states: "The ninth [category], the three types of abandonment (trividha-prahāṇa)," refers to these five mental states, such as the object-determining consciousnesses (*viśeṣaṇa-viṣaya*), which also pertain to all three types of abandonment.

Since their nature is not that of afflictive, defiled dharmas, they do not pertain to abandonment by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*). If they are abandoned within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one abandons the bondage of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) because one abandons the afflictions that arise simultaneously with them.

If they are of a wholesome or neutral nature, they are abandoned within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) through the abandonment of the bondage of the object (*ālambana-bandhana*). If there is no... [text ends]

Regarding "outflows" (*āsrava*): are they not subsumed under that which is not to be abandoned? Among the five universal [afflictions] within the five types of sensation, those associated with the suffering and other sensations at the time of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are bonds to be abandoned through association.
Among those to be abandoned by the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), those within the wholesome and neutral [states] are all bonds by way of object-condition (*ālambana*).

Initially, these are abandoned by their own nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*), similar to the particular mental objects (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*). Those that are pervasive and untainted (*anāsrava*) are indeed subsumed under that which is not to be abandoned.

Furthermore, it is explained as follows: those mental factors of the specific objects (*viṣayaviśeṣa*) that arise simultaneously with the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)—namely, the specific-object and universal (*sarvatraga*) factors—are of an unwholesome nature (*akuśaladharma*).

That which is of an unwholesome nature is abandoned by its very nature (*svabhāvaprahātavya*). If the five [mental factors] beginning with the specific objects arise simultaneously with the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they likewise include those abandoned by their own nature;
however, if they are untainted (*anāsrava*), they are not to be abandoned. Thus, one attains resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).

The Commentary states: "The eleventh [category] abandons nine faculties. This refers to those among the universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) mental factors that are recorded as being subsumed within the twenty-two faculties.
Specifically, among the object-specific factors, mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are subsumed within the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*);

that is, they are subsumed within the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. As for desire (*chanda*) and resolve (*adhimokṣa*), they likewise are not included among the twenty-two.

It is subsumed under two faculties. If, among the universal factors, it is categorized solely as feeling (*vedanā*), then it is subsumed under the five feeling faculties (*pañca-vedanendriya*) among the twenty-two faculties.

However, when associated with attention (*manasikāra*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), contact (*sparśa*), and mental formations (*saṃskāra*), it is not subsumed among the twenty-two faculties. If one asks whether it is discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) or non-discernment (*apratisaṃkhyā*)...

That is to say, among the five universal and specific-object mental factors: if they are of the indeterminate nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), they are subsumed under "discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā*);
if they are of the wholesome or indeterminate nature, such as minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), they are subsumed under "non-discernment" (*apratisaṃkhyā*).
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the outflow-tainted wholesome mind may not arise simultaneously,' etc.:

when an outflow-tainted wholesome mind arises, among the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayālambana*), it may at times give rise to one, two, three, or four; this is termed 'not simultaneous. At other times, it may give rise to all five;
this is termed 'simultaneous.'"
The commentary states: "It is not because of the distinction between the modes of joy (*abhirati*) and dejection (*daurmanasya*) within the afflictions (*kleśa*) [that they are excluded].

This means that it is not on account of the distinction between joy and dejection among the afflictions that the five object-specific mental factors (*pañca viṣayālambanāni*) do not associate with them; rather, this excludes only doubt (*vicikitsā*), as it cannot coexist with resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).

All others, however, can indeed associate. This passage thus provides a comprehensive clarification. It is not the case that among the mental afflictions there exists a mode of equanimity (*upekṣā*) characterized by joy.

Because hatred (*dveṣa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and so forth are of a nature of dejection (*daurmanasya*), and because among the wholesome states there are both those produced through application (*prayoga*) and those acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*), and because they take the three time periods as objects and take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as objects—these are specifically called the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣaya-niyata*). They do not associate with the aforementioned afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth.
Now it is stated that all of them can indeed associate with the object-specific factors; if the five object-specific factors were to associate with the root [afflictions], then...
It is so; it can also take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object.

The Commentary states: "Among the wholesome [mental factors], such as the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), they can specifically take both the conditioned and the unconditioned as objects; therefore, they are associated with them.

Furthermore, among the specific objects (*viśeṣālambana*), they also extend to the wholesome wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śrutamayī-, cintāmayī-, bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). The essence of these wholesome wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation is precisely the factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) within the category of mental objects.

It also extends to innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*). It can also take the three periods of time as its object, and it can also take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object; all of these are capable of association (*saṃprayoga*).
One should state that it is "not non-associated," yet the word "not" (*na*) has been omitted from the commentary.
The treatise states: Desire has aspiration as its nature and diligent application as its function. Resolve has the maintenance [of an object] as its nature and cannot be altered.
Mindfulness has clear recollection without forgetting as its nature and serves as the basis for concentration.
Concentration has the focusing of the mind without distraction as its nature and serves as the basis for wisdom. Wisdom has discernment as its nature and the severing of doubt as its function.

Question: Regarding this single category of mental factors (*caitasika*) with distinct objects (*viṣayaviśeṣa*), why is it that some have their own primary function as their activity (*karma*), while others have the function of another as their activity, such that they differ from one another?
Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun shu chao), Scroll Ten, Part One;
Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun shu chao), Scroll Ten, Part Two.
Composed by Dharma Master Lingtai of Beijing.

Regarding the establishment of the three factors beginning with equanimity (*upekṣā*), following the sequence already explained up to the establishment of these three: "establishment" refers to the remote [factors].
Equanimity and heedfulness (*apramāda*) are established based on the three roots of non-attachment (*alobha*) and so forth, together with vigor (*vīrya*).

Non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) is established based on the two roots of non-hatred (*adveṣa*). Therefore, it is said that the three beginning with equanimity are established. These are taken by means of the three roots, with vigor being mentioned last.
The Commentary states: "Because this is the equanimity (*upekṣā*) of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), it is distinct from the equanimity of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*).

To say "equanimity of the formations" means that it is the equanimity within the aggregate of formations, not the feeling of equanimity within the aggregate of feeling. In order to distinguish it from the equanimity within the aggregate of feeling, it is specifically designated as "the equanimity of the formations."

The Commentary states: "As for those who say 'the Vibhāṣā, Dharmatrāta, Dharmakīrti, Vasumitra, and the Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya,' these four masters—Dharmatrāta, Ghoṣaka, Vasumitra, and Buddhadeva—are the same as the *Vibhajyavādins* (the Evaluators) among the five hundred arhats in the *Vibhāṣā*."

Each of these four masters expounds different meanings. When these four masters explain their own doctrines, they may evaluate one another’s views regarding their specific characteristics and determine what is right or wrong.
For instance, Master Dharmatrāta composed the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-vaibhāṣā-śāstra*, while Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Although the *Mahāvibhāṣā* separately mentions dharmas such as 'aversion' (*vidveṣa*), Dharmatrāta and others do not mention them.

This means that although that treatise separately explains the existence of aversion and so forth, Master Dharmatrāta—who recorded these as the opinions of the *Vibhāṣā*-masters—did not adopt them. Therefore, Dharmatrāta also accepts aversion;
he establishes only ten types of bodhisattvas because he excludes 'non-delusion' (*amoha*), as its essence is simply wisdom (*prajñā*).
The Commentary states: "It is not that [the term 'pervasive'] is used because it refers to the pervasive wholesome [states], but rather it excludes those [other factors].

However, the Sarvāstivādins claim that the ten wholesome [mental factors] are called "pervasive wholesome" because they exist within all wholesome minds; although they belong to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) pervades all wholesome minds. As for the present Mahāyāna...

This concludes the explanation of the eleven wholesome [mental factors]. It is stated that they "arise only with a wholesome mind" and are thus called "wholesome mental factors," but it does not say they "pervade all wholesome minds.

This is because mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) does not pervade all wholesome minds; since mental pliancy is absent in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), five of the middle phrases are omitted. This clarifies the basis and the cause.
Regarding the five phrases: first, reality; second, virtue; third, capability—these three are the bases of faith.
[It is] because these three serve as the basis that faith arises. Fourth, patience is the cause of faith. Fifth, delight in the teaching is the fruit of faith.
As for the five phrases within "delight" which clarify the reality of the object of faith, its cause, and its function: according to my humble opinion, these are called the five phrases.
As for this, the full treatise states: First, "regarding the reality, qualities, and capacities" refers to clearly understanding the basis (*āśraya*).

Second, "stained patience and desire" refers to clearly understanding cause and effect (*hetu-phala*). Third, "having a pure mind as its nature" refers to clearly understanding the essence (*svabhāva*).

Fourth, "counteracting lack of faith," and fifth, "taking delight in the wholesome as its function"—these two phrases refer to clearly understanding the activity (*karman*) of clear faith. Thus, it is abbreviated therein.
Regarding the five phrases,
the Commentary states: "As for 'not separately distinguishing substance and so forth,' although that treatise contains only the expressions 'distinct from substance, quality,
and activity,' it does not analyze them as objects (*viṣaya*), nor does it reach the level of analysis found in this treatise."

The Commentary states: "The three—reality (substance), virtue (quality), and capacity (action)—are the bases for the expression 'is'; they are the objects, and thus belong to the seventh case. If one says "takes" (in the sense of *āśraya*), then "at" (*ā*) refers to the object;
that is, it is subsumed under the seventh case, the locative of the object. Because the three—reality, virtue, and capacity—are the objects of the cognition of faith, [they are the basis].
If one speaks of the "basis" (*āśraya*), then the "basis" (*āśraya*) refers to the sense-faculties; these are subsumed under the seventh case, the locative of the faculty.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states that the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* speaks of five types of activity. These range from "counteracting lack of faith" up to "arousing the path of goodness and increasing faith.
Regarding those five activities mentioned in that treatise: First, because it counteracts lack of faith; Second, because it can attain *bodhi*.

Since it is characterized by outflows (*sāsrava*), it is capable of accomplishing the goal; this is established because the provisions (*saṃbhāra*) are fulfilled. Here, the term "provisions" (or *saṃbhāra*) refers to...
The stage is called the "Provision" (*sambhāra*). Alternatively, the wholesome roots of humans and devas, which manifest wisdom, are also called provisions;

for example, by performing a single wholesome deed, one can obtain happiness for ten or five lifetimes. Fourth, because they benefit both others and oneself, all wholesome dharmas are beneficial; they either benefit future lives or others.
Fifth, because they give rise to the wholesome paths and increase faith, and because of this faith, one constantly attains birth in the realms of humans and devas, thereby increasing [virtue].
Regarding the *Poṣadha* (Uposatha) dharmas: these eleven wholesome factors all possess these five functions (*karman*).

If the first function is distinguished—as in the section on "shame" (*hrī*)—it is stated that they serve as the antidote to shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and so forth; the same applies to all subsequent cases. Furthermore, within the fifth function, one should also include the increase of shame and the other virtues.
However, this treatise states that their function is "delighting in the wholesome," which also subsumes the four functions mentioned in the aforementioned treatise.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "this is the firm faith (*dṛḍha-śraddhā*) within the treatise":

if faith possesses these five functions, it is also subsumed under "firm faith" in other treatises, because it is precisely through its firmness that one is able to reach discernment (*viniścaya*). However, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, and other works, there are three types of faith:
first, pure faith (*viśuddha-śraddhā*); second, firm faith (*dṛḍha-śraddhā*); and third, clear and pure faith (*prabhāsvara-śraddhā*). The present [case] refers to...

This is the second firmness (*dṛḍha*). It is as stated in that ninth [chapter]: "Faith is the basis for aspiration. This is clarified in the *Abhidharmapitaka* (Treatise on Correct Dharma), chapter nine.
If one speaks in general terms, all forms of faith are explained in the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Exposition of Ascertainment);

however, among the five types of ascertainment, the second—ascertainment of cause—is excluded. Yet, within the five activities, the second activity—the cause of enlightenment (*bodhi*)—is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*). This is the aspiration.

Seeking the fruit of Buddhahood may be designated as the cause of *bodhi*. If one were to discuss this comprehensively, other worldly virtues that produce the fruits of human or celestial rebirth, as well as those that generally attain the fruits of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), would then comprise the remaining four types of karma. These four types of karma can obtain worldly fruits;
thus, the second [type], the cause of *bodhi*, is excluded. Regarding the virtuous karma of humans and devas that induces good fruits over many lifetimes, all such merit and wisdom—
It is also called the "Provisional Accumulation" (*sambhāra*). The outflows (*āsrava*) themselves are not the stage of Provisional Accumulation;

rather, it is so named because they serve as provisions. The commentary states: "Whether phenomena or principles, faith and patience are both [included]. Here, "reality" (*bhūta*) does not necessarily refer to the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Excluding all phenomena, whether they be existent or non-existent, if they exist, one knows them as they truly are; if they do not exist, then likewise...
To know truly that there is no [substantiality] is called "knowing according to reality" (*yathābhūtam*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Because its essence is not real, it is also not a truth (*satya*)," the author of the commentary provisionally bases his argument on the fact that space is not included within the Four Noble Truths;
he uses this to challenge the established teacher. He does not rely upon the Mahāyāna, but rather treats space as being outside the Four Noble Truths according to the Hīnayāna perspective.
Regarding their subsumption: if it is taught within the Mahāyāna that consciousness transforms into space, this is subsumed under all four truths.

If the uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) transforms space, this is subsumed under the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*), and so forth, as explained previously in the second section on subsumption.
The Commentary states: "From 'the internal essence is subsumed within the distinct' up to 'also called the True Great' refers to the Three Jewels of Common Characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
As for the Three Jewels of Distinct Characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*): the Dharma-Buddha is named the Three Vehicles; the teachings, principles, and practices are named the Jewel of Dharma;

and the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and those of the two vehicles are named the Sangha. All of these are untainted (*anāsrava*). That which sustains the clay, wood, painted, or cast images is called the Jewel of Sustenance (*pratītyasamutthita-ratna*)."

These are the distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the Three Jewels with outflows (*sāsrava*). "True Practice" (*bhūta-caryā*) refers to this: "True" (*bhūta*) signifies *tathatā* (Suchness), and "Practice" (*caryā*) signifies the practice [of it].
Alternatively, "True Practice" refers to the Three Jewels of distinct characteristics as being without outflows (*anāsrava*), which are termed "True Purity" (*bhūta-śuddhi*).

Because they are like true purity, the Three Jewels of Sustenance (*pratiniṣṭhita-ratna*) are the skillful means (*upāya*) for the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and they are also termed "True Purity. Furthermore, among the Three Jewels, the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharma-ratna*) is...

Regarding this "Jewel," the Buddha stated that the Jewel of the Saṃgha is merely a provisional designation (*prajñapti*). This is because it is based upon such provisional designations that one speaks of the "Buddha" and "Saṃgha.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* asks: "For what reason do you only recollect the Prajñāpāramitā, and not the two [Jewels of] Buddha and Saṃgha, which are both quiescent?
The answer is: "The Buddha and Saṃgha are provisional designations; whereas the quiescence of phenomena (*dharmatā-śānti*) is the reality. Within the quiescence of phenomena..."
This effectively includes both the Buddha and the Saṃgha. In the older sūtras and śāstras, it is called *gārāma* in Sanskrit, which here means "place of maintenance.

In the newer sūtras and śāstras, both terms [vihāra and gārāma] are used (the question remains). As for the term "temple" (*si*), it corresponds to the nine temple-gates within the Saṃgha, where the nine *yúnqīng* (cloud-ministers) are stationed.
Just as these ministers assist and support the Son of Heaven, so too do the monks within the temple now assist and support the Buddha-Dharma. This is because...
The answer is the same as before. There may be different names for it, such as "True Purity" (*bhūtapariśuddhi*) or "Skillful Means" (*upāya*).

The commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "Now, that which can obtain [the former] and can accomplish [the latter], [refers to] the accomplishment of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the obtaining of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

This refers either to the accomplishment of the unconditioned and the obtaining of the conditioned, or to the new accomplishment and the subsequent wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) that penetrates [reality]. Furthermore, this "obtaining" does not refer to the obtaining of non-associated [formations] (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The commentary explains:

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (the *Dui-fa*) merely states, "those who claim 'I have power,'" which implies that since there is already the "blowing" of one's own school, this refers exclusively to oneself.
Question: In the present text, since it clarifies the locus of the Dharma, one type [of person] should be established; why then is it said that three types are established? If...
The middle [category] also subsumes the first two actual virtues (*dravya-guṇa*). If the first actual [virtues] are included within the middle, they also subsume the latter two.

Furthermore, regarding what is identical upon the actual [virtues], faith in the cause is also patience (*kṣānti*). If the latter two are placed below, they are spoken of solely as the Buddha-fruit; that is, they are the objects of aspiration and desire.
If the latter two are placed below and are spoken of solely as the Buddha-fruit—referring to aspiration, desire, and so forth—what is the reason for this? It could also be the case that the former...
The first [of these three recollections] refers exclusively to faith in the fruit; the latter two refer exclusively to faith in the cause. Furthermore, the question is valid:

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that one should "only contemplate the Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā, and not contemplate both together," yet it also says that the Dharma is the reality and the Saṃgha is the user.
Thus, since the precious Dharma is indeed real, why is it that among the objects of mindfulness one contemplates only the Buddha? Or perhaps there are other sūtras [that address this].
The three [factors] are quiescence and mindfulness; reflect upon this according to its meaning. That is to say, at the time of the cause, faith arises as distinct from the mouth (speech).

They mutually and simultaneously take outflows (*āsrava*) as their object. Faith is the cause, and [the subsequent stages] are the fruit. Faith is the cause, and the praises are the fruit of the fruit.

This is because knowing [the truth] further reveals that faith serves as the basis for desire (*chanda*) and as the basis for diligence (*vīrya*); such is the sequence. Question: How are these three factors [related]?
Regarding simultaneous cause and effect: these three dharmas arise by mutually supporting one another, just as two feet walk at the same time, each providing strength to the other;
this is also simultaneous cause and effect. This is likewise true for the causal relationship at the time of the cause. As for asynchronous cause and effect:
