having first given rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), faith in the Buddha arises; after faith has arisen—
It is also obtained through the arising of desire, because the mind is pure. This is an *upapada-ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive dependent compound). Regarding the third case (*tṛtīyā-vibhakti*):
if one says, "Devadatta gives the robe" or "the recipient accepts the bowl," this is called an *upapada-ṣaṣṭhī*. It is subsumed under the seventh case (*saptamī-vibhakti*).

What is its meaning? "Discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is the instrument; it is that which acts as the instrument. Because discernment serves as the instrumental basis, one subsequently realizes cessation (*nirodha*).
The third turning is also an instrument; this [turning] is likewise so. Faith is the instrument by which one is able to harmonize the mind with purity;
therefore, it is subsumed within the third turning.
The *Śāstra* states: "Because the mind is pure, it is explained by the *tatpuruṣa* compound using the third case ending. Regarding the third case ending, it is the "instrumental" (*karaṇa*) case;
that is, the instrument of action. This signifies that superior resolve (*adhimukti*) is the cause and effect of faith.
By means of faith as the instrument—possessing this very instrument—one is able to believe and thereby purify the mind.
The Commentary states: "Faith alone is that which can purify; all others are that which are purified.

This means that this faith can purify the mind, and when it reaches other universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) and their simultaneous occurrences, the other ten types of wholesome factors—such as faith and so forth—can purify it.

This is because they possess the functional capacity to universally purify other wholesome mental concomitants (*caitasika*), just as attention (*manaskāra*) is able to [pervade] all minds and mental factors. As for the others, such as shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*)...
If there were ten types [of faith], they could not possess a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Rather, one would desire for each to have its own distinct characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

If, according to your view, faith exists when there is good or evil, but that faith is non-existent within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), this refers to the intended meaning of "receiving" [the teaching].
If your faith is such that you believe good can be cultivated and you believe evil dharmas can be leaked away, then regarding evil dharmas—

It should be granted that lack of faith is a defiled dharma that can be loathed, whereas faith may exist. If that were so, then regarding indeterminate dharmas (*avyākṛta*), there would be no outflows (*āsrava*).

The commentary states that this is illustrated by the "water-clearing jewel" (*vimalaprabhā-maṇi*): if such jewels were common among humans, one might say that water is of the same category as the jewel.
The blue, yellow, and red pearls are all within the category of crystal pearls (*sphaṭika-maṇi*) that are capable of producing water; each is cherished for its respective pearl.
If a pearl can produce fire from within it, it is called a "flaming pearl" (*jvālā-maṇi*). Therefore, that which can clarify turbid water is called a crystal pearl.
The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "It is also like a loach stirring the mud and turbid water. This refers to the loach fish. When this fish dies, it becomes mud;
when it stirs its tail, it turbidizes the water. The *Śū* further asks: "If one has faith in the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), what prevents one from loving the three?

Why then do you claim that only [one] nature is good? The intent of this defense is as follows: just as in the Mahāyāna one has faith in phenomena that are wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, yet one maintains faith in that which is exclusively wholesome.
Because of its intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*). I believe that only craving is of the three natures; what prevents it from being wholesome? To refute such views, the treatise states:
"Furthermore, regarding suffering and its origin, [craving] is not the basis for faith. This is the interpretation of Master Chao.

The Commentary states: "If they were to offer this defense, saying that both [desire and resolve] have faith as their essence, then it would follow that the two dharmas of 'indicating' (ni-darśana) and 'conforming' (anu-vidhāna)—namely, desire and superior resolve—are both faith; yet, they would still not be desire and resolve."
The commentary states: "Acceptance (*kṣānti*) and desire (*chanda*) are the requisites of faith (*śraddhā*). Reflection (*cintā*) is the fruit of faith, and desire is also the fruit of faith;
therefore, they are the requisites of faith. Regarding the phrase "with respect to oneself": it means that one esteems oneself and exerts oneself with respect to the Dharma.

That is to say, regarding the excellent Dharma, one trains oneself personally. The intended meaning is: "This Dharma is to be mastered; if my own person should train in it, then now, this very body of mine [must do so]."
Because it gives rise to virtue and morality; because it engenders reverence for the Dharma; and because it engenders self-respect within oneself.
Thus, with respect to both the Dharma and the body, it serves as a superior standard of conduct.
The Commentary states: "Thus, that which carefully prevents evil refers to the *dharma* (the law). There are five types of such [punishments]:

first, the *chāyā* (flogging), such as when a crime is punishable by fifty strokes or fewer of the staff, it is termed *chāyā*; second, the *daṇḍa* (staffing), such as when sixty strokes or fewer are prescribed, it is termed the 'six kings' of the staff."

Third are the offenses involving penal servitude. As with penal servitude for obstructing, there are also five types: first, three years of penal servitude; second, two and a half years of penal servitude; third, two years of penal servitude;
fourth, one and a half years of penal servitude; and fifth, one year of penal servitude. Fourth are the offenses involving travel restrictions (*yuan-zui*).

There are three categories of travel distance: first, a restriction of three thousand *li*; second, a restriction of two thousand five hundred *li*; and third, a restriction of two thousand *li*. If it is a restriction of one thousand...

One *li* is one thousand five hundred *li*. None of these are called "conditions" (*pratyaya*); they are merely called "transferring one's residence. Fifth, regarding the two types of "offense upon offense":
first, death by condition; second, death by root. The *Lun* (Treatise) says: "To perfume the worthy and good, and to expose the violent according to their actions.

However, the distinct characteristics of shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*) both contain the chapters on persons and phenomena. "Worthy" (*xian*) means that a person of virtuous character is held in high esteem; "good" (*shan*) refers to a single [instance of] virtue.
"Shame and remorse for all wholesome dharmas" refers to learning from evil and censuring unwholesome dharmas.

The commentary states: "When that treatise says that the *Abhidharma* takes the stages of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*) as its essence, and when it says that [this practice] takes shame and remorse as its essence," [it means the following].

However, it is the distinction [between them] that constitutes their essence; there is only *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). To explain the distinct characteristics of shame (*hrī*) and modesty (*apatrāpya*), the commentary states:
"The *Vyākhyāyukti* says that 'supremacy in the world' refers to the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); this also generally refers to the object-conditions of shame and modesty.
Furthermore, the following refutes the ancient explanation. Question: Regarding the phrase "the ancient explanation," does "ancient" refer to those from the distant past of this land?
The "ancient teachings" (*pūrvācārya*) mentioned by the Master refer to the doctrines of the various masters of antiquity in the West (India).

If one were to call the doctrines of the masters of antiquity in this land (China) "ancient teachings," then how could the authors of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (the *Cheng weishi lun*) be considered "ancient masters" when they were far removed in time from those Western masters?
The answer is that these [doctrines] are indeed the ancient teachings of the West. Question: If the arousal of shame toward one's own evil deeds is called "moral dread" (*hrī*), then...
In the two higher realms, it is recorded that there are no evil persons or evil dharmas; how, then, can shame (*hrī*) arise?

Furthermore, non-conceptual wisdom takes true suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, yet true suchness is eternally devoid of evil persons and evil dharmas; how, then, can one give rise to shame and remorse (*apatrāpya*) while relying upon true suchness?
Again, it is asked: since the two upper realms and the three [lower] realms both lack gods and humans and lack dharmas, being in every respect similar to one another, [how is this distinction made]?
How can one give rise to reverence for the noble and the good, as well as a superior sense of worldly reproach and aversion, such that shame and remorse arise?
In the Great Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), how can there be wholesome dharmas, and how can humans give rise to shame?

Furthermore, since speech does not exist in the Formless Realm, how could one revere the noble and honor the good? One should further examine whether this can be established by comparing the higher and lower realms.
The Commentary states: "Although [the roots] such as greed (*rāga*) increase through their own power, they are indeed conditions for dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Regarding one's own person and one's own dharmas, these are the conditions for the arising of shame (*hrī*); regarding worldly dharmas, these are the conditions for the arising of dread-of-blame (*apatrāpya*).

One understands shame and dread-of-blame by way of their initial arising-conditions, just as it is stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* concerning the severing of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*): "The superior roots of non-goodness (*akuśalamūla*) are capable of severing [them]."

Regarding the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*): speaking according to reality, it is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) that can sever the roots of goodness; yet now, the superior unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*) are said to be able to sever the roots of goodness.

Speaking according to reality, the statement that "wrong view can sever the roots of goodness" refers to the specific conditions and occasions from which the severance of the roots of goodness arises.

It is like saying "the bandits burned the village. The bandits themselves cannot burn the village; it is the fire that can burn it. Yet, when one says "the bandits burned the village," it is said in reference to their role as the causal condition.
In the same way, shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) are explained by referring to the conditions from which they arise.

Specifically, feeling shame regarding one's own nature in accordance with the Dharma is "shame," while feeling dread of blame regarding the superior qualities of others in the world is "dread of blame"—this is merely a distinction based on the subjective perspective.
"Understanding" refers to oneself and others. For example, suppose a person performs a good deed or possesses great skill;
although they have done this, it is not as if they did not do it themselves, yet they wish to avoid taking credit for it. To take credit for it by means of wholesome dharmas is called "self-ability.

Having already answered thus, it is like a person who performs a certain act, and another person asks: "Although you performed this act, and although you did it yourself, you are nonetheless unwilling to acknowledge it."

Grasping is likewise regarding unwholesome dharmas, for they are able to harm oneself. Grasping designates unwholesome dharmas as "other. Wholesome dharmas benefit oneself, whereas unwholesome dharmas are like a forge.

As for the specific characteristics of *hrī* (moral shame) and *apatrāpya* (moral dread): veneration of the noble and good, and the rejection of the violent and evil—these are the specific characteristics of *hrī* and *apatrāpya*.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "If one were to say that the distinction between self and other objects arises from their causes—namely, that what pertains to one's own person is called *hrī* (shame), and what pertains to another's person is called *apatrāpya* (embarrassment).

The Commentary further states: "The Master of Right Reasoning (*Nyāyācārya*) says: 'Because there is a difference in the causes of present offenses, and so forth, up to the fact that they are not distinct in the present. This refers to the differentiation of offenses.

Because it is distinguished by the present body, it is called *hrī* (shame). If the fruit of a sinful, unwholesome act is to emerge in a future body in a different state of existence, it is called *apatrāpya* (embarrassment).
The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'the three unwholesome roots, because they are countered by their opposites and do not require a separate antidote':
if one refers to the three roots of greed, hatred, and delusion, there are indeed specific antidotes; for instance, non-greed is the antidote to greed, and non-hatred is the antidote to hatred."

Non-delusion (*amoha*) is the specific antidote to delusion (*moha*). There are two types of general antidotes, namely right wisdom (*samyak-prajñā*), which can generally counteract greed, hatred, and delusion.
If non-delusion were itself wisdom, then we would now establish the following formal argument (*prayoga*):

Delusion must necessarily have a distinct antidote, because it is included within the triad of greed, hatred, and delusion that are to be countered; this is due to the causes of greed and hatred, just as delusion has a distinct antidote called non-delusion. If...
It is permitted that afflictions are countered only by their specific antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), whereas taking [the object] is correct wisdom (*samyag-prajñā*) and has no separate antidote.

The commentary states: "Regarding 'general' and 'specific' as being opposed to these, and 'distant' as being generally opposed"—if the three roots of goodness are directly opposite [to their respective afflictions], they are called "near."
If wisdom (*prajñā*) does not oppose the three wholesome roots, it is categorized as "distant" (*viprakṛṣṭa*).
The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "These two [categories] exclude all forms of grasping (*upādāna*) that are not unwholesome roots.

According to my humble opinion, this is because, for instance, although the universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) mental factors pervade the six consciousnesses, their essence is not subsumed under the afflictions (*kleśa*), as they do not possess both [necessary] conditions.
The universal objects are not faculties. Furthermore, if they were indeterminate, they would not be present throughout the five consciousnesses;
nor are they subsumed under the primary afflictions. Lacking these two criteria, they are also not faculties. As for delusion, pride, and the five views, although they are primary afflictions—
However, among these five consciousnesses (pañca-vijñāna), they do not exist; nor do they pervade the six consciousnesses. Because they lack these two criteria, they are not faculties (*indriya*).

As for the ten minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*), they are established as mental factors (*citta*) alone and do not pervade the five consciousnesses; furthermore, because they are not subsumed under the primary afflictions (*kleśa*), they are not faculties.

These are not the root [afflictions]. Although the middle two [of the ten great afflictions] and the eight [secondary afflictions] pervade the substance of the six consciousnesses, they are not subsumed under the category of primary afflictions, because their minds are not rooted [in the defilements].
These two points distinguish them from all other mental factors that act as concordant causes;

only those that are *sāsrava* (tainted) are [included here]. Question: If wholesome karma can be called "greed," then if unwholesome karma is named "greed," consider this: what serves as the condition?
Because they also grasp at *nirvāṇa* and give rise to greed and other afflictions, they too are "possessors" [of such faults].
Furthermore, those with the false views of non-Buddhists give rise to greed and hatred toward dharmas such as *nirvāṇa*. Again, it is asked:

Why is it that only the dharma of *nirvāṇa* is wholesome and so forth, yet one is born into the three evil destinies? If *nirvāṇa* is what is possessed, why does one not take up *bodhi*? Reflect upon this and ask further.

Regarding the statement that "analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and nirvāṇa are also [included] because they arise from delusion regarding the principles of suffering": Question: Are the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) and nirvāṇa identical or distinct?

Furthermore, what is the difference between the certainty of suffering (duḥkha-niyama) and the factors that possess suffering (duḥkha-vastu)? The explanation is as in the commentary. The three types of suffering (duḥkha) are:

the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā), the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā), and the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā). Question: Regarding the three sufferings in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), can it be said that they are produced by the desire realm? [Is it also produced by] hatred (dveṣa)?

Because it pertains only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). If [suffering] in the two higher realms is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), how could it be produced by hatred (*dveṣa*)? This should be considered (further inquiry required). The Commentary states:
"Greed and wisdom arise from the three realms as the factors for producing karma and moistening rebirth; therefore, they are called the 'suffering of suffering' and its instruments.
If greed predominantly moistens rebirth and only slightly produces karma, and if greed predominantly moistens rebirth and only slightly... [the text repeats].

Regarding the initiation of karma: while hatred (*dveṣa*) for the most part initiates karma, it can to a small degree moisten rebirth. The *Śāstra* states that "the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) all effect rebirth.

The *Sub-commentary* explains that "hatred is discussed only with respect to heavy objects among sentient beings. However, that treatise further states that hatred applies only to [sentient] existence...
Regarding the case where anger arises toward a sentient object: if one intends to strike or harm the object of resentment, this constitutes a full karmic path (*karmapatha*).

However, if anger arises toward a non-sentient object and there is no intention to strike or harm, it is merely a mixed state. Now, when consciousness gives rise to anger, it applies to both sentient and non-sentient objects.
Question: Can the greed of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) give rise to unwholesome karma? If so, what about the merit of the three realms?
Regarding the karma of movement (*iriyāpatha-karma*): consider how it is initiated by greed.
The commentary states: "The dharmas that can now act as obstacles pertain to all three realms; that which is called hatred (*dveṣa*) is the specific counteragent for the desire realm."

Non-hatred (*adveṣa*) pervades both realms. Question: Why is it that greed (*rāga*) and delusion (*moha*), which are able to counteract the Buddha [as objects], are said to pervade all three realms, whereas the hatred (*dveṣa*) to be countered is restricted to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while non-hatred pervades all three realms?
Answer: Because evil dharmas must be guarded against from their very depths, there is this distinction between the counteracting subject and the countered object.
Non-hatred (*adveṣa*) pervades the three realms; that is to say, it is exclusively of the nature of the mental realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The *Yuanji* (Commentary) states that according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, this has the nature of the definitive discernment of wisdom as expressed by the teaching. However, that *Samuccaya* says:

The non-deluded root of goodness takes the wisdom that arises from the realization of the teachings as its essence. Therefore, this treatise cites scriptural authority and logical proof. The commentary states:
"Because it is obtained through the fruition [of past karma] and is acquired immediately upon birth, it is termed 'fruition' (vipāka) by way of its basis. As for "fruition":
This is the body of maturation (*vipāka-kāya*). The body is the basis (*āśraya*); because there is a body, there is a self. This is appropriately termed the "wholesomeness of the body of maturation.
Now, to realize this name is what is called "wholesomeness of retribution" (*vipāka-kuśala*).

The Commentary states: "If the term 'cultivated wisdom' (bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā) is named after its cause, which is meditative concentration (samādhi), it is because wisdom is able to be produced by taking concentration as its cause;
thus, this very wisdom is what is here called 'cultivated wisdom,' named after its causal concentration."
The Commentary states: "It is not a fault that [the sūtra] does not say that equanimity (*upekṣā*) and so forth are subsumed within the eleven wholesome factors (*kuśalamūla*).

If one were to claim that obtaining the eleven factors as causes results in obtaining equanimity and so forth, this would constitute the fallacy of uncertainty (*aniyata-doṣa*). Therefore, it is stated that equanimity and so forth are added, and thus they are subsumed within the eleven wholesome factors."
If equanimity (*upekṣā*) and so forth have no separate substance, does non-delusion (*amoha*) also have no separate substance?

Or, when it is included within the eleven wholesome factors such as non-attachment (*alobha*), does non-attachment have a separate substance while non-delusion has a separate substance? Now, if it is subsumed under the three roots of goodness, would there not be no fault?

The Commentary states: "Regarding this Great Compassion, as previously mentioned, it should be subsumed under the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) among the twenty-two faculties, such as wisdom (*prajñā*).
However, when one reaches the stage of Buddhahood, within the three untainted faculties, it is subsumed solely under the faculty of 'one who has already known' (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

Furthermore, if the faculty of 'one who has already known' at the stage of Buddhahood is based on the fourth dhyāna, it takes seven factors as its essence, namely, the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*)."

The faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) constitutes the essence of the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*). If this faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge exists within the lower three dhyānas, its essence consists of the cessation of activity, or alternatively, it consists of nine factors.

If it exists in the third dhyāna, its essence consists of eight factors: the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), the faculty of mind, the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).

If it exists in the first or second dhyānas, its essence consists of nine factors, adding either the faculty of joy (*prītindriya*) as a preparatory application (*prayoga*). [In these cases], the "great" [elements] do not constitute its activity.

Its essence consists of the two dharmas of non-delusion and non-hatred. If the essence of non-delusion is itself wisdom (*prajñā*), then it should be subsumed under the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) among the faculties of knowledge, as well as among the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).

The Commentary states: "The absence of delusion [applies] to both cause and fruit, as it pervades all four types of wisdom; furthermore, this is because it is an outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and a dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Regarding the "four types of wisdom," these refer to innate wisdom (*upapatti-labdha*), wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī*), and wisdom derived from reflection (*cintā-mayī*).

Alternatively, one must add "wisdom of natural skillfulness" (*prakṛti-kauśalya*) for them to fully accord with the principle. "Natural skillfulness" is precisely untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*). These various forms of wisdom are either the absence of delusion itself...
As for its causes: it may be the result of non-delusion, or it may be a simultaneous cause-and-effect, or a sequential cause-and-effect.
When it functions as a cause, there are two among the six causes: namely, the root-cause (*mūla-hetu*) and the associated-cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).

When it functions as a result, there are two among the five results: namely, the virile-result (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the outflowing-result (*niṣyanda-phala*). As for the dominant-result (*adhipati-phala*)...

Regarding the result of all [causes] being simultaneous: if the cause and result were simultaneous, then because a preceding similar-type cause (sabhāga-hetu) draws forth a subsequent outflowing result (niṣyanda-phala), and since a similar-type cause and its outflowing result must necessarily be at different times, within those causes and results that occur at different times, there are also efficient causes (kāraṇa-hetu) and dominant results (adhipati-phala). To speak according to the actual reality, as for that similar-type cause:

This refers exclusively to the production of seeds from seeds and does not refer to the manifest. This is because the manifest is considered a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) only in relation to the manifest. As the preceding treatise states:

"Seeds produce their own kind in succession, just as a homogeneous cause draws forth its concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*). If one considers the manifest in relation to the manifest, it is through cultivation.

Regarding the statement that the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) has an outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), this is not precluded; for instance, when the acquisition of a mark (*lakṣaṇa-pratilambha*) or the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) arises from a mark, these are all metaphorically designated as the similar cause and the outflow fruit.
As for simultaneous cause and effect, they obtain the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*) by virtue of the three causes:
the co-existent (*sahabhū*), the enabling (*kāraṇa*), and the associated (*samprayukta*). However, in the Mahāyāna, [these distinctions] are not emphasized.

The relationship between cause and effect is distinguished by means of the six causes (*ṣaḍ-hetu*). In the Hīnayāna, the relationship between cause and effect is likewise distinguished by means of these six causes.

Now, that which is "wholesome acquired at birth" (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) is precisely the "wholesome pertaining to merit" (*puṇya-bhāgīya-kuśala*). However, while the wholesome pertaining to merit is broad, the wholesome acquired at birth is narrow;

the wholesome pertaining to merit subsumes the wholesome acquired at birth, yet the wholesome acquired at birth does not subsume the wholesome pertaining to merit. This is because the essence of the wholesome pertaining to merit is...
It is clear, sharp, and superior because it is the excellence of the three realms. If it were innate wholesome [states], their essential nature would be obscure and inferior.

As for karma that accords with the three realms, the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation are all subsumed under the category of "wholesome states conducive to merit" (*puṇyabhāgīya-kuśala*).

However, these wholesome states conducive to merit have as their essence a portion of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, such as physical joy and aversion; they do not exist [in this way] among the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

The wisdom consisting of the six aspects, such as "arising" and so forth, or that which involves "aversion toward the lower" and "delight in the higher," refers to aversion toward the suffering, coarseness, and obstruction of the lower realms, and delight in the tranquility, subtlety, and detachment of the higher realms.

Since the wisdom of hearing and reflection (śrutamayī-prajñā and cintāmayī-prajñā) must first be acquired before one can obtain the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā) that brings about the fruit, the wholesome factors conducive to merit (puṇya-bhāgīya-kuśala) take as their essence a portion of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
While they properly include a portion of the wisdom of cultivation, in terms of their essential nature, they are also [classified as] the wisdoms of hearing and reflection.

Therefore, if it is the wholesome [state] of the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), it is precisely the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*); for although this wisdom includes a portion of the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī*) and reflection (*cintāmayī*), it is categorized as the wisdom of cultivation with respect to its essential nature.

If it is the wholesome [state] of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), it refers to the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*), cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) of the three vehicles.

These are the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*). According to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is explained by extension that Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward possess the wisdoms of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) and reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*).
They are called "wisdom of hearing" because they hear the meaning of the Dharma, and "wisdom of reflection" because they reflect upon the meaning of the Dharma.

However, speaking in terms of their essential nature (*svabhāva*), these are exclusively cultivation (*bhāvanā*); thus, even for them, there is no [separate] wisdom of hearing or reflection. Regarding the distinction between the two meanings in the Hīnayāna, the Hīnayāna Śrāvakas...
The master Bhadanta [Vasumitra] maintains that there are five reasons for distinguishing [the latent dispositions] from greed, hatred, and delusion:

First, because when greed, hatred, and delusion are heavy, they can give rise to coarse and heavy unwholesome karma of body and speech. Second, because greed, hatred, and delusion act as the powerful preliminary application (*prayoga*) for the severing of the roots of virtue.
Third, because they pervade all six consciousnesses; whereas doubt, pride, and so forth do not pervade all five [of the first five]. Fourth, because they are latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). Fifth...
"Universal" refers to those that follow along; that is, they pursue sentient beings. "Mental states" (*ākāra*) refers to their being obscure and difficult to discern, resembling a state of sleep.
Fifth, "because they pertain to all five categories of abandonment" means: the four categories of analytical afflictions under each of the Four Truths;

the four categories of analytical afflictions under the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*); and the five classes of afflictions under the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Taken together, these constitute [the universal afflictions].
The five abandonments are also called the five gates. By means of these five meanings, the sense in which greed, hatred, and delusion constitute "roots" is explained.

In the present context, because the arising of consciousness toward evil is predominant, it is said to be subsumed under the afflictions (*kleśa*). In the *Abhidharmakośa*, this refers to the "body that severs the roots of goodness," which is either strongly acquired through application (*prayoga*) or subsumed as such;
that is, it arises from extremely grave bodily and vocal karma, or is subsumed by both. In the present commentary, it says:

Regarding the three points used to distinguish the Hīnayāna, these were the master of the commentary’s own division of the text. Now, by adding further [points], five points of distinction are established.
When the commentary states, "If that is so, then the three applications of mindfulness are likewise," this represents the latter teacher raising an objection against the former teacher. For now...

Regarding the three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): suppose, for instance, that one person applies fragrant ointment to the Buddha’s body, yet the Buddha feels no attachment toward this person who applies the ointment, remaining in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension (*samyak-smṛti-samyak-saṃprajanya*). Furthermore, suppose another person were to strike the Buddha on the right side with a sword.
The Buddha felt no anger toward the person who was being cut with a knife; he remained with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
Furthermore, there was another person who neither anointed his body with perfumes nor cut him with a knife; the Buddha felt no delusion toward this person who neither anointed nor cut him;

he remained with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension. Thus, these three foundations of mindfulness consist precisely of non-attachment, non-aversion, and non-delusion, along with right mindfulness.

Right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) constitutes its essence. As for right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), it is subsumed under the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) within the faculty of one who possesses full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) among the twenty-two faculties.
Right knowledge, likewise, is subsumed under the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) within the faculty of one who possesses full knowledge among the twenty-two faculties.
However, the three applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are subsumed within the twenty-two faculties (indriya). Subsequently, the later master challenged the earlier master, saying:
"Great compassion (mahākaruṇā) has non-hatred (adveṣa) and non-delusion (amoha) as its two essential natures."

Regarding the treatise’s statement that great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is comprised within the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) by way of being non-hatred (*adveṣa*): it should also [be comprised] within the three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Furthermore, its essence consists of the mind being free from greed (*alobha*), hatred, and delusion (*amoha*). According to the treatise, since it is non-greed and non-hatred, one should say it is comprised within the three foundations of mindfulness, not within the twenty-two faculties.
Moreover, the latter master counters the former master, saying: "No, for great compassion is based on the four..."

Immeasurable compassion (*karuṇā*). The four immeasurables of compassion take non-hatred (*adveṣa*) alone as their essence; they should also be subsumed under the root of compassion within Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

The Commentary states: "It is not so; for this Great Compassion is [subsumed] within these immeasurables because its compassion, up to its non-abiding, relies upon wisdom (*prajñā*), and thus its root is [wisdom]."

Regarding "that which is subsumed": this is the interpretation of the former master. Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) is, among the four immeasurables, that which takes non-hatred (*adveṣa*) as its essential nature.

Because Great Compassion possesses characteristics (*sanimitta*), and because possessing characteristics leads to confusion, the treatise [distinguishes it] from the compassion within the immeasurables, which both take non-hatred as their essential nature.
Since Great Compassion and [ordinary] compassion would otherwise be confused by virtue of sharing these characteristics, the treatise [specifically] refers to non-hatred.

It is said that the three foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are included within the root of great compassion (mahākaruṇāmūla). Because they are signless (animitta), and because the signless might otherwise be confused [with other states], the treatise states that the three foundations of mindfulness are subsumed among the twenty-two faculties (indriya).
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "For now, this is based on the text which clarifies that the reflection is not the actual principle. This refers to the previous master’s interpretation.

Furthermore, regarding the explanation of texts such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which says that great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is not subsumed under the faculties (*indriya*), this is said because it takes non-hatred (*adveṣa*) as its essence;

thus, it is called "not subsumed under the faculties. However, speaking according to the actual reality, since great compassion takes non-delusion (*amoha*) as its essence, and non-delusion is itself wisdom (*prajñā*).

A portion of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is in fact subsumed under the faculties (*indriya*). However, because its essence is unreal, the treatises state that great compassion is not subsumed under the faculties;
this is merely a way of indicating that great compassion is indeed subsumed under the faculties, rather than being a statement that exhausts the full principle.
Regarding the statement in the treatise that the three foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are subsumed under the faculties (indriya), they now take non-hatred (adveṣa) as their essence.

Regarding the statement in the treatise that great compassion (mahākaruṇā) is not subsumed under the faculties, this also implicitly reveals that great compassion is indeed subsumed under the faculties.

Regarding the statement in the treatise that the three foundations of mindfulness are subsumed under the faculties, these three foundations of mindfulness are themselves the abiding in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension (samprajanya), taking non-delusion (amoha) as their essence. The aforementioned [total] is twenty-two.
Regarding their inclusion among the faculties (*indriya*): they also indirectly manifest the three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Since they take non-hatred (*adveṣa*) as their essence, they are also not included among the twenty-two faculties. The treatise’s indirect manifestation does not fully exhaust the principle.

If the treatise were to state that of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and the applications of mindfulness, half are included among the faculties and half are not, then it would be an exhaustive treatment of the principle.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "If that is so, how does one distinguish the three mundane [factors] from the textual passages? The latter master challenges the former, saying:

"The treatise states that non-harming (*ahiṃsā*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and vigilance (*apramāda*)—these three—are mundane existents (*saṃvṛtisat*). How do you reconcile this with the [notion of] discernment (*pravicaya*)?"
The Commentary states: "As for the statement that 'the essence of those [factors] possessing sound is wisdom,' the former master replied: 'Non-delusion depends on a single wisdom;
since one dharma can have five aspects, wisdom is substantially existent, and non-delusion is likewise substantial.

However, if equanimity and non-negligence were established based on four dharmas, these two would take multiple dharmas as their essence; therefore, non-negligence and equanimity are nominally existent.'"
The Commentary states: "The question is: if the essence of non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) is none other than non-aversion (*adveṣa*), it should not be a provisional existence. The latter master objects:

"If non-delusion (*amoha*) is established based on a single wisdom (*prajñā*) and non-delusion is substantial, then non-harming—which likewise relies upon a single non-aversion—should also be substantial, as it is not otherwise."
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The response regarding 'conventionally existent' (*saṃvṛti-sat*) applies to both the provisional (*prajñapti*) and the substantial (*dravya*).

The former master replies: "If the treatise says 'conventional,' it applies to both the provisional and the substantial. If one says 'provisionally existent,' this refers to that which lacks an essence (*asvabhāva*).

If one says 'possessing an essence,' this refers to having a distinct essence. This, too, is not correct; as explained in the section on the five views within the category of wisdom (*prajñā*), they are [treated] as worldly.

Regarding the statement, "As it is with the conventional existence of the cause, so it is with this non-delusion (*amoha*)," the former master explains that non-delusion takes a single wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence;
thus, non-delusion is substantially real. The five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*) likewise take a single wisdom as their essence, and thus these five views are also substantially real.
However, if equanimity (*upekṣā*) and heedfulness (*apramāda*) take multiple factors as their essence, then equanimity and heedfulness are merely designations (*prajñapti*).
[The opponent] stands up. This commentary states that the latter master raises a counter-objection to the former, saying:

"This is also not so. Those five views are established based on a single wisdom (*prajñā*); those five views are precisely the five views mentioned in the context of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

As for [the statement] 'it is conventional,' the same applies to the statement that there is no delusion (*amoha*): non-delusion is also established based on a single wisdom, and it likewise serves as an antidote to delusion."
If delusion (*moha*) were a mind-factor existing as a conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-sat*), it should also have been stated in the treatise that "delusion is said to exist as a conventional reality.
Since the treatise does not treat non-delusion (*amoha*) as a conventional reality, non-delusion is not established based on conventional designation.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "That which is 'discriminating' and 'discriminative' refers to the perfection of abandonment.

This means that from the initial entry into the fundamental dhyānas up until the point of extreme clarity, it is like someone who can enter meditative absorption but cannot discern whether they are abiding in it or emerging from it.
It is said that for the sake of perfection, one must later become even clearer before one can properly know the entry and emergence and attain mastery."
This is called "conducive to the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*). In this manner, it is likewise for those who enter the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), and so forth.

According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, regarding those who have perfected the excellence of discernment (*pravicaya*): suppose there is a person who, while sitting, attains the first dhyāna but has not yet attained the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*);

this is not called "perfected. Only upon attaining the fundamental concentration (*maula-samādhi*) is it called "perfected. How, then, is it said to be "accomplished"? Even though one sits and attains the first dhyāna concentration, [it is not yet perfected].
Whatever meritorious wholesome dharmas exist within the stage of the first dhyāna are all accomplished through cultivation; the concentration now attained becomes even more luminous and pure.

It is like a person who has newly built a house and named it "Full," yet must still refine it by sweeping the floors, plastering the walls, and so forth, so that the house becomes increasingly luminous and pure. The refinement of concentration is also like this.

When one attains the fundamental concentration (*mauladhyāna*) of the second dhyāna, it is called "fulfilled" (*paripūrṇa*); this applies likewise up to the fundamental concentrations of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "This merely refers to the cause, whereas that [text] refers to a portion within the actual cause, up to the ultimate stage of fruition.
That *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* says: "As for 'fulfillment,' it is spoken of in terms of practice during the causal stage; that is, having attained a portion of the first dhyāna."
The fundamental concentration (*mauladhyāna*) is termed "fulfillment" (*pūrṇa*). Subsequent concentrations that counteract [defilements] are termed "accomplishment" (*siddhi*).
This means that attaining even a single portion of the fundamental second dhyāna is called "attaining a partial concentration," which is termed "fulfilling the root.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) speaks only of "fulfilling existence" (*pūrṇabhava*) and does not mention "fulfilling non-accomplishment" (*apūrṇapūrṇa*); this is based on the perspective of reaching the stage of Buddhahood through cultivation.
Because perfect wisdom has not been cultivated and purified, one does not achieve mastery over syllables. Whether it be the practice of a śrāvaka, proceeding until the fruit of no-more-learning;
or the practice of a pratyekabuddha, proceeding until the ultimate fruit of a pratyekabuddha; or even the practice of a bodhisattva, proceeding until the fruit of Buddhahood.

Furthermore, because there is no further cultivation or refinement, it is called "fulfilling the good. This does not refer to the name "fulfilling" as applied to the practice of conduct within the causal stage.

As the Commentary states: "Alternatively, if one performs virtuous deeds with completeness, they may be called 'fulfilling,' for they are able to fulfill the roots of goodness; it is not necessary that their fruit [be realized]."

Alternatively, regarding the term "fulfillment of wholesome qualities" (*paripūrṇa-kuśala*) within the *Vijñaptimātra* [tradition], on what basis does it refer to the cultivation of wholesome qualities? "Fulfillment" refers to the completion of a single lifetime’s limit.
This interpretation is identical to that of the *Abhidharma* treatises; it does not speak in terms of the ultimate fruits of the three vehicles.
The *Śāstra* states: "That which consists merely of the cultivation of preparatory attention (*prayoga-manasikāra*) is not 'refined' (*praṇīta*).

Although among the four types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*) there are those such as deportment (*iryāpatha*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), which are like the worldly arts and crafts, even if one were to apply diligent effort to them for a hundred or fifty years, they would yield no benefit whatsoever.
Furthermore, [the Buddha] is also capable of performing such things as the deeds of a Tathāgata. Question: Why is this not called "refined"? Is it because it is not "pure" (*śuddha*)?
What is the distinction? (Consider this. The *Śāstra* states:

"The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* contains only the five names that serve as evidence—namely, 'possessing power,' 'possessing diligence,' and so forth—and lacks even one name from the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* that is present in both.

This means that in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, there are only the five names that serve as evidence, such as "possessing power" (*sabalatva*) and "possessing diligence" (*sodyamatva*), but it does not include the five names found in the [Abhidharma] *Madhyama-śāstra*, namely: [...the five names... (Note: The specific five names from the *Madhyama-śāstra* are omitted from the source text provided, but the structure indicates they are the standard set of five qualities corresponding to the five faculties/factors.)

These arise through application and so forth; furthermore, in the Abhidharma treatises, the middle five names are also referred to as "concomitant" (sahabhū) within those treatises, and thus there are two names for them.

The Commentary states: "Those of superior rank are called 'non-retrogressive. As for those who retrogress, it is like someone who, upon encountering these four superior stages—which belong only to Bodhisattvas and superior persons—thinks, 'I am a base person and cannot study this,' and thus falls away.
Those who are non-retrogressive are like one who says, 'He is a man of integrity, and I am likewise'; they should not disparage themselves and succumb to despondency."

The Commentary states: "Next, 'the person contemplates with clarity,' etc. This refers to the period prior to entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), which is termed "contemplation with clarity" (*tīkṣṇaprekṣa*).
Regarding the term "Nirvāṇa," this Nirvāṇa is the place where one rests the body; therefore, it is called by the name "Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, this Nirvāṇa is also called a "dwelling" (*gṛha*).
The Commentary states: "Regarding the statement that 'in the practice of cultivation, one has never realized that [the names] are derived from metaphors':
if one examines them closely, both 'donning the armor' and 'not relinquishing the yoke of virtue' are names derived from metaphors."

The Commentary states: "For example, regarding the equanimity of the stage of practice (bhūmi-caryā), there are those who first generate the mind [of awakening] at the lower, middle, or superior levels.

As for the phrase 'for example,' it refers to the generation of the mind prior to entering the first bhūmi; this is what is meant by 'donning the armor' (saṃnāha-pratipatti), or it may refer to its power within that stage."

Having entered the first bhūmi, there are three types of mind: the mind of entering, the mind of abiding, and the mind of emerging. The mind of entering is called the lower grade; it is the preparatory application (*prayoga*) and is also called the "mind that diligently abides.

The mind of abiding is called the middle grade; it is the state of non-mind (*acitta*) and is also called "courageous emergence. The mind of emerging is called the upper grade; it is the state of non-abiding and is also called "firm and fierce.
When one desires to enter the second bhūmi, one gives rise to the mind of superior progress (*viśeṣa-citta*); this is the state of non-attainment and is also called...
"Not abandoning the yoke of virtue" means that from this point forward it is always thus.
The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "The 'initial generation of the mind' refers to the initial generation of the bodhicitta.

'Cultivating for a long duration' refers to cultivating the causes over three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas. 'Uninterrupted cultivation' refers to diligently practicing within the mind at every single moment."
It is appropriate. As for its cultivation: whatever one practices, it is because the mind holds it in high esteem. Regarding "cultivation without remainder":

this means that all meritorious qualities and wholesome dharmas are cultivated to their full extent, with nothing left over. Furthermore, one attains the five powers, such as the power of armor and so forth, which correspond respectively to the following:
the five paths of the provisions and so on, all of which are accomplished through the power of donning the armor. This is diligence.

There are three [categories]. As for that which subsumes these four, it is also like that which subsumes them. Regarding those three, they are: donning armor (*saṃnāha*), gathering what is wholesome (*kuśala-saṃgraha*), and benefiting and bringing happiness (*hitasukha*).
Among those three, "donning armor" is a provisional designation for subsumption; this is the first of the five, namely armor-like diligence (*saṃnāha-vīrya*).
Therefore, it is said that [the latter] subsumes four, but not five types. As for the diligence of gathering what is wholesome (*kuśala-saṃgraha-vīrya*), it is...

This includes the other four types of diligence. As for the diligence of benefit and happiness (*hitasukha-vīrya*), it does not include the five stages; rather, the diligence of benefit and happiness is distinguished separately from within those five. Regarding the "Bodhisattva-bhūmi of the Main Section" (*Maulī Bhūmi*), this refers to the Bodhisattva-bhūmi within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Although all six perfections (*pāramitā*) are present there, diligence is not omnipresent across all six; for this reason— [The text continues: ...this diligence... [is explained as follows]. It is the diligence that is not distracted by other activities, and it is the diligence that is not distracted by other mental states. Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by external objects. Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by internal afflictions. Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by signs (*nimitta*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of a living being (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of a soul (*jīva-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of a creator (*kartṛ-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of a feeler (*vedaka-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of a knower (*jñātṛ-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of a seer (*draṣṭṛ-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of non-existence (*vibhava-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of grasping at rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of pride (*māna-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of arrogance (*adhimāna-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of overweening pride (*abhimāna-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of conceit (*asmimāna-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of inferiority (*ūnamāna-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of superiority (*atimāna-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of equality (*samamāna-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of difference (*viśeṣamāna-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of non-self (*anātma-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of signlessness (*animitta-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of non-arising (*anutpāda-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of non-ceasing (*anirodha-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of non-defilement (*asaṃkleśa-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of non-purification (*avyavadāna-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of non-birth (*ajāti-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of non-destruction (*avinaṣṭa-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of non-origination (*anutpanna-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of non-extinction (*aniruddha-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of non-existence (*abhāva-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of existence (*bhāva-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of oneness (*ekatva-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of multiplicity (*nānātva-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of identity (*tattva-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of difference (*anyatva-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of eternity (*nitya-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of transience (*anitya-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of pleasure (*sukha-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of suffering (*duḥkha-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of purity (*śubha-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of impurity (*aśubha-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of non-self (*anātman-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of permanence (*dhruva-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of impermanence (*adhruva-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of bliss (*śiva-dṛṣṭi*). Moreover, it is the diligence that is not distracted by the view of non-bliss (*aśiva-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is the diligence that is not distracted
"Advancing" means being able to pervade the remaining five perfections through superior activity; therefore, it is said that diligence is present in all six perfections.

Regarding the "two destinations"—the fruits of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*)—and the stage of benefit and happiness, these are simply not mentioned because they are [either] abbreviated or non-existent [in this context].
As for those capable of attaining the fruits of the two vehicles, they are those of fixed nature who proceed toward tranquility (*śama*), namely those destined for the third or fourth fruit.

However, among those śrāvakas who have entered into tranquility (*śama*), there are both those of dull faculties and those of sharp faculties. Likewise, among the four types of great śrāvakas, there are also those of sharp and dull faculties.

The intent of this passage is to state that, although the text mentions only the ultimate path of the two vehicles, because they aspire toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), it clarifies only those of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*)—namely, those śrāvakas who turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle. This is not [the case for] those in the treatise... (Note: The final sentence fragment appears to be incomplete in the source text.)

This is to clarify the two types of vehicles that seek quiescence (*śama*). Now, the commentary states: "Among those śrāvakas who seek quiescence, there are those of non-retrogressive dharma (*avinivartanīya-dharma*), who are called *pāramitā-śrāvakas*.
Residing in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they are able to manifest the form of meditative fruition (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) and can also, to a small degree, benefit other sentient beings;
however, because the text is abbreviated, this is not mentioned. As for the two vehicles that seek quiescence, if they seek quiescence..."
Among the śrāvakas, there are those who follow the Dharma through ignorance; these are not arhats, as they are entirely incapable of benefiting others.
A second interpretation states: if a person of indeterminate lineage attains Buddhahood, they can, until the end of the future, attend to the minds of other sentient beings.

The treatises speak of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) of indeterminate lineage in this context. As for those of determinate lineage, at the time their nature is fixed, they [are unable to] benefit others.
Sentient beings are few and cannot endure for long; they immediately dissolve their bodies and withdraw their wisdom.

Since there is no longer any matter of benefit or joy—both because it is minimal and because it is non-existent—it is considered "non-existent" in the treatises, and thus the "attainment of tranquility" (pratisaṃvid) is not mentioned. Now, as for the correct interpretation:

when it speaks of the "two fruits," these refer to the Śrāvakas who have attained tranquility—the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) and the fruit of the realization and awakening of no-more-learning. Thus, one does not take the [third]...

The third fruit. Because those who have attained the third fruit possess a mind that progresses toward further realization, the treatises speak only of the ultimate principle of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Thus, in this present commentary, we take as our subject those who have attained the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) within the two vehicles.

Among those of the two vehicles who have entered quiescence (*śamaikāyana*), there are noble ones of the *pāramitā* path who are not deluded regarding the Dharma; these individuals are able to bring a small measure of benefit and happiness to others. However, in the present case...

Because this section is concise, the two vehicles that seek tranquility (*śama*) are not mentioned. If those of the dull-witted among the two vehicles who have attained the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) were included, they would be entirely incapable of benefiting others;
since they lack the capacity to benefit others, they do not exist [in this context], and thus are not mentioned in the treatise.

Within the establishment of the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), they do not exist, and therefore the treatise does not mention them. There are two types [of such beings]: first, those who are untainted (*anāsrava*), which is accepted...

Regarding "outflows" (*sāsrava*) and "the heaviness of outflows" (*sāsrava-dauṣṭhulya*), it is because they pervade all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*). This is due to the fact that afflictions take phenomena of the three natures as their objects;
consequently, upon all phenomena of the three natures, there exists both heaviness and the state of being unserviceable (*akarmanyatā*).

When practitioners of the Two Vehicles give rise to the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*), they are directly able to sever the fixed obstructions (*niyata-āvaraṇa*) within the afflictions, and they are also able to incidentally suppress the heaviness within the cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*). This is certain.
Characteristics do not arise; subsequently, one enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, which is the extinction through wisdom (*prajñā-kṣaya*).

If a bodhisattva gives rise to the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*), it directly counteracts the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) regarding phenomena—namely, the aforementioned heavy impediments (*dausthulya*) that are meditative obstructions—and concurrently severs the heavy impediments of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
This untainted [wisdom] can eliminate the fixed nature of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). As for the two types of tainted [wisdom], they are merely... [up to] only this.

Regarding those of a wholesome nature: however, according to their mode of arising, wholesome states associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) can only suppress the obstacles to concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) that are unwholesome;
yet they may later regress and are unable to suppress the obstacles to higher concentrations that are wholesome or neutral (*avyākṛta*), because their power is inferior.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Thus, regarding the *Abhidharma*’s statement that all other obstacles [are abandoned] up to the tenth [stage], the same applies.

This means that in the tenth chapter of the *Abhidharma*, it is either the same as the others, exhausting the nature of the treatise on phenomena; or, the tenth chapter of the *Abhidharma* is the same as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (or *Yogācārabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*), because it eliminates the coarse and heavy afflictions (*dausthulya*).
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Alternatively, it may be that which is merely a 'countable obstruction' (*saṃkhyeya-āvaraṇa*).

For example, when one who practices meditative cultivation attains the first dhyāna, they experience its inferiority and are unwilling to further cultivate the higher meditations; this is precisely the experiencing of an inferior dharma."
The Commentary states: "That which is prevented therein encompasses all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena.

Among contaminated phenomena, it prevents only those that are distinct from unwholesome (*akuśala*) phenomena, for there is nothing else apart from those four categories of phenomena. ... Furthermore, regarding the phrase "simultaneously establishing both non-substance and function":

"substance" refers to non-diligence, while "function" is diligence itself; the three faculties constitute its substance. As for "function," it is non-laxity, serving to prevent evil and cultivate goodness.

Regarding "function": it means that the essence and function of non-dissipation are not separate from those four dharmas. If there were a distinct essence for non-dissipation, then its non-dissipation would constitute a distinct function.
Since the essence and function of non-dissipation are no different from those four dharmas, non-dissipation does not exist outside of them.
If it were external to the four dharmas, then both [essence and function] would be established as having no distinct essence or function. "Four" refers to others; this, then, is one.
Regarding the statement that "all [schools] separately maintain that there is a substantial entity (*svabhāva*)," this text represents the Sarvāstivāda position.
The Sarvāstivāda school establishes that all phenomena (*dharmas*) possess a substantial entity; alternatively, other sources also establish that phenomena have a substantial entity.

This may refer to the entire Sarvāstivāda school’s teaching, which does not allow for a separate substantial entity [beyond the dharma itself]. Alternatively, "all" may refer to [the consensus] within both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
The various masters state that non-laxity (*apramāda*) has a distinct substantial entity.
The *Śāstra* commentary says: "The 'basis' refers to the locus that sustains and causes [wholesome factors] to increase. This means that real dharmas are the basis for provisional dharmas;
taking real dharmas such as non-attachment (*alobha*) as the sustainer, they cause provisional dharmas such as non-laxity to cause wholesome factors to increase.

The Commentary states: "The distinct capacities of wisdom can ultimately not be found" means that while the four dharmas—non-attachment and so forth—collectively possess the capacity to prevent evil and cultivate goodness, their distinct capacities are as follows:
non-attachment serves as the antidote to attachment; non-hatred serves as the antidote to hatred, and so on;
and diligence serves as the antidote to laziness.
The *Śāstra* states: "Because among the distinct explanations immediately preceding this, non-attachment (*alobha*) is primary, it is used as the proximate basis for the summary.
This means that even if the three roots—non-attachment and so forth—are added to the enumeration, and non-attachment serves as their essential nature, the treatise’s specific analysis states:
"If one distinguishes them according to their support, then non-attachment and the others likewise have non-attachment as their primary [basis]. This is the text of the treatise.
In the *Saṃyukta-āgama*, it says: "Apart from non-greed and so forth, [the roots] cannot ultimately be found. Thus, non-greed is also taken as the foremost.

If greed, hatred, and delusion are termed "roots" (*mūla*), their meaning of "root" differs from that of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*). If greed, hatred, and delusion can produce unwholesome and evil factors of body and speech, they are termed "unwholesome roots" (*akuśala-mūla*).
If, among the twenty-two faculties, the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) specifically has the capacity to illuminate objects, it is distinct [from the aforementioned roots].

They are clearly understood. "Dominant" (indriya) refers to that which exercises sovereignty. If it is the male or female faculties, they exercise sovereignty over the secular household. If it is the five feeling faculties, they exercise sovereignty over the experience of the fruits of karma.

If it is the life faculty, it exercises sovereignty over maintenance and sustenance. If it is the three untainted faculties, they exercise sovereignty over the ability to produce enlightenment and nirvāṇa.
If it is the five faculties beginning with faith, they exercise sovereignty over worldly transcendence.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), [it refers to] equanimity (*upekṣā*). This is to distinguish it from the equanimity within the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*). The phrase "the measure of formations" does not mean the aggregate of formations itself.

Looking at the current passage, that which "should be practiced" refers to the aggregate of formations; the "equanimity within the aggregate of formations" is the equanimous feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*) within the aggregate of feeling.

Regarding the statement "now, practicing equanimity" (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*): this does not mean that it is a "formative force" (*saṃskāra*) simply because the word "formation" (*saṃskāra*) appears [in the compound].

Here, "formation" (*saṃskāra*) refers to volition (*cetanā*). This equanimity is not like volition, which is called a "formation" because it is capable of performing actions such as creating good or evil;
rather, volition is designated as a "formation" because it is the primary and most eminent factor within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Thus, volition is said to be the formation.

The Commentary states: "Because it is free from sinking. The initial mind’s joy and so forth still involve preparatory application (*prayoga*). The subsequent mind is upright regarding the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) in defilement.
As for the final "absence of function," these three stages refer specifically to the first entry into meditative absorption (*samādhi*);

they do not exist during other moments of distracted mind. Regarding the initial mind’s sharpness and so forth, this occurs within the stage of preparatory application; should there be sinking, [it must be countered].
Its mind is not sharp. Within the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga*), if one is free from the state of mental sinking, it is therefore said that "the initial mind is sharp," and so forth.
Regarding "far removed from preparatory application, subsequently upright": this refers to the mind that has entered meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).

Since within the mind of preparatory application there is still seeking and striving, there is a sense of high and low; being free from such preparatory application, it is called "upright. Regarding "uncontaminated by defilement" (*kliṣṭa*):...
Regarding the phrase "after the nature": as for that which has no immediate function, this is also precisely the mind entering meditative concentration immediately thereafter.
If, during the state of a distracted mind, one is invaded by superior defiled dharmas, the mind is weak in its nature and must exert effort.
Now, being in the state of concentration, since one does not even believe in superior defiled dharmas, the mind is neither timid nor weak, and there is no need for effort.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Or, although what is now being explained is simultaneous, it is not [merely] simultaneous; this explains its characteristics. As for the statement that "the others are explained in terms of the increase of benefit":
if, within the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), one is able to eliminate defilements (*saṃkleśa*), then the non-distraction (*avikṣepa*) increases simultaneously.
There are cases where it is explained in terms of the increase of benefit; although those two preceding and succeeding dharmas are in reality simultaneous, the Commentary speaks of their abandonment.
It arises either simultaneously with or prior to or posterior to [the object], being pleasant at both times.

Regarding the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Treatise on the Treasury of Abhidharma), Chapter Ten, which speaks of "extinguishing greed through equanimity" (*upekṣā*), that treatise refers to the equanimity of the higher realms or untainted (*anāsrava*) equanimity.

It is capable of removing the craving and discursive thought of the desire realm. Question: Since non-negligence (*apramāda*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are both established based on the same four factors, and their essential natures (*svabhāva*) are superior and middling, they should be identical without distinction. What is the reason for this? Answer:

Although these two dharmas are equally established based on the same four factors, their functions (*kāritra*) are each different. Non-negligence has the nature of guarding and cultivation as its essence; it acts as an antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Heedlessness accomplishes all [unwholesome states]. Its function is to act as an obstacle to supramundane wholesome states.

If one practices equanimity (*upekṣā*), its nature is to cause the mind to be even, upright, and to abide without effort. Its function is to counteract restlessness and to bring about peaceful abiding.

Furthermore, it is asked: should that which depends (*āśrita*) resemble its basis (*āśraya*)? Why? Because the dependent factors—heedfulness, non-heedlessness, and the practice of equanimity—are each distinct. If...
The four dharmas borrowed [from the roots] differ both in essence and function. That is to say: non-attachment has non-clinging as its essence and performing wholesome deeds as its function;

non-hatred and non-malice have non-ill will as their essence and performing wholesome deeds as their function; non-delusion has clear understanding as its essence and performing wholesome deeds as its function;

and heedfulness has vigor as its essence and fulfilling wholesome deeds as its function. As for anger, resentment, and so forth, they likewise depend upon hatred and the like; this should be understood accordingly.

Question: Regarding "equanimity, rectitude, and effortlessness. Since it has already been stated that these ten factors arise with every wholesome mind, when such a mind arises, there is necessarily equanimity of application (*praśrabdhi-upekṣā*).
When a mundane wholesome mind (*vyākṛta-kuśala-citta*) arises, how can it also possess equanimity, rectitude, and effortlessness?
If a mundane wholesome mind were to arise without equanimity and rectitude, then its equanimity of application and so forth would not [be present].

Regarding the "universally wholesome mind," the commentary states: "In order to eliminate the mind that harbors craving, one relies upon equanimity (*upekṣā*). Here, the "mind" is that which is to be pacified;
thus, equanimity is the basis (*āśraya*), and the mind is that which depends upon it (*āśrita*).

The *Śāstra* states: "The *sūtra*s' 'removal of covetousness and concern' (*lobha-pratigha-citta-vinodana*) extends even to equanimity (*upekṣā*). Because the mind arises even when the objects of covetousness do not return, it is called 'covetousness and concern.

When that treatise speaks of 'equanimity' and 'the removal of covetousness and concern,' it refers to the equanimity of the two upper realms (*dhātu*s), which can remove the covetousness and concern within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This applies either to those bound to the desire realm alone, or, alternatively, to untainted (*anāsrava*) equanimity, which can remove [them]."

The "outflow-tainted craving" (*sāsrava-rāga*) of the realms refers to deliberation (*vitarka*). To speak according to reality, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), equanimity (*upekṣā*) can also coexist with deliberation;
for example, when one feels longing and sorrow for the Unsurpassed Dharma, since there is no wholesome mind, deliberation likewise arises together with equanimity.

The Commentary states: "Because it is taught within the Eightfold Path (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*) in the *Abhidharma* (the *Dharmapada*), it refers exclusively to the untainted (*anāsrava*). This is an erroneous citation by the author of this Commentary.

It is only among the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) that they are exclusively untainted; since [the factors] are taught within the Eightfold Path, there is no such thing as [an exclusively untainted] equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The Commentary states: "Hatred seeks to destroy in general, not merely those who cause harm. If hatred intends to sever life, it does not merely intend to damage property;
its transgression exceeds that of damaging property. Therefore, hatred is said to be 'severing life.'"
The Commentary states: "Since this is so, [the case] where wind and the like do not sever the life-force of beings is as follows:

when one harbors malice toward sentient beings, the arising and ceasing of the preceding sentient being's mind and so forth constitute a course of action (*karmapatha*). This is because it can summon the general and specific retributions for the body in the three evil destinies in the future.
Whether it discards the general retribution-body, or is capable of inducing a general or specific retribution-body, all are termed courses of action. If it only summons..."
The individual body is not called a karmic path (*karmapatha*), just as the *saṃskāra* member [of dependent origination] does not induce an individual retribution-body.
All that can induce an individual retribution are called karmic paths; yet, just as the *saṃskāra* member induces an individual retribution, it is not itself called the *saṃskāra* member.

Only that which can induce a collective retribution-body, or that which can induce both a collective and an individual retribution-body, is then called the *saṃskāra* member. If one discusses consciousness or hatred as being karma and so forth, they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

[The action] arises; it can only induce a specific retribution (*vyavasthita-vipāka*) and cannot summon a collective retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*), and thus it is not called a course of action (*karmapatha*).

Furthermore, as in the case of a bhikṣu’s ordination platform: when he is formally receiving the precepts, after the three *karmavācanas* are completed in a single day, this precept can induce a collective retribution, or it can simultaneously summon both a collective and a specific retribution for the body.
