There are five [factors]. The commentary explains that the gods such as Vijñānātman (Jue Tian) calculate the sequential stages of the mind. If one speaks of them individually, there are feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*).

For instance, at the first moment when one is provoked by an object and experiences it, this is called feeling (*vedanā*). Next, in the second moment, when the mind conditions the object and establishes names and words to grasp its image, this is called perception (*saṃjñā*).
Next, in the third moment, when the mind conditions the object and engages in formative activity (*abhisamskāra*), this is called... [volition].

Next, when there is the cognition of an object, that is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). Thus, within the single substance of consciousness, the distinct temporal stages of its engagement with an object are designated as feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Apart from the mind itself, there are no separate mental factors (*caitta*); other states such as greed (*lobha*) or faith (*śraddhā*) are likewise [mere states of the mind].

All [of these] are conventionally established based upon volition (*cetanā*). Thus, one should know that there is no separate mind that apprehends [them]; rather, it is the preceding and succeeding states that are said to constitute the five aggregates.

If the Sautrāntikas posit the existence of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*) such that the five aggregates are already established, this is not what is being refuted here. Furthermore, consider this:

if Bhadanta Buddhadeva does not posit feeling, perception, volition, and so forth, then why is it that this refutation is directed against the system of Bhadanta Buddhadeva? It is not a refutation of something else; reflect upon this.
The Commentary states: "Because their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are distinct, their substance (*svabhāva*) must also be distinct. Now, I raise this objection:

since you already admit that the characteristics of feeling (*vedanā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and perception (*saṃjñā*) are distinct, then the substances of feeling, perception, and formations must also be distinct, because substance is not separate from its characteristics.

The Commentary states: "That [opponent] reckons that the substance of the six consciousnesses is one, yet they are spoken of as six because their bases are distinct states; this aggregate is likewise so.

This refers to the Bodhisattva’s reckoning that it is but a single mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Furthermore, that [opponent] reckons that the six consciousnesses are identical in substance as one, yet are spoken of as six because they are drawn forth through the gates of the six faculties, such as the eye, which serve as their common basis—just as a single monkey [is seen in six different places] at six windows.

The same applies to these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). It is definitively established that they are only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*); however, because there are distinct states (*avasthā*) at preceding and succeeding moments, one speaks of the five aggregates of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Now, by way of a digression, I shall cite a certain class of Bodhisattvas to directly refute the view of Deva.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "Because a single present moment possesses various different aspects (*ākāra*), it is designated as having many stages (*avasthā*).
If these were distinct [moments], there would be further difficulties. It further raises the objection: "That is to say, within a single moment of consciousness, there are multiple aspects;

namely, within one moment, there are the aspect of experiencing (*vedanā*), the aspect of grasping secondary objects, the mind that performs the primary action, the aspect of discernment (*vijñapti*), and so forth. Since..."

It is granted that there is only one consciousness which is with outflows (*sāsrava*). Therefore, one should reflect upon this single moment of consciousness: it possesses manifold aspects (*ākāra*), and its causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) are likewise manifold.
Regarding the meaning of this, the Commentary (*Śāstra*) states:
"That is to say, even when many moments undergo transformation and the sense organs and objects are similar, the causes and conditions are no different; the same fault applies to what precedes."

Furthermore, there is the difficulty of manifold transformation. Even if you grant that there are many moments before and after, such that a single consciousness is led to possess various mental aspects, we now raise this objection:
Consider, for instance, a preceding moment of visual consciousness and a succeeding moment of visual consciousness. Both rely upon the eye-faculty;

the preceding moment of visual consciousness takes color-form as its object, and the succeeding moment of visual consciousness likewise takes color-form as its object. Since the visual consciousness takes [the same object] in both the preceding and succeeding moments...

[Objection: Since the faculties and their objects are similar, what basis is there for [the distinction between] preceding and succeeding moments? Thus, a single visual consciousness would possess various mental formations such as discrimination, reception, grasping of images, and volitional activity across its preceding and succeeding phases.
If these were distinct [moments], it would entail the same fault as previously established.
The Commentary states: "That greed has no defiled mind upon which it relies" means that greed has no consciousness upon which it relies;

as for "no consciousness upon which it relies," the Commentary further states: "Moreover, the subsequent sutra speaks of contact, feeling, and perception together. Since the sutra states that there exist contact, feeling, and perception, we know [that they must have a basis].
There are no separate mental factors (*caitta*).

The commentary states: "Furthermore, it is said that these various dharmas are in conjunction and not non-conjunction. If there were indeed many separate mental factors, one could speak of their conjunction;
however, just as a single person cannot be called a "conjunction" even though they are composed of many parts, [a single dharma] cannot be termed a conjunction.
[Objection: Since there is only a single consciousness and no mental factors (caitta), how can it be called "conjunction" (saṃprayoga)?
Since you speak of "conjunction," we know that there must exist many distinct mental factors.
The Commentary states: Furthermore, the Sūtra speaks of the analogy of the lamp’s light, up to "like a traveler proceeding.
Just as many rays of light exist depending on a single lamp, so too do many manifestations resembling the long practice exist depending on a single mind. This is as previously cited.
The preceding treatise states: "The analogy of light and sunlight is similar to the analogy of illumination. Just as there are many rays depending upon the sun, the commentary (*shu*) states:
"Furthermore, from the three analogies of speed... until it is established that there is only perception (*saṃjñā-mātra*). Here, it says: "Now, taking up the latter three..."
The phrases correspond to the three realms as previously established. Regarding the "Hearers" (śrāvaka) dwelling in the realm of sound: what is meant by "those who are awakened alone"?
This refers to those who, having previously discussed desire, [assert] that within the desire realm the four great elements are taken as the self.

Since it is asked whether the desire realm consists only of form, [the answer is] that there are also mind and mental factors, or perhaps only mind. These correspond to the Form Realm (rūpadhātu). Within the Form Realm, since it is said to be "mind-born," [it refers to] the mind.

That which is "this" is precisely the mind. How could it be that within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) there is only mind? Therefore, the ground [of that realm] must also possess something resembling an object.
As for the statement that "there is only perception," this corresponds to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Within the formless realm, since it is said that "formless perception arises," how could it be that within the formless realm there is only the perception of form without mental factors (*caitta*)? Thus, the ground of the formless realm possesses other minds and mental factors; this refers to "milk."
"From curd and ghee up to those possessing perception"—this analogy is now cited. Its intended meaning is to demonstrate that where there is mind, there must also be mental factors (*caitta*).

How could it be that wherever there is form, there must necessarily be mind alone? There must also be perception (*saṃjñā*), feeling (*vedanā*), and so forth. "Form produced by the mind" (*manomaya-rūpa*):
"produced by the mind" means it arises according to the will of the mind.

The Commentary states: "Regarding those who take the aforementioned three coarse great elements as the self—this refers to humans and devas in the desire realm, all of whom grasp these coarse great elements and regard them as the self."
The *Śāstra* says, "about to determine. The commentary explains: the five active paths (*pañca-pratipad*) are also called "about to determine" because the mind arises immediately upon its inception;
thus it is said that the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is the sovereign and the support, distinguishing it from that which lacks activity, namely the five aggregates (*skandha*).

First, as explained according to their nature, these are the phenomena of greed, hatred, and so forth. Second, in the subsequent sutra, they are contact, sensation, perception, and so forth. Third, it further states, "such a conjunction."

[The text continues with] "and so forth. Fourth, the Sūtra speaks of the analogy of the lamp and its light in conjunction. Furthermore, the three preceding analogies together constitute what is called the "Five Sūtras.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "There is only perception" (*saṃjñā-mātra*). The Explanation says: Since it says "there is perception," there must therefore be other mental factors (*caitasika*), such as contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.

When the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*) are taught, they are intended solely to reveal the basis for the arising of form, motion, mental factors (*caitta*), and so forth; thus, the term "mind" (*citta*) is used because it is preeminent.

However, the "six elements of the person" (*puruṣa-ṣaḍ-dhātu*) mentioned here refers exclusively to the functional processes within the internal sentient body, and does not refer to functions occurring upon external objects such as mountains or rivers.
Since it specifically speaks of the "person," it is clearly understood to be internal. First, [the element of] form is the basis for appropriation (*rūpa-upādāna*).
This refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the body. That which serves as the supporting basis (*āśraya-dharma*) consists of eleven factors:

namely, the five sense-faculties (*indriya*), the five objects (*viṣaya*) of the body, and the previously mentioned manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*). These eleven dharmas all depend upon the four great elements of the body as their cause.
As for external objects, the external supporting bases consist only of the five objects; thus, there are eleven dharmas in total. These two [categories] are the bases of motion.

This refers to the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*) within the joints of the body. Because there is an empty space between the joints, the internal body is able to sustain inferior activities and past events;
the other mental factors (*caitta*) may likewise be understood as depending on their respective elements (*dhātu*). "Element" (*dhātu*) refers to the nature [of the cause].
As for the physical body of form and mind moving in dependence upon space, it is like a person who, at the time of acting, gives rise to a flow [of action] through the power of a respectful mind.
Only when form (*rūpa*) exists can there subsequently be spontaneous and effortless activities such as "carrying" (*vahana*). The *Śāstra* states:

Furthermore, the sutra cited previously regarding the analogy of milk and so forth should be used to pose a counter-interrogation. Buddhadatta and others maintain that after the eleventh moment, the mind undergoes transformation;
if the five aggregates were to arise separately, they would be distinct entities. Now, the counter-interrogation is posed: [Regarding] milk, curd, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and so forth.
Regarding the transformation of milk into curd, butter, and so forth over time, this is what is meant by "identity" (the same entity).

Since you admit that the substance of the mind undergoes transformation from prior to subsequent states, the substance of the mind would likewise have to be called "matter" (rūpa). This does not mean that the underlying substratum (*dravya*) and so forth are non-existent.

If the mind-king itself is designated as "that which can resemble" (*nirbhāsa-kṣama*) and the mental factors (*caitta*) are designated as "resembling," then when a defiled mind arises following that [pure] mind, it should be identical to that resemblance, and so on. If the mind...

When the King (the mind-king) arises as pure, the mind-king itself appears as if it were faith and so forth. The verse states that the mind appears as two; this means the mind-king is capable of appearing [as such].

It may appear as the objective substance (the *ālambana*) and so forth, or it may appear as faith and so forth. These are the objects of appearance—the substances such as the mind—and they possess no separate essence.
As for the phrase "up to what is manifested," this refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), which exist apart from the external essence of the self.

There are no separate seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*); they arise from the self-substance-part (*svabhāva-bhāga*). Thus, the transformation of contact gives rise to the appearance of the two parts—the seeing and the object-like.
Although these two have distinct entities, their substance arises only from the mind; because they are subordinate to the dharma [of the mind], they are described as "resembling" it.

This passage refers to the mental factors (*caitta*). Apart from the sovereign mind-king (*citta-rāja*), they do not possess a separate substance; rather, the mental factors arise from the sovereign mind-king, and thus they are the "subordinate dharmas" (*dharma-guṇa*) of the king.
[They] can arise. If that is so, as for those things such as greed and faith, up to those which resemble greed and faith—what are they?

The intent of this question is: since greed, faith, and so forth are already included within the mental states (*citta*) that resemble them, what other distinct entities resembling greed and faith could there be?
"What is capable" refers to the mental factors (*caitasika*) such as faith, desire, and so forth, which are included therein; this is the answer. Regarding the term "mental factors":
while the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is capable of giving rise to both defilement and purity, these [factors] are the specific objects of defilement and purity, such as desire, faith, and so on.

Herein it is taught that the mind-king itself is also capable of attaining the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of defiled desire, pure faith, and neutral dharmas; that is, the mind-king’s self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*).
Within the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) manifested upon the self-verifying aspect (svasaṃvedanabhāga), there are dharmas of the three natures—greed, faith, and the indeterminate.

This faith is also able to take as its object the essence of greed and indeterminate dharmas, as well as the actual faith and so forth, within the objective aspect that arises upon the self-verifying aspect.

There are also faith, greed, and dharmas of the indeterminate nature (avyākṛta). These [afflictions] such as greed can likewise take as their objects the essential natures (svabhāva) of faith and so forth, which belong to the three natures including the indeterminate.
However, upon the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) manifested by the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-cognizing aspect) of greed and so forth, there also exist greed and the indeterminate three natures.

It is accepted that within the collection of mental states (*cittopakleśa*) associated with the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), there are mental factors (*caitta*) arising simultaneously; this explains the greed associated with the mind-king.

The mind can resemble greed or faith; this is distinct from the [preceding] explanation. Among indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena, there are those that accord with defilement and those that accord with virtue.
As for those that accord with virtue, even in this case it is just as when a virtuous mind takes an indeterminate phenomenon as its object:

it takes the aspect-part (*nimittabhāga*) of the indeterminate phenomenon as its object, and that aspect-part of the indeterminate phenomenon is itself termed "accordant with virtue. It is the same when a defiled mind takes an indeterminate phenomenon as its object. Now, in the verse:
It is simply stated that they resemble dharmas of greed and defilement, and resemble dharmas of faith and purity; it does not say they are indeterminate (avyākṛta) dharmas.
Regarding those indeterminate dharmas: if one gives rise to a defiled mind toward these indeterminate dharmas, then those indeterminate dharmas accord with defilement.
If, on account of these indeterminate dharmas, a pure mind arises, then those indeterminate dharmas accord with purity. If they accord with defilement, then...
Indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena are designated as "defiled. If those indeterminate phenomena accord with the wholesome, then those indeterminate phenomena are designated as "wholesome.

The verse does not mention them as being indeterminate. For example, the Mahāsāṃghika, Ekavyāvahārika, Lokottaravāda, and Gokulika—these four schools establish the existence of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, but do not establish indeterminate phenomena. Furthermore, for instance...
With virtue as the cause, one experiences the fruit of level, excellent mountains and rivers.

Although these mountains and rivers are strongly induced by this virtuous karma, since they are produced by that virtuous karma, the mountains and rivers themselves are "conducive to defilement" (anuloma-kuśala).

Furthermore, those dharmas such as the mountains and rivers—which are the causes capable of inducing virtue—are also called "virtuous. [Likewise,] with unwholesome karma as the cause, one experiences...
Mountains, rivers, worlds, hells, and so forth—even those malevolent mountains and rivers—accord with the causes of the evil karma that brings them about;
thus these mountains and rivers are termed "malevolent. Regarding the second interpretation, one might ask: what distinguishes it from the first? The former is broad and superior;

one should therefore set aside the *Zongchao*. What is now being explained is the second of the four types of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), namely, the conventional truth of reason (*yukti-saṃvṛti*). Now...
Regarding the point that it is not logical for cause and effect to be identical according to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*):

this treatise states that if one relies on the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) categories of aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), the primary mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) are each distinct; this is explained according to the second type of conventionality.

Furthermore, when the treatise says that if one relies on the ultimate (*paramārtha*), the mental factors are neither identical to nor separate from the mind, this is based on the fourth type of ultimate truth.

Within the section on meaning, the second is the explanation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). According to this second ultimate truth, all phenomena are neither identical nor distinct [from one another].

Taking the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) as the cause and the mental factors (*caitta*) as the effect, they are neither identical nor separate; alternatively, taking the mental factors as the cause and the mind-king as the effect, they are likewise neither identical nor separate.
This is because, when the mind-king and mental factors are compared, they can possess the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Nor does it rely upon the first ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). In the first ultimate truth, it is taught that all phenomena are like illusions;

furthermore, it does not clarify the gate of non-identity and non-difference. It is by relying on the second ultimate truth that one speaks of non-identity and non-difference, thereby establishing the fourfold conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
This is explained definitively in relation to all phenomena: if it is the second conventional [truth], then jars and basins are still dependent [upon their parts]. If it is the third...

The second is the conventional [truth], which refers to the aggregates, bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu*). The primary minds (*citta-rāja*) each definitely exist, and their essences are distinct.

If one relies on the third type of conventional truth, the Four Noble Truths function as cause and effect: that which is an effect is definitively an effect and not a cause; that which is a cause is definitively a cause and not an effect.
Furthermore, a virtuous cause will certainly result in a pleasant fruit; likewise, virtuous and non-virtuous causes are determined [to produce their respective results].
One obtains the fruit of suffering; cause and effect are distinct. If one relies on the fourth conventional truth, then the two types of emptiness are each distinct:

by severing the grasping at a self, one attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). If one relies on its four doors of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), then it cannot be said that phenomena are fixed;
all phenomena are non-fixed. Regarding the first ultimate truth, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are all like illusions and like magical transformations.

The eight similes, such as that of the self and so forth, are all not the true tenet. If one relies on the second [level], the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), cause and effect are neither identical nor separate;
the cause is itself the effect because suffering and pleasure are one. The mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is the effect and the mental factors (*caitta*) are the cause;

or the mind-king is the cause and the mental factors are the effect. The seed and the consciousness are cause and effect in terms of their substance, yet they are likewise neither identical nor separate.

If one relies on the third ultimate truth, the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is one; however, because it is manifested through the first mode of expression, it is conventionally described as two types of concentration (*samādhi*).
If one relies on the fourth ultimate truth, it is the single Dharma-realm of the mind, for it transcends the path of both mind and speech.

Regarding the second conventional truth and the first ultimate truth, although their dharma-essence is one, there is a distinction in that the former is like an illusion and so forth. As for the others...
It should be understood accordingly. The three mundane virtues following the [three] gates and the three true [virtues] are all identical in essence as suchness (*tathatā*).
Within a single dharma, I distinguish between the conventional and the ultimate. If that dharma is one, it is merely for the sake of those to be taught that distinctions are made.

Thus, for sentient beings who have newly entered the Buddha-dharma and for other *manomaya-kāyas*, the Buddha speaks of four conventional dharmas, asserting that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) definitely exist.

Phenomena such as cause and effect truly exist, each being real in its own right. If the Buddha, for the sake of practitioners wishing to enter the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*), speaks in accordance with the sequence of contemplative practice, he describes all phenomena as being like illusions, where cause and effect are neither identical nor separate; these are the four types of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*).

The latter [conventional] and the former three [ultimate] realities are non-different in essence; they differ only in that the initial stage of contemplative practice has not yet reached the level of the faculties (*indriya*).
They are not the same; that is to say, there is a difference. Furthermore, regarding the third level, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*):

even if one were to argue that they are identical in terms of the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*), the eight [categories] are not necessarily distinct from it. Although *tathatā* (suchness) is a single essence, it is manifested through its designations (*vyavahāra*).

For example, one speaks of the *tathatā* of wholesome phenomena, the *tathatā* of unwholesome phenomena, and the *tathatā* of indeterminate phenomena—all of which are manifested through their designations. The present two layers are likewise so.

First, regarding the explanation: there are eight [aspects] corresponding to the eight consciousnesses. If one considers them in terms of the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*), all eight consciousnesses possess these two selflessnesses;

thus, the essence of the eight consciousnesses is not distinct. Furthermore, when one investigates them within the primary ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they are neither identical nor separate.
Even if one were to suppose there could be a real separation, here, in relation to the primary ultimate truth, they remain neither identical nor separate. Since all phenomena are thus...

Like an illusion or a magical transformation, it is neither true nor real; it is distinct yet inseparable. Regarding the statement that "the first truth, which is principle (*li*), is superior to the second, the conventional (*suk*)":
the commentary (*shu*) says this may refer to the fourth [truth], and so forth, as the text itself clarifies. If one relies on the fourth ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the mind...
The King did not provide a definitive statement. If one were to say they are identical, it would contradict the explanation given regarding the eight consciousnesses, which states:

"The intrinsic nature of the eight consciousnesses cannot be said to be definitively one, because their modes of activity (*ākāra*), bases (*āśraya*), objects (*ālambana*), and associated mental factors (*samprayukta*) differ; furthermore, when one ceases, the others do not necessarily cease," and so forth.
Nor can they be said to be definitively distinct, for the Sūtras state that the eight consciousnesses are without differentiation, being like water and its waves. Therefore, they are definitively...

Otherwise, they would not possess the nature of cause and effect; therefore, even the eight consciousnesses cannot be definitively described as being either identical to or separate from [the ultimate].
At that level of true ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the path of both mind and speech is cut off; this will naturally become clear from the text itself.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the question, 'Although there is only the manifest arising... according to the meaning of the basis and the concomitance,' if one examines the text, it asks only how one should understand the stages of manifest arising;
it does not ask about the meaning of the basis and the concomitance mentioned in the subsequent section. The reason it does not ask is as follows:"

The Commentary states: "Having already explained the second verse concerning the defilements of the third transformative consciousness, and continuing up to where it says 'the mental factors are said to be concomitant,' this refers to the previous explanation of the defilements of the third transformative consciousness;
specifically, the single verse beginning with 'Next, the third transformative consciousness' is taken as the first [section]."
The subsequent passage states: "This mind is omnipresent" (*sarvatraga*). This refers to the first verse.

Regarding the phrase "relying upon the fundamental consciousness" (*mūlavijñāna*), it means that even the six consciousnesses rely upon the eighth consciousness as their basis. This is expressed in the verse by:

"The five consciousnesses appear according to conditions," and "the mental consciousness always arises. Because these preceding six consciousnesses all rely upon the eighth consciousness, they may be either simultaneous or not simultaneous with it, as follows:
The two lines beginning with "Waves depend on water" explain the meaning of simultaneous occurrence (*sahabhāva*). According to the verse of the treatise, there should be three lines in total.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The words 'without mind'... until 'the arising and establishing of the mental faculty'," this refers to the two characters "without mind" (*acitta*) in the verse.

This applies to the four lower stages. One should state that these are the mindless attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the mindless attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), mindless sleep, and mindless fainting.

If, regarding the other four stages, one does not say they are "mindless," it is because in those four stages there is mental activity due to the presence of a distracted consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
To claim that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can arise in these four stages is erroneous. Since it has already been stated that there are five such states...

If there is no mind, how can you allow the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to arise therein? Since "no-mind" applies to all four lower stages, would it not follow that these four lower stages are themselves states of no-mind, and thus there is no fault?

The Commentary states: "The source from which the root arises" refers to the beginning of understanding; this is the meaning of "root. It is the causal basis for the arising of the eighth consciousness.
Furthermore, within this first-born body, the eighth consciousness is also the source from which [this life] initially arises;
it cannot be said to have a beginning since beginningless time. The eighth consciousness is itself beginningless; it merely arises for the first time in this present manifestation.
Within the limits of a single lifetime, the beginning and end are established.
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are both clarified, even up to the passage on 'mutual manifestation.

Regarding the eighth consciousness being 'both clarified,' this refers to its state during the out-flowing (impure) stage; as previously explained in the verse on the eighth consciousness, it is like the position of the *Rāga-kūpa* (or 'offering' stage). Thus.

This clarifies the stage at which the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) abandons its contaminated (*sāsrava*) portion. Furthermore, as previously stated in the verse concerning the seventh consciousness (*manas*), it says:
"In the Arhat and in the supramundane path, it does not exist. This precisely clarifies the stage at which the seventh consciousness abandons its contaminated portion.

Thus, regarding the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, the verse clarifies only the stage at which the seventh consciousness abandons its contaminated portion, and does not clarify [the abandonment of] the seventh and eighth consciousnesses [simultaneously]. The seventh and eighth consciousnesses...
Regarding the stage of cessation: here, the six evolving consciousnesses clarify only the stages of their arising and ceasing.

This refers to the verse stating that the five consciousnesses appear according to conditions, and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is constantly manifest, except when one is born in the Heaven of Non-conception, or during states such as sleep and fainting.
This refers to the six evolving consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*) alone, which clarify the stages of arising and ceasing, and clearly distinguish the stages of severing the outflows (*āsrava*).
The commentary states: "The seventh and eighth consciousnesses perform all functions constantly and without interruption;

therefore, while the seventh and eighth consciousnesses clarify the stages of severing the outflows, they do not clarify the stages of arising and ceasing. This, in turn, reveals that the six evolving consciousnesses likewise [possess these stages]."

At the time of abandonment, the six consciousnesses merely clarify the stages of arising and ceasing. Furthermore, although they manifest the mutual manifestation [of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses], even though only the stage of abandoning outflows (āsrava) is clarified for the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, this also implies that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses likewise possess stages of arising and ceasing;

that is, at the very moment the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are correctly abandoning outflows, they are also termed "arising and ceasing. Now, although the six evolving consciousnesses merely clarify [this]...

The "different states" (bhinnāvasthā) reflect the six impure states of the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). This refers to the arising and ceasing as mutually reflected throughout the preceding and following treatises.

Regarding "ceasing," this refers to the five states of mindlessness (*acittaka*). Regarding "arising," it says, "the mental consciousness manifests," which will be explained in its own place within the section on the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) below.
Question: In which passage is this found? Answer: The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) below states: "It is the mental consciousness that is constantly manifest."
Regarding the phrase "giving rise to the lower transformation of the basis," this single line applies to both verses.

As for the two lines "this very [consciousness] relies upon the fundamental consciousness," these two lines apply to the following two stanzas. Within those two subsequent stanzas, the six evolving consciousnesses are clarified; it is shown that all six evolving consciousnesses rely upon the fundamental consciousness.
The Commentary states: "The two [consciousnesses] share the same object of form" refers to the five types of sensory objects (pañca-viṣaya) which are material forms.

The Commentary further states: "If, according to the Hīnayāna, the five consciousnesses have three categories based on arising from four, five, or three conditions," these three categories are as follows:
first, visual consciousness constitutes one category, because visual consciousness arises by way of five conditions—namely, light, clarity, the sense organ (indriya), [the object, and attention].

The object and mental attention constitute one category. Second, auditory consciousness constitutes one category; auditory consciousness arises from four conditions, namely: the ear-organ, the object, and mental attention.
Third, the three consciousnesses of the nose, tongue, and body constitute one category; these three consciousnesses arise from three conditions, namely:
the organ, the object, and mental attention. Regarding the divine eye, it excludes light and clouds. Question: Does the divine eye exclude light and clouds? [Does] the nose and body consciousness...
Furthermore, if it also removes clouds, how does it differ from the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*)? One would expect that the divine eye can see even in the dark and through obstructions;

the eye perceives objects within its range of contact. Again, if the divine eye removes clouds, what is the difference between this eye and the physical eye (*māṃsacakṣus*), and what is the difference with the ear?

The Commentary states: "There is no fundamental support whatsoever. If one refers to the first six consciousnesses, according to this Commentary, the eighth consciousness serves as their fundamental support.
However, if the seventh and eighth consciousnesses depend upon one another, they possess only a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) and lack a fundamental support.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Some say that the eighth [consciousness] depends on four conditions and the seventh depends on three, and so forth.

According to the correct principle (*samyak-artha*), if it is said that the seventh consciousness arises depending on all four conditions, this is precisely the incorrect doctrine of the first three masters, as previously stated at the beginning of the fourth section.
The first master asserts that the seventh consciousness takes the cognitive substance (*vijñapti-tattva*) of the eighth consciousness as its object, and also takes the... [and so forth].
The second master asserts that the eight consciousnesses are simultaneously associated with mental factors such as perception (saṃjñā) and the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika).

The third master asserts that the seventh consciousness takes the two parts—the seeing-part and the seen-part—of the eighth consciousness as its object. Furthermore, [the third master] asserts that the seventh consciousness takes the substance of the eighth consciousness and its subsequent seeds as its objects.
The three masters mentioned above state that the seventh consciousness relies upon the eighth consciousness;

this seventh consciousness universally takes the five universal mental factors (*pañca-sarvatraga*) and the seeds of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its objects. Thus, the support (*āśraya*) and the object (*ālambana*) of the seventh consciousness are each distinct.

This seventh consciousness arises from four conditions (*catasraḥ pratyayāḥ*); the arising from four conditions is explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*). As for the explanation of the fourth master, regarding the seventh [consciousness]...
The *vijñāna* (consciousness) relies upon the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) and takes that seeing-portion as its object.

Thus, the seventh consciousness relies upon the first root (*indriya*), which is precisely its objective sphere (*ālambana*). That the seventh consciousness arises solely from three conditions (*pratyaya*) is the correct interpretation.
Regarding the phrase "like a great torrent of water": [the questioner] asks, "In the sūtra, why is only the 'torrent of water' taken up, and not [other examples]?"

The pool water—its sweetness and the non-flowing of its current—can be understood through this analogy. That is to say, it is like the reflection of many images appearing upon the surface of a clear, bright mirror.
Question: Within the Mahāyāna, there is the doctrine that objects do not exist; how then can this sutra speak of "mirror-images"? Furthermore, what is meant by "images" in the context of a mirror?
It is like a person walking within the four [elements], where other forms arise; these are called "shadows. What is the distinction between these?
Therefore, in this sutra, the term "intermediate image" (*pratibimba*) is explained as a shadow.

Regarding the answer that "there may be the arising of one shadow, or even many shadows," since a clear mirror is being discussed here, what appears within the mirror is an image (*bimba*), not a shadow. This is especially so when one is walking in the sunlight.

There is another form that arises, which is called a shadow (*chāyā*). Regarding the phrase "In this [context], one should say 'up to' within the dharmas," etc., this refers generally to the *saṃjñā*, *cetanā*, and so forth.
A third interpretation states: In this treatise, it should have said "this dharma, the analogy, and so forth," as explained at length in the Sūtra.
Thus, it would not have used only "this dharma" or "this analogy. Now, the fact that it uses only "these dharmas and analogies" refers to the *dharma*.

Within the middle [category], there are only the five bases of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) for which no corresponding phenomena exist. If, within the analogies, one were to raise individual examples for each, then within those analogies there would be corresponding analogies to match;
that is to say, the taking of sensations (*vedanā*) and so forth is illustrated by the analogy of a reflection in a mirror. This refers to these corresponding phenomena and their analogies.
The Commentary states: "Up to the stage of Buddhahood, the five consciousnesses possess a momentum similar to that of the cause. The Explanation says:
Regarding the five consciousnesses at the stage of Buddhahood, the number of conditions they require is similar to those of ordinary beings in the causal state;

furthermore, the consciousnesses of a Buddha are frequently interrupted and only partially continuous, because the various conditions upon which they depend are often not fully present. Moreover, within the Buddhas, the physical eye (māṃsa-cakṣus) arises by means of nine conditions. Since...

This is called the flesh eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). It necessarily possesses nine conditions for consciousness. If it is the Buddha’s divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), it possesses seven conditions, excluding cloud and light.
The commentary states that the word "also" (*api*) indicates the sense of non-fixity; therein are four interpretations.

The Commentary states: "Or [it arises] by taking the mind as its object, or by taking something else as its object. "Or by being weary of the mind" refers to the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
"Or by [the state of] maturation" refers to the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñi-deva*), as well as sleep and fainting.
The Commentary states that the eight consciousnesses differ from one another, and so forth, up to the point where it says they are "constantly manifest.

This means that the sixth consciousness differs from the first five consciousnesses in its coarse and agitated nature; the conditions upon which it relies are frequently incomplete, such that it arises for a short time and remains unarisen for a long time.

Furthermore, the sixth consciousness differs from the latter two; the seventh and eighth consciousnesses have subtle modes of activity (*ākāra*) and are constantly continuous at all times, whereas the sixth consciousness is said to arise manifestly at all times.
The *Śāstra* states: "Regarding the second turn [of the commentary] below, it says:

'For this reason, the middle [verse] among those in the *kārikā* does not mention this sixth [element], up to the point where they are both concluded. This refers to the end of the second turn of the explanation in the treatise, which concludes:

'For this reason, it is not mentioned. The sixth is mentioned here because it manifests according to conditions; it should likewise be explained in the first turn of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and its conclusion should also be made there. By means of this...
This [text] does not state that "this appears according to conditions. In the present treatise, this phrase is not attached at the end of the first alternative;
it is only attached within the second explanation. Because it is not stated here that "this appears according to conditions," the initial double conclusion summarizes the two preceding explanations.

The commentary states: "As for the principle of seeds and faculties," "seeds" refers to the seeds [of consciousness], "faculties" refers to the six sense faculties, and "principle" refers to the principle of the Four Noble Truths.

The commentary further states: "Regarding 'by what basis,' etc., or 'when there is a deficiency,' etc.": this refers either to the five material sense faculties which serve as the bases for the five consciousnesses, or...

Regarding the five material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*), there are times when they are absent; for instance, while in the mother’s womb during stages such as the *kalala*, because the five faculties have not yet arisen, one is said to be "deficient in faculties," and the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) likewise cannot arise.

Furthermore, in cases such as congenital blindness or deafness within the womb, the non-arising of the five consciousnesses is due to the deficiency of the five material sense-faculties that serve as the bases for the five [consciousnesses].
The commentary states: "Regarding 'the principle, phenomena, and so forth': 'principle' refers to the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*) and the unestablished truths (*avyavasthāna-satya*).
'Phenomena' refers to internal things; that is, the five sense objects are called external, while the faculties and their spheres are called internal.

Regarding the statement 'because the eighth and seventh consciousnesses are the same as them': this means that the five consciousnesses, the eighth consciousness, and the seventh consciousness are all the same."

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it cannot be explained in terms of being internal or external. If the seventh consciousness were to take only the internal as its object, while the five sensory consciousnesses took only the external as their objects, then [the claim that] "perception (*saṃjñā*) constitutes the interior of birth and death" would be untenable;
for even the non-Buddhists do not separately establish mental factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) or volition (*cetanā*).

Only perception (*saṃjñā*) is able to take all objects as its conditions and grasp their characteristics. Just as with perception, beings are born into birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) because of perception;
they undergo the body of birth-and-death by training in it. Because this perception exists within birth-and-death, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) particularly loathe it.

Furthermore, they undergo the cultivation of the various dhyānas and the cultivation of the formless realms (*ārūpya*). Those who cultivate the dhyānas are born into the first dhyāna; they should emerge from the second to transcend suffering, and emerge from the third.

There are three kinds of joy arising from bliss: first, the joy and bliss born of concentration in the first dhyāna; second, the joy and bliss born of seclusion; third, the sublime bliss born of seclusion.
Fourth, there is the tranquil bliss of mindfulness and equanimity, which is the attainment of the immovable and unconditioned, free from the fluctuations of sensation.

The cultivation of the formless perceptions refers to the perception of the sphere of infinite space, the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness, and so forth, up to the perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Because one is free from unchanging sensations, one attains the cessation of sensation and perception without distinction.

Regarding the statement that there is a separate high tower, both the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and other treatises state that within the Heaven of Great Reward (*Bṛhatphala*), there is a separate high tower where the Brahmā King resides. First...

The Śuddhāvāsa and Brahmapurohita [heavens] are the same as the Brahmakāyika heaven; they share one *parvata-saṃsthāna* (mountain-like) cloud-ground. It may be granted that on this ground one may separately establish high towers.

As for the fourth dhyāna outside [the first three], since these are heavens that dwell in obstructed space (*sāvaraṇa-vihārin*), how could one separately establish high towers within the Bṛhatphala heaven?
Answer: Just as with the Yāma heaven and the Āsaṃjñika heaven, although they each dwell in separate locations, because they consist of high towers upon the ground, [they are possible].

They share the same name and belong to the same stage (*bhūmi*). However, the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) is slightly higher than the Heaven of Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*), by one hundred *li* or fifty *li*;
therefore, it is called the "High Tower" (*kūṭāgāra*). Each of these non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*) resides individually in a single high tower;
it is not that many people dwell together in one tower. Just as in the lower three dhyānas there are clouds that merge densely, so too within the fourth dhyāna...
It is named the Heaven of the Abodes of Stars (*Tārakāvati*). Thus, the first heaven is named "No Cloud" (*Anabhraka*); by this example, the remaining eight heavens above it are also named "No Cloud.

These names exist because they are designated according to their specific characteristics, just as the Four Noble Truths are uniquely termed "Establishment" (*vyavasthāna*). By citing the first, the subsequent ones are revealed:

the Truth of Origination is termed "False Practice," and so on, up to the Truth of the Path being termed "Right Practice. Now, although the Brahmā King and the Brahmā-purohitas share the same level (*bhūmi*), if...
During that interval, the Brahmapurohitas could not see the Brahmā King; however, when the Brahmā King intended for them to see him, they were able to see him.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The interpretation provided contradicts the literal text as it was explained," this refers to the immediately preceding commentary which states, "As in the assembly of the second master."

There is only the factor of "possessing form" (*rūpin*), which refers to the intermediate long duration—that is, both at the time of initial birth and at the final moment—during which the mind is present.

Furthermore, although it serves as an analogy for the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), it is the long duration that is similar [to them], and thus it is taken as the analogy for the subsequent state.
The Commentary states: "The Sthavira school and others maintain that even the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for those born there is devoid of mind.
That school asserts that the intermediate state for those born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) is likewise without mind."

The *Śāstra* says: "In the Mahāyāna, it is subsumed under the branch of birth (*jāti-aṅga*). The commentary explains: If one speaks according to the Hīnayāna, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is subsumed under the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*).
This is because the Hīnayāna does not establish the existence of seeds (*bīja*). From the stage prior to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)—namely, the intermediate state—it is called "consciousness.
When this branch of consciousness enters the mother’s womb, it is called the branch of name-and-form. As the fetus gradually grows, it is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). And so forth...

This should be omitted from the separate copy. It asks: among those [factors] that reach the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*), are all those that have not yet undergone decay and change subsumed under the "limbs of birth" (*jātibhāga*)? The commentary states:

"It is not the case that [they are included] at the second moment following the existence at birth, nor even until the time of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the existence at birth. Regarding this:
Those who desire to be born in the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva-deva) possess a mind; however, this does not mean that they possess a mind at the very moment of birth.

Neither the first moment nor the second moment [of the birth-existence] are called "possessing a mind" because those first and second moments of the birth-existence lack a mind, just as the first and second moments of the prior existence (pūrvakālabhava) likewise lack a mind. This is because...
[They] faint. However, with respect to their fundamental state of mind (*mūlacitta*), which persists for a long duration, it is said that they possess consciousness.
That is to say, having been born in that heaven, for one full lifespan of five hundred *kalpas*, the period is divided into three stages.

Regarding the first stage, from the beginning up until one hundred and sixty-seven *kalpas* have passed, they all give rise to mental factors (*dharma*). Thus, within that single lifespan, when divided into ten parts, the initial portion consists of fifty-six *kalpas*.
In all cases, there is very little mention of the state of possessing mind (*sacittaka*). Furthermore, there is the state of possessing mind for a hundred years or fifty years.

If one refers to the first and second moments of both the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) and the fundamental existence (*mūlabhava*), these are said to possess mind; however, this does not apply to the initial stage of the fundamental existence.

Within that initial phase, from the beginning up until the completion of one hundred and sixty kalpas, it is designated as "possessing mind. This refers to those born from eggs and so forth, at the very moment they first receive birth, during the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*).

In the first thought-moment, the second thought-moment, and the many thought-moments of the prior existence (*pūrvabhava*), no consciousness arises. Because of this, one is sustained by a state of fainting.
Only subsequently, in the [moment of] the prior existence, does mind arise. Therefore, it is known that the same applies to birth in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*).
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, it is not that at the end of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) one can give rise to a mind of perception (*saṃjñā-citta*).

This means that even at the final stage of the intermediate state, one cannot give rise to a mind of maturational indeterminate (*vipāka-avyākṛta*) nature. This is because at the final stage of the intermediate state, one invariably gives rise to a "conception of rebirth" (*pratisaṃdhicitta*).

This conception of rebirth is itself a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*), not a mind of perception. As for the phrase "at the time of the state of no-mind which induces maturational indeterminate [states]": this refers to the capacity [of the mind].

It draws forth the seeds of the maturation-unspecified (*vipāka-avyākṛta*). Six factors are always present: namely, the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) together with the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
The remaining five may or may not be present. These differ from the five object-specific factors (*viṣaya-niyata*), which sometimes arise as one, two, or more.

It is precisely these aforementioned factors that serve to give rise to the substance of the maturation-unspecified mind. However, such an unspecified mind mostly does not give rise to the object-specific factors; it gives rise to them only rarely.

Regarding the object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*): if a wholesome mind arises, it mostly gives rise to these object-specific factors, though there are also instances where they do not arise at all.
However, if it is a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) or an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), it invariably gives rise to all five object-specific factors.
The Commentary states: "Now, this division establishes the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñika*) upon the cessation of the sixth consciousness. Question:

Why do the preceding treatises establish the maturation of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*) based upon the eighth consciousness, whereas here it is established within the sixth consciousness?
Is the establishment of the maturation of the non-conceptual state within the sixth consciousness therefore distinct [from the former]?

Regarding the statement "perception is this perception," etc., the previous [explanation] was based on the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), wherein the maturation of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is established as the fruition of the activity of the mental formations (*saṃskāra*).
This present [explanation], however, is established without contradiction based on the seeds of the mind of aversion within the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

The Commentary states: "As with the Vaibhāṣikas, who also maintain that [the mind] arises for a long duration," this refers to the statement that one is born in the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva).

This likewise maintains that the mind arises for a long duration; subsequently, however, it is the distinct, neutral, resultant (*vipāka*) real dharma that obstructs the mind and mental factors, preventing them from arising.
According to the Mahāyāna school, this occurs precisely when the sixth consciousness does not arise. At that time, [it is...]
The seed of the mind of revulsion is established as the "retribution of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya*).
The commentary states that the same applies to the two heavens below the fourth dhyāna; these are not the inferior or middling perfumings of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

The heaven of True Cloudlessness (*Anabhraka*) is called the inferior grade, the Heaven of Merit-Born (*Puṇyaprasava*) is called the middling, and the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) is called the superior. These six heavens above the heaven of Non-Conception are [the result of] perfuming.

The cultivation [of these] occurs only within the Bṛhatphala Heaven and not in the two lower heavens. If one allows for them to exist within the three dhyānas, each of those three heavens possesses the six types of perfuming—lower, middle, and upper.
For example, within the first dhyāna, the Brahmakāyika Heaven is called the lower six, the Brahmapurohita Heaven is called the middle six, and the Mahābrahmā Heaven is the upper.
The same applies to the three heavens in the second and third dhyānas; the lower two [dhyānas] are likewise.
As for "the heavens are likewise," this refers to the two heavens of Anabhraka (Cloudless) and Puṇyaprasava (Merit-born).

These are also coarse and active; it is not that these two heavens themselves give rise to a different type of sensation called "likewise. This is because these two heavens also consist of lower and middle grades. Furthermore, those born from the six lower dhyānas are born in Anabhraka;

those from the six middle ones are born in Puṇyaprasava; and those from the six upper ones are born in Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit). As for those born as non-Buddhists who do not know [this], [it is as follows].

Question: According to the *Śāstra*, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) resides in the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*), if they attain the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) or the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), do they also separately know the five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsakāyikā devāḥ*)?

Furthermore, if Bodhisattvas or those in the latter two fruits of the path reside in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or up to the Heaven of Vastness (*Bṛhat*) within the fourth dhyāna, do they likewise not know [the Pure Abodes], or can they know them by means of their own bodies? Indeed.

Regarding the passage "Now, this is precisely before meditative concentration... up to what is explained in the *Mahā-śāstra* (Great Treatise), fascicle 56," there are three interpretations in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) below;
this is the first interpretation, which states: "If it is 'before the preceding concentration,' then at the time when the mind gradually [arises], the seeds obtained through perfuming..."
This seed, while in the state of having consciousness (*sacittaka*), possesses the capacity to induce the ideation of that celestial realm.
This is the seed acquired through perfuming by the eighth consciousness during this gradual process of the mind.

Once this seed reaches the state of being without consciousness (*acittaka*), that very same seed is able to induce the retribution of specific phenomena within that celestial realm. Thus, the sixth consciousness alone can, as a single cause, summon distinct results.
The interpretation that [the seeds] are the two fruits of the two types of *saṃjñā* (perceptions) is incorrect. Therefore, the second and third interpretations provided below are taken as correct.

Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that these are the volitions (*cetanā*) capable of inducing meditative concentration, and so forth, up to the distinction between the two causes and two fruits:
this second interpretation states that if, at a previous time, when [the mind] was sharp and subtle, seeds were perfumed within that subtle state of mind, those seeds [are what remain].
The potency [of these seeds] is capable of inducing the fruit of the eighth consciousness—the state of having thought and mind—at that time.

When seeds are perfumed during moments of subtle mind or extremely subtle mind, these seeds, while in a state with mind and subsequently until the state without mind, are all able to summon their respective retributions.
Furthermore, even when the sixth consciousness is in its preceding state of extremely subtle mind, the seeds can still summon [their results].
When one is born in that heaven, at the initial moment there is a distinct dharma-mind, which is the fruit of the sixth consciousness.
If these seeds reach the state of being without mind, they can produce the subsequent distinct retribution of that heaven;

when the sixth consciousness is in the state of the mindless maturation-fruit, [the seeds] can produce the fruit of having mind during the state of having mind, and produce the fruit of being without mind during the state of being without mind. This is the intended meaning of these passages.

That is to say, the preceding *anubhūta* (subtle) mind is powerful enough to attract the *ālayavijñāna* as the collective retribution (*saṃghātabhoga*). If, at the time of the *anubhūta* mind, it is weak and feeble, it can only induce individual retribution (*vyaktibhoga*).

This is like when, during the formal ritual of the one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-tricaturtha-karman*), the fundamental path of action (*maulakarmapatha*) is established, which is capable of inducing the corresponding mental phenomena.
If the preceding preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) and the subsequent attained mind (*pṛṣṭha-labdha-citta*) either perceive or maintain [the vow], [the retribution is likewise induced].

Question: How is it that while a state of mind can only bring about a distinct retribution, there is a case where, having brought about that distinct retribution, when one reaches a state of no-mind, it can bring about the fruit of five hundred kalpas of no-mind? Answer: It is like the storehouse of firm causes established by giving.
When one first resolves to give, one feels joy; when one gives away material things, one feels joy; and when one gives the gift itself, one feels joy. By receiving this joy, one attains [the result].
Regarding the mutual firmness of the objective conditions across the three times: if one moment is not favorable, then the karma will not have a fixed result. This case is also like that.

At the initial time, there is karma with a mind (*sacittaka*), which induces a sixth consciousness with a mind; at a later time, during a state without a mind (*acittaka*), that very karma is able to induce that sixth consciousness without a mind.
Furthermore, the thesis states that this refers specifically to a single day, [distinguishing] between the time when there is a mind and the time when there is no mind.
Regarding the distinct states: they are capable of separately inviting both a collective retribution and a specific retribution.

That is to say, when this sharp volition (*cetanā*) exists before or after the state of meditative concentration, once the mind has entered the state of concentration, this volition is able to invite the specific retribution of the sixth consciousness within the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*).
This applies to the state with mind prior to concentration and the state without mind subsequent to it; if at that time there is sharp volition during the state with mind preceding the concentration.

At that time, the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is the resultant retribution (*vipākaphala*) of the mind of that deity, is admitted to be capable of being summoned by a single volition (*cetanā*) as a distinct retribution.

Whether in a state with mind (*sacittaka*) or a state without mind (*acittaka*), because one asks: "What is this karma that can induce both the material and the non-material?"—the material refers to the physical body (*rūpakāya*), and the non-material refers to the matured mind and mental factors (*vipākacitta-caitta*). The first and third interpretations may be understood accordingly.
The *Śāstra* states: "The previous explanation already grants that a single volition (*cetanā*) can bring about two types of retribution; furthermore, this principle does not exclude it.

This refers to the first interpretation, which asserts that a single volition is capable of inducing both collective and individual retributions. "Form" (*rūpa*) refers to the body; "non-form" (*arūpa*) refers to that which is apart from the sense faculties.
Just as based on a single karma one can experience both the physical body and the sense faculties, we know that a single volition (*cetanā*) can produce distinct retributions.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the statement that this thought and the preceding thought possess only the 'form-possessing members' (*rūpin-aṅga*)," this refers to the fact that among the six consciousnesses, they do not function [simultaneously];
it describes the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), which possesses only the form-possessing members.

The Commentary states: "If one were to establish this for a single period, it would be the same as the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Regarding the Lesser Vehicle, they assert that there are definitely three [stages];

even when referring to the subsequent [stage], it is called "mind" (*citta*). This is because the subsequent existence mentioned in the following text is not like this prior [existence]. The Mahāyāna refutes this, saying: "There is no fault in [the intermediate state] lasting for a long duration."

The Commentary states: "That those sentient beings born there must necessarily have karma for the desire realm and so forth, up to the karma for being born as a deva after death," means that, for example, certain non-Buddhists first cultivate and attain the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) during their first birth in the desire realm.

Having died in this desire realm, they are reborn in their second life in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*). They remain in the Heaven of Non-conception until it is fulfilled; from that point...

Upon death, one is reborn in the second life immediately falling into the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). This is because, among the [three types of] karma in the desire realm, there is the "later-retribution" (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*) karma;

this is as explained in common by the Hīnayāna. For example, when a person is born in the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*), that person who dies in the Northern Continent necessarily possesses karma for later retribution, such as the karma for birth in the six heavens of the desire realm.

This is just like the case of a mountain-dwelling meditation master who, while practicing contemplation, is able to observe his own body and perceive that within the six realms of existence there is no real self (*ātman*).
"All phenomena exist; these arise through causes and conditions, with the sole exception of the grasping at dharmas"—this is the practice of those who favor existence.

If one maintains that all phenomena are entirely without essence, this is the grasping of those who favor non-existence. They do not uphold the Buddha's teaching because they claim all phenomena arise rootlessly from the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru).
Because they previously observed the absence of a real self, they were reborn in the Northern Continent; thus, regarding all phenomena, they [hold such views].

There is no grasping at a self. Because, through the previous conditions of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) prior to sitting in meditation, there was some wholesome merit from hearing and reflection;
having passed away from that Northern Continent, they are subsequently born among the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as a result of their karmic retribution.
The Commentary states: "The meaning of this passage—that from the previous existence here up until the necessity of being born in the desire realm—is the interpretation of the Hīnayāna.

Because various non-Buddhists, in a previous life within this desire realm, cultivated the state of non-conceptual absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), they must have previously performed wholesome karma belonging to the desire realm;
since they were established in that [karma], they receive birth in the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings (asaṃjñisattva-deva). They will certainly be reborn in the desire realm."
Within the desire realm (kāmadhātu), one may be born among gods, humans, ghosts, animals, or in the Avīci hell, and so forth. The Upādhyāya, employing the Mahāyāna school, challenges the Hīnayāna:

"If you say that when one cultivates meditative concentration (samādhi), having previously created karma of the desire realm during the preparatory stage, one is subsequently reborn in the desire realm as a result of that maturation, we now challenge this:
even when cultivating the 'attainment of non-conception' (asaṃjñisamāpatti), one likewise creates [karma] of the three lower realms during the preparatory application."

Regarding the practice of dhyāna: when one first attains the state of non-percipient absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), at the very time one first begins to cultivate this non-percipient absorption, it is said that one has already attained the first dhyāna through birth.
Having attained the first dhyāna, one then cultivates the second dhyāna; having attained the second dhyāna...
Furthermore, the third and fourth [arguments] are the same as before. Only then does one actually produce the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

Since one has already established the central thesis within the fourth dhyāna prior to entering that concentration, one ought to be reborn in that state of non-conceptualization. However, because of subsequent retributive karma, one is instead born into the lower four dhyānas.

If they were to argue that the desire realm is inferior and thus one is reborn there, we now raise this objection: when compared to that state of non-conceptualization, the three lower dhyānas are likewise inferior.

The three lower heavens are likewise inferior; one ought to be reborn in those three lower realms. Furthermore, regarding their claim that it occurs before meditative absorption, or that the Śākyas enter nirvāṇa and so forth, and that one who dies in that Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva) is subsequently born in the desire realm due to karma of subsequent retribution—now I shall challenge this:

if the Śākyas possessed fixed karma (niyata-karma), they certainly could not have been born in the Heaven of No-Thought. Since they attained the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), [their karma was thereby severed].
The various karmas, such as those of proclivity (*anuśaya*) and so forth, combine to form indeterminate [karma]. Therefore, it is known that one can be reborn in all three lower dhyānas.

The commentary states: "This differs from that; it is only the present dharma... up to "...karma to be experienced in subsequent lives. This means that in the Mahāyāna, this is not the same as the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

If, according to the Small Vehicle, the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) is exclusively karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*), then one may say that one goes to the Heaven of No-Thought.

After death in the heavenly realm, one is reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) by means of subsequent retribution karma (*paścādvedanīya-karma*); that is, it is the first birth within the desire realm.

Having cultivated and attained the state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), one then experiences the karma of the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*) through the second birth, which constitutes the karma of subsequent retribution. Thus, the third birth may be described as the "subsequent karma," whereby one is born again into the desire realm.

In the Mahāyāna, since the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings is understood to involve subsequent retribution, there is no such thing as "karma to be experienced in a subsequent life" (*paścādvedanīya-karma*).
Born within the Desire Realm.
The Commentary states: "Thus we know that being born there encompasses birth from both determinate and indeterminate karma, up to the point where none exist.

Now, regarding birth among those in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), it encompasses birth from retributive karma (*vipākakarman*), subsequent retributive karma (*paścādvipākakarman*), and indeterminate retributive karma (*aniyata-vipākakarman*). As in the case of the [first]...

During one lifetime, having cultivated and attained the state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one dies here in the desire realm and is immediately reborn in the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*);

this is called the "thought-activity of birth. Just as in the first birth within the desire realm, after attaining non-conceptual absorption, while manifesting the precepts and manifesting differentiation, one then regresses from that prior state;
the non-conceptual absorption arises from the lower three dhyānas, and after dying in the desire realm, [one is reborn] for the second time.

While in this present body, having been born within the lower three dhyānas, one further cultivates the previously attained state of non-conceptual absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) during the first birth.
Immediately after dying within those lower three dhyānas, one reaches the third birth, being born for the first time in the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings (asaṃjñi-sattva-deva);
this is called "karma of subsequent retribution" (aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karman). Furthermore, within this present body, one cultivates and attains the non-conceptual absorption, which manifests...

Having passed away from that body, one is reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). In a second birth, having cultivated and attained the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), one dies here;
only in that second birth is one born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*). This is also called "retribution in a later life" (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*).

Furthermore, it is like a person who first attains the attainment of non-conception in the desire realm, but subsequently regresses from that prior attainment of non-conception; after his death, following three or five births, [he is finally born there].

Furthermore, after one has attained it through renewed cultivation, the state of non-conception arises first; thus, the name "Non-Conception Heaven" (Asaṃjñisattva) refers to karma of indeterminate retribution, which encompasses all three types of karma.
If, after passing away from that Non-Conception Heaven, one is reborn in the lower [heavens] such as Anabhraka, or within the third dhyāna, [this applies].

They may also attain rebirth throughout the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Furthermore, they may die in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) and immediately proceed toward the Heaven of Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*), or reach the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (*brahmapārṣadya*);
in all such cases, they attain birth in succession. This is because this person has previously cultivated the karma for each successive stage within the four dhyānas.
For instance, when previously cultivating the concentration of the Heaven of Non-conception, one must first subdue the defilements of the desire realm to attain the lower level of the first dhyāna.

The six concentrations: having attained the lower six concentrations, one immediately cultivates the middle six concentrations; having attained the middle six, one cultivates the upper six concentrations;

and having done so, one gives rise to a mind of revulsion, feeling revulsion toward the suffering, coarseness, and obscurations of the first dhyāna, and so on, until one cultivates the lower six concentrations of the second dhyāna.
Up to the point of subduing the defilements of the third dhyāna, one attains the four dhyānas and the lower six concentrations (*samādhi*). Next, one cultivates the middle six concentrations;

next, one cultivates the attainment of the upper six concentrations. Within these upper six, through specific and intensive cultivation, one attains the supreme of the supreme: the six states of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

Thus, it is known that prior to the non-conceptual absorption, one has already cultivated and attained the karma of the middle stage of the fourth dhyāna to go to the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), having been born there separately.
They attain rebirth in succession, descending from the Bṛhatphala heaven through the fourth dhyāna, down to the Brahmakāyika heaven of the first dhyāna;
however, they cannot be born in the Cloud-Abode (Abhāsvara) or the Heaven of Consciousness (Vijñānānantya), because they have never previously cultivated those levels.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "It is said that 'only' [is used] because there is no mind in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), and thus one knows that it must be distinguished [from other states] lest it be confused with those that possess mind.

If the Heaven of No-Thought exists solely in the single location of the Great Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) and experiences no distinct perception of dharmas, then since there would be no confusion, it need not be emphasized;
however, it is distinguished by the term "no-mind" (*acittaka*). Therefore, the verse simply says: "excluding those born in the Heaven of No-Thought," and "excluding the four states of no-mind."
Those who hold erroneous views claim that there are also states of meditative absorption with mind (*sacittaka-samādhi*), as well as sleep and fainting with mind.

Since the present context speaks of "mindless" (*acittaka*), it excludes those states involving mind; thus, it refers to the two mindless absorptions (*acittaka-dhyāna*) and mindless sleep, fainting, and so forth.

However, among humans in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), for the most part, there is mindless sleep due to the consumption of heavy,黏稠 (*guru*) foods. Among the six classes of gods in the desire realm...

There is also a small portion of mindlessness; specifically, in the Sañjīva (Reviving) Hell, there is also a slight degree of mindless sleep, whereas in the other hells, there is no such mindless slumber.

The treatise states: "To subdue the pervasive purity is also to subdue both the pure and the defiled. If one attains the contaminated concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*) of the first dhyāna, one then subdues the craving of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
