This is a dream-object; because it is realized through correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*), there is no fault of *tathatā* (suchness) being unreal. That treatise states: "In this very context, up to this point...
In response, the difficulty regarding the determination of time is established through formal inference (*pramāṇa*). Only the former [inference] is stated:

"When you see a garden and so forth in a dream, you should also not see them, because you admit that dream-objects are not substantially existent (*dravyasat*), just like other [non-existent things]."

When one does not see a garden and so forth within a dream, or at a time when one does not see a garden and so forth in a dream, one should likewise perceive the mental formations of "having a garden" and so forth;
for dream-objects are not substantially real, just as when one sees a garden and so forth in other dreams.
If there were no sentient beings within the garden itself, yet one says that there are sentient beings within the garden, one thereby knows that the determination of time also applies [to the dream].
Sentient beings, you admit that dream objects are not substantially real. However, this reason [you provide] is directed against the Sautrāntikas.
The Sautrāntikas maintain that within a dream there are no non-existent external objects at all, because dream objects are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*).

In the previous commentary, it was stated that this response is made from the perspective of the Sautrāntikas; this reason does not apply to the Sarvāstivādins, for the Sarvāstivādins assert that dream objects are all substantially real.
There is. The Commentary states: "That treatise says, 'It is like hungry ghosts... up to those who are not permitted to obtain food.

This means that when various hungry ghosts inquire about karma, the objects perceived by those with common karma are the same, whereas the objects perceived by those with distinct karma are different. Or, there may be a certain class of beings..."

Because many hungry ghosts share the same karma, they all collectively perceive other things such as excrement as being obstructive. Yet, for all those ghosts, pus is perceived by them all simultaneously;
what power of harm could it possibly have? Thus, they do not perceive the other excrement and such things.

For this class of hungry ghosts, that other excrement and so forth possesses no power of harm. Alternatively, there may be a certain class of many hungry ghosts with shared karma who all collectively perceive only...
They see excrement and the like, which have the function of causing harm; yet they do not see other pus or similar substances.
For these hungry ghosts (*preta*) of this class, such [substances] lack the function of causing harm.

Alternatively, there is a class of many hungry ghosts with a common karma who all together see only numerous hell-wardens—sentient beings wielding swords and staves—who guard rivers and the like, preventing them from obtaining [them].
When one drinks, the prison-wardens have a harmful effect upon sentient beings; toward this class of hungry ghosts, they likewise possess a harmful function.
However, for other pus-rivers and the like, these prison-wardens have no harmful effect upon this class of hungry ghosts.

Although these prison-wardens are not mentioned in the sacred scriptures (*āgama*), if one examines them through reasoning, they are also insentient (*anipita*). If a person sees such evil things and drinks, they will be reborn in the future as an inverted being.
Regarding "life and so forth," the Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Establishing the formal argument (*pramāṇa*)," and the Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says:

"In the same place, at the same time, and so forth, just as hungry ghosts see a river of pus. This means that in one place and at one time, there are many people; if they are all... [the text continues].
Regarding "obscuration" (timira): when it exists, one sees things such as hair and flies; if it does not exist, one sees only the hair and so forth, but does not see flies and the like.
This is analogous to hungry ghosts who, due to their shared karma, see only rivers of pus, whereas those with different karma do not see the rivers of pus and so forth.

The *Śāstra* says: "Establishing the formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to explain: 'Whether with an optical defect or without an optical defect, what is seen... even as in a dream, where one loses consciousness,' and so forth.

This answers the three types [of objections] mentioned previously regarding their function. That is to say, the formal inference states: For one with an optical defect, seeing hair and the like has no practical utility;
for one without an optical defect, what is seen is actual hair, which does have practical utility. Furthermore, regarding food, drink, or a sword seen in a dream...
The staff and such would then be useless; however, other things—such as food, drink, knives, and staves that exist at times other than during a dream—do possess real utility.
Furthermore, while the City of Gandharvas (Gandharvanagara) lacks real utility, the drinking vessel and so forth within it do possess real utility; the principle here is the same.
The reason given is that because one admits there is no real object, it is like [the objects] within a dream. If semen, blood, and so forth are lost, they then possess utility, whereas others do not.
The emission of semen, blood, and so forth is useless. This emission of semen and blood is shameful; one must not speak of it before an assembly.

One should instead say, "It was like seeing excrement and urine in a dream. Excrement and urine have practical utility, whereas other things—those not seen in dreams—are not excrement or urine; thus, they lack practical utility.
The *Śāstra* says: "Establishing the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to explain: 'In other states, place is fixed,' and so forth, up to 'like those in the hells.
All of these are now merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). Although there are no real objects external to the mind, place and time are nonetheless fixed.

While the body may be indeterminate, the establishment of its being functional or non-functional, and its loss or gain, is achieved. This is because we admit that there are no real objects, yet this consciousness arises—just as in the case of the hells."
Within the prison, although there are no actual sentient beings such as hell-dwellers or hungry ghosts, those who see them perceive them as being equal [to real ones].
While hungry ghosts have the capacity to inflict harm upon others, those who have emerged from hunger do not have the capacity to inflict harm.
The Commentary states: "Now, by citing one dream and so forth, it includes the other two distinct metaphors and one type of metaphor. Here, the treatise cites the metaphor of a single dream-object;

the phrase "and so forth" (etc. encompasses the remaining two metaphors—namely, the metaphor of the hungry ghost (*preta*) and the metaphor of the emission of semen within a dream—and furthermore, the single type of metaphor of hell.
Although the infernal guardians are insentient, they possess the quality of pressing and resenting sentient beings.

Sentient beings take insentient things as instruments of suffering. If the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) were to see the true nature of the realm, they would find no pleasure;
yet, when they see other men and women, they experience joy. The female deities of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations are all comprised within the category of sentient beings.

Now, by way of analogy, even in the midst of suffering, the most extreme suffering in the *tālapatra* hells consists of taking insentient objects that resemble sentient beings as instruments of pain. Likewise, in the midst of pleasure, the highest degree of bliss extends to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations.

One might object that non-sentient things appearing as sentient beings serve as instruments of pleasure; now the answer is given: in the heavens, one attains mastery and thus takes sentient beings themselves as the instruments of pleasure.

In the hells, however, because they are summoned by evil karma, non-sentient things appear as sentient beings and serve as instruments of suffering. Therefore, it is not permissible to raise this objection.
Among pleasures, the ultimate pleasure extends up to the third dhyāna. In that which is insentient yet resembles the sentient, it serves as an instrument of pleasure.

If, however, one considers the meditative bliss of the third dhyāna, it pertains solely to the internal sphere and does not take external objects such as forms and so forth as instruments of pleasure. This is also the case among the gods of the desire realm.

In the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*), sexual desire and pleasure are moderate. This is because the celestial maidens and other beings of that heavenly realm are taken as the instruments of pleasure.

One might simply object that while "pleasure within pleasure" extends up to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, these instruments of pleasure must be insentient things appearing as sentient.

If the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Tathāgata is also included among sentient beings, then all categories perceived by those in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations would likewise possess [sentience].

Regarding "sentient beings" (*sattva*): the question is asked, "How can magically created men and women, as well as emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), be sentient beings? One should ask this. The *Shu* (Commentary) states:
"The 'Old Yogācāra' says... the 'Old Consciousness-Only' says... This refers to citing sūtras as authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*) to raise an objection;
specifically, it refers to taking the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) from the four Āgamas as authoritative scripture within the "Old Twenty Verses on Consciousness-Only."

It is taught that there are no phenomena external to the mind. For what reason did the World-Honored One teach the twelve bases (*āyatana*)? In the *Āgama* sūtras, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases, and elements (*dhātu*) are explained in detail.

These aggregates, bases, elements, and so forth, were originally taught for the sake of those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), in order to cause those of the two vehicles to abandon their attachments to other [inferior] vehicles.
This constitutes entering into my midst. I shall explain the six pairs of dharmas. Some say that what is called *āgama* refers to Mahāyāna sūtras;
it is also termed *āgama*, but this does not refer to the four *āgamas* of the Hīnayāna.

This is because within the Mahāyāna, the teachings, principles, practices, and so forth of the three vehicles are each distinct, and there are inferior, middling, and superior grades of spiritual capacity. Regarding the distinction of teachings: for those who seek the Śrāvaka...
Regarding those who hear [the Dharma]: for those seeking the state of a Pratyekabuddha, it is taught that they should practice the Dharma according to the Four Noble Truths.

As for Śrāvakas and the two vehicles, from the beginning until the end, they all loathe suffering and aspire toward cessation. Regarding Bodhisattvas, although at the initial stage of cultivation there is a slight degree of loathing for suffering and aspiration for cessation, in later stages they do not loathe suffering nor aspire toward cessation.
According to the Vaibhāṣikas, the three vehicles differ solely by virtue of the superiority or inferiority of their faculties and dispositions.

Middle and inferior. Because their faculties are distinct, there are three vehicles (*yāna*), and thus the vehicles have distinctions. The teachings and practices of the three vehicles are all identical in that they are all the same three vehicles;
they are all identical in observing the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), because the practice of the three vehicles is the same.
The Commentary states: "The manifest consciousness appearing as form, from the conjunction of its own seeds up to the bases of body and contact.

This now refers to the manifest consciousness appearing as form within the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect). The *nimittabhāga* is not itself form, yet it appears as form; because the *nimittabhāga* arises from consciousness, it is termed "manifest consciousness" (*darśanavijñāna*).

If it were the *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect), it would be called "consciousness appearing as form. Conditionally arisen phenomena are like illusions and transformations; they are not [ultimately real].

This is actual consciousness (*vijñāna*). However, because it resembles consciousness, and because the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of consciousness can transform and give rise to form (*rūpa*), it is called "manifesting form.

In the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, it is said that the mind (*manas*) is identical to the image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*); this is called the five image-portions. What are currently active are named the five sense objects (*viṣaya*), such as form;

these are the seeds of the image-portion. Through the transformation of seeds due to the convergence of conditions, the seeds of the Buddha’s image-portion arise, which are explained as the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) within the Buddha-dharma’s image-portion.

Because they manifest, they are called the "form base" (*rūpāyatana*). Alternatively, it is said that the seeds of the seeing-portion (*darśanabhāga*) are called the "material faculties" (*rūpendriya*), while the seeds of karma are called the "five faculties.

This is as explained previously in the fourth fascicle. Regarding the above explanation that the seeds of the object-portion (*nimittabhāga*) are called the five faculties, this still follows the lower [interpretation].

According to the lower interpretation, there should be seeds of the five faculties; all manifestations of the five faculties are likewise called the five faculties. If [this applies to] the first six...

The characteristics of consciousness (*vijñāna-lakṣaṇa*) and the objective portions (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness and so forth are termed the "fivefold colored objects" (*pañca-rūpa-viṣaya*).

Although this verse is cited from the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, although the intent is the same, the details differ, as in the first fascicle where the citation of the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*) and other points refutes the theory of atoms (*paramāṇu*).

In the second fascicle, the citation of the five sense organs and other points is for the purpose of establishing that [consciousness] possesses functional activity (*savyāpāra*); subsequent instances follow this precedent. Furthermore, it is explained that [this system] is established based on these principles.
"Because of the eighth consciousness. Regarding the statement that "the faculties of the five consciousnesses, and so forth, are all transformations of consciousness":

this refers to what is stated in the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Twenty Verses on Consciousness-Only), where seeds are said to be the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the five faculties, and their manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) constitutes the five objects (*viṣaya*).

This is explained from the perspective prior to the establishment of the eighth consciousness, concerning the five material faculties (*rūpa-indriya*), where seeds are designated as the "faculties. This was likely done out of concern that the Hīnayāna schools might [cling to] something external to consciousness.

There are five sense-faculties (*indriya*). In this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the statement that they "rely on what is transformed [by consciousness] and do not exist as separate transformations" sets forth the correct doctrine.
Its meaning is as follows: the five material sense-faculties manifesting as active states (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) arise from the transformation of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*);

these serve as the support (*āśraya*), while the five objects manifesting as active states serve as the objective condition (*ālambana*) through their aspect of appearance (*nimitta-bhāga*). This treatise differs from the text of the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. This treatise...
It is taught that the five faculties, the five objects, and consciousness are all transformations [of the mind].

The Commentary states: "As for the phrase 'if one knows individually, from the six pairs of dharmas up to the knower,' it means that if there are sentient beings who can know, they arise from the six faculties and six objects as the six consciousnesses;
these are conventionally designated as a 'body' through their provisional combination, but there is no real self that acts as the knower."
There is no truly existent self that sees; in this way, sentient beings are able to enter into the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*). The Commentary states:

"This is because it breaks the mark of a unitary, substantially real self, thereby causing entry into the emptiness of self. It further explains that while ten [bases] such as form (*rūpa*) were previously mentioned, there are now said to be twelve bases (*āyatana*).
Thus, one knows that the body consists of ten distinct bases; this is precisely the refutation of the attachment to the body as a substantially real self.

Because it is a single composite mark (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*), we know that the body possesses the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*). Each [base] serves as a support for those to be converted, even down to sentient beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*).

However, in the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the Blessed One relied upon the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) of those to be converted, so as to lead those of the two vehicles into the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmyadhyāna*).
Therefore, this was the Blessed One’s intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*); subsequently, [he taught] the twelve [bases].

[This is] the section. Just as the Blessed One, in order to refute the views of non-Buddhists, spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) that there are beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*). [Regarding the statement] "There are sentient beings;

there is the transition of consciousness," the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "To say that there are no sentient beings or self (*ātman*), but only the causes of phenomena (*dharma*)," these two phrases are from the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
The middle verse states: This verse intends to convey that there are no real sentient beings and no real self; there are only various phenomena arising from causes and conditions.
"Causes and conditions" refers precisely to the five causes, the four conditions, and so forth.

The Commentary states: "As for the question regarding sentient beings' attachment to a self and the teaching of the 'dharma-sphere' (*dharmāyatana*) in order to refute a substantial self—this 'dharma-sphere' refers to the ten spheres of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). The Commentary further states:

"Furthermore, based on this, one explains the teaching of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*); the remainder concerns the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and the three absences of nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*)."
The *Xingjiao* (Teaching on Nature) is entirely an exposition of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as being empty of a self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

The commentary states that by teaching "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*), it eliminates the view of phenomena (*dharma-dṛṣṭi*). This "view of phenomena" is precisely the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

The Commentary states: "It is not that apart from the reality of the thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), there is another statement that designates it as 'dharma-śūnyatā' (the emptiness of phenomena).

This means that apart from the phrase "reality apart from the thoroughly imagined," there is no further explanation to be found elsewhere regarding the uncontaminated fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms being designated as "dharma-śūnyatā.

Rather, it is simply the emptiness of the grasping at phenomena that is called this "emptiness. Question: Does this statement mean that the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms realize only...?

Regarding the nature of consciousness (*vijñapti-tathatā*): it is termed the "nature of representation-only" (*vijñapti-mātratā*) because it takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object-condition; it is also termed the "nature of representation-only" in reference to the "basis of names" (*nāma-adhiṣṭhāna*).

The answer is given to address the questioner’s inquiry; furthermore, there is no contradiction in referring to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) in relation to the grasping of True Suchness.

The Commentary states: "If one were to say that even the essence of phenomena is beyond words based on dependent [designation], then although there are dependent words capable of expressing them, the essence of those phenomena is nonetheless beyond words.
The Commentary further states: "Among the fourfold conventional truths, the first three are conventional truths... up to 'the two truths depend upon existence. This refers to...

Fayun’s commentary states: It should simply be said that among the four conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the first conventional truth is exclusively conventional and does not extend to the ultimate;
among the four levels of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the fourth ultimate truth is exclusively ultimate and does not extend to the conventional.

The latter three within the conventional and the former three within the ultimate extend to both the ultimate and the conventional. This passage [indicates] that the ultimate and the conventional are mutually dependent.
This clarifies that within the fourfold conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are likewise dependencies upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Just as within the fourfold conventional truth, if the first three conventions are termed the "conventional within the conventional," the fourth convention is termed the "ultimate within the conventional.
Since the former three conventions rely upon the latter ultimate, there is likewise [an ultimate] within the four conventions.

The conventional truth relies upon the ultimate. Among the four types of ultimate truth, the first three ultimates are termed the conventional truth within the ultimate truth, while the fourth ultimate is termed the ultimate truth within the ultimate truth.
Thus, the fourth ultimate truth also relies upon the preceding three conventional truths.
This explains that among the four ultimates, the ultimate truth—namely, the fourth ultimate truth—likewise relies upon the preceding three conventional truths. This is what is taught.
The four ultimate truths also depend upon conventional truth. The treatise states:
"The ultimate and the conventional are mutually dependent. If one were to establish only the four conventional precepts and not the four ultimate ones, they could not be called mutually dependent.

One must establish both sets of four—the four truths and the four conventionalities—in order for them to be called "mutually dependent. Here, too, mutual dependence is explained according to coarse characteristics.

To explain each in detail: within the four conventionalities, if one takes the preceding [conventionality] as the standard, that which precedes is the conventional; if one regards the subsequent in relation to the preceding, the subsequent is the truth.
Furthermore, the first conventionality may depend upon the second conventionality, and the first conventionality may also depend upon the third.

Regarding the conventional (*saṃvṛti*): first, one may rely on the fourth conventional, and the conventional itself is also attained. If one relies on the second conventional, one may also attain the third conventional;
relying on the second conventional, one may also attain the fourth conventional; and relying on the third conventional, one may also attain the fourth conventional.

In this context, that which is capable of being relied upon is entirely conventional, while that which is relied upon is termed the ultimate (*paramārtha*). However, in the commentary, for the time being, it is treated according to the four conventional levels.

Among the first three conventional [truths], one relies on the fourth conventional; furthermore, among the four ultimate [truths], one immediately relies on the subsequent ultimate upon the preceding ultimate.
Thus, by relying on the fourth ultimate, one also attains reliance on the first ultimate. If the fourth ultimate relies on the second ultimate, that is also attained.
If the fourth ultimate relies on the third ultimate, that is also attained. If the third ultimate relies on the first...

The ultimate can also be established. If one takes the third ultimate as the basis for the second ultimate, it is also established; if one takes the second ultimate as the basis for the first ultimate, it is also established.
Now, among these four ultimates, that which is the basis is termed the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), while that which is based upon it is termed the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
Since each of the four ultimates and four conventions possesses this mutual dependence, the former is called the ultimate and the latter three are called the conventional. And so they are named.

It is the ultimate (*paramārtha*). Because it is contrasted with each preceding conventional (*saṃvṛti*), it may also be called conventional; because it is contrasted with each succeeding ultimate, it may also be called ultimate.

This is like the three characters [of the word *pāramitā*]. If one takes "ordinary" (*pā*) alone, it is neither Mahāyāna nor Hīnayāna. If one takes "only" (*ra*) alone, it is neither Mahāyāna nor Hīnayāna.

If one takes "rejecting" (*mi*) alone, it is both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Why? If one pairs "ordinary" (*pā*) with "rejecting" (*mi*), "ordinary" is named only Mahāyāna, just as the fourth is the ultimate (*paramārtha*).

The first three correspond to the True [Dharmadhātu]. The fourth is exclusively True and not Conventional. If one contrasts "Rejecting" (qì) with the ordinary, that rejection is only Small and not Great.
This is because, just as the initial Conventional corresponds to the subsequent Conventional, that initial Conventional is exclusively Conventional and does not penetrate the True.

If one contrasts "Rejecting" (pái) with the ordinary and the holy, it is called Small; if one contrasts "Rejecting" (pái) with "Rejecting" (qì), it is called Great. Therefore, it is said that "Rejecting" (pái) is both Great and Small.

Small. Because the first three are ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the latter three are conventional (*saṃvṛti*). If these three pairs are compared with the initial conventionality, these three are designated as merely ultimate;
yet if these three are compared with the fourth ultimate, these three are then designated as conventional. Thus, the middle three ultimates are also conventional.

If one considers all four conventionalities and ultimates in relation to one another, even down to the two truths that exist therein, it is said here: if the four conventionalities are all conventional...
The fourth conventional truth can also be based upon the fourth ultimate truth. If all four are ultimate truths, then the four ultimate truths can also be based upon the first conventional truth;
this is because the fourth ultimate truth is exclusively ultimate and not conventional, whereas the first conventional truth is exclusively conventional and not ultimate.
In this context, "mutual dependence" (anyonya-āśraya) refers to mutual correspondence; therefore, it is called mutual dependence. To explain in detail: if the first...

The conventional has four levels of reliance: namely, the first conventional relies on the first ultimate; the first conventional relies on the second ultimate; the first conventional relies on the third ultimate;
and the first conventional relies on the fourth ultimate. Thus, the first conventional has four levels of reliance.
If the second conventional has three levels of reliance, they are as follows: the third conventional relies on the second ultimate, and the second conventional relies on the third ultimate.

[The first] conventional [truth] relies on the fourth ultimate; the second conventional relies on the fourth ultimate. If the fourth conventional relies solely on the fourth ultimate, it is said that the four conventional truths rely on the ultimate.
If the four ultimates also rely on the conventional, this means: the fourth ultimate exists; the fourth ultimate relies on the first conventional;
the fourth ultimate relies on the second conventional; the fourth ultimate relies on the third conventional; and the fourth ultimate... [relied upon by the fourth conventional].
Regarding the four [levels of] truth, the fourth is the conventional (saṃvṛti). Furthermore, for the third ultimate (paramārtha), there is a formal proof (pramāṇa):
namely, the third ultimate relies upon the first conventional; the second conventional, the third [ultimate], and so forth, follow the same method of formulation as before.

If there are two ultimates with two layers of reliance—namely, the first conventional and the second conventional—the first ultimate relies solely upon the first conventional. However, this is stated in the commentary (*śāstra*) in terms of their general characteristics.
The Commentary states: "The meaning of the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* is the same as this. This means that within the *Viṃśatikā*, it is also said:

"The 'real' (*satya*) refers to being established in mutual dependence," and so forth. Furthermore, the statement, "That which the Buddha taught as 'unattainable' (*anupalabdha*)," is identical in wording to the text of this *Vijñaptimātratā*.
The Commentary states: This question concerns the reason why matter and consciousness are said to abide in continuity. An externalist asks:

"If all material phenomena arise from the transformation of consciousness and take consciousness as their essence, such that these material phenomena are termed 'matter-consciousness' (rūpavijñāna), then what is the basis for this? [The author] answers: All material dharmas arise from the transformation of consciousness; they take consciousness as their substance. Thus, the various categories of material phenomena are designated as "matter-consciousness."

For what reason do the mind and mental factors themselves undergo interruption, while their supporting bases—the material objects—do not undergo such distinct interruption as the mind and mental factors?
Regarding the term "of one kind," the opponent asks again: "If all matter is a transformation of the mind, [then why is this so?]"

Why is it that the transforming mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) permeate all three moral natures (trividha-svabhāva) and are not of a single category, whereas the transformed matter (rūpa) is of only one category—indeterminate (avyākṛta)—and does not permeate the three natures?
Regarding the statement "due to the force of the perfuming of names and words" (nāma-vāsanā-vaśāt):

it is like when, upon the consciousness-mind of a sentient being as it perceives these five objects (viṣaya) and five sense organs (indriya), the consciousness-mind forms hundreds or thousands of interpretations.

Through this practice and understanding, form itself becomes a seed. Later, when the active manifestation arises from this seed, the five sense organs and the five objects that are produced also continue to evolve for a hundred years.
While Vasubandhu of the Heaven of No-Form possessed only the intention of understanding, he lacked the textual exposition.
Question: When the sixth consciousness perceives the sense organs and objects, does it immediately perform a thousand-year practice upon the mind?

[Objection: It is explained that [the cognition] perfumes [the storehouse consciousness] to form seeds, and when those seeds later give rise to actualized states (*pravṛtti*), they obtain a duration of a thousand years.
[Response: When the five consciousnesses perceive the five objects, they do not necessarily form the conceptualization of a "thousand-year activity.

If the seeds of the sensory objects planted by the five consciousnesses were not to produce actualized states later on, they would fail to continue and would instead become interrupted. Furthermore...
When the seventh consciousness takes the eighth consciousness as its object, that seventh consciousness likewise cannot form the conceptualization of a "tongue for a thousand years.

The seventh consciousness perfumes seeds for the transformation of the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness; these seeds later give rise to the seeing-division of the eighth consciousness.

[If this were not so,] the seeing-divisions of the eight consciousnesses would fail to maintain continuity. It is through the power of the perfuming of names and words (*nāma-vikalpa-vāsanā*) that [the seeing-division] arises.

Question: Why, among the three types of perfuming (*vāsanā*), are the two perfumings of the "factors" (*aṅga*) and "self-grasping" (*ātma-grāha*) not mentioned, while this treatise specifically discusses only the perfuming of "linguistic designations" (*nāma-kāya*)?

Furthermore, consider this: does this term "linguistic designation" refer to the linguistic designation that expresses meaning, or to the linguistic designation that manifests objects? Reflect upon this.
The treatise states: "If defiled phenomena were the basis, then there would be neither affliction nor pure phenomena.

The intent of this passage in the treatise is extremely remote [from the current context]. This refers to the five faculties and five objects as being the bases for the removal of both defiled and pure phenomena.
This refers specifically to a portion of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and also to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); it does not refer to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This is because within the formless realm, the five sense faculties and the five objects of the senses—matter (*rūpa*)—do not exist.

How could one refer to the presence of the five sensory objects in the desire realm such that they would immediately trigger a non-object-reflecting mind? That is to say, when the five sense faculties give rise to the five consciousnesses...
Regarding the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*): if there are the five sense objects of sentient beings, one immediately gives rise to craving and desire toward those five objects.

One gives rise to craving for forms and sounds, and even craving for pleasant tactile objects and other such realms; thus, afflictions arise and the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*) are fully committed.

Furthermore, if one encounters the five objects as adverse conditions, the consciousnesses arise through the five sense faculties, and one gives rise to a mind of anger; likewise, the ten unwholesome actions arise and various afflictions are produced.

Affliction. If there were only the five sense objects (*viṣaya*) and no five sense faculties (*indriya*), afflictions could not arise, nor could one perform the various inverted evil karmas of affliction.
This is because, without the consciousnesses that take them as objects, one would be unable to fully commit the ten non-virtuous actions (*daśākuśalakarma*).

Consequently, one would be born in the three evil destinies (*durgati*). Therefore, the Sūtra states that both the five faculties and the five objects are called "confused appearances" (*vikṣepa-nimitta*). If one can...
The consciousness conditioned by these [objects] is itself the essence of distraction; this refers to external forms and so forth, which serve as the basis for defiled phenomena.

Furthermore, because human beings reside in the desire realm, they may develop a slight degree of weariness toward the five sensory objects and maintain the five precepts, thereby being reborn among humans.
Furthermore, by observing a small portion of the precepts and the ten wholesome actions, one is reborn among the devas.

Moreover, because one possesses a superior degree of weary detachment (*nirveda*) toward the five objects and five faculties of the desire realm and does not give rise to a mind of craving, one practices both appreciation and aversion (*abhinandanā-nirvedanā*) as well as contemplation of the truths (*satya-vipaśyanā*), thereby attaining the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the form realm.
In this way, one becomes weary of the form realm and attains the meditative absorptions of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhyāna*). Thus, one comes to know that all three realms are...
Realizing they are unreal, one then performs contemplation of the truths and gradually practices until attaining entry into the ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*).

It is taught that the five objects (*viṣaya*), the five faculties (*indriya*), form (*rūpa*), and so forth, serve as the basis for pure phenomena (*śukladharma*). If the five objects did not exist, there would be no objects of the five desires to be craved.
These are the five objects of desire that one loathes. Furthermore, there are the five faculties, which are the five bases for generating the mind of pure dharmas.

These formless and other such dharmas constitute both defilement and purity. If there were no sound-dharmas, pure dharmas would likewise not exist; consequently, there would be no birth in the human or celestial realms, nor any supramundane dharmas.
All of these arise from the five sense objects and the five faculties. If there are the defiled dharmas that are to be remedied, then there will naturally be that which can remedy them.
Regarding pure phenomena (*śukla-dharma*): even within the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), one cherishes one’s own physical body, and because of that form, afflictions such as craving arise.
Furthermore, within the form realm, by giving rise to a mind of revulsion toward form, one immediately gives rise to the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*).

Within the form realm there are also signs of distraction (*vikṣepa-nimitta*) and the essence of distraction; however, in the sūtras, these signs and essences of distraction are discussed only with reference to the two realms of desire (*kāma-dhātu*) and form (*rūpa-dhātu*).
The Commentary states: "Inversion refers to the various consciousnesses and so forth, up to being produced by karma. This means that one gives rise to inversion while perceiving objects such as form;
this passage from the treatise specifically concerns sentient beings of the desire realm who give rise to afflictions while perceiving the object of form.

A small portion of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) also gives rise to afflictions by taking the objects of the form realm as their conditions; however, the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) entirely lacks the arising of afflictions by taking the objects of the form realm as their conditions, because the mind has no form-dharmas.
Regarding this, there are two interpretations in the commentary (*ṭīkā*). The first states that it refers specifically to the outflow-tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*).

When the mind does not realize that its objective referent, form, is unreal, then all the tainted (*sāsrava*) and false minds and mental factors of the three realms are termed "inversions" (*viparyāsa*).
From this point onward, the afflictive obscurations (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), karma, and so forth arise; thus, inversions arise first, and the obscurations arise later.
If one gives rise to the four inversions regarding the object of form, and the afflictions such as craving are termed "inversions," then it is as follows:
First, one gives rise to the afflictive defilements (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*) through attachment to the four inversions (*viparyāsa*). This is precisely what constitutes the afflictions.
How then can the treatise state that "if there were no inversions, there would be no defilement"? This implies that the inversions arise first, and the afflictions arise subsequently;

therefore, we know that the inversions are not themselves the four inversions within the category of afflictions. Rather, it is the tainted (*sāsrava*), false mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that are termed "inversions."
The second explanation states: Alternatively, the essence of inversion is itself the inversion produced by karma. Among the afflictions, these are the four inversions.

For example, when taking a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*) as an object, one grasps it as permanent; this "permanence" is actually the conceptualization of the impermanent, and is thus subsumed under the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).

Likewise, when taking a material phenomenon as an object, one grasps it as a self (*ātman*); this is the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). Or, when taking a material phenomenon as an object, one grasps it as pleasurable (*sukha*).

To reckon suffering as pleasure is subsumed under the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Alternatively, to take conditioned phenomena (*rūpadharma*) as pure, thereby reckoning the impure as pure, is subsumed within the [clinging to views].

The *Śāstra* says: "Regarding 'confused appearances' (*luanxiang*), does 'xiang' mean 'appearance' or 'cause'? The commentary explains: "Confused appearances" refers precisely to the objective aspect (*xiangfen*).

This objective aspect acts as the causal condition of the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), because it is able to give rise to the subjective mind that perceives it. Therefore, the object is itself the cause of the mind.
These "confused characteristics" (*vikṣepa-lakṣaṇa*) and "confused essence" (*vikṣepa-svabhāva*) are all explained in reference to the two realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and form (*rūpadhātu*).

The commentary states that the text is "interrupted" for the sake of conforming to the rules of verse composition (*śloka-bandha*). Regarding this "interruption in verse composition," one takes the second line;

it should be understood as "form-consciousness" (*rūpa-vijñāna*). This connects with the two characters "upper confused characteristics" (*ūrdhva-vikṣepa-lakṣaṇa*) from the first line above. That is to say, one takes the... [second line].
The three phrases and the phrase "non-material consciousness" conclude the first sentence above, specifically the two characters "disordered essence" (*luan-ti*).

That is to say: if there is no disordered appearance (*luan-xiang*), the disordered essence is likewise non-existent. If one were to follow the method of sequential verse composition, it should state:

the disordered appearance is material consciousness, while the disordered essence is non-material consciousness. If there is no disordered appearance, the disordered essence is also non-existent. Now, this is discussed from the perspective of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect).
Regarding "consciousness of form" (*rūpa-vijñāna*): form arises through the transformation of consciousness; thus, form is called "consciousness of form.

The commentary states that "the object serves as the cause for the production of the result, which is the mind" means that the object acts as the *ālambana-pratyaya* (objective condition) cause, which is capable of inducing the determinate result that is the cognizing subject.

The Commentary states: "When all phenomena are determined as existent or non-existent by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this refers to authoritative testimony (*āptavāda*) and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which are capable of determining the existence or non-existence of all phenomena.

The Commentary further states: "The Master of the Treatise, relying on the response 'it is as I am,' [explains that] the five consciousnesses and the simultaneous mental consciousness obtain time and so forth through direct perception."
However, according to the Mahāyāna’s own tenet, it is taught that the six consciousnesses arise simultaneously.

The commentary states: "In accordance with the interpretation of other schools, the five consciousnesses perceive their objects through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) at the same time, yet they do not grasp them as external [objects].

Regarding the subsequent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which falsely generates the appearance of objects existing outside the mind, this is also in accordance with the interpretation of other schools. This refers to the Sautrāntika and... [the Vaibhāṣika].
Regarding "many" and so forth: since it is not admitted that the six consciousnesses arise simultaneously, the present treatise explains in accordance with that view as follows.

The first five consciousnesses perceive their objects through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and do not grasp them as external. Once the five consciousnesses have ceased and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) subsequently arises, it falsely discriminates its object and falsely gives rise to the appearance of an external object.
Furthermore, according to the Mahāyāna school, when the five consciousnesses perceive objects such as form (*rūpa*), the five consciousnesses [do not...].
It forms the conceptualization of blue or yellow, yet it spontaneously takes this as its object without forming the conceptualization that it is an external object.

Regarding the explanations of the two schools of the Hīnayāna, they state that the five consciousnesses form the conceptualization of blue or yellow regarding color-form and so forth, and that these constitute external direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This is said according to the majority view; however, in reality, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises simultaneously with the five consciousnesses also possesses grasping.
The Commentary states: "Thus, although the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are indeed accompanied by the consciousness of mind (*manovijñāna*), there is false clinging...

even until the subsequent five [consciousnesses] arise, what is it that clings and ceases? However, at the same time as the five consciousnesses, the mental consciousness also arises with clinging. It is just like the continuity of the five consciousnesses:

while the mental consciousness is correctly perceiving objects such as form (*rūpa*), and the five consciousnesses take those objects such as form as their causal conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), suddenly from the side there is an enemy.

Regarding the discourse on the household: once the ear-consciousness has heard these sounds of resentment, the mental consciousness immediately gives rise to grasping. This grasping takes it to be real anger and resentment;
as this conforming consciousness continues in a stream and focuses its attention, it becomes attached to this stream of ear-consciousness characterized by resentment.

As this conforming consciousness continues in a stream and focuses its attention, it becomes attached to this stream of ear-consciousness characterized by resentment. This resentment is then grasped by the mental consciousness as being real.
[It is] an enemy. Therefore, one knows that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) simultaneous with the five sensory consciousnesses also possesses grasping (*samanvāhāra*).

If the mental consciousness simultaneous with the five sensory consciousnesses were without grasping, then after hearing the sound of an enemy, the mental consciousness simultaneous with the five [sensory consciousnesses] would not grasp it as an actual perception of an enemy;

yet, in reality, there is the perception of an enemy. Since the mental consciousness simultaneous with the five sensory consciousnesses grasps it as an actual perception of an enemy, [it follows that it possesses grasping]. Thus, the five sensory consciousnesses...
At that same time, there is grasping within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
If it is as your later statement suggests—that grasping arises in the mental consciousness only after the five sense-consciousnesses have ceased—then another objection may be raised:

if grasping arises in the mental consciousness only after the five sense-consciousnesses have ceased, then when the subsequent five sense-consciousnesses arise, for what reason would they cause the mental consciousness to be interrupted? Therefore, we know that when the subsequent five sense-consciousnesses arise...

If grasping within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not severed, one knows that at times when the five sensory consciousnesses have not yet ceased, the mental consciousness simultaneously gives rise to grasping alongside them.
Thus, one knows that the mental consciousness occurring simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses can possess grasping.

The Commentary states: "However, it can be said that there is a difference only insofar as [the mental consciousness] firmly eliminates [attachment]; it is not the case that when the five [sensory consciousnesses] are present, all are without attachment.

If, at the time the five sensory consciousnesses are simultaneous with the mental consciousness, that mental consciousness does not firmly eliminate attachment, then this mental consciousness simultaneous with the five sensory consciousnesses is, like the five sensory consciousnesses, a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If, at the same time as the five sensory consciousnesses, the mental consciousness..."
When consciousness arises with firm grasping, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is not termed direct perception (pratyakṣa).

It is therefore distinct from the five sensory consciousnesses that arise simultaneously, because while the five consciousnesses are direct perceptions, the simultaneous mental consciousness is not. "Firm grasping" refers to grasping that is not firm;
"removal" refers to the absence of grasping.

The *Śāstra* states: "In various places it is merely said that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) co-arising with the five sensory consciousnesses is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), but it is not stated that this is necessarily so;

therefore, there is no contradiction. This means that while various treatises all state that the mental consciousness co-arising with the five consciousnesses is direct perception, they do not definitively state that the mental consciousness co-arising with the five consciousnesses is invariably direct perception.

Furthermore, the statement that the mental consciousness co-arising with the five consciousnesses possesses grasping (*sasaṃprayoga*) is likewise not contradictory. [This concerns] the object (*viṣaya*).

[This is] an explanation. Furthermore, within the Mahāyāna school, it is also taught that after the five consciousnesses have ceased, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) arises. This is mutually consistent with both our own and other schools’ tenets. The commentary states:

"Among the four divisions, there is the self-characteristic division. As for these "four divisions," they are the image division (nimittabhāga), the seeing division (darśanabhāga), the self-witnessing division (svasaṃvedanabhāga), and the witness-to-self-witnessing division (svasaṃvedanasaṃvedanabhāga).
...and so forth. These are the aspects of the fourfold division (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The Commentary states: "Among the five consciousnesses, anger and the like are mutually 'proximate' (*sākṣāt*) but do not accord with the objective essence (*bhāva-viṣaya*);

they are merely called 'proximate' because they transform their own aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), and are not the 'universally imagined' (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Now, the Master of the Commentary says that when greed, anger, and the like within the five consciousnesses take an object, [they do not accord with the objective essence].

To say that [the five consciousnesses] accord with the essential nature (svabhāva) but do not accord with the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) is merely an explanation based on coarse characteristics; it does not fully capture the meaning.

For instance, if one suffers from the kāmalā disease, which impairs the visual faculty such that the eye-consciousness perceives blue as yellow, this is a case of not acceding to the essential nature of the blue color, yet both [the perceiver and the object] are said to accord with the yellow objective aspect. According to the actual state of the five consciousnesses, since they are direct perception (pratyakṣa)...
Regarding the objective sphere, one speaks only of the substantial essence (*svabhāva*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).

When a person presses on their eye with their hand and sees a second moon, this is actually the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Within the gateway of the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), the cognition of the second moon is not, in reality, a second moon.
This case is likewise. Because of this affliction, it is the mental consciousness that perceives blue within the gateway of the visual faculty.
Yellow. When the visual consciousness perceives yellow, this interpretation is the best. It is also like the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of a Bodhisattva;

when it takes the knowledge of others' minds as its object or takes conventional objects as its object, since these are both direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*), they are both termed "objective aspects corresponding to the primary essence" (*svabhāva-nimitta-bhāga*).

The same applies to the objects perceived by the five sensory consciousnesses. The five consciousnesses are exclusively direct perception; thus, when the five consciousnesses perceive their objects, they are all termed [as such].

The objective aspect of the primary substance (*mūla-vastu-nimitta-bhāga*). Furthermore, when a direct-perception consciousness (*pratyakṣa-citta*) takes an object as its condition, it is simultaneously called the objective aspect of the primary substance;

this is because the perceiving consciousness is free from names and words, and is therefore termed the objective aspect of the primary substance. However, if this same perceptual consciousness takes an object [in a different context], it is called merely the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).

It does not correspond to its essential nature (*svabhāva*). As stated previously in the treatises, conventional cognition (*prajñapti-jñāna*) and its designations are themselves valid cognition (*pramāṇa-jñāna*).

If a non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa-citta*) takes an object as its condition, then both [the subjective aspect and] the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) fail to correspond to the essential nature. Nevertheless, it is universally accepted that minds of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) can all be non-valid;
for example, cognitions apprehending things such as jars or garments are all non-valid.

The Commentary states: "The reason the five consciousnesses do not accord with the primary object (bimba) but only with the image-part (nimitta-bhāga) is that within the five consciousnesses there must also be inference (anumāna).

Since it is admitted that they do not accord with the primary object, and given that the three types of minds within the five consciousnesses are all exclusively direct perception (pratyakṣa), we know that when the five consciousnesses take an object, they both accord with the primary object and the image-part.
Question: If one suffers from the disease of *kāma* (cataracts) which impairs the eye, then... [the second...]
Regarding the six consciousnesses: based upon the eye-faculty as its gateway, it is the sixth consciousness that perceives blue as yellow, whereas the eye-consciousness still perceives blue.

Thus, the eye-consciousness is said to perceive the objective image. An objection is raised: if the sixth faculty [the mind] is impaired by the kāmalā disease, it may be granted that the sixth consciousness perceives blue as yellow;
however, since the eye-faculty is impaired by the disease, it should be the eye-consciousness that perceives [it as such].
If blue is perceived as yellow, yet the sixth consciousness and the mental faculty (manas) are not impaired, then that sixth consciousness ought to perceive blue as blue.

Furthermore, it is objected: since you claim the eye-faculty is afflicted and damaged, or that the visual consciousness perceives blue as yellow, or that the mental consciousness, relying on the gateway of the eye, perceives blue as yellow, then by the same logic, the ear-faculty should also be damaged by illness, and the auditory consciousness should likewise [perceive sounds erroneously].
A pleasant sound may be perceived as unpleasant; consciousness, relying upon the ear-faculty as its gateway, takes a pleasant sound as its object and perceives it as an unpleasant one.

This principle should be understood to apply even to cases where it harms the body-faculty. Furthermore, one asks: according to what meaning does the *Śāstra* state that within the five consciousnesses there are greed, anger, and so forth, yet these do not correspond to their objective essence (*bhāva*)?
Likewise, when the five consciousnesses give rise to wholesome or neutral states of mind, they too should correspond to their objective essence.
The Commentary states: "Present awareness is like a dream," etc. The Explanation says: "Awareness" (*jñāna*) is a term applied to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

For example, when one perceives objects within a dream, one does not say, "I am in a dream. Likewise, when the mind of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is correctly perceiving an object, it likewise does not conceive, "I am able to perceive this object."
The commentary states: "The Saṃmitīya school accepts that while objects persist through a continuum, the various consciousnesses arise and perish moment by moment.

This means that the Saṃmitīya school maintains that there are long-lasting four characteristics—such as the persistence of the world for kalpas—and they likewise accept that the cognizing mind arises and perishes from moment to moment.

That is, when an object gives rise to a mind, they both take the previous object as their common focal point. However, the Saṃmitīya school maintains that even after the five consciousnesses have ceased, the subsequently arising mental consciousness (manovijñāna) can still be considered direct perception (pratyakṣa).

The Commentary states: "Regarding the claim that the five consciousnesses, as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), can perceive [an object] while the mind has ceased and no longer exists—this now refutes the Saṃmitīya school.
Even if one were to grant that the perceived object does not cease, since the mind has already ceased, the five consciousnesses would still be unable to perceive it."

How could the subsequent mental consciousness (manovijñāna) possess direct perception (pratyakṣa)? However, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that once the five sensory consciousnesses have ceased, the subsequent mental consciousness arises and likewise attains direct perception.
The commentary states: "In this passage, the general meaning contains two types. This means that within this treatise, the general intent contains both [types of] refutations.
The Saṃmitīya school has two types [of arguments]. As the verse states: "Direct perception is like a dream, etc.

This is because when the mind of direct perception arises, both the time of awakening and the object are already non-existent. This primarily refutes multiple schools while simultaneously refuting the Saṃmitīya.

The Commentary states: "These two types of direct perception (pratyakṣa) are non-conceptual and non-apprehending. Regarding "the two types of direct perception," this refers to the direct perception of the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) and the direct perception of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises simultaneously with them; hence, it is called "the two types of direct perception."
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Now, herein, 'according to the majority' refers to the mental consciousness that arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses.

The Commentary further states: "Because there are also two [types], there are no many faults. This means that because it is stated that the mental consciousness arising simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses possesses grasping (*sagrāha*), there are likewise no many faults.
An opponent asks: "If, at the limit of all moments of awakening... and so forth, up to this point.

Regarding the phrase "thereby citing and determining the opponent's school": A question arises—since this text is from the Hīnayāna coming to challenge the Mahāyāna, the Hīnayāna should be termed "the other" (para) and the Mahāyāna "one's own" (sva).
Thus, it should be citing and determining the Mahāyāna’s own school; why then does this text say it is citing and determining the opponent's school?
Answer: The explanation follows below. Why [is it said that] during the waking state, with respect to one's own visual objects...

Regarding those who do not understand *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), when it is asked how one speaks within the context of dependent phenomena (*pratyaya-dharma*), the follower of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) must consider this:

by what means can they demonstrate that their own mind is consciousness-only, both during the state of dreaming and during the state of waking? The outsider asks: "As long as one does not depart from consciousness...
This is a formal restatement of the opponent's position. The commentary explains: this is a provisional designation (*upacāra*) used within the Mahāyāna.
This establishes the opponent’s Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) thesis as the object of refutation.

Specifically, within the Mahāyāna refutation of the Hīnayāna thesis, since all Hīnayāna schools admit that there are forms and other phenomena external to the mind, this section provides only the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) but lacks the formal application (*upanaya*). The underlying intent of the question is:
"If the dream-objects cease to exist upon waking from a dream, why is it that when I am awake in my ordinary state, the preceding objects of form do not likewise cease to exist?"
This means they are eternally present. The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "The functioning of all phenomena is without utility; there is neither function nor an agent who acts. The explanation says:
If one takes the person as a whole aggregate, they are called the "agent"; if one uses the hands, body, and so forth, these are called the "function. Therefore, there is no reality [to them].
The agent of action, as well as the hand and so forth which lack substantial reality, are both merely different names for the self (*ātman*).
The treatise states that this is not like the hand directly grasping external objects, nor like the sun extending its light to directly illuminate external realms; [the former] is not [the case].
"Just as the hand and so forth directly grasp external objects"—these two phrases refute the Saṃmitīya school. The Saṃmitīyas do not establish the existence of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect).
That school asserts that the mind and mental factors directly apprehend the preceding object, like an object within a bowl; [the text] refutes this by stating:
It is not like the hand or similar [senses] that directly grasp external objects, nor like the sun and so forth that directly illuminate external objects by emitting light.

These two phrases constitute the refutation of the argument; they refute the claim that when visual consciousness arises, it emits light to directly illuminate the object before it, as the sun emits light to directly illuminate its object.
Now, the refutation states: when the mind and other [faculties] perceive objects, it is not like the sun and so forth emitting light to directly [illuminate them].
It illuminates external objects. Regarding these external things, the sun and moon are their names and substances.
The Commentary states: "It is simply like your own [view in the] *Zhengjingshi*: when objects are illuminated, they appear as if they were external realms, even appearing upon one's own mind.
However, both the Mahāyāna and the Sautrāntika schools do not establish the existence of reflections in mirrors or moons in water; there is no such reality within the mirror.
There is no image. In reality, there is no moon in the water. It is like when a person faces south and looks into a mirror;
because the surface of the mirror is bright and pure, it causes the visual consciousness to see one's own face facing north.

Again, when looking at water, because the water is bright and pure, it causes the visual consciousness to see the moon in the sky. It is just as if one were looking at a basin from within the sun or the moon. Furthermore—
Because water and the surface of a mirror are clear and bright, they cause the sunlight to appear reflected back toward the rafters of the house.
That which appears within the mirror is called the "image-division" (*pratibimba-bhāga*); light arises therein, while other visible colors are termed "obstructions" (*āvṛti*).

Now, regarding what is called an "image" (*pratibimba*) within the mirror, this is spoken of by borrowing the shadow of another object that exists elsewhere; it is described as being within the mirror. This is established according to both schools.

There are mirror-images that are real and the moon in water. Now, the commentary states: According to the Mahāyāna, it is merely because, according to both of your two schools, a real mirror-image appears within the mirror, that this knowledge of others' minds is likewise so—it is simply a reflection of another's mind appearing upon one's own mental continuum.
Now, within the Mahāyāna, the two teachers are refuted by stating that there is no real image in a mirror.
It is said: Furthermore, it is like two people dwelling on opposite banks of a narrow body of water; each person sees both banks clearly reflected in the water.
If these were substantial forms (*dravya-rūpa*), how could two substantial forms occupy the same location? [They must therefore be] extremely subtle forms (*paramāṇu-rūpa*).
Regarding the analysis of matter as that which is capable of being perceived and that which is perceived:

either the human body is the perceiver and the wall is the perceived object, or the wall and the obstruction are the perceivers and the human body is the perceived object. Second is the matter of extreme distance (*paramāṇu-rūpa*), which refers exclusively to the matter obtained through analysis;

it is called "matter of extreme distance" because it is extremely subtle. This "perceived matter" refers to the matter of the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*) existing between the two types [of bodies] and between the two walls.
When obstructed by persons or other objects such as grass and trees, the form of the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*) that is perceived is made non-manifest.
According to the explanation of both [Hīnayāna] schools, the form of the space-element is also composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*);

being situated near empty space, it acts as the primary creator, meaning the four great elements are the creators and the form of the space-element is their derivative (*upādāya-rūpa*). According to the Mahāyāna, however, this is not fixed; at times it is simply empty space.

Within [the earth], there are the material forms of the space-element (ākāśadhātu) produced by the four great elements. Sometimes, the material forms of the space-element in the distant sky are produced by the four great elements within the earth.

Consequently, in some cases, the productive great elements may be many while the produced derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is few; in other cases, the productive four great elements and the produced five sense-faculties (pañcendriya-rūpa) may be equal in size.
This can be known when one perceives that a wall completely obstructs [vision]. Conversely, when one sees the azure color of the heavens from afar, it is because the obstruction is absent.
This is called the "single manifest color of emptiness.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the mutual relationship between the perceived object (nimitta-bhāga) and the self-body when consciousness undergoes transformation, etc.:

if one's own consciousness takes the perceived object-color of another person as its substantial cause (ālambana-pratyaya), it likewise transforms itself into both a perceived object-part and a self-body."
The first six consciousnesses and so forth take the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by the eighth consciousness as their substantial basis (*ālambana-pratibimba*).

These six consciousnesses then themselves transform and give rise to their own *nimitta-bhāgas*. Thus, for the six consciousnesses and so forth, [the objective aspect] serves as the direct object-condition (*sākṣād-ālambana*).

Question: While it is acceptable to call the *nimitta-bhāga* a "reflection" (*pratibimba*), how can the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect) be called a reflection? Answer: It is because that [aspect] arises from...
"Because it arises from its own substance.
The Commentary states: "Just as one sees the original object by taking that object as a condition, so too one sees one's own mind by taking the mind as a condition.

This is like when a person looks into a mirror: taking the face of their own original substance as the condition, they see the face of their own original substance reflected back by means of the mirror's surface.

Because it is luminous and pure, the agitated visual consciousness turns back to see its own fundamental face. Just as when one perceives external objects and the like, one actually takes one's own mind as the object;
thus, "seeing one's own mind" means that within one's own mind, the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving portion) sees the reflection of the *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived portion) upon the mind itself.
Since the *nimitta-bhāga* is not separate from the mind, it is called "one's own mind. It is not that [the mind] sees itself.
This is because it perceives its own seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as a distinct portion.
The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "How does the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) know its object as it truly is? It does not know it as the objects known by a Buddha, and so forth.

This passage explains that when the knowledge of others' minds belonging to other vehicles or to Bodhisattvas on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) takes another's mind as its object, [it does not perceive it as it truly is].
It cannot accord with reality as much as one would wish, because the essential nature of another's mind is not clearly manifest;
just as when one's own mind takes itself as its object, it likewise cannot be made to accord with or become clearly manifest.

This is inferior to the Buddha’s knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), which, when taking another's mind as its object, can cause that mind to be known in accordance with reality and allow for the full comprehension of the essential nature of that other mind.

Question: If it is taught in the Mahāyāna that Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh bhūmi give rise to a contaminated knowledge of others (*sāsrava-paracitta-jñāna*) and thus cannot know those who have attained the four fruits [of the śrāvaka], then those with uncontaminated minds (*anāsrava-citta*) within the first six bhūmis should likewise be unable to perceive the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of those who have attained the four fruits, just as the post-attainment wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of a Buddha or the post-attainment knowledge of others' minds of a Bodhisattva on the tenth bhūmi cannot perceive it. Furthermore—

From the ninth stage (*bhūmi*) downwards, there is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). This is because fundamental wisdom is superior, whereas subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is inferior. Furthermore, it is asked:

if a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), having given rise to an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), is able to know the tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*) of a Bodhisattva of the second stage, then if one says he knows it, how can it be said that a Bodhisattva of the first stage does not know the second-stage Bodhisattva’s lifting and lowering of his feet? Conversely, if one says he does not...

Regarding the knower: how can it be said that the knowledge of others' minds belonging to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is able to know the contaminated mind (*sāsrava-citta*) of one who has attained the first fruit, up to the contaminated mind of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*);
and that it is able to know other contaminated minds of the first stage, up to the uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) of the first stage;
and that it is able to know the uncontaminated mind of the first stage, up to the contaminated mind of the first stage; and that it is able to know other uncontaminated minds of the first stage?

Regarding the mind: Furthermore, when it is asked whether the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) within the Mahāyāna can take another person’s mind as its object and also take that other person’s mental factors (*caitta*) as its objects—does this refer to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or does it refer to those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*)?
It is also like one person taking another as an object; for example, just as the first person takes the second person as an object, the second person’s mind is the object of cognition.

The first person’s mind is a mind capable of cognition (*ālambaka*). By this principle, it can be known that the first person’s mind takes the third person’s mind as its object (*ālambana*), and so on, up to the ninth person’s mind taking the tenth person’s mind as its object.

Thus, each preceding mind is the cognizer and each succeeding mind is the object of cognition; this applies even to ten million people. These bodhisattvas and others thus give rise to the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

When taking the mind of another’s first [level of] realization as an object, does this bodhisattva’s knowledge of others’ minds take the mind of the third [level] as its object, or does it also take the mind of the tenth level as its object?
This question should be applied analogously even to the knowledge of others’ minds regarding Buddhas and those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).

The answer is given in verse twenty of the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*: "What is this phrase?"—this constitutes the introductory question. It asks concerning the other vehicles and bodhisattvas...

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): is it a knowledge that accords with reality, or is it a knowledge that does not accord with reality? The answer is contained in the following three phrases: namely, "knowing the object as it is not," and so forth.
If it is the knowledge of others' minds belonging to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it does not equal that of a Śrāvaka;

the Śrāvaka does not equal that of a Pratyekabuddha; the Pratyekabuddha does not equal that of a Bodhisattva; and the Bodhisattva does not equal that of a Buddha’s knowledge of others' minds—excluding the case of [knowing] other humans.
When the mental faculty takes another person’s mind as its object, it knows it only in its general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), rather than in detail.

It does not know each individual instance of affliction arising in the preceding person’s mind prior to the arising of the knowledge of others' minds. Specifically, regarding which of the eighty-four thousand gateways of conduct requires a specific antidote for abandonment—since this involves the abandonment of those afflictions—the knowledge of others' minds belonging to other persons does not know them as they truly are (*yathābhūtam*). This is because it functions by taking [the object] as one would take one's own mind as an object.

Regarding wisdom (*jñāna*): when a subsequent thought-moment takes a preceding thought-moment as its object across four time-periods, it likewise cannot truly know [it] as it is, nor can it know it truly in the same manner that one's own mind takes itself as an object.

However, if it is the Buddha’s knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), he knows each and every detail, including the eighty-four thousand modes of conduct and understanding, as well as the remedial and counteractive dharmas for the afflictions within these various mental states. Furthermore, if...
The Hīnayāna school asserts that the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) takes only the mind and mental factors of others as its object;

it does not take what those other persons themselves are taking as objects. When a person takes another person as an object, they do so by means of the Bodhisattva’s mind as the objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
At the time of the Bodhisattva’s mind, when the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of others' minds takes this person's mind as its object, he knows only the person's capacity to cognize [the object].
Whether it is associated with wholesome states or associated with greed and so forth, this is the bodhisattva’s knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

It does not take as its object the focal domain (*ālambana*) of another person's mind. If it were to take the focal domain of another person's mind as its own object, then the bodhisattva’s mind would fall into the error of taking itself as its own object;
for the bodhisattva would then be the very locus that serves as the focal object of that other person's mind, and thus that bodhisattva’s cognition would have to be called "self[-cognition]."

The mind of another cannot be called "knowledge of others' minds. Furthermore, if the preceding person’s mind takes only form (*rūpa*) and so forth as its object, then those forms and so forth belonging to that preceding person’s mind become the objective sphere (*ālambana*).

If a Bodhisattva’s knowledge of others' minds were to take those forms and so forth—which are the objects of that preceding person’s mind—as its own object, then that Bodhisattva’s knowledge of others' minds would have to be called "knowledge of form" rather than "knowledge of others' minds. Moreover, the preceding...
Regarding the objects of another person's mind: [these include] dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and so forth.

If a bodhisattva’s knowledge of others' minds takes as its object that which was previously taken as an object by another person’s mind, and since that former person had already employed dissociated formations and unconditioned phenomena as their objective sphere, then that bodhisattva’s knowledge of others' minds should be called "knowledge taking dissociated formations and unconditioned phenomena as its object," rather than being called "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*). This applies to other arhats as well.

The knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) of Pratyekabuddhas and others should also be understood according to this principle. Therefore, the knowledge of others' minds takes only the minds of others as its object;
