All of these are equally termed "co-existent factors" (*sahabhū-dharma*). If one speaks of the mind in its general sense, it consists solely of the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) and the perceived and perceiving portions (*nimitta-grāhaka-bhāga*).
If one speaks of the mind within each specific category (*citta-kalāpa*), it is both broad and inclusive, encompassing the mental factors (*caitasika*) as well as the self-verifying portion.

The characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the four characteristics such as acquisition (*prāpti*), etc., all belong to the same category. If one says that "coexistent dharmas" (*sahabhū-dharma*) and "dharmas possessing dharmas" (*dharmin*) are extremely broad, they likewise include acquisition, the four characteristics, and so forth.
The commentary states: "In persons lacking the nature [of enlightenment], the seventh manas-consciousness also possesses power, as has already been recorded above."
Sentient beings who lack [a specific] nature also have their seventh consciousness able to perfuse seeds, because within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna),

there exist its own seeds from which the eight consciousnesses arise as manifest activity once the causes and conditions are present along with their own essence. Indeed, since there are already the seeds of the eight consciousnesses within the fundamental consciousness,
the eight consciousnesses arise as manifest activity from their respective seeds.
The Commentary states: "Regarding results that are either simultaneous or of a different time and a different category":

this refers to when a seed is considered in relation to a simultaneous seed of a different category—such as the seed of visual consciousness in relation to the seed of auditory consciousness—or in relation to a long-term manifestation of a different category—such as the seed of visual consciousness in relation to the manifestation of auditory consciousness, or the manifestation of visual consciousness in relation to a simultaneous auditory consciousness of a different category.

Regarding the manifest [dharmas] and so forth: either seeds in relation to seeds of a different time or a different category—such as the seed of a preceding moment of visual consciousness in relation to the seed of a subsequent moment of auditory consciousness—or seeds in relation to manifest dharmas of a different category, these are not, in this context, of the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

In the *Abhidharma* treatises, within the discussion of causal conditions, six causes are taught; however, regarding those that are causal conditions, the *Abhidharma* speaks of them in terms of these six.
Based on this, the various dharmas are clarified; the six causes are explained as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and so forth.

In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the causal conditions and others are elucidated by means of ten causes and two modes of operation. For example, when barley produces a sprout, the characteristic of the seed is manifest in the active manifestation (*pravṛtti*).
This is not the case when [the sprout] arises from chaff or is pulled up; rather, it is when the sprout arises from a barley seed that the active manifestation perfumes and forms a seed.

Regarding the meaning: this text explains that when the eighth consciousness acts as the causal condition (*pratyaya*) for the other seven consciousnesses, those seeds belong to the eighth consciousness;
thus, the seeds enter into the eighth consciousness as its cause and become its seeds.

Since they are the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, it is said that the eighth consciousness serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the preceding [seven] consciousnesses. As for the seven consciousnesses...

It acts as three types of conditions for the eighth consciousness. Furthermore, the seeds within that fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) also belong to the seeds of the seven consciousnesses, because they enter into the functioning of the seven consciousnesses;
thus, the seeds pertain to both locations. However, the ālayavijñāna acts as two types of conditions for the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*):
first, the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the eighth consciousness serves as the support (*āśraya*) for those seven evolving consciousnesses; second, [the seeds...]
The seeds within consciousness act as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses;

that is, the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) directly produce the seven consciousnesses. Furthermore, the preceding seven consciousnesses also act as conditions for the *ālaya-vijñāna*:

first, because the seven consciousnesses can grow and nourish the seeds within that consciousness, namely by means of the perfuming of the manifest activities (*pravṛtti*). This causes new perfumed seeds to arise.
Regarding the phrase "the seeds produced by the sons": the original text contains the term *bīja-dīrgha* (long seeds).

Second, because the seven consciousnesses are able to contain and plant those seeds—that is, through the actual manifestation (*pravṛtti*) of the seven consciousnesses—they perfume and form seeds, from which the eighth consciousness manifests.

Now, it is explained that the first seven consciousnesses act as the two types of conditions for the eighth consciousness; this is all stated in reference to the perfuming actual manifestations of the first seven consciousnesses. This...
Regarding the statement in the *Madhyāntavibhāga* that the sixth and seventh consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness serve as mutual causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*):

this is because the sixth and seventh consciousnesses can perfuse (*vāsana*) and thereby generate the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness. It does not state that the five consciousnesses or the fifth consciousness separately can perfuse and generate the seeing-part and so forth of the eighth consciousness.
Therefore, with respect to the seven active consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) in relation to the eighth consciousness, they are considered to be mutually [causes and conditions].
It is not that the seeds of one's own names within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) can produce actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*) without such a restriction;
rather, it is said that the seven consciousnesses and the fundamental consciousness mutually perfuse (*vāsanā*) one another to serve as mutual causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Although these seeds produce the manifestation of the fundamental consciousness, the manifestation of the fundamental consciousness cannot, in turn, perfume them to form seeds. Thus, their mutual functioning as causes and conditions does not hold. Now, we adopt the former [view].

The seven manifesting consciousnesses do not serve as mutual conditions for one another. Furthermore, it is explained that the seeds of those seven evolving consciousnesses themselves cannot produce the manifest eighth consciousness;
thus, one cannot say that the evolving consciousnesses and the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) act as mutual causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Now, if the seeds of the seven consciousnesses were to produce their own manifest seven consciousnesses, they could be termed causal conditions. [End of previous section]
The active manifestation of the seven consciousnesses produces their own seeds; this may be termed the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Likewise, if the seeds of the eighth consciousness produce the active manifestation of the eighth consciousness itself, this may be termed the "causal condition. The former interpretation is superior.
As for the "immediately antecedent condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it possesses the function of cognitive apprehension (*ālambana-manasikāra*).
The Commentary states: "Those previously arisen that are subsumed under 'opening and guiding' refer to the preceding moments of mind and mental factors;
they are so called because, as the opening and guiding [conditions], they are able to induce and sustain the subsequent moments of mind and mental factors."

The Commentary states: "Thus, it is not merely because they are provisional that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth are excluded... [and so on] until: 'those that mutually possess this condition'. An opponent asks:

"If the life-faculty and so forth are provisional, they are not equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*). Likewise, since the essence of heedfulness (*apramāda*) and so forth is also provisional, they too should not be equal-and-immediate conditions.
The answer is: "It is not merely because they are provisional that the life-faculty and so forth are excluded."

These are not equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), because they lack the function of taking an object as a cognitive focus (*ālambana*). By excluding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and others on this basis, there is no fault.
Although factors such as heedfulness (*apramāda*) are nominal (*prajñapti-sat*), they are nonetheless equal-and-immediate conditions.

The Commentary states: "Therefore, regarding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth, there is the sense of 'equal and immediate antecedent' (*samanantarapratyaya*), but not the sense of 'object-condition' (*ālambanapratyaya*).

This means that if the essence of the preceding moment of the life-faculty is one, and the essence of the subsequent moment of the faculty is also one, then there exists only the sense of being an equal and immediate antecedent, but not the sense of being an object-condition.

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'immediately preceding' (*samanantara*), this indicates that although the preceding moment serves as the condition for the succeeding one without interval, it would follow that even [a mind] that ought not to be such a condition [would be so].
As for 'equal and immediately preceding' (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it means there is no interval within the moments of consciousness;

even if separated by a hundred years of moments, provided there is no intervening mind of a different category, it is still called 'equal and immediately preceding. A separation of moments, however, constitutes a non-immediate condition."

Regarding the argument that "one who has entered the mindless absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*) cannot be considered a homogeneous immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) in relation to the mind of that absorption," even if a hundred years have passed since the interruption,
it is still called a homogeneous immediate condition; it is simply because there is no interval between the preceding mind and the subsequent mind that it is termed a homogeneous immediate condition.

The Commentary states: "Therefore, one should know that [the *samanantarapratyaya*] is defined only in relation to consciousnesses of its own kind... even if there are the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, how could they not be this condition?
If one follows the masters of the orthodox school (*samyak-artha-vādin*), the *samanantarapratyaya* is established only in relation to consciousnesses of its own kind.

Thus, although the seventh and eighth consciousnesses persist during the attainment of the mindless states (*acittaka-samāpatti*), they do not serve as the *samanantarapratyaya* for the preceding six consciousnesses. If the former [six] were not correct...
Regarding the Master of Meaning (Yi-shi): this refers to the eight consciousnesses acting as mutual *samanantara-pratyaya* (equal-and-immediate conditions) within their respective categories.

As for these mutually preceding and succeeding paths of cause and effect: the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the preceding moment are the cause, while the mind and mental factors of the succeeding moment are the effect.
"Equal" (*sama*) means that both cause and effect are alike; they are both equal.
The Commentary states: "This immediately excludes the meaning of a 'śramaṇa' who merely resembles [the true one].

In that case, each primary mind (*citta*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) are considered in relation to themselves, not in relation to others. Now, regarding 'equality' (*samatā*), there are two meanings. First is equality of essence (*tattva-samatā*):

the preceding moment consists solely of one primary mind and five universal mental factors, and the succeeding moment likewise consists solely of one primary mind and five universal mental factors; thus, the preceding and succeeding moments..."

First, equality of substance (*tulya-dravya*): the mental king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) have a similar number of instances; this is called equality of substance. Second, equality of function (*tulya-kāritra*):

if a preceding moment consists of a single mental king, it possesses the power and force capable of acting as an opening and guiding condition (*āvajjana-avakāśa-dāna*) for the subsequent moment’s mental king and mental factors.
Regarding the arising of the mind and mental factors in the subsequent moment following a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*):

it is precisely the force and power inherent in the single mental factor of the preceding moment that is able to draw forth and cause the simultaneous arising of the numerous mind-kings (*citta*) and mental factors of the subsequent moment.

Thus, although the preceding moment’s mind is a neutral (*avyākṛta*) phenomenon, it possesses the capacity—consisting solely of universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viniyata*) mental factors along with the mind-king itself—to give rise to the subsequent moment.

The eleven wholesome mental factors (*kuśala*) and so forth are brought into arising by many mental concomitants (*caitta*). Furthermore, as in the case of the eighth consciousness during the stage of a cause (*hetu-avasthā*), it possesses only the five universal mental factors (*pañca sarvatraga*);

upon reaching the time of Buddhahood, it can induce the five object-specific mental factors (*pañca viṣaya-niyata*). The eleven wholesome factors and many other mental concomitants bring them into arising.

These all consist of the "equality of function" (kāritra-samatā). If one is merely similar to a śramaṇa, they are called a "nominal śramaṇa. In such cases, there is only the "equality of substance" (dravya-samatā) without the "equality of function.
Upon attaining Buddhahood, the eighth consciousness possesses five universal mental factors (sarvatraga) and induces eleven wholesome factors. This takes the final retribution as its object.

Just as there are many types of form and non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra), so too among those that arise, there are many types of arising within the category of non-associated formations.
Furthermore, it is like how within a *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class), many similar [phenomena] arise together;
or as within a body there exist the *dhātu-sabhāga*, the *gati-sabhāga*, the *cakṣu-sabhāga*, and so on up to the *śrāmaṇera-sabhāga*, all of which arise simultaneously.
It is also like how within a body, the four characteristics of arising, abiding, change, and cessation—numbering in the hundreds of thousands—arise at one and the same time. It is likewise one.
Regarding the statement that "although the eight consciousnesses of the body are called many types, up to [the analogy of] fruits and so forth":

although within a single body there are eight consciousnesses whose essence and function each have their own distinct activities, they are termed "equal" and so on. Their forms and other qualities arise as hundreds or thousands of similar instances;
for example, the nourishing matter (*aupacayika-rūpa*) within the body also arises simultaneously in hundreds or thousands of instances. It is also like many blades of grass.

Once it has fallen into the pit, it immediately becomes a small amount of ash; thus, a small color draws forth [the result of] much color. Furthermore, it is like burning grass, from which immeasurable smoke arises;
thus, much color draws forth [the result of] much color, and all are unequal. This causes that [result] to arise determinately and instantaneously as the subsequent fruit.

Although the sūtra text speaks of "far off," even until that which is to arise determinately—such as when one is born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), where after eighty thousand kalpas one must [attain] non-perception.

When one who has died in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) is born into the intermediate state (antarābhava), after one or two moments have passed, at the very moment visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna) arises, this is precisely at the time of death in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) eighty thousand kalpas prior. At that time, visual consciousness serves as the opening path;

acting as the supporting equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya), it draws forth the arising of visual consciousness within this intermediate state. If one asks what the support for the equal-and-immediate condition is, it is—

It refers exclusively to the preceding moment of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*). If one speaks of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it then encompasses both the preceding moments of the mind-king and its mental factors (*caitta*).

While the preceding moments of mind and mental factors serve as the equal-and-immediate condition for subsequent moments, subsequent moments of mind and mental factors cannot be taken as the equal-and-immediate condition for preceding moments.
That which functions as a cause—whether simultaneous with or prior to [the effect]—is the cause; that which follows is the effect.

Regarding the principle of "non-associated [conditioned phenomena]," whether it be in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* or in later works, the *Śāstra* states: "If non-associated [phenomena] are provisional, this is the tenet of our own school.
If my Mahāyāna and the Sautrāntika both allow that non-associated [phenomena] are provisional, yet the school [in question] allows them to be real, [then there is a discrepancy].
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "If it is granted that the eight consciousnesses mutually serve as conditions for one another’s pleasure, and even that this should apply to the category of seeds...

If the aforementioned heterodox masters grant that the eight consciousnesses serve as mutual equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), such that the eighth consciousness, acting as a condition, draws forth the other seven consciousnesses, then they must also grant that multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously. Now, the objection is raised: "The same should apply to seeds."
The name "equal-and-immediate condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is used because many types of seeds arise simultaneously.

The *Śāstra* states that this is not the case for the eight consciousnesses regarding their modes of activity (*ākāra*), objects of perception (*ālambana*), or even their "opening-and-guiding support" (*kṣaṇika-āśraya*). In the explanation of the opening-and-guiding support, it says:

namely, visual consciousness relies on the eye-faculty; the five consciousnesses each rely individually on the five material faculties; the sixth [consciousness] relies on the seventh; and the seventh...

The consciousnesses do not rely on the eighth consciousness, nor does the eighth consciousness rely on them; they cannot serve as one another’s equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), as explained previously in the fifth fascicle regarding the "mutual reliance" (*paraspara-āśraya*). The commentary states: the five consciousnesses have four bases (*āśraya*):

namely, their own respective objects, the sense organs, the sixth consciousness, and the seventh consciousness. The sixth consciousness has two bases: namely, the seventh consciousness and the eighth consciousness.
Regarding consciousness: the seventh consciousness has one support, namely the eighth consciousness; the eighth consciousness has one support, namely the seventh consciousness.
Since the supports of the eight consciousnesses differ in this way, is it not the case that they do not serve as mutual conditions for one another?
The Commentary states: "Regarding the eighty-first [fascicle], it says 'entering the mind of nirvana without remainder' and so forth, even including other interpretations.
To take an example, such as an Arhat liberated through both parts who has previously attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*):

when he subsequently desires to enter parinirvāṇa without remainder, he first enters the nine successive absorptions (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) by means of his prior power of aspiration—namely, the eye, the inverse, the even, the interval, the skipping, and so forth—and thus first...

Having entered the meditative absorption with mind (*sacittaka-samādhi*), one next enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Only after this attainment has ceased does one enter *nirvāṇa-with-remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

Thus, the attainment of cessation is designated as "meditative absorption. One practices this attainment of cessation in the interval between the preceding absorption with mind and the state of being without [mind], prior to *nirvāṇa-without-remainder* (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*). Because it is asked regarding the state within *nirvāṇa-without-remainder*, the attainment of cessation is so named.

This is indeed a practice of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). If others do not attain the concentration of an Arhat, they enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) as previously described regarding the non-attainment of the cessation-concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

As stated in the fifth fascicle, at the end of life, one who craves existence must necessarily abide in a distracted state of mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), not in a mindless concentration (*acittaka-samādhi*).

The meaning of this passage is that if one is in a concentrated state of mind (*samāhita-citta*) at the time of death, one cannot pass away; it is only by abiding in a distracted state of mind that one can do so.
"Death at the end of life" refers specifically to the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). Regarding this treatise, it should state:

"Other Arhats, through the power of their vows, enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and attain death while in that state of mind. Other persons must abide in a distracted state of mind (*vikṣipta-citta*);

they do not attain death while in a mindless meditative attainment. Furthermore, when an Arhat abides in a mindless meditative attainment, he attains death immediately, just as in the case of one who has previously entered the attainment of cessation."

Only upon entering the concentration of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) does one enter the nirvāṇa without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa). If an Arhat abides in the concentration with mind (sacittaka-samāpatti), they likewise cannot pass away.
Just as when one has not entered the concentration with mind while sitting in meditation for others to see the Path, one is immediately seized by the powerful demon Lambā;
because one has not entered the concentration with mind, one cannot pass away. Since it is permitted that the fruit-dharmas (phala-dharma) may extend through a single [moment],...

It is also appropriate that the dharma of the aggregate is the condition for the dharma. This being so, since there are both mind and mental factors within the subsequent moment, we know that within the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) of the prior moment, there must likewise be a single aggregate of mind and mental factors.

The *Śāstra* states: "Two individuals in the general realm. The commentary explains that these are the two types of Bodhisattvas: those of sudden enlightenment and those of gradual enlightenment. The *Śāstra* states:
"All ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are those of sudden enlightenment. This means that those of sudden enlightenment enter directly into the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Bodhisattva and so forth.

Such a person is called a bodhisattva who is an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*). If one of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*) first attains the fruit of a noble one in training (*śaikṣa-āryaphala*) of the two vehicles, or attains the fruit of a noble one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-āryaphala*), and later turns the mind to enter the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), they are then called a bodhisattva who is a noble one (*ārya-bodhisattva*).

The Commentary states: "Those who attain Buddhahood through the benefit of successive future retributions in the Form Realm and are born in the abode of the wisdom of Maheśvara" refers to those Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment.

"Those who receive the status of Buddha through the benefit of the present retribution" refers to Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*) who attain Buddhahood within their current physical body;
this is called the benefit of the present retribution. The benefit of the future retribution refers to [those born in] the abode of Maheśvara... [text fragment ends].
Regarding those born from the abode of Śiva’s wisdom, these are present-day bodhisattvas of the tenth stage who are born within the fourth dhyāna and act as kings therein.
This karmic activity of the king was performed previously, while still on the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi, during the position of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*).

Having entered the first bhūmi by performing these ten wholesome karmas, they do not create further karma thereafter; thus, from the stages prior to the bhūmis, they have accomplished the karma of the ten kings.

Having passed through hundreds and thousands of births up to the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), one is born into the fourth dhyāna; it is only then that one experiences the sovereign karma of the fourth dhyāna accumulated prior to reaching this stage.
As for those "born in the abode of wisdom," these are the bodhisattvas of the tenth stage who reside in the palace of Maheśvara.
Because it is the source from which all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñā*) arise; or alternatively, because it is the source from which wisdom and vision arise.

Regarding the ten royal stations: a Bodhisattva on the first stage (*bhūmi*) acts as a king of Jambudvīpa; on the second stage, he acts as a Cāturmahārājika king or a golden-wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).

Question: Why does he not act as a silver-wheel-turning monarch and so forth? Answer: Because here we are considering a progression where each successive stage is one-fold superior to the preceding one, starting from the iron-wheel-turning monarch.
He immediately transcends to become a Cakravartin King of the Golden Wheel, yet he does not become one of copper or silver. In the third bhūmi, he becomes a King of the Śakras;
although he rules over the four continents, he is merely a minister and not a sovereign king.

If a Bodhisattva is born among the Four Great Kings, since the Four Great Kings are themselves the rank of ministers, he attends upon Śakra once every day. In the fourth bhūmi, the Bodhisattva becomes a King of the Yāma Heaven.

The fifth becomes a Lord of the Assembly; the sixth, a King of Music; the seventh, a King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations; the eighth, a King of the Heaven of Meditative Concentration.

If a Great Bodhisattva is born as a King of the Caves, he becomes a Mahābrahmā King; however, Lesser Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles are never born in the Heaven of Mahābrahmā, because it is a place of biased attachment.
The ninth becomes a King of the Second Dhyāna; the tenth becomes a King of the Fourth [Dhyāna].

Question: Why does the King of the Dhyānas not become the king of the third dhyāna? Answer: Because the third dhyāna is the ultimate bliss (*sukha*). Therefore, he does not become the king of the third dhyāna.

Alternatively, there may be a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*bhūmi*) who becomes an Iron Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*), or an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) who becomes the king of the fourth dhyāna.
Although this ordinary being becomes the king of the fourth dhyāna, his meritorious qualities do not even equal those of one prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*).

This applies even to Bodhisattvas at the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*), let alone those Bodhisattvas at the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) who possess the moral conduct of an Iron Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*).
Next, one should now consider the status of the Ten Kings; however, it is not necessarily the case that one immediately attains the status of a Ten King.

There is a class of Bodhisattvas at the first stage who are of sudden awakening (*tongwu*) and whose wisdom (*jñāna*) predominates; such individuals do not become Iron Wheel-turning Kings, but are instead reborn within the Fourth Dhyāna, where they are born among the Anabhraka gods (*Anabhra-kāyika*).

The three heavens of the Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit) rely upon the most excellent support to undergo the transformation of birth-and-death (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*). This continues up to the bodhisattvas who attain sudden enlightenment;

upon reaching the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), they do not become kings of the first dhyāna, but are born directly into the three heavens of Anabhraka (Cloudless), Puṇyaprasava (Merit-Born), and Bṛhatphala within the fourth dhyāna, where they undergo the transformation of birth-and-death.
Therefore, one should know that bodhisattvas of the ten stages do not necessarily receive the status of the ten kings.

Regarding the stages: if those of the two vehicles, whether in training (śaikṣa) or beyond training (aśaikṣa), turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle, they cannot newly create the karma of the ten kings prior to reaching the [first] bhūmi.
This is because the treatise states that the various noble ones in training have eternally severed the non-common ignorance and thus do not create new karma.

The Commentary (*Shu*) states: "The eightieth [fascicle] speaks of 'transformative birth and death' (*parināmika-jarā-maraṇa*). The 'retained birth-body' (*sthita-janma-kāya*) is precisely within this continent. The Explanation (*Jie*) states:
"This means that one undergoes transformative birth and death specifically within the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa)."
The Commentary states: "If one must necessarily reach the palace of Maheśvara, it refers only to those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who are subsequent to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

If one reaches the palace of Maheśvara, this refers to a bodhisattva of the tenth stage who has attained sudden enlightenment; that is, immediately following the form realm, the eighth consciousness induces the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state.

This refers to those ordinary beings who seek the Buddha-way. [Question: Regarding those who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), they have severed a small portion of the afflictions (*kleśa*). When...

They are named "Noble Ones" (ārya). How much more so for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) who have severed both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*)? Yet they are still called "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*). Answer:

They are named according to their cause, as explained above. Question: If one attains the fruit of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) while the body remains in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*) or within the mastery of the body in the third dhyāna, and then withdraws that mind to enter the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), having already attained entry from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) onwards—[how is this possible]?
Can that person also be called a king of the Four Heavenly Kings and a king of the third dhyāna?
If you say he is included among these kings, how can it be said that a bodhisattva of the tenth stage does not become a king of the Four Heavenly Kings or a king of the third dhyāna?
If he is not included, what kind of form is he? Furthermore, in the *Rājapuruṣa-sūtra*, it is stated that bodhisattvas of the tenth stage also become kings of the Four Heavenly Kings.
And regarding the King of the Third Dhyāna: he further asked, "I do not yet know how the Four Heavenly Kings can be called 'Four Heavenly Kings' when they are merely ministers.

He also asked, "Among the Four Heavenly Kings, there are those who have attained the fruit of Arhatship; do they also attend the court and offer sacrifices to the ordinary Śakra? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 50, states:
"Regarding the death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāma-cyuti*), even down to those in this very continent... [Question: What?

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is stated that only this continent (Jambudvīpa) undergoes the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmiki-jarāmaraṇa*), while the six heavens and the two continents are not mentioned.

Reflecting upon this, one considers that in those form realms (*rūpadhātu*), there are no Buddhas to provide instruction. Question: Since there are indeed Buddhas of Other-Enjoyment (*parasaṃbhoga*) within the form realm, how can it be said that there are no Buddhas?
Regarding the palace of Maheśvara: Question, how is it that beneath the Akaniṣṭha heaven there is the ocean-fire?
There is a specific number. As for that Palace of Maheśvara, is there also a number below it? Furthermore, regarding this term "Maheśvara," by what is he so named?
Is he called "Maheśvara" (the Sovereign) in reference to his acceptance of the name of a Buddha, or is he called "Maheśvara" in reference to a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage?
Since those prior to the seventh stage have already accepted a body of segmented birth (*paricchinna-deha*), I do not yet know [the status of] the seventh stage.
Previously, within the *parabhogakṣetra* (land of enjoyment for others), were there parents or women? If there were, how could it be called a "pure land"?
In a pure land, there are no women. Furthermore, regarding bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) within a defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭakṣetra*):

Regarding those who receive a womb from their parents, how can it be that the subsequent text states that Bodhisattvas of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) are constantly born within the great assemblies of all Buddhas?
It cannot be said that a Bodhisattva receives a fetal body within a defiled land and yet is simultaneously constantly born within the great assemblies of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, if one says that there are no women in the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* (other-enjoyment) lands, how then can it be explained?
"Amitābha Buddha" refers to the names of his parents. Question: Since the Great Brahmā King and those of the Two Vehicles are not reborn there, why does the sutra not exclude the Great Brahmā King?

Answer: It excludes only the Five Pure Abodes. As for the passage below, the commentary explains that the sutra does not mention them because they have not yet resolved their minds toward Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*). This is the interpretation found in the treatise.

The Commentary states: Regarding those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], they do not go to birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth, up to the point where they do not go to be born there.

If a person who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) turns their mind while still subject to the maximum of seven rebirths (*saptakṛtvobhava-parama*), they possess fixed karma (*niyata-karma*) for seven births.

Upon turning their mind until the seventh birth is exhausted, they undergo the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) within the desire realm. As for those such as the "one who goes from family to family" (*kulaṃkula*), they likewise undergo fixed karma according to their specific mode of rebirth.
Once these are exhausted, one immediately receives a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) within the desire realm.

If one who has attained the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) has received the fixed karma for coming and going between the human and heavenly realms, they then receive the cycle of transformation birth-and-death (*pariṇāmika-jarāmaraṇa*) within the desire realm.

This continues until the birth-and-death of the desire realm is exhausted for one who has attained the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), at which point they receive a transformation body within that very body of the desire realm. Within the first [dhyāna] of the desire realm...
The tenth stage: one immediately proceeds to the palace of Maheśvara in the Akaniṣṭha heaven and attains Buddhahood. Those in training (śaikṣa) must do so within the desire realm;
they certainly do not generate the mind for transformation and receive a change-of-constituent body (*pariṇāmikakāya*) while born in the form realm.

If, like an Arhat, one wishes to prolong one’s life, it is necessary to attain the "limiting concentration" (prāntakoṭika-samādhi) of the fourth dhyāna before one can achieve the practice of extending life.

If one undergoes the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), or if one is a Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) or Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), even though they have not yet attained the fundamental dhyānas, they can still undergo the cycle of birth and death as a transformation body upon attaining the initial "not-yet-arrived" concentration (anāgamya). If they attain the fundamental dhyānas, they are likewise able to undergo such a transformation.
It is easy to undergo birth and death.

The *Śāstra* states: "While other ordinary beings [may attain] bodies in the formless realm and eventually receive a superior transformation body (*pariṇāmikakāya*), a Bodhisattva whose compassion has increased prior to the seventh stage is born in the desire realm and receives a body of segmented existence (*prādeśikakāya*). Upon reaching the eighth stage..."
One will certainly be born among the three heavens of the fourth dhyāna—the Cloudless (Anabhraka), the Merit-born (Puṇyaprasava), and the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala).
Within these three heavens, one assumes one of these bodies and, having taken birth in a superior body, only then receives the extraordinary transformation body (nirmāṇakāya).

Alternatively, for a Bodhisattva of the first stage whose wisdom is predominant, they are born immediately in the lower three heavens of the fourth dhyāna—namely, the Cloudless and so forth—and only after obtaining a superior body [do they proceed].

They receive a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). However, it is now also taught that a Bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment reaches the eighth stage and is born among the three lower heavens of the fourth dhyāna in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) to receive a transformation body; this is stated with reference to those who are certain.
All Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment who reach the eighth stage are certain to be born within the fourth dhyāna. Alternatively, there may be those at the first stage whose wisdom is predominant.
The *bhūmi* also gives rise to the fourth dhyāna, whereby one receives a transformation body (*pariṇāmikakāya*). As explained in the eighth fascicle of the treatise:
Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery receive transformation bodies based on their certainty; however, among them, there are also those at the first fruit and so forth.
Those in training (*śaikṣa*) belonging to the first three fruits also receive transformation bodies, because within the state of being in training, there is no fixed certainty.

Regarding meditative concentration: among those in training (*śaikṣa*), there are some who do not turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] and thus do not receive the transformation body (*pariṇāmika-kāya*).

It is said that only those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) obtain the transformation body; this case is likewise so. Furthermore, it is stated that the Bodhisattva of Sudden Enlightenment is born into the fourth dhyāna at the eighth stage.
According to the *Niyata-nirdeśa*, among them there are those for whom wisdom increases in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), and who are born into the fourth dhyāna even in that first stage.
If compassion increases, however, one is not born into the fourth dhyāna in the first stage.

Alternatively, there may be those who, from the first stage, are born into the three heavens—Anabhraka and so forth—within the fourth dhyāna, where they receive a body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*). Or there may be those who are born into the fourth dhyāna from the second stage downward.

The Three Heavens of No Cloud (*Anabhraka*). Bodhisattvas of the third stage, as well as those from the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh stages who have been reborn within the Four Dhyānas in the Three Heavens of No Cloud and receive the body of transformation (*pariṇāmikakāya*), are all called Bodhisattvas of Increasing Wisdom (*jñānavardhana*).

If those of the eighth stage are reborn in the Four Dhyānas in the Three Heavens of No Cloud and so forth and receive the body of transformation, they are called [Bodhisattvas of] Increasing Compassion (*karuṇāvardhana*).
Regarding the increase of Bodhisattvas: these Bodhisattvas, having received a *pariṇāmika-kāya* (transformation body), no longer undergo actual rebirth in other places.
The commentary states that some claim the Palace of Maheśvara exists within the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, while others say it arises from the very beginning.
This Palace of Maheśvara is located above the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens; thus, the *Ṣaṇmukhadhāraṇī-sūtra* says: "The Bhagavān..."
Brahmā resides in the Heaven of Pure Abodes, dwelling supported by space. This pure land is adorned with the seven kinds of exquisite jewels;

it is called the Land of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakṣetra*). Within this Land of Enjoyment for Others at the tenth stage, one attains the Body of Equal Enlightenment and becomes the Buddha of Self-Enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
If a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage does not perceive the self-enjoyment lands of the Buddhas, [he cannot attain this].
Only the Buddhas are able to know this. Regarding this palace of Maheśvara: if one discusses its bondage, it is a phenomenon that is unbound;
if one discusses its location, there is a distinct place above the Akaniṣṭha Heaven;
if one discusses its inclusion, this palace of Maheśvara is included within the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; if one discusses its stage...
The body of a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) is precisely the body within the three heavens beginning with Anabhraka.

If the tenth-stage Bodhisattva has not yet attained Buddhahood, they proceed to receive a land of enjoyment for others; if they have already attained Buddhahood, their sense faculties pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "This refers exclusively to the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* realm, where the *vipākakāya* (retribution body) of the *daśabhūmi* bodhisattvas proceeds there.

However, because their *vipāka* (maturation) belongs to the same stage, this Palace of Maheśvara is precisely the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* realm. It is the *vipākakāya* of the seventh-stage bodhisattva who proceeds to the Palace of Maheśvara;
it is not that they are born there. This refers to the tenth-stage bodhisattva [proceeding] to the Buddha’s *paranirmita-vaśavartin*..."
Within the land of enjoyment (*saṃbhogakāya*), one becomes the Buddha of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*). This is born from the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*).

It is the body of the three heavens—Cloudless (*Anabhraka*) and so forth—within the fourth dhyāna. Subsequently, one proceeds to the palace of Maheśvara. Although there are distinctions among these heavens, they are all bodies of the same single level within the fourth dhyāna.
As for the term "retribution" (*vipāka*), it is a name for the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*); it does not refer to the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Among these three bodies, this is the *saṃbhogakāya*.

The commentary states: "According to reality, those who undergo transformation (*pariṇāmikī-kāya*) and reside in the lower three heavens but have not yet attained birth in the Pure Land—such as those of the eighth stage and above who are of sudden enlightenment—undergo transformation within the four dhyānas, specifically in the lower three heavens such as Anabhraka."
It is easy [to understand]. One does not attain birth in the palace of Maheśvara until the tenth stage (daśabhūmi) is fulfilled; only then does one attain birth in the palace of Maheśvara.
Because one proceeds toward that state in this life, it is called "birth."

The Commentary states: "Those who attain birth therein by means of the ultimate cultivation of the tenth stage" refers to those who, as non-returners (*anāgāmin*), must cultivate the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) through a mixture of the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) in order to be born in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). Now, the Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage do not perform this mixed cultivation of the meditative absorptions;
rather, they achieve it through the ultimate cultivation of the power of their vows, the power of concentration (*samādhi*), and the power of wisdom (*jñāna*).
They proceed to the palace of Maheśvara; however, the five Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa) do not arise anywhere upon the earth.

Because the Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage are perfected, they are called "thoroughly cultivated" (atyabhyasta); whereas the Bodhisattvas of the preceding nine stages are merely called "cultivated" (abhyasta).
This is not called "ultimate.
The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "When attaining Buddhahood, one must necessarily proceed to the Palace of Mastery (*Īśvarabhavana*) to achieve enlightenment in that supreme location.

However, for a Bodhisattva of gradual enlightenment, while still in a body within the Desire Realm, they proceed directly to the fourth dhyāna of the Form Realm upon reaching the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
[He] attains Buddhahood in the Palace of Sovereignty (*vaśavartin-vimāna*).
The *Śāstra* states: "Later, he goes to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), which refers to the various Pure Lands.

Regarding these various Pure Lands, Bodhisattvas from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward are born within the Pure Lands of Other-Enjoyment (*para-sambhogakāya*), specifically the ten [stages] where Ten-Ground (*daśabhūmi*) Bodhisattvas dwell.

Regarding the second-order *paranirmita-vaśavartin* lands: now, those of the two vehicles—both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] and have already received a *nirmāṇa-citta-vaśitā* body, will at a later time enter the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
Having done so, they immediately exercise supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and travel to the second-order *paranirmita-vaśavartin* land of the first stage to make offerings to the Buddhas.
Once the first stage is perfected, they again exercise supernatural powers and travel to the second-order *paranirmita-vaśavartin* land of the second stage.
This applies to the earth realm, and so on up to the tenth level of the *parabhogakṣetra* (land of enjoyment for others).
For a bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment, the true body is born within the lotus of the *parabhogakṣetra* by transformation. Within that *parabhogakṣetra*, there are no women;
thus, there is no birth from a womb.
The Commentary states: Some say that the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* permits the existence of multiple transformation births (*pariṇāmika-janman*).

This refers to the explanation of the ancient masters and others, who maintain that after a transformation death has occurred, one again receives a transformation body; and after that transformation body has died, one again receives another transformation body.
In this way, there are indeed multiple transformation bodies.
The Commentary states: "It is granted that the Buddha goes to where Bodhisattvas are born. However, there are generally three types of transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*).
First, those who manifest as various bodies, such as the *rūpakāya*, in order to go to other realms of existence and act as Buddhas. Second, the six-foot transformation Buddha;

this refers to the single six-foot Buddha who acts as a Buddha within one four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*). This small transformation Buddha transforms those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and...

Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth, as well as Bodhisattvas in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) prior to the *Vaibhāṣika* [level], and Bodhisattvas who have transformed themselves to enter the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), are all minor transformation-Buddhas of a single four-continent world-system (*cāturdvīpaka*).

If there are many sentient beings whose faculties have matured, then a minor transformation-Buddha of a single four-continent world-system emits light from an inferior ground and proclaims: "I am the All-Knowing Deva."

Above the heavens, I alone am honored. If, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there should be one or two individuals whose faculties have matured, or if at times there is a Buddha or a Bodhisattva who conceals their form and secretly guides them—transforming them as if they were the Buddha—then after my parinirvāṇa, there may be Arhats of indeterminate nature who wish to enter the nirvāṇa without remainder; or at times there may be a Buddha.
At times, there was a bodhisattva who manifested as an old monk; at other times, he lived together with a manifested elder.
On one occasion, a visiting monk asked that arhat, "What practice does a person cultivate to realize what fruit?
The arhat replied, "I have now attained the fruit of arhatship and my afflictions are exhausted. Being aged and infirm, I now wish to enter the nirvana without remainder."
That manifested monk replied: "Regarding this nirvana without remainder, I have entered this nirvana without remainder hundreds of thousands of times since beginningless time;
yet afterwards, my mind-consciousness arises once more. As for 'a person,' they enter [this state] at a later time."

The mental consciousness will certainly arise again; it is merely that those who would delay and hinder the extensive cultivation of the Path should turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle and cultivate unsurpassed Bodhi.
At that time, when this Arhat hears this, he shall not enter Nirvana but will turn his mind toward the Great Vehicle.
As for the form [of the Buddha], if the faculties of sentient beings are mature, the Buddha will surely come to transform them. Thirdly, the Buddha of Great Transformation is precisely...

In each trichiliocosm, there is only one Great Transformation Buddha (*mahā-nirmāṇa-buddha*). This Great Transformation Buddha teaches only those Bodhisattvas at the stages of *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and *laukikāgra-dharma* within the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) prior to the grounds. These Bodhisattvas are able to see this Great Transformation Buddha of the trichiliocosm.
Even when they are about to enter the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they likewise see this Great Transformation Buddha, who leads them from here into the Path of Seeing.

When one subsequently emerges from meditative absorption and beholds the manifestation of the Path, what is seen is not the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Buddha; rather, it is the enjoyment-body for others (parasaṃbhogakāya).
This enjoyment-body for others appears to bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi) and teaches exclusively that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations.
Although these Bodhisattvas on the stages also see [the Buddha] preaching the Dharma for the two vehicles and the ten transformation Buddhas prior to the stages, they do not receive this Dharma.
This is because they already know that this Dharma is intended solely for the faculties of Bodhisattvas prior to the stages, and thus does not accord with the faculties of Bodhisattvas on the stages.
As explained in the text, although they are seated beneath him hearing the preaching of the Dharma, they do not receive it.

...and so on, up to a Bodhisattva of the second stage. Even if they see the Buddha manifesting as a Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) to preach the Dharma for a Bodhisattva of the first stage, it is not commensurate with them, nor do the faculties of the Bodhisattva of the second stage receive it.
However, if they see the Buddha preaching the Dharma as a Body of Enjoyment for those of the second stage, they then receive it, because it is commensurate with their faculties. And so forth...
If a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage sees the Buddha’s Body of Enjoyment for Others (parasaṃbhogakāya) preaching the Dharma for a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage, they receive it;
if they see [the same Buddha] preaching the Dharma for a Bodhisattva of the ninth stage, they do not receive it.
Furthermore, once one has attained the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) of the first fruit, there may be some Arhats.

This is the body of fragmented birth (*prādeśika-kāya*). Even with the arising of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), one cannot see it. This is the body of transformation (*pariṇāmika-kāya*) belonging to those who have attained the first fruit (*phala*).
Because the body of transformation is subtle, from those who have attained the first fruit up to those who have attained the fourth fruit, all undergo transformation.

Although there are distinctions between those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they are nonetheless similar enough that they can see one another with their ordinary physical eyes (*māṃsacakṣus*), being of the same kind.

Therefore, they are able to see one another. It is not so for Bodhisattvas; if there are two Bodhisattvas of the same first stage who have both received a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), even though they possess only the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*), they are still able to see one another.

However, a Bodhisattva with a transformation body of the first stage cannot see a Bodhisattva with a transformation body of the second stage, because the Bodhisattva of the second stage is superior. If...
A Bodhisattva of the second stage manifests a body through supernormal powers (abhijñā) so that this Bodhisattva of the first stage may see it.

A Bodhisattva of the first stage is likewise able to see the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) of a Bodhisattva of the second stage, and so on, up to a Bodhisattva who has entered the mind but does not yet know how to abide in the mind.
A Bodhisattva who abides in the mind cannot see a Bodhisattva whose mind is perfected in the stages; this refers to the transformations within the ten stages.
Regarding the Bodhisattva-body: because after that which cannot be seen, one attains the vision of what precedes it in subsequent stages;

furthermore, once the first fruit has undergone transformation (pariṇāmanā), there are no longer wives or children. Moreover, among those in the first stage (bhūmi), some receive a transformed body, while others receive a body of segmented birth (prādeśika-śarīra);
some are those of sudden enlightenment, while others are those of the stage of training (śaikṣa) who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]. Or there are...

Regarding those who have turned their minds from the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*): these various classes of bodhisattvas who together enter the first bhūmi likewise see a hundred buddha-worlds and are able to transform a hundred types of sentient beings.

Although there are differences between the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma-vibheda* (transformative) [bodies], all their remaining merits, wisdom, and so forth are entirely similar, and they are likewise established in their manifestations. However, they cannot be equated with the Enjoyment Buddha (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) and others.

This Bodhisattva of the first stage who has received a body of transformation (*pariṇāmikakāya*) is able to see many Buddhas, whereas one with a body of fragmented birth (*bhinnabhava*) must see few Buddhas;
it is impossible for the latter to see as many. This remains true up to the Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage.
Furthermore, if one has received a body of transformation, even the divine eyes of other beings cannot perceive it. Moreover, this applies to Bodhisattvas from the first stage up to the eighth stage.

Since beginningless time, those who receive a body of segmented birth may be born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and undergo birth from a womb, in which case they have parents; or they may undergo apparitional birth (*upapāduka*).

Or they may be born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), taking birth in each respective stage (*bhūmi*), with the sole exception that they cannot be born in the five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ*) or in the palace of Maheśvara.
Even Bodhisattvas up to the seventh stage, having been born in the form realm, do not relinquish their meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and return [to lower realms].

He was born in the desire realm. Furthermore, whether in the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation) lands or the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense) lands, all the Tathāgatas manifest having parents, wives, and children;

this is solely for the sake of transforming bodhisattvas prior to the [eighth] stage, the ordinary beings of the two vehicles, and those bodhisattvas from the seventh stage downward who still undergo the body of segmented birth (*pariccheda-śarīra*).
Therefore, the Buddha manifests having parents and a wife; it is for this reason that Śākyamuni Buddha displayed them.
Manifestation: For the sake of ordinary beings who are to be converted, [the Buddha] manifests parents, wives, and children.

Furthermore, when a *paranirmita-vaśavartin* Buddha exists within a *saṃbhoga-kāya* realm to convert Bodhisattvas from the first up to the seventh bhūmi who still undergo the body of segmented birth (*bheda-deha*), that *paranirmita-vaśavartin* Buddha likewise displays the appearance of having parents, wives, and children, in order to serve as objects of conversion for those from the first up to the seventh bhūmi who still experience the desires of the desire realm.

The body of aggregates (*skandha-kāya*) likewise has parents and so forth. However, regarding the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifested by a Buddha, or the transformation bodies received by Bodhisattvas within the Pure Lands—even the name of "woman" does not exist there, nor are there parents, wives, children, and so on.

Since these things do not exist for the Bodhisattvas who have received such transformation bodies, if one were to claim that even a Buddha goes [to those lands], yet upon examining the sūtras, although form (*rūpa*) is seen...
The devas of the various realms look downward toward the Buddha in the desire realm; upon first hearing [the Dharma], they resolve their minds and attain the fruits [of the path].
Nor is there any mention in the sūtras of the Buddha traveling to the form realm to transform sentient beings of the form realm.

Nevertheless, the śrāvakas of the form realm—both those still in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa)—also turn their minds toward the Buddha-way in the desire realm and, redirecting their resolve toward the Great Vehicle, receive the body of transformation (nirmāṇakāya).
The Commentary states: "Only those in the first two fruits and the pratyekabuddhas lack the arousal of the mind for the higher realms.

This means that within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are no individuals in the first two fruits, nor do they arouse the mind for [the path] up to that of a pratyekabuddha. As for those in the first two fruits, they exist only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Among them, those who follow the *gaṇacārin* (group-dwelling) type exist only among humans—excluding the northern continent (*uttarakuru*)—and thus pertain to all three continents.
There is. If it is like a rhinoceros horn, it exists only in Jambudvīpa. If it is within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), only non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and arhats can manifest it through the body.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that it does not say "only in the desire realm" to exclude its absence in other realms, this latter master says: according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, however...
It is accepted that both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) possess the transformation body (*pariṇāmikakāya*).
The commentary states: "Is it not the case that [this] does not exist in other continents?

This means that, with the exception of Uttarakuru, all three continents are accepted as possessing the transformation body; thus, one knows that there are also Śrāvakas who turn back [from the path] within the form realm.
The mind subsequently induces the outflow-free state within the form realm. The commentary states:
"All [beings] below obtain non-analytical cessation of the form body. This means that if one is born within the form realm, one obtains non-analytical cessation regarding the body of the form realm;
if one is born within the formless realm, one obtains non-analytical cessation regarding the bodies of both the desire realm and the form realm.
All attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

The commentary states: "It is not that matter produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can be used to form a body that remains [in the world]. If one transforms and gives rise to matter that is the fruit of concentration within the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there would only be the objects of the sense-fields of form and so forth;
furthermore, there would be neither actual five sense-faculties nor actual objective fields that support those faculties. This cannot be [the case].
This is because the body is maintained through the form resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*).

Regarding the statement in the commentary that the *Antarābhava-sūtra* says the Buddha dwells in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and even the sūtras of the Mahāsāṃghika school do not accord with the Mahāyāna doctrine:

the Mahāsāṃghikas assert that in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there exist eyes, ears, and so forth, and they possess the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñānakāya*).

Furthermore, the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) also possesses the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Thus, the Buddha simultaneously knew that after his death as a deva, he would receive birth within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), where for twenty years he would transform sentient beings of the formless realm.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the claim that the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and the *Mahāvibhāṣā* say that bodhisattvas are not born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)," this refers to the fact that bodhisattvas from the first bhūmi upward are all said to be born in the formless realm.

If it were also permitted for bodhisattvas prior to the bhūmis to be born in the formless realm, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* treatise would likewise state that bodhisattvas on the bhūmis are not born in the formless realm.

The Commentary states: "One interpretation says that those born in the formless realm who are reborn in the form realm are unwilling to undergo even one more birth in the higher realms, let alone many.
This first explanation is inferior to the second; it is the interpretation of the first master mentioned previously.
The intention of that former master is to say that it is absolutely impossible for one who has already generated the bodhicitta in the desire realm to die there and be reborn in the form realm."
One receives a body subject to transformation (*pariṇāmikakāya*) within the realms. For example, suppose there is a person who, while in this present body, attains the first fruit (*prathamaphala*).

Without undergoing further rebirth, they immediately attain the third fruit. They do not undergo further births within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); having passed away from the desire realm, they are born directly into the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
A noble one (*ārya*) in the form realm certainly does not pass through a birth in the desire realm. This applies even if there are those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
A person who has attained either the first fruit or the second fruit may, within the desire realm itself, pass through one birth, two births, or even many births.
Having passed through these births in the desire realm, these individuals of the first and second fruits will not be reborn in the higher realms.
Because they have already undergone births in the desire realm, they will attain the fruit of Arhatship right there within the desire realm. Both [cases] are the same.
The *Śārasamuccaya* states: "A noble one (*ārya*) who has undergone rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) does not go to be born in another realm.

Alternatively, there may be a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) in the desire realm who, having generated the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), attains the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*) and the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), thereby knowing that their karma in the desire realm is exhausted."
Feeling weary of the coarse body, they suddenly draw forth a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Or, among those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm who have attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), although they may have generated the bodhicitta, they do not attain the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*) of the higher realms, nor do they attain the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).

Consequently, they do not know that their karma in the desire realm has been exhausted; merely feeling weary of the coarse body, they immediately and urgently draw forth a transformation body. Thus, within the desire realm—

Regarding the stage of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) within the realm: one undergoes the death and rebirth of *pariṇāmikī-jāti* (transformative birth) while still possessing a body in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

This is because it is absolutely impossible for one who has already generated the mind of enlightenment within the desire realm to subsequently be born in a higher form realm (*rūpadhātu*) before undergoing transformative birth;

therefore, the fruit of a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) differs from those of the first two fruits. This is because, in the case of those with the first two fruits, the karma of the desire realm has not yet been exhausted. Thus, although they possess the first or second fruits, [they remain in the desire realm].
They attain supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) by virtue of the power of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).

There are some who are also able to know the number of births resulting from karma in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), yet there are also those in the first and second fruits (*phala*) who cannot know the number of births resulting from karma in the desire realm.

These individuals in the first and second fruits are drawn along by the force of their own karma; some may even undergo the death-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmiki cyuti*) at the very moment they resolve upon awakening (*bodhicitta*).

There may be those who, having already generated the bodhicitta, undergo the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) only after passing through one, two, or even up to seven births within the desire realm.
These first two fruits [of the path] attain the state of undergoing the death and rebirth of transformation while still in the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of the first dhyāna;
they undergo the body of transformation in a single lifetime, let alone over many lifetimes.

The *Śāstra* states: "Regarding the second [interpretation], since there is no textual prohibition against receiving [the precepts] as in the case of those who have seven more births (*saptakṛtvah-parama*), it is not necessarily the case that the generation of the bodhicitta and the retention of the body occur simultaneously;
thus, there is no contradiction even with respect to the noble ones (*ārya*). Therefore, the second explanation is superior. This refers to the interpretation of the second master mentioned later.

The intention of this latter master is to say that since there is no scriptural passage prohibiting it, one may indeed generate the bodhicitta while still within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and subsequently take birth.

In the higher realms, one undergoes the transformation body (*pariṇāmikakāya*). This is like those who, having attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and being destined for seven more births, resolve upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) and retain their bodies to undergo transformation.

It is not necessarily simultaneous; "not necessarily simultaneous" means it is not fixed. There are cases where at the very moment one resolves upon *bodhicitta*, one undergoes the transformation body and retains the body;
thus, the resolution of the mind and the retention of the body are simultaneous. There are also cases where one resolves upon *bodhicitta*...

Once the mind has been resolved, one may receive a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) after one lifetime, or receive a transformation body after two lifetimes, or after three, four, five, six, or seven lifetimes;
the resolution to resolve the mind and the retention of the body do not necessarily occur simultaneously.

The same applies to the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*): the resolution to resolve the mind and the retention of the body are not necessarily simultaneous. Thus, there are [beings] in the desire realm...

Upon generating the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), one immediately receives a body of transformation (*nairmāṇika-kāya*) within the desire realm; this is called "generating the resolve while retaining the body to receive a body of transformation.

Because the karmic force of the body in the desire realm belonging to the stage of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) is exhausted, and because one has not yet attained the fourth dhyāna’s *prāntakoṭika-samādhi* (the meditative concentration of the ultimate limit) which could support the previous karma, one is able to retain the body.
This is done with the intent to be born in the form realm, relying upon a superior body to receive a body of transformation.

By this principle, having first generated the mind of awakening in the desire realm and taken birth in a single Brahmakāyika heaven, one receives a body and immediately thereafter receives a transformation body (*pariṇāmikakāya*).
Or, after taking two bodies in two places—the Brahmakāyika and the Brahmapurohita—heavenly realms—one then receives a transformation body.
Or, one may take birth in three heavenly realms before receiving a transformation body, and so on, up until taking birth in all [heavens] that receive [such births].
Regarding the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*): one may receive a transformation body in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna stages, or even as far as the Bṛhatphala heaven;
none of these are prohibited. Upon reaching the fulfillment of the tenth stage of a bodhisattva, one immediately proceeds to the palace of Maheśvara and attains the state of Buddhahood.
There are some who, having experienced only one birth in the fourth dhyāna, receive only one body before receiving a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

This is due to their determinate karma (*niyata-karma*). Although they have attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), they resolve their minds on bodhi and proceed toward the stages of the Mahāyāna;

yet they cannot be reborn again because they will not receive another body in the place of their birth, as they have not yet attained the "limitless concentration" (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*) that can serve as a support. This...
The meaning of the commentary (*śāstra*) states: If one attains the ultimate concentration (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*) within the fourth dhyāna, one then receives a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Since a person who has attained the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) has not yet attained the ultimate concentration, they do not rely on past karma to receive a transformation body.

However, this commentary also speaks only from a general perspective and does not exhaustively address the principle. Now, we raise an objection: there are also those in the first three fruits who rely on the first [dhyāna]...

Within the *anāgamya-samādhi* (preparatory concentration), one attains the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). How then can it be said that those who have attained the fruit of *anāgāmin* (non-returner) cannot enter the transformation body because they have not yet attained the *prāntakoṭika-dhyāna* (ultimate limit concentration)?
However, according to the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), six types of dharmas arise solely in dependence upon the ultimate limit concentration:

first, prolonging life; second, the *araṇā-samādhi* (concentration of non-contention); third, the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*); fourth, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*); fifth, the [analytical knowledge of] meaning...

The analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). The sixth is the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*). However, there are two kinds of limits: first, the limit of the stage (*bhūmi-paryanta*), which refers to the fourth dhyāna;
second, the limit of the fruit (*phala-paryanta*), which refers to the highest of the high grades (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) of the fourth [dhyāna] concentration.

The commentary does not fully explain this; it should rather state that one who has attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*) and generates the aspiration for the Mahāyāna within the desire realm is immediately reborn in the form realm.
In the middle [section], it is stated that one relies upon a superior body to receive the *pariṇāmi-kāya* (transformation body).

The Commentary (*Shu*) says: "As the discussion arises from the discussion: Is it the case that above the Śuddhāvāsa heavens there is a *vipākaphala-bhūmi* (retribution-realm) where those of the tenth stage dwell, serving as a location within the triple world, or is it not so? Herein, the same principle applies: above the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens, there is a *vipākaphala-bhūmi*."
The Earth. Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage dwell here. Is this Palace of Maheśvara included within the realms of the three worlds (*tridhātu*), or is it not?
The *Fodi lun* (Buddhabhūmi-śāstra) states that this is the "other-enjoyment" (*parasaṃbhoga*) [body], and that it is subsumed under the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. This...
The Enjoyment Body Buddha dwells in the Enjoyment Land and preaches the Dharma for Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage.
If discussed in terms of its location, this Enjoyment Land is subsumed within the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. If discussed in terms of its bondage, this Enjoyment Land is unconditioned (unbound).
Even when it comes to ascending the great jewel-flower king throne, the duration of time is exceedingly long—ten thousand [eons].
When the majestic deportment and other qualities of a thousand Buddhas of a kalpa are complete, ten kinds of signs appear. First, the sign of the Great Jewel Flower King Throne appears.
This continues until the tenth stage, when the Bodhisattva has ascended the Great Jewel Flower King Throne;

immediately, the Transformation-Bodies of the Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage throughout all worlds, as well as the Enjoyment-Bodies of all Buddhas, gather together like clouds and rub the Bodhisattva.
The crown [of the head] vibrates seven times, and so forth. At that moment, the Bodhisattva enters the Vajropama-samādhi (diamond-like concentration).

Within a single kṣaṇa, he suddenly severs all seeds of the two obstacles of the three realms until they are exhausted. By the second thought-moment, having attained Buddhahood, he pervades the Dharma-realm, as described in detail in the "Ten Stages" chapter (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
These bodies of the Buddhas are subsumed within the ten locations and ten realms, and they also possess the five sense faculties.
Regarding the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*): because they are unobstructed, they resemble the "non-resistant form" (*apratigha-rūpa*) within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

This specifically refers to the palace of Maheśvara, which exists solely in the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca-śuddhāvāsa*). However, if one discusses pure lands, such forms exist throughout the *dharmāyatana*.

Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that [the Buddha] constantly dwells on Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*), and that there are palaces of Maheśvara in all ten directions, just as there is one on the southern mountain of Rājagṛha.
A Zen master was practicing meditation within a cave when he suddenly saw a beautiful woman emerge from a small hole.
Upon seeing her, the master immediately sat down beneath the hole and called out to her. Hearing him, groups of young men, ten or fifteen at a time, came and sat inside that hole.
After a short while, the master again saw the woman emerge from the small hole, whereupon the young men spoke to her.
He said, "Could we not immediately call for each other to meet and become one? The woman called him to enter;
Confucius entered with the man, and they traveled thirty *li* together. They saw a great river and a city. The woman spoke to the man, saying:
Desiring to enter the city to bathe in the central pool, the people entered the water to wash and were not aware of what was happening.
Once they opened their eyes, they found themselves sitting within this opening in the southern part of Rājagṛha; this is the asura-opening.
Such asura-openings exist everywhere, and even small holes are designated as such locations. If one is above the palace of Maheśvara...
Each of the ten [heavens] below possesses [such a realm]. This also refers to the palaces existing above the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca-śuddhāvāsa*).

Therefore, the Sūtra states that there is a wondrous pure land transcending the triple world (*tridhātu*). As for those Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage who are destined to be born within these heavens, this is the pure land of the palace of Maheśvara.
If it is a transformation produced by the consciousness of a Buddha, or by the untainted (*anāsrava*) [consciousness] of a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage...

That which is transformed by wisdom—the palace of Maheśvara—is not subsumed within the three realms (*tridhātu*). This is because the sutra refers to that which is transformed by uncontaminated consciousness (*anāsravavijñāna*);

thus it says there is a wondrous, pure land that transcends the three realms.
