However, if the eighth contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-aṣṭamavijñāna*) of a Bodhisattva on the ten stages transforms the pure land of Maheśvara’s palace, then that transformation of Maheśvara’s palace as a pure land is indeed within the three realms.
[Included] because it is that which is transformed by outflow-tainted consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*).

The commentary states: "Whichever realm's defiled or non-defiled consciousness induces the arising of untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) in whichever stage, the 'defiled' refers to the Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment (*tadānī-bodhisattva*);
some maintain that the 'non-defiled' refers to those of the Two Vehicles who have turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna] after reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)."
There is only the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). That is to say, these two persons reside in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);

their seventh *kliṣṭa-manas* (afflicted manas), which follows the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), is likewise bound to the desire realm. When they enter the first dhyāna, the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) arises;

this is the seventh consciousness—whether defiled or non-defiled—of the desire realm that induces the wisdom of equality of the first dhyāna, and so on, up to inducing [the wisdom of equality] of the second and third dhyānas.
The same principle applies to all stages from the first dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) regarding the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).

Alternatively, when the body is in the first dhyāna, one may immediately give rise to the wisdom of equality of the second dhyāna; that is, the seventh consciousness—whether obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) or unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)—of the first dhyāna induces the wisdom of equality of the second dhyāna. The remaining cases should be understood accordingly.

The Commentary states: "To say that what is 'obscured' (nivṛta) is called 'defiled' (kliṣṭa) and what is 'unobscured' (anivṛta) is called 'non-defiled' (akliṣṭa) is based on a general understanding. Why is this?

This attachment to phenomena (dharma-grāha), when viewed from the perspective of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), is called 'unobscured' and thus 'non-defiled. However, when viewed from the perspective of the bodhisattvas, it is 'obscured' and thus called 'defiled.
What is said here regarding its ability to induce the outflow-free (anāsrava) state is all made with reference to the latter [the bodhisattva path], and does not apply to the former two."

This is explained according to the vehicle [of the teaching]. Therefore, it is known that attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is designated as "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*) only by name. One should ask: from which realm does the defiled [seventh consciousness] arise?
And what kind of untainted (*anāsrava*) seventh consciousness of which realm does it project?

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Regarding the claim that this master [Dharmapāla] asserts that there is mutual generation between the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*) and the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), this refers specifically to the explanation of Master Dharmapāla.

He maintains that the seventh consciousness possesses both the grasping at a person and the grasping at phenomena. When it is now said that within the seventh consciousness there is defiled attachment to the grasping at a person while the grasping at phenomena is non-defiled, this is stated from the perspective of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). It is also like the case where the seventh consciousness first exists..."

Regarding the human realm: later, when one enters the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-darśana*) and so forth, the seventh consciousness is then non-obscured (*anivṛta*). This means that the non-obscured induces the obscured.

Furthermore, for one who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) while still in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and has not yet entered the contemplation of the emptiness of persons, that seventh consciousness is an obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) state belonging to the desire realm.
However, upon entering the contemplation of the emptiness of persons, it becomes the obscured [state] of the desire realm.

The seventh consciousness gives rise to the non-obscured seventh consciousness within the desire realm, and so on, up to the stage of the "family-to-family" practitioner who has attained the fruit of once-returning;

all cases should be understood accordingly. Furthermore, as with the fruit of non-returning, when one’s body is in the first dhyāna stage of the form realm and enters the contemplation of the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

Furthermore, at the time following the realization of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-darśana*), and during the state of the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the obscured (*nivṛta*) seventh consciousness of the first dhyāna induces the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) seventh consciousness of the first dhyāna.
Subsequently, upon emerging from that contemplation, the unobscured-neutral seventh consciousness of the first dhyāna induces the obscured seventh consciousness of the first dhyāna.
This continues until the body first attains [the state of] the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

At the time of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is precisely the seventh consciousness—which possesses ideation (*saṃjñin*) and is obscured (*nivṛta*)—that induces the non-ideational (*asaṃjñin*) and unobscured (*anivṛta*) seventh consciousness.
Regarding which stage’s untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousness is induced by the defiled or undefiled consciousness:

[this concerns] the sixth consciousness of the Bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment (*tadānīṃ-bodhisattva*). Previously, he enters the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-darśana*), because he relies upon the seventh consciousness, which is defiled by the notion of self (*ātman*).

Regarding the grasping of the seventh consciousness, there remains only the non-defiled attachment to phenomena (*dharmanirmāṇa*). Immediately thereafter, one gives rise to the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) within the sixth consciousness.

When the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is induced to arise, it may also be termed "the non-defiled attachment to phenomena of the seventh consciousness inducing the outflow-free state" (*anāsrava*).
The answer is as explained previously.

The Commentary states: "That is to say, the seventh [consciousness] of the two lower realms, which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), is bound to the same level (*bhūmi-bandhana*) as the eighth consciousness.
Bodhisattvas from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward are never born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); they are born only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)."
If the seventh consciousness is with outflows (sāsrava), it is necessarily bound to the same level (bhūmi) as the eighth consciousness.

This is also like a bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment, or a bodhisattva of gradual enlightenment who has attained the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), whose body resides in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).

When their sixth consciousness enters the first dhyāna as the wondrous observational wisdom (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna), this is precisely the obscured-without-outflows (nivṛtāvyākṛta) seventh consciousness of the desire realm that induces the untainted (anāsrava) equanimity of the first dhyāna.

Regarding the seventh consciousness, up until the sixth consciousness arises as the wondrous observational wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) in the stage of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-bhūmi*), this constitutes the defiled, afflicted, and obscured seventh consciousness of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). It induces the equality wisdom (*samatā-jñāna*) of the stage of non-perception.

This ability to induce the equality wisdom from the defiled seventh consciousness refers exclusively to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) equality wisdom induced by that which is bound to the desire realm; it extends throughout both the form and formless realms.

Regarding the realm: when the body of a bodhisattva is in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the sixth consciousness gives rise to the wondrous observational wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) of the form realm;

this is precisely the seventh consciousness of the form realm, which is obscured and defiled (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). This [seventh consciousness] is able to give rise to the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) of the form realm. Subsequently, upon emerging from meditative observation:

This is the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), which induces the production of the obscured seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manas*) of the form realm, up to the sixth consciousness arising as the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) in the stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*). This is precisely the obscured and defiled seventh consciousness of the form realm.
It induces the wisdom of equality of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (asaṃjñisattva-bhūmi).

When subsequently emerging from meditative observation, it is precisely this wisdom of equality of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception that induces the seventh consciousness of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), which is obscured and defiled.
The obscured seventh consciousness of the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu) cannot induce the outflow-free (anāsrava) state, because Bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi) are not born in that Formless Realm.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The statement 'also the defiled seventh consciousness' refers to its general characteristics; it should rather be stated as 'only the defiled seventh consciousness.

This is because, from the perspective of a Bodhisattva, both the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) and the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) are obscured and defiled (*nivṛta-akliṣṭa*). However, if the grasping at phenomena were discussed from the perspective of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it would be termed non-obscured and non-defiled (*anivṛta-akliṣṭa*).
Here, however, both are discussed from the perspective of the Bodhisattva."

The Commentary states: "Because Bodhisattvas extinguish and depart from birth in the formless realm" means that because Bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi) extinguish birth in the formless realm, they depart from it.
The Commentary further states: "The untainted Wisdom of Equality (samatājñāna) cited here also extends, as appropriate, to the formless realm and beyond."

It cannot be said that the seventh [consciousness] belongs to the lower stages (*adhobhūmi*). To explain: the seventh consciousness that induces the obscured and defiled (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) state is bound to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*);
however, the Great Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) that it induces pertains to both the Form and Formless Realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Furthermore, during the stage of a Bodhisattva through the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), this seventh consciousness follows the sixth consciousness, as is the case for Bodhisattvas from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) upward.

While abiding in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the sixth consciousness gives rise to the dharma-contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the first dhyāna, and its seventh consciousness gives rise to the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).
This [seventh consciousness] then accords with the dharmas of the same stage as the first dhyāna of the sixth consciousness.

When the sixth consciousness gives rise to the dharma-contemplation of emptiness of the second dhyāna, its seventh consciousness gives rise to the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), which then accords with the sixth consciousness.

In the second dhyāna, the dharmas of the same stage [arise], continuing up until the sixth consciousness arises in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) or the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

At that time, the seventh consciousness gives rise to the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), which follows the sixth consciousness in being of the same stage as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

If it is the state of Buddhahood, the wisdom of equality of the seventh consciousness follows only the eighth consciousness as its same stage; thus, the seventh consciousness does not [follow the sixth].
The sixth consciousness conforms to its own level (*bhūmi*). This is precisely what was explained in the three interpretations within the preceding commentary.
Some say that the Tathāgata relies solely upon the fourth *dhyāna*, as explained in detail previously.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the fact that the contaminated (*sāsrava*) states of the three realms and nine stages can each serve as conditions for the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and so forth, there are four categories:

first, the three realms in relation to one another as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*); second, the nine stages, whether superior or inferior, in relation to one another as equal-and-immediate conditions;
third, the contaminated and the uncontaminated as equal-and-immediate conditions; fourth, the wholesome and the unwholesome..."

The nature [of the mind] serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Regarding the statement "good and evil," this refers to the three natures within the first realm (the desire realm) in relation to one another acting as equal-and-immediate conditions;
it does not refer to the upper realms, because there are no unwholesome dharmas in the minds of those in the upper realms. The commentary explains:

if one dies in the desire realm and is reborn again in the desire realm, one obtains death in all three natures, which induces and gives rise to the obscured-unwholesome state of the desire realm and the craving that moistens rebirth.

Furthermore, it is as when one dies in the first dhyāna and is reborn in the first dhyāna: at the moment of death, the mind—whether it be obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), unobscured-unwholesome (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), or wholesome (*kuśala*)—induces the birth-attaining consciousness (*upapattipratilambhika*) of the first dhyāna, which is obscured and moistened by craving. This applies likewise up to the point of dying in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and being reborn in the Peak of Existence.
If one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the form or formless realms, one cannot [die] with an unwholesome mind or... with an obscured mind.

Regarding the obscured mind (*nivṛta-citta*): since one must first become detached from the defilements of the lower realms before being able to be born in the higher realms, if one has not yet become detached from the defilements of the lower realms, one cannot be born in the higher realms.
One can only die with a non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) or obscured-unspecified mind.

It is the obscured [mind] that possesses the moisture of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), which is capable of projecting and producing the self-body (*ātma-bhāva*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and causing it to arise in continuity. However, this is not of a single level (*ekabhūmika*), and so forth...

Regarding the mutual relationship between the nine stages (*bhūmi*): if one dies in a lower stage and is reborn in a higher stage, at the moment of death, only an obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) or wholesome (*kuśala*) mind can arise;
this induces the craving that moistens birth in the higher stage through an obscured mind.
If one dies in a higher stage and is reborn in a lower stage, the mind at the end of life may be obscured, unobscured, or wholesome; this induces birth in the lower stage.
Being covered and moistened gives rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all three natures—wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth—are fully present.

In the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), there is only the wholesome nature, as well as the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*) and unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*) natures. Furthermore, according to the Mahāyāna school, as stated in the treatise:

when one dies in a lower realm and is to be reborn in a higher realm, at the moment of death in that lower realm, craving for the higher realm arises. The same applies when descending from a higher realm to a lower one.
That is so. According to the Hīnayāna school, when one passes away from a higher realm to be reborn in a lower realm, the mind at the moment of death cannot give rise to craving for the lower realm;
it is only upon reaching the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that craving for the lower realm can arise. The same applies when being born from a lower realm into a higher one.

Furthermore, when being born from a lower realm into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), although there is no intermediate state, it is only upon reaching the moment of birth in the formless realm that the initial mind of that realm first arises.

Craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu-tṛṣṇā*). Question: Since it has already been stated that the three realms encompass the nine stages (*navabhūmi*), and that the nine stages likewise encompass the three realms, why are the "three realms" and "nine stages" mentioned again?
Answer: The distinction between their breadth and narrowness can be understood according to reason.
The Commentary states: "As for the ability to induce the sixth consciousness, the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) exists only in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

This means that if one refers to the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) of those in the three vehicles, these include both the wisdom arising from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as well as the wisdom arising from hearing and cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) throughout the four dhyāna stages.

However, if one refers to the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*), which consist of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), these exist only in the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna. If not...

Regarding the fruit of returning (*pratipannaka-phala*): when one first suppresses the afflictions through the six stages of the mundane path and, bypassing the first two fruits, directly attains the third fruit, this refers to the wholesome states of the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
These pertain to five stages, namely: the fundamental dhyāna concentrations and the initial threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).

Alternatively, they may pertain to six stages, including the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*). As for the wholesome states of the stage of penetration belonging to a Bodhisattva, they are [the same as] those of penetration.

The "shared roots of goodness" (sādhāraṇakuśalamūla) exist throughout the stages of Heat (uṣmagata), Summits (mūrdhan), and Patience (kṣānti) up to the lower levels; they are present within all three lower dhyānas. However, at the stage of Supreme Patience (agradharmakṣānti), they exist only in the fourth dhyāna.

As the subsequent text states: "Although during the time of preparatory application (prayoga) they extend through all the meditative concentrations (dhyāna), it is only by relying on the fourth that they reach fulfillment.
As for the "rheumy-like" (khadgaviṣāṇakalpa) four roots of goodness, these exist only in the fourth dhyāna, as they constitute a single [uninterrupted] state.

When seated, one must not rise from the lower three dhyānas of the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (stages conducive to penetration). As for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it lacks the *mokṣabhāgīya* (stages conducive to liberation) and the *nirvedhabhāgīya* stages of the Three Vehicles.
Question: After attaining the first fruit [of the path], does one still possess the *nirvedhabhāgīya* stages of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)?
Answer: No. These exist only prior to attaining the first fruit and so forth, during which they are designated as such within the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
The roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) are so called because they lead toward the true penetration of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

Within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—whether it be the stage of the first fruit or that of a Bodhisattva from the first bhūmi upward—there exists only the concentration of the peak of penetration (*mūrdhan-nirvedhabhāgīya-samādhi*).

As the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "There are four types of concentration: first, the part conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*), which refers to emerging from pure concentration and entering the second dhyāna."

This is precisely what is called "conforming to superior progress. The same applies to the second dhyāna and above. Regarding the four concentrations conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-samādhi*):

this refers to the state of having already attained the concentrations conducive to penetration at the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). However, Mahāyāna bodhisattvas also cause these four concentrations to exist; the method of practice is as before.

Furthermore, if one speaks of the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), it refers to the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*)—Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), and so forth—which are termed "application."

Regarding the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*): if one speaks of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), then all Bodhisattvas from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward possess the path of preparation, which refers to the paths of preparation, uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), and so forth.
If one speaks of the knowledge of preparation (*prayoga-jñāna*), this refers to Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage who possess the knowledge of preparation.

Question: When the three vehicles (*triyāna*) first give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*) state, they do so by using only the tainted wholesome mind (*sāsrava-kuśala-citta*) of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) as the inducer. If...
Afterwards, when the untainted [state] arises, it may temporarily be induced by tainted wholesome minds of the form realm or the formless realm;
this need not be questioned, as one should consider it in light of the preceding and following context.

The Commentary states: Regarding the first three among the five consciousnesses, the terms "upper" and "lower" refer to their own respective categories, up to the point where it cannot be said that they are "tainted" (*āsrava*) when restricted to a single realm.
If these are the three consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and body, they belong to the Desire Realm and the First Dhyāna; thus, they serve as mutual conditions across upper and lower realms.
As for the two consciousnesses of the nose and tongue, they exist only in the Desire Realm and not in the upper realms; therefore, one cannot speak of them as being "upper."

The lower realms serve as mutual conditions for one another. If the three natures—wholesome and so forth—of the two consciousnesses of smell and taste in the desire realm are also mutually [related] as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the Commentary states:
"The mention of 'wholesome and so forth' here follows what is appropriate for the respective upper and lower realms. This refers specifically to the wholesome eye-... [in the desire realm].

With consciousness as a condition, it induces the arising of the indeterminate [mind] of the first dhyāna. When the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna first arises, because it is a mind of sudden encounter (*ābhoga*), it is indeterminate.
Alternatively, the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna may induce the arising of the eye-consciousness of the desire realm; the same applies to body-consciousness.
The commentary states: "Non-common" (asādhāraṇa) is used to distinguish [the eighth consciousness] from the contaminated eighth consciousness, which is "common" (sādhāraṇa).
Regarding the eight consciousnesses as a whole, the eighth consciousness is the common support (*āśraya*), while the remaining seven consciousnesses are termed non-common supports.

If the consciousnesses are compared individually, the five physical sense organs serve as the non-common supports for the first five consciousnesses; that is, the visual consciousness relies exclusively upon the visual faculty, and so forth. As for the sixth consciousness...

It is also called the "common support" (*sādhāraṇa-āśraya*). That is, the first five consciousnesses have the sixth consciousness as their common support; the seventh consciousness is likewise a common support, in that the preceding six consciousnesses have the seventh consciousness as their common support.

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'sharing the same object' (*sabhāga-viṣaya*), this excludes the seventh consciousness. Although the six [consciousnesses] have the aforementioned sense of being supports, they do not share the same object.
If the eye and visible forms are such that the eye-faculty can perceive the forms, this constitutes a support sharing the same object.

If the sixth consciousness relies upon the seventh consciousness, the seventh consciousness is an uncommon support (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*). It also relies upon the contaminated (*sāsrava*) seventh consciousness as its faculty to produce the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) sixth..."

Regarding the six consciousnesses: the seventh consciousness relies solely upon the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, whereas the sixth consciousness universally takes all phenomena as its object;

thus, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses do not share the same objective domain. If one follows only the former master’s view—that within the seven stages one attains untainted (*anāsrava*) five-sense consciousnesses, and from the eighth stage onward one attains the death and rebirth of transformation (*nirmāṇa-cyuti*)—then this master intends to cite these examples as evidence to establish his position.

Regarding the statement that from the eighth bhūmi onward, Bodhisattvas definitely attain the wisdom of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and that once Bodhisattvas have attained the first bhūmi, they definitely attain the five untainted consciousnesses (*anāsrava-vijñāna*):
although their initial arising must necessarily occur in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), their subsequent arising also extends to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

This is the explanation of the first master. Furthermore, the text of the ninth fascicle of the treatise states that for Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment (*tad-ekābhisamaya*), when they first enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)...

Regarding the Path: when entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), it arises solely in dependence upon a body that has produced wholesome roots; that is, at the very moment of first entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Since this is the initial induction of the five untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses within the five sensory consciousnesses of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is said that although its initial arising must necessarily occur in the desire realm.

If a bodhisattva, having entered the first stage (*bhūmi*), is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and receives a body of transformation (*nairmāṇika-kāya*), they give rise to the five untainted consciousnesses (*anāsrava-vijñāna*).

Therefore, it is said that "subsequent arising also extends to the form realm. As for the claim that when a person of different lineage attains Buddhahood, the eighth consciousness of the form realm necessarily induces the untainted [consciousness] afterward—this refers to the case where a bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment attains Buddhahood after being in the form realm, thereby inducing [the untainted consciousness].
Regarding the five untainted consciousnesses (*anāsrava-vijñāna*): for Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onwards, there are no olfactory or gustatory consciousnesses.

As for the previous explanation regarding their distinction, here it is stated that for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages whose bodies belong to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are no olfactory or gustatory consciousnesses.
However, for Bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment whose bodies are in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they possess all [six consciousnesses] from the eighth stage up through the tenth stage.

Regarding the five consciousnesses: it is asked, "Does a bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment who is born in the form realm lack the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses, whereas a bodhisattva of gradual enlightenment whose body remains in the desire realm possesses all five consciousnesses?
Thus, the bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment would not equal the one of gradual enlightenment? The answer is: "Not so.

According to the teachings of the Hīnayāna, those who practice through gradual stages attain a greater amount of unconditioned analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), while those who practice by leaping over attain [less]."
A small portion. Furthermore, the Buddha also attains a small portion of the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

That is, one who attains the first fruit through successive practice (*ānupūrvika*) further gives rise to six uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and six deliverances (*vimukti-mārga*), thereby severing the first six categories of afflictions of the desire realm and attaining the second fruit. Such a person has already attained the first fruit;

within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they have attained the eight instances of analytical cessation corresponding to the eight aspects of the four truths in both ascending and descending order, as well as the severance of the six categories of afflictions of the desire realm.

The six lower [categories] are cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). For one who practices according to the successive stages, having attained the first fruit (*phala*), they further give rise to nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) to sever the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm and attain the third fruit. That person then attains the cessations through deliberation pertaining to the eight truths within the previous path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

If they attain the cessation through deliberation for the severance of the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm—nine such cessations through deliberation—and sever the afflictions of the nine stages...

One attains eighty-one instances of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). If it is claimed that one who has "leaped" from the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) attains the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*), such a person would attain only the eight instances of analytical cessation corresponding to the eight truths of the Path (*mārga-satya*), but would not attain the six instances of analytical cessation corresponding to the six grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) abandoned through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
It is impossible for such a person to attain the second fruit while having already abandoned the six [grades of afflictions] of the Desire Realm prior to the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).

One obtains six types of analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Furthermore, suppose there is a person who, in a previous life, had completely severed the nine grades of the desire realm through the Path;
at a later time, this person enters the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and immediately bypasses the first two fruits to attain the third fruit.

This person obtains only the eight analytical cessations pertaining to the eight truths of the Path of Seeing, but does not obtain the nine analytical cessations pertaining to the nine grades of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

It is impossible for one who has already attained the third fruit to subsequently give rise to the Noble Path and, by abandoning the preceding nine grades [of afflictions], attain analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, there are those who first use the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) to abandon the afflictions from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) downward;

and there are those who later enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and likewise transcend the first two fruits to attain the third fruit. Such a person, however, does not [attain the abandonment] within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The ninth is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). That person attains nine instances of analytical cessation within the first dhyāna, up to and including nine instances of analytical cessation in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

While this person is on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they must first give rise to the noble path (*āryamārga*) in order to eliminate the nine grades of afflictions and subsequently induce the second dhyāna;
the same applies to the third dhyāna and so forth. This is also like the vision of a Buddha.
Once the sixteen moments of the Path have passed, one immediately transcends the seven higher stages and proceeds directly to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Therein, one gives rise to the nine non-returning paths and nine deliverances, thereby completing thirty-four moments of mind and attaining Buddhahood.

This allows for the attainment of the eight analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) within the Path of Seeing, as well as the nine analytical cessations within the stage of the Peak of Existence; thus, a total of seventeen analytical cessations are attained. How could this not be the Buddha?
Because one attains the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), one does not equal those who practice in successive order (*anupūrva-kārī*) or those who leap over stages (*vītarāga*).

Since those of sharp faculties attain fewer analytical cessations, how could they possibly equal those of dull faculties? Therefore, it is known that [the object] is not necessarily perceived by the five consciousnesses, and that when perceived by the three [higher] consciousnesses, it is inferior.

The Commentary states: "Alternatively, at the location of the two faculties, the body-faculty hears the fragrance. This means that since the body-faculty is already present at the locations of the nose and tongue faculties, it is by means of the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) that the fragrance is perceived.
This is because the two consciousnesses associated with the nose are cognitions through contact (*saṃsṛṣṭajñāna*), and the body-consciousness is likewise a cognition through contact;
therefore, one perceives the fragrance by means of the body-consciousness.
The Commentary states: "Although this interpretation exists, because of such reasoning, it does not avoid the objections raised against the former master's explanation.

Although this latter interpretation holds that the nose and tongue consciousnesses of the desire realm depend upon the nose and tongue faculties within the form realm, we do not adopt this latter view.

Rather, we adopt the former view—that the eye, ear, and body consciousnesses function interchangeably to perceive odors—which is superior in principle. Question: If both the former and latter masters maintain that [the faculties] exist...
When the five contaminated (*sāsrava*) consciousnesses first give rise to the five uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses,

by means of which stage’s contaminated five consciousnesses do the bodhisattvas of sudden and gradual enlightenment employ them to subsequently induce the uncontaminated five consciousnesses of which stage? The answer may be understood by referring to the preceding section and the commentary below.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the nature of being wholesome or indeterminate, while most are exclusively wholesome in nature, there are some that also pertain to the indeterminate. This passage explains:

when a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage is on the verge of attaining Buddhahood, by means of which nature do the five sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) induce the arising of the untainted (*anāsrava*) five sense-consciousnesses?

Therefore, the present commentary states that [the five consciousnesses] pertain to both wholesome and indeterminate natures. Within these five consciousnesses, they are for the most part exclusively wholesome in nature, with only a small portion being indeterminate.
This does not mean that at the time of attaining Buddhahood, all five consciousnesses are entirely indeterminate; rather, they are entirely wholesome in nature.
What is here termed "wholesome nature" is comprised within that which is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), beginning from the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*).

From the sixth bhūmi onward, because the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) state continues uninterruptedly within the sixth consciousness, the five sensory consciousnesses from the eighth bhūmi onward possess only that which is produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), and lack that which is produced by hearing (*śruta-maya*) or reflection (*cintā-maya*). This is precisely because the wisdom of cultivation within the sixth consciousness induces [the corresponding states] within the five consciousnesses;
thus, either two or three of them are of a virtuous nature. Alternatively, since two of the consciousnesses are states of sudden occurrence (*tātkālika-citta*), they are...
This is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). Therefore, within the five consciousnesses, half are of a wholesome nature (*kuśala*) and half are of an indeterminate nature.

From this point onward, one then brings forth the untainted (*anāsrava*) five consciousnesses, just as Maudgalyāyana’s sixth consciousness entered the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

The ear-consciousness hears sounds of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). If a wholesome nature (*kuśaladharma*) arises within that ear-consciousness, it is produced by cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

Since the ear-consciousness hears a sound and gives rise to a sudden, impulsive mind (*ābhoga-citta*), this is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*); an indeterminate nature is not included among those produced by cultivation.
However, that which is produced by the three types of wisdom is exclusively of a wholesome nature. Now, this case is also like that: for a Bodhisattva of the ten stages... the first...

Among the six consciousnesses, those that are eternally untainted and wholesome [belong to this category]. As for the five sensory consciousnesses, if they arise as a sudden, impulsive state of mind (*ābhoga-citta*), they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

An indeterminate mind is not comprised within what is produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*). This is the case for the five consciousnesses belonging to a Bodhisattva who has already attained the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
It possesses no unwholesome nature; it has only wholesome and indeterminate natures. It frequently arises as wholesome and frequently arises as indeterminate.

The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "This combines the eight consciousnesses into twelve mental states to constitute the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). As for these twelve mental states, if..."
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are four types of mind: first, wholesome mind; second, unwholesome mind; third, obscured-neutral mind; and fourth, unobscured-neutral mind.
In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are three types of mind: first, wholesome mind; second, obscured-neutral mind; and third, unobscured-neutral mind.
Regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*) [mind], there are two types: first, the untainted mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*); second, the untainted mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), there are twelve minds in total. As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "In the desire realm, nine arise; from these, eight subsequently arise.
The defiled arises from ten, and four [arise] from it, etc. These may serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the three realms and so forth.
If one considers the distinctions within the Mahāyāna: in the Mahāyāna, the non-obscured neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) of the desire realm can induce the arising of those above.
The non-obscured, neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) of the two higher realms serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for that which is the eighth consciousness;

this applies when one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the two higher realms, and likewise when one descends from the higher realms to be born below. Furthermore, this also applies to the obscured-neutral mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) of the lower realm.
It can induce the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds of the form and formless realms and serves as their equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*;

i.e., the seventh consciousness). When one passes away from the lower desire realm and is reborn in the higher form or formless realms, these principles exist only within the Mahāyāna and not in the Hīnayāna.
In the Hīnayāna, [this applies only to] the unobscured-unspecified mind of the lower desire realm.

At the end of life, one is reborn in the higher form and formless realms. Within the desire realm, an unobscured-neutral mind takes up the hearing [of teachings] regarding the two higher realms and gives rise to a defiled mind.
According to the Hīnayāna school, the mind lacks an unobscured-neutral mind of a lower stage that could induce the arising of an unobscured-neutral mind of a higher stage.
If one dies with an obscured-neutral mind of a lower stage, one cannot be reborn in the two higher realms, because... [the text is incomplete].

Because one cannot be reborn in a higher plane by being free from the defilements of a lower realm, in the Hīnayāna there is certainly no obscured mind (*nivṛta*) of a lower realm that can induce the birth-inducing obscured mind.
Furthermore, within the Hīnayāna, it is taught only that a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*) can induce an outflow-free mind (*anāsrava-citta*);
there is absolutely no instance where an obscured or non-obscured neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) can induce an outflow-free mind. However, in the Mahāyāna, this is also permitted.
This is just as, from the first bhūmi onward, the obscured mind within the seventh consciousness gives rise to the untainted *samatājñāna* (wisdom of equality);
and likewise, at the moment of initial Buddhahood, the unobscured eighth consciousness gives rise to the untainted eighth consciousness.
In the Hīnayāna, there exists a meditative mind of the higher stages that prevents defilement;

that is, when one arises from a cultivated wholesome concentration and engages in those defiled activities, the stage constrained by that concentration gives rise to a wholesome mind of a lower stage from that defiled mind, so as to rely on the wholesome [mind] of the lower stage to guard against falling back into defilement.
Furthermore, within the desire realm itself, there exists in the Hīnayāna a mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*), which is induced from a wholesome concentration of the form realm.
One gives rise to the indeterminate mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Furthermore, from the indeterminate mind of supernormal power in the desire realm, one induces wholesome meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the higher realms. These meanings exist only in the Hīnayāna schools and not in the Mahāyāna;

therefore, according to the Hīnayāna schools, there are four types of indeterminate states in the desire realm—namely, those of deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), supernormal power, and maturation (*vipākaja*)—while there are three in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Excluding the *kṛtaka* (artificial) mind, there are three other types. In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is only the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and the mindless state (*acittaka*); there are no other three types.

Regarding the Mahāyāna, there are three types in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), excluding the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala-citta*). As for the defiled minds, they are similar in both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.
The treatise states: "The mind may be associated. The term "may" (vā) signifies that the three natures are indeterminate.
This means that the mind-king (citta-rāja) is associated with mental factors (caitta) of the three natures in varying degrees; it is not fixed.

At times it associates with wholesome mental factors such as faith (*śraddhā*) while taking an object; at times it associates with unwholesome [factors] such as greed (*lobha*) while taking an object; or at times...
It is associated with obscured minds, or at times associated with unobscured minds; thus it says "or.
Regarding the phrase "therein are two masters" up to "or those who take only the real as their object," this refers to two interpretations among the masters of the Western [tradition].

This specifically excludes the Sautrāntikas, who hold that the eye-consciousness takes a composite form as its object, asserting that such a substance is a conventional (provisional) phenomenon and not a real one.

Regarding "taking that which lacks intrinsic nature as its object": A question arises: Is the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) permitted in this Mahāyāna system to take provisional phenomena such as length as its objects the same as the Sautrāntika position, where eye-consciousness takes as its object a provisional existence consisting of a combination [of atoms]? Consider this.

"Carrying" (*ādāya*) means that the mind bears an image resembling that object. As explained previously in the second volume, "carrying" has the sense of relying upon or leaning on, just as a sick person [relies on a staff].

Just as a person must rely on a staff to stand up, so too do the mind and mental factors arise by relying on objects; that is, the mind and mental factors depend upon the support of an object to arise.
This is also called "carrying" (or "bearing"). "Carrying" means that the mind bears an image resembling the subsequent object.

Thus, when there is a cognizing mind that possesses an image resembling the object of cognition, this is precisely the direct *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part). If this *nimitta-bhāga* is considered from the perspective of the Hinayana...

According to the explanation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the "aspect" (*ākāra*) is named the "mode of activity" (*ākāra-vṛtti*). This refers to the cognizing mind itself. The external phenomena subsumed within that mind are the "object of cognition" (*ālambana*).

If one follows the two-tiered model of the Mahāyāna: when the objective realm is designated as the "object of cognition," then the "aspect-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*) is said to be the object, and the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) is named the mode of activity.

This is the "contracted head" [position]. Alternatively, if the primary essence (*bimba*) is designated as the "object of cognition," then the aspect-part is named the mode of activity. This is the...
"Manifesting" (*chūtóu*) carries two meanings. These are the two meanings explained by the ancient masters of the West and by the Tripiṭaka masters regarding the etymology [of *tathatā*].
That is to say, when right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and so forth arise, they do so while "carrying along" the essence and characteristics of *tathatā*.

This means that right knowledge arises precisely because it takes *tathatā* as its object. Regarding "neither identical nor different," if this is explained according to the various categories [of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*], it refers to *tathatā*.

This is that which is realized (*prameya*). Since correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) is that which realizes, there is a distinction between the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Now, this is explained from the perspective of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). When correct wisdom realizes *tathatā*, it does not, within the scope of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), form conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding oneness or difference, nor does it form conceptual constructions regarding the existence of marks or the absence of marks; therefore, it is said to be "neither mark nor non-mark."

That which is characterized is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it the case that it is not non-characterized. Furthermore, one does not perceive the characteristic itself as a characteristic.

If its essence were to constitute a characteristic, then there would be mental factors (*caitta*) arising simultaneously [with the mind]. Even though there may be something upon which [the mind] relies, it is not that which is being cognized.

The meaning of this passage is that if any phenomenon possessing an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were designated as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), then at the time when the mind and its mental factors arise simultaneously—
Mental factors (*caitta*) also possess substantial reality. Furthermore, the mind-king (*cittarāja*) likewise depends upon mental factors to arise.

Thus, one might argue that mental factors should be the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the mind-king. To this, the answer is given: from the perspective of the mind-king, mental factors possess only the capacity for "discernment" (*vitarka*) and lack the capacity for "deliberation" (*vicāra*).
Since the mind-king cannot directly take mental factors as its object, it is said that mental factors are not the object-condition. [End of previous section]

Regarding the phrase "the sentence is the condition" (*pratyaya*): this refers to what the treatise states, that if there is a phenomenon which serves as a condition. Regarding the phrase "the sentence is the object-condition" (*ālambana*):
the treatise says it is the mind bearing its own aspect, or that which is associated with it, and that which is contemplated or relied upon;

this is the object-condition. Furthermore, regarding the previous phrase "condition" and this phrase "object-condition": True Suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth are precisely those previously mentioned phenomena possessing substantial existence; this is the meaning of "condition."
That which is "concerned with" (*ālambita*) and "entrusted to" (*āśrita*) refers to the latter phrase;

it carries the meaning of "object-condition" (*ālambana*). The Commentary states: "Alternatively, these associated dharmas are the fruit of the object-condition," because there exists an objective sphere (*ālambana-viṣaya*).

That is to say, the mind and mental factors that take [an object] as their condition arise; the objective sphere (*ālambana*) serves as the cause, while the mind and mental factors that take it as their condition are the effect.

The commentary states: "That which can act as a condition to produce that which illuminates the phenomena. As for "that which illuminates the phenomena," this refers to the five material sense organs (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

All such things are termed "dharmas that can illuminate. If one speaks of "dharmas that can be cognized," these refer exclusively to consciousness and so forth; the sense organs (*indriya*) cannot be so cognized.

The Sub-commentary (*Śū*) states: "Even if they serve as the basis upon which [consciousness] relies and from which it arises—such as the five material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) in relation to the five consciousnesses—they function merely as the objective support (*ālambana-āśraya*) upon which [consciousness] relies, and are not themselves the objects (*ālambana*) of the five consciousnesses."
The Commentary states: "Since masters such as Sthiramati lack the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part), how can they explain the *ālambana* (object of cognition)?

If Master Sthiramati lacks the *darśana-bhāga*, then there is no capacity for cognition (*cintana*) or reliance (*niśraya*), because the *nimitta-bhāga* (image part), such as form and so forth, is absent; consequently, there would be nothing to be cognized or relied upon.
However, this passage refers to the fundamental and reflected [aspects] as the two branches (*dvaya-aṅga*) in order to contrast with the tenets of the Hīnayāna schools. This is the Mahāyāna position.

Regarding the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and its image (*pratibimba*), each has two branches. If one understands the tenets of the Mahāyāna’s own school, it is unnecessary to speak of the essential nature and the image each having two branches;
rather, one should further inquire into how the cognizing mind takes its object.

The Commentary states: "The first is the conditioned, which is that which is internally apprehended and relied upon by consciousness; this refers to the immediate *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), which is the immediate object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). The Commentary further states:

"This is like the self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) taking the seeing part (*darśana-bhāga*) as its true object," meaning it is like the self-witnessing part taking the seeing part as its object.

The self-cognizing aspect (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) takes the self-cognizing-of-self-cognizing aspect as its object; the self-cognizing-of-self-cognizing aspect takes the self-cognizing aspect as its object;
and non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) takes suchness (tathatā) and so forth as its objects—all of these are direct objective conditions (sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya).
The Commentary states: "Although space and so forth are subsumed under the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and even if, according to their fundamental substance, they are *tathatā* (suchness)...

Regarding "space and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the immovable (*āniñjya*), and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).
These five unconditioned phenomena, when functioning as objects transformed by consciousness, are at that time transformed as objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) which are directly perceived.

Because the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by consciousness is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), these five unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are provisionally established upon the ultimate reality (*tathatā*).
When correct wisdom takes *tathatā* as its object, it is also said to take the five unconditioned phenomena as its object.

The essence of the unconditioned is precisely *tathatā*, which is itself provisionally established upon the unconditioned. This is as stated previously in the second fascicle of the treatise: "It is free from all manifest obstructions."

Therefore, it is called "empty space" (*ākāśa*). However, if this were either provisional or substantial, it would be subsumed under the category of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). This is precisely what was stated in the previous two fascicles: that empty space is a transformation of consciousness.

Since empty space as a transformation of consciousness possesses arising and ceasing, it is subsumed under the category of the conditioned. If, however, one judges its arising from the perspective of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

This unconditioned phenomenon transformed by consciousness is exclusively a "solitary image" (*kevala-chāyā*) and arises solely from the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*). As for its intrinsic nature, it is...

The three natures are determined based on the perceiving consciousness (*ālambaka*). If a master includes the "ineffable unconditioned" (*avaktavyam asaṃskṛtam*) within [the category of] cessation, then according to Śubhagupta, it is exclusively cessation;
this phenomenon is included within the "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*). If one perceives and clings to something apart from the aggregates (*skandha*), its nature is also determined by the perceiving mind;

this too is a "solitary image" (*kevala-nimitta*) arising solely from the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*), and is thus included within the "homogeneous. This applies whether it is the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of a past mind, or if one perceives form (*rūpa*).
The objective part (*nimittabhāga*) is subsumed under form (*rūpa*). If one takes the objective part of the mind as an object, it is subsumed under mind (*citta*).
The commentary states: "It does not say that the internal mind arises [from it], because this is the meaning of being an object.

This means that if the primary object (*ālambanavastu*) were to directly give rise to the seeing part (*darśanabhāga*), then the seeing part would arise only by taking [that object] as its condition. However, the primary object of the seeing part—which is the apprehending subject—is unable to directly give rise [to it].

Regarding the aspect of mutual perception (*anyonya-darśana-bhāga*): as for the statement that "one also transforms the basis (*āśraya*) of another," "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) refers to becoming similar [to it].

As for the first master’s view—that [the transformation] does not depend on the other for its arising—it is like the case where, when a person is bound, the *upādāya-rūpa* (derived matter) [of the binding agent] arises upon the body of that person;

at that same location, the *upādāya-rūpa* of all other sentient beings in other places likewise arises upon the body of that person who is undergoing the transformation. At that time, those other people each transform [their own matter] upon the body of that person who is undergoing the transformation.

Regarding the *upādāya-rūpa* (derived matter): when a person transforms the *upādāya-rūpa* of another person as its own essential nature, that transformed *upādāya-rūpa* is "appropriated" (*sopādāna*).

However, if another person transforms the *upādāya-rūpa* derived from the body of that first person, that *upādāya-rūpa* is "not appropriated" (*anupādāna*). This same principle applies when others look at one another.
It is likewise so; self and other do not serve as mutual supports or bases.
The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "That is to say, seeds and so forth mutually rely on the transformations of others, and even when viewed from the perspective of another, they constitute images.
This is the intended meaning of the second master: that one's own eighth consciousness must rely upon the seeds of the five sense organs within the bodies of others.

Taking the receptacle world and so forth as the objective basis (*ālambana-pratibimba*), one's own body then transforms into the reflected images of the five sense faculties, their seeds, and the receptacle world;
within one's own body, the five sense faculties, their seeds, and so forth, are themselves reflected images when viewed from the perspective of another.
Furthermore, the eighth consciousness of other persons likewise takes my own body—the sense organs, their seeds, and the receptacle world—as its objective basis.

Since others likewise give rise to images such as the sense organs, the body, seeds, and the receptacle world, it is said that others also serve as the objective basis (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for my own self.
The Commentary asks: "Why is it not permitted that the enjoyer takes [the object] as a condition, while that which cannot be enjoyed does not? Now...

The Master of the Treatise challenges him, saying: "Regarding your claim that seeds, vessels, and so forth are not equal as conditions and thus are not objects of cognition, it should now also apply to the eighth consciousness.
That is to say, while other lands and other sense-bases (indriya) along with their supporting dust (viṣaya) may be experienced [by others], they are not objects of one's own eighth consciousness;
likewise, if other five sense-faculties and seeds are being experienced [by others], one's own eighth consciousness does not take them as its objects. This is also the case here.
The seed is difficult to establish. Furthermore, since the five sense faculties (pañcendriya) lack the nature of being experienced [by another], how could they transform into something else?
However, in this treatise, the seed is used as an objection; likewise, the five sense faculties should also be used as an objection. One should further object as follows:

"Since another person’s five sense faculties cannot be experienced by oneself, nor can they take the five sense faculties of another as their substantial basis, they [cannot transform into one's own]."

Regarding the statement that the existence [of an object] is not fixed because one takes unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) and phenomena of the three times as objects: if one takes unconditioned phenomena of the three times and so forth as objects, there is no objective essence (bhāva).
If one takes other conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) as objects, then there is an objective essence for the aforementioned object-condition (ālambanapratyaya).

The Commentary states: "Regarding the five [sensory] numbers within the causal state, they rely solely on what is transformed by the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) as their objective basis (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

This interpretation by the Master of the Commentary is incorrect. Zhefa says: "The five numbers within the causal state also rely on what is transformed by the eighth consciousness, the mind-king, as their objective basis.
These five numbers can now rely on phenomena such as those transformed by other persons as their primary objective basis. As for the seeds of the five numbers and the five sense organs..."

This is precisely a transformation through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-vipariṇāma*), which lacks practical utility. If it were a transformation of form and so forth, it would constitute the function of material obstruction and the like;

this is a transformation through causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-vipariṇāma*). Furthermore, these five categories, such as tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*), are also capable of transforming by relying upon the forms and other phenomena transformed by another person.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the statement here that 'the text of this section, though it speaks generally of the mind and its associates, is not so':

although the treatise speaks generally of the 'mental category' (*citta-pakṣa*), this refers specifically to the eighth consciousness, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), which is able to take another as a substantial basis (*bhāva*) and then transform itself.
However, the five mental concomitants (*caitasika*), such as contact (*sparśa*) and the rest, cannot take another's substance as a basis for transformation."
The Commentary states: "Since it is neither a karmic fruit nor a karmic entity, it arises supported by matter.

The Master of the Commentary here adopts the first of the two positions presented in the preceding treatise regarding the explanation of the eighth consciousness. That first position states: "It transforms spontaneously through the power of any single cause;
since the substance of the seventh consciousness is not a karmic fruit, it arises supported by matter. If this were the case...

Regarding the nature of the fruit of karma (*karmaphala*), it does not rely upon a material substrate (*dravya*). If the Master of the Commentary (*ṭīkākāra*) were to provide this interpretation, it would not be identical to the aforementioned incorrect position.

Now, the objection is raised: [If it were so], it would also be permanent—just like the grasping and objective conditions within the eighth consciousness that allow for the notion of a self apart from the aggregates (*skandha*).

Although it is not the substance of the fruit of karma, it likewise does not rely upon or transform based on a material substrate; rather, one should say it is the co-emergent seventh consciousness that relies upon [the substrate]. Thus, it relies upon [the substrate].

Taking the true suchness (tathatā) and empty space as their objective support (ālambana). Regarding the statement that "fundamentally there is no external object, even up to the point where there might be an external object": Question:

If fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) takes true suchness and empty space as its object, it may be said that there is no external object, because it directly perceives [the reality] itself. However, if it is subsequent wisdom (prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna), [how is this so]?
Regarding the taking of suchness, space, and so forth as objects: how can there be an external substance (*bāhyārtha*) when one takes them as appearing transformations (*pariṇāmākāra*)? Question:

If it is said that one takes present phenomena as objects while there is an external substance, consider this: just as within the present moment the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) takes the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*) and so forth as its object, how could there be an external substance in such a case? Reflect upon this.
The Commentary states: "Therefore, the existence or non-existence of the fundamental substance (mūla-vastu) relied upon by all modes [of cognition] is not fixed.
Here, "all modes" does not refer to seeds (*bīja*), but rather to all categories of objects (*ālambana-jāti*).

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Alternatively, when the external substance transformed by the sixth consciousness arises, this refers precisely to the actual matter (*rūpa*) and so forth that are the fruits of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*) transformed within the sixth consciousness.
The five consciousnesses also take as their object this actual matter transformed within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Therefore, the second treatise previously stated: 'and the actual matter appearing within the sphere of mental objects. The meaning of this passage is that it refers to the stage of the ten bhūmis."

In the middle [section], it is stated that the pure sixth consciousness—the *suvicāra-jñāna* (wonderful observation wisdom)—transforms and gives rise to actual meditative fruits and so forth, which serve as the objective essence (*ālambana-svabhāva*) for the five sensory consciousnesses.
Therefore, the commentaries on the first four wisdoms state: "It is also said that the gold, silver, and other such things transformed within the ten stages possess practical utility.
Furthermore, the preceding treatise states: "However, those real forms (*rūpa*) included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are all, in terms of the *suvicāra-jñāna*..."

The results of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*) manifested within wisdom are indeed real. Furthermore, the tenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The characteristics of consciousness regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth do not necessarily all correspond.
This is because the pure lands manifested by the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of Bodhisattvas possess actual utility.

Therefore, we do not include the determinate-resultant form (*niyata-phala-rūpa*) manifested within the sixth consciousness of Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) or those of the two vehicles (*yāna*).

Although the determinate-resultant matter (*niyata-phala-rūpa*) manifested within the sixth consciousness of Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and those of the Two Vehicles exists as a semblance, its substance is not real;
therefore, it does not exist. As for the statement that "it cannot be obtained," this refers to what is taught in the tenth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

The Buddha’s five sensory consciousnesses lack fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and cannot take suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth as their objects; they possess only subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), which takes other conventional phenomena as its objects.

However, according to this text, once the stage of Buddhahood is reached in the Mahāyāna, everything becomes an object of cognition, even excluding the associated mental factors themselves, because these too serve as objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
This passage states that upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, [the Buddha's cognition] is identical to the [mental] aggregate.
The mind and its mental factors can also take one another as objects. This is just as with the twenty-two dharmas that arise simultaneously with visual consciousness;

these twenty-two dharmas serve as mutual objects for one another. The mind-king (citta-rāja) can also take feeling (vedanā) and the other factors as its object, and feeling and the others likewise take the mind-king and the rest as their objects.

The self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the mind-king (*cittarāja*) itself does not take its own nature as an object; likewise, even the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*) cannot reflexively take its own substance as an object.
The same applies to other mental factors (*caitta*). This also holds true for all minds and mental factors gathered together within the eight consciousnesses.

Regarding the mutual functioning of the sense faculties (*indriya*), there are two views: one says it is attained in the first stage (*bhūmi*), while another says it is attained in the eighth stage; both views are accepted.

Correct. Once a bodhisattva has attained the mutual functioning of the primary faculties (*mūla-indriya*), each of the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) takes all eighteen realms (*dhātu*) as its object.
Thus, the visual consciousness also takes the auditory consciousness as its object, and so on, up to taking the eighth [consciousness] as its object;

it can even give rise to the cognition of the five faculties and the six sense-objects (*viṣaya*). However, the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) that coexist with the visual consciousness cannot [do so].

Regarding self-characteristic conditions (*svalakṣaṇa-pratyaya*): the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) of visual consciousness cannot take its simultaneous mental factors (*caitta*) as an object, nor can the simultaneous mental factors take the mind-king as an object.
This applies likewise to the four consciousnesses from auditory consciousness up to tactile consciousness.

Therefore, it is said that, with the exception of the inability to take external phenomena as objects due to their association (*samprayoga*), all [factors] are indeed objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The Commentary states: "To serve as a condition for a subsequent dharma of a different nature, rather than for the preceding master-dharma, is like frost being able to damage crops and so forth.
It causes all preceding things, such as the arising of blue color, to perish; subsequently, they wither and die.

Frost, lightning, and so forth act as concordant conditions for the subsequent yellow of the withered state, but they do not act as conditions for the preceding [state] that has already perished, such as the formation of blue color."
The Dharma acts as a contrary condition (*virodha-pratyaya*) for the production of blue; externally, there is no further predominance (*adhipati*).
Even when the four conditions are explained through these distinct entities, they are merely the predominant condition, which is itself the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

For example, when the eye correctly perceives a form in the south, all other unperceived locations—east, west, north, and so on—are subsumed under the predominant condition. However, according to the Hīnayāna...
[In the] Middle [Section]. Question: Between the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), which is broader and which is narrower?

Answer: It is said that the dominant condition is broader, while the object-condition is narrower. What is the reason for this? It is as follows: take, for example, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
The faculty of faith cannot serve as a dominant condition for itself. Excluding its own essential substance, the faculty of faith serves as a dominant condition for all other phenomena.

This applies to conditions (*pratyaya*), and so it is for all other phenomena as well. Therefore, regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), with the exception of its own self-nature (*svabhāva*), it cannot act as a dominant condition for itself.

The dominant condition is broad; if the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) were narrow, it would be like performing the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths (*catur-āryasatya-vipaśyanā*), where there are twenty-one preceding minds capable of observation:
namely, the eleven universal (*sarvatraga*) and specific-object (*viṣayaviśeṣa*) mental factors, plus the eleven wholesome (*kuśala*) factors, making twenty. The [twenty-first] is... [text fragment].

O Mind-King, when these twenty-one factors reach the first moment of thought, one contemplates all that is wholesome; at that time, one takes the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) of the three realms as its object, and does not take the other three truths as objects.

If one takes any contaminated cause (*sāsrava-hetu*) as an object, one takes the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) of the three realms as its object, and likewise does not take the other truths as objects.
If one takes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as an object, one takes the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) of the three realms as its object. If one takes...

Regarding the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*): this refers to the Truth of the Path within the three realms. If taken in its broadest sense, it means that when one practices the contemplation of emptiness and non-self (*śūnyatā-anātman*), one universally takes all four truths as objects, exhausting them entirely, because all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty and without self.

However, because the twenty-one factors of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) at that very moment cannot take themselves as objects, the designation "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is considered narrow. As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)...
Except for its own single dharma, it can serve as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for all other dharmas.

When the contemplation of emptiness and selflessness reaches the second moment, it likewise takes as its object the subsequent aggregates (*skandha*), mind (*citta*), and mental factors (*caitta*) of the preceding first moment. Thus, the first moment is termed "narrow."
Question: In the Hīnayāna, how is it said that the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is broad while the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is narrow?

For instance, when one contemplates the emptiness and selflessness of the twenty-one factors within a single moment of consciousness, one takes those twenty-one factors as the object; yet those twenty-one factors are themselves empty and without self.
Answer: The explanation is as stated above. However, according to this correct principle, the object-condition does not include the others.

Regarding "conditions": as for the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), a question is raised: In the Mahāyāna, when one contemplates emptiness and non-self within a single moment of consciousness, one takes all other phenomena as well as the twenty-two factors of mind and mental concomitants as objects.
How can it then be said that they do not take [those] as objects, yet are subsumed under the dominant condition? The answer is as explained throughout the commentaries.
The Commentary states: "The 'resultant phenomena' herein refer to the faculties (*indriya*). That which is established by superior conditions is called the *adhipati-phala* (dominant fruit).
Taking its own seeds as the precursor, it serves as the basis for that which is non-material, up to the emergence of the phenomena of the three realms. Question:

Among [the four stages of] arising, abiding, establishment, and attainment, it is only within the latter, "establishment," that the second phrase establishes [the meaning], while the fourth phrase establishes the meaning of "attainment."
They are distinct. Now, in this context, what is the difference between the second and the fourth phrases?
Furthermore, when a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*) arises, what serves as its precursor, what serves as its foundation, and by what dharma’s conjunction is the material phenomenon established?

Moreover, regarding its duration, since you have already mentioned the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) and so forth, why do you not state what dharma serves as its precursor and what serves as its foundation?

The four propositions—establishment, conjunction, abiding, and so forth—are set forth. Furthermore, it is asked: what is meant by the "wind-circle" (vāyu-maṇḍala), and what is the meaning of the "water-circle" (jala-maṇḍala)?
The Commentary states: "Taking its own seeds as primary, the other dharmas—both material and immaterial—act as establishing assistants; the objects of perception serve as the conjunction."
Regarding the arising of phenomena within the three realms: just as the seed of form (*rūpa*) serves as the precursor, it is the cause;
the establishment of form and so forth is the result; and the accompanying factors constitute the conjunction, namely the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as well as odor, taste, and tangibility.

And the four characteristics such as acquisition (*prāpti*) are all auxiliary material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*). When there is first an objective referent (*ālambana*), it is termed a material phenomenon;
this gives rise to its actual manifestation (*samudācāra*). The fourth characteristic, arising (*jāti*), is identical to the second characteristic, establishment (*sthiti*).

Just as with mental phenomena, where the seeds of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) come first—acting as the cause—and the formless [states] act as the establishment—acting as the result—the term "formless" refers to...
The four aggregates of mind and mental factors constitute a combination through their mutual assistance and a common object of cognition (*ālambana*).

"Mutual assistance" refers to the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) such as volition (*cetanā*), attention (*manasikāra*), and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) including acquisition (*prāpti*), all of which act as assistants.

Regarding the "object of cognition," when the mind and mental factors arise, they necessarily have an object; it is only when there is an object that these mental phenomena can arise. Because the objective sphere serves as the cause, the mental phenomena are able to arise.
