When other material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) arise, they have no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). However, this sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) possesses the functions of arising, abiding, accomplishing, and obtaining.
In this context, regarding which sovereign condition is it? It is the non-confounded sovereign condition. What is its nature?

If, within the process of arising, seeds already exist beforehand—as it is stated below that "the seeds of the dharmas of the three realms arise," and that "seeds give rise to manifest activity"—this is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Now, it is said that "arising" (*utpāda*) is designated as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). This refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), which is also called the dominant condition; this is explained according to the inclusive sense of the dominant condition.

If the subsequent abiding (*sthiti*) and accomplishment (*niṣpatti*) attain three [factors], these are exclusively the exclusive dominant condition (*asaṃkīrṇa-adhipati-pratyaya*), as they all depend upon the previously mentioned conditions.

Therefore, although there are seeds of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) even within what is attained, at the time of attainment, one attains *nirvāṇa*; this is explained according to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the seeds: those who attain unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nirvāṇa also obtain them. This is an explanation based on the predominant (*adhipati*) sense.

Because unconditioned seeds give rise to unconditioned active manifestations (*pravṛtti*), one only then attains nirvāṇa through unconditioned manifestations; therefore, it is said that the three—attainment, abiding, and realization—are all exclusively predominant conditions without admixture.
If one speaks of "attainment" according to the latter interpretation, one also attains the twenty-seven types of noble ones (*ārya*) of enlightenment.

The uncontaminated seeds that produce uncontaminated manifest activities are also called "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*); therefore, they may also be considered "mixed sovereign conditions" (*miśra-adhipati-pratyaya*).
Among these four dharmas, if one speaks of "birth-obtained" [dharmas], it is explained in terms of mixed sovereign conditions;

if one speaks of the two dharmas of "subsistence" and "maintenance," it is explained in terms of unmixed sovereign conditions. Regarding the statement that "other dharmas take formlessness as their establishment," the explanation is as follows:
Since the remaining [phases of] arising, abiding, and ceasing all possess these four dharmas, it is clearly known that this phase of arising likewise possesses the four dharmas.

Since it was stated below that the arising of dharmas within the three realms refers to their actual manifestation (*samudācāra*), the present mention of the form and formless realms means that "formless" refers to the mental faculty (*manas*),
while "form" refers to both the physical faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and the objects of form.
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'abiding,' as in the *Abhidharmakośa* (Treatise on the Treasury of Abhidharma), Chapter Five:

'The wind-circle abides upon the water-circle, etc. This means that the wind-circle abides by depending upon space; the water-circle abides by depending upon the wind-circle; the gold-circle abides by depending upon the water-circle;
the earth-circle abides by depending upon the gold-circle; and all other things, such as grasses, trees, and the myriad phenomena, all abide by depending upon the earth."

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "That which is preceded by the understanding and appreciation of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and is established by means of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Regarding "understanding the object of knowledge": this refers to having properly understood the phenomena (*dharma*) and their meanings (*artha*) prior to establishing the argument. Regarding "appreciation": this refers to that which accords with one's own inclination;

it is precisely what the proponent of the argument desires to establish, such as the impermanence of sound (*śabda-anityatva*). The "establishment" consists of these three: the thesis, the reason, and the example.

This refers to the meaning of the ancient expositions. That is, the three members—thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—are the "means of proof" (*sādhana*), while the meaning [of what is to be proven] is the "object of proof" (*sādhya*).
Regarding the phrase "the object of proof is established," this follows the interpretation of the ancient masters that the meaning is the object of proof.
Furthermore, when this treatise speaks of "establishment" (*siddhi*), it encompasses the establishment and accomplishment found in other treatises.

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'internal and external correct mental attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) and so forth,' the phrase 'and so forth' includes practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*).
In the older sūtras, this is termed 'correct mental attention,' because one attends to the mind in accordance with reality.

In the newer sūtras and śāstras, it is termed 'right mindfulness and reflection. Here, 'right mindfulness' is equivalent to 'in accordance with reality,' and 'reflection' is equivalent to 'mental attention.'"

Although the terminology differs between the old and new [traditions], their meaning is similar. In the older sūtras and śāstras, it is termed "practicing in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmacaryā*), meaning practicing exactly according to the teachings.
In the newer sūtras and śāstras, it is termed "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*).
Regarding the term "practice in accordance with the Dharma," there are two interpretations found in other treatises. One states that "all dharmas" refers to the *nirvāṇa* to be realized...
"Following the Dharma" refers to the practice capable of realizing the Noble Path; that is, by practicing the practice, one is able to realize *nirvāṇa* through the Noble Path.
Therefore, this is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma. Second, "all dharmas" refers to all the supramundane dharmas of the Noble Path.
"Practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*) refers to the mundane wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāprajñā*) that is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).

Because one must first practice mundane dharmas in order to subsequently attain the supramundane, it is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma. Furthermore, "Dharma" refers to *nirvāṇa*, while "in accordance with the Dharma" refers to the teaching (*śāsana*).
By practicing in accordance with the teachings, one is able to realize the dharma of nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, it is explained that "dharma" refers to the untainted noble path (anāsrava-āryamārga), while "conforming to the dharma" refers to the teachings (deśanā-dharma). By practicing in accordance with these teachings, one is able to attain the untainted noble path.
This is as explained in the treatise regarding the distinctions of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga); this path of seeing is also termed "Right [View]."

The nature [of the first dhyāna] is the departure from birth (*jāti-viveka*). "Right nature" (*samyaktva*) is precisely *nirvāṇa*. Because one internally realizes and attains *nirvāṇa*, one is able to distance oneself from the unwholesome dharmas of saṃsāra, or is able to depart from birth.
All afflictions (*kleśa*) are termed "birth. That is to say, the various afflictions—whether arising as harshness or smoothness—are evil that can harm the phenomena of existence (*bhava-dharma*).
Therefore, the first dhyāna is called "joy and bliss born of departure from birth. In the desire realm... [one is not so].
All evil and unwholesome dharmas are termed "birth. The first dhyāna is able to abandon the evil and unwholesome dharmas of the desire realm;
alternatively, when the faculties have not yet matured, this is termed "birth."

The Commentary states: "That [explanation] is for the time being based on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); in reality, it also extends to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because all twenty-seven types of worthies attain it.
This means that while those great treatises and others speak of attaining *nirvāṇa* by way of the unconditioned, in actual fact, this also applies to the conditioned.

Now, one should understand that the uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) of the three vehicles serve as the primary cause; the internal factors establish [the result], while the external factors and so forth act as the conditions.
Through this conjunction, one realizes the first fruit, up to the fruits of the twenty-seven noble ones (ārya-pudgala), including the fruit of arhatship.
The commentary states that "attainment extends across all three natures" means that attainment can also extend across the unwholesome nature (*akuśala-dharma*).

For example, taking past unwholesome karmic seeds as the primary cause, with improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) acting as the establishing condition, and external factors such as evil teachers and bad associates serving as [cooperative conditions].
“Concordance. One should understand that this applies analogously to how evil karma results in the attainment of wholesome dharmas.
The commentary states: “That treatise further asks what the function (*kāritra*) of a dharma is... [it continues] until it says that it merely provides a partial summary.

The explanation says: Within the *Mahā-śāstra*, the function is generally added; thus, there are only four types of functions—namely, arising (*janana*), producing (*nirvartana*), attaining (*prāpaṇa*), and functioning (*kāritra*)—which lack the function of abiding (*sthiti*). If...

In the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, there are only four [characteristics]: arising (*jāti*), abiding (*sthiti*), decay (*jarā*), and impermanence (*anityatā*). They lack any separate functional activity (*kāritra*). The first interpretation states:

Regarding "functional activity" in the Great Treatise (*Mahāśāstra*), there is no distinct entity for functional activity; it is simply the functional utility of the four entities themselves—arising, abiding, decay, and impermanence.
The second interpretation states: Functional activity exists only in the third [characteristic], decay (*jarā*). The fourth [characteristic], impermanence (*anityatā*), is the cessation itself.

One attains the supreme unconditioned state which is devoid of functional activity (*kāritra*). This *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* exhaustively encompasses all phenomena through [the categories of] arising, abiding, establishment, attainment, and inclusion.
If the *Abhidharma* does not mention functional activity, or if the *Mahāśāstra* does not mention abiding, these two treatises may be mutually abbreviated.
What has been explained here refers to the concordant causes that produce their respective fruits. If one asks how all discordant fruits are universally applicable—
as stated in the Mahāyāna treatises where it is said that the cause concordant with the departure from defilement acts as a discordant cause for defiled phenomena,
and likewise, the concordant cause for pure phenomena is both concordant and discordant— then [it follows that] when these two types of concordant causes, the defiled and the pure, arise:
At that time, there are both those that accord and those that oppose. That which arises from the cause of neutral opposition possesses only opposition and lacks accord;
it is like frost and the like, which can only damage rice and the like, and thus act only in opposition to the rice. Answer:
That which arises from a neutral cause also possesses both accord and opposition; for example, although frost and the like act in opposition to the initial rice and so forth...
As for the cause: frost and the like serve as the concordant causes that produce later states such as withering and death.
This is because it is precisely by taking the preceding frost and so forth as causes that one subsequently brings about the withering and death of later times.
The Commentary states: "The verse says: 'Grasping objects, continuing the lineage,' and so forth, up to 'based upon these measures, the faculties are established.
'Grasping objects' refers to the five material faculties and the mental faculty (*manas*). 'Continuing the lineage' refers to the two sexual faculties.
'Sustaining life' refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). 'Experiencing the fruits of karma' refers to the five feeling-faculties (*vedanendriya*). If one is within the hells..."
One should experience the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), which is the experiencing of the fruits of unwholesome karma and the arising of the sensation of suffering.

If one is among humans or devas, the sensations of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and joy (*saumanasyendriya*) are the experiencing of the fruits of past wholesome karma. As for the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), it pervades all five faculties within the world.
These are the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*). That which is supramundane and pure refers to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Regarding their measure, the twenty-two faculties are established based on seven components.
As the treatise states, "taking the full and partial portions as their nature," this means that the male and female [faculties] are constituted by partial portions of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).

Regarding the essential nature of the two faculties (*dvindriya*), the *Śū* (Commentary) states: "It either pervades the eight consciousnesses or it does not; therefore, it is said 'according to circumstances' (*yathāyogam*). The *Jie* (Exegesis) explains:

"Now, regarding the two characters 'according to circumstances' (*suíyìng*) in the main treatise: 'it pervades the eight consciousnesses' means that the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is present within all eight consciousnesses."

Regarding sensation (*vedanā*): otherwise, if the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the wholesome faculties exist only within the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), whereas painful and pleasant sensations (*duḥkhavedanā* and *sukhavedanā*) exist in all five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), then the text of the treatise states "according to what is appropriate.

However, Master Hufashi maintains that the five sensations exist within the sixth consciousness, and he allows for the existence of painful sensation there; whereas other masters maintain that within the sixth consciousness there is only...
These are the four feelings, excluding painful feeling.

Regarding the statement in the treatise that "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (ājñāsyāmīndriya) up to its stage as the root of the necessities of life," the fact that the treatise explains three stages for the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' refers specifically to the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
The Commentary states: "Not taking the preceding stages" means not taking the preceding stages of the *sambhāra-mārga* (provisioning path) and *prayoga-mārga* (preparatory path).
The Commentary further states: "Therefore, within the *darśana-mārga* (path of seeing), as in the ninth [chapter] of the *Abhidharma*, there are sixteen moments of mind;

excluding the final moment here refers to excluding the sixteenth moment of the *mārgānvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge of the path) from the *darśana-mārga*, and taking the preceding fifteen moments, which are termed 'not-yet-known' (*anājñāta-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)."
One should know the faculties (*indriya*).
The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Question: Why is it that while the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) encompasses sixteen moments of mind, these faculties exist only during fifteen of those moments?
The intent of this question is to provide an answer based on the Path of Seeing of practitioners of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). If one were to ask regarding the Bodhisattva...
Why is it that the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is said to comprise two sets of sixteen moments of mind, and both sets of sixteen moments are called the path of seeing?

Why is it that within the first set of sixteen moments, the first fifteen moments are still termed the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), whereas upon reaching the sixteenth moment of the second set, it is only then termed the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*)?
Question: For those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), [how does this apply to] one set...
Regarding the sixteen moments of mind: why are there sixteen moments of mind in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and why are all sixteen moments collectively termed the path of seeing?
Up to the fifteenth moment, they are designated as the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*); however, the sixteenth moment is not so designated.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "As for the statement that the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is so called because it proceeds by observing the truths through vision, and thus all sixteen moments of mind constitute it—this also answers [the question regarding] the sixteen moments of mind of the path of seeing for those of the three vehicles.
Within this path of seeing, there exists the untainted noble eye of wisdom (*anāsrava-āryaprajñā-cakṣus*), which is able to see the principle of the four truths;
therefore, all sixteen moments of mind are designated as the path of seeing. 'Proceeding by truth' (*satyacara*) refers to [the progression through] suffering and so forth..."

Regarding the sixteen moments of mind beginning with "constant" (*nitya*), the commentary states: "This faculty has something yet to be known which is to be known by the faculty of 'to-be-known' (*ājñātāvy-avaijñeya-indriya*), and so on up to the body.

As for "that which is to be known," this refers to the faculty of "the unknown-to-be-known" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*); because there is something yet to be known that is to be known, only the first fifteen moments of mind are termed "unknown."
Regarding the faculty of "to-be-known" (ājñātavya-indriya): as for the sixteenth moment of mind, all noble paths (āryamārga) involve a repeated knowing.
Since, in that sixteenth moment of mind, there is nothing further unknown that remains to be known, the sixteenth moment of mind is therefore called the faculty of "already-known" (ājñātāvīndriya).
The Commentary states: "In this context, the 'subsequent patience' (*anvaya-kṣānti*) takes the preceding mind as its object;

as for the statement that 'the fifteenth mind, up to and including it, takes only these fifteen minds as its root,' this means that when one reaches the fifteenth mind—the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*)—this patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path is able to universally take all noble paths of the three vehicles as its object and explain them extensively. Although [it previously took] the three truths of suffering, origin, and cessation..."
The receptivities to the subsequent knowledge of the truths (*satyānvayajñānakṣānti*) and so forth are all explained as having a double objective support.

However, when the fifteenth mind—the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*)—universally takes all noble paths of the three vehicles as its object, that *mārgānvayajñānakṣānti* has only a single objective support;

all noble paths have a double objective support. This *mārgānvayajñānakṣānti* refers to having universally taken other remaining noble paths as its object and completed [that process]. *Mārgānvaya*...
The receptivities of the knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) cannot take their own associated factors as objects.

The receptivity of the subsequent knowledge of the path can only universally take the noble paths of the other three vehicles as its object; it cannot take itself as an object, meaning that the receptivity of the subsequent knowledge of the path cannot know itself.
Therefore, it is known that the preceding fifteen moments of mind are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind, the *mārga-anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge of the path), one again repeatedly takes as object all the noble paths of the three vehicles.

Having completed this second round of universal observation of the noble paths of the three vehicles by means of the preceding *mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti* (receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path), that sixteenth moment of mind, the *mārga-anvaya-jñāna*, once again...
The sixteenth moment of mind, the Knowledge of the Path (mārgānvaya-jñāna), doubly and universally takes as its object the preceding Patience of the Knowledge of the Path (mārgānvaya-jñānakṣānti).
Thus, it doubly takes as its object all the sixteenth moments of mind of the noble ones of the three vehicles, and doubly takes as its object all the noble paths of the three vehicles.
For this reason, the sixteenth moment of mind, the Knowledge of the Path, is called the faculty of one who has perfect knowledge (ājñātāvīndriya). Although...

The sixteenth moment of mind, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), universally takes as its object the noble paths of the other three vehicles; thus, it is an object of two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

As for that subsequent knowledge of the path taking the preceding acceptance of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) as its object, it is a single instance of double-objectification. At this time, within this context, we speak of double-objectification in terms of the Truths (*satya*), not in terms of moments (*kṣaṇa*).
Although the acceptance of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path take the path as their object in a single instance, if it were otherwise...

Because all noble paths (āryamārga) take both types of valid cognition as their objects, the sixteenth moment of mind is designated as the ninth faculty, the faculty of one who has full knowledge (ājñātāvīndriya).

Furthermore, within the true path of seeing (darśanamārga), having completed the severance of the seeds of the two obscurations, the subsequent moments of "subsequent patience" (anvaya-kṣānti) therein all take the preceding moments of mind as their objects.
As it is stated in the ninth fascicle of the treatise: there are two sets of sixteen moments of mind.

If, in the first set of sixteen moments, eight contemplate *tathatā* (suchness) and eight contemplate correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*), this constitutes taking the preceding moments of mind as the object, up to the uninterrupted path and the path of liberation within the true dharma-seeing path (*dharmadarśanamārga*), wherein one perceives the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*). This continues up to the second set of sixteen moments, wherein one contemplates the manifest realm.
The dharmas of the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering and so forth, do not appear before one in the realm [of the ultimate].

This differs from the Hīnayāna school’s position regarding the sequential observation of the truths during the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) within the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). If the Hīnayāna did not posit that afflictions are abandoned through the true path of seeing, it would consist only of these sixteen moments of the path of seeing.
As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The pure [path] does not exceed sixteen; that is to say, in the Hīnayāna, the dharma-knowledge of suffering..."

The patience of knowledge (*jñānakṣānti*) is the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) that abandons the afflictions of the desire realm; the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) is the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) that realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
That is to say, the subsequent patience of knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvayakṣānti*) is the uninterrupted path that abandons the afflictions of the two higher realms;

the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvayajñāna*) is the path of liberation that realizes the unconditioned. This should be understood by analogy for the subsequent patience of knowledge regarding the path (*mārga-anvayakṣānti*) and so forth. As the *Abhidharmakośa* verse says: "The pure path..."

The nature of the *sa* (sands) is the fruit of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Herein there are eighty-nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). By the cessation of five causes, the four fruits are established. One abandons and attains the superior path;
through the attainment of the abandonment of the aggregates (*saṃyojana*), one acquires the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) instantaneously and accords with the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).
Taking these aspects as the verse for abandonment, that text explains them, which corresponds to the meaning here. Question: In the Mahāyāna, do the sixteen moments of mind possess liberation?
The Path—does it not realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? Again, one asks: do the types of patience (*kṣānti*) not take the preceding mind as their object?
If they do not take it as an object, how can they be designated as the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*) and so forth?
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "Question: This 'Path of Vision of Characteristics' (*lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga*) occurs after the 'True Path of Vision' (*tattva-darśanamārga*).

Since within the True Path of Vision there are the 'uninterrupted' [moments] and so forth, could it be that even those in the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) possess these faculties? Answer: "This question is posed according to the Mahāyāna school; it is not based on the Hīnayāna school.
According to the Hīnayāna school, the preceding twelve moments of mind are called the 'Path of Vision,' while the sixteenth moment of mind is called the 'Path of Cultivation' (*bhāvanāmārga*)."
Regarding the Path: within the Mahāyāna, even the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) has already abandoned the afflictions through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in previous births.
Consequently, the subsequent sixteen moments of mind, such as the *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*, all constitute the "path of seeing with signs" (*sanimitta-darśanamārga*). Here, a question is raised:

since the path of seeing with signs occurs after the [first] path of seeing, and because the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) already existed within the preceding true path of seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*), it was the uninterrupted path that abandoned the afflictions.

[This concludes the section on] the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Since one has already attained the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) through that [path], why is it that during the subsequent path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the preceding fifteen moments of mind are still subsumed under the faculty of "the unknown yet to be known" (*ājñātāvya-jñendriya*)? Does this imply that even in the first fruit there exists this faculty of "the unknown yet to be known"?
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "To answer this, it is not so; as for the meaning that one attains the first root [of faith] up to the stage of the first fruit (*prathamaphala*)," he answers:

"This objection is not valid. From the first fruit up to the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), it is only when the sixteenth moment of mind—the perfection of the aspect of seeing the truths—is reached that one can establish the first fruit.
It is not within the Path of True Vision (*abhisamayamārga*), nor can it be called the first fruit during the Path of Liberation (*vimuktimārga*). Therefore, the preceding..."

The fifteen moments of mind are subsumed by the faculty of "that which is yet to be known" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*). However, one does not obtain this initial faculty upon attaining the first fruit (*prathamaphala*).

The Commentary states: "In meaning, it refers only to Bodhisattvas; from after the True Vision (*tattvadarśana*), they likewise do not emerge from meditative absorption until they are subsumed by the second faculty."
Regarding the "three minds" of a bodhisattva, there are three interpretations. The first states: if it refers to the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is called the first mind;

if it refers to the first set of sixteen moments of mind, these are established as sixteen distinct types of mind—eight of the apprehended and eight of the apprehender—based on the contemplation of the grasped object and the grasping subject.

This is called the second mind. If one establishes sixteen distinct minds of dharma and category based on the contemplation of the lower and upper truths within the second stage, this is called the third mind.
Within this path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), both types of sixteen minds are termed subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
This is precisely when the Bodhisattva enters the true path of seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*); following the true path of seeing, it is also...
Without emerging from meditative absorption, one immediately enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) through its characteristics.

Within the first set of sixteen moments of mind, based on the gate of the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*), one separately establishes the sixteen moments of mind regarding the factors of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and their subsequent realization (*anvayajñāna*).

As for these first sixteen moments of mind, when one reaches the fifteenth moment—the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*)—it is still subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*). This continues up until the sixteenth moment.
The path-subsequent knowledge (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) is subsumed under the faculty of "that which is yet to be known" (*ājñātāvya-indriya*), because its aspects and views have not yet been perfected.
This very first set of sixteen moments of mind is then designated as the second set of moments. When the Bodhisattva enters this second set of sixteen moments of mind...

This refers to the establishment of sixteen distinct types of mental states—comprising both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*)—based upon the lower and higher levels of the truths (*satya*). Regarding this second set of sixteen mental states:

if one possesses the first fifteen moments of mind, they are subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), because the aspects (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) have not yet been fully perfected.
When one reaches the sixteenth moment of mind, the aspects and objects are finally perfected, at which point the vision is completely fulfilled; thus, it is no longer "unknown."

The faculty of "knowing what is to be known" (*ājñātavyendriya*) is subsumed under the second, the faculty of "already knowing" (*ājñendriya*). This second stage consists of sixteen moments of mind, which are designated as the third moment of mind.
As for the "nine-moment path of seeing" (*navacitta-darśanamārga*), it is merely a widespread convention within the holy teachings regarding the first sixteen moments of mind;

it is spoken of according to the meaning established within the Dharma. In reality, there is no separate nine-moment path of seeing apart from that. Regarding the practice of contemplation (*bhāvanācaryā*):
Within the mind, one also does not form the nine mental activities of conceptualization; for this reason, it is not established as a fourth mind. The second interpretation states:
regarding the three minds, the first mind refers to the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), while the second mind refers to the path of seeing consisting of the three minds.
This refers to the internal wisdom that eliminates the conceptual designation of sentient beings as its object.

This master asserts that these three moments of mind constitute the *lakṣaṇa-mārga* (path of characteristics), while the preceding single moment of mind constitutes the *tattva-darśana-mārga* (path of seeing reality).

If other masters assert that these three moments of mind constitute the *tattva-darśana-mārga*, they then establish the preceding single moment of mind as the *tattva-darśana-mārga*, thereby substituting this path of seeing consisting of three moments for the path of seeing consisting of a single moment.

Regarding the "locations": the third mind refers to the sixteen moments of the latter two stages; specifically, within the sixteen moments of the third stage, the first fifteen moments are still subsumed under the faculty of "the knowledge of what is yet to be known" (*ājñātāvyajñāsyāmīndriya*).
Only upon reaching the sixteenth moment does it become subsumed under the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*).
A third interpretation states that the "three minds" exclude the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and refer only to the path of semblance (*pratibhāsadarśanamārga*).
The first set of sixteen moments of mind constitutes the first stage; the second set of sixteen moments of mind constitutes the second stage;
and the third set of sixteen moments of mind constitutes the third stage. This principle follows the preceding pattern. All three of these interpretations are excellent.

The Commentary states: "In this context, the terms 'preparatory application' (*prayoga*) and 'provisional equipment' (*sambhāra*) do not merely refer to those two which encompass the fundamental [path].

Here, 'preparatory application' and 'provisional equipment' do not merely refer to the equipment and the preparatory application; the terms 'equipment' and 'preparatory application' also include the fundamental path and the path of vision (*darśanamārga*)."

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: As it says in [the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*] 57, "one [meaning] is that which is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-saṃprayukta*) and that which is unbound (*asaṃprayukta*);
all that is bound and unbound constitutes the meaning. That which is bound to the realm of form refers precisely to the wholesome factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśala*).

These factors conducive to penetration are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*) wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), and thus they are exclusively bound to the realm of form. That which is unbound refers precisely to uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas. All that is bound and...
"Bound" (*baddha*) is the meaning; "meaning" (*artha*) refers to the object (*ālambana*). That is to say, it is the absence of an object of cognition.
"Bound" refers to the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and its origin (*samudaya-satya*); "unbound" (*abaddha*) refers to the truths of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the path (*mārga-satya*).

This refers to a Bodhisattva in the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), who takes all the truths of suffering and its origin as objects, and takes all the truths of cessation and the path as objects. This treatise is abbreviated; if stated in full, [it would be]: first, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Regarding the definition of "bound to the form realm," "unbound," and "all that is bound and unbound": if it refers to what is bound to the desire realm, this refers to the wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*).

These are comprised of the wholesome roots of reflection and wisdom (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*) within the desire realm that are conducive to liberation, as well as the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) within the intermediate dhyāna of the form realm, which is also conducive to liberation. This [includes] the intermediate [dhyāna] of the form realm and the [desire realm]...

The wholesome roots conducive to liberation within the realms (*dhātu*) also take the truths of suffering and origination as their objects; they also take cessation and the path as their objects. It is taught that the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) is also subsumed under this first root;

therefore, this commentary states that this first root begins from the stage of the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*). The answer is as follows, as will be understood from the commentary:
"From the fundamental stage up to that which can remotely support the fundamental stage. Why, then, is this reception not derived from the preceding stage of equipment? It is because...

First, one attains liberation through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and only thereafter does one attain liberation from the stage of the provisions (*sambhāra-avasthā*). Furthermore, it was asked:

"If one only attains the path of seeing after first completing the fundamental stages of the aforementioned provisions (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*), then those two preceding stages should be called the 'fundamental' (*mūla*).

Why, then, is the path of seeing alone designated as the fundamental stage? Regarding the designation of the path of seeing as "fundamental," although it may be so named in relation to [the subsequent paths], it is [considered fundamental] because it is the root for [attaining the path of cultivation].
Examine this fundamentally. The *Śāstra* states:
"In the Mahāyāna, from the entry into the kalpas onwards, it is the same for the Hīnayāna as well.

Regarding those who, within the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), give rise to a resolute and superior desire for the wholesome Dharma: in the Mahāyāna, these are precisely the Bodhisattvas who have already entered the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa."

Regarding dharmas such as bodhi and nirvāṇa, one gives rise to a mind of resolute and supreme desire for wholesome dharmas; at that point, one no longer clings to previously inferior wholesome states.
As it is said in the *Yúyún* (The Traveler): "The ninth [chapter] of the Sūtra says: 'From the generation of the profound and firm great bodhicitta,' etc. This refers to that very state.
If it pertains to the Hīnayāna, it is the entry into the wholesome states conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), from the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) onwards.
To initiate a superior and wholesome desire for the Dharma (dharmakāma) after having entered a kalpa corresponds to a Bodhisattva entering the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa;
to initiate a definitive and superior wholesome desire for the Dharma upon the clear realization of the Truths (satyābhisamaya) corresponds to the Hīnayāna.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Regarding the question in the fifty-seventh [verse], 'What is the meaning of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)?', the intent of this inquiry is:
what is the meaning of the term 'unknown' (*anājñāta*) in relation to this faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'?"

The Commentary states: "Regarding the answer concerning those who cultivate the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), from the stage of desire for wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*) up to the stage of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*):
this means that for one who cultivates the clear realization of the truths, from the stage of desire for wholesome dharmas onward, throughout all paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*)."
The five faculties, such as faith that arise—these five faculties of faith and so forth are precisely the meaning of this faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Therefore, it is known that the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" also extends to the stage of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

As for other ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet entered the desire for wholesome dharmas, nor those who have not yet generated the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), although they may give rise to...
The five faculties, such as faith, concentration, and wisdom, are not subsumed under the faculty of "the unknown to be known" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

As for the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga*), it refers to the means for proceeding toward enlightenment; thus, both the stage of provisions (*sambhāra*) and the stage of application (*prayoga*) may also be termed the path of skillful means.
If one speaks specifically of the stage of application, it is subsumed within the stage of application among the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*); it cannot be [anything else].
It extends through other stages. If one speaks of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), it is present in all Bodhisattvas of the ten stages;

that is to say, Bodhisattvas of the ten stages possess the path of preparation, the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), and so forth. If one speaks of preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*), it extends only to Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage;
Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward no longer possess the path of preparation.

The Commentary states: "This is not named in relation to *nirvāṇa*; this shall be understood below. This means that the faculty of "knowing what is yet to be known" (*ājñātavyendriya*) is named only in relation to the faculty of "already known" (*ājñendriya*) within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). That is to say, in relation to the faculty of "already known" within the path of cultivation, this is given the name "faculty of knowing what is yet to be known.
Since this faculty of "knowing what is yet to be known" has not yet attained the first true liberation, it is therefore not named in relation to *nirvāṇa*.

"Parinirvāṇa" is the name [for the goal]. Nirvāṇa is true liberation. If one follows the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), they are named "conducive to liberation" by looking toward Nirvāṇa from afar;

because they accord with Nirvāṇa from a distance, they are called wholesome factors conducive to liberation. As for the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), they are named solely by looking toward the factors such as the awakening-factor of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-sambodhyanga*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The treatise states: "In these three stages, from the five faculties beginning with faith up to being 'for the sake of this faculty'... Question:
Throughout the preceding sections of the treatise, only the initial untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) of the two vehicles have been explained.

Since practitioners of all three vehicles enter the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) based on the initial *anāgamya* concentration, they should possess only seven faculties—namely, faith, mind, and the five wholesome faculties. Why, then, does this passage state that there are nine faculties? Answer: It says:
The nine faculties refer to the five beginning with faith, as well as the mental faculty (*manas*), joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

However, if a bodhisattva, during the preceding stage of preparation (*prayoga-avasthā*)—specifically within the sequence of one [moment] preceding and following [another]—is able to attain the four dhyāna concentrations, they are then able to attain the nine faculties.

This is because the six sense bases of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) possess the first untainted faculty (*anāsrava-indriya*). When a bodhisattva relies upon the fourth dhyāna to enter the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they [attain them] exclusively...

Seven faculties arise: namely, the five beginning with faith, the mental faculty (*manas*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). If one considers practitioners of the Two Vehicles during their prior stage of application (*prayoga*), they should also give rise to nine faculties.
If one speaks in terms of the general possibility for different individuals within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is said that nine faculties may be obtained.
However, if speaking of a single individual, only [certain] arising faculties are possible. What is the case? It is when one enters the path of seeing based on the initial *anāgamya* concentration.
There are only seven faculties, namely: the five beginning with faith, the mental faculty (*manas*), and the faculty of joy (*saumanasya*). Answer:

There are those who, relying on the fundamental dhyānas of the first and second stages, enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); they also give rise to these seven faculties—the five beginning with faith, the mental faculty, and the faculty of joy.

If there are those who, relying on the third dhyāna, enter the path of seeing, they likewise give rise to seven: the five beginning with faith, the mental faculty, and the faculty of pleasure (*sukha*). If there are those who rely on the [fourth dhyāna]...

Entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) within the fourth dhyāna likewise gives rise to only seven faculties: the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), the mental faculty (*manas*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). Question:

Since the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is common to the four dhyānas as well as the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya*), one should know that a person attaining the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) based on the preliminary concentration actually possesses eight faculties at present:
the five beginning with faith, the mental faculty, the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity. This applies even if a person relies upon the third dhyāna.

Upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are likewise eight faculties: the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), the mind faculty (*manas*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Even if a person enters the Path of Seeing by relying on the third dhyāna, there are still these same eight faculties—the five beginning with faith, the mind, joy, and equanimity.

Why, then, is it said that when entering the Path of Seeing by relying on the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya*) or the third dhyāna, there are only seven faculties? [This refers to] the faculty of thought (*vitarka*).

Because it can be understood through general application, the *Śāstra* states: "That which has eighty faculties as its nature," and so forth, up to "many are concordant with that. If the preparatory (*prayoga*) faculty of grief (*daurmanasya*) is considered, it has ten faculties as its nature:

namely, the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), the mental faculty (*manas*), joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and grief itself. If [the view of] Sthiramati is also...
It is so. It is also stated in the *Abhidharma-kośa* (Treatise on the Abhidharma) that the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) has ten faculties as its nature.

Since the Bodhisattva Sthiramati largely follows this *Saṃgrahaṇī* (Compendium), and since the Bodhisattva Asaṅga composed the *Saṃgrahaṇī* and it is also stated therein that the faculty of grief has ten faculties as its nature;
furthermore, it says that Sthiramati follows the Hīnayāna in asserting the existence of the faculty of grief—this too is consistent [with that].
This is a divergent explanation, which agrees with that of Sthiramati.

The commentary states that it is not frequently mentioned in the *Mahāśāstra* and other texts because there is no sorrow (*daurmanasya*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) at the fundamental stage.

Therefore, the *Mahā-śāstra* (Great Treatise) frequently does not mention the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*). The Buddha taught nine faculties: the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), as well as the mental faculty (*manas*), joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

The commentary states that there is one who is able to enter [the path], namely the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*); and there is one who is unable to enter, namely the faculty of "already known" [in its preliminary stage].
Regarding the faculties (*indriya*): there is one that cannot enter [the path], namely the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

If one possesses the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñendriya*), one is able to enter entirely. The commentary (*śū*) states: "Although this characteristic is already understood, it is explained separately for a specific reason.

However, the *Mahā-śāstra* (Great Treatise) states that the lower three formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*) possess the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown. Therefore, this treatise provides a double reconciliation, stating that the former [case] refers specifically to the lower three formless realms.

There exists the seed of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). Now, upon entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one causes those seeds to increase by practicing them as collateral cultivation.

Regarding the second treatise, the *Lunhui* (Commentary on the Treatises) states: "Alternatively, for those in the stage of the two vehicles who turn toward the Mahāyāna to realize the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)...

up to 'those included within this faculty'. The meaning of this passage is that, alternatively, there may be none [of these seeds] in the stage of the two vehicles; or, having previously attained the untainted (*anāsrava*) state, they are fully endowed with it.

The faculty of full knowledge (*ājñātendriya*). Now, turning toward the Great [Vehicle], for the sake of realizing the emptiness of the dharmas of a bodhisattva, that person—while still on the stages prior to the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi*)—possesses the faculty of full knowledge consisting of the nine uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) faculties of the emptiness of persons across the six form realms and three formless realms.

Those same faculties of full knowledge consisting of the emptiness of persons, which were produced by the two vehicles, are also subsumed within the bodhisattva’s faculty of "that which is not yet known but will be known" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*). Therefore, it is said that the lower three [faculties] are [uncontaminated].

Regarding the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) in relation to form (*rūpa*): furthermore, one who has attained the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) first acquires the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*)—the untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledge of the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*).

Later, when they turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) to realize the dharma-emptiness (*dharma-nairātmya*) of a bodhisattva, that non-returner, upon reaching the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), likewise gives rise to the untainted faculty of "having known" regarding the emptiness of arising across the nine grounds.
That non-returner also gives rise to the [untainted faculty of "having known"] regarding the arising of the lower three formless realms (*ārūpya*).
The faculty of having already known the empty and outflow-free [states] is subsumed within the bodhisattva’s faculty of "that which is yet to be known.
Therefore, it is said that from the three lower formless realms up to the first outflow-free faculty.

The Commentary states: "It is said that there are bodhisattvas who, while previously in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), [attain these concentrations] up until the point where, even though they have not yet entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is no fault.
This means that bodhisattvas, while previously courageous in the stage of an ordinary person, cultivate the four dhyānas and eight samāpattis later on.
Regarding this, there are two interpretations. The first says: these are precisely the bodhisattvas who, from time immemorial, have repeatedly cultivated and attained them.
Regarding the four dhyānas and eight samādhis: one immediately attains those three lower formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). This interpretation is not accepted here.
Second, it is said that even while in the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*), one repeatedly practices and attains the four dhyānas and eight samādhis;

thus, although the four dhyānas and eight samādhis arise during the stages of equipment and application, one immediately attains those three lower formless attainments. This [is] with the equipment...

In the stage of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the [attainment of] food, there arise interspersed the four dhyānas and eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), which are conducive to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states that there are four types of meditative concentration:

first, the concentration of the part conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya-dhyāna*), which, upon emergence, is conducive to the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*); second, the concentration of the part conducive to maintenance (*sthiti-bhāgīya*).

This refers to: (1) the concentration that accords with one's own level; (2) the three concentrations that accord with superior progress, which involve emerging from the first dhyāna concentration and entering the second dhyāna concentration;

and (4) the concentrations that accord with the stages of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), which, upon emerging from concentration, accord with untainted (*anāsrava*) concentration and cause one to attain the concentration that accords with the stages of penetration—namely, the eight concentrations arising in an alternating manner during the stage of equipment and application (*sambhāra-prayoga*). These are able to accord with [the path].

Regarding the untainted meditative absorption (*anāsrava-samādhi*), we now adopt the second interpretation. During the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*), the arising of the meditative absorptions of the eight stages and so forth is preeminent.
That is to say, at the time of the Bodhisattva’s subsequent path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), one incidentally cultivates those seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) previously arisen.
Because these seeds of conventional knowledge serve as the auxiliary support for that other untainted [knowledge], the seeds of the tainted conventional knowledge thus obtain [cultivation].

It is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*). Therefore, it is said that below those [stages], the seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) within the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*) are called the faculty of "knowing what is to be known" (*ājñendriya*).
Thus, it is stated that below those, in the three formless realms, there exists the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.

Subsequently, at the stage of the Path (*mārga-avasthā*), one can also give rise to the seeds of conventional knowledge so that they manifest as actual activity. This occurs precisely within the stage of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Because they emerge from various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and traverse various attainments (*samāpatti*), they give rise to the seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), causing them to manifest in actual activity (*pravṛtti*).
It is not an error to hold that conventional knowledge can arise in actual activity during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
however, one cannot produce the seeds of conventional knowledge within the path of seeing.

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "In the thirteenth chapter of the *Abhidharma*, the true realization (*tattvābhisamaya*) is explained... until this conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) finally manifests.
However, the explanation in the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* is also similar to the explanation found in the preceding passage of this *Śāstra*.

If one speaks of the realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), that realization is the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and not the non-conceptualized truths (*avyavasthāpitasatya*). Since it is said, "the knowledge at the limit of realization" (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna*), [it refers to] the truths.
Abhisamaya refers to the time of the sixteen moments of the *darśanamārga* (path of seeing).
It is precisely at the time of taking the *vyavasthāna-satya* (established truths) as an object that the seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) are nourished and increased.

Because these seeds of conventional knowledge are nurtured by the power of the supramundane dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is said that one "attains" this conventional knowledge. Within the stage of the path of seeing, conventional knowledge...

The seeds [of this conventional knowledge] cannot manifest, because during the sixteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is no interruption, and thus there is no room for the manifestation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) within the clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
However, if one is in the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), then this conventional knowledge can indeed arise as a manifest activity.

Thus, within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one enters and emerges from the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) while dwelling in the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā*). Question: What dharma is now employed as conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)? Answer:

It is precisely the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that can perform the contemplations of attraction and aversion.

Therefore, the wisdom of hearing and reflection in the desire realm is designated as conventional knowledge. It is by means of this wisdom of hearing and reflection in the desire realm that one performs [the contemplations].

Because of the contemplation of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-vipaśyanā*), one is able to give rise to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Furthermore, one takes up the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation within the form realm;

these wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation within the form realm are also capable of performing the contemplations of delight and revulsion. Therefore, the wisdom of hearing and the wisdom of cultivation within the form realm are termed conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

There is no wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) in the form realm. Moreover, one takes up the wisdom of cultivation in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); [this applies to] the wisdom of cultivation in the formless realm.

Wisdom (*prajñā*) is also capable of performing the contemplations of attraction and aversion. Therefore, the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) likewise causes conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

For all noble ones (*ārya*), upon entering the stages of the provisions (*sambhāra*) and the preparatory application (*prayoga*), they rely upon the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī*) and reflection (*cintāmayī*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as well as the wisdom of hearing and cultivation in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the wisdom of cultivation in the formless realm.
These collectively comprise three types of mental attention (*manaskāra*): first, attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanaskāra*).

First, attention through mental reflection (*manasikāra*), which refers to contemplating the five aggregates (*skandha*)—such as form and feeling—as well as the three categories of phenomena (*dharmaparyāya*), namely the aggregates, bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

Second, attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*), which refers to contemplating all phenomena through the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, up to the path, suchness, practice, and emergence.
Third, attention through resolute conviction (*adhimuktimanasikāra*), such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*).

The contemplation of the skeleton and so forth—these three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) are precisely those employed by the noble ones (*ārya*) and others when entering the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*).
Although these three types of mental attention are themselves contaminated (*sāsrava*), they all accord with the uncontaminated noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*).

Furthermore, these three are not necessarily characterized by the contemplations of either delight or aversion; however, if non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) were to practice such delight and aversion, [they would be different].
These six modes of practice belong exclusively to the mundane path; thus, one does not perform these three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*). These three types of mental attention consist of:

the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) cultivated in the desire realm; the wisdom derived from hearing and the wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) cultivated in the form realm; and the wisdom derived from cultivation cultivated in the formless realm.
All are able to produce these three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
The Commentary states: "This faculty is neither an access-faculty (*prāyogika-indriya*) nor an outflow-free faculty (*anāsrava-indriya*) in its actual manifestation;

yet it exists in the cultivation of that [state], because in the cultivation of that stage there are no four wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*). If within the lower three formless stages (*ārūpya-bhūmi*), those stages lack outflow-free [faculties], one cultivates the mundane [faculties] as collateral practice.
The seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). These seeds of conventional knowledge are termed the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

These aforementioned seeds of conventional knowledge belonging to the three lower formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) are not subsumed under the wholesome states resulting from application (*prayoga-kuśala*).

This is because the four wholesome roots of application do not exist in the three lower formless realms; the four wholesome roots of the stage of application exist only within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). Thus, these aforementioned [seeds] in the three lower...
The seeds of conventional knowledge regarding form are both outflowing phenomena (*sāsrava*) and not non-outflowing phenomena (*anāsrava*). Question:

Since it is already admitted that during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the seeds of conventional knowledge are cultivated in a secondary manner and allowed to increase, it is not yet known [how this occurs] within the path of seeing.
Furthermore, regarding the seeds of virtue from the stages of prior provisions (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*) cultivated during the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*):

do they increase when one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)? Moreover, after entering the path of seeing, do those virtues from the stages of provisions and application arise as actual manifestations (*samudācāra*) once again?
Answer: At this point, within the path of seeing, one merely cultivates them in parallel with the intermediate stage between the stages of provisions and application.
The seeds of the mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) arising from the four dhyānas and eight samāpattis are made to increase;

likewise, during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the seeds of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) consisting of the accumulations (*sambhāra*) and the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) are also not cultivated incidentally, yet they are made to increase. Why is this?

One who has attained the fruit does not cultivate the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), because it has already been previously attained. Furthermore, the virtues of the provisions (*sambhāra*) and the preparatory application (*prayoga*) are all subsumed under the path of preparation;

therefore, they are not cultivated. Moreover, once one has entered the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), all virtues of the provisions and preparatory application never again arise as manifest activity (*samudācāra*).

As for the incidental cultivation of the seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) to cause them to increase, this is like having previously generated the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

This is because, while within the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*), the merits practiced such as giving and ethical discipline (*śīla*) are all able to indirectly support the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*),
causing them to increase. If other persons have not yet resolved upon bodhicitta and have not entered the stages of equipment,
application, and so forth, then even though they practice giving and ethical discipline, they are unable to provide support for the untainted seeds.
This means to cause it to increase.

The *Sūtra* commentary (*Shu*) states: "In this context, it is taught that cultivation consists solely of 'cultivation by acquisition' (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), and not 'cultivation by practice' (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*); [therefore] cultivation does not necessarily arise.

Herein, when the mundane wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is cultivated during the path of insight (*darśana-mārga*), it is exclusively cultivation by acquisition; that is, it is termed cultivation by acquisition because it accords with the seeds [of that wisdom].

Now, one only cultivates the seeds of that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) so as to cause them to increase, rather than conforming to the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of that conventional knowledge.

This is because, during the untainted path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it is impossible for the tainted conventional knowledge to arise in actual manifestation; this is also termed "cultivation by acquisition" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*).

That which is not the cultivation of practice is also the manifestation of practice. Question: Why are there two instances of the term "cultivation" (bhāvanā) and why are there two instances of the term "training" (śikṣā)?

Answer: Regarding the statement "cultivation of cultivation," it is called cultivation because one attains cultivation; regarding the statement "cultivation of practice," it is called cultivation because one practices cultivation.
Therefore, in both phrases, there are two types of persons who cultivate. This is according to the Bodhisattva-pudgala.
One immediately cultivates the mundane [knowledge] of future lives so that it may increase.

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Cultivating by way of differentiation through lateral observation, even up to that which is not concordant," refers specifically to the sixteen moments within the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

One laterally cultivates the seeds of that mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) as a concordant factor for the subsequent [Path of Meditation]. This is because the Path of Differentiation (*viśeṣa-mārga*) exists.

[The text] distinguishes [the following]: the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that accords with characteristics is not the conventional knowledge that can be cultivated within the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

This is because the true path of seeing is without characteristics (*animitta*), undifferentiated, and lacks the characteristics that accord with [conventional reality], and for this reason it does not cultivate it.
This first interpretation is superior.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*) is also cultivated, yet it is not mentioned because its duration is brief and there is no differentiation.
This is the second interpretation: within the true path of vision, one is also able to incidentally cultivate the seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

Because the duration within the true path of vision is brief, and furthermore because there is no aspect of differentiation, it is therefore not mentioned. Thus, conventional knowledge is incidentally cultivated within the true path.

It merely states that within the path of insight (*darśanamārga*), one incidentally cultivates the seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). This second interpretation does not equal the former. The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states:

"In this context, it is said that one may also cultivate the higher [stages] while dwelling in the lower; that one first becomes detached from the desire realm of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth, gradually becoming detached from desire—this is said to be an unreal principle.
However, this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states that one enters the path of insight based upon the fourth dhyāna.

The seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) for the three lower formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) cultivated alongside [the higher ones] are precisely those by which a lower stage can cultivate a higher stage.
This means that the lower can cultivate the higher, and these are all of the superior grade (*adhimātra*).

Thus, while Bodhisattvas in the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*) intermittently give rise to the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of the eight stages, they first and foremost become detached from the desires within the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), thereby attaining those four formless attainments.

Regarding meditative concentration (*samādhi*): one is able to cultivate the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the lower three formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). There are superior paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) that do not entail all paths of seeing being thus.

If one has previously attained and mastered the cultivation of the lower three formless concentrations, then upon subsequently entering the path of seeing, one simultaneously cultivates the seeds of that conventional knowledge of the lower three formless attainments.
This applies whether one is a follower of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*) or otherwise.

Regarding those who cannot attain the three lower formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*): they are unable to concurrently cultivate the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of those three lower formless absorptions within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
If the Yogācāra (Vijñaptimātra) school asserts that one can cultivate a higher stage based on a lower stage, this refers exclusively to those of superior grade who have already attained mastery;
that is, those of superior grade who have already attained mastery rely upon the fourth dhyāna.

When entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one is also able to incidentally cultivate the seeds of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) and conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) of the three lower formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Now, one is able to incidentally cultivate the seeds of the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*)—which are conventional wisdom—within the lower desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

One who is capable of generating delight and aversion is able to incidentally cultivate the seeds of the wisdom of hearing and wisdom of reflection within the lower desire realm, which are conventional wisdom, and is thus capable of generating delight [and aversion].
Regarding "aversion" (*nirveda*): it is able to cause the seeds of conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) within the lower three dhyānas to increase through lateral cultivation.
If one follows the explanation in the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, this refers to the gradual departure from the desires of the lower realms at the present time.

Once one has attained the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of a higher stage, the seeds of wholesome dharmas—the conventional wisdom of the lower stages—can then be cultivated and increased within that higher stage; this refers specifically to the medium grade of the lower [realm].
This "category" refers to what is taught for those who have not yet attained mastery. One in a higher stage can cultivate the seeds of wholesome dharmas belonging to a lower stage.

If it concerns the cultivation of the seeds of wholesome dharmas of a lower stage by one in a higher stage, then all noble ones (*ārya*) are capable of this, just as ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones alike, upon entering the initial *anāgamya* concentration, are able to simultaneously cultivate all the seeds of wholesome dharmas within that initial *anāgamya* concentration.

It causes all seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) to increase. It is also able to incidentally cultivate the seeds of wholesome factors consisting of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) and reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*) within the lower desire realm;

those who are capable of generating delight and aversion cause these to increase. This is like entering the fundamental concentration (*mauladhyāna*) of the first dhyāna, which is also able to incidentally cultivate the seeds of the wholesome factors belonging to its own level—the first dhyāna—including the wisdom derived from hearing and the wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), as well as [incidentally cultivating] other...

The seeds of mundane conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) within the wholesome dharmas of the lower preliminary concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*), as well as the seeds of mundane conventional wisdom arising from hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*) regarding the wholesome dharmas of the desire realm, all attain growth.

This is likewise true for all higher stages, even down to all noble ones (*ārya*) and all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), whenever they enter the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). All [seeds] therein...
They are able to cultivate, as a secondary practice, the seeds of wholesome dharmas of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception so that they increase;

they are also able to cultivate, as secondary practices, the wholesome dharmas of the lower three formless attainments, the four dhyānas, and the wisdoms of hearing and reflection belonging to the desire realm, and these too can increase.

If the higher [levels] can cultivate the lower, this applies to those of middling or inferior grades; if the lower can cultivate the higher, they are also able to cultivate the lower, which constitutes a person of superior grade. Or...

There are ordinary worldlings who, having attained the four formless attainments, when subsequently entering the fourth dhyāna concentration, are also able to concurrently cultivate the seeds of mundane conventional knowledge regarding the wholesome dharmas within the four formless attainments, causing them all to increase.

They are also able to concurrently cultivate the seeds of the wisdom of hearing and reflection pertaining to the lower three dhyānas and even down to the desire realm, causing them all to increase; all of this is reckoned according to the present moment.
The preceding passage explains the gradual departure from desire.
The commentary (*śū*) states: "Having cultivated and attained the meditative concentration (samādhi), up to the seeds of conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) that are produced. Question:

As it is said that the three lower formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are called conventional wisdom, yet wisdom (*jñāna*) is not itself concentration (*samādhi*), this must therefore refer to the seeds of wisdom cultivated through meditation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).

"Son, as for the latter two [knowledges], their arising is permitted. Since there is no fault in their arising even though they do not arise during the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), this refers to the arising of the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that arises mixed with the practices within the preceding two stages.
It does not refer to the arising of the wholesome dharmas within those two stages. Question: One attains the superior and abandons the inferior;

one attains the fruit and abandons the previous [path]. Just as when one has attained the purity of entering the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), one might again give rise to the previously practiced provisions (*sambhāra*) and applications (*prayoga*)."

Regarding the seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) that arise within the state [of the path], these seeds of conventional knowledge give rise to their actual manifestation (*samudācāra*).

If it is asserted that these seeds of conventional knowledge—which are not included within the stages of the provisions (*sambhāra*) or the preparatory application (*prayoga*)—can nevertheless produce their actual manifestation while one is in the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), an objection is raised: if the seeds of conventional knowledge are neither part of the provisions nor the preparatory application...

As for "the wholesome": the seeds of conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) should not be subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*). Since it is stated that the seeds of conventional wisdom are subsumed under the first faculty, it is clear that they are included within the wholesome [states] of the stages of accumulation (*sambhāra*) and preparation (*prayoga*). How, then, can it be said that conventional wisdom arises as an actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) prior to [the attainment of] the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*)?
