Those of the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*) may also have previously practiced [the formless attainments], such that it is not the case that all those on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are like this.

Regarding this second interpretation: if a person of the two vehicles has previously attained the three lower formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), that person should first use the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) to suppress the afflictions of the three lower formless realms, and subsequently enter the path of seeing based upon the fourth dhyāna. Thus...

Regarding the non-returner (anāgāmin) who transcends the first three fruits to attain the third fruit: one who proceeds by gradual stages does not obtain the superior fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

If such a person of gradual progression has not previously attained the three lower formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), they cannot subsequently cultivate the seeds of the lower pure formless wisdom or the superior conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
The answer is likewise [if they have not]. Furthermore, this applies to those who have abandoned desire for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) as well as to Bodhisattvas.

As for this: the question is, since this text first discusses the separation from desire in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it should correspond to the second explanation in the preceding commentary regarding the two vehicles (*śrāvakayāna* and *pratyekabuddhayāna*) practicing auxiliary cultivation, as well as the attainment by Bodhisattvas—which is precisely the first explanation in the preceding commentary regarding Bodhisattvas practicing auxiliary cultivation.

Furthermore, within the three lower formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), there exist seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); these are termed "subsumed under the initial faculty" (*mūlendriya-saṃgṛhīta*) and thus enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Question: Since the stage of that cultivation-by-association (*pārśva-bhāvanā*) also contains seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), why is it not said to be subsumed under the first faculty (*indriya*), nor is it said to enter the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) as a cultivation-by-association?
Answer: It is indeed a cultivation-by-association; however, it was stated previously according to the sequence [of the faculties].

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the three formless stages (*ārūpya-bhūmi*) of a Bodhisattva also possess the untainted path of vision (*anāsrava-darśana-mārga*), up to and including those who rely solely on the stages of concentration, compassion, and wisdom.
The intended meaning here is that the seeds of the path of vision in the lower three formless realms are made to increase;
just as within the lower three dhyānas there are also seeds of the path of vision which merely increase, yet they never actually arise."
This is a miscellaneous point. This interpretation is because the Master of the Commentary himself refutes it within the text of the commentary itself.

Since it is stated that the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is characterized by an increase in wisdom (*prajñā*), whereas in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) there is an increase in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom is deficient, the Path of Seeing cannot exist in the three lower formless realms.
This is because the Path of Seeing specifically depends on a stage where concentration is increased and wisdom is deficient, and such a stage does not exist [in those realms].

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Alternatively, it is said that since one has already admitted the desire for wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*) and beyond as being named this 'root,' then those who possess the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*)—namely, Bodhisattvas—also arise therein;

it is not [only] the proponent [who holds this view]. Since one has already admitted that from the stage of entering the desire for wholesome dharmas onward, one is named the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), then those Bodhisattvas in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) who are in accordance with liberation [are included]; thus, the time [of their arising] is distinguished by its duration."

Furthermore, one may also be born into the lower three formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*). When a bodhisattva is in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), this period is distinguished as being long and distant, lasting for one great eon (*mahākalpa*).
Once born into the lower three formless realms, one then newly perfumes (*vāsana*) the seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

It is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*). Therefore, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" exists within the three lower formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*).

This is as stated in the *Mahāśāstra*, the *Pāramitā*, and the *Bodhisattva* [treatises]. Whether by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or by birth (*upapatti*), one fully comprehends all phenomena within the formless realm.
Regarding "by concentration," this refers to when one attains those four formless absorptions while residing in a lower realm. Regarding "by birth," this refers to when—

Among these, when a bodhisattva is in the stage of the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) within the stage of the accumulations (*sambhāra*), they may be reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Therefore, it is accepted that there are also roots of goodness conducive to liberation for bodhisattvas in the three lower formless realms.

If the aids to liberation in the desire and form realms are termed "direct aids to liberation" (*samyag-mokṣabhāgīya*), then those in the formless realm are termed "auxiliary aids to liberation" (*anugrāhaka-mokṣabhāgīya*); they are not "direct. If...

Regarding the previous commentary’s explanation that "in those stages, these seeds exist by their very nature (*dharmatā*)," this refers to the fact that the lower three formless realms possess the original seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Now, in this current commentary, since liberation is permitted to exist within the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), [the same principle applies].

Regarding the statement that "a Bodhisattva born in the formless realm perfumes and establishes the seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)," this refers specifically to seeds produced through new perfuming (*navasaṃskṛtabīja*).

In those Bodhisattvas of the three lower formless realms, there exists the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), which is acquired through the cultivation following the superior path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
The Commentary states: "Because the number of kalpas for those of the Two Vehicles is short, it cannot be said that they possess the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
If those of the Two Vehicles are in the stage of the factors conducive to liberation, they may pass through three births at most, or at the very longest sixty kalpas;

since the time for attaining the Noble Path is thus brief, there is no possibility for those of the Two Vehicles in the stage of the factors conducive to liberation to be born in the Unsurpassed [Heaven]."

Regarding the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*): since persons of the two vehicles (*śrāvakayāna* and *pratyekabuddhayāna*) have a brief duration while in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) during the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), they do not take birth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Within the formless realm, there are no roots of goodness conducive to liberation for those of the two vehicles, nor the faculty of "knowing the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

These [roots] consist of the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*) within the desire realm, as well as the wisdom derived from hearing and cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) within the realm of form.

Regarding the two vehicles (dviyāna) practitioners who cultivate the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*): these exist only within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

As for those from the third fruit onward who turn toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), if one asks about those of the first and second fruits who have already turned their minds [toward enlightenment], since they have already passed through one great eon (*mahākalpa*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), they should also be able to give rise to the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātāvindriya*), which is the untainted knowledge of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*) across the nine stages. Furthermore—

This is comprised within the bodhisattva’s initial untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*). Why does the Commentary state that it refers exclusively to the Sūtra on the Fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmi-phala*), saying "it has already departed but not yet attained"?

Furthermore, the Commentary asks: "However, because the two vehicles have not yet realized the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-darśana*), they give rise to the untainted [state]."

The commentary explains: Although it is said that those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) practice the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmas), because they have not yet realized [this realization] when giving rise to outflow-free wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) prior to the stages (bhūmi), this [text] does not state that they also obtain [the status of] a faculty (indriya).

The Commentary states: "Regarding the previous mention that all three stages consist of the faculties of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*)," this refers to what was stated earlier in the treatise:

that within these three stages—the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*), the stage of application (*prayoga*), and the stage of vision (*darśana*)—there are all those possessing the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*). This is explained in reference to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" as it pertains to persons of the two vehicles.
The Commentary states: "Although it is likewise for those of the two vehicles, even the stages prior to the path of seeing cannot be cited as an example.

This means that although the duration of the path of seeing for those of the two vehicles is brief, the durations of the stages of accumulation (*sambhāra*) and preparation (*prayoga*) prior to their path of seeing are all equally brief.
Therefore, the *Mahāśāstra* says: "For those of the two vehicles, the stages of accumulation, preparation, and [seeing]..."
The three stages of the Path all possess the faculty of "the unknown yet to be known" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).

Since the two stages prior to the Bodhisattva grounds—the stages of Accumulation (saṃbhāra) and Application (prayoga)—span many kalpas, the *Mahāśāstra* states that those on the Bodhisattva stage of "Conduct through Resolute Belief" (adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi) possess the faculty of the unknown yet to be known;
it does not state that Bodhisattvas on the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) possess this faculty. Therefore, the cases are not comparable. Furthermore, [regarding] the turning back...

Regarding the minds of those of the Two Vehicles and others: a person who has attained the first fruit [of the śrāvaka path] requires eighty thousand kalpas before reaching the initial mind of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) of a bodhisattva.

For those who have attained the second fruit, it takes sixty thousand [kalpas], and so on, up to the comparison between the four branches (*catur-aṅga*) and the ten branches (*daśāṅga*) and the initial mind of the ten stages of faith.
Once these persons of the Two Vehicles have attained their respective fruits, they do not fear the three evil realms; they wander about, lacking the resolve to progress and cultivate the path.
Therefore, the duration of the kalpas is long; if a bodhisattva practices the path for either thirty or sixty kalpas, they reach the initial stage of the Ten Faiths.
These aforementioned kalpas are all calculated based on the kalpas of formation and destruction.
Although there are distinctions such as seven kalpas of fire-disasters followed by seven kalpas of water-disasters before a wind-disaster occurs, [the calculation] regarding fire, water, and wind...

The three kalpas are each comprised of eighty *antara-kalpas* (increasing and decreasing kalpas), which together constitute one kalpa of formation and destruction (*vivarta-saṃvarta-kalpa*). The three kalpas of water, fire, and wind are all similar in this regard.
The commentary states: "The nine faculties and ten faculties are both explained as before. The sub-commentary explains: "If a Bodhisattva prior to the seventh stage has not yet..."

Those who have departed from the desire realm also possess the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), which has ten faculties as its nature. If they are Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage or above, they lack the faculty of sorrow, and their nature consists of nine faculties.
If they are persons of the first two vehicles who have not yet departed from the desire realm, they also possess the faculty of sorrow.

These consist of ten faculties (*indriya*) within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). If one has already abandoned desire for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) from the third fruit upward, there are only nine faculties.

Regarding the first two faculties, those that are also associated with outflows (*sāsrava*)—namely, the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) and so forth—are also termed the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

Furthermore, the faculty of mental distress and the five outflow-associated faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*) present in the bodies of those on the first two fruits are all termed [the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"].

Regarding the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*): if, within the body of an adept (*aśaikṣa*) of the two vehicles, there exists the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the five faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*) that are with outflows (*sāsrava*), these are all termed the faculty of one who has already known.
Furthermore, the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) also extend to those that are with outflows.
*Cheng weishi lun shu Taichao*, Scroll 12.
This *Taichao* was missing from the sutra repository of Yakushi-ji.
Recently, when Kihan of Jizō-in was preparing to lecture on it, he obtained a copy from the sutra treasury of Fukuen-in at Kōfuku-ji and requested my assistance with the transcription. Although...
I am ashamed of my poor calligraphy, yet I rejoice in this not a little. To ensure that the Dharma may endure for a long time, I have transcribed this during the reign of Emperor Zhongzong.

May the merit from this act cause my teachers, fellow practitioners, dharma companions, parents of seven generations, internal and external kin, and all beings within the dharma realm, to never let their residual influence go to waste, and may we together attain the infinite bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

the brushwork and meaning are clear and harmonious.

The Commentary composed by Dharma Master Lingtai of Beijing states:
"Regarding the meaning that the manifest conditions exhaustively encompass all phenomena, there are further four distinct conditions established separately to exhaustively encompass all phenomena."

These are the four conditions (*catasraḥ pratyayāḥ*), which exhaustively encompass all phenomena (*sarvadharmāḥ*). These are also the fifteen bases (*pañcadaśa-āśrayasthānāni*), which likewise exhaustively subsume all phenomena.
These are the four conditions; based upon the fifteen bases, they are explained as exhaustively subsuming all phenomena through their specific meanings.
Upon these specific meanings of the fifteen bases, ten causes (*daśa-hetavaḥ*) are established; these too are distinctions of meaning based upon the fifteen bases.

They are distinct; therefore, they are established as ten causes. The fifteen bases (*āśraya*) are the substance (*svabhāva*) of the phenomena. These ten causes are the functional meanings (*artha-vṛtti*) upon those fifteen bases.
Since function is not separate from substance, the treatise states: "Because there are distinctions in meaning based on the fifteen bases, they exist as ten causes.
Regarding the distinction between cause and substance: it is now said that the ten causes depend upon the fifteen bases; thus, their meanings are both general and specific.
Therefore, as for establishing them as ten causes, this is explained in terms of essence and function: the fifteen bases are the essence, while the ten causes are their functional meanings.
Since function does not depart from essence, the ten causes do not depart from the fifteen bases.

The Commentary states: "That which relies" (*yanni*) uses the seventh case suffix for both meanings. Regarding the phrase "relying on sound and form" (*yi shengse*), if one says "at" (*yu yu*), it applies generally to both the object (*viṣaya*) and the supporting faculty (*āśrayendriya*). If it applies generally to the object...
The Commentary states: "In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 38, there are only three kinds of ten causes (*daśa-hetu*) and five fruits (*pañca-phala*).

As for the statement that their essence is the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*): the three kinds of ten causes are as follows: first, the ten causes of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), which refers to things such as seeds; second, the ten causes of purification (*viśuddhi*), which refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas of the Three Vehicles;
third, the ten causes of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), which refers to these twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) within the cycle of birth and death. 3.
There are ten kinds of causes, as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 38.
However, while that fascicle mentions only the ten causes and five fruits, it does not clarify the fifteen bases (*āśraya*).

The Commentary states: Because names precede all phenomena and are universal as that which precedes them, they are said to be the "causes for the sequential designation" (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*) of those various phenomena.
Since the substance of all phenomena exists first, names are then produced; that is to say, one designates: "This is mind," "This is form," "This is a person," and so forth.
Once these have been designated, there arise within the mind mental concomitants that function simultaneously with them, namely, the various names, perceptions, and sounds.

Perception is like the nature of perception. Once perception has arisen, awakening immediately follows. That which takes the essence of all phenomena as its fruit and is able to abandon defilement as its cause—this very [perception] is also taken up and expressed in words;
thus, it is taught as the causal essence. If the three factors are designated as "perception," this is precisely the source from which defilement arises.
This is identical in meaning to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only). Such is the intent of this passage.

It is said: Because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) have existed from the beginning, once the Buddhas and Tathāgatas have realized these all-encompassing phenomena, they subsequently give rise to designations based upon them and establish names for all phenomena.

Accordingly, they teach the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and so forth. Once these names exist, Maitreya and the other Bodhisattvas all rely upon these names and teachings.
[This is] finished. It arises within the Bodhisattva’s mind and is immediately grasped as a basis. Yet, what is called "name" and what is called "all"? That is to say:
"this is the name," "this is the mind," and so forth. When the Bodhisattva speaks to other sentient beings, first a conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) arises within the Bodhisattva’s mind.
Conceptualization has the function of being able to bestow various conventional designations (*nāma-pada*). Having thus conceptualized, he then speaks.

Therefore, the designation "arising" applies only to the Buddha; the "conception of arising" belongs to the Bodhisattva. Thus, that which is grasped as the arising of *sā* (existence) is taken as the essence of the cause for conventional discourse (*vyavahāra-hetu*), being beyond words.

Alternatively, because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) have existed from the beginning and are thus exhausted [in their ultimate nature], the Buddha, having realized these all-encompassing phenomena, now—in this present time—proclaims the twelvefold division of the teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) as Śākyamuni Buddha. Now...

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha took up the names and teachings spoken by all the Buddhas of the past. He then gave rise to mental conceptions within his own mind based on those ineffable teachings that had been established, thinking:
"This is the name; this is the name; this is the mind," and so forth. Having thus given rise to these conceptions, he...
However, it is for the sake of other sentient beings that verbal expression arises. This refers to the broad, successive transmission [of the teaching].
That is to say, the arising of the designation "present Buddha" based on the past Buddha, and the arising of speech—this speech so produced is called "conforming to the cause" (*anuvartaka-hetu*).

Although the force of that treatise’s phrasing seems to take that which is devoid of all phenomena, up to three phenomena, as its essence, such is not the case in treatises like the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (or *Xianyang lun*).

Regarding the force of the argument: it appears that [the author] takes the name, conception, and expression that exist above all phenomena, and takes these three factors—name, conception, and expression—as the essence of the cause for conventional designation;
he does not take merely the arising of speech as the essence of the cause for conventional designation.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Now, this present text correctly explains that meaning... down to 'the mind is the cause for the separation from all phenomena.

Now, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) text correctly explains that the aforementioned treatise takes only the speech arising from the three—names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and mental representations (*vyañjana*)—as its basis;

this speech thus arisen is the very essence of the "cause of conventional designation" (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*). Why is this so? Because it exists solely in dependence upon the cause of conventional designation.

Speech is taken as the essence of the cause for subsequent expression (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*). If speech alone were not taken as the cause for subsequent expression, then the treatise should have stated:

"based on non-conceptualization, the three are expressed. Since it says, "that which expresses in accordance with speech is speech itself," we know that only the speech produced [by the mind] is taken as the essence of this cause.
In this context, that which is capable of acting as the cause for speech is the signified (*abhidheya*).
All phenomena constitute the fruit. One takes names and concepts as the basis for speech; is it that speech arises precisely by depending on names and concepts?
Thus, language is indeed the very cause for the expression of all phenomena.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the statement that 'the nature of speech generally refers to all three natures,' and even that its substance consists of two natures:

if this is considered from the perspective of the conventional (prajñapti), because vocal sounds can express the wholesome and the unwholesome, they are conventionally designated as such; and because they are conventionally designated as wholesome or unwholesome, it is said that vocal sounds pervade the three natures.
Second, regarding the perspective of the substantial self: vocal sounds pervade two natures. If, in the case of a Buddha, one relies upon vocal sounds, these are [then]..."

The nature of untainted goodness (*anāsrava-kuśala*). The speech-sounds of all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and of Bodhisattvas from the first stage up to the tenth stage are all of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).

Regarding the commentary which states: "Alternatively, in the Mahāyāna, sound may lack an intrinsic essence," and so forth, up to "the objection by analogy is the same as that regarding the substratum (*āśraya*)," if...

The previous explanation stated that names consist of only two natures (*dvaya-svabhāva*), which refers to their ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*). Now, regarding the conventional designation (*prajñapti-vyavahāra*), they pertain to all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).

Alternatively, since names and so forth in the Mahāyāna are designated based on speech, and names lack any essence apart from sound, and since the sound upon which they depend pertains to all three natures, these names—being named after their dependent sounds—likewise pertain to two natures, just like arising, change, and cessation.

Regarding the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): just as that which is characterized is of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*) as the essence of the dharma (*dharma-tattva*), so too these characteristics—arising, abiding, change, and cessation—are wholesome by virtue of depending upon that which they characterize, the essence of the dharma.

Furthermore, when the essence of a conditioned dharma (*saṃskṛta-dharma-tattva*) is unwholesome (*akuśala-svabhāva*), these characteristics of arising, abiding, change, and cessation are likewise unwholesome, in accordance with the essence of the dharma upon which they depend. How, then, is this obtained? [It is obtained] through the dharma.

Since its essence (tattva) permeates all three natures (trisvabhāva), that which enables it to be attained likewise possesses the three natures. The acquisitions (prāpti) of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), the homogeneous character (nikāyasabhāga), and analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha)—which serve as the bases for non-acquisition and so forth—as well as the acquisition of the Path (mārga), are [of these three natures].
In the Mahāyāna, there is no such thing as attaining a dharma before the dharma exists or attaining it after the dharma has arisen;
rather, it is merely a conventional designation (prajñapti) of "simultaneous acquisition" (sahajā-prāpti) occurring at the very same time as the essential body (dharmakāya) of the dharma.
The Commentary states: "One cannot say that the three characteristics are co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), because their meanings all apply [beyond this].

If the Sarvāstivādins maintain that the four characteristics—arising (*jāti*) and so forth—are co-existent causes in relation to the essence of a dharma, then since these four serve as the basis for the arising of the dharma and their own essences also pertain to all three natures (*tri-dharmatā*), they can be obtained both before and after the dharma; thus, they are established based on the dharma that is obtained.
[The previous discussion] held that the "attainment" (*prāpti*) which is capable of acquiring [a dharma], as well as the dharma that is acquired, both pervade the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
However, in the Hīnayāna schools, attainment is not established as being a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) with the essential body (*svabhāva*) of the dharma. Why is this?

If the essential body of the dharma exists in the future, then the attainment would arise prior to the dharma; when [the dharma] reaches the past, the attainment and the dharma would no longer be simultaneous. Furthermore, if the essential body of the dharma exists in the past...

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of that dharma also exists either in the future or in the present. Since the essence of the dharma does not belong to the same temporal period, it cannot function as a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Furthermore, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), such as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), do not encompass the three time periods;

however, the acquisition of these unconditioned phenomena does encompass the three time periods. As for the three—name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and syllable (*vyañjana*)—if they are by nature indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), then as for the name...

In relation to the three dharmas—their substance—phrases, words, and phonemes are not simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*). Furthermore, they cannot serve as the "attainers" (*prāpaka*) that acquire those dharmas.
Therefore, phrases, words, and phonemes are by nature indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); moreover, phrases, words, and phonemes are also distinct from deportment (*airyāpathika*).

Within deportment (*airyāpathika*), there is a mind that takes deportment as its object; thus, the names and phrases of the mind of deportment and so forth do not arise from craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).

Within craftsmanship, too, there is a mind that takes craftsmanship as its object and a mind that initiates craftsmanship; the names and phrases of these are likewise not different from those of maturation (*vipāka*).
This is because maturation is either wholesome or unwholesome and is subject to cessation; therefore, it is intrinsically neutral (*avyākṛta*). However...

The Hīnayāna establishes five kinds of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) factors; that is, in addition to the other four types of indeterminate, it further posits "intrinsic indeterminate" (*svabhāvāvyākṛta*), namely names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*).

Now, the Mahāyāna objects: one cannot say that the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*), for the three characteristics pervade all three natures (*tridharmasvabhāva*).
Names and so forth are not co-existent causes; names and so forth are exclusively indeterminate phenomena. I shall now [explain] this extensively.

The three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the vehicle are provisional; their underlying substratum is the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Names, phrases, and syllables are also provisional, as they likewise depend upon sound.
Since sound itself permeates all three natures, names, phrases, and so forth also permeate all three natures. Therefore, with respect to names and phrases...

These are inherently simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*). The three characteristics of arising and so forth, as well as the dharmas themselves, are also simultaneous causes. Attainments (*prāpti*) and the like are conventional;

they arise from the dharmas they attain and likewise pertain to all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). However, when the Mahāyāna states that names, phrases, and so forth pertain to the three natures, it is as follows:

This is also a designation made by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). Furthermore, the Mahāyāna does not state that names and so forth, nor that the primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the four secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*), act as co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
This is merely a provisional adoption of the tenets of other Hīnayāna schools; thus, the Mahāyāna provisionally speaks of the existence of co-existent causes.

Therefore, it is said that names (*nāman*) and so forth pertain to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*). However, when the Abhidharma states that names, phrases (*pada*), and so forth are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*), this is because it follows a provisional gate of reasoning (*anuvartana-yukti*).
Now, the Mahāyāna teaches that names and so forth pertain to all three natures, because within the Buddha’s body, names, phrases, and so forth are untainted and wholesome (*anāsrava-kuśala*).
Furthermore, as the Abhidharma also states that the five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) are indeterminate, this too is [a case of] following [provisional reasoning].

The *parivṛtti-dvāra* (door of transformation). If one possesses the faculties of middle capacity within the Mahāyāna, these are also of a wholesome nature, because the five faculties within the Buddha-body are untainted (*anāsrava*) and wholesome.
The commentary states:

"That which is attained by following what is seen, heard, sensed, and known is based precisely upon this realization. This refers to the phrase "if one follows what is seen" (*yadi dṛṣṭam anuvidhīyate*).
The eye obtains [objects] by seeing; the ear obtains sounds by hearing; the nose, tongue, and body obtain smells, tastes, and tangibles respectively.

Following what is known through these, one perceives all phenomena according to their meaning, and subsequently gives rise to speech to express those various meanings. Therefore, the expressive words are taken as the cause, and all the phenomena expressed are the result.

In the Mahāyāna, seeing with the eyes is called "seeing," while hearing with the ears and so forth are all termed "hearing. The three faculties of nose, tongue, and body are termed "sensing" (or "contact").

Because this is based on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is termed "cognition" (*buddhi*). However, mental consciousness may also include non-valid cognitions (*aprāmāṇya*) and so forth;

therefore, in the Hīnayāna, the views regarding clarity are the same as before. If the three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body are termed "cognition," it is because the three objects—odor, flavor, and tangibility—are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), being like a corpse.
Since these [consciousnesses] now reach those [objects], it is said that the nose, tongue, and body are also "cognitive. As for mental consciousness...
This is called "knowledge. This is explained in terms of the one who perceives. Once all such perceived objects have been seen, this person says:
"I see this object," "I [know] all these things," "I am aware of this thing," or "I am able to know this thing. Thus, it is explained in terms of the one who perceives.
Alternatively, according to those perceived objects and so forth, all are spoken of as... [the various phenomena].

Meaning. Therefore, this passage explains that all which is seen is merely phenomena (*vastu*). That is to say, regarding the "self-phrase" (*ātma-pada*) that has come forth, what is seen—such as forms, men, women, and so forth—is explained as being based on the meaning of phenomena. Thus, this passage takes up the explanation that all which is seen is merely phenomena;

namely, regarding the "self-phrase" that has come forth, what is seen is like seeing such phenomena as forms, men, women, and so forth. Or, regarding all that has previously come forth, it is likewise [the case for] the tongue.
Or it refers to the flavors and so forth previously perceived.
The Commentary states: "This speech is the cause of all that is spoken; all that is spoken is the result of the vocal karma that speaks."
The Commentary states: "The ancient masters say that all dharmas thus spoken are the essence of the cause. The explanation says:

If the ancient masters say that because everything serves as a cause, speech is subsequently initiated, then the essence of all dharmas constitutes the causal essence for the sake of discourse, while language itself is the result.
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the causes for the designation of outflowing, neutral, and so forth, up to defiled and pure,' this cause can only be understood in this way.
Now, the Master of the Commentary, having already observed that there are three types of causal seeds within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, has here provisionally glossed the meaning accordingly.

Having already seen this "cause of conventional designation" (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*), [the text] uses it to distinguish it from the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); that is, it uses the cause of conventional designation to distinguish it from the indeterminate cause of conventional designation.

It uses it to distinguish it from the defiled (*saṃkleśa*); that is, it uses the universal cause of designation (*sāmānyavyavahāra-hetu*) to distinguish it from the defiled cause of conventional designation.

It uses it to distinguish it from the pure (*vyavadāna*); that is, it uses the cause of conventional designation to distinguish it from the pure cause of conventional designation. If it were indeterminate, it would simply be the cause of conventional designation.

"Cause" (*hetu*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound; it refers to the expressive speech itself. This cause is of a contaminated (*sāsrava*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature. The various resultant phenomena (*phala-dharma*) expressed by it, however, encompass all three natures—contaminated, uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and indeterminate.
This is because, with the exception of the Buddha’s speech, which is exclusively uncontaminated and wholesome (*kuśala*), all other results may be of any of the three natures.

Therefore, for Bodhisattvas from the remaining ten stages [of the path] onwards, as well as for all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth, the vocal sounds that serve as the expressive medium are exclusively of a contaminated (*sāsrava*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature.
However, among the resultant phenomena (*phala-dharma*) that are expressed by these sounds, there can be both uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) and wholesome (*kuśala*) natures.
Furthermore, the contaminated and indeterminate speech of Bodhisattvas from the ten stages onwards, as well as that of ordinary beings and so forth, is likewise...

It is capable of expressing phenomena such as the defilements (*saṃkleśa*) of birth and death; thus, among the resultant phenomena that are expressed, there exist defiled and unwholesome (*akuśala*) dharmas.
Furthermore, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth, as well as for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) outflowing (*sāsrava*) sounds;

these are also capable of expressing the dharmas that serve as seeds and causes, such as rice and barley. These resultant phenomena that are expressed possess the nature of being indeterminate. This is the capacity [of sound].
The "cause of conventional designation" (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*) is of a tainted and indeterminate (*sāsrava-avyākṛta*) nature.

The resultant phenomena designated by it include tainted phenomena, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and those of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*). That is to say, while the cause is exclusively an indeterminate phenomenon, the result encompasses all phenomena.

If the term "indeterminate cause of conventional designation" is analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound), it refers to the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

The terms "outflows" (*āsrava*), "the three natures," and so forth are causes of designation (*prajñapti-hetu*). Just as [the terms] "rice" and "barley" are non-informative (*avyākṛta*) causes, even so, the terms for the outflowing, non-outflowing, and the three natures are causes of designation that express non-informative results. These are the expressive causes (*vācaka-hetu*) which apply to all phenomena;
the expressed results (*vācya-phala*), however, are exclusively of an outflowing and non-informative nature. If they are defiled (*saṃkliṣṭa*), they are accordingly designated.

"Causes" (*hetu*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound. It refers to the defiled, contaminated speech of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and others, excluding the Buddha, which expresses resultant phenomena (*phala-dharma*) that are contaminated, conditioned, and characterized by the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).
These are the "causes of conventional expression" (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*), which are exclusively of a defiled nature.
Among the resultant phenomena expressed [by these causes], they encompass all contaminated and uncontaminated, conditioned and unconditioned phenomena across the three [times].
It is of the nature of equality (*samatā*). If it refers to the causes for the conventional designation (*prajñapti-hetu*) of defilement (*saṃkleśa*), it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

That is to say, the expressions regarding the three natures—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—used by all Buddhas, bodhisattvas of the ten stages, and all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to denote the phenomena of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and defilement, are precisely the causes for the conventional designation of the three natures, such as those with and without outflows, which serve to express them.

The phenomena of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and so forth are the causes for conventional expression (*vyavahāra-hetu*), which pertain to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*) as well as both outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) states.

The resultant phenomena that are expressed (*abhidheya-phala-dharma*) are exclusively of an afflicted nature. If it refers to purification (*viśuddhi*), then the cause for conventional expression is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound);
the resultant phenomena that are expressed include all dharmas of the three natures, both outflowing and non-outflowing, with the exception of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and others.

The explanations regarding birth and so forth—namely, all things that are contaminated or uncontaminated, conditioned and so on, as well as all matters that are pure, defiled, or indeterminate—are themselves the causes for the conventional designation of uncontaminated purity. The results expressed by these [terms], however, encompass results that are both contaminated and uncontaminated, including those of the three natures (tri-niḥsvabhāva).
If [the term] "cause for the conventional designation of purity" is analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound, it is as follows:

These are the words—whether tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*), and belonging to the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*)—of the Buddhas, bodhisattvas on the ten stages, and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
They speak of matters such as enlightenment (*bodhi*), nirvana, and the purification of outflows (*āsrava-viśuddhi*).

These are the causes for conventional designation (*prajñapti-hetu*) based upon the tainted three natures and so forth, which express matters such as the untainted fruits of the pure dharmas. Thus, they are the expressive language (*vācaka-śabda*) that applies to both the tainted and the untainted.
Regarding the three natures and so forth, the phenomena that are the expressed results (*phala-dharma*) are exclusively pure. Now, in this context, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is not included;

rather, there is the defiled *vyavahāra-hetu* (conventional cause) and the pure *vyavahāra-hetu*. This is because the term "conventional cause" (*vyavahāra-hetu*) as used [in other contexts] is too narrow.
Here, only the indeterminate *vyavahāra-hetu* is taken, as well as the defiled and the pure [vyavahāra-hetus].

This refers to the cause for conventional designation (*prajñapti-hetu*), because this capacity to express (*abhilāpa*) is broad, encompassing the three natures such as the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
According to the *Cherppal Chopyo* (Jeppeopcho), it is the cause for the seeds spoken by all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), bodhisattvas of the ten stages, and the Buddhas.
Grains such as rice and barley are non-informative (*avyākṛta*) things. These types of forms are called "informative causes of conventional designation" (*vyavahāra-hetu*).

If all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and buddhas speak of the defilements (*saṃkleśa*) of saṃsāra, these are called "informative causes of conventional designation for defilement.
If the buddhas, bodhisattvas of the ten stages, and ordinary worldlings speak of bodhi and nirvāṇa...
[This is] an indeterminate [explanation regarding] the untainted (*anāsrava*). These are precisely what are called the causes for pure conventional expression (*viśuddha-vyavahāra-hetu*).

Regarding the statement that "the fruit extends to all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) [phenomena]," one asks: Since the treatise states that the unconditioned is "cut off from the path of speech" because its nature is beyond words, and furthermore is not a basis for speech, how can it now be said that the unconditioned is the same as the conditioned in being the fruit of what is expressed (*abhidheya*)? Reflect on this. Question: Based on the preceding [discussion],...

Within the context of the teaching-body (*śāstra-deha*), it is stated that the sixth uncontaminated consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) of a bodhisattva on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is such that all names and so forth upon which it relies are exclusively uncontaminated and virtuous (*kuśala*).
Why, then, is it stated here that all contaminated [phenomena] belonging to a bodhisattva on the ten stages are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
This refers to the "conformity-explanatory cause" (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*). Furthermore, it is asked: does this conformity-explanatory cause take the sound that serves as its basis (*āśraya-śabda*)?

If one takes names, phrases, and syllables as the essence [of speech], or if one takes the Buddha’s voice as the essence—since the essence of the Mahāyāna voice consists of the names, phrases, and syllables that function as the expressive means—then if one takes names and phrases as the essence, the "causal basis for conventional discourse" (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*) would necessarily be a conceptual construct (consider this). Question:
Do the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and those of the two vehicles not also possess a causal basis for conventional discourse that is free from defilement? (Consider this). Question.

As previously stated regarding the *anuvāda-hetu* (cause of subsequent statement), since there exists an indeterminate *anuvāda-hetu*, this indeterminate *anuvāda-hetu* is also present among the ten causes, even within the *avirodha-hetu* (non-contradictory cause). That is to say, the *avirodha-hetu* itself may be indeterminate.
One should reflect that the non-contradictory cause of the indeterminate is itself the non-contradictory cause of defilement;
the non-contradictory cause of defilement is itself the non-contradictory cause of purification.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Just as names and so forth are the fruits of that explanation," up to "attachment arises from seeing names.
If this is said to be the *Asaṃjñisamāpatti* (attainment of non-perception), then this passage is identical to the original version in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

If it is not [the attainment of non-perception], but rather attachment to grasping signs by means of names, then this passage is the text of Haribhadra. The intended meaning of that treatise is stated by...

Because the name comes first, one immediately gives rise to a conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) that establishes a portion of deliberation. However, it is only after this conceptualization that an interpretation (*vyākhyā*) subsequently arises.

Just as when one grasps an object based on a signifying name, one clings to the preceding [name] itself as not being the real name, yet clings to the color, sound, and so forth signified by that name as being real, because they are what can trigger speech.
Having seen that such clinging arises, one then clings to the conceptualization previously produced as being a "real conceptualization."
When speech is about to arise, one takes the triad of name (*nāman*), concept (*saṃjñā*), and view (*dṛṣṭi*) as the causal substance for that which follows the discourse;

what arises is called "speech," which serves as the effect. Thus, these three dharmas—name, concept, and view—are established as the basis of speech, because speech arises in dependence upon these three dharmas.
Now, when it is said "like the names that can express [meaning]," this also applies to the conventional designations (*nāma-vyavahāra*) that express meaning through indication.

"Name" refers to the expressive term; "now" refers to the perceiving subject and the perceived object. Here, it merely concerns the moment when the view arises as described in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*:
just as with an object expressed by a name, one simultaneously gives rise to the characteristic of grasping.
The Commentary states: "As for the question, 'What is the reason that these two treatises contradict each other?'—the question here asks:

Why is it that in the *Abhidharma*, the three factors of name (*nāman*), characteristic (*nimitta*), and view (*dṛṣṭi*) are taken as the substantial nature of the cause of verbal expression (*vyavahāra-hetu*), while name, characteristic, and view are said to give rise to speech, which is then termed the fruit?

And why is it that in treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the three factors of dharma (*dharma*), name (*nāman*), and conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) are employed [as the cause]?"

Regarding the origin of the arising of speech: speech arises from its source, and that very speech which has arisen serves as the cause for subsequent expression, while all phenomena (dharmas) expressed thereby serve as the result. Therefore, there is no contradiction between the two treatises.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the two treatises' explanations of cause and effect—those of the *Abhidharmapitaka* and Asaṅga—up to their being non-contradictory, each is based on a single meaning.

This means that if, according to the *Mahāśāstra* and other texts, verbal expression is taken as the self-nature and all phenomena expressed [by those words] are taken as the fruit; [then this is one perspective].
Regarding the relationship between the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*): the signifier is taken as the cause and the signified as the effect;

conversely, the signified is taken as the effect of the signifier, and the cause of the signifier is likewise established. Thus, in terms of the signifier and the signified, there is both the effect of the signifier and the cause of the signifier.
This constitutes the causal relationship based on the signifier and the signified. As it is stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*:
Taking origination as cause and effect: that is, based upon name, conception, and view, one gives rise to verbal expression.
Thus, these three factors—name, conception, and view—are the "originators" acting as the cause; the speech that is originated is the "result.
That is, based upon name, conception, and view, one gives rise to verbal expression; thus, these three factors—name, conception, and view—are taken as the originators acting as the cause.
It is the cause; the speech that arises from it is the effect. Each of the two treatises relies on one specific meaning, and thus they do not contradict one another.

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) says: "Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: 'In accordance with conventional expression'... up to 'the capacity for conventional expression,' the 'contingent condition' (*apekṣā-kāraka'), and so forth."
"Acting and so forth" refers to speech, which is that which is expressed. "The agent" refers to the three factors of name (*nāman*), conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), and view (*dṛṣṭi*).
These three factors—name, conceptualization, and view—are able to produce speech. This is like the sequential establishment of the ten causes;
specifically, it is like the first cause-and-effect correspondence, where the second, the "cause of expression," is termed the "signifier. All nine subsequent causes are likewise [signifiers].
The "agent" (*kartṛ*) refers to the result that is to be expressed. Third, regarding the pairing of the two—the agent and the object—one establishes the dependence-condition (*apekṣā-hetu*).

That is to say, within the dependence-condition, the subject that experiences is the cause, while that which is experienced is the result, and so forth. Third, regarding the pairing of the distant and the near, one establishes the two causes:

the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and the producing cause (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*). Thus, between these two—the projecting cause and the producing cause—the projecting cause is distant from the result.

The cause of arising is proximate to its result. Fourth is the pair of the immediate and the remote: this establishes the appropriating cause (*parigraha-hetu*) and the cooperative cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
If based on the appropriating cause, it is termed remote; the cooperative cause is termed immediate. Fifth is the pair of the homogeneous and the heterogeneous:
this establishes the productive cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and the determinate cause (*pratiniyama-hetu*). As for the productive cause, it exclusively induces that which is homogeneous.

This is called "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*). If the cause were definitively distinct [from its effect], then even wholesome and unwholesome karma would have as their cause a resultant fruit that is ethically neutral (*avyākṛta*), which would mean they are of different natures.
This is the sixth [point]: the contradiction regarding causes that are either concordant or discordant.

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, when the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains [the relationship] from 'taking speech as the cause' up to 'not being mutually contradictory,' it does so by taking the realm that penetrates all phenomena as its basis.

If the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* bases itself upon the 'signified' (*abhidheya*)—which encompasses all contaminated and uncontaminated, conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, such as the three natures (*trisvabhāva*)—then because the signified realm is broad, it takes 'speech' as the cause and the 'signified phenomena' as the result. If, however, [it is] in relation to..."
In the *Dharmaparyāya*, based on the arising of the defiled aspects (*saṃkleśabhāga*), name and appearance (*nāmanimitta*) are taken as the cause and speech (*abhilāpa*) as the result;
that is, seeing leads to attachment, and attachment is itself the defiled aspect. Therefore, this does not apply to the pure [aspects].
The Commentary states: "Some say that the three feelings alone constitute its essence... yet within the act of experiencing, it encompasses both the subject and the object. Furthermore, some say:
"It is subsumed under the category of feeling-in-general, which constitutes its essence... yet within the act of experiencing, it encompasses both the subject and the object.
Moreover, there is an interpretation which says: "It is subsumed under the categories of feeling-in-general, painful feeling, and pleasant feeling, etc., and is taken as the object of contemplation."

To claim that the essence of the cause depends [on something else] is incorrect. If it were the case that one first seeks and then seeks union only after a desire arises within the mind, one might say that feeling (*vedanā*) constitutes the essence of the cause;
yet this too is flawed. It would then follow that desire arises only because of feeling, and thus the union with what is felt would be the cause while desire would be the effect.
Furthermore, since that which is felt and the union are not three distinct entities, we know [this position to be untenable].
One must not hold that only the three feelings of suffering, pleasure, and so forth can serve as the essential nature of the condition of relative dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*).

However, within the condition of relative dependence, that which is experienced (*anubhūta*) serves as the cause and that which experiences (*anubhavitr*) serves as the effect; yet it is also the case that that which experiences serves as the effect. Therefore, one should know that its essential nature encompasses both the experienced and the experiencer.
The commentary states: "One cannot say that because desire (*chanda*) is not pervasive and is not of the nature of feeling (*vedanā*), it is not [the essence of] speech.
This means that since the preceding statement refers to the seeking of and union with objects of affection and desire, it takes desire as its essence.

To say it is "not feeling" is because this term does not apply to the mind; for when the mind exists, there is no [such thing as] speech, whereas that which is capable of feeling is a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika-citta*).
Because there is sensation (*vedanā*) at the very moment of arising, sensation is taken as its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
The Commentary states: "One observes that, according to the capacity of the subject and the object, one experiences the fruit that is capable of being experienced.

Within this capacity to experience (*vedaka*), there is also that which is experienced (*vedya*); thus, the capacity to experience acts as the cause, and the experienced fruit acts as the effect. In this context, the capacity to experience is the cause, and the experienced fruit is the effect.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "Alternatively, regarding 'arising, abiding, and attainment,' these [factors] act as causes for that which is produced and so forth. This means:

if a seed acts as the counter-correlative cause (*pratigha-hetu*) for the sprout it produces; or if the water-circle (*jala-maṇḍala*), by depending on the wind, is able to abide, then it [acts as a cause] for the water.
The wheel constitutes a relative condition (*apekṣā-hetu*). All of these take what is received as the cause and what is received as the result. Question:

However, regarding this relative condition, since all of these are found only in the commentary (*vṛtti*), and since external seeds in relation to sprouts and internal seeds in relation to the manifest [result] and so forth are not considered relative conditions, how can the first phrase of this text be explained as referring to the seeds of the Three Vehicles?
Nature (*prakṛti*) comes first. Regarding the fourth phrase: if it refers to the attainment of the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, the fourth phrase is subsumed under this "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*).
However, if the fourth phrase refers to the attainment of the fruit of *nirvāṇa* in terms of seeds giving rise to manifest activity (*samudācāra*), it is not subsumed under a direct contingent cause;
rather, it emphasizes the stages of arising, abiding, and ceasing. If it pertains to that which is acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*), then it takes the parts (*aṃśa*).

Regarding the division into the second and third phrases and so forth, all are subsumed under this "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*). If one provides this interpretation, it is superior in every respect.
Nevertheless, as for the water mandala and the wind mandala, the wind mandala serves as the cause; that wind mandala is precisely the contingent cause upon which [the former] depends.
The water-circle is the "supported effect" (*pratītya-phala*). This continues until the earth-circle rests upon the gold-circle;
here, the gold-circle is the "supporting cause" (*pratītya-hetu*), and the earth-circle is the "supported effect. Regarding the statement that the "supported" and the "produced" act as causes:
the "produced" is the "supported effect," while the "supported" is the cause. Thus, the "supported" and the "supporting" function as cause and effect for one another.
Furthermore, regarding "seeking" or "taking": "seeking" refers to the arising of emotional speech, such as saying, "I shall eat," or "It is appropriate.
"Taking" refers to engaging in various activities and fabrications.
The Commentary states: "Thus, regarding 'that which is depended upon' (*pratītya*), 'that which depends' (*pratīti*), and so forth, up to the fourfold distinction (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The general meaning of this passage is as follows: If that which is depended upon is termed the "cause" (*hetu*), it is because the effect arises by virtue of being supported by it.

If that which depends is the "effect" (*phala*), it is because the effect is only produced by means of the power of that cause. Therefore, in its causal state, [the cause] is always that which is depended upon. Its...
The fruit always acts as that which is "awaited. To "await" means to rely upon. Therefore, the present fourfold formulation is as follows:

there are cases where that which is capable of receiving [feeling] serves as the cause, and that which is capable of receiving [feeling] serves as the fruit. This is like awaiting pleasure while suffering from pain. For example, suppose a person experiences the painful sensation of illness;

they look toward the recovery from the illness and seek a pleasant sensation. Since they do not yet see a physician, they await pleasure while still possessing pain. This, then, is the use of that which is capable...

That which is depended upon is the "receiver" (the subject), and that which depends [upon it] is the "result. There are cases where the receiver is taken as the cause and that which is received is taken as the result;

for example, first giving rise to desire as the cause and subsequently seeking union and so forth. This is precisely using the receiver—which is depended upon—as the cause, and that which is received—which depends [upon it]—as the result.
There are also cases where that which is received is taken as the result; for example, when a person wishes to travel far and observes...

It means that taking language as the cause, one obtains coming and going as the result. This is thus taking what is received and what is depended upon as the cause, and taking that which receives and that which depends as the result.
There are cases where what is received is taken as the cause and that which depends is taken as the result;

for example, as previously explained, taking the reception of food as the cause and subsequently giving rise to the result of sensual desire. Here, there are cases where what is received and what is relied upon [are the cause].
The cause is that which is capable of experiencing, and this constitutes the fruit; such is the general meaning of this passage. The *Śū* (Commentary) states:

"The two [causes] differ in their fivefold stages. The *Jie* (Explanation) says: "If 'experience' refers to the presence of suffering and pleasure, it refers to the distinction between the five feelings (*pañca-vedanā*): joy, sorrow, equanimity, and so forth."
The Commentary states: "Regarding the four mental factors beginning with attention (*manasikāra*) up to [feeling], they do not function as feeling does in the case of experiencing pleasure.

Although attention, contact (*sparśa*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*) are also constantly and universally present in all minds, contact has as its nature merely the touching of an object;
it cannot experience pleasure in the manner that feeling can. It is only feeling that is capable of experiencing pleasure."
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Excluding only those dharmas that serve as seeds and conditions... otherwise, one should say they obtain 'concordant fruits' (*niṣyanda-phala*).

If it refers to the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*), it is only when there is a remote mutual dependence that it constitutes a contingent cause; therefore, the preceding text says they "obtain dominant fruits" (*adhipati-phala*).
This means that by excluding the dharmas that serve as seeds and conditions, [the result] is like a rice or barley seed in relation to its sprout—sharing the same kind.
The seeds in relation to their manifest activity are all not *apekṣā-hetu* (dependent causes).

If one were to take these seeds in relation to the seed within the sprout, or in relation to the manifest [sprout], and call them *apekṣā-hetu*, then it would follow that they "attain a result of uniform outflow" (*niṣyanda-phala*), as stated in the subsequent text.
Since the subsequent text does not state that they attain a result of uniform outflow, other causal factors such as seeds are all not *apekṣā-hetu*.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Question: Why is it said that only the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is the drawing-in cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) up until the very end?
What fault would there be [in this]? [Answer: Herein, why is it said that the causal condition is subsumed under the drawing-in cause and the producing cause (*abhinirvartaka-hetu*)?

Furthermore, this causal condition is also subsumed under the four causes of mutual inducement (*āvāhaka*), determination (*pratiniyama*), common function (*sahakārin*), and non-contradiction (*avirodha*). Receiving the objective-condition cause (*apekṣā-hetu*) is also subsumed under the objective-condition. Moreover...
This is subsumed under the four causes: producing, differentiation, commonality, and non-contradiction.

This cause of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*) should also be subsumed under the causes of attraction (*ākṣepa*) and arising (*abhinirvṛtti*). What fault would there be in this? "Ultimately" (*anta*) means "finally" (*niṣṭhā*).

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "The answer is that this is not so; because it is already termed 'distant,' it is called the 'contingent cause' (*apekṣā-hetu*), and so on, up to 'because the name is common.
The Explanation says: This first interpretation states that only that which is related through a remote distance, rather than being immediate, is the contingent cause.
Thus, the term 'contingent' (*apekṣā*) refers to what is remote. If the immediate were also included, it would encompass both the remote and the immediate."
This is because the name applies universally.

The *Śāstra* states: "Another interpretation holds that if even direct mutual dependence is considered this cause, and so on up to not mentioning 'equal outflow' (*niṣyanda*), then this interpretation is superior.
This refers to the second interpretation, which also takes direct dependence as the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*). It is explained as follows:
The seeds that are expected to manifest and the internal seeds upon which they depend are all subsumed under the category of the immediate *apekṣā-hetu* (condition of dependence).

In the following section explaining the results, it is stated that the *adhipati-phala* (dominant result) is obtained based on remote [conditions]; however, while the *kāritra-phala* (result of activity) is mentioned, the *niṣyanda-phala* (result of outflow) is not explicitly stated as being "obtained" from the immediate cause.

If one were to claim that the *niṣyanda-phala* is not obtained from this *apekṣā-hetu*, that would be incorrect; for this *apekṣā-hetu* also obtains the *niṣyanda-phala*. This interpretation is superior to the previous one, as it is like the case of a fool.
It seems that the second interpretation in the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) on this matter accords with the *Śāstra*.

This is because the *Śāstra*, in its exposition of the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*), states that within both "abiding" (*sthiti*) and "attainment" (*prāpti*), seeds give rise to manifest activities (*samudācāra*).

Therefore, it is logically superior to hold that the contingent cause encompasses direct causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). As for the textual explanation of the "contingent [cause] of desire," it refers to the state of being contingent upon [desire].
Regarding the phrase "the meaning [is such that] it is not the cause for this," there is no further separate explanation in the commentary (*śāstra*) itself;
it merely reiterates the second of the two previous interpretations. Within that single interpretation, only those that are remote are designated as the *apekṣā-hetu* (contingent cause).

Thus, the subject that experiences (*anubhavitṛ*) is the cause, while the preceding experience (*anubhava*) is the effect; the object experienced (*anubhāvya*) is the cause, while the experiencing subject is the effect—this constitutes the relationship between the agent and the object.

The nature of sensation (*vedanā*) is subsumed under the condition of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*). For example, when internal seeds are compared to manifest states, or seeds are compared to sprouts, these are not matters of emotional desire, because they function as the mutual dependence between the object and the subject of observation.
As for that which is "proximate" (*pratyāsanna*), it is not subsumed under the condition of dependence;
just as a seed produces a sprout, even without depending on emotional variation, the distinct type of seed is nonetheless capable of producing the sprout.
The Commentary states: "Question: If this is so, why is it that having feet serves as the cause for the karma of coming and going? This is a question posed from my own perspective.
The intent of this question is as follows: if one must depend upon sensual desire, and this dependence constitutes the "conditioning cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*), then such [desire] acts as the cause.
If there is the karma of coming and going, how could it be that the feet themselves come and go? Is this also due to emotional desire (*kāma*)?
The Commentary states: "The answer is that it is also dependent upon internal emotional desire. This refers to dharmas such as seeds, active manifestations (*samudācāra*), causes, and conditions."

Because it is not that which is awaited by the sentient being, it is not an "observed-dependence cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*). If it were at a time when it is awaited by the sentient being, it would not be a "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*).

The Commentary states: "Since the previously explained correct principle has already established within the 'appropriated' (*upātta*) that which is awaited as the cause, the sprout likewise awaits the seed."
Regarding this "distant cause" (*viprakṛṣṭa-hetu*): since there is no distinct meaning for it here in the commentary, this serves to re-establish the second interpretation.
The second interpretation states that seeds producing manifest activity (*samudācāra*) are both direct causes (*sākṣāt-kāraṇa*) and also dependent causes (*apekṣā-hetu*).

The subsequent text, for the time being, refers only to the distant cause, stating that it obtains the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), but does not say that it obtains the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). It also obtains [the fruit of] the dharma.

Regarding the "flowing fruit" (*niṣyanda-phala*): among those that are "received," that which is awaited also serves as the cause. For example, as actual manifestation awaits its seed, and a sprout awaits its seed;
likewise, that which is received serves as the cause, and that which is received serves as the fruit.

Although there are two interpretations within the *Śāstra*, the more distant one is taken as superior. In the present case, we consider the "remote condition" (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*) because it is a remote dependence;
we do not take the immediate one.

The *Śāstra* says: "Furthermore, if an indeterminate cause were itself indeterminate, then that cause would possess only the nature of being either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)," and so forth.
"All [terms] should be understood according to this. If it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), then the cause is exclusively of a contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) nature;
all [subsequent terms] should be understood according to this. If it is indeterminate, it is the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*). This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

Its cause is exclusively a contaminated sentient entity, while its fruit encompasses the three natures—contaminated, uncontaminated, and so forth—just as with the case of seeds and other such causes. This is non-existence (*abhāva*).
This explains the *apekṣā-hetu* (contingent cause). For example, when someone wishes to sow seeds such as rice or wheat, they first make a vow, saying:
"Once I have successfully sown these seeds of rice, wheat, and so forth, I shall then purchase sheep and oxen to perform labor and engage in the business of selling meat.
Such activities are the *avyākṛta-apekṣā-hetu* (indeterminate contingent causes), for their results are *sāsrava* (tainted).

It can be understood that wholesome natures have suffering as their fruit, and this applies to indeterminate (avyākṛta) factors as well. If the "condition of dependence" (*apekṣā-hetu*) is an indeterminate factor, it is analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound;
in this case, the condition of dependence itself may be of any of the three natures—defiled, wholesome, or indeterminate—while its fruit is exclusively defiled and indeterminate.
If the condition of dependence is a defiled factor, it is analyzed according to the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound; in this case, the cause is exclusively defiled.
Its nature [is such that] its fruit may pertain to all three natures—outflowing (*sāsrava*), non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), and so forth.

For example, there was a person who, having already encountered the consequences of having committed evil karma, subsequently gave rise to a virtuous mind; this is like the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, who, after having committed various evil deeds such as entering the palace, attained realization through diligent practice.
Having seen that others were ultimately killed, Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva contemplated this evil event and immediately resolved to leave the household life to attain the Noble Path;
this constitutes the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*). Its result encompasses the untainted wholesome nature (*anāsrava-kuśala-dharmatā*) and so forth.

There are those who, having committed the evil karma of sexual misconduct, immediately return to lay life to take a wife and children; this constitutes the "contaminated contingent cause" (*saṃkleśa-apekṣā-hetu*). Its [result]...

The fruit thus includes both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the unwholesome (*akuśala*). As for the phrase "the remaining factors only," it is understood that they include the neutral (*avyākṛta*) fruits of maturation (*vipāka*).

If it refers to the objective condition (*apekṣā-hetu*) of defilement, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound; its cause thus includes all three natures—tainted, untainted (*anāsrava*), and so forth—and its fruits.
This is exclusively of a defiled nature. As explained in a certain sutra, if a non-Buddhist sees either the Buddha or the Dharma and gives rise to slander, they immediately fall into hell;
this refers to the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*) of purification. Its result encompasses both the seed and the fulfillment. The others should be understood accordingly.
If it is a cause of purification, it is called a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). This contingent cause is exclusively pure and...

[The cause] is with outflows (*sāsrava*). Its fruit is common to both the outflowing and non-outflowing [states], and possesses the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*). If it is the dependent cause (*apekṣā-hetu*) for purification, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound;
its cause is common to both the outflowing and non-outflowing [states] and possesses the three natures, while its fruit is exclusively non-outflowing and pure (*anāsrava-viśuddhi*).

However, since this commentary states that "the indeterminate is itself the cause," and so forth, up to "it is called the remaining outflows (*āsrava*) and so on," it does not explain [the causes] according to the three types of ten causes found in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

If one were to rely on that text, if the indeterminate cause were itself untainted (*anāsrava*), then the phrase "difficult to defile as a cause" would imply that tainted phenomena of the three natures are collectively termed "defiled" (*saṃkleśa*). Defiled...

Because the cause-stage also subsumes the aforementioned indeterminate causes, and because the commentary (*śāstra*) itself addresses the three natures—wholesome and so forth—the causes and effects have already been explained.
One should therefore state: "indeterminate causes and wholesome causes" (reflect further and consult the commentaries). As for those defiled by the power of wholesome arising and so forth:
if they are uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), they arise from the defilement of wholesome arising and so forth; if they are contaminated phenomena of the three natures, they are all...

Regarding the question of whether [the seeds] are defiled or undefiled from the perspective of observation, and why they are called "cause and effect" based on the designation of their common and distinct characteristics and natures:

if they share the same nature, then wholesome seeds produce their own manifest results, such as wholesome states; if they are of different natures, it is like how wholesome and unwholesome karma serve as causes.
And it induces its own result, which is the indeterminate (avyākṛta) maturation (vipāka).
The commentary states: "It also obtains, within the cause, that which is superior and pure. This refers precisely to the manifestation of the noble path (āryamārga), which is untainted (anāsrava).
Since the noble path is the means of realization and nirvāṇa is the dharma to be realized, the noble path is so named.

The pure dharma is, at present, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Based upon the uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) within the locus, these act as the causal conditions for the manifestation of the uncontaminated noble path (*ārya-mārga*) that realizes nirvāṇa.

Since the manifest noble path arises from causes, the uncontaminated seeds do not act as the causal conditions for the nirvāṇa that is realized; for nirvāṇa does not arise from causes. Do not [view it otherwise].

The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "This cause is the cause for attaining the purity of nirvāṇa; it is immediately said that the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) acts as the cause by which the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*) is obtained.

Since the unconditioned is not produced by a cause and because the unconditioned is remote [from causal processes], the subsequent treatise does not mention the basis of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Because the projecting cause obtains the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga*), it is known that this cause merely..."
It is capable of realizing nirvāṇa, taking the manifestation of the untainted noble path as its causal condition. The lower treatise discusses only the locus of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*):
the projecting cause consists of seeds producing seeds, and seeds producing manifest activities (*samudācāra*), whereby one obtains the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).

If it is a karmic seed, one obtains the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*); if it is an external object such as sound or grain, one obtains the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*). Now, this [treatise] concerns the immediate...
Regarding the phrase "the cause of the three natures... up to because it can induce the concordant and dominant fruits":

the meaning of this passage is that if the cause is wholesome, the fruit is also wholesome; if the cause is unwholesome, the fruit is also wholesome; if the cause is unwholesome, the fruit is also unwholesome;
