if the cause is indeterminate, the fruit is also indeterminate; and even an indeterminate cause can obtain a dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

Regarding the fruit: because it is like external grains and the like, the fruit conforms to the nature of its cause. All of the above concerns how causes and conditions can produce *niṣyanda-phala* (concordant fruits).
Alternatively, if the cause is of an untainted (*anāsrava*) wholesome nature, the fruit may also be neutral (*avyākṛta*).

If the six perfections (*pāramitā*) are tainted (*sāsrava*), they obtain only four fruits, excluding the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*). If the six perfections are untainted, they obtain four fruits; as for the remaining *vipāka-phala* (ripening fruits), they are excluded.
If the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [factors] mutually support one another across six aspects, one shall obtain the five fruits.

This is just as the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is produced by the support of uncontaminated karma, thereby eliciting a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*). That which is obtained through uncontaminated karma is actually a dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Furthermore, when uncontaminated factors manifest, they induce a similar flow (*niṣyandaphala*) through mutual succession; if they are attained simultaneously, they possess the four characteristics.
At the same time, the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) are termed the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*). Therefore, untainted acquisitions (*anāsrava-prāpti*) obtain two fruits.

If they are tainted wholesome states, they likewise obtain two fruits: the dharmas that are outflowing (*niṣyanda*) obtain the outflow fruit; the preceding and succeeding marks (*lakṣaṇa*) obtain the outflow fruit;

and the simultaneous mind, mental factors, and their outflows obtain the four marks, which are termed the sovereign fruit. It should be understood that the nature of being wholesome or unwholesome applies to all three natures (*tri-śīla*).

If wholesome states serve as the cause, two fruits are obtained: they produce a wholesome fruit, which is the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), and they also produce an indeterminate fruit, which is the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
If unwholesome states serve as the cause, two fruits are likewise obtained; namely, the acquisition of an unwholesome fruit.
This is the *niṣyanda-phala* (outflow fruit). It is also obtained as an *avyākṛta-phala* (neutral fruit), which is the *vipāka-phala* (ripening fruit).
If it is a neutral cause, the cause may pertain to all three natures while the fruit is exclusively neutral. If one knows that a neutral cause yields a neutral fruit, this is the *niṣyanda-phala*.
If a wholesome or unwholesome cause results in a neutral fruit, this is the *vipāka-phala*.
The Commentary states: "As for 'the pure cause acting as a condition for being near to Bodhi,' this is an explanation.

In this commentary, it is provisionally based on the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) at the time of attaining Buddhahood acting as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*);

it does not refer to the [realization of] the Truths during the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and so forth that precede it. The Commentary further states: "This condition is as previously distinguished regarding the cause; whichever nature the fruit belongs to, it pervades all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*)."

This is as previously explained regarding the absence of an interval; it is further clarified here: for instance, when a preceding moment of contaminated mind induces a subsequent moment of uncontaminated fruit, this should be understood according to the method established for the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

The commentary states: "If one takes the future as cause and effect, it is not the present," and so forth; this establishes the principle that while the meaning resembles the future, there is no actual future.
Within this commentary, "not being before the cause" constitutes one point, because the effect does not exist prior to the cause.
Furthermore, "being the effect" constitutes another distinct point, because it exists after the cause while being identical to what preceded it. If...
When the mind takes a future object as its focal point (*ālambana*), the cause exists in the future, yet the resulting mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are not in the present.
This is because a result cannot exist prior to its cause; only when a result depends upon a preceding cause can it be designated as a "result.

However, this is not the case here either. Although the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) exists in the present, it resembles the future in its meaning; thus, it is the result of the perceiving mind and mental factors.
This is also the present; it is also called cause and effect. That which serves as the cause may be simultaneous with or prior to [the effect];
that which serves as the effect may be simultaneous with or posterior to [the cause]. As I understand it, if the present mind takes the past as its object:
This means that the cause precedes the effect; however, if the present mind takes a future object as its condition, then the effect would precede the cause.
Thus, it would not be the case that "the cause is prior and the effect is posterior. Such is the intent of the objection.

The Commentary states: "Its substance consists of the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), which thus pervades the eight consciousnesses; the five faculties constitute its substance, and the fruit is exclusively that which is known by mind and mental factors.

If it pervades the eight consciousnesses, then the substance consists of the mental faculty (*manas*) and the five material faculties; thus, it employs the six faculties. The Commentary further states:
"Regarding these first three fruits, their nature as fruits is identical; the causes may be inferred accordingly. This refers to the basis of the immediately preceding cessation.

The bases: the basis of objects, and the basis of faculties. These first three bases are results; all phenomena that are results of these three bases are identical to the results of these three bases.

These results are exclusively mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). Since they are mind and mental factors, they encompass the three natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral) as well as the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) categories.
For instance, within the basis of objects, if a Śrāvaka subsequently gives rise to untainted mind and mental factors, they are exclusively...

Regarding the establishment of truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*): if a bodhisattva gives rise to uncontaminated mind and mental factors (*anāsrava-citta-caitasika*) through subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), these are of an uncontaminated wholesome nature.
If they are the immediate cessation, the basis, and the cause, they are also the fruit of the mind and mental factors, and they are themselves mind and mental factors;
that is, the mind and mental factors of the preceding moment that have ceased serve as the cause and the basis, while the mind and mental factors of the subsequent moment constitute the fruit. If...

The objective field (*ālambana*) is divided into the basis (*āśraya*) and the cause (*hetu*). This encompasses all phenomena, both material (*rūpa*) and mental (*citta-cetasika*). For example, when another’s mind arises taking another’s mind as its object, that objective field serves as both the cause and the basis.
If the result consists solely of minds and mental factors, then the objective field is divided into the cause as the basis, while the cognizing minds and mental factors constitute the result.
If the root is the basis and the cause, it then encompasses both the material and the mental; the material is, for instance, as follows:

Regarding the five material faculties (*rūpīndriya*): the mind that cognizes them is itself the faculty. If the fruit consists solely of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), then the six faculties serve as the causal basis (*āśraya*), and the mind and mental factors constitute the fruit.

Question: Since the immediately preceding mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) already exists within the basis of the faculties, it would already include the basis of the immediately preceding cessation (*anantara-niruddha-āśraya*). Why, then, is this separately established as the fifth [basis], the "immediately preceding cessation"?

Regarding the basis (*āśraya*): the answer is that this [basis] pertains to both matter and mind. In terms of the faculties, it refers exclusively to the uninterrupted succession of mind and mental factors.

The *Śāstra* states: "As for 'direct and auxiliary conditions,' whether their results are broad or narrow, their functional activity (*kāritra*) and their efficient operation (*puruṣakāra*) must necessarily be identical to that which is produced.
The meaning of this passage is that if there is a basis of functional activity and a basis of efficient operation, these two bases obtain the result.

In terms of both breadth and narrowness, they are all similar. If one considers their activity (*kāritra*) and their specific efficacy (*puruṣakāra*), they all equally obtain the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
However, there are differences in terms of intimacy and remoteness. For example, when felling a tree, the location where it occurs is called the "place of action" (*karmapradeśa*).

The human effort and exertion that are most intimately connected to the activity is called "human efficacy" (*puruṣakāra*). Excluding the axe and other such items, which are called "instruments of action" (*karaṇa*), the activity itself is remote; this refers specifically to the person.
The functions of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and the axe, etc., are similar to the actions performed when cutting down a tree and so forth.
The commentary states: "These two fruits encompass both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), as well as all three moral natures (*tridhātu*); the causes are likewise.

These two fruits refer to the fruit obtained through the basis of human effort (*puruṣakāra-adhiṣṭhāna*) and the fruit obtained through the basis of functional activity (*kāritra-adhiṣṭhāna*). These two fruits encompass the contaminated and uncontaminated, as well as the three moral natures.

In nature, it is also like when a preceding contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind acts as the cause to project and produce the subsequent moment of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
At that time, the preceding moment’s associated contaminated mind and mental factors are termed the "agent" (*kartṛ*).

The simultaneous attention (*manaskāra*), the attainment (*samāpatti*), the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and so forth, are termed the "instruments" (*karaṇa*). Thus, the contaminated mind and its associates constitute the agent, the action (*karman*), and the instruments; the action serves as...

Regarding cause and effect, these may both be untainted (*anāsrava*). If a preceding moment of tainted mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) acts as the cause, it can induce a subsequent moment of tainted mind and mental factors;
in this case, the preceding moment of tainted associated mind and mental factors is termed the "agent" (*kartṛ*).

At the time of the cause, the act of attention (*manasikāra*) that attains the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) is termed the "instrument" (*karaṇa*). These two results produced by this instrument are both tainted. (3)

Regarding the statement, "The nature of the mind and mental factors is the fruit; by analogy, the cause is likewise," this means that the cause also encompasses the three natures—leakage (*āsrava*), non-leakage (*anāsrava*), and the neutral (*avyākṛta*).
These minds and mental factors of the three natures, whether leaking or non-leaking, all take the associated mind and mental factors as their agent.

Furthermore, the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) such as attention (*manasikāra*) occurring simultaneously are termed the instruments of action. For example, when an unwholesome mind arises, the associated mind...

The mental factors (*caitta*) are called the "agent" (*kartṛ*), while the simultaneous attention (*manasikāra*), the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and so forth, are called the "instruments" (*karaṇa*).
The Commentary states: "Thus, these two, along with the five previously mentioned [factors], constitute the 'uncontaminated record' (*anāsrava-vyākaraṇa*), which is the cause;

even this [process] conforms to the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) in its operation based on the six consciousnesses. Now, regarding these two: they refer to the basis of activity (*kāritrāśraya*) and the basis of human effort (*puruṣakārāśraya*). And...

The first five are: the basis of speech (*vāk-āśraya*), the basis of experience (*anubhava-āśraya*), the basis of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-āśraya*), the basis of seeds with moisture (*sasneha-bīja-āśraya*), and the basis of objects (*viṣaya-āśraya*).
These exclude the five bases of immediate cessation (*samanantara-niruddha*) and the basis of the faculties (*indriya*).

All these aforementioned bases are universally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); that is, their causes and effects encompass both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). As for the basis of activity (*kāritra-āśraya*)...
The basis for human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). That which is both cause and effect and is untainted (*anāsrava*) is as follows:

when the tainted, indeterminate eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) induces the arising of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), the preceding moment’s mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) associated with that tainted, indeterminate eighth consciousness are called the "agent" (*kartṛ*), while the simultaneous attention (*manasikāra*) that attains the four marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth is called the "reaction" (*pratipatti*). It induces [the wisdom].
The subsequent moment of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is itself an indeterminate cause that gives rise to an outflow-free (anāsrava) fruit.
If the preceding speech-reliance is indeterminate, it is a "conformity-to-explanation" cause; its fruit may be either with-outflows or outflow-free, yet it is itself indeterminate.

Here, the expressive signifier serves as the cause, and among the resultant phenomena expressed by it, there are those that include outflow-free resultant phenomena. If it pertains to the sphere of the reception of phenomena...

Commentary: This refers to the condition of relative dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*). Its results encompass both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), all of which are remote [results].

Regarding the locus of the perfuming habit-energy (*vāsanā*), there is the locus of the moistened seed. If it is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) seed, then that cause is capable of producing contaminated or uncontaminated results.
Since it is a seed, it must be an indeterminate seed acting as the direct cause (*sākṣāt-kāraṇa*) that gives rise to the uncontaminated dharma-result.

If one examines it from a more remote perspective, these are also empty of inherent existence. This is just as in the stages of the profound *sambhāra-mārga* (provisional equipment) and *prayoga-mārga* (preparatory application), where the seeds of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the seeds of the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are perfumed within the eighth consciousness.

Since these seeds of the factors conducive to liberation and penetration are themselves contaminated (*sāsrava*), when their characteristics are subsumed under their nature, they are identical to the [ultimate] nature.

The eight consciousnesses are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). These very seeds of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the factors conducive to discernment (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are termed "indeterminate.
These same factors conducive to liberation and conducive to discernment can, from afar, act as conditions;

with the outflowing indeterminate seeds as their cause, they are also able to indirectly support the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) seeds, thereby giving rise to the manifestation of the uncontaminated in this life. These very factors conducive to liberation...

The seeds of the stages of liberation (*vimokṣabhāgīya*) and the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) draw forth and give rise to the manifestation of uncontaminated minds (*anāsrava-citta*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
This is neutral (*avyākṛta*); it is produced by a neutral cause; it is produced by a neutral cause; it is produced from a neutral cause to yield an uncontaminated fruit.
This interpretation follows the second fascicle of the *Śāstra*, which states: "The various contaminated seeds and the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) are [identical] in substance..."

Because there is no distinction, it is subsumed under the indeterminate (avyākṛta) nature. If, within the sphere of objects (viṣaya-dharmāyatana), that which is also indeterminate serves as the cause, its fruit may be either contaminated (sāsrava) or uncontaminated (anāsrava).
For example, when contaminated minds and mental factors take the five sense objects and so forth as their objects, these [objects] are themselves indeterminate.

That fruit may be either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*). If it is neutral, then when an uncontaminated fruit arises from a cause, if it arises subsequent to a Śrāvaka’s uncontaminated [attainment], it takes only the established truth (*prajñaptisatya*) as its object.

If it arises subsequent to a Bodhisattva’s uncontaminated [attainment], it can take the established truth as its object, and it can also take as its objects the mundane realms such as the five contaminated sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). This is the contaminated [fruit].

The objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is itself indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and constitutes the cause; its result, however, extends to include uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Excluding the immediately preceding basis (*samanantara-āśraya*), there is necessarily no indeterminate [result]; thus, both cause and result extend to the uncontaminated.

Regarding that immediately preceding basis, the two pairs of results produced are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), because those two causes—the immediately preceding basis which is contaminated—are themselves indeterminate.
Therefore, it does not produce an untainted (anāsrava) fruit. This is just as within the context of the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya):

if a preceding neutral (avyākṛta) mind serves as the cause, it can certainly not induce the subsequent moment’s untainted mental fruit; for if the cause is neutral, the fruit must necessarily be tainted (sāsrava).
However, if a preceding neutral mind serves as the cause, it can indeed induce the subsequent moment’s tainted wholesome (kuśala) mental fruit.

Alternatively, it refers to the results of unwholesome minds and so forth. Within the locus of the faculties (*indriya*), there is absolutely no case where a result such as a pure mind (*anāsrava-citta*) arises with a faculty that is a contaminated indeterminate (*sāsrava-avyākṛta*) fivefold consciousness as its cause. This is because a faculty that is indeterminate does not produce a pure result.

In this present interpretation, excluding the locus of the faculties as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), there is no instance where [a result] fails to arise due to an indeterminate cause.
Regarding the untainted fruit (*anāsrava-phala*): this follows the method of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) based on the preceding six consciousnesses.

In the system of the Lesser Vehicle, the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) must necessarily have a neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind of the preceding moment as its cause to induce the fruit of an untainted mind in the succeeding moment.
It is certainly not the case that tainted (*sāsrava*) neutral faculties (*indriya*) can serve as the cause to produce the fruit of untainted fivefold sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna*).

The Commentary states: "If the seventh and eighth consciousnesses take the indeterminate as their immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), then cause and effect both encompass the untainted (*anāsrava*);

that is, while seven [of the faculties] are tainted (*sāsrava*), six are untainted. This means that within the Mahāyāna, when the seventh and eighth consciousnesses function as immediate conditions, they are indeterminate in nature;

yet, as for the effect, it encompasses the untainted. This is just as the non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) eighth consciousness becomes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*mahā-ādarśa-jñāna*).
At the time of wisdom, it is the preceding moment of the indeterminate eighth consciousness acting as the cause that draws forth the subsequent moment of the untainted fruit.

If the obscured-indeterminate seventh consciousness transforms into the Wisdom of Equality, it is the preceding moment of the indeterminate seventh consciousness acting as the cause that draws forth the subsequent moment of the untainted fruit. All such instances are termed "indeterminate."

This refers to the cause and effect [of the transformation of the basis], which encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). This interpretation concerns the sequential relationship between cause and effect.

If one interprets it as simultaneous dependence, then the sixth consciousness relies upon the seventh consciousness—which is contaminated and neutral (*avyākṛta*)—as its root; yet the sixth consciousness gives rise to the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (the wisdom of wondrous observation).
Thus, it takes this neutral root as its cause. This excludes the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the root-cause (*hetu-pratyaya*).

As for the statement that "even its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and cause (*hetu*) also extend to the untainted (*anāsrava*)," the intent of this commentary is as follows:
the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), being untainted, serve as causes and give rise to results of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). These include:

the basis of speech (*vāk-āśraya*), the basis of experience (*anubhava-āśraya*), the basis of moistening seeds (*sneha-bīja-āśraya*), the basis of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-āśraya*), the basis of objects (*viṣaya-āśraya*), the basis of activity (*kāritra-āśraya*), and the basis of human effort (*puruṣakāra-āśraya*).
These seven aforementioned bases (āśraya) have causes that span both the outflowing (sāsrava) and non-outflowing (anāsrava) natures, as well as the three moral natures.

Their fruits, however, span the indeterminate (avyākṛta) nature. Excluding five causal factors (though this may not yet be understood, it can be understood through reflection), if the seeds of the latencies (vāsanā) and the two bases of the "intercalary" (saṃvartanīya) seeds are non-outflowing causes, then their fruits—which span the indeterminate nature—can never arise from a non-outflowing cause acting as the direct cause (sākṣāt-hetu).

"Result. This is explained here in terms of remote causality. That is to say, within the context of *pariṇāma-cyuti* (transformative birth-and-death), uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma involving conceptualization serves as the cause, which is able to produce the result of the maturation (*vipāka*) of transformative birth-and-death, which is ethically neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Thus, an uncontaminated cause gives rise to a neutral result. Furthermore, it is like how a preceding moment of uncontaminated [consciousness] acts as the inducer for subsequent moments of contaminated consciousness.
This excludes the fruit of an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*). The present explanation is given in terms of remote conditions.
If one considers the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), then it refers only to the exclusion of the basis of the immediate condition and the basis of the faculties (*indriya*).

It is absolutely impossible for a preceding moment that is untainted (*anāsrava*) to induce a subsequent fruit of an indeterminate mind. If a preceding moment of untainted mind acts as a condition, it can only produce a subsequent wholesome [mind].

The mind is the fruit. Furthermore, there is no occurrence of an indeterminate mental fruit arising from the five material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) as its cause—provided one excludes the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the basis of the faculties (*indriyāśraya*). This is formulated based on the six consciousnesses.

If, however, it relies on the immediately preceding condition of the seventh consciousness, then for a Bodhisattva in the stage of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*), it is induced from the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) as its cause, giving rise to the indeterminate.

Regarding the seventh consciousness: it takes the preceding moment of outflow-free (anāsrava) [consciousness] as its cause and draws forth the subsequent moment of outflow-possessing (sāsrava) and indeterminate (avyākṛta) fruit.

Thus, while taking the outflow-free as its cause, its fruit is of an indeterminate nature. When acting as a cause for the indeterminate, with the exception of the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) and the faculty-condition (indriya-pratyaya), the remaining causes encompass both the outflow-possessing and outflow-free, as well as all three natures (tridhātu). If this dharma is discussed in terms of the six consciousnesses, the question is as follows, like Maudgalyāyana:

One enters the untainted meditative absorption (*anāsrava-samādhi*) of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Yet, one gives rise to the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which is sudden and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Furthermore, from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, the sixth consciousness of Bodhisattvas constantly enters the indeterminate state, yet they also give rise to indeterminate five-fold sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).

These five consciousnesses rely upon the sixth consciousness as their basis for discernment; thus, they are both outflows (*sāsrava*) and causes. Since their fruits are generally indeterminate, how is this [to be understood]?

One should understand that the middle section relies on the six consciousnesses to establish its method, yet excludes the sense organs (*indriya*) and their bases (*āyatana*). Furthermore, the preceding commentary explains:
"Thus, these two and the five preceding neutral [factors]... and so forth, up to "...this conforms to the Lesser Vehicle. The meaning of this passage is as follows:

"these two" refers to the activity (*kāritra*) and the human effort (*puruṣakāra*); "the five preceding" refers to the three factors—the immediately ceased [consciousness], the object (*ālambana*), and the sense organ (*indriya*).
Together with the aforementioned two—the activity (*kāritra*) and the virile efficacy (*puruṣakāra-śakti*)—these are called the five.

Among these five, excluding the immediately preceding cessation and the basis of the faculties (*indriya-adhiṣṭhāna*), the remaining three are all neutral (*avyākṛta*) and are thus causes. Regarding whether they are contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it is as in the case of objects (*viṣaya*):
if a contaminated, neutral object serves as a cause, then if a contaminated mind and mental factors take it as their object, they become contaminated. If...

The subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) untainted (*anāsrava*) mind and mental factors of a Bodhisattva take this as their object; thus, the fruit is untainted. This interpretation is also acceptable. The sub-commentary states:

"If there were a difference between the material faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and the mental faculty (*manas*)," meaning that if the five material faculties were tainted (*sāsrava*), they would be of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).
As such, while they serve as causes for the five faculties themselves, they cannot act as causes to produce untainted fivefold consciousnesses. That is, the indeterminate [faculties]...

A cause does not produce an untainted (anāsrava) fruit. If the six consciousnesses take the preceding moment as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the mental faculty (*manas*), and if the mind lacks a preceding untainted mind as its cause, it draws forth a subsequent moment of neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind as its fruit; likewise, a neutral mind serves as the cause to produce a subsequent untainted fruit.
This is discussed based on the first six consciousnesses, and this is the same in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. However, the *Sautrāntika*...

Vasubandhu: The five consciousnesses possess the five material sense-faculties as their simultaneous (sahabhū) bases. The five consciousnesses also possess the mind-faculty (manas-indriya) as their immediately preceding (samanantara) base.
However, the sixth mental consciousness possesses only the immediately preceding mind-faculty of the prior moment, and thus lacks a simultaneous mind-faculty.
In the Mahāyāna, within the mental faculty (*manas*), both [the tainted and untainted] coexist.

Just as the sixth consciousness takes the seventh consciousness—the root of non-cognition—as its cause, the sixth consciousness is able to enter the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state. The seventh consciousness takes the eighth consciousness, which is tainted and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), as its cause;
the seventh consciousness thereby induces the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*). If the immediately preceding mental faculty (*samanantarāśraya-manas*) serves as the cause, then its...

The seventh consciousness has the indeterminate as its cause, while its effects may be both pure (anāsrava) and impure; for example, the indeterminate seventh consciousness induces the arising of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).

Alternatively, it may have the pure as its cause, while its effects may be both indeterminate and pure; for example, the pure seventh consciousness induces the arising of the indeterminate seventh consciousness.
The eighth consciousness has [the seventh] as its cause, while its effects may be pure; for example, the indeterminate eighth consciousness.
It becomes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
The Commentary states: "In this context, the function of 'human effort' (*puruṣakāra*) refers exclusively to the activity of sentient beings as persons;

it does not refer merely to internal sentient beings alone. If one speaks of the fundamental basis of human effort, it refers only to the activity of persons as individuals. Thus, it is called "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*).
It is "function" (*prayoga*). This refers to a person being called a "man" (*puruṣa*). The physical strength of this man is able to construct houses and rooms;
when these houses and rooms are successfully completed, it is termed the "fruit of human function" (*puruṣakāra-phala*). Tools such as axes and hoes are termed "instruments of action.

Furthermore, because the person serves as the cause, they are able to perform functions such as reaping grain, weeding rice, or harvesting other crops; this is termed "functional utility" (*vṛtti-prayoga*). Therefore, the text below speaks of "attaining the fruit of functional utility" and so forth.

It is not said that the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) is attained. Now, this also includes the "human-effort" (*puruṣakāra*) fruit; it is not only sentient beings who occupy the position of human effort.

There are four kinds of human-effort fruits regarding phenomena (*dharma*): first, the simultaneously-arisen human-effort fruit, which refers to seeds producing actualities (*pravṛtti*) and actualities producing seeds;
second, the immediate human-effort fruit, which refers to seeds; third, the transcendent human-effort... [text truncated]

"Purushakāra-phala" (the fruit of human effort) refers to the vipākaphala (ripened fruit). Fourth is "non-arising purushakāra," which refers to the severing of afflictions through the Noble Path and the realization of the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*), and so forth.
Furthermore, another interpretation states: "Now, this also includes not only internal sentient beings.

This means that the various stages of the earth and so forth serve as the basis for *purushakāra*; since each stage is the direct cause for sprouts and the like, it is said: "and the plowshare acts as the agent."

[It is] "by means of. Now, as for the statement that both "activity" (*kāritra*) and "function" (*puruṣakāra*) are expressed by the third case ending (*tṛtīyā-vibhakti*): Question: It is said that the instrument and activity are expressed by the third case ending;

how then can "human function" (*puruṣakāra-kāritra*) also be included under the [third] case ending? Answer: Indeed, both "activity" and "human function" are subsumed under the third case ending, the instrumental (*karaṇa*).

This is because a person, being a conventional designation (*prajñapti-pudgala*), possesses activity; thus, it is included within the category of words denoting hearing (or verbal expression). This is just like the case of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*).
Cessation (*nirodha*) is also included within the third oblique case (*tṛtīyā-vibhakti*). "Discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā*) refers to wisdom (*prajñā*). Wisdom is the instrument for realizing *tathatā*;
it is precisely by means of wisdom that one is able to realize *tathatā*. This is like the case where, once visual consciousness has arisen, the eye-faculty and its seeds [are said to be the cause];
this is explained here as the "agentive function" (*puruṣakāra*) of dharmas. However, regarding the Master of the Commentary’s (*ṭīkā-kāra*) interpretation, there is a difficulty to be discerned.

If the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is the locus of support for the preceding faculty, and the seed is the locus of support for the preceding habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and so on up to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), all of these are the loci of support for the preceding faculties, the immediately preceding conditions, and the objective spheres.
Now, the Upādhyāya’s interpretation states: "Just as at the time of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one grasps the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that is able to awaken the mind."
"O King, it is because [the mind] is proximate through its mental attention (*manasikāra*). This mental attention is precisely the basis for the activity of the person (*puruṣakāra-adhiṣṭhāna*).
As for other simultaneous minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), they are remote; thus, they are termed the basis for the function of the instrument (*karaṇa-kriyā-adhiṣṭhāna*).

Furthermore, it is said: 'However, this remoteness is also explained as being ultimately [due to] the seeds. It is also like visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), which is called the 'agent' because the eye-faculty and its seeds are proximate."

The efficient cause (*puruṣakāra*) and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) are remote; therefore, they are termed "instrumental action" (*karaṇa-kriyā*). The current text uses the word "like" (*yathā*);
it does not say "is identical to" (*eva*). According to the commentary (*śāstra*), this constitutes a case of "separation" (*viyoga*).

If the eye-faculty were identical to the locus that serves as the basis for the preceding faculty, or if seeds were identical to the locus that serves as the basis for habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), then—since we now treat them as efficient causes—they would constitute a case of "separation."

The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is subsumed within the aforementioned basis of the immediately preceding [condition]. If it is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it is subsumed within the aforementioned basis of the objective field (*viṣaya*).

Now, because it functions as an instrument for production, it is established as being distinct [from the others]. Regarding the explanation that the sense of shame (*hrī*) excludes [the other factors]:
it is also like visual consciousness, which relies upon the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, and thus employs the sixth and seventh consciousnesses as its instruments.

Consciousness functions as the *puruṣakāra* (human effort) cause, as it lacks direct intimacy [with the result]. Other conditions, such as space, light, and so forth, function as the *karaṇa* (instrumental) cause.
The Commentary states:
"In relation to a person lifting a toothpick, the person is the *puruṣakāra* cause, while earth and water are the 'other' causes; these 'other' causes are more remote than the person."

Regarding "all that is produced" (*sarva-kṛtaka*): this refers to the relative distinction between the immediate (*pratyakṣa*) and the remote (*parokṣa*). From the perspective of an external person, the human being is the "instrumental agent" (*puruṣakāra*), and thus the human being is the immediate factor.
Because human effort and power can weed out and eliminate evil tendencies such as the "fangs" (*daṃṣṭrā*), it is defined according to the sense of the remote.

As for earth, water, and so forth, these are termed "auxiliary instruments" (*karaṇa-vyāpāra*); earth and water are therefore remote. Although they are also included within the category of the instrumental agent (*puruṣa*), they are [distinguished as remote] because they function as seeds.
Regarding the cultivation of grain: if there is no human effort to weed and tend the seedlings, there will be no good fruit.
Furthermore, when axes and such tools are used to cut down trees and the like, the person is termed the "human agent" (*puruṣakāra*), while the axe and such are termed "instruments.
Thus, the person is direct, whereas the axe and such are remote.
The Commentary states: "If one follows the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 38, regarding the causes of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), up to the point where 'plowing' is taken as the function;
that treatise regards earth and water as the sovereign efficacy (*puruṣakāra*), while the sun and plowing are regarded as the instrumental function (*karaṇa*)."
This refers to explaining it according to the actual principle.

The *Śāstra* states: "That is to say, all untainted views (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*), all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and even those included within the category of productive causes (*ākṣepa-hetu*)—these constitute the basis for true vision (*tattva-darśana*).
In this context, the preceding moment of untainted vision acts as the cause for the manifestation of the subsequent moment of untainted [vision]."
When one perceives the active manifestations and realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), these are distinct from the very dharmas of birth and death.
Thus, within the present basis for grasping causes, because the first five [bases] consist of tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas, they differ from the sixth, which is the distinct basis for true vision.
Furthermore, the first five tainted dharmas differ from those that lack the six bases; this remains so even though they are untainted (*anāsrava*).

When [an uncontaminated state] manifests, there are likewise the first five bases (*āśraya*). When the uncontaminated manifests, there is an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), which is precisely the base of the objective sphere (*viṣayāśraya*).
When a preceding mind takes up a succeeding mind, there is also the base of the immediately preceding cessation (*samanantaranirodhāśraya*).

Furthermore, when the uncontaminated manifests, there is also the faculty that serves as its support (*āśrayendriya*), as well as attention (*manaskāra*) and the attainment of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, which function as the instruments of its activity. That is to say...

It is also the basis for activity (*kāritra*). Although true seeing (*tattvadarśana*) possesses the aforementioned five bases, as for how those five bases are subsumed within the [six] bases—given that the five bases do not include the sixth, the basis of true seeing—they lack an object apart from that.
This excludes those who perceive the cause and effect [of seeds], whereby their own fruits become seeds; although they lack [an external object],...
When outflowing views (*āsrava-dṛṣṭi*) manifest, they likewise arise as manifest outflows from their own uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) acting as cause and condition.
Now, by excluding the uncontaminated seed as the cause, the uncontaminated [result] acts as the cause and condition; thus, it is subsumed within the category of the "arising cause" (*janaka-hetu*).

This is the production of a manifest state from a seed, which is subsumed under the category of the "originating cause" (*utpādaka-hetu*). Although it is an uncontaminated manifest state, it nevertheless perfumes and forms [a seed].
Regarding the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*): here too, we exclude those seeds that arise simultaneously with their own manifest activity (*samudācāra*).

Since they function as causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), they are subsumed within the category of "projecting causes" (*ākṣepaka-hetu*). In the present context of the basis for true vision (*tattva-darśana-āśraya*), we refer only to the untainted manifest activities that project subsequent moments of untainted manifest activity.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Regarding 'the subsequent conditioned, untainted [states] can induce subsequent dharmas,' one asks:
what is the distinction between this basis of true seeing—which is the inducing of a present state by a present state—and the equal-and-immediate basis (*samanantara-āśraya*)? Answer:

If that equal-and-immediate condition refers specifically to the preceding moments of mind and mental factors, then the subsequent moment serves as the basis for opening the way; however, the present [basis] is the basis of true seeing."

That which precedes and induces what follows is the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). Within the True Path of Seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*), the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) induces the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) and the sixteen moments of the Path of Seeing.
That is to say: the preceding "Dharma-knowledge-acceptance" (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) induces the subsequent "Dharma-knowledge" (*dharmajñāna*);

Dharma-knowledge induces the subsequent "Subsequent-knowledge-acceptance" (*anvayajñānakṣānti*), and so on, until the "Subsequent-knowledge of the Path" (*mārgānvayajñāna*), where each preceding moment acts as the cause that induces each succeeding moment of seeing.
It is the Path (*mārga*). Since beginningless time, the realization of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) is the most difficult to attain.
Once this has been attained, one is then able to enter the second stage and so forth, up to the stage of a Tathāgata. Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

Just as when a bamboo stalk is split, the second knot can be broken by first breaking the first knot; so too, having attained the first stage (*bhūmi*), the remaining stages are realized through the subsequent overcoming [of obstacles].
Regarding this, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that from the "seed" (*bīja*) four arise as five, and from the "unraveling" (*vibhaṅga*) five arise as four; the meaning of this passage is as follows.
If there is a learner’s (śaikṣa) untainted mind, it arises immediately after four other minds, namely:
from a preceding moment of a learner’s mind, or from a wholesome mind of the three realms. As for this learner’s mind, it can immediately give rise to five other minds.
That is to say, it gives rise to the wholesome minds of the other three realms; it gives rise to subsequent moments of the *śaikṣa* untainted mind; and it gives rise to the *śaikṣa* untainted mind.
That is to say, the *aśaikṣa* untainted mind arises from five types of minds: namely, from the wholesome minds of the other three realms, and from the *śaikṣa* mind and the *aśaikṣa* mind.
That is to say, immediately following the untainted mind, it is able to give rise to the other [minds].
The four minds refer to the arising of wholesome minds in the three realms of others, as well as the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).

The commentary states that those which assist in the formation of causes and conditions are termed "appropriated" (*parigṛhīta*). If the five bases (*āśraya*) are considered remote conditions, they can assist in the formation of contaminated (*sāsrava*) causes and conditions;
however, regarding the seeds of the mind and mental factors, these seeds must currently exist within the body before they can arise.

The causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the outflowing (*āsrava*) [dharmas] is so called because it refers to the manifestation of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). The first five bases (*āyatana*) are termed "appropriation" (*upādāna*).

They are termed appropriation because the seeds of the outflowing produce the manifestation of outflowing mind and mental factors; this is what is meant by the "causal condition. Therefore, it is said:
"It means to appropriate the five conditions for outflowing dharmas. Furthermore, by means of these six bases, the remote dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is able to assist.
The seeds of mind, mental factors, names, and phrases that constitute the direct causes for the attainment of the untainted (*anāsrava*) are now empowered;

it is from these seeds that the manifest outflows (*āsrava*) arise. It is precisely by means of these six bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*) that one is able to sustain the seeds which are the causes and conditions for the untainted, and the arising of the manifest from the seeds is termed "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Therefore, the treatise states: "It fully sustains the six as well as the untainted dharmas. As for the remaining causes...

Regarding "those conditions that can produce dharmas through intimacy," this refers to all [conditions] within the context of the six causes, with the exception of the direct cause-condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "According to what is appropriate, there may be five or six, or even none at all for those that are not mind or mental factors.
If they are contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors, they possess five bases, excluding true vision (*tattvadarśana*). If they are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds...

Regarding mental factors (*caitta*), there are six bases (*āśraya*): namely, the immediate [preceding moment], the sense faculty (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), activity (*kāritra*), human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and true vision (*samyag-darśana*).
These aforementioned six bases are explained solely with respect to the capacity to sustain tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors;

they are not explained with respect to the capacity to sustain the five [aggregates] as being either tainted or untainted. It is not the case that all phenomena (*dharma*), whether tainted or untainted, possess these [bases].
Regarding the five bases: if a contaminated mind or mental factor arises, it possesses all five bases.

If there is contaminated matter (*rūpa*) or contaminated factors dissociated from matter (*viprayukta-dharma*), they possess two bases: the base of contaminated activity (*kāritra-āśraya*) and the base of human effort (*puruṣakāra-āśraya*).
This is also like when matter arises; necessarily, there are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that act as its producers. From the perspective of these producing great elements...

Regarding derived matter (upādāya-rūpa), the primary elements (mahābhūta) that produce it are termed the "agent" (kartṛ) and the "basis" (āśraya). It is not so for the functional efficacy (puruṣakāra) of derived matter itself.

Furthermore, there are other derived matters that arise simultaneously with it, such as other derived matters, the acquisition of the four characteristics (catur-lakṣaṇa), and homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu).
From the perspective of this [primary] matter, these other derived matters, the acquisition of the four characteristics, and so forth, are termed the "instrument" (karaṇa) and the "activity" (kriyā).

Furthermore, when the four great elements arise, they all proceed from the transformation of consciousness. Thus, both consciousness and the seeds of the four great elements are designated as the "agent" (*kartṛ*) and "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*).
The four great elements do not arise independently; when the four great elements arise, there are also other factors present. [Objection:

Are not the four great elements and their four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) all called "instruments" (*karaṇa*)? [Response: The expression "the activity of another" does not apply to the gates of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Regarding "without cause": when a contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind or mental factor arises, there are five bases (*niśraya*).
However, when that which is neither mind nor mental factor—namely, the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*)—arises, there are no five bases.
As for matter (*rūpa*) and the dissociated factors, they possess only two bases. Among these, the first five are causes of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), while the last one is not.

Regarding these: if one refers to the first five bases of reliance—namely, the object (*ālambana*), the uninterrupted [succession], the faculty (*indriya*), the activity (*kāritra*), and the human effort (*puruṣakāra*)—these five bases all pertain to the three moral natures.
If one refers to the latter single base of reliance, which is true vision (*tattvadarśana*), it is exclusively of an untainted wholesome nature (*anāsrava-kuśala*).
Furthermore, when this true vision realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is called true vision; when it abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is also called true vision.
If a preceding thought induces a succeeding thought, this is also called "true seeing.

The commentary states: "This means that the three dharmas are all untainted (*anāsrava*). Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), even within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) there are those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), as well as those of deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and supernormal power (*nairmāṇika*).
This is because each preceding state is inferior, while each succeeding state is superior. That is to say, [the latter] differs from the former.

That which is matured (*vipāka*) and that which serves as the cause for maturation are called "equal" (*sama*). That which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and that which serves as the cause for deportment (*airyāpathika*) are called "superior" (*viśeṣa*).
Deportment and deportment are called "equal. Deportment and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) are called "superior. Craftsmanship and craftsmanship are called "equal.
Craftsmanship and that which is produced by supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*) are called "superior. The supernormal power of the first dhyāna and the [mind] of the first dhyāna...

Regarding the names and so forth: the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) resulting from the first dhyāna serve as causes for, and are superior to, those resulting from the second dhyāna; this should be understood accordingly up to the fourth dhyāna.
As for dharmas of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala*), they function only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), for there is no unwholesomeness in the two higher realms.
Thus, within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the lower levels are termed unwholesome; because they serve as causes for the inferior grades of unwholesomeness, they are called "superior."
That which is middling is also not wholesome. When it serves as the cause for middling unwholesome states, it is called "equal.

When middling unwholesome states serve as the cause for superior unwholesome states, they are called "superior. If superior unwholesome states serve as the cause for inferior unwholesome states, they are called "equal."
"If the nature is untainted (*anāsrava*)," and so forth, refers to the self-arisen dharmas (*svayaṃbhū-dharma*).

The *Śāstra-vivaraṇa* (Sūtra Commentary) states that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle five, and other texts say: "The indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) serves as the cause for the defiled and the wholesome;

even in relation to the active manifestations (*samudācāra*), they are of the same nature. However, regarding the seeds of the three natures within the outflowing realm (*sāsrava*), when their characteristics are subsumed under their nature, they are identical to the eighth consciousness.

It is subsumed under the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). Nevertheless, because it gives rise to seeds and active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of the three natures, and because its causes and effects are simultaneously associated with the wholesome and so forth, it is also called "wholesome seeds.
Accordingly, the active manifestations that arise from them are also of the same nature. Thus it is said: "The indeterminate takes the wholesome and the defiled as its cause."

The Commentary states: "Regarding the dharmas of the desire realm acting as causes for the [dharmas] of the three realms and the outflow-free (anāsrava): if, within the desire realm, the innate wholesome (upapatti-labdha-kuśala) acts as a cause for the innate, this is called 'equal' (sama).

When the innate wholesome acts as a cause for all wisdom (prajñā), it is called 'superior' (viśiṣṭa). When that same wisdom acts as a cause for the wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā), it is called 'equal.
When the wisdom of reflection acts as a cause for the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā) in the form realm, it is called 'superior. At the beginning of the form realm...

The wisdom cultivated through meditation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā) is designated as "equal" when it serves as the cause for the wisdom cultivated through meditation in the first dhyāna. It is designated as "superior" when the wisdom cultivated through meditation in the first dhyāna serves as the cause for the wisdom cultivated through meditation in the second dhyāna, and so on, up to the untainted (anāsrava) state. This should be understood by analogy.
The Commentary states: "This refers only to those of the same nature (*svabhāva*). Even if they were of different natures, they would still be mutually inclusive;

therefore, it is not the case that things of different natures do not include one another. This is the reason for their definitive difference. All [cases] are explained in terms of being of the same nature;

even if the natures were different, they would still be mutually inclusive. That is to say, wholesome or unwholesome karma brings about neutral (*avyākṛta*) results. Although these are of different natures, they are nonetheless congruent in their *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena). For this reason, there is a definitive difference."
Regarding the causal stage: there are causes of wholesome and unwholesome karma that bring about neutral (*avyākṛta*) results. It is on this basis that the subsequent commentary states:

"In terms of nature (*svabhāva*), it is broad. As for mutual inclusion: wholesome karma definitely induces the eighth consciousness of the human or celestial realms, but does not induce the eighth consciousness of the evil destinies, because they are mutually exclusive in their characteristics. If wholesome karma were not to induce [the latter],...

Because it is not concordant with the eighth consciousness of the evil destinies. If determinate evil karma were to project the eighth consciousness of the three evil destinies, it would not project the eighth consciousness of humans or devas, because they are discordant later on; evil karma does not project the eighth consciousness of humans or devas because they are not concordant.
Within its own category (*svabhāga*), that which has self-nature as its cause: as for "self-nature,"...
This means that the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—are each considered in relation to their own nature.

Just as wholesome and unwholesome karma induce neutral results because they are commensurate with one another, so too is the neutral nature considered a "nature" in relation to wholesome and unwholesome karma.
The Commentary states: "The internal serves as the cause for the internal; that which is nurtured serves as the cause for that which is nurtured," and so forth.

"The internal" refers to the sense-bases that support the faculties (*indriya-adhiṣṭhāna*). Thus, the sense-bases that support the faculties serve as the cause for the sense-bases that support the faculties. Within this, the nurtured matter (*aupacayika-rūpa*) serves as the cause for nurtured matter.
Matured matter (*vipākaja-rūpa*) serves as the cause for matured matter. Similarly, matter of uniform outflow (*naiṣyandika-rūpa*) serves as the cause for matter of uniform outflow.
Therefore, it says "such as these. The Commentary states:
"These causes, whether contradictory or non-contradictory, apply to both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) results;

this is likewise even down to the point where they cause conditioned uncontaminated phenomena not to arise and unconditioned phenomena not to manifest. This refers, for example, to those such as the inhabitants of Uttarakuru or the long-lived gods (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva*).
In these states, conditioned phenomena that are untainted do not arise, and unconditioned phenomena are not manifested. These states thus act as contrary causes to the Noble Path.
Once the Noble Path has been attained, one is no longer reborn in the Northern Kuru continent or among the long-lived gods;
having already ceased such rebirth, the Noble Path acts as an antidote to evil.

Regarding the contradiction with the cause: the Commentary states that the "reception" (*anubhava*) and these latter three causes are the same as those mentioned in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (15), which speaks of the results such as arising and abiding therein, but does not mention others because their nature is narrow. However, this applies to both the upper and lower sections of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

The textual locations differ. If one consults the fifteenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, its account of the basis for prior reception and the subsequent three causes—namely, the cause of commonality (*samāna-kārya-hetu*), the cause of contradiction (*viruddha-hetu*), and the cause of non-contradiction (*aviruddha-hetu*)—is identical to that in this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

In the fifteenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is stated that within these four causes, each brings about arising (*utpāda*), abiding (*sthiti*), accomplishment (*niṣpatti*), and attainment (*prāpti*).
Because these four causes are broad, whereas the other six causes are narrow; furthermore, among the remaining causes, there is no arising, abiding, accomplishing, or obtaining.
Moreover, there is another passage in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* likewise states:

however, within these three causes—namely, the cause of common function (*ekārtha-hetu*), the contradictory cause (*virodha-hetu*), and the non-contradictory cause (*avirodha-hetu*)—there is indeed arising, abiding, accomplishing, and obtaining. If...

Regarding the *apekṣā-hetu* (contingent cause), it does not produce or sustain that which is non-outflow (*anāsrava*) or acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*). However, within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, all four causes possess the functions of producing, sustaining, establishing, and acquiring;
thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* is broader than that [other] treatise, which states regarding the *apekṣā-hetu*: [it does not produce or sustain the aforementioned types].

Because it relies solely on the aspect of expectation and because it establishes its own mode of operation, that treatise [the *Abhidharmakośa*] treats the condition of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*) as being narrow in its essential nature. Regarding "its nature is narrow":

"nature" refers to the essential nature (*svabhāva*). As for the statement that among the thirty-eight [conditions], it is "only this" that is predominant within the category of non-contradiction (*avirodha*), and thus it is called "non-contradictory":

furthermore, within that treatise’s discussion of the contradictory cause (*virodha-hetu*), it mentions only "arising" and does not mention "abiding. This constitutes the establishment [of the distinction].
It is so obtained. Furthermore, within the context of what is contradictory (*viruddha*), because it is predominant, only "arising" (*utpāda*) is mentioned.

Within the context of what is non-contradictory (*aviruddha*), because arising is most excellent therein—since it is that which can produce phenomena—it is specifically termed "contradictory arising" even within the contradictory. This accords with and clarifies the text of the *Saṃprayukta-saṃgraha* (or *Samuddeśa*), which speaks of "arising" based on what is predominant.

The Commentary states: "One should know that although the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) in the Mahāyāna does not depend on causes, nor even acts as a cause for the cessation of preceding phenomena—just as when one is separated from the full set of ten causes, or separated from the full set of concordant causes—it nevertheless [acts] toward the preceding pure phenomena."
The concordant cause for the state of separation acts as a discordant cause for fulfillment; it is precisely that which can produce the successive states of separation and fulfillment.
Conversely, the concordant cause for the state of purification acts as a discordant cause for the states of separation and fulfillment;

that concordant cause for purification is precisely what can produce the successive states of purification. Among the ten causes of the indeterminate, those such as frost and snow are able to cause damage.

Regarding the destruction of crops and the like: the preceding states, such as the arising of the green color and so forth, cannot occur; rather, they cause the subsequent states—such as the yellowing, death, and withering—to arise.
Thus, the yellow color and its like act as the cause for production (*janaka-hetu*), while the nature of arising and ceasing acts as the contradictory cause (*virodha-hetu*).

Furthermore, [the preceding states] act as the concordant cause (*anukūla-hetu*) for the subsequent states of withering and yellowing. This same principle applies even to the death of the crops and other subsequent phenomena.
It acts as a concordant cause (*anuloma-hetu*) for the manifestation of the characteristic of blueness.
If that were so, death would also act as a concordant cause for subsequent states such as grain, causing the characteristic of blueness to flourish because the final state arises;

thus, the preceding states of withering and yellowing could not arise. Therefore, it acts as a discordant cause (*virodha-hetu*) for those preceding states, while [acting as a concordant cause] for the subsequent ones.
The subsequent dharma serves as the cause of arising.

Regarding the statement in the Commentary that "the first interpretation is largely the same as the general meaning of the ancients," if one examines the first skillful interpretation in the text concerning the meaning of *vitarka* (applied thought) and so forth in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, it differs greatly from the ancient interpretation; namely, [it] takes [the factors] from among the six causes.
The seeds of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) serve as the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*).

This refers to employing the seeds of karma and so forth found within the remaining causes, specifically the two causes of projection (*ākṣepa*) and actualization (*abhinirvṛtti*). As for the second alternative, it is largely identical to the explanations of the ancient masters.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The question asks: How is it known that the productive cause possesses seeds such as karma? ... up to:
'because it does not state that there is a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)'? The intent of this question is: How is it known that the productive cause possesses the seeds of karma?

Regarding the two locations in the treatise: the first is the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* (the Treatise on the Bodhisattva Stages), and the second is the *Savitarkā Bhūmi* (the Stage with Discursive Thought)."
In these two passages from the treatise, both state that the cause of arising (*utpattihetu*) is subsumed under the productive cause (*janakahetu*).
They do not say that within the cause of arising there exists the karmic seed as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "The answer to this is that it is not so; there are also scriptural passages...

up to "...in the passage concerning 'arising' (*utpatti*), there are also seeds that are not causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Here, the response says: "Within the causes for arising, there are also seeds of karma as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Now, there is also a scriptural passage from the *Mahā-śāstra* (Great Treatise), Volume Ten, which asks: "If [the twelve links]..."
Regarding "mutually awaiting without causes and conditions": for what reason is it said that they await without causes and conditions?

For what reason is it said that the twelve links of dependent origination are established based upon the twelve causes and conditions? If they were subsumed under the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the twelve links would consist of the three causes of attraction, production, and instigation.
As for saying they do not exist as causes and conditions: this refers to the cause of attraction (*ākṣepa-hetu*).

Namely, ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are called the "projecting factors" (*ākṣepaka*). Consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the other five fruits are called the "projected factors" (*ākṣipta*).
Therefore, both the projecting and the projected are termed "projecting causes" (*ākṣepahetu*). As for the "producing cause" (*abhinirvartakahetu*):

craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) are called the "producing causes," while birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are called the "produced. This refers to the stage when the seeds of the five fruits have already been established.
Regarding the name "arising cause" (*utpatti-hetu*), within it there is the "textual" [explanation], which includes the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) of karmic seeds.
Thus, one should know that within the arising cause, there is also the dominant condition of karmic seeds.
As for the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*), it is subsumed within two causes: namely, the projecting cause contains the projecting cause, and the arising cause also contains the projecting cause.

This refers to the causal origin. Therefore, that treatise, within the context of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), states that there exists a "projecting cause" (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) and a "generating cause" (*abhinirvartaka-hetu*).
The Commentary (*Śū*) says: "Furthermore, regarding the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and other texts, who would claim that the 'generating cause' mentioned therein is this very [causal] factor?
As for the meaning of the text: the intention here is to state that although it is said in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* that there is a generating cause, it is exclusively...

The causal conditions that are capable of producing [a result] are subsumed under the category of causes; specifically, within the "Arising" section of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, there is also the seed of karma as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).

This is just as stated in the tenth fascicle of this great treatise (*Mahāśāstra*), and furthermore, within the proof for the cause of arising, there is also the seed of karma as a dominant condition.
This corresponds to the passage from the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāśāstra* cited immediately above, which states that the twelve links of dependent origination effect the drawing forth of birth.

The inclusion [of seeds] within the three causes that initiate and project is the proof for this. Excluding the seeds of manifest activity and the seeds of a different nature that project manifest activity:
"seeds of manifest activity" refers to the seeds from which manifest activity arises; "projecting manifest activity" refers to manifest activity itself;
and "different nature" refers to the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma that produce neutral results, and so forth. As for the cause of initiation, it takes...
"Seeds project their own seeds; how then do they project actualities? ... up to "...because they take the preceding causes as their own essence. Question:

Since this passage takes up the seeds that have not yet been moistened among the four causes—such as the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) and so forth—and since seeds that have not been moistened cannot produce actualities, these must be subsumed under seeds that have already been moistened.
It would therefore be incorrect for them to be included within the projecting cause. Answer: If [they were] already...

The "intercalary" (*rūṇ*) refers to the inclusion of that which has arisen; it also lacks the fault of [including] the past and future. The "intercalary" is the inclusion of what is projected (*ākṣepaka*). The commentary states:
"Excluding those that project their own continuum, as well as the matured (*vipāka*), augmented (*adhipati*), and outflowing (*niṣyanda*) fruits. Regarding the projection within one's own continuum:
If uncontaminated seeds give rise to uncontaminated manifest activity, they are taken here as well because they function as causes and conditions.
However, the seeds of uncontaminated manifest activity are not taken here. If uncontaminated manifest activity realizes the unconditioned, it is not a cause and condition;
therefore, the realization of the unconditioned through the Noble Path is excluded here. Regarding the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), there are two kinds: first—
First, when a seed produces a seed, a seed produces a manifest activity (*samudācāra*), and a manifest activity produces a seed, this is called a "result of outflow" (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Since it is a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is now included here. Second, there is the "figurative result of outflow":

if one receives a retribution of a short life in the present body due to the karma of killing committed in a previous life, this is also called a result of outflow; thus, it is termed a "figurative result of outflow. In reality, it is...

The *adhipati-phala* (dominant fruit) is also excluded here and not taken up. Alternatively, it may be included within the cause for initiating karma (*karmārambhahetu*), specifically that which currently perfumes the seeds.

Regarding the two explanations for the term "lower" (*adhara*) found in the commentary: if one follows the current text of this preceding sub-commentary, which takes only the arising of seeds from seeds and the arising of manifestations from those [seeds], this corresponds to the first of the two lower explanations, which states: "Although there is actual manifestation, it is capable of producing [the result]."

Regarding the cause (*hetu*): among the four types of causes, that which produces its own seeds is frequently interrupted; thus, it is omitted here for brevity. However, the present commentary states:

"Alternatively, taking the currently functioning perfuming seeds within the 'inducing' [cause] as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is precisely what the second explanation in the lower section of the treatise says:
'Alternatively, that which directly accomplishes the fruit is also designated by the name "seed," just as one speaks of the currently manifesting seeds of grain, wheat, and so forth.'"

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Regarding 'a small portion of the first four causes within the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*), excluding the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*),' this means that within the projecting cause, one excludes the seeds of karma and the dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and takes only the seeds of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). This is because [the projecting cause] projects...

Among the seeds of the causal conditions within the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*), none have yet been moistened, as they are distant from the fruit; therefore, it is said here that the projecting cause is taken in its entirety.

However, among these four causes—namely, the producing cause (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*), the specific cause (*viśeṣa-hetu*), the concurrent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the non-obstructive cause (*aviruddha-hetu*)—one likewise excludes karma, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and so forth, and takes only the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Nevertheless, within these four causes, regarding the seeds of the causal condition:
There are two kinds: first, seeds that have not yet been influenced by the conditions of intercalation; second, seeds that have already been influenced by the conditions of intercalation.
Here, we do not take the seeds that have already been influenced by the conditions of intercalation among these four causes.

Now, we take only those seeds among these four causes that have not yet been influenced by the conditions of intercalation; therefore, it is said to be "one part of the four causes," which is to say, one cause.

The four causes of gold are but a partial portion [of the causal process]. That is to say, the productive cause (janaka-hetu) is excluded, because it has already been moistened and because it is proximate to the fruit;
that is, it is the drawing-in cause (ākṣepa-hetu). Furthermore, among these four causes, the seeds of the fully moistened conditions (paripūrṇa-pratyaya-bīja) are likewise not included.

The Commentary states: "If [a seed] has already been affected by the intercalary month, it is all termed 'already matured. Regarding the statement that the generative cause consists of the entirety of the four causes minus a portion of the drawing-in cause:

within these generative causes, one must also exclude the karmic seeds of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Now, among these four causes, within the seeds of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), there are those that are manifest and those that have not yet been affected by the intercalary month.
1. Seeds of the causal condition that have not yet been affected by the intercalary month. 2. Those that have already... [text fragment ends]

Regarding the conditions for being "intercalated" (*vārṣika*): here, we take only those seeds among the four causes that have already been intercalated, because they are similar to the fruit that is about to arise and are proximate to it.

We exclude those among the four causes that have not yet been intercalated. These [excluded] causal seeds belong to the prior projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*), as they are subsumed within the four causes.
Therefore, the productive cause (*abhinirvartaka-hetu*) consists entirely of the minor portions of the four causes, excluding the causal portion within the projecting cause itself.
It is the seed as a condition (*pratyaya-bīja*). Furthermore, it is not included within the "arising cause" (*utpāda-hetu*).
Among the four causes, that which has not yet been moistened by conditions is also a seed that is subsumed under the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*). It is the seed.

The commentary states: "Since these two seeds are both causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*)," referring to the two seeds as the projecting seed (*ākṣepaka-bīja*) and the producing seed (*abhinirvartaka-bīja*).
The commentary further states: "Because these two causes consist solely of seeds," since the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* speaks of the projecting seed.
[This refers to] the seed of origination (*utpatti-bīja*).
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Because these two causes consist solely of seeds. This refers to what is said in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
"The projecting seed (*ākṣepa-bīja*) and the seed of origination (*utpatti-bīja*). Since it says that seeds comprise only seeds—that is, only seeds produce seeds—it refers to the seed.

Regarding the arising of actualized activity (*samudācāra*): since the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* does not mention actualized activity, it does not include the seeds that arise from actualized activity among the other four causes, such as the cause of production (*ākṣepaka-hetu*), which serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

The Commentary states: "Regarding the four causes, such as 'inducing' (*āvāhaka*) and so forth, from among which the 'manifesting cause' (*abhinirvartaka*) is able to produce seeds, [the author] has omitted them for brevity.
Now, in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, it speaks only of the "projecting seed" (*ākṣepaka-bīja*) and the "producing seed" (*janaka-bīja*).

This is because these seeds are infused within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), where they form a single class that continues constantly and without interruption. Even if one cuts off the afflictions (*kleśa*), the seeds of the afflictions [remain].
Because it is only when the Path of the Sage arises that the non-continuity is severed, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* speaks of only two types of seeds.

Although among the causes such as "inducing" (*ākṣepa*) there are also cases where a manifest state (*pravṛtti*) perfumes a seed to serve as its causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), this is because the manifest states that act as perfumers are generally characterized by frequent interruptions.
Furthermore, although the manifest state of the seventh consciousness is also constantly continuous at all times...

Regarding the perfuming agent (*bhāvakatva*): since the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the first six consciousnesses are frequently interrupted, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* briefly does not state that these active manifestations serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Although it states that seeds are the "capable seeds" (*bīja*), they function as the generative cause (*janaka-hetu*).
The Commentary states: "Because this very active manifestation directly produces the fruit... even those subsumed under the other four causes.

Now, since the production of seeds by an active manifestation constitutes a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), and there is no such active manifestation that can directly take the seed as its object-fruit, it is not said that this active manifestation is metaphorically designated as the "fruit of the seed.
