Furthermore, this production of seeds by an active manifestation is not subsumed under the category of the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*). As [the verse] says:
Since the seeds within the causal stage of arising have already been perfumed, those perfumed seeds are incapable of immediately producing a fruit;
therefore, at the very moment this manifestation arises, it does not perfume a seed, nor does this manifestation itself produce a fruit.
Therefore, the arising of actualized phenomena (*pravṛtti*) is subsumed under the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*). Thus, the arising of actualized phenomena produces seeds;
it is not subsumed under the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*), because the projecting cause and its fruit are distant from one another.

Furthermore, the second [interpretation] explains that this arising of actualized phenomena producing seeds is not subsumed under the latter four of the six causes—namely, the four causes among the initiating (*abhinirvṛtti*), specific (*anyathābhāva*), concurrent (*sahabhū*), and non-contradictory (*avirodha*) causes. It is subsumed under these four causes.

The Commentary states: "These causal conditions for the means (*upāya*) also include the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and so forth;

there is not even a slight lack of distinction [from other causes], as will be explained below. These four causes constitute the entirety [of the immediate and object-conditions], while the six causes constitute a partial portion.

Within the means, there are also the immediately preceding condition and the object-condition; namely, the dependence cause (*apekṣā-hetu*), the support cause (*parigraha-hetu*), the co-operative cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the non-associated cause (*viprayukta-hetu*). These four...
Within the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*), there are also the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

For the time being, however, because we are addressing them in contrast to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), we speak of the immediately preceding condition and the object-condition as being subsumed under the general category of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Regarding the remaining factors in the causal stage—the first, second, fifth, and ninth—it may be asked: since the causal condition of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*) already includes arising, abiding, accomplishing, and acquisition, and within that arising and acquisition...

Furthermore, there are cases where seeds giving rise to manifest activity constitute the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Why, then, is it stated here that the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*) is subsumed solely under the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)?
Answer: This refers to taking a small portion from among those [causes] acquired at birth, as has already been explained previously.

If, within the ninth [category], the "contradictory" [cause], it is stated that apart from other concordant causes, there is no contradictory cause for purification; then, regarding the characteristic of purification—

[The seeds] that are conducive, as well as those that are non-concordant and those separated from other pure [seeds], are likewise subsumed under the condition of causal origination (*hetu-pratyaya*).

How then does the treatise state that discordant causes (*virodha-hetu*) are also subsumed under the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)? (Reflect upon this further; it is also appropriate to include this in the text.)
The Commentary states: "If it were to include only two [causes] and exclude others, it would be too narrow;

if it were to include all two causes—namely, the projecting (*ākṣepaka*) and the actualizing (*abhinirvartaka*) causes—and designate them as 'binding causes' (*bandhana-hetu*), there would be the fault of being overly broad, because these two causes contain the seeds of karma.

Furthermore, if it were to include only the projecting and actualizing causes while excluding the seeds of the other four causes, such as the inducing (*āvāhaka*) cause and so forth, [it would likewise be incorrect].
Your [position], my son, would then incur the fault of being too narrow, because among the other four causes (*hetu*), there are also causal conditions (*pratyaya*) capable of producing [an effect].

Regarding the statement in the Commentary, "Because those exist but are not subsumed under the category of 'expedient means' (*upāya*) as causal conditions," if one were to take only the eight causes as being named "expedient means," then the two causes of projection (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and production (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*) would not be included.
Furthermore, regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), such as karmic seeds and so forth, [if they were excluded], there would then be...

The fault of being too narrow: since those two causes—projecting (*ākṣepaka*) and actualizing (*abhinirvartaka*)—include factors that are not causal conditions (*pratyaya*), the present method is too narrow because it does not include within the two causes those factors that are not causal conditions.

If [one objects]: "If the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) includes only the actualizing cause and excludes the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and so on up to excluding the seeds of karma that actualize [results], this constitutes the fault of being too narrow," then [the response] follows in the preceding commentary.

In the main text, the faults of being overly broad or overly narrow have already been explained. Why, then, does this current commentary explain the fault of being overly broad or narrow regarding the interpretation of "human perfuming" (*puruṣa-vāsanā*)?
How does this subsequent interpretation differ from the previous one? The answer is that it is also the same as the general interpretation of "perfuming."
The Commentary states: "In this context, 'shadowing and omitting' (yinglüe) is explained as being neither exhaustive nor too narrow. To 'shadow' [the meaning] is to take up the broader sense.

For example, although it is known that if there is a stage of seeking (mārga-paryeṣaṇā), one speaks only of the cause of birth-and-death as the cause of linking rebirth (pratisandhi-hetu), this fails to exhaustively include all causes and conditions;
thus, it is an overly narrow abbreviation. Although it is said that the cause of arising is the cause of linking rebirth..."

Furthermore, among the five causes such as the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) and so forth, the seeds of the various causal conditions (*pratyaya*) are termed the "cause of linking rebirth" (*pratisandhi-hetu*); this is the complete explanation of the principle.

Although the other nine causes are said to be the "causes of expedient means" (*upāya-hetu*), they do not exhaustively include all non-causal-conditional phenomena (*apratyaya-dharma*) subsumed within the "cause of origination" (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*).
Thus, [the former] is too narrow and is therefore called "abbreviated. Now, we shall also implicitly include those non-causal-conditional phenomena within the cause of origination. All...
The seeds of karma and so forth are called the "causes of expedient means" (*upāya-hetu*); thus, the principle is exhausted.

If, as in the preceding *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, one were to designate only the seeds that project and produce [existence] as the "cause of linking birth" (*pratisandhi-hetu*), it would fail to encompass all the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) within the remaining four causes and would therefore be too narrow.

Furthermore, it would merely be a brief indication; thus, among the other four causes—such as the cause of production (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and so forth—the seeds of the various causal conditions are designated as the "cause of generation" (*janaka-hetu*).

Alternatively, in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, it is taught that only the projecting seeds (*ākṣepaka-bīja*) and the actualizing seeds (*abhinirvartaka-bīja*) are termed the "cause of linking rebirth" (*pratisandhi-hetu*), while the production of seeds from manifest activity (*samudācāra*) is not termed the "cause of generation" (*janana-hetu*); this is what is meant by "concise.

Although seeds are stated to be the cause of linking rebirth, this also implies that the seeds produced from manifest activity are included within the category of the cause of linking rebirth. This remains true even though the other eight causes are mentioned.

The cause of skillful means (*upāya-hetu*) is termed "concise" (*saṃkṣepa*). It also refers to the "indirect inclusion" (*pratibimba-grahaṇa*) within the causes that project and produce [results], namely the seeds of various virtues, deeds, and so forth that are not direct causes (*hetu-pratyaya*);
these are called "induced by skillful means."
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "Question: Why are the causal conditions (*pratyaya*) of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* divided into two?
Why is the cause of rebirth (*janmanidāna*) also called the 'projecting seed' (*ākṣepabīja*), and why does it encompass both the projecting and the actualizing seeds? The intent of this question is:

how is it that the causal conditions of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, through these two [types of causes], can produce [results]? Why is the productive cause also termed the "arising seed" (*utpādabīja*) and the "projecting seed"? Although there is projection...
It produces two kinds of seeds: namely, the production of seeds from seeds through grasping, and the production of manifest activity from seeds through non-grasping.

Because manifest activity does not produce seeds through grasping, the causal conditions are not exhausted. In the stage of applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra-bhūmi*), only the cause that produces [activity] once is established;
subsequently, both manifest activity and seeds are completely exhausted through grasping.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The answer concerns whether or not there is an intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*), and because it discusses only the seeds, there is no contradiction. This response is explained as follows:
In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, two stages—namely, with and without an intercalary month—are distinguished, and thus two kinds of generative causes (*janaka-hetu*) are established.

That which has not yet been intercalated is called the "projecting seed" (*ākṣepaka-bīja*); that which has already been intercalated is called the "arising seed" (*abhinirvartaka-bīja*). Therefore, the treatise...

This is divided into two parts concerning the productive causes (*janaka-hetu*). Since the treatise’s text speaks of "projecting seeds" (*ākṣepa-bīja*) and "arising seeds" (*abhinirvṛtti-bīja*), and since the treatise’s text mentions only seeds and does not speak of manifest activities (*samudācāra*), the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* includes only the acquisition of seeds and the production of seeds from seeds.
That seeds produce manifest activities constitutes the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), and it does not include the production of seeds from manifest activities.
This refers to the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*). If there is a stage characterized by vitarka and vicāra, that which is capable of producing the resultant entity is the causal condition.
Since the treatise speaks only of the "producing causal condition" (*janaka-hetu-pratyaya*), it is subsumed under the "conditioning cause" (*pratisandhi-hetu*);

because it does not explicitly mention seeds and manifestations, it includes both seeds and active manifestations. Whether it is a seed producing a seed, a seed producing a manifestation, or a manifestation producing a seed, all are [included].
That which is capable of producing the essence of the fruit is the *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition). Furthermore, there is no distinction between whether an intercalary month has been added or not;
rather, they are distinguished by their relative proximity. That which is proximate is termed "arising" (*janaka*), while that which is remote is termed the "expedient cause" (*upāya-hetu*).
Therefore, when investigating the stages (*bhūmi*), one establishes only a single "arising cause. Thus, there is no contradiction with the two treatises.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'not including those subsumed under predominant karma,' the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* speaks only of causal seeds;
these are subsumed under the 'projecting cause of birth. Thus, it does not state that seeds of predominant karma and so forth are subsumed under the projecting cause of birth.

How can this commentary be correct? It is simply that the character "what" (何) has been erroneously substituted for the character "that" (即). The Treatise says: "Although [these are] within the two causes..."
There are causes that are not the cause of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*), yet because their seeds are particularly prominent and manifest, they are specifically mentioned. The commentary explains:

these two causes are called the "cause of rebirth-linking" because their seeds are immediate conditions and are particularly prominent and manifest; therefore, the treatise mentions them specifically.
Among these two causes, the dominant seeds are remote and subordinate, and thus the treatise does not mention them. As for the other eight causes, they are simply dominant, remote, and manifest.

The treatise speaks of eight causes as a provisional means (*upāya*). Although the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is also present among the other four conditions, this is because it follows upon the direct causal condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Thus, the treatise does not state that the causal condition is included within these eight causes.

The *Śāstra* says: "Attention (*manasikāra*) does not receive [the fruit] simultaneously. The commentary explains: This is a scriptural passage. It means that when one commits an evil deed, the retribution is not received immediately—that is, not at that very same moment (*kṣaṇa*).

For example, after having committed an evil karma, one must wait until ten, five, or even a hundred mental moments (*citta-kṣaṇa*) have passed before one finally receives the fruit of that evil karma.
The Commentary states: "That which is not a cause for linking rebirth is actually of only one kind; that which is a cause of skillful means is only ninefold. This is incorrect.

It is not the case that what is not a cause for linking rebirth is subsumed solely under the cause of origination (*janaka-hetu*), nor is it the case that what is not a cause of skillful means is subsumed solely under the other nine causes.

Furthermore, this text does not fully capture the principle. One should rather say: among the six causes, those that function as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) are all subsumed under the cause for linking rebirth. If...
The cause of skillful means (*upāya-hetu*) comprises the entirety of four causes and a portion of six causes; this is the complete explanation of its inclusion.

The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Although there have been two textual passages above," these two passages refer to the ten bases and fifteen locations within the preceding treatise, wherein ten causes and twenty causes were established, along with their mutual inclusion within the [two] causes.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Furthermore, excluding the conditions of attraction and arising. Since this passage follows the four conditions based on the fifteen bases (*āśraya*), it should have stated:
"Furthermore, excluding the basis of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), there are also seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-bīja*).

This is because the ten causes are the function (*kāritra*) and the fifteen bases are the substance (*svabhāva*); since substance and function are not separate from one another, [the seeds] are also present within the fifteen bases. Thus it is clarified.
There is no contradiction in stating that [the seeds] lead to and give rise to [existence].
As for the statement in the treatise that "the term 'seed' belongs exclusively to the fourth [basis]," this master’s intention is as follows:
when taking up the seeds now, they belong only to the fifteen bases; the fourth [basis], the "intercalary seed basis," is included because the name "seed" is identical.

Therefore, it belongs exclusively to the fourth [category], namely the seeds with intercalary [factors]. Although the third category, the locus of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), is mentioned, habitual tendencies are merely another name for seeds;
they are not included here because the names "habitual tendency" and "seed" are distinct.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "In this [system], among the bases with intercalary seeds (*sāntara-bīja-āśraya*), one does not distinguish the seeds of karma (*karman-bīja*); rather, it includes the seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-bīja*).

Regarding the causes and conditions from 'depending on' (*niśritya*) up to 'taking up or discarding' (*ādāna-tyāga*), these are as previously explained regarding the inclusion of the two causes. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says:

If this master’s position is stated thus, he speaks only of "seeds" (*bīja*), which belong exclusively to the fourth base of intercalary seeds. Furthermore, within the base of intercalary seeds, seeds of karma are not established.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that the seeds of causes and conditions among the other five bases—such as the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and so forth—are not included, the process of selection and exclusion is as previously described.

Although within the "intercalary" seeds there are also karmic seeds that are not dharmas of causes and conditions, the karmic seeds and others are mentioned specifically because they are closely related to and proximate to the fruit, following the seeds of causes and conditions.
Although the habitual tendencies follow along with the distinct functional capacities (*śakti*), they are integrated [with them].

There is no obstruction. Within the remaining five bases (*āśraya*), there are also causal seeds; that is, among the remaining five causes, the seeds of predominant karma (*adhipati-karma*) are manifested, yet they follow the causal seeds.

As for the reason why two causes are not mentioned—namely, the producing cause (*janana-hetu*) and the instrumental cause (*upāya-hetu*)—it is because of their distinctions such as being distant or remote.
Regarding the term "distinction" (*bheda*): herein it refers to the distinctions between the distant and the near, or the intimate and the remote; it follows the manifestation of these distinctions.
The Commentary states: "That which is here [presented] is precisely the meaning of the first master mentioned previously.

However, within this section explaining the ten causes and so forth, it corresponds to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* (Chapter on Having Discursive Thought) in the upper and lower volumes of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

Even passages that appear contradictory—such as those concerning the four conditions based on the fifteen locations—are all explained through the combined interpretation of these two masters. If, within various passages, the initial...

The "Master" (*ācārya*) refers collectively to a single master; this is a comprehensive and exhaustive explanation according to the principles of the text of the chapter. Within the text of the chapter, there is no separate master.
This is not the same as the "First Master" mentioned in the preceding text, nor is it distinct from the "First Master" appearing later in the text.

As for the "Second Master" found throughout various sections of the text, these are all collectively the First and Second Masters; there are no further distinct masters beyond them. This is not the case with the preceding text.
The "second master" refers to the second master mentioned later in the text.

Regarding the phrase "the remaining [factors of] reception (*anubhava*) and the subsequent conjunction (*saṃprayoga*), up to the point where the object (*viṣaya*) is common to all four [conditions]," according to the commentary (*śāstra*) below, it states that reception and conjunction do not obstruct [the arising of consciousness], as well as the immediate antecedent (*samanantara*) or the objective basis (*ālambana-adhiṣṭhāna*), etc.; all of these are said to depend upon the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

The equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya) all possess these four bases. It is an error for the present commentary to state that there are three bases for the equal-and-immediate condition;
it should state that there are four. Question: How can the equal-and-immediate condition exist within the basis of reception (anubhava)?

Because it is impossible for a preceding thought-moment to exist within the state of being induced by feeling (*vedanā*), one should ask the Dharma Master regarding the subsequent thought-moment of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that if there is an experience (*anubhava*) that is not obstructed within the three bases of conjunction (*saṃnipāta*), there are also both the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
This is like the case of the basis of experience, which awaits what previously existed; that is, the preceding thought-moment of past feeling induces the subsequent one.

Because it has not yet been received, it is called the "equal-and-immediate condition as the basis for reception" (*samanantara-pratyaya-upādāna*). This means that it is also obtained as an equal-and-immediate condition.

Alternatively, because it exists within the mind, it is "sentient form" (*rūpa*); thus, it is also obtained as an equal-and-immediate condition. Or, because it exists within the mind, it is "sentient color.
That is to say, it seeks to manifest conjunction and so forth; since it also takes manifestation and conjunction as its objects within the mind, it perceives them as its objective field (*viṣaya*).

Feeling (vedanā) has an object of cognition (ālambana) based on the internal. Regarding the statement that "the two [aggregates] are combined with the preceding [aggregate] to constitute its essence":

this refers to the basis of conjunction (saṃyoga-āśraya) and the basis of non-obstruction (anāvaraṇa-āśraya). These two bases constitute the external substance of form (rūpa); that is, they are the bases prior to their combination.

This is considered to be the essence of non-obstruction. However, it manifests as the four bases: the basis of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarāśraya*), the basis of conjunction (*saṃprayogāśraya*), and the basis of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇāśraya*).
Yet, these four bases all possess the immediately preceding condition; thus, the immediately preceding condition has four bases. Nevertheless, the commentary states:
"The three [types of] immediately preceding conditions" refers to the immediate [condition], or alternatively, to the bases.
The self-substance [of the mind] merely manifests the cognition and reception of the conjunction [of conditions], and does not obstruct the three bases;
this refers to the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). If it concerns the objective base (*ālambana-āśraya*), it receives the conjunction without obstruction.
Among these four bases, all possess an object of cognition (*ālambana*); therefore, the commentary states: "The objective sphere pervades all four."

The Commentary states: "Because the names of these two bases are also fully manifest. This means that if it is the basis of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it is exclusively an immediately preceding condition;
there is nothing else here that is not an immediately preceding condition. If it is the basis of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it is exclusively an object-condition;
there is nothing else here that is not an object-condition. Thus, in these two bases, there are no other conditions present. That is to say:

In these two cases, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) are further explained as being the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
Regarding the bases for experience and so forth, some are object-conditions while others are not;
some are immediately preceding conditions while others are not.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Regarding 'those based on the remainder,' because they are easy to understand, they are omitted;
this continues until 'because all are predominant. However, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "Those based on the remainder are predominant.

Since this text is easy to understand, it is not explained here. If one were to explain it exhaustively: among the fifteen bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) pervades all six.

This refers to a portion of the sixth *āśraya* (basis). That is to say, among the six bases—the third being the basis of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the fourth being the basis of seeds with intercalary [factors], the eleventh being conformity, the twelfth being specific functional capacity, the thirteenth being conjunction, and the fifteenth being non-obstruction—a portion of these six bases constitutes the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). As for the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)...

The condition by way of object (*ālambana-pratyaya*) pervades all four bases of dependence (*āśraya*). That is to say, it exists in its entirety within the base of immediate antecedence (*samanantara-āśraya*), and partially within the other three bases:

the base of experience (*upabhoga-āśraya*), the base of harmony (*sāmagrī-āśraya*), and the base of non-obstruction (*anantarāya-āśraya*). As for the condition by way of object (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it likewise pervades all four bases of dependence.
That is to say, it exists in its entirety within the base of the objective field (*viṣaya-āśraya*), and partially within the remaining three bases: experience, harmony, and non-obstruction.
A portion of it exists. However, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is broad while the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is narrow.

Regarding the dominant condition, with the exception of its own self-nature—one dharma—it acts as the dominant condition for all other dharmas, just as in the state of Buddhahood. This has already been distinguished regarding the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).

Otherwise, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes itself as its object; the seeing-part, excluding its own self-nature part (*svabhāva-bhāga*), is able to take all other dharmas as objects, even up to the mind...

The objective aspect (*grāhyabhāga*) is also thus. However, as for the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), it pervades six bases in their entirety and nine bases in part. Regarding the six bases in their entirety:

these are the basis of experience (*anubhavasthāna*), the basis of the faculties (*indriyasthāna*), the basis of function (*kāritrasthāna*), the basis of human effort (*puruṣakārasthāna*), the basis of true vision (*tattvadarśanasthāna*), and the basis of obstruction (*pratibandhasthāna*).
These six bases are entirely the predominant condition. As for the nine [bases] in part: [they are as follows...]

Regarding these [conditions], they consist of: (1) dependence on experience, (2) difference in habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), (3) immediate cessation, (4) the object, (5) conformity, (6) differentiation, (7) functional integration, and (8) non-obstruction.
Among these nine bases, each possesses a portion of the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
If, within the state of immediate cessation, a mind or mental factor arises through grasping, then from the first moment to the second moment of mind, this is [the case].

It is subsumed under the condition of equal immediacy (*samanantara-pratyaya*). If the first moment of mind is considered in relation to the fourth or fifth moments of mind, it is subsumed under the condition of equal immediacy.
If the first moment of mind is considered in relation to the fourth or fifth moments of mind, it is subsumed under the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Alternatively, it may be said that because it serves as the object (*ālambana*) for both [the preceding and succeeding moments], it is further described as a dominant condition upon the basis of these two locations.
This refers to the condition (*pratyaya*). If one does not fully understand the mutual relationship of causes and conditions, there is a fourth basis that serves as the locus for all seeds.

Although the other five bases also possess causal conditions, they are not mentioned here because they manifest as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and thus do not follow the nature of causal conditions.

As for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it pertains exclusively to the fifth basis, the immediately ceased [consciousness]. As for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it pertains exclusively to the sixth basis, the objective field.

Regarding the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*): although they do not obstruct the experience of the composite [aggregates], and since the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) also exist within the bases, the predominance condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is emphasized because it is more prominent among the intermediate conditions; thus, they are not mentioned. There is further difficult text regarding the inclusion of other [conditions].
Apart from the three bases of the immediately preceding cessation and the object, the remaining twelve bases are all subsumed under the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Although the dominant condition is also present within the base of the seed that is augmented by intercalary factors, it is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) that makes the dominant condition manifest.

It is not mentioned because it follows [the others]. Although the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), conformities, and specific functional capacities are received, and although there are also remaining bases for the combination that do not obstruct, the other three conditions are not mentioned because they are manifested by following the predominant [condition].
If one does not fully understand how the four conditions subsume the ten causes, [it is because] the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is simply the cause itself.

It is subsumed within the *janaka-hetu* (productive cause). Although the other five causes also contain the *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition) within them, it is not mentioned here because the *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant condition) is manifest while the *hetu-pratyaya* is latent.
As for the *samanantara-pratyaya* (immediately preceding condition) and the *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition), they are subsumed solely within the *parigraha-hetu* (appropriating cause).

Although the other functions—namely *apekṣā* (contingency), *sahakārin* (cooperative action), and *avirodha* (non-contradiction)—also possess the nature of the immediately preceding and object-conditions, they are not mentioned because the *adhipati-pratyaya* and the two intermediate conditions [the *samanantara* and *ālambana*] are predominant.
As for conditions (*pratyaya*): because they are implicit, they are not explicitly stated. As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is subsumed within the arising of other factors.

Apart from the two causes (*hetu*), the remaining eight causes combined are all dominant conditions. Although there are also dominant conditions within the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), this reveals the dominant condition through the productive cause;
because it is implicit, it is not mentioned. Furthermore, although there are also dominant conditions within the appropriating cause (*parigraha-hetu*), yet the dominant [condition]...

The superior [condition] follows [the object]; the two intermediate conditions are not mentioned because they are already manifest. If one were to explain them exhaustively, they would be subsumed under the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*):
a portion of the six causes is subsumed under the two intermediate conditions; a portion of four causes is subsumed under the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);

and the two causes in their entirety—the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and the opposing cause (*virodha-hetu*)—as well as a portion of other causes, are included. The treatise states that the causal condition is capable of producing the cause.
The sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is subsumed [within the causes]. The nature of the sovereign condition is subsumed within the two intermediate conditions among the [four] conditions.
Regarding its subsumption under the causal factor (*hetu*), this treatise on Yoga explains this meaning by means of the three causes.

Having clarified how the four conditions are mutually subsumed with the two causes, one should state that the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is subsumed under the generative cause (*janaka-hetu*), while the remaining three conditions are subsumed under the instrumental cause (*upāya-hetu*). If...

The four conditions (*pratyaya*) and the ten causes (*hetu*) are mutually inclusive. They should be subsumed under the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), which is itself comprised of the [ten] causes. The two intermediate conditions are subsumed under four causes.
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) comprises the entirety of two causes, namely the cause of designation (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*) and the contradictory cause (*virodha-hetu*);

the remaining eight causes are partially subsumed [under it]. This treatise clarifies that the causal and dominant conditions are comprised within the means of production (*janaka-upāya*); thus, [the other conditions] are not mentioned.

The middle two conditions are subsumed under the two causes. Herein, the phrase "the former [two] are sparse" means they are sparsely cited. The remaining nine causes are subsumed under the three conditions.

As for the statement that the treatise does not mention them: although other types of appropriating causes (*parigraha-hetu*) are included within the aforementioned nine causes, they already encompass the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains only their inclusion within the ten causes.

[The remaining causes] are subsumed under [the three conditions]. The two intermediate conditions are not mentioned; the other nine causes are subsumed under the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
That is to say, a portion of the six causes constitutes the causal condition, while the remainder constitutes the dominant condition.

Regarding the statement that "the non-expedient cause does not subsume the two conditions because the matter of the contingent cause (*apekṣā-hetu*) is not contradictory and is subsumed under the expedient," the meaning of this passage is that it speaks of the non-expedient...
It follows that the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) are not included [within the efficient cause].

Since it is stated that the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*) does not contradict the four causes, and since these two intermediate conditions are already present within this [efficient] cause, the object-condition and the immediately preceding condition are not included.

Furthermore, since it is stated that there is no contradiction regarding the "matter" (*vastu*) within the efficient cause, and since these two intermediate [conditions] are already present among these four causes...
Regarding the conditions (*pratyaya*): it is further stated that these four causes also pertain to the cause of application (*prayoga-hetu*).

Since the two intermediate conditions exist, one knows that the two intermediate conditions are likewise subsumed under the cause of application. Because the other two conditions are also termed dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), these three conditions are also subsumed under application.
If this were not the case, then the "generating cause" (*janaka-hetu*) mentioned in the *Mahā-śāstra* would be [inconsistent].

Regarding "by way of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)," the *Mahā-śāstra* states: "That which is taught as a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), being already a cause, is not further designated as a dominant condition. The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says:

"Within causes, the preparatory means (*upāya*) subsume the three conditions; that which is productive subsumes the efficient cause (*hetu-pratyaya*). This means that the preparatory means subsume the three conditions.
This refers to the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), as well as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The Commentary states: "If one were to speak merely of 'maturation' (*vipāka*), it would only encompass the retribution within the six consciousnesses that is not the true maturation;
therefore, the term 'born of maturation' (*vipākaja*) is used. If the treatise had spoken merely of "maturation," it would have captured only the sixth consciousness. The sixth consciousness...

Only the true maturation (*vipāka*) is excluded [from the category of "born of maturation"]. Therefore, it is judged that [the term] does not include the mind born of maturation among the first six consciousnesses that is acquired through karma.
This is because that which is produced by karma within the first six consciousnesses is exclusively "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) and cannot be termed "true maturation" (*vipāka*).
Consequently, this treatise speaks only of "born of maturation," which thereby includes what is acquired within the first six consciousnesses.
Regarding that which is induced by karma, it is exclusively non-heterogeneous maturation (*vipākaja*) and cannot be termed true maturation (*vipāka*).
Therefore, this treatise refers only to "maturation-born" (*vipākaja*), which subsumes the aforementioned six consciousnesses; among these, that which is induced by karma is maturation-born.
This also subsumes the eighth [consciousness], because the eighth consciousness is likewise maturation-born, as previously stated in the second [section].

This is a detailed exposition from the treatise. Question: Since there is wholesome karma in the formless realm that brings about fruition, is there a body characterized by a continuous stream of maturation (*vipāka*)?
If there were none, how would the preceding passage in the treatise explain that "without a body and life, there is nothing capable of sustaining [them]"? Answer:
Although there is no remaining form-body (*rūpakāya*), it may still be called a "body" (*kāya*).
The Commentary states: "This passage clarifies that the argument that 'the Dharma produced by the Path does not well receive retribution' is incorrect.
Now, this "Dharma produced by the Path" refers to a person from the Jin dynasty. He was originally a humble official from Hezhou who respected the Way. [His secular...]
His original surname was Li (登). Later, having left the household life, he served the Dharma Master Zhu Fahu as his *upādhyāya*.
Consequently, Dao-sheng’s original surname was changed; he adopted Zhu Fahu’s surname and thus altered his own. With the surname Zhu, he was named the Dharma Master Zhu Dao-sheng.
This was taken from the Buddha’s clan name (*gotra*) because he served that *upādhyāya*. His appearance resembled that of the assembly of monks.
Regarding the Buddha’s clan name, the monks and others likewise did not explain it as "some. This refers to the Dharma Master Daosheng; he was indeed the Dharma Master Daosheng.

Together with Sengzhao, Tanrong, and Fayong, they were contemporaries. Specifically, among Daosheng, Sengzhao, Tanrong, and Fayong, the Dharma Master Daosheng composed one fascicle of the *Wuzhong lun* (Treatise on the Five Kinds).
In his *Shan bushouqi lun* (Treatise on Goodness Not Being Subject to Arising), this master’s intention is to state that wholesome karma does not bring about [retribution].

Furthermore, non-neutral (*avyākṛta*) resultant karma does not produce a non-neutral resultant fruit. This master’s intention is to say that this is identical to the doctrine of the Mahāsāṃghikas within the Hinayana.
The Mahāsāṃghikas assert that there are only two types of phenomena—wholesome and unwholesome—and no phenomena of a non-neutral nature.
Thus, things such as mountains, rivers, and the great earth are exclusively of the nature of either wholesome or unwholesome. If wholesome karma brings about a human birth...
The human body, as well as mountains, rivers, the great earth, and so forth—these mountains, rivers, the great earth, and so on—are collectively termed "of a virtuous nature" (*kuśala-svabhāva*).
The karma capable of producing these results is of a virtuous nature; and that which is produced—the body, the mountains, the rivers, and so forth—is all termed "of a virtuous nature.

If, by means of mental karma (*manas-karma*), one brings about the acquisition of a hellish body, or implements such as hoes filled with smoke and charcoal, or swords—that is, blades—and the hellish body itself along with the hoes filled with smoke and charcoal [are all of a virtuous nature].

The sword is subsumed under the category of blades. As for the seals (mudrās) such as the plow, the earth, the mountains, and the rivers—all these seals, including the plow, the earth, the mountains, and the rivers—are termed "unwholesome in nature" because the karma capable of inducing them is unwholesome in nature.
Since they induce the attainment of the hellish sword-mountains, the mountains and rivers are likewise unwholesome in nature.
This applies to all afflictions; how much more so for those designated as unwholesome in nature? This includes even the form realm and the formless realm.

The realms (*dhātu*). There are also phenomena of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala-dharma*), because afflictions (*kleśa*) also exist within the two higher realms. According to this master [Dharmakīrti], the path (*mārga*) possesses only the two natures of wholesome and unwholesome.

Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are also included as the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Now, in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, it is accepted that there are phenomena of the three natures;
that is, it is accepted that there are wholesome and unwholesome karmas capable of summoning the neutral fruit of maturation (*vipāka-vipāka-phala*). Thus, the ancients...

Dharma Master Daosheng is incorrect. Regarding the discussion of the twenty thousand kalpas, this master’s intention is to say that all the mountains and rivers within the human body are equal to [the state of] no momentary arising or ceasing.
Within the same Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) schools, the Saṃmitīya school asserts that the subject and object are one.

Furthermore, it speaks of the three types of nirvāṇa—such as the "equality" and so forth—and the four conditions of the *Anabhilāpya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Nameless). If it refers to the theory of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), then [it is as follows].
The *Śāstra* states: "Regarding the point that, as in the Hīnayāna, even contaminated wholesome [karma] brings about retribution—this is now stated only according to our own school.
That wholesome and unwholesome karma can bring about the fruit of neutral maturation (*vipāka-avijñapti*) is likewise consistent with the Hīnayāna tenets.

However, the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna asserts that the dharma of neutral maturation belongs to sentient beings; since it exists within sentient beings, it is exclusively non-obscured neutral (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*)."
Within the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, it is stated that there is "maturation" (*vipāka*). The fruit of maturation is comprised exclusively of sentient beings;

that is, because all contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome and unwholesome karmas, as well as unwholesome karmas, are able to take up the fruit of maturation, they are called "contaminated acquisitions" (*sāsravopādāna*).
From these wholesome and unwholesome karmas, this fruit of maturation arises.
The Commentary states: "This stage is called 'prolonged. Upon reaching the Vajra-mind, one suddenly attains the level of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) among the Two Vehicles.

This clarifies the eighth consciousness. If it is termed the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), this retributive consciousness is only then suddenly severed upon reaching the final moment of the Vajra-mind at the completion of the ten stages.
This retributive consciousness likewise extends to the stage of those beyond training among the Two Vehicles."

The *Śāstra* states: "The mention of 'thirty-eight' and so forth all refers to the increase of dharmas as being the self-result. This also clarifies the results of equal conditions (*sabhāga-pratyaya*) within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
It is also the case that the cause is inferior while the result is superior; for example, when an inferior grade of wholesome dharma serves as the cause, there are three grades of results, namely:
an inferior-grade result, a middle-grade result, and a superior-grade result. If a middle-grade dharma serves as the cause, [there are likewise three grades of results]...
There are two grades of fruit: namely, the medium-grade fruit and the superior-grade fruit; there is no inferior-grade fruit.
If a superior-grade wholesome dharma serves as the cause, there is only a superior-grade fruit, and no medium- or inferior-grade fruits. The same applies to unwholesome dharmas and neutral dharmas.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The Abhidharma (*Abhidharma*) refers exclusively to wholesome dharmas. The Explanation says: However, within the Abhidharma, wholesome dharmas are also cited as examples;
this [category of] outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) should properly encompass dharmas of all three natures.

The Commentary states: "This refers to the retribution of short life for killing, and so forth. Furthermore, since these are called *niṣyanda-phala* (outflow fruits), they are not *sabhāga-phala* (homogeneous fruits).
For example, suppose there is a person who, due to having committed the karma of killing, dies and enters hell, where they undergo immeasurable suffering.
Later, he emerges from hell because the remaining karma of his residual acts of killing has not yet been exhausted. Otherwise, he would be cut short within the human realm;
this too is certainly the result of induced wholesome karma, which causes the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) to remain for a brief duration.

For example, when a person practices giving or cultivates wholesome deeds, if there is no regret during the three periods [of preparation, execution, and completion], that wholesome karma becomes "fixed" (*niyata*). This is like the case where the remaining karma of a teacher’s evil deeds, as well as water...
Fire, weapons, and so forth, are all capable of harming the provisional [person] and causing their life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) to be shortened.

If one performs acts of giving or cultivates wholesome deeds, yet at one time, two times, or even three times feels regret, this causes those wholesome karmas—such as giving—to become indeterminate (*aniyata-karman*).
Although the person born from such wholesome karma should have a lifespan of one hundred years, that very same [person] is [subjected to] the remainder of the killing and other [non-virtuous acts].
Regarding karma: having subtracted fifty years, the remainder is the lifespan of five years that one receives through governance.

To speak according to reality, the length or brevity of a human life is determined solely by the maturation of determinate wholesome karma (*niyata-kuśala-karma*). Determinate wholesome karma definitely brings about a long life, while unwholesome karma definitely brings about a short life.
This is just like the remaining evil karma from killing and so forth, which is indeterminate and brings about a shortened life.
To cause another to obtain a short lifespan is what is subsumed under the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).

When it is now said that one obtains a short life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) due to the karma of killing, this refers to a concordance of characteristics; it is described as a "fruit" in a single sense because it accords with its cause.

Since the life of another is shortened by the act of killing, through that very same karma of killing, one's own life is also shortened; this is metaphorically designated as a "concordant fruit" (*niṣyandaphala*).
Because the nature of the karma that shortens existence (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) differs from that of unwholesome karma, this shortening is not a result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).

This is because the duration—whether short or long—of neutral (*avyākṛta*) results corresponds to the similarity between the wholesome or unwholesome karma that was experienced. One should understand that the same principle applies to acts such as theft and the performance of rituals.

Regarding the "gate of conforming characteristics," it is so called because the fruit conforms to its cause; it does not follow the explanation of the Hīnayāna, and thus it is termed "conforming" (*anuvartin*).

This is the section on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Question: Regarding the other virtuous actions (*śubha-karma*) and their results of similar outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), what are their modes of activity (*ākāra*)? Furthermore, it is asked:
Just as non-killing has longevity as its result of similar outflow, should this [result] also be considered a conventional designation (*prajñapti*)?

The Commentary states: "The meaning of 'similarity' refers to that which is conventionally designated as a 'concordant result' (*niṣyanda-phala*), though it is actually produced by karma. This fruit is called the 'karma of killing.

It brings about the retribution of a short life among human beings. While this is conventionally designated as occurring 'among humans,' the actual concordant result—the length or brevity of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) among humans—is truly produced by wholesome karma, not by the unwholesome karma of taking a single life."

The Commentary states: "This fruit encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and is exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); it pertains to both ordinary beings and noble ones.

Regarding these, the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) that pertains to the contaminated refers to cases where the wholesome produces the wholesome, the unwholesome produces the unwholesome, and the indeterminate produces the indeterminate;

within the wholesome uncontaminated, the uncontaminated produces the uncontaminated, and so forth—all instances where things of the same nature produce one another are called the fruit of uniform outflow.

"Both ordinary beings and sages are permeated by it" means that within the bodies of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there is also the manifestation arising from seeds, the activity arising from seeds, and seeds arising from seeds;

this is likewise true for the bodies of noble sages (*ārya*). The Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) also speaks of "permeation as a natural outflow" (*niṣyanda*), which is similar to the "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*).

Its resemblance to the Mahāyāna is also evident in its descriptions of the self-arising [of seeds] and their production prior to the stages [of the path], as found in the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts.

Regarding the statement that "the basis of reliance (āśraya) applies to both the preceding and the succeeding": as for the "basis of reliance," it refers to the basis of conformity (anuloma-āśraya). The meaning of this passage is as follows:

that which is the basis of conformity—namely, a preceding moment of dharma in relation to a subsequent moment of dharma—is termed the "basis of conformity" when considering the former in relation to the latter.
This basis of conformity attains its result of outflow (niṣyanda-phala), and this also applies to the drawing forth [of the effect] by the preceding moment.
The subsequent thought does not refer to simultaneous dharmas when it speaks of the "concordant basis. The *Śāstra* states:

"Taking the immovable aspect within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the cessation of sensation, and the suchness (*tathatā*) of the three natures as the fruit"—all these unconditioned phenomena are fruits of disconnection (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
The intention here is to explain that, if one distinguishes between the provisional and the real, [the fruit] pertains to the removal of one [obstruction].
That is to say, within the context of the abandonment of afflictions regarding suchness, it is termed "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Within cessation through deliberation, one distinguishes between the immovable [attainment] and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*). Here, we refer exclusively to the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling obtained through ultimate abandonment;
we do not refer to the immovable cessation of perception and feeling obtained through suppression (*vibhava*). This [latter] is what is obtained through suppression...

Because it is exclusively cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), this cessation through deliberation within [the category of] the "unshakable" (*āniñjya*)—referring to the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*)—is, when considered in terms of its essential nature, exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*).

These three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are all fruits of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*). Now, neither space (*ākāśa*) nor cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are included here;
these two are merely established as designations based upon the supportless *tathatā* (suchness). In terms of their actual reality, these two unconditioned phenomena are...

Regarding their moral nature: with the exception of one [unconditioned phenomenon] considered as a designation, namely space and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), these are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Therefore, the *Abhidharma-śāstra* states: "In the ultimate sense, the indeterminate refers to the unconditioned phenomena of space and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Furthermore, both of these unconditioned phenomena are not manifested through the abandonment of hindrances. If, within the state of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there is no location of form, this manifests space.

Space (*ākāśa*) is the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) obtained where conditions are absent. For this reason, space is not a non-analytical [cessation], nor is it a fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*).
Since the treatise states that it is a virtuous unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) manifested by the abandonment of obstructions, this has already been fully explained.
If one subsumes the provisional under the real, the first five unconditioned phenomena are all the essence of the suchness (tathatā) of the three natures.
This very suchness is termed the "fruit of disentanglement" (visamyoga-phala). To speak according to the ultimate reality, the essence of this suchness is exclusively of a wholesome nature;
this is designated by way of exclusion and manifestation as the suchness underlying wholesome dharmas, the suchness underlying unwholesome dharmas, and the suchness underlying indeterminate dharmas.

It is so. The *Śāstra* (Commentary) says: "As for the interpretation that this fruit consists solely in the severance of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), even up to [the view] that it does not contradict [other positions], this too is not contradictory.
The intention of this master is to say that afflictions are fetters; therefore, by severing the afflictions, one attains [liberation].
Regarding the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*): if the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) cannot bind, then for that reason the cognitive obstacle is not severed.

Even if one were to sever the obstacle of grasping (*upādāna-jñeyāvaraṇa*), one would not obtain the fruit of disconnection; likewise, even if one severs the obstacle of meditative absorption (*samāpatty-āvaraṇa*), one would not obtain the fruit of disconnection.

This master’s position is precisely what is stated in the following passage: it refers to the meaning of being subsumed within the two types of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) within True Suchness (*tathatā*). If the second...

The Master explains that by severing the two obstacles—the afflictive (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) and the cognitive (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*)—one attains the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*). This Master’s position is as follows:

in the passage below, it is stated that by severing the cognitive obstacle, one also attains analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Among these, the first [result] is True Suchness (*tathatā*), while the latter three are all analytical cessations; such is the Master’s doctrine.
To speak according to reality: by abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*), one attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

By abandoning the fixed [afflictions], one attains the unconditioned of non-agitation (*āniñjya*) and the unconditioned of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*). The "obstructions to meditative concentration" (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) are precisely feeling (*vedanā*).

Because one abandons changeable feeling, one attains the unconditioned of non-agitation; because one abandons unchangeable feeling, one attains the unconditioned of the cessation of perception and feeling. If one abandons that which is...
One realizes the suchness (*tathatā*) of wholesome phenomena, the suchness of unwholesome phenomena, and the suchness of indeterminate phenomena upon knowing the obstacles.

These unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) states are all attained by means of the abandonment of obstacles. As for the unconditioned state of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is not attained through abandonment, but rather is obtained through the deficiency of conditions.
Likewise, the unconditioned state of space (*ākāśa*) is also not attained through abandonment; it is merely...
It does not obstruct; therefore, it is not empty space. The *Śāstra* (commentary) states:

"Regarding the thirty-eight [factors] and so forth, they only mention 'human effort' (*puruṣakāra*) up to 'the fruit of human effort,' but do not say that they are obtained like the co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) and so forth.
That treatise says: "As for 'human effort,' for example, suppose there is a person who is able to practice divination."
At that time, the person is the agent; all the counting beads, divination charts, and written documents are called the instruments.

When one obtains a teacher from another, that teacher is also called the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*). When a person, by means of tools, engages in activities such as buying and selling, the person is the agent;
all the carts, pack animals, and carrying poles are the instruments. That which is obtained—the bowl—is in all cases called the "fruit of human effort."
Furthermore, it is like a person who can build a house. At the time of building the house, the skillful person is called the agent;

all the axes and other tools are called instruments of action. The completion of the house is also called the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). This applies even up to [results] produced by the power of a person.
When one plants field crops such as rice and grain, the person is called the "agent. All items such as pens, ink, and documents are the "instruments of action" (*karaṇa*).
If one obtains the result known as "harvest," these are all termed "fruits of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*). Regarding "planting" (*kṛṣi*) and "reaping" (*sasya*):
"planting" refers to the day of sowing, while "reaping" refers to the day of harvesting. As for "planting": when a person is planting, they cast seeds such as rice and wheat into the earth. Thus...

When [the grain] has reached [maturity], and before the fruit has fully formed but the process is already established, all of this is called "planting" (*jia*). "Planting" refers to the cultivation of grain crops.

When the rice, wheat, and other grains have formed fruit and reached maturity, and have been harvested outside the threshing floor (*hao*) and are situated upon the threshing floor, having been processed through threshing and so forth until completion—all of this is called "reaping" (*se*).
This refers to the "human utility" (*puruṣakāra*) of the day of the plowing. This above clarifies the human utility of the person;
that *yoga* [of the cause] also does not state, as the Hīnayāna does, that the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) obtains the fruit of human utility.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "That which is produced simultaneously and without interval, being a fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), refers to the following four types;
these are the fruits of human effort pertaining to dharmas (*dharma-puruṣakāra*). These four types are the doctrine of the Hīnayāna, as explained therein:

first, that which produces only the fruit of human effort consists of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*); the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) are termed 'simultaneous' (*saha*)."

First, the productive activity (*puruṣakāra*) that gives rise [to a result]; second, the immediate productive activity, which refers to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) of mind and mental factors;

third, the delayed productive activity, which refers to when wholesome volitional karma acts as the cause and, after being separated by many moments and a long period of time, finally attains its matured fruit (*vipāka-phala*); fourth, the non-productive activity, such as the severing of afflictions.
The non-arising of further affliction is the realization of the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).

These four fruits are so named because they are designated as "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*), though in reality they are not human effort. Only that which is obtained by a conventional person (*pudgala*) is called the fruit of human effort.

This is like the worldly expression "drunk from the foot of the rice stalk" (*śāli-pādaka*); although it is not the foot of the rice stalk itself, there is a three-year-old plant that resembles the foot of the rice stalk, and thus it is called "the foot of the rice stalk. This is definitive.

It is not that they are sufficient [in themselves]. If one gives much wine to those who are intoxicated, or kills them with a sword at the neck, or breaks them apart like the aforementioned thieves—this is merely the case where there is such a "sufficient power" (*puruṣakāra*) for defeating the thieves;
it is truly not this [power] itself, but rather it is subsumed under the category of weaponry.

It is just as when one is among a troop, one is part of that troop. If it were the person themselves who could lead the troops and perform such functions, then this [power] would be co-emergent (*sahaja*).
The four types of *puruṣakāra* (human effort) mentioned previously are merely said to be "like" *puruṣakāra*; in reality, they are not true *puruṣakāra*.

Now, according to the doctrine explained in the Mahāyāna, there are likewise four kinds of *puruṣakāra*. For example, actions such as those of a master (*pradhāna*), a companion (*sahaja*), or a producer (*janaka*) are designated as "simultaneous arising and ceasing.

However, when one performs acts such as giving birth or providing treatment for another person, and only on the following day or subsequent days does one receive the designation [of being their cause], this does not qualify as *puruṣakāra*.

It is said that what is sown during the period of "extinction" (nirodha) is harvested during the period of "maturity" (vṛddhi), thereby receiving the name "grain" (sasya). Likewise, the cessation [of suffering] which severs the afflictions receives the name "disconnection" (visamyoga).
It does not produce "human effort" (puruṣakāra). This cessation may also exist within the Mahāyāna; there are four kinds of dharmas that constitute human effort.
First is simultaneous arising (*sahaja*), which refers to seeds giving rise to manifest activity (*samudācāra*). Regarding seeds, there are two types of immediate *puruṣakāra* (human effort):

namely, the immediate condition of seeds [themselves] and the immediate condition of preceding and succeeding minds and mental factors. As for the remaining functions, one should first hear about the Hīnayāna.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "First, that which is obtained solely by a person (*pudgala*) acting as the cause is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*);

the cause is merely a conceptual construct (*prajñapti*), not a small, substantial dharma. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says: This first master definitely takes only the conceptual person (*prajñapti-pudgala*) as the agent.

That which is obtained—the barley—is the fruit of human effort; it is not the human effort of a [substantial] dharma. Thus, he takes only the conceptual person as the "effort-maker" (*puruṣakāra-puruṣa*). This conceptual person...
The substance [of a person] consists solely of the five aggregates in combination; there is no small, substantial entity. Therefore, the four conditions do not encompass a nominal person (pudgala).

Because a nominal person lacks a substantial entity, it is only when the four conditions—such as the causal condition and so forth—are all dharmas possessing substantial entities that this principle holds.
The Commentary states: "The intention of the second master is that the mind and mental factors together, up to the conventional agent, possess the various activities and tasks to be accomplished.
This second [position] generally includes both persons and dharmas, neither of which possesses *puruṣakāra* (human effort).

Thus, when the mind and mental factors arise simultaneously, they are also called the *dharmapuruṣakāraphala* (the fruit of human effort as a dharma). Within the category of the *dharmapuruṣakāraphala*, this extends even to those that are co-arising or non-arising.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The former masters take only a portion of the conditioned as the essence of the fruit, because it is produced by the power of the person (*puruṣa*).

If this is the intention of the former masters, they mean that they take only a portion of the conditioned—namely, only the conventional person (*prajñapti-pudgala*)—as the cause from which [the fruit] is sown.
Obtaining fields and grain, the production of stumps, boats, and so forth; the construction of houses and dwellings through divination;
and even such things as when a person makes clothing and it is completed—all these are termed "fruits of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*).

If, for instance, wild plants grow spontaneously without being sown by human labor—whether from within, below, or above—they are not called fruits of human effort. Therefore, [the text] takes only those [cases] as a partial illustration.

This master takes only the conventional person (*pudgala*) as the cause; that which is obtained is termed the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*). He does not take dharmas as the fruit of human effort.
Question: Since the former master takes only the conventional [person] as the cause, how can it be the fruit of human effort?

It is not yet known whether the fruits of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), such as the noble fruits (*ārya-phala*) and meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), obtained through the wholesome karma practiced by the conventional person—namely the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and so forth—are all the fruit of human effort.
"Result. This is because that which is not an answer is also such. The *Śāstra* says:

"The second master [holds that] it also encompasses the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and many are also results. As for the essence, even up to being named 'human effort' (*puruṣakāra*) from its function:
the second [master] thus universally includes the human effort of dharmas; that is, he takes both the co-arising and the immediate [conditions], as well as those that do not arise."
The "function of the noble person" (*puruṣakāra*) refers to the realization of the attainment of disjunction from the afflictions, which is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Since the unconditioned is that which does not arise as a cause or effect of things, it is said to "pervade the unconditioned. It is also the essence of the fruit; that is, taking the untainted seeds as the object and the dharmas of the field as the agent.

Simultaneously, one obtains the four aspects of attention (*manasikāra*) as the instruments of action. "Simultaneous" means that they function together with wisdom; thus, they are called instruments of action.

Here, the noble instruments of action and so forth are explained as being named after the conventional person who employs them for the purpose of giving. As for being named after their function: [the following applies].
Regarding "predominant" (*adhipati*), this refers to the remaining [conditions] other than the previous four. As for the statement that "the other four conditions have results":

if one asks how it can be said that there are other phenomena outside the four previously mentioned results—namely, that phenomena other than those four results are called "predominant results"—and what further constitutes a predominant result outside of those four results:
[it is as follows]. Furthermore, in the preceding explanation, regarding the inclusion of the ten causes within two causes and so forth, although...
In this context, throughout the preceding and following passages, all the "first teachers" (pūrvācāryas) refer to the meaning of a single teacher.
The phrase "the matter of habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) reveals the various bases (*āśraya*), and so forth, up to the designation for all that attains the predominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).

However, what is here called "efficacy" (*sāmarthya*) refers to the fact that all phenomena, acting as causes, are able to obtain the five [fruits]; therefore, these causes are termed "efficacy. If...

The "basis of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-adhiṣṭhāna*) also attains this fruit; that is to say, it is attained through six bases. Within the category of dharmas, this is a fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Since it is a fruit of human effort within the category of fruits of human effort, it is combined with the five preceding bases, thus making six.

However, although the commentary mentions the "activity of dharmas," one should understand it as the fruit of human effort consisting of the "functioning of dharmas" (*dharmakārya-puruṣakāra*), which attains the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
In the *Śāstra*, the function of phenomena (*dharma-kriyā*) is not explicitly answered; furthermore, the term "function" (*kriyā*) is used broadly.

If "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) is also termed "function," then it refers to human effort as an instrument of action. Furthermore, there is also the "function" of the superior grade, which refers to the function of the instruments of action.

Therefore, by taking "human effort" as the function, the six bases (*āśraya*) of the preceding [consciousnesses] are identical to their maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*). However, some say that herein...

Since it has already been stated that the seeds of karma obtain the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*), [the claim] that the remote operation obtains this fruit is therefore merely a "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*).
If you argue that human effort is "proximate," that is not so; for the latencies (*vāsanā*) and their fruits are also proximate, and thus they too would not be considered ripened fruits.
This is incorrect. Alternatively, the operation may be considered human effort, establishing the first five bases.
"Abiding" refers to the attainment of the seven stations (*sthāna*). Within this "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*), there are four types;

however, within the "activity of the instrument," these four types cannot exist. Nevertheless, when it is said here that human effort obtains a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*), this is simply a way of speaking regarding the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).

The Commentary states: "If one subsumes the five [bases] to include all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena, both mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are subsumed under the two bases, because they subsume everything that is contaminated.
If mind and mental factors are themselves the subsumption of the five, this means that mind and mental factors possess five bases:

the basis of the support (*āśraya-āyatana*), the basis of the object (*ālambana-āyatana*), the basis of the inquiry (*pṛcchā-āyatana*), the basis of the human effort (*puruṣakāra-āyatana*), and the remaining mind and mental factors, which are the other [bases]. If they are the remainder, they are the other [bases].

The intermediate, the boundary, the faculties, and the three supports are all fruits of the mind and mental factors; as for other dharmas, such as the non-associated formations, they possess only the two [conditions] of activity and locus.
Therefore, it is known that the *dharmadhātu-prayoga* (the functional application of phenomena) also possesses seeds and thus attains the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "How is it known that there are five [causes]? ... up to "...there are two explanations; this also applies here, and it should be understood in the same way.
How is it known that the five bases obtain the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*)? This is based on the ten causes explained below:

the five causes—namely, the projecting cause (*ākṣepahetu*), the producing cause (*abhinirvartakahetu*), the determinative cause (*pratiniyamahetu*), the non-obstructive cause (*avighnabhāvahetu*), and the co-operative cause (*sahakārihetu*)—obtain the ripening fruit, whereas the sustaining cause (*parigrahahetu*) is not mentioned.
Because it obtains the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), it does not take up the activity of human effort (*puruṣakāra*). It obtains the fruit of maturation.

Furthermore, according to the two explanations regarding the activity of human effort found below, if one follows the former master’s view that the four causes have the activity of human effort as their fruit, this refers exclusively to the activity of human effort belonging to a person (*pudgala*).

This is because, in this context, based on the five bases (*pañcāśraya*), one obtains the fruit of maturation. In this regard, the first master also does not speak of the activity of human effort belonging to a person.

The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) is obtained. If the second master says that eight causes obtain the fruit of human effort, this refers generally to the fruit of human effort regarding phenomena (*dharma-puruṣakāra-phala*).

This is the second interpretation herein; or rather, it is the fruit of human effort within the operation of phenomena (*dharma-vyāpāra-puruṣakāra*), which also includes the obtaining of the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) from karmic seeds.
This is precisely the fruit of human effort within the fruit of human effort regarding phenomena; that is, the seven supports (*saptāśraya*).
The ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) is obtained in five bases. Now, according to the commentary (*śāstra*), the ripening fruit is obtained in five bases;
the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) is obtained in seven bases; and the fruit of disjunction (*visamyogaphala*) is obtained in five bases.

Some say that the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) is obtained in five bases; others say it is obtained in eleven bases. These interpretations are all based on the ten causes explained below.
Attaining the fruit within the middle [state] and, conversely, performing many minor ritual acts are both correct principles.

If other interpretations suggest that one attains the five fruits by relying on increased or additional bases, these are all secondary meanings and not the primary ones. Regarding the true explanation, this too refers to what manifests within its own category.
If, within the true explanation, the preceding moment of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) manifestation induces the subsequent moment of uncontaminated manifestation...
[This refers to] activity. Alternatively, according to one interpretation, it is also expected that [a result] manifests within its own category.

If interpreted according to the ultimate truth, the manifestation of a subsequent moment of untainted [dharma] is induced by the manifestation of a preceding moment of untainted [dharma]; or, as in the case of the Path of Seeing inducing the Path of Cultivation and so forth, these are all termed "outflow results" (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Some say that the locus of the functional operation (*puruṣakāra-vṛtti*) also obtains this result; even this master relies upon [this view].
Regarding that which obtains the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*): among the four types of functional activity (*puruṣakāra*) of this master, the first three are said to be co-arising.
Within the fruit of functional activity, there is the seed producing the manifest and the manifest producing the seed; these are also considered fruits of outflow in this context.
Furthermore, within uninterrupted functional activity, there is the production of seeds from seeds, and the cause of the manifest producing the manifest, and so forth.
This is also a result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) within this context.
The Commentary states: "Because the perspectives regarding the dharma that has just ceased differ... and for this reason, it cannot also be a result of uniform outflow."

If a result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) were restricted solely to its own realm and its own stage, then a superior fruit being induced by simultaneous inferior dharmas as its cause would constitute a case where the cause is inferior while the fruit is superior; such could indeed be called a result of outflow.

Now, regarding this basis of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the three types of mind serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*): a wholesome mind induces an unwholesome mind, and an unwholesome mind induces...

An indeterminate mind serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Therefore, in the case of the "equal-and-immediate basis" (*samanantara-āśraya*), a subsequent wholesome mind cannot produce a result that is a similar outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) for a preceding wholesome or unwholesome mind of the same class.
