As for that which acts as the immediately preceding condition by inducing a subsequent state:

it is when a superior state of mindfulness (*smṛti*) that has just ceased acts as the cause to induce a subsequent moment of inferior mind; thus, in this case of the immediate basis, no result of similar outflow is obtained.

If one maintains that the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala) is obtained when both the phenomenon and its human effort coincide, this teacher is the same as the second teacher mentioned previously.
Furthermore, there are four types of phenomena that constitute human effort. If one takes the activity of the phenomenon’s human effort as the fruit of disconnection (visamyoga-phala):
This is the explanation of the fourth fruit, the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).

If one analyzes the operation of human effort, the first five fruits correspond to the seven bases (*sthāna*), as they are likewise the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*) and the cessation [of suffering]. That which leads to the basis for experience is the eighth base.

As for "not being established through realization" (*na prāpti-siddha*): this is because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not arise by depending on realization; rather, it already exists prior to its realization. Furthermore...
The fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) is established based upon the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it is not established based upon the untainted conditioned (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*).

This is because that [unconditioned] possesses the dharma of liberation as its causal condition for purification. However, among the causal conditions of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*), there are birth, abiding, accomplishment, and attainment.

Within attainment, the seventh "birth" (the birth of birth) occurs first. According to the commentary, this refers to the attainment of the fruit of *nirvāṇa* and the attainment of the fruit of *bodhi*.

Therefore, what is now attained is exclusively the attainment of bodhi, as it is a conditioned fruit (*saṃskṛta-phala*). Thus, it is said that within the context of the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*), the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) is attained.

The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Furthermore, depending on the means of realization (*sākṣāt-karaṇa*), there is that which is realized; regarding the arising, abiding, and so forth, up to the conditioned fruit... This [passage]...

The meaning of the passage is as follows: Within the "basis of reception" (*anubhava-āśraya*), it is also established that one attains the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is equivalent to attaining the fruit of dissociation within the six bases. Specifically, within the basis of reception, there is the arising, abiding, and accomplishment of attainment;

therein, one first possesses the lineage (*gotra*) of the three vehicles. With internal correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) as the primary factor and external conditions as the secondary factor, the Buddha appears in the world and one comes to know well.

Consciousness and so forth act as the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that realizes the fruit of nirvāṇa, which is dissociation (*visamyoga*). Therefore, it is said: "Among the [four] acquisitions (*prāpti*), there is the fruit of dissociation.
Thus, among the six bases (*āśraya*), the acquisition of the fruit of dissociation is established. According to the ten causes discussed below, five fruits are obtained;

however, the treatise mentions only five bases as obtaining the fruit of dissociation, and does not state that the fruit of dissociation is obtained from the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*). Therefore, now...

Regarding the basis for reception: among the five bases, there is the attainment of the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*). According to the second master, the fruits are said to be obtained even up to the eleventh basis.
If one receives [the result] within the midst of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it is only through human agency that it is designated as the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Furthermore, this second master asserts four kinds of human effort, two of which are mentioned here, as well as the fourth, as explained in the section on habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
That is, seed produces seed, and seed produces seed; the seed itself is the immediate *puruṣakāra-phala* (human effort fruit).
Within the state of immediate cessation, the preceding mind induces the subsequent mind, which is also an immediate *puruṣakāra-phala*.

In the true explanation, there is also the case where the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) induces the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), which is likewise an immediate *puruṣakāra-phala*. If one realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), that is the fruit of non-arising (*anutpāda-phala*).

Regarding the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*): within that which conforms [to its cause], there is also the realization of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This is the "non-arising" fruit of human effort.

Furthermore, where there is functional capacity, there is also the realization of the unconditioned; this too is the "non-arising" fruit of human effort. Conjunction (*sāmagrī*) has as its essence the non-obstruction of the preceding factors combined together.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Regarding the bases (*āyatana*) and phenomena (*dharma*), the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*)...
[omitted] ...therefore it is known that the same applies to the bases. This means that within the category of bases, there is no fruit of human effort;

rather, because all phenomena that serve as causes do not have a fruit of human effort, and because the resulting fruit is not closely connected to its cause, and furthermore, because this fruit of human effort must necessarily be something produced (*janya*), it can only manifest the phenomenon itself.
In the ten causes listed below, it is nowhere stated that the *anuvāda-hetu* (the cause of subsequent expression) obtains a *puruṣakāra-phala* (the fruit of human effort).
Therefore, we know that the *vāk-āśraya* (the basis of speech) likewise does not obtain a *puruṣakāra-phala*. Now, the objection is raised:
If a *puruṣakāra-phala* must necessarily arise from something else, and since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is said to produce a *puruṣakāra-phala*, how can the unconditioned itself arise?

The Commentary states: "If [the definition] 'that which is not karma' refers to the third [category], the basis of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), then it would be excessively broad (*ativyāpti*) because it includes causes, conditions, seeds, and results of similar outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) that are not karma.
If such things were to obtain a ripened result (*vipāka-phala*), this would constitute the fault of being too broad."

The Commentary states: "Because it follows the statement that [the basis] extends only from the eleventh [ground] onwards, and because it is not a result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), there is the fault of being too broad.

This means that within the present eleventh basis of conformity (*anukūla-āśraya*), it also cites the *Nirvāṇa* as being the result of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*), rather than a result of outflow.
Furthermore, within the basis of conformity, it is not of the same class (*sabhāga*) nor is it different; it is untainted (*anāsrava*).

Regarding "similar dharmas" (*sabhāga-dharma*): for instance, when innate wholesome states (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*) induce [subsequent] acquisitions (*prāpti*), these [acquisitions] are similar outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) that are not of the same category [as their cause].

However, those things induced by innate wholesome states—namely, both wisdom derived from reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*) and wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*)—are not of a different category and are not outflow fruits; since they are all induced by wisdom, they are all termed "similar" (*sabhāga*).
When wisdom induces wisdom, it is called "dissimilar" (visabhāga); when wisdom induces contemplation-wisdom (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), it is called "similar" (sabhāga).

When contemplation-wisdom induces contemplation-wisdom belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is called "dissimilar"; when contemplation-wisdom belonging to the first dhyāna induces contemplation-wisdom of the first dhyāna, it is called "similar.

When contemplation-wisdom of the first dhyāna induces contemplation-wisdom of the second dhyāna, it is called "dissimilar," and so on up to the induction of existence (*bhava*); all cases should be understood accordingly.
Now, those factors above that are of the same category, the same nature, and the same level, which mutually induce one another, are all termed "fruit of equal outflow" (*niṣyandaphala*).
If they are of different natures, different categories, or different levels, and thus mutually induce one another, this is the "predominant fruit" (*adhipatiphala*).

Alternatively, when contaminated wholesome states induce the arising of contaminated wholesome states, it is called the "fruit of equal outflow of the same category. When contaminated wholesome states induce the cessation of uncontaminated wholesome states, this is the predominant fruit.

Regarding the fruit: if the mind and mental factors are simultaneous, they may be either *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort) or *niṣyanda-phala* (fruit of outflow). Furthermore, when a contaminated [cause] induces an uncontaminated [result], it is likewise not a *niṣyanda-phala*.

If one were to include within this category of "conducive bases" those of different types and different realms, as well as that which induces *nirvāṇa*—such as a contaminated cause inducing an uncontaminated *niṣyanda-phala*—then there would be the fault of being overly broad (*ativyāpti*). Nevertheless, among those things that are conducive, there exists the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, subsequent [moments] are not induced by those of a different category. That is to say, among the four types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*), if a maturation-born state induces a state of its own kind, or if a state of its own kind induces a higher state, or if a state of its own kind induces a state resulting from application (*prayoga-ja*), these are all not results of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). Furthermore, regarding the induction of wholesome states, the treatise says:

Within each category of the wholesome, wisdom induces thought-wisdom (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and induces cultivation-wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Furthermore, within all that is wholesome, wisdom induces the wholesome of application (*prayoga-kuśala*).
Within all that is wholesome, wisdom induces thought-wisdom and so forth; these aforementioned instances are all not results of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Moreover, within the unwholesome, greed induces anger, and anger induces delusion (*moha*); thus, factors of different types induce one another. It is also said that factors of different realms induce one another.

This means that within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), both wisdom-born from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and wisdom-born from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) exist. Furthermore, the wisdom-born from reflection in the desire realm induces the wisdom-born from cultivation in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Again, the wisdom-born from cultivation in the form realm induces the initial wisdom-born from cultivation;

this initial wisdom-born from cultivation induces the wisdom-born from cultivation of the second dhyāna, and so on up to the third dhyāna inducing the fourth dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna inducing the untainted (*anāsrava*) states and so forth.
Moreover, from the wisdom-born from cultivation in the form realm, one is induced into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), such as the sphere of infinite space.

The cultivation of wisdom in the sphere of infinite space gives rise to the cultivation of wisdom in the sphere of infinite consciousness. The cultivation of wisdom in the sphere of infinite consciousness further gives rise to [the cultivation of wisdom] in the sphere of nothingness.

The cultivation of wisdom in the sphere of nothingness gives rise to the cultivation of wisdom in the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). The cultivation of wisdom in the peak of existence gives rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*) [wisdom].

All of the above are not results of similar outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). Furthermore, within the untainted, the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) gives rise to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the path of cultivation...
They induce the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*). These [dharmas] of different realms are likewise not of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*).

Regarding these aforementioned dharmas: if they are of the same category, those of the same category induce one another; if they belong to the same realm, those of the same realm induce one another. Furthermore, the superior induces the superior, the superior induces the intermediate, and the intermediate induces the superior.
Only when the superior induces the superior is it called a result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). Moreover, among the indeterminate states, if there is a superior maturation (*vipāka*)...
Superior maturation draws forth superior maturation; superior maturation draws forth middling maturation; middling maturation draws forth superior maturation.

These are just as in the case of the superior maturation among the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); it should be understood that the "superior-superior" follows the same pattern. These are the results of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Furthermore, within the functional (*airyāpathika*), the superior draws forth the superior, the superior draws forth the middling, and the middling draws forth the superior. This is...

These are results of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). This applies even up to the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Furthermore, among the innate wholesome states and those induced by the innate wholesome states, there are likewise three grades.
Moreover, within the categories of wholesome states analyzed in the treatises, all those induced by wisdom (*prajñā*) also consist of three grades before they constitute results of outflow.
Furthermore, regarding those induced by the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), it is only when they mutually induce one another in three grades that they constitute results of outflow.
Furthermore, among the wholesome states of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), all are induced by wisdom (*prajñā*); that is, they are induced by wisdom.

It is because they are induced by the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) that they constitute a result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). Moreover, within the first dhyāna, all are induced by wisdom; these too are results of outflow.

This continues up to the fourth dhyāna, where all are induced by wisdom, and only then do they constitute results of outflow. This extends even to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), which induces [the corresponding] existence.

Only when [the wisdom of cultivation] belonging to a higher stage induces [the wisdom of cultivation] belonging to that same stage is it a result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). If the wisdom of cultivation of the first dhyāna induces the wisdom of cultivation of the second dhyāna, it is not a result of uniform outflow;

this continues up to the point where the wisdom of cultivation of the sphere of nothingness induces the wisdom of cultivation of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), which likewise is not a result of uniform outflow.

Within the untainted (*anāsrava*) realm, when the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) induces the Path of Seeing, it is indeed a result of uniform outflow; the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is also the same.

The outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*). All that has been discussed above constitutes the outflowing fruit. Although it conforms to its cause, even when factors from different realms mutually induce one another, provided they are not contradictory, this is termed "conforming" (*anuloma*).
For example, within the category of innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*), all are comprised of the portions of volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Within the wholesome [states] that well-induce preparatory application (*prayoga*), there is wisdom; within wisdom, there is wisdom. Wisdom induces the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*);

the wisdom of reflection induces the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*) of the higher realms; the wisdom of cultivation induces the untainted (*anāsrava*). Through the untainted, one realizes *nirvāṇa*.

All of these are mutually non-contradictory and are in accord with one another; therefore, they are called "causes of sequential explanation" (*anusahitahetu*). They also include those of their own stage, as well as all similar phenomena (*sabhāga-dharma*) that are simultaneous or subsequent.

[The term] "that which" refers to the noble minds and mental factors that arise simultaneously in correspondence, as well as their four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and the subsequent outflowless states induced by preceding moments;

none of these are results of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*). If it is argued that only the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the result of disjunction, then regarding the term "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*), it applies exclusively to the ninth [ground], and so forth, even including the induction of superior and concordant results (*niṣyanda-phala*). However, within the context of human effort...

Thus, there is no result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). As for the claim that there is only the dominant result (*adhipati-phala*), within the category of "functioning of phenomena" (*dharmasya puruṣakāra*) there is also the result of uniform outflow.
For example, among the four types of functioning of phenomena: in the case of simultaneous functioning (*sahabhū-puruṣakāra*), seeds produce actualities (*samudācāra*), and actualities produce seeds;

furthermore, in the case of uninterrupted functioning (*anantara-puruṣakāra*), the preceding moments of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) induce the succeeding moments of mind and mental factors.
Regarding the statement that "seeds produce seeds," these are termed *niṣyanda-phala* (outflow fruits). There are other [interpretations] among the remaining [categories] that are too broad;
even if [a category] is not included, it would then be too narrow. In this commentary, there are two explanations. The first is the aforementioned fruit;
it does not explain the *adhipati-phala* (dominant fruits). Among the fifteen [obstructions], the four obstructions regarding objects (*viṣaya*) are precisely these four locations.
Regarding the eleven minor divisions, if one claims that all those which are predominant (*adhipati*) are subsumed under the predominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), this refers only to the four [bases].
Since the eleven minor divisions would then likewise be the predominant fruit, this definition is too narrow (*atisaṃkṣipta*).

Conversely, if one claims that the eleven external bases—wherein the latencies (*vāsanā*) conform to the human effort (*puruṣakāra*) of true vision—are the predominant fruit, this incurs the fault of being too broad (*ativyāpti*). These eleven...

The intermediate states also include those who have attained the four fruits; if the intermediate states were not to include the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), then the four intermediate states would differ from the previous four fruits, and furthermore, if there were a separate superior fruit (*adhipatiphala*) that was not included, this would result in the fault of being overly restrictive.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'inducing subsequent similar types,' this means that within true seeing (*tathā-darśana*) there is also the manifestation of the untainted (*anāsrava*).

This induction of the untainted manifestation is not itself the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*). Furthermore, within the category of 'receiving' (*vedayita*), there are also cases where the 'human effort' fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*) is not obtained.
However, according to the preceding treatise, since it speaks of the locus of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) is obtained therein."
Up to the point where one attains dissociation (*visamyoga*) through true vision; now, in this passage, it reverses that text. It should be stated:

"Just as in the case of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) is not obtained, so too in the case of true vision, the fruit of dissociation is not obtained. Furthermore, it should also be stated regarding the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*):
"In the midst of [the process], there is also the non-obtainment of the fruit of human effort. This is what is meant in the commentary by the phrase "the locus of experience" (*anubhava-āśraya*).
It is as follows: among the *puruṣakāra* (human efforts), there are those that do not obtain the fruit of *puruṣakāra*.

For example, suppose a person’s original intention is to go to another's house, but they do not perform the act of giving birth to a child for that family. If they were to perform the act of giving birth to a child, they would not only obtain the status of being that person’s relative;
if they obtain this fruit of *puruṣakāra*, then if that person does not obtain it, what is obtained is called the *adhipatiphala* (dominant fruit). If one performs this external [act]...

This also contradicts the following passage. The following passage states: "Although it is a fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), it is also obtained as a dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*). Answer:
Regarding the fruit of human effort that has been obtained, it is designated as a dominant fruit by way of its functional significance.

According to my understanding, even within the category of fruits of human effort, there are cases where one does not obtain the fruit of human effort; for example, when a person provides a livelihood for others. Its...

Although a person may perform actions for others through various means such as cultivation and so forth, they cannot attain [the result]; therefore, among the results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), one does not obtain the result of human effort.
Alternatively, this predominance (*adhipati*) should be understood as being strictly limited to the four bases of reliance (*pratisaraṇa*), because it is by these that the fruit is attained.
This is the second interpretation; it is the explanation regarding the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
If fifteen bases are called the dominant fruit, or if the remaining four bases are [included], or if one takes only eleven bases as the dominant fruit, then it would be too narrow.
Is it not the case that it is merely narrow and lacks the fault of being too broad, because it fails to include the four bases? For even within the eleven bases, they are indeed included.
The four fruits are collectively termed the "predominant fruit" (*adhipati-phala*). Attaining the four fruits in four locations is collectively termed the "predominant fruit.

Why is it not [merely] called the "predominant fruit"? Thus we know that although the four fruits are attained in four locations, these four locations and the four fruits together are collectively termed the "predominant fruit";
it is not narrow [in scope]. This is because the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) has matured.
Regarding the statement, "At that time, one knows the characteristics of the fruit, up to the point of obtaining the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*)," the answer is as follows:

At the time of ripening, the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma are called "ripening causes" (*vipāka-hetu*) because, in terms of their nature and characteristics, they stand in relation to the neutral (*avyākṛta*) ripened fruit.

Furthermore, since the locus of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the fruit's characteristics has not yet been known, it is said that the ripened fruit is obtained within those habitual tendencies.

The Commentary (*śāstra*) states: "Because a cause of outflow (*niṣyanda-hetu*) must be an inferior or equal dharma [in relation] to a superior or equal dharma... and so forth, up to: "Therefore, the treatise says.

This means that while the cause is inferior, the result is equal; furthermore, if it is concordant (*anuloma*), the result is even superior. Since conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) also have results that are superior to their causes, it is said that they obtain a result of outflow when they are concordant.
The Commentary states: "However, where there is necessarily a *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort), it cannot be the same as what was said previously.

This [present] case is also not [restricted to that], nor can even the *puruṣakāra-phala* obtained here be [limited to] the fruits of increase (*adhipati-phala*) and so forth. Nevertheless, among the other four bases (*sthāna*), there are four types of cause-and-effect, some of which are not [obtained].
For example, regarding the 'conducive base' (*anuloma-sthāna'), it is said that one obtains the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala'). This conducive base is also [subject to this]."
It is not a result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). Among the "bases of true vision" (*satya-darśana-sthāna*), it is said that one attains the result of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*);

yet within this same basis of true vision, one also attains what is not dissociation. Furthermore, among the "bases of prior habitual tendencies," one also attains the ripening result (*vipāka-phala*);

yet in reality, this also includes what is not a ripened result. This is consistent with other passages in the treatise, where it is stated that these are likewise not bases. Regarding the "basis of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-sthāna*), the treatise states:
The presence or absence of the term "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) does not mean that it is not the fruit of human effort; it merely states that it is the locus of human effort.

This locus also includes the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) and others, yet it is specifically the locus of human effort. It cannot be said that it is also not [the fruit of human effort] because one has forgotten that it is the fruit of human effort.

Regarding the meaning of the fruit of human effort, it is also the dominant fruit. If one regards it as a cause for phenomena, then it is also taken [as such]; thus, it takes the phenomena of human effort.
The "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) is subsumed within the "functioning" (*kāritra*); it also obtains the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).

The Commentary states: "Since the treatise does not explicitly state that [the cause] obtains [this fruit], there is no contradiction in our current interpretation, as it merely differs regarding the specific category (*sthāna*).

Furthermore, because the 'contingent cause' (*apekṣāhetu*) and the 'human effort' (*puruṣakāra*) would otherwise be confused, we take all eight categories of meaning within the eightfold classification."
In relation to human effort (*puruṣakāra*), other causes do not act as a supervising factor, and thus they are not [the cause].

The commentary states: "In the Mahāyāna, the arising of causes is not by way of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). This means that within the Mahāyāna, the maturation of wholesome and unwholesome karma, as well as neutral (*avyākṛta*) and nominal (*nāma*) phenomena, are not [produced] by the causal condition.
Even in the Sarvāstivāda school, although there are other [types of] causes, they function as the creative cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).

Regarding the remaining five causes: since the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is entirely of the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the verse identifies the five causes as being of the nature of the causal condition by means of the "human agent" (*puruṣakāra*).
However, this is not done with respect to the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*). As for why the "attainment" (*prāpti*) is not mentioned:

since the contingent cause has already been stated to be a conventional designation (*prajñapti*), and because the human agent depends upon that which is depended upon, the human agent cannot obtain a fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*). Therefore, the contingent cause is not mentioned [in that context], yet it is obtained.

The fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*). Question: Since arising, abiding, and attainment are already included within the condition of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*), and since nirvāṇa is said to be among these attainments, why is it said that the condition of dependence does not obtain the fruit of dissociation?
One should ask the Dharma Master: because it is induced by pure conditioned phenomena (*samskrta*).
This is because True Suchness (*tathatā*) itself is designated as the fruit of dissociation; thus, among the ten causes of purity, it is the "inducing cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*).

Regarding the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*): why is this so? Because among the ten causes that are exclusively pure, it is designated as the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*) because it takes only the conditioned, untainted seeds as its fruit.
As for the projecting cause—the untainted seeds—the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not the fruit of disjunction.
The actualized manifestation produced by the uncontaminated seeds drawn forth therein is able to realize the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) because it is free from afflictions;

therefore, the unconditioned is termed the fruit of dissociation (visamyoga-phala). Consequently, among the ten causes of purification, it is not said that the fruit of dissociation is obtained through the cause of drawing forth.

The Commentary states: "Since this is so, the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the remaining three conditions may even be called 'human effort' (puruṣakāra), including those that do not produce results.
This refers to the second master’s explanation of the "fruit of human effort" (*dharma-puruṣakāra-phala*). It explains the eight causes and the three conditions.

And thus one obtains the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). This is because, apart from the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), there is nothing within external objects that functions like human effort.
Although previously it was established that the seeds of bondage and so forth are bound by human effort, these are all merely figurative designations.
How, then, can the other three conditions be fully present? Within the four types of human effort, specifically within the simultaneous (*sahaja*) human effort, the seed itself exists.

The arising of actual manifestation, the seeds produced by actual manifestation, and the human effort (*puruṣakāra*) produced immediately thereafter—within these, the seeds and so forth are all causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
If there is no [actual] function within [the process], then there is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is pervasive.
Therefore, the *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort) also obtains a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*), yet it is not obtained here [in this context]. Fourth, the *puruṣakāra-phala* does not arise.

Below this, the ten causes and four conditions are clarified as obtaining five fruits; all are as previously stated regarding the fifteen bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*). The attainment of the fruit of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is identical in all cases.
The Commentary states: "Regarding these dominant fruits up to the four conditions": because these are dominant fruits, it is not otherwise;
the functions previously employed as the four fruits differ from those obtained through external causes, as their respective fruits are distinct.

This is the second interpretation, which does not speak of dominant fruits. That is to say, among the ten causes, one takes only the *anuvāda-hetu* (conformity cause) and the *virodha-hetu* (contradiction cause). This...

Regarding the two causes: when the primary cause is significant and the secondary cause is minor, the first four fruits are established; the remaining external factors are then designated as the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).

However, since the category of non-contradiction (*avirodha*) includes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), how can these be considered sovereign? The intent of this question is to take the "cooperative cause" (*sahabhūhetu*) as the basis for the sovereign fruit here.

Within the non-contradictory cause (*avirodha-hetu*), there is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); and within the appropriating cause (*parigraha-hetu*), there is also the unconditioned in the sphere of the object (*viṣaya-sthāna*).
The unconditioned serves as the cause for the arising of the fruit, which consists of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*). Thus, the unconditioned functions as a cause.

Since that causal entity—the non-contradictory cause—already takes the preceding sphere of the object as its essence and does not grasp [the unconditioned] as a separate factor, it is merely described in terms of being a cause and is not [explicitly] mentioned [as a distinct category].
Within the context of the *anuvāda-hetu* (the cause of subsequent designation), although there are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, they are not included.

This is because those unconditioned phenomena are exclusively effects; since they are intended as effects by virtue of being designated as causes, within the *anuvāda-hetu*, the unconditioned does not function as a cause for others.
Rather, because it is solely an effect, it is not taken [as a cause]. Within the context of true vision (*tattva-darśana*), although there are unconditioned phenomena...
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*). Furthermore, it is not a cause for anything else, because it acts as a fruit for others;

therefore, it is not included [in those categories]. Consequently, it is only included within "appropriation" (*parigraha*), "commonality" (*sabhāga*), and "non-contradiction" (*aviruddha*), because the unconditioned serves as a cause from which the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) is obtained.
Now, a question is asked: Within these three categories, how does the unconditioned obtain the dominant fruit?
In this commentary, for now, I have cited only those [factors] that are not contradictory; this is merely to provide a general indication of the direction.
Regarding the response, "All ten causes obtain their fruits, and even the 'contingent' cause and so forth are likewise," the intended meaning here is as follows:

If all ten causes obtain their fruits and there is none that does not, then among these three causes, the statement that the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) obtains a sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala) applies to it simultaneously with all phenomena.
They do not obstruct one another. That which is attained as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is called the attainment of the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).

When it is said here that the unconditioned attains a fruit, this unconditioned also possesses the functional capacity to take and bestow a fruit, just like the *anuvāda-hetu* (the cause of subsequent mention).
Since all phenomena act as causes for their respective fruits, whatever [fruit] exists in its own primary locus is also bestowed by them; thus they are called "causes."
They do not reach one another and are remote. This same applies to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) acting as causes. Furthermore, it is like the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*);
although it is a remote contingency regarding its effect, it is still called a cause because they do not reach one another.

This unconditioned phenomenon acting as a cause is not like the unconditioned phenomena of the Hīnayāna, which are neither cause nor effect and thus cannot be termed cause and effect. It should therefore not be explained in the same manner as in the Hīnayāna.

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is both cause and fruit. Within the six causes, when the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) subsumes the unconditioned as a cause, it does not obtain any of the five fruits.
Among the five fruits, the unconditioned is subsumed as the fruit of disconnection (*visamyogaphala*) when the unconditioned is taken as a fruit.
It does not arise from the six causes. Now, the Mahāyāna also teaches that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) possesses cause and effect. It is realized precisely because it is noble (*ārya*):
the noble unconditioned is the cause, and the unconditioned is the effect. Because the unconditioned serves as the object (*ālambana*), the mind and mental factors take it as their objective support;
thus, the unconditioned is the cause and the mind and mental factors are the effect.
The Commentary states: "The passage concerning 'the phenomena produced by conditions' should clarify the conditions themselves.

Therefore, the statement that "abiding in the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is the correct treatise" means that "produced by conditions" refers to the fourth alternative: the arising of various respective conceptualizations (*vikalpa*).
Because the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that arise from conditions are immediately produced as the substance of the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*).

Although the *Catuṣpratyaya* (Treatise on the Four Conditions) clarifies that which is produced by conditions, it does not clarify the conditions themselves. As for the second [section] stating, "although it clarifies that which is produced," etc., it does not clarify the meaning of how various specific discriminations (*vikalpa*) arise through the four conditions.
Therefore, since this treatise already establishes the characteristics of phenomena produced by conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma-lakṣaṇa*), [the four conditions must be explained].

Regarding the phrase "acting as conditions" and so forth, up to "why is it used for liberation": because the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) act as three types of conditions, the four conditions are the correct doctrine.

As for "discerning the essence," this refers to the four conditions themselves. Regarding "the function of the four conditions": because the seeds within the fundamental consciousness act as three conditions, the four conditions are the correct doctrine.
Discerning the essence means that these are precisely the four conditions; the four conditions are [the essence]. The four conditions are...
Regarding the various entities and functions: this refers to the second master following the passage "by means of all-seed consciousness" in the [second] fascicle.
The treatise states: "These are the results of outflow, maturation, increase, and dominance; therefore, the four results are termed 'entities,' and 'all seeds' are termed 'functions.

If there were no entity as the basis for the four conditions, how could the functions of the four results be distinguished? According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts, that which is obtained by the agent (*puruṣakāra*) is [the result of human effort].
Regarding the phrase "the fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and so forth, up to "thus both masters [are correct]":

the intended meaning of this *Yogācārabhūmi* passage is that, in deliberating upon what constitutes the fruit of human effort according to this treatise, there are two masters. However, although the treatise explains that what is obtained by a person (*puruṣa*) constitutes the fruit of human effort, it does not contradict the *Mahāśāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*), which also treats such things as the fruit of human effort. Therefore, within this context, there are two masters.

All of these are correct. However, regarding the ten causes—whether they are with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—there is a distinction between those with and without outflows.

Among the ten causes, three are common to both the without-outflow and with-outflow categories; namely, the cause of verbal expression (*nirukti-hetu*), the cause of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*), and the cause of contradiction (*virodha-hetu*).
Within the cause of verbal expression, for instance, the Tathāgata’s verbal expression that is without outflows serves as the [verbal] expression.

Regarding the causes of speech: the teachings on causes and the principles of dharma state that tainted (*sāsrava*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) speech constitute the cause of conventional expression; this is what is meant by "discourse.

As for the condition of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*), or when there are causes such as the Tathāgata’s untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) and dharmas such as *tathatā*, these serve as conditions of dependence.
If one gives rise to a mind of slander toward these, one will follow [the path to] the hells and other realms. Furthermore, within the category of contradictory causes (*virodha-hetu*)—

There are those that are untainted (*anāsrava*). Because the untainted and tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas are indeed contradictory causes, among the ten causes, the *anuvāda-hetu* (cause of subsequent statement), *apekṣā-hetu* (contingent cause), and *virodha-hetu* (contradictory cause) apply to both the tainted and the untainted. Seven causes are exclusively tainted and do not apply to either the tainted or the untainted.
If, within the ten causes of purification, one considers them as well, three of these causes also apply to both the tainted and the untainted.
This refers to the "cause of conventional designation" (*vyavahāra-hetu*). That is, the speech of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and others serves as the cause of conventional designation;
it also designates pure, untainted (*anāsrava*) resultant phenomena. Furthermore, the tainted (*sāsrava*) serves as the cause of conventional designation for pure phenomena and so forth.

Within the context of the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*), untainted results are likewise produced with defiled phenomena and the like acting as their causes—just as, for example, a person acts out of evil [intentions].

When one encounters such circumstances, one immediately attains the state of a sage. As for contrary causes: because all evil matters are contrary causes to untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), they are also contrary causes to purity.
Furthermore, among the ten causes of purity, tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) may also exist as contrary causes.

Among the seven causes that are with-outflows (sāsrava), there are those that are exclusively without-outflows (anāsrava). Within the ten causes that are indeterminate (avyākṛta), the explanatory cause (nirukti-hetu) and the dependence cause (apekṣā-hetu) are both common to the without-outflows;
these include the pure, outflow-free speech of a Buddha as well as the speech of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), which serves as the explanatory cause.

Furthermore, there are neutral (avyākṛta) matters such as sowing fields, wheat, and so forth. If one sows fields and the like while contemplating giving or cultivating merit, or if one sows fields and the like while contemplating unwholesome karma, these fall within the category of neutral "contingent causes" (apekṣā-hetu), which include both contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava) phenomena.
However, within the category of neutral "contradictory causes" (virodha-hetu), uncontaminated phenomena are not included; it refers only to things such as frost that cause damage.
In reality, frost and lightning are equivalent to the crops themselves, as they serve as opposing causes. Question:

The treatise states that there are six types of "appropriating causes" (*parigraha-hetu*) within the context of the [six] bases (*āyatana*). What about the "appropriating cause" included among the ten causes and the ten indeterminate causes?
Within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), there is that which exists. How can there be a basis for true vision (*samyag-darśana*)? The basis for true vision is untainted (*anāsrava*).
If, within the indeterminate, the appropriating cause (*parigraha-hetu*) lacks a basis for true vision, how can one speak of the essence of the basis while discerning the function of the ten causes?
Furthermore, how could it be called "true vision"? Answer: It is simply the cause of the five bases of feeling (*pañca-vedanā-sthāna*). Thus, true vision may be known.

Second is the distinction between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Regarding the ten causes—namely, the cause of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*), the cause of appropriation (*parigraha-hetu*), the cause of commonality (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the cause of non-contradiction (*avirodha-hetu*)—among these four, the unconditioned serves as the "commonality" (*samāna-darśana*).

That is to say, by depending on the unconditioned as a cause through the cause of dependence, one practices wholesome dharmas. Yet, if one separately slanders the unconditioned—that is, the dharma of cessation—one falls into hell.

In all cases, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) serves as the relational cause (*apekṣā-hetu*). Within the category of the appropriating cause (*parigraha-hetu*), regarding the objective sphere (*ālambana*) and its locus, there likewise arises no cause consisting of an object of cognition;
rather, it is the unconditioned that serves as the object-cause (*ālambana-hetu*), while the cognizing mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*) serve as the resultant phenomena.

Thus, the unconditioned object is the cause and the cognizing mind is the result. Because these two causes—the "common function" (*ekakārya*) and the "non-contradiction" (*avirodha*)—have the former [the unconditioned] as their essential nature, they are identical.
Regarding the two causes that do not contradict their effects (*kārya*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) can also serve as causes.

Although unconditioned phenomena exist among the causes such as "production" (*ākṣepaka*) and "specificity" (*anyathātva*), they are excluded from being included within the category of causes because they are themselves the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).

Thus, among the four [projecting] causes, unconditioned phenomena can function as causes; however, the remaining six causes consist exclusively of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). If [one considers] the ten...

Regarding the five bases (*āśraya*): namely, the basis of experience, the basis of objects, the basis of conjunction, and the basis of non-obstruction—each of these may have the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its cause.
This follows the method established among the ten causes. As for the remaining eleven bases, none have the unconditioned as their cause.
Furthermore, regarding the "consequent cause" (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*) spoken of by the Tathāgata, this accords with what is taught in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.

The three bodies (*trikāya*). If one acts as a person of the three types of karma and so forth, these are the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and others, for whom only the three categories of dharmas—bases (*āyatana*), aggregates (*skandha*), and elements (*dhātu*)—are taught.
As for the dharmas such as the six *pāramitās* of giving, upholding, and emerging, these pertain to the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha;

that is to say, they are the dharmas of the ten stages of Bodhisattvas, such as the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the activities of all worlds. Question: How is this explained in the *Mahāśāstra* and other texts?
That which is cultivated on the stages (*bhūmi*) is called the Great *Pāramitā*. Furthermore, how does one attain the ten correspondences (*yoga*) to manifest the ten stages?
Answer: It is according to the correspondence with the named [Dharmakāya]. Answer: It is the Dharma-gate of non-arising and non-ceasing taught by the Dharmakāya Buddha.

However, a portion of the Dharmakāya is ineffable; it is taught by the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. It is according to the correspondence with the Nirmāṇakāya, that is, the Dharma-gate of transformation. According to the Dharma-gate of transformation, it is also...

This is precisely the dharma-gate of the bodhisattvas of the ten stages. Whether it be the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) or the reward body (sambhogakāya), when the Buddha speaks of non-arising and non-ceasing—the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing—this is the dharma-gate of the transformation-body and the dharma-body Buddhas.

The *Śāstra* states: "Regarding the statement that the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) can serve as conditions for the arising of manifestations and the arising of manifest discrimination, etc., the passage from 'by means of the all-seed consciousness' in the preceding seventh fascicle up to 'one should correctly discern the treatise' is precisely an instance of revealing the cause by citing the effect.
The 'effect' refers to the arising of various respective discriminations; the 'cause' refers to the conditions."

Regarding the ten causes, two causes, fifteen bases, and so forth: these first cite the various fruits of arising and differentiation in order to reveal the four conditions and other factors that produce them.
Now, in this fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the passage from "the seeds within" (*madhye bījāni*) onwards cites the cause in order to reveal the fruit;
the "cause" refers precisely to the seeds within the fundamental consciousness, while the "fruit" refers to the manifestation of the actualized portion (*pravṛttibhāga*).
The phrase "others and so forth" (*ādi*) here refers to the fact that [the term] "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) encompasses both mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*).

If it is argued that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) consist only of their own substance, we reply: when manifesting through discrimination (*vikalpa*), there are also factors dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-dharma*) within that discrimination.

Since the object-part, the seeing-part, and other such dissociated factors all have consciousness as their substance, the treatise itself declares that "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) is its central tenet.
This refers to the manifestation of arising conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
The commentary states, "There is nothing that is not a seed of consciousness. This means that all phenomena arise from the seeds of consciousness;
there is not a single phenomenon that does not arise from the seeds of consciousness.

The Commentary states: "In general, all phenomena such as the aspects (*nimitta*) and the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) possess this condition, for there is nothing that arises without seeds of consciousness.
What is now referred to as "arising manifest discrimination" also extends to the arising of the knowledge of phenomena and their associated mental factors.
The aspects and the seeing-part are *hetu-pratyaya* (causal conditions), not merely the arising of consciousness itself that is termed a causal condition.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the fact that among the seeing-parts (*darśana-bhāga*), the remaining five consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness—even up to the sixth—sometimes take [seeds] as their objects:

now, as for the remaining five and the seventh consciousnesses, these five and seventh consciousnesses cannot take seeds as their objects. This was already established in the previous fourth fascicle according to the interpretation of the Five Masters (*pañca-ācārya*):
it is the seeing-part of the fifth consciousness that takes seeds as its object. However, the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness is capable of [taking them all]."

Regarding the timing of the conditions for seeds: when the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the sixth consciousness has seeds as its object, there are times when it does not have seeds as its object.
The Commentary states:

"That is to say, when seeds exist in relation to manifest phenomena (*pravṛtti-dharma*), and even in relation to those distinct from manifest phenomena, they all constitute dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*)."

Regarding "conditions" (*pratyaya*): these are the factors that assist and provide [the cause], namely the faculties and seeds. They assist in sustaining the seeds of consciousness and so forth; the seeds of mental attention (*manasikāra*) assist consciousness and so forth.
As for "consciousness and so forth," this refers to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*), and is therefore called "the two.

This is as stated previously in the third fascicle: "Although these are also capable of inducing the arising of mental factors, because the mind is the primary [factor], it is said only that they induce the mind. This...

These are called "auxiliaries" because they provide assistance; therefore, they are termed "dominant conditions" (*adhipatipratyaya*). Furthermore, even in the absence of assistance, that which is merely non-contradictory is also a dominant condition.
For example, the seeds of visual consciousness can be known, and all manifest activities are likewise non-contradictory; thus, they are subsumed under the category of dominant conditions.
The Commentary states: "Thus, it is not the case that the untainted seeds and the tainted active manifestations are not [mutually related]; therefore, it is not [the case that they are unrelated].
This is the first interpretation: the untainted seeds are also a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and are also subsumed under the category of non-contradictory causes (*avirodha-hetu*).
However, uncontaminated seeds do not serve as non-contradictory dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the production and so forth of contaminated manifest activities.
When uncontaminated [states] arise as manifest activities, they are able to impair contaminated phenomena;
since those uncontaminated states do not act as causes for contaminated phenomena, uncontaminated seeds are not the cause of contaminated phenomena. Therefore, the uncontaminated...
Dharmas and contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas do not act as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for one another; therefore, [the text] excludes uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas.

Regarding the commentary’s statement: "Alternatively, this condition also refers to that which acts as an obstacle in the present or future, even to the point of being a condition that prevents [them] from arising"—this second interpretation of the uncontaminated seeds also functions as a non-contradictory [condition] for contaminated dharmas.

Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*): although the uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) of the three vehicles exist within the bodies of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), they do not obstruct the arising of the manifest activities (*samudācāra*) of the contaminated [dharmas] of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). This is because all contaminated afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth are able to arise;
furthermore, even though these uncontaminated seeds exist, they are not mutually contradictory. It is also like receiving a body of transformation (*pariṇāmika-kāya*), which is uncontaminated...
There is conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). First, because it can induce the subtle fruit of maturation (*vipāka*) of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);

and because it manifests as such; and because it necessarily does not arise. This means that when a contaminated (*sāsrava*) state arises in its active manifestation (*samudācāra*), since contaminated phenomena such as afflictions (*kleśa*) already exist, and once the contaminated afflictions have been destroyed, [that state] cannot arise. Thus it is said: "because it does not arise. In this context...
However, when a contaminated (*sāsrava*) manifestation occurs, it is simultaneously an uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) manifestation; thus, it does not cause the contaminated to cease.
Therefore, it is said that uncontaminated phenomena and contaminated phenomena also function as non-contradictory dominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*). This latter interpretation is superior.
The commentary states: "This general statement regarding the 'seeing-part' (darśana-bhāga) applies both universally to all [consciousnesses] and specifically to the individual.

If one reaches the stage of Buddhahood, when uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) give rise to actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*), these are likewise [produced by] the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This refers to the seeing-parts of the five consciousnesses, the sixth consciousness, the seventh consciousness, and the eighth consciousness at the stage of Buddhahood.

All [of these] are able to take seeds as their objects. As for the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the seventh consciousness’s *samatājñāna* (knowledge of equality) and the seeing-division of the eighth consciousness’s *ādarśajñāna* (great perfect mirror knowledge) at the stage of Buddhahood, they always relate to seeds; although this is not the understanding [intended here] regarding the stage of Buddhahood.
It is superior in principle to hold that the eight consciousnesses take seeds as their objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

The *Śāstra* states: "This passage is a general [statement]; it does not [specify] that the small aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of a consciousness belonging to its own level act as the three conditions. This refers to a general explanation within this treatise;

it does not distinguish between self and others regarding the number of conditions possessed. One should rather say: "The aspects of one's own and the eight consciousnesses of others [act as conditions]."

There is only the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Regarding the mutual relationship among the eight consciousnesses within one's own continuum, it is as follows: the eight [consciousnesses] exist in relation to the seven, while the seven do not exist in relation to the eight, and so forth; this will be clarified in the text below.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Regarding the presence or absence of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), in the preceding general section (*sāmānya-mukha*), it was said that 'the remaining ones' [refer to] those that are fixed.

As for the "general section," it refers to the statement in the preceding treatise: "Manifest conceptualization (*vikalpa*), when viewed in relation to one another, can serve as three types of conditions, because there is no lack of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*)."

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "In this context, since 'discrimination' (*vikalpa*) encompasses the perceived aspect (*nimittabhāga*), the perceiving aspect (*darśanabhāga*), and so forth, up to 'it is the perceiving aspect,' does this statement that 'discrimination arises' include matter (*rūpa*), as well as the associated mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), the perceiving and perceived aspects, and so on?

These arise from other seeds and so forth; it is not only the arising of the perceiving aspect that is called 'the arising of discrimination. [This includes] matter, non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and other phenomena, because they are consciousness..."

As for their substance, they are all designated by names that do not differ. Now, regarding "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*), the term is raised to illustrate the arising of present conceptualization; it specifically refers to consciousness.

The Commentary states: "That is, the preceding six consciousnesses, or alternatively, the eighth consciousness, because it resembles other places. This refers to the five [consciousnesses], such as the eye-consciousness, and so forth.
Consciousness also takes other sense organs and objects as its substantial basis (*bhāva*) and gives rise to its own objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).

In the case of the sixth consciousness, it can take all phenomena associated with the auxiliary sense organs (*indriya-sahakārin*) as its substantial basis and actually give rise to its objective aspect.

For the most part, the eighth consciousness can only transform other auxiliary sense organs and so forth into its substantial basis as a remote object-condition (*parokṣa-pratyaya*); it cannot transform them [into its direct objective aspect].
The seeds refer to the five faculties and so forth.

The Commentary states: "Among the four conditions, two are definitely absent," namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and others; the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is also absent.

The Commentary states: "If the eighth exists, the seventh must necessarily exist. This means that if the eighth consciousness is taken as the object of perception (*ālambana*), it is because it universally relies upon both the sense faculties and objects; therefore, because there is an eighth consciousness, the seventh must necessarily exist.

To speak according to reality, if the eighth consciousness exists, the seventh must necessarily exist, because the seventh consciousness is constantly uninterrupted. As for the seventh consciousness...
Because it is conditioned by the eighth consciousness: when the eighth consciousness exists, the first six consciousnesses must necessarily arise as well.

For instance, when the eighth consciousness arises in a higher realm, it is stated that the two consciousnesses of the nose and tongue are bound exclusively to that realm; as for the three consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and body—
In the first dhyāna, which is bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), although the eighth consciousness exists, the five sensory consciousnesses do not.

Furthermore, when one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) or the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), although the eighth consciousness exists, the sixth consciousness does not. Question:

According to this treatise, the eighth consciousness does not support the preceding seven consciousnesses. How is it that other passages state that within these attainments, the sixth consciousness first undergoes transformation?
There are no [defiled] images, etc. Its eighth consciousness assists the sixth consciousness upon the pure (*anāsrava*) objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*);

only then does the eighth consciousness transform and produce [images]. The mention of "outflows" (*sāsrava*), etc., is intended to allow other sentient beings to partake in [the experience]. Answer: It certainly exists prior [to that].

The Commentary states: "Because this is a teaching on a single dharma, the eight [consciousnesses] are not questioned. This refers to the gateway of practice (*caryāmukha*). It is formulated specifically with respect to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Regarding the other seven consciousnesses: there are seven that exist within the eighth, but none that exist within the seventh; there is one that exists within the sixth, but none within the other five. Thus, the eighth consciousness is questioned in relation to the seventh consciousness.
Regarding the six consciousnesses: there is one that exists within the seventh, but none within the other five; and all six exist within that [eighth].
In all cases, they do not exist [within one another]. That is to say, regarding the remaining seventh consciousness, it is the sixth consciousness that is questioned:

the five consciousnesses do not exist within the sixth, while the other five exist within it. This is because the sixth consciousness and the five consciousnesses, etc., do not take one another as objects.
This applies up to the point where minds and mental factors of the same category but different entities are considered equal; one should understand all cases of "one action" accordingly.

As in the sixth fascicle above regarding the ten afflictions and so forth, when the view (*dṛṣṭi*) is taken as the question, the remaining nine afflictions obtain the two conditions of association and predominance (*sahabhū* and *adhipati*), because they necessarily do not arise simultaneously. When greed (*lobha*) is taken as the question, the remaining eight afflictions [function similarly].

Regarding the outflow (niṣyanda): some say that the seventh [consciousness] is discussed solely from the perspective of its single mode of activity (ākāra), whereas the eighth possesses other modes of activity that are non-conceptual;

therefore, they are not the same. This explanation is superficial. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "The sixth [consciousness] lacks the five [objects] without remainder, and the five [objects] lack it [the sixth consciousness] without remainder."

Regarding the statement that "the other five [consciousnesses] have five consciousnesses therein, as they rely solely upon the characteristics of the eighth [consciousness]," this treatise currently explains this in terms of karma and its fruit.

The first five consciousnesses do not take the sixth consciousness as their object. However, if one considers a Bodhisattva who has already attained realization, within their untainted (*anāsrava*) sixth consciousness, the five sense-objects such as visible form—which are fruits—arise in reverse;
these are subsumed under the *dharmāyatana* (sphere of mental objects). Thus, the five consciousnesses of actual matter are also able to take them as objects.
Within the sixth consciousness, it is the matter of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*).
The Commentary states: "The preceding sixth aggregate may serve as three conditions for the subsequent sixth consciousness-aggregate, which is the remaining cause and condition.

This refers to the mental consciousness mentioned in the treatise; if the preceding moment of the sixth consciousness induces the subsequent moment of the sixth consciousness, it is [an equivalent condition].
The immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) remain;
only the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is excluded. Regarding the commentary’s statement, "In this context, the final mind of an Arhat is not [treated as] an immediate condition":

if it refers to the final mind of the sixth consciousness—the very last moment of an Arhat—and if a subsequent moment takes that preceding moment as its object, then for that subsequent moment, there would indeed be an object-condition.
There is also the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). As for the other sixth consciousnesses, the remaining consciousnesses possess only the dominant condition.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “all are not seeds”: these are now all manifest activities (*pravṛtti*). The reason why manifest activities are not seeds is as follows: [they lack the capacity for continuity and transformation].

The Commentary states: "If the former serves as a condition for the latter by inducing its functional capacity," this is a verse from the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* (Treatise on the Investigation of the Object).
"Functional capacity" refers to the seed; that is, the seed of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the manifesting consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) from the preceding moment.

The Commentary states: "As for the claim that 'because the Sautrāntika school holds that cause and effect occur at different times, and since [the object] is not a present objective field, it cannot give rise to the five consciousnesses'—this is because the Bodhisattva here follows the Sautrāntika master’s view that cause and effect occur at different times.

Therefore, a subsequent moment of the five consciousnesses takes the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the preceding moment as its object. Indeed, according to the tenet of the Sautrāntika school, a subsequent moment of the five consciousnesses does take the *nimitta-bhāga* of the preceding moment as its object."

The meaning is as follows: There is no need to argue that the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) of a subsequent moment take the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of a preceding moment as their object.

However, according to the Sautrāntika masters who maintain that cause and effect occur at different times, it is because the seeds of the preceding moment give rise to the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) of the subsequent moment, and the manifest activity of the subsequent moment arises from the seeds of the preceding moment.
That is to say, the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*) of the preceding moment give rise to the five consciousnesses of the subsequent moment; thus, the causal seed must necessarily cease.
The fruit arises only later; therefore, it is called "a different time.

The Commentary states: "Because the subsequent moment of consciousness carries the preceding aspect (ākāra) as its manifestation. This means that the "preceding aspect" which is the object of apprehension and the basis for the subsequent moment of the five sensory consciousnesses is what is termed the "object-condition" (ālambana).

The Commentary states: "Taking the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-aspect) as the mode of apprehension (*ākāra*) and the objective essence (*vastu*) as the distant objective condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*)" means that the *nimitta-bhāga* of the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) produced by the preceding moment is called the "mode of apprehension.

The *nimitta-bhāga* of the preceding moment's manifest activity serves as the objective essence, which is the distant objective condition. It does not take the seeds of the *nimitta-bhāga* from the preceding moment as the object-condition (*ālambana*).

[This is] a condition (*pratyaya*). Because the five consciousnesses do not take seeds as their objects, it is not the correct principle for this Bodhisattva to say that the preceding aspect [of the object] is the cause for the subsequent moment of the five consciousnesses.
Therefore, regarding those who hold the "subsequent seeing" view, the question is: how is this named?

Furthermore, among the former masters, since they assert that for a Bodhisattva—following the Sautrāntika position—the cause and effect occur at different times, then the first moment of the five consciousnesses would necessarily be a manifest aspect (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*).
It is perfumed in portions. The seeds of the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) of the first moment of mindfulness can produce the objective aspect of the second moment of manifest activity;
only then is it perceived by the five consciousnesses of the third moment. This applies likewise up to the seventh consciousness.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "If that which follows takes what preceded it as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), such that one's own eight consciousnesses—even those [consciousnesses] that simultaneously infuse seeds into both parts [of the object and the subject]—then this subsequent passage in the treatise follows the Sautrāntika masters in asserting that cause and effect occur at different times when discussing the five consciousnesses.
When the first moment of thought perceives the five sense-objects, there is the objective part (*nimitta-bhāga*) within the five consciousnesses."

The active manifestation perfumes and forms the seeds of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). As the Master [Yogācāra] states, from the first moment until the subsequent second moment, the objective aspect arises immediately.

In the subsequent second moment, the five consciousnesses take the objective aspect of the preceding moment as their object; thus, the five consciousnesses across these preceding and succeeding moments also possess the three conditions.

Now, regarding the statement that the five consciousnesses of the subsequent moment take the objective aspect of the preceding moment as their object: sometimes this occurs, and sometimes it does not.

All [of these] exist at all times. That is to say, based on the preceding [moment], the five consciousnesses of a Bodhisattva subsequently perceive by taking the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) of the preceding moment as their object.

This principle corresponds to the meaning of "lateral engagement" (*pārśvavāhana*). Thus, one understands that the first seven consciousnesses, in relation to the eighth, may contain seeds that resemble those which perfume the *nimittabhāga* and *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect) of that eighth consciousness.
If the first seven consciousnesses perfume the seeds of their own respective *nimittabhāga* and *darśanabhāga* within the seven consciousnesses...
My son, there is immediately the aforementioned first moment of thought, which perfumes the seeds of the seeing and seen portions within its own kind, the seventh consciousness.
When these seeds of the seeing and seen portions reach the subsequent second moment, they immediately give rise to the actual manifestation of the seeing and seen portions.

Because this is not produced by karmic retribution, it is said that the seventh consciousness of the preceding moment perfumes the seeds of the seeing and seen portions of its own kind, and in the subsequent moment, the actual manifestation arises. This is precisely so.

Just as in the case of the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) of preceding and succeeding moments, when they take the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the preceding moment as their object, the mental force (*manas-śakti*) relies upon the preceding moment;
this is also an *ābhāsa-nimitta-bhāga* (reflected objective aspect). The succeeding moment is likewise an *ābhāsa-nimitta-bhāga*, which is precisely the *nimitta-bhāga* of the preceding moment.

This perfumes a seed (*bīja*) until the second succeeding moment, at which point it gives rise to the actual manifestation (*pravṛtti*). This is the object of the succeeding moment’s five consciousnesses. Now, if the seventh consciousness...

Having perfumed the seeds of the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) and *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part) of that eighth consciousness, once these seeds of image and seeing have produced their respective manifest activities (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), if the image-part is perceived by the seeing-part of that other eighth consciousness, and that other eighth consciousness’s *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying part) takes it as its object, this is called the eighth consciousness taking the preceding seven consciousnesses as its object.
Thus, the manifest activities of the seven consciousnesses are capable of perfuming; the manifest activities of the seven consciousnesses are termed [the perfumers] with the eighth...

The eight consciousnesses serve as the remote objective condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*). When the eighth consciousness takes its own seeing and image divisions (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*) as objects, these are called the immediate objective condition (*sākṣātpratyaya*).
That is to say, within the image divisions of the preceding seven consciousnesses, they act as the perfuming agents for the seeds of the image and seeing divisions of that eighth consciousness.
Regarding the seeds of the seeing and seen aspects: until the second moment [of consciousness], they have not yet reached the stage of manifest activity (*pravṛtti*).
Since the seeing and seen portions of the eighth consciousness have not yet been induced by karmic retribution, the manifest activities of the seeing and seen aspects do not arise.

These seeds of the seeing portion of the eighth consciousness must pass through hundreds or thousands of years, and after two lifetimes have elapsed; only when they are summoned and induced by the power of wholesome or unwholesome karma does this eighth consciousness [arise].
Only when the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) possesses the seeing and image aspects does the actualization of the seeing and image aspects arise.

Therefore, while the preceding moment of the seven consciousnesses perfumes the eighth consciousness, it is not itself produced by karmic retribution; thus, in the subsequent second moment, the seeing-consciousness of the eighth [consciousness] does not arise.

This refers to the manifestation of the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect). Furthermore, when the five consciousnesses take as their object the fundamental reality (*mūlapratibimba*) transformed by the eighth consciousness, they perfume seeds of the *nimittabhāga* within the objective aspects of the five objects—form and so forth—within the fivefold *nimittabhāgas*.

Just as in the case of the preceding image-aspect (*pratibimbabhāga*), these seeds are perfumed until the second moment, at which point the fundamental reality of mountains, rivers, and so forth—the five objects such as form—is produced. Therefore, one knows that the former...
Even though the seven consciousnesses perfuse the seeds of the seeing and image divisions of the other eighth consciousness, in the subsequent moment,
they are unable to produce the image and seeing divisions of that eighth consciousness.

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "If the seeds of the self-witnessing [portion] (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) arise from the self-witnessing [portion], it should likewise apply to the case where the sixth consciousness takes the self-witnessing portion of another’s eighth consciousness as its object.

That is to say, if the sixth consciousness takes the self-witnessing portion of another’s eighth consciousness as its object, then the image portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) of that sixth consciousness acts as the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*) for the seeds of the self-witnessing portion of that other person's eighth consciousness.
Even after those seeds of the self-witnessing portion have passed through a hundred or a thousand years, they may already have been affected by the evil karma of that other person.

When the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the feeling-producing [consciousness] manifests, it serves as the direct objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for the eighth consciousness’s self-verifying portion when the latter takes that self-verifying portion as its object.

If the manifest image-portion (*nimittabhāga*) of the sixth consciousness—which acts as a perfuming agent—is taken by the eighth consciousness’s self-verifying portion, it likewise serves as an objective condition.
Furthermore, if the sixth consciousness takes the self-verifying portion of another eighth consciousness as its object...

At that time, the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the sixth consciousness acts as the perfumer (*vāsaka*). It perfumes the seeds of the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-cognizing aspect) of the eighth consciousness.
Later, when the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) is produced by the maturation of those karmic seeds, it is then apprehended by the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* of the eighth consciousness;
