this refers to the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga*. Thus, within the eighth consciousness, there is the manifest activity that acts as the perfumer.
The image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) serves as a remote objective condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*) for the self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of another person’s eighth consciousness.

When the self-witnessing-of-self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the perfumed eighth consciousness arises as a manifest state, it serves as an immediate objective condition (*sannikṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*) for the self-witnessing part of that eighth consciousness.
Regarding these [conditions] whereby the first seven consciousnesses serve as objects for the eighth, all such arguments are the assertions of different masters; they are not [the definitive view].
This is the correct principle (*nyāya*). That is to say, the preceding eight [consciousnesses] are [the objects] of the eighth [consciousness] in eight ways;

this is the correct principle. The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "If one takes empty space, as well as mind and mental factors, and so forth—even up to the sixth consciousness—these possess the latter two phrases;

they should be understood according to reason. Regarding the first phrase: there are those that are related to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness only as a remote object-condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*).
The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). This refers to the objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) within the first five consciousnesses that act as perfumers;

these serve as the remote object-conditions for the seeing part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness. Just as with the five consciousnesses, when they take the actual objects (*bhāva*)—the five sensory objects transformed by the eighth consciousness—as their conditions, they perfume the five types of objective parts within the eighth consciousness. These five are the objective parts of the eighth consciousness.
The seeds of subsequent karma produce the manifest aspect (nimittabhāga) of the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

This manifest aspect serves as the direct object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) of the eighth consciousness. Furthermore, within the five sensory consciousnesses, the manifest seeds that act as perfumers serve as the indirect object-condition (*asamantarapratyaya*) for the eighth consciousness.
As for the second phrase, it refers exclusively to the self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) of the eighth consciousness.

It acts as a remote object-condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*). That is to say, when the seventh consciousness takes the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its substantial basis (*bimba*), it simultaneously transforms a direct image-part (*sākṣāt-nimitta-bhāga*); this manifest image-part of the seventh consciousness then serves as the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*).
Within the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) of the seventh consciousness, the seeds of the *darśanabhāga* (perceiving aspect) of the eighth consciousness are perfumed.
Later, these seeds of the eighth consciousness’s *darśanabhāga* give rise to the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) of the eighth consciousness’s *darśanabhāga* through karmic retribution.

This manifest activity of the *darśanabhāga* serves as the immediate *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition) for the eighth consciousness’s *svasaṃvedanabhāga* (self-verifying aspect). Furthermore, the manifest *nimittabhāga* within the seventh consciousness that acts as the perfumer is, in turn, related to the [eighth consciousness’s *svasaṃvedanabhāga*].
The self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses serves as a remote object-condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*). Regarding the third phrase:
there are also those that serve as remote object-conditions for both the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*) and the self-verifying portion of the eighth consciousness;

these are the object-aspects (*nimittabhāga*) within the sixth consciousness that possess the capacity to perfuse (*vāsana*). For example, when the sixth consciousness takes the seeing portion of the eighth consciousness as its object, it is the sixth [consciousness]...
The objective aspect within consciousness acts as the perfuming agent that perfumes the seeds of the seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the other eighth consciousness.

When the seeds of the eighth consciousness’s seeing portion subsequently give rise to the actual manifestation of the seeing portion, this seeing portion of the eighth consciousness is then [conjoined] with the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.

It acts as a direct objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Within this sixth consciousness, the perfuming image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) serves as an indirect objective condition for the self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.

When the sixth consciousness perceives the five objects—form and so forth—which are transformations of the eighth consciousness, as well as the five fundamental substantial entities, the manifest image-part within the active state of the sixth consciousness can perfume the eighth.
Consciousness perfumes the seeds of the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) within the eighth consciousness, such as the five sense objects and the five sense organs.

When these seeds of the objective aspect subsequently give rise to the manifest activity (pravṛtti-vijñāna) of the objective aspect—namely, the five sense objects and the five sense organs—they serve as the direct objects of apprehension for the seeing aspect (darśana-bhāga) of the eighth consciousness.
If the objective aspect within the sixth consciousness is capable of perfuming, it likewise serves as [the object] for the eighth consciousness.

The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) acts as a remote objective condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*). Therefore, within the sixth consciousness, the perfuming image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) acts as a remote objective condition for the seeing-part and the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness. As for the fourth case:

there are instances where neither [the seeing-part nor the self-witnessing-part] acts as a remote objective condition for the seeing-part and the self-witnessing-part of the eighth consciousness; that is to say, when the sixth consciousness does not take the eighth as its object.
The eight consciousnesses do not infuse seeds into the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part) and *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived part) of the eighth consciousness.

Question: Since the eight consciousnesses and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are each distinct, what then does another single sixth consciousness take as its object?

The sixth consciousness can perfumate the seeds of the other eight consciousnesses. These seeds of the eight consciousnesses, in turn, give rise to the manifest activities (*pravṛtti*) of the eight consciousnesses and so forth.

It is not yet known whether the five consciousnesses can perfuse seeds of the three natures within a single-nature mind. Answer:

The five inferior [consciousnesses] cannot perfuse the five kinds [of seeds] within a mind of a single destiny (*ekāyana*). It is seen that they do not function within another mind of the desire realm.
Can seeds of the nine stages (*navabhūmi*) be perfumed? This question and answer apply analogously even to the three realms (*tridhātu*) and the four natures (*caturvidha-svabhāva*).

The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "If it refers to other conditions, they do not share a single object of cognition (*ālambana*); they are collectively received [by the mind], yet they do not share the same object as the mind."

This is because it is the Mahāyāna. The Mahāsāṃghika school objects: "If, when other mind-kings (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) take an object, the nature of the feeling (*vedanā*) is different from that of the object-feeler, then there would be a lack of identity.
However, since the object is common to both the mind and its mental factors, when these phenomena take an object, they must logically share the same object."
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Thus, because they are extremely close, they do not take all phenomena as their objects. The explanation says: "In this *Śāstra*, there are two interpretations;

this is the first interpretation. The meaning of this passage is that the Sarvāstivāda, Mahāyāna, and other schools state that the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) [do not take all phenomena as objects] because the mind and mental factors are extremely close to one another, just as many people facing the same direction look at the sun together."

Furthermore, as with people watching a performance together, because their faces are extremely close to one another, they do not mutually perceive each other's minds or mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).

It is the same in this case: although the mind and its mental factors take the same preceding visible object (*rūpa-viṣaya*) as their object, because they are so closely situated, they likewise do not perceive one another.
Moreover, the mind and its mental factors cannot perceive coexistent phenomena (*sahabhū-dharma*), such as the acquisition (*prāpti*) or the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Because they are extremely close to one another, just as the eye-consciousness cannot see its own eye because it is too close, so too [the objection applies].

However, once the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) is established as having itself as its object, the aforementioned fault no longer applies. As for the subsequent deficiency, this passage represents the second interpretation.
The meaning of this passage is that the self-cognizing part of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and the seeing parts (*darśana-bhāga*) of the other mental factors (*caitta*).

The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) that shares the same object of cognition (*ālambana*), as well as the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) of the mind and mental factors (*caitta*), are likewise so.

That is to say, the mind and mental factors all share one and the same object of cognition; thus, there is no prior [distinction] and no lack of identity. Regarding the fault of "the object being prior" or "not being identical":

if one were to allow that they do take it as an object, this refers to the textual passage concerning the fault of not sharing one and the same object of cognition. This explains how the self-verifying part of the mind-king is common to the other minds.

Regarding the "perceiving portion" (*darśana-bhāga*) that shares the same object as the perceiving portion of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*): this would entail the aforementioned fault. That is to say, the subsequent treatise states:

"Let it not be that the objects of the perceiving portions differ from their respective substrates. This passage from the treatise would then contradict the principle that the perceiving portions of the mind and its mental factors (*caitta*) share the same focal object (*ālambana*).

Nor does it rely on the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) being called "identical" because it shares the same object as other seeing portions (*darśana-bhāga*); therefore, it is said that there is a subsequent fault.
To speak according to reality, within the stage of the cause (*hetu-avasthā*), it is superior for each mind and mental factor not to cognize one another. As I, the fool, understand it:

since it has been stated that the self-cognizing portion of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) [cognizes] its own seeing portion, and that the seeing portions of the other mental factors likewise cognize their own mind-king's seeing portion...
At the time of division, there would be no preceding sensation (*vedanā*) that shares the same object as the mind; therefore, it is said:

"Since the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the mind-king has already been explained, [it follows that] it shares the same object as the other [factors] such as sensation and the seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*). Regarding the subsequent statement:

'However, because they are extremely close, share the same objects, and possess equal functions,' this fault arises because, due to their proximity, the mind and mental factors harmonize together. They do not [function independently].

Regarding the "condition" (*pratyaya*): The *Śāstra* commentary states that it is not the case that many seeing-aspects (*darśana-bhāga*) together take a single, direct objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) as their object, thereby constituting a unified whole;
rather, each individual seeing-aspect individually realizes its own direct [objective aspect].

"Because it is an objective part (*nimittabhāga*). If that is so, then just as the eighth mind-king (*citta-rāja*) cannot [function in such a way], how can they be said to have the same object of cognition (*ālambana*)?
This passage represents the opponent's objection: "The eighth consciousness, being a mind-king, does not take its associated mental factors (*caitta*) as its object."

If the five *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspects) are divided into distinct entities (*dravya*), how can they be said to be identical? Furthermore, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) itself lacks an objective aspect as its own substance.

that is, the objective aspects of both the primary minds (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) do not serve as objects for one another. This extends even to the eighth consciousness, where the mind-king and its mental factors likewise do not take each other’s objective aspects as objects. Each...
