the *Śāstra* commentary states: "The two aspects are similar and share the same name," referring to the mind-king and its associated mental factors (*caitta*) that coexist with the eighth consciousness, and so forth. This...
Regarding the "ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha*): it is called "identical" because they are currently similar. This is the doctrine of the first master.

According to the doctrine of the first master, when explaining simultaneous occurrence, all aspects of the perceiving portions (*darśana-bhāga*) of both the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) do not take one another as objects.

Question: According to the first master, since the five objects associated with the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) do not take the perceived portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the mind-king as their object, [how is this so]?

Regarding the essence: there are five cases where a distant object-condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*) does not exist. Answer: Even if it does not exist, one can still attain lower levels of understanding; it is not strictly necessary for it to exist.

As for the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) stating, "Because there is no simultaneous seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of another [mind], this [condition] exists in the stage of a cause (*hetu-bhūmi*), whereas for a Buddha it is not so"—this is the intended meaning of the second master.
He explains that within the causal stage, it is only when the mind and mental factors are simultaneous that [the condition] applies to their respective aspects (*nimitta*).

The objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) arises from the essential nature (*svabhāva*). If the objective aspects of simultaneous minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) were to mutually perceive one another, they could not do so at the same time.

This refers to the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) of the mind. However, within the correct doctrine regarding the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhatva*), simultaneous minds and mental factors are able to mutually perceive one another;
that is, the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the mind-king and the subjective aspect of the simultaneous mental factors perceive the same object simultaneously.
The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), or likewise among the mental factors (*caitta*), is similar to the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*):
it takes as its object the same seeing-part that experiences itself, which occurs simultaneously with the seeing-parts of the minds and mental factors.
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "The mind takes that which is reflected by the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as its substantial object (*ālambana-svabhāva*);
this principle applies equally to all primary minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). Regarding this second master’s distinct example:

for instance, the five mental factors associated with the eighth consciousness take the actual seeds, the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*), and so forth, of the eighth consciousness—the mind-king—as their substantial object; it is only then that the five mental factors [arise].

From this self-reflection, the image-aspect (nimittabhāga) arises. As for the seeing-aspect (darśanabhāga) of that eighth mind-king (citta-rāja), it does not take the mental factors (caitta) as its object.

Rather, the seeds of the five aforementioned categories of image-aspects take their own [original] nature as the objective basis (ālambana-pratibimba), and from these, the eighth mind-king itself gives rise to the image-aspect. Thus it should be known.

At the same time, the mental factors (caitta) take as their object the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*). This is analogous to the preceding seven consciousnesses. It is likewise with the mind-king:

it relies upon the *nimitta-bhāga* of the mental factors, while the mental factors rely upon the *nimitta-bhāga* of the mind-king; this refers to how they arise by mutually serving as the objective basis (*ālambana-pratibimba*) for one another.

The Commentary states: "Thus, the intention of the former masters is that each [mental factor] individually takes as its object the seeds reflected from itself, up to the point where there is no capacity for the function of producing consciousness.
Thus, the eighth consciousness, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), does not rely on another substrate; it takes only the seeds reflected from itself as its object.
As for the five mental concomitants (*caitta*), they likewise do not rely upon or depend on the seeds reflected from the mind-king; the five mental concomitants take only... as their objects.

This refers to the provisional seeds that are themselves inverted. Because the *bhāga* (objective parts) do not mutually serve as objects for one another, the same applies to the preceding seven consciousnesses.
This former master’s position represents the correct doctrine. As stated in the treatise regarding the previously mentioned "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*):

"In all cases of the 'directly apprehended object-condition' (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*), there must be something apart from what is internally relied upon; otherwise, [the cognition] would necessarily not arise. As for the 'remotely apprehended object-condition' (*parokṣa-ālambana-pratyaya*), it is either the subjective perceiver..."

Since there are cases where [cognition] arises even when separated from external objects of reliance, the former masters and the latter masters alike maintain that the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) must mutually support one another and be differentiated.
However, both the former and latter masters exclude the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) as the mind-king and its factors;

rather, they hold that seeds possess actual utility in being able to produce the manifest mind-king and its factors, as well as the five sense organs, and that the mind possesses the actual capacity to give rise to the various consciousnesses and so forth.

Regarding function: if, within the eighth consciousness, the five mental factors (caitta-dharma) were to lack functional seeds and the five sense organs (indriya) likewise lacked functional seeds, they would be unable to produce manifest states (pravṛtti). Furthermore, the five sense organs would lack the function of initiating consciousness and so forth.
If, however, the seeds associated with the mind-king (citta-rāja) and the five mental factors all possess functional efficacy, then within a single moment, there is production.
This avoids the faults [of having] six tusks and so forth; it avoids the fault of producing six visual consciousnesses and so forth. This latter master is distant from the former;
there may be textual evidence for the idea that the remote object-condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*) is the object of the cognizer (*ālambaka*).

The commentary states that this master raises the objection: "Why is it that a single object of cognition (*ālambana*) is divided into two meanings, while the eighth consciousness and its five mental factors lack a substantial basis (*bimba*)?
The latter master then rebuts the former, asking: "Why is it that a single object of cognition is divided into two?
First, because their substantial basis is identical, they are called 'a single object of cognition'; second, because they are similar, they are called 'a single [object]'."

It is also a condition (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, it does not exclude the eighth consciousness, its five associated mental factors (*caitta*), or the objective parts (*nimittabhāga*) of those mental factors which serve as the substantial seeds and the fundamental essence (*ālambanapratibimba*). The former master’s explanation states:

"If there must necessarily be a fundamental essence, how then can [the image] be identical to that essence? The former master says: "If the sixth consciousness takes space (*ākāśa*) and so forth as its object..."
By what would it have as its essential nature? Therefore, one knows that it likewise lacks an essential nature. Furthermore, he challenges the latter master, saying:

"If you claim that they share the same object of cognition (*ālambana*) because they all mutually depend upon one another, then how can you say they share the same object of cognition when the eighth mental king (*citta-rāja*) does not depend on the five mental factors (*caitta*) and their associated features (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its essential nature? Regarding this, there is another master who says in this commentary:

If all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) must rely upon an objective essence (*bimba*) when they arise in order to obtain their objects of cognition, then when they take empty space as an object, they take its name as that essence.

For example, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), the eighth consciousness, relies upon the simultaneous mental factors (*caitta*)—such as the provisional seeds and so forth—as its objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) to serve as its essence; only then does the eighth consciousness itself reflect back upon its own direct objective parts.
If the five mental associates (*caitta*) also rely upon the mind-king (*cittarāja*), they must first take the seeds, the objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*), and so forth, as their substantial basis;
only then do the five associates each individually give rise to their own direct objective images. This applies equally to the preceding seven consciousnesses.

Just as with a teacher, when the seeing portions (*darśana-bhāga*) of the various mental associates perceive this direct objective image of the mind-king, the seeing portion of the mind-king [is likewise perceived].

It also takes its own immediate objective aspect (sākāra) as its object; this is precisely what is meant by "having the same object. The objective aspects of mental factors (caitta) are likewise so called, meaning that these various objective aspects arise with [the primary consciousness] as their substantial cause (ālambana-pratyaya).

The Commentary states: "Regarding the claim that the object of the self-witnessing division (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) is not admitted to be the same as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), but rather [is the same as] its own seeing-division (darśana-bhāga)—and so forth, up to 'this meaning should be reflected upon'—the intention of the latter master is as follows:
if the object of the self-witnessing division were not the same as its object-condition, it would be just like the self-witnessing division of the mind-king (citta-rāja)."
It takes only the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of its own mind-king as its object; it truly cannot take the seeing-parts of other minds and so forth as objects.

As for the self-verifying parts (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the various mental factors (*caitta*), each takes its own respective seeing-part as an object. Therefore, it is said that "the objects of the self-verifying part are not shared with others.
Even regarding the direct image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), it likewise does not share the same object as the mind-king’s seeing-part; it can only directly or indirectly [take]... [the object].

The mind-king (*citta-rāja*) directly perceives its own immediate objective aspect (*sākṣāt-svabhāga*). It cannot, however, directly take as its object the immediate objective aspects of other mental factors (*caitta*).

If it were so for the mental factors as well, then they would likewise be identical in their basis. For instance, in the case of visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*), the mind and its mental factors share the same basis;

the same applies to other consciousnesses. Furthermore, their objective referents (*ālambana-pratibimba*) are also identical, just as in the case of visual consciousness and its simultaneous mental factors.

That upon which they both rely is one: the objective sphere of the essential nature of form (*rūpa-svabhāva-viṣaya*). The objective sphere of the essential nature of form is likewise the same for both. All other cases are similar.
Therefore, it is said that this meaning should be reflected upon.
The commentary states: "Having the same object of cognition is called 'identical' because they are similar; each is the opposite [of the other], and so forth...
therefore, the views of the former masters are all worthy of contemplation. This passage from the current commentary refers to the second master. As for the second master:

All arising minds possess a fundamental essence; this is termed "having the same object of cognition" (*ekālambana*). That is to say, when minds and mental factors arise, they all have a remote object-condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*).
Regarding the principle of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only), we now adopt the interpretation of the former master:
because the various minds and mental factors directly perceive their own respective image-aspects (*nimittabhāga*), which are similar to one another, they are said to "have the same [object]. Each...
Because each [position] is individually refuted, these arguments are all superior. Therefore, the first master’s establishment of the "wondrous" (*yan*) is excellent;

indeed, the first master’s extraordinary view is truly marvelous. Thus far, these two masters have explained that the simultaneous seeing and image-aspects (*jiansiang erfen*) do not mutually apprehend one another.
The Master [Asaṅga] explains that the aspect (nimitta) constitutes the substantial basis (dravya), while the arising and so forth constitute the function;

these two masters both speak with reference to Bodhisattvas from the causal stage up through the ten bhūmis, as well as ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) who lack the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).

The commentary states: "If it is said that the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) and the other parts serve merely as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and that even the remote object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) does not apply because the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) and the *nimitta-bhāga* are not similar—this is the first interpretation.

If it is said that the *nimitta-bhāga* [relates] to the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-cognizing aspect), and the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* to the *svasaṃvitti-svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-cognition of self-cognition), they possess only the dominant condition. If one says that the *darśana-bhāga* acts as a direct [condition] for the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga*..."

Regarding the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): it is not the case that the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) act as a remote objective condition for one another.
Why? Because the image-aspect and the self-cognizing aspect are similar to the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*).
For instance, when the seeing-aspect takes an external object such as blue color as its essence, it subsequently gives rise to an image-aspect of blue; thus, the essence is itself the color.

Therefore, the appearing aspect (nimitta-bhāga) is also blue; that is, because both the appearing aspect and the primary object (ālambana) are similar and both are blue, one may say that the primary object—such as the color blue—is the remote objective condition (*parokṣa-ālambana-pratyaya*).
That is to say, the aforementioned primary object is the "objective aspect" (*ālambana-nimitta-bhāga*), while the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) is called the "functional aspect" (*ākāra*).
The appearing aspect, such as the color blue, is the immediate objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*). Now, as for the seeing...
The image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and so forth are dissimilar [to the self-witnessing part]. As for their dissimilarity:

the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) is the mental aspect that acts as the cognizer, while the image-part is the objective aspect that is material form. Furthermore, because the seeing-part consists of only four aggregates (*skandha*), whereas the image-part consists of all five aggregates.
Since the seeing-part and the image-part are thus dissimilar, the image-part does not serve as a remote object-condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*) for the self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Alternatively, it may be said that because the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) arises by taking the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its condition, this is the second interpretation.

The seeing-part acts as the direct objective-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), and the image-part likewise acts as the indirect objective-condition for the self-witnessing-part."

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): by way of its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), it serves as the condition for arising; thus, the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*)—which is the self-witnessing aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*)—is also able to arise.
This is because both the subjective aspect and the self-witnessing aspect are equally capable of being the cognizing subject (*ālambaka*).

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that when the subjective aspect perceives the immediate objective aspect such as blue or yellow, the subjective aspect itself is not [itself] understood as blue or yellow; rather, both the subjective aspect and its objective aspect possess the quality of blue or yellow.

Therefore, because the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) and the image-part (nimitta-bhāga) are also similar to one another, the image-part serves as the remote objective condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*) for the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*), while the seeing-part serves as the immediate objective condition (*sākṣālambanapratyaya*) for the self-verifying part; this is identical to the aforementioned image-part.
That which is the object of cognition is the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect); that which is named the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) is the objective entity (*vastu*).

Now, if it is argued that the *nimitta-bhāga* (image aspect) and the self-cognizing aspect function as a remote object-condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*) for one another, we now raise this objection:

Why is it that while the fundamental essence (*bimba*) is separated from the immediate image aspect, yet the fundamental essence itself serves as a remote object-condition for the perceiving aspect? Therefore, we know that the image aspect is separated from the perceiving aspect.
It is not contradictory for the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) to act as a remote object-condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*) for the self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).

Thus, one should know that while the image-part acts as a remote object-condition for the self-witnessing part, it does not act as a remote object-condition for the witnessing-of-self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvittisaṃvittibhāga*), because the image-part is separated from the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) by the intervening layer of the self-witnessing part. Although this is stated in the *Śū* [the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śūtra*],...

There are two interpretations; the latter interpretation is superior. This is a loose [explanatory] text. It should rather say: "Alternatively, it may be said that [the self-cognition] arises by taking the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) as its condition (*pratyaya*).
If it were to mean that the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) arises by taking the *nimitta-bhāga* as its condition, then the [logical] limit would be lost;

why then would one need to speak of "hearing"? If [it refers to] the *darśana-bhāga* and the fourth *sākṣin-saṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying aspect), they are merely *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant conditions).
[This concludes the section on] conditions. All that follows above has been explained in terms of the immediate objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

If, however, one speaks in terms of the remote objective condition, then the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) and the witness-to-self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvittisaṃvitti-bhāga*) serve as the immediate objective condition for the seeing division (*darśana-bhāga*). As for the seeing division and the witness-to-self-witnessing division...

It acts as a remote objective condition (*viprakṛṣṭālambanapratyaya*). If it were the prior stage of seeing, then the aspect of form would be the object and the cognizing mind would be the seeing-part;

thus one could speak of the seeing-part and the aspect-part being dissimilar. However, in the present case, both the seeing-part and the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) are similar [to the object].

Therefore, in the *Śūtra* (the *Triṃśikā-bhāṣya*), it does not state that the seeing-part and the self-witnessing-part are dissimilar. This is when considering the immediate objective condition (*sannikṛṣṭālambanapratyaya*).
That is to say, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) act as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
If considered in terms of the remote object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), then the seeing-part and the self-cognizing part are both the remote object-condition and also the dominant condition;

therefore, there is no contradiction. However, when the self-cognizing part takes the seeing-part as its preceding object, then the seeing-part acts as [the object-condition] for the self-cognizing part.
The image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) act as the immediate objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

When the self-cognizing part subsequently cognizes the self-cognizing-of-self part (*svasaṃvittisvasaṃvittibhāga*), at the time of cognizing that [third] part, it acts as the immediate objective condition for the self-cognizing part; there is no fifth part that acts [as such] for the self-cognizing part.

It is also a remote object-condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*). It functions as two conditions through a successive process because they obtain mutual conditionality. Regarding the phrase "when the self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) takes the cognition (*vijñāna*) as its object":

when the self-cognition takes the cognition as its object, it serves as both the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for the self-cognition part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).

When the self-cognizing cognition (*svasaṃvittisaṃvitti*) takes the self-cognition as its object, the self-cognition likewise serves as these two conditions for the self-cognizing cognition part; that is to say, the object-condition and the dominant condition.

This refers to the superior condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). The Commentary states: "Thus, while the preceding discussion of the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) as two conditions does not mention that the seeds also serve as the object-aspect or even as a condition, all of the foregoing has been based upon the manifest aspects of the object-aspect, the seeing-aspect, and so forth."

It is said that the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) serve as two conditions for one another, namely, the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).

If the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness takes the seed-image-part as its object, then the seed-image-part and the eighth consciousness’s seeing-part function as three conditions for one another:
the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*), the object-condition, and the dominant condition. As for "one's own and others' eight consciousnesses," this refers to one's own...

One's own body and the bodies of others; the eight consciousnesses each have their respective characteristics. If one speaks of "one's own" and "others' consciousnesses," it means that within one's own body, the characteristics of the eight consciousnesses are taken as "self."
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "That which manifests through its functional capacity is precisely the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). The second fascicle of the Treatise (*Śāstra*) says:
"Upon reaching the stage of outflow-free purity (*anāsrava*), the objective aspect of superior wisdom should be described as being realized through non-conceptualization;
therefore, it is said that although there is no actual utility [in the objects], they nevertheless manifest. Otherwise, the Buddhas would not be equal.
*Cheng weishi lun shu chao*, Fascicle Thirteen, Part One;
*Cheng weishi lun shu chao*, Fascicle Fourteen. The commentary (*shu*) states:

"That which is induced by those [actions] gives rise to the three types of karma. The sub-commentary (*jie*) explains: "The three types of karma refer to either merit (*puṇya*), non-merit (*apuṇya*), or..."
Movement is called the three karmas, namely those of body, speech, and mind. Quoting a verse from the *Abhidharmakośa* as an ancillary reference:
"One who constantly harbors poisonous thoughts, delights in accumulating the faults of movement, and finds joy in seeing the suffering of others, shall become a demon executioner after death."
"Evil karma [leads one] to become a hell-warden. The commentary states:
"Regarding 'assisting those who preside over their respective tasks,' the question is: Is there a distinction among those who assist? Furthermore, what do those who assist individually receive?
Moreover, does this constitute the primary cause for the manifestation of the collective retribution, or is it the karma for both collective and individual retribution? (As follows...)
[Commentary on the] *Vyākhyā*:

Regarding karmas of immediate retribution (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), although transforming a human body into that of a beast or a dull-witted person cannot cause the continuity of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it can nevertheless cause five types of continuity to arise:
[a human] may turn into a beast, or a beast may turn into a human. This refers to the karma of immediate retribution.

It should be called "karma of collective retribution" (*saṃnipāta-vipāka-karman*). It may also be called the "limb of volitional formations" (*saṃskāra-aṅga*) and should be called "projecting karma" (*ākṣepaka-karman*). Furthermore, it is asked:

If there are women who have transmigrated from another realm, there should also be those who have transmigrated into both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), as well as women who have not [previously] belonged to that realm. Just as one who has transmigrated from the human realm becomes an animal, the same should apply to the five [destinies].
How could a body of the desire realm produce a mind of the form realm, or the bodies and so forth of each of the various heavens? The answer says: Regarding women...
By making offerings to the Buddha in one's present body, one obtains the status of a Wheel-Turning Monarch (*cakravartin*) through karma that ripens in the present life.
Furthermore, as stated in the sūtras, there was a householder named Sthūla who was previously poor; because he made offerings to the Buddha, he suddenly became immensely wealthy in his present body.

Such instances of retribution in the present life only result in specific fruits (*viśeṣa-phala*); karma that ripens in the present life cannot induce the primary projecting fruit (*ākṣepaka-phala*). Therefore...
Karma to be experienced in the present life is excluded from the member of "formative action" (*saṃskāra*). This is just like karma to be experienced in the next life or in subsequent lives;

that which can induce a collective retribution (*vipāka*) is able to cause the continuity of birth and death, and thus may be designated as the member of "formative action. However, this does not apply to karma to be experienced in the present life or karma that merely projects [a future existence].

It merely brings about retributive fruits such as the present body; this retribution for present karma cannot bring about a total retributive fruit, and thus there is no continuity of birth and death.
Therefore, it is said that the fruits of present retribution and the karma of distinct retribution are both not the member of "formative action" (*saṃskāra*).

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: The *Abhidharma* (Dharmapada) seventh [chapter] says that there is no real meaning in the non-creation of unwholesome karma because one does not encounter [the conditions for it];

thus it says, "Because the Noble Ones lack the delusion regarding what is unreal. As for the latter statement, "The Noble Ones do not create [unwholesome karma]," this refers to karma that results in general retribution—namely, meritorious and immovable karma.
If so, could the Noble Ones also create karma that results in present retribution? [They can.]

The *Śāstra* states: "The tenth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says that the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpādāṅga*) are subsumed under 'neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee' (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), yet they are not [exclusively] distinct retributions.
The commentary explains: However, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the twelve members are subsumed under "neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
Are the karma of retribution and the distinct retribution-karma of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) all included within the member of formations (*saṃskārāṅga*)?

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "In this context, some say that those who have already generated the initial resolve take the 'factors conducive to liberation' (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and so forth as their essence, and none of them create future [rebirths].

Regarding the phrase "none of them create future [rebirths]," it refers to *ākṣepaka-karma* (projecting karma). The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says: However, there are others who explain that the essence of the "faculty of knowing the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) exists in three stages:
first, the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*); second, the stage of Application (*prayogamārga*); and third, the stage of Provisions (*sambhāramārga*). These three stages are all termed...

Regarding "that which is yet to be known": these three stages, such as the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) and the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*), are all designated by the essence of "one in training" (*śaikṣa*).

Therefore, it is known that after first generating the mind of awakening and entering the stage of equipment, since one is already termed "one in training," all [subsequent actions] are termed "non-creating."
Thereafter, there is the karma of total retribution (*vipāka-karma*), none of which is subsumed under the branch of *saṃskāra*. The explanation says: Question:

Why is it said here that during the stages of equipment (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*), one is able to create the first immovable *saṃskāra* within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), whereas other authoritative scriptures state that these stages of equipment and application are comprised within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*)? Answer: In other authoritative scriptures, the emphasis is on the aspect of initial compliance and engagement [with the path].
It is taught that the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and the application (*prayoga*) are subsumed under the first faculty.

However, according to the actual meaning in this treatise, it is stated that within these two stages, one is able to perform meritorious and immovable karma; furthermore, these two stages are contaminated (*sāsrava*) and capable of producing the karma of birth and death.

Regarding the cause for that person, the tenth fascicle of the *Mahā-śāstra* states that the factors of dependent origination (*aṅga*) are not subsumed under the category of those in training (*śaikṣa*). Consequently, it is interpreted as follows:

since the stages from the "part conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*) onward are subsumed under "that which is yet to be known" (*ajñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*), it is clear that liberation itself is subsumed within the state of existence (*bhava-sthiti*), and thus one does not create new projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*). This, however, is not correct. The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* does not speak of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in terms of internal dharmas; rather...
"Up to the point of 'within the indeterminate, internal dharmas, ordinary beings do not create new karma. The commentary explains:

"The following sections of the sub-commentary (*śū*) are all the author’s refutations of the divergent interpretations of the preceding opponents. Furthermore, there are four types of ignorance (*avidyā*): first, that which is associated and also non-common;

third, the ignorance of the turning of the *sūtras*, which refers to manifest ignorance (*samudācāra-avidyā*); and fourth, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), which refer to seeds (*bīja*). This is according to the actual reality."

It is said that ignorance (*avidyā*) has only two types: first, the associated (*saṃprayukta*), and second, the non-associated (*asaṃprayukta*). The non-associated [ignorance] is said to exist both as manifest activity (*samudācāra*) and as seeds (*bīja*), and is divided into four types.
Regarding "ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of internal phenomena," this refers to those who have reached the tenth stage, the seventh stage of mind (*citta*).

They are thus called "inner dharmas" and "ordinary beings. Upon reaching the seventh stage of mind within the tenth level, they no longer regress to become icchantikas, non-Buddhists, or followers of the two vehicles.
According to the statement, if one belongs to the lineage of those subject to regression (*parihāṇa-dharman*), this occurs prior to the sixth mind of the tenth abiding.

They also all possess regression; thus they are termed "ordinary beings of the external dharma" (*bāhyadharma-pṛthagjana*). One must reach the seventh mind of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) before one is called an "ordinary being of the internal dharma" (*adhyātmadharma-pṛthagjana*).

Those prior to this belong to the lineage of non-regression (*avinivartanīya-gotra*); upon entering the ten stages, from the first moment of mind onwards, they do not regress and are all termed ordinary beings of the internal dharma.
However, according to the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, ordinary beings of the external dharma can indeed attain [realization].

The four types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)—associated, unshared, occasional, and continuous—are capable of producing karma that results in total retribution; these are subsumed under the member of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

If, within the initial stage of the Mahāyāna, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) of the internal dharma does not produce [the other three], then among the four types of ignorance (*avidyā*), only the latent ignorance arises.

This [latent ignorance] produces the karma of total retribution and constitutes the member of volitional formations. It is capable of [producing] the three types of [karma] through association, non-sharing, and occasional binding.

[The term] "clear" (*ming*) [refers to the following]. Among those of the internal dharma (*adhyātmika-dharma*) who are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and negligent, there are four types of equanimity (*upekṣā*) that correspond to the three kinds of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)—namely, those associated with the arising of [afflictions], those bound by the sūtras, and those that follow along.

These are subsumed under the branch of formative action (*saṃskāra*) which produces karma leading to general retribution (*vipāka*). By analogy, this excludes the non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) that does not give rise [to such karma].

This [non-common ignorance] is mostly produced by those of external paths (*bāhyaka-mārga*). If, however, an ordinary being of the internal dharma who is negligent does not commit the ten unwholesome karmas, they are not arrogant.

Regarding "advancing on the path with heedfulness," the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states that although among those born as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the internal dharma there is heedfulness, their meritorious and immovable formations (*puṇya-aniñjya-saṃskāra*) do not have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their condition.

This is because it is only the three types of non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) that arise in association with active manifestation (*samudācāra*) which are not permitted; in order to exclude those actively manifesting ignorances, it speaks of those meritorious and immovable [formations].
It is *saṃskāra*, not the link of ignorance (*avidyā*). The preceding seeds of ignorance are precisely what can give rise to those meritorious and immovable [karmas];

thus, they attain the status of being subsumed under the general category of the *saṃskāra* link. Regarding the forty minds of the Mahāyāna and the seven preparatory stages (*saptaprayoga*) of the Hīnayāna: as for the seven preparatory stages, they are: first, the contemplation of the five stabilizing practices (*pañcanivaraṇa-pratipakṣa*);

second, the mindfulness of specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*); third, the mindfulness of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*); fourth, *ūṣmagata*; fifth, *mūrdhan*; sixth, *kṣānti*.
The seven dharmas of the world’s foremost stage are as explained in the assembly. There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
those who do not regress from their initial resolve and those who, later on, are able to manifest the eight phases of transformation tenfold. At the seventh mental stage, one does not regress;

furthermore, one does not sever the roots of goodness nor commit the five deeds of immediate retribution, and thus does not fall into the Avīci Hell of Immediate Retribution according to the mind. If such a person reaches the fourth dwelling within the ten dwellings:
Furthermore, they do not give rise to non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*), and they are cautious regarding the three evil destinies.

In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, this refers to the stage of "non-retrogression from the lineage" (*gotra-anivartana*), which describes matters such as being a true son of the Buddha born of noble birth in the fourth stage.

If one were to retrogress from the lineage, then prior to the sixth stage, one would sever the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), commit deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), and fall into hell—such individuals are exemplified by Śreṇika and others. If one reaches the [sixth] stage...

It is only upon reaching the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) that one truly believes in non-retrogression, does not sever the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), and does not commit the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*).

Consequently, one does not enter hell; however, thereafter, it is not impossible for one to enter other evil destinies (*durgati*). It is only upon reaching the fourth *pariṇāmanā* (dedication of merit) that one no longer follows the three evil destinies, nor even a single ground within them.
Furthermore, one subsequently experiences [retribution] in a manner corresponding to the body and so forth. This is just as when the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was in the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.

During that kalpa, he became the Buddha Muni-jaṭi-ratna-keśa and received his prediction [of enlightenment]. Now, speaking according to the general rule, only those from the seventh stage (bhūmi) onward are termed "inner-world ordinary beings" (adhyātma-prthagjana).
Even if there were a person who, having first resolved their mind [on awakening], [proceeded further...]
That is, the non-arising of the associated ignorance (*sahagata-avidyā*). Or, speaking in terms of general principles regarding the present and the past:

as for those who are heedful (*apramāda*), their meritorious and immovable formations (*puṇya-aninjya-saṃskāra*) do not have ignorance as their condition; they do not give rise to the manifest activity of the associated ignorance.
However, those who are heedless (*pramāda*) first fail to give rise to the unique ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*). It is with reference to those who are heedful that this [text] speaks. But...

It is said that ignorance associated with non-arising [is meant]. Even if one has attained the state of an Arya, if [ignorance] subsequently serves as a condition, one does not create karma that results in total retribution (*vipāka*).
"The wise" refers to those who are untainted (*anāsrava*) and heedful (*apramāda*), distinguished from this [ignorance]; therefore, it speaks of those formations (*saṃskāra*).

As for the statement that even ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within internal phenomena do not create new karma: herein, "heedfulness" (*apramāda*) is used to distinguish the present activity within this [state] from that [ignorance].
This explains the teaching on the undertaking of practice. For one who is heedful, ignorance does not serve as a condition [for new karma].

Although such a heedful person still possesses the seeds of ignorance capable of producing karma that results in total retribution (*vipāka*), it should be understood that ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) within the internal Dharma are also able to create new karma.
The sūtras merely state that noble learners (*śaikṣa*) do not create new karma; they do not say that ordinary worldlings within the internal Dharma do not.
Regarding the capacity to create new karma, a question is asked concerning those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the Buddhist fold (*adhyātmika-dharma*).
Whether they are heedless or not heedless, do they all equally employ the seeds of non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) to project the formative forces (*saṃskāra*)?

If those ordinary beings within the Buddhist fold employ the seeds of non-common ignorance to project the branch of formative forces, how do these ordinary beings within the Buddhist fold differ from the outsiders (*bāhya-tīrthika*), since the outsiders also employ [them]?

Regarding the branch of the projecting cause consisting of the seeds of non-concomitant ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*): the answer is that for outsiders, it exists both manifestly and unmanifestly. Question:

Why is it that ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) within our own Dharma who are not heedless do not give rise to the manifestation of associated ignorance (*saṃprayukta-avidyā*), yet after attaining the state of an Arya, they may again give rise to the manifestation of associated ignorance?
Associated ignorance is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Furthermore, regarding the provisions prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva-sambhāra*)...
It is also admitted that both innate and conceptual afflictions manifest during the stage of the path of accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*). As the sub-commentary below states:
"Only within the stage of accumulation can one suppress coarse conceptual afflictions"—referring to those arising from teachers or false teachings;

whereas those arising from subtle conceptualization, or from what is termed "self-delusive conceptualization," are suppressed by the preceding path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*). Thus, both [types of conceptual afflictions] are addressed in the paths of accumulation and preparation.

Regarding the stage [of the path], the ninth fascicle of the *Śāstra* states: "While a Bodhisattva abides in this stage of the equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), although the two coarse types of manifest activity are suppressed, the subtle types and the two latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are not yet abandoned;
because the power of mental observation is weak, they cannot yet be suppressed or extinguished. It further states:

"In the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), a Bodhisattva is able only to suppress and eliminate the two types of conceptual grasping (*vikalpita-dvaya-grāha*); as for the innate [grasping] (*sahaja*) and the two..."

Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*): because the mind that contemplates the outflows (*āsrava*) still apprehends objects and involves conceptual discrimination, these dispositions have not been fully subdued or eliminated;

since they have not been fully subdued or eliminated, they have not yet been extinguished. If one does not admit that the afflictions arise from the provisions (*sambhāra*) and the preparatory application (*prayoga*), this would contradict the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
Would it not be certain that at the time of death for such individuals, the craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*) that link one to rebirth would not arise? If [one] admits [this]...
Regarding "arising": when afflictions arise, there must necessarily be a corresponding ignorance that arises simultaneously with them, because delusion (*moha*) pervades all defiled minds.
Therefore, one should know that even for those who give rise to non-negligence within internal dharmas, a corresponding ignorance still manifests as an active state (*samudācāra*).

If one were to allow that [ignorance] arises [in this way], it would contradict the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*. For that sūtra states that for one who is heedful (*apramatta*), ignorance does not serve as a condition.

Question: While it may be the case that the ignorance giving rise to non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya-karman*) in the desire realm is exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*) by nature, how can the ignorance that gives rise to meritorious karma (*puṇya-karman*) of humans and gods in the desire realm be exclusively unwholesome by nature? Furthermore, as in the internal...

Regarding the case of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who are heedful (*apramatta*), though their bodies reside in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they initiate karma solely by means of the seeds of ignorance (*avidyā*). How can it be that ignorance is exclusively of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala*)? Furthermore, regarding internal ordinary worldlings who are heedless (*pramatta*), though their bodies reside in the desire realm, they initiate formative forces (*saṃskāra*) solely by means of associated ignorance (*saṃprayuktāvidyā*). How can it be that this is exclusively unwholesome? As stated below in the initial verse: [The text continues with the verse: "Even for those who are heedful, when they are in the desire realm, Karma is produced by the power of ignorance;

How could it not be unwholesome? And: "For those who are heedless, when they are in the desire realm, Karma is produced by associated ignorance; How could it not be unwholesome? Thus, as explained in succession, the first [verse] states: [the verse follows].
The *Zhongshu* (Middle Commentary) explains:

"From this it should be known that the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*) and the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*), up to [the point stated], are thus the practices that induce the collective retribution (*saṃbhāra-vipāka*).

This is the first interpretation. Furthermore, the meaning of 'expedient means' (*upāya*) here refers to the wholesome roots of expedient means; these constitute the provisions (*saṃbhāra*) and the preparatory application (*prayoga*)."
Within these two states, one is able to oppose the evil dharmas of birth and death within the three realms and is able to proceed toward nirvāṇa.
Within these two states, one can also create karma that results in collective retribution; this refers to the members of ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*).

When it is said that these two dharmas are "innate wholesome dharmas" (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*), this does not mean that "innate wholesome" is merely a name for obscure goodness. What is here called "innate wholesome" is, in fact, the *sambhāra* (provisional equipment).
The roots of merit acquired during the stages of preparation (*prayoga*) and accumulation (*sambhāra*) are not roots of merit acquired by birth (*upapatti-lābhika*).

This means that the essence of the roots of merit of accumulation and preparation produced within these two stages constitutes the limb of volitional formation (*saṃskāra-aṅga*), which is capable of producing a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
Furthermore, it is not contradictory to say that there is obscurity within these two stages; indeed, obscurity arises within these two stages.

Question: Is the wholesome [karma] identical to the wholesome obtained within the bodies of other ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), such that both are equally the member of volitional formations (*saṃskāra-aṅga*)?

Answer: In this context, the intention is that in the two stages of the provisions (*sambhāra*) and the preparation (*prayoga*), the wholesome [karma] has as its essence the member of volitional formations; it is capable of inducing a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).

This is the first interpretation in this commentary, which states that during the stages of the provisions and the preparation, one is able to create the karma that constitutes the total retribution (*nikāyasabhāga*). This is also the correct meaning. If one explains it according to the sequence:
The stages of liberation (*vimokṣabhāgīya*) and the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are both termed "the nature of the preparatory means" (*upāyabhāva*).

These provisions (*sambhāra*) and applications (*prayoga*) can oppose the existence of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the existence of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the existence of the formless (*ārūpyadhātu*); yet they still possess a collective retribution (*vipāka*). This is subsumed under ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*).

Therefore, all innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) existing within those two stages of provisions and application are categorized as "wholesome pertaining to merit" (*puṇyabhāgīya-kuśala*), which suppresses [defilements] through the six modes of practice consisting of joy and aversion.
Delusions and so forth are all branches of *saṃskāra* (volitional formations) that can induce a collective retribution (*sāmānyavipāka*).

If one considers the actual reality, if the innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) produced in the desire realm possess functional power, they can induce a collective retribution fruit and are thus subsumed under the branch of *saṃskāra*.

However, because the innate wholesome states produced in the form and formless realms lack such power, they induce only individual retributions (*prātibhedavipāka*) and cannot induce a collective retribution fruit. If...

The wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) can also induce a collective retributive fruit (*sāmānya-vipāka-phala*), and they are also part of the member of practice (*pratipad-aṅga*). The wholesome roots conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) induce only a specific retributive fruit (*viśeṣa-vipāka-phala*).

The Commentary states: "Some say that these [roots] are also wholesome dharmas of the preparatory stage (*prayoga-kuśala-dharma*); otherwise, there would be the fault of lacking a corresponding precedent for specific retribution."

This is the second interpretation: it maintains that within the stage of the mere accumulation and application [of merit], one can only create specific karma (*viśeṣa-karman*) and cannot create general retributive karma (*sāmānya-vipāka-karman*);
thus, it does not designate [this stage] as the "limb of formation" (*saṃskāra-aṅga*). Now, in this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, we only take into account the karma that brings about general retribution.

Only then is it established as the member of volitional formations (*saṃskāra-aṅga*). Therefore, when the Sūtra says that those who do not create [karma] regarding internal phenomena are [liberated], this does not mean that they do not create karma for total retribution (*vipāka*) during the two stages of ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations.

Although the Sūtra speaks of non-negligence during the stage of the practice of provisions (*sambhāra-caryā*), the meritorious and immovable formations (*puṇya- and āniñjya-saṃskāra*) that produce such results are indeed not total retribution;
rather, they are causes for individual retribution (*pratyeka-vipāka*) and are likewise not the member of formations.

If it is not admitted that karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*) and so forth is called the "member of formations" (*saṃskāra-aṅga*), then [the argument] that it separately assists karma to be experienced in the future would be subject to the same logical fallacy.

Conversely, if it is asserted that karma to be experienced in the present life is indeed called a "member," then [the claim that it does not assist future karma] would likewise be subject to the same logical fallacy.

If it is argued that karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma*) is called the limb of formations (*saṃskāra-aṅga*), then karma that assists future karma should also be called the limb of formations;

yet, since it assists future karma, it cannot be called the limb of formations, and thus the karma to be experienced in the present life is likewise not called the limb of formations. This interpretation is also incorrect.
The Upādhyāya states: "Because there is much distraction and negligence during the stage of accumulation (*sambhāra-avasthā*), one can also produce total retribution (*vipāka*)."

Regarding karma: if, during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one exclusively practices calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), although one can create karma for specific retributions (*vyaktika-vipāka*), one cannot create karma for general retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*).

This is because the resulting birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) would not be of a superior nature. Furthermore, as for the argument that the causal substance of "not-yet-reported" (*anabhisankhata*) should be designated as the limb of formations (*saṅkhāra-aṅga*): if...

Karma that produces collective retribution (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka-karman*) and karma that produces both collective and individual retribution (*sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇa-vipāka-karman*) are fully capable of producing the collective and individual retributions of birth and death—that is, the body of birth and death.

This karma of collective retribution and this karma of collective and individual retribution are termed "excellent" (*viśiṣṭa*); they are subsumed within the factors of right practice (*samyak-pratipatti-aṅga*).

If these two types of karma do not assist the karma of the present life, and yet birth and death are produced, they are not excellent; they consist only of karma of individual retribution (*asādhāraṇa-vipāka-karman*) and so forth, and do not constitute the twelve [links of dependent origination].
Regarding the inclusion within the factor of right practice (*samyak-pratipatti*) and not being included within non-practice:

since this karma of distinct retribution (*vipāka*) is capable of producing the fruit of a future distinct retribution, that karma of distinct retribution is also included within non-non-practice; that is, the karma of distinct retribution is also included within the factor of right practice as an auxiliary (*anugraha*).
If one does not admit that distinct [karma] is an auxiliary to the karma of the present life and is thus included within the factor of right practice, then, for example:
Throughout a single lifetime, sentient beings experience only one karmic action that constitutes a total retributive maturation (*vipāka*).

This very action brings about the entirety of the consciousness link (*vijñāna-aṅga*) within the fruit of total retribution, as well as the mental attention (*manasikāra*) and contact (*sparśa*) associated with the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) within the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Regarding the branch of sensation (*vedanā*), that portion which corresponds with the eighth consciousness is the sensation-branch.

If the first [category] is of a composite nature, it takes the sixth sense-base (*manāyatana*) from among the six bases; on the eighth consciousness, these are all results of collective retribution (*vipāka*).
When there is a single karma capable of producing both collectively and individually retributive results, this very same single karma can induce the mind of the eighth consciousness.

Regarding mental factors (*caitta*): just as with form (*rūpa*), these are each a portion of the total retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*) consisting of feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth. Furthermore, by means of this karma, they are also able to bring about specific retributive fruits (*viśeṣa-phala*).

That is to say, within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), there are the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) and the mental factors associated with the remaining six consciousnesses—namely, perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*manasikāra*), and the five object-specific mental factors (*pañca viṣaya-niyata-caitta*).
Within the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), there are the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) and the sixth consciousness, together with the apprehension of the six [objects].

The factors such as contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) that arise simultaneously with consciousness—all these are termed "distinctive retributive karma" (*pratiniyatavipāka-karma*). Delusion (*moha*) possesses only one type of distinctive retributive karma;

it only brings about the acquisition of the "distinctive retribution" consisting of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the four sensory objects that support the sense organs, and the five specific-object mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyatālambana*) and the five omnipresent mental factors (*sarvatraga*) that arise at the time of the first six consciousnesses, as well as those six consciousnesses themselves. This distinctive retributive karma, however, cannot bring about "collective retribution" (*sāmānyavipāka*).
Regarding the fruit: this excludes the eighth consciousness and its associated mental states from among the five fruits. Here, the intended meaning is as follows:

if that which is produced by the power of general retributive karma and specific retributive karma—namely, name-and-form, sense bases, contact, and feeling—is what constitutes the branches of name-and-form, sense bases, contact, and feeling, then these very factors of name-and-form and so forth are designated as "name-and-form," "six sense bases," "contact," and "feeling. These are the factors of name-and-form and so on.

This is precisely what is called "volitional formations (saṃskāra) inducing specific auxiliary causes for future karma. That which is induced is termed the "specific retributive fruits" of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), feeling (vedanā), and so forth.
Clothing is not called "induced by volitional formations," and likewise, it should not be termed "name-and-form," "the six sense bases," and so on.

Since these are exclusively the causal substance that serves as specific auxiliary causes for future karma, they are also designated as the "limb of volitional formations" (saṃskāra-aṅga). All of the above concerns the drawing forth of causes by means of results; this is the distinction between the primary and the secondary.

Regarding the matured branch of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): even those formative forces (*saṃskāra*) that result only in specific retribution (*bié bào*) are included here. This also cites the fruit to reveal the cause.

If, within the name-and-form and so forth that constitute the actual maturation (*vipāka*), there were only that which results in general retribution (*zǒng bào*), then there would be only a single karma.

It only brings about the fruit of total retribution (*sāmānya-vipākaphala*). "Total retribution" is a name for *vipāka* (maturation). This means that among the five fruits, it takes up the eighth consciousness along with its associated mental states (*citta-caitta*).

If one also includes those that bring about specific [retributions], then there is karma that can simultaneously bring about both total and specific fruits, thereby fully encompassing all five fruits—namely, the fruit of total retribution and the fruit of specific retribution. If one also includes the branches of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), it is merely a fulfillment.

If the fruit is also this [same], then it is further designated as the "exclusively distinct retribution karma" (*kevala-vipāka-karma*). That which is induced is termed "name-and-form," "the six sense bases," "form," and "feeling," and these are also the "fulfillment fruit" (*pūri-phala*).

Now, the same applies to the member of "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*). If one takes the member of volitional formations as the primary factor—just as when the "total retribution maturation fruit" (*sarva-vipāka-phala*) is the primary factor—it consists of both the total retribution karma and the karma that induces both total and distinct retributions. If, however, one includes the "exclusive volitional formations" (*kevala-saṃskāra*) as well...

Regarding "karma that produces specific retribution": this refers to karma that specifically assists future karma and produces only specific retribution—namely, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*).
All such karma that produces only specific retribution is also a specific retribution of the auxiliary factors of the [twelve] links;
thus, it is subsumed within the link of name-and-form. This is not contradictory, because it is produced solely by karma that yields specific retribution.
[Result]. This distinct retributive result (*vipāka-phala*) consists of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*).
This distinct designation of the results as name-and-form and so forth is also inconsistent with their inclusion within these twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*), as they are already subsumed therein.
Furthermore, this treatise only takes up the primary practice; otherwise, there would be the same logical obstacles as mentioned before. The reason it is profound is that this treatise only...
The karma that brings about the general [rebirth] is taken as the primary; the karma that brings about specific retribution is designated as "correct" (*samyak*).

This means that it is not separately taken as merely the karma for specific retribution, but rather it is subsumed under the "limb of correct practice" (*samyak-pratipatti-aṅga*). This is because the karma for specific retribution cannot by itself draw forth the general retribution of a future existence (*punarbhava*).

Nevertheless, the essence of the karma for specific retribution is also subsumed under the "auxiliary limb of practice," though it is not subsumed under the "limb of correct practice. Therefore, the auxiliary [karma] for specific [retribution] is excluded.
Karma is subsumed under the branch of right action (*samyak-karmānta*); otherwise, there would be the same fault as previously explained.

The Commentary states: "Since this is so, it conversely reveals that even what is included within habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)—by means of the principle just mentioned—reveals that within ignorance (*avidyā*), if there is no beginningless karma capable of producing the general retribution (*vipāka*), this ignorance is doubly capable of producing specific retribution."
All such instances of ignorance (*avidyā*) are subsumed within the "ignorance" link (*avidyā-aṅga*) among the twelve links of dependent origination.

This being so, conversely, it is revealed that if ignorance were capable of producing only the specific [retribution], then the ignorance that produces only the specific retribution would not be the "ignorance" link among the twelve links.
If the retribution produced by this ignorance were exclusively specific retribution and specific karma, that would constitute the permeation of the "constituent of existence" (*bhavāṅga*).

That which is subsumed within the "habitual" (*vāsanā*) is not included within the "correct practice" (*samyakpratipatti*) branch among the twelve links. Regarding the statement that the first two branches are subsumed under the "maturation fruit" (*vipākaphala*):
these two branches refer to ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*). This commentary merely provides a general explanation at the outset and does not fully capture the underlying principle.

What is the matter? If it were not for the branch of ignorance—which is neither naturally wholesome nor unwholesome—that would fail to produce the non-meritorious karma (*apuṇyakarma*) through which [the result] is induced.
Within the three miserable destinies, there is the ripening fruit of suffering (*duḥkha-vipāka-phala*).
This ripening fruit of suffering acts as the cause of ripening for the preceding members, ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), such that cause and fruit correspond. Why is this?

Because ignorance and formations are of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala-svabhāva*), whereas the ripening fruit of suffering is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); thus, compared to the [first] three members, it is of a different nature, and for this reason it is called "different" (*visadṛśa*).

Regarding the matured fruit: if unwholesome ignorance of the desire realm gives rise to meritorious formations, it brings about the ripened fruit of karma for humans and devas within the desire realm.
This ripened fruit of human and celestial karma acts as the ripened fruit for those meritorious formations, but it does not act as the ripened fruit for the preceding ignorance.
Why is this? Because cause and effect must be commensurate. If the meritorious karma is wholesome...

As for its nature: it can obtain the ripening fruit of pleasure among humans and devas. However, since the member of ignorance (*avidyā*) is of an unwholesome nature, it cannot obtain the ripening fruit of pleasure among humans and devas, because the cause and the effect would not correspond. The fruit of suffering is experienced through unwholesome karma;
the relinquishing of the fruit through wholesome karma is obtained by both the wholesome and the unwholesome. All ignorance that initiates karma in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is unwholesome.

As for its nature: it does not obtain the fruits of happiness of humans or devas. Since the fruits of happiness of humans and devas are obtained only by looking toward meritorious karma (*puṇya-karma*), the ignorance that is of an obscured nature (*nivṛta*) within the two upper realms—namely, the factor of ignorance associated with immovable karma (*āneñjya-karma*)—obtains the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of the upper realms.
This ripened fruit of the upper realms functions solely as the ripened fruit of the aforementioned immovable karma. This is because...

The cause is of a wholesome nature (*kuśala*) while the fruit is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); thus, cause and fruit correspond. As for the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of pleasure, it does not function as the ripened fruit for the preceding member of ignorance (*avidyā*).
This is because ignorance is of a nature that is obscured and defiled (*nivṛta-kliṣṭa*), and therefore cannot produce the ripened fruit of pleasant sensation belonging to the higher realms.
Furthermore, since a ripened fruit must be pervasive (*sarvatraga*), it is not appropriate here. By this reasoning, this is the former... [text ends].
The maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) does not depend upon ignorance; thus it is called a maturation fruit.

Regarding the statement that "the entire link of consciousness (*vijñāna*), as well as the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and so forth up to the rest, are all exclusively individual retribution (*pratyeka-vipāka*)," while "the middle mind is the substance of the collective retribution fruit (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*)," if one defines the substance [of the fruit] without mixing [the two], one takes the entirety of the link of consciousness.
Within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), one takes [only] the perception (*saṃjñā*). As for the middle... one takes [only] that which corresponds with...

The perception associated with the eighth consciousness; furthermore, within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it refers to the attention (*manasikāra*) associated with the eighth consciousness;
and within the factors of contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*), it takes the contact and feeling associated with the eighth consciousness.

Among these, one takes the mind and mental factors that arise simultaneously with the eighth consciousness and names them the "total retribution" (*vipāka*). As for the "giver," it refers to the five sensory consciousnesses and...

The Commentary asks: Why does the first fascicle of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra* state that "one part—namely, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—is also called 'that which is produced' (*janyamāna*)"?
Answer: This statement is made based on their future actualization (*samudācāra*), not to say that the seeds themselves are called "produced. The Explanation says: Why?

The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states: "One portion of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) is called 'that which is projected' (*ākṣepaka*);
another portion of name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling is called 'that which is produced' (*abhinirvartaka*). Answer:

If the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* speaks of one portion of name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling as being "produced," this is said with reference to their state of actualization (*samudācāra*) in the future; it does not refer to the seeds (*bīja*) of name-and-form and so forth.

Form (*rūpa*) is that which arises from name (*nāman*); the various types of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are merely subsumed and drawn forth by name. Furthermore, when it is said that name-and-form enters the mother’s womb, this refers only to the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

If this second contact (*sparśa*) is explained as being comprised within the seed-state of the future arising of the links of birth, then the manifest name-and-form, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact, and feeling within the mother’s womb—namely, the single state of name-and-form and so forth—are what is meant.

It is also called "that which is produced" (*jāta*). Furthermore, it is not because one can enter the stage of being in the mother’s womb while still in the seed-stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) that this is so;
rather, it is clarified that the consciousness link (*vijñāna-aṅga*) itself is subsumed under the category of seeds, and it is not said that the consciousness link is "produced."
The *Śāstra* says: "The World-Honored One said that they arise in a sequence of before and after; it is thus explained. The commentary says:
If one speaks according to reality, the seeds of the five fruits—consciousness and so forth—are perfumed by the member of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) simultaneously;

this is the sequence of before and after. If one speaks figuratively regarding the sequence of before and after, it is because of the explanation concerning the single delusion; therefore, it is so stated.
The five types of consciousness have a sequential order of priority. Regarding the two delusions, there is a sequential order of priority in the state where the factors of the future birth manifest.
As stated in the subsequent treatise: at the time of rebirth, the characteristic of consciousness is prominent, and thus the limb of consciousness is explained first.

Next, when the sense faculties are not yet fully developed, the characteristic of name-and-form increases, and thus the limb of name-and-form is explained next. Subsequently, when the sense faculties are fully developed...

The sixth station is clearly described. Immediately following, the limb of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is explained. Because new contact arises, the limb of contact (*sparśa*) is explained immediately thereafter.

Because sensation (*vedanā*) arises from contact, the subsequent stations are explained. These represent the sequential order of the five factors, beginning with consciousness, as they are conventionally designated within the state of the future place of birth.
Regarding the phrase "whether intercalary or non-intercalary, they must not coexist": the character "intercalary" (*rùn*) mentioned above refers to sensation (*vedanā*).

The essence of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) is the meaning of "intercalary" (*vyañjana*). The character "intercalary" (*vyañjana*) here signifies the sense of being "sustained" or "incorporated. The meaning of this passage is as follows:

if craving and grasping have not yet sustained or incorporated the seeds of the five fruits, such as formative forces (*saṃskāra*), then the projection [of the future existence] and the actual birth cannot occur simultaneously.

Therefore, it is said that "the intercalary and the non-intercalary karma do not coexist. This treatise can also be understood in this way: once the five fruits, such as formative forces, have been intercalated, then birth occurs.
Regarding "drawing forth at the same time": if there is no intercalary month, then it arises as drawing forth at a different time.
The commentary states: "Even after eighty thousand kalpas, the fruit will ultimately not arise. The explanation says: This commentator cites the case of Udraka Rāmaputra.

Due to falling away from the eight higher meditative attainments (*dhyāna*), he practiced those higher attainments again. He was tormented by birds and beasts: first, while in the forest, he was troubled by flying birds;

they manifested as hawks devouring various birds. Later, in an open space, he was troubled by rats; he wished to become a cat. He was troubled by fish in the water; [the fish] devoured the *jian* (crabs/shrimp).
Afterward, he was reborn in the upper realms for eighteen thousand kalpas. Thereafter, being born again in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), he once became a winged weasel. There was one...
The Sūtra speaks of "transforming the cat-like cognition.
The Commentary states: "If it were able to produce the manifest [result] at the very moment of initial perfuming, then craving and so forth would already exist during the stage of initial perfuming.

If this were so, how could one explain the difference in the timing of their formation? For instance, within a single thought-moment, ignorance arises and initiates the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)."

The "branches" (*śākhā*) are precisely these seeds capable of bringing about the five fruits. Only after a long period of time do they receive the "intercalary moisture" (*upasecana*) of craving and grasping, and only then do the actual manifestations (*samudācāra*) arise.

If it were said that at the very moment of initial perfuming in a single instant, the seeds of all five fruits could produce their manifestations, then at the time of initial perfuming, craving and the other factors would have to arise as intercalary moisture to produce them. If that were so, how could the performance of karma and the intercalary production [of the fruit] be distinguished?
Because the timing differs, we know that within a single moment, when ignorance arises and karma is created, it cannot simultaneously give rise to the "moistening" factors such as craving.
At the time of the initial perfuming, the actual manifestation cannot yet be produced; only after being moistened by subsequent factors such as craving can the actual manifestation arise.
The *Śāstra* says: "It is only at the stage when [the result] is about to arise that the projecting [cause] and the projected [result] are admitted to exist simultaneously;

because they are distinct entities, it is said that there is a distinction between the projector and the projected. The commentary explains: The meaning of the text is that at the stage of future birth and old age, one metaphorically designates the projector and the projected as being simultaneous with the produced [result].
That is to say, even within the present stage of birth and old age, there exists the projecting consciousness (*ākṣepaka-vijñāna*).
Because the seeds of the five fruits give rise to the actualities (*samudācāra*) of birth and aging, they are conventionally designated as "existent" within their respective states.

The projecting causes (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) and the projected [causes] (*ākṣipta-hetu*) are simultaneous with that which is produced. However, according to the actual path, the actual projecting causes and so forth cannot be simultaneous with that which is produced.

This is because, prior to being conditioned by the moisture [of karma] and before the actualities of consciousness and so forth have arisen, they are designated as the projecting and projected causes.
If [a limb] has already been "intercalated" (*upasaṃhita*) at the time of its manifestation, it is then designated as a "generating limb" (*janaka-aṅga*).

Since the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) and the "projected" (*ākṣipta*) differ from the "generating cause" (*janaka-hetu*) and the time [of their occurrence], they cannot all exist simultaneously. Furthermore, it says:

"The intent of this passage is to state that if the 'formations' limb (*saṃskāra-aṅga*) and the seeds of the five [limbs] beginning with 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*) have been intercalated, they are then subsumed under the category of generating limbs. They are obtained simultaneously; in reality, the actual practice and the seeds of the five fruits are of one essence. Because they differ at the initial stage, they receive two distinct names based on the different meanings of "projecting" (*ākṣepa*) and "producing" (*abhinirvṛtti*).
