It is conventionally taught that the "projecting" (ākṣepaka) and the "projected" (ākṣipta) are simultaneous with the "producing" (janaka) acquisition; therefore, the acquisition receives the two designations of "projecting" and "producing.

If one follows the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, all instances of projecting and producing are conventionally said to be simultaneous. However, if speaking according to ultimate reality, the projecting and the projected [are not so].
It cannot exist simultaneously with the "projecting" (ākṣepaka) factors. That which has not yet been supplemented by the seasonal intervals is called a projecting factor;
that which has already been supplemented is called a producing (abhinirvartaka) factor, because the seasonal intervals are distinct.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The Sūtra also intends [the causes and effects] to be simultaneous. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says:

"In this Sūtra, it is not definitively stated that the projecting factors (*ākṣepaka*) and the projected factors (*ākṣipta*), or the producing factors (*janaka*) and the produced factors (*janya*), must necessarily be simultaneous.

The Sūtra merely states that if the projecting factor—the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)—and the seeds of the five projected results, such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth, have not yet been moistened by conditions and have not yet given rise to their actual manifestations (*samudācāra*), they will nonetheless give rise to [their effects] in the future."
If, at the time of their actualization, one speaks of the "projecting" and the "projected," do the "producing" and the "produced" arise simultaneously?

This is explained in terms of the distance or proximity between them and the resulting fruit that they produce. The commentary states: if it refers to the projecting and the projected, then they are distant from the fruit.
If that which is the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*) is indeed close to the fruit it produces, the Commentary (*Śāstra*) states:

"Although both craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) can also nourish the substance of the preceding projecting causes (*ākṣepa-hetu*), they are called 'nourishing' (*anugrāhaka*) because they are proximate to the future;

however, [the preceding causes] are only described as 'productive'. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states: "Craving and grasping can also nourish the branch of formations (*saṃskāra*) which is the preceding projector."

If there were seeds for the five fruits, such as consciousness and so forth, then craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) would also have to be subsumed under the "moistening cause" (*paripuṣṭa-hetu*).

However, in this system, while craving and grasping are indeed moistening factors for the link of existence (*bhava*), they possess only the designation of being a "generative cause" (*janaka-hetu*) for that link.

Within the link of existence, the seeds themselves constitute the primary cause that generates the two subsequent links of birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) in the future. Consequently, craving and grasping cannot be classified as generative causes for those two links.

Because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) moisten the link of existence (*bhava*), they are capable of producing its actual manifestation; therefore, craving and grasping can cause another birth.
Furthermore, because craving and grasping are proximate to the link of existence and serve as the causes that produce it, these two are also subsumed under the category of "causes of production."
"If that which induces and that which is induced are the distant fruit," the *Śū* (the Commentary) says;
this refers back to the previous interpretation, stating "this restates the preceding treatise. This means it cites the prior discussion to introduce the subsequent one. Question:

If this section had merely clarified that craving and grasping are the factors that moisten, without mentioning the factors previously moistened, then although it would be understood from the text that craving and grasping are capable of moistening, one would not yet know what specific factors they moisten.

Therefore, in order to clarify that craving moistens, the treatise first restates the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which were the factors previously moistened, and subsequently shows how craving and grasping moisten them. Thus, [the sequence is established].
"Clouds rise in front and form behind. The Commentary states:
"These six [consciousnesses] are all capable of being proximate to 'existence' (bhava) and so forth," which refers precisely to the existence of non-existence. This is not the body;
it is called "possessing grasping" (sa-upādāna). "Existence" here is the name for the body itself. Furthermore, when experiencing objects, one is unable to discern that which is known.
Regarding the object (*viṣaya*): when defiled feeling arises, craving and so forth increase. Now it is said that being deluded regarding external [objects] is also a result of ignorance (*moha*).

Taking the feeling of the object as a condition, one gives rise to craving and so forth. If one takes the causal body—the cause and effect—as a condition, this is called being deluded regarding internal maturation (*vipāka-phala*).

If one perceives the pleasure and so forth to be experienced in a future birth as being the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), this is called ignorance regarding the external dominant fruit (*bāhya-adhipati-phala-moha*).

This gives rise to the perception of a superior realm (*adhika-dhātu-vedanā*). When one is about to die from the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) with the intention of being reborn in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), that person’s mind at the point of death, though directed toward the sphere of infinite space, also takes as its object the future place of rebirth, thinking:
"Will my body experience pleasure there? Even in the sphere of infinite space, there is thus an object-condition directed toward an external realm.

Regarding the elements and sensations (*dhātu-vedanā*): they do not separately and definitively depend upon their objects as conditions to give rise to craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*), because [such a condition] is not universal.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "It is not so; while this maturation (*vipāka*) is the seed of conventional designation (*nāma-vyavahāra*), it has not yet produced its fruit. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says: "If [it refers to] the five [aggregates], such as consciousness (*vijñāna*)..."
The seeds of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-bīja*) that produce the five fruits are the seeds of names and phrases induced by the performance of karma and so forth;
these seeds of names and phrases are capable of producing actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*).

If, however, the seeds of names and phrases that constitute maturation (*vipāka*) were not induced by karma, then those seeds of names and phrases of maturation, even while residing within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), would necessarily be unable to draw forth and produce actual manifestations.
Yes. This karma is induced by the preceding ignorance; such is the meaning of "relying upon" used as an analogy.

The *Śāstra* says: "In this context, the meaning of 'delusion increasing' (*anuśaya*) is explained as follows: up to the point where the delusion regarding cultivation is divided into two distinct parts that increase separately. The commentary explains:

Karma can also nourish rebirth, because it fully involves the defilements that link one birth to the next. Regarding "delusion concerning internal maturation" (*vipāka-sammoha*): this refers to the affliction of conceptualizing what is not the Path;
it is the affliction of being deluded regarding the principle (*nyāya*). This occurs because ignorance is deluded regarding the principle of the fruit of suffering that is maturation.

Furthermore, being deluded regarding the manifestation of the causes and effects of future birth-and-death, one immediately craves the body that is the fruit of future suffering, and thus performs meritorious or non-meritorious karma.
The three types of karma—meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable—induce the fruit of future suffering;

therefore, delusion regarding the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) is precisely the affliction that deludes one regarding the principle (*tattva*) upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). Hence, it is called an "affliction of the Path of Seeing.

While not entirely deluded [regarding phenomena], these afflictions of the Path of Seeing are mostly deluded regarding the principle and only slightly deluded regarding phenomena. That which is slightly deluded regarding phenomena follows the pattern of views concerning self and others, as appropriate to each case.
The arising of greed, hatred, and pride constitutes afflictions associated with the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) that take as their objects the views regarding self and others;

these are abandoned by the path of seeing. Furthermore, delusion regarding external objects refers to innate (*sahaja*) afflictions associated with the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) that arise during moments of confusion.

For example, the afflictions that arise taking external objects such as the five sensory realms—form and so forth—as their objects are termed "afflictions deluded regarding phenomena" (*vastu-moha-kleśa*). Delusion...

Ignorance regarding external objects. Since ignorance regarding external objects is an ignorance that arises during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it gives rise to afflictions concerning phenomena.
For example, the afflictions arising from taking external objects such as the five sensory realms—form and so forth—as their conditions are called "afflictions concerning phenomena.
Ignorance regarding external objects, being an affliction of the path of cultivation, is both directly productive and auxiliary to [rebirth].

It can give rise to non-meritorious karma. However, regarding the afflictions cultivated through practice (*bhāvanā-heya*), there is more delusion regarding phenomena (*vastu*) and less delusion regarding principles (*tattva*).

That which is less deluded regarding principles refers to the innate views of self and what belongs to self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi* and *antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), as well as the adjacent greed, pride, ignorance, and so forth; these are termed "delusion regarding principles.

As for the two types of increase that are distinct from the two views abandoned through practice (*darśana-heya*), the present treatise [states]: [The text continues: ...the two views abandoned through practice are exhausted; the two types of increase that are distinct and follow along with them are as follows: now, the treatise...
The delusion regarding internal maturation (*vipāka*) refers to the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); it is described according to what can give rise to karma.

The delusion regarding internal maturation that is "clear" (*vidyā*) refers only to those [afflictions] that can give rise [to karma]; this too is a description according to their increase (*anuśaya*).

As for the delusion regarding external increasing realms, this refers to the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) that nourish rebirth. Now, the delusion regarding external objects is said to be only that which can nourish rebirth. It is also...

This is explained according to the principle of "increasingly pervasive" (*anuśaya*). However, in the Mahāyāna, if afflictions are conceptual (*vikalpita*), they are abandoned solely by the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*);
these include greed, hatred, pride, and so forth, which arise based on views concerning oneself and others, and which can be abandoned even while on the Path of Seeing.

If, however, the afflictions are innate (*sahaja*), they are abandoned solely by the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Yet, while the Path of Cultivation primarily abandons those afflictions that are deluded regarding phenomena (*vastu*), it is also capable of abandoning [conceptual afflictions].

Afflictions that delude one regarding principles (*nyāya*) refer to the innate views of self and extremes (*satkāyadṛṣṭi* and *antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), as well as the closely associated pride (*māna*) and so forth.

According to the Sarvāstivādins, afflictions that delude one regarding principles are abandoned solely through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), whereas afflictions that delude one regarding phenomena (*vastu*) are abandoned solely through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Therefore, the two subsequent afflictions both universally induce [the karma] and universally moisten [the rebirth]. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says: This refers to what the lower treatise states:

"If it is an affliction of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it is that which directly induces karma and assists in moistening rebirth; if it is an affliction of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), it is that which produces and moistens rebirth."
[The phrase] "assists in the arousal of karma" refers to this.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states: "These twelve links [of dependent origination] have no causes or conditions, because they are based on the arising cause as it is subsumed under the predominant factor.
The commentary explains: Regarding those treatises such as the *Yogācāra-bhūmi*, when they state that the twelve links have no causes or conditions, it is precisely based on...
Regarding the cause of origination: it is explained through ten examples of predominant karmic seeds.

If one were to say that only karmic seeds are mentioned and there are no [other] links, then would it not follow that one is not speaking of the five effects—consciousness and so forth—as being the links of designation within the causal conditions of the cause of origination?

That which arises is precisely the "arising cause" among the ten causes. As for why the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* speaks of this when the result is proximate, yet does not mention the other causes, it is because those other results are remote.
The *Śāstra* says: "Below that, it further states: 'The karma subsumed under grasping (*upādāna*) is called the superior differentiation of existence (*bhava*), etc. The commentary explains:
"Karma subsumed under grasping" refers to the karma of the formations (*saṃskāra*) branch, which is moistened by the two branches of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping.

Because those [branches] of craving and grasping moisten and sustain it, the formations-branch karma transforms into the existence (*bhava*) branch. Once the existence branch has been moistened, it immediately produces the future fruit.

Therefore, it is called "existence with a superior portion. In this context, since the link of grasping (*upādāna*) is proximate to the link of existence (*bhava*), the karma subsumed under grasping is mentioned;
furthermore, the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is also included therein.

The Commentary states: "Although the five kinds [of seeds] are causes capable of producing, they are not designated as 'existent' because they lack the power to actually produce [the result]. The Explanation states:

"Although the seeds of names and phrases (nāma-vyañjana-bīja) regarding the five results—consciousness and so forth—are the direct causes and conditions for the five seeds of the manifest consciousnesses, such as birth and old age, in the future, if they do not receive the impetus of karma, they necessarily lack the power to produce."
The five seeds, such as the self-arising consciousness and so forth, must be induced by the karma of others before they can produce their actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*).

If it is only the seeds of karma that are designated as the "limbs of existence" (*bhavāṅga*), does this not mean that the seeds of names-and-words (*nāma-vyañjana*) for the five fruits— consciousness and the rest— are not called limbs of existence?

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "In the fifth [chapter], 'The Grounds' (*Maulī Bhūmi*), at sections thirty-eight and so forth, it is taught that the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*) and the generative cause (*janana-hetu*) subsume the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) as their nature;
thus, there are only five types, and the karmic factors (*karma-aṅga*) are not mentioned. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says:

In those works such as the *Yogācārabhūmi*, within the initial discussion of the productive cause, it is explained that the generative cause refers specifically to the arising from the immediate causal condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). It speaks only of the seeds of designations (*nāma-kalpa-bīja*) for the five fruits, beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The *bhava-aṅga* (existence link) directly gives rise to birth and old age; it does not depend on the dominant karmic seeds within the causal factors of birth.

Thus, the seeds of karma are not designated by the name "existence link. Regarding the state of decay: for however long the duration may last, the simultaneous deterioration of both mind and form is called "old age.

This is the intended meaning within the Dharma: in the Formless Realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), it is only the mind that decays; in the Desire and Form Realms (*kāma- and rūpa-dhātu*), both mind and form decay.
It is simply decay; therefore it is said that there is no time when mind and form are not [subject to] increase or decrease.

If one is born as a human or a deva in the desire realm, being half-old like a human, the period prior to having reached one hundred years is termed the branch of birth (*jāti-aṅga*). If it has already passed beyond this, all of it is the branch of old age (*jarā-aṅga*).

As for the six classes of desire-realm devas, they are mostly subsumed under the branch of birth; once they are about to die, even if only one or two days have passed [since their birth], [they are considered to be in the branch of old age].

The day is named *jarā-śī* (the branch of old age). If one is in the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) or the formless realm (*arūpa-dhātu*), one passes away only after ten or five moments of consciousness (*vijñāna*) have elapsed following the onset of old age.

The commentary states: "There are six kinds of birth, up to and including 'growth-and-maturity birth' (*paripūrṇa-jāti*). The explanation says: "The first kind of birth is from the semen and blood of the parents."
1. Conception (*saṃyoga*): entering the mother’s womb. 2. Growth (*vivardhana*): having entered the mother’s womb, the gradual growth until emerging from the womb.

3. Birth (*niḥsaraṇa*): emerging from the mother’s womb and the gradual growth and maturation thereafter. 4. [Omitted in original numbering]. 5. Full development (*paripūri*): continuing until the onset of decay and transformation.
However, within this context, five types of birth and six types of death are taught; these all refer specifically to the human realm and to those born from a womb.
This is the explanation of death according to the Left (Vāma). It does not restrict the five types of birth to humans alone; animals and hungry ghosts also possess all five.
This applies to the Form and Formless Realms, the six heavens of the Desire Realm, and likewise within the hells, where only the fifth type—birth by transformation—is present, lacking the first four.

As for those born by transformation, their sense faculties arise spontaneously. Apart from these, among other hungry ghosts, animals, and humans, if they are born from a womb or by external birth, [they likewise possess the five].

Thus, these five types of birth are fully present. If one considers moisture-born and transformation-born beings, there are only two [of these five], namely: birth by gradual growth (*anupūrva-ja*) and birth by transformation (*aupapāduka*).

Furthermore, excluding the time at the beginning of a world-cycle (*kalpa*), humans at the beginning of a cycle are exclusively transformation-born, just like the gods of the Form Realm (*rūpāvacara*) at the beginning of a kalpa; they possess only the fifth type, birth by growth.

Although among the six heavens of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) there are likewise these five types up to the twelfth existence (*bhava*), [the specific focus here is on] the ten recollections (*daśa-smṛti*) and the five [preliminary stages].
[The author] reflects: Since there is a force that gradually increases even slightly, there must be a gradual growth of birth. Here, the meaning of gradual growth over ten or five years is taken;
[this applies to] the six heavens of the desire realm prior to the fourth birth.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "This refers to the decay of the beard and hair, up to the decay of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). The Explanation says: "The greying of the head is called the decay of the hair;

the wrinkling of the face and the skin of the body is called the decay of physical appearance (*rūpa*); the inability to engage in worldly activities is called the decay of functional capacity (*karma*);

the inability to enjoy food, drink, wealth, or sensual pleasures is called the decay of enjoyment (*upabhoga*); and the gradual approach toward death is called the decay of the life-faculty. Now, regarding this...
Regarding those who give rise to many benefits within the intermediate [realm]: humans possess the five signs of decay; the inhabitants of the Northern Continent now have white hair;

and in the two upper realms, it is the life-faculty that decays. Among the gods of the six desire heavens, there are the signs of the great five decays and the minor five decays, which are subsumed under physical decay.
The aging of the head, the withering of flowers, and so forth, are also signs of physical decay; there is likewise the decay of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Among animals, there are days when the aging of white hair occurs, and their thoughts regarding their destination are the same [as humans]. Among humans who possess the four modes of birth (*yoni*), all have the five signs of decay. In the hells, there is only the decay of the life-faculty.
If one hears of death and feels joy, thinking, "I shall abandon this root of suffering through that cause," [the question arises: "Are there large and small [lifespans] in the higher realms?"
[Question: "Are there not the five signs of decline?
[The Master] asked further. The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "There are six kinds of death, including those who die at the six times or at improper times.

The *Jie* (Exegesis) explains: First is "ultimate death" (*niṣṭhā-maraṇa*). There are two interpretations. One says: when an Arhat enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, it is called ultimate death. [Regarding] the Arhat...
First, there is that which is called "ultimate death," wherein only this single body dies; after death, no further subsequent body arises.
Second, it is said that when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) dies, consciousness departs from the body, and after the breath has ceased, it is called ultimate death.
As for the second type, non-ultimate death, this refers to those born through various karmic conditions who, although they die in this body, [possess] yet another...
Within this present life, there are hundreds of thousands of returns to death; these are called "incomplete" deaths. Third, regarding death by its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*):
this refers to the period immediately preceding death and the moment of actual death, when consciousness is about to depart from the body; this is called death by its own characteristic.

Here, one does not take the state after the breath has ceased and consciousness has already departed from the body to be "death by its own characteristic. Fourth, the specific characteristics of the various stages leading to incomplete death.
This refers to the distinctions among the stages of the dying, the actual dying, and the already dead for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and others.

There are five distinct characteristics of the final stage of death: namely, at the time of an Arhat’s passing away, there are likewise the distinctions among the stages of the dying, the actual dying, and the already dead, along with their preceding and succeeding phases. To know these and take [the death of] an Arhat as the standard is called "final" (*niṣṭhā*).
Death is, in principle, superior. There are six types of timely and untimely death. When the lifespan of a hundred years is fully exhausted, it is called timely death;
when it is not yet complete, it is called untimely death. The desire realm possesses all six types of death. The six heavens also have six types of death;

instances such as beheading, severing the waist, or dying from rage are termed untimely. The two higher realms lack untimely death, because they lack the power of physical techniques that can contravene external conditions.
Therefore, in the hells, death occurs at specific times; since there is still a remainder of the body, there are five types of death.

In the three evil destinies as well, death occurs at non-specific times, and there are four types of death, excluding only the ultimate [death]. Furthermore, for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in the first three fruits, there are four types of death.

There is no first death or fifth death; rather, death gives rise to the factors of birth. For those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there are only four types of death, excluding only the second and third.
Question: How can an Arhat experience untimely death? Answer: Even for Arhats who have attained the realization of contact, there is untimely death, such as being killed by others.
However, this does not contradict the established definition of death as the cessation of one's own constituent characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
There are five types of death. Although untimely death also encompasses the other five types, the first distinction is made such that six types of death are enumerated.
Here, we take only the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*): "death" refers to the time when one is about to die or is in the process of dying;

it does not refer to what has already died. Question: By inferring from the east and west, is there the production of action? Furthermore, there are five types of birth in the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*).

No. Do the five types of old age and six types of death exist among the eight classes of beings? Do those in the four fruits and ten stages experience these five births, six deaths, and five types of old age through their respective modes of birth—whether *pariṣandaja* (segmented) or *nairmāṇika* (transformative)? Question: Do the gods of the six heavens have white hair?

As noted above, this refers to those who die from self-love (*ātmasneha*). Question: Regarding the link of death (*maraṇa-aṅga*) within the twelve links of dependent origination, is it the same as the aforementioned death characterized by its own specific mark (*svalakṣaṇa*)? If...
Regarding the branches of birth, death, and old age: do they take five births and five old ages?

The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "This is based on the stages. If there were no manifesting consciousness (*vijñāna*), it would still be subsumed as 'consciousness' because it serves as the basis for the drawing-in cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*)," and so forth, as explained at length therein;
this does not contradict the present context. The *Jie* (Explanation) says: "If one speaks according to the principle, that which is drawn-in by consciousness and the other [factors]..."

The five fruits are exclusively seeds; they do not include manifest states (*samudācāra*). As for those cited in the preceding treatise, they refer to the five kinds—consciousness and so forth—contained within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) which are subsumed under the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) to be produced in the future. Thus, one should know that the five fruits are exclusively seeds.

If we speak according to reality regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it is subsumed solely within the link of birth-and-death (*jātimaraṇa*). The first passage states: "That is to say, from the intermediate state..."
Up until the point when one has not yet undergone decay within the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), all [factors] are subsumed under the members of birth (*jāti*).

This means that, with respect to the stage of future manifestation, if they are provisionally designated as five resultant members: at the time of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*), the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*) becomes manifest; next, before the sense faculties are fully developed, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) increases in its characteristics;

next, at the time the faculties are complete, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are experienced; based on this, contact (*sparśa*) arises; and due to contact, feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth arise. These five—
Speaking in terms of their actual status, they are subsumed under the "arising" (*jāti*) branch; that is, they are conventionally designated as the five resultant branches.

Now, if one were to conventionally designate the currently functioning consciousnesses and so forth as the five branches from the moment they first arrive in the state of manifest activity, this would contradict the principle of the intermediate [existence] having power.

From the very first moment of taking birth, everything is both consciousness and subsumed [within it]; thus, one speaks of the manifest consciousness as being conventionally designated [as the branches].

Regarding the limb of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*): it is taught that the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) is subsumed under the limb of consciousness. Furthermore, if one speaks of the manifestation of consciousness, it should likewise be subsumed under consciousness;

thus, at the stage of the [twelve] limbs, what is manifest as consciousness is metaphorically designated as the "limb of consciousness. From the time of entering the mother’s womb until the completion of the first twenty-eight days, this is the limb of consciousness.

Subsequently, before the sense faculties are fully developed and while the characteristics of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are increasing but not yet complete, it is metaphorically designated as "name" (*nāman*).
The branch of form (*rūpa*). Next, when the sense faculties are complete, the characteristics of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) increase; this is metaphorically designated as the branch of name-and-form.

Next, when the sense faculties are complete, the manifestation of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is clearly perceived; this is metaphorically designated as the branch of the six sense bases. From this, contact (*sparśa*) arises; this is metaphorically designated as the branch of contact.
The sensation that arises from prior contact is conventionally designated as the "limb of sensation. These five stages are, in reality, the limb of birth;
they are conventionally designated as the five resultant limbs, such as consciousness and so forth.

If one conventionally designates the manifest consciousnesses and so forth of the stage of birth as the five resultant limbs, then both the eighth retributive manifest consciousness and its seeds exist within the eighth manifest consciousness. This [process] induces...
The causal seed refers to the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, which is the actualized eighth consciousness itself.

The basis for the drawing-forth cause refers to the name-base (*nāma-āśraya*) of the actualized eighth consciousness. The "capable" [cause] refers to the seeds of the drawn-forth and that which is drawn-forth;

specifically, it refers to the actualized name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the actualized six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the actualized contact (*sparśa*), and the actualized feeling (*vedanā*) as the causes capable of producing [the result]. This is based on...

The active manifestation of the causal basis gives rise to the active manifestation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Name-and-form brings about the active manifestation of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The six sense bases produce the active manifestation of contact (*sparśa*).

Contact produces the active manifestation of feeling (*vedanā*). From the active manifestation of feeling, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises. The exhaustion of [feeling] gives rise to grasping (*upādāna*). Grasping gives rise to becoming (*bhava*).

This craving, grasping, and becoming constitute the productive cause. It is precisely upon this productive cause—the active manifestation of name-and-form and so forth up to contact and feeling—that [the subsequent links] arise.

This refers to the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*). That which is named the "basis" (*āśraya*) consists of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth, up to contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*), because these serve as the basis for [the subsequent stages].

Therefore, it is said to be the "basis for the cause of production. According to the Sarvāstivāda school, the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is also subsumed under the member of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Just as the two past members are causes and the five present members are results, the body of the intermediate state is likewise subsumed under the present member of consciousness. This is because...
Next, upon entering the mother’s womb, from the fourth week onward, it is designated as the limb of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the entire group of dependent origination is subsequently established through five aspects. Regarding the basis for the projecting cause, this refers to [the process] within the present life.

With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise without interruption. All foolish worldlings, not knowing this basis and its locus, give rise to delusion regarding their own internal bodies;

this is the textual definition of ignorance (*avidyā*). With ignorance as condition, there subsequently arise mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and at a later time, there is feeling (*vedanā*) conditioned by contact (*sparśa*).
In this context, the six sense bases are the causal factor induced by ignorance and the other [links].
Regarding the "basis" (*āśraya*): this passage refers to the stage of future birth and aging, wherein name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) first arises;

from that, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) come to exist. As long as these six bases are not severed, all foolish worldlings, regarding their own internal bodies, give rise [to cognition] based upon the six bases.
Without a basis for the arising of ignorance (*avidyā*), they would not produce the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). It is through these formative forces that [the subsequent stages] are acquired.

Regarding the seeds of the five fruits: herein, both the ignorance that induces [the result] and the seeds of the five fruits that are induced all arise only when the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are present.

Therefore, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the six sense bases are said to be the basis for the inducing cause. Within this context, contact (*sparśa*) and sensation (*vedanā*) are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Contact and feeling are included among the factors. Regarding the statement that they are the basis for the arising of the two types of suffering:
it means that for all foolish commoners, with contact as a condition, feelings arise in the present life; taking those feelings as a basis, they give rise to craving toward external objects.
With craving as a condition, there subsequently arises grasping; with grasping as a condition, there subsequently arises becoming. Thus it is.

Regarding the statement that "the three kinds of causes for the arising of craving and so forth depend upon feeling as their condition, with contact as their basis," the meaning of this passage is as follows:
because of the existence of contact, the five types of feeling arise within the present body of ordinary worldlings; this contact serves as the basis for those feelings.
Regarding external objects, one gives rise to greed, craving, and so forth; subsequently, there is grasping (*upādāna*). With grasping as a condition, there is then "existence" (*bhava*).
This craving and grasping constitute the productive cause. All productive causes arise in dependence upon contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*).
In this context, one takes the contact of ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*) and the feeling born thereof as "contact" and "feeling. Regarding the basis for the three categories of suffering:
it refers to the sequence from ignorance as a condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), up to contact as a condition for consciousness (*vijñāna*) arising in the present life.

This [consciousness] is followed by the successive perfuming of seeds—namely, meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable karma—which is capable of drawing forth the arising of further bodies, consciousness, and so forth, in the future.

The suffering of death. Therefore, when it is said that "this is the cause of grasping," the meaning of this passage is that ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling constitute the cause of grasping.
By means of these five results, one is able to draw forth the future stages of birth, aging, and death.
Regarding the cause for the arising of the fourfold mass of suffering: this refers to craving conditioned by feeling, and grasping conditioned by craving; this is called the [future]...
The cause for the arising of future suffering is precisely the karma previously performed, which is grasped by the afflictions (*kleśa*), because birth in a future life is about to manifest.

That which is called "existence" (*bhava*) here refers to the three—craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*)—which serve as the causes for the arising of the five aggregates of suffering.
The arising of the five aggregates of suffering means that, following the conditions of birth, there arise aging and death; this is what is termed the arising of the aggregates of suffering.
That is to say, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling;

when these exist as seeds according to their respective supports, they receive the designation of "the cause that draws forth all suffering. Now, as for the designation of the "fruition" as the suffering of birth, aging, and death:

among these five [categories], the first two are merely conventional designations applied to the states of birth and aging within the manifest [process]. As for the latter three, the first one is explained by means of the twelve links. This is because...

Regarding that which has improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) as its cause: although it is not included [in the category of universal factors], it is logically consistent to designate it as "improper mental attention.
The essence of mental attention is itself the mental attention among the universal factors (*sarvatraga*), which can serve as a cause herein.

Thus, it is said that improper mental attention acts as the causal condition for ignorance (*avidyā*). To speak according to the actual reality, improper mental attention is associated with all afflictions (*kleśa*).
It serves as the cause. Whenever any affliction arises, it never accords with reason; whenever any delusion arises, it does so only through improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
Because ignorance (*avidyā*) is all-pervasive, it is said that ignorance takes improper mental attention as its cause.

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Because that [ignorance] is solely a cause for non-cessation and not a cause for the departure from defilement (*vairāgya*), the members [of dependent origination] are explained in reliance upon the causes of defilement.

The *Exegesis* explains: Within the *Śāstra*, there are three layers of established reasoning. Regarding the "cause for non-cessation": it arises with the production of improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) as its cause.
That is to say, each teaching gives rise to ignorance and improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), which causes ignorance to continue in succession or to be interrupted.
This improper mental attention acts as the cause for the non-interruption of ignorance, ensuring that ignorance does not cease.

Because ignorance is not severed, ignorance is able to give rise to karma, and karma is able to produce the seeds of the five fruits [of maturation] and so forth, causing them to arise in a continuous succession that is never interrupted;
therefore, it is said that it is "only the cause that is not severed. However, this refers to improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
This is also identical to the defiled wisdom (*kliṣṭā prajñā*) among the five object-specific mental factors (*pañca viṣaya-niyata-ālambana-citta-dharmāḥ*), which constitutes its essential nature.

Since wisdom that is not defiled does not constitute this nature, improper attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) is not stated to be a constituent factor. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is a constituent because it gives rise to karma that is free from defilement and serves as the cause for the arising of defilement.
It is said: By means of perfuming these seeds of karma, it causes the five fruits—consciousness and the others—to become capable of producing their actual manifestations.

Furthermore, through the moistening influence of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) among the afflictions, this becomes the link of becoming (*bhava*), which gives rise to birth, aging, and death.
This karma has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its cause; improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) is not mentioned [separately].

The Commentary states: "The Buddha said that ignorance also induces improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) and serves as a condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). The Explanation says:
Ignorance is also able to induce improper mental attention; ignorance is also able to serve as a condition for volitional formations.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "If there were [further] existence (*bhava*), it would be infinite; furthermore, this must be explained. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says:
If old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) had a fruit, and that fruit were further existence (*bhava*), then the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*) would have to become twenty or thirty-four links.
If old age and death have a fruit, why is it not stated at this time that old age and death have a fruit?

The commentary states: "When an elder undergoes separation, the foolish person’s mind becomes feverish with craving... [this] up to 'the many types of afflictions bound by suffering'. The explanation says:
When a fool witnesses the death or separation from a wife or child, all six sense faculties experience suffering. This is stated in terms of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Here, however, it is based on association with the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) that they are termed "suffering" and so forth; therefore, it says that when the five faculties encounter their objects, it is called suffering. As for [its] association with the mental faculty (*manas*)...

Regarding the term "should be named" (*ying ming*): it is therefore said that the mutual correspondence of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is called "correspondence" (*ying*). Furthermore, herein, when the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) is severed and one directly experiences suffering, its correspondence with the mental faculty is termed "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*).

This refers to the mental object (*dharmaviṣaya*) being associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), whereby the mental consciousness, taking objects such as wife and children, gives rise to sorrow (*daurmanasya*).
If one speaks of the mutual correspondence of the five faculties versus the mutual correspondence of the mental faculty, the older translations distinguish between sorrow and suffering. However...

Many are called "suffering" (*duḥkha*). That which is called "affliction" (*upāyāsa*) is a phenomenon that causes distress; it is not the same as the preceding "concomitant affliction" (*anuparivartin-upāyāsa*). Upon seeing a person die, one merely feels vexation in the heart.
As for "lamentation" (*parideva*), it occurs only within the sixth consciousness. "Lamentation" (*parideva*) means to sigh or wail.
Lamentation can pertain to all three types of karma—body, speech, and mind—referring to the act of uttering words of wailing and sighing. This is what is meant by "the self as an entity."
The Commentary asks: "Why is it not mentioned? Why is it that old age and death are not said to have the fruit of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction?
Regarding "sorrow and lamentation due to separation": if one encounters an object of separation as previously described, only then do sorrow and lamentation arise.
The Commentary (*Śū*) states: "The consciousness that goes to the various realms of existence. The Explanation (*Jie*) says: "It should go to the five realms, such as humans and devas;
this is the meaning of 'various realms' (*sarvagati*). The Commentary states: "'Dharma' refers to what is common with the Old [School] and the Hīnayāna. The Explanation says:

"If the Hīnayāna also teaches that sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction are the fruits of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), it still does not teach that perception (*saṃjñā*), sorrow, suffering, and affliction are subsumed within the twelve links [of dependent origination]. "Old" refers to the Old [School].

The sutras and śāstras state this; the commentary (*shu*) says: "How is this intended to be revealed? It means that either birth arises from karma, or that from karma there arises the [resulting] entity, and so on, up to revealing that subsequent ignorance also arises from prior ignorance.
The explanation states: This cites the meaning of the ninth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*, which says: "[Ignorance] arises from afflictions (*kleśa*)."

Or suffering: this refers to the arising of the *upādāna* (clinging) link from the *tṛṣṇā* (craving) link; the arising of karma from afflictions, which refers to the arising of the *bhava* (existence) link from the *upādāna* link and the arising of the *saṃskāra* (formative activities) link from the *jāti* (birth) link;
the arising of things from karma, which refers to the arising of the *vijñāna* (consciousness) link from the *karma* link and the arising of the *jāti* link from the *bhava* link;
and the arising of things from [the aforementioned], which refers to the arising of *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form) from the *vijñāna* link and the arising of the six [sense bases] from *nāmarūpa*.
From the link of contact (*sparśa*) arises the link of sensation (*vedanā*), and from the link of birth (*jāti*) arise the links of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

From activity (*karma*) arises affliction (*kleśa*), namely, from the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises the link of craving. By means of the link of existence (*bhava*), the principle is solely that of phenomena (*dharma*).

However, the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) is free from the term "affliction" (*kleśa*); in the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*), there is no text [explicitly] excluding "affliction," and it likewise cites this principle of "what need for affliction? (*kiṃ kleśena*).
If one considers the five fruits according to the stage at which they are about to arise as actualities (*samudācāra*), they are also called "limbs" (*aṅga*).

Later, just as the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises from the object obtained through sensation (*vedanā*), this demonstrates that [craving] arises from the preceding old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) as its cause.
This very present ignorance (*avidyā*) arises from the preceding old age and death, just as grasping (*upādāna*) arises from craving; this demonstrates the preceding ignorance.

At present, ignorance arises from prior ignorance. However, the intended meaning here is that it is only through the arising of *bhava* (existence) or the stage of birth and old age (*jāti-jarā*) that one can produce [subsequent] non-existence; that is, the twelve links revolve through birth and death.
Furthermore, one does not take the arising of *bhava* from [prior] ignorance as the production of present ignorance from prior ignorance; such is not the characteristic of the twelve links.
"...continues the cycle of transmigration.
The *Śāstra* states: "If the self-nature of old ignorance (*avidyā*) is defiled, and if other conditions—even those that do not diminish it—are not present, it is not called [a cause].
The commentary explains: "If one says that ignorance acts solely as a cause for ignorance and there are no further ten conditions (*pratyaya*), this..."

If ignorance were the cause for the arising of ignorance itself, it would neither be able to cause the twelve links of dependent origination to continue and increase in the cycle of birth and death, nor would it be able to cause the phenomena of birth and death to diminish.

It is only by taking ignorance as the cause that one can produce the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and furthermore bring about the five results such as consciousness (*vijñāna*). Only when these five are moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) do they lead to old age and death. Thus, [ignorance] causes...
Birth and death increase [thereby]. For this reason, it is not stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of ignorance.
The intention here is to say that it is not by means of a preceding ignorance that subsequent ignorance and so forth are made to increase or established as diminished.
Rather, at the very beginning there are other conditions: namely, the seed of ignorance, as well as the objects of perception known as consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth; thus...
This causes ignorance to increase. If there were any other noble path capable of severing ignorance and its manifestations, then [ignorance] would be diminished.
The Commentary states: "By this, one may likewise infer that old age and death have results which serve as the causes for ignorance, and so on, up to their outflows."
This serves as an analogy. The explanation says: it is analogous to how old age and death act as causes that can produce ignorance (*avidyā*) and give rise to the delusions that initiate karma;

that is, old age and death serve as causes for ignorance, just as feeling (*vedanā*) gives rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Although one knows that while the substance of the delusions that initiate karma does not have [old age and death] as their cause, yet old age and death act as causes capable of producing ignorance—and ignorance is precisely the substance of the delusions that initiate karma—just as feeling gives rise to craving, so too is craving [the result].

This refers to the "defilements that cause rebirth" (*upapatti-saṃyojana*). Although the ignorance that initiates karma (*karmābhisamskāra*) and the craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth that cause rebirth within the *vedanā* link are distinct in their nature as the two types of defilements—namely, those that initiate karma and those that cause rebirth—they are both equally outflows of affliction (*kleśa-niṣyanda*).
If *vedanā* acts as the cause capable of producing *tṛṣṇā*, this is likewise a case of a specific defilement arising from another. As for old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)...

It serves as the cause for the arising of the link of ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore, because it arises from a phenomenon (*dharma*) to produce a defilement (*kleśa*), it is said to be "an outflow similar to that" (*sabhāga-niṣyanda*) as an analogy.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "It is not that the ignorance of the Hīnayāna takes the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as its condition; craving and the others are likewise," or [it refers to] their characteristics.

For example, the commentary explains: In the Mahāyāna, it is held that ignorance alone can give rise to the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and that feeling (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) alone give rise to grasping (*upādāna*).
In the Hīnayāna, however, it is held that at the moment of ignorance, the five aggregates simultaneously give rise to the link of volitional formations;
and at the moment of craving, the five aggregates simultaneously give rise to grasping. All of these are based on the dependent origination of discrete stages (*avasthika-pratītyasamutpāda*). As...

Regarding the "foolish view": since ignorance (*avidyā*) takes the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as its condition within the links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and since craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) likewise take the five aggregates as their conditions, ignorance and craving are analogous because they share the same nature—the five aggregates.
Furthermore, this passage refutes those two types of folly regarding permanence and annihilation by clarifying that these are present fruits; [it shows] the present fruit.
The ten causes from the past produce [the present]; this refutes the view of permanence (*śāśvata*). The ten causes in the present can produce two fruits in the future;

this refutes the view of annihilationism (*uccheda*). The Commentary states: "It is not that those two factors both lack fruit and cause. The Explanation says: "It is not that old age and death lack a fruit, nor that ignorance [lacks a cause]."
There is no [independent] cause. That is to say, old age and death have ignorance as their fruit, and ignorance takes old age and death as its cause.
Regarding the question, "What is this birth, etc., from which birth, old age, and death arise? there are four intended meanings in this inquiry.

First, it asks whether birth, old age, and death are the three marks (*lakṣaṇa*); they are not non-existent, for they are subsumed within the three marks. Second, it asks again: if birth, old age, and death...
Regarding these three characteristics: for what reason is the characteristic of "abiding" (*sthiti*) not taught as a constituent (*aṅga*)?
The term "lower aggregates" (*adhara-skandha*) is used because "abiding" would be confused with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which is not included [among the constituents]. A third question asks:

if "abiding" is not taught because it is confused with the unconditioned, then in the Hīnayāna it is taught that the characteristic of arising (*jāti*) exists in the future, while abiding, change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*nirodha*) exist in the present. Now, in the Mahāyāna, it is taught that arising, abiding, and change...
The third [mark] is cessation in the present, while its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) resides in the past; this refers to the ten causes in the present.

The two branches of the fruit [of suffering] are in the future, and their characteristic—namely, the characteristic of death—resides in the future. How could the characteristic of cessation in the past be the characteristic of death in the future world?

This concludes the passage from the *Rājakaumudī*. Regarding the fourth passage, the question asks: "If birth, aging, and death are not the three characteristics, one does not yet know what these 'birth' and so forth are."
Regarding the inclusion [of birth, aging, and death] within the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) that are not associated with the three characteristics of arising, aging, and cessation:
since birth, aging, and death are not themselves those three characteristics, it is not yet known what kind of "birth" and so forth are also included therein.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "How is it that the subsequent objection well explains the preceding objection? The Explanation says: The subsequent objection refers to Subhūti’s [question] which states:

"Are birth, old age, and death the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)? Now, since the arising, aging, and death of the aggregates (*skandha*) are subsumed under these three characteristics, the previous question asks:

"How is it that aging is prior? and further asks: "Why is 'abiding' (*sthiti*) not stated as a characteristic? This is because at present, the aggregates have not yet arisen; therefore, it is said that the preceding objection is like this.

"What?"—this question is answered by the preceding [section]. This is subsumed under the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*). That is, it concerns the first objection regarding the aggregates (*skandha*).

Regarding the three objections concerning the non-aggregates (*askandha*), it asks: "How is that previous objection well-explained? How does the commentary (*ṭīkā*) reconcile the objection so that the previous objection is well-explained?
How do the aggregates manifest the former name as being subsequent, and the former name as being prior to the latter? Furthermore, ask again."
The *Śāstra* states: "Only aging (*jarā*) is not the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*). The commentary explains:

If one takes "aging and death" (*jarāmaraṇa*) to mean the moment of impending death, as well as when the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and so forth depart from the body, then the characteristic of death (*maraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is a dharma possessing a substantial entity (*sadravya-dharma*) existing in the present; the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), however, is without a substantial entity.
Since the characteristic of cessation belongs to the past, according to the aforementioned treatise, the latter [of the two characteristics] is non-existent; therefore, it resides in the past.

The Commentary (*Śū*) states: "This refers to the final moment of actual death as well as the stage of 'conforming to death' (*anuloma-maraṇa-avasthā*) prior to it. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states:

"Actual death" refers to when warmth has not yet departed from the body; this is precisely when the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) is about to depart from the body, which is termed "actual death.
Regarding the "stage of conforming to death" mentioned during illness, it may last for five days, ten days, or more.

The Commentary states: "The nature of the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) is non-existent; it is established only with respect to the past and cannot [function] as such, for it is also without substance.

This means that the characteristic of cessation and the characteristic of death (*maraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) are not to be explained by analogy. The four characteristics of a single [moment of] disintegration (*viccheda*) endure for a long duration, whereas the four characteristics of a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) perish immediately after arising.

Thus, although their temporal divisions differ, they are one in this regard. Among these four characteristics, [this refers to] the characteristic of cessation and the four [characteristics] of a moment."

Among the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) and others are established in the past time (*atīta-adhvā*). In the Mahāyāna, the characteristic of cessation is established in the past time;

therefore, it is said that "the characteristics are established based on time. The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Although both are conventional (*prajñapti-sat*), they differ in their reliance on time. The *Jie* (Exegesis) explains: "If the member of death (*maraṇāṅga*) were also conventionally existent (*prajñapti-sat*), then..."

Upon the manifestation of the aggregate collection of the five *skandhas*, the factors of birth, aging, and death are provisionally established. This is like how, based upon the four types of sensory objects (*viṣaya*), one speaks of them collectively as a "vase.
The vase is a mere designation (*prajñapti*), whereas the four [objects] are substantial (*dravya*). Now, the five *skandhas* are substantial, while birth, aging, and death are provisional.

Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "Nine are substantial; three are provisional. Since the six factors have already been included and combined to form "existence" (*bhava*), if [one were to consider] only one...

Among the four characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*). Since the characteristic of cessation is conventional (*prajñapti-sat*), although both [the characteristic of birth and cessation] are conventional, they differ according to their temporal basis (*adhvan*).
That is to say, the characteristic of death exists only in the present; as for the characteristic of cessation, its temporal basis differs.

The Commentary says: Question: If birth and so forth are themselves the characteristics of birth and so forth, then the latter two members [of dependent origination] should be subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and so on, until:

"yet they cause one to feel revulsion, for their substance is not subsumed under those three characteristics. Explanation: The question concerns the three characteristics of arising, change, and cessation.

This is subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). If birth, aging, and death were the three characteristics of arising, change, and cessation, then these subsequent three members—birth, aging, and death—should be seen as included in the aggregate of formations.
Answer: By means of those [characteristics of] having already arisen and ceased, the three characteristics manifest these three members of birth, aging, and death;
it is not that these three members of birth and so forth are the three characteristics of the subsequent birth and so forth. These [members of] birth, aging, and death...
The three entities of death are the five aggregates (*skandha*) in their active manifestation (*samudācāra*). Therefore, birth, aging, and death are collectively subsumed within the five aggregates.

The three members—birth, aging, and death—are not themselves subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Although these three names, birth, aging, and death, are based upon the three characteristics of arising, transformation, and cessation;

There is a distinction in their substantial reality (*dravya*). Regarding this distinction in substantial reality: the three [factors] of birth, aging, and death have the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as their substance;

the three branches of birth, aging, and death have the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as their substance. This is like the designation "death-contact" (*maraṇa-sparśa*) within the sphere of contact (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).

That is to say, among the discussion of smoothness, roughness, lightness, heaviness, softness, laxity, tension, hunger, thirst, satiety, strength, and weakness—within these two types of contact, [the term "death-contact" refers to] sickness, aging, fatigue, and labored breathing.
There is death. Among these twenty-two kinds of contact (*sparśa*), death is not itself the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*).

Rather, at the very moment of dying—when the "wind of the blade" (*śastra-vāyu*) dissolves the joints and limbs—it is designated as the "contact of death" among the twenty-two kinds of contact. Death is a constituent part of birth; it is within these contacts that death occurs.
How could the death among the twenty-two kinds of contact be the essential nature of the characteristic of cessation? It is for this reason that there is birth, aging, and death.

The three [links] are designated based on the three characteristics such as arising (*jāti*), in order to induce revulsion. However, the three entities of birth, aging, and death are not subsumed under those three [characteristics].
The commentary states: "Now, birth, aging, and death should be called two links; here they are called two links because both consist of birth, aging, and death."

Third, the distinction. Therefore, it is called the "three branches. Question: If the branch of death among the twelve links is subsumed under the "death-contact" among the twenty-two kinds of contact, then the branch of death within the twelve links and the branch of death within the two [branches] should be subsumed under the volition of death-contact among the twenty-two kinds of contact;
yet, if the branch of death within the twelve links were to depend solely upon that which possesses form (rūpin), [this would be inconsistent].

Regarding the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) within the aggregates (*skandha*): why did the preceding commentary state that the factors of birth, aging, and death are subsumed under the present five aggregates?
Furthermore, since there are no twenty-two types of contact (*sparśa*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), by which contact are one who is about to die or who is in the process of dying subsumed?

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "In the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, old age and death are also established as a single member [of dependent origination] in order to demonstrate that even when separated from birth, they still exist;

therefore, they are each established as distinct members. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states: The meaning of this passage is to ask: why are old age and death combined and established as a single member?

Answer: This is to clarify the process of separation and combination. Old age is followed by death; even those who die young undergo old age before dying. Therefore, the factor of death is established as being preceded by old age.
It is not the case that within a womb-born body, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and so forth can exist independently of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the other factors.
Thus, this passage conversely demonstrates that for an infant in the womb, or for those born from eggs and so forth, there must first be name-and-form.
Only after the five faculties have matured do the six sense bases arise; these occur within the womb.
Thus, the six sense bases are manifested based upon the limb of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and the limb of the six sense bases cannot exist apart from the limb of name-and-form.

While name-and-form and the six sense bases are each established as distinct limbs, in the case of the two types of birth—moisture-born and transformation-born—the various faculties are manifest and complete from the outset; therefore, it is not said that they arise based on name-and-form.
Regarding the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the treatise asks: why are they not considered branches [of the path], and why are they neither universal nor fixed? Question:

Among the twenty-seven noble ones (*āryapudgala*), as well as those who practice with joy (*prīticārī*) and the rhinoceros-like [solitary realizers] (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa*), and the ten-stage bodhisattvas—whether those ten-stage bodhisattvas receive a body of fragmented birth (*pariccheda-kāya*) or a body of transformation (*nirmāṇa-kāya*)—as well as the asuras and the eight classes of beings, do all of these possess illness? Or not?
[Question: Do the four wheel-turning kings have illnesses? [Question: When asking whether the Buddha can have illnesses according to the teachings of the Hīnayāna, one asks:

Are these illnesses all the individual retributions for unwholesome karma—so-called results that fail to be fulfilled—or, since Arhats have already severed unwholesome karma, how can they still have disease?

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "Question: This dharma of illness does not pervade the world; [it is said] that one has never suffered even a minor ailment. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says: "In the two upper realms, there are no illnesses.
Even among the six classes of desire-realm devas, there are none; yet those devas who possess great merit all die when the five signs of decay (*pañca-vyasanāni*) manifest."
This is not a disease. As for "hell," it refers to the intense suffering of oppression and acute pain; in comparison, [the latter] is merely subtle suffering.
Since there is no suffering of disease in hell, disease does not pervade all realms and destinies. It exists only among humans, animals, and hungry ghosts. Furthermore, disease is not constant;
for example, Kula was eighty years old and never suffered even the slightest ailment.
The Commentary states: "Those who do not engage in intercourse at midlife" refers to those whose faculties and consciousness have declined prior to the end of life. The Explanation states:

"Not engaging in intercourse at midlife" refers to the elderly and others. This is because when the elderly and such reach the end of their lives, their faculties and consciousness necessarily become weak.
Old age pervades the three realms; those with little sexual intercourse do not grow old.

The treatise states: "Because they are fixed, the stages [of the embryo] are established as branches; this applies even to those born from moisture until they are designated as the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*).

Question: Regarding this dialogue, why are the characteristics of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) explained solely in terms of their manifestation during the stage of the future birth?

Furthermore, among these five fruits, why is there a question and answer concerning only name-and-form and the six sense-bases, while no such question or answer is provided for consciousness (*vijñāna*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*)? Answer:
Regarding the question and answer concerning whether one will be reborn in another existence, the *Shu* (Commentary) states:

"The ninth [section], etc., nine [sections], etc., state that for the moisture-born and egg-born, excluding those remaining in the mother’s womb, the sequential arising is as certain as that of the womb-born.
The *Jie* (Exegesis) explains: "If one is moisture-born or egg-born and emerges from the mother’s womb, since it was within the egg [or moisture]..."
Yellow fluid and the like are called the "mothers" of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). When they are about to be joined to this egg, the name-and-form within the egg gradually increases.
Furthermore, regarding moisture-born beings—such as King Māndhātṛ and the various ranks of his attendants—all are moisture-born.
Although moisture-born beings do not reside in a mother’s womb, they possess name-and-form; and name-and-form likewise gradually increases. Therefore, it is said that moisture and eggs [are similar].

Regarding the two types of birth [moisture-born and egg-born], with the exception of those in the mother’s womb, if they are egg-born, it is only within the mother’s womb that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) can begin to grow slightly.
These two types of birth—moisture-born and egg-born—with the exception of those not in the mother’s womb, are like the womb-born;
while in the mother’s womb, their name-and-form and so forth gradually increase.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "As for those sentient beings with form who take birth in the realm of desire within the realm of form, because their sense faculties are complete at the moment of initial birth and they differ from others, [the name-and-form] is not universal.

The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says: This refers to the celestial realms and the hells in their entirety; in these other births, the six sense faculties are present at the moment of initial birth, and there is no such thing as name-and-form that is entirely absent.
Furthermore, humans, animals, and hungry ghosts at the beginning of a kalpa are all born by transformation (*upapāduka*); in their initial birth, they likewise lack [name-and-form].
Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). All its characteristics are complete.

The commentary states: "Question: Why is it said here that all three types of birth possess a sequential order, yet for moisture-born and transformation-born beings, the parts of the body arise instantaneously?
The explanation says: This question asks, "Why is it that among these three—moisture-born, egg-born, and [womb-born]—it is said here [that they arise sequentially]?"
Regarding the statement that "name-and-form (nāmarūpa) gradually and subtly increases," why does the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explain the branch of birth (*jāti*) as follows?
It asks: "What is emergence (*abhinirvṛtti*)? It answers: "Emergence is called birth. The underlying question is: "How does it manifest in that place? The answer is:

"It refers to the sudden manifestation of the bodily parts of moisture-born and transformation-born beings. This explains that the bodily parts of moisture-born beings arise all at once; this arising occurs within this [context].
The statement that "in moisture-born beings, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) increases very gradually" is contradictory [to the following].
The *Śū* (Commentary) says: "This refers to the general case where those born by moisture or transformation all attain their full form instantaneously. The meaning of this passage is as follows:

if at the moment of birth, moisture-born beings possess only hands and feet but lack the five sense-faculties (indriya), then the initial state of transformation-born beings likewise possesses both hands and feet. Furthermore...
The five faculties arise suddenly in two distinct ways. The *Śāstra* states: "At the stage of initial conception, one possesses only the faculties. The commentary explains:

Why is it not said that one possesses all six faculties, but rather that one possesses five? Because the five material faculties (*rūpīndriya*) are complete, this is termed the limb of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

As long as the five material faculties are not yet complete, even though the mental faculty (*manas*) is present, it is not called the six sense bases. This refers to the very moment of initial conception.

At that time, there are already the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) and the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*). If, at the moment of the first thought-moment, the body-faculty were absent, one would be like wood or stone, being insentient.
Even when the body-faculty and mind-faculty are first acquired at the time of conception, they are not yet designated as the "limb of the six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana-aṅga*).

It is only now, at full completion—stated to be after four weeks (twenty-eight days)—and once the remaining four faculties (the eye-faculty and so forth) have been achieved, that it is properly called the "six sense bases."
Zhi’s commentary states: "If this is so, how is it that those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) in the realm of form have their sense-faculties (*indriya*) complete from the very beginning?
This passage poses a question regarding those born by transformation in the realm of form, concerning their developmental stages, and so forth. The following is the answer.
The *Śāstra* says: "All [factors] and a portion of those in the two upper realms. The commentary explains: "All" refers to the twelve links.
"A portion" means that within the desire realm there is a portion of all twelve links; this is because within the desire realm there are no [links] belonging to the two upper realms.
Thus, "a portion" refers to those present in the form realm, which consists of a portion of all twelve links—specifically, ten links.

The two branches exist within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Since they do not exist within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is said that they constitute "one part.
The same applies to the form realm.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Regarding the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, it says: 'If there were only names and no form at all, what fault would there be?
... up to: 'It may also be called dependent on names; logically, there is no error. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states: That sutra asks:

"If, during a single lifetime of a sentient being, there were only its name and no form whatsoever, what fault would there be? It answers: "If, during a single lifetime, there were only the four [mental aggregates]..."

Regarding the name "warmth": it is said that the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is entirely absent in the realm of non-perception (asaṃjñika). To claim that the name does not depend upon form for its existence would be illogical.

This explains that name and form are mutually dependent. According to the Master Sthiramati, there are three interpretations regarding the intent of that sūtra passage which states that "the name depends on form for its abiding.
The first interpretation holds that this refers to the two realms of desire and form, specifically concerning the physical basis (āśraya) within the realm of existence (bhavāgra).

Manifest speech. One interpretation states that there may also be no seeds of form (*rūpa*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Within the form realm, the eighth consciousness is called "cognition" (*vijñāna*);
the five mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) that arise simultaneously with the eighth consciousness are termed "name" (*nāman*), while the seeds of form are termed "form" (*rūpa*).
This same principle applies to the eighth consciousness in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which likewise coexists with the five mental factors and—
The seeds of form (*rūpa*) abide in mutual dependence. That which is called "the seeds of name-and-form being the support for consciousness" refers to these seeds of form;

although they are the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) within the eighth consciousness, when the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) takes those seeds of form as its object, it abides by relying upon the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.
Thus, it is said that the seeing aspect of the eighth consciousness also indirectly relies upon the seeds of form as its objective aspect.

The mutual support [of the mind] refers to the five mental factors associated with it, such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth; therefore, it is said that the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) in the formless realm serves as the seed for form and acts as the support for consciousness.
It does not state that the eighth consciousness depends upon the seventh consciousness, because the seventh consciousness is not produced by karmic retribution (*vipākaja*).

Because it is not subsumed within the twelve links [of dependent origination]. This refers to the name (*nāman*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) of the upper realm (*ūrdhvadhātu*), which depend upon the seeds of form (*rūpa*) in the lower realm.
Zhe says: "However, these seeds are not themselves subsumed within the twelve links of the formless realm. A third interpretation further states:

The formless realm possesses seeds of the form that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). These seeds of the form that is the fruit of concentration are likewise not said to be included among the [twelve] members.

If this were so, then noble ones (*ārya*) would possess seeds of form; furthermore, when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are born in the formless realm, they would be unable to take the form of the lower realms as an object.
Consequently, ordinary beings would not be endowed with all twelve members, or else the seeds of form must also be designated as "form."
Regarding the phrase "even unto those designated as belonging to other realms": this passage clarifies only the *rūpa* (form) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
