It refers generally to the formless realm as a whole, where there is the mutual dependence of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and so forth; it does not refer specifically to the seeds of name-and-form within the formless realm.
That is to say, these are subsumed under the members of name-and-form and the six sense bases within the twelve links of dependent origination. Why is this? If...

The seeds of form belong to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). It is not admitted that the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth are subsumed under the "name-and-form" member (*nāmarūpa-aṅga*) among the twelve links of dependent origination.
Since these [seeds] consist of the five sense-faculties and four objects belonging to the lower realms, they cannot be subsumed under the twelve links as they exist within the formless realm.
If one considers the stage of name-and-form in terms of birth in the formless realm, then the seeds of the faculties and objects are what is termed "name-and-form."

Among the aggregates, that which is matter is subsumed under the aggregate of matter (*rūpa-skandha*). If it subsequently exists in the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), then the seeds of the faculties and so forth are subsumed under the five faculties within the six sense bases.

Furthermore, regarding those who possess the seeds of meditative concentration (*samādhi-rūpa*) and volition (*cetanā*), even within the body of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), these likewise depend upon the seeds of the matter produced by the fruit of innate meditative concentration.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "World-Honored One, if one were to say that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) alone is the condition for grasping (*upādāna*), and that grasping does not take [craving] as its condition, what fault would there be?

The Explanation says: If it were said that craving conditions grasping, or that craving does not condition grasping such that grasping does not arise from craving—what fault would there be in severing [this connection]?

To delineate the characteristics, [it is said that] craving exists in the evil destinies, and so on, up until the arising of these two fruits; yet even there, [grasping] would not take craving as its condition.
There are two kinds of persons here. The first is one who has committed evil karma; at the time of death, such a person does not desire the miserable realms but seeks birth in a happy realm.
Due to their non-meritorious karma, this person is instead reborn in a miserable realm—desiring a happy realm but being born in a miserable one.
Nevertheless, if this person gives rise to attachment toward their own self, that attachment will nourish the seeds of the miserable realms.

Son, if one loves the wholesome but cannot proceed toward either *saṃyojana* (fetters) or *upapatti* (rebirth)— just as with the two types of self and person— when one is among the seven stages of preparation (*saptavidha-prayoga*) and the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*),
and practices the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), deeply loathing the body of birth-and-death, and within a mind that does not love the body of existence,

desires to obtain a body that has no further existence, this is called "seeking non-existence" (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*). Although such a person seeks the non-existence of that [existence], because of this person, existence still persists.
Whether it be meritorious karma or immovable karma, upon death, contrary fruits arise within the cycle of rebirth among gods and humans.

This very seeking after the fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is what is called "contradiction. Therefore, the pursuit of non-existence occurs only during the stage of the seven preparatory practices (*saptaprayoga*).

If one attains the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), one knows for certain that one will be born in a favorable realm; thus, it is not the case that there is no existence [therein], because one knows that the number of births is many.

Because it is slight. Furthermore, regarding what was said about "one who has no craving": when there is seeking for non-existence and seeking for the time of non-existence, the explanation is as follows:

as stated in the sūtras, those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) while in the stage of provisions (*sambhāra-avasthā*) and the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catur-nirvedhabhāgīya*), are at the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Having not yet attained [the fruits], they are now attaining them for the first time; having not yet attained the truths, they are those heading toward the first fruit (*prathamaphala-pratipannaka*). This refers to those who, in relation to entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), are focused on the desire [to enter].

At that time, one generates the intention and aspiration to attain the realization of the fruit. When attaining the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), one immediately severs the future existence within the three evil destinies.

If one subsequently becomes a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), one severs the six grades of afflictions in the desire realm; if one does not return to the desire realm, one no longer possesses a body of existence there.
If one attains Arhatship, one severs the future existence within the cycle of birth and death across the three realms. Therefore, it is so named.

Because they do not give rise to craving even when seeking existence as a deity. If one follows the literal meaning of the sūtra, these are exclusively ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who seek a future body;
however, according to the underlying principle, those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have attained the first three fruits also aspire to sever future existence within saṃsāra.
Thus, there is no contradiction in referring to those in training who have attained the first three fruits as being "without further existence."

The Commentary states: "If that were so, would this not contradict [the teaching] up to the point of the Non-returner? This passage cites [the case of those who have overcome craving] to refute [the objection regarding] craving and so forth.
Subsequently, it says that once the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) has arisen, craving no longer exists. The first two refer to these same two types of persons:

(1) those who are born in the miserable realms, and (2) those who seek non-existence. Regarding those who seek non-existence, it is permissible to grant that they attain the meditative attainment of cessation.

There is no manifest craving or grasping. If other non-returners (anāgāmin) do not suppress the afflictions of the lower realms and have not attained the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), would they manifest grasping to nourish rebirth? Furthermore, this treatise states that non-returners nourish rebirth through craving.

Although one who has not suppressed the lower fetters may attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) and be a non-returner (anāgāmin), if within their full mental state there is no manifest activity of grasping (*upādāna*),
then even if they are born in the three higher realms, they may still give rise to manifest activity of craving and grasping as a non-returner. Conversely,

if one has not suppressed the lower fetters and does not attain the meditative absorption of cessation, then even at the stage of the full mental state of that level, they may also give rise to manifest activity of craving and grasping.
"Rebirth through an intercalary birth (*antarābhava*) does not occur because the ground is not accumulated and the mind is absent.

The *Śāstra* states: "If one who has attained the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) is born in another realm, although the craving [associated with that realm] does not manifest during the intercalary birth, it nevertheless exists as a seed, just as in the case of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
The commentary explains: This passage from the treatise refers specifically to a Non-returner who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
It is said: For example, one who has attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*) has completely severed the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm.

Having suppressed the afflictions from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), they attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Thus, they do not give rise to afflictions as a non-returner.
Later, at the time of death, they are reborn in the first dhyāna or various other realms where there are afflictions; immediately, the seeds of craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*) [arise].

Regarding "intercalary birth" (*vṛddhi-janman*): Furthermore, from the Brahmakāyika heaven one is born into the Brahmapurohita heaven; it is solely by means of the seeds of craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*) that intercalary birth occurs, and the actual manifestations (*samudācāra*) of craving and so forth also arise.
This applies likewise to all higher realms. Thus, they are subsumed under the category of intercalary birth through the seeds of craving.

Just as the seeds of grasping within one's own continuum can effect intercalary birth, there is no case where one has not been born in a higher realm and yet severs the possibility of being born in a lower realm. Or is there not? [There is not.]
[This refers to] the fruit [of the non-returner]. Having suppressed the afflictions from the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, at the time of death, one is immediately reborn in the first dhyāna.
Although there are seeds of affliction present, the seeds of craving and grasping likewise serve as the "moistening" condition for birth.

This discussion concerns all cases of the non-returner fruit who have suppressed the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of the afflictions of the first dhyāna and so forth, and thus speaks of the seeds of craving and grasping acting as the moistening condition. This applies even in the case of a non-returner who is an "upward-streamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*).

Having completely severed the afflictions of the desire realm but not yet subdued those of the higher realms such as the first dhyāna, when one later dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the first dhyāna, one uses the active manifestation of craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*) to provide the "moistening" for birth.

This continues even when being reborn from the Brahmakāyika heaven into the Brahmapurohita heaven, using the active manifestation of craving and grasping to provide the moistening for birth; and likewise when proceeding from the Ābhāsvara heaven to the Parīttaśubha heaven.
Regarding the statement, "Hearing [of rebirth] manifests; craving and grasping act as the incubating conditions for growth and development in the realm of hungry ghosts":

although such a person does not crave the place where they will be born, up until the point of encountering present objects, this individual—despite having no craving for their future place of birth—still gives rise to craving conditioned by their present self.
Thinking, "May my body die right now," they further give rise to craving for the five types of sensory objects currently being experienced, such as clothing and so forth.

Regarding "the realm of dust" (*dharmāyatana*): the Commentary states, "Although the seeds and the manifest are distinct, their substance is not different. This means that although the seeds and manifest forms of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are distinct, both seeds and manifest forms alike constitute the member of name-and-form;
and although the seeds and manifest forms of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are distinct, both alike constitute the six [sense bases].

Regarding the stage: although the seeds and the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) previously mentioned are both subsumed under the member of consciousness (*vijñāna*), even though they differ in their manifestation, is there no distinction in their essence?
That which occurs prior to the four seven-day periods is the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Since this stage of name-and-form occurs within the first four seven-day periods, it corresponds to the *kalala* stage during the first seven days, the *arbuda* stage during the second seven days, and the *peśī* stage during the third seven days.
The first seven days are the stage of *nāmarūpa*. The next four weeks are the stage of *ṣaḍāyatana*. These four stages are all called the stage of *nāmarūpa*.
The commentary (*śāstra*) states: "In this context, from the five [aggregates] prior... [it is said] in order to explain the text so that it may apply to what follows. The explanation says:

Here, only the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is mentioned, saying "at the time of linking rebirth" because consciousness is manifest as the cause. Now, the character "cause" (*yin*) applies throughout the following four stages. That is to say:

At the time when rebirth is to be continued, it is manifested through the causal consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth; because the sense faculties (*indriya*) are not yet mature, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) increases its characteristics.

When the causal name ceases and the characteristics subsequently reach the stage where the faculties are mature, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) become clearly manifest. Because the stage of the six sense bases is manifested, this gives rise to contact (*sparśa*);

because of contact, the characteristics of sensation (*vedanā*) become manifest. Now, at the time when the five fruits arise as active manifestations, they cause the five fruits to exist as the fruit-time.
This is clarified by means of characteristics. "Praśākhā" is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as the "stage of possessing the faculties.

The Commentary states: "The World-Honored One, if old age and death, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are the characteristics [of this stage], for what reason does he designate this birth-body as 'old age and death'?
The Explanation says: This passage explains that within the stages of birth and old age...

Some say that rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) occurs first; next, the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*) becomes manifest; next, while the sense faculties are not yet complete, the characteristic of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) increases;

and so on, until, conditioned by grasping (*upādāna*), contact (*sparśa*) arises, and conditioned by contact, feeling (*vedanā*) and the rest arise. These are explained as occurring during the two stages of birth (*jāti*) and old age (*jarā*).

Since these five stages already have their respective names, they should simply be designated as the stage of consciousness, the stage of name-and-form, and the five stages of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact, and feeling.
The names are assigned to the stage of what is about to arise; they are merely the names for birth and aging. Question: Why is the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna*) not mentioned here? Answer:

The branches were previously explained in relation to the aggregates (*skandha*). That was done by referring to the seeds of the branch of consciousness, which encompass both the projecting and the projected factors.

Since that is not mentioned here, this passage instead refers to the manifest states (*samudācāra*) of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) as they enter the mother’s womb, specifically describing these four stages. According to the actual reality...
It is said: "If one follows the treatise, the link of name-and-form exists only after the link of consciousness has first arisen. As the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* states:
"If one does not enter the mother's womb, name-and-form cannot grow."

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Birth is the beginning of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*); old age is the beginning of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*); death is the beginning of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*).
This applies even up to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), wherein these three characteristics are manifested. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states: A question is raised:

Why does the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Treatise on the Abhidharma) state that birth, old age, sickness, and death are all termed "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), whereas here [in this text] birth, old age, and death are termed the "three sufferings"? These two treatises appear to contradict one another. Regarding the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is based upon... [the aggregates].
To speak according to reality, all four types are called *duḥkha-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of suffering). This is because even while in the womb, there is the contact of suffering.
Birth is also *duḥkha-duḥkhatā*, namely the subsequent contact with heat, craving, and other forms of suffering. In this treatise, the emphasis is primarily on what increases [suffering]:

that is, since the constituent parts possess form, they are termed *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of conditioned formations); the loss of pleasure due to middle age and old age is termed *vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of change); and [it is so] by virtue of death and cessation.

The body is itself the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). Within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), all three types of suffering are present; within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there is only the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*);
and within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is only the suffering of conditioned formations.

The *Śāstra* says: "If the production of the fruit were in the future, in order to cause sentient beings to develop revulsion and detachment, it is taught only by way of its general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

From birth, old age, and so forth, up to the characteristic of belonging (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*), [the nature of] suffering is made manifest. The commentary explains: This indicates that although there are many causes, they are comprised within the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*).

For example, just as there are ten links as causes in the present, there are two links as causes in the future. These two links as causes in the future are, in fact, [contained] within the future itself.

Regarding the two branches of birth, aging, and death as results in the future life, they are explained only in terms of their general characteristics and designated as the two branches of birth, aging, and death to induce a sense of revulsion toward them.

As for the ten branches of causes in the past and the two branches of results in the present, within these very results of birth, aging, and death in the present life, the five results beginning with consciousness are also taught.
This refers to the fact that the characteristic of consciousness, which is the cause for the continuity of rebirth, becomes manifest; subsequently, the faculties are not yet fully developed.
These are called the five stages, beginning with "increase" (*vṛddhi*) and so forth. Now, all of these are mutually analogous.

If we follow the latter [classification], which posits the two links of birth and old age/death (*jāti-jarāmaraṇa*) in the future, then within the present resultant stage of consciousness and so forth, one may likewise designate the two links of birth and old age/death by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

Thus, using the future to analogize the present, there is no impediment to speaking of these two. If, however, we follow the present five stages, then regarding birth and old age/death in the future...
Within the two stages of death [and birth], there are likewise five types of fruit-differentiations of the five consciousnesses as explained.

That is to say, by classifying the present [stage] into five, these five are not excluded. This is formulated based on the possession of the twelve links, just as in the two stages of the present life and death.
For example, when a person dies and does not pass through the intermediate stage, but is born and reaches old age, being able to exhaust their full lifespan—this is precisely...

Within the stage of the birth-constituent (*jāti-aṅga*), four stages are subsumed; however, one stage is made very brief. That is to say, from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the single moment of entering the mother’s womb, it is called the consciousness constituent (*vijñāna-aṅga*).

Next, from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and contact (*sparśa*), up until the point where suffering has not yet been distinguished, all are called the stage of the contact constituent (*sparśa-aṅga*).
From this point onward, once one is able to discern suffering, up until the age of fifty, all are called [the stage of the feeling constituent].
Regarding the stage of the *vedanā-aṅga* (feeling limb): because it encompasses the stages prior to birth, it includes four stages;

thus, a small portion of the single stage of feeling—from this point until the onset of aging, decline, transformation, and finally death—is all designated as the stage of the *vedanā-aṅga*. Consequently, the *jarā-aṅga* (aging limb) encompasses only a small portion of a single stage.
Alternatively, for example, there may be someone who undergoes an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and dies within that intermediate state; such a person likewise possesses all ten [limbs].

Regarding the two branches of birth and death and so forth: for example, there may be a bhikṣu of little learning who, having attained the fourth dhyāna, passes away while in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*);
such a person also possesses all twelve links. Or, there may be one who passes away after only one or two moments of entering the mother’s womb.
There may be those who enter the womb and pass away while still in the stage called *nāmarūpa*; there may be those who pass away while in the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*);

and even those who pass away while in the stage of experiencing painful sensations associated with the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*). In all such cases mentioned above, although they possess the intermediate factors, they are nonetheless complete with the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*).

The Commentary asks: "Why, within the internal [factors], are craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) not differentiated as two distinct types, whereas ignorance (*avidyā*) is established as such? The Explanation says:
"Why, within the link of ignorance, are there not two separate types established as there are for craving and grasping? 'Within the link of ignorance' means within the very link of ignorance itself."
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "As explained in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, there are eleven excellences. First, the excellence of the object (*ālambana-viśeṣa*):
it refers to the fact that this ignorance universally takes as its object all four truths, encompassing both defiled and purified phenomena.

Suffering (*duḥkha*) and origination (*samudaya*) are termed 'defiled,' while cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are termed 'purified. Second, the excellence of the aspect (*ākāra-viśeṣa*): namely,"
This ignorance can obscure *tathatā* (suchness) and manifest *saṃsāra*. It excels in three causal conditions:
namely, this ignorance can serve as the root of all afflictions (*kleśa*), and it can also serve as the root of karma and birth.

Regarding its excellence in immediate origination (*hetu-samutthāna*), this ignorance directly initiates and draws forth the six streams of the *saṃskāra-aṅga* (volitional formations). Regarding its excellence in remote origination...
"Arising" also refers to that which induces the factors to be produced and the factors reached; these are all of a similar class. "Equal arising" refers to cause and effect.

Regarding the five types of transformational distinctions: this ignorance is itself able to transform into four kinds of ignorance—namely, those associated with the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), the fetters (*bandhana*), and the non-associated [ignorance].
Regarding the distinction of the sixfold wrong practice: this ignorance consists of the grasping or doubt regarding the first four Truths.

That which is "I" and "mine" is termed the augmentation of the aggregates (*upacaya*). If one gives rise to false views that deny the Four Noble Truths as they manifest, this is termed diminution (*apacaya*).
Regarding the excellence of its seven characteristics: the essence of this unique ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*) proceeds toward subtlety and is difficult to discern.
How is it subtle? For instance, when a person’s mind arises in a general state, if root afflictions such as greed or pride arise—

At that time, there is simultaneously the associated ignorance (*avidyā*). When minor afflictions such as anger or joy arise, the delusion (*moha*) co-arising with them is termed "non-dominant ignorance.
Among the four types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*), when one is focused on deportment (*īryāpatha*), it is termed the "mind of deportment," and so forth;

when focused on craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), it is termed the "mind of craftsmanship"; and when one is merely indifferent and not focusing on deportment or craftsmanship, [it is termed the "mind of the unmanifest"].
Even when performing crafts or arts, one does not give rise to afflictive defilements, nor does one give rise to the eleven virtuous mental states such as faith and shame.

Rather, it is a mind that arises spontaneously, functioning without deliberate attention (*amanasikāra*) and merely engaging with its object in a general way. This mind is called a "mind born of maturation" (*vipākaja-citta*).
Who would think so strongly through deliberate attention that they could discern cause and effect? To speak according to reality, such a mind truly does not understand the path of cause and effect.
As for those who, despite [understanding] principle, nevertheless remain deluded regarding the principles of cause and effect: this mind is termed "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇikī avidyā*).

Only non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) give rise to this unshared ignorance; as for ordinary worldlings within the Buddha's teaching (*ādhyātmika*), they correctly understand the principles of cause and effect.

There arises a distinct, unique ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*). The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of this ignorance is subtle; it is the state of mind that pervades [the perception of] the agreeable, the disagreeable, and that which is neither agreeable nor disagreeable.
As for its general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), it is precisely that which is neither agreeable nor disagreeable, and is thus termed the "unique characteristic.

Now, regarding this general characteristic, one does not speak of the ignorance of the general characteristics such as suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self. If it were associated with craving and so forth, [it would not be termed unique].

It is called "loved" (*priya*). If it is associated with aversion (*dveṣa*), it is called "unloved" (*apriya*). If it is not associated with other afflictions—that is, neither loved nor hated—it is called the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the excellence of its function: this ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as the basis for the process of transmigration within the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and its origin (*samudaya-satya*).
Furthermore, this ignorance also [acts as the basis] for the True Suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma of tranquility, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the mind, and so forth.

The Section on Action. Regarding "seeking the tranquil": this refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*). Regarding "the mind of meditative concentration or tranquility": this refers to the mind of nirvāṇa. Regarding "the path that exists":
this refers to the path capable of bringing unwholesome dharmas to rest. Regarding "the overcoming of the nine obstacles": this refers to this very ignorance (*avidyā*).

It can obstruct the dharmas of supreme enlightenment and the extensive dharmas of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all divisions. Regarding "supreme dharmas," this refers to the dharmas of enlightenment consisting of the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*).
Regarding "extensive dharmas," this refers to true suchness; because true suchness pervades all phenomena, it is called "extensive dharmas."
Eleventh, regarding the excellence of the antidote: it refers to two kinds of sublime wisdom (*prajñā*), which alone are capable of counteracting the phenomena (*dharma*).

Regarding these two kinds of sublime wisdom, there are currently two interpretations. The first says that fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) are called the two wisdoms; this interpretation is incorrect.

The second says that the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) and the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*) are called the two kinds of sublime wisdom, and they are able to sever [the afflictions].
Ignorance (*avidyā*). Subsequently, it becomes predominant. Question: Regarding these four wisdoms (*jñāna*), how many constitute the path of abandonment or the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*)?

How many possess the untainted path of contemplative observation (*vicāra*)? In relation to the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (wisdom of accomplishing activities) and the *ādarśa-jñāna* (great perfect mirror wisdom), these two are exclusively the untainted path of contemplative observation;
they are not called the path of abandoning afflictions. These two wisdoms are attained only upon becoming a Buddha. If [it is] wondrous...
The wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) is either the path of abandonment or the untainted (*anāsrava*) path; it is capable of severing all afflictions.

As for the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), speaking according to reality, it likewise cannot sever afflictions. If one were to say that the wisdom of equality can sever delusions, [it would be incorrect].
Because those of the two vehicles lack the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), it is known that they are likewise unable to sever [the afflictions] that are common [to both].

Now, these are explained in conjunction: this wisdom of equality is also called the path of abandonment or the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). This refers to the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) within the sixth consciousness;
when it correctly severs the afflictions, the wisdom of equality within the seventh consciousness also acts in concert with the wisdom of wondrous observation.
Wisdom serves as the basis for activity and also functions as a remote support for the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) in its severing of delusion.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that the wisdom of wondrous observation itself directly severs delusion at that time;

rather, the wisdom of wondrous observation is designated as the "path that severs delusion," while the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) that arises simultaneously with the wisdom of wondrous observation is designated as the "untainted path of contemplative play. Therefore...
The wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) is that which directly severs [afflictions]; thus, the wisdom of wondrous observation is itself called the "path of severance.
Furthermore, the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) that arises simultaneously with the wisdom of wondrous observation is also called the "path of severing delusions."

Furthermore, another interpretation states that the "two kinds of sublime wisdom" refer to the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*) and the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*).

Therefore, when practitioners of the Two Vehicles give rise to the wisdom of the emptiness of persons, they are also able to sever this ignorance (*avidyā*). As for the mention of "two wisdoms," these are not the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*);

for the subsequently attained wisdom cannot sever the ignorance that deludes regarding the principle (*tattva*). In this context, all [ignorance] refers to that which deludes within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
The ignorance that gives rise to karma is not the wisdom of wondrous observation; these two are called the "two wisdoms. Furthermore, the wisdom of equality cannot sever afflictions.

If one were to claim that the wisdom of equality is also called "severing afflictions" by way of association, then the mundane path would likewise be called "severing afflictions" by way of association.
Therefore, it is known that [this wisdom] does not take up the wisdom of equality or wondrous observation.
2. The Commentary states that the various treatises speak only of four types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*): first, "craving for craving" (*tṛṣṇātṛṣṇā*), which is the general designation;

second, the person who practices virtue, who craves a future existence in a favorable realm and thus practices [the path] with craving; third, craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*); and fourth, craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*). Third, reconciling [these views with] the virtuous...
"Concomitant craving" refers to those who are deluded regarding unwholesome karma; they constantly experience it together with the objects of the five sensory realms.
"Craving for various delights" is that which gives rise to the mental aspiration and pursuit of offspring in those who possess excessive greed.

As for why the treatises state that these four types of craving alone constitute the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), this is said in terms of their predominance. In reality, however, all other afflictions (*kleśa*) and karmas are also [included].
This is subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
The Commentary states: "It can moisten itself. "Moistening" means to nourish. The Commentary further states:
"In reality, there are many active manifestations (*samudācāra*). The Explanation says: "Speaking according to the actual fact, there are many active manifestations. The Explanation says: [The same].

To speak according to reality, there are many active manifestations of afflictions and craving (*tṛṣṇā*). For the time being, based on the initial and final stages, craving and grasping (*upādāna*) are divided into two types.

The Commentary states: "Whether it be that which grasps (*grāhaka*), or that which is grasped (*grāhya*), or that for the sake of which one grasps—all these are called grasping. The Explanation states: "That which is able to grasp..."

That which is "the grasper" (upādātṛ) is precisely the craving that serves as the objective condition for the four graspings (*catvāry upādānāni*). That which is "the grasped" (*upādāna*) refers to the four graspings themselves by way of analogy.

That which is "that for the sake of which one grasps" (*yasyārtham upādānam*) refers to all other afflictions (*kleśa*), such as ignorance (*avidyā*), anger (*dveṣa*), and pride (*māna*), for which the graspings are undertaken.

Because the graspings first arise as the objective conditions for these [afflictions], it is said that they give rise to the remaining afflictions; therefore, they are called "that for the sake of which one grasps. These...

All are termed "appropriation" (*upādāna*). The commentary (*śū*) states: "The question regarding the dependent origination of phenomena, up to the point where there are [factors] belonging to other stages. The intent of this question is to introduce the following textual discussion.

Since the ignorance (*avidyā*) of this stage can give rise to [factors] of higher stages, this question arises. The meaning of the question is: for the purpose of generating [factors] within this stage?

Regarding the twelve links: while those belonging to the same stage (*bhūmi*) serve as conditions for the twelve links of that same stage, there are also instances where they serve as conditions for the twelve links of other stages.
As for the commentary’s question, "What fault is there in this?", this section of the sub-commentary should address both points together to demonstrate that each position possesses its own defects.
The *Śāstra* says: "If [the factors] of dependent origination belonged exclusively to this stage, how would one reconcile the following passage?
... it would not be logical; it would not be its object. The commentary explains: The intent of this objection is as follows:

If, when discussing the members of dependent origination in relation to a particular stage, all of them were to belong exclusively to that stage, then how would one reconcile the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*? For in that *Sūtra*, an objection is raised to the Blessed One: [text continues].

The three links of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are all afflictions (*kleśa*). Thus, it is said that the link of ignorance serves as the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

For what reason is it not stated that the two links of craving and grasping are the same as ignorance, such that both craving and grasping can give rise to the link of volitional formations within their own realm (*svabhūmi*), or that craving and grasping can give rise to the link of volitional formations in another realm (*parabhūmi*)? The Blessed One replied: "As for the two types, craving and grasping..."

Because they possess a limited scope (*avacara*). This craving and grasping can only serve as the cause for the formative factors (*saṃskāra*) and the seeds of the five fruits belonging to their own respective levels.
Why is this so? If craving and grasping of the desire realm were to act as the originating cause for the immovable formative factors of the two higher realms, it would not be logical.
Why? Because they are not within its range (*agocara*). "Not being within its range" means that they do not fall within its scope.
If ignorance functions as an impelling cause, it acts as the equal-and-immediate cause for the formations (*saṃskāra*).
If craving (*tṛṣṇā*) functions, it acts as the supporting cause for the five types of seeds belonging to the formations within its own realm.

Furthermore, the statement that "ignorance acts as the equal-and-immediate condition for the dependent origination leading up to the capacity to produce [birth] in those who have abandoned desire" is a general description; "those who have abandoned desire" refers to the first [stage].
Regarding the *anāgamya-samādhi* (the preparatory concentration), it is taught that it can bring about detachment from the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Ignorance (*avidyā*) of the desire realm, occurring simultaneously with the initial *anāgamya*, also acts as a causal condition for the arising of its factors (*aṅga*). That is to say, by means of the ignorance of the desire realm, one can give rise to the factor of volition (*saṃskāra*) of the initial *anāgamya*.
Alternatively, regarding those belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is said that ignorance can give rise to the factor of volition of the initial *anāgamya*. Or...

Regarding those belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), this refers to the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of the second dhyāna, up to the preparatory concentration of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

What is their function? It is because the ignorance of the first dhyāna can give rise to the formations (*saṃskāra*) of the preparatory concentration of the second dhyāna, acting as their equal-and-immediate cause (*samanantara-hetu*);

and so on, until the ignorance of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) can give rise to the formations of the preparatory concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
[Ignorance] acts as the cause of origination.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Furthermore, it is said that this ignorance, accompanied by the irrational mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) arising from it and its results, serves as the condition for the formless (*ārūpya*) formations (*saṃskāra*) of that realm;
thus, ignorance is distinct from the formations of other realms. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says: "This..."
The meaning of the text is as follows: it is admitted that ignorance (*avidyā*) of one stage can give rise to the limb of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) of another stage.
For example, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because the cause—the arising of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*)—gives rise to ignorance, that ignorance itself is the fruit.
That is to say, the two types—cause and fruit—are called "companions. Furthermore, the simultaneous mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta) that are associated are also called "companions.
Thus, the ignorance (avidyā) of the desire realm can give rise to the factor of "volitional formations" (saṃskāra) within the initial "access concentration" (anāgamya-samādhi) of the first dhyāna;

however, the factor of ignorance belonging to the desire realm cannot necessarily give rise to the factor of volitional formations within the fundamental concentration (maula-dhyāna) of the first dhyāna. [The text continues: Ignorance of the desire realm...
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is likewise unable to produce the factors of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) of the second dhyāna, and so on up to the higher stages.
However, the factor of ignorance within the first dhyāna can only produce the factors of the preparatory stage of the second dhyāna;
that is, the ignorance of the first dhyāna cannot produce the factors of the preparatory stage of the third dhyāna. The same principle should be understood for all higher stages. Only...

They must be contiguous; they cannot be separated by an interval. Furthermore, within the stage of the first dhyāna, ignorance arises with improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) as its cause.
Improper mental attention is the cause and ignorance is the fruit; these two are termed "companions."
By means of the factor of ignorance within this first dhyāna, one is able to give rise to the factor of the practice of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) within the second dhyāna.

In this manner, it continues until, by means of the factor of ignorance in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one is able to give rise to the factor of the practice of the threshold concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
However, if these eight stages were each to possess their own independent factors of the practice of the threshold concentration, they would all [arise] from the ignorance of the lower stages.

Regarding "arousing": just as the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the desire realm can arouse the formations (*saṃskāra*) that constitute a branch of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna, and so on up to the ignorance of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) which can arouse the formations that constitute a branch of the preparatory stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), for what reason are these eight [levels] called "preparatory" (*anāgamya*)?

One cannot give rise to the afflictions and ignorance belonging to one's own level; because the aggregates are like a crown prince who has not yet attained his position, one cannot engage in unwholesome conduct.
Question: Since one has not yet reached the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) that possesses consciousness, why does one not employ the ignorance belonging to that same level?

When one practices the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) of one's own level, having exhausted the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm through the abandonment of the aggregates, one is then able to give rise to the defiled states within the preparatory stage.

Furthermore, these defiled states within the preparatory stage can also serve as the causal conditions for the practice of the factors (*aṅga*). As for the factors practiced in the fundamental concentrations (*mauladhyāna*) of the eight higher levels: [the same applies].
It arises solely from the ignorance of its own level. If one attains a fundamental dhyāna, all afflictions of that same level can arise.
Just as a crown prince who has attained the royal throne is able to commit evil deeds, the factors of the fundamental dhyāna of the first stage arise solely from the ignorance of the first stage;
likewise, up to the fundamental dhyāna of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it arises solely from the ignorance of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, in this context, the factors of the practice of the *anāgamya* concentration of the eighth stage can be initiated by the ignorance of a lower stage;
however, the mind of a higher stage, being free from the ignorance of that higher stage, cannot initiate any of the factors of practice belonging to a lower stage.
If one regresses and gives rise to [defilements] of a lower stage, there are immediately the afflictions of that own stage;

since it is due to the ignorance (*avidyā*) of that own stage that the formative factor (*saṃskāra*) of that same stage is produced, the member of ignorance belonging to a different stage can produce the formative factor of a different stage.

The *Śāstra* says: "If one obtains a limb belonging to a different stage (*bhūmi*) after having arisen from a limb belonging to another realm (*dhātu*), it should be known that such limbs are subsumed within this very [category].

The commentary explains: This is a challenge. [It concerns] how ignorance (*avidyā*) of one stage gives rise to the limb of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) of another stage. Now the challenge is posed:
If you allow that ignorance of one stage gives rise to the limb of volitional formations of another stage, for what reason is this so? Furthermore, the fifty-sixth [chapter] states: "Again..."
What is the "pervasion" (abhisamaya)? That treatise states: "One should know that the factors of existence (bhavāṅga) follow according to birth, according to realm, and according to stage.
Specifically, the ten factors and two branches of the Desire Realm ground follow accordingly; that is, they are bound to the Desire Realm. This applies likewise up to the two higher realms.

The *Śāstra* says: For example, when ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth of a lower stage give rise to practice in a higher stage, the five [faculties] take the nine grades of ignorance of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) belonging to the lower stage and ascend.
Is it by means of the ignorance of the path that one gives rise to the upward movement?

Suppose there is a person who has suppressed the first eight grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower stage; could the remaining one grade still give rise to the upward movement? Answer: It is not like the case below.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "All members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are dharmas belonging to their own stage (*svabhūmi*), sharing the same homogeneous character (*sabhāga*)," spanning fifty-six characters. It further states: "There is that which initiates activity;

depending on the stage, ignorance (*avidyā*) arises together with grasping (*upādāna*) as its condition. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says: "If all members of dependent origination depend upon their own respective stages..."

This refers to taking fifty-six phrases. Regarding the statement that "in whichever realm or level one is born, the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are all subsumed under that same level," this is said by way of the majority.
That is to say, among the twelve members, eleven members in their entirety and a small portion of one member are entirely of the same level.
This excludes only a small portion of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is capable of giving rise to the formative action (*saṃskāra*) member of a higher level.
Regarding the statement that "ignorance (avidyā) has an object and functions by depending on a specific stage (bhūmi)," this is identical to the scriptural passage from the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.

However, within the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, it is taught—referring only to a small portion of a single member—that a member belonging to one stage can serve as a condition for a member belonging to a different stage;

yet, it is specifically stated that only the member of ignorance belonging to a lower stage can give rise to members of higher stages. These two [the Sūtra and the Śāstra] each rely upon one of these two seeds.
The meaning is not contradictory either. The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "How is this?
One should categorize such matters accordingly; [the case where] one [factor] becomes many, or where there is only one, is as follows:

for example, when ignorance (*avidyā*) of a lower stage gives rise to formations (*saṃskāra*) of a higher stage. The explanation says: This question asks: "Since it is already admitted that the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-aṅga*) of different stages can [function together],..."
Regarding the condition of the factors of dependent origination belonging to a different level (*bhūmi*): this matter should be clarified.
Do all twelve factors of a different level serve as conditions for the twelve factors of another level? Or is it that only a single factor among the twelve serves as such a condition?
It can serve as a condition for the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) belonging to a different level (*bhūmi*). As stated in the *Skandhaka*:

"Among these twelve factors, only one factor can transform the dependent origination of another level into a condition. For example, a factor of ignorance (*avidyā*) of a lower level can give rise to a factor of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) of a higher level.
This occurs when one has completely abandoned the nine categories of desire; only at a later time does the ignorance of that higher level arise. If this were not permitted...

In the attainment of the intermediate state (*dhyānāntara*), there is also defilement; furthermore, it is necessary that one has exhausted the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm before one can first give rise to the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*).
Within the preparatory stage (*anāgamya-samādhi*), with the exception of the defilements within that preparatory stage itself, one is also able to project karma.

This is as when one arises in the preparatory stage: whether one has suppressed three or four grades of the desire realm, or has already suppressed them—if they have been suppressed, they cannot manifest as active afflictions (*samudācāra*).

If [the defilements] have not yet been subdued, they can still arise as active manifestations. Regarding the *anāgamya* concentration, if it is defiled, one must first abandon the nine grades of the lower stage, or eliminate them entirely, before the defilements within the *anāgamya* itself can arise.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "This meaning is the same as what is explained in the fifty-sixth [fascicle], which says that based on the many branches, the intent of the Sūtra is to provide a general discussion;

thus, there is no contradiction in [the present case] also being based on the stages (*bhūmi*). The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states: 'If the fifty-sixth [fascicle] explains that whichever realm or stage one is born into, all conditions precede [it]...'"

The statement that "all are comprised within both self and other" is made from the perspective of the majority. That is to say, eleven of the twelve links in their entirety, along with a small portion of one link, are all comprised within their own respective levels (*svabhūmi*).

This excludes only the link of ignorance (*avidyā*), which can give rise to formations (*saṃskāra*) belonging to different realms. Aside from this, the remaining eleven links are all comprised within their own level.

Furthermore, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states that a link of dependent origination belonging to one level may serve as a condition for a link of dependent origination belonging to a different level.

Regarding "having a member as a condition": this refers generally to only a small portion of a single member. For example, as when ignorance (*avidyā*) of a lower stage gives rise to the member of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) of a higher stage.

The Commentary states: "The meaning here is that [ignorance] enters into the manifestation of ignorance within the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration; or, one who has not attained the fundamental concentration will certainly not [give rise to it]."

"Because they arise. The commentary explains: This refers to the fact that in the contaminated *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration of the upper eight stages, there are no defilements or seeds [of defilement].
This is because one has not attained the fundamental concentrations (*mauladhyāna*) of those stages; therefore, the defilements of the upper stages cannot arise. As the preceding treatise states:

"When one is born in a lower stage and has not yet abandoned the defilements of that lower stage, the defilements of the upper stages cannot manifest, even if one attains the fundamental concentration of those [upper] stages."

Regarding "concentration" (*samādhi*): since that stage can manifest before one, we know that although one who has attained the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) has not yet reached the *anāgamya* concentration, they are able to abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Nevertheless, there still remain innate unwholesome afflictions belonging to the desire realm.
This is just as within the *anāgamya* concentration: because there are afflictions of the lower stages, it does not follow that the higher stages are free from afflictions.
The Commentary states: "However, whenever the first arising of the *anāgamya* (unattained) concentration occurs on any lower stage, it is always like this. The Explanation says:

For example, when one is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the first arising of the *anāgamya* concentration of the first dhyāna involves the factor of volition (*cetanā*). This very volition of the desire realm—which is unwholesome and characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*)—is capable of giving rise to the volitional factor of the first *anāgamya* concentration.
This is just as in the case of the *anāgamya* concentration within the second dhyāna of the first stage; it is precisely due to the [volition of the] first...

The factor of ignorance (*avidyā*) within the dhyānas can give rise to the factor of formations (*saṃskāra*) in the "not-yet-attained" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of the twelve dhyānas, up to the "not-yet-attained" concentration of the first stage, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
That is to say, the factor of ignorance in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) can give rise to the factor of formations in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Regarding both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, it is universally accepted that at the moment of death, the mind is exclusively associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Within the Mahāyāna, [this is further specified as follows:]...

It is taught that within the fundamental meditative attainments (*mauladhyāna*) of the first and second dhyānas, there are feelings of joy (*prīti*), pleasure (*sukha*), and also equanimity (*upekṣā*).

However, in the fourth dhyāna, there is only the feeling of equanimity. For example, suppose a person whose body resides in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) attains the fundamental dhyānas of the four higher stages;
this person may then pass away while in the state of mind of the fundamental dhyānas of those four stages. Thus it is said.

Within the three fundamental dhyānas, it is universally accepted that there is the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). It is likewise the case when descending from those four dhyānas to the lower stages;

although the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) undergoes death and rebirth, these are all instances of the sensation of equanimity. Here, however, we are speaking specifically of the sensation of equanimity within the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, the fundamental dhyānas of the first and second stages consist exclusively of the sensation of joy (*prīti-vedanā*) and lack the sensation of equanimity. As for the third dhyāna...

Within the fundamental dhyānas, there is only the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*). If the mind is in the eight preliminary concentrations (*anāgamya*), it is only the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
For example, suppose a person’s body resides in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), yet they have attained the fundamental dhyānas of the lower three realms.

When this person later passes away in the desire realm and is reborn in the lower three dhyānas, this mind of death (*cyuti-citta*) immediately enters and emerges from the fundamental dhyānas of those lower three realms.

In the three lower dhyānas, one attains death only through the mind of the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration, because the fundamental dhyāna states of the three lower levels lack the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), whereas the *anāgamya* state does possess it. One passes away from those three lower dhyānas by means of that [equanimous] mind.
However, since the sensation of equanimity exists within the fundamental dhyāna states from the fourth dhyāna upward, one may also attain death directly within those fundamental dhyāna states.

End. According to the Sarvāstivāda school, it is admitted that death may occur with a mind of any of the three natures (kuśala, akuśala, or avyākṛta). In the Mahāyāna, however, the mind at the moment of actual death is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta);
yet, even this final death-mind can likewise pertain to all three natures. This is because there are those who, due to the influence of habitual practice (*abhyāsa*), [experience such states].

As the treatise explains regarding the mind that receives rebirth and the mind that dies: these must necessarily exist within a state of distracted consciousness (*vikṣipta-citta*), and not in a state of no-mind (*acittaka*).

Regarding meditative concentration (*samādhi*): how is it explained in the Mahāyāna? For example, if a person dwelling in the desire realm attains the four *dhyāna* concentrations and, having attained the fundamental mind of the fourth *dhyāna*, passes away, this is permitted. Within the lower three *dhyānas*, the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is permitted.

However, in the Hīnayāna, one passes away only upon reaching the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of the lower three *dhyānas*. This is stated with reference to the sixth aggregate (*skandha*).

Following that treatise, it is because [the discussion] refers to the eighth [dhyāna]. Furthermore, a question is asked: within the eight fundamental dhyānas, one attains the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*);

does one also attain the distracted mind within the eight preparatory stages (*anāgamya*)? If the preparatory stage were exclusively a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), how could afflictions arise?
The *Śāstra* says: "The acquisition of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) also takes as its object the feeling (*vedanā*) of a future birth. Question:

Does this text refer to the craving that arises toward the feeling of a future birth within a single set of the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*), such that one generates craving for a future birth based on that feeling?

Or does it refer to two sets of the twelve links, where one first experiences a defiled feeling in the present and subsequently generates craving? Answer: Here, "taking as an object" (*ālambate*) means "relying upon" (*upādāya*). That [feeling]...
By means of what feeling (*vedanā*) does craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arise? For what reason is this question asked?

Since it is accepted that the member of feeling arises conditioned by feeling, and so on up to the point where it is granted that [factors] of different stages (*bhūmi*) can serve as conditions, the explanation is as follows: Just as it is granted that ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as a condition for the member of formations (*saṃskāra*) of a different stage, so too should the member of feeling of a different stage be able to serve as an example for the member of craving of a different stage.

The *Śāstra* says: "According to what is appropriate, that [feeling] also takes as its object either the feeling of a future birth, or a feeling currently manifesting simultaneously, or a feeling existing as a prior seed.

The commentary explains: If it is a defiled feeling (*kliṣṭa-vedanā*) that is associated with a presently manifest craving (*tṛṣṇā*), then this defiled feeling can also serve as a condition for the arising of craving.
This feeling associated with craving is precisely the "feeling of the objective field" (*viṣaya-vedanā*). It is the feeling of the objective field.
This refers to the defiled feeling produced with ignorance-contact as its condition; it is this defiled feeling alone that can serve as the condition to produce craving.
Alternatively, "the preceding seeds" refers to the seeds of the maturation-feeling and the seeds of objective-field-feeling contained within the five resultant factors, such as consciousness;
these are also able to serve as conditions to produce craving.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "From the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanabhūmi*), even when moving to another stage, it is fixed that one relies on a feeling of the same stage. The Explanation says: This is the first interpretation.

If one dies in one's own stage and is reborn in one's own stage, one relies on a feeling of that same stage as the condition to give rise to craving; this is the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇāṅga*), which is fixedly dependent on a feeling of the same stage.
If one dies in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is reborn in the First Dhyāna, one then relies on a feeling of the First Dhyāna stage and so forth, which belong to a different stage.

And craving arises; furthermore, this craving is also necessarily based upon feeling belonging to the same level (*bhūmi*). This feeling of the same level is what was previously included [in the definition].
Moreover, there is the sense that feeling present in one's current abode can even serve as a remote condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*). Regarding this second interpretation, it says:

for example, when one dies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is reborn in the first dhyāna, the feeling within the desire realm also serves as a condition for the craving in the first dhyāna, just as ignorance does.

The practice of a different stage arises. This craving conditioned by sensation in a different stage is not itself a [dependent origination] limb. This is the second interpretation, as well as the first interpretation:
if craving and grasping in a different stage cannot act as the "intermediate link" (*vṛddhi*) for the existence-limb (*bhava-aṅga*) of that different stage.

Regarding the statement that "sensation conditions craving and thereby indirectly connects different stages," this refers to my previous second interpretation: the indirect connection of sensation in a different stage with [craving].
"Taking craving for the realm as a condition"—this is the question.

The commentary (*śāstra*) states: "The question is: why is it that consciousness and the others differ in their expansion and contraction (i.e., being detailed or summarized), and yet how can they both exist together as one?
The explanation says: "The intent of this question is: why do the members [of dependent origination] cited here differ in their expansion and contraction, while those that lead [the process]..."
Regarding the link of formations (*saṃskāra*) and the link of existence (*bhava*): are they combined into one? The Commentary (*Śū*) states:
"Therefore, there are three types of karma which, when taken together, are named 'formations' and 'existence. The Explanation (*Jie*) says:

"The three types of karma refer to meritorious (*puṇya*), non-meritorious (*apuṇya*), and imperturbable (*āniñjya*) karma. These—meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable—are collectively named the links of formations and existence."

The Commentary states: "The Sarvāstivāda and others... Regarding the two causes and five fruits: indeed, the Sarvāstivāda school establishes that all twelve links are present within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
For example, at the time one commits the act of killing, the ignorance occurring simultaneously is called the link of ignorance;

the volition (*cetanā*) occurring simultaneously is called the link of formations (*saṃskāra*); if consciousness occurs simultaneously, it is called the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*); and if [name-and-form] occurs simultaneously...

The conceptualization that supports the sense faculties and their objects is termed the limb of name-and-form (nāmarūpa). If the five sense faculties exist simultaneously with the immediately preceding mental faculty (manas), this is termed the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana).
When contact exists simultaneously, it is termed the limb of contact (sparśa); when sensation exists simultaneously, it is termed the limb of sensation (vedanā).
At that same time, greed is called the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). At that same time, the remaining entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) among the afflictions are called the limb of grasping (*upādāna*).

At that same time, bodily and vocal actions are called the limb of becoming (*bhava*). The characteristic of arising is called the limb of birth (*jāti*). The characteristic of change is called the limb of aging (*jarā*). The characteristic of cessation is called death (*maraṇa*).

"Within this present section" refers to the following passage in the treatise: "That is, within this present person’s vehicle-section (*yāna-varga*), it is the causal factor of the middle member (*madhya-aṅga*) from the past."
The commentary states: "That which causes contact with the body and birth and death. The explanation says: This refers to the ten links [of dependent origination] created by the present body;
once this present body has died, one will only then receive the fruits of two links in a future life.
The Commentary states: "If this is discussed in terms of temporal divisions, then [the link of] birth and old age would even exist until [the end of the future];

for would it not be the case that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) coexist with birth and old age in the future? Thus, if one explains the meaning of the three periods of time based on broad temporal divisions, it would be indeterminate.

This passage of the Commentary is erroneous. It should read: "As in the case of the karma of a future rebirth: having created the causes of the first seven links in the past, one gives rise to craving, grasping, and becoming (*bhava*) in the present world."
The three causal factors [of the past] result in the two resultant factors of birth and old age in the future. This constitutes the fixed determination across the three times.

If one creates the first seven causal factors in the present body, then through a second body, craving, grasping, and becoming arise; and through a third birth, the two resultant factors of birth and old age are experienced.
If one interprets it in this way, there would be no [fixed sequence of] the three times, as [the factors] would not yet exist in the present.

In the future life, one creates the causes for the seven branches—namely, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), existence (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—all of which reside in the future life.

Thus, there are only two [lifetimes]: the present and the future. However, the intent of the commentary (*śāstra*) provisionally concerns the four types of birth resulting from karma with subsequent retribution;

it is not contradictory to state that, according to the actual fact, one undergoes three lifetimes. Now, one should say that the past consists of the first seven branches, while the present corresponds to the final three branches.
The future gives rise to the three branches of the fruit; thus, the three time periods are explained in terms of the moment of arising.

Furthermore, according to the Mahāyāna, it is as if there were someone who, having committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*) such as slandering the Dharma, receives retribution in this very life. For instance, a single karma may bring about a hundred successive births in the bodies of those undergoing immediate retribution;
that is, a single karma brings forth the seeds for the five fruits across a hundred bodies. Thus, in this present life, one performs the first seven branches [of karma].
The ten causal links of craving and grasping lead to the first birth in the future, which is the immediate reception of a hellish body.
This occurs because one has created the ten preceding causal links in the present; thus, there are two resultant links in the future, spanning only these two lifetimes.

When one receives that first birth as a hell-being and is about to die, craving and grasping arise once more, thereby acting as the "intercalary" cause for the second birth as a hell-being, resulting in the consciousness and subsequent links.
The five fruits are said to be the seeds. Furthermore, one receives a body in the second hell; the karma produced in this life is thus complete across the three periods of time.

That is to say, in the past one creates the causes for the first seven links; in the present one gives rise to the causes for the [next] three links; and in the future there are the two links of the fruit.

This continues until the time when one in the ninth hell is about to die, at which point one again separately gives rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) as intercalary factors.
The five fruits, such as the ten body-consciousnesses, are termed "seeds. Only then does one receive the tenth birth, the body of hell.

This karma of retribution in this life likewise possesses all three time periods: namely, the causes of the seven branches previously created in the past, the causes of the three branches in the present life, and the two branches in the future.
Subsequent methods of practice are to be understood by analogy. This applies even up to the first intercalary body.

However, the arising of craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*) in three ways is likewise so. Or, a single karma may produce one complete set of seeds for names and phrases (*nāma-pada-bīja*), which contains the five types of seeds for names and phrases.

After having experienced one body in hell, if one again gives rise to craving and grasping to moisten these seeds of names and phrases, one will once more experience a body in hell. This continues until this entire set of names and phrases...

Regarding the seeds of the five fruits, it is not even an obstacle to undergo one hundred births repeatedly. For example, a person of the Dharma who slanders those who uphold their practice and causes them to turn the wheel [of suffering] enters hell and so forth, remaining there for a full kalpa;
when that kalpa ends, they are reborn again for another kalpa. This cycle of increase and decrease is what is termed "one kalpa."
Within a single kalpa, one undergoes one full lifetime and then dies; thereafter, one undergoes yet another hell.

That which is "undergoing [suffering] for one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*) without interruption" refers to the abiding kalpa (*sthiti-kalpa*) within one cycle of increase and decrease. During twenty such cycles of increase and decrease, one undergoes twenty hellish bodies.
If hells exist only during the abiding kalpa, then they do not exist during the kalpas of formation (*vivarta*) or destruction (*saṃvarta*).

Hell. Furthermore, after this sinner has undergone [retribution] in this world for twenty kalpas, when this world’s kalpa is destroyed, they immediately go to undergo it within the hells of other worlds. In this manner, they pass through the hells of the ten directions. Question:
Since the force of this single karma has already brought about a body in hell, should one not experience the remaining force of that karma only after having finished experiencing the first portion?

It does not cause further death; that is, once a single body for rebirth in hell has been received, its karmic connection is fully exhausted. Why, then, during the intermediate kalpas, is there a small amount of returning death?
Furthermore, regarding the "receiving of few bodies" upon rebirth—does this mean receiving distinct individual bodies? Answer:

Although by means of this single karma one may experience many bodies in hell, when calculated as a whole, it is considered that the exhaustion of the connection occurs within a single body. Nevertheless, [the seeds] are extended.
Because he fell into a deep sleep immediately upon receiving his life-span, he did not obtain a hellish body through a single karma;
thus, within twenty kalpas, he experienced only one body. Therefore, we know that he must have undergone twenty bodies in succession.
This is just as Aniruddha, by giving a single meal as an offering, obtained the experience of bliss among gods and humans for ninety-one kalpas—how could this have been from a single [act]?
The retribution for the physical body has already been exhausted; how could it be that while others receive a lifespan of one hundred years, this person alone receives ten thousand?
Thus we know that [longevity] depends upon the category [of karma]. Only through eye-medicine, divine mantras, and the like can one obtain a long life.

Furthermore, by hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Constantly-Minimizing Bodhisattva obtained a single karmic action for his lifespan. One obtains a single karmic action, yet one may obtain many bodies. [This applies to] humans.
Among the gods, there may be cases where a single karma produces many bodies; this follows the same principle as the method previously explained for the hells.

Furthermore, the Sarvāstivādins state that a kalpa of abiding consists of twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*). In the first kalpa, there is only decrease and no increase; in the twentieth kalpa, there is only increase and no decrease;
and in the eighteen intermediate kalpas, there is both increase and decrease. Regarding the kalpa of abiding in the Mahāyāna:

Throughout twenty kalpas, there are both increases and decreases, distinguished by their magnitude. Within the Mahāyāna, a single karma can bring about the bodies of one hundred or even one thousand lifetimes;
even the final hundredth body still produces retributive karma, which is designated by the name of the first body.

It is produced by the same karma. Since the first body is called "karma to be experienced in the next life" (*upapadyavedanīya-karma*), so too are all bodies up to the hundredth called "karma to be experienced in the next life.

If there were a single "karma to be experienced in a subsequent life" (*aparaparyāyavedanīya-karma*) capable of bringing about one hundred individual lives, such that the final one experiences the hundredth body, this too would be called "karma to be experienced in a subsequent life," as it is named from its beginning. Question: If it is granted that a single karma [produces many results]...

It is capable of inducing ten lifetimes or a hundred lifetimes; it must likewise give rise to a single set of craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*) that can nourish the seeds of the five fruits for ten lifetimes or a hundred lifetimes.
The power of the karma that initiates [rebirth] is able to induce results at a great distance;

therefore, while karma induces many bodies, the nourishment of those births must necessarily be immediate and direct. Thus, within a single lifetime, the set of craving and grasping directed toward a single destination is exclusively...

The *rūṇ* (intercalary) [factor] is adjacent to the five resultant seeds—consciousness and so forth—within a subsequent existence. Through craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), it is able to intercalate a further birth.

Alternatively, within a single lifetime among humans or animals, craving and grasping during the process of dying can intercalate the five aggregates of a subsequent intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).

This occurs when one dies prematurely in the human intermediate state and is killed by another; unable to complete the natural death process, one gives rise to the craving for rebirth that constitutes the intercalation. However, this does not occur in the case of those in the hells.
They die prematurely. In a single lifetime, one takes up birth and gives rise to craving and grasping as the intervening conditions. If one asks about this single body:

if it were granted that a single karma could produce many distinct results, then one would also have to admit that numerous collective retributive karmas and afflictions could produce a single body; yet, in reality, there is only a single karma [that produces it].
One can certainly produce many [results]. It is impossible that karma and afflictions which constitute a collective retribution for multiple bodies would produce a single body;
rather, each of the many karmas of collective retribution is capable of producing its own individual body. Questioning the Sarvāstivādins:

"If that is so, and many karmas of collective retribution cannot be lost and each produces a single body, why is it that the Bodhisattva, having cultivated the karma for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) for a hundred eons, produced only a single body?"
Answer: These marks and signs cultivated by this bodhisattva over a hundred kalpas are all individual retributions (*pṛthag-vipāka*).

It is thus admitted that many individual retribution karmas can produce a single body; however, there is absolutely no case where many collective retribution karmas (*sāmānya-vipāka*) together induce a body. Question:

Suppose, for instance, a single karma of retribution in the present life (*upapadya-vedanīya-karma*) induces ten successive births. At the time one receives the body of the first birth, what of these [ten]...?

Karmic actions that produce birth, when moistened by craving and grasping, are termed the "existence" (*bhava*) link. Since these [actions] can induce ten future births, why do they not produce ten bodies all at once?

Furthermore, since this karma is moistened by craving and grasping within the first body (the present life), and the previous "existence" link has already occurred, how could it again be moistened by the craving and grasping for individual retribution (*prātibhāṣika-vedanīya*) when reaching the second body (the future life)? How could it be moistened a second time?
