Regarding karma: although craving and grasping arise within the first body of the aggregates (*skandha*), this karma that invites [rebirth] throughout the ten directions is simultaneously conditioned by them.
Since this karma has been so conditioned at one time, the five fruits—such as consciousness (*vijñāna*)—within the bodies of the remaining nine births are termed "seed-karma."

Although it is "intercalated" by craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*), it is nonetheless able to suddenly give rise to the manifestation of the ten bodies in both the preceding and succeeding stages.

Furthermore, although this karma is intercalated by craving and grasping during the first birth, there is no impediment to its being further and repeatedly intercalated by craving and grasping within the second birth.
Moreover, regarding what the karma depends upon: if one considers this karma in relation to a single lifetime, it has already been intercalated by the craving and grasping of the first birth.
Because of the intercalary [existence], this karma, in relation to the first existence, is termed a "link of becoming" (bhava-aṅga).

If, however, it is related to the remaining nine existences, this same karma can induce those nine existences and is thus termed a "link of volitional formations" (saṃskāra-aṅga). Furthermore, although this single karma induces ten existences...
That is to say, the five types of seeds for the results—such as the first consciousness of the ten bodies—are each distinct.
One cannot take the nominal seeds of the five results of the first body-consciousness and only receive them within the second body.

In the Hīnayāna, a single karma that produces only one body cannot produce the bodies of multiple lifetimes; that is, a karma of immediate retribution (*upapadyavedanīya-karman*) pertains only to a single birth.
The *saṃbhogakāya*. The remainder are all subsequent retributions of indeterminate karma and so forth. Question:
Since a Bodhisattva in the stage of application (*prayoga*) possesses a body of segmented birth (*paricchinna-deha*), is it burned by the fires at the end of the eon?

Furthermore, when the great three [calamities] destroy the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), will the great [Bodhisattva] who is about to attain Buddhahood be destroyed by the great three calamities before long? Question: From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, [the body is] of segmented birth...
Do the Bodhisattvas' bodies suffer damage from the three great calamities? It is not yet known where they are reborn when the kalpa is destroyed.

Furthermore, do the ten types of contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*) of the Bodhisattva suffer damage from those three calamities? Consider this. Question: Since wind has motion as its nature, why is it said that the substance of wind is "turning"? Answer:
When we say that wind has motion as its nature, this refers to the wind that, within other worlds, is capable of producing the myriad things.

Regarding "things": they are able to bring all things to completion. This refers to the winds that move through space (*ākāśa-gata-vāyu*), not to those spoken of in relation to the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).

Furthermore, among the winds of the world, there are also those that have a basis; for example, gross winds are capable of differentiation. If one considers them by way of the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, there are three kinds of wind:

first, the formative wind (*abhinirvartaka-vāyu*), which refers to the ordinary winds moving through space that constitute the world; second, the sustaining wind (*dhāraka-vāyu*)... [text fragment ends].
The "sustaining wind" refers to that which, by means of the substance of the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), is able to sustain and cause the world-system to remain stable.

Third is the "destructive wind," which is the arising of a wind that possesses the power to shatter the world-system. However, the Sarvāstivādins maintain that the wind-circle must necessarily consist of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) in equilibrium.
The four great elements are never separate; there is never a case where the earth element alone exists apart from the other great elements, such as wind.
Now, this wind-wheel that we perceive is simply the earth element in its state of extreme increase, just as the Mahāyāna establishes the existence of the four great elements acting in isolation.

This wind-wheel is precisely the wind element acting in isolation. Regarding the five heinous crimes, such as harming one's father, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that "harming" merely refers to causing injury.
Sentient beings do not sever their own life-span. This statement regarding "harming one's mother and father" refers to the severing of another's life and the injury of their body.

The answer states that "harming the mother" is a synonym for "killing. Killing the father is distinct from killing the mother; there are general names and specific ones, just as the term "light" has both general and specific designations.
Generally, they are called "light" (*āloka*). Furthermore, the moon, stars, fire, and so forth are also designated by the name "illumination" (*prabhā*).

If one uses specific names, that which is the sun is only called "light" and cannot be called "illumination. That which is the moon, stars, fire, and so forth is only called "illumination" and cannot be called "light. Now, this case is likewise:
if one considers them collectively, killing (*vadhya*) is also called "harming" (*hiṃsā*), and harming is also called "killing. Killing is the severing of life; harming is not.
Because life has been severed, the seeds of volition (*cetanā*) produced by other karmas may repeatedly manifest as active states (*samudācāra*) throughout a single lifetime.
However, the seeds of volition produced by the karma of killing one's father or mother will manifest as an active state only once during that lifetime, because it is impossible to kill two parents.

The Commentary states: "The Sārvastivāda masters maintain that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*)—among the three [links]—are necessarily not of the same time-period as the first two of the aforementioned seven types.
This refers to the Sārvastivāda teaching: the two links of the past are the cause; the five links of the present are the fruit; the three links of the present are the cause;
and the two links of the future are the fruit. Thus, in the present life, there are actually eight links which are necessarily obtained within the same time-period, namely:

The five fruits beginning with consciousness, as well as craving, grasping, and becoming—if craving, grasping, and becoming were necessarily of a different time period from ignorance and formations—then in the Mahāyāna system, within the present life, these [factors] would necessarily be comprised of ten members, seven members, or three members occurring simultaneously. However, they are indeed simultaneous.
Now, it is certainly impossible for eight members to attain the same temporal period (*adhvan*). That is to say: ten members of the present serve as the cause for two members of the future;

or, one creates the causes of the seven members—ignorance (*avidyā*), formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and so forth—in the present, followed by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) in the subsequent life, and finally the fruits of birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*);
or, the three causes of craving, grasping, and existence arise in the present, while the two members of birth and aging-and-death arise in the future.
This refers to the fruit.

The Commentary (*Sūtra*) states: "It is not that the present [factors] arise and are able to intercalate such that the future branches of existence (*bhava-aṅga*), which are the objects of intercalation, are only then established at a different time. The Explanation (*Jie*) says:

"It is not that the present [factors] arise and are able to intercalate craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), and only then do the future branches of existence, which are the objects of intercalation, arise. However, this commentary provisionally discusses this in terms of the "intercalating" [factors].

Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) exist in the same temporal period as the *bhava* (existence) factor that they condition. Furthermore, there are cases where craving and grasping arise in the present and are able to condition [future existence] while being in the same period as the seeds of the latter ten links of the body;
thus, there is no contradiction in the conditioning agent (*upakāraka*) and the conditioned object (*upakārya*) being separated by different periods.

Likewise, when the seeds of the latter ten links and the five links of the body act as the conditioning agents for the conditioned objects, there is no inconsistency in the conditioning agent and the conditioned object being separated by different periods. As it is said: [like...]
As previously cited, the *Śāstra* states:
"The cause is in the past while the fruit is either in the present or the future; the cause is in the present while the fruit is in a future life.
The commentary explains: For example, if one creates a karma that ripens in the next birth (*upapadyavedanīya-karma*) capable of inducing ten successive births, if one were to receive the first...
In one lifetime: ten factors of the cause exist in the past, while two factors of the fruit exist in the present.

If one undergoes the body of a second or third rebirth and beyond, then seven factors of the cause exist in the past, three factors exist in the present, and two factors of the fruit exist in the future.

Alternatively, regarding karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya-karma*), ten factors of the cause exist in the present, and two factors of the fruit exist in the future; or [karma] to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).
Karma: seven branches have their causes in the past; three branches have their causes in the present; two branches have their results in the future. The *Śū* (Commentary) states:
"Speaking in general terms, this refers to dependent origination across two lifetimes. The *Jie* (Explanation) clarifies:

that is, the ten causal branches of the past and the two resultant branches of the present; the ten causal branches of the present and the two resultant branches of the future. Although seven branches belong to the past, they arise in the present.
The three links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) give rise to the two links of birth (*jāti*) and so forth as their future fruit.
These seven links beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*), along with the aforementioned three links of grasping and existence—these ten links are all of the nature of causes.

Although the preceding seven and the subsequent three belong to different lifetimes, since all ten links are now established as being of the nature of causes, it may also be said that these ten links share the same time period as their causes. (2)
The branches (*aṅga*) are distinct fruits across [different] time periods (*adhvan*). They may also be said to span two time periods.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states that, according to principle, they also span three time periods. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says:
namely, the seven branches of the past as causes, the three branches of the present, and the two branches of the future as fruits; thus they may also possess the three time periods.
The *Śāstra* states: "The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle eight, says 'the twelvefold dependent origination'... up to "...this translation is erroneous. The commentary explains:
However, the old *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the sūtra on the twelve links is the method for [analyzing] the three periods of time, which is identical to the Hīnayāna.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "That is to say, the two links of past ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are causes;

the five links of the present are effects; the three links of the present are causes; and the two links of the future are effects. This is an error of the translator. In the Mahāyāna, there is truly no such meaning.

In this current translation from the Sanskrit original, it accords with the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; it merely speaks of the "three time periods" (*trikāla*), and does not mean that there are specifically "three links" [in each period]. Thus asks the Old [Commentary]: [End of excerpt]

I am now translating the eighth fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. Regarding the various "three times" (*tri-kāla*), the new *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks instead of the "three limits" (*tri-koṭi*).

What is the difference between the characters *jiè* (limit) and *shì* (time)? Furthermore, what is the distinction between the "three limits" of the *Yogācāra* and the "three times" of the *Daśabhūmika*? To ask further:

it simply mentions the "three limits," extending even to the limit of the future (*paścima-koṭi*) regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). "The first limit" refers to the past; "the middle" refers to the present.
"Subsequent departure" refers to the future. This means that, following the pattern of the initial and middle limits, "departure" arises;

that is, the ten factors of the cause in the past and the two factors of the fruit in the present. Regarding dependent origination from the middle limit to the subsequent limit: the ten prior causes in the present and the two factors of the fruit in the future.
The *Śāstra* says: "Now, [the author] departs from this interpretation of the previous masters. The commentary explains:

If one follows the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, which states that the three members of the past are causes, the five members of the present are effects, the three members of the present are causes, and the two members of the future are effects—thus establishing the sequence of cause and effect across the three periods of time—then this would be equivalent to the old interpretation, which accords with the teachings of the Hīnayāna. Regarding the statement that "present effects arise from causes," this refers to the present...

Regarding the fruit of birth, aging, and death, it arises from the ten causes of the past. As for the phrase "the cause must proceed toward the destination," this refers to the ten causes of the present, which are capable of producing birth, aging, and death in the future.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The essence of *adhyavasāna* (clinging) is a synonym for *tṛṣṇā* (craving); furthermore, because it serves as the essence of the member of clinging (*upādānāṅga*), it is not a mere designation (*prajñapti*).

The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states: Question: The seeds of the five resultant consciousnesses and so forth constitute the member of existence (*bhavāṅga*), and since the member of existence is a mere designation, why is the member of clinging (*upādānāṅga*)—which is the intensification of craving—not also a mere designation?
Furthermore, if the three lower types of craving are [the essence], why is it not so? If [it were] merely a name...

Regarding the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā*): if craving is of the highest degree, it is designated as the limb of grasping (*upādāna*). Because the limbs of grasping and craving each possess their own distinct substantial entities, they are not merely nominal existents (*prajñaptisat*).

Even when the three lower grades of the limb of craving are transformed into the limb of grasping, because they each possess their own distinct substantial entities, they are not merely nominal existents.
Furthermore, when the three lower grades of craving are transformed into the highest grade of craving, and that highest grade of craving becomes the limb of grasping, [the same principle applies].

It may be said that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) transforms into grasping (*upādāna*); it may be said that the limb of grasping is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*). However, in this case, the superior and inferior grades are each distinct and cannot be transformed [into one another].
Since the inferior grade of craving does not constitute the limb of grasping as a conventional designation, the inferior grade of craving is indeed the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā-aṅga*).

Superior-grade craving is termed the "appropriation" (*upādāna*) limb; therefore, the appropriation limb is not merely nominal. Furthermore, the appropriation limb takes other afflictions as its essence.
Among the five [limbs], these are ignorance, consciousness, contact, sensation, and craving. Regarding the limbs of contact and sensation:

do they consist of the contact and sensation associated with the six consciousnesses, or the contact and sensation associated with the eighth consciousness? These constitute the essence of the contact and sensation limbs.

How is it that this is not merely a single matter? Furthermore, [the text] asks: since the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) also includes craving associated with the six consciousnesses, how can it be designated as a single matter? Reflect on this.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The formations (*saṃskāra*) pertain to both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) asks: "If, within the member of formations (*saṃskārāṅga*), the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—are called 'matter,' then is volition (*cetanā*) called 'mind'?"

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Some explain that 'five' refers to the appropriation and non-appropriation of the *vijñāna*-link; the appropriation is governed solely by the predominance of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The *Vyākhyā* (Exegesis) explains: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* lists the names of both "one matter" and "not one matter," yet speaks of them in general terms as "five.
Here, in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the explanation of "one matter" and "not one matter" refers specifically to their individual names.

Regarding the ancient great Dharma masters such as Master Jing and others, they had not yet seen the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) explaining how a single matter is [simultaneously] not a single matter.
Consequently, the Great Master composed the *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the *Yogācārabhūmi*). The text of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"The five 'single matters' refer to ignorance (*avidyā*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*); that is, superior-grade craving is named the limb of grasping (*upādānāṅga*). Thus, the limb of grasping is a single matter."
That is to say, one does not take the consciousness that cognizes as the member [of dependent origination]; rather, one takes all six consciousnesses as the consciousness-member.

This is the "consciousness-member of manifold activities," not a single activity. Now, the Commentary states: "If the Master [Vasubandhu] and others were to take the members collectively and call this 'a single activity,' it would contradict the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other such authoritative scriptures (*āgama*)."
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The five types of form are not [included in] the category of non-form; the formations (*saṃskāra*) pertain to all three types of action and are thus termed 'form';

the six bases (*āyatana*) and two aggregates (*skandha*), up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), pertain to both [categories]. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states: "If, within the member of formations (*saṃskāra-anga*), there are both mental actions as well as bodily and vocal actions—since bodily and vocal actions are subsumed under 'form'—the 'six bases and two aggregates' refers to the five sense organs being the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and the base of mind (*manāyatana*) being the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). The Formations (*Saṃskāra*).

These six branches are further designated as the "existence branch" (*bhava-aṅga*). The existence branch encompasses both the material and the non-material. The manifestation of the five aggregates is termed the "birth branch" (*jāti-aṅga*);
the birth branch likewise encompasses both matter and mind. The same applies to the "aging branch" (*jarā-aṅga*).
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "If the sixth and seventh [categories] were not [respectively] contaminated (*sāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), then this section would be rendered useless.
The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states: This refers precisely to the sixth category, the gate of the contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and the seventh, the gate of the conditioned. Question:

Since it has already been stated that these are the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-anga*), it is clear they are contaminated and conditioned. Why, then, are the gates of the conditioned and unconditioned, as well as the contaminated and uncontaminated, discussed here?
The Gate of the Untainted (Anāsrava). Answer: The reason for establishing these sixth and seventh gates now is to address the Mahāsāṃghika and Kṣemaka schools.

As stated in the Sūtra, the World-Honored One said: "Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the nature and characteristics of the principle of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) remain eternally constant.

Regarding this sūtra, both the Mahāyāna and the Sarvāstivāda provide the following interpretation: [The remainder of the text follows the technical analysis of the two schools' views on the nature of dependent origination.]

It is said: Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear in the world, the factors of dependent origination remain as "ignorance conditions volitional formations," and so on, up to "birth conditions aging and death.

When a Buddha teaches the Sūtra on Dependent Origination, the dharma of dependent origination remains as "ignorance conditions volitional formations," and so forth; even if a Buddha does not teach it, it remains thus.

At that time, there is also [the formula] "ignorance conditions volitional formations," and so forth. A sūtra states: "The nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā*) is eternally abiding.

If the teachers of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravāda school explain this sūtra as meaning that the nature of the phenomena of dependent origination is eternally abiding, then we know that there exists a distinct limb of dependent origination called ignorance.

Therefore, when the Blessed One says that the nature of dependent origination is eternally abiding, it is clearly understood that there is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) limb of dependent origination.

Because that illumination relies on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is unconditioned; its nature is non-ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, non-ignorance is able to project the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

Because the link of volitional formations also relies on the unconditioned, the link of volitional formations is able to induce the five fruits, beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), up to birth (*jāti*) as the condition for aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Thus, there are distinct links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) that are unconditioned. Furthermore, dependent origination itself also extends to the unconditioned.

[These] are untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas. Now, regarding those two categories mentioned in the Mahāyāna, it is stated that the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-aṅga*) are exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and tainted (*sāsrava*).

In contrast to those two groups, these sixth and seventh [factors] are established here as being clear. These two gates are not without the function of being "conditioned" in relation to all [dharmas].
To say they are "conditioned" means they are produced by causes and conditions and so forth; to say they are "unconditioned" means they are not...

That which is produced by karma is both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This means that the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*) is called "conditioned" because it arises from causes and conditions;
it is called "unconditioned" because it is not produced by karma and the like. If one interprets it in this way, this exists only in the Mahāyāna and not in the Hīnayāna.
Regarding "intercalary births and the obscured," this refers to the innate greed and delusion (*sahaja-rāga-moha*) within the three realms.

The two views—view of a self-identity and extreme view—are absent [among the afflictions arising from the Noble Ones]. These arise either as correct or as derivative; they are of the nature of being obscured. This excludes only the anger arising from the Saṃgha, because it causes harm to oneself and others.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "There are multiple proofs that the four types of grasping (*upādāna*) in the desire realm are unwholesome (*akuśala*). The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says:

"In the Mahāyāna, it is taught that if a defilement (*kleśa*) belongs to the desire realm, it is termed 'grasping of the desire realm' (*kāma-upādāna*); if it consists of three views, it is termed 'grasping of views' (*dṛṣṭi-upādāna*)."

Within the three realms, the clinging to precepts is called *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to rules and observances). Within the three realms, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is called *ātmavādopādāna* (clinging to the doctrine of self).

In the desire realm, all four types of clinging are present; when the four clingings of the desire realm are analyzed, they are exclusively of an unwholesome nature—namely, clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmopādāna*), clinging to rules and observances, clinging to views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*), and clinging to the doctrine of self.
In the two higher realms, there is only clinging to views, as well as [the remaining portions of] clinging to rules and observances and clinging to the doctrine of self.

There is no grasping for desire (*kāma-upādāna*). Grasping for desire refers to the grasping of sensual craving (*kāmarāga*). According to the Sarvāstivāda school, grasping for desire exists only within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).

Because there are afflictions in the realm of desire, one predominantly grasps at external objects of form through greed. Since grasping for desire exists in the realm of desire, the two upper realms possess only grasping for self-existence (*ātmavāda-upādāna*).
This is because the afflictions of the two upper realms belong to the meditative stages (*samāpatti-bhūmi*) and predominantly take [internal states] as their object.
Because one gives rise to craving and attachment toward the internal body as "mine," there is the clinging to the discourse of self (*ātmavādopādāna*) within the two upper realms.

If the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) are both considered the clinging to the discourse of self throughout the three realms, it is because when one clings to a real self, the essence of a self does not actually exist;
there is only empty talk, which is termed the clinging to the discourse of self. Furthermore, among the afflictions of discrimination within the desire realm, all are of an unwholesome nature.

Is the factor of ignorance within the desire realm of an unwholesome nature? And is it this factor of ignorance that can give rise to the first *anāgāmya* concentration and the factor of immovable formations (*aniñjya-saṃskāra*)?
The Commentary states: "In the higher realms, these three are all exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). The Explanation says:

"If, within the two higher realms, the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) and the grasping at self and precepts (*ātma-śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*) are of an indeterminate nature; furthermore, it is also possible for ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) in the higher realms to be of an indeterminate nature."

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: Question: If one takes up the "clinging" (*upādāna*), since it already transcends the four types of clinging, why then speak of the "path of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmārga*) as either the primary or secondary views, or as the assistance for the "existence-branch" (*bhavāṅga*) being named "assistance"? The Explanation says:

The intent of this question is that since there are four types of clinging within the clinging-branch, and these four types of clinging are themselves conceptual discriminations (*vikalpa*), and since there are thus conceptual afflictions within the clinging-branch, then now—[it follows that...]

It is said that the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are the primary [defilements], while those of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are secondary. How then can it be said that the path of cultivation is either primary or secondary?
Furthermore, the path of seeing is a secondary defilement; moreover, if there is the link of grasping (*upādāna*), it is called a secondary defilement.
The *Śāstra* says: "The answer to that [objection] regarding the auxiliary question is that they are collectively termed the 'appropriation member' (*upādāna-aṅga*). The commentary explains:

The present response states that if within the appropriation member there is superior-grade craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and since superior-grade craving is itself named the appropriation member, then within the appropriation member, only superior-grade craving is designated as the "primary" (*maula*) [member].

If the appropriation member consists of the four types of grasping (*catvāry upādānāni*), then these four graspings are designated as the "auxiliary" (*sahakārin*) [members]. Thus, the primary and the auxiliary are combined into two.

Is it called the "appropriation link" (*upādāna*)? The Commentary (*Śū*) says: "Question: What prevents [the view] from also being designated as 'aiding and promoting' (*sahakārin*), or being combined with [ignorance] and named 'ignorance' (*avidyā*)? The Explanation (*Jie*) says: "The present objection states:

Since within the appropriation link there are both the primary (*maula*) and the auxiliary (*sahakārin*), and since the primary and auxiliary together are named the 'appropriation link,' it should likewise follow that [the karma-forming volition] is what promotes [rebirth]."

Among these, there is ignorance (*avidyā*) that can only produce a specific auxiliary for future karma. This ignorance, which assists future karma, should properly be designated as the "member of ignorance" (*avidyā-aṅga*).
The *Śū* (Commentary) states:

"The answer to Gao’s interpretation is also acceptable; however, here we rely solely on what directly produces [the result], or because the text of the treatise itself permits it. Thus, the phrasing is abrupt.

"As before, it follows the subsequent. The commentary explains: The intent of this explanation is that within this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the ignorance (*avidyā*) that directly gives rise to both primary and secondary karma is designated as the "limb of ignorance" (*avidyā-aṅga*).
However, the ignorance that gives rise to specific auxiliary karma for future births is not subsumed under the limb of ignorance.

Now, taking the aforementioned limb of ignorance as a standard to compare with the subsequent limb of grasping (*upādāna*), since within the limb of grasping there are both primary and auxiliary factors of grasping:
These are collectively designated as the "appropriation link" (*upādāna-aṅga*). Now, this very [link] is precisely what initiates and assists the initiation of the "ignorance link" (*avidyā-aṅga*);

thus, they are collectively designated as the "ignorance link. This also obstructs the five resultant links. Regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the stages (*avasthā-lakṣaṇa*) in the place where one is to be reborn:

although that place of rebirth is actually within the stage of the "birth and old age and death links," it is conventionally said to possess five resultant links in succession. That is to say, while still in the mother’s womb, during the stage of linking existence (*pratisandhi*).

The characteristics of consciousness are manifested due to these causes. Next, while the sense faculties are not yet fully developed, they are designated as the "increase of the five characteristics" and so forth.

Within the various stages [of the five positions], wholesome and defiled states also arise, and thus the five fruits are taught. This is because wholesome and defiled states arise based on specific phases [of development]. Question:

Since minds of the three natures can arise within the mother’s womb and other such states, one wonders what kind of nature the mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) arises with. Question: Regarding Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Wheel-turning Kings...

O King and others: while in the mother’s womb, one may not yet know the arising of the wholesome states acquired through application (*prayoga-labdha*) or those acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha*), nor the four types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*), nor the innate afflictions (*kleśa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that arise simultaneously with the mind.

However, if the body of a Bodhisattva prior to the seventh bhūmi is of the nature of *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented existence), then while in the mother’s womb, they can give rise to the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), as well as abide in the first two fruits [of the path].

Can one give rise to untainted (anāsrava) thought? Answer: When an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is in the womb, they can only give rise to innate wholesome states (upapattilābhika-kuśala), not those acquired through application (prāyogika).
They can only give rise to afflictions (kleśa) that arise simultaneously with birth. They can only give rise to mental action (manas-karman); they cannot initiate bodily or vocal actions.

Only the neutral state born of maturation (*vipākaja-avyākṛta*) can arise; it may also be divided into that which can give rise to the category of minds associated with deportment (*airyāpathika*) and those that cannot.

Because one is within the womb, one cannot initiate deportment. If a Bodhisattva is in the womb, they are able to initiate applied wholesome states (*prāyogika-kuśala*) and so forth, whereas others cannot.
Furthermore, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not recall the events of their previous lives at the time of birth.

Regarding the statement, "Old age and death [arise] from two meanings... up to 'two or many should likewise arise,'" here, if it is said that the state of old age gives rise to defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and gives rise to compassion (*karuṇā*) and so forth, all such texts are consistent with the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which states that [the state of old age] is exclusively defiled (*kevalasaṃkleśa*).
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The twelve [bases] in their entirety are subsumed under the Desire Realm;

a small portion of the twelve are subsumed under the Formless Realm, as well as the formless [factors], the non-formless [factors], and the absence of the three feelings. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says: "If it is said that the twelve are entirely subsumed under the Desire Realm..."

This means that within the factor of ignorance (*avidyā*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is both delusion regarding the conventional (*saṃvṛti-moha*) and delusion regarding the ultimate (*paramārtha-moha*).

Delusion regarding the ultimate gives rise to meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*) within the desire realm, and these also possess an unwholesome nature (*akuśala-svabhāva*). Furthermore, among the formations (*saṃskāra*) of the desire realm, there are both meritorious and non-meritorious formations;
however, there are no immovable formations (*āniñjya-abhisaṃskāra*) in the desire realm. Moreover, within the desire realm, there are also the three types of bodily [actions].

These are equivalent karmas. Among the formations (*saṃskāra*), they also encompass both wholesome and unwholesome natures. Within the consciousness link (*vijñāna*) of the desire realm, all five destinies (*gati*) and four modes of birth (*yoni*) are present.
Within the name-and-form link (*nāmarūpa*) of the desire realm, there are likewise the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as well as the five destinies and four modes of birth.

Within the six sense bases link (*ṣaḍāyatana*) of the desire realm, which is fully complete, there are also the five destinies and four modes of birth. Furthermore, within the contact link (*sparśa*), there is also agreeable contact (*manojña-sparśa*).
Unpleasant contact and disagreeable contact likewise exist. There are also the five destinies and four modes of birth.

Within the branch of feeling (*vedanā*) in the desire realm, there are present the feelings of suffering, pleasure, joy, and equanimity, excluding the feeling of grief (*daurmanasya*). The feeling of grief is exclusively of a wholesome or unwholesome nature;

it does not extend to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and thus cannot be termed a maturation (*vipāka*). As for the branch of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in the desire realm, it also extends to the unwholesome nature as well as the obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Regarding their nature: the *upādāna* (clinging) link within the desire realm is also of an unwholesome or obscured-unspecified nature.

Furthermore, the *upādāna* link comprises both root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), as that which clings, that which is clung to, and the object of clinging are all termed "clinging.
As for the *bhava* (becoming) link in the desire realm, it consists of the synthesis of the preceding six links; however, it functions solely as the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). If...
Birth, old age, and death are also to be understood according to the preceding [explanation]. As for the twelve links within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they possess only one aspect:

the link of ignorance (*avidyā*) consists solely of delusion regarding ultimate truth (*paramārtha-moha*), lacks delusion regarding conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-moha*), and is not of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala*); it is exclusively of the obscured-unspecified nature (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Regarding the link of formations (*saṃskāra*): there are only immovable formations (*āniñjya-saṃskāra*) and no formations of the two [other] types. Within the first dhyāna, there are the three karmas of body, speech, and mind;

in the second dhyāna, there are only mental karmas, and these are exclusively wholesome dharmas. Regarding the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*): it exists only in the heavenly realms and is exclusively of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*).
Within the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the two objects of smell and taste are absent; thus, within "name" (*nāman*), the nose and tongue faculties are absent.

Regarding the two consciousnesses: from the second dhyāna upward, all five sensory consciousnesses are absent. Furthermore, there is only birth by transformation (*upapāduka*), which is subsumed under the destinies (*gati*).

If, within the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), there is only birth by transformation, it belongs exclusively to the heavenly destiny (*devagati*) and consists solely of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which is termed the mind base (*mana-āyatana*). This does not apply within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
At the moment of initial conception, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) exists first; it is only after four weeks have passed that the four faculties of the eye, ear, nose, and tongue arise.

When one is about to die, one first relinquishes the four faculties of the eye, ear, nose, and tongue, and only at the very end does one relinquish the body-faculty and the mind-faculty (*manendriya*).
Furthermore, in the desire realm, these are not fully present at the moment of initial conception; they are likewise absent then.
The faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are fixed roots. When one first takes birth in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), these five faculties arise simultaneously.
When one dies with wholesome desire, one abandons the five material faculties all at once. If one is born in that realm of form, all five material faculties are fully possessed.

There are certainly no cases where the five faculties are not fully present. Regarding contact and feeling in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is only contact that is agreeable and contact that is neutral;
there is no disagreeable contact. Nevertheless, it should now be explained: speaking in general terms, agreeable contact gives rise to feelings of joy and pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*);
disagreeable contact gives rise to feelings of suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*); and neutral contact gives rise to...

It gives rise to the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). If one follows this interpretation, from the fourth dhyāna upward there is only the contact that is "concordant and discordant" (*ubhaya-vipakṣa-sparśa*), which can give rise to the feeling of equanimity;

there is no other contact. Within the category of equanimity, since there exists both the equanimity that is favorable (*anugrāhaka*) and the equanimity that is detrimental (*upaghātaka*), it should also be stated—according to a specific sense—that agreeable contact (*iṣṭa-sparśa*) can give rise to favorable equanimity, while disagreeable contact (*aniṣṭa-sparśa*) gives rise to [detrimental] equanimity.
The contact associated with aversion (*pratigha*) produces equanimity that is accompanied by distress; the contact associated with renunciation (*upekṣā*) produces equanimity that is neutral.
Since these three types of equanimity pertain to both of the upper realms, their corresponding three types of contact likewise exist in those two realms.

Furthermore, when newly born gods in the Form Realm first behold the calamities of fire from the lower realm, they experience fear; likewise, when gods in the two upper realms are about to die, they also harbor [such thoughts] in their minds.
It is not so stated. Since it must be admitted that there is no [feeling] in the upper realms, it is clear that this refers to the abandoning of [feeling] through impairment.

Within the factors of feeling, in the three lower dhyānas there are the three feelings of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*); from the fourth dhyāna upward, there is only the feeling of equanimity.

If the links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are exclusively of the nature of obscured-unspecified (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*), then the links of existence (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) follow the same principle as previously explained.

If within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are fewer of the twelve links—namely, the link of ignorance (*avidyā*) consists only of ultimate delusion (*paramārtha-moha*) and is of the nature of obscured-unspecified;
if among the link of formations (*saṃskāra*), there are only immovable formations (*āniñjya-saṃskāra*) and only mental karma (*manaskarma*); if the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*)...
These lead exclusively to rebirth in the heavenly realms. As for the limb of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), there is only name and no form.

Within that name, furthermore, there are no five consciousnesses. Within the limb of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), there is only the mental base (*manāyatana*). Within the limb of contact (*sparśa*), there is only contact that is neither [agreeable nor disagreeable].

Within the limb of feeling (*vedanā*), there is only the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Within the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), there is only that which is obscured-neutral (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*). Since the limb of grasping (*upādāna*) already encompasses one [of these],...

Regarding all afflictions (*kleśa*): if one refers to the ten root afflictions, *dveṣa* (hatred) belongs exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while the remaining nine pervade all three realms.

Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the seven of the "small" category and two of the "medium" category are of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala*) and thus belong only to the desire realm. *Māyā* (deceit) and *śāṭhya* (guile) pervade the first fruit [of the path] as well as the desire realm;
the remainder pervade all three realms. Therefore, it is said that in the two upper realms, there is only the appropriation of a portion of the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
The members of birth, aging, and death can be understood [as they are]. In the two higher realms, there are only a portion of twelve members.
Regarding the statement in the current commentary that "the defilements of the form and formless realms are entirely non-existent," this is not so;

rather, one should say that while the nature of unwholesomeness is absent in the two higher realms, the faculties present there are of the nature of obscured-neutral (nivṛtāvyākṛta). As for those in the desire realm that pertain to both the defiled and the pure, these are indeed present.

There are branches that are both defiled and pure; these are called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). Regarding the statement that name-and-form possesses the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), there are two interpretations of its essential nature (*svabhāva*).

If one considers the essential nature as being produced through a mixture [of defiled and pure elements], then name-and-form possesses the five aggregates. Here, we follow the interpretation of the mixed essential nature, whereby name-and-form possesses the five aggregates.

If one considers the essential nature as being produced through transformation, then name-and-form is not without the possession [of the aggregates]. In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all branches are present. And so forth.
Regarding "concordant origination" (*samutthāna*): "concordance" (*sāmagrī*) refers to mutual conformity, or rather, it is only when the twelve links are in concordance that origination occurs.
This "concordance" refers to all factors; if one dies in an upper realm, only a portion [of the links] originates. "Origination" refers to the simultaneous and equal arising of all twelve links.
Regarding the phrase "the six sense bases possess the various consciousnesses," among the six sense bases, there is the divine sense base (*devāyatana*).
There are thus the six consciousnesses that arise immediately following the preceding moment. However, speaking in terms of the eight consciousnesses:

there are eight in the desire realm, six in the first dhyāna, and three from the second dhyāna upward. Regarding the discussion of the factors of practice (mārgāṅga) in higher stages being able to rely upon lower stages:

The meaning of the question is as follows: Just as the six paths of practice of the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya*) can rely upon the desire realm and coexist with cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), so too can the factors of immovable cultivation (*āniñjya-saṃskāra*) rely upon the twelve links of the desire realm. Furthermore, it is asked:

just as the factors of the second dhyāna can rely upon the twelve links of the first dhyāna, could there not be the principle that the defiled states of a higher stage can rely upon those of a lower stage? How could there possibly be wholesome states of a higher stage [relying on a lower one]?

Regarding the "immovable formative factors" (*aniñjya-saṃskāra*): wholesome immovable formative factors based on the first dhyāna, up to those based on the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), are likewise [immovable] for those based on the lower stages.
The commentary states: "This applies to both the Form and Formless Realms, because one initiates those formative factors in order to seek rebirth in higher [planes]. To explain this: if the first...
The factors of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna can completely abandon the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Likewise, the factors of the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) can completely abandon all defilements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Although the factors of the preparatory stage of the second dhyāna can abandon the defilements of the first dhyāna and so forth, here the discussion concerns complete abandonment of defilements rather than partial abandonment. Is this not the case?

The *Śāstra* says: "Taking the lower realm as the object of contemplation constitutes the 'obstructing' [contemplation], while taking the upper realm as the object constitutes the 'excellent' contemplation. The *Commentary* explains:

This refers to the sixfold practice based on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration or the path; that is, contemplating the lower realm as suffering is the *ānantarya-mārga* (path of immediate succession).
Contemplating the upper realm as tranquil is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). That is to say, contemplating the lower realm as coarse form is the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*);
contemplating the upper realm as sublime is the path of liberation. Contemplating the lower realm as an obstruction is the uninterrupted path;

contemplating the upper realm as deliverance is the path of liberation. Regarding the mention of "suffering" here, it does not mean that the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhā-vedanā*) is called suffering.
If there were painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), then there would be no painful feeling in the higher realms.

For instance, just as being separated from the desire realm is considered suffering, so too the feelings of joy, pleasure, and equanimity associated with the desire realm are termed "suffering" because they are objects of aversion. This is like the case of the "ground of non-characteristics" (*alakṣaṇabhūmi*); likewise, in the *anāgamya* concentration, one regards the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) as suffering. It is not that the feeling itself is called "suffering," but rather that it is designated as such [due to its nature as an object of aversion].
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "This refers to the factor of 'arising' (*samudaya*), which is produced by the factor of 'ignorance' (*avidyā') below. The Explanation says:
For instance, within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), the factor of ignorance of an unwholesome nature can produce the factor of 'arising' in the First Dhyāna.

The factor of 'arising' in the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) of the First Dhyāna, once it has arisen, is able to suppress the innate delusions of greed and ignorance within the Desire Realm. Question: Is this not yet the preparatory stage?

Regarding the question of how many factors of practice (*pratipadāṅga*) exist within meditative concentration (*samādhi*): the answer is that, for instance, in the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of the first dhyāna, there are nine.
These correspond to the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Thus, there are twenty-seven such factors of practice within these concentrations—three sets of nine—which are capable of producing the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) of the first dhyāna. As for the path of further advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*), it is not fixed.
According to the Abhidharma and other treatises, there are three types of the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*).

First, immediately after the paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*), uninterrupted (*ānantaryamārga*), and liberation (*vimuktimārga*) have arisen from within the *anāgamya* concentration, one gives rise to the scattered (*vyagraka*) wisdom of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*) belonging to the desire realm as the path of superior progress.
Since this path of superior progress consists of the scattered wisdom of hearing and reflection belonging to the desire realm, this path of superior progress does not—

It can induce the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) within the first dhyāna. If this interpretation is adopted, there would be no path of superior progress consisting of meditative concentration and cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*);
rather, only the nine preparatory (*prayoga*), uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and liberation (*vimukti*) paths would constitute cultivated wisdom. Second, it is said:
just as one has previously given rise to the preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths, one subsequently employs the preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths that arise thereafter.

The path of equality (*samatā-mārga*) serves as the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) for each preceding path. Within the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*), there are three, nine, and twenty-seven [moments]. Regarding the "three":

it is said that after first arising the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one then separately enters the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-manaskāra*) as part of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) as the path of superior progress. If the wisdom of cultivation constitutes the path of superior progress, then that itself is the path of superior progress.

One also experiences the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) within the first dhyāna. If one explains it in this way, from the initial stage up to the threshold (*anāgamya*), there are nine paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and nine paths of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*). These constitute thirty-six factors of the branch of cultivation-wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*).
Since the first dhyāna cultivates the threshold concentration, one must specifically give rise to the path of preparation within that initial threshold stage. Within the initial threshold...

There are thus nine paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*). When one arises in the access concentration (*anāgamya*) of the second dhyāna, there are likewise these three kinds of paths of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*);

however, in this case, the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) within the first dhyāna is taken as the path of excellence, because there is no wisdom derived from reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*).

The remaining two causes are as before. Up until the arising of the *ākiṃcanyāyatana* (sphere of nothingness) or the *anāgamya* (preparatory stage), there are likewise three types of *viśeṣamārga* (paths of distinction) for the *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing) arising within the fourth *dhyāna*.

If one arises in the *vijñānānantyāyatana* (sphere of infinite consciousness) and so forth—since within the four formless realms (*ārūpya*) there is only *bhāvanāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from cultivation) and no *śrutamayī* or *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing or reflection)—there are only two types of *viśeṣamārga*. This is for the purpose of employing the successive stages of preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Immediately following [the first], one performs two *viśeṣa-mārgas* (paths of excellence) with the preceding path. One separately arouses the *manaskāra* (mental attention) that realizes characteristics through cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) as the path of excellence;

this applies likewise up to the higher stages. If, from the second stage upward in the *anāgamya-samādhi* (preliminary concentration), one arouses a single *prayoga-mārga* (path of preparation), then one immediately arouses two *ānantarya-mārgas* (uninterrupted paths), two *vimukti-mārgas* (paths of liberation), and two *viśeṣa-mārgas*; this is termed "collectively. Or, one may arouse a single [set].

The preparatory stage (*prayoga*) can give rise to only one path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), which is termed "distinct birth" (*visabhāga-jāti*). This is the same as that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Whether these preparatory stages are taken collectively or individually, [it is asked: herein, when the *anāgamya* dhyāna is produced, there are thirty-six factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*).
Does one definitely attain a single fruit, or does one attain the subsequent thirty-six fruits? Answer: It is not fixed.
If one enters the *anāgamya* concentration with a sharp and intense mind, or through a single factor of the path (*ekāṅga*), one may obtain many fruits.

For example, a bhikṣu who prostrates to the Buddha with a sincere heart may thereby attain the immeasurable status of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). However, this is not the case for one who enters the *anāgamya* concentration with a wandering or distracted mind.
This refers to the multiple practice-branches (*bahulīkāra-aṅga*) which subsequently constitute a single fruit. Regarding the statement "all that is below serves as the objective sphere":

this means that taking all that belongs to the lower realm as an object constitutes an obstruction to the vehicle of suffering (*duḥkha-yāna*). Although one may take all that belongs to the higher realm as an object, this involves taking all that is above as tranquility (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*);
"tranquility, excellence, and renunciation" is also termed "wonderful emergence" (*praṇītaniḥsaraṇa*). Therefore, it is said that by relying on this, one also abandons the lower realm.

Regarding the "limb" (*aṅga*): it is asked, [if] the essence of the sixfold practice of subduing or the Path is wisdom (*prajñā*), and wisdom is able to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower realms, why does this treatise state that the limb of practice belonging to the higher realms is able to subdue the afflictions of the lower stages? Answer:

To speak in terms of reality, the essence of wisdom is indeed able to subdue the afflictions. However, in the present context, it refers to the volition (*cetanā*) associated with wisdom, which is also capable [of such subduing].

The afflictions of the lower stages are suppressed not only by wisdom (*prajñā*), but the mental factors (*caitta*) that arise simultaneously with it, such as the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), are also capable of suppressing the afflictions of the lower stages.
Here, however, we speak of the auxiliary function of association; thus, we state only that the factor of volition (*saṃskāra-aṅga*) can suppress the afflictions of the lower stages.
Therefore, the preceding text states: "The attendants of karma are also designated by the name 'karma,' just as in the case of the fifteen [factors] within the mental consciousness."

Among the various types of karma, there is that which can bring about detachment from desire; this is exclusively wisdom (*prajñā*). Therefore, it is said that the mind (*manas*) can sever the roots of goodness.

This refers to the severing of the roots of goodness by wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). It is said that the mind can reconnect the roots of goodness; this refers to the reconnection of the roots of goodness within a state of doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Although this is another mental factor (*caitta*), it is now designated by the name "arising" (*jāti*) as the specific function of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

This case is likewise. Furthermore, as it is said that the mental consciousness can bind the mind and initiate activity—wherein binding the mind and initiating activity is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*) initiating activity—so too here it is named after its arising. Thus, it coexists simultaneously with wisdom (*prajñā*).

The twelve factors are all capable of subduing the afflictions of the lower stages. The answer regarding their "aspects" (*ākāra*) is that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is as previously explained;
even up to the point where it says "like the sixteen aspects," this is the intended meaning of the response.
However, while all minds and mental factors possess only a single aspect, if it is wisdom (*prajñā*), it possesses six aspects and so forth—how is this so? It is like the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).

There is only one aspect of discernment (*vijñapti*). If feeling (*vedanā*) has only one aspect, and perception (*saṃjñā*) likewise has only one aspect—namely, the aspect of grasping an image—then wisdom (*prajñā*) alone possesses six aspects: suffering, coarseness, hindrance, tranquility, excellence, and detachment.
Therefore, these six aspects are said to belong exclusively to the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*). Furthermore, they are also like the sixteen aspects [of the four noble truths].

Wisdom (*prajñā*). This means that all sixteen aspects, such as suffering, the absence of dust, and so forth, are wisdom. Other mental states and mental factors do not possess these sixteen aspects in association;
rather, it is wisdom alone that receives the name "sixteen aspects. Furthermore, these sixteen aspects encompass both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
However, even within the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), they are not exclusively contemplations of the contaminated sixteen aspects; therefore, the sixteen aspects apply to both.

[They are] outflows (*āsrava*). However, in the present case, all six aspects (*ākāra*) take wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence. Because wisdom is able to discern (*viveka*), it is able to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower stages;
thus, it is wisdom itself, as well as the factors that function simultaneously with wisdom—namely, wisdom and its concomitants—that subdue the afflictions of the lower stages.
Therefore, these six types of aspects take wisdom as their essence, just like the sixteen aspects, such as suffering (*duḥkha*) and impermanence (*anitya*).
The sixteen aspects, such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), non-self (*anātman*), cause (*hetu*), origination (*samudaya*), condition (*pratyaya*), and so forth, all have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence.

Therefore, it is said that these aspects consist of wisdom and its concomitant mental factors (*sahabhū-saṃskāra*). The treatise states: "The factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*) of the higher stages can suppress those of the lower stages."
The Commentary states: "The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter ten, asks: 'Is there one who, relying on the factors of origination (*pratītyasamutpādāṅga*), attains detachment from those very factors?

... up to: 'Neither untainted (*anāsrava*) nor ultimate. That treatise further poses the question: "Is there one who, relying on the superior arising factors, attains detachment from the factors of dependent origination?"

Answer: It is said that by relying on the practice of a higher stage (*bhūmi*), one becomes weary of and detached from the defilements (*kleśa*) of a lower stage. Is this not the ultimate ability to abandon them?

Furthermore, it is not the case that the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)—ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)—of a higher stage can abandon the defilements of a lower stage. This is because the members of ignorance, craving, and grasping in a higher stage are themselves afflictions;

thus, they do not become weary of or detached from the defilements of a lower stage. If the members of existence (*bhava*) in a higher stage were of the nature of karma that perfumes (*vāsana*) [the mind], then they would indeed be "existence" (*bhava*).
The nature of the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*) consists solely of the seeds of karma; they are not the nature of currently manifest karma.

Furthermore, the factors of existence belonging to the higher stages cannot themselves be free from the defilements of the lower stages. However, the present contaminated preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) takes all the factors of existence as its manifest activity.

It is only through this manifest wisdom that one can exercise the six types of mental aspects (*ākāra*), namely, feeling revulsion toward the six lower stages and aspiring toward the higher stages. Yet, regarding the higher...

The five resultant seeds, such as those of the ground-consciousness (*bhūmi-vijñāna*), as well as the factors of birth and aging, are both of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*);

furthermore, they do not transcend the defilements of the lower stages. Since the remaining eleven factors of the higher stages are not the path that acts as an antidote, they cannot transcend the defilements of the lower stages.

Therefore, it is known that only the factor of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) of the higher stages is called the "factor of transcendence. This factor of volitional formations is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*). Only then...
It is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*). These exist only temporarily as a reliance upon the defilements of the lower stages and are not ultimate.

If they were untainted (*anāsrava*), they would not be subsumed under the member of volitional formations. As for the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) maturations (*vipāka*) such as consciousness and so forth, which are capable of ultimately abandoning defilement—[it is asked:

since there is already wisdom (*prajñā*) within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), why is it unable to suppress the afflictions of the lower stages? [The answer is: the member of volitional formations is of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*).

It is able to subdue the afflictions of the lower stages. If the wisdom within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), it does not subdue the afflictions of the lower realms.

Regarding the statement that the desire realm possesses all "concordant conditions" (*sahajāta-pratyaya*): "concordant" means all meanings. If it were the higher realms, one should say it is "partially concordant.
"Concordant arising" (*samutthāna*) refers to the twelve links arising simultaneously and equally. That treatise asks:
As for the statement: "Those [factors] that exist within the outflowing (sāsrava) body—why are they not karma? ...

Why are they not included among the members (aṅga)?"—here, "members" does not refer to the twelve members; rather, it is simply a part that is designated by the name "member. The intended meaning here is this:

if the outflowing factors within the bodies of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) were [to be categorized], why are they not called "of training" or "beyond training"? The answer follows below: if taken collectively from the perspective of...
"Learning" (*śaikṣa*) refers to contaminated wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*), which are also termed "Dharma-learning" (*dharma-śaikṣa*).

If one considers the actual substance (*dravya*), only uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are designated as "learning" or "beyond learning" (*aśaikṣa*). This is consistent with every question and answer in this commentary. The intent of the question is:

why are the contaminated wholesome factors within the person of one in training (*śaikṣa-pudgala*) not subsumed under "learning"? In the response, it is stated that the contaminated wholesome states within the person of one in training...

Because it takes clear knowledge (*vidyā*) as its condition, it is not subsumed under the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*); therefore, it is not equivalent [to the other factors]. Answer: Since it is not a factor of existence, by extension it is also not "learning" (*śaikṣa*).

The Commentary (*Śū*) states: Some explain that in this Mahāyāna system, once one has attained the desire for wholesome dharmas, such a person is called "one in training" (*śaikṣa*). This is the explanation.

It is said: This refers to Master Taisi and Master Shunjing. In their *Commentary on the Yogācārabhūmi*, regarding the aforementioned stages of the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), and the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga-avasthā*)—these three stages are all termed "that which is yet to be known" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), as they are all designated as "those in training" (*śaikṣa*).

Once the mind has been generated, internal ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) no longer create karma that results in total retribution; none of these are triggered by ignorance (*avidyā*), and none constitute the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

As for internal ordinary beings who are heedless, they exclude one type [of ignorance]. Furthermore, even for those in training (*śaikṣa*) whose three trainings have ignorance as their condition, [the same applies].
Regarding the previous statement about "heedless persons within the Dharma," this refers to excluding the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*). What is used [as the condition]?

The other three [types of karma] have ignorance as their condition. That text states that internal factors—namely, non-negligence and the noble trainees—also take the three types of ignorance as their conditions.
What is the difference between these two? Just as with the mind, if internal factors involve negligence, they are all conditioned by ignorance;
likewise, if an internal factor involves a person who is not negligent yet creates meritorious or non-meritorious karma, it is also conditioned by ignorance.
That is to say, taking the three types of ignorance as conditions: if one performs meritorious, immovable karma, that meritorious karma likewise takes the three types of ignorance as conditions;

it also takes the true Dharma and appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) as conditions, and thus there is also a distinction. Although one may understand it in this way, one should further practice the Dharma slightly more.
Once the state of an Ārya has been attained, one gains mastery, and the non-arising of [defilements] through correspondence (*anuloma-samprayoga*) also arises.
This clarifies the manifestation [of karma].

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Furthermore, when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who do not practice heedlessness within the internal dharma perform meritorious actions, up to those for which ignorance does not arise as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), this text refers exclusively to the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*). Taking the True Dharma as a condition, they create [karma] that results in distinct retribution (*vyañjanavipāka*)."

Regarding meritorious and immovable karma: because it gives rise to a mind of appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) which induces the untainted path of vision (*anāsrava-darśanamārga*), it is not said that ignorance serves as its condition.
Although there may be cases where one attains a superior birth in a fortunate realm (*sugati*), these are all categorized as distinct karmic results (*vipāka-karma*).
As for the statement that "taking skillful explanation as a basis," this refers to the mind’s focused pursuit of excellence, taking the wholesome dharmas of the True Dharma as its foundation.

If one is not heedless, while in the stage of accumulation (*sambhāra-avasthā*), one takes the seeds of ignorance as conditions to perform general retributive meritorious and immovable formations (*saṃskāra*).
Regarding this, the *Śu* (Commentary) states: "This is not the [standard] dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)," and further states: "External dharmas and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)."
"...up to: 'It is clearly known that once the desire for wholesome dharmas has departed, it is entirely due to the factors of volitional action (*saṃskāra*).

Regarding this, the preceding commentary states: 'This establishes the stage of accumulation (*sambhāra-avasthā*); [at this stage] one is able to create karma that results in a general retribution (*vipāka*).

Furthermore, the aforementioned commentary all establishes that within the stage of accumulation, one creates karma that results in a general retribution. Among those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the internal Dharma who are not negligent, they do not create [karma that results in a general retribution].

When performing meritorious karma, one takes the three types of ignorance as conditions. However, when performing meritorious or immovable karma, one relies on the true Dharma and appropriate mental attention (yoniśo-manasikāra) induced by the mind and mental factors; thus, one does not take ignorance as a condition.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "Thus, as in the *Nirvedhabhāgīya* [the 'Aids to Penetration'], although the wholesome [karma] is distinct, there is no textual passage definitively establishing that it produces only a collective retribution;

even if it were not a factor of the path of action (*karmapatha*), it would not necessarily fail to be a direct cause for [rebirth]. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says: The following section clarifies the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).

It creates only karma for individual retribution (*pratyekavipāka*). However, if one belongs to the Three Vehicles during the stage of the equipment (*sambhāra*), because the duration of time is long, one is able to create collective [karma].

Regarding distinct karma (*pratyeka-karman*): for those of the Three Vehicles during the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), the time remaining is brief, consisting of only two or three births before they enter the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Therefore, they do not create formative actions that result in collective retribution (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*). It is logically superior to hold that they create only those actions that result in distinct retribution (*asādhāraṇa-vipāka*).
Now, one must not simply say that Noble Ones (*ārya*) do not perform any action; this passage intends to show that such a claim is also untenable according to the Sūtras.

The statement that "Noble Ones do not create karma for total retribution" refers to the stage of preparation (*prayoga-avasthā*). Since they are still ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) at the stage of preparation, it follows that they do create karma for total retribution.
Although the Sūtras state that Noble Ones do not create karma for total retribution, this applies only until they reach the stage of preparation.

Yet, transformation is not something newly created. According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, Chapter Seven, this applies even to those who have not yet seen the Truths, up to the point of performing meritorious and immovable karmic formations (*puṇya-āneñjya-saṃskāra*).

However, within the text of this *Abhidharma*, it is also clarified that for one who practices heedfulness while in the stage of the Requisites (*sambhāra-avasthā*), manifest ignorance does not arise;

rather, such a person performs meritorious and immovable karmic formations that constitute total retribution (*vipāka*) solely by means of their seeds (*bīja*). These very [formations] are what are meant here.
The seed of ignorance is also called "existence through delusion" (*avidyā-bhava*). Now, this seed of ignorance is also a branch of ignorance. The *Śāstra* states:
"By means of the mixed cultivation of *dhyāna*, one utilizes karma from lower realms to be born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, etc. The commentary explains:

"However, there are four kinds of cultivation that serve as a basis (*upakaraṇa*): first, purely impure cultivation, such as when an Arhat, at the end of his life, uses the wisdom of death and rebirth to observe the future."

This causes their practice to progress or their life-span to be extended. Furthermore, when observing sentient beings in the present, if one observes those who harbor no thoughts of benefit toward the Buddha-dharma and do not form the intention to receive future existence, nor are willing to extend their lives—meaning they are free from craving and do not cherish their own bodies—and who, at the point of death, joyfully relinquish the body as if discarding a grave illness, thereby attaining what has never been attained before and entering the nirvana without remainder; if one observes such present cases...

There is benefit. He cherishes his body and, using it as a resource, gives it away as an offering to the great assembly. This enables him to prolong his life, complete his tasks, and maintain the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) without decline.
Desiring to dedicate this merit—arising from the distracted body, speech, and mind of the desire realm—he forms a mental vow: "May this merit cause my life-force and formations to extend.
He then enters the fourth dhyāna, the limit of the contaminated (*sāsrava*). Through the twofold provision of meditative concentration and merit, he prolongs his life-force and formations.

Having emerged from meditative absorption, one issues forth a vow regarding the three karmas to support the life-force and the causes for manifesting the body, so that the resulting fruits may continue without interruption for a long duration.
Furthermore, upon re-entering meditative absorption, one issues a vow to extend this life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) for a hundred years, a kalpa, or more.

This [vow] involves only the contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind supporting the body of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Two types are purely uncontaminated (*anāsrava*): namely, those of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*) among the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta enters exclusively into untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*). He transforms his segmented body (*bheda-kāya*) and enters a transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), or else he uses untainted meditative concentration to support this body.
First, he brings forth through mindfulness a superior and wondrous support; this is the support of the six grades of the body.
[The Buddha] causes [them] to spend many kalpas of body and life over hundreds of thousands of kalpas inquiring about the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Regarding the women such as Yaśodharā and Utpalavarṇā who were granted the prediction of Arhatship and will attain Buddhahood—when will these women abandon their female bodies? Answer:

It is precisely at the moment they are about to receive the *parināmika-kāya* (the transformation body). Even when entering the *parināmika-kāya* from the *aupapaduka-kāya* (segmented body) of a woman, it is permitted that they are able to abandon it.

Feeling [the sensation], one knows the transformation of rebirth and also abandons the female body. Regarding the three bases of transformation, these pertain only to ordinary women who, having cultivated the medium grade of concentration in the first dhyāna and practiced it repeatedly, are born in the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude (Brahmapāriṣadya).

Having cultivated the medium grade of concentration in the first dhyāna and practiced it repeatedly, they are born in the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita). As for cultivating the superior grade, they are born in the Heaven of Great Brahmā (Mahābrahmā). II.

The same applies to the dhyānas. Regarding the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), such as the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and so forth, although there are no three [distinct] heavens, they constitute the four formless heavens.

Within these formless heavens, there are all three grades.
