The practitioners who cultivate the four contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mixed meditations as their provisions—namely, those who have attained the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*)—utilize contaminated and uncontaminated concentrations to provisionally support the karma of the three heavens: the lower Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, and Bṛhatphala heavens.

There are five grades [of practice] by which one is born into the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). If categorized according to the time of mixed cultivation (*vyavakiraṇa*), when one has not yet attained mastery, one enters ten moments of untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) following ten moments of untainted concentration; this is because at the initial stage of practice it is not so.

One enters one moment of tainted concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*) and then enters one moment of untainted concentration, continuing in this manner until entering three moments of untainted concentration, followed by entering three [moments of tainted concentration].

One contemplates the contaminated concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*). Then one enters the three moments of uncontaminated concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), gradually entering one moment of uncontaminated concentration, immediately followed by entering one moment of contaminated concentration, and again entering one moment of uncontaminated concentration; this is called the perfection of the mixed cultivation (*vyavakiraṇa-paripūri*).
Regarding the five grades—namely, the inferior, middling, superior, excellent, and supreme—the first, the inferior grade, consists of the cultivation of three moments of mind:
the first moment is untainted (*anāsrava*), the second is tainted (*sāsrava*), and the third is untainted. By cultivating these three moments of mind, one is reborn in the Avṛha heaven.

Second is the middling grade, which consists of six moments of mind; by generating these, one is reborn in the Atapa heaven. As for the six moments of mind, they consist of four applications of mindfulness...

The fifth thought-moment is with outflows (*sāsrava*); the sixth thought-moment is without outflows (*anāsrava*). The third [category] is the "superior" grade, which means being born into the nine grades [of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens], namely, being born in the Sudarśana Heaven.
Regarding the twelve thoughts: six are without outflows and three are with outflows; this follows the same method of application as before.
The fourth is the "superior-superior" grade, which means there are twelve thoughts, namely, being born in the Sudṛśa Heaven. These twelve thoughts...
This refers to the eight untainted (anāsrava) minds and the four tainted (sāsrava) minds, as previously established. Fifth, there are fifteen minds of the supreme, most excellent category;
one is born in the Heaven of Ultimate Purity (Akaniṣṭha). Among these fifteen minds, ten are untainted and five are tainted.

Question: Within this context, what are the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of both the impure (*sāsrava*) meditative mind and the pure (*anāsrava*) meditative mind? Answer: As for the modes of activity of the impure meditative mind, they function through three types of attention (*manasikāra*): first, attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanasikāra*), which refers to observing the aggregates, bases, and elements, or observing form, blue, and so forth; second, attention to general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*), which refers to [observing] suffering, impermanence, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth. The third is... [the attention to] the sign (*nimittamanasikāra*). Regarding the pure meditative mind, its mode of activity consists solely in the attention to the sign. Why is this? Because it is by means of the attention to the sign that one enters into the state of non-conceptualization. Furthermore, regarding the impure meditative mind, its mode of activity consists in the attention to the sign and the attention to specific characteristics. Why is this? Because it is by means of the attention to the sign that one enters into the state of conceptualization, and it is by means of the attention to specific characteristics that one attains the state of tranquility. Therefore, the impure meditative mind possesses these two modes of activity. However, the pure meditative mind does not possess these two modes of activity. Why is this? Because the pure meditative mind is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). It is by means of the attention to the sign that one enters into the state of non-conceptualization. Therefore, the pure meditative mind possesses only the single mode of activity consisting in the attention to the sign. Consequently, the impure meditative mind possesses three modes of activity, while the pure meditative mind possesses only one. This is the distinction between the two. Furthermore, regarding the impure meditative mind, its mode of activity consists in the attention to the sign, the attention to specific characteristics, and the attention to general characteristics. Why is this? Because it is by means of the attention to the sign that one enters into the state of conceptualization; it is by means of the attention to specific characteristics that one attains the state of tranquility; and it is by means of the attention to general characteristics that one attains the state of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
