Regarding the three aspects: the contemplation of the white bone through the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*) consists of impure meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*) that takes only the aspects of suffering, impermanence, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth as its objects.
Question: Do Bodhisattvas in the tenth stage, who are born in the palace of Maheśvara, practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna (*vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna*)?

Answer: No. It is the fruit of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who, by means of the mixed cultivation, utilizes the karma of the lower stages to produce a body of fragmented birth (*prādeśika-kāya*) within the five [desire realms].

Regarding birth in the Śuddhāvāsa [Heavens]: if a bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment is certain to be born within the fourth dhyāna, they will take on a *pariṇāmika-kāya* (body of transformation) in whichever of the three heavens—Anabhraka and so forth—they are born into. Once the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are fulfilled, they then employ their compassion and vows to support those below;
thus, through the residual karma from the three heavens such as Anabhraka, they manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and proceed to the palace of Maheśvara.

If it is a Bodhisattva of gradual enlightenment who has turned their mind from the Two Vehicles, since they still possess a residual birth-body (*janma-deha*) within the Desire Realm, they receive a body of transformation (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) within that Desire Realm.

Once the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are fulfilled, because they look toward the Desire Realm through compassionate vows, they employ intermediate karma to manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and proceed to the palace of Maheśvara.
If the Second Dhyāna is described as the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), there too are those of the Two Vehicles.

The "turning of the mind" refers to the bodhisattva of gradual awakening (*anupūrva-abhisamaya*). Within one of the heavens of the four dhyānas, they take birth and receive a body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Subsequently, in the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), according to the previous account, they are born in the palace of Maheśvara. As the aforementioned treatise states:

"Either by means of the sixth consciousness, the eighth consciousness is drawn forth by compassion and vows to become untainted (*anāsrava*)," and so forth. Therefore, it is known that the bodhisattva of the tenth stage does not practice the mixed cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

If one who has attained the fruit of Non-returner possesses a body of fragmented birth (*paricchinna-śarīra*), then by practicing the mixed meditative absorptions (*dhyāna-vyavakiraṇa*), they are born in the five Pure Abodes;

because this is an actual birth, it is called "birth. If a Bodhisattva, having already received [the body] and undergone the transformation of the body (*parivṛtti-kāya*), then whether receiving birth or not receiving birth, merely going [to those realms] is called "birth.
Although those from Stream-enterers up to Arhats receive the body of transformation (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), since they only perceive... [it is as follows].
In one set of four continents, the small transformation Buddhas and those bodhisattvas who have attained sudden enlightenment prior to the [first] bhūmi see the same.

If they reach the four roots of goodness (catvāri kuśalamūlāni), then in each of the three realms there is a great transformation Buddha. Although those of the two vehicles undergo the transformation of change (*parināmikī cyuti*), what is seen by the bodies of sudden-enlightenment bodhisattvas, who are still in the stage of fragmented existence (*bhavasaṃdhi*), is identical for all Buddhas; these are all termed "prior to the bhūmis. If, from the first bhūmi onward...
What was seen above applies equally to the Buddha in the form of the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).

The Commentary states: "Regarding the karma of suffering as a collective retribution and the seeds of conventional expression (*nāma-vyavahāra*): at the time they are spoken, one has already created present karma and the seeds of receiving past names.
Because these are conjoined with and attached to the karma that produces and evokes [results], they support the karma of the lower realms and..."
One gives rise to the names and phrases [of existence] and is born in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).

Once the four fruits [of the path] have been attained, as well as during the stages of the contaminated mind prior to the seventh ground, and the contaminated five consciousnesses from the eighth ground upward—within these states, although new perfumations do indeed form the seeds for the five fruits of names and phrases, one can no longer newly initiate karma.
Although that which is newly acquired... [five]... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment. The translation reflects the available portion.)

Regarding the fruit: because there is no mutual resonance between names and words and karma, this term "name-seed" (nāma-bīja) establishes that there is no commonality [with karma] and thus cannot produce a manifest state (*pravṛtti*).
As for the previous interpretation—that "immovable" (*aniñjya*) refers only to the name of the stage—it actually applies to all [stages]. However, the previous explanation states:

"Because of the fixed nature of the object, and so forth, none of these possess such [karmic] activity. This interpretation is based on the fact that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can cause the mind to dwell single-pointedly upon its object.

A single object is called "immovable" (*āneñja*). If one understands that the subtle meditative absorptions (*sūkṣma-samādhi*) can cause the mind to be focused exclusively on a single object, then the eight higher dhyāna stages are all termed "immovable.
This is to say that the scope [of the term] is broadened. As for the phrase "if it is not different and furthermore immovable...

this too should be so," however, since the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is already admitted as a state of distraction (*vikṣepa*), it is included within the range of the [four] form realms (*rūpadhātu*). In humans...

It is experienced within the middle [realm], for this is a scattered stage (*viprakṛṣṭa-bhūmi*). However, since the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) is a different stage, it attains [the experience] as being of the same stage, yet it is distinct in its location within feeling (*vedanā*).

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "If it were not in a different place, it would be called 'immovable feeling' (*aniñjya-vedanīya*). This is mostly explained as being like the karma of hell, which cannot be altered;

yet it is still permitted that heavy fetters (*bandhana-guru*) constitute the bodily experience of an Arhat. The Explanation says: The *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states that it cannot be otherwise.

Regarding the statement that "experiencing [retribution] in this life is called immovable karma," this is said in terms of the majority of cases, just as it is said that hellish karma cannot be altered.

Nevertheless, the possibility of transforming hellish karma is permitted; this too is said in terms of the majority of cases. If one follows the scriptural text, it states that upon attaining the fruit of Arhatship, one may experience the fires of hell.

According to the principle, however, this refers to those in the first two fruits (Srotāpanna and Sakṛdāgāmin). Because they have not yet abandoned desire within the Desire Realm, there remains the potential for evil.
Because of the nature of karma and so forth, Non-returners and Arhats certainly do not undergo retribution.

If it is said within the Mahāyāna that an Arhat may experience the suffering of hell, then how can it be explained within the Mahāyāna that the seeds of an Arhat’s evil karma have already been completely severed?
Furthermore, since there are no past or future evil karmas, how could an Arhat experience the suffering of hell?
Moreover, it is not as in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), where there exists that which does not belong to bodily karma yet can induce a result.
For example, when a person receives the *prātimokṣa* vows, although these [moments] are momentary and each preceding moment enters the past, they constantly give rise to subsequent dharmas.
The name belongs to the body. For example, when a person’s life comes to an end, there is the relinquishing of this [name] that induces the *prātimokṣa* vows;

once the *prātimokṣa* vows have induced [their cessation], the aggregates fall away into the past, and the name no longer belongs to the bodily action. Although these *prātimokṣa* vows have fallen into the past, [they remain].

Yet it does not belong to bodily action (*kāyakarman*). Because the maturation (*vipāka*) of the karma that brings about rebirth has not yet been completed, there can be an Arhat who still possesses evil karma for which he must undergo suffering in hell.
Furthermore, according to the Sarvāstivāda, there are dharmas that cannot be made to be seen, nor can they be made to arise.
If, as in the Mahāyāna, the seeds of evil karma perish in each moment and are produced anew in each subsequent moment, then if one were to give rise to the Noble [Path]...
The Path. That is, to exhaust all sensations without remainder. How could an Arhat be subject to the experience of suffering?

Therefore, it is known that for the first two fruits [of the path], sensation is not present; rather, non-sensation is superior. As for the tenth-stage Bodhisattva, they shall be born in a favorable realm.
Even until they attain birth there, according to reality, it is merely due to their nature that they are said not to be newly born in that place. In that treatise:

Since there is the statement regarding "birth," the Master [of the Commentary] follows that treatise in stating that the six words induce the eight consciousnesses, whereby one attains birth in the Palace of Great Sovereignty (Maheśvara).
Although there are thirteen layers within this single location, they do not obstruct one another; what is the nature of this matter?

First, it refers to those who act as the two vehicles prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). Regarding the explanation of the "lesser transformation" (*kṣudra-nirmāṇa*) within the *Unsurpassed* (*anāgamya*) stage, it is said within that lesser transformation: "Within it..."

There are outflows and defilements. That which is called a "pure kalpa" refers to the time when the aeon is increasing; that which is called "defiled" refers to the time when it is declining. These two serve for the purpose of transformation.

Within the great transformation land of a Bodhisattva of the four roots of goodness situated in a single trichiliocosm, others—that is, the devas during the period of increase—are entirely pure devas.
Next, the lands received by the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are considered to have ten layers. Furthermore, as for the Tathāgata himself...

Regarding the Land of Enjoyment (*saṃbhogakāya-kṣetra*), because it consists of one hundred and one layers, there are thirteen layers. To take, for example, a single trichiliocosm, there are four heavens.

Within these four heavens, there is always a minor cloud of emanation (*pariṇāmika-nirmāṇa-megha*). Bodhisattvas who practice their preparatory applications (*prayoga*) in the same location constitute one such minor cloud of emanation, while those who encompass many others constitute one major cloud of emanation (*mahā-nirmāṇa-megha*).
Thus, one minor cloud of emanation serves as one major cloud of emanation; however, this is not the case for those within the minor clouds of emanation themselves.

One sees the inhabitants of the transformation lands. One sees the inhabitants of the transformation lands; one is able to see those within a small transformation land. While those above can see, those below cannot see those above; after this, it is the same for all.
Furthermore, although a Bodhisattva of the first stage (prathamabhūmi) shares the same location as a hundred great transformation lands, they perceive them as one.
This is what is called the "other-enjoyment" (parasaṃbhoga) of a Bodhisattva of the first stage. It is thus. Regarding the second stage, within one...

Regarding the ten locations of the first bhūmi, if one refers to the *parabhogakṣetra* (land of enjoyment for others), it is said that a single [location] is transformed as the dwelling place for a bodhisattva of the second bhūmi, and so on up to the tenth bhūmi.
Because this is explained both generally and specifically, there is no mutual obstruction among them.
It is certainly not the case that two [bodhisattvas] of the first bhūmi occupy the same location; they would obstruct one another if they were in the same place.
There is obstruction. Up to this point, it has been said that there can never be two bodhisattvas of the tenth stage dwelling in the same place because they would obstruct one another;

thus, even two cannot exist together. Now, the *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Transformation) states that they can indeed dwell in the same place, which implies that within a single cloud there may be many bodhisattvas of the same class, such as those of the first stage. If there were two bodhisattvas of the first stage... one... [text fragment].
One is established here in this world-system. Thus the treatise says: "Or in another world-system. This refers to the various pure and wondrous clouds of this realm;

it means that some are in the first bhūmi in another world-system, some are in the first bhūmi in this world-system, some are in the second bhūmi in another world-system, some are in the second bhūmi in this world-system, and so on up to the tenth bhūmi—it is the same for all. Therefore, they are of the same kind.

They cannot occupy the same location. If one speaks of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) as being identical, they may indeed share common characteristics. Regarding the Buddha’s own enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), it is said that they reside in the same place;
regarding the transformation enjoyment body (*nirmāṇasaṃbhogakāya*), it is said that they are inclusive. As for the self-enjoyment body, it is defined by mutual non-obstruction.

However, to dispel [the misconception regarding] the other-enjoyment body (*parasaṃbhogakāya*), it is stated that this is precisely the tenfold pure clouds of the Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage. Question: Regarding the self-enjoyment bodies of the many Buddhas...

It is said: "They attain identity in one place. If they attain identity with the Buddhas in one place, or if they themselves possess their own self-enjoyment clouds, they attain identity in one place because all these pervade the Dharma-realm. As for the aforementioned twelve layers of clouds, they have distinct domains and sizes;
therefore, although they are of different types, they exist in the same location. This is like the dimensions of a small manifested cloud, which is indeed one.

The four continents are called the "Great Transformation Cloud" (*mahā-nirmāṇa-megha*), which is equivalent to one trichiliocosm. If it is the "Cloud" of the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is equivalent to a hundred trichiliocosms.
This continues up to the tenth stage, each having its own specific extent. Therefore, those of the same category cannot occupy the same location.
However, a Bodhisattva in the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*) perceives both the small transformation clouds prior to the stages and the great transformation clouds.

It says: "If one is at the first stage (bhūmi), one sees the purity of that very stage, as well as the minor [realms] prior to that stage. However, when the great transformative clouds appear, one sees the three layers;
when the seven [clouds] appear, one sees below them."

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Regarding the distinction of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is said that [afflictions] either produce only meritorious or immovable karma, while those on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) produce non-meritorious karma.

The *Vyākhyā* (Exegesis) explains: How could it be that the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) on the path of seeing are exclusively of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala-svabhāva*) and thus able to produce meritorious or immovable karma?
Rather, the afflictions on the path of cultivation—whether they are of an unwholesome nature or of a hindered-neutral nature (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-svabhāva*)—are able to produce non-meritorious karma.

The *Śāstra* says: "Furthermore, among these two explanations, it is stated that the ignorance (*avidyā*) which directly initiates karma is severed only by the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). The commentary explains:

"In this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, there are two masters who both state that the ignorance which directly initiates karma is severed only by the Path of Seeing, while that which assists in initiating karma is not fixed.
That person later says: 'The delusion of the immature and the confusion regarding the first eight sufferings... [and so on]... until the remainder is severed by the Path of Seeing.'"
Regarding the phrase "The refutation is not so": all the preceding passages consist of the Master Tàifǎjǐng and others establishing principles and citing scriptural texts to prove their eight points.
The Commentator (Sūzhǔ) previously applied his critique to the latter two masters; therefore, he did not record their names by origin, but merely set forth their incorrect interpretations.
The refutation begins with the words "In the Commentary, it is not so," and from this point onward constitutes the work of the Commentator himself.
The eight types of suffering begin with birth and extend to the five types of sensory suffering. Is this because the aforementioned worldly sufferings are identical?

Even up to the point of generating non-meritorious karma, those who engage in the worldly—this is the intended meaning of this passage. However, within this treatise, it speaks of being deluded regarding the worldly.

The performance of non-meritorious action (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*) is due to delusion regarding the conventional; the performance of meritorious and immovable actions (*puṇyāneñjyābhisaṃskāra*) is likewise explained in terms of the performance of karma.
One performs meritorious and non-meritorious actions through delusion regarding the three types of suffering and the seven types of suffering, which is termed "delusion regarding the conventional.

One performs immovable actions through delusion regarding the superior fruits of humans and devas, which is termed "delusion regarding the ultimate" (*paramārtha-moha*). The *Abhidharma* treatises state that the first seven types of suffering are called "suffering of delusion regarding the conventional."

The eighth suffering is called ultimate suffering (*paramārtha-duḥkha*). This refers to the eight types of suffering and, by extension, to difficult-to-understand meanings and easily comprehended Dharma-gates, thereby distinguishing between the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate.

Furthermore, minor and subtle non-meritorious actions (*apuṇya*) and so forth are termed "conventional" even though their names are identical; thus, while the names are the same, their meanings differ.
If it were not so, then among the aforementioned seven types of suffering, why would one not create non-meritorious karma?

If one does not interpret it as explained previously—that which is below [the seventh] is the explanation—since there is already the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), there is also the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).

Among the eight sufferings, the sixth and seventh are the suffering of change. Since the previous seven sufferings have been explained, these are conventional; that which is capable of creating non-meritorious karma is what follows.

That which is experienced within the third dhyāna is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). If there were such suffering of change therein, why would those in the three lower dhyānas not create non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya-karman*)?
However, according to the ultimate meaning, it is only when one is born from within those three lower dhyānas into the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that [suffering arises].
All those born [there] attain the first dhyāna concentration, and so on, up until they attain the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Later, when encountering conditions that lead to regression from the concentrations of the fourth dhyāna and above, their active mental states immediately descend to the levels of the lower three dhyānas.

It is therefore said that within these lower three dhyānas, there is likewise the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks. Furthermore, it is taught in the Hīnayāna that the body of an Arhat may reside in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), where [the following] is fully present:
Due to five kinds of conditions for retrogression, one born in the desire realm may encounter conditions for retrogression and may also undergo the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).

However, if one is born within the form or formless realms, there are no instances of retrogression from the meditative attainments obtained; likewise, there is neither retrogression nor the refinement of faculties.
The sixth and seventh are the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). That is to say, even within the lower three dhyānas, there is the suffering of change.
Furthermore, how could the evil destinies lack the eighth, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)? And so on, up to:

since those who perform meritorious and immovable actions also experience the eighth—the suffering of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-duḥkha*)—within the three evil states, why is it that one does not perform meritorious or immovable karma within the three evil destinies? Question: Why?

In the sūtras and śāstras, when clarifying the twelve links [of dependent origination], it is stated only that "name-and-form conditions the six sense bases" (ṣaḍāyatana), and not that "name-and-form conditions the six elements" (ṣaḍdhātu) or the aggregates (skandha).

Furthermore, it is asked: it is stated only that "name" refers to the four non-material aggregates (arūpin-skandha), and again, it does not mention the bases (āyatana) or the elements (dhātu). Furthermore, it is asked:

It is said that only the "consciousness link" (*vijñāna-aṅga*) is mentioned, not the "mind" or "mental faculty" links. Regarding the example of afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and so forth arising from [the same] conditions as views:
if craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises as an intervening factor during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it arises by taking the future body as its object, not by taking views as its object.

If craving arises within the context of discrimination, it arises by taking views as its object. This is just as the preceding text stated: "taking the views of its own level as its object," which should be applied accordingly in each case.

Regarding the inquiry into greed, hatred, and pride: as for the arousal of karma, there is one class [of afflictions]—namely, the ignorance associated with the path of seeing—which can directly arouse the karma that produces the general retribution of the five destinies.

Furthermore, there is another class of afflictions associated with both the paths of seeing and cultivation which can assist in arousing the karma that produces the general retribution of humans and devas.

Moreover, there is yet another class of afflictions associated with both the paths of seeing and cultivation which can directly arouse the karma that produces the specific retribution of humans and devas. And there is still another class...

The defilements of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are capable of assisting in the production of the collective retributive karma (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka-karma*) that leads to the three evil destinies.

Furthermore, there is a class of afflictions belonging to both the paths of seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*) that can also produce the specific karma (*asādhāraṇa-karma*) for the three evil destinies. Now, regarding the "intercalary" defilements (*upasaṃhāra-lobha*), there is also a class of those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) that is capable only of directly moistening the karma of the five destinies.
Moreover, there is a class of afflictions belonging to both the paths of seeing and cultivation that is capable only of assisting in the moistening of human [karma].
There are certain afflictions of the paths of seeing and cultivation that can only assist and moisten the specific retributive karma of humans and devas.
Furthermore, there are certain afflictions of the path of seeing or [cultivation] that can only assist and moisten the general retributive karma of the three evil destinies.

Regarding the nine types of mental life-faculties (*jīvitendriya*) produced by the minds of cultivation within the three realms: Question: For what reason does the treatise establish these nine solely in reference to the three realms?

Regarding the mind at the end of life (*cyuti-citta*), it is not established in terms of the nine stages (*bhūmi*), the five destinies (*gati*), or the four modes of birth (*yoni*). Answer: The treatise explains this in terms of general characteristics;
there are only nine minds within the three realms (*tridhātu*). Furthermore, regarding the five destinies and four modes of birth, it may also be said:
if one calculates by way of the nine stages, there would be nine times nine, or eighty-one minds; if one calculates by way of the five destinies, there would be twenty-five. Now, as for this mind...

Approximately four types of birth constitute sixteen moments of mind. Among these, the innate craving (*sahaja-tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) that arise simultaneously with those [moments] are abandoned only through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

However, according to the former masters, because innate ignorance arises simultaneously with the arising of innate craving, both the craving and the ignorance occurring at that same time are the defilements that moisten rebirth (*janma-sneha-kleśa*), and are thus abandoned only by the path of cultivation.
Question: What about the innate pride (*sahaja-māna*) and the views of self-existence (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*)?

It is also capable of moistening rebirth. Why, then, is ignorance (avidyā) alone singled out for mention? Answer: Although other afflictions such as pride (māna) and so forth are not invariably present, ignorance is said to be invariably present throughout all defiled states of mind.

Regarding the "two difficulties" concerning the matters discussed below: the first difficulty concerns the link of ignorance (*avidyā*), and the second difficulty concerns the links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*).
The *Shu* (Commentary) states:

"If he should offer a defense, saying that the tenth fascicle of the *Mahā-śāstra* merely relies on the 'extreme' case and speaks according to the majority," the *Jie* (Exegesis) explains: [as follows].

The first master’s *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states: "Regarding the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) as having abandoned 'one portion' of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*), this is said according to the majority [of cases].

Excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*), the remaining nine links are abandoned through both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). This is the intention of the former master."

The first teacher asserts that only the primary ignorance which assists in the production of karma is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), while only the primary moisture (*upakleśa*) that assists in the maturation of rebirth is abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
This contradicts the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*. As for the second teacher, he maintains that both the primary and the auxiliary [ignorances] are abandoned accordingly.

It is taught that ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are common to both what is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). The second master follows that treatise. Question:

Regarding the four types of grasping, why is it that the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭi-upādāna*) and the grasping of precepts and vows (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa-upādāna*) are not included among the other types of grasping?

If the grasping of desire (*kāma-upādāna*) is also common to both abandonment through seeing and abandonment through cultivation, and if the grasping of the doctrine of self (*ātma-vāda-upādāna*)—which is the view of a transitory collection (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*)—is also common to both types of abandonment, then why are the two graspings of "I" (*ātman*) and "mine" (*ātmiya*) abandoned solely through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)?
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "It is not only the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) that can project karma leading to the miserable realms (*apāya*).

For the afflictions abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are also capable of projecting karma leading to the happy realms of humans and gods (*sugati*). If one were to argue that it is only karma that produces specific retributions (*pratyeka-vipāka*) for humans and gods which is projected by cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and that [the afflictions of the path of seeing] do not project [karma for] humans and gods at all, the former master offers this defense: "However, the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are indeed capable of projecting [karma for] humans and gods."

Regarding karma that results in specific retribution (*pratiniyata-vipāka-karma*): if one perceives the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it may give rise to karma that produces the general retribution (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*) of humans and devas; this thus encompasses both general and specific retribution. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* does not state that discriminating afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*) give rise to the fundamental karma of humans and devas, but rather says that discriminating afflictions give rise to karma leading to the three evil destinies. This implies that the specific retribution karma of the evil destinies should be abandoned through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Furthermore, when the treatise discusses only general retribution, it refers to the following: [The text continues with a passage on the relationship between the nature of phenomena, the path, and the cessation of suffering. In summary, the distinction between general and specific retribution is established based on whether the resulting fruit is shared across categories or restricted to a particular realm of existence.

Thus, while the Path of Seeing primarily eliminates the seeds of the general retribution of the three realms, the Path of Cultivation is required to eliminate the seeds of specific retribution within those realms, particularly those pertaining to the evil destinies. This demonstrates the progressive refinement of the practitioner's realization as they traverse the stages of the path.

This passage represents a later master challenging a former master. If it were as the former master said, then afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) would only be able to produce karma for distinct retributions as humans or devas;
afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation would not be able to produce karma for distinct retributions in the three evil destinies.
Since afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation can indeed produce [retribution] in the three evil destinies, we know that the *Mahā-śāstra* speaks only of merit and only of merit.

Since the five retributions are collectively termed "total retribution" (vipāka), we know that those which assist in producing the total retribution of the evil destinies are also exclusively the afflictions of conceptual discrimination (vikalpa-kleśa).

That [text] merely states that karma leading to the evil destinies follows from conceptual discrimination; however, the afflictions of the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-heya-kleśa) can also assist in producing the karma for the total retribution of humans and devas.

The treatise states: "That which links rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) is precisely that which unites with suffering. To unite with suffering means that, through craving and grasping, the five fruits are moistened, thereby causing the succession of future bodies to continue without interruption.
Therefore, regarding the karma that properly initiates the linking of rebirth, it is only when one perceives continuity combined with intensity [that it functions].
Furthermore, as for the statement that there is no contradiction when speaking in terms of the majority, this is reconciled within the text of this treatise.
Regarding the two treatises, the *Abhidharma* and the *Yogācārabhūmi*, both agree on the following:

the ignorance that gives rise to the general karma for rebirth in the heavenly realms, as well as the ignorance that gives rise to the general retributive karma for the three evil destinies, are both exclusively abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*). The *Abhidharma* states:
"The two types of evil—conventional and ultimate—are both auxiliaries abandoned by seeing. This is not subject to regression. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* likewise [confirms this].
It is said: If it is one who assists in the development [of the teaching], *Cheng weishi lun shu chao*, Scroll Fourteen, Part One;
*Cheng weishi lun shu chao*, Scroll Fourteen, Part Two.
Generally speaking, karma that produces collective retribution (saṃvartanīya-karma) pertains to both what is abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya) and what is abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).

Furthermore, karma that assists in producing the specific retributions of humans and devas also pertains to both abandonment by seeing and abandonment by cultivation; this is because innate (sahaja) afflictions that arise spontaneously can also assist in producing the collective and specific retributions of humans and devas.
However, the ignorance (avidyā) that assists in producing the collective retribution of the miserable realms (durgati) is abandoned solely by the path of seeing, because...

Only when one gives rise to intense afflictions (*kleśa*) born of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) can they serve as the auxiliary cause for projecting the general retributive karma (*vipāka-karma*) leading to the miserable destinies (*apāya*), as well as the specific retributive karma leading to the miserable destinies.

While these afflictions generally include those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*), the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that only afflictions arising from conceptual discrimination can project the conduct leading to the miserable destinies. This passage [refers to] precisely that.

Regarding the three evil destinies of the subterranean realm and the three evil destinies among humans—these two types of three evil destinies are all brought about by the afflictions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), which assist in the manifestation of the two types of retribution for the three evil destinies;
this is because the karma that constitutes their collective retribution is entirely abandoned through the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
The commentary states: "Those [afflictions] are exclusively afflictions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

They give rise to the karma that produces the specific retributions of the two evil destinies, as they pertain to both what is abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) and what is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Question: Are the eight classes of beings, such as the *asuras*, abandoned by insight? Answer: [They are.]

All of these are abandoned through the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Having attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), one will never again receive a non-deva body or the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*).
These are mutually abandoned through the worldly wisdom of seeing (*laukika-jñāna*). They are abandoned through seeing because they arise from the discrimination of mutual false views.

As for the long-lived devas (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva*), this refers to the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñi-sattva-deva*), as it includes the birth of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Regarding the four dhyānas and the four form heavens (*rūpa-dhātu*), with the exception of the noble ones (*ārya*)...
Those such as certain external worldlings (*bāla*) are all termed "long-lived gods" (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva*).

These worldlings, because they cannot attain [the path] while within the two upper realms (*ūrdhva-dhātu*), must necessarily enter the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) from the state of a worldling while in the Desire Realm (*kāma-dhātu*).
There is no entry into the Path of Seeing in the two upper realms; one does not leap over the first two stages from the level of a worldling while in those two upper realms.
As for the fruit, one attains the third fruit. This is because, compared to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), one has transcended the first and second fruits;
thus, this dharma attains an increased fruit within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). For those ordinary beings of the two upper realms, these are all difficult stages.
Furthermore, the five *pañca-śaka* are all categorized as hungry ghosts among humans. These five *pañca-śaka* are all called *pandaka*.
"Yellow" (*panda*) means "middle"; because they guard the center of the inner palace, they are called *pañca-śaka* in the newly translated scriptures.
In the old *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, he is called a *caṇḍāla*. A *caṇḍāla* is one who drives away the women of the inner quarters. The new translation calls him a *śvapaca*.
According to a high interpretation, the palace gates of ancient emperors were all coated with yellow orpiment (*haritāla*) to signify their noble lineage, while those of commoners used red earth.
Furthermore, in front of the halls of ancient sovereigns, the ground was always covered with pearl-dust (*vālukā*). Thus it was established.

This is called "red. Among the karmas that produce total retribution, there are both the primary and the auxiliary; even for those of the upper and lower realms, there are likewise the primary and the auxiliary.

The auxiliary consists of what precedes and follows; these preceding and following auxiliaries are able to trigger the karma. Question: If it triggers rebirth in the evil destinies, does it also involve greed, hatred, and delusion?
The treatise states: "Regarding the limb of ignorance (*avidyā*), that which directly initiates karma is exclusively abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). Answer:

Although craving, hatred, and so forth can also directly initiate the karma for the general retribution of the three evil destinies, ignorance pervades both meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable formations (*saṃskāra*).
For this reason, the treatise specifically mentions ignorance.
The Commentary states: "The initiation of karma may consist solely of seeds, because [karmic factors] such as non-negligence continue to arise as manifest [phenomena] until the time of death.
The Explanation states: This contradicts the scriptural passage which says that karma and afflictions are seeds; there are indeed sacred teachings that state this.

This refers specifically to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the internal dharma. Regarding those who are "heedful," they produce meritorious or immovable karma by means of the seeds of ignorance.
Alternatively, in the Noble Teachings, it is said that there are "seeds" for birth in the *asaṃjñisattva* heaven;

this refers to the seeds of one who has attained the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), explained in terms of the seeds nourishing rebirth. Furthermore, as previously stated in the seventh fascicle regarding the *asaṃjñisattva* heaven, the first master explains "birth" [in this context].
In the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), as well as in those cases where neither mind nor mental factors arise, only the seeds (*bīja*) provide the moisture for rebirth.

It can be said that for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) within the internal dharma who is not heedless, karma is initiated solely by means of seeds. Regarding the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is the seeds of non-associated ignorance (*asamprayukta-avidyā*) that properly initiate karma.
If one is an ordinary person within the internal dharma who assists in initiating karma, this refers to the ten preceding moments of thought.
Regarding the time of the remote cause (*dūre-hetu-samutthāna*), it is also the time of the momentary cause (*kṣaṇa-samutthāna*).

Furthermore, at the time of simultaneous arising (*sahaja*), there must be the manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*) which assists in the production of karma; therefore, it is called the "remote cause. This is because [ignorance] is also present at that time.

Moreover, when this refers to those who have attained the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*), humans, or those emerging from the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and who produce birth through the maturation of seeds (*bīja-paripuṣṭi*), this is based on the actual maturation of birth. If it concerns assisting in its accomplishment...
Regarding the non-returner (*anāgāmin*): even before the end of their life, they may still give rise to active afflictions (*kleśa*) that are capable of assisting in the prolongation of rebirth.

The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "The nature of form (*rūpa*) is not defiled; this [affliction] is severed, which applies universally to all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). The *Jie* (Exegesis) explains:

This statement means that if the nature of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) were not defiled, there would be no phenomenon that constitutes a binding condition. Thus, what is severed is not a severance of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If it concerns the mind...
The nature of mental factors (*caitta*) is defiled. Mind and mental factors are subsumed under the category of abandonment by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*). Question:

Just as one’s own eighth consciousness, in the same location as another person’s body, transforms into the supporting sensory objects (*bhautika-rūpa*), so too do the six preceding consciousnesses of one’s own body take as their object the mind that has extinguished afflictions.

From the eighth consciousness upward, even when it transforms into the *nirbhāsa* (objective image) of the sensory objects (*viṣayapratibimba*), can it constitute the meaning of being bound by conditions? Furthermore, [the questioner] asks:

Does this mean that the meaning of being bound by conditions is established when afflictions bind the immediate *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect), or does it mean that the meaning of being bound by conditions is established when afflictions bind the original object (*mūla-vastu*)?
If it were only the case that the immediate *nimittabhāga* of each of the first seven consciousnesses constitutes being bound by conditions individually, then its...

The objective essence (bhāva) of the eighth consciousness should not be bound individually. If it is considered a condition by way of its objective essence, then the external physical environment (rūpa-pratibimba) belonging to another’s body should be called "bound" (baddha), as it follows the objects of those seven consciousnesses—whether tainted (sāsrava), wholesome (kuśala), or otherwise. If that is the case, [the objection remains].
In this context, when a defiled mind takes a wholesome object or an unobscured-neutral object as its focus, that very object is the "object-condition of bondage" (*ālambana-bandhana*).

This is because wholesome and neutral objects are not themselves bound by others; rather, it is the subject that binds them. Thus, the binding power of the subject is subsumed under the category of the "object-condition of bondage.
If a defiled mind takes a defiled or obscured-neutral phenomenon as its object, it is [bound] by its own lower [level].

The nature of the fetter of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) pertains to the faculties (*indriya*). This is because the very essence (*svabhāva*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that serve as the objects of perception (*ālambana*) constitutes the fettering dharma itself;

it does not depend upon the afflictions that act as the perceiving subjects (*ālambaka*) to constitute a fetter. However, unwholesome (*akuśala*) and obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) dharmas are precisely the fetter of association.

The fetter of association is subsumed within the "nature" (*svabhāva*) discussed in the subsequent question. Yet, the *Mahāyāna-pañcavastuka* states: "Since they are neutral (*avyākṛta*), they are the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*)."
Among these, the afflictions [of the first five consciousnesses] can only take the five types of indeterminate sensory objects as their objects.

If they are the afflictions of the sixth consciousness, they can take dharmas of the three natures as their objects. Within the afflictions of the seventh consciousness, they take indeterminate objects.

Among these afflictions within the seven consciousnesses, taking Bodhisattvas and others as objects constitutes being bound by the object of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*). Furthermore, in this context, the general objects perceived by the seven consciousnesses are—

The five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) within one's own continuum, as well as wholesome and indeterminate phenomena, constitute the meaning of "bondage" (*bandhana*). Furthermore, this does not refer to the seven consciousnesses themselves.

Rather, by taking the wholesome and indeterminate natures of the five sense-objects belonging to another's continuum as their objects, they become "object-bondage" (*ālambana-bandhana*). The treatise states:

"One does not become 'with-outflow' (*sāsrava*) due to bondage by another, nor does one become 'without-outflow' (*anāsrava*) due to liberation from another. This refers to the time when afflictions exist within the seventh consciousness. At that time, its...

The eight consciousnesses are also attained [in this context]. Regarding the statement "the attainment of the severance of the bonds of objects," it does not mean that they are attained through severance.

The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Regarding the 'attainment of various afflictions,' this means that when the seventh consciousness gives rise to afflictions, up until the time the afflictions of the seventh consciousness are severed, the dharmas of the six consciousnesses and so forth each attain severance. The explanation says: This is the first interpretation within this *Śū*. It concerns the outflows (*āsrava*).
Regarding the phrase "both are called 'mixed' with those afflictions": this also refers to wholesome states that are shared with transgressions.

In the commentary (*shu*) immediately following, from the point where it says "furthermore, that which arises intermittently is termed 'mixed'," up to "that which arises interspersed with outflows (*āsrava*) by its very nature is termed 'mixed,'" [the meaning is explained].

The commentary explains: This second interpretation regarding "intermingling with those afflictions" means that within the first six consciousnesses, wholesome states and non-obscured neutral states are termed "intermingled" because they arise in alternation—preceding or following—the afflictions.
Due to the poisonous power of the afflictions, these preceding and succeeding wholesome and neutral states that have arisen all become of the nature of being outflowing (*sāsrava*).
This is called "intermingling with those afflictions. An external objection is raised:

"If that which arises intermittently is called 'intermingled,' then when a seeker (śaikṣa) turns their mind toward the Great Vehicle and attains sudden awakening upon reaching the first stage (bhūmi), the Bodhisattva gives rise to the Wisdom of Equality at that first stage."

It arises intermingled with afflictions; that is, either an affliction of a preceding moment gives rise to the wisdom of equality of a subsequent moment, or the wisdom of equality of a preceding moment induces an affliction of a subsequent moment. Consequently, the wisdom of equality should also be called "intermingled.

However, when one who has attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) turns their mind toward enlightenment, the wisdom of equality they give rise to does not [arise from] the afflictions of the seventh consciousness, which have already been severed.
It is called "mixed" (*miśra*). This designation as "mixed" applies only with respect to the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and not with respect to the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

However, the commentary explains that those which share the same nature of outflow (*sāsrava*) and are mutually concordant are each termed "mixed. The sixth and seventh consciousnesses, when untainted (*anāsrava*), are not afflicted;
because they are directly contrary to affliction, they are not termed "mixed. Furthermore, if there is an outflow that obscures...
Wholesome karma that is active is initiated by the factor of ignorance; that is, wholesome karma is produced as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) by ignorance.

This is called the "causal motivation" (*hetu-samutthāna*). One may say that contaminated wholesome karma is "mixed. As for uncontaminated [karma] and the sixth consciousness, as well as the six types of informative karma (*vijñapti-karman*):
That which is produced and arises as the sixth uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousness does not have afflictions or ignorance as its cause; therefore, it is not called "mixed.

When the commentary states that the uncontaminated sixth consciousness is "intermingled" with afflictions, this is said in terms of their general characteristics. Herein, the explanation of "intermingling" refers specifically to immediate succession.
If, for instance, an affliction within the seventh consciousness of a preceding moment induces [a state], and in the immediately subsequent moment, [the mind] becomes equanimous...
Regarding conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*): immediately following the knowledge of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), it can further induce the arising of afflictions;
thus, one may say that the seventh [consciousness], being untainted (*anāsrava*), does not accord with the afflictions and so forth. If it were the sixth consciousness, this would not be the case.

When the sixth consciousness is about to enter the untainted state, it first gives rise to a virtuous mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) before it can induce the arising of the untainted sixth consciousness. Even a virtuous mind acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*) cannot induce it.
If even the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) mind cannot give rise to a sixth consciousness, how much less could an afflicted mind?

Furthermore, from an outflow-free mind, either a preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) arises in succession, or at times a naturally acquired wholesome mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-upapatti-labdha-kuśala*) arises.

Even in immediate succession to the outflow-free mind, a naturally acquired wholesome mind of the two higher realms cannot arise. Therefore, the sixth consciousness is both cognitive (*jñāna*) and outflow-free.
It cannot be produced by the immediate proximity of afflictions (*kleśa*). If it arises from a remote cause, it is as follows:

immediately after the prior arising of an affliction, there arises a contaminated preparatory wholesome state (*sāsrava-prayoga-kuśala*), and immediately thereafter, the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [state] arises. From this uncontaminated sixth consciousness, the sixth consciousness [arises].

When [the mind] emerges from that state, it gives rise to contaminated wholesome states; only after these contaminated wholesome states do afflictions subsequently arise, so there is no contradiction.
If "mixed" refers to being mixed with the motivating cause (*hetu-samutthāna*), then it is narrow, applying only to contaminated wholesome karma which is termed "mixed.

However, since the motivating cause must necessarily be present for the factor of initiating wholesome conduct, yet only contaminated wholesome karma is termed [the "mixed" factor], the factor of ignorance (*avidyā-aṅga*) does not [qualify as such].

The karma that produces ignorance is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), such as the dharmas of the indeterminate class; thus, it should not be called "mixed. According to the actual interpretation, this excludes the seventh consciousness.

Within the seventh consciousness, there is only the admission that the pure *samatājñāna* (equality-wisdom) and the afflictions arise alternately; it is this alternating arising and non-arising that constitutes "mixing.

Within the seventh consciousness, there is only the obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), which is itself the outflow of impurity (*sāsrava*) and is distinct from the wholesome and the unobscured-indeterminate.
The term "mixed" (*miśra*) refers to arising in alternation with the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Now, excluding the seventh consciousness, it is not called "mixed.

If "mixed" were defined simply as arising in alternation, it would be too broad, referring only to wholesome (*kuśala*) and indeterminate dharmas within the six consciousnesses that cause afflictions to arise in alternation before and after them.
This definition thus encompasses both contaminated wholesome dharmas and unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) dharmas.
All those that arise interspersed with afflictions—namely, tainted wholesome states and indeterminate states—are called "mixed.
Thus, the nature of these tainted wholesome and indeterminate states, being in conformity [with afflictions], is termed "mixed."
The Commentary states: Furthermore, regarding "the mixed," this refers to the fact that wholesome contaminated karma and afflictions bring about a contaminated nature.

Through the link of ignorance (*avidyā*), one is able to give rise to the links of meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable wholesome karma; these links of formative action (*saṃskāra*) thus establish a contaminated nature that differs from neutral phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*).
Neutral phenomena do not arise through afflictions; rather, the link of ignorance gives rise solely to wholesome and unwholesome karma.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that one cannot attain the state of "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) after [the defilements] have been severed. That ignorance lacks wholesome karma; this is what is termed "severance through detachment from bonds.
This is the second interpretation in this commentary. Regarding the phrase "intermingled with those afflictions," it refers to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena.

"Wholesome and indeterminate" is broad in scope. If it follows the second interpretation of the commentary, "intermingled" means being led by contaminated wholesome karma and afflictions, which is due to ignorance.
The wholesome karma that produces immovable merit is called "mixed" (*miśra*). It is called "mixed" because it does not include indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena.

The second interpretation—that the indeterminate is not produced by ignorance and afflictions—is narrow; now, this [third] interpretation subsumes the second and applies it partially to the third, which is superior in principle.
The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "That which is called 'condition' (*pratyaya*) among those afflictions refers to the 'condition' as in 'relying upon' (*ālambana*).

The *Śū* further explains: "Another interpretation says that the binding associated with the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga-caitta*) are not defiled dharmas (*kliṣṭa-dharma*).

[The author] notes: "This interpretation contradicts the text below which states they are 'only abandoned by cultivation' (*bhāvanā-heya*); for how could there be no associated binding in the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*)? [The *Śū*] explains: "This is..."

The fourth explanation: It is mixed with those afflictions (*kleśa*). That is, the universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viniyata*) mental factors associated with the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) are neither defiled nor pure in their essential nature.
These factors—the universal ones and so forth—arise simultaneously with afflictions such as greed (*rāga*).

Once these universal factors and others have been designated as "affliction-bondage" (*kleśa-bandhana*), if one severs them, the afflictions such as greed that arise simultaneously with the mind-king and the other factors are also completely exhausted.
At that time, those [factors] such as the mind-king (citta-rāja) are designated as having attained the severance of the mind-king’s universal mental factors (sarvatraga).

Although they are associated with defiled phenomena such as greed and reach the nature of the mind-king and so forth, because they are neither defiled nor pure, the mind-king itself is not severed of its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva).

If the severance of associated fetters (*saṃprayukta-bandhana*) were subsumed under the category of severing new afflictions (*kleśa*), and if the severance of associated fetters were called "mixed with those afflictions," this interpretation would contradict the subsequent passage stating that "those mixed with those afflictions are severed only by the path of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmārga*).

If associated fetters are severed both by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation, then [the statement that] "those mixed with those afflictions are severed only... [would be inconsistent].

Regarding the abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*): if one were to say that the abandonment of associated fetters (*saṃprayukta-bandhana*) is called the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*), then would the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) not also abandon associated fetters?

Therefore, this interpretation is not the meditation of the Upādhyāya. The Master of the Commentary (*Vṛttikāra*) asks: "Why [is this so]? For in the previous section of his commentary, while explaining abandonment by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*), he stated:
"This also includes the abandonment of all defiled minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*); all are abandoned by intrinsic nature. Now, in this subsequent [section],...

The commentary states: "The mind-king (citta-rāja) arises simultaneously with the mental factors (caitta-dharma)—namely, the universal (sarvatraga), the object-specific (viniyata), and the afflictions (kleśa) such as greed (rāga).
If the mind-king is universal or its essence is non-defiled, yet it arises together with these afflictions, then if one were to sever those simultaneous afflictions..."

Regarding those [factors] such as the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) that coexist with the afflictions (*kleśa*), if you do not admit that their substance (*svabhāva*) persists even while they are being severed, we now raise this objection:

If the mind-king and the universal factors associated with the afflictions arise and are currently being severed along with them, yet the substance of the associated defiled mind-king and the universal factors remains unsevered and its substance still persists—then we ask: [how can this be?]

It is asked: It is not yet known whether this [mind] is associated with the afflictions (*kleśa*). At the same time as the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) such as the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), are these universal mental factors and so forth themselves defiled in their essence, or is their essence not defiled?
If they were defiled, then the universal mental factors and so forth would have to be of a defiled intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

All defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are abandoned by their very nature (*svabhāva-prahīṇa*). If it is claimed that what is non-defiled is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*), the objection is raised as follows:
The universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) and so forth, when associated with afflictions (*kleśa*), give rise to the universal mental factors and so forth within the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).

If their essence is not defiled and is thus of an indeterminate nature, they would fail to constitute defilement. [Furthermore,] those mind-kings and so forth, when associated with the eleven wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-citta*)...

Regarding those that are associated with equality: the universal mental factors (*citta-dharmas*) such as the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) would not be subsumed under the nature of wholesomeness (*kuśala*), nor would they be subsumed under associated wholesomeness.

Their essence would consequently have to be exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, the universal and object-specific mental factors (*sarvatraga* and *viṣaya-niyata*) could likewise not be established as untainted wholesome (*anāsrava-kuśala*) names.
If they were subsumed under untainted concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), then the eight mind-kings, the universals, and so forth—[would follow these same consequences].
Because their nature is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, although the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) and others arise simultaneously with the afflictions,

if those universal mental factors are by nature exclusively indeterminate, then the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its associated mental factors (*caitta*) that arise at the same time as the afflictions—

speaking according to reality— would mean that when the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) are severed, the eleven wholesome [factors] are severed, and these [indeterminate ones] would also be severed.

Regarding the term "excluded" (*pratiṣiddha*): it refers to the eleven wholesome [factors] and the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) such as the mind-king (*cittarāja*) that arise simultaneously. Master Heshang explains:

if those universal mental factors associated with the mind-king arise together with afflictions (*kleśa*), then the essence (*svabhāva*) of that mind-king and its concomitants is itself defiled (*kliṣṭa*).

When the afflictions are severed, the mind-king and its mental factors that arise simultaneously are also severed; since the essence of the mind-king and its mental factors is already defiled, [they are excluded from being wholesome].
This is because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is severed. As for the universal mental factors (*citta-dhātu*) and so forth:

if these defiled factors arise simultaneously with afflictions, they are likewise associated with unwholesomeness. If the universal mental factors and so forth arise simultaneously with the eleven wholesome factors, they may also be termed associated with wholesome roots;
they may also constitute untainted (*anāsrava*) concentration and wisdom, or be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Is this not possible?

It is known that when a person who has severed the roots of goodness severs the eleven wholesome factors, they also sever those mental states— such as the universal and particular-object mental factors— that are associated with the eleven wholesome factors and arise simultaneously with them.
The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "By this, one should know that the first two explanations [are correct]. The *Jie* (Exegesis) states: "This passage in the *Śū* is erroneous. It should now be read as:

'By this, one should know that the second and third explanations are correct. That is to say, regarding those wholesome [states] which take afflictions as their objects, within the full analysis of those mixed afflictions, there are four interpretations.
Only the second interpretation allows for wholesome and indeterminate dharmas to be interspersed with afflictions."
The third interpretation—that a small portion is called "mixed afflictions"—is superior in terms of principle. The *Shu* (Commentary) states:

"If one says that the seven consciousnesses are called 'mixed afflictions,' then from the stage of being free from desire through the nine grades until one has not yet attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), as long as they can take the cessation of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) as an object, these are said to be abandoned;
they are not abandoned mixed afflictions. The *Jie* (Explanation) states: "Regarding the afflictions within the seventh consciousness..."

Although the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) involves the exhaustion of all defilements from the desire realm up to the exhaustion of the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), it cannot sever the essential afflictions of the seventh consciousness;
these must be severed simultaneously and instantaneously along with the lowest-of-the-low (mṛdumṛdu) afflictions of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).

Because their power of aspiration and so forth are equal, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and others may, by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), suppress everything from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) downward, exhausting it;

yet they cannot suppress the defilements of the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭamanas*) of the lower realms. This is explained in the context of the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) when one abandons the afflictions of the desire realm through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
When the afflictions of the nine grades are exhausted, one attains the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmiphala), which is termed "detachment from sensual desire" (vairāgya).

If the afflictions within the first liberation of the seventh consciousness arise simultaneously with the three natures—wholesome and so forth—of the preceding six consciousnesses, they are then said to be "associated with outflows" (sāsrava).

Regarding what is called "being mixed with those afflictions": it is as follows. When one who has attained the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmin) dwells in the desire realm, because they have exhausted the nine grades of defilement of the desire realm but have not yet attained the body of a non-returner of the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa), they nevertheless possess wholesome dharmas of the desire realm within that very body of a non-returner.
Thus, within the body of a non-returner, the wholesome dharmas of the desire realm should not be said to be "mixed with those afflictions" [in the sense of being abandoned], because they still exist.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the seventh consciousness is intermingled with those afflictions (*kleśa*). Because they have been severed from the outset, if one considers the afflictions within the seventh consciousness—specifically those "afflictions intermingled with views"—then at the stage of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), when the nine grades of detachment from desire are exhausted, one is only able to sever the afflictions that take defilement as their object at the time of being stained;
this is what is termed "severance. One cannot, however, sever the afflictions that are themselves the nature of defilement, because the seventh [consciousness]...
"Because the consciousness-afflictions (vijñāna-kleśa) exist.

The commentary (*shu*) states: "If this is so, then even for noble ones born in the higher realms who do not abandon the mixed afflictions, these [afflictions] are naturally absent, just like the afflictions of the view of a self (dṛṣṭi-kleśa).
Even when the bonds of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) are not yet exhausted, they are considered abandoned; one should reflect upon this meaning. The explanation says: "That is to say..."

Just as in the case of the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), although one cannot exhaustively sever the various afflictions within the seventh consciousness, if one is born into the higher realms, the active afflictions of the seventh consciousness belonging to the desire realm do not arise.

Thus, based on the fact that they do not arise in their active state, they are naturally absent; this does not mean that the seeds of the afflictions within the seventh consciousness of the desire realm are non-existent.

Therefore, each is naturally so. Although the substance of the seventh consciousness of the desire realm does not exist [in that state], it is like seeing secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) which are bound by the category of afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

The afflictions abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) are each bound by their respective objects of perception (*ālambana*), while the afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation are the perceiving subjects (*ālambaka*).
How could one wait until the perceiving subject—the afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation—is entirely severed before the objects...?
The afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) that bind through objects of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*) are as follows:

the afflictions of pride (*māna*), bodily conduct (*kāya-mārga*), and anger (*dveṣa*) of a person who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), along with the conceptualized false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) within the bodies of others or non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), are the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) of the first fruit.
These are each capable of binding the afflictions of non-Buddhists and are termed "binding through objects of perception. If non-Buddhists and others subsequently sever them...

When [discussing] the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), how could one wait until a person of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) has exhausted the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) before non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and others can exhaust the afflictions of the path of seeing?

Therefore, we know that although a person of the first fruit has not yet exhausted the binding afflictions of the path of cultivation, those non-Buddhists are nonetheless able to exhaust the object-bound afflictions of the path of seeing. Furthermore, it is like [the case of] desire...
Regarding the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) within the realms, there are nine grades.

Specifically, when an affliction of the superior grade on the path of cultivation is bound by an affliction of the middle or inferior grade belonging to another [path of cultivation], if one subsequently gives rise to an inferior grade of the noble path (*āryamārga*), one immediately severs that superior grade affliction of the path of cultivation.
Although the middle and inferior grades exist as binding objects, they remain subordinate to that superior grade affliction.

They are mutually termed "abandoned. Now, it is likewise mutual: although one does not abandon the various afflictions within the seventh consciousness of the desire realm, those wholesome and other dharmas of the desire realm are also each abandoned and bound.
Furthermore, regarding the afflictions under the four truths of the Path of Seeing, there are nine grades;
among the superior-grade afflictions, there are hundreds of thousands of types, as are the middle and inferior-grade afflictions, each [having their own categories].

Regarding the statement that there are hundreds of thousands of afflictions (*kleśa*) and that one should now perform a fourfold classification (*catuṣkoṭi-vibhāga*): there are bonds within the same category (*sva-nikāya-sabhāga-bandhana*).

For instance, take the afflictions under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) during the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). If there are the four higher-grade afflictions under the same category of the Truth of Suffering, they take the Truth of Suffering as their own object;
since these higher-grade afflictions are of the same grade, they are termed "of the same category" (*sabhāga*). Thus it is said: "the same category and the same [grade]."

There is the bond of the same category with different names (*ekadeśa-nāma-bheda-bandhana*): this refers to the nine grades of afflictions under the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Because they share the same category as the afflictions under the truth of suffering, they are called "the same category as the afflictions under the truth of suffering.

Because they take the superior-grade afflictions of the truth of suffering belonging to others or oneself as their objects, yet differ in their respective grades, they are called "the same category with different grades" (*ekadeśa-bhinna-prakāra*).

There is also the bond of different categories with the same grade (*bhinnadeśa-sama-prakāra-bandhana*): for example, the [afflictions] of the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path within the path of seeing.

Because the Four Truths differ, they are called "different categories" (*visabhāga*). That is to say, the superior-grade afflictions associated with each Truth—such as those associated with the Truth of Origination or Cessation—are "different categories" when they take another Truth as their object.

For example, superior-grade afflictions associated with the Truth of Origination taking the Truth of Suffering as their object, or those associated with the Truth of Cessation taking all four Truths as their objects: although the Truths are different, they are all "superior-grade," and are therefore termed "the same category" (*sabhāga*).

There is binding by way of different categories and different degrees, such as the truths of origin, cessation, and the path, or lower and middle-grade afflictions binding [the mind] through the object of the truth of suffering, or lower and upper-grade afflictions;

these are called binding by way of different categories and different degrees. Within the Śrāvaka vehicle, this refers to the afflictions regarding the four truths during the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

It is not permitted for there to be simultaneous, sudden abandonment. That is to say, there is only the abandonment of the same category (nikāya) and the same grade (prakāra), and the abandonment of different grades within the same category.
This is because, in the path of seeing (darśanamārga), one abandons the nine grades of afflictions under the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya) all at once.

There is abandonment of the same class (jāti) and the same grade, and abandonment of different grades within the same category; however, there is absolutely no abandonment of different categories and different grades. Even if the abandonment of the same grade within the same category has already been completed beforehand, [the process continues].

When one is at the stage of the nine grades of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) during the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one has still not abandoned the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the three truths of Origin, Cessation, and the Path within the Path of Seeing.
As for the afflictions of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), only those of the same category (*nikāya*) and the same grade (*prakāra*) are abandoned;

thus, when one is at the stage of the superior grade (*adhimātra*) of the Path of Cultivation, one has still not abandoned the middle and inferior grades of affliction. These are the nine grades of afflictions of the Path of Cultivation.

Before and after [attaining the fruit], one certainly does not [fall back from] the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). Once born in a higher realm, one must follow the seven [consciousnesses] that arise in those eight places of birth.

Although one does not sever the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manas*) of the lower realm—which is mixed with afflictions—once one has been born in a higher realm, the afflictions of the seventh consciousness of the lower realm no longer function, nor can they arise;
furthermore, the contaminated wholesome and neutral dharmas of the lower realm do not manifest.
"Practice" (*caryā*) is called "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*). This is not a name applied merely in reference to what has been cultivated.

However, it is not the case that, as when afflictions associated with the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) take afflictions associated with the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) as their object, those afflictions of the path of seeing are thereby bound by the afflictions of the path of cultivation—whereby the path of cultivation would be the binding agent and the afflictions of the path of seeing the object bound—at a later time, when the afflictions of the path of seeing that were the objects of bondage are severed.

At the time of the afflictions (*kleśa*), although the fetters (*bandhana*) that take them as objects have not yet been abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), how could it be that the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are not called "abandoned"?
Therefore, one should know that even if the afflictions of cultivation have not yet been abandoned, the afflictions of the path of seeing are nonetheless termed "abandoned.

Thus, one should know that the object-fetters (*ālambanabandhana*) are so designated in contrast to the self-nature fetters (*svabhāvabandhana*) and the associated fetters (*samprayuktakabandhana*). This point ought to be analyzed; for in the Hīnayāna, it is taught that [the afflictions] are abandoned by the path of seeing.

Beneath the Four Noble Truths, there are four categories of afflictions: namely, the afflictions to be abandoned beneath the truth of suffering, the afflictions to be abandoned beneath the truth of the origin, and so on, up to the afflictions to be abandoned beneath the truth of the path.

Just as the afflictions to be abandoned beneath the truth of suffering are bound by the binding of the objects of the three grades of afflictions to be abandoned by the [subsequent] views of the origin, cessation, and the path, so too are the afflictions beneath the truth of suffering [bound].

If one does not accept this interpretation, then the nine entities of the mental factors would themselves be the essence of the afflictions and thus the binder, with no further dharma to be bound.
