How can the four types of grasping (*upādāna*) arise? At the time of death in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there also arises the innate (*sahaja*) craving for a self and for one’s own person.
Most treatises state that among the members of dependent origination, the four graspings are conceptual (*vikalpita*); by this standard, they do not refer to the innate four graspings.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that at the time of death one must necessarily give rise to craving for craving to condition rebirth; for example, a person may suddenly die from being struck by a wooden club.
How can craving and grasping arise? Therefore, we know that the craving and grasping arising during youth are certain to moisten rebirth.
The treatise states that because nine types of death-moment consciousnesses arise together with craving, this refers to those who die gradually, not all those who die suddenly.
Regarding the deceased: the two factors of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) that arose during the stage of youth are here specifically explained as the two factors of craving and grasping;

these are termed "distinct characteristics. Craving does not produce grasping as a manifest activity (*samudācāra*) from its seeds; otherwise, there would be the logical fallacy of craving and grasping being without causal conditions.

At the time of death, the preceding moment of arising craving is called "craving," and the subsequent moment is called "grasping. The seed of craving in the preceding moment is able to produce the [subsequent] one.

The manifestation of the thought of grasping (*upādāna*) is the causal condition for the existence of grasping (*upādānabhava*). The craving that arises at the moment of death is called the limb of grasping (*upādānāṅga*);

however, it is not yet capable of giving rise to the four types of grasping. In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, it is stated that at the time of rebirth, the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*) becomes manifest;

subsequently, before the sense faculties are fully developed, the characteristic of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) increases, and so on until this gives rise to contact (*sparśa*), from which feeling (*vedanā*) arises—this is identical to the verse in the *Abhidharmakośa*.

It is said: To establish the correct linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), the aggregates (*skandha*) exist prior to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). From the preceding moment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the eye and other faculties arise; the conjunction of these three is called "contact" (*sparśa*).

Regarding the cause and effect of the three types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) within the first six bases, that which has not yet been fully understood is called contact. It exists prior to sensual craving (*kāmatṛṣṇā*) and precedes feeling (*vedanā*).

Greed for requisites and sensual craving constitute two branches; although their specific meanings differ, their essential intent is the same. Furthermore, another interpretation asks: In the previous treatise it was stated that there is craving...

If one considers that "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) does not possess the same characteristics as "grasping" (*upādāna*), yet later in the treatise it states that craving acts as the causal condition for grasping, this would constitute a confusion of characteristics and thus a contradiction between the preceding and following passages of the treatise. Answer:

If the preceding and subsequent passages of the treatise were both the teaching of a single master, then we would indeed admit such a contradiction. However, since these represent two distinct masters, there is no contradiction. If the master [of the latter passage] speaks of grasping...
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) does not possess a heterogeneous character (*miśralakṣaṇa*). According to the former master, craving does not serve as a causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) for grasping (*upādāna*).

According to the latter master, craving and grasping do not constitute causal conditions; however, if the latter master asserts that craving serves as a causal condition for grasping, then he cannot maintain that the preceding craving, in relation to grasping, lacks a heterogeneous character.
Thus, according to the latter master, craving in relation to grasping also possesses a heterogeneous character.

It is not so; regarding consciousness in relation to name-and-form, and so forth, up to its being established as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) based on the stage of its future arising—this passage refers specifically to the "mixed" members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) within the *Abhidharma*.
It explains that consciousness serves as a causal condition for name-and-form and the other factors in terms of their sequential stages (*avasthā*).
This is based on the temporal sequence of the five resultant stages (*phala-avasthā*) within the process of the actualization of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) in the future.

It is said that in the future, within the link of birth (*jāti*), from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) until the initial stage of birth, this is designated as the stage of the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
At that time, the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth are collectively termed the link of consciousness.

When it is clearly understood that the seeds of name-and-form arise as the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) of name-and-form simultaneously with the link of consciousness, it is then stated that consciousness acts as the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) for name-and-form. If one looks toward [the point when]...
At the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the seeds of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are subsumed under the member of form (*rūpāṅga*).
From these seeds of the six preeminent [bases], which exist simultaneously with the stage of name-and-form, the actual manifestation of the six sense bases arises;

this is explained as the transformative cause and condition for name-and-form and the six sense bases, up until the stage of contact (*sparśa*). At the stage of contact, the seeds of sensation (*vedanā*) are subsumed under the member of contact. From the stage of contact...

When the seed of the feeling aggregate (*vedanā-skandha*) arises as the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) of the feeling aggregate, it is said that contact (*sparśa*) acts as the cause and condition with respect to feeling.

This passage refers to the *Abhidharma* system of the "intermingled" (*vyavakīrṇa*) dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), wherein the five fruits are conventionally described as being in a relationship of cause and condition when viewed in relation to one another.

However, according to the actual reality, since these five fruits are seeds when viewed in relation to one another, they do not constitute a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). If one considers the case of [temporal] separation...
Regarding the "exceeding" [of the factors]: the link of ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as the cause for the links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*).

This is explained in terms of the manifest activity (*samudācāra*) of afflictions arising simultaneously with craving and grasping from the seed of ignorance. Furthermore, the afflictions of the *kāmadhātu* are all capable of effecting rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*).
Moreover, the seeds of the five fruits act as causes and conditions for the future links of birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*). That is to say, from the seeds of the five fruits—

Furthermore, the *jāti* (birth) link manifests; furthermore, the *saṃskāra* (volitional formations) link manifests. Moreover, the *saṃskāra* link and the *bhava* (existence) link can also function as causes and conditions;
that is to say, from the seeds of the *saṃskāra* link, the *bhava* link arises.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* says that what is produced and what induces are simultaneous. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states:

The *Śāstra* says: "This is explained in terms of the mutual proximity of seeds. The commentary states: "In this context, regarding the seed of consciousness in relation to the seed of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), neither is a causal condition (*hetupratyaya*).

The seed of name-and-form is not a causal condition for the seed of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and so on, up to contact (*sparśa*) in relation to the seed of sensation (*vedanā*), which is not a causal condition.
Furthermore, it says: 'This text of the *Śāstra* is erroneous; it should rather say: "Now, regarding seeds in relation to [their respective fruits]..."'"

Regarding the explanation of the "present" and "adjacent" links: it is understood that, within the context of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*), the five types of resultant seeds, in relation to the manifest activities (*samudācāra*) of the immediately subsequent link, function as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

The Commentary states: "In this context, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains the ten stages of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) differently by specifying that karma is the causal condition for the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Based on this, the *Abhidharma* (Dharma-lakṣaṇa) school asserts that the seeds of karma constitute the link of consciousness; thus, the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) also acts as the causal condition for consciousness.

It is not the cause; therefore, it is said that "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) are to be understood accordingly.

The commentary states: "As explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*, regarding this seed of karma within the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*), 'formative action' (*saṃskāra*) is called the 'cause-condition' (*hetu-pratyaya*) in relation to consciousness."
Regarding "manifest activity" (*pravṛtti-vṛtti*): it is so called because it precedes the seeds of formative action (*saṃskāra-bīja*) within consciousness. To explain:

for instance, there may be seeds of karma that have existed from the beginning, or there may be those that produce maturation results (*vipāka-phala*). These include seeds of past karma or seeds of ancient karma; such are the seeds of karma existing from the outset or the seeds of ancient karma.
They immediately arise as active manifestations (*samudācāra*). These manifestations, in turn, perfume a heterogeneous collection of karmic seeds capable of producing ripened results (*vipākaphala*).
Because these karmic seeds are perfumed by the activity of karma, within the link of *saṃskāra* (formative forces), both the manifest and the seed aspects are included as the link of *saṃskāra*.
As it is said in the ancient sūtras and śāstras: "The link of *saṃskāra* exists at the time of the seed and at the time of the fruit."
There are three factors: first, the seeds of afflictions from past karma, which are the seeds of karma existing by nature; second, the actualization of karma;

The same applies up to the link of ignorance (*avidyā*). If there is ignorance, it can only correctly give rise to this specific link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "This is based on a distinct entity, not on a state (*avasthā*). The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says:

The commentary states: "That treatise takes ignorance as the primary example; the others should be understood accordingly. Thus, it first treats ignorance as the model.

Regarding the Dharma: in the Abhidharma, it is taught that ignorance (*avidyā*) in relation to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) can serve as four conditions; this applies likewise up to birth (*jāti*) in relation to aging (*jarā*). Therefore, it says, "by analogy, the others should also be so.

This means that the volition (*cetanā*) simultaneous with ignorance is able to produce volitional formations; thus, ignorance in relation to volitional formations possesses the condition of cause (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, because the ignorance that follows volitional formations in the preceding moment induces the manifestation of the subsequent moment, [ignorance serves as the condition of object (*ālambana-pratyaya*), etc., for the formations].
Regarding the volition of action (*saṃskāra*): with respect to ignorance (*avidyā*), it serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Because the currently active volition of action can take the preceding ignorance as its object, ignorance serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for volition; the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is likewise to be understood.

Thus, with respect to consciousness (*vijñāna*), volition also possesses all four conditions. That is to say, the seed of consciousness that exists simultaneously with the volition is able to produce the branch of consciousness; therefore, volition [is the cause].

thus, the *saṃskāra* factor serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the *vijñāna*. Its role as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is likewise to be understood. This explanation does not refer to the seeds of the five fruits associated with consciousness and so forth. That is to say...

Regarding the stage of the *bhava-aṅga* (existence), the five stages beginning with the active consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are conventionally designated as having four conditions (*catuḥ-pratyaya*) in relation to the *saṃskāra* (formative forces) and so forth, up to the relationship between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and form (*rūpa*), which likewise possesses four conditions.
Following the method established previously, this applies even to the relationship between birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), which also possesses four conditions.
As stated in the previous method, the Master says: "That treatise merely states that ignorance (*avidyā*) in relation to form and formative forces..."

The predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) serves as three conditions for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of the formless realm—namely, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the predominant condition—and likewise serves as three conditions for the formless realm itself—the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, and the predominant condition. The commentary explains:

Since karma is a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*), it cannot take the preceding moment of ignorance as its object; therefore, it lacks an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Since bodily and vocal karma are material phenomena, they do not arise from an immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*); thus, they lack an immediately antecedent condition.

Ignorance, in relation to material formations (*rūpa-saṃskāra*), possesses only one condition: the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). As for ignorance in relation to immaterial formations (*arūpa-saṃskāra*), it possesses two conditions.

The presently active factor of ignorance (*avidyā*) has three conditions with respect to the mental karma of volition (*manas-karma*), which constitutes the factor of formations (*saṃskāra*). These are:

first, the presently active ignorance of the preceding moment induces the manifestation of the mental volition of the succeeding moment; therefore, there is the condition of immediate antecedence (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Second, the mental volition of the succeeding moment, while manifesting, takes the ignorance of the preceding moment as its object; thus, there is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Question: Why is it not... [text ends]

Regarding the statement that ignorance (*avidyā*) takes formations (*saṃskāra*) as its object, it is said that formations have ignorance as their condition. The answer is: this is stated here according to the sequence of the arising of characteristics.

The result, which consists of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that act as the subject of cognition, arises from the cause, which is the object. If it is said that formations have ignorance as their condition, then since the cognizing mind arises from the object, this means that ignorance produces the formations. This means that ignorance arises from formations (*saṃskāra*); thus, [the claim that] ignorance does not arise from formations would be contradicted.

This means that the manifest mind and mental factors existing at the stage of aging-and-death are able to take as their objects those [factors] existing at the preceding stage of the birth-link.

The currently functioning aggregate of form within the stage of aging-and-death cannot take as its object the mind and mental factors within the stage of the birth-link.

Because it lacks a basis, there is no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). In the stage of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) do not arise from an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*);

therefore, there is no immediately preceding condition. Alternatively, regarding ignorance (*avidyā*) in relation to bodily and vocal karma: this is a case of the formless (*arūpa*) relating to the formed (*rūpin*), and the formless relating to the formless, serving as three conditions.
This refers to the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) in the stage of birth (*jāti*) in relation to the stage of old age and death.

The mental factors associated with the central [consciousness] (*maulī-vijñāna*) take as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) the preceding mental states and mental factors that functioned as concomitants during the stages of the prior members [of dependent origination].

Furthermore, because the mind and mental factors at the stage of old age and death can arise in immediate succession (*samanantara*) to the mind and mental factors of the preceding stages, they possess the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

The manifest mental karma of intention arises from preceding instances of ignorance as an immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), while the manifest appropriation arises from preceding instances of manifest [craving].

Because craving arises, there is the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). From this point upward, all [explanations] are based on reality and refer to the actual manifestation of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

Within the name-and-form link, the aggregate of form—in relation to the five material sense-faculties and so forth within the six sense-bases, as well as the five fruits beginning with consciousness and the existence link—is entirely a seed.
If one relies on what is subsumed under the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), or even speaks only of the dominant condition, then the preceding seven links are the "projecting" factors.

Regarding the inclusion within the causes: the *Abhidharma* states that both the "inducer" (*ākṣepaka*) and the "induced" (*ākṣipta*) are the projecting cause (*ākṣepahetu*). The *Abhidharma* states that both the "producer" (*abhinirvartaka*) and the "produced" (*abhinirvṛtta*) are the producing cause. This refers to the producing cause and the projecting cause.
That which is exclusively a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) refers to the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and the producing cause (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*) among the twelve links;

these are exclusively dominant conditions and do not constitute the ten causes. Furthermore, within the ten causes, both the projecting cause and the producing cause are also subsumed under both the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition.

The Commentary states: "Regarding ignorance in relation to the link of formations (*saṃskāra*), craving in relation to grasping (*upādāna*), and birth in relation to aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—these three have two remaining conditions, namely, the condition of immediate succession (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the condition of object (*ālambanapratyaya*).

The Explanation states: Regarding ignorance in relation to formations, this means that the preceding moment of ignorance acts as a condition to induce the succeeding moment of mental volitional action (*manasaḥ saṃskāraḥ*), which constitutes the link of formations. Therefore, there is the condition of immediate succession. As for the succeeding moment of mental volition...

Regarding the factor of karmic formations (*saṃskāra*): it takes the preceding moment of ignorance as its object; thus, there is an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Regarding craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in relation to grasping (*upādāna*):

that is, the preceding moment of craving serves as a condition to give rise to the subsequent moment of the factor of grasping; thus, there is an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Since the subsequent moment of grasping can take the preceding moment of the factor of craving as its object, there is also an object-condition. Regarding birth (*jāti*) in relation to aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*): this refers to the factor of birth.
In the stage [of birth], the mind and mental factors act as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the mind and mental factors of the stage [of aging and death] that they bring about;
these possess the object-condition. In this context, the mind and mental factors capable of cognizing are termed the "fruit," while the objective sphere (*ālambana-viṣaya*) is the "cause."

The Commentary states: "From 'volitional formations' (*saṃskāra*) in relation to 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*), up to 'contact' (*sparśa*) in relation to the 'feeling' (*vedanā*) limb, [these are not causes] because they are not objects that can be apprehended by a presently active mind.

The Explanation states: In this context, if a presently active mind or mental factor is the fruit of a mind or mental factor that acts as the apprehending subject, then the object-conditioned phenomena are termed the "cause.
Now, in the case of volitional formations in relation to the consciousness limb, it is seen that the mind acts as the apprehending subject.

Regarding the results: since the *vijñāna* (consciousness) link is neither a presently functioning mind nor mental factors (*citta-caitta*), it cannot take the *saṃskāra* (formative) link as its object;

thus, there is no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for it. This continues up to the *tṛṣṇā* (craving) and *bhava* (existence) links, which likewise are not presently functioning minds or mental factors, and therefore cannot take their respective "appropriated" links as objects.
These are all not object-conditions. As for the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it refers to the preceding moment of the present...
Mental states and their concomitants (citta-caitta) that function with intervals have the capacity to induce subsequent mental states and their concomitants to arise;

Within the stage of the member of birth, the currently functioning mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are able to take the preceding members as their objects; therefore, they possess an object-condition.
The limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is able to take the preceding limb of sensation (*vedanā*) as its object; therefore, it possesses an objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

The commentary states that "the sequence of cause and effect based on function" means that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the effect, continuing thus until birth (*jāti*) is the cause and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are the effect.

If, however, they are actual constituent members (*aṅga*), they are subsumed within the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*). If...

if it is actually subsumed under active manifestation (*samudācāra*), it is so designated. As for that which is mixed with both, although it is not itself a member, [it is nonetheless included].

If one considers ignorance in relation to the aggregates of form (*rūpa-skandha*) within the state of birth, old age, and death (*jāti-jarā-maraṇa*), there is only the single dominant condition;

because material phenomena cannot take ignorance as an object, there are no others. If one considers ignorance in relation to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) within the state of birth, old age, and death...

[The link] possesses two conditions: namely, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). This means that during the stages of birth and old age, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are able to take ignorance as their object;

As for the matter and mind within the stage of birth...

The *bhava-aṅga* (existence factor) acts as a mere dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for [the arising of birth], because the seeds of the *bhava-aṅga* cannot take the *jāti-aṅga* (birth factor) as their object.

The *bhava-aṅga* acts as two types of conditions for *upādāna* (clinging). *Upādāna* is able to take other *bhava-aṅgas* as its objects; thus, *upādāna* and *tṛṣṇā* (craving) also act as two types of conditions for one another, because *tṛṣṇā* takes *upādāna* as its condition.
*Tṛṣṇā* and *tṛṣṇā* act as a single dominant condition. *Vedanā* (feeling) and *sparśa* (contact) likewise act as a single dominant condition. This continues down to *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form) and...

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) also has one predominance (*adhipati*). If consciousness is a mental factor (*caitta*) within the link of formations (*saṃskāra*), it possesses both objective support (*ālambana*) and predominance;

if consciousness is the form (*rūpa*) of body or speech within the link of formations, it possesses only predominance. Formations (*saṃskāra*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) also possess objective support and predominance.

Since old age is not necessarily present [in all births], it is established as a link in conjunction with death; thus, old age and death together constitute a single link. These two obstacles are transcended.

As for this: if *jarāmaraṇa* (old age and death) and *bhava* (existence) act as conditions, they do so solely as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*). This remains the case up to and including *jarāmaraṇa* acting with respect to *vijñāna* (consciousness) and the others;
because these seeds are incapable of taking [unwholesome] objects. If the limb of *jarāmaraṇa* acts with respect to the limb of *upādāna* (clinging), it acts as two types of conditions.

This means that the *upādāna* (clinging) link can take the *jarāmaraṇa* (old age and death) link as its object, and so on, down to *tṛṣṇā* (craving), *saṃskāra* (formative forces), and *avidyā* (ignorance);
all of these possess two conditions. As for the immediate succession, according to the *Abhidharma*, each preceding link serves as four conditions for each subsequent link.
That is to say, just as *avidyā* acts as four conditions for *saṃskāra*, the same applies to *saṃskāra* acting as four conditions for the *vijñāna* (consciousness) link, and so forth.

Birth and old age and death are also like this, following the same method as previously described. Although there is an interval [between them], they do not differ from the actual conditions mentioned before.

Furthermore, regarding those factors that correspond to what is to be produced according to their respective modes of arising, the intervals herein—when considered in terms of actual meaning—are explained solely as seeds for the five effects, such as consciousness and so forth;
thus, they do not become confused with the explanation of the actual links of dependent origination.

In this regard, it is the same as before; one should also state that they are "immediate" (*samanantara*) and "intervened" (*vyavahita*). For instance, ignorance (*avidyā*) and the five [factors] beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) may possess only a single dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Ignorance and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) function as two conditions, namely, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition.
All such meanings are as explained in the previous notes. Therefore, it says: "It does not [contradict] the actual conditions mentioned previously."

Furthermore, this is also explained in terms of the five factors beginning with consciousness. If it refers to the present state of what is to arise, the meaning intended here is that it is explained in terms of the various links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

If it refers to the stage of the "birth-link" (*jāti-aṅga*) in the future, then the five results—consciousness and so forth—and the "existence-link" (*bhava-aṅga*) are all in their active manifestation (*samudācāra*); thus, these twelve links are entirely in a state of active manifestation. Therefore, one should say:

Ignorance (*avidyā*) and the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), as well as the link of existence (*bhava*), serve as two conditions—namely, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

This is because these five, beginning with consciousness, are all capable of taking ignorance as their object. Ignorance, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) all possess both conditions:

the object-condition and the dominant condition. One should apply this principle by analogy to those that follow in reverse order, whether they are immediate or separated by an interval. However, now, in reverse...

Next, regarding the "intermediate" [sequence], this refers to the remaining conditions, namely the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). As for the "reverse intermediate" sequence, it refers to the object-condition and the dominant condition.

Now, since we are explaining based on their mutual intermingling: the five fruits such as consciousness and the links of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) are exclusively seeds, meaning they lack actual manifestation (*pravṛtti*).

As for the mind capable of cognitive apprehension, these five fruits such as consciousness and the links of existence—given that they are treated [in this way]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.]

At the stage of birth (*jāti*), all may be described as the branch of actualization (*samudācāra*). As the text states: "By this, consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the others are also said to be actualized.

This means that the five fruits, such as consciousness, along with the branches of existence (*bhava*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) arising simultaneously, can all be said to possess actualization.

Regarding form and mind within the members of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) and the mind within the member of birth: they possess both conditions as dominant conditions.

The existence-factor (*bhava-aṅga*) also has two conditions, namely the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

This means that the existence-factor can take the subsequent birth-factors as its objects, up to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), which likewise function as these two conditions—namely the object-condition and the predominant condition—and so on, down to the formations (*saṃskāra*) and ignorance (*avidyā*, *moha*), which also function as these two conditions.
Even when there are intervening gaps in the reverse order, since this concerns the twelve factors in their disordered sequence, all of them possess both conditions.

That is to say, old age and death (jarāmaraṇa) and the link of existence (bhava) also possess two conditions. Following the same principle as the preceding dharmas, everything up to old age and the five fruits of consciousness (vijñāna) all function as two conditions.

Regarding the "intervening and non-intervening" [conditions] mentioned below, they possess two conditions, namely the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).

As for the statement that the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* explains these in terms of the dominant condition alone, this refers to the lower fascicle of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, which states that the twelve links involve only the dominant condition.

Regarding conditions (*pratyaya*): there are no three conditions. However, there are those that are distant and those that are proximate. If one proceeds in regular order (*anuloma*) or skips one or two links, it is called "proximate," as when ignorance (*avidyā*) is related to consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and so forth;
in such cases, how many conditions can it act as? If one skips four or five links, it is called "distant," as when ignorance is related to feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth;
in such cases, how many conditions can it act as? Alternatively, skipping [a few links] is called "proximate," while skipping [many links] is called "distant."

The twelve links and so forth are termed "distant. Following the method established previously, just as it is with the direct (anuloma) sequence, there are also distant and near instances in the reverse (pratiloma) sequence when skipping over intermediate stages;

these should be understood according to the method applied in the direct sequence. However, within this context, the five factors beginning with consciousness are separated by the various links of their respective future and present positions.

Regarding the instruction to apply this principle to each individual case: however, the five [factors] beginning with consciousness and the link of existence (*bhava*) are explained as being identical to birth and old age/death when referring to the state of the future life.
In the direct order (*anuloma*), these constitute the twelve links in immediate succession, such as the four conditions (*pratyaya*) described in the *Abhidharma-kośa* and so forth;

all of these follow the method previously established. In the reverse order (*pratiloma*), whether they are separated by one interval or by multiple intervals, they are also to be understood according to the previous explanation.

The Commentary states: "Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the path of karma; ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are the path of afflictions (*kleśa*); the remaining seven are the path of suffering (*duḥkha*).
The Explanation states: "What is here called 'path' refers to a principle—that is, the principle of karma, the principle of afflictions, and the principle of suffering.
What is here called 'path' does not mean a path in the sense of being traversed."

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Because of the difficulties of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*). It further notes that in the new translation, these are termed "defilements" (*saṃkleśa*). The explanation says:

"What is here called 'difficulty' (*durga*) refers to the 'obstacles' (*vighna*) mentioned in the Sūtra, or rather 'impediments' (*antarāya*). Because afflictions and karma act as impediments, they cause sentient beings to revolve [in saṃsāra] and prevent them from escaping the three realms (*tridhātu*).
The old translation speaks of "affliction-obstructions," "karma-obstructions," and "roots and intentions"; this accords with the meaning and intent of the term "difficulty."

It is similar. In the new sūtras and śāstras, these are termed the "three defilements," namely: the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and the defilement of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*).
The sub-commentary states: "Because it contains even a portion of the seeds of consciousness and so forth. The explanation says:

Since the branches of existence (*bhavāṅga*) already contain the seeds of the five fruits—consciousness and the rest—as well as karma, when the branch of existence here specifically clarifies the grasping of karma, it is said to "contain a portion."

If it were not so, that treatise would have to make a distinction; it should be as in this treatise, where karma constitutes one part [of the truth of origination], rather than being like "some karma," which is also subsumed under the truth of suffering and also subsumed under the truth of karma.
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, it is for the sake of producing weariness [with cyclic existence] so that one does not give rise to or create karma. The Explanation says:

"If one does not produce weariness toward the three realms, one will then give rise to or create karma, which consists of the two types of birth and death. If one produces weariness toward the three realms, one will then neither give rise to nor create karma."
The Commentary states: "Regarding the reason for the name," this refers to the basis for the two characters *yin* (cause) and *yuan* (condition).

"Cause" (*yin*) refers to the primary impelling; "condition" (*yuan*) refers to the auxiliary impelling. Regarding "the karma of projection and fulfillment": herein there are two types of karma. The first is projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*).

Only [karma] capable of projecting the eighth consciousness is the "projecting karma" (*ākṣepaka-karman*). The two types of "fulfilling karma" (*paripūraka-karman*) are capable only of fulfilling the fruit.

However, among the twelve links previously mentioned, there is one type of karma that is designated solely as "projecting," which is also subsumed under the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). There is another type of karma that pertains to both projecting and fulfilling, which is likewise subsumed under the link of volitional formations.
Question: Why is it that among the twelve links previously mentioned, only the projecting karma is also subsumed under the link of volitional formations, whereas here...

"Location" refers here to the two types of karma: projecting (*ākṣepaka*) and completing (*paripūraka*). The answer is that within the twelve links, this location serves as the "ornament" (*vyūha*) for the continuity of birth and death;

each is established according to a specific meaning. Within uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma—excluding non-conceptual fundamental wisdom (*nirvikalpa-mūla-jñāna*), subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), and the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) leading up to the arising [of cognition] based on objects—the question is:
are the preparatory, fundamental, and subsequently attained stages all termed "attaining non-differentiation"?
Is it not so? Answer: If it is the preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*), it is free from inverted conceptualization and is thus called non-conceptual fundamental knowledge (*mūla-jñāna*).

It is free from conceptualizations such as seeking and so forth. As for the subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), there is no [inverted] conceptualization. These three are all termed "non-conceptual.

However, in the present context, we take only the subsequently attained knowledge that takes phenomena as its object, and do not take the subsequently attained knowledge that takes the four truths as established by linguistic convention (*prajñapti*) and so forth as its object.

Regarding "wisdom": the phrase "it is precisely because of this that birth and death continue" indicates that it is by means of this—namely, both untainted (*anāsrava*) and tainted (*sāsrava*) karma—that the two kinds of birth and death are able to continue in succession.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Regarding 'untainted' (*anāsrava*), it is said that they 'directly induce' [results] because they are like the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*).

The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says: For instance, tainted wholesome and unwholesome karma acts as the cause of maturation and directly induces its own matured fruit (*vipāka-phala*). Once the matured fruit has been obtained, it continues in a succession.
As for untainted karma with conceptual differentiation, it is just like the case of tainted wholesome and unwholesome karmic causes; such untainted karma with conceptual differentiation...
It can also cause the body to obtain continuity, as in the case of the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
The Commentary states: "The afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) refers to all [afflictions] that assist in the production of existence (*janma-saṃdhāna*).

Although the grasping for karma (*karmopādāna*) initiates the action, once the action has been initiated, it brings about the seeds of the five fruits; however, here we refer only to all primary and auxiliary afflictions that assist in the production of existence. Question: For what reason?

One takes only the delusions that act as "intercalary" [conditions] for rebirth, not the afflictions that trigger the karma. If one were to take the [afflictions] that trigger the karma, then they would not be equivalent to uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
That contaminated karma is triggered by ignorance (*avidyā*); what dharma then serves as the trigger for uncontaminated karma? They are not equivalent.
If one takes the delusions that act as intercalary conditions for rebirth, then they are equivalent; these are the same as the obstacles to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which are contaminated karma.
It is the same as [the obstruction] regarding untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).

The Commentary (*Śū*) states: "Regarding the obstructions to the knowable (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*): although there are many such types, one takes only those that arise in relation to the Buddha and sentient beings, or those that arise in relation to all [phenomena].
The Explanation (*Jie*) states: "Although the categories of what is obstructed are numerous, here we take only those that relate to the Buddha and to sentient beings."

Regarding the "obstructions to the objects of knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): this refers to the subsequent treatise [which states that] if one does not grasp at sentient beings and bodhi as being substantially real, there is no basis for giving rise to intense compassion and vows.
A second interpretation says: alternatively, it may refer to all obstructions to the objects of knowledge; however, they serve as the conditions for the *pariṇāmika-maraṇa* (transformative death).
Because they cause all realms to be able to moisten and sustain birth, all obstructions to the objects of knowledge can thus provide assistance.

Regarding "because of birth-and-death through transformation," the commentary asks: "How many kinds of birth-and-death are there? This is the first question. How many types of birth-and-death are there?
The answer below states that there are two kinds of birth-and-death. The second question asks: "What is the reason why there are two kinds of birth-and-death?"
The *Śāstra* says: "Because it is easy to see, because it has fixed limits, and because it is easy to understand. The commentary explains:

"Easy to see" refers to having previously seen through direct visual perception those who possessed specific life-spans; that is, from a maximum of eighty thousand years down to a minimum of ten years.
"Easy to understand" refers to knowing this by means of the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

The Commentary (*shu*) states: "Because it consists of distinct portions and segments, it is called 'segmented' (*fēnduàn*). The Explanation (*jiè*) states: "When this body dies and a subsequent body is born—specifically, this very death of the present body followed by the birth of a subsequent body—is what is termed 'segmented.'"

The Commentary states: "It is not within the realm of those worldly beings, nor of the *śrāvakas* who have turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna], nor even can it be seen by the eyes of the various devas.

The Explanation says: "Even if one who has attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* were to enter the body of transformation (*pariṇāmikakāya*), they would still possess a body of segmented existence (*aupapādukakāya*).
Although Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas possess the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), they likewise cannot perceive this. Even if a person of the first fruit were to enter the body of transformation..."
Regarding the body: this fleshly eye can also see those of its own kind, namely the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of those who have attained the first and second fruits.

Furthermore, if a person who has attained the fourth fruit enters the state of birth through transformation, then those who have attained the first and second fruits—being of the same class—can also see one another.

The transformation bodies of those who have attained the first and second fruits can see the transformation bodies of those who have attained the non-returning fruit (*anāgāmin*) and the arhat fruit, as well as the transformation bodies of those who have attained the non-returning fruit themselves.

The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) can see bodies of its own class that have undergone transformation, and it can also see the transformation bodies of those who have attained the first three fruits.
One who has attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*) cannot see the body of an arhat, yet they can see those of their own class and also see those who have attained the first three fruits.
Furthermore, those at the stage of the Ten Faiths can see the *pariṇāmika* (transformative) heavens, yet they cannot see the *pariṇāmika* bodies of the ten stages (*bhūmis*).
Even those at the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), by means of this preceding *pariṇāmika* body, are able to see one another despite possessing only the physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*);

even if an ordinary person possessed the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), they would still be unable to see them. Question: Regarding the *pariṇāmika* body of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), can the *paricchinna-vidha* (segmented) body of the second stage and above [perceive it]?
Do you see the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the first stage? If you do, how can it be said that the transformation body is subtle?

Since one sees what is below from above, Bodhisattvas from the second stage upward—possessing the physical eyes born of their parents, which are already of sharp faculties and endowed with wisdom as explained in the *Ten Treatises*—are able to see the transformation body of the first stage.
As the Sūtra says: "The pure physical eyes produced by the parents of Bodhisattvas are able to see..."
They perceive the three realms of existence. However, Bodhisattvas differ from those of the Two Vehicles because their wisdom is limited and their faculties are dull.
Even with the divine eye of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, they cannot perceive the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of one who has attained the first fruit.

Yet, among these [Bodhisattvas], some in the first stage (*bhūmi*) receive a body of segmented birth (*pariccheda-kāya*), while others receive a transformation body (*pariṇāma-kāya*). Furthermore, that body of segmented birth itself cannot...

Regarding the vision of the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the same stage, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that they are perceived through the eyes of the same class of divine sight (*divyacakṣus*).

Furthermore, within the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*), the eyes of a Bodhisattva with a body of segmented existence (*prādeśika-kāya*) cannot see the transformation body of one who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), even though such a person is a noble one (*ārya*).
This is because the Bodhisattva in the four roots of goodness is still an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), unlike those noble ones from the first bhūmi upward. (2)
Regarding the segmented body of the stages: one may see the segmented body of the first stage.

Furthermore, although a bodhisattva of the first stage excels in virtue and conduct over those of the same stage, such a bodhisattva of the first stage cannot even see the land where a bodhisattva of the second stage dwells, much less see their body.
This is just as, for example, among the six heavens of the desire realm, although they are all equally ordinary beings and belong to the same realm, [they cannot see one another].
All are surpassed by even a small amount of merit. The Four Heavenly Kings cannot see the bodies of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, and so it continues likewise;
how much less could they see noble Bodhisattvas?

The Commentary states: "As previously mentioned in the seventh fascicle, there are already two interpretations. The Explanation says: "However, in the seventh fascicle, there are two masters' teachings. One says:
'A Bodhisattva who speaks of suddenness leaves behind a body only in the Form Realm; if it concerns the Śrāvakas of the Two Vehicles,' [it is otherwise]."

Regarding the second master’s position that one may leave behind a body in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) after [death], he also permits that those born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) may hear the Dharma from their former sons and turn their minds [toward awakening], with the exception of the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).

As for the statement that "this karma, this continent, and even the humans and devas of the desire realm are likewise," it means that within the category of *paricchinna-vedanīya* (karma to be experienced in a specific period), the karma, the continent, the realm, and the stage are all fixed at the time of birth; that is, such karma is the very cause, namely, impure wholesome action (*sāsrava-kuśala*).

Regarding "evil karma" and so forth: "this continent, this world-system, this land, this earth" refers to the place where one receives a body that undergoes the fruit of fragmented existence (*bheda-phala*).
That is to say, by such karma, one is born among humans in Jambudvīpa and lives for a certain number of years; the same applies to the other three continents.
Furthermore, by such karma, one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); that is to say, by such karma.
Therefore, the nine stages of birth and death are all fixed. Within the transformation-rebirth (*parināmi-kāya*), this karma is the cause; there is no subsequent karma.
The "provincial boundaries" and "stages" refer to the place where the fruit is received, or it refers to the body within these provinces.

That is, the untainted (*anāsrava*) karma within the four dhyānas serves as the causal support; or, even for the body in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it likewise employs the untainted karma of the four dhyānas [as its support].

As for the cause: it may be the body of the first dhyāna, and it also takes the untainted (anāsrava) states of the upper three dhyānas as its cause. Transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) are all indeterminate;

however, if they are based on untainted karma, their level is fixed. Since the *Śūchā* states that "the four limit-dhyānas (prāntakoṭika-dhyāna) can support transformation," we know that untainted concentrations of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) cannot directly produce transformation bodies, such as the body of a deva in the Bṛhatphala heaven.

They experience [the results] for five hundred kalpas, and their bodies are all five hundred yojanas in height. If they enter meditative absorption (samāpatti) or the fruit of concentration (samādhi-phala), they extend their lifespan for five or six hundred kalpas;
this is called "increase. Alternatively, if they sustain it for three or two hundred kalpas, this is called "decrease.
It is the same in other places regarding the sustenance of the body; there is only increase and no decrease.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "For example, the bodies of the Bṛhatphala (Great Fruit) devas in the Fourth Dhyāna exceed five hundred *yojanas* in height, and their lifespans exceed five hundred kalpas.

This is likewise true for those [devas] therein, and even for humans and devas in the Desire Realm. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) says: "Now, we shall first cite the Bṛhatphala devas within the Fourth Dhyāna;
because they represent the highest grade (*uttama-prakāra*), they are cited specifically. For instance, the bodies of the Bṛhatphala devas are five hundred *yojanas* in height, and so forth."

For five hundred kalpas. If a bodhisattva, relying on the body of a god of the Bṛhatphala Heaven, undergoes a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya), and if that body increases to exceed three hundred yojanas, it is then called "decreasing.

Furthermore, just as the people of Jambudvīpa are six feet tall and have a lifespan of one hundred years, if a bodhisattva, relying on the body of a god of the Bṛhatphala Heaven, undergoes a transformation-body and that body exceeds three hundred yojanas, it is then called "decreasing."
Furthermore, suppose a person from the Southern Continent is six feet tall and has a lifespan of one hundred years.
If a Bodhisattva, relying on such a body, enters the *pariṇāmika-kāya* (transformed body), and if this life-span exceeds one hundred years and the body exceeds six feet, it is called "increase.

If the life-span is thirty years or less and the body is four feet or less, it is called "decrease. Alternatively, some commentaries state that it is like the body of the *Akaniṣṭha-bhavana* (the Highest Heaven), which exceeds ten thousand [yojanas].
It is six thousand *yojanas* [in height]. After passing through sixteen thousand kalpas, the two periods differ.
This commentary distinguishes between the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, up until their attainment of the inconceivable realm and the untainted *dharmakāya*.

However, because this text clarifies the matter in relation to the *aśaikṣas* (those beyond training) of the three vehicles, it does not mention that Bodhisattvas attain the *pariṇāmikakāya* (transformation body). The intent of this passage is to censure the two vehicles for their lack of...

Regarding the transformation of the mind through study: although one has not yet attained the first bhūmi nor realized the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), because one has already attained the body of transformation (*nairmāṇikakāya*) upon transforming the mind prior to the bhūmis, it is said that one has "not yet realized the non-self of phenomena" and "has not yet attained the state beyond the body of transformation.

However, even though a bodhisattva has realized the non-self of phenomena, because this realization is not yet perfected, they have not yet attained the state beyond the body of transformation. Only a Buddha realizes the non-self of phenomena in its full perfection.
Because it is full, it is free from change and transformation. The *Shu* (Commentary) states:

"That which is born refers to the arising of various sensations (*vedanā*) and perceptions (*saṃjñā*); that which dies refers to the cessation of the various sensations and faculties (*indriya*). The *Jie* (Exegesis) explains:

"Sensation" (*vedanā*) either refers to the enjoyment of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) or to the grasping and maintaining [of the body], which is called sensation. "Faculties" (*indriya*) refers to the five forms. Thus, "that which is born" refers to the various sensations and the five forms.
The faculties arise. As for "one who has died," this refers to those possessing the five material faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*).
The commentary states: *Mālikā* is translated here as "niece"; she is none other than Queen Māllikā, and even Vaiśravaṇā (Śrīmālā).
The commentary explains: It was asked why Queen Mallikā was called Śrīmālā. She replied: "I was originally a flower-girl;
by making offerings to the Buddha, I manifested in this life as the daughter-in-law of King Prasenajit. Because I surpassed the king in excellence, I am named Śrīmālā (Victorious Garland).
King Virūḍhaka is Śrīmālā’s younger brother."

The Commentary states: "That explanation is 'as if' using the objects of perception as the very afflictions, and so forth, up to this point where the cause and fruit of the *paricchinna* (limited) realm are cited to illustrate the *pariṇāma* (transformative) realm.
Here, the body of the limited realm is cited as a metaphor for the body of the transformative realm; therefore, it is said to be 'as if.
For instance, regarding the category of the limited body: by taking impure wholesome and unwholesome [karma] as the cause, one brings about the five fruits, such as consciousness."

When the seeds of the afflictive hindrances arise, they take the "appropriation" (*upādāna*) link as a condition to moisten the seeds of the five resultant fruits—consciousness and so forth—from the preceding links, thereby producing the body of future existence within the three realms. Now, this same principle applies to the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*):
it takes uncontaminated karma with conceptual differentiation as its cause and the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as its condition, whereby the transformation [of the basis] is brought about.
The Commentary states: "The three types of mind-made bodies (manomayakāya) produced in this life and after death. The Explanation states:
These are the mind-made body of an Arhat, the body of a Pratyekabuddha, and the body of a Bodhisattva who has attained mastery; these are the three.
The *Śū* (Commentary) states: The *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* says, "Outside the three realms, there are three kinds of persons who undergo transformation (*pariṇāmika*).

Although these persons are indeed [within] this [world], they are not outside the realms. The *Jie* (Exegesis) explains: As for the statement "outside the three realms," this is spoken by way of an indirect cause (*paryāya-hetu*).

That is to say, it refers to the cause capable of inducing [rebirth], namely, untainted karma with conceptual differentiation (*anāsrava-savikalpa-karman*), which is designated as being "outside the three" (*tri-bahis*). Since this body of transformation (*nairmāṇika-śarīra*) is...
That which is with outflows (sāsrava) is not outside the three realms. As for the three types of persons, they are the Arhat, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Bodhisattva who has already attained mastery.
The Commentary states: "From the dwelling of ignorance up to the arising of the afflictions. These five should be designated as both self and other; "self and other" refers to the seeds.
All five dwelling-grounds (*pṛthagjanabhūmi*) are seeds. However, within these, there are two layers: first, the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) serves as the locus upon which they dwell;
second, if it is the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it constitutes that which dwells and that which is dependent.

The second [point] is that the seeds of the two obstacles (*dvividhāvaraṇa*) serve as the basis (*āśraya*) for what is supported; if the two obstacles manifest, they are the supported (*āśrita*). The commentary states:
"His intention is to say that there is one [type of body], which takes 'appropriation' (*upādāna*) as its condition. The explanation says:

"The transformation body (*pariṇāmikakāya*)—each and every dharma-function—is like the body of the *bhavasaṃdhi* (segmented existence), taking the member of appropriation (*upādānāṅga*) as its condition and contaminated karma (*sāsravakarma*) as its cause. Now, regarding the transformation [body]..."
The body is likewise. It takes the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as its condition and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) conceptualized karma as its cause;
therefore, it is said that "the one is like grasping.

The *Commentary* states that the second fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* says that for those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, [the path] may eliminate seven births up to three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

"Cultivating the causes for Bodhi throughout kalpas is without fault. The commentary explains: The meaning of this passage is that those who have attained the first three fruits receive a *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body).
Alternatively, it refers to those who have eliminated seven births, or those who are destined for seven more births and receive a *nirmāṇakāya*.

Or, for example, one who has attained the first fruit may possess the determinate karma for seven births within the realm of segmented existence (*prādeśika-karma*). [This continues] until the end of the Dharma during the ten-thousand-year period.
Once [the afflictions] have been extinguished, that which has attained the state of non-attainment through conditions alone is called a *pratyekabuddha*.

If one refers to the previous time when they were first generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), it was by listening to the Dharma from the Buddha that they subsequently generated the mind of a *pratyekabuddha*.

If there is someone who plants the roots of goodness for the four fruits of a *śrāvaka* and attains the first fruit of a *śrāvaka*, yet acts as one who returns to existence at most seven times, that person will reach their seventh birth.
Those born in the human realm, if they encounter a world where the Buddha-Dharma does not exist for seven lifetimes, will manifest in the form of a *śrāvaka*.
If born in the heavens, they manifest as *śrāvakas*, for it is by virtue of having the *śrāvaka* faculty-nature that one is able to be born in the heavens;

those with the *pratyekabuddha* faculty-nature cannot be born in the heavens, but exist only among humans. The Mahāyāna and the Sarvāstivāda agree in this teaching regarding the three vehicles of persons.
Having planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), one may also be reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) or among the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
If a *śrāvaka* plants the wholesome roots of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, they may likewise be reborn in the formless realm.

If one speaks according to the practitioners who follow the *śrāvakas*, as for the *khadgaviṣāṇakalpa* (rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddha), they cannot plant the stages of "warmth" or "summit" (*mūrdhan*) at this present time; rather, they plant "patience" (*kṣānti*) and the subsequent stages in a future life, within that single lifetime.

He attains enlightenment in a single sitting. According to the Sarvāstivāda school, the application of the Bodhisattva’s four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*) is identical to that of the rhinoceros-like [Pratyekabuddha].

Whether one plants the wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*) for śrāvakas over the course of one or two lifetimes, or plants the four roots of goodness for śrāvakas and so forth, such a person may emerge in a world where no Buddha exists and manifest as a rhinoceros-like [Pratyekabuddha], or else remain with only one birth remaining.

This refers to those who have attained the second fruit (sakṛdāgāmin) and receive a *pariṇāmika-kāya* (transformation body) with only one more birth remaining. These are those who go once between the human and heavenly realms;

this is called "one birth. Just as there is one birth for a *sakṛdāgāmin*, they must first exhaust the karma of their final *prātibhājika-kāya* (segmented body)—the fixed karma for one lifetime—before they can enter the *pariṇāmika-kāya*. Alternatively, they may exclude certain places within the human realm.

The "one who is born" (*upapadya*) refers to a person who has attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). Having attained the transformation body (*pariṇāmikadeha*), they are like those who attain parinirvāṇa with effort (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*) or without effort (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*).
Alternatively, having passed through one birth in a single celestial realm of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they undergo the dharma of transformation; this is the fruit of non-returning.
If they are born in a higher celestial realm, there is only one birth within that heaven, never two. There is no place where one can undergo two births, just as [in the case of the aforementioned].
Having received one birth among the Brahmakāyika devas as a result of the stage of Non-returner (anāgāmiphala), one is not born again among the Brahmakāyikas.
After dying from the Brahmakāyika realm, one is immediately born among the Brahmapurohita devas and so forth; one will certainly never again be born among the Brahmakāyikas.

One who possesses karma fixed for two births does not attain the first fruit [of stream-entry]; rather, they attain it while still in the body of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), having exhausted this [remaining birth].
Once one has attained the karma for only one more birth within the heavens, one then attains the fruit of Arhatship. The same applies to other fruits of the heavens.

For those in the Unreturning Fruit (*anāgāmin*) who are of indeterminate nature, there is only one more birth in various places within the higher realms. Among those in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are four types of Unreturning Ones who flow upward (*ūrdhvasrotas*):

those who attain contact with the peak of existence, those who attain it without practice, and those who flow upward; these may all receive a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This refers to the Unreturning One who flows upward.

Furthermore, there are those who attain the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmin) through either "leaping over" (*pluta*) or "half-leaping" (*ardhapluta*), as well as those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*). Such individuals do not receive a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
If a Non-returner attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), they must necessarily belong to the fixed nature of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*).

Moreover, some Non-returners are born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and only after eleven births do they receive a transformation body. As for those in the fruit of Non-returner who are born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), [they likewise do not receive a transformation body].
Those born in the [five] Pure Heavens (*śuddhāvāsa*) also do not undergo transformation (*pariṇāma*). All such beings are Śrāvakas of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*).

If they are persons who have attained the third fruit, once they have exhausted their determinate karma (*niyata-karma*) pertaining to the body of segmented existence (*bhava-āntara*), they immediately undergo transformation.
Although they previously possessed indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karma*) produced by various afflictions (*kleśa*), all of these attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The *Śāstra* says: "Ultimate non-arising does not mean never arising. The commentary explains:

"Ultimate non-arising" means that once one has received the body of transformation (*pariṇāmika-kāya*), the indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karma*) regarding the body of fragmentation (*prādeśika-kāya*) can no longer produce it; thus, one ultimately cannot produce the body of fragmentation.
This is not "never arising," for by means of untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*), the body of transformation is sustained, and thus the body of transformation is indeed attained.
Because they are born, their transformation body (*pariṇāma-kāya*) is immediately born; it is not that they will never be born again.
The Commentary states: "The eightieth [chapter] says that those Śrāvakas who subsequently turn toward Bodhi, even up to the wheel-turning [kings], this passage is not reasonable.

The Explanation states: "The eightieth [chapter] speaks in terms of general characteristics, or refers to those within the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) who are already capable of discerning [the truth]."
Regarding "renunciation": this refers to those of the two vehicles who, having attained the first three fruits, turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna;

they indeed renounce the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented body) and receive the *parināmika-kāya* (transformation body). Alternatively, it refers to those at the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) who are then able to renounce it;

these are the practitioners of the two vehicles at the stage of no-more-learning, who renounce the segmented body and attain entry into the transformation body. Thus, one knows that [this applies to] the first three fruits.
If one attains the body of transformation (*pariṇāmika-kāya*), and considering the text of this *Śrīmālā-sūtra* as well as the treatises on Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*),
it is taught that only those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward attain the body of transformation.
It is not reasonable to claim that those who have attained the first three fruits [of the Śrāvaka path] attain the body of transformation.

The *Śāstra* states: "Regarding those of determined nature prior to the seventh stage, because it does not mention these three kinds of certainty—such as 'receiving this birth' and so forth—it is so described.
The commentary explains: "As for the Bodhisattvas of determined nature prior to the seventh stage, they possess a body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Now, in this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, only the Arhats of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage onward [are discussed]."
Regarding the statement that "Sāgaramati receives the transformation body (*pariṇāmikakāya*)," this is spoken in reference to those who possess a fixed nature.
Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, as well as those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), definitely receive the transformation body.

As for those in the first three fruits of the śrāvaka path and bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage, they may either receive the transformation body or not; because they are not fixed, it is so stated.

This *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* treatise does not explicitly state that the three types of persons—the two vehicles at the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward—are fixed;
it does, however, imply this. Question: Regarding Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage, what is meant by "fixed nature" (*niyatatva*)?
If they possess a fixed nature and thereby attain the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), there must also be those with an unfixed nature who do not attain the transformation body.
Answer: If those from the seventh stage and below are called the Buddha-lineage, then Bodhisattvas with predominant wisdom are called those of "determined nature.
From the eighth stage and the first [of the ninth] stage onwards, they immediately receive the body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The treatise states that some attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) from the very first stage (*bhūmi*). If a Bodhisattva is one for whom compassion is predominant, they are said to be of "indefinite nature" (*aniyata-gotra*);

such a person only undergoes the transformation of birth (*pariṇāmiki upapatti*) upon reaching the seventh stage, when their mind is still subject to outflows (*sāsrava*). Therefore, the aforementioned treatise says: "Or there are those who, even until the completion of the seventh stage, only then enter the meditative absorption of cessation."

The Commentary states: "From the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) onwards, the Bodhisattva takes on the suffering of the three categories [of beings] as a true body, which cannot be known [as such by others]. The Explanation says:

Regarding those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) with a fragmented body (*paricchinna-śarīra*) prior to the seventh stage, when they take on the suffering of sentient beings on behalf of the three categories, they are either in a human body as a Bodhisattva or in a celestial body.
When facing the taking on of suffering for the three categories of sentient beings, there is also the experience of painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*). If the Bodhi...
Sāṃkṛtyāyana felt weary and distressed. He then gave the others food and clothing and spoke of various benefits. [The interlocutor asks:

"If those in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) experience suffering due to the existence of fragmented states of suffering, how can there be the sensation of suffering for those in the form realm (rūpadhātu)?

What is the answer? [The reply is: Bodhisattvas of Great Compassion are constantly born in the desire realm to save sentient beings; they do not frequently appear in the form realm. In the form realm, there is no sensation of suffering, because the body in the form realm...
Because their bodies are so subtle, they cannot be burned by fire; even if they were to enter a fire, it could not consume them.

Due to the subtlety of their bodies, they attain the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding all the fruits of the three evil destinies associated with the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Those with transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) prior to the seventh stage may manifest such bodies within the three miserable realms to undergo suffering on behalf of sentient beings.
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says that at the eighth stage one 'discards the insect-body,' meaning one discards the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence).

The explanation says: Generally speaking, this refers to discarding the segmented body; specifically, it means that the gods of the desire realm, humans, and deer are all considered "corpse-villages" (*śiva-grāma*).

They either dwell within or consume them. According to the scripture, within every single hair there are corpse-villages where they dwell; "discarding" refers to discarding the bodies [of those who dwell] in the desire realm heavens.

The human body, as well as the bodies of those in the form realm heavens, are both *pariccheda-kāya* (segmented bodies). They are radiant and pure like light, and thus lack the fire of putrefaction (*kuṇapa-agni*).

Those who dwell in the desire realm heavens—including the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven—also include yakṣas, spirits, ghosts, nāgas, and so forth; likewise, there are nāgas and others in the Tuṣita heaven.
These are *pariṇāma-kāya* (transformable bodies) and are likewise without the fire of putrefaction. In the hells, there is no door, only fire.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "If one provides this interpretation, it is because according to this context, it is not the case that [the transformation body] is absent prior to the seventh ground;

even those in the first three fruits may also receive it. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states: "While Bodhisattvas from the eighth ground upward definitely receive the transformation body (*pariṇāmikakāya*), in reality, those from the seventh ground downward, as well as persons within the three realms, may also obtain and receive the transformation body."
The Commentary states: "Since those who have attained the first stage and above must no longer possess determinate *paricchinna* (segmented) karma, they are like Arhats.
The Explanation states: "There are Bodhisattvas on the stages who attain the *parināmita* (transformative) body; these individuals lack determinate *paricchinna* karma."
Just as it is at the time of being an Arhat, there is definitely no karma of fragmented existence (*bheda-karma*).

If there were definite karma of fragmented existence, then an Arhat would have two births among the Brahmakāyika gods; thus, the karma of a fragmented body would certainly exist even during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Only after feeling has arisen does one attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*). If this interpretation is adopted, there may be bodhisattvas in whom wisdom predominates who possess determinate *paricchinna-karma* (segmented karma);
such individuals would not receive a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward. Alternatively, there may be bodhisattvas in whom compassion predominates;
although they lack determinate segmented karma from the first stage upward, they still receive a body resulting from indeterminate karma. That is to say:
In the first stage (*bhūmi*), one does not yet receive the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Some, for whom compassion (*karuṇā*) is predominant, do not seek out afflictions (*kleśa*);

thus, from the first stage upward, they receive the body of segmented existence (*paricchinna-kāya*). Others, for whom wisdom (*jñāna*) is predominant, do seek out afflictions; thus, from the first stage upward, they receive the transformation body.
The Commentary (*Śū*) states: "Mahāmati speaks of the basis of tranquility, and so forth, yet this is not stated here with absolute certainty. The Explanation (*Jie*) states:
"That which speaks of the dharma of tranquility is precisely the Buddha’s teaching on the principle of traversing space; it refers to the Bodhisattva of the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi (the Far-Reaching Stage)."
Having attained and realized this characteristic of non-self, the Bodhisattva of the seventh stage obtains the sovereign body of birth at will (*yathā-kāmopapatti-deha*).
Therefore, it is known that Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage also obtain this body of transformation (*pariṇāmi-śarīra*).

Nevertheless, Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage have not yet universally attained the body of transformation; that is to say, among those Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage, there are some who have attained it...

Regarding the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*): there are those who do not obtain it and those who do. In this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, it is not stated that bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage obtain the transformation body;

rather, it is said that from the eighth stage onward they invariably obtain it. This treatise and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* state that those in the eighth stage and the two vehicles at the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) obtain the transformation body, while it is also stated that [bodhisattvas] obtain the transformation body in the seventh stage.
The Commentary states: "First, because one attains the bliss of samādhi, up to the bliss of the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) as they truly are.
The Explanation says: "Samādhi" refers to the three samādhis—emptiness (śūnyatā), signlessness (animitta), and wishlessness (apraṇihita).

"Old" [tradition] uses the term *samādi*, which is an error; the new name is *samādhi*. *Samādhi* is equivalent to *samāpatti*. *Samāpatti* refers to the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvasamāpatti*).

Next is concentration (*samādhi*). This was previously called "mixed" (*miśra*); the new translation is *samāpatti*, which means "equilibrium" (*tingzhì*). Previously, it was stated that one delights in equilibrium;

the bliss of the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*) is the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Regarding the two points concerning knowing the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena as they truly are:
this refers to being able to correctly and appropriately realize the principles of all phenomena. Furthermore, "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) means "nature" (*svabhāva*). That is to say—
The principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is that which can be realized as it truly is. Regarding the phrase "three types arise simultaneously and not otherwise":

"types" refers to Bodhisattvas of the ninth and tenth stages (*bhūmi*), who are able to know all phenomena across the manifold categories of form and mind, or who are able to manifest as sentient beings of the types found on Mount Sumeru; yet these arise all at once and simultaneously. This is...
