That which is non-defiled (*anupalipta*) refers to wholesome (*kuśala*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas. Regarding "not produced by the sixth [consciousness]":

this means that if afflictions (*kleśa*) are not produced from the sixth consciousness, it implies taking those afflictions produced from the five consciousnesses, as well as the five sense objects such as visible form (*rūpa*), these wholesome and neutral dharmas, the afflictions produced within the five consciousnesses, and the dharmas of the five material sense organs (*pañca-rūpīndriya*). These are not [objects of] vision (*darśana*).

They are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Among the five consciousnesses, there are only afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation; there are no afflictions abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) within the five consciousnesses.
Furthermore, it is reckoned that among the five consciousnesses, there is only innate goodness (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*), and no acquired goodness (*prāyogika-kuśala*).

They reckon that within the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), there is also the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) or the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), as well as innate virtue (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) and virtue acquired through application (*prāyogika-kuśala*).

Now, because this concerns the Mahāyāna, they further reckon that within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) there is also the path of seeing, since [the latter] arises only when induced by the mental consciousness;
and that within the five sensory consciousnesses there is also the path of cultivation. Within the five sensory consciousnesses...
There is innate goodness (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*), and there is also acquired goodness (*prāyogika-kuśala*).

For instance, when the sixth consciousness grasps innate goodness, it simultaneously induces innate goodness within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). Likewise, when the sixth consciousness gives rise to acquired goodness, [it induces it in the five sensory consciousnesses].

That is to say, among the five consciousnesses, there is also "wholesome by application" (*prayoga-kuśala*). This wholesome [state] within the five consciousnesses is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the sixth consciousness;
it cannot be said that the wholesome by application arises within the sixth consciousness while the wholesome acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) arises within the five consciousnesses.

This cannot possibly be the case. One must not say that this mind of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is without ignorance (*avidyā*), just as the mind of attachment to a person (*pudgalagrāha*) is accompanied by ignorance.

Regarding this, Dharmapāla and Sthiramati state: "If you claim that within this wholesome or neutral mind there is an affliction of attachment to phenomena, yet this attachment to phenomena does not coexist with ignorance, then you would be describing the characteristics of delusion (*moha*) and non-delusion (*amoha*) as being identical."

[This is] contradictory. If you claim that when the grasping for phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) arises within an unwholesome mind, it is necessarily accompanied by ignorance (*avidyā*), then we raise this objection:

Just as it is accepted that when the grasping for a person (*pudgala-grāha*) arises, it is accompanied by ignorance, why is it that when the grasping for phenomena arises, it is not accompanied by ignorance?

Since both types of grasping are equally forms of attachment, when the grasping for a person arises, it is accompanied by ignorance; likewise, when the grasping for phenomena arises, it should also be accompanied by ignorance.
Both. The *Śāstra* states:
"The World-Honored One, regarding this wisdom, [arises] in association with the momentary mind that gives rise to afflictions," and so forth.

This passage refers specifically to that which gives rise to afflictions; it means that this mind arises in association with active (*samudācāra*) afflictions. This is the intended meaning of the text.
It is said that all moments of mind in which active afflictions arise are associated with and grow depending upon the ground of the seeds of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
There is nothing that does not depend upon the ground of the dwelling of ignorance. Is this "ground of the dwelling of ignorance" the same as the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)?
If the cognitive obstruction is designated as that which initiates karma, then because it depends on that designation for initiating karma, it is untainted (*anāsrava*).
It is likewise. For instance, when Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward enter meditative absorption, they are constantly in a state of outflow-free (anāsrava) consciousness.
Because it is induced by that outflow-free state, they are also able to give rise to the five types of cessation-consciousness and perceive forms or hear sounds and so forth.

These five consciousnesses are all induced by the outflow-free state; thus, these five consciousnesses are designated as "outflow-free" in name. However, in reality, these five consciousnesses are actually with-outflow (sāsrava), because [the five]...

The five material sense-faculties that serve as the supports for consciousness, as well as the eighth consciousness, are with-outflow (sāsrava); therefore, the future is truly without-outflow (anāsrava).
Regarding the phrase "the beginningless ground of ignorance non-associated with the mind" in the World-Honored One’s teaching, the meaning of this passage is that when the mind arises—
It is associated exclusively with the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); its mind is not associated with the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, regarding those factors that exceed the sands of the Ganges and are to be abandoned by the wisdom of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas—this "intention" (*manas*) refers to the wisdom of the Bodhisattva as the antidote, which serves to reveal the cognitive obstructions.
When the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) is severed, all that is to be abandoned is likewise eliminated.

"Furthermore, they are abandoned along with [the cognitive obscurations]. Question: This sutra states that when the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are abandoned, the remaining afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are abandoned along with them.
Why is it that Bodhisattvas on the ten stages abandon only the cognitive obscurations and do not abandon the afflictive obscurations?
If that were so, they would necessarily be simultaneous, just as the two types of grasping function together. This passage is Dharmapāla’s critique of Sthiramati.

However, Sthiramati maintains that within the sixth consciousness there exist both the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), whereas regarding the seventh consciousness, he allows only for the afflictive hindrances and does not allow for the cognitive hindrances.

Dharmapāla challenges this, saying: "If the sixth consciousness possesses the afflictive hindrances, it must also possess the cognitive hindrances; thus, the two hindrances would necessarily [coexist]."

If it is argued that because they arise together, the two obstacles (āvaraṇas) must each have distinct entities, then the seventh consciousness would necessarily have two distinct entities for its twofold grasping (*grāha*) arising simultaneously;
and within the seventh consciousness, there would likewise be the dual functioning of the two types of grasping, just as there is in the sixth consciousness.

According to the view of the foolish [opponent], this passage leads directly to the following section of the treatise: "Question: If that is so, wherever there is the obstacle of the cognizable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), there must necessarily be afflictions (*kleśa*)."
Regarding the "obstructions" (āvaraṇa): the essential natures of these two obstructions each have their own distinctions.

Within the seventh consciousness, the two types of grasping (grāha) should arise simultaneously, because they are both forms of grasping, just as [causes and effects] arise together. Next, the treatise is cited to answer: "Although their essence is not different, their functions are distinct."
Regarding the fact that these two obstacles vary in their degree of excellence or inferiority according to the noble paths of the three vehicles:

because both [the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha] are able to sever the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*) is termed "excellent. Because they cannot sever the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*) serves as an auxiliary.
Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because bodhisattvas of the ten stages sever only the cognitive obstacle, it is the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena [that is predominant].
It is superior [to the Śrāvaka], yet it cannot sever the afflictions (*kleśa*); therefore, the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*) is inferior.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra*, "the thorn or the subsequent," the word "or" (*vā*) here is used as an indefinite term; thus, it means that the wisdom of the emptiness of persons is "inferior or" [not severed], rather than the afflictions themselves being called "or.

This refers to the seeds (*bīja*) and not to the latent predispositions (*dausthulya*). If one does not sever the seeds of the afflictions throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*), [the wisdom remains inferior].

Therefore, it is said that the afflictions (*kleśa*) are not severed throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Within these ten stages, one is also able to sever the "heavy residues" (*dausthulya*) of the afflictions;
"heavy" refers precisely to this lack of functional capacity (*akarmanyatā*). Because two fruits are attained, it is necessary to sever both. As for these two fruits:
This refers to the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), which are called the two fruits. Furthermore, it says:
"Bodhi and Nirvāṇa. This means that by abandoning the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one attains nirvāṇa; and by abandoning the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one attains bodhi.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not sever the seeds of the heavy latencies (*dausthulya*) of the two obstructions.

The meaning of this passage is that ordinary beings are not capable of severing the seeds of the karma of the two obstructions; rather, it means they cannot sever either the seeds or the heavy latencies of the two obstructions.

Regarding the statement that "the seeds and the manifest [states] are one in essence but different in substance": if ordinary beings and others give rise to the manifest afflictions (*kleśa*), [they do so while possessing these seeds].

[This] activity is accompanied by the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Thus, the seeds of the predominant obscuration within a single manifesting state of both obscurations are the same as the seeds of the two manifesting obscurations; they possess the same essential substance (*ekadravyatva*).

If an Arhat has already severed and exhausted the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and subsequently gives rise solely to the manifestation of the cognitive obscuration, [that] cognitive obscuration...
The seeds obtained from what is currently active constitute the seeds; these seeds follow along with the active manifestations. There are only seeds of the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
These seeds of the cognitive hindrance are distinct in essence from the seeds of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*). There are those who possess only the cognitive hindrance.

The seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are of the same substance as the seeds of the non-common afflictions (*āveṇika-kleśa*). This refers to all cognitive obstructions present within the body of an Arhat;
they possess seeds of afflictions that are exclusive [to them], and these seeds do not share the same substance as the seeds of the cognitive obstructions.

This refers to Bodhisattvas on the ten stages (*bhūmi*) during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), who sever only the cognitive obstructions and do not sever the seeds of the afflictions; thus, [the latter] remain exclusive.

Regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*), there are two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) that share the same substance; this refers to the seeds of the two obstructions within the body of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*). This is the meaning of "being the cause.

Therefore, the seeds of the two obstructions each possess their own distinct substantial entities and do not share a common substance. As for the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of these two obstructions, they may occur either individually or simultaneously.
If it is the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it occurs as a manifestation of the cognitive obstruction alone, while at the same time...
If there is no manifestation of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it is as in the case of an Arhat; that is, only the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) manifests.

Since each [type of] afflictive hindrance arises, their manifestations are necessarily simultaneous; thus, whenever there is a cognitive hindrance, there is necessarily a manifestation of the afflictive hindrance, and there is no manifestation of the afflictive hindrance alone.

Regarding those who lack the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): if there were only the seeds of the cognitive obscuration, even though they do not share the same seeds as the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*), those solitary seeds of the cognitive obscuration would still be able to produce manifest activity (*samudācāra*). This is just like the solitary cognitive obscurations present within the bodies of Arhats.

They are able to produce manifest activity. If there are various types of afflictive obstructions that do not share the same seeds with the cognitive obstructions, those individual types of afflictive obstructions cannot each produce manifest activity on their own.
This is just as when, for example, the seeds of the two obstructions previously shared the same substance;
at the time a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage abandons one portion of the seeds of the cognitive obstructions, there remains one portion of the seeds of the afflictive obstructions.
Furthermore, because it cannot give rise to active manifestation [of afflictions], when afflictions are manifesting, there must necessarily be the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

This is just as, according to the previous principle, one who is deluded regarding the shallow must necessarily be deluded regarding the deep. When afflictions are manifesting, there must necessarily be the cognitive obscuration;
however, there may be delusion regarding the deep without delusion regarding the shallow, which occurs when the cognitive obscuration is present while afflictions are not actively manifesting.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "it is not the other three types": Question: If the unwholesome nature (*akuśala-svabhāva*) of deportment (*iryāpatha*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) arises simultaneously with afflictions (*kleśa*), it must necessarily involve the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Why, then, does the text say it is not the other three types?

Furthermore, if the cognitive obstruction is comprised within that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*), among the four types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*), under which category is the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) subsumed?

The Commentary states: "Although it arises simultaneously with unwholesome [states] and the generation of the resolve for awakening, and one does not attain the two vehicles, it is nonetheless termed 'unobscured' (anivṛta). Question:
Since the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is of the same substance as unwholesome and obscured afflictions (*kleśa*), how can it be "unobscured-neutral" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)?

Question: Since the cognitive obstruction is of the same substance as the afflictions, it would be just like an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) giving rise to the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
One creates evil karma such as killing living beings. At the same time as these afflictions (*kleśa*), there is also the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

If the cognitive obscuration is of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala*), it is likewise of an unwholesome nature. If an affliction arises, it is of a nature that is obscured (*nivṛta*); the cognitive obscuration is also of a nature that is obscured.
This is because the seeds of the cognitive obscuration must necessarily arise simultaneously with the afflictions; therefore, they cannot be one and the same.
Within the mind, afflictions (*kleśa*) are of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala*), while that which is obstructed is of a concealed nature (*nivṛta*).

As in the case of an Arhat, since they have not only severed the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) but have not yet severed the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and since the cognitive obstruction pertains to both the unwholesome and the concealed natures, how can this cognitive obstruction be considered "unconcealed" (*anivṛta*) from the perspective of the two vehicles? Answer: This cognitive...

Obstruction. If it shares the same substance as the afflictions (*kleśa*) and arises simultaneously with them, this cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is of an unwholesome and obscured nature (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*).
If the afflictions are severed and only the cognitive obstruction remains, then in relation to the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), the cognitive obstruction is unobscured (*anivṛta*).
This is like a person who, possessing both hands and both feet, is able both to kill others and to come and go.
One performs various kinds of activities. Suppose that person were to have one hand or one foot severed by another, or even have half their body cut off;
since they would then lack half of their bodily parts, they could no longer perform various activities such as walking or coming and going. This is the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
However, this has been difficult to understand in the past. As for this cognitive obscuration, when viewed from the perspective of a Bodhisattva, it is likewise non-arising.

Regarding its nature as being "obscured" (*nivṛta*): there is an external objection. It is argued that because it is an obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and because it obstructs the fruit of a Bodhisattva, it is "obscured";

yet, because it does not obstruct the fruit of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), it is "unobscured" (*anivṛta*). To this, one should object: if the obstacle to knowledge is defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and yet does not obstruct the fruit of the two vehicles, it would consequently become "unobscured.
Furthermore, this may be addressed within the stages of the equipment (*saṃbhāra*) and application (*prayoga*), where it serves to assist the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

The path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) may be admitted as virtuous (*kuśala*). However, if it does not assist toward the fruit of Buddhahood, it should be established as non-obscured (*anivṛta*). There is no difficulty regarding external [objects].

For example, when the seventh consciousness takes the eighth consciousness as its object, it is called "possessing a substantial basis" (*sadravyālambana*) and is said to be "common to both the affective and the fundamental.

If the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) of the seventh consciousness belongs to the perceiving seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*), it is of an obscured nature (*nivṛta*). If it belongs to the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness which is the perceived object, it is non-obscured (*anivṛta*).
Regarding its nature as obscured (nivṛta): how could a single objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) be half-unobscured and half-obscured? If one were to provide another interpretation:
if the object of cognition (ālambana) is predominant, it belongs solely to the object and is thus unobscured;

if the cognizing mind is predominant, it belongs solely to the seventh [consciousness] and is thus obscured. This interpretation has some degree of reasonableness. Furthermore, an objection is raised: "If [the interpretation is]..."

Just as the sixth consciousness is based upon the retributive-undetermined (*vipāka-avyākṛta*) mind within the second consciousness, which serves as the fundamental locus for both the physical basis (*āśraya*) and the mental objects (*ālambana*).
One should inquire of the Dharma Master regarding the commentary’s statement:
"The former masters do not admit that there is dharma-grasping (*dharmanirūpaṇa*) within the seventh consciousness, because two difficulties would be equalized."

However, Master Sthiramati maintains that while the seventh consciousness contains the attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*), he does not admit that the seventh consciousness contains the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
The current correct interpretation states otherwise. Why? Because it contradicts the inference (*anumāna*) within my own orthodox school.
If there were an attachment to birth (*jāti-grāha*) within the seventh consciousness, the two difficulties would be equal. If [there is no such attachment] in the seventh consciousness...

In the middle [state], there is no clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*); thus, they are not equal. To say they are equal means that while the seventh consciousness contains clinging to birth (*jātigrāha*), the sixth consciousness realizes the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*);

while the seventh consciousness contains clinging to phenomena, the sixth enters the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). When the seventh consciousness [realizes] the emptiness of phenomena, they are equal.

If they were not equal—if the seventh consciousness possessed clinging to phenomena—then when the sixth consciousness performs the contemplation of the emptiness of persons, the seventh consciousness...
Why does it not enter the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)? Because within the seventh consciousness there is no grasping at phenomena, it should therefore be the emptiness of phenomena.

Furthermore, as with the seventh consciousness of an Arhat, which lacks grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), when the sixth consciousness performs the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), the seventh consciousness should likewise enter the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena. This point should be further questioned of the Dharma Master; thus it is like the case of a fool.

The meaning is that the seventh consciousness within the causal state must necessarily possess attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), because it possesses the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*) just as the sixth consciousness does.
Regarding the commentary’s statement,

“It does not rely on the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Yingluo jing) because it is not universally established,” this refers to the fact that the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Weishi lun) only cites the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Shengweishi lun).
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* serves as the scriptural authority, because the meaning explained therein is comprehensive.
As for the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, it does not cite the *Aṣṭottaraśata-śikhara-sūtra* (or *Ratna-śikhara-sūtra*), because the meaning of that sūtra is not comprehensive.

Therefore, regarding the statement "there remains a remainder" up to "that which is not yet accomplished has been done": by attaining *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder), it is said that "the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established. The holy...
This refers to *nirvāṇa*. One practices the Eightfold Noble Path; it is by practicing the Eightfold Noble Path that one attains *nirvāṇa*. "Brahma" signifies tranquility (*śānti*).
The intended meaning is that *nirvāṇa* is tranquil and that which is to be accomplished has been fulfilled. This is because it arises from the Truth of the Path. As a verse says:
"The Brahma-faring has been established" means the Brahma-faring has been set up; "the Noble Path has been well-cultivated" means that which was to be done has been completed.
Regarding the "seven types of learners among humans and devas": this refers to the three fruits and four paths, which are termed the seven types of learners.
These seven types of learners consist entirely of human and celestial bodies.

The Commentary states: "There are two kinds of afflictions, namely, the afflictions of the dwelling grounds (*sthānabhūmi-kleśa*)... up to those that cannot be reached even by analogies such as the number of flowers.
Regarding the afflictions of the dwelling grounds, these refer to the seeds (*bīja*). Regarding the arising afflictions, these refer to the active manifestations (*samudācāra*).

That is to say, within the five dwelling grounds, there are both active manifestations and seeds. The intent of this passage is to explain that among the [first] four dwelling grounds, the afflictions...

The afflictions (*kleśa*), whether in their latent state (*bīja*) or manifest state (*samudācāra*), as well as the fifth, the manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*), have from time immemorial all depended upon the *avidyāvāsabhūmi* (the ground of the latency of ignorance), whether in its latent or manifest state, as well as the fifth, the manifestation of ignorance.
From time immemorial, these have all grown and developed by depending upon the seeds of the *avidyāvāsabhūmi*. Therefore, [it is called] the *avidyāvāsabhūmi*.

The earth element possesses the greatest power and serves as the basis for the higher afflictions—that is, the superior-grade afflictions. As for "ignorance," it refers to the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The Upādhyāya remarked: "The commentary must be erroneous; one should further consult the scriptural text."

There is the nature of falling away (*pāta-dharman*). This can obstruct the first dhyāna. One must employ the six modes of practice (*ṣaḍ-ākāra*)—either through suppression (*vibhava*) or the Path—to suppress the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm;

only then does one attain the first dhyāna. Just as all the afflictions present within the stage of the first dhyāna can obstruct the second dhyāna, so it is for the stages from the second dhyāna upward. That is, by suppressing the afflictions of the first dhyāna, one attains the [second].

The second dhyāna-samādhi; the subsequent stages should be understood accordingly. In this context, "ordinary beings" (pṛthagjana) refers to those who possess afflictions (*kleśa*) that can serve as the attainment of meditative concentration.

This person, having attained the initial threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*), experiences within that threshold concentration a subordinate, partial joy and bliss (*prīti-sukha*) that arises from separation.

Having experienced this intermediate joy and bliss within the threshold concentration, they are unwilling to progress further. Subsequently, they give rise to the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*) and so forth to suppress this concentration.

Regarding the hindrance to meditative concentration (*samādhy-āvaraṇa*): one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is the attainment of the fundamental dhyāna. This only serves to suppress the hindrance to concentration;

it cannot sever it, because analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)—has already been attained previously. Thus, this inferior nature is termed the "hindrance to concentration.

By abandoning the sensation of change (*vipariṇāma-vedanā*), one attains the unconditioned state of the "unshakable" (*āniñjya*). By abandoning the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), one attains the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not mentioned in the treatise because it is minor. The two vehicles (*dviyāna*) are able to sever the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

They obtain only contaminated and uncontaminated sensations. Regarding the three fruits: one obtains the pure concentration (*śuddhadhyāna*), the flavor-tasting concentration (*āsvādanādhyāna*), and the uncontaminated concentration (*anāsravadhyāna*).

If one is an Arhat, one obtains only the pure concentration and the uncontaminated concentration, but not the flavor-tasting concentration, because all afflictions (*kleśa*) have been completely severed.

The Commentary states: "When afflictions are suppressed, the dharma-grasping associated with them also does not arise; thus, from the suppression of afflictions and dharma-grasping up to the suppression by the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*).
The meaning of this passage is that when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) suppresses [afflictions] using the sixfold path of contaminated cultivation (*sāsrava-mārga*).
The cognitive obscurations that coexist with the afflictions are called "subduable," as they are prevented from arising by countering their momentum through the identity of their substance.

Furthermore, within the dharmas practiced by the noble ones prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), those that accord with rebirth in the world are the contaminated preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*), which is likewise capable [of such subduing].

This refers to the subduing of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Where there is clinging to birth (*jātigrāha*), it necessarily does not coexist with clinging to phenomena, because one who is deluded regarding the shallow must necessarily be deluded regarding the deep.

However, where there is clinging to phenomena, it does not necessarily entail clinging to birth; for example, when those of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*) who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) give rise to clinging to phenomena, they lack clinging to birth.

Regarding the three types of self, to erroneously grasp the permanent as the self constitutes all forms of *ātman-grāha* (clinging to a self).

However, speaking according to reality, clinging to the twenty-three *tattvas*, the six categories, and so forth, are all afflictions of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

[This] is subsumed under [false view]. This is because all verbal expressions that take what is not a cause to be a cause are subsumed under false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and are not subsumed under the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*).
Only the grasping at "I" and "mine" is termed the grasping at a self. For example, the master of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, Siṃhacandra, was originally ordained within the Sāṃkhya school;
later, he attained ordination within the Buddha-dharma and [became] associated with the Sautrāntika masters.

He became a disciple and immediately composed the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, still employing the terminology of the Sāṃkhya school. [According to them,] the five objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) give rise to the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*), and the five great elements give rise to the "appropriating existence" (*upādāna*).

If that person were an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), his assertion that these five objects give rise to the five great elements and so forth would all constitute wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) and an afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
it would not be subsumed under the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), because it is only when one clings to a "self" that it is truly grasping.

If such a person attains the fruit of Arhatship, yet still speaks of these five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) as giving rise to the five sense-objects or the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*), this is precisely the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) consisting of attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

There are many Arhats who cling to the existence of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*); their views are identical to those of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and all are subsumed under the cognitive obscuration of attachment to phenomena.

The Commentary states: "That which can subdue the two subtle types of discrimination, both manifest and seeds," means that it can subdue the manifest activities so that they do not arise, and it can also suppress the seeds, impairing their power so that they cannot produce manifest activities.

The Commentary states: "As for those [afflictions] that are both innate (*sahaja*) and manifest (*vartamāna*), as well as those that are seeds (*bīja*), even when they are slight, they can be suppressed.

This means that if the innate views of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arise independently (*mukta*), because they are extremely subtle, they cannot be suppressed during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).

However, if the innate views of self and extremes arise together with greed (*rāga*), delusion (*moha*), or pride (*māna*), because they are somewhat coarse, they can also be suppressed during the stage of preparatory application. If...
Furthermore, it can also suppress those co-arising [afflictions] such as greed, delusion, pride, and confusion that arise from objects;
their seeds are likewise subdued, and because the power of the seeds has been weakened, the two [seeds and afflictions] cannot produce manifest activity.
The Commentary states: "Because Bodhisattvas do not sever the lower realms, or because they arise from meditative absorption to be born in the higher realms.

This means that various Bodhisattvas, being non-retrogressive in their meditative attainments, may return to be born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Alternatively, they may give rise to the higher realms without having subdued the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm, because they have attained superior meditative absorptions.

If it were otherwise—such as when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) use the six practices of overcoming (*abhibhava*)—they must first completely subdue the afflictions of the lower realms before [proceeding].

One attains the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and is born into the higher realms. If one is born into the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one will necessarily regress from the higher meditative absorptions. Question:

Bodhisattvas in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) also practice the path of subduing afflictions through the six modes of practice, yet they are born within the three realms. This is just as a Bodhisattva in the stage of equipment, throughout the eon...

At the time of its destruction, one may also cultivate the path of suppressing afflictions through the six modes of practice, whereby one is reborn in the two higher realms or in other world-systems, and in all such cases, the afflictions do not become coarse.
However, upon reaching the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one will certainly not cultivate the path of suppressing afflictions through the six modes.

In this stage of practice, one predominantly cultivates the contemplation of the three natures of non-essence (*tri-niḥsvabhāva*). This is because, as stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, one intends to enter the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Question:
For instance, a Bodhisattva in the stage of application (*prayoga-mārga*) has not yet attained the untainted (*anāsrava*) state;

therefore, they cannot be reborn in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), nor do they perform the path of subduing through the six modes of conduct, and thus cannot be reborn in the two higher realms. If this stage of application reaches the time of the kalpa’s destruction, what then?

In what place is he born? The answer is: at the time when this kalpa is destroyed, this bodhisattva in the stage of preparation (prayoga) is reborn within the desire realm (kāmadhātu) of another direction.

This is because, according to the treatises, it is only within the desire realm that a body belonging to a fortunate rebirth (sugati) arises for a bodhisattva who intends to enter the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
They are born within the desire realm of other directions. The Sūtras state that two kinds of persons are born in other directions: first, those who slander the Dharma;
having entered the Avīci Hell of this world, they are born in the Avīci-hetu Hell of other directions when the kalpa reaches its destruction.
As stated in this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, at the end of a kalpa, beings are reborn again, and so on in succession for incalculable kalpas.

Second, regarding sentient beings of this realm who are born in other lands, they attain rebirth there; apart from these cases, there is no other textual passage stating that one is born into another realm [without such conditions].
Question: How is it known that Bodhisattvas who have accumulated the provisions (saṃbhāra) are born in the higher realms?
Answer: As stated in the sūtras, regarding the *pāramitās*, the śrāvakas, and the *vipaśyanā* of bodhisattvas:

whether in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) or in birth (*upapatti*), they comprehend all phenomena with a mind belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). If this refers to meditative absorption, it means that one attains only the higher realms.
If it refers to birth, it means that one is actually born within those higher realms. This explains the two truths in relation to the various schools.

Regarding mutual inclusion: according to this tenth [chapter], it says, "These eleven hindrances are subsumed within the two hindrances. It also refers to the method of mutual inclusion among the various sections.

When the treatise says "it is also thus," it refers to the levels from the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) onward; as for the word "also" appearing in the treatise, it does not refer to the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*).

Within these seven stages, they are subsumed under the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*). The factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*) are likewise subsumed under the stage of practice through understanding within these seven stages;

the treatise uses the word "likewise" (*api*) for this reason. Furthermore, the stages of equipment (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*) are also subsumed under the stage of practice through understanding among the thirteen abodes (*trayodaśa-vihāra*).
The treatise states: "Those whose nature consists of the conceptual resolution of the mind during a state of distraction. The meaning of this passage is that if one is in the stage of equipment...
For the most part, this occurs within the state of distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), yet it is also capable of being a definitive mental engagement (*adhimukti-manasikāra*) by nature.

To a minor extent, it also occurs within tainted meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*), yet it is likewise capable of being a definitive mental engagement by nature. Since it is called the "stage of practice through resolute belief" (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), it also includes the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).

In the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), there is only contaminated wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*); thus, it is known that even within contaminated meditative concentration, one is able to definitively resolve through the nature of reflection (*cintāmayī*).
Below, the mutual inclusion of merit and wisdom within the one hundred and forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) is clarified.

The Commentary states: "That which arises is the ten powers and all-knowledge. Regarding this passage in the Commentary, it says that all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) is not the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), yet it is designated as "all-knowledge. However, these ten powers are all subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
What is called "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*) is likewise subsequently attained wisdom. Within this fundamental wisdom, there are neither the ten powers nor the four fearlessnesses.

Within the wisdom attained subsequent [to meditative equipoise], one gives rise to the ten powers for the sake of the Māra-kings; and one gives rise to the four fearlessnesses for the sake of subduing those who hold false views.
Within these ten powers of a Buddha, there is already included all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*). This refers to what is stated among the ten powers:
namely, all-encompassing wisdom, stainless wisdom, pure wisdom, and the wisdom that is free from the conceit of superiority. If [one speaks of] the hundred and forty... [the text continues].

Within the ten non-dharmas, the "sublime wisdom of all aspects" (*sarvākāra-prajñā*) and the "objects of the sublime wisdom of all aspects" encompass both fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

If, as stated elsewhere, "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) and "knowledge of all aspects" are distinguished such that "all-knowledge" is the wisdom that takes reality as its object (*tattva-ālambana-jñāna*) and "knowledge of all aspects" is the wisdom that takes phenomena as its object (*vastu-ālambana-jñāna*),
then the one hundred and forty qualities of the unique dharmas (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) refer to the three— [the three bodies].

The thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, the fourteen fearlessnesses, the three foundations of mindfulness, the three ways in which he needs no protection, great compassion, the quality of never forgetting,
the permanent eradication of habitual tendencies, the sublime wisdom of all modes, and the four purities of all aspects of the buddha-field.
This refers to the one hundred and forty dharmas. Furthermore, there are eighteen distinct unshared dharmas (*āveṇika-dharma*), which are as follows:

the body is not preceded by mental deliberation; the mind is not preceded by mental deliberation; there are no diverse faculties; there are no harsh sounds; and there is no impairment due to lack of discernment—these constitute six.
Moreover, there is no decrease in aspiration, no decrease in resolve, no decrease in mindfulness, no decrease in diligence, and no decrease in [the power of] truth.

[The Tathāgata] diminishes [defilements] and so forth. Furthermore, the Tathāgata awakens to the arising of karma; because he knows the arising of the *jñānacakṣus* (eye of wisdom), it proceeds in accordance with that arising.
He has also eternally and thoroughly realized the transcendence of body and mind; he is without attachment and without equal. This is likewise true for the present and the future.

The above are all the uncommon dharmas (*āveṇika-dharma*) of the Mahāyāna. As for the eighteen uncommon dharmas within the Hīnayāna, they refer to the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four kinds of fearlessness (*catur-vaiśāradya*).

The three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) constitute eighteen [qualities]. If one speaks according to the Hīnayāna regarding shared merits (*sādhāraṇa-guṇa*), this refers to the thirty-two marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and eighty minor characteristics (*anuvyañjana*);
all these are subsumed under shared merits. These thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics are also possessed by a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
If one considers those who possess the eight meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they exist within the first five of the six realms of existence (*gati*).
It is also present among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Among the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the first seven liberations are shared by ordinary beings.

Regarding "the purification of all aspects" (*sarvākāraviśuddhi*), there are three types: first, the purification of the basis (*āśrayaviśuddhi*), which refers to the six sense faculties and the physical body of a Buddha;

second, the purification of the object (*ālambanaviśuddhi*), which refers to the pure lands manifested by a Buddha as well as the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*); third, the purification of the mind (*cittaviśuddhi*).

"Purity" refers to concentration (*samādhi*). "The purity of the four knowledges" refers to various forms of wisdom (*prajñā*). This refers to the mind and its objects, as well as concentration and wisdom. The Commentary states:
"Furthermore, among the Buddha’s ten powers, those subsumed under the faculty of wisdom and the faculty of knowledge are exclusively wisdom. The Sub-commentary explains:
"However, according to the actual fact, these ten powers take the five factors beginning with faith as their essence; they do not consist of wisdom alone."

It is taught that the ten powers (daśabala) are subsumed under wisdom (*jñāna*). However, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there are five ways of establishing their essential nature (*svabhāva*).

First, regarding the most excellent establishment of their nature, the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states that the ten powers have the faculty of knowing all (*sarvajña-indriya*) and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) as their nature when possessed by a Buddha. Second, regarding the nature of what is produced [by them].

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that their essence consists of either meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*). When defining their actual substance, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that they have the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) as their nature;

however, because the mental faculty (*manas*) is predominant, it is said that the ten powers (*daśabala*) have wisdom as their intrinsic nature. Therefore, they are referred to simply as the "power of knowledge regarding the bases" (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*) and so forth.

As for the powers of faith (*śraddhā*) and diligence (*vīrya*), they are subsumed within the textual explanations of "discernment" (*viniścaya*). Regarding the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), their essence is established through contemplation.
The Abhidharma further states: "Furthermore, associated dharmas have the four aggregates of mind and mental factors as their nature;

In the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one should know that the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is established upon the basis of the nine dharmas mentioned above.

That is to say, in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) is established upon the basis of those same nine dharmas. Furthermore, in the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is established upon the basis of these nine dharmas;
therefore, it is said that the ten powers (*daśabala*) are subsumed within the faculty of one who has known.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the four fearlessnesses being subsumed within the faculty of 'one who has already known' (*ājñātāvīndriya*), by whom is this universally known?
These four fearlessnesses are indeed subsumed within the five faculties, such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth; they are also subsumed within the faculty of 'one who has already known.

If they are subsumed within the five faculties, then among the five faculties—faith and the others—vigor (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and concentration (*samādhi*) are subsumed under merit (*puṇya*). As for the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) among the five faculties, it is subsumed under knowledge (*jñāna*). Therefore, the four..."

The fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) are subsumed under merit and wisdom. If one considers the four fearlessnesses, they are based upon the faculty of perfect knowledge (*ājñendriya*), with the five consciousnesses and so forth as their substance.
Thus, fearlessness is both fearlessness and also merit and wisdom.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'the various marks and secondary characteristics, the tongue faculty, and the locations of the four faculties, up to those subsumed under the four combined,' this refers precisely to the tongue faculty and does not include the other faculties.
It specifically includes the 'supporting bases' (*upastambha*) for the remaining four faculties and their objects.

The 'supporting bases' for the remaining four faculties refer to the locations upon which the body faculty, eye faculty, and tongue faculty depend. These 'locations' are precisely the four types of sensory objects (*viṣaya*) that support the faculties."

Regarding the primary elements (*mahābhūta*): here, the selection of the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*) is because, among the thirty-two marks, the Tathāgata’s tongue-faculty is in constant accord with the supreme flavor among all flavors; thus, only the tongue-faculty is taken.

Furthermore, the selection of the locus of the tongue-faculty is because, among the thirty-two marks, the Blessed One’s mark is thin, broad, and long, capable of covering the face up to the hairline. This is [the mark of the broad and long tongue].
The tongue-root (jihvā-indriya) is that which supports the sensory object upon the root. Now, regarding the location where the roots reside:

among the thirty-two marks, the World-Honored One’s eyes are deep blue-black with a bright white sclera, and the red-white iris is pure, clear, and distinct. These are precisely the auxiliary objects (upādāya-rūpa) supported upon the eye-root.

If one were to say that the eye can perceive distant objects, one would take the eye-root itself [as the subject]; however, since it is not stated here that there is "seeing from afar," [the root is not taken].
This refers to the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). Now, regarding the inclusion of the sense-fields (*dhātu*), faculties (*indriya*), and objects (*viṣaya*):

among the thirty-two marks, the Blessed One’s male organ is concealed within a sheath, pure and hidden, like that of a dragon-horse or a thoroughbred horse; thus, it possesses the supporting object (*āśraya*) of the male faculty.

As for the remaining marks among the thirty-two, they all depend upon the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) as their supporting object. This applies likewise to the supporting objects of the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) and the ear-faculty (*śrotrendriya*).
Because it is deep within the nostrils and ear canals, it is not explicitly mentioned among the thirty-two marks [of a Great Man]. Now, one should also take sound;
that is, among the thirty-two marks, the World-Honored One’s vocal body vibrates like a celestial drum.

In the commentary (*śāstra*), it should state that [sound] is comprised of the four sense organs (*indriya*) and their corresponding objects (*viṣaya*). Now, however, we take only the tongue faculty (*jihvendriya*) as the cause for taking the other four faculties.
Regarding the "basis" (*āśraya*): it is upon the basis of the tongue-faculty that the thirty-two marks are established. The thirty-two marks take the basis of the tongue-faculty as their substance.
In reality, the Buddha’s five material faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) are all untainted (*anāsrava*), and are thus merit (*puṇya*).
Among other persons, the five faculties are tainted maturation (*sāsrava-vipāka*) and are not merit; they are already of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).

If it is said that by virtue of meritorious karma one obtains the five faculties within the realms of humans and devas, these five faculties of humans and devas are named after the karma capable of producing them;
thus, they may also be called "fields of merit" because they are produced by the meritorious karma of others.
However, as for the five faculties within the three evil destinies, they are all produced by non-meritorious karma; this is why [the faculties] of the three evil destinies...
The five faculties belonging to the [five] destinies cannot be called "merit. Regarding the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*):

it is asked whether the Buddha’s *svasaṃbhogakāya*, which eternally dwells in the fourth dhyāna, can possess a male faculty. If one says that it does, it would contradict what is stated in the treatises.

Because the two sexual organs of male and female are unsightly and subject to leakage, and because there are no males or females in the form realm (rūpadhātu), there are four logical possibilities (*catuṣkoṭi*).
First, there are those who are male but not female; this refers to those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who possess the male organ. Second, there are those who are female but not male;

this refers to those in the desire realm capable of giving birth and nurturing offspring. Third, there are those who are both male and female; this refers to those with dual sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*). Fourth, there are those who are neither female [nor male]; this refers to those in the two higher realms.

The gods [of the form realm] are such. Therefore, it is known that the male and female faculties do not exist in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). If one asks: "If they do not exist, how can it be said that the Buddha possesses the thirty-two marks? The answer is:
Within the body of the Tathāgata’s own enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), the male faculty also exists, because it is a mark of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
If one says that all other gods of the form realm lack the male faculty, [the response is: Since the Buddha resides in the fourth dhyāna, the Buddha...

Regarding the second point, the characteristic of lacking the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*): as an analogy, it is stated that just as the tainted (*sāsrava*) nose and tongue consciousnesses are admitted to be bound exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), so too the color realm lacks these two types of consciousness.
Furthermore, the tainted eye, ear, and body consciousnesses are reckoned as being bound to the first dhyāna; thus, in the fourth dhyāna, the three consciousnesses beginning with the eye are absent.
Once Buddhahood is attained, the five untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses are admitted; all of these are admitted to be [bound to the first dhyāna].

Regarding the fourth dhyāna: some say that this case is likewise. Although the male organ (*puruṣendriya*) of the defiled type (*sāsrava*) certainly does not exist among the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), what prevents the Tathāgata’s body from possessing an undefiled (*anāsrava*) male organ? Thus, we know that the male organ exists within the body of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
Furthermore, the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the other-enjoyment (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) also possesses the male organ. However, it must not be said that it is of the nature of form (*rūpa*).

Regarding males: Bodhisattvas who attain sudden enlightenment do not possess male organs upon receiving their *parināmika-kāya* (transformation body), nor do they possess them when they later achieve Buddhahood.

Those who rely on the gradual enlightenment process within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and receive a *parināmika-kāya* do possess male organs, and they likewise possess them when they later achieve Buddhahood.
An objection is raised: since a bodhisattva of gradual enlightenment in the desire realm already possesses male organs beforehand, [they should likewise possess them afterwards].

At the time of attaining Buddhahood, they possess the male organ. This is because those Bodhisattvas who awaken based on the afflictions of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) have no prior transformation; thus, when they later attain Buddhahood, they immediately possess the male organ.

As for those who, at the time of attaining Buddhahood later, do not possess the male organ, this should also apply to those Bodhisattvas of the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu) who awaken gradually. They too [have no prior transformation].
There are five consciousnesses. It may be granted that one who attains Buddhahood later possesses the five consciousnesses; since that [attainment] is not the case for him, how could this be so?

Therefore, we know that when a Bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment later attains Buddhahood, he is fully endowed with the male organ, the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*).
"Secondary signs" refers to the eighty kinds of minor marks, which adorn the thirty-two primary marks; these are thus the "signs of the signs."

The Commentary states: "The three forms of non-protection (trīṇy arakṣāṇi) are like the fearlessnesses. Regarding the three forms of non-protection: they are non-protection of body, non-protection of speech, and non-protection of mind.

Within these three forms of non-protection, if there is non-protection of body and speech, this refers to bodily and vocal karma, which are subsumed under the categories of form (rūpa) and sound (śabda).
If there is non-protection of mind, this refers to mental karma, because it is the volition (cetanā) that arises simultaneously with the mind. These are the three forms of non-protection.
If one takes up the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, these constitute merit alone.

If this merit consists of the three types of non-protection (agupti), taking the five faculties such as appropriation and relinquishment as its essence, it then encompasses both the roots of merit and wisdom—namely, the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya). Thus, faith, diligence, mindfulness, and concentration are themselves merit.
If, however, it pertains to other persons, there are the three protections (gupti), namely, protection of the body and protection of the mind.

The Commentary states: "The three applications of mindfulness are not included among the faculties; being subsumed by non-attachment and non-hatred, they are exclusively meritorious. Regarding the three applications of mindfulness:
if there is a class of sentient beings who take up a blade and strike the Tathāgata’s right flank, the Tathāgata, taking this as an object, does not give rise to hatred.
This is non-aversion (*adveṣa*). Furthermore, there is a class of sentient beings who smear sandalwood paste upon the Buddha’s left side;

the Tathāgata, conditioned by this, does not give rise to attachment (*rāga*). This is non-attachment. Furthermore, there is a class of sentient beings who neither harm the Buddha with a blade nor smear him with incense;

the Tathāgata, conditioned by this, likewise does not give rise to delusion (*moha*), but knows it all through right mindfulness. Thus, [the absence of] both non-attachment and non-aversion [constitutes non-delusion].
These are subsumed within the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*). These three types of mindfulness (*smṛti*) are subsumed solely under merit (*puṇya*);

if they are right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), they are subsumed under both merit and the faculties; if they are right clear comprehension (*samyak-saṃprajanya*), they are subsumed under wisdom (*jñāna*) and the faculties. However, in the commentary (*vṛtti*):

All [of these] are explained in terms of "increasing along with" (*anuśaya*). Therefore, since the three mindfulnesses possess right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and right awareness (*samyak-samprajanya*), they should be subsumed under the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).

However, in this context, one takes only those factors that serve as causes for generating the mind; thus, non-attachment (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adveṣa*) are taken, even though they are not included among the faculties.
The commentary states: "Regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣa-dharma*): this quality of non-forgetfulness consists of both wisdom (*prajñā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*).

Because of the presence of mindfulness, there is no forgetfulness; that is, there is the wisdom capable of discernment. Due to the presence of mindfulness, among the five faculties (*pañcendriya*)..."
This is subsumed under the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*). This is merit arising from wisdom; it is subsumed under the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) among the five faculties.
The three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) are subsumed under the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*); thus, they possess both merit and wisdom.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the statement 'as with power, so too with all-aspect wondrous wisdom' when speaking of [defilements] increasing accordingly:

among the one hundred and forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), only all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is comprised solely of pure wisdom. The remaining ten powers and so forth all pertain to both contaminated merit and wisdom.
As for the permanent abandonment of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-prahāṇa*), it is not something cultivated by the six faculties; this is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)."

Alternatively, it may be the sixth faculty, the mental faculty (*manas*), which is capable of cultivating the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Because it is that which initiates what is cultivated, it is called "cultivated by the six faculties.

In reality, however, it is cultivated by nine faculties: namely, the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), along with the mental faculty, joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Since joy, pleasure, and equanimity are three types of feeling (*vedanā*) and cannot arise simultaneously, at the moment of realizing the unconditioned, only the seven [faculties]—namely, the five beginning with faith—are discussed.
Regarding the faculties (*indriya*) and among the three feelings (*vedanā*), one should take whichever feeling is appropriate.

That which is the "permanent severance of habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā-prahāṇa*) is precisely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) such as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Because it arises from the unconditioned, it is able to permanently sever habitual tendencies.

Since the permanent severance of habitual tendencies is unconditioned, it is not subsumed within the twenty-two faculties. As for the six faculties, they are those that are able to [function] from the unconditioned dharma; thus it should be understood.
These are the seven faculties: namely, the five faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, as well as the mental faculty (*manas*) and the equanimity faculty (*upekṣā*).

All of these are dharmas capable of realization. Alternatively, since this branch excludes the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), the mental faculty is not included; only mental factors (*caitta*) are taken, specifically the five faculties beginning with faith and the equanimity faculty.

Thus, there are only six faculties. Although the three feelings of joy, pleasure, and equanimity are distinct, [the first two]— (Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated at "然二," suggesting the sentence is incomplete. The translation reflects the available portion.)
Feelings do not arise simultaneously. Furthermore, because they belong to the same category of feeling, the three feelings are combined and counted as one. The commentary states:

"Among the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), and the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*)—even down to their minor components—a small portion is merit (*puṇya*);
the remainder is merit alone and not wisdom (*jñāna*). As for the four foundations of mindfulness, since they have wisdom as their essence, the four foundations of mindfulness are [merely]...

This wisdom is subsumed [by merit]. The essence of the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*) is diligence (*vīrya*); if they are the essence of the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), they are exclusively concentration (*samādhi*).
Therefore, the four right efforts and the four bases of power are subsumed solely by merit. As for the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) among the five faculties:

Among the five powers, it is the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*); among the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), it is the factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*); and within the eightfold noble path, it is right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

Right view, the factor of the investigation of phenomena, the power of wisdom, and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) are all knowledge (*jñāna*). Therefore, it is said that they are not differentiated as being [merely] knowledge.

If there are other factors such as faith, energy, and so forth, up to right mindfulness and concentration, they are all subsumed under merit (*puṇya*). Question: How many faculties (*indriya*) does a Buddha possess? Answer:

Within the body of a Buddha, he possesses the five faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*), the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the mental faculty (*manendriya*), and the faculties of joy (*sukha*), pleasure (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*);

and he also possesses the faculty of one who has final knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*). Question: Among the celestial abodes (*divyavihāra*), in which alone does the Tathāgata abide? Answer: [He abides] only in the middle [abode].

While abiding in the fourth dhyāna, there is only the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Since the lower three dhyānas possess the sensations of joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*), how can it be that within the Buddha’s body these sensations of joy and pleasure exist in a perfected state yet do not manifest? Question: If he does not give rise to the sensation of pleasure, why does the subsequent text state that the Buddha enjoys the great Dharma-pleasure (*mahāyāna-dharma-sukha*)? Answer: It is said: The Buddha’s body is always in a state of meditative equipoise; therefore, the sensation of pleasure does not manifest. However, because the Buddha has attained mastery over all phenomena, he is able to experience the flavor of the Dharma at will. Thus, although the sensation of pleasure does not arise, he experiences the great Dharma-pleasure through the power of his mastery. Furthermore, the term "pleasure" here refers to the bliss of liberation (*vimukti-sukha*), which is the ultimate happiness of the Tathāgata. It is not the same as the worldly sensation of pleasure associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Therefore, there is no contradiction. This is called the "inconceivable transformation-body" (*nirmāṇa-kāya*). Because he possesses inconceivable power, he can manifest various forms according to the needs of sentient beings, even while remaining in the fourth dhyāna. This is the meaning. Thus, it is established that the Buddha’s body is endowed with the perfection of the sensation aggregate. This concludes the explanation of the perfection of sensation. Next, we shall explain the perfection of the mental formations aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Regarding this, there are two types of mental formations: first, those associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*); second, those dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta*). Among these, the formations associated with the mind consist of fifty-one factors, such as contact (*sparśa*), volition (*cetanā*), and attention (*manasikāra*). The formations dissociated from the mind consist of fourteen factors, such as acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), and the life-faculty (*jīvita-indriya*). Within the Buddha’s body, all these factors are perfected and function without obstruction. This is called the perfection of the formations aggregate. This concludes the explanation of the five aggregates. Next, we shall explain the perfection of the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*). Regarding this, there are six internal bases and six external bases. The six internal bases are the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) up to the mind-base (*mana-āyatana*). The six external bases are the form-base (*rūpa-āyatana*) up to the dharma-base (*dharma-āyatana*). Within the Buddha’s body, these twelve bases are perfectly pure and free from all defects. This is called the perfection of the twelve sense bases. This concludes the explanation of the twelve sense bases. Next, we shall explain the perfection of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). Regarding this, there are six elements of consciousness, six elements of objects, and six elements of faculties. The six elements of consciousness are the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣur-vijñāna-dhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness element (*mano-vijñāna-dhātu*). The six elements of objects are the form-element (*rūpa-dhātu*) up to the dharma-element (*dharma-dhātu*). The six elements of faculties are the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*) up to the mind-element (*mano-dhātu*). Within the Buddha’s body, these eighteen elements are mutually harmonious and function without obstruction. This is called the perfection of the eighteen elements. This concludes the explanation of the eighteen elements. Next, we shall explain the perfection of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Regarding this, there are twelve links of dependent origination: ignorance (*avidyā*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). Within the Buddha’s body, these twelve links are transformed into the path of cessation and do not produce further suffering. This is called the perfection of dependent origination. This concludes the explanation of the twelve links of dependent origination. Next, we shall explain the perfection of the four noble truths (*āryasatya*). Regarding this, there are four truths: the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), the truth of the origin (*samudaya-satya*), the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), and the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). Within the Buddha’s body, these four truths are perfectly realized and fully understood. This is called the perfection of the four noble truths. This concludes the explanation of the four noble truths. Next, we shall explain the perfection of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). Regarding this, there are seven groups: the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*), the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅga-mārga*). Within the Buddha’s body, these thirty-seven factors are fully cultivated and perfected. This is called the perfection of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. This concludes the explanation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Next, we shall explain the perfection of the ten powers (*bala*). Regarding this, there are ten powers: the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*) up to the power of knowing the recollection of past lives (*pūrvenivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-bala*). Within the Buddha’s body, these ten powers are unimpeded and sovereign. This is called the perfection of the ten powers. This concludes the explanation of the ten powers. Next, we shall explain the perfection of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Regarding this, there are four fearlessnesses: the fearlessness regarding the realization of full enlightenment (*abhisambodhi-vaiśāradya*) up to the fearlessness regarding the teaching of the path leading to the cessation of suffering (*mārga-nairyāṇika-vaiśāradya*). Within the Buddha’s body, these four fearlessnesses are firm and unshakable. This is called the perfection of the four fearlessnesses. This concludes the explanation of the four fearlessnesses. Next, we shall explain the perfection of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). Regarding this, there are eighteen qualities: the absence of error in physical action (*kāya-karma-aviparīta*) up to the absence of loss of mindfulness (*amuṣita-smṛtitā*). Within the Buddha’s body, these eighteen qualities are eternally present and never diminish. This is called the perfection of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. This concludes the explanation of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Next, we shall explain the perfection of the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Regarding this, the Buddha’s great compassion is impartial, pervasive, and uninterrupted. It takes all sentient beings as its object and seeks to deliver them from suffering. This is called the perfection of great compassion. This concludes the explanation of the perfection of great compassion. Next, we shall explain the perfection of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Regarding this, there are thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs on the Buddha’s body. These adorn his physical form, making it supremely sublime and worthy of veneration by gods and humans. This is called the perfection of the marks and signs. This concludes the explanation of the marks and signs. Next, we shall explain the perfection of the voice (*ghoṣa*). Regarding this, the Buddha’s voice is melodious, clear, and reaches all realms. It can teach the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings, causing them to attain understanding and liberation. This is called the perfection of the voice. This concludes the explanation of the perfection of the voice. Next, we shall explain the perfection of the emanations (*nirmāṇa*). Regarding this, the Buddha can manifest various bodies—whether as Buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, or ordinary beings—to guide sentient beings according to their needs. This is called the perfection of emanations. This concludes the explanation of the perfection of emanations. Next, we shall explain the perfection of the light (*prabhā*). Regarding this, the Buddha emits immeasurable rays of light that illuminate all worlds, destroying darkness and revealing the true nature of phenomena. This is called the perfection of light. This concludes the explanation of the perfection of light. Next, we shall explain the perfection of the lifespan (*āyuḥ-pramāṇa*). Regarding this, the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable and cannot be calculated by time. He remains in the world for as long
The "joy of the Mahāyāna Dharma" is precisely the joy of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), not the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*). Question: Having sought the name, one understands its meaning;

since it is called the "joy of the Mahāyāna Dharma," how can it be the joy of pliancy? If you say that the joy of pliancy is the joy of the Mahāyāna Dharma, then ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles (*dvayayānika*) also attain the joy of pliancy; would these ordinary beings and others all then be said to have attained [the Mahāyāna Dharma]?
Regarding the Mahāyāna Dharma-bliss: if one says it is attained, how does it differ from that of the Buddha?
If one says it is not, how can it be said that the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is itself the Mahāyāna Dharma-bliss? One should question the Dharma Master. Regarding the male and female organs:

since these are both considered ugly and foul, why does the Tathāgata’s body of self-enjoyment possess a male organ? The answer is: the male organ of the Buddha’s body is... [the remainder of the text follows].

Among the thirty-two marks, the mark of the horse-like concealed organ (kośagatavastiguhyatā) is absent. Because the Tathāgata possesses the thirty-two marks, there is a male organ within the Buddha’s body.
Question: Within the Buddha’s body, the five faculties such as the eye, as well as the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), are already untainted (anāsrava).
Why are the five faculties, such as the eye, not subsumed under the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*)? Answer:

Because, just as there exists the untainted (*anāsrava*) within the stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), yet it is not clear and sharp, so too the untainted path within the stage of the Peak of Existence is not subsumed under any of the three untainted faculties—the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), or the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*). The five material faculties of the Buddha’s body are likewise; although they are...

The untainted [faculties] are not subsumed under the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*). Furthermore, the five faculties beginning with the eye are material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), whereas the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge is a mental phenomenon (*cittadharma*).
Since matter and mind are distinct, the six material faculties are not subsumed under the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge. Question:

Regarding the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*) of the Mahāyāna and the one hundred and forty unique qualities, how do they relate to one another in terms of subsumption? The three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are not subsumed under the faculties.

Regarding that which is subsumed by non-attachment and non-hatred: A question is raised concerning the third application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). If one does not give rise to delusion toward sentient beings who are of equal temperament, this constitutes the presence of non-delusion (*amoha*).

Why, then, is it stated here only that there is no attachment or hatred? Regarding the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), there are desire (*chanda*), effort (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*).
Since desire is truly [the basis], how can the commentary state that the four bases of psychic power are merely merit (*puṇya*)? Regarding the eight consciousnesses in relation to the two...

Among the twelve faculties (*indriya*), by which faculty are these subsumed? Question: Regarding the one hundred and forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) explained above, do these refer to the merit and wisdom attained through the Buddha’s own cultivation, or do they refer to the merit and wisdom produced in other sentient beings?

There are also those that arise solely as non-merit, up to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhi-jñāna*). Question: What is meant by the "knowledge of aspiration"? It refers to the Arhat...
The "pure vow-knowledge" (*praṇidhijñāna*) first arisen by the Han [master] refers to the vow-knowledge among these ten perfections (*pāramitā*).

According to the subsequent treatise, after the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of the ten perfections have been presented, the latter five knowledges take cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) as their nature, because they are said to be fundamental and subsequently attained knowledge (*mūla- and prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
One interpretation holds that the eighth [knowledge] takes the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) and faith (*śraddhā*) of the desire realm as its nature, for these three constitute its very essence.
Furthermore, other holy teachings also state that [the nature of this knowledge] consists precisely of desire (*chanda*), resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), faith (*śraddhā*), and wisdom (*jñāna*).

How then can it be said in the *Śāstra* (commentary) that the "knowledge resulting from prayer" (*praṇidhi-jñāna*) and so forth are wisdom and not merit? Moreover, regarding this knowledge resulting from prayer:
