Because there is a single essence of wisdom (*prajñā*), three names are established for it: it is called "seal-conformity" (*mudrā-anukūla*), it is called "patience" (*kṣānti*), and it is called "knowledge of reality as it is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).

The original text states that "seal-conformity" and "concentration" (*samādhi*) are distinct; thus, it is not concentration itself that is named "seal-conformity," but rather the actual concentration that occurs simultaneously with seal-conformity.
This is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound meaning "the concentration of seal-conformity" or "the concentration belonging to seal-conformity."

The wisdom of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) can be called "seal" (*mudrā*) because it is compliant (*anuloma*); it seals what precedes and conforms to what follows. Since the preceding [wisdoms] cannot seal or conform by their very nature, they are not said to be such.

Because this [Peak of Existence wisdom] definitely possesses the power to seal and conform, based on this sealing and conforming concentration, one necessarily gives rise to subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) that accords with reality.

This should be explained according to the previous case. If one is in the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), then within that single moment of wisdom, the three [subsequent knowledges] no longer exist.

Since it is a concentration (*samādhi*) that is immediate (*ānantarya*), "immediate" is itself the "concentration. This admits both the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) and *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) analyses, because wisdom (*prajñā*) lasts for only a single moment and there is no further interval to be subsumed. Alternatively, some take "immediate" as the "concentration" using the *karmadhāraya* analysis;

however, since both concentration and wisdom possess the sense of being "immediate," one generates the superior knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) by relying on this immediate concentration. This follows the previous explanation.

The Commentary states: "Phenomena have no names, and names have no referents. This means that although within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) there are names that express phenomena, these names lack the reality of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Thus, the name is the dependent [nature]. Furthermore, beneath the name that expresses the phenomenon, there is no real referent (*artha*) that is the object of expression belonging to the imagined nature.

The Commentary states: "The 'one part of the samādhi of entering the true meaning' mentioned in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Liang translation) refers to the 'one part where there are no names for what is apprehended.

That mention of 'one part' corresponds to the stage of 'lower patience' (*mṛdu-kṣānti*) within the system of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), because it realizes that there are no objects as they are grasped."
The Commentary states: "Because it conforms to and thoroughly penetrates the basis. As for the "basis," this does not refer to the body;
rather, each preceding phenomenon serves as the basis for its respective succeeding phenomenon, because the former induces the latter.
The Commentary states: "Among these three stages, wisdom established within the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*) is designated as 'patience' (*kṣānti*).

Now, regarding the term "roots of goodness," it does not refer to the four roots of goodness known by the names *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and so forth. Furthermore, what are called the "four roots of goodness" are:

first, lower patience; second, middle patience; third, upper patience; and fourth, the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). These four are called "roots of goodness" because each of them possesses the quality of patience.

The treatise states: "When the object of patience is realized as empty of consciousness, this is the 'lower patience' (mṛdu-kṣānti), which confirms that the grasped object is non-existent. When consciousness itself is realized as empty, this is the 'middle' and 'upper patience' (madhyama- and adhimātra-kṣānti), wherein one contemplates that the grasping subject-consciousness is also non-existent."

The treatise states: "Regarding the phrase 'herein, because of correct patience (samyak-kṣānti) and conforming patience (anuloma-kṣānti)': if one possesses lower patience (mṛdu-kṣānti) and higher patience (adhimātra-kṣānti), these are termed 'correct patience.

Lower patience confirms the non-existence of the grasped (grāhya), while higher patience confirms the non-existence of the grasper (grāhaka). If one possesses middle patience (madhya-kṣānti), it is simply termed 'conforming patience.'"

The Commentary states: "That which is 'uninterrupted' (*ānantarya*) is precisely 'concentration' (*samādhi*). This refers to the expression "the path of uninterrupted transition" (*ānantaryamārga*) within that single moment;

it enters the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), and thus is called "uninterrupted concentration. "Uninterrupted concentration" means that "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) refers to time, while "concentration" (*samādhi*) refers to the essential nature of concentration;
hence, it is termed "uninterrupted concentration."
The *Śāstra* states: "That which conforms to and approves of pleasure during the stage of medium patience" refers to the superior patience of the subsequent stage of conforming to pleasure;
that is to say, it refers to the stage of superior patience following medium conformity to pleasure, as well as the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
The Commentary states: "As for 'characteristics,' these are the characteristics of what is grasped as empty, the characteristics of the dependent nature, and even the true ultimate nature.
Regarding 'emptiness possessing characteristics': when this bodhisattva, while in this stage, contemplates the emptiness of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)."
"This Bodhisattva [perceives] the characteristic of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as empty. Regarding "when it appears before the mind":

when this Bodhisattva correctly realizes that the imagined nature is empty, there arises within the mind a transformation of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), which he then takes as his object; this is called "having a characteristic" (*sanimitta*).

Within the mind of this Bodhisattva, a thought arises and he speaks these words: "This characteristic of meditative concentration is precisely the true ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*)."

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Regarding 'conformity' (*anuloma*) herein, even the ancients have said that the *Vibhaṅga-vyākhyā* (Discourse on Distinct Contemplation) is merely a rough description;

its specific name is *Vibhaṅga-sākṣāt-kriyā* (Realization through Distinct Contemplation). If translated according to the broad sense, it is named *Vibhaṅga-yoga* (Yoga of Distinct Analysis), which is precisely contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

These two verses were originally taught by Maitreya Bodhisattva for the purpose of instructing bodhisattvas in the four roots of goodness (*catvāri nirvedhabhāgīyāni*) so that they may enter the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Therefore, now..."
Having become a Buddha, he then conferred upon him the prediction of enlightenment as a bodhisattva, just as Śākyamuni Buddha conferred the prediction upon Maitreya.
Nevertheless, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga cited two verses of instruction composed by that [Maitreya] and placed them within his other Mahāyānasaṃgraha treatises.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Because the duration is brief, it is explained from the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*).

However, while the verse mentions only Middle Patience and Superior Patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), it does not mention the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*). This is because the duration of the Supreme Worldly Dharmas is so short that they are not mentioned;

indeed, the Supreme Worldly Dharmas are what is referred to in the treatise as "Superior Patience. Regarding the phrase "subsequently touching the non-apprehendable" (*anupalambha*): "touching" (*sprśati*) here means "following" (*anu*).

The subsequent stage is the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), which is precisely non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). There is one interpretation that since all eight consciousnesses possess grasping (*grāha*), they are bound by the objective aspect (*nimittabandhana*);
this passage represents the view of Sthiramati. There is another interpretation stating that it is not so, up to the point where it says "that which is called being bound by the objective aspect";
this passage represents the reasoning and inquiry of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla. [This applies] even to wholesome and indeterminate minds.

Because there is no grasping. As for those who hold that there is a bond of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*), their subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) would also necessarily possess the bond of signs.
If it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called subsequently attained wisdom; if it is tainted (*sāsrava*), it is not called subsequently attained wisdom.
The following [passage] also concerns Dharmapāla’s position regarding the bond of signs.

If it were not the case that [the four] are so, and even if they were to take all objects as conditions, yet one did not attain liberation through discourse, then the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) would only be obtained once the outflows (*āsrava*) are severed—that is, only upon severing the outflows of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, we know that even with a mind associated with outflows, there may be a temporary cessation of those outflows.

Second, regarding the fact that its essence is neither hard nor rough and is not augmented by the outflows: this refers to when minds associated with outflows are wholesome or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Because they are conditioned by the afflictions (*kleśa*), the poisonous breath enters into the contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) and thus becomes outflows (*āsrava*).

That is to say, the essence of contaminated phenomena consists of a nature that is rigid, harsh, and unstable. Uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) are the opposite; therefore, they are not bound by characteristics.
It is not an object of false conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*). If there are contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), they are objects of the mind and mental factors that are themselves false.

The four types of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) take all appearances as their objects for the sake of realization and understanding. "Realization and understanding" refers precisely to the subsequently attained wisdom taking other cognitions and phenomena as its objects, regarding them as being like illusions, transformations, and so forth.
However, when a contaminated mind takes the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as its object, it does not treat it as being like an illusion and so on.

Explanation: Regarding "those that are associated with the characteristics [of outflows]," these are the contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas, which are always associated with the seventh [consciousness], the afflicted manas.
For this reason, uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas are not bound by characteristics; only contaminated dharmas possess the bondage of characteristics.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "because the dharma and the outflow are associated with characteristics," this refers to the contaminated objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*), which is simultaneously capable of being the object for the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) that is augmented by the outflows.
Regarding the term "hence" (*gù*): it is because after afflictions, those [subsequent states] take them as objects and increase their faults.

The *Shū* (Commentary) states: "If, within wholesome or non-obscured neutral minds, there are only direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), while defiled minds include non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), this text does not fully capture the principle. To speak generally for the time being, non-neutral minds do possess direct perception and inference."

A defiled mind is exclusively non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). However, speaking according to reality, if it is a wholesome or indeterminate mind, there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), and it is not non-valid cognition.

Within a wholesome mind, when taking objects such as a jar or clothing as its object, there is valid cognition. Within a defiled mind, there is also that which is non-valid cognition, namely the [erroneous] cognition of a jar or its basis within a defiled state of mind.
Furthermore, within a defiled mind, there is also direct perception, such as when afflictions arise within the five sensory consciousnesses.

When the object of affliction (*kleśa*) is perceived, it is termed "active manifestation" (*samudācāra*). Within that defiled mind, there is also inference (*anumāna*). However, regarding the commentary (*ṭīkā*), there are two interpretations:
one holds that it is also bound, while the other holds that it is not. These two interpretations are equally valid and neither is superior.

As for what is called "bondage by signs" (*nimitta-bandhana*), it refers to all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*); minds of the three natures—wholesome and so forth—are all termed bondage by signs, as they bind the cognizing subject.
The "mind" refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Its apprehension of the seeds of afflictions and so forth is also termed "bondage by signs" (*nimitta-bandhana*).

With the exception of untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), it is not bondage. Therefore, all four parts [of the consciousness] are termed "bondage by signs," because they possess phenomenal characteristics; it is not that the objective part (*nimittabhāga*) alone is called bondage by signs.

The Commentary states: "When an Arhat abandons the afflictions of the path of cultivation, up to and including the state of unfitness—viewed in relation to all afflictions, whether manifest or latent—these are all the essence of the outflows (*āsrava*). That is to say, they exist within the conscious bodies of all sentient beings."

Due to the presence of the seeds and the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of afflictions, there arises a state of physical and mental lack of stability and a lack of functional capacity (*akarmanyatā*).

Regarding the statement in the *Śūchao* (Commentary): "When the outflowing grossness (*sāsrava-dauṣṭhulya*) and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are abandoned, that which is produced from the outflows...

all become attenuated," the term "outflowing" (*sāsrava*) refers to all outflowing phenomena of the three natures—wholesome and so forth—including the mind and mental factors as well as form (*rūpa*). However, [only]...
Excluding the untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) entities, because they are not tainted (*sāsrava*).

This means that one fears that, just as with the entities of the three natures of mind such as the wholesome (*kuśala*), even though these phenomena are not themselves afflictions (*kleśa*), they are bound by association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) when coexisting with the taints;
and being objects of the taints, they are bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*). Consequently, the poisonous vapor of the wholesome phenomena enters into them, whereby they become [tainted].
It is hard, rough, and lacks lubrication by nature, just as when a snake bites a person, its venom permeates throughout the body, causing a lack of peace and stability.
These three natures—wholesome and so forth—are produced from the outflows (*āsrava*) of ignorance and afflictions.

That which is produced from outflows is the realization of the phenomena of the outflow of ignorance, which then gives rise to the outflows of formations (*saṃskāra*) and so on, being perfumed and activated by them through their active manifestation.

The afflictions (*kleśa*) perfume the seeds of outflows (*āsrava-bīja*) within the eighth consciousness, causing the eighth consciousness and the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*) to become a state of insecurity.

That which is "originally obtained" refers to the very essence of these dharmas of outflow; it is the nature of being an outflow that is originally established as what is obtained, and no other nature can be obtained.
Furthermore, it is said that "the nature originally obtained" refers to the cause. As for the dharmas of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), they arise from...
The two fundamental natures constitute its essence. That which arises through conditions and constitutes the nature of instability in contaminated phenomena refers to its essence.
Its state of dependence is its fruit. That which resembles it pertains to this state of dependence.

Because they resemble the essential nature of those original outflows (*āsrava*) and share the same heavy quality of poison, their lack of functional flexibility (*akarmanyatā*) all gradually becomes attenuated.
This is because they do not possess the essential nature of the outflows themselves; yet, due to the gravity of their faults, this scriptural passage is cited as being most thorough in its reasoning.
As for "all become subtle and thin": once the fruit of Arhatship is attained, these outflows and the tainted outflows (*sāsrava*) all become subtle and thin.

The Commentary states: "Arhats possess residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*). Because they already possess these defects, what is called "habit-energy" is not the seed of afflictions (*kleśa-bīja*), but rather refers to a state of lack of functional pliability (*akarmanyatā*). It is precisely because they possess this habit-energy that it is termed a "defect.

This refers to the passage in the preceding text stating that while the followers of the Two Vehicles eliminate the seeds but do not eliminate the habit-energies, only the Buddha alone is able to transcend them.
The meaning of transcendence is as stated elsewhere regarding their respective numbers: "An Arhat has fear and has a refuge;
a Tathāgata has no fear and has no refuge.

The commentary states: "Only the Buddha alone is able to deliver others and serve as a refuge for sentient beings. This teaching implies that if the Buddha is able to sever even the residual impressions (*vāsanā*).

Because [the Tathāgata] has eliminated habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), he can serve as a refuge for sentient beings. Since the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot eliminate habitual tendencies, they are not called a refuge.
Therefore, it is said that his desire to exhaustively eliminate attachment is an unshared Buddha-dharma (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).

This is because the Tathāgata is able to eliminate the habitual tendencies of outflows (*āsrava-vāsanā*); thus, among the one hundred and forty unshared dharmas, there is the "knowledge of the desire to eliminate" (*icchājñāna*).

Regarding habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 2, states that within one's own consciousness, up to "therefore the Buddha says they are 'those who dwell in formations'.

This passage refers to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Whether virtuous or non-virtuous, they are all subsumed under seeds. These are then categorized into three grades according to their superiority or inferiority.
If they are included in the category of afflictions (*kleśa*), they are the purification of afflictions, whether in their state as seeds or as manifest activity (*samudācāra*).

"Coarseness" (*dausthulya*) refers to that which is contrary to subtlety and lightness. It follows along with the nature of sentient beings, residing within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

When the fruit of karma ripens, it is categorized according to the five fruits, as well as other types of indeterminate seeds related to deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and the supernormal powers of the outflows (*kliṣṭābhijñā*).
These are termed "coarse" because they are produced from the outflows of affliction (*kleśāsrava*) and because their nature is one of non-tranquility; thus, they are not [termed] "light."

As for the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), their essence is not that of the afflictions (*kleśa*) or the outflows (*āsrava*). Therefore, all wholesome states and so forth are neither termed "heavy dysfunction" (*dauṣṭhulya*) nor "latent dispositions.
Nevertheless, in this particular passage, the method of exposition is based on contrasting superior and inferior qualities; it does not exhaustively capture the full nature of the principle.
However, unwholesome dharmas do not equal those of the formless realm; dharmas of the formless realm do not equal innate wholesome dharmas;

innate wholesome dharmas do not equal the wholesome dharmas of the merit-portion consisting of the wisdom of hearing and reflection; the wholesome dharmas of the merit-portion consisting of the wisdom of hearing and reflection do not equal the wholesome dharmas of the merit-portion consisting of the wisdom of cultivation;
and the wholesome dharmas of the merit-portion consisting of the wisdom of cultivation do not equal the worldly requisites conducive to rebirth in successive lives.

The wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) within the stage of accumulation (*sambhāra-avasthā*) is inferior to the wisdom of reflection within the stage of accumulation that accords with the arising [of the path] from life to life.
That wisdom of reflection is inferior to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) within the stage of accumulation.

The wisdom of cultivation within the stage of accumulation is inferior to the wisdom of cultivation within the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*). That wisdom of cultivation is inferior to the wisdom of cultivation within the stage of application. Application...

The wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) during the stage of practice does not equal the wholesome qualities of hearing, reflection, and cultivation within the contaminated preparatory wisdom (*sāsrava-prayoga-jñāna*) from the first bhūmi up to the seventh bhūmi;
it is a thousandfold or ten-thousandfold inferior. In this context, the former does not equal the latter; the latter is entirely superior to the former, being a thousandfold greater.
Furthermore, this does not refer to the wisdom of cultivation prior to the bhūmis, which is inferior to that of the bhūmis.
Higher rebirths are acquired through innate wholesome states (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*), because these innate wholesome states are characterized by obscurity. Question:

Why is it stated that among the wholesome states conducive to merit (*puṇya-bhāgīya-kuśala*), there is the cultivation of wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī prajñā*), as well as the wisdom arising from hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā-mayī prajñā*) which is dispersed within the stage of the provisions for transcendence (*lokottara-saṃbhāra-avasthā*) in the desire realm? Answer:

Regarding the cultivation of wisdom within the wholesome states conducive to merit, it must have been previously attained; that is, it has been obtained thousands and tens of thousands of times since beginningless time. Furthermore...
Because it conforms to the laws of birth and death within the three realms, it is not superior. If it were to conform to supramundane wisdom, such has never been attained since time immemorial.

Furthermore, because it can oppose the laws of birth and death, and because its essence is superior as it accords with the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) of the Three Vehicles, by this principle, even the wisdom cultivated from the category of merit (*puṇya-bhāga*) within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is likewise [not superior].

[This refers to] the portions [of wisdom] within the desire realm that accord with supramundane [wisdom], as well as mundane wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Question:

How is it that the wisdom cultivated prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) does not include the wisdom derived from hearing, reflection, and cultivation while in a distracted state (*vikṣipta-citta*) among the mundane wholesome states of application (*prayoga-kuśala*) prior to the stages? Answer:

If one cultivates wisdom prior to the seven stages, it cannot serve to initiate, draw forth, or lead into the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state; therefore, it is inferior. However, to speak according to the ultimate principle:
That is to say, all wholesome and neutral dharmas are also called "heavy impediments" (*dausthulya*), because they are augmented by afflictions.
Furthermore, when these wholesome and other dharmas arise, the very physical basis of the body becomes capable [of their production]. However, for these bodhisattvas...
Furthermore, because they are described as being heavy (dausthulya), the wholesome and other dharmas are said to exist moment by moment as active formations. The commentary states:

"The cognitive hindrance (jñeyāvaraṇa) is subsumed under the category of heavy maturation (vipāka). Regarding this, the cognitive hindrance refers to that which is included among the four types of neutral (avyākṛta) states.
This is subsumed under the category of maturation (*vipāka*).
The Commentary states: "Experiencing the heavy (*dausthulya*) includes all contaminated feelings (*sāsrava-vedanā*); thus, even wholesome feelings are included therein.
Furthermore, it includes the neutral feelings of deportment (*airyāpathika*) as well as other neutral feelings. This refers to the equanimity associated with pleasure and joy.

One abandons the five feelings (*vedanā*). Regarding the three natures of feeling—wholesome and so forth—it is called "coarseness" (*dausthulya*) when the reception of objects causes the mind to be unsettled.

As for that which is "fatigue and coarseness," it refers to the physical exhaustion caused by long periods of maintaining the postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, as well as other neutral states (*avyākṛta*), specifically referring to the neutral state of craftsmanship; if one engages in craftsmanship for a long time, it likewise results in fatigue.
These cause physical exhaustion. Among these twenty kinds of contact, it is subsumed under the category of "exhausting contact," as previously described;
it may either be harmful or beneficial.

The Commentary states: "According to the text of [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] fifty-eight, from 'coarse and heavy fetters' (*dausthulya-bandhana*) up to 'not yet severed,' this text is exhaustive in its principle.
That is to say, afflictions (*kleśa*) and all other contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena of the three natures, including wholesome ones, are all termed 'coarse and heavy.

However, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, fascicle sixteen, is also not exhaustive in its principle; it speaks primarily in terms of 'grasping' (*parigraha*), which refers precisely to that which is acquired."

This is because, by severing the fetters of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*), it is called "non-apprehension. That which is the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and that which is without anything seen refers to being free from the fetters of signs (*nimitta*);
thus, it is "without anything seen. This occurs during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

The Commentary states: "Regarding the statement that 'the bond of characteristics' (*lakṣaṇabandhana*) refers to active manifestations (*samudācāra*), while 'the bond of heavy dullness' (*dauṣṭhulyabandhana*) refers to seeds (*bīja*):

this text exhausts the principle and accords with reason. If seeds are also termed the 'bond of characteristics' and the 'bond of heavy dullness,' then when the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) takes the seeds of afflictions as its object, the seeds are termed the 'bond of characteristics. If there are active manifestations, they are also termed the 'bond of heavy dullness.'"

The *Śāstra* states: "Regarding the term 'bondage of signs' (*nimitta-bandhana*) here, up to its being identical with the 'defiled heaviness' (*sāsrava-dausthulya*) in the fifty-eighth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, this text exhausts the principle.

As for the phrase "severing the bondage of heaviness": just as in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), which is "distant from dust" and "coarse," it constitutes the very essence of an obstacle;
although the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) counteracts it, that which is counteracted is itself heaviness—the state of being unserviceable (*akarmanyatā*).

This is so. Therefore, the subsequent passage states: although there is no longer any principle of affliction (*kleśa*) at the time of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), one has not yet abandoned that state of unfitness (*akarmanyatā*).

Because this [unfitness] is what constitutes the nature [of the afflictions], it is known that the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) involves the coarse as the object (*viṣaya*) and the subtle as the sphere (*gocara*). It is like washing clothes:
first the coarse grime is attacked and removed, and only then are the fine stains stripped away. Now it is the same; such is the Dharma of the Noble Path.

The coarse is eliminated first; the subtle is severed later. However, in this context, "coarse" (*dauṣṭhulya*) may refer to the essence of the afflictions, or it may refer to the state of unserviceability (*akarmanyatā*).
Alternatively, the three natures of phenomena—such as tainted wholesome states—are called "coarse. Generally, these constitute the categories [of *dauṣṭhulya*].

The *Śāstra* says: "Attaining partially in the first stage" means that within the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), one abandons the two obstacles of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognizable objects (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as they exist in their conceptualized form, as well as the conceptualized heavy residues (*dausthulya*), the lack of functional capacity (*akarmanya*), and the lack of nature (*abhāva*). This also applies to the [subsequent] stages up through the seventh.
The six consciousnesses are bound by both the fetters of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-bandhana*) and the fetters of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*).

Through wisdom, one reaches the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), where the indeterminate activities of the sixth consciousness are freed from these two fetters, because the sixth consciousness is then constantly uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Its seeds, however, persist until the stages above the eighth.

As for the seventh consciousness, when all forms of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) cease to function, it is also said to be "partially non-existent. Nevertheless, the cognitive obscuration (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) still remains therein.
Regarding the bodhisattva who, within the established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*), does not merely practice the differentiated contemplation of the Four Truths:

rather, the bodhisattva may perform the general contemplation of emptiness, non-self, and true suchness (*tathatā*); or contemplate only the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*); or contemplate only the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);
or perform the three mental states, such as the wisdom that internally eliminates the provisional designation of sentient beings. Having performed these and the like, all of them are...

The contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). Furthermore, when a bodhisattva is in the stage of equipment (*sambhārāvasthā*), they also take the truths as objects in a scattered and intermittent manner.

If they are in the stage of application (*prayogāvasthā*), they also take the truths as objects in their entirety, performing the contemplation of the eight truths across the upper and lower realms. They also take the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) as an object in seven cycles and the practice of cessation (*nirodhamārga*) in three cycles;
even before attaining [realization], they practice the non-established truths (*apratiṣṭhitasatya*) by way of emptiness and selflessness.

The Commentary states: "Either one treats [the object] collectively as the single reality of *tathatā* (true suchness), or one treats it distributively as the two emptinesses. Regarding these collective and distributive terms:
first, because one collectively contemplates that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without marks, it is called the contemplation of the single reality of *tathatā*.

Second, whether it be a bodhisattva or a follower of the two vehicles, contemplating that the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*) is entirely empty is called the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Third, the bodhisattva contemplating that the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is entirely empty is called..."

The contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). These three types are called the "three minds" and are the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*). According to the view of the ignorant:
if among the three consciousnesses the first two minds are named individually, the third mind is named collectively, because it dispels sentient beings by relying upon phenomena.
The Commentary states: "The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* speaks of the four truths of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

However, although the term "unconditioned" is established when citing the four truths from the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, this question is not analogous to the establishment of such names. This is because it pertains to the transcendence of linguistic expression (*nāma-vyavahāra*).

It is not so. For that sutra speaks of both the "constructed Four Noble Truths" (*saṃskṛta-catur-āryasatya*) and the "unconstructed Four Noble Truths" (*asaṃskṛta-catur-āryasatya*), each having four aspects.

Since they are named "non-established truths" (*avyavasthāpana-satya*), how could there be [the conventional] Four Truths? Therefore, one should know this regarding both the sutras and the *Abhidharma-kośa*.
The non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*) consists of only one level, namely the single true *dharmadhātu*.

The established truths (*pratiṣṭhita-satya*), however, consist of four levels, because they include the aforementioned truths as being exclusively real and exclusively central. Now, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* is taken as the most authoritative source.

As for the claim that the unconditioned Four Noble Truths (*anabhisaṃskāra-āryasatya*) are the non-established truths: that treatise, however, speaks of the "Four Truths" by way of the gate of conventional expression (*vyañjana-mukha*).

It is not established [as a conventional truth]. This refers to the true suchness (*tathatā*) underlying the Four Noble Truths. If this treatise were to rely solely on the principle of "discarding the expression to reach the meaning," it would state that the single true suchness is called the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).
Therefore, this treatise and that treatise each rely on one specific sense and are not mutually contradictory. Furthermore, that treatise states:
regarding the Bodhisattva’s teaching of the four non-established truths, that which is free from the body of transformation (*pariṇāma-kāya*) is called the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

The abandonment of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is called the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*). In relation to non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*), it is called the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

The attainment of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*) constitutes the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). This is designated according to its actual nature as the "unestablished" (*apratiṣṭhita*).
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Furthermore, because they cannot subdue the obstacles to the two kinds of truths (*satya*). The explanation says:
"The two kinds of truths refer to the established truth (*vyavasthāna-satya*) and the non-established truth (*avyavasthāna-satya*); these are called the two kinds of truths.

Since the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), when they directly obstruct the Four Truths, constitute an obstruction to the established truth, one establishes one hundred and twenty-eight [subdivisions] within the context of the four established truths.

The afflictions. These two types can also obstruct *tathatā* (suchness). While *tathatā* functions as the non-designated truth (*avyavasthāpita-satya*), [the other] functions as the non-designated truth;
yet in the Mahāyāna school, that which is designated as the non-designated truth by the Hīnayāna is treated differently.
However, within the present Mahāyāna school, even those [afflictions] of the Hīnayāna are treated as both designated (*vyavasthāpita*) and non-designated truths. Nevertheless...

Regarding persons of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), there is also the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*) of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), which is capable of severing afflictions that contradict the principle. Question:
Bodhisattvas, while in the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), study and observe both the established truths (*pratiṣṭhita-satya*) and the non-established truths;

they are thus able to induce both types [of results] in the future. This is not like the two vehicles, who observe only the established truths. Since persons of the two vehicles enter the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*)...
When practicing the path, one can also attain the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*) and thereby sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).

As for those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), since they do not practice the contemplation of the non-established truth while in the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), how can they attain the non-established truth within the true path of vision (*darśana-mārga*)? Answer:

If we follow the explanation in the Hīnayāna, during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), the contemplation of the truths as objects of indeterminate perception (*vyāpyālambana*) is the most extensive; this continues up until the stage of application.

Regarding the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*): proceeding from the end toward the beginning, one reduces the objects of the truths (*ālambana-satya*) through seven cycles and reduces the modes of practice (*ākāra*) through twenty-four cycles, until only a single mode—such as impermanence (*anitya*)—remains.
One then enters the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), which consists of the sixteen moments of mind and so forth established by the truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*).
Now, according to the Mahāyāna, those of the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*) within the stage of preparation (*prayoga-bhūmi*) reduce the remaining three truths and [the modes of practice].
The four aspects of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) in the higher realms and so forth all decrease from back to front, as explained in the Hīnayāna.
If one intends for the four lower aspects of the Desire Realm, they decrease from front to back; that is, the aspects of suffering (*duḥkha*) and impermanence (*anitya*) are subtracted.

Because suffering and impermanence do not accord with non-conceptualized (*apratiṣṭhita*) *tathatā*, the two aspects of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and selflessness (*anātman*) are retained and established as the addition.

One enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) by means of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and selflessness (*anātman*), which accord with suchness (*tathatā*). Since emptiness and selflessness also exist within suchness,

and it is through the gateway of emptiness and selflessness that suchness is revealed, the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) are likewise able to induce the contemplation of the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*) within the path of seeing.
The treatise states: "Although during the stage of the preparatory means one may access all the dhyānas, it is only by relying on the fourth dhyāna that full accomplishment is attained.

For instance, when a bodhisattva first cultivates the stages of *ūṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti*, they likewise access the three lower dhyānas; however, at the time of full accomplishment, they rely specifically on the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, when first cultivating *ūṣmagata*, one proceeds gradually from the first dhyāna toward the *anāgamya* (threshold) state, moving progressively toward higher excellence.
Drawing forth the heat (*uṣmagata*) of the fundamental dhyāna, one subsequently cultivates the heat of the fundamental dhyāna, thereby drawing forth the heat of the second dhyāna.
Having reached the second dhyāna, one subsequently cultivates this heat, thereby drawing forth the heat of the third dhyāna.
Once the third dhyāna is attained, this subsequent heat draws forth the fourth dhyāna. Having reached the fourth dhyāna, one subsequently cultivates this heat until it is brought to full completion.

In this way, one again relies on the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna to cultivate the Peak (*mūrdhan*). Next, one reaches the fundamental concentration (*maula*) of the first dhyāna to cultivate the Peak, and so it continues up to the fourth dhyāna.

When cultivating the lower degree of patience (*kṣānti*) in the preliminary concentration, one immediately cultivates the lower degree of patience in the fundamental concentration of the first dhyāna—which is slightly superior to the lower degree of patience in the initial preliminary concentration—and next cultivates the lower degree of patience of the second dhyāna, and so forth.

The cultivation of medium-grade patience within the fourth dhyāna is likewise. As for the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata), Summits (mūrdhan), and the lower and medium grades of Patience (kṣānti), these pertain to all four dhyānas.

However, once their essential nature is fully realized, they rely solely upon the fourth dhyāna; this is designated as the upper grade of Patience (adhimātra-kṣānti) and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma).

These do not rely on the three lower dhyānas, but rely solely upon the fourth dhyāna because their duration is extremely brief. According to my humble opinion, if one attains sudden enlightenment to Bodhi...

Sā. Those whose bodies reside in the three continents of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as well as śrāvakas of gradual enlightenment whose bodies reside in nine locations of the desire realm or in the first dhyāna, and pratyekabuddhas who have turned their minds toward awakening while among humans—these individuals cultivate the four bodhisattva roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) based upon the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and thereby enter the bodhisattva path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
As for bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment whose bodies reside in the second dhyāna, [they do so] exclusively...
A Bodhisattva of gradual awakening who cultivates the lower three dhyānas and the four roots of goodness has their body in the third dhyāna;
they cultivate only the lower three dhyānas and the four roots of goodness. If a Bodhisattva’s body is in the fourth dhyāna, they cultivate only the fourth dhyāna and the four roots of goodness.

It is held that when one’s body resides in a higher stage, [the mental states] are exclusively those borrowed from other stages—namely, the consciousnesses borrowed from other stages, the vitarka and vicāra borrowed from lower stages, and the noble paths of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) borrowed from lower noble paths.
Question: Do the four roots of merit (kuśalamūla) of the two vehicles ever arise in a different stage? Answer: It is not so.
If a bodhisattva, for the sake of training thoroughly in all paths, relies upon the four dhyānas, they cultivate the four roots of merit throughout every stage. Second...

The four dhyānas are only fully perfected [through this process]. If a person of the Two Vehicles practices based on only one stage, they do so by relying on this single stage as the point where the summit (mūrdhan) is fully perfected;
they cannot practice based on different stages, because those of the Two Vehicles are unable to study all paths exhaustively.

Furthermore, for example, a practitioner who proceeds by gradual steps may also cultivate roots of goodness while relying solely on the preliminary concentration (anāgamya-samādhi) of the first dhyāna.

Upon completion, one necessarily cultivates *ūṣmagata* within the fundamental state of the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna. One cultivates the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) based on the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna;
it is not possible to cultivate them in any other stage. Although the seeds of the four roots of goodness exist within all five stages, [the actual cultivation occurs only as described].
That person cultivates only the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*) of a single stage. Among the fundamental dhyāna concentrations, one cultivates the four roots of goodness;
these four roots of goodness are fulfilled only by relying upon the fundamental stage of the first dhyāna.

This person also cannot rely upon the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), nor the second dhyāna and those above it, to cultivate the four roots of goodness. Even for one who has transcended [the stages], they rely upon the second...

The cultivation of the four dhyānas and so forth is likewise. If it concerns a *khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa* pratyekabuddha, they rely solely on the fourth dhyāna when entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
At that time, such a person cultivates and brings to fulfillment the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) based exclusively within the fourth dhyāna;
they cannot, however, cultivate and attain these roots of goodness by relying on the three lower dhyānas.
The Commentary states: "In section 69, among the explanations of the three vehicles, it is said that the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of those belonging to the three vehicles occurs.
If those of the two vehicles are gradual practitioners, their factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) are exclusively bound to the desire realm;

they take the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*) within the desire realm as their factors conducive to liberation. Question: Do the wholesome factors conducive to liberation for gradual practitioners also extend to the form realm?

No. If one follows the gradual practitioner (*ānupūrvika*), the essence of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) comprises both the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and the wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) within the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya-dhyāna*).
This refers to those who, as individuals already possessing the fruit [of the path], enter the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) based solely upon the preliminary concentration.

If, however, one follows the leaping practitioner (*vyutkrāntaka*), who has previously suppressed the afflictions by means of the worldly path (*laukikamārga*), the factors conducive to liberation pertain to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) as well.

The first dhyāna-stage, the *anāgamya*, has the wisdom derived from hearing and cultivation as its essence. Such a person may rely upon any of the four fundamental dhyānas and all enter the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
However, a rhinoceros-like solitary realizer (*khadga-viṣāṇakalpa pratyekabuddha*) enters the path of vision relying solely on the fourth dhyāna.

As for a Bodhisattva’s skillful means, they enter the path of vision by relying on all the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), yet [the text specifies] only the fourth dhyāna. Question: Relying on the first...

Question: How many people can enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*) by means of the *anāgamya-samādhi* (the preparatory concentration)? Answer: By relying on the initial path of the *anāgamya*, one may attain the first two fruits, the third fruit, and the fourth fruit.
Question: By relying on the fundamental dhyānas from the first up to the fourth, how many noble ones can there be?
Answer: By relying on the fundamental dhyānas of the four stages, two fruits can be attained; namely, the *anāgāmin* and the [Arhat].
This refers to the fruit of Arhatship.

The commentary (*shu*) states: "If there were one who clings to the intermediate [state] here," meaning that if there were a teacher who, while clinging to dharmas, could enter the path of seeing (darśanamārga) through the intermediate dhyāna, this very passage of the commentary refutes such a claim.

The Commentary states: "If there are those who cling to the intermediate [dhyāna] and so forth," which means that if there are other Dharma masters who cling to the intermediate dhyāna as being deeply involved in the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), this passage of the Commentary refutes them.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Regarding these [levels] which can be obtained based on the *anāgamya* (preparatory stage), up to and including the *ākiṃcanyāyatana* (sphere of nothingness)"—this refers to the six types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*). It asks: among the nine stages (*bhūmi*), which clear realizations are attained?

Why, then, does the question specify only from the initial *anāgamya* up to the *ākiṃcanyāyatana*, rather than asking about the *naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana* (sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception)? Answer:
This is explained here in terms of the untainted path that abandons afflictions (*kleśa*), not in terms of the untainted path of contemplative observation (*paryāya*).

Although the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) possesses the untainted path of contemplative observation, it lacks the untainted path of abandonment that severs afflictions; therefore, one cannot inquire about the stage of the Peak of Existence in this context.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "One reliance is not a reliance upon which all can be attained; furthermore, there are three reliances and five reliances from which [realization] arises. The Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states:

"'One reliance is not a reliance' refers to the contemplative realization (*cintā-abhisamaya*). It does not rely on the stages of the form or formless realms. This contemplative realization relies solely on the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
within the desire realm, the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā* and *cintā-mayī-prajñā*) are termed 'contemplative realization. The remaining [realizations] rely on all [stages]."

"Based on what is attainable" refers collectively to the names of the remaining five types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*). Furthermore, "the three based on five bases arise" is a specific explanation of the five types of clear realization.

The "three bases" refer to the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), the clear realization of the limits (*koṭyabhisamaya*), and the clear realization of ethical discipline (*śīlābhisamaya*).
The "five bases" refer to the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*) and the fundamental dhyānas from the first through the fourth. These three types of observation are thus comprehensive.

Based on the initial *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage and the four fundamental *dhyāna* concentrations, these three types of insight (*vipaśyanā*) are generally explained as pertaining to all three vehicles.

For instance, when a person of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), this wisdom—whether as a single momentary insight or as the threefold insight (*trividha-abhisamaya*)—arises solely based on the initial *anāgamya* concentration.
However, for practitioners of the two vehicles who practice by means of "leaping over" (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*), these three insights arise based on all four fundamental *dhyāna* concentrations.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva’s three types of clear realization arise, they do so solely in reliance upon the fourth dhyāna. Regarding both the established truths (*prajñapti-satya*) and the non-established truths (*aprajñapti-satya*), their respective dharmas must belong to the same level (*bhūmi*).

For example, if one gives rise to the non-established truth by relying on the wisdom of the first *anāgamya* concentration, one must subsequently give rise to the established truth by relying on that same wisdom of the first *anāgamya* concentration;
one must first rely on the wisdom of the first *anāgamya* concentration to give rise to the non-established [truth].

Established. Based specifically on the fundamental concentration (*mauladhyāna*) of the first dhyāna, one gives rise to the wisdom of establishment (*vyavasthāpanajñāna*), which necessarily lacks a [substantial] object; all instances above this are likewise so.
If it is the faith-realization (*śraddhābhisamaya*) or the ultimate realization (*niṣṭhābhisamaya*), these are untainted (*anāsrava*) and arise based on the wisdom of all ten stages (*bhūmi*).

That is to say, they rely upon the six stages of the form realm—namely, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the four fundamental dhyānas—as well as the four stages of the formless realm. If it is the small...

Regarding the vehicle school (*yāna-naya*): this means that one may also enter the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) by relying on the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), which is to say, by relying on the six stages (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi*).
The answer states: "One relies, does not rely, or neither relies nor does not rely; even a single type or a single part is likewise so.

However, the clear realization through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*) relies solely upon existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and does not rely upon existence in the higher realms; thus, it is "one who relies, but does not rely. All others rely upon everything.

Regarding "based on what is attainable," this means that the latter five types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) are based on all nine stages—namely, the six form realms and the three formless realms.

However, because both fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) are present within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and because clear realization is thus attained within that stage of cultivation, the attainment of wisdom regarding the truths (*jñāna-satya-prāpti*) extends across the nine stages.
This is not limited to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), as there is specifically the presence of the wisdom of the limit of knowledge (*jñānakoṭi-jñāna*).
This is the truth. If it refers to ultimate clear realization (*abhisamaya*), it also extends through the nine stages, as the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) exists based upon all nine stages.
If it refers to clear realization by faith (*śraddhā-abhisamaya*), it likewise extends through the nine stages; therefore, it is said that "the remainder may be obtained based on any basis. Question:
Regarding the clear realization of ethical discipline (*śīla-abhisamaya*), how can it extend to the higher realms? Answer: This should now be analyzed. If so, within the Hīnayāna itself—
[The author] says: [The opponent] asks, "How is it that the vows associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*) and the path (*mārga-saṃvara*) are established in the form realm?

He answers, "It is in order to eliminate the mind that would break the precepts through the power of equalizing wisdom; therefore, the vows of concentration and the path exist in the higher realms. How is this so?

For example, when one receives the *prātimokṣa* vows, one merely refrains from committing the seven fundamental offenses of body and speech which are natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). One does not...

It is capable of subduing and eliminating the power of the desire realm that gives rise to the breaking of precepts. This is because the preliminary application [of such breaking] contains minds such as anger;
it is only through the presence of desire for the five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) of the desire realm and through anger that one kills living beings, thereby breaking the precepts.

For instance, when receiving the five precepts, one must not give rise to even a single branch offense or a fundamental natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). When receiving the two hundred and fifty precepts, however—

At the time of the five hundred precepts, one is immediately able to subdue the ten branches of natural transgressions— namely, the three of body and the four of speech— and although one has received the prātimokṣa vows,
one thereby subdues the natural transgressions that might arise. However, if one does not subdue the fundamental [afflictions] such as those of the form realm,
when greed and other afflictions arise, because of the presence of greed and other afflictions of the form realm, one will subsequently be able to commit transgressions of body and speech.

Regarding the sevenfold nature of the offenses of natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), although the Prātimokṣa vows have not yet attained clarity and purity, for the sake of augmenting the power of the Prātimokṣa vows, one immediately gives rise to the restraint concomitant with the initial *anāgamya* concentration.
This serves to suppress the afflictions (*kleśa*)—such as attachment or grasping—that can give rise to [transgressions] within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Because these cannot arise, and because the initial *anāgamya* concentration is able to sever the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is thus at the very beginning...
In the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*), there exists the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*).

Although the afflictions of the desire realm are suppressed and do not arise, because the afflictions of the first dhyāna exist as a condition, they immediately give rise to the afflictions of the desire realm. To give rise to the afflictions of the desire realm is to transgress the precepts.
If the afflictions of the first dhyāna were absent, the afflictions of the desire realm would likewise be absent. Now, for the purpose of eliminating this transgression of the precepts—
Because the obstacles are further removed, one immediately gives rise to the *anāgamya* concentration of the second dhyāna and suppresses the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the first dhyāna.

This continues until, by virtue of the existence of the afflictions of the third dhyāna, one gives rise to the second dhyāna; the afflictions of the second dhyāna give rise to the afflictions of the first dhyāna;
and the afflictions of the first dhyāna give rise to the afflictions of the desire realm, whereby one violates the precepts. Now, in order to make these obstacles even more remote:

He immediately enters the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of the fourth dhyāna; because he thereby suppresses the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the third dhyāna, the obstacles to the fourth dhyāna become even more distant.
He immediately enters the threshold concentration of the fourth dhyāna; because he thereby suppresses the afflictions of the third dhyāna, the obstacles to the fourth dhyāna become even more distant.
He immediately enters the threshold concentration of the fourth dhyāna; because he thereby suppresses the afflictions of the third dhyāna...
Because of affliction (*kleśa*). In order to cause the obstacles to become even more remote, the fourth dhyāna possesses the "distant-part antidote" (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*).

For this reason, within the fourth dhyāna there is the concentration-associated precept (*samādhi-saṃvara*). As for the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), because they possess four kinds of remoteness, the formless realms do not establish the existence of concentration-associated precepts.
Although the concentration-associated precepts have arisen above and suppressed [the defilements], and although the four abandonments (*prahāṇa*) have been severed...
Regarding the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-vyāpatti*): if one later regresses and gives rise to afflictions, one again commits a transgression of the precepts.

If one wishes to permanently sever such transgressions of the precepts, that which can give rise to the afflictions and assist in purifying the *prātimokṣa* vows must be the arising of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
By means of this principle, one initiates the initial stage of *anāgamya*; through this, the Noble One is able to sever the afflictions of the desire realm.

Regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*): although one has severed the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), in order to cause those obstacles to become even more distant, one immediately gives rise to the noble path (*āryamārga*) of the second dhyāna to sever the afflictions of the first dhyāna, and so on, until one gives rise to the untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) of the fourth dhyāna to sever the afflictions of the three lower dhyānas.
Thus, within the fourth dhyāna, one employs the antidote of "distant differentiation" (*dūrabheda-pratipakṣa*) to cause the obstacles to become even more distant; therefore, within the fourth dhyāna—

There is the *dharmasamvṛti-śīla* (precept of co-arising with the path). Because there is no *dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa* (counteractive of the distant) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and because of four kinds of distance, the *dharmasamvṛti-śīla* is not established in the formless realm.

However, among the nine vehicles, the four *dhyānas* possess the *samādhisamvṛti-śīla* (precept of co-arising with meditative concentration), as previously explained in the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
Thus, both the fourth *dhyāna* and the three lower *dhyānas* all possess this co-arising precept, and so on.
Furthermore, there are those who transcend by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) and are able to suppress the afflictions from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) downward.
Later, when entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they do so based on the fundamental dhyānas of the four levels.

At the time of entering the path of seeing, every single path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) is capable of [abandoning] the transgressions of the desire realm and the afflictions associated with both seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*). Thus, all four dhyānas possess this capacity.
Regarding the precepts associated with the Path (*mārga-samvara*):

however, the Mahāyāna states that just as in your Hīnayāna system, only the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya*) is able to sever the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whereas the four fundamental dhyānas of the higher realms cannot sever the afflictions of the desire realm—because they serve as "distant counteractives" (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*) that further distance the obstacles—it is taught that within each of the four higher dhyānas there exists the precept of meditative concentration and the Path. This is so that...

In our Mahāyāna, since the fundamental dhyānas of the four *dhyānas* are all capable of severing the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), what prevents the same from being true for the three lower formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*)?

This would cause the obstacles to be further removed, constituting a "counteractive of distant separation" (*dūrībhāvapratipakṣa*). Thus, the three lower formless attainments likewise possess the morality concomitant with the path (*mārgasaṃvarasīla*);
therefore, the clear observation of morality (*śīlābhisamaya*) applies to all stages (*bhūmi*).

Furthermore, regarding the "three based on five" (*trīṇi pañca-sanniśritāni*): this text refers exclusively to the three types of clear observation (*abhisamaya*) within one's own path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).

It explains that the wisdom within this path of vision, in terms of the truths (*satya-pakṣa*), or the three clear observations, rely solely upon the five stages (*pañca-bhūmi*). As for the remaining one type and its partial aspect:
This refers to the abiding in the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) that assists the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), which likewise relies solely upon the five stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, that Brahmā king’s realm is characterized by much distraction; however, because the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is a stage of biased attachment, it is termed "distraction.
Therefore, those of the two vehicles (*yāna*) are not born in that heaven. Question: If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) becomes a Brahmā king, is this possible?
To eliminate distraction: if a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage becomes a Brahmā King, for what reason would there be distraction? It is not that the ground of pure purity is free from it;

could one not also say, "I am a knower," and so forth, as afflictions? If it is said that when he is a Brahmā King of the tenth stage, he does not grasp at being born as a son of Brahmā, then he would lack [the state of] "different bodies with the same perception" among the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). If it is said that the Bodhisattva also manifests...

If you currently maintain that the vehicle which can produce you [is the Mahāyāna], how could it be that a Bodhisattva teaches sentient beings to give rise to afflictions and karma such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*)?

Furthermore, it was asked: "If it is within the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), then it possesses out-flowing phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*); it is only the Great Brahmā King who can be compared [to it]."
Other devas cannot arise [therein]. It may be said that the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is the primary abode of Brahmā-rāja, yet it is not a stage of absolute purity.
Furthermore, since the Brahma-parṣadya and Brahma-purohita devas can also arise in the first dhyāna, how can it be said that the intermediate dhyāna is the primary abode of Brahmā-rāja?
Moreover, if Brahmā-rāja were to give rise to other untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas within the intermediate dhyāna, then that intermediate dhyāna would be untainted.

One does not enter the Path of Seeing while remaining in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*). Since the Brahmā King, while seated in the intermediate dhyāna, can give rise to contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas but cannot give rise to uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas—given that the essence of uncontaminated dharmas is dissociated from the wholesome—how could there be uncontaminated [dharmas] in the intermediate dhyāna?
Furthermore, it is asked: since the intermediate dhyāna of the Mahāyāna is not a stage of pure purity (*viśuddha-bhūmi*), one likewise does not enter the Path of Seeing from it.

Question: How is it that by relying on the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), one abandons the co-emergent afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) and attains the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) of the Two Vehicles?

Furthermore, why are the merits of a Bodhisattva not even equal to those of the Two Vehicles? Answer: However, the Bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the ultimate path of seeing rely exclusively upon the fourth dhyāna.
As for the Bodhisattva’s path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) and the merits of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), these universally rely upon all ten stages.

This means that while six [stages] involve form and four are formless, it is said that they primarily rely on the fourth dhyāna. If, however, it concerns the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the two vehicles, it then relies on five stages:

namely, for those in the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), it relies on the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) and the fundamental states of the four dhyānas. If referring specifically to the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), it is taught that the Small Vehicle’s path of seeing relies on six stages, adding the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
As for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) of the two vehicles, they likewise rely on all [six] stages.

It relies upon the nine stages, namely the three [stages] of the form and formless realms. As for the seeds of the various conventional wisdoms previously cultivated, these refer to the seeds of conventional wisdom cultivated while previously abiding in the stage of equipment (sambhāra-avasthā) through the practice of the four dhyānas and eight samādhis.

Through that cultivation, they all attain purification; this is also termed "cultivation. This is what is called "at the conclusion of the clear observation of the truths" (satyābhisamaya-paryavasāna). That is to say:

Within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), when subsequently contemplating the eight truths—both lower and higher—during the subsequent path of seeing (*anvayadarśanamārga*), one concurrently cultivates the seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), gradually causing them to become increasingly distinguished; this is called "attaining purity.

Because one enters the subsequent path of seeing while the mind is established upon the truths (*satya*), the seeds of conventional knowledge cultivated concurrently possess a distinguished power capable of producing their actual manifestation (*samudācāra*).

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "If that were so, then in the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the seeds of the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) would not be superior.

The intent of this objection is as follows: for instance, within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one incidentally cultivates the contaminated mundane seeds of the three formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
"Son, the seeds of worldly, outflow-tainted knowledge are called the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

These very same three [faculties], which possess no seeds of worldly knowledge and have been cultivated for a long time alongside the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), reach the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);

at that point, these seeds should be termed the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown. The answer is: although the substance of the seeds of worldly knowledge is one, with respect to the two stages of seeing and cultivation, they are not [identical]."
If one sees that the path is nourished by a single layer [of seeds], it is designated only as the faculty of "that which is yet to be known" (ājñātavya-indriya).

Upon reaching the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), when it is again further nourished, one should know that these seeds are precisely the faculty of "that which has already been known" (ājñendriya). The intent of this question is that once a fruit is attained, the preceding question does not arise.

If, while previously in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), all seeds of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) were subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), then after these seeds of conventional knowledge have been cultivated in the vicinity of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they subsequently give rise to the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of conventional knowledge within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Thus, the specific and general aspects of the stages of seeing and cultivation are one; now, these seeds of conventional knowledge are subsumed within the path of cultivation.

In the middle [of the path], it should be called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*). Regarding its stages and its modes of activity (*ākāra*), there are distinctions in both;

even when it is subsumed under the name of the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*), this is still the case. Now, although the essence of the seeds of this conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is a single seed, it is distinguished according to the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
That which was previously arisen during the stage of the path of seeing is not yet able to take [all objects] as its universal object.

Therefore, it is subsumed under the faculty of "the unknown to be known. When one reaches the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), because one again employs the wisdom of the path of cultivation to know [it] repeatedly, these very conventional seeds are said to be subsumed under the faculty of "the already known."

Furthermore, the sixty-ninth [treatise] states: "From the moment the first cognition of the path of seeing arises, up until it is subsumed under this faculty, this text refers to the three lower formless realms.
There are also untainted seeds of the path of seeing therein, which are subsumed under this initial faculty.

If one correctly enters the fourth dhyāna and the cognition of the path of seeing arises, one is then able to concurrently cultivate the path of seeing within the remaining three lower formless realms."

The seeds of the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of the Path all attain growth. Furthermore, the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in the three lower formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) is likewise unable to produce [these] in their active state (*samudācāra*).

Question: Since the seeds of the Path of Seeing already exist within the three lower formless realms, why were only the previously mentioned "three bases" (*tri-āśraya*) and "five bases" (*pañca-āśraya*) stated?
Should they not rather be called "three bases and eight bases"? As for the previous mention of "five bases," this refers specifically to the five [realms].

Within the [four] dhyāna stages (*bhūmi*), there exist seeds of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) because they are capable of producing manifest activity (*samudācāra*); therefore, only these five bases (*pañca-āśraya*) are specifically mentioned.
As for the seeds of the path of seeing in the three lower formless realms (*ārūpya*), they cannot produce manifest activity; therefore, the eight bases are not mentioned. Question:

While it may be possible for the seeds of the path of seeing to exist in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) through the presence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), how can this be so in the formless realm where emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is predominant and wisdom is weak?

Is there a seed of the path of seeing? One should ask the Dharma Master. Furthermore, it is said that the meaning of this passage is that at the very moment of first entering the path of seeing, one is also able to cultivate the path of meditation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Moreover, the seeds of the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) possess such power that they all give rise to their actual manifestations (*samudācāra*).

Although there is no subsequent [seed] capable of producing a manifestation, at this time [the seeds of the path of meditation] do not immediately produce a manifestation; therefore, the path of meditation does not exist [at that moment].

The seeds of the path of cultivation cannot be said to be subsumed under the path of seeing. However, once the seeds of conventional wisdom have been treated by the antidote of the path of seeing, they too are occasionally able to produce their actual manifestation.
For this reason, the seeds of conventional wisdom are said to be subsumed under the faculty of "knowing what is not yet known" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Question: Suppose there are contaminated dharmas of the path of cultivation that undergo increase; for instance, suppose one practices the lower grade of the first dhyāna.
At that time, one is able to cultivate the lower grades of the higher stages, as well as cultivate and increase the three grades of seeds belonging to the desire realm.
When cultivating the middle grade of the first dhyāna, one is able to cultivate the middle and lower grades of its own stage, but cannot yet cultivate the upper grade of the causal stage;
furthermore, one cultivates the three grades of the desire realm in a coarse manner. When the cultivation of the first dhyāna reaches the upper grade, one is then able to cultivate...
One can cultivate the three grades of one's own stage, as well as the three grades of the desire realm, and also cultivate the dharmas of the second dhyāna.

Why is it that entering and emerging from the fourth dhyāna enables one to cultivate these dharmas? Why is it that upon entering the fourth dhyāna, one is able to cultivate the three lower formless attainments and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*)? This point should be further questioned; reflect upon it.
The Commentary says: Question: If that is so, how is it that the noble path of those stages also abandons the desire realm?

That is to say, a person who has attained the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmin), while residing in the form or formless realms, is also able to sever the afflictions of both realms and thereby attain the fruit of arhatship (aśaikṣa).

He asked again: "If the Śrāvaka’s mind of reflection awakens gradually, and the Bodhisattva sits within the four dhyānas with a mind of aversion that is already weak, how can they enter the Mahāyāna path of seeing (darśana-mārga)?
He asked further: "Only humans in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) attain the clear realization (abhisamaya) when a Buddha appears in the world.
Clear realization is precisely the path of seeing. This means that one may enter the path of seeing in nine locations within the desire realm; namely, the East...
The three continents of the southwest and the six heavens of the desire realm—these nine locations are also where Buddhas appear in the world.

Regarding "the east and so forth," this refers to the inclusion by wisdom (*jñāna-saṃgraha*), because it encompasses the six aspects of *tathatā*. Since the preceding statement spoke of mutual inclusion by *tathatā* and inclusion by wisdom, the subsequent statement mentions "the east and so forth";
thus, the terms "mutual" and so on are repeated. Alternatively, if one were to exclude only the post-attainment wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), then...
It refers to contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Furthermore, it is said:

"Although contaminated subsequently attained wisdom is induced by the power of the preceding uncontaminated wisdom, this contaminated subsequently attained wisdom is merely designated as 'subsequently attained wisdom' by convention;
in reality, it is not truly subsequently attained wisdom. Only that which is truly uncontaminated is called subsequently attained wisdom."
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Regarding the *Buddhabhūmi*, there are two theories; this [first theory] does not exist here.

However, concerning those who assert that all uncontaminated minds (*anāsrava-citta*) function in unison (*sahakāra*), the subsequent treatises do not mention the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), or the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).
