Within that explanation, there are two masters’ views. One interpretation holds that all fundamental wisdom possesses both the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*)."
There is an interpretation that all fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) perceives existence and perceives non-existence.
The *Śāstra* states, "This is not so," yet even within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, it refers to the fundamental wisdom within the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
"Clearly seeing the existence and non-existence of the image (*nimitta*) and so forth.
The Commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "The wise person thoroughly realizes that both are non-existent, and so forth, abiding in the true *dharmadhātu* which is devoid of both.

This first master explains this verse as follows: "Thoroughly realizing" refers to entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). "Both are non-existent" refers to the two parts: the image (*nimittabhāga*) and the vision (*darśanabhāga*).

"Abiding in equality" refers to the self-cognizing division (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) arising from *tathatā*. "The two are non-existent" means that the two divisions—the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) and the image-part (*nimittabhāga*)—are absent.

"The true dharma-realm" is precisely *tathatā*. If one adopts the interpretation of the third master regarding this verse, "both are non-existent" refers to the grasping subject and the grasped object (*grāhakagrāhya*) as they are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*). The meaning of the logical inference (*anumāna*) is established through repeated application.
That which is cognizable: your cognition of form should not be a cognition of form, as it lacks the objective aspect of form, just like a cognition of sound.
Furthermore, a cognition of sound should not be a cognition of sound, as it lacks the objective aspect of sound, just like a cognition of form.

The *Śāstra* says: "Although there is no direct realization (*abhisamaya*), from the absence of conceptual characteristics (*nirvikalpa-lakṣaṇa*) up to the non-attainment of any other cognition, it is called 'proceeding from suchness' (*tathatā-anusārin*).

The commentary explains: The intention of this master is that although true reality (*tattva*) is indeed manifest from the perspective of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), when it takes suchness as its object, there still exists a subtle aspectual division (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Because this aspectual division is extremely similar to that suchness, it does not apprehend any other cognizing mind-king (*citta-rāja*).

This refers to the coarse aspect-part (*nimitta-bhāga*). A separate commentary states: "Just as although there is no direct [apprehension], that which is similar to the non-conceptual aspect [is apprehended].

This means that when fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) takes true suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, although it does not directly derive from true suchness, fundamental wisdom nevertheless arises from reality (*dharmatā*) with a subtle aspect-part and thus takes true suchness as its object.
This wisdom that takes true suchness as its object carries true suchness along with it (*sahagata*).
Regarding the statement that it is called the "object-condition" (*ālambana*) because it is the substance of wisdom: the term "clinging" (*xié*) carries the sense of "relying on a staff.

This is because the mind can only arise by relying on the object of True Suchness (*tathatā*). What is the meaning of this? To speak of "clinging" is like a sick person who cannot rise up by themselves.
It is necessary to have another strong person use their hand to support [the patient] under both armpits;
only then can this weak person cause the sick person to rise. This case is likewise. Fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) is like the sick person who cannot rise by themselves.
True Suchness (tathatā) is likened to the strong person; it is through True Suchness supporting Fundamental Wisdom under its "armpits" that Fundamental Wisdom is finally able to arise.

Regarding the term "girdle," it is like a counting-bag (*gaṇanā-puṭa*). It cannot stand up by itself; it must be fastened around a person's waist by someone, and only then can the counting-bag stand upright.
Now, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is like the person’s waist-girdle, and Fundamental Wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is likened to the counting-bag.
Fundamental wisdom cannot arise by itself; it arises only because True Suchness (tathatā) brings forth this fundamental wisdom. The Commentary states:

"If that were so, the mind-king (citta-rāja) should be called 'that which does not manifest its own reflection as an object of cognition,' for it is that which brings forth the wisdom whose essence and characteristics are derived from it."

Since the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) must arise by mutually supporting one another, this question is asked for the sake of their arising. Regarding the statement "seeing itself is the path" (*darśanaiva mārgaḥ*):

it refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). Because these constitute the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), they are termed the "path of seeing," and so forth.
What is here called the "path" does not carry the sense of "traversing. Furthermore, the *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Regarding 'seeing itself is the path,' [the word] path..."
The Truth (*satya*) is itself untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). All phenomena traverse this wisdom before one can attain Buddhahood;

therefore, this wisdom is called the Path (*mārga*). Regarding the "True Path of Vision" (*darśana-mārga*), the treatise states that it is the non-differentiated wisdom of the aforementioned divisions, even up to the general description of the single mind (*ekacitta*).
The subsequent text explains that there is a True Path of Vision consisting of three minds, as well as a True [Path of Vision] consisting of a single mind.
The Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is all explained here based on the True Path of Seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*).

Regarding the mention of "three moments," this refers to the three types of wisdom, such as the wisdom that internally eliminates the conceptualization of sentient beings. Although the treatise states that there are many moments (*kṣaṇa*), it is clearly understood that these constitute multiple minds;
a single mind is not called "two" or "three," but rather "many. Therefore, all three moments are termed the True Path of Seeing. Based on...

This is the established position. If one maintains that a single mind constitutes the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), then although it is said to consist of many moments (*kṣaṇa*), they are equal in nature.
Since they are said to be equal in nature, it is clear that there is only a single mind. Whether it is described as three minds or as a single mind, both are explained based on this very text.
The Commentary states: "That which is called 'sudden severance' (頓斷) refers to the three grades [of afflictions] being severed without separately arousing a contemplative mind;

this is what is meant by 'sudden. This master’s interpretation thus incorporates the text. Alternatively, it may mean that once the contemplative mind has arisen, one immediately severs these three grades of delusion, which is called 'sudden.

Furthermore, another explanation is that the third stage universally dispels the wisdom regarding the false conditions of all phenomena pertaining to sentient beings; since this corresponds to the superior grade of afflictions, it is known [to be the superior grade]."

Because the obstructions are severed in a single location, it is called "sudden. Regarding the rational obstructions of persons and phenomena, the former masters state that a bodhisattva first [realizes] the principle of the emptiness of persons and subsequently [realizes] the principle of the emptiness of phenomena; thus, they first sever the afflictive obstructions and later sever the cognitive obstructions.
First, one gives rise to the coarse wisdom of the emptiness of persons; subsequently, one gives rise to the subtle wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena.

According to the later masters, within the Bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one certainly does not separately give rise to the contemplation of the emptiness of persons, but practices only the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena.
The *Śāstra* states: "There is an interpretation that the two emptinesses and the two obscurations are abandoned simultaneously.

However, regarding the designation of the path of insight (*darśana-mārga*) as "simultaneous" (*tun*), although it consists of many moments of mind that continue over a long duration, it is called "simultaneous" because no further contemplation arises [afterward]. Nevertheless, within the *Vyākhyā* (the commentary), there are two interpretations for the term "simultaneous":
one interpretation states that attaining the three moments of mind is what is meant by "simultaneous," which refers to a single uninterrupted state; this is one interpretation.
[The phrase] "liberation" (vimokṣa) [is used]. Regarding the "one superior progress" (viśeṣa-mārga), the second interpretation states that this refers to the two minds taken as simultaneous;

that is, one gives rise to one path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) and one path of liberation (vimokṣa-mārga), excluding the superior progress. As for the statement, "for the sake of a provisional twofold explanation, there are eleven liberations in total," it may refer to the seven minds taken as simultaneous;
that is, the superior-grade afflictions (kleśa) and the superior-grade objects of knowledge (jñeya) are combined into a single superior grade, while the medium-grade afflictions... [and so forth].
The afflictions (*kleśa*) are combined into one medium grade, and the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are combined into one inferior grade.

Since there are thus three grades of affliction—superior, medium, and inferior—there are seven [moments] consisting of three paths of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), three paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and one path of special progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*). One mind constitutes the first solution;

alternatively, excluding the path of special progress, six minds are called "sudden" (*tad-ekakṣaṇika*), which is the second solution; or else, it refers to the subsequent path of uninterrupted realization.

The preceding path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is identical to the three paths of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*). Just as with the third moment of mind’s liberation, together with one further advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*), these five moments are termed "simultaneous.
This refers to the third [set of] liberations, excluding the further advancement; or, if the two obstacles are distinct, there are two grades for each of the upper and lower [obstacles].
Since the obstacles consist of three grades, there arise two paths of non-interruption and two paths of liberation, plus one further advancement.

Progression. The five moments of mind are called "sudden progression. That is, the fourth [moment] is the liberation; that is, the fourth liberation. Excluding the liberation, the four moments of mind are called "sudden.
The sixth is the liberation, or the subsequent immediate [moment], which is the aforementioned liberation. That is, the three moments of mind are called "sudden."
The seventh interpretation: "Excluding" is as explained in the Chapter on the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). The *Ṭīkā* states:
"It is not correct for the ancient masters to say that there are three explanations. This refers to Dharma Master Tái’s commentary on this passage, which says:

"That is to say, it is precisely the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) as described above, which truly realizes the ultimate truth manifested by the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), and so forth. Furthermore...
This is the interpretation of the first master. There is another view that within this context, the two emptinesses and the two obstructions are realized and abandoned gradually;
this is the interpretation of the second master. There is yet another view that within this context, the two emptinesses and the two obstructions are realized and abandoned instantaneously;

this is the interpretation of the third master. However, my own explanation is not thus. That is to say, the passage concerning non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and so forth serves as the subject heading.

This does not mean that they are distinct teachers. Regarding the subsequent text, there are two [interpretations]. One interpretation holds that these are questions posed by the two aforementioned teachers to an ancient master.
Is it not the case that Dharma Master Tai saw this very passage in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) and [commented] upon it himself?

Why, then, do you now present three different explanations? Please ask further: regarding this initial general discussion of the "aspected" (*sākāra*) and "aspectless" (*nirākāra*) paths of vision (*darśanamārga*), within that very path of vision, it is provisionally...
It is taught that there are three moments of mind in the vision of the path (darśanamārga), and not that there are no three moments of mind in the vision of the path.

Furthermore, regarding the determination that there are definitively three moments of mind—this refers to those who maintain that the vision of liberation consists of three moments of mind; "liberation" here refers to the vision of characteristics (lakṣaṇadarśana) within which there are definitively three moments of mind.

The Commentary states that these are combined into four categories: this means that within these three minds, which are to be abandoned by the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), each of the two obstructions (āvaraṇa) has both superior and inferior grades.
Here, however, in terms of the Noble Path (āryamārga) itself, there are only three minds.
The commentary states: "At the time of the third mind, its wisdom is of the superior grade and is able to extensively take as its object all internal and external self and dharmas.
Now, among the three minds, the third mind excludes the internal and external self and dharmas. How so? Taking the Brahmā King to be eternal constitutes the grasping at an external self;

taking all such [beings] to be emanated selves constitutes the grasping at an external self. Alternatively, it refers to grasping at all external five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and so forth as [an external self].
Because it belongs to what is "mine," it is now categorized as being subsumed under the external self (*bāhmātman*).

The commentary states: "This explains the meaning of the two true paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*). This refers to the teacher’s position that the three moments of mind constitute the true path of seeing.
Regarding the statement, "Each speaks of the provisional [nature], up to the second wisdom which is superior and capable of extensively [disclosing] the Dharma": this is...
The explanation of the three minds all pertains to the meaning of the masters who maintain that [the path] is characterized by the severance of signs (*nimitta*).
The *Śāstra* commentary states: "This refers to the general explanation as the path of vision characterized by signs (*lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga*).

Because they are similar to the preceding "patience" (*kṣānti*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) that took [the truths] as their objects, it is called "subsequent knowledge. The subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*) takes the previously [realized] objects as its focus.

The wisdom regarding the suchness of suffering is called "subsequent patience" (*anvaya-kṣānti*). If it is subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), it takes as its object the preceding subsequent patience regarding suffering; thus, it is a wisdom that takes [patience] as its object.

If it is the patience regarding the dharma (*dharma-kṣānti*) or the knowledge of the dharma (*dharma-jñāna*), both take suchness as their object. Regarding the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*): "suffering" refers to the truth of suffering within the three realms;
"dharma" refers to the teaching that expresses the truth of suffering; and "knowledge" refers to that which expresses suffering...

Regarding the teaching on the Truths (*satya*): "Wisdom" (*jñāna*) refers to the three types of wisdom—arising from hearing, reflection, and meditation—that occur within the contaminated mind during the stage of the Path of Application (*prayoga-mārga*).

"Patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to uncontaminated patience; specifically, it is the patience regarding the dharma of suffering, the wisdom regarding the dharma of suffering, and the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the dharma of suffering.
All of these are analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the [Truths of] Origination and Cessation.

The same applies to the three truths regarding the path (*mārga*). Regarding "patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of the path" (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*): "path" refers to the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*); "dharma" refers to the teaching that can express the path;

"knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the contaminated knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*) within the stage of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*); and "patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to uncontaminated patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*). All these are analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.

Following the previous case of "dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*): "suffering" refers to the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); "dharma" refers to the suchness of suffering (*duḥkha-tathatā*); and "knowledge" refers to the knowledge that takes suffering as its object.
Such wisdom is called the "knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*).

The *Vyākhyā* (Shū) states: "The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* XVII explains that the knowledge of the dharma (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the four truths do not differ by way of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The meaning of this is that there is no differentiation of the sixteen moments of mind based on the aspects (*ākāra*) of the objects they apprehend; rather, [the distinction lies elsewhere].

Within the essence of principle (*tattva*), there is already the implicit meaning of the sixteen moments of mind (*ṣoḍaśa-citta*). Thus, when discussing the essence itself, one speaks of the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) of wisdom, which are analogous to the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*).
If these were established separately: it is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) because it takes as its object the thorough investigation of the absence of self-nature.

It takes as its object all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). Because it cannot be grasped, it is called "without grasping" (*anupādāna*). Because it is the quiescence of nirvāṇa and possesses ten characteristics, it is called "signless" (*animitta*).

To explain this according to its meaning: within nirvāṇa itself, three [characteristics] are also taught. Specifically, because within nirvāṇa there is neither self nor what belongs to a self, it is called "empty" (*śūnya*).
Furthermore, this very nirvāṇa is called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) because it is free from names and transcends signs; thus it is known to be signless.

If there are contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), they likewise possess three aspects. On the basis of the *paratantra-svabhāva*, the absence of the grasped object of false attachment is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).

That very *paratantra* is, from its own nature, devoid of the capacity for grasping; this is called "signlessness" (*animitta*). Since there is nothing to be grasped, it cannot be known [as an object];
thus, because this *parikalpita-svabhāva* does not exist, it is called "emptiness. Since it lacks substantiality, it is called "signlessness" because it possesses no characteristics. Since...
That which has no substantial entity and cannot be grasped or sought is called "indeterminate grasping" (*avyākṛta-grahaṇa*). This very *tathatā* (suchness) is named the Four Truths;

the same applies to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and so forth. Because the cognizing wisdom takes the objects of these categories as its range of activity, one knows that at their source there are the four truths and sixteen moments of mind.
Thus, it is known that within *tathatā* there are also the distinctions of the Four Truths. This is the interpretation of Master Chao.

One should further inquire of the Dharma Master regarding the two types of realization: first, the patience of realization (*abhisamayakṣānti*), and second, the knowledge of realization (*abhisamayajñāna*). Now, these subsequent sixteen moments of mind are also termed the "patience of dharma-knowledge" (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) and "dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*), up to the "patience of subsequent knowledge of the path" (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) and "subsequent knowledge of the path" (*mārgānvayajñāna*).

These constitute the sixteen moments of mind. As for the term "patience of realization," it refers to the eight patiences: namely, the patience of dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*), and so forth, up to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*). Regarding the phrase "patience of realization," this refers precisely to the eight patiences, beginning with the patience of dharma-knowledge of suffering and the dharma-knowledge of suffering, and the patience of subsequent knowledge of suffering... The patience regarding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*); the patience regarding the knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*); the patience regarding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*);

the patience regarding the knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*). [Furthermore,] the patience regarding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*).

these constitute the arising of the sixteen moments of mind. The designation "path of seeing" and so forth is a conventional description; in truth, there are eight moments of true [wisdom].

Furthermore, regarding the Path of Seeing with signs (*sanimittadarśanamārga*): within this Path of Seeing with signs, the training in the realization of what is to be abandoned and realized by the True Path of Seeing consists entirely of the conventional and the real.

Since these are conventional phenomena (*prajñaptidharma*), how can they be called an "agent"? It is for the sake of subduing those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) that [these designations are used].

The intention is this: at the time of performing their activities, the bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion (mahākaruṇā) for the sake of benefiting others.
